en: Regarding the beginning and end of this sequel to my dream: I previously annotated the *Fahua zhizhang* (The Lotus Sutra at a Glance), commencing in the second year of the Yongzheng era, the Jiachen year, and completing the draft in the eleventh year of the Qianlong era, the Bingyin year.
When I was about to have it carved for printing, I failed to do so because my efforts were insufficient. Later...
In the winter of the Xinwei year, I was honored by the petition of the Prince Zhuang of Huosuo,
who recommended me for the position of abbot of Xiangjie Monastery. A year later, Biankong Yuan and others arrived from Xiuyun Monastery.

"Please explain the *Lengyan zhengmai* for us. When he first expounded the ten gates, [the Master] immediately took exception to its excessive polemical disputation, noting that its sequential order differed greatly from that of Qingliang and thus did not accord with the ancestral methods of the Xianzong school.
As for the redundant words in the title that distract the mind—such as the eight meanings beginning with "vast and expansive" (*hongkuo*)—these were also not adopted by my private judgment.
Nevertheless, disregarding my own meanness, I have hastily provided annotations and explanations. The students rejoiced in their clarity and requested that I compose a new commentary.
Thereupon, I applied myself with refined diligence and exhausted all thought; though three years passed, including both cold and heat, the draft was begun but not yet completed.
He revised it once more.

Furthermore, he was honored by Prince Zhuang with an appointment as Vice Director of the Office of Buddhist Records (Senglusi) and concurrently served in the Institute for Sūtras and Mantras (Jingzhouguan).

Subsequently, he assisted in the administrative affairs of the office and engaged in the oral recitation of mantras and sūtras. He again raised funds to carve woodblocks for his previous prefaces, and thus produced new prefaces for these sūtras.

I had no leisure to inquire further. In the summer of the Guiwei year, my duties at the monastery were briefly suspended; I went to a mountain hermitage to escape the heat, which is the present-day Samsan-am.
Its former name was Maga-am, but over many years it had fallen into ruin and could no longer shield one from wind and rain.

I expanded its foundations and renovated it, changing its name to its current one. While supervising the construction work, I felt a deep sense of longing for my two sons and passed some time lecturing on this sutra.
Having just finished one reading of my newly revised commentary, I lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* for my two sons.
Therein I explained that the Bodhisattva Asanga had formerly received the eighty-line verses directly from the Venerable Maitreya in Tuṣita Heaven.
Thereupon, a new work was produced consisting of a commentary on the sutra verses titled *Xinyan shu jing ji hejie* (A New Eye Commentary: Sutra Verses Combined with Explanation).
On the day the draft was completed, it happened that Master Du Bohui visited at Wanshou Jitan Temple; he took full responsibility for its publication.
The record of these events dates to the thirtieth year of the Qianlong era. In the thirty-first year, the cyclical year Bingxu, Zhengyin Xiuweng passed away. Furthermore, I received...

Prince Zhuang was appointed as the Director of the Office of Monastic Records (Senglusi Zhengyin). Before long, however, his talent proved insufficient for the responsibilities, causing his chronic illness to flare up;

his four limbs became numb, making it difficult for him to perform his duties. Shortly thereafter, he requested leave to return to the mountains to quiet his mind and调养 (nourish and restore) his health.

On the day of Dinghai, my illness slightly improved. On the day of Wuzi, I took up the original manuscript and practiced calligraphy over it; it was sufficient for my own confidence. I intended to solicit funds to carve it into woodblocks, when I was unexpectedly favored by the General Manager of the Office of Buddhist Records (Sengdaoluosi).

The Sixth Imperial Prince issued an edict ordering the cancellation of his leave and the re-engraving of the woodblocks, while concurrently petitioning for the appointment of a new abbot for Nianhua Temple. Thereafter, Liu Xingzi remained at the mountain hermitage to transcribe the text, while Huanzi accompanied him to Nianhua Temple to proofread the characters.
They subsequently raised funds and prepared the long-life jujubes. In the year of Gengyin, [the work was] respectfully...
As was the custom,
he performed his devotions at the Buddhist Hall in the Yuanmingyuan. In the thirty-sixth year, the Xinmao year,
he respectfully attended the grand celebration for the Empress Dowager’s longevity.
I was granted the purple robe to serve at the Imperial Altar. Reflecting upon this, I consider myself a poor man who has left the household life;

how could I have been destined to encounter such magnificent grace? I feel profound shame and am utterly unable to repay it in kind. This remains so until the present year, the Bingshen year of the Qianlong era, the forty-first year.

The carving of the blocks is now complete. I shall retire from the printing work to practice in seclusion, offering prayers for the Emperor’s longevity to repay the grace of the state, and spend the remainder of my years in this way;
this is truly my aspiration. I previously composed the "Preface to the *Fahua zhizhang bian*" (Compilation of the Lotus Sutra at the Fingers’ Tip).
At the end, it is said: "For over twenty years, I have regarded my own life as if it were a dream. Whether dwelling here or there, looking back, I am like a person within a dream.
Nearly four hundred thousand words have been spoken—all are but the mutterings of sleep in a dream.
Whatever occurred therein, whether contrary or favorable, was all a realm of dreaming. Even now, as I compile and arrange this from beginning to end, it remains still a discourse within a dream."
A dream. Yet, since it is said that one is "dreaming within a dream," this is simply one dream that has not yet awakened.
Now, having spent more than twenty years of labor to compose this new commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, is this not likewise one dream that has not yet awakened?
This is yet another continuation of my dream. I reflect that when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, he never uttered a single word;
how much less could he have uttered a single word within these sutras and commentaries, which do not even total six hundred thousand words?
I humbly entreat those who read these sutras and peruse these commentaries hereafter: may you please refrain from speaking of them as such.
This is a refutation of [erroneous] assertions and also serves as a commentary on the nature of real phenomena (*dharmas*).
Written on the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony for the monastic community in the year of Bingshen, the forty-first year of the Qianlong era.
Recorded respectfully by the purple-robed śramaṇa Xiànzōng, his junior disciple Tōnglǐ. Regarding the general principles for reading this commentary:

since this sūtra was transmitted to Zhèndàn (China), commentaries, records, treatises, and exegeses have become exceedingly numerous. In selecting the finest gold and gathering the finest jade, I truly defer to the *Huìzhǎo* (Compendium of Insights).

[This is] an explanation. In discerning the pulse and tracing its source, there is nothing comparable to the *Jiaoguang*. Now, for the purpose of guiding beginners to gradually enter the inner sanctum, this work differs from previous expositions;
fearing that new readers might be startled by these differences, you should peruse it thoroughly and not easily harbor doubts.

This commentary is titled "Fingers and Palms" (*Zhǐzhǎng*) because it seeks clarity and ease of understanding. I have not avoided philological explanations, even if they occasionally involve prolixity.
Since the realization of wisdom transcends conventional boundaries, one may freely abandon the complex for the essential; yet, in establishing these principles, I must support the foundational walls.
Furthermore, one must proceed from the coarse to the subtle; do not disdain examining the leaves and tracing the branches, lest you omit nine-tenths while hanging onto but a single strand.

(Tongli: Relying on a sense of shame, I have studied through learning; my wisdom does not surpass that of others. I have been unable to consult extensively with the highly enlightened or to peruse the vast corpus of ancient writings.
Consequently, every word and phrase in this commentary flows from my own breast. As I am not skilled in the styles of other authors, I did not dare to incorporate them haphazardly.
This was not out of any intention to exclude them, nor should you insist upon judging them as right or wrong.
The entire textual structure of this scripture possesses both main headings (*kāṇḍa*) and sub-sections (*varga*).

Within these sub-sections, there are further headings and sub-sections, much like the successive generations of an imperial lineage—such as the Son of Heaven, his father, and his sons and grandsons—which unfold one after another without the slightest disorder.

As for the relationship between heading and heading, or sub-section and sub-section, they follow one another like brothers, with their sequence being perfectly appropriate. By dividing the text according to these categories, a natural hierarchy is established. (The Śūraṅgama Sūtra)

Zhengmo has largely grasped this key point; my current commentary follows his lead. However, Master Jiao’s analysis is excessively detailed, often interrupting what should be continuous and thereby causing the meaning to lose its coherence for beginners who fail to perceive this. My present commentary distinguishes these matters.
This commentary, in order to avoid excessive detail, occasionally contains within a single section two or three distinct meanings.

Without clear headings, one could not decisively distinguish their connections; therefore, I have used circles (○) in the main text to mark them, and in the commentary, I have individually indicated each meaning.
For instance, at the beginning, it says "First, such-and-such meaning," and upon completion of the explanation, it further states "Under such-and-such, [the next] such-and-such."
I hope that by avoiding excessive subdivision, the essential points will be clearly distinguished.
In the ancient commentaries, the topical outlines (kōmoku) generally do not list all sub-sections; for instance, if a section is divided into three parts, only the first is indicated.

The text was then further divided into sections or paragraphs, which made it particularly difficult for beginners to cross-reference and verify. Now, following the structural format of the *Annotated Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*, each division has been clearly marked.

Once marked, the corresponding passages from the sūtra have been cited in sequence. At the conclusion of each commentary section, the end of that specific section (e.g., "Section X Complete") is noted;
however, if two sections are immediately adjacent, this concluding notation is omitted for the sake of ease of reading, so as not to... [interrupted].

Turning back the preceding and flipping to the following, the *Lengyan Zhengmai* (The True Pulse of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) employs characters such as "A," "B," and so forth to distinguish the headings and their hierarchical levels;

the Elder Boting also frequently adopted this practice. In the present commentary, I have fully designated all headings, and furthermore, at the conclusion of each section, I have tied together the preceding and following parts.
The sequence is clearly evident; therefore, I have not further employed characters such as "Jia" or "Yi.
A single sound is universally encompassed, yet diverse interpretations each manifest. As with the pestle, mortar, rope, and winnowing basket, all together describe the likeness of an elephant's body;
among the crane, snow, conch, and rice, which can clarify the true color of milk? Seeking the root through the branches, each selects its own rationale for entering the Way.
The conditions [for this work] are manifold and sufficient in themselves. Do not say that the original commentary is overly prolix and would hinder the widespread dissemination of this sutra.
Among the commentaries written by ancient masters, there are occasionally those that accord with my own views; these I have also slightly excerpted.
If I were to use their words in their entirety, I would cite them by name, such as saying "Zhengmo says," and so forth. If I have made even slight modifications, [I have indicated this].

Thus, I have merely highlighted the essential meaning as it was understood; for instance, when I refer to the "meaning of the *Zhengmai*" and so forth, it is because I dare not conceal the excellence of the ancients.
When gold and brass are set side by side, or jade and stone are displayed together, those with discerning eyes can naturally distinguish them; there is no need for deliberate disparagement or praise.

While the established doctrines of the *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) are indeed refined, its excessive refutation of past authorities causes later students to spend their efforts solely on calculating right and wrong, rather than seeking the meaning at the vital junctures.
Thus, they remain confused about the fundamental and obscure the source; this error is no small matter.
Therefore, in this present commentary, I have merely borrowed its essential meanings, while refraining from any polemical language that would seek to engage in combat.

Furthermore, Zhengmo (the Correct Pulse) is overly detailed regarding difficult points and overly brief regarding easy points; it accommodates only those of sharp intelligence and does not reach those of dull faculties.

This present commentary, however, provides clear instruction on difficult points without omission, and likewise elaborates upon easy points as necessary, so that all three types of faculties may be benefited and both the sharp and the dull may find it suitable.
*The Finger-Palm Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Fascicle One.
Respectfully composed by the junior disciple Da Tian Tong Li of Xian Zong of Nianhua Monastery in the Capital.
Transcribed by the dharma-heir disciple Xing Zong Zu Wang; proofread by Qing Huai Ren Zu Yu.
The ninth section provides a general explanation of the title. This means that a name is the guest of the reality it denotes, while a title is the mainstay of a scripture.

Since the great meaning of an entire sutra is concentrated within its title, it is called a "general explanation. That is to say, it is a general explanation of the great meaning of the entire sutra contained within the title.
Furthermore, "name" refers to the name of the translator, and "title" refers to the title of the translated scripture; thus it is said:
Regarding the general explanation: this refers to explaining the title of the scripture by means of its name. It is divided into two parts:
first, the title of the scripture; second, the translator. First:
*The Great Buddha-Crown Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, the Definitive Meaning of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Volume One: Explaining the Title of this Sūtra. This is briefly presented in five sections: first, a preliminary reconciliation of the five names; second, the formal explanation of the current title;
third, a brief preparation of the ancient methods; fourth, a renewed presentation of the Western (Sanskrit) name; and fifth, an appended explanation of the sequence of the volumes. First:
According to what the Buddha himself has taught in the sutra, there are five titles. First:
"The Great Uṣṇīṣa Śītavana-bhadrā Unsurpassed Jewel Seal, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions. (Zhengmo says: These are names based on both object and wisdom;

that is, "Great" and so forth refer to the object, while "Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions" and below belong to wisdom. Second: "The Savior and Protector of Kinsmen and Causes, Who Delivers Ānanda and Those in This Assembly."
1. The Female Bhikṣuṇī of Neutral Sex attains the Bodhicitta and enters the ocean of universal knowledge. (Zhengmo states: This is named after the recipient and the benefit;

that is, the female bhikṣuṇī Ānanda is the recipient, while "attaining bodhicitta" and so forth constitute the benefit. 2. The Tathāgata’s Secret Cause: The Definitive Meaning of Cultivation and Realization. (Zhengmo states: This is named after both nature and cultivation;

the "Tathāgata’s secret cause" pertains to what is inherent by nature, while the "definitive meaning of cultivation and realization" pertains to what is attained through practice. 3. The Great Vaipulya King of the Wondrous Lotus, the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions.
Dhāraṇī-mantra. (Zhengmo says: "Excellence" serves as its name; for the seven characters above are manifest and most excellent, while the eight characters below are esoteric and most essential.

Fifth is the "Chapter on the Sentences of Consecration," the Śūraṅgama of the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas. (Zhengmo says: "Cause and effect" serve as its name; the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas are the cause, and Śūraṅgama is the fruit.
This present title takes nineteen characters from among these five names, selecting the essentials to encompass the vast.
The *Sūtra on Sequential Compendium* was skillfully composed by the compilers. Second, the correct explanation of the title has four parts:
first, pointing to the fundamental essence of the Dharma, which is the single character "Great" (*mahā*). That which is called "Great" is precisely the mind of sentient beings.
This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena; therefore, it is called "Great. In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is the One True Dharma-realm (*eka-tathatā-dharmadhātu*).

This One True Dharma-realm subsumes the four dharma-realms and universally integrates the causes and effects of cause and fruit, as well as immeasurable wondrous gates and boundless wondrous meanings—is this not truly great? In various sutras, it is sometimes designated as...
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is sometimes designated as the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), sometimes as perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), and sometimes as suchness (*tathatā*).
In reality, all these are but the one mind. In this very sutra, it is the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*. Yet, this *tathāgatagarbha-citta* is not any dharma;
no dharma can encompass it. At the same time, it is all dharmas; yet no dharma can [contain] it.
It eludes and transcends; it is neither "is" nor "is not," neither "is" nor "is not. The path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity ceases.

Having no other recourse, we forcibly name it "Great. This is not "great" spoken in opposition to "small"; for if "great" were spoken in opposition to "small," then the great would have limits, and thus would not be the true Great.
Nor is it that it was small first and becomes great later; for if it were small first and then became great, then the great...

It has a beginning and an end, for it is not that its essence is originally great. Know, therefore, that this Greatness is inexhaustible throughout the ten directions and unfathomable across the three periods of time.
In delusion, it is the secret cause of the Tathāgata; in awakening, it is the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization.

As a cause, it is the myriad practices of the Bodhisattva; as a fruit, it is the Śūraṅgama King Samādhi. The essential and subtle points of this single sutra do not exceed this principle. The ten realms...
As for the pivotal axis, nothing surpasses this essence; there is indeed a profound reason for placing it at the head.

Second, to manifest the supreme excellence of the Dharma, there are the two characters for "Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. Regarding what is called "Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa," it refers to the invisible crown of the head atop the *uṣṇīṣa* mark.
This *uṣṇīṣa* mark is one of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), situated upon the blue-black curls of hair.
The hair at the center of his head is like the sun emerging from a spring mountain, yet its crown cannot be seen. It was as when the Buddha first descended from the Tuṣita heaven;
the forest deity of Lumbinī, acting as the Buddha’s wet nurse, held him up and gazed intently, yet could not see the crown of his head.
Furthermore, after the Buddha attained enlightenment and traveled to Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisattva Pūrṇa of the East sought to fathom the limit of the Buddha’s crown, ascending through the sands...
Even the Buddha’s eye cannot see it; it is but one of the eighty secondary marks, namely the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdha*).
To manifest the Dharma by means of this [mark] has, briefly, two meanings: first, because the Buddha’s crown is most supreme and unsurpassed, it manifests that this Dharma is likewise most supreme.

By practicing in reliance upon it, one proceeds directly toward unsurpassed bodhi. Second, "the most wondrous and invisible crown of the Buddha" (buddhoṣṇīṣa) reveals that this dharma is supremely sublime;

it is exhausted only by a Buddha, for it cannot be fully comprehended by anyone else. Furthermore, while the preceding [passage] merely revealed its greatness, this further reveals its excellence and subtlety.
It is a direct pointing to the essence of the dharma as being both great and the crown of the Buddha. Moreover,
The Buddha’s crown (uṣṇīṣa) may also serve as a metaphor; however, it is not as direct or intimate as pointing directly [to the reality].
Third, the detailed analysis of the distinct meanings is divided into four parts.
First, the secret permeation of the primary cause (*dharmatā-hetu*), which corresponds to the phrase "the secret cause of the Tathāgata. "Tathāgata" is one of the ten titles [of a Buddha].

The title “Tathāgata” (如來) is modeled after the designations of former virtuous teachers and contains two meanings. First, the explanation according to phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): this means that the Way of all Buddhas is identical.

When a later Buddha appears in the world, he is exactly like a former Buddha returning; therefore, he is called Tathāgata. Second, the explanation according to the penetration of principle (*tattva*):

depending on the depth of the teachings, there are many varieties that cannot be fully exhausted here. Now, based on the ultimate reality, "Thus" (*tathā*) refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), and "Coming" (*āgata*) refers to initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*).
Ultimate initial awakening is identical to the original awakening; this also follows the interpretation of the former masters.
In contrast to the bodhisattvas mentioned below, this refers to those who have attained the fruit, a title applied after the path of the various bodhisattvas.

Regarding the "secret cause," this is the true causal Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), which all sentient beings equally possess. Although they are deluded and do not know it, because of the power of internal permeation (*paripāka*), [they are led toward awakening].
Encountering the right conditions, faith is awakened; through this, one can ultimately attain Buddhahood. Precisely because one can become a Buddha, it is called the "cause of the Tathāgata.

Because those in delusion do not know this, it is further termed "mysterious" (*mi*). Furthermore, the reason the cause is called "Tathāgata" and also termed "mysterious" is to eliminate the errors of two types of people:
first, the term "Tathāgata" eliminates the adherents of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) of the Lesser Teaching who harbor delusion.
Regarding the fault of self-condemnation: because they do not realize that "mind is itself Buddha," they resign themselves to being excluded from the path and sink exclusively into emptiness.

Now, hearing that the cause is itself the Tathāgata, they suddenly awaken from their dream and sober up from their intoxication; turning away from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, they possess the potential to achieve Buddhahood.

Regarding the fault of abandoning cultivation for the sake of the "one word" of the two secrets: by means of this, the wild wisdom of the Perfect Teaching is dispelled, and one proceeds to actual practice.
As soon as he believed that his own mind was the Buddha, he abandoned cultivation entirely. Now he hears that it is merely the "secretly endowed" (mi-jù);
he knows for himself that it is not yet the perfected state, and that one must initiate cultivation from the fundamental nature, hoping to attain the capacity of fruition.

This, however, is precisely the true root among the two roots—namely, the original luminosity of the essence of consciousness (shí-jīng yuán-míng), which is capable of giving rise to all conditions; it is that which is lost amidst those conditions.

In the text, the ten instances that reveal the seeing are first pointed out from the faculty of the eye; by taking this one as an example for the other five, it is shown that all six faculties possess it.
If this principle is expanded and applied, it is evident that this seeing is not only present within the immediate faculties, but in fact encompasses all phenomena at a distance.

Subsequently, the four categories were synthesized and the seven elements were harmonized. The causes for the continuity of birth were clarified, and the reason for their perfect interfusion was revealed.
The entirety of the Three Baskets was fully manifested as not departing from the one mind; thus, the purport of the Tathāgata’s secret cause was expounded without any remainder.

The sutra text begins with the request for stabilization and continues through the first half of the fourth fascicle. [The practitioners] attain physical and mental pliancy, experiencing what they have never had before.
The Tathāgata repeatedly provides instruction, causing them to cultivate *śamatha*; only then do they respond with faith and compliance.

Within the four sections, the instruction on *śamatha* constitutes the "Section on Establishing Faith," and its meaning concludes here. Second is the manifestation of the "causal factor of realization" (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*), which is cultivation.

It is the realization of the words of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). To give rise to contemplation through faith is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*); this means that the practice of contemplation itself constitutes cultivation, rather than cultivation being achieved through the gradual performance of various tasks.

To attain understanding through practice is called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*); this means that awakening through understanding itself constitutes realization, rather than realization being attained by traversing successive stages.
This is because for a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, at the time of faith, understanding and awakening are simultaneous; at the time of understanding...
Since there has already been entry into realization, it was granted at the end of the preceding section that Ānanda and others had awakened their minds to the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Yet, this present section speaks of "cultivating and realizing the definitive meaning" (*yathārtha-nītārtha*). In truth, what preceded was faith (*śraddhā*), while this is understanding (*prajñā*).

This is because the sequential arrangement (*pratipatti-paṭala*) does not obstruct the perfect interfusion (*yuganaddha*); the statement is made by taking the superior aspect as the primary focus. Furthermore, regarding what is called "definitive meaning," there are two senses.
First is the realization of the preceding meaning; second is the realization of the meaning without remainder. Regarding the realization of the preceding meaning:

because of the faithful compliance with the teaching in the preceding section, although one knows that there is the secret cause of the Tathāgata, one has not yet been able to realize it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Therefore, he used a metaphor for himself, saying: "I am now like a traveler who has taken temporary lodging. Suddenly, I have been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King.
Although I have obtained this great residence, I must enter through the gate. (Please observe the gate; it signifies seeking awakening and entry.

Thus, the Tathāgata distinguished the gates to establish two meanings and provided verification to resolve two doubts. He tied the headcloth to demonstrate the proper sequence and... [the text continues].

He was granted the selection of the fundamental source. This was intended for him to practice and realize through the samādhi of the ear-gate, thereby awakening to the meaning of the "Secret Cause of the Tathāgata" discussed in the preceding section.
The phrase "nothing further remains to be understood" refers to the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty.

Transcending the twenty-four sages, it alone is wondrous. By relying on this for cultivation and realization, the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause.
In a single cultivation, all are cultivated; in a single realization, all are realized. There is not a single further meaning remaining to be cultivated or realized.
As for the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas that follow, they do not exceed a brief demonstration of the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) within the context of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).

The meaning of the sūtra text is divided into two sections. The first begins from the latter half of the fourth fascicle with the request for the door of the jeweled house, extending through the middle of the sixth fascicle to the passage where ten *asaṃkhyeya* *sahasra* of beings all recover their original mind, become free from dust and defilement, and attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.

To reveal the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*), the text proceeds from the latter half of the sixth fascicle with the request to establish the ritual site (*maṇḍala*) until the middle of the seventh fascicle, where the "Light on the Crown" (*uṣṇīṣa*) explains the mantras, demonstrating the benefits, the vows of protection by the two assemblies, and so forth; this serves to reveal the ritual procedures (*shi-yi*).

This is intended generally to cause one to cultivate *samādhi*. Among the four divisions, the division that elucidates the accomplishment of the understanding of *samādhi* concludes its meaning at this point.
The three conditions, causes, and aids for cultivation are precisely the phrases concerning the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas. "Bodhisattva" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term;
in full it is *bodhisattva*, which is translated here as "Awakened Being. There are three interpretations of this: first, with respect to oneself...
First, regarding self-benefit: although awakening is partially realized, one still possesses emotional consciousness (*saṃjñā*). Second, regarding the benefit of others:
it means awakening those sentient beings so that they may become like oneself. Third, regarding both benefits: it means seeking great awakening above while transforming sentient beings below.
In relation to the Tathāgata above, this refers to the stage of a causal practitioner; it is a designation used prior to the path of the Tathāgata. Thus, it is called "all... [bodhisattvas].
This refers generally to the fifty-five stages of the various sages who have attained partial realization within *dhyāna*. The practices cultivated throughout these stages are immeasurable:
for instance, in the ten faiths, one plants the seeds of Buddhahood through the full power of the faculties; in the ten abidings, one is born into the Buddha-family and becomes a child of the Buddha;
in the ten practices, one extensively performs Buddha-works through the six *pāramitās*; and in the ten dedications, one dedicates [merit] to the Buddha...
Taking phenomena as they are and turning toward the Buddha-mind, the four stages of application (prayoga) dissolve both mind and Buddha, extinguishing all numerical distinctions.

The ten stages (bhūmi) accord with True Suchness (tathatā), encompassing nirvana; Equal Enlightenment (samyak-sambodhi) reaches the limit of Buddhahood, destroying the mark of birth. One contains all; principal and satellites are layered upon one another;
dependent origination is unimpeded, like the net of Indra. What is now called "ten thousand luminosities" is manifold and not restricted to a fixed number.
This is a numerical exposition. According to the previous explanation of the "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*), it states: "In one practice, all are practiced; in one realization, all are realized.

This signifies that there is no further meaning remaining to be practiced or realized. Now, to speak again of the "ten thousand practices" is truly because the sequential arrangement (*pratipatti-vyavasthāna*) does not obstruct the perfect fusion (*pariniṣpanna-yoga*), and the perfect fusion likewise has no cause for disparaging the sequential arrangement.
The preceding section was intended to honor and exalt those at the initial stage of the path. As for the interpretation...

At that time, one immediately speaks of "realization and entry," so as to let [the practitioner] know that the principle is realized through sudden awakening; this serves as an antidote to wild wisdom (*prajñā*).

To say that all matters are "ultimate" (piàn-jìng) means to exhaustively penetrate the very root and source of all phenomena (*dharmas*), as in the meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra* regarding the ultimate reality-mark (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena.

First, the method of establishing titles. This refers to the way titles are established for various sūtras, which may consist of a single element—person, dharma, or metaphor—or combinations thereof, up to all three together.
There are seven such types as examples: first, a single person, such as *Vimalakīrti*; second, a single dharma, such as *Nirvāṇa*; third, a single metaphor, such as *Ratnakūṭa*.

This must be a recollection of what was heard in the past; it is merely said that "that was at one time. *Buddha* (佛) means the master of accomplishment. In the Sanskrit language, it is *Buddha*; here it is translated as "the Awakened One" (*Jue-zhe*).
It is one of the ten universal titles [of a Buddha]. There are three meanings of "Awakening" (*Jue*): first, self-awakening, which distinguishes [the Buddha] from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

second, awakening others, which distinguishes [him] from those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); third, full awakening, which distinguishes [him] from bodhisattvas. As for the character *zhe* (者): [The character *zhe* is used here as a nominalizing particle.]

"Person" (pudgala) generally refers to one capable of awakening. However, in the context of the present sutra, it specifically refers to Śākyamuni, as he is the presiding master of the *Śūraṅgama* assembly and not any other Buddha.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Only the Tathāgata is that to whom we return. Thus, he is the fourth [reliance].
He was accomplished in a dwelling within a house; Śrāvastī is the full form of Śrāvastī-ṣṭhī. [The old translation...]
It is called Śrāvastī; sometimes it is called Śāvatthī. This translates as "Abundant Virtue" (Puṇyavatī) or "Renowned Object.

This means that the kingdom abounds in the four virtues—wealth, the five desires, extensive learning, and liberation—and because it is an object of renown. The Jetavana Vihāra is located in the vicinity of Śrāvastī.
"Jetavana" refers to Jeta, also known as Śuddhodana’s son, who was the Prince of King Bimbisāra. This translates as "Victorious in Battle" (Jita). Because...

When the Crown Prince was born, King Bimbisāra returned in triumph, and thus it was named the Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak). Because it was there that he made his offering, the vihāra is called the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden.
A residence was established within the garden; as it was the most exquisite and marvelous, it was referred to by the name of the residence rather than the garden.
Originally, both the garden and the grove belonged to the Crown Prince. The Elder Anāthapiṇḍada purchased the garden and built a monastery, inviting the Buddha to preach the Dharma;
he did not decline the expense of covering it with gold, and consequently moved the Crown Prince to donate both the land and the grove.

Since the sovereign is honored and the subject is humble, the former (the grove) comes first, followed by the latter (the garden). Many sūtras refer to this as "Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park," which is more elegant; the subsequent text states that it "belongs to."

"O Bhikṣus, the summer retreat has ended and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony was performed. It is not possible for the Buddha and the Saṃgha to remain in retreat without this; therefore, this constitutes the fifth [requirement].

(The account of the elder purchasing the grove is detailed in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Āgama*, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, and other texts; it is not recorded here as it is not urgent. The general presentation of the five accomplishments is concluded.
II. The specific enumeration of the assembly: 1. The assembly of Śrāvakas; 2. The assembly of Pratyekabuddhas. The first [of these] has three parts."
First, the categories are raised to indicate the number; second, the stages are clarified and their virtues extolled; third, the principal leaders are briefly set forth. Regarding the first:
"Together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty people."

The initial citation of categories reveals his excellence. "Together with" (*saha*) means "in conjunction with," carrying the sense of inclusion. "Great" (*mahā-*) distinguishes him from the small, as he is not one in training (*śaikṣa*).

Furthermore, there are three senses in which he is called "great": namely, great in scale, great in number, and great in excellence. He is "great" because he is revered and honored by celestial kings and great men alike, for he does not possess merely minor virtues.
He is "great in number" because regarding internal and external scriptures, there is nothing he has not mastered extensively; he is not one of meager understanding.
Therefore, the "Victorious One" (Jina) transcends the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths; he is not an inferior vessel. The term *bhikṣu* contains three meanings:
first, the mendicant (*bhikṣu*), meaning one who begs for food and begs for the Dharma to nourish and benefit body and mind;

second, the destroyer of evil (*bhettā pāpasya*), meaning one who destroys [wrong] views and destroys [unwholesome] thoughts, thereby washing away all evils; third, the terrifier of Māra (*bhīṣaṇo māram*), meaning that by leaving the household life and crossing the boundaries, Māra is terrified.
Because they have lost their faction. "The assembly" (zhòng) is *saṃgha* in the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "harmonious assembly. There are two kinds of harmony:
first, harmony of affairs (*vastu-sāmagrī*), meaning that the six matters of precepts, views, livelihood, body, speech, and mind are all in accord;

second, harmony of principle (*dharma-sāmagrī*), meaning that they equally realize the unconditioned dharma of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Now, when only "assembly" is mentioned and not "harmony," it is because [the term] "assembly" already implies...
"Must be harmonious. Without harmony, there is no assembly. The second line indicates the number to manifest their unity. The *Bao’en jīng* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states:
First, he converted Cunda and the five others; next, he converted fifty disciples of Yaśas; next, he converted five hundred disciples of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa;
next, he converted three hundred disciples of Gayā-Kāśyapa; next, he converted the disciples of Nadī-Kāśyapa.
Two hundred. Next, he converted one hundred disciples of Śāriputra; next, he converted one hundred disciples of Maudgalyāyana.
Altogether, this totals one thousand two hundred and fifty-five people. The current reduction of five persons is due to the omission of minor figures. "Jù" (俱) means "together" or "the same.
These individuals had all long practiced heterodox paths, gaining nothing from their emptiness. Upon meeting the Buddha, they obtained benefit and were moved [to faith].
Their grace constantly follows them; now they likewise listen together, hence it is said they "go along with" [the Buddha]. This concludes the section on citing examples and indicating the number.

Second, the explanation of their status and praise of their virtues: they are all untainted (*anāsrava*) Great Arhats. "The Sons of the Buddha abide in the maintenance [of the Dharma], skillfully transcending all realms of existence (*bhava*); they are able, within the kingdom..."

He has perfected the majestic deportment of the earth and followed the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma. Wondrously worthy of being entrusted with the legacy, he strictly purifies the *vinaya* and establishes a grand model for the three realms.
With immeasurable transformation bodies, he delivers sentient beings, rescuing those of the future and causing them to transcend all worldly defilements.
First, based on their outward traces, their stages are clarified. "All of them" refers to the fact that there is no difference among the assembly. "Outflows" (*āsrava*) refers to the three outflows:

the outflow of desire (the afflictions of the desire realm), the outflow of existence (the afflictions of the two upper realms), and the outflow of ignorance (the ignorance of the three realms). Those who possess these are like a leaking vessel that is unfit for use;
furthermore, because they fall into the cycle of birth and death due to these outflows, this assembly has already severed them, and thus it is so called.

There is none. There are three meanings of "Mahāsattva" (Great Being): first, to distinguish [him] from those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*), for he is capable of turning his mind [toward enlightenment];

second, to distinguish him from those of actual practice (*satya-pratipatti*), for he is a provisional manifestation (*upāya-nirmita*); third, to distinguish him from those of the same class, for he is called the "Foremost. The term "Arhat" also has three meanings:

first, "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*), because he is fit to be a field of merit (*puṇya-kṣetra*); this is the fruit of the "Beggar" (*bhikṣu*). Second, "Slayer of Thieves," because he slays the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*); this is...

"Destroying evil fruits": the third is "non-arising," because it eternally severs future existence; this is precisely the fruit that terrifies Māra. The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) has long monopolized this name, so it serves as a provisional trace (*traces*).

Regarding the section beginning with "O Son of the Buddha," this praises his virtues based on his fundamental nature (*mūla*), while clarifying that his position is established through provisional traces.

To praise virtues based on the fundamental nature is to lead those of the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*); thus, he outwardly manifests as a Śrāvaka while inwardly conceals his status as a Bodhisattva.

Therefore, they are called "sons of the Buddha. Since they are called sons of the Buddha, they do not disdain to maintain their presence in the world rather than merely withdrawing themselves for self-preservation;
thus, it is said they "abide and uphold" (*zhuchi*). This means they dwell in the world to uphold the Buddha-dharma and transform sentient beings.

Although they dwell in the world, they are not bound by any worldly phenomena; therefore, it is said they "skillfully transcend" (*shanchao*). If one were to sink solely into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence, even such transcendence would not be skillful. Regarding all worldly phenomena...
Briefly explained, there are three; explained in moderation, there are nine; and extensively expounded, they become twenty-five.
Because cause and effect are not lost therein, it is called "existence" (*bhava*). It refers to kingdoms and royal capitals, where splendor dazzles the eyes and superior desires entice the mind.
To possess both majestic power and dignified deportment is not easily attained. One who is said to be "capable" or "accomplished" is one who acts as a master amidst the dust of the world;
they cannot be compared to those who merely exert themselves through forced pretension. "From" (cong) means to follow.

When the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings, this assembly constantly follows him, drawing in and gathering those of a similar kind. To transcend existence is to remain unattached to existence.
Possessing the ritual protocols, one does not sink into emptiness; because emptiness and existence are unrestrained, it is termed "wondrous.

Furthermore, because [the Buddha] turned the wheel of Dharma following the Buddhas and his karmic ties were long-established, he was worthy of being entrusted with the legacy. This refers to the entrustment to achieve Buddhahood and the charge to deliver sentient beings;
as he is capable of both, this above praises the virtue of self-benefit. Although it concurrently involves benefiting others, it merely borrows from external objects.

Once accomplished, it still pertains to self-benefit. *Vinaya* is the general name for the precepts and discipline. To discipline the body is called "rigor" (*yan*); to discipline the mind is called "purity" (*jing*).

Furthermore, regarding the precepts of phenomena (*dharma*), there is rigor; regarding the precepts of principle (*li*), there is purity. Now, to manifest the simultaneous upholding of both principle and phenomenon, and the concurrent disciplining of both body and mind, they are thus termed "rigorous" and "pure.
Yet, this is not merely for self-benefit; therefore, it is said to "establish a grand model for the three [realms]."
"Realm" (*dhātu*) means extensively opening the model of the Dharma within the three realms. "Response-body" (*nirmāṇakāya*) refers to manifesting in response according to the capacities of beings.
"Immeasurable" means that because capacities are immeasurable, the response-bodies are likewise immeasurable.

"Liberating sentient beings" refers not only to manifesting the body but also to preaching the Dharma, such as in the cases of Gadgadasvara and Avalokiteśvara in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. "Future" refers to the totality...
"Exhausting the ultimate limit" (*jìn-jì*) refers to the comprehensive inclusion of all worldly defilements (*chén-láo*).

It means that sentient beings are burdened and fallen by these defilements, transmigrating through birth and death as if falling into a deep abyss or sinking into a great deluge. This assembly is able to pull them up and enable them to cross over;
therefore, they are said to "extricate" (*bá*) and "rescue" (*jì*). The above praises the virtue of transforming others; although it also encompasses self-benefit, it is...
To accomplish things for others by means of oneself still belongs to the category of transforming others (*parārtha*). Within these virtues of transforming others:

first, it is said that "the broad model [of conduct] pervades the three realms," which seems limited to a single land; next, it is said that "the response bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are immeasurable," which encompasses the ten directions;

finally, it is said that "they rescue and deliver those of the future," which extends to the very limits of existence. Thus, there are no sentient beings—whether horizontally or vertically—who cannot be transformed. (Question: In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the praise of virtues is clearly [expressed as... sound...)

I have heard that this sutra praises his virtues and clarifies that he is a bodhisattva. Based on this, the ancient masters judged the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* to follow the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which seems to accord with reason. If it were placed before the *Lotus Sutra*, how would one reconcile this? The compilers used skillful means (*upāya*), casting shadows of both the fundamental and the manifested aspects upon one another.

In the *Lotus Sutra*, the fundamental aspect is revealed everywhere; therefore, its praise of virtues concerns only the manifested aspect. In the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the manifested aspect appears in every instance; therefore, its praise of virtues concerns only the fundamental aspect. The fundamental and the manifested are originally unimpeded; only by casting their shadows upon one another are they fully revealed without omission. Were it not so, [the sequence would be untenable].

Thus, the Lotus Sūtra emphasizes only the fundamental [truth], failing to manifest the provisional means for gathering and transforming sentient beings; the Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra emphasizes only the traces [of the Buddha's career], remaining entirely deluded regarding the profundity of actualizing the reality. How could these be considered fully excellent? Yet, there are other sūtras that are not thus, as some are intended solely for those of a particular capacity.
This concludes the clarification of the stages and the praise of virtues. Third, the brief presentation of the foremost disciples.
Their names were the Greatly Wise Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila,
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Upāliśata, and others who served as the leaders.
Śāriputra was the son of the Venerable Śārī. This name is translated as "Sparrow-Heron" (Śāri). Because his mother’s eyes were pure and her speech sharp, she was comparable to this bird;
thus, he was named after her. It is not translated as "Son," for the Venerable One was born from her, and the name combines the mother with the child.
He is also called "Body-Son" (Shenzi), because his mother’s physical form was upright and graceful, as if she were one who possessed a perfectly formed body.
For this reason, the *Āgama* states: "Within my Buddha-dharma, Śāriputra is foremost among those whose wisdom is inexhaustible and who resolve all doubts;
therefore, he is now honored by the title 'Great Wisdom' (*Mahāprajñā*). As for Maudgalyāyana, this is translated as "Bean-gatherer" (*Mudgalagotra*). It is his clan name (*gotra*).
In ancient times, there was a rishi who lived in the mountains and ate beans he gathered; thus, he took that as his surname. He is revered.
He was merely a descendant of that [lineage]. His name was Nyagrodha, which in this language means "knotless tree.
Because his parents had no son, they prayed to the tree deity and he was born; thus, they named him accordingly. The Āgamas state:

"Within my Buddha-dharma, regarding those who possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and can fly lightly to the ten directions, Maudgalyāyana is foremost," because he possesses great divine transformations.
Therefore, his personal name was not mentioned; he was distinguished by the prefix "Mahā" (Great) attached to his clan name.

Mahā-Kauṣṭhila—translated here as "Great-Thigh"—was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra. Formerly, he had excelled his sister in debate; however, once she became pregnant with Śāriputra, he could no longer surpass her.
Recognizing that the person she carried would surely be superior to himself upon birth, he became indignant and traveled to South India to study.
He studied eighteen types of sūtras so intently that he had no leisure even to trim his nails; thus, the world called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail).

Having completed his studies, he returned home and went to the Buddha to seek his nephew. The Buddha directed him to establish a formal thesis, whereupon he declared: "I take the non-acceptance of all dharmas as my tenet."
The Buddha asked, "Do you still accept this view? He reflected to himself: "If I accept this view, it contradicts my own tenet (for I have established the tenet of non-acceptance).

If I do not accept this view, my own tenet collapses (because by not accepting it, I would be identical to the common views of the masses, and thus I should not have established this tenet). His argument fell through and his words were exhausted; he apologized to the Buddha.
The Buddha permitted him to go forth as a monk, whereupon he realized the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*). The *Āgama* says: "I, the Buddha..."
Among those who have attained the four types of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*) within the Dharma and are able to answer whatever questions they encounter, Kauṣṭhila is foremost.
Pūrṇa—translated here as "Fulfiller of Vows"—is the father of the Venerable One. Maitrāyaṇī—translated here as "Compassionate Woman"—is the mother of the Venerable One;
he was born from her. Because the designation is abbreviated, he is simply called "Maitrāyaṇīputra" (Son of Maitrāyaṇī).
The Āgamas state: "Within my Buddha-dharma, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is foremost among those who are well able to extensively explain and analyze the principles and meanings.
Subhūti—here translated as 'Born of Emptiness' (Kōngshēng)—was so named because when the Venerable One was born, the storehouses of his family were all empty.
His parents were suspicious of this, but the storehouses appeared once more; therefore, he was also named 'Well-Appearing' (Shànxiàn). An interpreter of physiognomy [divined]..."
It is said: Because he was both virtuous and auspicious, he was also named Shanji (Good-Auspicious). He constantly cultivated the Samādhi of Non-contention.
Among the Buddha’s disciples, he was foremost in understanding emptiness. Upānisaṭha—translated here as "Dust-Nature"—attained the Way by contemplating the emptiness of the nature of dust.
He is also called Jinshao ("Close-to-Little"), because the color of his white bones and subtle dust was nearly exhausted. He personally testified to his realization of the Perfect [Enlightenment].

The *Tongwen* states: "From the impure, through the white bones and subtle atoms, one returns to empty space. When both emptiness and form are non-existent, one achieves the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The Tathāgata has certified my name as Niṣadha. Because other members of the assembly cannot be listed exhaustively, the term 'and others' (*ādi*) is employed.
All are the foremost peaks of the Dharma-gate and the guiding pillars of the great assembly; therefore, it is said that they serve as the leaders."
The assembly of Śrāvakas concluded. Second, the assembly of Pratyekabuddhas:

there were also immeasurable Pratyekabuddhas who had attained the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), together with those at the beginning of their practice, all coming to the place where the Buddha was. It happened to be the time when the Bhikṣus were concluding the summer retreat through the ceremony of self-examination (pravāraṇā).

The first section formally describes those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Since the audience at the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* assembly was not limited to the single class of *śrāvakas*, it says "furthermore there were.
The term "immeasurable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) is used to express their vast number. *Pratyekabuddha* is the full form of *pratyekakalpa*; the name contains two meanings:
first, the "Solitary Realizer," who appears in an age without a Buddha, observes the transformations of time, and attains self-awakening by discerning the nature of things.

Second, the Pratyekabuddhas. There are those who appear during the era of a Buddha and, having received his teachings, contemplate dependent origination; when their conditions are severed, they realize the Truth. Ci'en states:
"When Śākyamuni appeared in the world, five hundred Pratyekabuddhas came from the mountains" (referring to those who appear in an era without a Buddha and dwell in the mountains awaiting a Buddha).
The *Renwang jing* states: "Eight million billion Pratyekabuddha Great Sages all assembled. Thus, both of these two categories exist.

The term "existence" (*asti*) is preserved in the Sanskrit. Those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have reached the ultimate truth and exhausted all delusions; because they have nothing further to learn within their own class, they are so designated.
The word "and" (*bing*) serves to clarify those still in training (*śaikṣa*) as well. A teacher accompanies his disciples, hence the use of "and.

Those at the initial stage are precisely those in training, meaning they have first resolved to realize the state of a *pratyekabuddha*. As for "coming together," the disciples follow their teacher; thus it is said [they come together].

"The wind blows and the grass bends" is the underlying principle (*artha*). ○ "Belonging to the subordinates" (*zhǔ zhū xià*) generally states the purpose of their arrival. "Belonging" (*shǔ*) means to attach oneself to.

This means that since this group is not part of the regular retinue and has been permitted to observe the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) in a different location, they have now come together with the intention of attaching themselves to the resident bhikṣus to perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) rite. "The various bhikṣus" refers to the regular retinue; thus, these are śrāvakas.

This concludes the section on the Sangha of Vinaya-discipline. The Buddha ordained that bhikṣus observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*). This serves two purposes: first, to establish the formal boundaries for cultivating the Way;
second, to protect living beings and avoid suspicion. Now, as the summer days come to an end, it is the time to release the boundaries after ninety days.

The Buddha ordained that the retreat be released on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, or alternatively on the fourteenth or sixteenth. [The following concerns] the examination and adjudication...

Regarding the meritorious deeds of the ninety-day retreat: those who recognize their own transgressions declare them themselves; those who do not recognize their own transgressions allow the Sangha to point them out at will.
Thus it is called *pravāraṇā* (Self-Indulgence). This is because one fears that even the slightest flaw or blemish might defile the pure assembly.
However, within this context, both the pratyekabuddhas and the aforementioned śrāvakas belong to those who are the intended audience (*yathābhavyatā*).

This is because the original purpose of this sutra is to harmonize their limited minds and bring them to the fulfillment of the great resolve. As an ancient master said: "When Ziqi was not encountered, Boya snapped his strings."

If there were no person [to hear], for whom would the Dharma be preached? Therefore, this constitutes the sixth [element]. (The six elements above constitute what is also called the "General Preface," as they apply universally to all sūtras; they are also called the "Postscript to the Sūtra," as they were established during the compilation.

The causes and intentions behind the establishment of the compilation have been extensively discussed in various commentaries and are not recorded here. The first part, the narrative establishing the testimony of faith, is concluded.

Second is the narrative of the two conditions for the origination [of the teaching] (in the arising of the various teachings, there are respective conditions that inspire them, whether few or many, each with its own intended meaning; here, both conditions are provided).
II. Two [types of arousal]: 1. that of a bodhisattva; 2. that of a śrāvaka. The first [of these] has two [parts]: 1. a brief indication by way of analogy and induction; 2.

the arousal of the faculties of both new and old practitioners. The first [part] consists of: (a) resolving doubts through inquiry to induce the training in morality (*śīla-śikṣā*); (b) arranging seats in peaceful comfort to induce the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*); and (c) proclaiming the profound [teachings].

This initiates the training in wisdom. That is to say, when the Tathāgata was about to reveal the true precepts, concentration, and wisdom, he first employed a certain type of causal condition to stir the fundamental capacity [of the audience]. When the time came for the formal teaching, it was like the transformative power of a timely rain.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions consulted one another to resolve their doubts; they reverently honored his compassionate yet majestic presence, seeking the profound meaning.
At that moment, the Tathāgata spread his seat and sat in tranquil ease, proclaiming the deep and mysterious principles for those in the assembly.

At the beginning, the subtle capacity [of the sentient beings] responded in silent resonance. The Bodhisattvas, having received their mandate to deliver living beings, each presided over a specific realm; thus they are designated by the ten directions.

Having been separated from the Buddha for a long time, they lacked the conditions to attain the ultimate truth. Regarding the various Mahāyāna codes of discipline (*vinaya*), they were unable to be free from doubt or apprehension in their hearts.
Now, as the summer retreat has ended, they have returned to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; hence it is said they "consult for resolution," meaning they inquire of [the Master].

"Buddha" means to request a definitive resolution. "Respectfully receiving" means to reverently follow and rely upon. The Buddha possesses the two gates of subduing (*nigraha*) and gathering (*saṃgraha*):

regarding that which is requested for resolution, he is as stern as a father toward those who must be analyzed and subdued, and as compassionate as a mother toward those who should be gathered and nurtured.
Thus, the Bodhisattva respectfully receives and relies upon this, not daring to transgress it, taking it as the fundamental basis for his own self-discipline (*svairatā*).
Because [the conditions] have come together, the *pravāraṇā* has been completed. The wondrous faculty moves in the dark, hence it is called "about to seek.
"About to seek" means that it resides within the mind but has not yet reached verbal expression. "The secret meaning" refers to the principle of the equalization of *samādhi* and *prajñā*.

This is because followers of the Two Vehicles do not realize that their own nature is fundamentally in a state of concentration; even if they cultivate meditative stillness, they all fall into partiality and deficiency. Upon reaching *prajñā*, [they attain realization].

Yet, because they still exclusively valued empty wisdom (*śūnyatā-prajñā*), the practice of balancing meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā-samatā*) was transformed into a secret meaning.
The Bodhisattva, knowing this and wishing to bring it forth, had not yet manifested it in speech, but its intent was already clearly revealed; thus he recorded it directly, saying:

"He is about to seek the secret meaning. ○ Immediately below, there is a deep resonance with the timing, like pecking at the right moment. The Buddha’s wisdom discerns the capacity of the beings and responds accordingly.

Not missing the proper moment, it is therefore called "immediate. This is truly the non-contradiction between the pecking hen and the chick. As for "spreading the seat," it means sitting upon the prepared mat.

"Tranquil and at ease" means being peaceful and settled; this is because he intends to preach, so he enters meditative concentration for a short while to examine the capacities of his audience and contemplate the Dharma, thereby demonstrating the proper method for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, describing him as "tranquil and at ease" implies that he is composed and natural, requiring no artificial effort.
"Manifestation" refers to the samādhi that is naturally and inherently possessed. One emerges from this samādhi to respond to the capacities of sentient beings;
hence it is said, "for all the assemblies. The term "assemblies" includes both the Śrāvakas, as both the primary leaders and those they lead are included therein.

"Proclaiming and indicating" means to expound and point out. "Profound and abstruse" means deep, subtle, and wondrous; this corresponds to the previous request for the meaning of the esoteric teachings. And...

Because it teaches the Dharma of the equalization of concentration and wisdom, following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s introductory narrative, he first preached the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, then entered the *Anantamukha-samādhi*, and thereby provided the formal exposition as an analogy. In this present sutra, concentration comes first, followed by the teaching.

However, the specific title of the scripture has not yet been identified. Judging by its meaning, it must belong to the same category as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, that which "first moves through concentration and subsequently gives rise to wisdom. This concludes the brief indication of related citations.
Second, both new and old karmic conditions were stirred;
the pure assembly at the Dharma feast attained what they had never experienced before. The *kalaviṅka*’s celestial voice resounded throughout the ten directions.
Countless Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, gathered at the site of enlightenment, with Mañjuśrī as their leader.

At the beginning, the resident monks (*pūrvavāsika*) initiated the occasion; they spread the seats and prepared the mats to preach the Dharma for the assembly, hence it is called a "Dharma feast" (*dharmāsana*).

As for the "pure assembly" (*śuddhasaṃgha*), this refers to the regular followers and those who had arrived previously. Because they had already completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, they are called the "pure assembly.
