Now, to suddenly beg in sequential order—what is the underlying intention? Therefore, it is explained by the phrase "initially seeking within the mind," and so forth.
*Tanyue* (donor): this is translated as "giver" (*dānapati*). Alternatively, *tan* is translated as "giving" (*dāna*), while *yue* is a Chinese term meaning "by means of the merit of giving."
Because he has crossed the ocean of poverty. Regarding the term "last," it refers to a family that is most defiled and most lowly.
Although they are most defiled and most lowly, if one observes them with an impartial mind, they are all *dānapati* (donors). Previously, he did not beg from them;

now, for the first time, he has conceived this thought, desiring their offerings to serve as the host for his fast. Therefore it is said: "In his heart, he first seeks [alms]; even the defiled and lowly..."
How much more so for those who are pure and noble? Therefore, [the Buddha] addressed them collectively without distinction. As for *kṣatriya*, the full term is *kṣatriya*;

this translates as "royal lineage" (*wangzhong*) or "lord of the fields" (*tianzhu*). It refers to the imperial clan whose descendants have inherited the throne for generations and govern the lands of the state;
they are the most honored among the four castes, hence they are called the "noble caste. These are the pure and noble ones. As for *caṇḍāla*, this...
The butcher is also called the "one with the decorated banner" (*yan-zhi*). This refers to one whose profession is slaughtering; they are not permitted to dwell among the common people.

When traveling, they carry a banner as a mark of their trade so that those who see them may avoid them. These are the defiled and the lowly. Regarding the subsequent explanation of the practice below, it first addresses the intent of the initial seeking.
It states that because the power of the fruit of the first stage (*srotāpanna*) is subtle, when begging for food, one should adhere to the regular rules. First, one seeks the most...
Regarding the subsequent section on the *dānapati* (donor): what is its purpose? It is therefore explained by means of "universal practice" (*fangxing*) and so forth.

As for "universal practice and compassion," this refers to emulating the Bodhisattva’s practice of impartial compassion. One who practices impartial compassion ought naturally to have nothing to exclude or discard;

hence it says, "without discriminating between the lowly and the humble. The phrase "arousing the intention" explains the meaning of "universal practice," stating that even those of minor status find peace.

[The donor] is small. If one necessarily wishes to practice the bodhisattva path, what benefit would there be [in such a limited act]? Therefore, it is explained by means of "arousing the aspiration" and so forth.

"Arousing the aspiration" means arousing the mind of the Mahāyāna. "Perfectly accomplishing" means achieving complete fulfillment. "All sentient beings" includes, in their entirety, those who are pure or defiled, noble or lowly.
It is said that the bodhisattva begs with universal compassion, while sentient beings give as they please; thus, each obtains [their respective result].
Immeasurable merit [is gained]. If the beggar were to exercise discrimination, it would cause some among all sentient beings to achieve perfection while others would not.
Ānanda did not disdain this; thus he proceeded as a bodhisattva.
While this is indeed virtuous, one fears that rescuing someone from a well may not be the conduct of a wise person. This is the successive explanation of the meaning.
[The section] concludes. Third, it summarizes the reasons for this.
Ānanda already knew that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for having minds that were not impartial as arhats.
He then reverently looked up to the Tathāgata to reveal and expound the unobstructed [teaching], thereby resolving all doubts and slanders.
Previously, he was once rebuked, as stated above. It is already known that the intention behind begging for alms in successive order has been understood;
however, the intention does not arise spontaneously, but rather through a specific cause for its inspiration. Thus it is said, "Ānanda already knows," and so forth.

Regarding the rebuke of the two sages, ancient masters point to Vimalakīrti. Furthermore, in his own assembly [the Buddha] said: "Vimalakīrti rebukes them, and one thereby knows that the Tathāgata likewise [rebukes them]."
"Hā! Furthermore, it is said: 'He is the Tathāgata Suvarṇabimbaka; how does he differ from Śākyamuni?
While this explanation may also be tenable, it is ultimately not entirely consistent. I, the ignorant one, say that it need not be pointed out with certainty.

This is because there are still many scriptures of the Tripiṭaka that have not yet reached this land, and even among those already present here, there are some beyond the reach of our eyes. How can we know for certain?"
In other sutras and treatises, there is no separate place where these two sages are rebuked; let us await further reference on this point.
"Tathāgata" is the first of the ten epithets, and "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) is the last of the ten epithets; both are mentioned together here in order to include those in between.

Zhengmo says: Subhūti renounces the poor to beg from the wealthy; his intention lies in bestowing [wealth] so as to sustain their roots of goodness, fearing they might fall into ruin, yet there is no difficulty of diminishing [his own merit]. Mahākāśyapa renounces the wealthy to beg from the poor;

his intention lies in pitying those who have long suffered and bestowing [alms] so as to plant the causes for happiness, yet there is no concern regarding the pursuit of wealth. Therefore, he occupies the honored position of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This was an uneven matter; therefore, the Buddha rebuked it as being wrong. ○ Regarding "reverently admiring" and "changing one's course":

the Tathāgata’s reprimand of those two sages still rings in our ears. How could we dare not be reverent? The Buddha acted to dissolve their partiality and selfishness, merging them back into equality.
How can one not look up to and admire this? It is precisely because of such reverence and admiration that [the realization] is suddenly attained.
I shall set forth the great intention: first, to open and propagate the universal mind that is free from all limitations;
second, to deliver the world from difficult-to-explain doubts and slanders. For when the mind is limited, doubts and slanders are unavoidable.

That is to say, those who are excessively poor often give rise to doubt, while those who are excessively wealthy often give rise to slander. Having finished their vain emulation of the Mahāyāna, they approach the matter with artificial pretension;
passing through the city’s moats and ramparts, they hasten slowly toward the outer gates. They solemnize their deportment and reverently observe the rules of purification.

The ritual for first entering a city: Regarding the *chéng-huáng* (city moat), when there is water it is called a *chí* (moat-pool); when there is no water it is called a *huáng*. One enters from the outside, and thus passes through this first.
Regarding the *guō-mén* (outer gate), this refers to the protective structure outside the gate, which is what is now known as the *wèng-chéng* (瓮城) gate.
As one is about to enter the interior of the city, one slightly increases their self-restraint; hence it is said "to walk slowly," meaning with composure and deliberation.
He walks with slow and measured steps. ○ Regarding the formal etiquette for begging: "Strict" (*yan*) means being careful of one’s appearance; "orderly" (*zheng*) means gathering one’s robes.
Being careful of one’s appearance ensures there is a dignified majesty that inspires awe; gathering one’s robes ensures there is a decorum that one may look up to.
Thus it is called "dignified demeanor" (*weiyi*). "Solemnity" (*su*) refers to strictness of mind; "reverence" (*gong*) refers to respect for the task at hand. Strictness of mind—
Sincerity in fasting is undisturbed. By revering one’s duties, the Dharma is not lost; hence it is called the "Method of Fasting" (*zhāifǎ*). The *Śīla-sūtra* states:
"When I enter a village, I do not engage in any contrary or improper matters, but only observe my own bodily conduct—whether it is upright or not.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "When going out on alms-rounds, look ahead only a fathom’s distance; with mindfulness gathered, go forth to beg for food."
It is like a bee gathering nectar from flowers. Now, Ānanda’s conduct was not inconsistent with the prescribed rules;

rather, it was because he had long been accustomed to these essentials that, when the occasion arose, he naturally acted with composure and according to the Middle Way—without thought or effort. Look at the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*:
when the World-Honored One was about to go on his almsround, he simply donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī. How could there ever have been even a thread [of deliberation]?
To exert even a slight effort of attention—yet here it is said that he passed through [the forest], that he walked slowly, that he was dignified and composed, and that he was solemn and reverent;
all with a single-minded intent, this is entirely a matter of artificial affectation. How could this not allow the woman Mādrī to find her opportunity?
This discourse concerns actual practice. As for those who manifest through skillful means, Ānanda was certainly not like this; it was merely a pretense.

To display such majestic deportment toward one who is free from self-importance is merely to follow in the tracks of those who have gone astray. This concludes the section on the causes of falling into error.
Second, the matter of falling into error:
At that time, Ānanda, while on his almsround, passed by a brothel and encountered a great illusionist, the woman Mātangī.

Using the *sāvikāla* mantra of the former Brahmā-deva, she was brought under his influence at the place of dalliance; as he personally caressed her with lustful intent, he was on the verge of destroying the integrity of his precepts.
At that moment, he immediately applied himself with solemn gravity. "Next" (*krama*) refers to the sense of following in sequence without transgressing or overstepping one another.
Because he was begging for alms, he did not bypass or overstep [the houses]. Without distinguishing between the pure and the defiled, he passed through a brothel;
thus he encountered [her], which means he fell into it unexpectedly. As for "illusory arts," these are deceptive incantations that dazzle the eyes and mind.
The *Maṅgala-sūtra* states: "There is a Maṅgalā who possesses divine speech and talismanic spells capable of shifting [one's state]."
"The sun and moon fall to the earth; he can even command Brahmā and the gods to descend by means of incantations—how much more so the śramaṇa Ānanda?

From this we know that this was not an ordinary magical artifice, and thus it is called 'Great. According to the *Śīlāṅga-pratyaya-sūtra*, 'Mātanga' translates as 'of low family stock' or 'of base birth';
this is the name of his mother. His daughter's name is Pārvatī, which translates as 'the Original'."

"Nature" (*prakṛti*) means that although she has fallen into the state of a courtesan, her fundamental nature is not lost. Alternatively, it refers to "stone-nature," meaning her nature is like stone and cannot be altered.
Among the laity she is called a "nature-woman" (*prakṛti-strī*); among those who have left the home life, she is called a "nature-nun" (*prakṛti-bhikṣuṇī*).
She is now called "Mātangī" because the name is designated based on her mother. This is used [as a term of address]. The upper [term] serves as the agent of the action; the lower [term] serves as...
Regarding the methods employed: Sāṃkhyas are non-Buddhist practitioners who follow the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
They are called "Yellow-Haired" (*Kapila*) or "Golden-Headed," because their hair is yellow like gold. "Former Brahmā" refers to a past Brahmā;
it refers to incantations that were originally heterodox spells falsely claimed to have been spoken by a past Brahmā. This is recorded in the *Suvarṇaśirṣa-sūtra*. 登 (Dēng).

Therefore, they are listed in reverse order. Regarding their inclusion [in the categories]: according to the *Śīlaskandha-pratyaya-sūtra*, Paṅktidatā said to her mother, "I wish for Ānanda to be my husband.
Her mother then smeared the ground with cow dung, adorned it with colorful decorations, and lit lamps.
As he burned incense and recited mantras, Ānanda’s mind became dazed; following the power of those spells, he eventually arrived at her house.
"The seat of lust" refers to the bed where Ḍākinī lay. "The body of lust" refers to Ḍākinī’s own body. "Caressing" means rubbing, kneading, massaging, and pressing.
This describes how, once Ānanda had entered the seat and approached her body, Ḍākinī’s own lustful flames flared up as she caressed him.
The manner of pressing with the hand is something that cannot be avoided by its very nature; it is simply like supporting a drunkard or embracing a corpse—one can do nothing about it.

As for the "precept-substance" (*śīla-tattva*), it is the unmanifest substance (*avijñapti*) of the restraint-precepts (*saṃvara-śīla*). This refers to the immense power of the mental force at the moment one receives the precepts.
It is capable of producing sublime, wholesome, and untainted (*anāsrava*) material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).

Because of this, from the seeds of volition (*cetanā*), there arises a specific capacity for restraint and initiation, which is termed "unmanifest form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*); hence it is called the "essence of precepts" (*śīla-tattva*). It is an aggregate that is neither matter nor mind;
when maintained, it flourishes, and when violated, it withers. If the root is broken, the essence of the precepts is destroyed. As it says below: "Though the mind..."
He was clearly aware [of his state], yet his power was not at his own disposal. Furthermore, it is said that because his mind remained pure, he had not yet sunk into ruin.

Thus we know that although Ānanda’s *śīla*-essence (*śīlaskandha*) was not technically destroyed, it had already reached a state of peril; hence it is said, "it was about to. (Question: Within the assembly of Śrāvakas, there were many monks and nuns.

Why was it specifically Ānanda and Dharmadinnā who initiated this sutra? Answer: There are two meanings for each. Regarding Ānanda, the two meanings are: first, to demonstrate that what one has heard is not to be relied upon; second, to demonstrate that others are not to be relied upon. As for "what one has heard not being reliable..."

As for "relying": Ānanda was foremost among those of great learning, yet when he encountered a single instance of illusory magic, he could not escape it; how much more so for one who has only just entered the lecture hall to study the texts? When encountering circumstances and conditions, how could one not feel fear? Others are not to be relied upon.

It is said that Ānanda was the Buddha’s cousin, having left the household life following the Buddha; yet even between such close kin, their bodies and minds could not substitute for one another. How much more so when one's teacher is neither a sage nor an arhat, meeting them as casually as a floating gourd upon the water? To rely on such a person while failing to cultivate oneself—is this not a grave error? Regarding the two meanings of "Dengqie" (Ḍākinī): first, it means to spur forth the initial resolve;

second, it means to encourage long-term cultivation. As for spurring forth the initial resolve: Ḍākinī violated the pure precepts of others and lacked any intention for self-cultivation; yet, by receiving the power of the mantra once, she immediately realized the third fruit of Arhatship, her craving for desire dried up, and she became a forest of diligence.

This being so, how much more would this be true for those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta and seek to benefit sentient beings through Buddhahood? If one further applies the empowerment of mantras, it is like a wind-filled sail sailing with the current; there will be no concern that one will not reach the ocean of Sarvajñā (omniscience). This is what is meant by encouraging long-term cultivation.

As for this, although Dhanika was formerly a courtesan whose karmic obstructions were most profound, because she cultivated untainted goodness (*anāsrava-kuśala*) for even a single thought-moment, she either escaped the bonds of affliction or received a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). How much more so for one who has long practiced pure conduct and whose delusive habits have already been thinned!

If such a person exerts themselves with vigor, they will sever the silken threads [of karma] and dye them [into liberation]. Who would say that the wheel of birth-and-death suffering cannot be exited? The conclusion of Ānanda’s accidental fall. Part Three:
The Tathāgata’s Deliverance, in three sections: 1. The Buddha returns to the assembly; 2. The Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*) recites the mantra; 3. The command to rescue and return.
First: The Tathāgata knew that the demon’s sorcery had been cast upon him; having finished his meal, he returned home.
The king, along with the great ministers, elders, and lay devotees, all followed the Buddha, wishing to hear the essential points of the Dharma.
The Buddha first knew that [the king] would quickly return; he was referring to Ānanda. The Tathāgata’s Dharma-eye is penetrating and clear, and thus he was able to know this.
Because the matter of the application of the art of lust was urgent and the essence of his precepts was about to be destroyed, there was no time for delay in saving him.

Therefore, having finished his meal, he returned immediately, saying that once the matter was concluded, he would return with speed. ○ The King and the assembly below followed, seeking benefit and support.

The text states: "It is the Tathāgata’s constant custom that after accepting an invitation for a meal, he always preaches the Dharma. Today, his swift departure suggests there must be a specific purpose;
therefore, the king, ministers, and others have all come to follow the Buddha, as they perceive that he has suddenly deviated from his usual routine."
They must surely discuss the most supreme Dharma, the essential meaning of the mind; everyone gazes upward in expectation. Hence it is said: "I wish to hear the essentials of the Dharma.
This is the great mechanism of the True [Dharma] moving in profound resonance. Second, the Transformation Buddhas recite the mantra.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness.
From within this light, a thousand-petaled jeweled lotus emerged, upon which a transformation-body Buddha sat in the full lotus posture and proclaimed a divine mantra.
Ānanda was under the influence of a spell, yet the King and his attendants acted with such promptness that the rescue was carried out without fail. Therefore, at this very moment, he emitted light.
As for the light being emitted from the crown of his head, it signifies that the divine mantra he has taught is supreme and unsurpassed, possessing a most wondrous and invisible intent.
The light, endowed with the colors of a hundred jewels and benefits, signifies that the mantra possesses the compassion of gathering and bestowing grace. There is no goodness [greater than this].
This is not established. The light possesses the marks of fearlessness and majestic power, signifying that the mantra possesses the severity of subjugation; there is no evil it does not crush.
The radiance has the function of destroying darkness and illuminating objects, signifying that the divine mantra has the utility of destroying delusion and illuminating the Truth.
Since it possesses the utility of destroying delusion and illuminating the Truth, it is naturally able to give rise to the unimpeded, perfect cause. By means of this—
The thousand-petaled lotus represents the unimpeded perfect cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*), for it is because one contains all and all is one.
Being able to give rise to this unimpeded perfect cause, one naturally achieves the wondrous fruit of non-action (*asaṃskṛta-phala*).

The presence of the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) represents the non-active nature of the wondrous fruit; it is neither empty nor existent (the Buddha is not empty, and the transformation body is not existent), being the non-obstruction of emptiness and existence.
Therefore, as for sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka-bandha*), one folds the feet double like the coils of a dragon;
among all methods of sitting, this is the most secure and restful, as it prevents exhaustion and keeps the hands and feet restrained so that the mind does not scatter.

The Buddha sits in this manner, and the emanation Buddhas do likewise, signifying that this mantra is the convergence of the provisional and the ultimate, being the unshakable Dharma. Since the symbolic representation is thus complete:
What was signified is now clearly manifest; therefore, it is proclaimed by the unobstructed mind of the transformation Buddha.
As for the term "divine" (*shen*) applied to the mantra, its power and function are inconceivable, as will be seen below. Third, the command to rescue and bring back.
The Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī to go with the mantra to provide protection. The evil spells were extinguished, and he led Ānanda and Mātaṅgī back to the presence of the Buddha.
"Command" (chì) refers to an imperial decree; it may be used for both secular kings and Dharma-kings. Mañjuśrī was the one who issued this command. The Buddha—
Regarding those who do not save themselves: this is sufficient to establish the Three Jewels as a model for the future.

The Tathāgata is the Buddha Jewel; the divine mantra is the Dharma Jewel; and Mañjuśrī is the Saṃgha Jewel. Although the Dharma was spoken by the Buddha, it would not have been transmitted were it not for the Saṃgha.

The significance of the Saṃgha Jewel is indeed great! As for the specific command to Mañjuśrī: because Ānanda was afflicted by the sorcery of a heretical spell, none but one of Great Wisdom could have awakened him from it.
Because one is bound by the delusion of lust for ḍākinīs, none but those of great wisdom can untie it; thus, "will" (*jō*) implies "to maintain. This meaning applies to both speech and mind:

that is, to recite and expound with the mouth, and to contemplate and visualize with the mind. If the body is also involved in going forth [to perform the rite], then the three karmas are maintained together.

"Guarding" (*go*) means to obstruct and protect; it obstructs heterodox arts and protects the correct mind. For true Dharma and illusory arts differ as vastly as heaven and earth in their power and function. Therefore—
As soon as the divine mantra reaches it, the evil spell is immediately dissolved; it may be compared to snow melting under the sun’s heat.
This is why its power and function are said to be inconceivable. "Ti" means to lift up and carry away; "wei" means to encourage and exhort.

It is said that Ānanda was like one who had just awakened from a drunken stupor and could not return to himself, and thus required to be lifted up and carried away. Dhaṅkā, knowing her error, felt ashamed and was not yet willing to comply.

Therefore, it is necessary to provide encouragement and exhortation. All this is manifested through great skillful means (*mahopāya*) to inspire actual practice and fully express the underlying sentiments.

(The above two conditions for the initiation [of the teaching] are also called the "Separate Introduction" because they pertain specifically to the present sutra; they are also called the "Preface Prior to the Sutra" because they precede the sutra. The Section on the Narrative is concluded. II.
The Main Body of the Teaching (the correct exposition of the fundamental nature and definitive purpose of this sutra). 2.1. Ānanda’s Entreaty for the Buddha’s Wondrous Samādhi.
Second, the Tathāgata provides a detailed exposition of the causes and effects from beginning to end, consisting of two parts: first, Ānanda’s sincere plea born of grief and remorse;
second, the universal aspiration for benefit shared by the great assembly. First: [The first part: Ānanda’s Sincere Plea Born of Grief and Remorse.

Ānanda saw the Buddha, prostrated himself, and wept with grief. He lamented that from time immemorial he had been devoted solely to extensive learning, yet had not fully perfected his power of the Way.

With earnest sincerity, he entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to reveal the initial expedient means for attaining the wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* that lead to the realization of Bodhi.

First, one feels sorrow and remorse for past transgressions. The specific mention of "beholding the Buddha" is because one has fortunately been granted the opportunity to see his face again. Regarding "prostrating," this refers to touching one's head to the Buddha’s feet;

although this is a standard ritual, it is also an expression of gratitude for the Buddha’s kindness. Regarding "weeping with grief," this refers to shedding tears and sobbing out of profound lamentation.

Although this was a state of shame and trepidation, it also evoked a sense of self-reproach and loss; as this reproach did not cease, it transformed into resentment. Hence, it is called "hatred" (*hen*).
Hatred is one of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); it obstructs loving-kindness (*maitrī*), assists anger (*dveṣa*), and, being contrary to the Way, ought not to exist.
Yet, the hatred felt today is truly indispensable, for it enabled Ānanda to turn from the Small Vehicle toward the Great, to reverse his delusions and return to the Truth, and so forth.
When they attain Buddhahood in the future, all shall take this resentment as their precursor. "Without beginning, consistently," etc., correctly describes that which is resented;
since its origin cannot be found, it is called "without beginning. This is said to express the extreme distance of their delusion. "Consistently" means a single-minded orientation.
"Much learning" refers to being abundant in hearing and retention. One must know that there is no fault in much learning, except for—
Tending toward the single flavor since beginningless time, there has been an error in true cultivation. That the power of the path of the four fruits has not yet been perfected is truly regrettable.
○ With earnest sincerity, he entreats for the wondrous samādhi. "Earnestly" means with repeated and pressing urgency; "to open and address" means to request.
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions," etc., correctly describes what is being sought. It states that Ānanda has already realized his former errors and [is now] once again...
A profound awakening arises. Even the attainment of the four fruits of the śramaṇa is not what is desired;
therefore, one seeks from the Tathāgatas of the ten directions the method for attaining bodhi. Herein there are two layers of discernment:

first, "attaining bodhi" distinguishes this from the Two Vehicles of the Hīnayāna, because although they may attain cessation through their practice, they do not achieve bodhi. Second, "the wondrous"—one.

[This] term distinguishes [this teaching] from the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*), for although they may enter into the state of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) through their practice, they do not achieve its perfect and wondrous realization.

This is because the three practices beginning with *śamatha* are common to all vehicles; yet, if practiced erroneously, a difference as slight as a hair’s breadth leads to a divergence of a thousand miles.

Therefore, it is necessary to distinguish them. *Śamatha* is here translated as "stopping" (*zhi*); it takes "quiescence" as its meaning, referring to the cessation of distraction and the entry [into concentration].
Because it is tranquil (*śānta*). According to this present sutra, the realization that consciousness is not mind is called "stopping" (*śamatha*);

because one realizes consciousness is not mind, there is no need for forced restraint, as it naturally does not follow [distractions], which is true stopping. That all phenomena of consciousness are by nature [empty] is called "tranquility" (*śānti*);
because all phenomena of consciousness are by nature [empty], there is no need for forced detachment, as they naturally do not move, which is true tranquility. Thus, one should know this.
This *śamatha* is vastly different from that forced suppression of the mind where one closes the eyes and visualizes emptiness.
*Samādhi*—its full Sanskrit forms being *samāpatti*, *samādhi*, *samāpatti*, or *samāpatti*—are all merely variations in the transcription of the Sanskrit sound.
This is translated as "equipoise" (*dengzhi*), meaning the dissolution of illusions; it refers to equality.

"Reaching Samādhi": because it dissolves illusory delusions. According to this present sutra, the names "movement," "stillness," "faculty" (*indriya*), and "understanding" (*samjñā*) are called "equanimity" (*samāpatti*).

This is because movement is not understood as non-existent, and stillness is not understood as existent; when the understanding of the faculty is profoundly settled, it is truly equanimity. "Awakening to emptiness and extinguishing understanding" is called "dissolving illusions.
This is because awakening-understanding is detached illumination, emptiness-understanding is detached stillness, and extinction-understanding is the manifestation of the nature. Thus...

Because it truly eliminates the illusory, one knows that this samādhi is vastly different from those "temporary abidings" that resemble meditative concentration (wherein the faculties are not yet exhausted, it is called "resembling concentration"), and from those who ultimately cling to what resembles the real (wherein cessation is not understood, it is called "resembling the real").

*Dhyāna*—here translated as "calm contemplation"—takes "quiescent extinction" (*śamatha*) as its essential meaning. This means that by arising from stillness, one engages in contemplation and cultivation until reaching quiescent extinction (which is *nirvāṇa*).
If one follows this present sutra, then the equality of śamatha and vipaśyanā is called dhyāna;
for it is through the adamantine observation of the ten profound metaphors that vipaśyanā within śamatha constitutes true dhyāna. From cause to fruit, it is called nirvāṇa (寂滅);
for it is because one has reached the state where no word such as "tea" (*ta*) can be spoken that it is true nirvāṇa. Thus one knows this...
Dhyāna is vastly different from that which takes awakening as its cultivation and regards partial realization as fulfillment.
Nevertheless, the sublime samādhi of Buddhahood is truly difficult to cultivate; one must understand the process of gradual progression in order to avoid the fault of leaping over stages.
Therefore, these are bound together under the heading of "Initial Expedient Means" (*ādikarmika-upāya*). This is because one wishes to rely upon expedient means to cultivate correct practice.
Although there have been many ancient commentaries, their points of agreement and divergence could not be resolved; their prolixity would only distract the mind, so none are recorded here.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you have said is indeed true and worthy of delight. It is because of the mind and the eyes.
If you do not know the location of the mind and the eyes, you will be unable to subdue the dust and toil of worldly afflictions. It is like a king who has been invaded by bandits;
he must dispatch troops to eliminate them, and those troops must first know where the bandits are located. This is what causes you to wander through the cycle of rebirth."
"You have made a mistake. I shall now question you: where do the mind and the eyes currently reside?
At first, Ānanda followed his words and remained fixed in his position. Previously, Ānanda had replied to the Buddha that the cause of attachment and delight lies in the mind and the eyes.
Wishing to dismantle this view, the Buddha then told him: "According to what you have said above, is it truly the case that the cause of attachment and delight lies in the mind and the eyes?"
As for this, I shall provide an illustration for you. This is merely to establish the terminology, fearing that it might be altered or misunderstood.
If one does not descend [into the depths], one should understand the manifest state. This is because, through the eyes one perceives, the mind gives rise to attachment and delight;

and because of this attachment and delight, the afflictions (*kleśa*) compete to arise. (Afflictions are so called because they possess the sense of defilement, termed "dust" (*rajas*), and the sense of agitation, termed "toil" [*klama*]). One must necessarily know the mind.
When the eyes are properly situated, one can finally subdue the dust-laden afflictions; hence it is said, "If one does not recognize and know," and so forth.
This is a reductio ad absurdum used to clarify the necessity of what should be known. The section beginning with "It is like" employs a metaphor to assist in illumination.

The king is a metaphor for the true mind of the nature of seeing; as they are fundamentally one entity, only the king is used as a metaphor. The matchmaker and the thief rely upon each other, and both are referred to as...

The "bandits" are a metaphor for deluded views and the deluded mind. Because deluded views give rise to the deluded mind, one chases after sensory objects (*viṣaya*) and engenders various afflictions (*kleśa*), thereby shrouding the true mind and disturbing the realm of inherent nature; thus, they are likened to being invaded by bandits.
The "soldiers" are a metaphor for wondrous *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*. This serves as a metaphor for practicing based on the truth, in order to suppress and eliminate [the afflictions].
The analogy of destroying the false to reveal the true means that when one employs troops, one must know where the enemy is located;

this is analogous to how, when practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one must necessarily know the place from which delusion arises. By severing its root, the branches and twigs will naturally perish.

From here below, the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) is investigated and refuted to reveal the seeing-nature (*darśana*). Subsequently, the false seeing is dissected; all of these are done so as to reach the source of the delusion and thereby destroy it.
"Suppose you were to lower your finger below the point of inquiry: the cycle of transmigration arises from worldly afflictions (*kleśa*); these afflictions originate from the deluded mind.
The mind does not initiate itself; it arises based on deluded perception. Thus, one knows that the eyes act as the intermediaries for the thief, while the mind is the master of the thief."
Worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) are the companions of thieves; they act as go-betweens that stir up movement, and these companions cause disorder.
The mind and eyes are at fault—this can be known through reflection. Once it is known that the mind and eyes are at fault, one must accordingly discern their location.

Therefore, one addresses the mind and eyes directly, double-interrogating both simultaneously. (The following section was originally intended to refute consciousness; however, there are three reasons for double-interrogating the mind and eyes: first, to reveal that the eyes are merely superficial dust-like phenomena, thereby causing one to perceive their distinction.)

Because there is the nature of seeing. For the eyes upon the face are merely ephemeral dust; since Ānanda has identified the act of seeing as the eye, he will inevitably neglect that very nature of seeing. Therefore, these two questions are posed together to cause him to observe the face and realize that the ephemeral dust has no power of seeing, so that he may personally awaken to the distinct existence of the essence of seeing.

Yet, alas, Ānanda does not understand; he must wait for ten successive demonstrations before gradually comprehending it. Second, this is to reveal that the eye is a "thief's intermediary," so that he may know how to guard against the intermediary and destroy the host.

Zhengmo says: Since Ānanda has mistaken the thief for his son, the Buddha wishes to destroy the thief and point out the delusion. Yet, alas, the eyes are truly the mediators of the thief; they lead consciousness to rush toward forms. To destroy that consciousness, one must guard against the eyes;

therefore, he poses these two simultaneous questions to make him realize that if the eyes do not roam, then consciousness has no use and will collapse of its own accord. Thirdly, it is to reveal that the eyes have a fixed location, so as to compel him to state that consciousness must likewise have a fixed location. Zhengmo says: The Buddha knows that sentient beings mistake consciousness for the mind and are certain to be deluded into thinking it resides within the physical body.

Fearing that Ānanda might evade the issue and refuse to speak plainly, he uses the eyes—which are evidently on the face—as an analogy to question where the mind is located. This is essentially to force him to reveal the location of the mind. It must...

Just as the eye is situated on the face, it is manifest and unmixed; these three meanings rely on the subsequent ten sections that reveal seeing. If there were a distinct nature of seeing apart from this, then the first meaning would be correct. If one relies on the upper [explanation]—that seeing occurs through the eyes and the mind gives rise to attachment and delight—then the second meaning would be correct.

If one relies on the lower [explanation]—that such a discerning consciousness actually resides within the body—then the third meaning would be correct. Some say that this section presents a double inquiry and the subsequent text provides a double refutation; this interpretation is also plausible, for after the ten sections that reveal seeing below, [the refutation follows].

Because there is a separate passage that analyzes and eliminates false views. Having completed the second section—following up on the previous inquiry to identify the locus—the text proceeds to provide the answer by citing a response.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all ten types of ordinary beings in the world alike take their consciousness-mind as their [abiding]..."
Within the body, even when looking outward, the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes are still upon the Buddha’s face.
Now, as I observe these four sensory objects of the floating faculties, they reside only on my own face; thus, this consciousness-mind truly dwells within the body.

First, another example is cited. Although all worlds generally comprise three types [of existence], for now we shall refer to the "receptacle world" (*bhājanaloka*) as the environment in which beings dwell.
The "ten kinds of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*) refers specifically to sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), meaning their primary retribution;

they are called "ordinary beings" because they are born differently according to the retributions induced by their respective karma. As for the term "ten kinds," this excludes the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) from among the twelve classes of living beings.
There is no characteristic of a body; there is no perception, nor is there any characteristic of mind. This is because one does not conceive of the mind as being located within the body.
"Consciousness-mind" (*vijñāna-citta*) refers to the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), distinguishing it from the first five, which therefore reside within the body.

This [text] cites the "generating mind" (*janaka-citta*) being within as an analogy for one's own mind. As for the "generating eye" being on the face, let it be set aside for now; hence it says, "even if one observes."
The Tathāgata and others: In the Western Regions there is the blue lotus (*utpala*), whose petals are slender and long; the Buddha’s eyes resemble these, hence they are so named.
Furthermore, this refers to the color-form of the physical sense-base (*bhautika-rūpa*) to distinguish it from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Therefore, it is also located on the face. This citation of the Buddha’s eyes being on the face serves as an analogy for one’s own eyes. ○ "I now," etc., points to the conclusion of the answer. It distinguishes [the Buddha's eyes] from the physical sense-roots (*mūla-indriya*).
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) consists of pure form (*rūpa*), which is invisible. That which is visible here is called "floating dust" (*bu chen*);
its substance encompasses form, fragrance, flavor, and touch, and is thus termed the "four dusts. This is because the name and the substance are each designated separately;

taken together, they constitute the "floating dust sense-organ" (*āśraya*). As for the phrase "only on my face," it means that although one's own eyes are inferior, they reside on the face alongside those of the Buddha.
There is no difference; it does not exist separately elsewhere. Therefore, the two characters "just so" (rúshì) are set forth alone. To take the eye as an analogy:
since the eye is identical to the Buddha, the consciousness-mind should likewise arise identically. By this analogy, one knows that the consciousness-mind truly resides within the body.
Zhengmo says: "This is the fundamental premise. As it says later: "One delusion constitutes the mind; it is a definitive delusion."

The fact that [the self] is within the physical body sufficiently proves this point. As for the other six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), they were merely forced into a revised position by the Buddha’s temporary refutation;
among them, there are also positions that are identical to externalist views, and thus they must all be eliminated.

Having completed the investigation to determine the location [of the self], section four refutes the seven [bases] individually regarding consciousness: first, the refutation of its being within; second, the refutation of its being...
1. Refuting the external; 2. Refuting the interior of the sense organs; 3. Refuting the rescue from within; 4. Refuting the point of conjunction;
5. Refuting the intermediate space; 6. Refuting non-attachment. Regarding the first four: 1. Secretly establishing the method of refutation; 2. Granting the settling of the mind; 3.

Determining that it is not a counter-refutation; 4. Pointing out the conceptualization to conclude the refutation. At the beginning [the Buddha did not directly refute its error, but rather proceeded according to what is presently perceived, distinguishing between the internal and the external, and further regarding the faculty of seeing...]

Regarding the sequence of "first" and "after," Ānanda responded spontaneously according to his own understanding, yet he did not know the underlying reason. When he was confronted by the Tathāgata with a series of counter-arguments, he realized for himself the error of his own calculations; only then did he understand that the Tathāgata’s words were no ordinary speech.
This is essentially a method for secretly establishing a trap so that there is no way to escape it. It is like Zhuge Liang’s Eight Arrays: when they were first set up, no one knew their purpose;
it was only later, when Lu Xun himself fell into them, that he realized Zhuge Liang’s arrangement at that time was by no means an ordinary deployment.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "You are now sitting here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall. Observe where the Jeta Grove is located now.
"World-Honored One," [Ānanda replied], "this great multi-storied pavilion, this pure lecture hall, is within the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden; the Jeta Grove is actually outside the hall.
"Ānanda, what did you first see within the hall just now? "World-Honored One, while I was in the hall, I first..."
He saw the Tathāgata; next he observed the great assembly; looking outward in this manner, he finally beheld the grove and garden.
"Ānanda, by what cause do you behold the grove and garden? "World-Honored One, because the doors and windows of this great lecture hall are wide open, I am able to gaze afar from within the hall."

Regarding the internal and external aspects of the objects of the first dhyāna: you pointed to Ānanda, who is currently in the lecture hall, to secretly reveal that the mind you postulate resides within the body;
it should be analogous to this. The Jeta Grove is clearly outside the hall;

thus, by intentionally posing these questions, you compel him to speak for himself, so that later, when confronted with the refutation, he has no place to escape. As for the "multi-storied pavilion," its eaves and corridors rise in successive tiers.
"Purified" means that the dust of afflictions does not reach it. "Lecture Hall" (kathā-śālā) refers to where the Buddha sits to discourse on the sutras;
"multi-storied pavilion" describes its physical form, while "purified" reveals its virtue. "Lecture Hall" designates its name. It is located within the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden.
"Secretly manifesting the body within the world" should be understood in this same way. "The grove outside the hall" secretly manifests all that exists before one's eyes.

All dharmas are equally external to the body; they should be understood in this same way. ○ When Ānanda first established that seeing occurs prior to the eyes, he asked what it was that was seen first.
He did so because he already knew the answer, yet he questioned him to prompt him to state it himself, thereby preparing for a potential rebuttal.
Regarding the sequence where one first sees the Tathāgata in the hall and subsequently observes the great assembly: this secretly reveals that the mind is within the body;
thus, one should first see the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach, and subsequently observe the growth of nails and hair, and the movement of tendons and pulses.
As for looking outward at the groves and gardens: this secretly reveals that the mind is within the body; thus, one should see what is outside the body only at the very end.

[The Master] refuted all dharmas (the "zhì" in "zhèqiè zhūfǎ" is pronounced with a retroflex *n* [zhì], as in the middle character of "nánzhōng"). One by one, none were as they appeared. Yet Ānanda merely knew how to answer according to the flow of conversation; he did not realize that his own calculations had already fallen into the World-Honored One’s net.
Ānanda subsequently determined that there was external seeing. Why is there seeing? This is also a question posed with full awareness of the answer.

The doors and windows of the lecture hall were wide open; thus, for one who could see from afar, the subtle manifestation of the mind within the body would be rendered impossible to establish, because this body is not as open as the doors and windows of the lecture hall.

Having thus completed the refutation of the doctrine, [the Buddha] provisionally granted the settling of the mind (as previously, Ānanda had entreated him for a wondrous samādhi, and the Tathāgata first questioned him regarding the arousal of the mind, likely because he feared that the mind might be divided into the true and the false, and samādhi distinguished as real or empty).

Ānanda mistook the delusory for the real and practiced in confusion, like steaming sand to make rice—there will never be a true result. Now, through this exchange of questions and answers, with repeated investigation and interrogation, we have identified the delusory mind that is employed and further probed the specific point of delusion upon which he clings.

As we are about to refute and dismantle it, I fear he might become alarmed; he might think that I am not granting him a fixed method of cultivation and see only refutations, leaving him empty-handed in his yearning and ultimately severed from the path.

Therefore, the Tathāgata permitted the existence of *samādhi* and so forth, whereupon Ānanda prostrated himself to receive the teaching. Thus, his inner mind being at peace, when the successive refutations follow below, he will no longer find them strange.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm from within the great assembly and stroked the crown of Ānanda’s head.
He announced to Ānanda and the entire multitude: "There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown, the King of Śūraṅgama.
It fully encompasses the myriad practices and is the wondrous path of sublime adornment through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend in a single gate. Listen attentively now, Ānanda."
I prostrate and humbly receive your compassionate instruction.

Regarding the general name for the initial emergence from meditative absorption (*samādhi*): extending the arm to touch the crown of the head signifies showing loving-kindness and bringing peace to the mind.

The meaning of *samādhi* applies both generally and specifically. If the three names follow one another in sequence, they carry a specific meaning; if *samādhi* stands alone as a singular designation, then—
This is the general meaning. As for the specific meaning, it is translated as *samāpatti* (equipoise), as previously explained.
The general meaning is translated as *samādhi* (concentration), or alternatively as "universal gathering and sustaining," because it universally gathers and sustains all samādhis.
As the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says: "All meditative concentrations that gather the mind are called *samādhi*. This refers to the general meaning, which subsumes what precedes.

Thirdly, it is also a general name because it applies universally to all meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). *Śūraṅgama* is a collective name in contrast to the preceding [names], yet a specific name in contrast to others;
for while it collectively encompasses the previous three, it is specifically situated within this very sutra. Its essence is precisely the one mind (*ekacitta*).
Therefore, it is called "Great" (*mahā*). Its logic is most supreme and most wondrous; thus, it is likened to the crown of the Buddha’s head (*uṣṇīṣa*). The meaning is detailed in the title.
As for the addition of the word "King" (*rāja*), there are two meanings: first, the sense of transcending, because it transcends all *samādhis*;
second, the sense of sovereignty, because one spontaneously attains Buddhahood without obstruction. [The section] beginning with "Endowed with" explains the subsequent meanings.
It possesses distinct categories. "Possessing" means being complete. This refers to establishing a state based upon which one cuts off delusions and realizes the Truth;
it is like cutting silk or dyeing cloth: when one part is cut, all is cut, and when one part is realized, all is realized.

This is precisely the meaning of the myriad practices within *dhyāna*. To abandon this and seek elsewhere, one will ultimately achieve no real fruit throughout kalpas. Therefore, it is called "one gate."
Cultivating according to this, one may transcend to the stage of no-more-learning in the mere snap of a finger; hence it is called "Transcendence.

This is further the secret cause within *śamatha* and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) within *samādhi*. Based on this, the arising of faith, the development of understanding, and the initiation of practice all rely entirely upon it;
therefore, it is called the "Path of Sublime Adornment" (the Buddha’s myriad virtues of adornment are fully cultivated as identical to nature, thus termed "sublime"). However, Ānanda requested—
While the "abodes" (*sthāna*) are exclusively distinct, the World-Honored One’s response regarding the "abodes" encompasses both the general and the specific.

This is because Ānanda did not recognize the unique name of *Śūraṅgama*; therefore, he requested the abodes using only the common names such as *śamatha* and so forth. To distinguish these, he specifically added the word "wondrous.
The Buddha’s wisdom, discerning his capacity, revealed them both collectively and individually; thus, the three distinct [abodes] and the one general [abode] were opened up in this great chapter.
In four parts. ○ From "You now" onwards, there is the admonition to listen, the prostration, and the acceptance. "Attentively" (*dṛḍha*) has two meanings:

first, the sense of careful examination, meaning one should examine the meaning of the words so as not to let anything be lost; second, the sense of reality, meaning one listens with a true mind, free from a mind subject to arising and ceasing.
"Prostrating" (*praṇipatya*) means to briefly express thanks upon hearing permission. "Humbly receiving" (*vinīya*) means to bow down and accept [the teaching]. The Buddha...
