The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is as you have said. While the body is in the lecture hall and the doors and windows are wide open so that one can gaze far out at the groves and gardens, there may also be sentient beings within this hall who do not see the Tathāgata but see what is outside the hall.
Ānanda replied: "World-Honored One, it is impossible for those in the hall to see the groves and springs while failing to see the Tathāgata."
First, the preceding answer is established by the phrase "As you have said," etc., which confirms what was stated so that there is no room for evasion.

Regarding the statement "The body was in the lecture hall," it implies one must have previously seen the Tathāgata; this is followed by the observation of the words of the great assembly, which are spoken in an abbreviated and transcendent manner.
The phrase "There is also... is a deliberate counter-question intended to clarify internal insight while observing external appearances.
Knowing that this is impossible, he therefore poses a counter-question to cause [Ānanda] to speak for himself. ○ From "Ānanda" onwards, he knows that the claim is illogical:
being inside the hall, one cannot see the Tathāgata while being able to see the groves and springs; this is not sequential. Knowing it is erroneous, he says, "There is no such possibility.
Since this is impossible, the fallacy of the mind being within the body becomes self-evident. By means of this—
One who is unaware of what is internal knows what is external; since you are the same as this, the second difficulty is that what is within would not be seen in sequence.
Ānanda, you are also like this. Your spiritual mind is all-knowing and clear.
If the mind that is currently clear and aware were actually inside your body, then at that time it should first perceive the interior of the body. Is there any sentient being who...?

Having observed the body within, one subsequently observes external objects. Even if one cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach, one certainly ought to clearly perceive the growth of nails and hair, the shifting of tendons, and the throbbing of the pulses;
how then can one not know them? If one certainly does not know what is within, how can one know what is without?
The first phrase rebukes the preceding error. Its meaning is that you perceive the external while being oblivious to the internal;

you claim that something does not exist, yet it must exist as a mental representation—indeed, you yourself are just like this. The section following "You" establishes the definitive principle to challenge the question.

"Your spiritual mind" refers to the nature of the mind, which is spiritually transformative. "All things are clearly understood" means that one penetrates matters as they arise; this truly exists within the body beforehand.
Regarding "one should know that which is internal": this is a judgment of correct principle. It is clearly known that there is no one who can ask whether such a person exists;
therefore, a difficult question is posed. "Poh" (頗) means "can it still be the case? This refers to observing the world universally: can such a person still exist?

The intended meaning is that if he exists, the principle of his being "internal" is established; if he does not exist, then the location one has calculated is incorrect. [The phrase] "縱不下" (even if not below) follows.

"Though one may let them go for a moment, they will ultimately seize [the mind] away. "The 'heart' (xin) here refers to the heart-flesh, which is the fire-organ (*tejo-dhātu*); the liver is the wood-organ (*dāru-dhātu*); and the spleen is the earth-organ (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). The stomach is the 'receptacle' (*koṣṭha*) for grain.
Among the organs (*dhātu*), three are cited; among the hollow organs (*koṣṭha*), one is cited. These are all those situated near the interior.

[This is said because] Ānanda might evade [the point] by saying, 'The eye does not see its own eyebrows precisely because they are too close. Now, the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach are likewise too close to the mind."
How could one possibly see them? Therefore, for the sake of argument, let us grant that they can see—namely, the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach—even if we concede that these cannot see.
This is a temporary concession; below, the position will be definitively refuted. To say that what is situated within and extremely close is not known may be plausible.
As for how the nails grow, how the hair lengthens, how the tendons turn, and how the vessels pulse—these all lie within the skin and outside the flesh, not being particularly close to the heart;
these are indeed matters that ought to be clearly understood. How is it that one cannot know even these?
It appears that one is ultimately unable to know what is internal; this error of regarding the internal as external may already be inferred.

It is seen. The final two lines turn to further expose its fallacy, stating that since it cannot know what is very near or even adjacent, perhaps it is obstructed by the heart, liver, spleen, and stomach; yet it certainly cannot possess cognition while remaining inside them.
If this were so, then external objects would likewise not be known, for one would not perceive the doors and windows of the lecture hall being opened.
Now, how can you conversely claim that it is able to know what is external? Does this not further reveal your error? This is certainly not a valid counter-objection;
the refutation of the "four-finger-width" calculation of the knots is now complete.
Therefore, you should know that your assertion—that the mind which perceives and knows resides within the body—is impossible.
"Because of this" means because of this internal ignorance regarding the external. "Should be known" means one should know that what has been conceptualized is erroneous.
"Awakened awareness capable of knowing" refers to the moment awareness first arises, it immediately discriminates as being capable of knowing;

this is said in reference to that which appears to be both manifest and the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and is intended to reveal the spiritual transformations of the nature of the mind.
The meaning of "all things being clearly manifest" is that they abide within the body; one should first perceive them within the body and only subsequently observe external objects.
Since this is not the case now, it is said that such a thing is impossible. This concludes the refutation of [the view that consciousness] abides within.

Second, the refutation of [the view that the mind] is external, which has two parts: first, Ānanda’s shifting argument that it is external; second, the Tathāgata’s refutation by citing examples. Regarding the first:
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying, "Having heard such a Dharma-sound from the Tathāgata, I have realized and understood my own mind."
It truly dwells outside the body. Why is this so? It is like a lamp burning within a room;
that lamp must first illuminate the interior of the room, and only thereafter reach the doorway and the courtyard.

Yet all sentient beings do not see what is within their own bodies, but see only what is outside their bodies—just as a lamp situated outside a room cannot illuminate the interior. This is the meaning.
It must be clear; may there be no further delusion. May it accord with the Buddha’s definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not be erroneous?
"First, receiving the previous shifting calculations": *jī-móu* (稽首) means prostrating oneself; that is, bringing the head to the ground and remaining there for a short time.
"Such a Dharma-sound" refers back to what was previously explained regarding the refutation of internal [views]. Regarding "awakening to and knowing," the Zhengmai (Correct Pulse) says:
When one does not see [the self] within the body, one realizes it is not within the body; when one clearly perceives it outside the body, one realizes it must be outside the body.
To reject the internal and grasp for the external is the inevitable tendency of ordinary sentiment. Therefore, what follows cites the analogy of the lamp.

The logical proof (*liṅga*) can be understood as follows. For example, once the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is established, an analogy is borrowed to clarify it. [The thesis is: "Consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is the subject (*dharmin*), resides outside the body.

[The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because it is dim regarding what is internal and knows what is external. [The similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is: "A lamp outside a room. [The dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is: "A lamp inside a room.

When a lamp burns within a room, it first illuminates the interior of the room and only afterwards reaches the courtyard (the space outside the screen). This constitutes the correct principle. Since consciousness is not like this, its cognition does not reside within. One.
All sentient beings fail to perceive what is within and see only that which is outside the body; they hold it to be the correct principle that consciousness resides outside the body.

Therefore, the analogy is drawn of a lamp placed outside a room being unable to illuminate the interior. Regarding the meaning below this, [the author] personally resolves that he is the same as the Buddha.

This meaning refers to the doctrine that the mind resides outside the body; through the union of the teaching (dharma) and the analogy (dṛṣṭānta), the thesis (pakṣa) and the reason (hetu) are fully established. This is so.

Because it serves as a true measure (*pramāṇa*), it is said to be "necessarily clear. This implies that one will indeed attain [realization]; it is not like a concordant semblance (*sārūpya-pramāṇa*), and thus there is no delusion.

The Buddha taught that [the mind] does not reside within the body; now, one likewise knows it does not reside within the body. Therefore, it is said to be identical to the Buddha’s definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

"Definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*) refers to that which is spoken by the Tathāgata, for its meaning is exhaustive and leaves nothing unexhausted. "To have attained [it] not" (*wude bu*) means "there is nothing that is not so.
The character *ye* is not a term of doubt; rather, it expresses the intention of pre-emptively silencing the Buddha’s mouth, fearing that he might be refuted.
[The opponent] says: "If mental discourse were not identical to that of the Buddha, it might contain falsehoods. Now that it is identical to the Buddha's, could it not still contain falsehoods?
Surely such a principle does not exist; you may have confidence in this. Ānanda then shifts his argument to the external [world], concluding with four points:
first, a question-and-answer session using an analogy; second, pointing out the fallacious reasoning.

Third, verifying the meaning so that it may be understood; fourth, pointing out the calculation and refuting the objections. Regarding the first two [sections]: first, the inquiry based on what is irrational;
second, the correct response according to principle. As for the first:
the Buddha told Ānanda, "These bhikṣus have just now come from the city of Śrāvastī, begging for alms-food by following the streets."
"I have already returned to the Jeta Grove and finished my midday meal. Observe whether the many people are satiated when a single bhikṣu eats.
These bhikṣus are spoken of solely in terms of the śrāvakas; for a bodhisattva, because all matters are unimpeded and self and others are fused as one, this does not constitute a non-question.
What was just said regarding "only now" refers to the Buddha and bodhisattvas attending the secret [assembly].
The King invited [the monks]. The Arhats followed the Buddha into the city to receive their respective portions from the hosts of the feast;

hence it is said, "following me. The two phrases "循乞" (xún qǐ) should be read as a single unit. "Xún" means to follow or accord with. This states that although they have now accepted the invitation, they still maintain the usual protocol.

Having obtained alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*), they returned to the forest grove to eat together with the assembly; thus, *piṇḍapāta* is also called "lump-food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), because it consists of physical lumps that can be grasped.

This distinguishes it from "contact-food" (*sparśāhāra*, as when spirits are satiated by contact with vapors), "volition-food" (*manahsañcetanāhāra*, as when the gods of the form realm sustain their spirits through meditative reflection), and "consciousness-food" (*vijñānāhāra*, as when the gods of the formless realm maintain the continuity of consciousness and perception).
It means to stay overnight. The bhikṣus all returned before eating; only the Buddha and the Bodhisattva...
Śāriputra, having finished his fast, returned home; thus he said, "I have already observed the fast," meaning that he had already remained for the fast within the royal palace.
By using this [example], with the exception of the Buddha, one also avoids the sense that self and other are neither fused nor identical, which would render the question invalid.
Although the bhikṣu was able to empty himself, he had not yet attained the extinction of the body. He clearly knew that while one person ate, the others were not satiated, and yet he intentionally—

This constitutes a rhetorical question intended to expose the fallacy of the mind existing outside the body; this will become clear later on its own. Having finished the inquiry as it is illogical, [the author] proceeds to the second part:
providing the correct answer based on principle.
Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Although these bhikṣus are all arhats, their physical bodies and lifespans differ;
how could one person cause the multitude to be satiated?"
The first part provides a direct answer; the phrase "For what reason" (*kasmāt*) introduces the inquiry; and the section beginning with "These bhikṣus... provides the explanation.

Although these bhikṣus have realized the fruit of Arhatship, their physical bodies and life spans are each different because, while the fetters of the seeds (*bīja-bandhana*) have been severed, the fetters of the fruits (*phala-bandhana*) still remain.
As it says later: "Each has a body, and all have their respective clans, lineages, and names."
This sufficiently proves the point. How can one person [claim] that it is certainly impossible for such a principle to exist? It is a pity for Ānanda;
he knew only how to answer offhand, unaware that his own tongue had already fallen into the hands of the World-Honored One.
The exchange of questions and answers regarding the analogy is concluded. Second, the erroneous reasoning is exposed by example.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If the mind that perceives and knows were actually outside the body, then since the body and mind would be external to one another and mutually unrelated, the body could not perceive what the mind knows, and the mind could not perceive what is at the boundaries of the body."

"Knowing" (*jñāna*) refers first to the verbal formulation of what has been determined. "Awakening and comprehending" (*vijñapti*) refers to the awakening to and comprehension of the preceding objects in accordance with the five sensory consciousnesses; this is the *manovijñāna* (the discerning consciousness).

To understand the meaning through the engagement with phenomena is called "knowing," which seems to refer to the *manovijñāna* acting independently (*svatantra*). To encounter an object and grasp its characteristics is called "seeing" (*darśana*).
This likely refers to the preceding five [aggregates], as they are equally illusory; thus, when refuted, they are all refuted together. "The mind is outside the body" is what he conceives.
By adding the word "real" (*shi*), it is fixed so that it cannot be shifted. ○ Regarding "body and mind," this follows the previous example of their lack of mutual interaction.
Since he says the mind is already outside the body, the body must likewise be outside the mind; therefore, it is said that "body and mind are mutually external. Since...

If the mind and body were external to one another, they would naturally not interfere with each other, just like two Arhats whose physical lives are distinct and whose food does not satisfy one another.
If this were so, then what the mind knows, the body should not perceive; and what the body perceives, the mind should not know.
Since they would thus be mutually unaware of one another, one could say that the mind exists outside the body. However, I fear this is not yet the case.
This is necessarily so. Having finished exposing the fallacious reasoning, I shall now provide three proofs to bring you to awakening.
I now show you my hand of *tūla* cotton; when your eyes see it, does your mind discern it?
Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Ānanda, "If they know one another, how can [the hand] be outside?"

First, he shows his hand to allow for verification. "Shows" means extending it to display it. In Western India there is a cotton called *tūla*, which, according to its meaning, is translated as "fine fragrance.
This is because it is fine, soft, fragrant, and pure; the Buddha’s hand resembles it, hence it is named after it.
Visual perception is the knowing of the body; mental discernment is the knowing of the mind. As soon as one sees, one discerns; this seems to be neither body nor mind.

[The Buddha] spoke outside [the context of the previous discussion]. He asked with full knowledge of the answer in order to let [Ānanda] verify it for himself. ○ "Ānanda" and below: he answers truthfully according to the question.
"In this way" means that it is exactly as the Buddha asked: that the eye sees while the mind discriminates; it is indeed so. ○ "The Buddha said" and below: he points out its error.
Since you say that the eye sees while the mind discriminates, then the body and the mind must know one another. If this were truly the case...
Body and mind are mutually aware; their principle is not like that of food, which does not satisfy one another through mutual consumption. How can you say that the mind exists outside the body?
You have simply failed to reflect upon this. Having verified and realized this through awakening, the four fingers of conceptual knots are thereby severed.
Therefore, you should know: your claim that the mind capable of conscious awareness dwells outside the body is impossible.
"Therefore" means because the eye perceives the mind as distinct [from the body]. Since the eye perceives the mind as distinct, it is clearly evident that this mind does not exist outside the body;
thus, it is taught that one "should know," while using the phrase "it is impossible" to refute [your position]. The refutation lies herein.
The end of the section on "Outside. Three points refute [the claim that the eye] is inside the root. First, Ānanda accepts the previous argument and shifts his position;
second, the Tathāgata uses an analogy to refute it. The first [section] has three parts: first, he acknowledges the previous shift to the position of "one location";
second, responding to the inquiry, he indicates that [the eye] is inside the root; third, he removes the two errors regarding its being internal. The first [of these].
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said, because it does not see internally, it does not abide within the body;
yet because the body and mind know one another and are not separate from each other, it does not exist outside the body. As I now reflect upon this, I know that it must reside in a single location."
"What the Buddha has said" refers generally to the teachings on refuting both the internal and the external; "not seeing" these two phrases specifically refer to the words refuting the internal;
and the three phrases beginning with "body and mind" specifically refer to the words refuting the external. "As I now contemplate" means:
Both [positions] are refuted. Seeking another locus for the mind, one realizes it resides in neither;
this is knowing that it does not fall into the two erroneous positions. Yet, the deluded mind fundamentally has no location, and the true mind cannot be grasped through discursive thought.
If even his contemplation was already incorrect, how much more so his claim to know the location [of the mind]? It is no wonder, then, that he was refuted by the World-Honored One.
Second, having accepted the challenge, Ānanda pointed to the location being within the sense organs.
The Buddha asked: "Where, then, is this location? Ānanda replied: "This cognizing mind, since it does not know what is inside, yet is able..."
It sees external objects. As I contemplate it, it lies hidden within the sense organ. It is like a person who takes a lapis lazuli bowl and covers both eyes;
although something is placed over them, there is no obstruction, and that organ perceives and subsequently discriminates objects as they appear.

The initial inquiry was based on the premise that the location [of the mind] had been established; however, the statement regarding "a single location" was refuted by the same logic used to challenge it. Therefore, the inquiry asks:
"Where, then, is this location now? ○ Ānanda, following the previous discussion on the fixed location, since he does not know it to be within, he certainly knows it is not within.
Yet it is able to see the external; moreover, it does not reside within the external. If I set aside these two paths and reflect further, it must surely be latent within the sense organ (*indriya*).
To borrow an analogy to clarify this principle: a crystal bowl or a pair of spectacles represents the eye-organ (*cakṣur-indriya*);
that which is joined with the eyes represents the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*). Now, although the crystal is...

There are objects that meet the eye, yet do not obstruct the eye's seeing; this is a metaphor for how the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya), though it possesses form and meets with the mind, does not obstruct the mind's knowing.
Therefore it is said: "That faculty follows the seeing, and as soon as it sees, it immediately discriminates.

This is because that faculty follows the seeing, just as when meeting with lapis lazuli, it can reflect objects according to them; it immediately discriminates, just as the visual faculty meets with the lapis lazuli.
[The opponent] is able to see [the fault]. Through the combination of principle and analogy, he claims that his own reasoning is fully established.

Regarding the three types of liberation, the former two were previously considered to exist internally; the Tathāgata refuted this by showing that one who is ignorant of the internal cannot know the external. Consequently, [the opponent] shifted his position and calculated that they exist externally, but now that position has been refuted as well.

Having no means to refute or rescue [the opponent], he then relies on the meaning of the Tathāgata’s teaching regarding "being oblivious internally while cognizing externally" to make his estimation. His intention is that if [consciousness] were to reside hidden within the sense organs, then both errors—being oblivious internally and cognizing externally—would be avoided.
However, as for this mind of mine that awakens and knows, its inability to see within is because it resides in the sense organs;
its ability to clearly perceive without without obstruction is because it is hidden within the organs.
"Awakened awareness is capable of knowing. This reiterates the preceding mind.
The reason this mind does not see the interior is that it resides in the sense organ (*indriya*) rather than within the body. This dispels the error of being oblivious to the interior.

Since one is already oblivious to the interior, yet clearly perceives the exterior without obstruction, it is because [the mind] is hidden within the organ; the organ is like a bowl. This dispels the notion of "knowing the exterior."

The error of this [position] must be understood as follows: the internal calculation merely deviates from one's own school, while the external adherence still accords with the tenets of other schools.
As for the error regarding the sense faculties, it is a successive delusion; thus, both one's own school and other schools are not without contradiction.
In general, because they rely on their own meager cleverness and fail to apply themselves to authentic cultivation, when questioned or pressed, they stumble here and there like a blind man.
How wondrous are those who possess the skillful means; they serve as a mirror for our school. Thus ends Ānanda’s succession of shifting calculations.
The Tathāgata refutes [the opponent's view] by means of an analogy in three parts: first, determining the observation based on the analogy; second, showing that the phenomena are not analogous;
third, pointing out the attachment to views and refuting it. Regarding the first:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "As you have said, that which is hidden within the faculties is like lapis lazuli. That person..."
"If one were to cover the eyes with lapis lazuli, would one see the mountains and rivers, or would one see the lapis lazuli? "World-Honored One, it would be so;
if this person were to have their eyes covered with lapis lazuli, they would indeed see the lapis lazuli."
First, let us establish the analogy. As you have stated, this is what was intended by his words; it was a stratagem based on a hidden premise.
The comparison with lapis lazuli (vaidūrya) was fundamentally not equivalent. Since the Tathāgata wished to refute this, he first established the point to elicit the opponent's argument.
[The passage] "That person" refers to the questioner who saw the lapis lazuli; it states that "that person" should have used the lapis lazuli...
The glass obstructs the eye. Yet, lapis lazuli certainly does not obstruct the eye. Even though it does not obstruct the eye, it is not a thing without substance.
Since that faculty of the eye can see mountains and rivers from afar, how could it not see the lapis lazuli nearby?
The reason for specifically asking whether he "sees" is to compel him to speak for himself, thereby providing a basis for raising an objection within the Dharma.
○ Regarding the phrase "Thus [he] answered below with what he actually sees": the term "thus" is an initial general response, meaning that it is exactly as the Buddha has asked.

This person is next to be questioned: namely, one whose eyes are covered by a lapis lazuli cage who actually sees the lapis lazuli. This is because he should provide an answer corresponding to his own experience.
Having thus concluded the application of the analogy to the certainty of seeing, there are two difficulties regarding the lack of parity between the phenomena.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If your mind were joined with the crystal [of the eye], you should see mountains and rivers;
why do you not see the eye itself? If you could see the eye, the eye would then be the same as the external objects, and it could no longer function as the faculty that follows them.
If you cannot see it, how can you say that this discerning mind is hidden within the sense organ like a crystal?"

At first, my formal objection was that the two cases were not equivalent. My intention was this: if you claim that your mind resides within the sense organ, such that it is like glass placed over the eye, then your mind would be identical to the eye, and the visual faculty would likewise be identical to the glass.

Yet, as your mind currently perceives mountains and rivers outside, why does it not first perceive the eye itself? Since the dharma (the subject) and the analogy (the example) are thus inconsistent—[for in the analogy, the glass actually covers the eye]—...

When one sees lapis lazuli, the eye-faculty within the dharma-encompasses the mind; because one cannot see the eye itself, that which you calculate to reside in the faculty is not established as ultimate.

If [you claim] "seeing" below, it is to simultaneously prevent error (for fear of the erroneous conclusion that when seeing mountains and rivers, one would also be able to see the eye; therefore, this prevention is made). It says:
"If your mind can see the eye, then the eye is identical to the object confronted. Even if we grant they are identical objects, it is a confrontation and not a following. You previously..."
What is said—that "those faculties follow seeing and immediately engage in discrimination"—is likewise not universally established.

[If this is not refuted by returning to the correct analysis, it is because one might fear that upon hearing that the eye does not see, one would instead reckon that it does not see at all; therefore, one returns to the correct refutation. It is said: if the mind cannot see the eye...

Thus, it is not a hidden root (*guṇa*), because it is not like the eye-root situated within lapis lazuli. Why, then, do you say that the mind is within the roots, as if they were joined with lapis lazuli?
This is a false calculation based on reality; it is like the knot imagined by three fingers, which is then destroyed [upon analysis].
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of cognizing and perceiving lies latent within the sense organs like a crystal—has no basis in reality.
Whether in the state of seeing or not seeing, neither possesses the meaning of being latent within the organs. For this reason, you should understand what has been calculated.
No. Therefore it is said: "There is no such possibility. This concludes the refutation of [the view that the mind] is within the sense organs.

Fourth, the refutation of the rescue [of the previous position] from within (formerly translated as "refuting both the internal and external"). Upon careful examination of the text, Ānanda certainly did not speak of a dualistic calculation, nor did the Tathāgata use words to refute them simultaneously.

Zhengmo (正脈) says: "To examine this calculation rigorously, it still returns to the initial attachment to [the mind] being within; it differs only in that the two previous errors have been removed. He further says: "Although the names are listed separately, in reality they are merely attempts to rescue the previous defeat regarding the [mind] being within. Therefore, the present commentary uses 'refuting the rescue' [to categorize this]."
(Internal Medicine) II. First, Ānanda attempts to rescue [the argument] from within; second, the Tathāgata refutes it by addressing the difficulty of the objection.
First: Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have now further reflected thus: this body of sentient beings..."
The viscera are within, while the apertures dwell without. Where there are viscera, there is darkness; where there are apertures, there is light.
Now, as I face the Buddha, when I open my eyes and see light, it is called seeing the external; when I close my eyes and see darkness, it is called seeing the internal. What is the meaning of this?
First, he reflects upon the principle of rectification. To seek it outside is certainly erroneous; to seek it within the sensory faculties is even more so.

Thus, he returns once more to the attachment of [seeking it] within, and further contemplates the principle of liberation from error. Therefore, it says: "Again, he reflects in this way. *Fù* is the same as *fǔ*, referring to the six *fǔ* (organs).

[These are: the stomach is the *fǔ* of water and grain; the small intestine is the *fǔ* for receiving and containing; the large intestine is the *fǔ* for the passage of matter; the bladder is the *fǔ* of fluids and essence; and the gallbladder is the *fǔ* of clarity and purity. Three...

The small intestine is the solitary *fu* (receptacle). The *Suwen* states: "That which transmits and transforms substances but does not store them is called a *fu*. *Zang* is also written as *cang*; it refers to the five *zang*. (The kidneys are the *zang* of essence.)

The heart is the repository of the *shen* (spirit); the liver is the repository of the *hun* (soul); the lungs are the repository of the *po* (soul); and the spleen is the repository of the *zhi* (will). The *Suwen* states: "That which can store the vital essence and qi without leaking it is called a 'repository' (*zang*). Therefore, the character *zang* (repository) is used immediately below.
Since the *fu* (organs) and *zang* (repositories) are all internal components of the body, they are said to be "within.

As for the "orifices" (*qiao*), this refers to the seven apertures and cavities (two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, and one mouth), all of which are located on the face; therefore, they are said to be "situated outside. "Repository" (*zang*) carries the meaning of enclosing and storing; thus, there is...
Where there is a location, there is darkness. "Orifice" (*qiao*) carries the meaning of being open and penetrating; therefore, where there is no location, there is light.

Here, Ānanda wishes to escape his previous error and first sets forth the principle that it is dark within and bright without. "Now, I... and below is the rescue from difficulty and request for a definitive resolution.

Because his previous calculation placed [the mind] inside, the Tathāgata rebuts him with two fallacies: first, the fallacy of being inside yet being oblivious to what is inside; second, [the fallacy of being inside yet not perceiving the internal].
To know the internal while erroneously claiming to see the external is a misconception. Now, because there are apertures, there is light; this is exactly like doors and windows being opened wide.
Thus, when one opens the eyes and sees light, it is called "seeing the external. This dispels the error of knowing the internal while seeing the external.

Furthermore, because there are internal organs, there is darkness; that which is dark refers precisely to the viscera. Thus, when I close my eyes and see darkness, it is called "seeing the internal. This dispels [the misconception].
This is the error of being internally obscured regarding what is internal. His intention was that the preceding objection by the Tathāgata was unreasonable;

he still maintained that "being internal" was correct, yet having been repeatedly refuted and disabused of his view, he did not dare to reach a conclusion on his own. Thus he asked, "What is the meaning of this?
This was yet another attempt to seek clarity from the very lips of the World-Honored One. Ānanda ultimately attempted to rescue the position that [the mind] is internal.

Second, the Tathāgata refutes [the opponent's position] by analyzing the terminology in three parts: first, opening the inquiry based on the terminology; second, forming the refutation based on that inquiry;
and third, concluding the refutation by pointing out the underlying presumption.
Regarding the first: the Buddha told Ānanda, "When you close your eyes and perceive darkness, is this objective realm of darkness facing your eyes?"
"It is not non-confrontational with the eye.

Since that which faces must be situated in front and thus established as external, the objection asks: how can it be established as internal? "If it were established...

This means that the *jiao* itself is simply a *fu*. If [the eye] does not face [the object], how can it constitute seeing?
Since facing is already untenable, and yet you yourself calculate that there is no facing, the text next challenges this by means of the lack of facing: "seeing occurs without facing."

This contradicts worldly consensus; therefore, it is difficult to establish how this constitutes "seeing. Second, this also serves to prevent erroneous arguments (fearing that one might erroneously argue:

"When I say 'seeing darkness with eyes closed,' I am referring to internal seeing. This means that at the time of closing the eyes, this mind has already departed from external seeing and turns inward to face the internal organs; thus, seeing is established. This is still a calculation that [seeing] ultimately resides within.
Therefore, the World-Honored One used this to prevent such views).
If [the body] were established by depending on an internal object apart from external vision, then when one closes the eyes and sees darkness, it would be called "within the body.
But when one opens the eyes and sees light, why does one not see one's own face? If one does not see one's face, then an internal object cannot be established.
To begin with, even granting your erroneous claim, my intention is this: if you erroneously maintain that when the eyes are closed,
this consciousness departs from external vision and turns inward to face the internal organs,

thereby constituting "seeing," then what you have calculated as "seeing darkness when the eyes are closed" is precisely what you call "seeing within the body" (the two lines concerning the eyes are a restatement of your prior calculation that seeing darkness when the eyes are closed is called "seeing internally," with the phrasing slightly altered).
○ Opening the eyes and taking this as an example reveals the fallacy. The intent is this:
when the eyes are closed, since this mind is already able to rotate and see the internal viscera, when the eyes are opened, it should likewise rotate and see the face and eyes.

Now that you are properly opening your eyes and seeing light, why do you not see your own face? If you claim that at the time of opening the eyes, one cannot see [the face], [then the previous case is also untenable].
The face cannot be turned around. Taking this as an example, when the eyes are closed, they likewise cannot be turned around;
thus, the meaning you propose regarding "facing inward" cannot be established.
Since facing inward is not possible, how can you claim that seeing darkness with closed eyes is called "seeing within"? It is clear, therefore, that what you have calculated is incorrect.
Third, the successive refutation of the error:
If the seeing of the face were established [as being external], then this cognizing mind and the eye-organ would reside in space; how then could they be said to be "within"?
If they were in space, they would not be your own body; consequently, the Tathāgata’s seeing of your face now would likewise [be something external].

Regarding your body: since your eye has already perceived that the body is not conscious when it comes into contact [with an object], if you insist that both the body and the eye must each possess consciousness, then this single body of yours would have to become two Buddhas.

The initial mind’s eye being in space is an error. (This was originally intended to clarify the mind; it incidentally involves the eye because ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle generally reckon that the mind follows the eye, as stated previously:

"Those faculties follow seeing, and they immediately engage in discrimination. The meaning is this: even if one were to grant that the eyes can rotate when opened, the principle of "seeing the face" would still be established.
If this were so, then the mind and the visual faculty would both reside in empty space, for it is only through their mutual confrontation that seeing can be established.
Is it not the case that what faces [the eye] must reside in space? If you concede that it resides in space, then it belongs to the external;

therefore, it is difficult to maintain that it exists internally. (Zhengmo says: Ānanda originally maintained that the mind still resides within; thus, he now concludes his refutation by showing that both the mind and the visual faculty cannot exist internally, thereby exposing the contradiction in his own words.)
If the argument is turned downward, it results in the fallacy of establishing the other's position as one's own. This means:

if you insist that the mind-eye exists within space, not only does it fail to exist within [the body], but by being in space, it is separated from you; it is not your own substance, but rather becomes the mind of another.

If the argument is turned downward immediately, it results in the fallacy of establishing the other's position as one's own. This means: if you forcibly claim that although it is separated from you...
"If it is not the case that it is nonetheless your own substance, then the Tathāgata seeing your face now would also be your body;
for since you have already conceded that it is nonetheless distinct from you, it must be universally admitted. These two preceding fallacies serve to reprimand him for destroying worldly conventions.
"If your eyes were below your body, this would constitute the fallacy of 'non-perception. This means that self and other would interchange positions.
The characteristics of the world have already been refuted; how much more so, then, your mind which follows the eyes?

Since those eyes are detached from the body yet possess conscious awareness, your body would consequently be equivalent to an insentient object and lack conscious awareness. This is because a single person possesses only a single mind;
when it resides in the eyes, it cannot reside in the body. [This] must be an error on your part to claim that one body has two fruits. The meaning is: you must hold such a view.
To say that awareness resides both in the body and in the eyes, such that both possess cognition, would mean, Ānanda, that you have two consciousnesses.

Since human beings rely solely upon this single cognition to cultivate causes and realize the fruit, if you now possessed two cognitions, then when you attain Buddhahood in a future life, you would become two Buddhas. This is logically impossible; it is nothing but a delusion.
The refutation based on the specific details is concluded. Third, the refutation by means of the three fingers.
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that seeing darkness is called "seeing the internal"—is untenable.
Because of the mutual contradictions between "facing the eye" and "not facing the eye," the principle of seeing the internal is not established;
thus it is said, "there is no such case. Since seeing the internal with eyes closed is already untenable, it is sufficient to refute his defense regarding the internal.
There is no need to further refute the principle of seeing the external with eyes open. *Zhengmo* says: "Single..."
The section on "Bondage and Views within" concludes that this calculation [of the self] must likewise reside within. This completes the refutation and defense regarding the "within.

Part Five: Refuting the Conjunction of Locations, in two sections: (1) Ānanda’s erroneous calculation based on scriptural citations; (2) The Tathāgata’s restatement of that calculation to challenge and refute it. First: [Ānanda’s erroneous calculation based on scriptural citations].
Ānanda said, "I have often heard the Buddha reveal to the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
and because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise. Now, as I contemplate this, I realize that the very essence of my contemplation is truly my own mind-nature."
Wherever there is a conjunction, the mind follows and exists there. It is also not found in the three locations of internal, external, or intermediate.

First, there is a mistaken citation of ancient teachings regarding that which is "constantly heard. These ancient teachings were previously heard; such statements as "with the arising of the mind, dharmas arise" apply universally to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as they are commonly taught in the ancient scriptures.
Now, referring specifically to the Two Vehicles (Hīnayāna), we shall provisionally designate the six consciousnesses as the "mind. Six...
"Dust" refers to phenomena (*dharma*). Guanding says: "Because one clings to external objects from within the internal mind, the objects arise in accordance with the mind;
therefore it is said that 'with the arising of the mind, phenomena arise. Because the internal mind is stimulated by external dust, the mind manifests in pursuit of the objects;

therefore it is said that 'with the arising of phenomena, the mind arises. Zhengmo’s *Yi* (Commentary) states: "'With the arising of the mind, phenomena arise' shows that phenomena do not arise of themselves. Regarding phenomena...
"The arising mind arises; the seeing-mind does not arise by itself. This correctly reveals that the mental dharmas depend upon one another and appear falsely, both lacking substantial reality.
Ānanda has missed the essential point and instead uses this as proof for a dependent mind, which exists whenever it encounters its conditions; this may be called extreme delusion.
"In my present [teaching] below, 'deluded calculation' refers to existence according to conditions. 'Contemplation' refers to the principle that the mental dharmas arise in mutual dependence."
Furthermore, at the very moment of contemplation, the functioning of deluded consciousness is clearly manifest;
one perceives that there is no separate mind-nature and takes this [consciousness] to be real. Thus, it is said: "This very substance of thought is truly my mind-nature.
Yet one does not realize that the Tathāgata has repeatedly refuted this, precisely because this perception is not true, and thus there is cyclic existence. This is Ānanda.
"You have failed the Tathāgata not a little. As for 'arising in accordance with what it encounters': whatever dharma it grasps as an object, the mind arises accordingly.
For example, when you currently contemplate the Dharma taught by the Buddha, the mind arises clearly; if you were to contemplate another dharma, the arising of the mind would be exactly the same.
By inferring from this analogy, is it not the case that the mind arises in accordance with whatever it encounters?"

Regarding "arising in accordance with conditions": the *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) cites the Sūtra as saying, "The mind gathers its objects and stirs within; it rushes outward and runs wild. This state of confusion and agitation is taken to be the nature of the mind.
The ancient masters remarked that such攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to objects) and 妄想 (wàng-xiǎng, deluded thoughts) are like a wild fire; how could they be called the true mind?
Now, Ānanda has been rebuked in four successive instances for identifying this state of "arising in accordance with whatever it encounters" as the mind; it is clearly [not so].
Internally agitated and externally distracted, it is truly called "confused turmoil. This is precisely the攀緣 (*pán-yuán*) of delusive thoughts; how is it any different from a wild fire?
It is simply because it has been repeatedly struck and probed that its true nature is exposed. Yet, one still does not realize its falsity, merely exhausting all manner of deluded states.
Furthermore, this phrase does not entirely negate the preceding errors. It means that while words follow and correspond to [objects], they do not exist where those objects are absent.

"Concentration (*samādhi*) does not reside exclusively within these three locations. For the time being, 'intermediate' refers to the interior of the sense organs; this is because the space between the internal organs and the external [body] constitutes the intermediate.
Ānanda has thus concluded his erroneous calculation by citing scriptural authority. Second, the Tathāgata restates his calculation and refutes it through difficulty.

This section has three parts: first, restating what he has calculated; second, dividing the thesis into two and presenting two difficulties; third, pointing out the calculation and concluding the refutation. First:
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have just said— that because phenomena arise, various states of mind arise, and that wherever they meet, the mind follows and exists—
although there were four propositions cited by Ānanda previously, his intention was to take only the latter two, setting aside the former two."

Because the mind already exists prior to the phrases, it cannot be said that it arises in accordance with their conjunction; therefore, this Tathāgata also refers to them by means of only the latter two phrases.
[The second section on the two-fold thesis and the two-fold refutation: First, the refutation that there is no essence because they do not conjoin.
The two objections regarding the existence of a substance lack any basis. First:

if this mind has no substance, then there is nothing with which it could conjoin. If it were possible for something to conjoin without having a substance, then the nineteen realms would conjoin with the seven objects; such a proposition is untenable.
The initial formal objection refutes the notion of "conjunction. Since mental states arise following the arising of dharmas, the mind lacks an intrinsic nature of self-arising.

If its very nature does not exist, upon what could one rely to speak of conjunction? Therefore, it is said that there is nothing with which to conjoin. Thus, even the idea of "following conjunction" is already incorrect;

how much more so the claim of "following existence"—is this not merely to increase delusion? ○ The passage beginning with "If there is no... serves to prevent such erroneous attachments, for fear that...

The erroneous objection states: "Although the mind lacks substantiality, it does not preclude its temporary manifestation as that which can conjoin; therefore, this [argument] is formulated as a safeguard. The intent is this:

generally speaking, whenever one speaks of conjunction, both factors must possess substantiality, as in the case of the eighteen *dhātus*, which are formed by the conjunction of the six objects (*viṣaya*) [with the six faculties and six consciousnesses].
This is what was permitted in the ancient teachings. If one insists that something can conjoin despite lacking substantiality...
This refers to the false calculation that, outside of the eighteen *dhātus*, there exists a nineteenth *dhātu*. Furthermore, it is claimed that this arises from the conjunction of seven particles;

however, neither the present teaching nor the former teachings permit this. Since the *dhātus* are strictly eighteen and the particles are only six, there has never been a doctrine of nineteen or seven.
How, then, could there be the principle of "conjunction"? Therefore, it is said: "This argument is not tenable. This constitutes the objection.
The refutation of the non-existence of an entity through the argument of non-conjunction is concluded. Second, the refutation of the existence of an entity due to a lack of basis has two parts:

first, the formulation of the refutation based on two meanings; second, the formulation of the refutation based on the four characteristics. Regarding the first of these two: first, the direct refutation of the two meanings; second, the simultaneous critique of erroneous arguments. Regarding the first [of these]: [End of section]
If it possesses a physical substance, then as you now strike your own body with your hand, does the mind that perceives this emerge from within, or does it enter from without?
If it emerged from within, it would see what is inside the body; if it came from without, it should first see your face.
First, I shall examine and verify its origin. Since it lacks an intrinsic nature when considered in relation to what precedes it, the conjunction is not established.
Because you nevertheless maintain that it possesses an intrinsic nature, I shall now challenge you by means of this very notion of an intrinsic nature. My intention is this:

if you now claim that this mind possesses an intrinsic nature, you should verify it for yourself. For example, when you touch your own body with your hand, at the very moment of contact, there is [an experience].
Regarding the mind that knows pain and knows itchiness: you must now examine the nature of this mind that is capable of knowing.
Does it emerge from within, or does it enter from without? It must necessarily have a basis; only then can one say it has a substantial body.

If, on the other hand, you take the lower part as a separate path and apply the previous example to refute it, the implication is that if it emerges from within, it would be the same as being previously inside, and thus it should return [to its original state].
First, one sees within the body; if [the object] were to come from outside, it would be the same as the previous internal correspondence.
First, you should have seen my face from afar, yet now neither is the case; thus, there is absolutely no basis for it. What is called "having a substance" is merely a false conceptualization.
Second, the simultaneous refutation of erroneous arguments, which has two parts: first, Ānanda’s erroneous argument; second, the Tathāgata’s refutation.
First, Ānanda said: "I see with this eye. [The Buddha replied: "To claim that the mind knows while the eye does not see contradicts the meaning of 'seeing.

Because you were confronted by the Tathāgata’s challenge regarding the difficulty of internal seeing emerging from within and external seeing arriving from without, you have consequently offered a fallacious argument, saying: 'I see...'"
This is the function of the eye; the mind can only know, it does not possess the same capacity for seeing as the eye. As the Buddha said:
"If what emerges from within sees the body, and what comes from without first meets the face," this was intended to challenge the notion that the mind is the seer.
"If it were able to see, it would not be the nature of the mind. Would the Tathāgata then be deceiving me?
This was the second refutation by the Tathāgata. The Buddha said:
"If the eye were able to see, could you see me while I am inside a room through the door? [The opponent replied: "No. [The Buddha continued: "Then as for those who have already died..."
If there were eyes remaining, all should see objects. If one sees objects, how can it be called death?

First, this refutes [the claim] that consciousness resides within a person's life by stating: if the mind is inside the body like a person inside a room, and the eyes merely provide the passage for light so that [vision] occurs, then it is the mind within the body that sees;
the metaphor is that the door merely provides the passage for light, while it is [the person inside] who sees.
This refers to the person inside the room. If one claims within the Dharma that the eye alone can see, then by analogy, the door must also be able to see.
While the fact that the eye can see is something even those of the Two Vehicles do not realize to be erroneous, the notion that the door can see is recognized as a fallacy by everyone in the world.
Therefore, he uses the analogy to raise an objection, causing [the opponent] to realize their own error for themselves. ○ Then, as for "all" below...

This refutes [the opponent's position] by means of the analogy of a dead person’s consciousness departing. Since you have already used an analogy to question me, yet still do not understand that [the eye] is not [the seer], you must maintain that the eye is capable of seeing.
Therefore, the analogy requires that it be a dead person who is capable of seeing; thus, the challenge is posed based on one who has already died.
This refers to the time when the mind has departed from the body. Although the mind has left the body, the eye still remains. At this time, if [the eye could see]...

If one sees for oneself, this is seeing with the eyes; therefore, it is difficult to claim that one must see all things. This is likely because one knows full well that such seeing is impossible, yet deliberately makes it difficult.
The final two phrases constitute a refutation based on the inconsistency between the meaning and the name.

It says that only when a person is unable to see objects can they be called "dead"; if they see objects, they are simply a living person. Therefore, it is difficult [to maintain the opponent's position].
What is meant by death? In this way, when a person dies, there is nothing seen; the eyes remain as mere emptiness because consciousness has departed.

One who understands this meaning can clearly perceive that what was seen was indeed the eye, and thus realize the error of thinking that the mind knows through the eyes. This becomes even more evident.
The refutation based on two meanings is concluded. Second, the refutation based on the four characteristics has two parts: first, restating the essence to pose a general inquiry;
second, posing specific refutations based on the characteristics. Regarding the first:
"Ānanda, furthermore, if this mind of yours that perceives and knows must have an essential substance, does it constitute a single entity, or..."
[The opponent claims it has] multiple bodies. Now, regarding these bodies within your own person, do they pervade the entire body or not?

The previous refutation of these two meanings has already exposed the fallacy of having [multiple] bodies; yet, fearing you may not yet be convinced and might still stubbornly cling to the notion of having bodies, I restate the point and inquire once more.
Below, each case shall be individually refuted. As for "a single body": this means that the four limbs share one common mental essence (*citta-tattva*).
Regarding "multiple entities": each of the four parts possesses its own distinct mental substance; this is an inquiry based on number. Regarding "pervasive entity":
a single mind pervades all four parts; regarding "non-pervasive": it is restricted to one part and does not pervade; this is an inquiry based on extent.

Indeed, a thesis that posits a substantial entity must necessarily possess both number and extent in order to be established. Second, there are two difficulties concerning the distinction between characteristics.
First, the two characteristics that are difficult to enumerate; second, the two characteristics that are difficult to measure. Regarding the first:
if it were a single entity, then when you touch one limb with your hand, all four limbs should feel it. If they all felt it, there would be no specific location for the touch.
If the touch has a specific location, then your "single entity" cannot be established. If, on the other hand, it were multiple entities...
[If] that were so, it would constitute many [entities]. What essence (*ātman*) could belong to you?

First, the objection regarding the non-establishment of a single entity: if the four limbs were a single entity, there would be the absurd consequence of simultaneous arising. Therefore, the objection is first formulated by way of a single entity. The intent is this:
if the four limbs shared the essence of a single mind, then at the very moment one limb is touched, the four [limbs]— [...would all experience the sensation simultaneously.]

The limbs should all be conscious, because they constitute a single entity. If you hear my words and mistakenly claim that all [limbs] are conscious, then the point of contact should not be localized; for it would be established as being conscious.
If, however, when the head is touched one knows it, and when the foot is touched one feels it, yet the point of contact is localized, then your conception of "one" is refuted.

The meaning of "substance" (*tattva*) cannot be established by itself, because the four factors are not shared [by a single entity]. If one were to argue that there are multiple substances based on the following objection, this would still be incorrect;
for while refuting the notion of a single substance, the mind inevitably resorts to the notion of multiple substances. Therefore, the objection is again formulated in terms of multiple substances.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I too have heard when the Buddha was discussing the true nature of reality with Mañjuśrī and other Dharma princes, that the World-Honored One also said that the mind is neither within nor without."

This has been frequently heard in the past; hence it is said, "I have also heard. Although it does not specifically identify which sutra, recounting what was previously heard, it should pertain to the first half of the *Prajñāpāramitā* assemblies and the period of the *Vaipulya* and *Saṃdhinirmocana*.

Regarding "with Mañjuśrī and others," this is because during the *Vaipulya*, *Saṃdhinirmocana*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* assemblies, Mañjuśrī and others were constantly the primary recipients of the teaching (*yathābhavyatā*).
Therefore, the Vaipulya sutras are like the *Vimalakīrti*, and the Prajñāpāramitā sutras are like those such as the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā*.

When referring to the various Dharma-Princes—such as Mañjuśrī’s class, including Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and others—who manifest traces as those adjacent to the ultimate, the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) they discuss can be briefly explained in three ways.
First is the characteristic of formlessness, which is called true reality, as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: [text follows].
"That which is the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is itself the absence of marks"—this is the intent of the Initial Teaching (śāstra). Second, "all dharmas are truly real," which is termed the true mark;
as the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* says: "Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha likewise. This is the intent of the Final Teaching.

Third, the absolute emptiness that transcends all marks is called the "True Mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As stated in the *Anantamukhanirhāradhāraṇī-sūtra*: "That which is the One Dharma is what is called 'marklessness.
That which is markless and yet not without marks is called the True Mark. This is the intent of the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*).

For example, the "Śāriputra Chapter" of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "The mind does not abide within, nor does it exist without. Ānanda, as for the distinction between the true and the false...
[This is] a division. To cite errors as evidence and for the learned to follow the names while remaining ignorant of the meanings is certainly to be expected.
As for his own view—that he once heard this in the past yet still calculates in terms of "internal" and "external"—it is no wonder that he was refuted by the World-Honored One.
This concludes the erroneous citation of past teachings. Second, establishing the Middle Way through reflection.
As I reflect upon this: because there is nothing seen within, it does not exist internally;

because the internal and external are mutually aware and inseparable, it is not logical for it to exist externally. Since they are now mutually aware, yet there is no seeing within, it must reside in between.
First, I reflect upon the two previous errors. As for my own contemplation, I rely on the Buddha’s former teachings to examine his present discourse.
Now, because I conceived of the "self" as being internal, the Buddha challenged me by stating that nothing is seen within;

this is because one cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, stomach, and so forth. Furthermore, because I conceived of the "self" as being external, the Buddha challenged me by stating that it would not be able to perceive [the body].
This is because it corresponds to the principle of the "single meal" (ekāśana) for those who do not eat to satiety.

According to the Buddha’s intention, [the mind] cannot be said to exist internally because there is no cognition within; nor can it be said to exist externally because body and mind are mutually cognizant and inseparable.

This thus accords with the meaning of the ancient teaching that [the mind] is neither internal nor external. ○ Now, the characteristics below depend upon one another to constitute the characteristics of the Middle Way.
The former teaching and the present discourse are already in accord. I have also verified this within myself:

because my body and mind are currently known to one another, I know that [consciousness] does not reside outside the body; yet, because it is not perceived within the body, I know it does not reside inside the body either.
Having set aside these two alternatives and reflected further, it must reside in between; there is no room for further debate.

The Buddha said: "You say that within the 'middle' one must not be deluded, and that it does not exist nowhere. Now, when you investigate this middle, where does it reside?
Does it reside in a location, or does it reside in the body?"

First, based on reason, it is established that [the capacity for speech] exists. Regarding the statement that one who speaks in the midst of things is certainly not deluded: this is because one who is deluded does not speak, whereas one who speaks must necessarily possess the power of comprehension.
It is not that there is no locus [for this capacity]. One who possesses the power of comprehension must necessarily be able to point and instruct;

one who points and instructs must necessarily have a locus. Now, in the passage beginning with "You," [the text] double-interrogates both loci. Although it is true that the locus is not non-existent, you should respond with due care.
Therefore, he instructs by means of "investigating the middle" (*madhyama*), which refers to minutely investigating the characteristics of the middle.
As for the question, "In what does the middle reside?"—that is, a general inquiry as to what constitutes the locus of the characteristics of the middle—is it in the locations and so forth?

This means that all phenomena do not transcend the internal body of the faculties and the external objects of the sense-fields; therefore, he specifically poses two questions regarding the body and the location. There must necessarily be a fixed [locus].
Only when it exists can one apply the refutation. Second, the difficulty regarding its existence in the established [position] has two parts: first, it is not established in the body;
second, it is also not [established] in the location. Regarding the first:
If it resides in the body, it is at the periphery and not in the center;

if it were in the center, it would be identical to the internal. The first phrase establishes that it resides in the body; in the following two phrases, both "periphery" and "center" are transcended. "Periphery" refers to the attachment to the skin, while "center" refers to the interior.
To say it resides in the body implies there is both center and periphery; yet if one speaks of the periphery, one cannot speak of the center. This is of its own... [text ends].
This contradicts the tenet. For instance, if one claims it is "in the middle," it would still be identical to being "inside," which has already been refuted above.
Since both positions possess faults, [the self] does not even exist within the body; how much less can it be said to be "in the middle"? Thus, the position itself fails to be established.
The second [alternative], that they exist in a location, is also untenable.

If they existed in a location, would they be something indicated or something non-indicated? If they were non-indicated, they would be identical to non-existence; if they were indicated, there would be no fixed determination.
Why is this? It is like a person using a marker to designate the center: when looking toward the east, it becomes west; when observing from the south, it becomes north.
Since the substance of the marker is thus confused, the mind should likewise become disordered.

The first phrase establishes the locus; the following two phrases inquire into and indicate presence or absence. "Presence" indicates the locus of manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*); "absence" indicates the locus of space (*ākāśa*).

To say that manifest form exists in its locus implies that there is both manifest and non-manifest form. If it were as in the case of non-manifest form, it would be identical to empty nothingness, and your mind would become subject to annihilationism.

This results in confusion. Since both positions possess faults and the context is already erroneous, how can it be established within the words?
Why is this so? This serves to interrogate and explain the meaning of the lack of fixedness in the *biao* (table/manifestation). It is because the words regarding "lack of fixedness" are muddled;

without an explanation, they cannot be understood. Therefore, an interrogation and explanation are required. Regarding the two characters for *biao* that follow one another, the preceding character for *biao* refers to...
The object that can signify expresses the sign; that is to say, it manifests the internal characteristic. Therefore, it is said: "using a sign to manifest a sign.
Zhengmo (Zheng-mu) says: "A 'sign' (*biao*) is a marking pole. Those who construct houses erect it to mark the central position. Guanding says: [as above].

This is like the *zhouguan* (Director of the Office of Sacrifices) using the *tuguī* (earth-gnomon) to measure shadows and establish markers: looking east, the west is formed; observing south, the north is established.
When the shadow-patterns shift, looking west, the east is formed; observing north, the south is established. This can be understood through reflection.

The final two lines speak of the substance that serves as the indicator: since the four directions are thus intermingled, how could the mind being indicated possibly establish itself as a fixed center?

Therefore, there would be confusion; that is to say, the four directions would intermingle and designations would become disordered. This is what is meant by "lack of fixedness. The formal objection concludes here.
Second, the simultaneous refutation of erroneous defenses, which has two parts: first, Ānanda’s erroneous defense regarding the characteristics within;
second, the Tathāgata’s refutation of that error regarding what is within. First:
Ānanda said: "What I have spoken does not fall into these two categories. As the World-Honored One has said: 'With the eye and forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises.
The eye possesses discrimination, while the objects of form are without cognition; when consciousness arises between them, that is what constitutes the presence of the mind."
The first section, "Different from the Buddha’s Manifestation," means that within what I have taught, there is another principle;
it is not the two kinds spoken by this Tathāgata, namely, those concerning the body and the middle [of the body]. "Like in the world," and so forth, accords with the Buddha’s former teachings.

it is consciousness alone that possesses discrimination. Even if one points to the nature of the faculty, the subsequent text also says: "Its..."
The eyes look around, but it is merely like [the reflection] in a mirror; there is no separate analysis. Your consciousness identifies and points out within that [reflection].

Third, what was previously stated—that the mind gives rise to affection and delight—belongs to the mental consciousness (manovijñāna); what is now stated—that consciousness arises therein—is the visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna). The point of inquiry lies with the former.

If one combines both, the entities of things become confused; since things are not the substance of cognition, they stand as two opposing forces.

Since it is neither within, nor without, nor in between, it has no location at all.
That which is called "mind" is the name for the non-attachment to all things. Is my non-attachment to all things what you call "mind"?
First, the previous teaching is cited: "In the past, I saw the Buddha point to the *Prajñā[pāramitā]*;

This is precisely the meaning of the Buddha’s command to transmit the teaching. The explanation of Maudgalyāyana and others, along with their Chinese and Sanskrit names, is found in the introductory section (*nidāna*).

Those who have studied [the Dharma] are called "younger brothers" (*di*), signifying that their learning follows that of the teacher. Those from whom the Dharma is born are called "sons" (*zi*), signifying that wisdom arises from the Dharma.
The leaders of the Saṃgha are addressed as "Great" (*da*), signifying that among the Buddha’s disciples, four are the foremost.

Because they receive the Buddha’s mandate and propagate the teaching on his behalf, the term "together" (*gong*) is employed. By preaching the Prajñāpāramitā Dharma, they destroy ignorance and delusion; therefore, [this title is used].

The metaphor of the wheel: as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "I, following the Buddha's teaching, act as a great bodhisattva; through various causes and conditions, I preach the unsurpassed path.
This refers to the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, signifying the meaning of receiving the Buddha’s command and together turning the wheel of the Dharma.
The Prajñā school takes non-abiding as its fundamental principle; hence it is called "the discourse on the eternal. Discernment and conceptual discrimination are precisely the deluded mind.

The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* refers to this as the "reflected shadow conditioned by the six sense-objects," while this scripture denounces it as a false and illusory mark of perception. Since it possesses no substantial reality, [it is ultimately empty].

However, since these are stated as conventional sayings, they appear to be citations of the general sense, or perhaps from various sections [of the sūtras].
The same statement also appears in the *Prajñāpāramitā*. [The Master said: "Regarding 'all things,' you have made a presumptuous conjecture and requested a decision.
You claim that the Buddha’s intention was to show that the consciousness-mind is illusory because it has no location whatsoever;
yet Ānanda did not understand this meaning, and instead took 'non-attachment to all things' to be the mind. This is truly relying on conjecture and making a false judgment. Although...
Having repeatedly been refuted and stripped of my positions due to making arbitrary and deluded judgments based on mere conjecture, I did not dare to consider myself correct.

As before, I requested a definitive resolution from the Buddha; hence it is said: "I am unattached," which is called "the mind being non-existent. (Formerly, the Second Patriarch requested peace of mind from Master Bodhidharma.

[The opponent] claims that it appears right here, yet Ānanda has not actually arrived at this place; he falsely asserts non-attachment while still not daring to realize it himself. Many of such types are like those whose feet do not even touch the ground.

[The Master] concludes by citing the scriptures to refute Ānanda’s erroneous calculations. Second, the Tathāgata refutes him through reasoning. First, he presses the point and poses a double challenge.
Second, both existence and non-existence are difficult to maintain. Third, the refutation of the calculation regarding the knots. First:

The Buddha told Ānanda, "As for what you said—that the nature of the mind which perceives and discriminates has no location—[if this is so], then all things in the world, including empty space, water, land, flying creatures, and all such objects and phenomena, are called 'everything. If you do not cling to these, where would they exist?"
There is none.
First, to establish what was said: although these are the words of the Buddha, because Ānanda cited them, they are the words of Ānanda;
therefore, it says, "you say. This is brought forward for refutation, having first established the point. ○ Below, "In the world," etc., is an inquiry.
Regarding the existence or non-existence of objects: your statement that both are "non-existent" implies that this is the state of universal non-attachment.
However, setting aside for a moment the matter of non-attachment, what constitutes "everything"? It is like the space of the world, which belongs to the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment);

the beings of water, land, and flight belong to the *sākṣāt-karma-vipāka* (retributive body). These two types of retribution—the environmental and the personal—distinguished by their various categories, are called the "various objective phenomena."
All things and phenomena are collectively and comprehensively encompassed; this is precisely what is meant by "all.

Regarding your previous statement that you do not cling [to them], is it because all these things are present and you yourself do not cling to them, or is it because all these things are entirely non-existent and you therefore do not cling?
You clearly know that neither case is tenable, yet you deliberately ask this question to initiate the discussion.
Second, both existence and non-existence are problematic: (as stated above, that which "exists" is precisely existence).

If it were non-existent, it would be identical to a tortoise's hair or a rabbit's horns; how then could there be non-attachment? That which exists cannot be called non-existent if one is not attached to it.
If there are no marks, then there is nothing; if it is not non-existent, then it has marks. If marks exist, then [the object] exists. How, then, can there be non-attachment?
This initial formal objection concerns existence and non-existence; its intent is that if one claims that the absence of both is called "non-attachment," then that intention is not established.
If [the mind] were non-existent, it would be identical to the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit; it would exist in name only but lack reality.

Regarding the section "Non-characteristic" (*animitta*) below, this further explains the objection. The meaning is: if I say it is non-existent, then it is the same as a tortoise's hair or a rabbit's horns.

Then one cannot be called "unattached. This is because "non-non-existence" is a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Where there is a characteristic, there is presence. To say that "non-non-existence" is a characteristic means that non-non-existence is itself existence;

This would mean it both exists and does not exist; since neither case is free from the fault of attachment, he challenges [the opponent] by asking, "How can there be non-attachment?
If even non-attachment cannot be described, how much more so is it a delusion to claim that this is the mind?
Having concluded the critique of both existence and non-existence, he proceeds to refute the analogy of the three fingers forming a knot.
Therefore, it should be known that it is impossible for one who is free from attachment to perceive the mind as existing or non-existing.

If one calculates that the mind which is free from attachment is the true mind, it is entirely non-dual and there is not a single instance where this is correct.

[Question]: A thief who changes his occupation becomes a good citizen; yet, to kill him for remembering his past [deeds], can that truly be called good governance? If one recognizes this as the mind, why must it be further destroyed?

[Answer]: The true mind is like the ocean; the deluded mind is like the waves. When the waves strike the boat, they cause harm. If they do not strike the boat, one must wait for the waves to subside.
