Furthermore, one leaves the sea only to seek the waves; now Ānanda has indeed realized his non-attachment, yet he naturally seeks the mind and finds it unobtainable. Since the mind is unobtainable, one spontaneously perceives the true mind. How could one then abandon the truth to identify with the delusion?

Since you still identify with the delusion, your claim to be "unattached" is likewise not worthy of trust. Therefore, as I said before, Ānanda has truly not yet reached this state. It is like a thief who speaks of having reformed his ways while his heart has not actually changed. One charged with the duty of apprehending thieves—how could they simply set him aside without investigation?

This is why the Tathāgata further refuted it. The *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Pulse) says: "Examining these seven instances that establish the locus [of the self], there are only four locations: first, the internal; second, the external; third, within the sense organs; and fourth, in between. Since three of these are still included within the internal, [the self must reside therein]."

The fifth [position] lacks a fixed location; the seventh lacks even a location altogether. Furthermore, the first four [positions] cite the common consensus of the multitude, while the second and third employ one's own reasoning for speculation. The latter three cite scriptural teachings yet provide erroneous interpretations. Gushan says: "Taken together, these seven rounds appear to refute the four natures (*catur-koṭi*).

Within, they secretly undermine the 'self-nature' (*svabhāva*); without, they refute the 'other-nature' (*parabhāva*); in between, they refute the 'common nature' (*sādhāraṇa-svabhāva*); and by following the union [of causes], they refute the 'natureless' (*asvabhāva*) without attachment. Nāgārjuna said: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another;

they do not arise from both, nor without a cause. Therefore, it is said that they are unarisen (*anutpāda*). Based on this, the seven rounds exhaust all conceptual attachments; when one completely lets go of the body, one enters the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Although Ānanda has not yet reached this state, what he has relied upon in his daily life...

[The text states: "As for what is considered the mind, it is likewise profoundly without a place of abiding that can be traced. This concludes the second section: "Secretly Showing that Deluded Consciousness Has No Abode. Next, the second [section]:

"Manifestly Rebuking Deluded Consciousness as Not Being the Mind" (whereas previously its nest was destroyed, here its guilt is formally pronounced). This has two parts: 1. Ānanda reproaches himself and requests instruction; 2.
The Tathāgata reveals the fundamental [nature] and rebukes the error. The first of these has two parts: 1. Self-reproach for one's own mistakes.
At that time, Ānanda, being thus bewildered, sought the Buddha’s instruction on the path of cultivation. First:
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly; he bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am the youngest younger brother of the Tathāgata, having received the Buddha's compassion..."

Āyuṣmat Ānanda, although you have now left the household life, you still rely on pride and affection; therefore, despite your great learning, you have not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
You were unable to subdue the *Sāvitrī* spell and were turned by it, falling into the house of lust. This must be because you do not know the destination of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
First, the sūtra narrator describes the ritual setting. "At that time" refers to the moment when the seven points had been refuted.
With his arguments exhausted and his stratagems depleted, he sought the Buddha’s compassion; thus, he rose from his seat. "Baring the flesh" means to expose the skin.
"Baring the right shoulder" means to partially expose the flesh on the right side of the shoulder. The right side signifies compliance and also expresses the intention of being ready for service.

Therefore, Guanding said: "In this land, one bares the shoulder when apologizing or obeying a command; in the Western Regions, one bares the right shoulder when having an audience with a king or seeking his favor.
Now, Ānanda seeks [instruction from] the Buddha; his etiquette is the same as that for an audience with a king, manifesting the utmost reverence.

Regarding the right knee touching the ground, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* provides three meanings: first, the right knee possesses strength, allowing one to kneel comfortably for a long duration; second, the right...
The knees possess strength, making it easy to rise and sit. Third, the right knee is restless; when placed upon the ground, it is made stable. An ancient master said:
"With three parts raised high, the right knee touching the ground is called *prāṇāma* (half-kneeling). Such a posture symbolizes humility, deference, and compliance.

Joining the palms symbolizes the gathering in of scattered movement. All of the above pertain to the activity of the body. To be solemn and reverent is called *gōng* (reverence); to hold in high esteem is *zūnzhòng* (respect)."

"Jing" (reverence) pertains to the mental karma (*manas-karma*). "Gao" (to announce) refers to what is shown above; "bai" (to inform) refers to what is initiated below; these pertain to the verbal karma (*vāk-karma*).

When the three karmas are practiced with such sincerity, they are sufficient to move the Buddha; therefore, this is specifically set forth as a narrative. The passage beginning with "I am... is a self-reproach for one's own errors.

Among the Four Heavenly Kings and their eight sons, Ānanda occupies the last position; thus, he is the youngest brother. Being the youngest, he was particularly favored with the Master’s special attention.
Thus, having received the Buddha’s compassionate love, I still retained worldly sentiments even after leaving the household life.

Consequently, I continued to rely on arrogance and pity—where "pity" refers to a feeling of compassion and concern. Because of this reliance, from the time I began attending upon the Buddha until now, I have not yet been struck by the harsh *ghanṭā* (monastic gong).
I have allowed myself to become spoiled and self-indulgent, focusing exclusively on extensive learning rather than striving for true cultivation. Not yet...

Having attained the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*), he was finally able to realize the first fruit of the path. Yet, upon encountering the *sāvitra* spell, he could not bend it to his will nor subdue it;
instead, he was turned by it and fell into a house of prostitution, unable to emerge on his own.

Had it not been for the protection of the Tathāgata’s spell and the guidance of Mañjuśrī, he would have had no choice but to flee far away—what face would he have had to see the Buddha? This was still a mistake of the past.
Yet it is already too late to turn back. ○ Regarding the character "由" (yóu) in the phrase "當由下猶慮當迷" (dāng yóu xià yóu lǜ dāng mí), many commentators fail to provide a definition.
Lecturers generally explain it in the sense of "cause" (yīn). However, upon careful examination of the preceding text, this interpretation lacks any basis.
This is because the previous errors were recounted in chronological order, each having its own specific cause; the first was caused by being the youngest, thereby receiving the Buddha’s compassion.

First is attachment; subsequently, because of being favored by that attachment, one long relies upon and becomes arrogant toward that affection. Next, because of relying upon and being fond of that affection, one still hears erroneous testimony.
Finally, because of that erroneous testimony, one’s power is unable to overcome the false. Thus, each stage arises from its own respective cause.

Furthermore, it says, "it shall be by way of. If this is taken in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), how can it be reconciled? Now, to explain "by way of": it refers to that which is to be traversed in the future.
"The Reality-limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*) refers to the true mind as the ultimate reality. This is to take deluded consciousness as the true mind and that which is occupied as the ultimate reality;
it is simply not realized that there exists separately a true mind and an ultimate reality. [One] arrives.

This refers to the ultimate locus. My intention is that since my previous errors were already committed and cannot be remedied, I hope that regarding the course of the future, it may still be possible to pursue the path.
However, I have personally realized that although the sevenfold delusions are exhausted, I still do not know the true mind, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), or the ultimate locus.
Upon what, then, can I rely for further cultivation? This is what I am concerned about. Observe the following:
I request instruction on the path of *śamatha*. As for the reasons for my concerns regarding the future, they may be understood by reflecting within myself;
I have already reproached myself for having fallen into delusion. Second, I seek the Buddha’s revelation of the path of cultivation.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will reveal to us the path of *śamatha*.
May this cause all those of icchantika nature to abandon their barbarian ways. Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground;
together with the great assembly, they waited expectantly with thirsting hearts, reverently awaiting his instructions.

At the beginning of the path of correct seeking and cultivation, there is no one to whom one may turn for refuge except for the Buddha alone; therefore, it says, "I only pray that the World-Honored One...

One does not seek the bliss of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), but rather looks toward Great Compassion and pity, because only by the certain arousal of Great Compassion can one be granted Great Bliss.
"Pity" (āi) refers to grieving over past errors, while "pitying" (mǐn) refers to taking compassion for future delusions. I request that you show me the sublime [path].
"Seeking the path" (mārga) means seeking to know the location of the mind. Because one does not know the location of the mind, there is no path of *śamatha* that can be cultivated.
However, Ānanda only knew how to seek the path, yet did not recognize seeing as the mind; this is like a person walking upon a broad, level highway.
He only knew how to seek its opening, yet did not realize that consciousness is not the mind; this is like a capable official who opens up the road. As it says below:

*Icchantika*—this is translated as "one who lacks faith. Because they do not believe in cause and effect and lack shame and remorse, they are also called "those who have severed their roots of goodness.

It is said that previously, because the path of *śamatha* was obstructed, those who practiced correctly perished, and most fell into the extremes of heterodoxy, accumulating evil views until they fell forever among the *icchantikas*. This realization of truth through the abandonment of delusion also causes those of the icchantika class to reform their own heterodoxy and return to the right path; thus, their evil views naturally collapse.

According to the records, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, whenever he encountered those who harmed him, he not only refrained from retaliation, but out of pity for their ignorance and delusion, he made vows to deliver them.
Now, Ānanda lacks the power to overcome the heterodox, and his body has received [the injury].
That he would deign to request instruction on the path and cause [his] evil views to fall away is itself the intention of a Bodhisattva’s vow to deliver others.

Ānanda, the time has arrived; before long, he will relinquish his body. Therefore, he manifests this through the six kinds of earth tremors.

This is a subtle indication that transforming others is identical to transforming oneself. The phrase "in this manner" refers back to the aforementioned shaking of a single world-system (*dhātu*).

When a single world-system shakes, it successively reaches others; thus, in such a continuous succession, the lands as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions all open up and manifest simultaneously.
If one were to interpret this as a symbolic teaching (*dharma-pratibimba*), it signifies that Ānanda has abandoned delusion, while the assembled multitude...

Although the above has been revealed, there still remains separation; although the scope of vision has become pervasive, the boundaries remain distinct.
Furthermore, by means of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he casts down the Iron Ring Mountains and lays flat Mount Sumeru, merging the rivers and lakes to connect them with the Fragrant Ocean.
There are no longer multiple lands, but only a single world-system; thus it is said that all worlds are combined into one realm. If one were to...

The various realms represent delusion, while the single realm represents the True. When these are brought together and fused, the signifier and the signified are likewise analogous in meaning.

the consciousness-mind is fundamentally unobstructed, and thus it is still represented by means of that realm. By transforming others to be like oneself, all sentient beings follow from this.
Because he has resolved his mind [for enlightenment], he is represented by the Bodhisattva. Since he has already returned to the truth, there is no further distinction between the real and the false;

The Fundamental Source of Delusion. First:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have undergone various inversions.
The seeds of karma arise spontaneously like clusters of akṣa fruits. Those practitioners who cultivate cannot achieve unexcelled Bodhi, nor even [the stages] beyond..."
Those who become śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; those who become non-Buddhist devas, māras, and their retinues;
and all sentient beings who, from the beginning, were ignorant in their creation of karma—these refer generally to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who do not know how to practice.

As for those who have followed ignorance since beginningless time, this refers to the period since the advent of their own deluded consciousness, during which they have opposed the truth and pursued the false.
Turning one's back on awakening and conforming to the sensory dusts, one reckons the non-self as self and the non-dharmas as dharmas;
thus it is said there are "various inversions. This belongs to the path of affliction (*kleśa-mārga*). Because of these inversions, one creates various karmas that serve as causes for the future;

thus they are called "seeds" (*bīja*). This belongs to the path of karma (*karma-mārga*). The path of affliction is like firewood, and the path of karma is like fire; depending on the wood, the fire spreads, each possessing its own characteristic.
It is ablaze; the body of phenomena (dharmakāya) is scorched by its fumes, and the life-force of wisdom (prajñājīvita) thereby hangs in peril.

This belongs to the path of suffering. One gives rise to delusion and creates karma, and the fruits of suffering follow accordingly. These three matters are mutually dependent; thus it is said to be like a cluster of *akṣa* fruits.
*Akṣa* is the name for a fruit in the Western Regions. Guanding says: this means "cotton-stringed beads," where three fruits share a single stem and are gathered together.
Thus, the three paths that arise are similar [to those previously described], and for this reason they serve as a metaphor. Regarding the phrase "Those who cultivate [the path] below":
ordinary beings who give rise to delusions and create karma, thereby revolving through birth and death, are certainly pitiable.

Yet, even those who possess the will to practice but whose progress on the Middle Way is circuitous remain objects of sorrow. The word "various" (*zhū*) generally conveys the sense that although one speaks of "cultivating the path," it is in fact...

This refers to those who do not rely on correct cultivation. "Bodhi" is translated here as the "Path of Enlightenment. It exists in all three vehicles (*triyāna*), though they differ in depth; only that of the Buddha is unsurpassed.
The reason one cannot achieve it is precisely because one does not cultivate based on correct enlightenment.
The phrase "and so forth" (*naiti*) excludes and abbreviates the Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings and the Mahāyāna. [The section on] Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas has been explained.
The introductory section concerns the Hīnayāna. Although they have separately achieved this [realization], they are still worldly sages and worthies.

Yet there are those who err even more severely; thus it says, "and those who become non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and so forth. Non-Buddhists are those whose minds wander outside the Way and who pursue perverted cultivation.
The various devas of the triple world are those attached to outflows (*sāsrava*). The Māra King dwells at the summit of the desire realm and is addicted to...

Regarding those who delight in sensual pleasures: the spirits and goblins that are the retinue of Māra, as well as those who associate with Māra—these too are ordinary worldlings dwelling in this life.
Yet, compared to those ignorant doers of karma, they are even more difficult to save; is it not tragic that they provide no benefit?
This concludes the identification of those lamented. Second, the indication of the fundamental basis of their delusion.
All this arises from practicing erroneously due to ignorance of the two fundamental roots. It is like boiling sand in the hope of producing a fine meal;
even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will never succeed.
The initial emergence [of these errors] stems from being misled by superficial signs, as described above. It goes without saying that those who act out of ignorance are to be disregarded;

however, as for those practitioners who originally intended to attain the Way and its fruits, yet instead encounter detours midway, becoming stalled and obstructed within provisional or inferior teachings, or even mistakenly entering the realms of Māras and externalists—desiring purity they become defiled, and seeking to ascend they instead fall. The reason for this is as follows:

Why is this? Therefore it is said: "It is all due to ignorance," and so forth. Regarding the two fundamental natures: the first is the True Fundamental, which is that which is revealed in the ten successive sections below.
The second is the Delusory Fundamental, which is that which was refuted in the seven locations above. The preceding passage on the "mind grasping at error" states:
"From beginningless time, the continuity of birth and death has occurred entirely because one does not know the eternally abiding Truth."
The mind employs various deluded thoughts; the meaning is the same here, though it has not yet been clarified that this [mind] is the source.
What is now called the "source" is so designated because all true causes and true fruits, as well as false causes and false fruits, do not arise apart from it.
Those who practice erroneously take deluded thoughts to be the true mind and point to counterfeit fruits as genuine realization; they do not merely mistake the true.
To employ delusion is, for the time being, to use the false to confuse the true. This is like the following illustration used to clarify the error:
it speaks of practitioners who take deluded thoughts as the causal mind while hoping to realize the true fruit—like boiling sand in the hope of producing a fine meal.
Sand is not the basis for food; though one toils in vain for kalpas, it is said that one will ultimately never obtain it. Falsehood is likewise not a true cause.
For this reason, one fails to achieve Bodhi and mistakenly enters the ranks of the provisional and inferior vehicles, as well as those of external paths, celestial demons, and Māras.

"Ānanda, the first is the root of birth and death from time without beginning—namely, that which you and all sentient beings now take to be their own nature:

The first phrase, "emerges from," means that throughout the beginningless succession of kalpas of birth and death, if one traces the current back to its source, it does not emerge from anywhere other than the deluded mind;

therefore, it is called the "root. The passage beginning with "Then you" (*zé rǔ*) indicates the manifestation [of this root]. It is intended to cause awakening to delusion by pointing to what is present before one;
hence it says, "Then you, now. Since all who have not yet realized the Truth inevitably identify with delusion, it says, "[it is] with all the multitudes."
"Arising" refers to the攀緣心 (pān-yuan xin), which is the mind of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).

As the six consciousnesses perceive objects, they give rise to attachment wherever they encounter them—like a monkey clinging to a tree or a caterpillar (*śalabha*) crawling along a branch; hence it is so named.

However, this is fundamentally neither the mind nor its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet sentient beings cling to it as the essence of the mind. Therefore, it was said previously: "It is precisely the substance of thought (*cintā*); truly, it is the self (*ātman*)."
Regarding the nature of the mind, it was previously stated that "that which is capable of deliberation" shall be taken as the mind.
Now, it is clearly pointed out to be the very root of birth and death; yet Ānanda still does not realize this—how truly pitiable he is!
Second, he subsequently reveals the true source.

This second point is the fundamentally pure essence of bodhi and nirvana from time without beginning. It is this very essence of the consciousness-essence (vijñāna-garbha) that is originally luminous and capable of giving rise to all conditions;
yet it is what is lost amidst those conditions. Because sentient beings have lost this original luminosity, although they [continue to] exist...
The sun moves on without one’s own awareness, yet [beings] erroneously enter the various realms of existence (*gati*).

"Emerging from the beginning" differs from the preceding section; while the preceding section encompasses the intermediate period—meaning from the beginningless past until now—this section refers solely to the initial limit, meaning the time of the beginningless. Bodhi.
There are three: first, real wisdom; second, skillful means; and third, true nature. This is the bodhi of true nature, because the nature is inherently self-awakened, which is itself bodhi.
Nirvana also has three aspects: first, purity of nature; second, purity of skillful means; and third, perfect purity.
This is the nirvana of purity of nature, because the nature is inherently pure, which is itself nirvana. Originally pure.

This does not mean that it is made clear by being clarified; rather, it means that it is primordially free from the turbidity of birth and death, thereby manifesting it as *prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa* (naturally pure nirvana).

"Primordial purity" (*yuanjing*) does not mean that it is made pure by being treated; rather, it means that it is primordially free from the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa*), thereby manifesting it as *tathatā-bodhi* (true nature enlightenment), which serves as the foundation for all pure phenomena. The meaning is: "I now merely dare not slander the Dharma; even if I were to be rebuked and give rise to anger, and consequently lose faith in the Buddha-Dharma."
On the contrary, they give rise to slander; consequently, they lose their roots of goodness and fall into the state of an icchantika.

Furthermore, they are driven by this very mind. Thus one knows that this mind is the chief culprit and the primary offender. Since it has gained power over the past, one knows it must likewise do so in the future.

Though one rebukes it as a non-virtuous mind, how can one truly forget its influence? Therefore, I have recounted these matters clearly and in detail, hoping that you will find some means to address them.
"You have taught me. You have exhaustively recounted how you attained this power.
You have opened me to the state where the two fears no longer exist and nothing is sought. If this revelation is not the mind, then I am as mindless as wood or earth;
apart from this awareness, there is nothing else at all. Why, then, does the Tathāgata say this is not the mind? I am truly terrified by this."
The great assembly was without exception filled with doubt and confusion. May you deign to bestow your great compassion and reveal the truth to those who have not yet awakened.
First, let us examine the Buddha’s words: the phrase "if it is like this" refers back to the previous reprimand and instruction.
Since the Tathāgata has already rebuked it as wrong and further denounced it as a false appearance and conception, he has clearly elucidated that it is not the mind. "I, therefore," and so forth.
I personally declare that fear arises from the mind; that is to say, the master of merit and the chief of sin are both this very mind alone.
Whether in the past or the future, it is necessarily employed by its own power. If this [mind] does not exist, then I become a person without a mind. If a person has no mind—
[He] should naturally be the same as earth, wood, or stone, because apart from this conscious awareness, nothing else exists. The section beginning with "How could...
correctly describes his alarm and fear. "Why do you say it is not so? expresses his astonishment that what the Tathāgata has said is inappropriate.
"I am truly alarmed and afraid" clarifies that he himself was rendered disoriented upon hearing it. "Along with this great assembly" still refers to those of the Hīnayāna.

There is a certain class of people who, because [the teaching] establishes the root of both defilement and purity solely through the six consciousnesses, will inevitably feel doubt upon first hearing that it is not the mind.
The final two lines conclude the request for instruction; their state of alarm, suspicion, and unease is truly pitiable.
Therefore, I only hope that you will bestow your great compassionate heart. There are two points regarding my lack of realization:
first, why this consciousness cannot be called "mind" (*citta*); second, how it can differ from earth or wood if it is separated from [the mind].

To dispel my own fear and resolve the doubts of the assembly, I seek the Buddha’s instruction. Upon reaching the section on "Consolation," he shows that [the mind] exists; now, he provides the formal instruction.

This is not like earth or wood; it dispels the alarm and fear. By examining the objects before one, their non-existence is revealed. Thus, the teaching that they cannot be named "mind" is clearly shown, and doubt is resolved.
Ānanda’s alarm and fear having reached their limit, he sought further instruction. The Tathāgata showed both the existence [of the mind] through examination and its non-existence through analysis.
First, he comforted him by showing its existence; second, he analyzed the objects to show its non-existence. Of these two, the first consists of: first, the touching of his head.
First, citing the teaching of "Mind-Only" to illustrate that the True Mind possesses substantial reality.

At that time, the World-Honored One revealed this to Ānanda and the great assembly, desiring to cause their minds to enter the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena).
On the lion throne, he rubbed Ānanda’s head and addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata has always taught that all phenomena that arise are manifested solely by the mind.
All causes and effects, and even the minute dust motes of the world, take their substance from the mind."
First, the Sūtra master sets forth his intention: he reveals [the truth] to Ānanda because of his state of alarm and terror, and to the great assembly because of their doubts and delusions;
he desires to trace the source of the words and reveal the Buddha’s original intent.

He says that while Ānanda and others previously used the consciousness-mind to discriminate, thereby giving rise to false views of arising and ceasing, this teaching now reveals that there is no substantial essence, so as to cause them to abandon such discrimination.
Then one enters the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). The *Avataṃsaka* says: "The patience of non-arising means not seeing the arising of even the slightest dharma.
The *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Renwang jing) says: "All dharmas are empty; thus one attains the patience of non-arising. Furthermore, "patience" (*kṣānti*) means faith;

it refers to having deep faith in the meaning that all dharmas are non-arising. [The Buddha] then placed his hand upon the disciple's head and spoke to him. As for the "Lion Throne" (*siṃhāsana*), its construction...

Regarding the "Teacher Seated Image" (座像師): it need not necessarily be an image; rather, the seat itself is designated by the name "Teacher" to signify the meaning of fearlessness in preaching the Dharma.
Because [the disciples] were struck with awe, he touched their heads while addressing them to demonstrate his intention of providing consolation.

That "the triple world is mind-only" and "all phenomena are consciousness-only" is the great tenet of the Buddha’s teaching; therefore, it is said that he "constantly preached. As for "all phenomena," the *Abhiṣeka* states: [All phenomena...]
Briefly stated, there are only two kinds: matter and mind. "That which is produced" refers to that which is able to arise.
Because it arises not apart from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), it is said to be "manifested solely by the mind. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The mind is also 'mind-only';

even that which is not mind arises from the mind. The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "The objects perceived by all consciousnesses are manifested solely by the mind. The subsequent text also says: [the same].

The various conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors (*caitta*) and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and all objects of cognition, are manifested solely by the mind; this sufficiently proves what has been constantly taught.

Regarding the phrase "all [phenomena] below," it is based on the teaching of severance. That is to say, based on what is constantly taught, one determines that the cause resides in the mind, because the meaning of the establishment of the essence [of phenomena] depends upon the mind.
Regarding all causes and effects, speaking in terms of the primary retribution (*vipāka*), there are two interpretations. First, both the noble ones and ordinary beings each have [their own].

Cause and effect: second, from the inferior toward the superior, where the cause precedes and the effect follows. The "worldly atoms" (*loka-rajas*) refer to the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment);
they also carry the meaning of cause and effect, for the accumulation of atoms is the cause and the formation of the world-realm is the effect.

All such things are manifested by the *ālayavijñāna*. This is intended to reveal that the mind is certainly not non-existent, as will become clear below. Therefore, it is said: "The substance is formed through the mind. *Ma*...
The explanation that "all is but mind" is concluded. Second, the true mind is shown to possess a substantial essence by way of analogy:
"Ānanda, if all things existing within all worlds—even down to blades of grass, leaves, threads, and knots—when their fundamental source is examined, all possess a nature and substance;
even empty space has its name and appearance. How much more so, then, for the pure and wondrous [mind]?"
The pure, luminous mind is the nature of all minds, yet it is itself without substance.
First, "all" (zhū) refers to the various entities that exist; here, "all" collectively encompasses all phenomena presently manifest.

Within this, there are both general and specific categories: the general refers solely to the world-system, while the specific refers to everything that exists. "Among them" (qí zhōng) refers to all that exists...
The term "middle" encompasses both the minute and the vast, as well as the subtle and the coarse. The word "even unto" (*yāvat*) is a term used for omission or abbreviation.

As for what is said to be "manifest" or "vast," they certainly possess their own substantiality; even down to the most minute and the most subtle—such as a single leaf of grass or a single knot in a thread—if one investigates their fundamental origin, all have a substantial nature (*svabhāva*) upon which to rely. For example, a leaf has the grass as its [basis].
Substance. Because it is composed of threads, its nature is that of a conditioned formation (*saṃskāra*). Yet even this belongs to the realm of the colored and the obstructive.
Even in the case of formless emptiness and unobstructed space, there are still characteristics by which they may be named and appearances by which they may be described;
for "emptiness" is its name and "azure-green" is its appearance. How much more so, then, does this illustrate the True Mind, which is pure within?
"Immediate" refers to the insight revealed by stripping away delusion, for its nature is fundamentally unstained.

"Sublime purity" refers to the reality that emerges from dissecting delusion, for it is uniquely sublime and pure, being free from defilement. Because it is pure, it is not obscured while within the bonds of saṃsāra;

because it is sublimely pure, it is perfectly luminous once obstacles are removed. Therefore, it is collectively termed the "Luminous Mind. Its nature pervades the four categories and the seven elements.
Since it constitutes the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is also called the "nature of all minds," unified as the single True Mind.
How could such a mind be without substance? To provide an analogy for clarification so that its nature may be easily realized:

even words and phrases possess an essential nature, and even empty space has names and characteristics. By what comparison can one describe the True Mind in contrast to these? Yet, if one speaks of the True Mind in reverse...

[The self] lacks inherent substance. This is because [the Buddha] deeply deplored that Ānanda should have made such a statement; thus he comforted him by demonstrating its existence. If you maintain that the nature apprehended by the discernment of vitarka and vicāra must necessarily be the mind, then this mind should exist as a complete,
independent nature, distinct from all objects of the senses— namely, the spheres of form, odor, taste, and touch, as well as their various activities.
First, one stabilizes the mind by means of what is grasped and what is clung to. "Grasping" refers to stubbornly adhering to old views; "clinging" refers to being miserly and unwilling to let go.
These refer to the mind that discriminates, applies vitarka (initial inquiry), and vicāra (sustained investigation). As for "discriminating," it is the arising of thoughts in response to objects;

as for "vitarka and vicāra," it is maintaining internal stillness in a secluded state. This will be seen for oneself later in the section on "Verifying Falsity. Guanding says: "The initial thought of the coarse mind..."
"Vicara" (discernment) is named "awakening" (jue). The subsequent thought of the subtle mind is named "observation" (guan).

As for the nature of that which is cognized, it refers to the capacity for cognition possessed at the very moment of correctly distinguishing between awakening and observation. However, this nature is entirely the consciousness-mind (vijñāna-citta);

it properly belongs to the root of delusion, yet Ānanda stubbornly clings to it and refuses to relinquish it, identifying it as his true mind. The Tathāgata, wishing now to dismantle this misconception, therefore...
First, establish the premise. As the text states: "If it is said that they must all be established," this refers to the mind.

This section below addresses the objection based on grasping; "that which should respond" is according to the principle of reasoning, because what was previously cited has already been made manifest. [This applies to] form, odor, taste, and touch.

Briefly stated, there are four sense-objects (*viṣaya*). There remain two others: sound and mental objects (*dharma*). These are collectively subsumed under the term "all sense-objects. Regarding "activity" (*karma*): it refers to worldly undertakings.
The initial stage of engagement is called "activity," while its completion is termed "work. It is said that all worldly activities and works are accomplished in dependence upon sense-objects.
Since this discusses both the agent and the object together, it is termed "the activity of all sense-objects. In contrast to this, there is "discriminative cognition" (*vikalpa-buddhi*).

[If] one observes that the nature of what is known is only manifested when the conditions are present, and that as soon as there is a moment’s separation [from those conditions], the knowledge is impaired—how could it possess a complete nature existing independently?
This is intended as a refutation. Second, one examines the objects of perception to verify their falsity.
As you now listen to my Dharma, this is a discrimination arising from sound.

Even if you were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be but a shadowy affair of discriminating within the dust of dharmas.
It is as when you point with your finger toward something present before you, intending to reveal that which is deceptive;

because you point to what is manifest as a verification, you listen to my Dharma, for there is a distinction based on sound. By analogy, one knows how to gaze up at my physical form, for there is a distinction based on color.

One smells the incense smoke from my burner, for there is a distinction based on fragrance, and so forth. To speak by way of abbreviation, it is said: "Even if [the senses] were extinguished," and so on. This refers to seeing and hearing.
The two consciousnesses of eye and ear, and the three of nose, tongue, and body, are collectively termed "feeling" (*saṃjñā*), because they are alike in being cognitions arising from contact.

This cognition is none other than the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Furthermore, this has two aspects: first, the "clearly manifesting consciousness," which arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses and is also called the "mental consciousness co-arising with the five" (*pañcaka-sahaja-manas*).
It perceives objects with clarity and directly apprehends the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena; therefore, it is so designated.
[The first] is named [the consciousness associated with the five sense organs]. Second is the independent consciousness (*mukhyavijñāna*). This, in turn, has three types:

first, the independent consciousness in the state of distraction (*vikṣiptāvasthā*), which takes as its object a purely imagined realm (*pratibimba-viṣaya*); second, the independent consciousness in dreams, which takes as its object the realm within a dream;

and third, the independent consciousness in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which takes as its object the realm within concentration. What is now called "extinguished" refers to the state of concentration, because in that state the eye does not perceive forms and the ear does not hear sounds, and so forth. Furthermore—
When there is no distracted mind nor dreaming, then the first five consciousnesses, the five concomitant mental states, and the independent [minds] of distraction and dreams all cease to function.

Nevertheless, even if one can achieve this, it is not yet true cessation, because there still remains the independent mind within meditative concentration that maintains the objects of that concentration;
thus it is said, "internally maintaining a profound stillness. This refers to the mind that internally maintains [the state].
This refers to the solitary mental consciousness within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Its profound depth and tranquil seclusion constitute the objects within concentration.

Although these objects within concentration are subtle, they do not depart from the objects of mental phenomena (*dharmārambaṇa*). This solitary mental consciousness within concentration is continuous and dense, and thus also belongs to the category of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

It is not merely a matter of conceptual discrimination, but rather belongs to the category of reflected phenomena (*pratibimba*), because apart from the objects of the mental faculty (*dharmāyatana*), it possesses no intrinsic nature.
Thus, the three teachings investigate and examine this with subtle precision.
I am not commanding you to hold that this is not the mind. Rather, you must examine the mind with subtle discernment:

if the nature of discrimination exists apart from the objective fields, then it is truly your own mind; if the nature of discrimination has no substance apart from the fields, then it is merely a reflected image of the discrimination of those fields.
The term "compulsory command" (*qiáng mìng*) refers to this. The Tathāgata’s intention is as follows:

although you previously clung to this as being the mind, and I have repeatedly refuted and stripped away that notion, I have not been forcibly commanding you to shift your clinging and regard this as non-mind.
Rather, it is simply that you must not mistake it. Examine the mind subtly and minutely for yourself; if there were a nature existing apart from objects, that would indeed be your true mind.

Because the true mind must necessarily have a substantial essence. If it were as I have stated above—that it has no essence apart from objects—then it would merely be a conceptual discrimination arising in dependence upon external objects, belonging to the realm of illusory shadows; how could it be the true mind?

The Tathāgata has demonstrated that although phenomena appear to exist, they are ultimately non-existent. The assembly of the three gatherings knows that this is not a lack of eloquence. Dust is not permanent;
if it were to undergo transformation and perish, this mind would be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit.
In that case, your Dharma-body would be subject to annihilation. Who then could cultivate and realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas? At that moment, Ānanda and the great [assembly...]
The assembly remained silent, overcome with self-reflection.

[The Master] first pointed out the errors in [the opponent’s] departure. He continued: Since what has been discussed above pertains to reflected images, and these depend solely upon external objects (*viṣaya*), yet you insist that they are the mind, there are two fallacies.
First, external objects are produced by conditions; they are not permanent phenomena. Suppose, for instance, that the conditions...
When all things undergo transformation and extinction, this mind has nothing upon which to rely; it would then be like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, reduced to non-existence.
This is the fault of having a name but no substance. Second, if the mind were identical to the Dharmakāya, it would belong to the category of inherent nature (*xingju*);

yet, practicing based upon it to realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) belongs to the category of that which is attained through cultivation (*xiude*). Since the mind would thus have no substance, the Dharmakāya would likewise [be non-existent].
Regarding cessation: upon whom does the patience regarding phenomena (dharmakṣānti) rely for cultivation and realization? This is the fault of losing both nature and cultivation.

"Immediately thereafter," [the text] says, meaning that after the Tathāgata had instructed him through investigation and examination, Ānanda knew that there was nothing to be argued. "Immediately thereafter" refers to the time when the Tathāgata taught him to scrutinize. Having subtly investigated and deliberated, he already knew there was no substance;
furthermore, hearing that [asserting existence] would constitute a fault, his emotions were exhausted and his words at an end. Since it was thus with Ānanda, so it was for the entire assembly.
It is likewise so. Thus it is said, "together with the great assembly. Since they do not know which is the true, yet dare not continue to recognize the false as such, they can only remain silent.
They perceive themselves as having lost both; the ram caught in the fence serves as an apt metaphor.
The comprehensive refutation of the three delusions is hereby concluded. Third, the summary rebuke of erroneous recognition.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Although all practitioners in the world may currently achieve the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*)."
They cannot exhaust their outflows to become arhats; this is entirely because they cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death, mistaking them for reality.
Therefore, although you have now attained much learning, you have not achieved the fruit of sainthood.
The first binding excludes the "learners of the world," who are those in the three lower fruits of the path. They are called "of the world" because they have not yet transcended the three realms;

they are called "learners" because they have not yet realized the fourth fruit. Those who are "present" are those who, proceeding from this point onward, achieve the successive meditative absorptions (anupūrva-samāpatti), which constitute the fourth fruit.

The former eight [absorptions—the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments] are accomplished while still at the level of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana); the latter one is the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

If only the six consciousnesses are ceased, it is called the "mindless absorption" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti); if the seventh consciousness is also ceased along with them, it is called the "absorption of cessation" (nirodha-samāpatti). Furthermore, because it involves a specific aversion toward sensation and perception, it is also called the "absorption of the cessation of sensation and perception" (saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti), as it is accomplished at the level of an Arya.
If we discuss the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path], according to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, one who has already exhausted the outflows (āsrava-kṣaya) is an arhat.

That it is said here, "although they have attained them, they do not obtain them," is because the previous [attainment] was granted as a provisional concession; in reality, they have not yet attained them.

This is entirely due to their attachment to these [provisional states], which causes them to manifest that they have not yet attained them. "Delusive thought" (vikalpa) refers specifically to the six consciousnesses, for these are the root of saṃsāra.
Therefore, it is called the delusive thought of birth and death; those who mistake this for reality do not understand that consciousness is empty.
Precisely because they do not understand that consciousness is empty, although they achieve cessation, it is no more than pressing grass down with a stone or binding a thief with a rope.

Even if one can pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, there will ultimately come a time of destruction. Since the meditative state of cessation is not ultimate reality, it is not what is meant by the "exhaustion of outflows" (āsravakṣaya).
"Are the Arhats truly real? Therefore, [the text] below concludes by rebuking Ānanda. 'Therefore' refers back to the statement that the Arhats are not truly real.
It says that although the Arhats have deeply cultivated the samādhi of cessation and their outflows are exhausted, this is still merely granted as a provisional status.
As for Ānanda, he has only been occupied with extensive learning; how could his realization of the noble fruit be a true attainment? Thus, he is rebuked by saying, 'Even though you have attained...'"

[Cheng] asks: Zhengmo’s commentary on the nine concentrations states, "The first eight are accomplished during the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); the ninth is accomplished during the stage of the untainted noble ones (*ārya*). Now, it is said that one cannot attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) and become an Arhat [at those stages].

One should know that what is called the "untainted stage of the noble ones" there is merely a provisional concession for the time being. Does the current sub-commentary (*shu*), which also says, "The former belongs to a provisional concession; in reality, it has not yet been attained," agree with or differ from Master Jiao? Answer: Although the words appear similar, the meaning is actually different.

It seems that Zhengmo regards the ultimate end of the five abidings (*pañca-vihāra*) as the exhaustion of outflows; therefore, he deeply approves of Changshui’s view that the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) constitute the exhaustion of outflows, and there is no room for doubt. However, he fails to realize that if the ultimate end of the five abidings were considered the exhaustion of outflows, then only a Buddha alone [would possess it].

Only a person may truly bear this title; thus, among the Ten Epithets, the second is named *Arhat*. The character *ha* (呵) is a phonetic transcription of the Chinese character [for "to strike" or "to eliminate"]. Even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*Samyaksambodhi*) still possess the mark of birth and have not yet exhausted their outflows (*āsrava*);

how much less so those in the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*)? My current explanation is simply that as long as the deluded mind is not eliminated, one’s severance of afflictions cannot be considered true. If one can realize that the essence of deluded consciousness is fundamentally empty, then once severed, it is severed forever; such total extinction precisely corresponds to the Fourth Fruit (*Caturthaphala*). One who possesses extensive learning is capable of entering the stream of the Sages.

This is what is meant by "only removing the illness, not destroying the body"—this is where he differs from Master Jiao. [This concludes the section] summarizing the major headings to refute and dismantle the grasping at the deluded mind, thereby opening [the path].

The path of *śamatha* concludes. Second, revealing the true nature that has been overlooked so as to cause one to see the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*. (Zhengmo says: "The preceding section concerns the root of delusion;

it has already been refuted and is no longer used. This section concerns the root of truth; it must be employed in correct cultivation. The Buddha said: 'Sentient beings have overlooked this original luminosity. Therefore, the title of this section uses the character 'overlooked' (*yí*). Nevertheless, within the six sense faculties currently possessed, it pervades all.")

The Essential Nature of the Dharmas. Therefore, this section begins with the revelation of the eye-faculty and extends through the four sections to the seven elements. (3) One: Ānanda abandons the false and seeks the true; Two: The Tathāgata fully reveals the true essence; Three:
The assembled multitude collectively believe in the Treasury of Space. Regarding the first two [sections]: One: Compassionate grief, repentance, and self-reproach; Two:
Recognizing one's faults and requesting instruction. Regarding the first:
Having heard this, Ānanda wept again with deep sorrow. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Since I followed the Buddha to leave the household life and develop the aspiration for enlightenment, I have relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, constantly thinking to myself that there was no need for me to practice."
"I thought that the Tathāgata had bestowed upon me samādhi; I did not realize that body and mind are fundamentally not interchangeable. Thus, I have lost my original mind.
Although I have left home in body, my mind does not enter the Way; it is like a destitute son who abandons his father and flees."

"First, he was moved by compassion for his former delusions. Regarding "Ānanda, having heard this": it means that after hearing how the Tathāgata had completely refuted the three types of delusion, Ānanda was inwardly moved;
unconsciously, he wept and shed tears. Facing the chamber where the sexual act had occurred, he returned, prostrated himself, and wept;
hence the words "once again. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) says: "Generally, those who have attained deep realization subsequently give rise to compassion; or, upon realization..."

One may grieve because of long-standing suffering due to delusion, or one may grieve because of long-standing loss despite having realized the truth; this present instance is the grief arising from the realization of delusion.

As for prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, it is because when there is something further to seek or attain, one ought to perform a double prostration. As for kneeling for a long duration, it means sitting with both knees level upon the ground.
"Joining the palms" means to take refuge with single-minded devotion and address the Buddha, fully recounting one's delusions and omissions;
all that precedes this constitutes the ritual for seeking advancement. The two phrases beginning with "Since I" start from the very outset, revealing that one was mistaken from the very beginning.
The majestic virtue of the Buddha can ward off demonic obstacles; the spiritual power of the Buddha can assist in the realization of the fruit.

Because one has already received the Buddha’s compassionate love, one takes this as a reliance. To "constantly contemplate" means to think that since there is a Buddha, there is no need for me to practice, believing that his empowerment alone suffices.
Little do they realize that such contemplation is itself a deluded thought (*vikalpa*); without cultivation, [enlightenment] will never be attained.
There is no actual realization; this is precisely Ānanda’s delusion, being turned by that which is false. Regarding the phrase "about to regret having manifested and left behind the truth":
when he was reflecting, he thought that the Tathāgata’s compassionate grace had bestowed upon him the samādhi, whereby the Way would be accomplished naturally.
What need was there for his own cultivation? This was his retrospective remorse for past errors, as he did not realize [the truth].
The two characters "jiāngwèi" (will presume) are the inverse of the preceding "jiāngwèi. This means that although he presumes it to be so, he ultimately fails to realize it.
The phrase concerning body and mind precisely clarifies the meaning of this failure. It states that although the Buddha and Ānanda belong to the same celestial kinship, [they remain distinct].
Body and mind are each distinct. Because the body is distinct, food does not satisfy one another; because the mind is distinct, wisdom does not illuminate one another.

When it comes to cultivating the causes and realizing the fruits [of enlightenment], how could they possibly substitute for one another? This statement can only be spoken today. Regarding the loss of my original mind, there are two interpretations.
First, that body and mind do not substitute for one another; this refers to losing my hope for the Buddha’s compassionate grace.
The fundamental mind of the original nature. This meaning seems consistent with what precedes, because above there is the notion that [the Buddha] intends to bestow wisdom upon me.
Second, one cannot attain samādhi; one loses the fundamental mind of tranquil, eternal, wondrous clarity.
This meaning seems appropriate for what follows, because below there is the request for tranquil, eternal, wondrous clarity. If one follows the latter, it is like abandoning one's father and fleeing.

Regarding the analogy of the deceased, the latter interpretation is correct. Although the text below states that one must undergo the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) as retribution, this is because one has lost the fundamental mind.

Thus, while one accumulates learning, it results in fault; one possesses the outward appearance of having shaved one's hair and donned the dyed robes, yet lacks the reality of cultivating the causes and realizing the fruit.

Therefore, it is said: "Though the body has left the household life, the mind does not enter the Way. Because the mind does not enter the Way, one continues to revolve in the cycle of birth and death as before.

Therefore, the following passage clarifies this through analogies. The "poor son" is Ānanda himself, who uses it as a metaphor for having lost the merit of *samādhi* and being destitute of the wealth of *guṇa*.
Thus, he is likened to a pauper. Fortunately, because his Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) remains uninterrupted, he may still be called a "son.

"Abandoning his father" is a metaphor for losing the [awakened] mind; "fleeing away" is a metaphor for turning one's back on the Path. Because he turned his back on the Path and did not enter it, he has needlessly undergone the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
This is no different from those who have fled to other lands and roam about in the four directions.
Yet Ānanda took the Tathāgata as his elder brother and, moreover, relied upon him to leave the household life; nevertheless, their respective bodies and minds could not substitute for one another.

Therefore, the Zhengmo (Correct Pulse) says: "Observing this, one can understand that those who do not know how to practice cultivation but merely seek the Buddha's empowerment [will find themselves in such a state]."
Be on guard! My feelings of sorrow, regret, and self-reproach are now complete. Second, acknowledging my transgressions and requesting instruction:

"Today I have finally realized that although one may possess much learning, if one does not practice it, it is equal to having heard nothing at all. It is like a person who speaks of food but can never satisfy their hunger.
"World-Honored One, we are currently entangled by the two obstacles (āvaraṇa). This is truly because we did not know [the nature of] tranquility (*śamatha*)."
The nature of the constant mind. ○ I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for one who is destitute and exposed, will give rise to his wondrously luminous mind and open my eye of the Way.
I first realized that hearing is without effort; it is only today that I truly know this, having come to understand it through the error of my previous fall.

This means that Ānanda had previously relied on the Buddha and devoted himself exclusively to extensive learning, believing that by merely hearing and being able to recite the Dharma taught by the Buddha, he had achieved his goal.
This is so. When the incident involving Ḍākinī arose, he finally realized that speaking about a *zhang* does not equal practicing even a single *chi*.
That a little practice is superior to much learning; hence it is said: "Though one has heard much, if one does not practice, it is equal to not having heard at all.
Ānanda personally suffered the consequences of this error and spoke thus. Yet, fearing that those who delight in hearing might not easily reform their habits, [the text] continues below with...
To clarify this through analogy: it is said that hearing and being able to preach the flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma is like describing the taste of food;

if one does not practice, there will be no merit, and one will lose hope for the holy fruit—how is this any different from remaining unsatiated? As the Master Nāgārjuna states in his Commentary on the *Amitābha Sūtra*:

"What benefit do talk of cakes bring to a hungry stomach? This is precisely the same meaning. Now, Ānanda was renowned for his extensive learning, having maintained [the teachings] in memory throughout kalpas.
Miaoyan further said: "If one does not practice, it is the same as never having heard [the Dharma]. Therefore, Zhengmo stated:

"Observing this, those who merely rely on their learning while neglecting actual cultivation can likewise be alerted. "World-Honored One," [the text continues], "know that the obstacles arise from delusion.
The phrase "we and others" refers to oneself and one's own kind; that is, those present here in this very place.
To speak of their positions: thus it is said, "now. Regarding the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: First is the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

This refers to the grasping at a real self as imagined by the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), with the view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—that is, the view of a self-body—as its primary [affliction].
It consists of the one hundred and twenty-eight root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) and their derivative secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). All of these disturb and torment sentient beings.
The afflictions of the mind and body that are able to obstruct *nirvāṇa* are called the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Second, the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*):
this refers to the grasping at the reality of phenomena as they are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its primary factor.

Along with views, doubt, ignorance, craving, hatred, pride, and so forth, these obscure the non-perversion of the objects of knowledge and are able to obstruct *bodhi*; thus they are called the cognitive hindrances. Furthermore, the afflictions...

The afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are also called the hindrances of phenomena (*vastv-āvaraṇa*); they cause the continuous succession of birth and death. The cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are also called the hindrances of principle (*tattvāvaraṇa*);

they obstruct right knowledge and vision. The *Awakening of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "If one first eliminates the hindrances of phenomena but has not yet severed the hindrances of principle, one can only awaken to and enter the realm of the two vehicles.
If the hindrances of both phenomena and principle have been eternally severed and extinguished, then one enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of great perfect enlightenment. Furthermore,
The afflictions (*kleśa*) refer to the views and thoughts within the realm of desire (*dhātu*). "Views" refers to those arising from discrimination; "thoughts" refers to those arising spontaneously.
The objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) refer to the "dust-sands" of ignorance beyond the realm. "Dust-sands" means failing to realize that external objects are nothing but mind.

When encountering circumstances, one gives rise to attachment. Ignorance (*avidyā*) refers to the failure to realize that the nature of what is cultivated and realized is emptiness, thereby giving rise to craving according to one's capacity.

Furthermore, the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is precisely the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*); it arises based on this grasping at a self and is able to obstruct the principle of self-emptiness (*ātma-śūnyatā*).

The cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is precisely the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*); it arises based on this grasping at phenomena and is able to obstruct the principle of phenomenon-emptiness (*dharma-śūnyatā*). At this time, Ānanda...
It is difficult to realize the first fruit [of the path]. While the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) certainly remain present, the afflictions (*kleśa*) have likewise not been entirely abandoned;

moreover, since one has not realized that consciousness is empty, what is severed is not a true severance. Therefore, the Tathāgata rebuked them for failing to achieve the fruit of an ārya, while they themselves claimed to be entangled by the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).
Yet, obstacles do not arise of their own accord, nor does this entanglement occur without cause; thus, the following passage clarifies this.
The reason for this is truly due to a lack of sincerity. The quiescent and eternal nature of the mind is what they seek within their thoughts;

yet, having personally realized that deluded consciousness is flickering, subject to arising and ceasing, and impermanent, they assume there must exist a separate, quiescent and eternal nature of the mind.

It is precisely because they do not know this true nature that they instead identify with that deluded consciousness, clinging to a self and clinging to phenomena, thereby finding no way to liberation. Thus it is said:
This refers to being entangled by the two obstacles (āvaraṇa). ○ From "I only pray" downward is a request for instruction and revelation.

The intent is that because one is entangled by the two obstacles, there is no means of liberation; lacking the wealth of merit, one is separated from the house of nirvāṇa. Hence, they are called "poor" and "exposed.
Being poor, they lack the resources for cultivation and realization, and thus they seek compassion. Being exposed, they have no refuge within saṃsāra, and thus they seek pity.
"Development" (*fa*) means to awaken or bring forth. As for the "wondrously luminous mind," it cannot be bound by the two deaths, nor can it be obscured by the two hindrances.
One must certainly seek to develop this because, without attaining this mind, deluded consciousness is difficult to abandon;

there would be no way to cultivate *śamatha*, and no opportunity to realize *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. [Question: Previously, one was deluded regarding quiescence and permanence; now, one develops the wondrous luminosity. For what reason are delusion and development not mutually consistent?

[Question: Yes. [Answer: Abiding in delusion, it belongs to original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*); once it has arisen, it becomes initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*). Original enlightenment is solely quiescent and eternal; initial enlightenment is then wondrous and luminous. These are different designations for what is, in reality, only the one mind. "Opening" means opening up and penetrating.

"The eye of the Way" is the eye that perceives the Way, which is precisely initial enlightenment; it is still that aforementioned wondrously luminous mind. Although the wondrous luminosity has been activated, the path ahead remains distant.
If there is even the slightest bit of stagnation or obstruction, this means the eye of the Way has not yet been opened.
Therefore, he seeks to have it revealed. This is because one proceeds from initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) to ultimate awakening (*niṣṭhā-bodhi*).
After Ānanda has abandoned the false and sought the true, the two Tathāgatas most clearly manifest the essence of reality. Part One: [The Manifestation of Signs].
Part Two: [The Verbal Explication]. The first [section] has two parts: (1) the actual manifestation of signs; (2) the instruction to personally receive and realize them.
First: At that moment, the Tathāgata emitted a precious light from the svastika on his chest.

This light shone brilliantly in hundreds of thousands of colors, pervading all Buddha-worlds as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions simultaneously. It universally drenched all [beings] within the ten directions.
The crowns of all the Tathāgatas of the Jewel Lands revolved and descended upon Ānanda and the great assembly.

At first, the entire body appeared both secretly and manifestly. Upon the chest of the Tathāgata there was a mark, a right-turning cross known as the "Auspicious Sign of Ten Thousand Virtues" (*sahasra-guṇa-śrī-lakṣaṇa*).
This is because one who possesses this mark must necessarily be endowed with ten thousand virtues and is thus a person of auspiciousness. For this reason...

It is translated as "ten thousand. However, only the sound is translated and not the character, because the character represents the marks of the Buddha; to translate it would cause one to lose those marks.
Previously, light was emitted from the mouth, symbolizing that the natures of the six sense organs are each distinct and localized.

Now, it surges forth from before the chest, symbolizing the holistic essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Since all the nature-virtues, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are fully possessed therein, [it is for this reason that...]
It is represented by the *svastika* (卍). ○ Its light shines downward, secretly manifesting the full revelation of its great function.

Since its essence has already appeared, its function naturally becomes evident; therefore, it is represented by this radiant brilliance. "Radiant brilliance" (*huàngyù*) carries the meaning of luminous splendor.

The "hundreds of thousands of colors" symbolize the meaning of function transforming in accordance with conditions. Since function transforms in accordance with conditions, every dharma is fully manifested;

therefore, it is further symbolized by the pervasive permeation of the sensory realms. Regarding "pervasively irrigating" and below, this secretly reveals that what is above corresponds with what is below.
Regarding "Jewel Realm" (*ratnakṣetra*): the *Mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Names) states that *kṣetra* is the correct pronunciation of *che-tuo-lo*.

This translates as "land" or "field," referring to the sphere of transformation of a single Buddha; thus, it still refers to a world-system of dust-motes. However, because it is a designation of honor for the Buddha, it is called a "Jewel Realm. As for "pouring down":
to universally pour [light] upon the Buddha’s crown signifies that this function manifests to harmonize with the Buddha-realm above. What is poured down is... [the text continues].
This refers to being of one and the same compassionate power as all Tathāgatas. "Revolve" (xuan) means to turn back and pour forth.
As for reaching Ānanda and the great assembly, it signifies that this function manifests not only by ascending to harmonize with the Buddha-realm, but also descends to accord with sentient beings;

this is what is meant by being of one and the same sorrowful longing as all sentient beings. Based on this, the nature of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna)— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
The entire body, its perfect penetration, and its supreme functions all manifest within this single ray of light. This concludes the section on the manifestation of signs.

Second, as for teaching through direct experience, he addressed Ānanda, saying: "I now establish the great Dharma banner for you, and shall likewise cause all sentient beings throughout the ten directions [to do so]."
One attains the wondrous, subtle, and esoteric mind that is pure and luminous by nature, and acquires the eye of purity.
This section of the meaning has two aspects: first, it points back to what has already been made manifest for direct realization; second, it permits future instruction through prior knowledge.
This section relies on the former meaning and should therefore be clarified first. Since the signs have already been manifested, the reason for speaking again is out of concern...

The esoteric is revealed yet not fully recommended, as it still employs the teachings of the Exoteric Vehicle. Thus, the entire substance of the *tathāgatagarbha* (the nature of the treasury) and its perfectly pervasive, supreme function constitute the Great Dharma.
When the nature of the treasury is revealed, deluded consciousness is crushed; when perfect penetration is established, deviant practices are extinguished.

Therefore, it is likened to a banner (*dhvaja*), for a banner possesses the meanings of being manifest, standing firm, crushing, and destroying. The flowing light from the *svastika* symbol is precisely intended to reveal this essence.
Therefore, it is called "establishing. Once the Dharma-banner has been established, its radiance will naturally spread;

however, that it must cause the dust-motes of the ten directions to be simultaneously and universally pervaded must signify something else. Thus it says, "and also cause the sentient beings of the ten directions...

(etc.). "Obtaining" refers to the nature of mind sought previously. The seven characters beginning with "wondrous" (*miao*) are alternative designations for the original and initial [nature], used when one is deluded.
To realize their identical substance is called "wondrous. This is a praise for the union of the nature and mind.

The "subtle and secret," "nature-purity," and "luminous mind" are each established as distinct names. "Nature" refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), which possesses no marks of movement, agitation, arising, or ceasing;

therefore, it is termed "subtle and secret"—this is the same meaning as the previously mentioned "quiescent and eternal. "Mind" refers to initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*), which possesses the function of internal brilliance and external illumination; therefore, it is termed "pure."
"Clarity" (*ming*) is precisely the meaning of the previously mentioned "wondrous clarity. Based upon this mind-nature, one gives rise to contemplative observation;
when the wisdom of observation manifests before one, one clearly perceives the mind-nature as the eye of purity—this is the meaning of the previously mentioned "eye of the Way" (*daoyan*).
Thus, Ānanda’s request for a single light is fully met. Fearing that he may still not understand, this is further explained with clarity to ensure he personally realizes it.
If one adopts the latter interpretation, the meaning extends to the passages concerning *śamatha* and *samādhi-dhyāna*.
As I now permit you to demonstrate the essence of *śamatha* so as to erect the great Dharma-banner, this encompasses the entire substance and function of the Three Tathāgata-garbhas;
it likewise permits the demonstration of *śamatha* throughout the ten directions and so forth.

The Path. By means of the subtle, secret, pure, and luminous, one immediately encompasses that which is near within the faculties and reaches far to the wondrous *tathatā* (suchness) nature of the myriad dharmas.
One who has attained the pure eye is permitted to be shown *samādhi* and *dhyāna*. Within *samādhi*, one enters the perfection from the faculties;
within *dhyāna*, one flows into the center of the centers—both are the pure eye. The Buddha’s voice is perfectly wondrous, or...
Whether leading from the front or standing behind, a single drop of ink-water forms two dragons; this is indeed possible.

Having concluded the section on the manifestation of signs through esoteric revelation, the second part concerns the manifestation through verbal expression. First, pointing to the true mind according to the capacities of the faculties.

In the second assembly, the four categories [of phenomena] are integrated to return to the nature of the Treasury; in the third, the seven greatnesses are harmonized to sweep away emotional attachments and conceptual reckonings. First, as for "pointing to the mind through the faculties":

this is because the most extraordinary point of this sutra lies entirely in its rejection of the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) and its non-employment thereof, instead taking the nature of the faculties (*indriya-svabhāva*) as the causal mind. This is truly because the employment of consciousness versus the employment of the faculties is the very basis for the distinction between the provisional and the ultimate teachings.

As it is said: "To take the arising-and-ceasing [mind] as the causal mind is like steaming sand to make rice; to take the non-arising-and-non-ceasing [nature] as the causal mind is like relying on gold to fashion vessels. Now, since Ānanda seeks unexcelled bodhi, the Buddha first points to the faculties to direct him toward it.

If one takes this as the causal mind, then the fruition stage of perfect accomplishment can be hoped for. Second: first, revealing the true by means of the delusory; second, extracting the true from within the delusory.
First (because the nature within the faculties is its very substance, which is the *ālayavijñāna*. It is a fusion of the true and the false, not pure truth alone.

Since Ānanda was urgently seeking to abandon the false to find the true, and because at the stage of an ordinary being there is no separate, purely true mind to point toward—if one had first said that the false exists, he might have feared to acknowledge it; thus, for the time being, the false is left in place, merely to reveal that this [nature] is the true).
Ten: 1. Revealing that seeing is the mind; 2. Revealing that seeing is immovable; 3. Revealing that seeing is indestructible; 4. Revealing that seeing is non-forgetting.
5. Revealing that seeing has no source from which it returns; 6. Revealing that seeing is not intermingled; 7. Revealing that seeing is unimpeded; 8. Revealing that seeing is indivisible; 9.

Although they are all equally one refined spirit, among the stations of sentient beings, nothing is more convenient for apprehension than the seeing-nature within the eyes. Therefore, the revelation proceeds solely from this; the others may be understood by analogy. Three. One: Taking an example to introduce [the subject].

First, the introduction; second, the formal presentation and analysis of the view; third, the conclusion revealing that this is the mind.
