Third, the manifestation that seeing is not extinguished, in four parts: first, the assembly, having attained awakening through causes, requests further instruction; second, King Bimbisāra, harboring doubts regarding cessation, seeks a definitive resolution;
third, the Tathāgata universally manifests the teaching for them; fourth, the king and others leap for joy in celebration. First:
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, felt their bodies and minds become serene.

They reflected that since beginningless time they had lost their original mind, mistakenly identifying with the discriminating reflections of conditioned objects. Today they have attained awakening, like a child who has lost its mother suddenly encountering her again.
With palms joined, they prostrated to the Buddha, wishing to hear the Tathāgata reveal the truth and falsehood regarding body and mind.
The illusory manifestation before one’s eyes reveals both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing as two aspects of the luminous nature.

At first, because of this awakening, there was a sense of joy and relief. Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard this instruction on the mind and further hearing this teaching on immovability, were instantly freed from the alarm caused by the name "non-mind" and the fear that nothing remained beyond this.

Therefore it is said, "body and mind are serene (*tai-ran*). "Serene" means peaceful and relaxed. This refers to the state where, because the inner mind is at peace, the outward appearance is also relaxed;

this is what is meant by "celebrating the fulfillment of one's entire life. Regarding "recalling from no-beginning": one recalls the past form as it is now, looking back to the very beginning until its origin cannot be fathomed;
hence it is called "recalling from no-beginning. The originally existing [nature] becomes obscured and transformed into...
The *ālayavijñāna*, though capable of generating all conditions, is itself beyond the reach of those conditions; thus it is said that one has "lost the original mind.
Internally wavering and externally rushing about, one takes this state of turbid confusion as the nature of the mind; thus it is said that one "falsely recognizes the objects of conditions.

These "objects of conditions" refer to the consciousnesses of the six sense bases. To speak of "discrimination" is to describe their function; to speak of "reflected phenomena" is to manifest their characteristics. Today, [this is] opened...

The awakened one awakens to the realization that the nature of the mind is its substance, which is immovable; thus the Dharma-body is reconnected and the life of wisdom is further extended. Therefore it is said:
"Like a child who has lost its milk suddenly encounters a compassionate mother. This conversely reveals that losing the original mind is like turning one's back on the mother and losing the milk;
falsely identifying with conditioned objects is like having one's life hanging by a thread. When the present and the past are contrasted, what joy could be greater than this?

The previous statement that "body and mind are at ease" refers to this. ○ Joining the palms below, the formal ritual and the hope for benefit, as well as the request to hear [the teaching], are not the words of the interlocutor;
rather, they are the scribe’s depiction of his intent. This is because, within the preceding section, the principle was easy to understand:

while the objects moved, the nature of seeing remained unmoving. As for the shaking of the head, the turning of the body, and the shifting of the mind—these were likewise [instances where the seeing-nature did not move].
However, the meaning of "one moves and one does not move" is difficult to distinguish. Therefore, he joined his palms and prostrated to the Buddha,
intending that the Tathāgata might reveal why this mind is true and real, and reveal why this body is delusory and empty,

This means that what is new again passes away, and having passed away, it becomes new once more. Since this is so for a single thought-moment, it is so for every successive thought-moment;
therefore, it is said to be "non-abiding. Because of this non-abiding, things undergo transformation and become new in an instant. Thus it is said: "Like fire turning into ash, the ash has no..."
It is constantly ash. In an instant it transforms from old to new; therefore, it is said that it gradually "wastes away and perishes" (*xiāoyǐn*).

This means that because it wastes away and perishes, the old ash is revealed and new fire appears. "To perish" (*máng*) also carries the sense of "to waste away. It is precisely because of this perishing that it is renewed, and because of this renewal that it perishes again.
Because there is no place of ultimate rest, it is said that "perishing and passing away never cease. As it is with the present, so it shall be for the future;
therefore, one must decisively know that this body is destined to be extinguished. The Zhengmo (Correct Pulse) states: "These few words alone are sufficient to awaken the mind to impermanence.

It will not be long before you see this comparison with the time of its full flourishing.

"Within a single thought-moment (*citta-ekakṣaṇa*), there are ninety *kṣaṇas*, and each *kṣaṇa* contains nine hundred instances of arising and ceasing. From this, one knows that a *kṣaṇa* is still contained within a thought.
[In the] middle: Since there is change in every *kṣaṇa*, not even for a single moment can anything remain stationary.

Since nothing remains stationary from moment to moment, it is verified that in the end, all things are impermanent. Therefore, one knows that this body of mine will ultimately undergo transformation and extinction.
Having thus concluded the demonstration that this body is illusory, [the text] next demonstrates the nature of this mind.
The Reality has two parts: first, the presentation through questions and answers; second, the manifestation by means of an illustrative event. Regarding the first:
The Buddha said to the Great King, "You see that transformations and changes ceaselessly occur; you realize and know your own extinction.
At the moment of that extinction, do you know that within your body there is something that does not perish? King Prasenajit joined his palms and said to the Buddha, "I truly do not..."
[The King] said, "I understand. The Buddha said, "I shall now demonstrate to you the nature of non-arising and non-extinction.
First, he restates the realization to provide the basis for his inquiry. The Buddha addressed the Great King:

"Because I wish to manifest the true nature of non-arising and non-extinction within this very mind, I take up what you have realized—that seeing change is knowing extinction—and use it as the starting point for my question."
That which does not perish within perishing is what the Righteous King was deluded about; his inquiry served as the catalyst for his awakening.

○ From "Pāsa" [the Persian] downward, they held their hearts with sincerity in response. King Nimi, fearing that [all things] were subject to annihilation, suddenly received the question regarding non-perishing and urgently sought its explanation.
Therefore, he joined his palms, held his heart with sincerity, and said: "That I truly do not know is no mere pretense of humility. If...
If one truly knows this, one will naturally not be deluded by the view of annihilation. The Buddha’s words below grant permission to demonstrate non-extinction:
"Since you do not know this, I shall now, within this very body subject to birth and death, reveal to you its nature of non-birth and non-extinction."

Second, manifesting [the truth] by means of an analogy, which has two parts: first, citing and recounting the observation of the river; second, using the water as an example to reveal the seeing. Regarding the first:

"Great King, at what age did you see the Ganges River? The King replied: "When I was three years old, my compassionate mother took me to visit the deity Jīva, and we passed by this stream. At that time, I immediately knew it was the waters of the Ganges."
The question regarding "at what time one sees water" intends to demonstrate that the vision of childhood and the vision of old age are not subject to change.
The answer, "one knows it at three years of age," precisely demonstrates that the nature [of the mind] at the age of a crawling child is already identical to its nature at the time of old age.
The correct Sanskrit pronunciation of Gaṅgā is *Gaṅgā*; this is translated as "Coming from Heaven. This is because—
This water flows from Lake Anavatapta at the summit of the Snowy Mountains; because its source is the highest, it is described as such.
*Ti bao* (提抱) means "to carry," and *zhao li* (朝禮) means "to pay court. *Jīva* is translated here as "Long Life"; according to the local custom, people sacrifice to it to pray for longevity.
Because the compassionate mother carried her son to pay court to this [deity], these two examples illustrate the manifestation of the two [aspects].
First, a preliminary discussion on the water used as the analogy; second, the actual manifestation of the vision being illustrated. Regarding the first:
The Buddha said, "Great King, it is as you have stated: at twenty years of age one declines from the state of ten years, and so on until sixty."
The sun, moon, years, and seasons shift and change from moment to moment. When you were three years old and saw this river, what was the water like when you reached the age of thirteen?
The King replied, "It was exactly as it was at age three, without any difference;
even now at sixty-two, there has been no change."

First, the statement "the body undergoes change" refers to the coarse analysis mentioned previously, such as at the age of twenty, based on the principle that there is one transformation every ten years.

The phrase "up to" (*naiji*) skips over three, four, five, or ten [decades] because it mentions sixty; thus, it cites the whole while omitting the remainder, which is why the number two is not mentioned.
The phrase "days, months, years, and seasons" refers to the subtle analysis mentioned previously, wherein even the shortest moments (*kṣaṇa*) do not remain still. This is "time."
This refers to the *kṣaṇa* (instant), as it is explained in reverse order from the year, month, and day. "Then you" and below provide an analogy by questioning the water in relation to the body.
From the age of three to thirteen, the inquiry is made approximately over a period of ten years. As for the question "What becomes of that water?":
since the body undergoes a transformation every ten years, the questioner asks whether the nature of the water also undergoes change within those ten years; thus, he inquires once more.
The King replied that there was no difference. To say "exactly as before, without difference" means simply that its moist nature remains unchanged and its azure color is the same as it was.
If one speaks in terms of the water's condition, there will naturally be variations of swelling and receding within ten years;
this applies even up to three, four, five, or ten years, and so on up to sixty-two.
I shall also answer you by saying that it remains unchanged over ten years. Second, [the Buddha] clarifies the vision being used as the analogy.
The Buddha said: "Now you yourself see your hair turning white and your face wrinkled; your face must certainly be more wrinkled than it was in your youth.
"In this present moment, as you look at this Ganges River, is there any difference between this vision and the vision you had when looking at the river as a child—any sign of aging?"
The King said, “No, World-Honored One.

The first citation concerns changes in the face; the preceding citation concerned the passage on the passage of years. This citation concerns the statement that the present and the past are distinct and different.
Based on what has been observed regarding the injuries sustained, it is concluded that the face must inevitably change.”
Thus, you have now asked about the nature of the face by comparing it across time—specifically, by contrasting its present state with that of childhood.
"Seeing" includes both the young and the aged; here, "aged" (*mào*) carries the meaning of senility rather than referring specifically to those ninety years old.
Since the face clearly differs between these two times, I do not yet know whether the seeing-nature that perceives the river also differs between these two periods. For this reason...
Childhood and old age are indeed different. [The Master] replied that they are not different, following the previous analogy of the unchanging nature of water.

He did so because he realized that the substance of the seeing-nature is identical; thus, he answered directly with "No. However, this applies only to the capacity for seeing throughout its beginning and end.
If one speaks in terms of the sense organ itself, then within those sixty years, there are certainly differences such as clarity and turbidity, or brightness and dullness.

(Question: In the section on "Immovability," it was already known that while the body moves, the nature remains immovable. How does this differ from the present case? Answer: Although it was previously known, it was merely a momentary awakening and illumination.

As for the actual presence of arising-and-ceasing versus non-arising-and-non-ceasing, there was truly no wisdom to distinguish them. Now, the Buddha has clearly revealed this through King Bimbisāra, so that what Ānanda and the others had previously awakened to and illuminated should naturally become even more luminous;
it is not as it was before. Having finished demonstrating the reality of this mind, the third part concludes by showing the two natures present before us. First, the formal conclusion.
[The Buddha] showed [this]. Second, the reprimand for the delusion of the wheel. First:
The Buddha said, "Great King, although your face has grown wrinkled, this essence of vision has never been wrinkled. That which is wrinkled is subject to change."
It does not wrinkle, nor does it change. That which changes is the cessation of sensation; that which does not change is fundamentally without birth or extinction.
"Wrinkling" refers to the countenance and is taken from the expression of distinct differences; "changing" refers to the passage of time and years and is taken from the description of transformation.

Yet, while the face wrinkles, the nature of the mind remains unwrinkled; the delusion of body and mind and the reality of the True Nature are clearly distinguished. Though there is wrinkling and changing—
The wrinkling and non-transformation of body and mind distinguish between the empty and the real. While transformation implies extinction, non-transformation implies non-extinction;
thus, the nature of arising and ceasing and the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing are each elucidated. The request of the assembly has been answered at this point.
Second, the two anomalies are censured for their deluded wandering.
"How can you undergo birth and death within this [body], yet still cite Makkhali Gosāla and others who claim that after the death of this body there is total annihilation?
The phrase "how can" is a term of reproach and wonder. Since [the body] possesses the nature of neither arising nor ceasing, one should rely upon it for cultivation and realization. Thus...

It transcends birth and death. Why do you not grasp this? Instead, you remain within bodies subject to arising and ceasing, willingly accepting your own cycle of birth and death and bringing about your own transmigration;

this is already an error. Yet you still cite those such as Makkhali Gosāla and other types of non-Buddhists who all claim that after the death of this body there is total annihilation—is this not an error upon an error? Truly, it is so.

The most extreme form of delusion is that of Makkhali Gosāla (translated here as "Not Seeing the Path"). This man claimed that sin and merit, as well as suffering and pleasure, are not obtained through action.

He shared the same school of nihilistic views (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) as Kātyāyana and others. Fearing that King Ajātaśatru might abandon those [other teachers] to follow him, the Buddha spoke of them interchangeably;
he stated that they were all identical, saying that for one who is completely extinguished, both body and nature perish.
"It perishes accordingly. In truth, this is not so; therefore, he rebuked him in this way. King Ajātaśatru’s doubts regarding annihilation were forever extinguished from this point on.
The Tathāgata had fully revealed the teaching, and the Four Heavenly Kings and others leaped for joy in celebration.

Upon hearing these words, the King came to believe that after death one abandons this life to transition to another. Together with the great assembly, he leaped for joy and experienced a state never before attained.
Although the initial hearing of the words and the resulting faith are understood through the preceding text, the point where the King truly gains mastery lies here.
The final two lines of this reprimand serve as a summary. For although King Bimbisāra did not originally seek the true mind, he was not delighted to hear that it is unchanging and indestructible;
and although he did not originally seek to transcend birth and death, he was not startled to hear that he would undergo birth and death.
It was only upon hearing the refusal of total annihilation and the revelation of a future world that his doubts were suddenly resolved.

To sever the doubt regarding the view of annihilationism, it is said: "I believe and know that after this life... and so forth. Passing from one birth and proceeding to another is precisely the "personality mark" (*pudgala-nimitta*) among the four marks;
because King Ajātaśatru was dwelling in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), he believed only in this. Regarding the phrase "Together with all," it means rejoicing with the multitude.
As for "the great assembly," this refers exclusively to the class of people centered on King Ajātaśatru—those situated within the realms of humans and devas who are attached to pleasure.
Fearing that birth and death would result in annihilation, he now realizes that because his faith is identical to the King’s, he cannot restrain the leaping in his body and the joy in his heart.
Previously, he believed that after death there was total emptiness; now he knows that after death there is a nature, and he can thus abandon this life to proceed to the next.

Therefore, it is said that he has attained what he never had before. (Question: The term "the great assembly" is broad in scope; why is it used here to refer specifically to those at the level of ordinary beings? Answer: For those of provisional or limited capacity, believing this would bring them joy, yet for them this would be a loss rather than a benefit.)

Nevertheless, it is not that he lacks joy; rather, he rejoices because this section is even more clearly elucidated than the preceding "Immovable" chapter. Since it is not a new realization, it is not explicitly described [as such].
According to the four meanings requested by Ānanda, this section precisely clarifies the meaning of permanence. This concludes the demonstration that the seeing-nature does not perish.

The fourth section clarifies that the seeing is not lost, consisting of two parts: first, Ānanda grasps this and doubts what preceded; second, the Tathāgata reveals that although there is perversion, the seeing is not lost. Regarding the first:
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated to the Buddha, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if this seeing..."
Upon hearing this, they will certainly not give rise to birth or extinction. Why, World-Honored One, do you say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of inversion?
We pray that You will arouse Your compassion to wash away our defilements.

First, regarding the protocol for rising from one’s seat: because this inquiry arises from a doubt concerning the Buddha’s words and is not an ordinary discourse, it is necessary to prostrate and kneel before making the request.
“World-Honored One,” [the disciple] says, pressing his hand down to stabilize the ground as he prepares to speak. “If it is like this” refers to what was previously stated.

While the previous section mentioned only what was seen, this section further includes what was heard; this is because, fundamentally, they constitute a single entity. Since that which was seen is neither born nor extinguished, so too is that which was heard.

Because the nature [of reality] can be explained by analogy, to say that it "certainly does not arise or perish" is precisely to rely upon the fixed words of the Buddha as a basis for raising doubts below.

○ The passage beginning with "How could... reverses the doubt regarding the previous statement. Its intent is to suggest that, according to what the Buddha has currently said, there should be nothing lost or omitted;
why then did the World-Honored One previously state that we have lost the true nature? Furthermore...
To reprimand them for acting with such perversity is something I do not understand. I pray that you will arouse [compassion] and seek Buddhahood to dispel my doubts.
"Arouse" means to initiate; it refers to the prayer that the Buddha will initiate a heart of compassion. A subtle doubt lingers in my thoughts, and defilements obstruct my mind.
If I am graced by your compassionate cleansing, I may perhaps attain the joy of non-extinction and emerge from the suffering of loss.
II. The two Tathāgatas manifest that there is no error in inversion. This has two parts: (1) clarifying through the combination of dharma and metaphor;
(2) universally revealing and instructing. The first [section] has two parts: (1) borrowing the arm as a metaphor; (2) applying it to the body. The first of these has three parts:
(1) lowering the arm as a metaphor for inversion; (2) raising the arm as a metaphor for correctness; (3) the metaphor of exchanging them without error.
First: At that moment, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm, pointing downward with his wheel-marked hand, and said to Ānanda:
"Do you now see my *mudrā* hand as upright or inverted? Ānanda replied: "To the sentient beings of the world, this is considered inverted."
I do not know who is upright and who is inverted.

Pointing downward with the arm hanging loose is a metaphor for turning away from the truth and pursuing delusion. Addressing Ānanda by name is intended to cause him to examine the Dharma in detail through this analogy.
*Mudrā* is translated here as "seal. The hand is called a seal because it can form seals according to various matters, thereby accomplishing [the purpose].
Furthermore, the destruction of evil spirits is achieved through the power of the inconceivable. Regarding the question as to whether this constitutes "correct" or "inverted":

this is intended to serve as a metaphor for the body of the Perfectly Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) and the body that is inverted by nature. The answer states that worldly sentient beings regard this as inverted;
this refers to the gateway of manifested transformation. Because they oppose the truth and pursue delusion, it is termed the "body inverted by nature."
Therefore, my not knowing who is upright and who is inverted reveals that the arm has no fixed characteristic; this serves as a metaphor for the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
For the body of inherent inversion is itself the body of the Perfectly Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), and the body of the Perfectly Enlightened One is itself the body of inherent inversion.
Although the text of this response here was spoken by Ānanda, it is nonetheless the Buddha’s intention expressed through his mouth as a metaphor.
Therefore, there is no impediment to this interpretation. Second, holding the arms upright serves as the primary metaphor.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people in the world consider this to be inverted, then what do people in the world take to be upright?"
Ānanda said, "If the Tathāgata raises his arm—his hand as soft as *tūla* cotton—and points it toward the sky, that is called 'correct.
Since the Buddha’s intention is to establish the gateway of transformation while heading away from the truth and pursuing delusion, which he calls the inversion of nature, he now asks:

regarding this gateway of transformation, what further thing can be called 'Perfectly Complete Knowledge' (*samyak-saṃbuddha*)? Therefore, he continues to ask within the context of the metaphor: 'If...'"

Worldly people consider this to be inverted; yet, what do worldly people take to be correct? The answer is that raising one’s arm upward to point is a metaphor for returning from delusion to the True.

This "returning from delusion to the True" is described, from the perspective of the gate of establishing transformation, as the Body of Universal Knowledge (Samantabhadra-jñāna-kāya). Therefore, it is designated by the metaphor of "correct."
Regarding the metaphor of the three phases being exchanged without error:

the Buddha immediately raised his arm and addressed Ānanda, saying, "If this inversion were to exchange its head and tail"—the Buddha’s raising of his arm serves as a metaphor for the gateway of transformation and manifestation, wherein there is the matter of returning to the truth by reversing delusion. If this...
This refers to pointing upward and holding it upright as the "correct" state.
The meaning is that if this upward orientation is considered correct, then what is called "inverted" is nothing more than exchanging the head of the hand—the top—and the base of the arm—the bottom.
How could there be anything else called "inverted" apart from the correct arm? Using this as a metaphor illustrates the establishment of transformation.

If one takes "turning back from delusion to return to truth" as *samyak-saṃbuddha* (Perfect Universal Knowledge), then what is called "the inversion of nature" is nothing more than deviating from truth and pursuing delusion, with truth and delusion intermingling.

How could there be such a thing as an "inversion of nature" existing apart from *samyak-saṃbuddha*? Thus, delusion is not outside of truth; it is because of the clinging to delusion that [truth] is said to be lost.
"Truth is the very basis of inversion. Because it turns its back on truth, it is called 'inversion.
One who understands this analogy will naturally not harbor doubts regarding what is termed 'loss' or being 'reproached with inverted speech. The illustration by means of the arm is concluded."
Second, regarding the body, there are two ways of synthesizing it: first, a general synthesis; second, a specific synthesis.

Regarding the first: when ordinary people of the world look at you with single-minded attention, they will realize that your body may be compared to and illuminated by the pure *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas.
"One-and-a-half times" means two-thirds more; it is equivalent to saying "one additional part. It is said that when held upright it is "correct," and when hanging down it is "inverted.
Most people in the world view things in this manner with one additional part, as if it were something to be relied upon.
If you take this as an example, then you will know that your defiled physical body and those of all Tathāgatas—[are not the same].

The pure Dharma-body is what is referred to as "inverted" or "correct. These designations do not go beyond using analogies to manifest the forms and clarifying the meaning by contrasting the contravention of truth and the pursuit of delusion with the reversal of delusion and the return to truth. How could there truly be such things as "correct" or "inverted"?
Second, the specific synthesis:
The body of the Tathāgata is called "Perfectly All-Knowing" (Samyaksaṃbuddha). Your bodies, by contrast, are designated as "inverted in nature.
As you observe your own bodies with discernment, where in the name of the Buddha-body is there anything to be called "inverted"? At that time—
Ānanda and the great assembly gazed at the Buddha with wide-open eyes, their pupils unblinking; they were unaware of where the inversion of body and mind lay.

Initially, the upright arm was used as a correct analogy: the Tathāgata’s body is the pure *dharmakāya*. If one uses Ānanda— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*

The body that is difficult to attain is manifested through its form by way of analogy; yet, when elucidated according to its underlying meaning, it is called the Body of Right Universal Knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha-kāya*).

This is because, by turning back from delusion and returning to the truth, one establishes right knowledge and vision to universally know all things—no different from that hand on the wheel-turning king’s arm pointing upward.
○ Your bodies below serve as an analogy for being inverted when the arms are hanging down. You, Ānanda, and...
These are the bodies of the multitudes. As long as they have not realized the pure Dharma-body, they all possess the defiled form-body (*rūpakāya*).
If one were to compare the body of the Tathāgata with these manifested forms and elucidate them according to their underlying meaning, they are termed "bodies of inverted nature.

This is because, by turning away from the Truth and pursuing the delusive, they have formed inverted views; they recognize the delusive while abandoning the Truth. It is like that hand of the wheel-turning [deity] pointing downward—there is none.

Different. ○ From "According to you" (*suǐ rǔ*) downwards, this is a metaphor for the interchangeability of characteristics without loss. The phrase "name and location" (*míngzì chù*) should be joined with the preceding as a single sentence.

The meaning is that while the analogies used to elucidate this may appear to have a correct order or an inverted one, in reality there is fundamentally no such distinction between correct and inverted.
If you do not believe this, examine it closely according to your own judgment: "This is your body; this is the Buddha’s body. As for why your body...
To speak of "inversion" is merely to provisionally establish a name by analogy with the Buddha-body; ultimately, where could it be designated as inversion?
It is because the Tathāgata clearly knows there is no such place that he intentionally poses this difficult question to cause [Ānanda] to awaken for himself.
"At that time" refers to the moment when the Tathāgata manifested the inquiry. Ānanda and the great assembly, receiving his instruction, contemplated with earnest attention.

Therefore, it is called "staring blankly" (*deng-meng*). "Staring" (*deng*) means gazing straight ahead; "blankly" (*meng*) means lacking clarity—meaning that after staring for a long time, one instead becomes dazed.

One who contemplates the Buddha first observes the Buddha’s body to seek the state of correctness. Because the correct and the inverted are in opposition, one seeks to recognize the inverted by means of the correct.
That the pupils of the eyes do not blink indicates that the state of correctness cannot be attained. Since the state of correctness cannot be attained, [the gaze remains fixed].

Looking back at one’s own body and mind, one does not know where the inversion lies; thus, it is understood that the Buddha-body and the birth-body are fundamentally free from both correctness and inversion.
Although they are termed "inverted," there is no error in this, for they are nothing more than the intermingling of the true and the false.
This is no different from the analogy of a golden arm, wheel, hand, and head being rearranged in various orders. The explanation through the union of principle and metaphor is complete.
Second, the universal revelation [of the truth] has three parts: first, showing by means of right view; second, rebuking for inverted attachments;
third, concluding with praise by means of a metaphor.
Regarding the first: the Buddha, giving rise to compassion and pitying Ānanda and the great assembly, uttered the ocean-tide voice to proclaim universally to those gathered together.
"O sons of good family, I have always said that all conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors and their motivations—
all objects of perception— are manifestations of the mind alone. Your bodies and your minds are both objects manifested within the wondrously luminous, true essence of the wondrous mind."

The initial passage sets forth the intent and issues the proclamation. "The Buddha gives rise to compassion" means he desires to bestow upon them the bliss of perfect universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and to extract them from the suffering of inherent perversion.
He gazes fixedly without blinking, appearing as if blind or as if deluded; thus, they are objects of pity. This applies not only to Ānanda but to the great assembly as well;
therefore, he includes them. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) states: "One who does not miss the proper time is called a sea tide."
Regarding "Sound": at this time, as Ānanda and the great assembly were precisely ready to be taught, the Buddha responded to that opportune moment.

Therefore, the meaning of the single sound universally pervading all those gathered in the assembly is proclaimed. Regarding "All wholesome [dharmas]" and below: this cites the teaching of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*). *Guǎngdìng* states:
"The 'Constantly Expounded' refers to Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana*. "Form" refers to the eleven [bases].

Regarding material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*): the "mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings (*citta-rāja*). As for the "conditions" that give rise to the mind, there are four conditions:

namely, the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). The arising of material form involves only two conditions, because it does not require an object-condition or an immediately preceding condition.
The "mental concomitants" (*caitta*) refer to the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) that follow the mind.

They are called "driving forces" (*niyojana*) because they compel [the mind]. All objects of cognition (*ālambana*) consist of twenty-four types of dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and six types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is because dissociated formations are also objects of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the six unconditioned phenomena are objects of wisdom (*jñāna*).
This is explained in detail in the *Vijñaptimātra-śata-dharma-śāstra*. Thus, they manifest through transformation.
The single word "mind" (*citta*), although it refers to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, points to the essence that is free from delusion and purely true.
When ignorance and non-awakening arise, the three subtle states suddenly emerge; with objective realms as conditions, the six coarse states vigorously manifest.

Therefore, it is said that "all is manifested by mind alone. One who performs this contemplation is said to possess right view. [The passage] beginning with "Your body... directly points to the finger to lead one to awakening. You—
"Body" refers directly to Ānanda’s body composed of the four great elements. "Your mind" refers directly to Ānanda’s mind consisting of the six consciousnesses.
Because all things are thus, there is nothing that is not so. That which has never been obscured is called "wondrously bright"; this is the illuminating function of the mind.
That which has never changed is called "true essence"; this is the quiescent substance of the mind. Quiescence and illumination are mutually integrated; [this is] the substance...
Because it functions without obstruction, it is collectively designated by the term "wondrous mind. According to the *Awakening of Faith*, this is the source of the one mind;

according to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is the one true dharma-realm. All phenomena are manifestations thereof. Ānanda’s own body and mind must likewise be objects manifested within this [dharma-realm].
This is the Tathāgata directly pointing out that Ānanda is none other than the very body and mind manifesting before him, thereby providing proof.
The fundamental substance of all dharmas constitutes right knowledge and right view. Having finished demonstrating right view, there follow two sections on the reprimand for inverted attachments:
first, the explanation through Dharma; second, clarification through analogy. The first section has two parts: first, contravening the truth while pursuing the delusive;
second, recognizing the delusive while neglecting the true. The first part [contravening the truth while pursuing the delusive]: [Text continues...]
"How is it that you have lost your original, wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind, and its bright, wondrous nature? You mistake the delusion within awakening for reality.

Through the obscuration of darkness, space arises; within the darkness of this empty space, the coagulation of obscurity forms matter. Matter becomes intermingled with false thoughts, and these conceptual appearances form the body."

The initial reprimand concerns the deviation from reality. The phrase "how can this be" is an expression of astonishment and reproach. "Neglecting" and so forth are all faults for which one is rebuked.
"Fundamentally wondrous" refers to the wondrous mind mentioned in the preceding section; it is fundamentally and inherently wondrous because it is not something acquired through cultivation.
"Perfect" (*yuan*) refers to the characteristic of pervasive integration and dynamic functioning. "Treasure" (*bao*) refers to the characteristic of the pure, firm, and substantial essence.
When functioning, it arises from the wondrous as clarity; thus it is called "wondrous clarity" (*miaoming*). This reveals that function is identical to essence.
Since the essence is itself wondrous within its clarity, it is called "clarity-wondrous" (*mingmiao*). This reveals that essence is identical to function.

Thus, while mind and nature may be temporarily distinguished as function and essence, they are also not distinct. Because their meanings are mutually integrated, their opening and closing are unimpeded; therefore, the Sūtra says:
In this context, the term "mind" (citta) may be mentioned alone, or "nature" (prakṛti) alone, or both "mind-nature" may be presented together.
When lecturing, establish the meaning according to the specific passage without being dogmatically attached to one interpretation. Recognize that within awakening there is delusion:

the aforementioned "awakened mind-nature" refers to the state of mind-nature at the time of awakening, while the subsequent "confused and agitated appearances" refer to the state of mind-nature at the time of delusion. Nevertheless, delusion arises depending upon the true, and confusion is born from awakening.
Therefore, this is delusion within awakening; if one does not fail to recognize it, then the false is immediately the true.

It is entirely deluded and entirely awakened precisely because of mistaken recognition, which is why one is forever at odds with the True and eternally separated from Awakening. [The passage] beginning with "Obscured and darkened" reproaches [the mind] for pursuing the false.
It says that the nature of the mind is fundamentally wondrous; how could it have been lost? Furthermore, being right in the midst of awakening, how could one suddenly...

Because of delusion, [the text] explains its origin by means of "dark obscurity as emptiness" and so forth. It begins with a single moment of deluded movement that obscures the fundamentally wondrous nature;
therefore, it is called "dark obscurity. This state is precisely the *ālayavijñāna*, because the time of dark obscurity is itself the time of the conjunction of the true and the false.
Next, from the *ālayavijñāna*, the "seeing-division" (*darśana-bhāga*) emerges. Regarding that which was originally non-existent...
Within the Dharma, one falsely constructs the appearance of emptiness, and thus it is called "emptiness. This refers to what was later stated:
"Due to delusive confusion, there is empty space. For emptiness is merely a state of inert vacuity and a characteristic of obscurity.

However, when the perceiving faculty does not maintain this characteristic of darkness but instead stubbornly clings to it as an object of perception, it then coagulates within the obscurity of emptiness to form the materiality of the world. Subsequently...

This refers to the statement that the world is established based upon space. Now, there are two kinds of worlds: first, the sentient (the subjective); second, the insentient environment (the objective). At this point, the three subtle states are fully present:
the *ālayavijñāna* is the aspect of karmic activity (*karma-lakṣaṇa*); the perceiving division (*darśana-bhāga*) is the aspect of transformation (*pravṛtti-lakṣaṇa*);

and the realm of space is the aspect of manifestation (*pratibhāsa-lakṣaṇa*). Below these are the six coarse states: form is that which is manifested by the aforementioned [aspects]; based on this as a condition, cognition arises.

Continuing with the two characteristics: it is therefore said that "form is mixed with false conceptualization. This means that within the form of objective realms, it is mixed with two kinds of false conceptualizing minds.
Regarding the characteristic of perception (*saṃjñā-lakṣaṇa*): one perceives those forms and grasps them by calculating names, thereby giving rise to karma.
Because this can induce future birth, it is said that "the characteristic of perception constitutes the body. At this point, the six coarse aspects are fully accomplished.

To take the body as being identical to the characteristics of suffering bound by karma is to reproach oneself for following delusion from the subtle toward the coarse, chasing after falsehoods without returning.
Thus ends the section on "contradicting the truth and pursuing delusion. Second is "recognizing delusion while abandoning the truth."
The aggregates of perception gather at the internal boundaries and waver; they rush outward in wild flight. One takes this state of confused turmoil as the nature of the mind.

Once deluded, one regards this as the mind and becomes firmly convinced that it resides within the physical body. Thus, one fails to realize that from the physical body outward—to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—all are objects within the wondrously luminous True Mind.
First, the recognition of delusion is clarified. The two phrases beginning with "gathering conditions" refer to the preceding seven consciousnesses.

Since there have already been internal and external distinctions regarding the characteristics of the body, the preceding seven evolving consciousnesses manifest upon the substance of the eighth consciousness.
The sixth consciousness gathers the reflected images of the objects perceived by the first five consciousnesses; its internal discrimination is termed "internal."
"Shaking. The first five consciousnesses pursue the five external objects; their galloping and unrestrained wandering is called "fleeing and running wild.

The seventh consciousness is not mentioned because it is subsumed under this meaning (taking the seventh consciousness as its own essence and function, internally relying on the eighth and externally borrowing from the six).

Because there is internal shaking and external fleeing with no moment of stillness or peace, it is called the "state of turbid agitation. Sentient beings do not realize this, and instead claim that there is a substantial entity.
For this reason, it is said that this constitutes the nature and mind. This is what is meant by "recognizing delusion within enlightenment.
Regarding the phrase "once deluded": "once" means just once. As for "fixed delusion," there is no one capable of liberating oneself from it.
It is said that sentient beings do not fail to become deluded; once deluded, they invariably claim [the mind] resides within.
There is no one capable of escaping this delusion, as Ānanda said: "All ten types of ordinary beings in the world alike maintain that the conscious mind dwells inside the body.
The physical body belongs to the primary retribution (*vipāka*), as well as to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth.
All these belong to the retributive environment (*pariṇata-niśraya*). These all manifest through the transformation of the wondrously luminous true mind according to conditions;

yet, because they are established in dependence upon that [mind], it is said that "they are all things within this. This is like sentient beings identifying the mind within their own bodies as the self.

This means that although it is capable of being vast and great, and possesses a substantial essence and function, one consequently fails to know the substance upon which the environment and its inhabitants universally rely—the originally vast mind. It is for this reason that one is said to have lost the fundamental wondrousness.
The teaching on the Dharma is concluded. Two analogies clarify this:
it is like setting aside a clear, vast ocean hundreds of thousands of miles across, and instead recognizing the substance of a single bubble as being the entire tide.
Exhausting the vastness of the oceans and seas—this is the virtue of the sea, which is used as a metaphor for the true mind being pervasive and pure.

Its measure of hundreds of thousands [of *qǐng*]—meaning hundreds of thousands of square leagues—is a metaphor for the true mind encompassing all phenomena. Because no other sea can equal it, it is called "Great. This serves as a metaphor.
The ocean of mind is not something that the ocean of consciousness can reach; because it is consistently lost, it is said to be "discarded.

This metaphor illustrates the deviation from the Truth, for one who deviates from the Truth necessarily pursues delusion; it does not illustrate the pursuit of delusion itself. A floating bubble on the water is a bubble;

it briefly possesses two meanings that can be used as a metaphor for the conscious mind: first, it appears temporarily based upon the ocean, which illustrates how the conscious mind depends upon both the True and the Delusive.
First, arising; second, the uncertainty of existence and non-existence. This is like the consciousness-mind, whose arising and ceasing never ceases.
Because it is consistently and erroneously grasped, it is called "merely recognizing. "The entire tide" refers to the full ebb and flow of the ocean tide.

Its boundless flooding can be understood as a metaphor for the wondrous functioning of the True Mind’s dependent origination. Since sentient beings merely recognize the delusory, they will inevitably rely upon discursive thought.

Grasping at objects of perception is regarded as the wondrous function of the true mind; thus it is said, "the eyes are its gateway. The vast ocean beyond the seas is that which only the sea itself can penetrate;
this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s ultimate awakened mind, which can only be secretly realized through fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi).

However, sentient beings, having already taken this deluded conceptualization and its objects of perception to be the wondrous functioning of the true mind, claim that by means of this very [delusion] they can attain Buddhahood;

therefore, it is said that they have "exhausted" [the truth]. This metaphor illustrates the recognition of the false; it does not illustrate the abandonment of the true, because the recognition of the false necessarily entails the abandonment of the true.
Having finished reprimanding them for their inverted attachments, the third section concludes with a summary and an exclamation based on the metaphor.
"You all are people who are doubly deluded. It is no different from my hanging down my hand. The Tathāgata calls you pitiable ones.
First, he uses a metaphor to reveal your inversion:
you violate the Truth by clinging to the false, yet you regard this as the wondrous function of the True Mind, even claiming—
That one can thereby attain Buddhahood is like abandoning the ocean to recognize a bubble as its essence; this is already delusion.
To then designate it as "the entire tide" and claim it exhausts the vast seas is to be deluded within delusion; thus it is called "a person doubled in delusion.
Because what is non-inverted is made inverted, and what is not an error is spoken of as an error, it is said: "It is like my hanging down my hand—there is no difference between them."
The final sentence concludes with an expression of pity. It says that if one possesses inversion or error, it is not even worth pitying;
rather, it is precisely because one lacks inversion yet establishes inversion—claiming what is not an error to be an error—that it is like reaching down a hand, and thus truly pitiable.

This shows that wishing for correctness is not difficult, for simply raising the hand is it; furthermore, returning to reality is easy, as there is nothing that is not non-delusion. Having heard the Buddha’s conclusion...

These words of praise should inspire deep reflection. (Question: "To manifest the True by means of the deluded has not yet been deeply understood; to suddenly point toward the source of Truth—will this not leave one as bewildered as gazing at the Milky Way? Answer: "The manifestation of seeing is fundamentally for the purpose of attaining harmony with the True.")

This is the Buddha’s intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). It was because Ānanda did not realize there was delusion that he was immediately shown its excellence, so that he might perceive and understand it.

According to the *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse), among the four meanings requested by Ānanda, this also suffices to precede the word "constant" (*nitya*). The previous section speaks in terms of the future, as in:
"reaching to the end of the future limit, ultimately never extinguished. This section speaks in terms of the past, as in: "from beginningless time, fundamentally..."
"There is nothing left behind. Since this refers exclusively to the vertical dimension, it undoubtedly belongs to the character "constant" (cháng).

This concludes the section on revealing that seeing is not lost. (Zhengmo says: "Returning" means "going away. The heading specifically highlights the sense of going, while the text also includes the sense of coming; thus, it reveals that there is neither going nor coming. Section Three: Ānanda Seeks Resolution Regarding What to Accept and What to Reject.
Part One: The Tathāgata Refutes and Reveals the Two Minds. Part Two: A Concluding Praise of His Own Realization.
The Wheel of Sinking. First:
Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s compassionate rescue and profound instruction, wept and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Although I have received such wondrous sounds from the Buddha and have awakened to the wondrous, luminous mind—the originally perfect and eternally abiding ground of the heart—yet my awakening..."
The Buddha manifested the sound of preaching the Dharma; we manifested our minds of discernment to look up to him in reverence.

Yet, having merely obtained this mind, we did not dare recognize it as our fundamental, original ground of the mind. We pray that the Buddha will take pity on us and proclaim his perfect voice to uproot our doubts and lead us back to the Unsurpassed Way.
At first, moved by compassion, he addressed the Buddha. Zhengmo says: "Compassionate rescue" means rescuing one from the drowning of inverted perceptions;

"profound instruction" means instructing one to fully comprehend the Perfectly All-Knowing One. There are two meanings to his shedding tears: first, being moved by the Buddha’s rescue and instruction such that his grief is deep and repayment difficult;
second, grieving for his own ignorance and delusion, as he has not yet resolved what to adopt and what to reject. From these two...

This is why Yi clasped his hands and addressed [the Buddha]. "I" refers to himself; "though" (*sui*) indicates a temporary concession, meaning he temporarily concedes that he has realized the true mind.
"Such wondrous sounds" (*ru shi miao yin*) refers to what was explained in the preceding section:

because this revelation in accordance with the nature (*xing*) is utterly different from past discourses, it is called "wondrous sounds. "Realization" (*wu*) means generating understanding according to the words, but it is not yet the ultimate truth.

[The Master] said: "Awakened. One can know from the phrase "I did not yet dare to recognize it" [found below] that this is so. "Wondrously luminous" (*miaoming*) and so forth refer to the true mind (*zhenshin*) indicated in the preceding section.

Above, it was called the "wondrously luminous true essence" (*miaoming zhenjing*); here it is simply called "wondrously luminous," for since function must have a substance, it need not be stated explicitly—it is already understood.
That which was "originally full and perfect" means that it is inherently and spontaneously endowed with all things, complete and lacking nothing.
This summarizes the meaning of the preceding section concerning how all phenomena manifest from the mind and how the Dharma resides within the mind.

Having heard this without error, yet forming erroneous views, one realizes that the fault lies in one's own explanation rather than in the teaching itself; therefore, it is called the "Ever-Abiding Ground of the Mind. Furthermore, the character *chang* (常) carries the sense of being difficult to apprehend.

Below, there is the "fear of abandoning" because one is reluctant to abandon that which is difficult to abandon. This intention refers to awakening to the Buddha’s present teaching; it means employing the presently active mind as the object of focus.

To abandon this focused mind—upon what could one rely for awakening? This is the meaning of the fear of abandoning. "Yun" (允) signifies sincerity. "Zhan-yang" (瞻仰) carries the sense of longing and devotion;
it means that out of such longing for the focused mind, one cannot bear to abandon it suddenly. This is the meaning of the difficulty of abandoning. In vain...
This refers to the ultimate distortion of meaning; that is, to have distortedly acquired this mind. "This mind" still points to the true mind.
Since it was previously stated that it is "originally perfect and complete," it is clearly known to be the fundamental ground of the mind.

Yet, the reason one still says "I do not yet dare to recognize it" is that recognizing this would necessarily entail abandoning that [the provisional mind], and there is a fear that if one later hears the Dharma and attains awakening, there would be nothing to rely upon. ○

I pray that the Buddha will descend; I seek the Buddha’s proclamation and instruction. This is because the deluded mind (*prapañca-citta*) is the root of birth and death, and I cannot suddenly abandon it;

yet the true mind (*tathatā-citta*), as the pure essence of the two fruits of enlightenment, I do not yet dare to identify with. Knowing myself to be ignorant and deluded, I therefore beseech the Buddha to look upon me with compassion.
Your perfect wheel of sound responds universally to all heights and depths; thus I seek the Buddha’s proclamation and instruction regarding this deluded mind.
That which is difficult to relinquish is the root of doubting the truth. Uproot and eliminate it; only then may you grasp the true mind and return to the Unsurpassed Way.
Ānanda sought a definitive resolution regarding what to adopt and what to abandon. Part Two: The Two Tathāgatas Refute and Reveal the Two Minds.
Section One: Refuting the Conditioned Mind as Having a Return. Section Two: Revealing the Nature of Vision as Having No Return. The first section has two parts.

First, the refutation of the object of perception (*ālambana-dharma*); second, the formal refutation of the perceiving mind (*ālambaka-citta*). Regarding the first, there are four parts: (1) a direct censure of that dharma;

(2) an indirect clarification through a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); (3) a formal elucidation through a similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*); and (4) a synthesis to awaken the student. As for the first: (Note from Zhengmo: "If one does not abandon the mind that perceives objects, since that mind is entirely devoted to the heavy dharmas, one must refute those dharmas;
once the dharmas are refuted, the perceiving mind will naturally abandon them. Regarding the first [of the four]: a direct censure of that dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind, this Dharma will also become a condition;

you have not attained the nature of the Dharma. Your words contain a profound sense of censure. The meaning is that I have repeatedly refuted and rejected [the use of] the conditioned mind, intending for it to be abandoned forever;
yet I did not expect that you would still listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind. This is truly a transgression.

This is indeed deeply pitiable. As for this teaching, since that which is able to hear belongs to the *pratyaya-citta* (the mind of conditions) and that which is heard belongs to the *pratyaya-viṣaya* (the objects of conditions), and since these are merely conditions, true wisdom is deluded by false conceptualization and suchness is obscured by names and marks;
therefore, it is said that "the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not attained. The nature of phenomena is the true nature of all dharmas. Because all [phenomena]...
This is because phenomena are manifested solely by the mind. Second, the dissimilar example serves as a negative illustration:
it is like a person pointing out the moon with their finger; that person, following the finger, should look at the moon.

Fearing that they might not yet be convinced by the refutation based on the failure to realize the *dharmatā*, [the author] first employs a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) to demonstrate it through contrast.
He states that the Tathāgata’s teaching was originally intended to reveal the nature of the mind (*cittaprakṛti*) and to instruct the wise.

It is like a person pointing out the moon to another with their finger: the upper character "person" (*jén*) symbolizes the Buddha; the "hand" symbolizes the teaching; the "moon" symbolizes the mind; and the lower character "person" symbolizes the listener.

The wise person says to the deluded one: "If you were truly wise, you would naturally be able to observe the mind according to the teaching, just as that person, because of the finger, ought to look at the moon.
This conversely demonstrates that Ānanda and the others were unable to do so, which sufficiently shows they had not attained the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
This is the third [part], the correct clarification through a similar analogy.
If one further regards the finger as the substance of the moon, this person not only loses the lunar disc but also loses the finger itself.
Why? Because they take the pointing finger to be the bright moon. Not only do they lose the finger, they also fail to recognize brightness and darkness. Why?
Because they take the very substance of the finger to be the nature of the moon’s brightness; thus, they confuse the two natures of brightness and darkness.

Because there is nothing to be fully understood, the heterologous example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) used by way of contrast may still leave one uncertain; therefore, he further clarifies it directly through a homologous example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

The text is divided into three sections. The first illustrates the delusion regarding the nature of the mind: it says that a foolish and deluded person, using the攀緣心 (*parikalpa-citta*, the攀緣心 or "clinging mind"), upon hearing the teaching...
This refers to awakening the mind. Suppose there were another person who looked at a finger and mistook it for the moon;

here, the "person" is a metaphor for the ignorant, clearly illustrating that Ānanda and others, in their delusion, are just like this. The passage beginning with "This person" below is a metaphor for being deluded regarding the essence of the teaching.
It states that such a deluded person not only fails to know the nature of the mind, but also fails to recognize the essence of the teaching, just as that person [mistook the finger for the moon].
One who points toward the moon not only loses sight of the lunar disk but also loses the finger itself;
here, "losing" refers entirely to a failure to understand the meaning. Why? In the analogy, one investigates the reason for losing the finger;

in the Dharma, one investigates the reason for being deluded regarding the teaching. Thus it is said that such ignorant and deluded people are called those who do not know the essence of the teaching.
Why is this so? Within the explanation, they take the teaching that expresses (*vācaka*) to be the mind that is expressed (*vācya*).
This is like a person who, when observing a finger pointing toward the moon, takes the finger used as the signifier to be the moon it signifies.
How could such a person understand the purpose of one who knows how to use the finger? One must know that the knower of the finger does not, in fact, [take] the finger [to be the moon].

It is for the sake of the moon. One who understands the teaching—how could they ever take the teaching itself as their core? How much more so does the following metaphor clarify that the two aspects are delusion:

brightness represents the aspect of the moon, which is a metaphor for the awakened spirit as the aspect of the mind; darkness represents the aspect of the finger, which is a metaphor for the insentient dust as the aspect of the teaching.
It says that such ignorant and deluded people not only fail to recognize the essence of the teaching, but furthermore—

The distinction between the conscious spirit and the insentient is like that person who mistakes a finger for the moon; not only do they lose sight of the finger, they likewise fail to recognize light and darkness.
Why, then, does the subsequent analogy inquire into and explain the reason for this failure to recognize light and darkness?
Within this Dharma, the inquiry and explanation concern the reason why such ignorant and deluded people do not recognize the distinction between the numinous and the insentient.

Why is it said that they do not recognize the numinous from the insentient? It is because, according to the teaching, the objective realm (dust) takes the form of the insentient, while the mind takes the form of numinous awareness.
Since these individuals take the substance of the teaching to be their own mind, the two characteristics of the numinous and the insentient are likewise [confused].
They cannot comprehend it. It is like those who, observing a finger as the moon, take the substance of the finger itself to be the luminous nature of the moon;
because they fail to discern the two natures of light and darkness, they not only fail to attain the Dharma-nature, but their extreme delusion and confusion become even more evident.
Fourth, the combined exhortation to awakening.
"You are also like this. Although these are words of conjunction, they carry a sense of admonition. The meaning is:
as I have said above, that which loses both the finger and the moon, and is obscured by both light and darkness—is this not you? Yet your minds and teachings are both...
The deluded spirit’s stubborn inability to discern is likewise so. You should fortunately awaken to this yourself; do not allow yourself to be ridiculed by the wise.

(The four preceding sections collectively constitute the refutation of the object-condition (*ālambana-dharma*). They need not be further subdivided; however, because the teachings and metaphors are so repetitive that they are difficult to explain, I have not grown weary of the detail and have analyzed them.
The refutation of the object-condition is now complete. Second, the formal refutation of the subject-consciousness (*ālambaka-citta*). Part Three: A Detailed Refutation of the Ear.

Consciousness. Second, briefly citing examples for the remaining five [consciousnesses]. Third, a general conclusion to refute [the argument]. Regarding the first [of these three], [it is noted that] because the mind that currently cherishes conditions and sounds cannot be abandoned abruptly, it must be refuted in detail.

This consists of two parts: first, refuting through a counter-objection based on their own tenets; second, clarifying through the application of dharma and analogy. Regarding the first [of these two]:
If you take this discriminative sound of my preaching the Dharma to be your own mind, then this mind ought to possess a discriminative nature even apart from the discriminative sounds.

Since its object of cognition (*ālambana*) is not the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), how could the subject that cognizes it be the true mind? I have spoken thus because I fear you might remain stubbornly attached to your views.
This is difficult. My intention is this: if you insist that you take the reflection of the sound of my teaching as your mind, then that mind must have a substantial nature.
Now, when this mind separates from the sound that was being discriminated, it ought to possess a distinct nature of discrimination in itself.
Yet, since we have already refuted this by examining the object, how can you so hastily forget it?
Second, the teaching and the analogy are combined for clarification.
It is like a traveler who stays overnight at an inn; having rested briefly, he departs and does not remain permanently. Yet the person in charge of the inn goes nowhere;
he is called the "master of the inn. This is also like that: if it were truly your mind, then it would have no place to go.
Proceeding, [the text asks]: "What is the nature of non-discrimination apart from sound?

The first analogy is explained as follows: the guest represents the mind that takes objects as its support (*ālambana-citta*); the roadside inn represents the objective realm (*ālambana-viṣaya*). The guest is not the master of the inn;

arriving by chance to take up temporary residence is called "staying overnight. This illustrates that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not the *dharmatā*. It is merely a momentary grasping of objects, relying [only] upon them.
This is an attachment. If a pavilion does not suit one’s fancy, one abandons it after staying for but a single night; this is to say that having stopped briefly, one departs immediately.
It is a metaphor for the conscious mind encountering sounds that are disagreeable: unable to endure them as objects of focus for long, they arise and then immediately perish.

That which never remains permanently—even if it is pleasing—is no different from a hometown; after three days or five, one must inevitably leave. This is a metaphor for the conscious mind, even though... [it may be favorable].
When one encounters sounds that are pleasing to the mind, yet once the journey has grown weary, the emotions shift with the circumstances; in the end, there comes a time of departure and cessation.
This is a common analogy, for the mind that conditions [objects] is exactly like this. The "person who manages the inn" refers to one who oversees a traveler’s lodging;
it serves as a metaphor for the true mind, which is able to establish all phenomena and is not like a transient guest. Therefore, it is entirely without [fixed location].
"Departure" serves as a metaphor for the true mind (*tathatā-citta*), which, unlike the conditioned mind (*pratyaya-citta*), is eternally abiding and indestructible.

Furthermore, because it has nowhere to go, it is called the "host of the pavilion. This serves as a metaphor for the true mind, which, being eternally abiding and indestructible, is termed the *dharmatā*.

This is a dissimilar analogy (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), because the conditioned mind is not like this. "This also," and so forth, is the application to the dharma (*dharma-saṃkrama*). "This" refers to the conditioned mind.
Whether it be subject to arising and ceasing, or whether it be eternally abiding, it should likewise be similar in this regard between the guest and the host. This is the general synthesis.
As for the specific synthesis following "If [the fruit] were real": the meaning is that if the fruit were truly your own mind, then it should be like the innkeeper, having nowhere to go.
This synthesizes the dissimilar example. The section beginning with "How could... synthesizes the similar example, based on the preceding refutation of its lack of substantiality.
[The Buddha] said: "Just as you now listen to my Dharma, this is a discrimination that exists because of sound;
apart from sound, it has no intrinsic nature. Ānanda already knows this, and therefore he raises an objection based on this point. His intention is to ask:
'If it is not like the host, why is it instead like a guest who stays for a while and then departs? As I previously stated, apart from sound there is no discrimination."
It is clear, then, that their nature is not real. The detailed refutation of the ear-consciousness is concluded. Second, a brief application of this principle to the remaining five [consciousnesses]:

(The present grasping of sound as an object has already been refuted in detail. Although the remaining five have not yet arisen as seeds while one is currently grasping them, they are still in a state of dormancy; because they are dormant, they must be refuted by analogy. Because they have not yet arisen, they are mentioned only briefly.)
This is not merely a matter of the discriminating mind of sound discriminating my appearance; it is the non-discriminative nature that is free from all marks of form (*rūpa*).
Thus, even until discrimination is entirely absent, there is neither form nor emptiness. Yet those such as Kauśika mistake this for the "Dark Ultimate" (*tamas-tattva*).
The nature of non-discrimination exists apart from the conditions of all phenomena;
this is a statement that cites the preceding as an illustration. That is to say, it is already known that the discriminating mind of sound lacks an intrinsic nature apart from sound.
How much more so is this true for the discriminating mind that conceives of a self or a physical form, which lacks discrimination apart from various material characteristics (*rūpa*).
A distinct nature is likewise merely like a guest who stays for a short time; it is not the host of the pavilion.

This is reiterated by using the two preceding cases as examples. Since both types of mind are thus, one may infer that the minds which discriminate fragrance, flavor, touch, and phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature apart from these four, following the same logic. To speak more concisely: ultimately, discrimination is entirely non-existent.

The internal maintenance of a mind that is secluded and tranquil is also like this. "To be entirely without discrimination" means that the six consciousnesses do not take the six sense-objects as their conditions;
there remains only the solitary internal maintenance within meditative concentration, which is secluded and tranquil. What is now called "neither form nor emptiness" refers to this.

Because it has already departed from the coarse characteristics of the six sense-objects, it is said to be "not form"; yet because there still exists the subtle realm of seclusion and tranquility, it is not emptiness.
It is said that this is not "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*). *Kosala*—here translated as "cowshed"—is an alternative designation for Makkhali Gosāla.

Guanding (Guǎndìng) maintains that it refers to his birthplace; Zhengmài (Zhèngmài) maintains that it is the name of his mother. I, the fool, believe that since it is an alternative designation, the interpretation of it being his birthplace is correct.
This follows the precedent in this region of establishing names based on one's place of birth, such as the case of [the term] "Nai" (Nǎi). This points to their shared views. As...
The Sāṃkhya teachers and others, by means of their power of meditative concentration, are able to penetrate beyond eighty thousand kalpas;

yet beyond that, everything becomes dark and indistinguishable, which they establish as *avyakta* (the unmanifest). Furthermore, because they claim this is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, they designate it as "Truth" (*satya*).

One must understand that this state of being dark and indistinguishable is precisely equivalent to that which is neither form nor emptiness. Even such a profound and secluded realm remains a subtle object of cognition (*dharmāyatana*). Because...
Because they do not understand this false establishment, it is called "obscuration" (*mèiwéi*). This false establishment and obscuration are identical to the mind that internally guards [the breath];
they are still subtle discriminations. Even when separated from the dharmas as objects, they remain without intrinsic nature.

They are no different from the discriminating mind regarding sounds and so forth. (According to the *Zhèngmò xuánshì*, the consciousness-mind briefly has five kinds of superior and wholesome functions: first, taking the physical marks of the Buddha as its object.)

First, the mind that perceives the Buddha’s physical marks; second, the mind that takes the Buddha’s verbal teachings as its object; third, the mind that hears the Dharma and attains realization; fourth, the mind that ceases distraction and enters stillness; and fifth, the mind that attains verification beyond the realms. I, the fool, say that these five kinds of mind have been completely shattered from the beginning of the "Principal Teaching" (zhengzong) up to this point.

As Ānanda previously said: "When I saw the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, my heart gave rise to love and attachment. The Tathāgata rebuked him, saying: "Because this perception is not true, there is cyclic existence.

And here [in the current text], it says: "To discriminate my appearance is to be detached from form and devoid of nature. Both of these passages shatter the first mind—that which takes the Buddha’s physical marks as its object. Furthermore, the previous text says: "As you now listen to my Dharma, this is discrimination arising because of sound. This shatters the second mind—that which takes the Buddha’s voice as its object.

"Sound and teaching are the mind. Furthermore, Ānanda said, "I perceive the Buddha’s present preaching of the Dharma with my conditioned mind," and when the Tathāgata showed him that listening to the Dharma with a conditioned mind means this very Dharma is also a condition—this refutes the third [delusion]: the mind that perceives and understands through hearing the Dharma. Furthermore, it was previously stated:

"Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and internally maintain a state of profound stillness, it would still be a mere shadow of the discrimination of dharma-dusts. Here, it says that discrimination is entirely absent and that by departing from the conditions of all dharmas, one possesses a nature free of discrimination—this refutes the fourth [delusion]: the mind that enters stillness by ceasing distraction. Furthermore, it was previously stated:

"Although you have now attained the nine successive meditative concentrations (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), you have not yet attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) to become an Arhat"—this has already refuted the fifth [delusion]: the mind that seeks realization outside the realms.

This is because all birth and death since beginningless time have arisen from mistakenly identifying with this mind. If one were merely to destroy its inferior and evil aspects, I fear its superior and wholesome aspects might still remain. Now that its superior and wholesome aspects have been destroyed, the inferior and evil mind will naturally know for itself that it is no longer fit for use.
This concludes the five remaining sections of the "Brief Examples. Third, the general conclusion of the refutation.
Thus, the natures of your minds each have their respective places of return; how, then, can they be the master?

Here, "the nature of your mind" refers collectively to the six types of consciousness that depend on conditions. Because they lack inherent nature apart from sensory objects, it is said that "each has its respective place of return.
Since this clarifies their status as guests, one asks, "How can they be the master? As they are not the master, you must urgently abandon them.
This section serves, for the time being, to uproot the seeds of doubt for Ānanda and others; it is only at the end that he is led to the Unsurpassed Way.

The first part, "The Refutation of the Returnable Nature of the Conditioned Mind," concludes here. Second, the manifestation of the nature of seeing as being without return. This has two sub-sections: first, Ānanda requests instruction on that which is without return;
second, the Tathāgata provides a detailed demonstration thereof. The first [sub-section].
Ānanda said, "If my mind-nature each has something to which it returns, then why does the Tathāgata say that the wondrous, luminous, original mind has nothing to return to?
I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain this for me."

The single character "ruò" (若) implies a lack of self-confidence. It suggests that if one follows the Buddha’s teaching that these six kinds of mind each have something to which they return, then since these [six] have a point of return, the wondrously bright primordial mind spoken of by the Tathāgata prior to this must itself be without a return.
Yet, not knowing how it is without a return, one's progress is uncertain and one retreats.
If one abandons [the teaching] without resolution, wisdom will fall between the two pillars like a sheep butting against a fence.

If it were not for the Tathāgata’s compassionate proclamation, by what means could one be liberated? Therefore, it says, "Only deign to... and so forth. Second, the Tathāgata clearly reveals [the truth]. Third.

First, the demonstration through suppression and affirmation; second, the dialectical analysis of subject and object; third, the exhortation to discern what to adopt and what to reject. Regarding the first:
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "Furthermore, as for your seeing me—this clarity of the faculty of sight—although this seeing is not the wondrous, supremely clear mind,"
It is like a second moon; it is not the reflection of the moon. You should listen attentively, for I shall now show you the ground where there is nothing to be returned.
First, I shall briefly provide a demonstration through suppression and exaltation. When the Buddha addressed Ānanda, he responded to his earnest plea for compassion. Furthermore, as for what you see—
We have accepted your request for this discourse. The Tathāgata’s intention is this:
since you have sought my compassion, I need not lead you through a long and winding path; let us simply speak according to your own perspective.
