End. Third, the ultimate exhaustion of deluded sentiments. (To speak of "is" is the opposite of "is not. Since the former was taken as creating prior characteristics, "non-existence" was manifested to show there is no "is. Yet, if one further clings to "non-existence" because of that non-existence, this is still deluded sentiment;

it has not yet been fully understood. Therefore, this simultaneously refutes the characteristic of "non-is" to preemptively block all such doubts. Indeed, when both "is" and "is not" are forgotten, and the mind that forgets is also forgotten, only then does the wondrous nature of the unified, interpenetrating essence manifest before one. Fourth.
1. Stepping upon the former [point] to press down and determine that it is not so; 2. Teaching by means of an object to clarify that it is not;
3. Ānanda responding that it is neither so nor not so; 4. The Tathāgata confirming what he has said. First:
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda: "As you have said, there is no visual essence that exists apart from all objects with a separate intrinsic nature;
therefore, among those objects you point to, none of them possesses this faculty of seeing."
What you have said repeats the previous statement that there is no seeing within the elephant; this is because that which cannot be extracted is considered non-existent.
Thus, in the following passage, you rely on this non-existence to establish definitively that there is no such thing as "seeing.

[Question: Why do you not rely on the statement that there is no seeing outside the elephant? [Answer: The absence of seeing outside the elephant might still exist within the elephant; one cannot determine with certainty that it is necessarily absent. It is only when it is certain that there is no seeing even within the elephant that one can establish it definitively.
Second, I shall clarify the error by teaching you through the objects themselves.
Now I tell you again: you and the Tathāgata are sitting in the Jeta Grove; look further at the groves and gardens, even up to the sun and moon.
The various elephants are distinct; surely the essence of seeing cannot be pointed out by you. You have again investigated which among these objects is not seeing.
To eliminate doubts regarding what is not seeing, he speaks again: "You and the Tathāgata shall together instruct one another to observe further."

"Regarding 'the former objects': 'Garden' (*yuan*) is a synonym for a park or grove; in meaning, it encompasses canals, streams, and palaces. The phrase 'and so forth' (*zhì yú*) abbreviates the Ganges River and the rest.

These are simply the previously listed internal and external, distant and near objects. Since there is no such seeing either within the elephant or outside the elephant, it is said that 'it must not exist,' and so on.
This means that the essence of seeing (*jian-jing*) must certainly not be something that receives what you have pointed out and attached to."
To depart from this [view] and assume that it is not a state necessarily reached by insentient things would be a mistake; therefore, he further instructed him to clarify what constitutes "non-seeing.
Ānanda responded that there was nothing that was not seeing.
Ānanda said: "I truly see this entire Jeta Grove, yet I do not know which part within it is 'non-seeing.'"
Why is this? If the tree is not seeing, how can one see the tree? If the tree is itself seeing, how can it still be called a tree?
This applies even to space: if space is not seeing, how can one see space? If space is itself seeing, how can it still be called space?
I further contemplated that within these myriad phenomena, when minutely examined and illuminated, there is nothing that is not seeing.
At first, he answered directly that he did not know. He said that one can only see what one has reached;
since he now sees the entire Jeta Grove, it is clear that the nature of seeing reaches everywhere. However, although this clarity reaches all that place, it cannot be separated from that place;
therefore, he answered directly with "I do not know. Why [the Master] subsequently repeated the question in detail? He said: if...
If the tree is not seeing, then there is no seeing upon the tree. If there is no seeing, then this and that do not encounter one another. Hence it is asked: "How can you see the tree?
Now, since you have seen the tree, it seems as though the tree and the seeing encounter each other; yet you cannot resolve this distinction. Is it not the case that the tree is itself the seeing?
If the tree were identical to the seeing, you would still be falling into the same error as before. Therefore it is asked: "Furthermore, how can there be a tree?"
The phrase "and so on, up to" (*iti yāvat*) abbreviates all other objects. The principle that "if it is empty, it is not seeing," and so forth, may be inferred accordingly.
Based on this, it is not merely that there is no "non-being"; furthermore, by means of this, one further comes to know that there is no "being.

[The text says: "I again... and below, this concludes the response regarding the absence of "non-being. To speak of "being" (*asti*) is to posit its opposite, "non-being" (*nāsti*). If there were such a thing as "being," only then...
One might say it is "not. Now, let us examine this with thorough detail: not only is there no "is" that is real, there is also no "is not.
Because there is no "is not," one turns back to contemplate "is. Yet, since "is" is definitively absent, "is not" is likewise ultimately non-existent. Therefore, I further reflect as follows:
within these myriad phenomena, when each and every subtle aspect is clearly illuminated, there is not a single dharma that is not [empty].
My view is that this "non-negation" is the principle of the single essence in harmonious fusion, transcending all dualistic oppositions;
it is a meaning that is inconceivable and beyond deliberation. The four Tathāgatas have sealed what they have taught.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.
Right and wrong are both severed; deluded sentiments are entirely exhausted. When the one essence is merged and fused, how could there be any prior characteristics?
Therefore, the Tathāgata also repeated 'So it is' to certify this, thereby extinguishing right and wrong and completely destroying the prior characteristics."

Second, regarding the failure to maintain [the teachings] and the instruction to contemplate with discernment, there are two parts: first, the failure of those in training (*śaikṣa*) to maintain them; second, the Buddha’s instruction to contemplate with discernment. As for the first:
at that time, the great assembly—excluding those who were no longer in training—heard these words of the Buddha and were utterly bewildered, not knowing the beginning or end of their meaning.
At that moment, they were struck with alarm and lost their composure.
Those who are not yet "beyond training" (aśaikṣa) are precisely those still "in training" (śaikṣa); this refers to Ānanda and his like.

While those beyond training might perhaps have a faint inkling of it upon hearing this, the wisdom of those in training is inferior, and they become even more like the blind and deaf. Therefore, it is said they were "bewildered," meaning they were utterly lost in a state of profound confusion and obscurity.
It is so. This meaning refers precisely to the two points: the absence of the view that there is, and the absence of the view that there is not. Zhengmo says:
"Generally, when a meaning is shallow, one can then see the end from the beginning; for by means of the end, one will certainly not obscure the beginning.
Now, regarding these two meanings, later [the text] states that because the Buddha had not yet spoken of them, one could not fathom their ultimate destination—this constitutes not knowing the end."
Previously, when investigating the Buddha, it was already stated that one should not seek his origins; this constitutes not finding his beginning.

Because this further increases confusion and distress, one becomes momentarily terrified. "Terrified" describes the state of fear. Since right and wrong are not resolved, one loses what one maintains.
Only by deciding upon a certainty—whether it be "it is so" or "it is not"—can one uphold and maintain [the truth].
The Buddha instructed them to contemplate this with earnest attention.
Knowing that their spirits were agitated and their minds cowed, the Tathāgata gave rise to compassion and comforted Ānanda and the great assembly.
"O virtuous sons, the Unsurpassed Dharma King speaks words of truth; he teaches exactly as it is, without deception or falsehood."
False. This is not the fourfold evasive discourse on immortality of Makkhali Gosāla. You must contemplate this carefully so as not to disgrace our shared grief and longing.
"Initially knowing fear and compassion" refers to the spirit's consciousness and deliberation; "changing alarm and trepidation" refers to further shifting into states of shock and dread.

This means that fear and trepidation remain within one’s heart. One who knows this is the Buddha, for by observing the external with his knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), he fully comprehends the internal.
"Compassion" refers to pitying those who have failed to maintain their guard; "consolation" refers to releasing them from their fear and trepidation;

and "to the great assembly" includes those of a similar kind—this refers to what was mentioned above regarding those who are not yet beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). ○ From "all the good [dharmas]" below, it reveals [the following].
It is said that one should have faith. Because he universally issues mandates regarding what is to be done, he is called "Good Sons.

Because he personally manifests his own credibility, he is called the "Unsurpassed Dharma King. If even the upright people of the world may be relied upon as trustworthy, how much more so the Unsurpassed Dharma King?
Such terms as "words of truth" do not rely solely on the person being trustworthy; rather, they show that what is spoken is likewise trustworthy. Thus it is revealed.
To speak of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called "true speech" (*bhūta-vāda*), as when one says, "That which does not exist, I see as it is.
To reveal conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is called "actual speech" (*tathya-vāda*), as when one says, "That which is not non-existent, I see as it is.

To reveal the Middle Way is called "speaking according to suchness" (*yathā-tathatā-vāda*), meaning to speak in accordance with the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) as it has been personally realized. As explained above, by repeating this in detail, both extremes of "is" and "is not" are severed, and delusion is eliminated.
"Sentiment and principle are both exhausted" refers to this. "Not deceiving" means not cheating those who are beginners; "not being false" means not treating this and that differently.
This demonstrates that the meaning is identical to the five kinds of speech associated with deep faith. How could the Buddha ever engage in self-aggrandizement?

○ Regarding the passage "It is not the end," it serves to distinguish [this teaching] from heterodox doctrines. "Non-death" refers to the meaning of non-determinacy. The "four kinds" are both changing and constant.

It is both arising and ceasing; it is both existent and non-existent; it both increases and decreases. This will be explained in detail later in the section on the Māra of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Because it is indeterminate, it is called "evasive confusion" (*vibhrama*), meaning a forced and disordered state.

The Buddha’s intention was that he feared if they heard "neither right nor wrong," they might instead cling to "neither wrong nor right," which resembles evasive confusion; therefore, he used "wrong."
Makkhali and others rejected this. Furthermore, regarding those who do not die, it refers to their false calculation that there exists a "Deathless Heaven" (Amarā-vimāna);

these four phrases are what they transmit. When someone asks whether one will be reborn in that heaven based on a single birth [of practice], the Tathāgata rebukes them as proponents of evasive sophistry (*vibhajyavāda*), because they do not understand the meaning of the Three Truths. Thus he instructs them, saying: "Reflect with truth."
Since this is neither deceptive nor confused, there must be a fixed principle. If you can examine and contemplate with earnest sincerity, why is it that there is neither "is" nor "is not"?
Look straight ahead until you reach a point where the mind has nowhere to rest; at that moment, the bottom of the bucket will naturally fall away.
This is precisely what the Tathāgata taught as investigating by departing from mind, intellect, and consciousness; it is not a teaching of conceptual discrimination.
Please reflect upon this and do not misunderstand it, lest you, who are already unworthy, further betray my intent.

When I said that Ānanda had sought the true from the false since he first renounced the deluded, his repeated and earnest entreaties were all rooted in his yearning for the wondrously luminous, quiescent, and eternal.

My intention was that if he could contemplate with true discernment, then the wondrously luminous, quiescent, and eternal would manifest within his own mind; thus, he would not have betrayed his earnest entreaties.
This is the spirit of yearning admiration. Because of the failure to maintain the precepts, the instruction on thorough contemplation is concluded.
Second, regarding the three conditions for the proxy inquiry that points to the true essence, there are two parts: first, Mañjuśrī’s compassionate proxy inquiry out of pity for the assembly;

second, the Tathāgata’s pointing to the essence to bring it forth. The first part has three sections: first, pitying the assembly and assuming the proper ritual demeanor; second, acting as their representative to express their sentiments.
Third, seeking the original source. First:

At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, rose from his seat amidst the great multitude, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and joined his palms in reverent homage.
"This time" refers to the time for contemplating the Buddha's teaching. Although he was instructed to contemplate, he remained terrified;

therefore, Mañjuśrī took pity on him, rose from his seat, and prostrated at his feet to express the sincerity of his inquiry on his behalf. Joining his palms in reverence, he demonstrated his intention to speak.
Now, as for why Mañjuśrī must act as the petitioner: it is because of the profound [wisdom] of the Unsurpassed Dharma King.

To say that one who has not attained the true sonship of the Dharma King lacks the fundamental great wisdom sufficient to illuminate the Buddha-sun and enlighten the fourfold assembly is to misrepresent the reality of those two generations. Their realization of the ultimate truth was profound.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, this great assembly does not understand the meaning of the Tathāgata’s clarification regarding the two kinds of refined vision—that which perceives form and emptiness, and that which does not perceive them.
World-Honored One, if these preceding objects such as form and emptiness were the seeing itself, there should be something pointed out;
if they were not the seeing, there should be nothing beheld. Yet now we do not know the meaning of this."
Because they returned [to their former state], there was still fear and dread. It was not that their past roots of goodness were slight or meager;
rather, at first, the assembly did not realize the meaning of Mañjuśrī’s intent. Mañjuśrī’s intention was this:

the Tathāgata’s two previous rounds of questioning were specifically intended to clarify the profundity of two things—namely, the meaning and the non-meaning of "refined vision" in relation to form and emptiness.

This is why it is so. Although Ānanda remained silent in each instance, the Tathāgata provisionally granted his approval out of skillful means, yet fearing he might still be deluded regarding the profound, he instructed him again to contemplate with earnest attention.
This was done in the hope that he would attain some realization to resolve his erroneous doubts;
however, observing that his demeanor remained as fearful and trembling as before, it is clear that he has ultimately failed to awaken to what the Tathāgata has revealed.
Because these two meanings are profound, only a Buddha can discern this capacity, and only a Buddha can awaken it.

○ From "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*) downward, he infers the [disciples'] sentiments and speaks on their behalf. Because he intends to speak on their behalf, he again addresses them as "World-Honored One," hoping that [the disciples] will have their circumstances taken into consideration.
The character "若" (*ruò*) above should be read as "如" (*rú*). This indicates that the assembly was terrified and did not doubt the Buddha.
Regarding "confused speech": his intention is as follows. Taking the preceding objects such as form and emptiness as examples, if it were a case of seeing, there should be something pointed out;

if it were not a case of seeing, there should be nothing perceived. Now, since there is neither a thing pointed out nor anything perceived—both meanings being absent—he ultimately does not know to which category this underlying meaning belongs. For this reason, he experiences alarm and fear.
Observing their spirits and anxieties, they were thus transformed by fear. "Whence did this come? refers to the two assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Vaipulya* (Prajñāpāramitā) in the past.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, they fainted and fell to the ground; in the *Vaipulya*, they willingly took up the task of removing filth. Both occurred because their roots of goodness were slight and meager.
Since the present is not comparable to the past, it is said that "this is not so. There are briefly two reasons why Mañjuśrī spoke these words.
The intention is threefold: first, to demonstrate that he has heard [the teaching] and is free from the fault of the Buddha’s deceptive equivocation;

second, to demonstrate that there is the benefit of further attaining understanding and clarity; therefore, in the following section, he immediately requests instruction on their behalf; third, to request instruction on the original source.
I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, will clarify this for me: what are these various objects and this essence of seeing fundamentally?
Within them, there is neither "is" nor "is not."
Since your roots of goodness are neither slight nor meager, your sublime mind should be further enlightened.

Therefore, I pray that the Tathāgata’s great compassion will clarify this inquiry into the ultimate source—asking what this fundamental substance is—so that we may exhaustively investigate its origin.

Regarding all material phenomena and this essence of seeing (*darśana-viśuddhi*), if they possessed two distinct natures, one could then speak of them as being either "identical" or "not identical. Now, since both [of these] meanings are absent...
"No. This must mean that there are not two distinct entities; it is simply that one does not know what the original substance is, such that within it, there is neither "is" nor "is not.
I myself do not know this, let alone Ānanda and the others; it is therefore no wonder they ultimately fail to awaken.
Yet Ānanda and the others only know how to speculate within the realm of "is" and "is not," and do not understand how to turn toward [the source].
Seeking neither the right nor the wrong, he traversed both extremes with sovereign ease yet remained fearful. He tested [the Buddha] by asking, "Observe this:
what, fundamentally, is Mañjuśrī? This was like a thunderbolt that struck, shattering the deafness of all who heard it.
It is said that one who reaches the ultimate bottom line is truly a master, and Mañjuśrī was such a one. Having finished his inquiry on behalf of the multitude out of compassion, Mañjuśrī departed.
Third, the Tathāgata points out the essence and elucidates it in three parts: first, directly pointing to the true essence; second, elucidating through metaphor;
and third, concluding by demonstrating the correct meaning. Regarding the first:
the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly, saying, "The Tathāgatas and great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions abide in their own [state]..."
Within samādhi, one sees that the seer, the objects of seeing, and the perceived characteristics are like flowers in the sky—originally non-existent.
This seeing and its objects are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. How could there be "is" or "is not" within this?
The address to Mañjuśrī is for the purpose of posing the question on his behalf; the address to the great assembly is because they were filled with awe and trepidation.
The mention of "Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas" brings forth those capable of perceiving the true essence, thereby demonstrating that what is taught has a valid basis.

When the Bodhisattva is referred to as "Great," it indicates a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching who has attained the stages (*bhūmi*), distinguishing them from those following provisional or gradual teachings, as well as those prior to the stages.

Samādhi is the general name for all meditative concentrations. To avoid confusion with other states, it is distinguished by the term "abiding in itself" (svayam-sthita), which reveals that it is the fundamental concentration of its own nature.
This distinguishes it from the provisional, gradual co-abiding of the forcibly constrained conscious mind; in its ultimate sense, it is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
"Vision" refers to the essence of vision, while "the objects of vision" refers to external phenomena. This is stated in accordance with the preceding text.

Furthermore, speaking in terms of the nature and objects of the eye-faculty, in reality, the seeing-nature also encompasses the six consciousnesses, and the conditions for seeing also encompass the six sense-objects.
Based on this, the "conceived characteristics" (*saṃjñā-nimitta*) refer collectively to the six consciousnesses, as they are the reflected images arising between the faculties and their objects.
All of these are manifested through the successive delusions of ignorance and non-enlightenment.
Now, through abiding in meditative concentration, one awakens to and understands that because phenomena arise from conditions and lack intrinsic nature, they are said to be like flowers in the sky.
These "flowers in the sky" are merely signs of visual fatigue; when observed with clear eyes, they cannot be found at all. Therefore, they are used as a metaphor.

That which is fundamentally non-existent has been so from the beginning, for it is not something acquired through effort. As it says later: "Observing these appearances is fundamentally false; there is nothing [to be grasped]."

This points out the truth. As for this "seeing" and its "conditions," they are not called "perception" (*saṃjñā*) or "characteristics" (*nimitta*), because these differentiated shadows have no ultimate substance;
they are like the reflection of the moon in water. This seeing-nature does not perceive objects through comparison; when emotional attachments are forgotten, it is the Truth (*tattva*).
Because it is like a second moon, it is fundamentally *bodhi*, and so forth—meaning that it is the entire reality of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Because it is the ultimate reality. Among the three types of *bodhi*, this is the *tattva-bodhi* (True Nature Bodhi).
From the very beginning, it cannot be constrained by delusive views, cannot be defiled by sensory objects, and cannot be obscured by discrimination;

therefore, it is designated as the "wondrously pure and luminous essence. As stated later: "Observing that the nature is fundamentally real, it is solely wondrous enlightened clarity. This is to be understood according to what precedes.
Mañjuśrī asked: "What was it originally that, within it, has neither 'is' nor 'is not'? This refers to the statement that it was "originally bodhi," and so forth.
Since it was originally bodhi, it is beyond all dualistic opposition; there is not even "is," let alone "is not. Therefore, it is said:
"How could there be [such things] within it? (Zhengmo asks: The Buddha initially took only seeing as the nature, yet he explained in detail that it does not correspond to the body...)

The mind takes all things as its companions. This seems to suggest that seeing alone is real while everything else is false, leading one to rely on the nature of seeing in isolation. Now, when discussing the false, it degrades the nature of seeing by equating it with empty flowers; yet when discussing the true, it elevates all phenomena to be the same as the true essence.

While this is indeed a discourse that reaches the ultimate principle, what can be done about how people apply their minds? To which direction shall they turn? The commentary now answers: Initially, because there is no purely true mind within the state of ordinary sentient beings, and because among the daily activities of common life, the visual faculty’s nature of seeing is the most convenient for pointing out, we have provisionally used the eye to reveal it.

Furthermore, fearing that they might mistake it for the myriad objects and confuse the sense organs with consciousness, thereby failing to establish the realization, we have again explained it through indirect means.

That it does not associate with the body, mind, or the myriad phenomena is because the initial resolve values single-mindedness and the discernment of dharmas requires precision; thus, it is said that seeing the solitary truth renders all else false, leading one to rely solely on the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*).

Now, fearing that one might consider a small attainment sufficient and no longer seek the true mind, this treatise treats the nature of seeing as equivalent to a flower in the sky when discussing the false. Furthermore, fearing that one’s vision may be restricted to the eyes and fail to universally integrate the myriad phenomena, it elevates all dharmas to be the same as the true essence when discussing the true.

This is because study prizes reaching the source and principle demands universal integration; therefore, this ultimate discourse on principle is provided to enable thorough realization and perfect enlightenment. Since practitioners’ applications of the mind differ, the administration of medicine according to their ailments must likewise vary; this is tailored to the specific symptoms.

There is no ailment that will not be cured by taking this medicine. As for the reasons for those [previous] omissions, there are replies within them; if you wish to know them, examine them (refer to the previous section).

Part Two: Elucidation through Parables. This has two sections: First, taking Mañjuśrī as the parable; Second, manifesting the meaning by applying it to the Dharma. The first [section] has two parts: First, two questions based on the parable;
Second, answering each according to the question. The first [part]: [The text continues with the specific questions and answers regarding the parable.]
Mañjuśrī, I now ask you: if there were another Mañjuśrī like you, would that Mañjuśrī be without Mañjuśrī?
This direct pointing is difficult to clarify; it must be made manifest through analogy. Therefore, he calls out his name again to pose the question: "If there were another Mañjuśrī like you..."
This borrows the original substance of Mañjuśrī as a metaphor for the true substance.

As for the question regarding whether there is yet another Mañjuśrī and so forth, the intent is that only if there were a Mañjuśrī distinct from this original substance could it be said [that he exists], just as one might say, "That is this.
As for the question regarding whether there is no Mañjuśrī, the intent is that only when even this original substance is absent can it be said [that he does not exist].
"No. It is as it is said: 'Fundamentally, he is not [Mañjuśrī]. Second, answering each question individually: 'It is so, World-Honored One;
I am truly Mañjuśrī, yet there is no such thing as Mañjuśrī. Why is this? If there were such a thing, there would be two Mañjuśrīs.
However, today I am not without Mañjuśrī. Within this, in reality, there is neither 'is' nor 'is not.'"
[The Master] said: "No. At first he answered that there was none. His intention was that it was just as the Buddha had asked: "World-Honored One, allow me to answer according to my own judgment.
I consider myself truly Mañjuśrī; there is only this single fundamental essence, and there is no other who is Mañjuśrī. Why?
This can be understood by examining the phrasing. Regarding the subsequent explanation, "If there were": unless there were two Mañjuśrīs, one could say that "he" is "this.

Now, since there is only this single reality, who is there to say it? Therefore, I say "none. Regarding the phrase "However, I next... and so forth, the answer to the objection of non-existence is as follows:
"It is not that Mañjuśrī does not exist," for "non-existent" does not mean that Mañjuśrī is absent. It means that he is not [a separate entity] alongside [the reality].

This fundamental substance is also non-existent. It is not that Mañjuśrī is entirely non-existent; the meaning is that since it is not entirely non-existent, one cannot say it is not [existent] either.
This can be understood without further words. Within this, the phrase concludes that both are non-existent.

Since it has already been stated that they are non-existent, yet it is also not the case that they are entirely non-existent, there is a concern that the audience might be confused. Therefore, he concludes by saying: "Within this, in reality, neither exists."

It is not of two aspects. "Within it" means within the single true essence. According to the Buddha’s own words and metaphors, his intention was that my true self, Mañjuśrī, is a metaphor for the wondrously pure and luminous essence of Bodhi, which truly possesses no two aspects. How could there be "is" or "is not"?
This will become clear when we reach the section on the application [of the metaphor]. Having finished taking Mañjuśrī as the metaphor, second, [he uses] the Dharma...
This reveals two points in combination: first, the unification with my own true self, Mañjuśrī; second, the unification with the reality that is free from dualistic characteristics.

Regarding the first: the Buddha said, "This seeing, which is wondrously luminous, is likewise with respect to all empty objects and sensory dusts. It is originally the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed *bodhi*, the pure, perfect, and true mind."
This "seeing" refers to the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*). Having existed in the state of entanglement since beginningless time, its numinous radiance remains as it is;
therefore, it is designated as "wondrous clarity. "Empty dust" refers to objective phenomena, for although these phenomena are manifold, they do not transcend emptiness and dust.

This corresponds to the word "I" within the preceding metaphor, which was stated above as "this seeing and its conditions. "Originally so" means that it has been thus from the very beginning; it is not something newly created.

It is attained through provisional cultivation. Precisely because it is not attained through provisional cultivation, it is called "sublime clarity. Even when reaching the fruit of Buddhahood, it does not transcend this; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed bodhi.
Because it remains unchanging while following conditions, it is called the "pure mind. Because it follows conditions while remaining unchanging, it is called the "perfect mind.
Its essence and function are without obstruction, beyond the reach of words or thought, and fundamentally distinct from that conditioned mind.
Because it is devoid of falsehood, it is called the "True Mind. This corresponds to the meaning of the "True Mañjuśrī" within the preceding analogy;
it is what was stated above as "originally being the wondrously pure and luminous essence of bodhi. Second, it is truly without dual characteristics.
To falsely conceive of form as empty, or of hearing and seeing, is like a second moon. Who can say which is the true moon and which is not?
O Mañjuśrī, there is but one true moon; within it, there is naturally neither "this is the moon" nor "this is not the moon."

The initial delusion falls into two reckonings: form and emptiness are the *bhājana-vijñapti* (objective aspect) of the *ālaya-vijñāna*, while hearing and seeing are its *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect).
All arise through the successive illusory manifestations of the non-awakening of ignorance; therefore, they are called "false. Because of this falsity, one reckons that there are two aspects.
Within these, one asserts "this" and denies "that," unable to transcend them; thus, it is further likened to the two moons.
The analogy: It is like the second moon, which arises because the eyes have been pressed;

since it is produced by the same delusion, one does not realize that once the pressure on the eyes is released, it is truly non-existent. Thus, through false conceptualization, one wonders which is the real moon and which is not.
This is exactly like Ānanda, who did not realize that form and emptiness, hearing and seeing, are the truth when free from conceptual thought;
he only knew how to calculate and deliberate within the realm of "is" and "is not. ○ When Mañjuśrī spoke below, his awakening transcended "is" and "is not.

He called out "Mañjuśrī" again to instruct him against becoming attached to mental effort, and also to provide a secondary warning to Ānanda. To speak of "is" and "is not" arises entirely from clinging to duality. If one knows...
There is only the true moon; within it, there naturally exists neither the proposal that it is this moon nor the argument that it is not the moon.
One who understands this analogy can then apply it by extension to the principle that form and emptiness, as well as hearing and seeing, are devoid of the distinction between right and wrong.

This was an analogy used to match an analogy; fearing it might still not be clear, the following section provides a further summary and demonstration. The explanation through the use of analogies is now complete.
The third section clarifies the correct meaning.

Therefore, when you now observe the various manifestations of the mind with respect to sensory objects, this is called deluded thought (*vikalpa*). You are unable to distinguish within it what is and what is not.
Because of this true, essential, wondrously enlightened nature of clarity, it is able to cause you to emerge from pointing at what is and what is not.
[The Master] points [to Ānanda]. This initial binding [of the analogy] demonstrates the fall into two attachments. Here, the word "you" still refers to Ānanda.
Having already established the metaphor and its application above, he now intends to provide a final summary; thus, he speaks again to Ānanda. His intention is that, based on what preceded—
Consider the analogy of the moon and the previous analogy of Mañjuśrī. Therefore, Ānanda, when you now observe the dust, you need only see what its original substance is;

there is no need for various kinds of elucidation. Even if one were to provide various kinds of elucidation, it would still be a matter of asserting "this" or "that," all of which belongs to discrimination and is called delusive thought. Even if one were to speak to the point...
Even in a donkey-year, one would still be unable to transcend within this the distinction between what is right and what is not.
This is similar to those who cling to the existence of two moons and falsely calculate which one is the true moon and which one is not.

From "By this" onwards, the conclusion demonstrates the awakening that transcends right and wrong. The intention is that since one cannot transcend right and wrong, I have previously questioned each point one by one.
You were ultimately unable to definitively point out who possesses this seeing and who does not.
This is because both the seeing and its objects are of one and the same true essence—the wondrously enlightened nature of clarity.

Because I questioned you based on this, I was able to lead you toward a vague realization that transcends the pointing-out of "this is seeing" and "this is not seeing," and to [lead you] beyond that...
The "True Moon" (the one moon) is, in its very midst, naturally devoid of any semblance of being either "this moon" or "not this moon.

Herein, the true essence (*tattva-sāra*) is precisely the original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). It is termed "wondrously enlightened clarity" because, although it is the causal mind, it is identical to the resultant essence;
for the nature of wondrously enlightened, perfect clarity realized by the Buddha is not separate from this. According to Ānanda’s request, this section [addresses]...

It remains the same wondrous character as before. It is precisely by transcending "is" and "is not" that the wondrousness of the essence of nature is revealed. The section on the non-differentiation of manifestation and seeing is concluded.
Part Nine: Revealing that this transcends conceptual thought, in two sections: First, Ānanda raises a doubt based on the confusion with external objects; second, the Tathāgata [responds].

The explanation that transcends ordinary emotion consists of two parts: first, acknowledging that the nature is pervasive and eternal; second, suspecting it might be conflated with externalist theories. Regarding the first:

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma King has said: that the awareness which conditions objects is pervasive throughout the ten directions of space, and is profoundly..."
However, the nature of eternal abiding is neither arising nor ceasing;

it is indeed the true fruit. What the Dharma King has taught generally refers to that which is revealed by the preceding eight [consciousnesses]. "The perceiving condition" (*jue-yuan*) specifically refers to the seeing-nature (*jian-xing*).

This means that, based directly upon the awakened mind (*jue-xin*), there arises the capacity for perception; because this is a fusion of the true and the false, it is termed the "perceiving condition."
In the section on Non-differentiation, form and emptiness share the same substance; in the section on Unobstruction, body and mind are perfectly luminous.
Hence it is said, "pervading the ten directions," which refers to the meaning of pervasiveness. In the section on Non-mixture, one stands independently apart from objects;
in the section on Mind, even the sense organs are liberated. Hence it is said, "serenely still. In the section on Non-abandonment, there has been no loss from the beginning; it is immovable.
In the section on "Non-Returning," it is said there is no coming or going; in the section on "Non-Cessation," it is said that it is ultimately inexhaustible.
Therefore, it is stated that its nature is neither arising nor ceasing. This summarizes the meaning of permanence.

Having concluded the summary of the pervasive permanence of nature, there are two points regarding doubts about confusion with externalist calculations: first, the doubt regarding confusion with external nature; second, the doubt regarding... [text fragment].
Regarding the external schools: first,
what difference is there between this and the "Ultimate Truth" (*tattva*) discussed with the former Brahmin Śāṃkara,
as well as the various non-Buddhist sects such as the ash-smearing ones who claim that a true self exists pervading the ten directions?
The "former brahmins" (*pūrvabrāhmaṇa*) refers to the ancient brahmins. They claimed to be descendants of Brahmā, aspiring to be born in the Brahma-heaven;
they are thus of the Brahmin caste. Regarding the name *Sāṃkhyakāra* (the author of the *Sāṃkhya*), the introduction states that he was a teacher of the *Sāṃkhya*.
As for "the vision of the *tattva* of darkness" (*tamas-tattva-darśana*), this refers to the first of the twenty-five *tattvas*. That *Sāṃkhya*...
The masters of the treatises (śāstrakāra) maintain that the primordial nature (prakṛti) is eternal and capable of producing the twenty-three principles, such as the Great One (mahat).

This bears a superficial resemblance to the meaning of what is now being taught—that the nature is profoundly quiescent, eternally abiding, and not subject to arising or ceasing. Regarding the practice of "throwing ash" (*tōhai*), some say it means "smearing ash" (*tōhai*);
this refers to sometimes throwing one's body into ash and sometimes smearing ash upon the body—both of which are fruitless ascetic practices. Furthermore...
These include such practices as plucking out one's hair, fumigating the nose, sleeping on needles, lying upon spikes, remaining naked, and self-starvation; thus, the word "etc. is employed.
All of these have their minds wandering outside the Way and each establishes its own lineage; therefore, they are called "various types of non-Buddhists" (*tīrthika*).

Regarding those who assert the existence of a true self (*ātman*), according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the non-Buddhists' conceptions of the self-characteristic are threefold: first, large; second, small; and third, neither [large nor small].

[The Buddha] said: "Pervading the ten directions is what is called the 'Great Self' (mahātman). This seems to overlap with the meaning of what is being taught here—that the object-condition of awakening (bodhy-ālambana) pervades the realms of the ten directions.

[The interlocutor] concludes the inquiry in the final sentence, saying: "The Buddha says the object-condition of awakening is eternal (nitya), yet the non-Buddhists also claim that primordial nature (prakṛti) is eternal.

The Buddha says the object-condition of awakening is pervasive, yet the non-Buddhists also claim that the self (ātman) is pervasive. Thus, the Buddha’s teaching and the non-Buddhist claims appear to be the same."

What is the distinction? If the unwholesome were treated as indistinguishable from the wholesome—like the difference between muddy water and clear spring water—I fear that even a deviation of a hair’s breadth will lead to an error of a thousand li.
Second, there is the doubt of being conflated with non-Buddhist schools.
The World-Honored One also once expounded this meaning on Mount Laṅkā for Mahāmati and others.
Those heterodox teachers constantly speak of spontaneity (*svabhāva*); I, however, speak of causes and conditions, which is not within their realm of experience.

I now observe that this nature of awakening is spontaneous, neither arising nor ceasing, and far removed from all false delusions; it seems, therefore, not to be a matter of causes and conditions. It is thus with them...
How does one naturally reveal how to avoid entering among the various heterodoxies and attain the wondrously enlightened nature of the true mind?
First, [the text] cites what was previously selected; "also once" means that in the past, he had also done so. Mount Laṅkā is the place where the Buddha preached the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
In Sanskrit, *Laṅkā* is translated here as "Inaccessible"; it cannot be reached by anyone who lacks supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Because they cannot reach it. Based on this, the sutra speaks of the excellence of the Dharma, which is not within the reach of those of the Two Vehicles.

When Mahāmati and others are mentioned, they represent the specific audience while encompassing the rest of the assembly. The reason for expounding this meaning is to distinguish the non-Buddhist schools and establish one’s own school.
Regarding the statement that those non-Buddhists and others constantly speak of "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*), Qingliang says: "The proponents of causelessness (*ahetuvādin*) reckon [it as] one."
All things arise and perish spontaneously, without cause and without condition. As that verse says: "Who opens the rivers and seas and piles up the mountains?
Who carves the thorns and paints the beasts and birds? There is no one at all who can produce them; therefore, I say they are spontaneous.
This is to deny cause and effect and to reject the establishment of cultivation and realization. [The Buddha, however,] by means of causes...
Because it is subverted by conditions, it is said: "The dependent origination I teach is not within the realm of those [other schools]. As a verse in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
"I teach that there is only a chain of links (the 'hook-and-chain' being the meaning of the non-interruption of the causes for grasping signs); this is free from the errors of the non-Buddhists.
If there were dharmas produced apart from the chain of conditions, that would be the doctrine of causelessness, which destroys the principle of the chain of links. (1)
All things in the world are nothing other than chains of causal links. Ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and karma constitute the internal chain of links;
seeds, clay, wheels, and so forth are called the external. Herein, the first phrase establishes my own school’s position regarding the formulation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The second phrase indicates that this is not the domain of others, thereby distinguishing it from external schools. As for the four phrases beginning with "if one is separated from," etc.:

The reason the six phrases beginning with "all" are used for exclusion is that [if they were not excluded], one would fall into the view of causelessness or spontaneous origination, thereby destroying the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The reason the six phrases beginning with "all" are established is that they accord with correct reasoning and are universally accepted in the world;
they do not fall into the errors of causelessness or false causes. Thus, both ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) act as causes, while karmic formations (*saṃskāra*) act as conditions.
That which can produce consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth, thereby forming the internal body of faculties, is called the "internal chain.
Just as a sprout arises with the seed as the cause and water and earth as the conditions, or as a jar is formed with a lump of clay as the cause and the wheel and rope as the conditions.

The other realms of existence may be understood by analogy with this; thus they are called the "external chain. Therefore, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) in the teachings are also termed the "twelve links" (*dvādaśa-śṛṅkhalā*).
[The section] beginning with "I now... clarifies that the current [explanation] might seem redundant; it concerns the phrase "the nature of awakening is spontaneous."

First, there is the confusion arising from the mistaken determination that [the teaching] is subject to superfluous application. Phrases such as "neither arising nor ceasing" are erroneously taken to prove the Buddha’s established doctrine;
however, the meaning within "neither arising nor ceasing, neither extinguished nor lost" is not what they claim.

Such notions as being mobile, returning, mixed, obstructed, or divisible all belong to delusion and inversion. It is rather non-movement, non-returning, non-confusion, and non-obstruction that constitute the truth.

The divisions and so forth are all for the purpose of distancing oneself [from conceptualization]. Now, as for what is called "distancing," it precisely reveals that which transcends emotional calculations and severs all frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Yet Ānanda did not understand this; instead, he wished to use this erroneous proof to establish "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, it is said: "It appears to be non-causal. His intention was: since it is neither causal nor spontaneous, what could it possibly be? [The passage continues: "With those below..."
He requested the Buddha’s instruction, saying: "Since the *Laṅkāvatāra* has already distinguished [the true from the false], how could I now allow myself to be confused?
Therefore, I seek the Tathāgata’s clarification regarding how what is taught here compares to that theory of spontaneity (*svabhāva*), so that I may determine what to adopt and what to reject."

Once what is to be accepted and what is to be rejected has been determined, one will not enter among the various heterodoxies but shall attain the wondrously enlightened and luminous nature of the true mind.
Ānanda’s doubt regarding the confusion with external objects is thus concluded; second, the Tathāgata provides the explanation by means of transcending worldly sentiments. (4)

1. Correctly explaining the preceding doubt; 2. Simultaneously refuting further attachments; 3. Generally dispelling delusive sentiments; 4. Concluding with a reprimand of discrimination. Regarding the first two [sections]: 1. Reprimanding the delusion and seeking its essence; 2. Detailed refutation through difficult questions. Regarding the first [of these two]: [The text continues as follows: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, if one asks: 'If all dharmas are without self-nature, how can there be birth and death? If there is no birth and death, how can there be nirvana? Mahāmati, it is because of the false attachment to the characteristics of self-nature that there is birth and death. Because of the cessation of the grasping at the characteristics of self-nature, there is nirvana. Mahāmati, it is like a person who, seeing a rope in the dark, falsely conceives it to be a snake. Because of that false conception, fear arises. Upon closer examination, the fear ceases. Mahāmati, the same applies to this: because of the false attachment to the characteristics of self-nature, there is birth and death. Because of the cessation of the grasping at the characteristics of self-nature, there is no distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome. Mahāmati, it is like an echo. It has no substance, yet because of the power of sound, people falsely conceive it to be speech. Mahāmati, the same applies to this: because of the false attachment to the characteristics of self-nature, there is the distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome. Because of the cessation of the grasping at the characteristics of self-nature, there is no distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome. [The text continues as follows: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, if one asks: 'If all dharmas are without self-nature, how can there be the distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned? If there is no such distinction, how can there be liberation? Mahāmati, it is because of the false attachment to the characteristics of self-nature that there is the distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned. Because of the cessation of the grasping at the characteristics of self-nature, there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned. Mahāmati, it is like a magical illusion. It has no reality, yet because of the power of mantras and drugs, people falsely perceive various forms. Mahāmati, the same applies to this: because of the false attachment to the characteristics of self-nature, there is the distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned. Because of the cessation of the grasping at the characteristics of self-nature, there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned. [The text continues as follows: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, if one asks: 'If all dharmas are without self-nature, how can there be the distinction between the world and the transcendence of the world? If there is no such distinction, how can there be the turning of the wheel of Dharma? Mahāmati, it is because of the false attachment to the characteristics of self-nature that there is the distinction between the world and the transcendence of the world. Because of the cessation of the grasping at the characteristics of self-nature, there is neither the world nor the transcendence of the world. Mahāmati, it is like a reflection in a mirror. It has no reality, yet because of the power of the object, people falsely perceive a face. Mahāmati, the same applies to this: because of the false attachment to the characteristics of self-nature, there is the distinction between the world and the transcendence of the world. Because of the cessation of the grasping at the characteristics of self-nature, there is neither the world nor the transcendence of the world. [The text continues as follows: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, if one asks: 'If all dharmas are without self-nature, how can there be the distinction between the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the bodhisattva? Mahāmati, it is like a person who, having entered a deep sleep, dreams of being in a palace or a forest. Upon waking, all is non-existent. Mahāmati, it is because of the false attachment to the characteristics of self-nature that there is the distinction between the dharma and the non-dharma. Because of the cessation of the grasping at the characteristics of self-nature, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Mahāmati, it is like a phantom city. It has no reality, yet because of the power of karma, people falsely perceive a city. Mahāmati, the same applies to this: because of the false attachment to the characteristics of self-nature, there is the distinction between the dharma and the non-dharma. Because of the cessation of the grasping at the characteristics of self-nature, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. [The text continues as follows: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, if one asks: 'If all dharmas are without self-nature, how can there be the distinction between the past, the future, and the present? If
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I have now thus revealed the skillful means and spoken the truth to you. Yet you still do not understand, and you are deluded into thinking that [this state] is spontaneous.
"Ānanda, if it were necessarily spontaneous, one must clearly discern whether there is a substantial body of spontaneity.
For the moment, observe this wondrously luminous faculty of seeing: what therein constitutes its own nature? Does this seeing take luminosity as its own nature?"
Taking darkness as self, taking emptiness as self, and taking obstruction as self—this initial exposition rebukes delusion.
Such an instruction refers directly to the preceding eight passages that clarify the nature of seeing.

Whether through indirect elaboration or lateral extension, or through explicit revelation or subtle implication, it is nothing but skillful means (*upāya*); thus it is called "expedient. This is the original intent of the Buddha.
[The Master] says: "I" [refers to the speaker]. This is spoken in total to demolish false conceptualizations and reveal the true source; therefore, he says, "I truly tell you.
This shows that the Tathāgata describes what he has taught as being without falsehood and thus worthy of trust. The two phrases beginning with "You still...

reprimand him for failing to awaken when he ought to have done so, and for being deluded when he should not have been. [The passage] beginning with "Ānanda" below follows his delusion to seek the essence. If it were necessarily spontaneous...
First, establish the point by means of a premise. One must personally discern and clarify [the nature of things] before being taught to personally investigate and examine them;
there must necessarily be a clear, vivid, and natural essence. "You, for your part," he says, addressing him from within this context to pose a question:
"The wondrously bright true vision perceives all phenomena universally. For your part, observe within this wondrously bright vision: what do you take to be the 'seeing'?"
"Is it the natural substance? This is a general inquiry. "Does this vision, moreover...

and so forth are individual questions asked one by one to clarify whether brightness constitutes its own nature—that is, to determine if vision takes only brightness as its natural substance—and likewise whether darkness constitutes its own nature, and so on.
This can be known by such examples. Second, a detailed refutation of the objection:
"Ānanda, if brightness were its own nature, it should not perceive darkness; if again emptiness were its own essence, it should not perceive obstruction.
In this way, even up to the various characteristics such as darkness—if these were taken as its own nature, then the nature [of seeing] would still be perceived at the time of brightness."
[This would be] annihilationism. What is meant by "seeing light"?

That which is "self-existent" does not undergo transformation according to conditions. If one were to see light as being the self, one should not see darkness, because it would not follow the conditions of darkness—just as a fish in water meets with land and perishes from exhaustion. This is to be applied by analogy to [the views that] space is the self, and so forth.
This can be understood. "In this manner, up to... refers to the abbreviation by skipping over [the intermediate stages].
As for "darkness and other such signs": midnight, the black moon, clouds, mist, and gloom—all these constitute the sign of darkness.

Since one takes seeing darkness as one's own [nature], one should naturally not depend on the condition of light; therefore, it is difficult to observe its cessation during times of light. Why is this?

If one sees light and necessarily raises such an objection—claiming that because the nature of seeing comes to see light and comes to see darkness, and so forth—then apart from what has been stated here, how could there be any sense of spontaneity? This concludes the formal resolution of the preceding doubt.

The second section comprises two parts that together refute a further misconception: first, Ānanda’s shift to the view of causes and conditions; second, the Tathāgata’s refutation based on that very view. Regarding the first:
Ānanda said, "If this wondrous nature of seeing is not spontaneous, then I now discern that it must arise from causes and conditions."
Still not clear, I inquire of the Tathāgata: how is this meaning consistent with the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?

It must be that this wondrous vision and so forth were previously established as not being self-originated; yet now, by clarifying them as "I have manifested," you instead cling to them as being dependently originated.
This is because dependent origination and spontaneity (*svabhāva*) are diametrically opposed. Previously, one harbored doubts because [the manifestation] appeared to be non-dependent origination.
This refers to "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*). Here, the Buddha again refutes spontaneity by turning toward the adherence to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

How could one know that both causes and conditions and spontaneity are equally mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*)? Ordinary people do not understand that all is but mind-only (*cittamātra*); there is no one capable of escaping this delusion.

What is called "clarification through illumination" refers to an illumination established through opposition; it is not true knowledge. Since it is not true knowledge, one must seek a definitive resolution.
Inquiry: This meaning refers to the nature that is not subject to arising and ceasing, and which is free from delusion and inversion. Originally, it is not conjoined with causes and conditions.
Although [the opponent] attempts to refute this by relying on causes, they instead cling to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which is difficult to reconcile logically.
Therefore, he asks again, "How [is it so]? Second, the Tathāgata refutes their clinging in two parts: first, refuting the meaning of the cause; second, refuting...
Regarding the meaning of conditions:
First, the Buddha said, "As for what you say regarding causes and conditions, I shall question you further.

Now, as this seeing-nature manifests before you due to your sight, does this seeing exist because of light? Does it exist because of darkness? Does it exist because of emptiness? Does it exist because of obstruction?"
Ānanda, if existence were dependent upon light, one should not perceive darkness; if existence were dependent upon darkness, one should not perceive light.
This applies likewise to everything from space to obstruction, which are analogous to light and darkness.
First, the thesis and the fixed cause are restated. Your statement "the faculty of sight" (cakṣur-vijñāna) is a general restatement of what you maintain.
I, moreover, [assert] that the fixed cause is seen to exist. *Zhengmai* says: After "seen," the characters "bright and dark" (*āloka-tamas*) should be supplemented;

this refers to the beginning of the manifestation in response to objects. The phrase "this seeing" and below generally interrogates four meanings. Regarding "because of brightness there is seeing": this takes brightness as the cause for the arising of seeing.
The rest may be understood by analogy. ○ [Section on] Ānanda: Refuting two examples. Second, because light exists, it is explained as the cause for the arising of seeing.

When the light departs and darkness arrives, the cause for the arising of seeing has already vanished. Since there is no principle by which one can seek a sprout from what is seedless, it is said that "one should not perceive darkness.
This is to be understood by analogy with the phrase "because of darkness existing," and so forth. Thus, even up to [the subsequent points], it should be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, by using the examples of light and darkness, the arguments that [the visual faculty] exists because of emptiness or exists because of obstruction are refuted. Second, the refutation of the argument regarding conditions:
Furthermore, Ānanda, this seeing again exists depending on light; it exists depending on darkness; it exists depending on emptiness.
Because of the obstruction, there is the perception of the wall. O Ānanda, if you perceive because of space, you should not see the obstruction;
if you perceive because of the obstruction, you should not see space. This applies even to perceiving light or darkness, which are the same as space and the obstruction.

First, the four meanings are collectively questioned. Regarding "having vision conditioned by light," this means that light serves as the condition for the arising of vision; the other cases should be understood accordingly.

○ From "Ānanda" onwards, there is the refutation of two examples, the second of which concerns "having [vision] conditioned by space," meaning that space serves as the condition for the arising of vision.

Since the exhaustion [of the eyes], though it arises from staring, is manifested by way of an object, the terms "concomitant," "together with," and "identical" are used as analogies to reveal this principle. This has two meanings: first, using analogy to believe in the truth.
To say that the nature seen within the eyes is fundamentally based on the true nature of Bodhi may be easily believed by people;
yet that the symptoms of fatigue produced by staring are also fundamentally based on the true nature of Bodhi is difficult for all to understand. Therefore, it is said that "both are equally Bodhi.

The Buddha’s intention is to use the fact that the nature of the sense organs is fundamentally true as an analogy to show that those symptoms of fatigue are likewise fundamentally true. Second, one knows the delusion through such analogical comparison.
It is easy for all people to understand that the appearance of visual fatigue resulting from staring is merely a false illusion without reality.

However, it may be difficult for some to believe that the nature of seeing within the eyes is likewise merely a false illusion without reality. Therefore, it is said that both are equally the result of visual fatigue.

The Buddha’s intention is to use the example of the falsity of visual fatigue to illustrate that the nature of seeing is also purely illusory. Through this analogy between these two meanings, one gains conviction.

"Truly. This serves to simultaneously resolve the previous doubts. Previously, it was stated that while floating dust and illusory transformations are of a nature that is truly the essence of wondrous enlightened clarity, these present signs of eye-strain produced by staring also belong to the category of floating dust and illusory transformations.

For those whose previous doubts remained unresolved, this provides a further explanation. By analogy, one knows that [the eyes] are false; this is the correct meaning of the main text. Observe the following passage:

This serves to distinguish the delusion so that it may be known. Second, the naming of the emergence and the discernment of the counterfeit. This has two parts: first, the naming of the emergence as a brief manifestation;
second, the detailed discernment through the investigation of its causes. Regarding the first:

based upon the two kinds of delusory objects—light and darkness—the faculty of vision arises in the interval between them. It draws in these objective images and names this process "the nature of seeing."
This seeing is ultimately without substance apart from those two objects of clarity and darkness.
At first, it seems to exist by relying on these objects; because clarity and darkness alternate with one another, they are called "delusive objects.

Because the seeing arises due to these objects and subsequently takes those objects as its condition, it is said to be "situated in the midst" [of them]. This means it draws in the images of the objects to constitute its own domain. This is the correct [explanation].

Because it possesses this functional capacity, it is designated as "seeing the nature. To say that it is "named" [as such] further reveals that it is merely a phantom and delusion, a designation for appearances.

Regarding the phrase "this seeing," below: apart from objects, it truly does not exist. If one discusses the two aspects of light and darkness, they are constantly continuous and there is no time when they are separated.
What is meant by "separation" refers to the realization that the apprehension of objects is solely mind.
When observing the mind, objects are forgotten. Since objects do not exist, from where could seeing arise? Therefore, it is said that they ultimately have no substance.
This is like the ear-faculty entering the stream and losing its object; motion and stillness do not arise. Even "the hearing and the heard being exhausted" is precisely aligned with this.
Among the six knots, one can only resolve the first three; yet if one can further awaken to the "awakened" and the "object of awakening," [then all are resolved].
When emptiness, up to and including cessation, manifests before one, it is precisely the wondrous true suchness-nature of the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha.
Thus we know that although it is said to be "without substance," this is merely for the purpose of suddenly realizing that appearances are false and advancing to reach the truth of the nature;

it is not the same as the ultimate destruction of the conscious mind mentioned previously. The remaining five entries should be understood accordingly. Second, a detailed analysis by inferring the causes. Part two.
First, a general indication that [the vision] has no source; second, a detailed analysis breaking down each part.
First: "Ānanda, you should know this: this seeing does not come from light or darkness; it does not emerge from the sense organ; nor is it produced in space."
Zhengmo says: "Based on worldly sentiments and faculties, this [first position] constitutes the primary argument; the other two merely serve to prevent its transformation.
The text divides them into two parts to refute each. Why is this?
If [the seeing] came from light, then it would perish along with darkness, and thus it should not be able to see in the dark. If it came from darkness..."
When light appears, it immediately ceases; thus, there should be no seeing of light. If [seeing] were produced from the sense organ, there would necessarily be neither light nor darkness;

likewise, this essence of seeing would fundamentally lack self-nature. If it emerged from empty space, then when one gazes at external objects before oneself, one should instead see the sense organ upon returning [to the source]. Furthermore, if empty space were observing itself, what would it have to do with your faculty of perception?
In this passage, there are four points. The first, which follows from the preceding inquiry, is easily understood. Second, [the text] refutes the notion that [vision] comes from external objects.
If one were to claim that this vision comes from light, then vision would have light as its cause. Since it would have light as its cause...
In darkness, light is extinguished; when it is seen, it is extinguished accordingly. Because there is no cause for its arising, the effect is extinguished along with it;
thus, one should not perceive darkness. How then can one continue to see darkness as before? This should be understood by analogy regarding [the view that] it comes from darkness and so forth.
(3) Refuting [the view] that it arises from the sense organ: If you claim that this seeing arises from the sense organ, it would necessarily have no dependence on light or darkness. It must...
Know that ignorance is without darkness, for the essence of vision is fundamentally devoid of self-nature; this has already been demonstrated above, as it has no substance apart from objects.
4. Refuting [the view] that it emerges from space: If you claim that this vision emerges from space, then space must enter the eye.
In that case, its gazing outward at external objects would indeed be appropriate. However, whatever emerges must have a place of return. If it were to return to space, [the vision would vanish].

On the contrary, one ought to perceive the sense-faculties (*indriya*). Since this does not occur, we know that [the cognition] does not emerge from space. Furthermore, even if one were to grant that it emerges from space, it would be space itself that is capable of observing;
what concern would this have with your "entrances" (*āyatana*)? This further reveals the error in their argument. The refutation of the false claim regarding its emergence is concluded.
Third, the conclusion through refutation and demonstration:
Therefore, one should know that the eye-entrance is false and illusory; it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor by a spontaneous nature.

Since it arises from nowhere within these three locations, it is entirely like a wearying appearance; hence it is called "false and illusory. Consciousness is Bodhi itself, appearing due to the fixed gaze [of the mind]. It does not...

When one stares, it remains as ever the Bodhi-mind; therefore, it is said that "the fundamental is not [dualistic] equality. This concludes the section on the Ear-entrance (2).
