The first is the meaning of "cause": because the conjunction of the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—produces karma, which serves as the cause for birth and death.
Second is the meaning of limitation (*sīmā*). This refers to the fact that the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—each have their own boundaries and do not interfere with one another.

The Buddha, wishing to break down the boundaries between the center and the periphery to reveal the essence of the treasury of emptiness (*śūnyatā-garbha*), and to sever the causes of birth and death while demonstrating the true fruit of the *nirvāṇa*, first poses a general inquiry.
Subsequently, he proceeds to demonstrate each of these in groups of three. This serves as an opening for those who are deluded regarding both mind and form.
The mind. Furthermore, this is taught for those of inferior capacity who attain awakening through broad exposition. Second, the specific presentation of the six [bases] consists of:

1. the eye, form, and visual consciousness element; 2. the ear, sound, and auditory consciousness element; 3. the nose, odor, and olfactory consciousness element; 4. the tongue, taste, and gustatory consciousness element; 5.

the body, tangibles, and tactile consciousness element; 6. the mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness element. Regarding the first three: first, they are established according to provisional [teachings].
Section on the Elements. Second, distinguishing delusion with respect to consciousness. Third, concluding the discussion by showing the fetters. First:
"Ānanda, as you have understood it, visual consciousness arises with the eye and forms as conditions."
There are two meanings to what you have clarified. First, it refers specifically to Ānanda;

for in the passage on the refutation of consciousness, he once cited these words, and we grant that he was already capable of such clarification. Second, it refers generally to the provisional teachings (*upāya-śāsana*);

that is to say, as clarified in your provisional teachings, the arising of consciousness from the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) is that which was taught in the provisional teachings of the past.

Because it is so stated, between these two meanings, the latter is more logically sound. This is because, among the various realms discussed below, Ānanda has never cited the arising of ear-consciousness and so forth based on the conditions of the ear and sound.
Zhengmo says: "That which is called the eye-faculty and the object of form are in relative opposition, internal and external;
within the space between them, eye-consciousness arises—this is the internal, the external, and the intermediate."
Thus, the three realms are established. All subsequent sections follow this pattern. Second, the analysis of delusion with respect to consciousness (*vijñāna*).

(The reason for analyzing it solely in terms of consciousness is that when the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) correspond, consciousness arises between them, much like three families living as neighbors. If the boundary wall of the middle family were removed, the boundaries of both the left and right families would cease to exist. Furthermore, according to the *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse), there are three types of distinctions in the method of breaking down the dharmas within the three categories of bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and aggregates (*skandha*).

The first is "breaking by way of conditions" (*pratyaya-bheda*). This means not restricting oneself to the primary dharma itself, but extensively breaking down external conditions. It is like extinguishing a fire not by directly striking the flames, but by removing the fuel; the fire will then extinguish of its own accord. This is because the fire...

They lack intrinsic nature. Second, they are mutually sublated. This means that when two phenomena are established in mutual dependence, they must be mutually sublated. It is like a water-demon (*nāga*) and water, which depend on one another and both become a source of affliction; to eliminate them, one expels the demon and cuts off the source of the water.

The draining of water is the destruction of the dragon’s dwelling. These three methods of "destruction by way of the essential" (*yāo-pò*) are of two kinds. First, the destruction of two factors by way of the essential: it is like two pieces of wood standing leaning against each other; if one side is pushed over, both fall together. Second, the destruction of three factors by way of the essential:

it is like sinew, horn, and glue joined together to form a bow, where the glue is the essential element; if the glue is removed, the sinew and horn can no longer function as a bow. To examine the aforementioned method of destroying the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it is entirely based on conditions (*pratyaya*), for the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are precisely those conditions.

Within the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the four bases of eye/form, ear/sound, nose/smell, and tongue/taste are mutually destroyed with one another. As for the two bases of body/touch, they are destroyed solely by way of the sense organs (*indriya*). The remaining six bases are destroyed solely by way of the sensory objects. All [of these] involve two [factors].

The Dharma is analyzed by means of its essential categories. Within these eighteen *dhātus*, the analysis of phenomena consists entirely of three essential categories; among these three, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the primary category. Although the text follows this essential approach, the underlying intent actually refutes all [categories] equally.

This differs from the case of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), where the primary intent lies in the sense organs (*indriya*). This can be clearly seen upon examining the concluding sections. Second: First, identifying consciousness to examine the *dhātus*; second, analyzing the text to refute each [category] individually. Regarding the first:
Does this consciousness arise because of the eye and thus take the eye as its element (*dhātu*), or does it arise because of form and thus take form as its element?
Here, "this consciousness" refers specifically to the consciousness that arises from a particular object. The phrase "does it... and so forth interrogates what constitutes its element.

This is because while the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) each have distinct names, consciousness itself has none. If it were not associated with the sense organs and their objects, [it would be impossible to identify].

There is no such discrimination. However, most sūtras clarify that [the sense-faculties] are the basis of attachment. Now, according to the provisional teachings, both the sense-object (*viṣaya*) and the sense-faculty (*indriya*) can give rise to consciousness;
thus, it would follow that the basis of attachment for the two is not fixed. Therefore, the text addresses both the faculty and the object to investigate which constitutes the "element" (*dhātu*).

The intent is this: that which arises because of the eye is called the "eye-consciousness element" (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*); by analogy, one should understand that which arises because of form (*rūpa*).

The two parts of the text each refute three [positions]: first, refuting that it is tied to the sense organ (*indriya*) as unestablished; second, refuting that it is tied to the object (*viṣaya*) as unestablished;
third, refuting that it is tied to both as unestablished. First:
Ānanda, if [consciousness] arises because of the eye, then since there is neither form nor emptiness to be distinguished, even if your consciousness were present, what would you have it serve?
Furthermore, your seeing is not blue, yellow, red, or white; having nothing to represent it, from where could its boundaries be established?
First, the direct refutation of the sense-faculties as the cause: If you claim that this consciousness arises from the eye, it should not depend upon form and space.
Since there is no form or space to be known, there would be nothing to differentiate; thus, to say it cannot produce consciousness is merely a pretext.

Even if one were to grant that it could produce it, what use would your "consciousness" have? When there is no place for its function, on what basis can you speak of consciousness? This clarifies [the point].

"Know that it does not arise from the eye. [The Master] provides this precaution against erroneous argumentation regarding "your seeing. Having been at liberty to hear the refutation of its arising from the sense organ, you have erroneously argued:

"What is called 'arising from the eye' does not refer to the physical sense organ (*rūpa-indriya*), but rather refers to the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*); therefore, this precaution was made.

This intention is based on the fact that whenever a realm (*dhātu*) is established, there must necessarily be a perceptible form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) upon which to rely; even if it were to arise from seeing...
Furthermore, what you perceive is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white; it cannot be designated. From what, then, could the realm of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) be established?
Thus, one knows that what is called the "eye-consciousness realm" is merely a false designation. Second, the attachment to the object (ālambana) is untenable.
If [your consciousness] arises because of form, then when space is devoid of form, your consciousness should cease; how then could it cognize the nature of emptiness?
If, when form changes, you also cognize the shifting and changing characteristics of that form, yet your consciousness does not shift, from what basis would its realm be established?
If it follows change, then the characteristics of its realm would naturally be non-existent. If it does not change, then it is constant; since it arises from form, it should not [be constant].
One cognizes the location of empty space.
Initially, one correctly breaks away from attachment to objects. If you claim that this consciousness arises because of form (*rūpa*), then it should be unable to arise apart from form.

One must know that form undergoes change and cessation; where there is change and cessation, there is emptiness. When you reach the state of emptiness where there is no form, your consciousness would not exist.
If [space] were caused by form, it would necessarily be subject to cessation. If it were subject to cessation, then even emptiness should not be cognized.
Yet, at the time when form undergoes transformation and ceases, how could one cognize this nature of space? This clearly demonstrates that [the cognition of space] does not arise from form.

The passage "If form... and below serves as a preemptive defense against erroneous arguments. Fearing that the difficulty raised by the question "How can one cognize space? might lead others to erroneously argue that "cognition arises from [form]," [the author] provides this clarification.
Form arises; though form changes, consciousness itself does not change. Why, then, do you not admit that consciousness is empty? It is for this reason that [the following] defense is offered:
If you claim that when form undergoes transition, you likewise cognize the transition of its form-characteristics, then your consciousness itself must be non-transient.
Even if one were to grant it is non-transient, it still cannot constitute a "constituent" (*dhātu*), because apart from form there is no basis upon which a constituent could be established.

Thus, one should know that what is called the "consciousness-element of form" is merely a false designation. From the phrase "from transformation," he employs a sophistry of equivocation (*kuhaka*) to block [the argument], fearing that his position will be refuted by the principle of change.
He thus equivocates, saying, "It proceeds from transformation. Then, fearing that this "proceeding from transformation" will be refuted, he further equivocates, saying, "It is unchanging.
Therefore, the refutation states: If you claim it proceeds from transformation, then it must undergo transformation and extinction, and would consequently lack substantiality.
If this were so, the characteristics of the elements would naturally be non-existent, rendering further verbal elaboration unnecessary.
If you claim that [consciousness] is unchanging, then its nature should be eternally constant. Being eternally constant, it should only perceive form since it arises from form;

it should not perceive the location of empty space. Since neither of these is the case, your argument is merely sophistry. How could there truly be such a principle as consciousness arising from form?
The three [defects] and the two [alternatives] would both fail to be established.

If the eye and form were to arise together in both ways, then when they are joined, they would be separated in the middle; when they are separated, they would be joined at both ends. With such a confusion of their essential natures, how could they constitute a "constituent" (*dhātu*)?

Fearing that neither the arising from the auditory faculty nor the arising from external objects would be established, one then calculates that they arise together; therefore, this refutation is made.
If it is claimed that this consciousness has both types as its cause, such that it arises together through the conjunction of the internal eye and external forms:
First, one must carefully determine whether this consciousness is conjoined with the sense organ and the object, or separated from them.
If it were conjoined with the sense organ and the object, then the consciousness in the interval between them would naturally be divided into two:

the half conjoined with the eye would belong to that which possesses cognition, while the half conjoined with the form would belong to that which lacks cognition; thus, its essential nature would be disordered. If...
If it were separated from both the sense faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*), then the consciousness in between would have to be half of the eye and half of the form.

These two halves would combine to produce a state where the sentient and the insentient are indistinguishable, just as when water and earth mix to form mud, their essential natures become intermingled.
Since they are thus mixed and disordered, how could they constitute a middle realm? This is analyzed with respect to consciousness.
The refutation of delusion is complete. Third, the conclusion is established through analysis and demonstration.
Therefore, one should know that although eye and form serve as conditions for the arising of the visual consciousness-element, these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the eye, form, and the visual consciousness-element—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.

Because neither individual arising nor simultaneous arising can be established, one should know that what was taught in the former teachings—namely, that consciousness arises conditioned by [the sense organs]—is entirely non-existent in these three locations. Since there is nothing in between, how could internal and external be distinguished?
If one traces back from the branches to the root, then this eye, form, and the realm of form—these three—are in their very essence not causes or conditions.

It is not of a spontaneous nature. The *Zhengmai* states: "The realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) refers to the realm of form-consciousness (*rūpa-vijñāna-dhātu*). This takes 'dust' (*viṣaya*) as its alternative name;
furthermore, the character 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*) is omitted, and the following two sections follow this pattern. The section on the eye, form, and consciousness-realm concludes.

Second, the three sections on the ear, sound, and the element of auditory consciousness: first, establishing the provisional nature of the elements; second, analyzing the delusion from the perspective of consciousness;
third, concluding the analysis with a summary and demonstration.
Regarding the first: "Ānanda, furthermore, that which you understand—the ear and sound acting as conditions to give rise to auditory consciousness."

Second, distinguishing delusion with respect to consciousness, which has two parts: first, identifying consciousness and examining its constituent elements; second, analyzing the text to refute each [element]. Regarding the first:
Is this consciousness produced because of the ear, taking the ear as its element? Or is it produced because of sound, taking sound as its element?

The two parts of the text each refute three points: first, refuting that [the cognition] is tied to the sense organ (*indriya*) as unestablished; second, refuting that it is tied to the object (*viṣaya*) as unestablished;
third, refuting that it is tied to both as unestablished. First:

Ānanda, if [the faculty of hearing] were produced by means of the ear, then since the two characteristics of motion and stillness are not present before it, the faculty would not constitute cognition; there would necessarily be nothing known.

If even cognition cannot be established, what form could consciousness have? If one takes the act of "hearing" as belonging to the ear, then because there is neither motion nor stillness, the act of hearing itself cannot be established.
How then can the physical form of the ear, along with the objects of color and touch, be called the element of consciousness? Thus, the element of ear-consciousness—
Furthermore, from whom is this established?
First, it correctly refutes the dependence on the sense organ. If one were to claim that this consciousness arises because of the ear, then it should not depend upon motion and stillness.
Since the two characteristics of motion and stillness must be known and yet do not appear before one, the sense organ alone cannot constitute cognition. It must...
It reaches a state of utter emptiness and voidness where nothing at all is known. Yet, consciousness manifests because of knowing;
now that even knowing is absent, even if consciousness were to arise, what form or appearance could it possibly rely upon? Thus, it is clearly understood that it does not arise from the ear.

○ If one adopts the former [position] to prevent fallacious arguments, there is a fear that since even "hearing" (*śruta*) has not yet been established as a cognition, what kind of form could there be to refute?
Consequently, a fallacious argument is raised: "The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) relies upon knowing, whereas the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) relies solely upon hearing.

Since there is no 'knowing' but there is 'hearing,' the auditory consciousness can thus arise. It is for this reason that [the author] provides this prevention. If one adopts the latter [position], it refers to the capacity for hearing within the ear.
The arising consciousness should likewise not depend upon movement or stillness; since one must know that there is neither movement nor stillness, the nature of hearing is also not established.
If even hearing is not established, how much more so the arising consciousness? It cannot exist naturally. The passage beginning with "How can...

serves to prevent further errors, guarding against the refutation that because hearing lacks movement and stillness, the nature of hearing is not established. Furthermore, it prevents a subsequent shift [in argument].

The erroneous [objection] states: "What is so wrong about simply taking the form of the ear as that which produces consciousness? Therefore, this [sūtra] provides a safeguard, stating that the producer and the produced must necessarily be of a similar nature.

Consciousness is capable of discrimination and thus belongs to the category of the sentient (saṃjñin); the form of the ear, along with color, odor, taste, and touch, belongs to the category of the insentient (asaṃjñin).

(The form of the ear has the four sensory objects as its substance—namely, color, odor, taste, and touch. In the text, two are mentioned explicitly, while the others are subsumed under the term 'sensory object' [viṣaya].)"

If one considers the auditory faculty (*śrotra*), its form, the various colors, and the tactile objects as the "element that gives rise to consciousness," this is difficult to explain because cause and effect are dissimilar.
The final two lines serve as a summary conclusion to this objection:
since both the arising of the ear and the arising of hearing are illogical, from what then does that which is called the "auditory consciousness element" (*śrotravijñānadhātu*) arise in the world?
It stands; this is merely a phantom and delusion designated as a "mark. Second, if it were attached to the dust [the object], it would not be established.
If it arose from sound, then since consciousness would exist because of sound, it would have no relation to hearing. Without hearing, the locus of the mark of sound would vanish.
If consciousness arises from sound, and you grant that sound exists because of hearing, then the characteristic of sound should be heard by the hearing-consciousness.

If it is not heard, it is not a sense-object; if it is heard, it is identical to sound. Since consciousness has already been "heard," who would know the hearing-consciousness? If there were no knower, one would ultimately be like grass or wood.

First, to directly refute the attachment to external objects: if one claims that this consciousness arises from sound, then since this consciousness would exist because of sound, it should have no relation to the hearing of the ear.
One must know that sound is manifested through hearing; if there were no hearing, the locus of the characteristic of sound would also be lost.
Since the characteristic of sound itself does not exist, how could consciousness arise? It is certain that it cannot.
[This is] so. ○ [The Master] anticipates a fallacious argument from below. Fearing that upon hearing the refutation that "there is no hearing and no sound," one might mistakenly argue:
"This consciousness certainly exists because of sound, yet the sound that produces it exists because of hearing.
It is like a grandfather being born from a father, and a son being born from a father; this is perfectly established by reason and requires no further words."

Therefore, this safeguard was established. If you claim that this consciousness definitely arises from sound, yet you only grant that this sound exists because of hearing, then one must also hear the consciousness when hearing the sound;
for if consciousness arises from sound, then since consciousness is present within the sound, both [sound and consciousness] should be heard together.
○ The section "Not hearing... below unfolds the errors in turn. There are four [points]. First:

It is not the case that there is no error in saying one does not hear what is not a constituent element (*dhātu*). Suppose it is claimed that one can only hear sound and cannot hear consciousness; this would mean that consciousness is absent within the sound.

Since consciousness is absent within the sound, the sound itself could not be the constituent element that gives rise to consciousness. If both [sound and consciousness] were heard, then the error regarding sound would apply equally.
Suppose it is claimed that hearing sound actually means being able to hear consciousness; then consciousness, like sound, would be something heard by the ear.

Third is the fallacy of hearing the unknown. You claim that what is heard by the ear can only be known by consciousness; yet now that consciousness has been heard, there would be no one capable of knowing it.
Therefore, it is difficult to maintain that "someone knows the hearing-consciousness. Fourth is the fallacy of being identical to grass and trees.
If you assert that the hearing-consciousness has no knower, and take this as a precedent, then the hearing of sounds likewise would have no knower.
[If you] know [nothing], since there is ultimately nothing known, you would eventually be like grass and trees, rather than belonging to the category of sentient beings.
Thus, the three refutations and two constraints are not established.

It is not appropriate for the Śrāvakas to intermingle and form a middle realm (*madhyadhātu*). If the realm lacks a middle position, then from what could the characteristics of "internal" and "external" be established?
Fearing that both the arising of the ear and the arising of sound would fail to be established, one then calculates that they arise together through conjunction;
therefore, this refutation is made. If one calculates that this consciousness arises through the conjunction of these factors, then sound and hearing would intermingle to form a middle realm.
When examined according to the logic of the matter, it cannot be so; for if they are intermingled, they are indistinguishable and thus cannot be established.

Because it has no middle. Since the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) thus lacks a middle position, from what could the internal characteristic of the ear-element (śrotradhātu) and the external characteristic of the sound-element (śabdadhātu) be established?
These three locations are all unestablished. This concludes the analysis of the falsity of consciousness.
Third, the conclusion is established through analysis and demonstration.
Therefore, one should know that when the ear and sound serve as conditions to produce the auditory consciousness-element (śrotra-vijñāna-dhātu), these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the ear, the sound, and the auditory consciousness-element—these three—are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
The explanation of the meaning follows the precedent above. This concludes the Ear, Sound, and Consciousness Elements. Next, the three [sections] on the Nose, Odor, and Consciousness Elements:
first, defining the elements according to provisional designations; second, discerning delusion based on consciousness; third, concluding the discussion with a summary indication. First:
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that the nose and fragrance serve as conditions to produce nose-consciousness—this consists of two parts:
first, identifying consciousness to examine its realm; second, analyzing the text to refute it point by point. First:
Is this consciousness produced by the nose and thus has the nose as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or is it produced by the fragrance and thus has the fragrance as its constituent element?

Each of these two textual divisions refutes three points: first, it refutes that [the consciousness] is tied to the sense organ, which is untenable; second, it refutes that [the consciousness] is tied to the object, which is untenable.
The three refutations of the two positions are not established. First, the two [positions]: first, the inquiry regarding the nose; second, the sequential refutation. Regarding the first:
"Ānanda, if it arises because of the nose, then within your mind, what do you take to be the nose? Is it the physical form of the flesh and the two nostrils?"
This is its characteristic. It takes up the nature of movement through smelling and knowing.

If the nose were produced by depending on your words, then what would those words be for the nose? To take up these two points, he poses two questions. "Fleshly form" refers to the floating root (the physical organ).

Later it says, "The four objects of the floating root are these. "Two claws" refers to... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist commentary discussing the nature of the sense organs and their relationship to consciousness and external objects. The translation reflects the technical terminology used in such contexts.)
Regarding the *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense organ): it is as described later, where the pure four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are like a pair of hanging claws.

"Smelling" refers to the nature of that which smells; "movement" refers to the fragrance being smelled. Before reaching the stage of consciousness (*vijñāna-bhūmi*), distinctions have not yet been differentiated;
there is only the appearance of movement. That which can smell and can know this is the very nature of the sense organ (*indriya*). As stated later: "The essence of smelling reflects."
This refers to fragrance. Second, each point is refuted individually in two parts: first, refuting the claim that the physical flesh constitutes the nose;
second, refuting the claim that the act of smelling constitutes the nose. Regarding the first:

if one takes the physical form and substance of the flesh to be the nose, then since it is known by the body, it is contact (*spraṣṭavya*); what is called the "body" is not the nose, and what is called "contact" is an object (*viṣaya*).
Since the nose itself lacks a name, how can one establish it as a distinct element (*dhātu*)?

As for its fleshy form, it also extends to both nostrils; although they differ in coarseness and subtlety, their substance is the same in that they consist of the four sense-objects (*viṣaya*). To refute [the opponent's] position:
if one takes the fleshy form to be the nose, then the fundamental substance of that fleshy form is what is called the body (*kāya*), or else one would have to take the body [itself] as the nose.
That which is known by the body is precisely what is called "contact" (*sparśa*). Since the fleshy substance is called the "body," it is not the nose.
If that which is known by the body is called "contact," then it must be the sense-object (*viṣaya*). Thus, both of these lack the name "nose.
If even the nose has no name, how can consciousness arise based upon it to establish the designation of the "nose-consciousness element"?

This is merely empty delusion. Second, refuting [the opponent] by means of the nose as the organ of smell has three parts: first, the direct refutation of the three meanings; second, preventing erroneous arguments; third, simultaneously preventing further erroneous shifts. First: The term "only" (惟) excludes the possibility that this is anything other than empty delusion. It is because the nature of the nose-organ is empty that it cannot perceive odors; therefore, the statement that "the nose can smell" is false. Furthermore, since the nature of the nose-organ is empty, it cannot be the agent of smelling. Thus, the claim that "the nose smells" is false. Moreover, since the nature of the nose-organ is empty, it cannot be the locus of smelling. Therefore, the assertion that "smelling occurs within the nose" is false. Consequently, the three propositions—that the nose itself smells, that the nose perceives odors, and that smelling occurs within the nose—are all false. This constitutes the direct refutation of the three meanings. Second, preventing erroneous arguments. Here, one anticipates the opponent's potential rebuttal: "If the nose does not smell, then what does smell? Is it not the case that the consciousness smells? To prevent this, the text states: "It is not the case that the consciousness smells. Why? Because the nature of consciousness is empty, it cannot be the agent of smelling. Therefore, the claim that "consciousness smells" is false. Furthermore, since the nature of consciousness is empty, it cannot be the locus of smelling. Thus, the assertion that "smelling occurs within the consciousness" is false. Consequently, the proposition that "consciousness smells" is also false. This prevents the opponent from shifting their argument to consciousness. Third, simultaneously preventing further erroneous shifts. Here, one anticipates the opponent's further rebuttal: "If neither the nose nor the consciousness smells, then perhaps the contact between the two smells? To prevent this, the text states: "Nor is it the case that the contact between the two smells. Why? Because the nature of contact is empty, it cannot be the agent of smelling. Therefore, the claim that "contact smells" is false. Furthermore, since the nature of contact is empty, it cannot be the locus of smelling. Thus, the assertion that "smelling occurs within the contact" is false. Consequently, the proposition that "contact smells" is also false. This simultaneously prevents the opponent from shifting their argument to the contact between the two. This concludes the first section.

If you claim that it is known through smelling, then in your mind, what constitutes this "knowing"? If the flesh constitutes the knowing, then the knowing of the flesh is fundamentally a matter of touch and not the nose.
If emptiness constitutes the knowing, then emptiness would know itself, and the flesh should not be perceived;
if this were so, then empty space would be you and your body would have no faculty of cognition, meaning that today, Ānanda, you would have no place of existence. If [the nose]...
"Perfume is what is known. Since knowing belongs to the perfume itself, what concern is it to you?

First, he generally challenges [the opponent] by asking, "What constitutes knowing? That which smells and knows is of a fluctuating nature. Since this nature is not without substance, he challenges him by asking, "What constitutes knowing?
[The text continues: "By means of the flesh," etc., first refutes the notion that the flesh constitutes knowing. By means of the flesh...
Regarding "that which is known by the knower": this means that what is known by the flesh is taken as the nature of olfactory cognition.
However, since olfactory cognition belongs to the nose, what is known by the flesh is fundamentally tactile rather than olfactory. As I stated above, bodily cognition is precisely tactile.
What is called "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*) is precisely the object (*viṣaya*). How could it be that there is no nature of olfactory cognition?

[The text] next refutes the notion that emptiness is the knower by means of the phrase "by means of emptiness. To say that emptiness is the knower means to claim that the emptiness within the nose constitutes the nature of olfactory cognition.
However, if emptiness were to possess cognition, then emptiness would know itself; consequently, the flesh of the nose would naturally not be sentient. Sentience is also cognition. For example...
In that case, empty space must be you, and your body is not the knower. By the example of the nasal cavity having cognition, one may infer that all cavities have cognition;
therefore, empty space is you. By the example of the nasal flesh being insentient, one may infer that the flesh of the entire body is insentient;
therefore, your body is not the knower. Based on these two principles, Ānanda, you should today be non-existent.
As for its location: since space is your emptiness and has no location, you likewise have no location. Your body is not consciousness; even if it had a location, it would not be self-aware.
How could this possibly be logical? Below this, [the text] refutes the notion that fragrance constitutes consciousness.
To say that fragrance constitutes consciousness means to claim that the fragrance within the nose is the nature of the faculty of smelling. However, as for fragrance...
If there is cognition, then that cognition belongs to the fragrance; what concern does it have with you? Yet you name it the "nature of your cognition. Here, "pre" (預) means "to interfere with" (干).
This second point is intended to prevent erroneous arguments.
If fragrant and foul odors must arise within your nose, then those two types of flowing air—the fragrant and the foul—would not exist in the *eranda* tree or the sandalwood tree.
Since these two substances do not come to you, you would have to smell your own nose to determine whether it is fragrant or foul; yet if it were foul, it could not be fragrant.
Fragrance ought not to be foul-smelling.
Fearing that [the opponent] might object, "How does the act of smelling concern your refutation? he then offers this fallacious argument:

"Although the cognition belongs to fragrance, the fragrance itself arises in the nose. How can you say it does not concern me? Therefore, I offer this defense. If one were to claim that fragrance arises in the nose...
For example, we know that odors also arise from the nose; thus, they must necessarily arise from your nose.
However, it is commonly accepted by the world that foul odors arise from *eranda* (Iraṇa) and fragrant scents arise from *candana* (sandalwood).

Now, if you insist that these arise from your nose, then those two kinds of moving vapors would not arise from those two substances—which is certainly impossible. Please test this for yourself. As follows:
When these two things do not come together, you yourself smell in the nose whether it is fragrant or foul.

If it is foul, it cannot produce fragrance; if it is fragrant, it should not produce foulness. Thus we know that the claim that the so-called fragrant and foul odors must necessarily arise from the nose is an error.

(The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisūtra* says: "On Mount Mālinda there is the eranda tree, whose stench is like that of a bloated corpse, and its scent pervades forty yojanas. Its flowers are red and most beautiful.")

[The Buddha said: "If anyone were to eat it, they would go mad and die. Even when *gośīrṣa-candana* grows from within a thicket of *elā* trees, while it is still small—like a bamboo shoot in Jambudvīpa—it cannot emit fragrance.

Only when the middle month of autumn is full does it suddenly sprout from the earth and become a *candana* tree; then all people smell the wondrous fragrance of the *candana*, and the foul stench of the *elā* is forever gone. (3) This also serves to prevent further errors.
If you were able to perceive both fragrance and stench simultaneously, then you, as a single person, would have to possess two noses. When I questioned you, I asked:

"Ānanda, there are two Ānandas here; which one is your true self? If the nose were a single entity and fragrance and stench were not two distinct things, then when stench becomes fragrance and fragrance again becomes stench, these two natures would not exist. From what, then, could the boundaries between them be established?

First, there is the error of claiming that both [fragrance and stench] are smelled simultaneously, which leads to the refutation: "If one smells stench, it cannot be fragrance; if it is fragrance, it should not be stench.

To avoid this error, one shifts the argument, saying: "Now, what prevents me from smelling both fragrance and stench at once? Why should both fragrance and stench not arise together from the nose? This is the defense being made.

It is stated that fragrance and stench are of different natures and the nose does not perceive them simultaneously. If one were to claim that the two gases of fragrance and stench are present together...
If it were possible for one to hear [both], then you, Ānanda, alone should have two noses:
one nose to smell fragrance and another nose to smell stench, so that they might not be confused. Yet everyone in the world knows that a single person has only one nose.
If there truly were two noses, then right now, as you question me, there should be two Ānandas. Even if you grant this...
Where there are two, there must necessarily be the true and the false. Furthermore, between these two Ānandas, which one is your true self?

You must have some means to distinguish them before you can say that there are two. Otherwise, it would be like having one nose below the bridge of the nose, which is the fallacy of possessing two noses;
it would lead to the refutation that if two noses hear, there should be two bodies. Moreover, you might further argue in error: "I am originally not two."
The nose is indeed one. Although it is but one, there is no impediment to its possessing both the two natures of fragrance and stench;

therefore, this [objection] is raised as a defense. If you claim that because the nose is but one, it must possess both the two natures of fragrance and stench, then fragrance and stench would naturally merge into one, and the two natures would not exist. Since the two do not exist, then as for stench, it would already be...
Fragrance may again become foul; as they mutually cancel each other out, both vanish and neither nature remains.

How much more so when fragrance is taken as the object of cognition or the nose itself—it is truly a case of successive delusions with nothing to rely upon. Regarding what is called the "establishment of the elements" (*dhātu*) based on the arising of consciousness:

let us ask, from whom are these elements established? Having finished refuting that the elements are not established by depending on the sense organs (*indriya*), we now refute that they are not established by depending on the objects (*viṣaya*).

If consciousness arises because of fragrance, and consciousness exists because of fragrance, then just as the eye has the capacity for seeing yet cannot see itself, so too, because consciousness exists because of fragrance, it should not know that fragrance.
To know it would mean it was not produced from it; not knowing it would mean it is not consciousness. If fragrance is not known, the fragrance-element (*gandha-dhātu*) is not established.
If consciousness does not know fragrance, then the element is not established based upon fragrance.
First, to correctly refute the attachment to objects: if you maintain that this consciousness arises because of fragrance, then this consciousness must necessarily exist because of fragrance.

Please clarify this with an analogy so that you may know for yourself that [your position] is incorrect. Just as that [consciousness] exists because of the eye, yet that seeing cannot perceive the eye;
so too is it with consciousness. Because it exists because of fragrance, it should naturally be unable to cognize fragrance itself. Furthermore...
Both knowing and not knowing entail faults. If it knows, then it does not arise from fragrance, which contradicts one's own tenet;
for it is one's own tenet that consciousness arises from fragrance. If it does not know, then it is not consciousness, which contradicts worldly convention.
This is because it is commonly accepted in the world that consciousness is capable of cognizing. [The phrase] "fragrance is not... serves as a precaution against fallacious argumentation.

Fearing that one might hear the refutation that "it is not cognized, therefore it is not consciousness," and thus mistakenly argue: "Even if it is said to be not cognized, there is no obstacle to its being consciousness," this precaution is established.
Since it has already been stated that it is not cognized, even if one were to grant that it is consciousness, when that fragrance-object (gandha-viṣaya) actually manifests, it would still [be so].
It is not that it knows existence. If this were so, the fragrance-element (gandha-dhātu) would not be established.

Furthermore, since consciousness does not know that fragrance exists, that which is called the consciousness-element (vijñāna-dhātu) established on account of fragrance would certainly not be established from fragrance.
If the three [elements] are destroyed, the two boundaries cannot be established.
Since there is no intermediate space, the internal and external cannot be established. Thus, those various natures of hearing are ultimately false and illusory.
Now, the reason the sense organs and their objects can be established as internal and external realms is because of the existence of the intermediate consciousness; since that is now absent...
Since there is no intermediate state, neither internal nor external can be established. Thus, it is not merely that the realm of consciousness lacks reality;
those natures of the hearing faculty and the heard objects are likewise ultimately false and illusory. How could there truly be any principle of the arising of consciousness?
This concludes the analysis of the falsity of consciousness. Third, the conclusion based on this analysis is presented.
Therefore, you should know that the nose, odors, and the nose-consciousness element arise with one another as conditions; yet in these three locations, none exist inherently.
Thus, the nose, odors, and the nose-element are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
Now, if the middle realm does not exist, that which is produced is fundamentally non-existent. If the internal and external are not established, how can there be a producer?
Therefore it is said that the three locations are entirely non-existent. One must know that delusion has no self-nature and that its entire substance is wholly true;

thus, it is still granted that this is fundamentally neither a nature produced by causes and conditions nor a spontaneous nature. This concludes the section on the realms of the nose, fragrance, and consciousness.

Regarding the fourth [aggregate], the tongue-taste-consciousness element, there are three parts: first, establishing the elements according to provisional designations; second, discerning delusion with respect to consciousness;
and third, concluding the discussion by showing the result. First:
"Ānanda, furthermore, as you understand it, with the tongue and tastes as conditions, tongue-consciousness arises."

Second, the analysis of delusion with respect to consciousness has two parts: first, identifying consciousness and examining its constituent elements; second, analyzing the text to refute each [element] individually. Regarding the first:
does this consciousness arise because of the tongue, taking the tongue as its element? Or does it arise because of flavors, taking flavors as its element?

The two sections of the text each refute three points: first, refuting that it is not established by being tied to the sense organ; second, refuting that it is not established by being tied to the object;
third, refuting that it is not established by being tied to both. First:
Ānanda, if [taste] were produced because of the tongue, then there would be no taste at all for the sugarcane, plum, yellow myrobalan, rock salt, fine pepper, ginger, and cinnamon found in the world.
You yourself might as well try to taste your own tongue—is it sweet or bitter? If the nature of the tongue were bitter, who would come to taste the tongue?
Since the tongue does not taste itself, what could be said to have cognition? If the nature of the tongue were not bitter, then taste would not arise of its own accord.
How are the elements established?
The first phrase determines that consciousness arises with the tongue as its cause; this clearly indicates that it does not depend upon flavor.
Regarding the subsequent passage, it teaches that one experiences the tongue apart from flavor: the sweet taste of sugarcane, the sour taste of the black plum, and the bitter taste of *huáng-lián*.

Rock salt has a salty taste; it is called "rock salt" because its lumps resemble stone. *Xi xin* (Acorus calamus) is a medicinal herb that possesses a slight pungent taste, while ginger is the most pungent among such substances.
Among medicinal ingredients, cinnamon (*rui gui*) also possesses a slight pungent taste. Of the six tastes, it lacks only the faint taste;
however, if one takes cinnamon blossoms, they may be considered faint. This is because the common name for *yan gui* (mountain cinnamon) is used here.
Osmanthus is used to impart flavor; it is valued for its subtle fragrance. It possesses no distinct flavor itself because, when all other substances are not present, all flavors are quiescent.

When the teaching asks you to taste your own tongue to see if it is sweet or bitter, the intent is that only when one is clearly distinguished from all flavors—sweetness and bitterness alike—can it be said that the consciousness arises dependent upon the tongue.
If the tongue were both painful and non-painful, it would be a contradiction.

If you claim that because the nature of the tongue is painful, the consciousness produced by it is also painful, then since pain does not perceive pain, who comes to taste the tongue for you? Do not say that the tongue can taste itself.
Judging by this principle, the tongue does not taste itself, just as the eye does not see itself; this may serve as an analogy.
Since the tongue cannot taste itself, what could come to possess the nature of cognition? Thus, we know that the claim that the nature of the tongue is suffering is erroneous.
If one were to say that the nature of the tongue is not suffering, then by applying this single case to all others, it would follow that all tastes [are likewise not suffering].

It would logically not arise. To claim that consciousness must depend on flavor for its manifestation, yet argue that since flavor does not arise, how can the designation "consciousness-element" be established—this too is erroneous.
Second, the refutation of the attachment to objects as being unestablished has two parts: first, the refutation by contradiction with one's own tenets;
second, the refutation by contradiction with the world. First:

If consciousness arises because of flavor and flavor itself becomes the object of that consciousness, then—just as it is with the tongue faculty—it should not be able to taste itself. How, then, could that consciousness discern whether something is flavor or not flavor?
If you claim that this consciousness arises because of flavor, then it would be like grain producing more grain; thus, your consciousness should become its own object.
Taste. Since consciousness itself is the taste, it logically follows that it cannot know the taste; it would be like the tongue-faculty, which cannot taste itself.
How is it that your consciousness is not thus, yet is able to cognize whether something is a taste or not? This contradicts your own tenet. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
The subject is "the consciousness produced from taste"; the thesis (*pakṣa*) is "it should not know the taste"; the reason (*hetu*) is "because consciousness is itself..."
Because it possesses the quality of taste, it would follow by analogy that the tongue-faculty itself could not taste its own flavor. How then could consciousness cognize [it]?
This directly rebukes the contradiction with one's own school and refutes the contradiction with the two worldly conventions.
Furthermore, all tastes do not arise from a single substance. Since tastes arise from many sources, the consciousness [of them] should likewise consist of multiple entities.

If the essence of consciousness were a single entity, it would necessarily arise from taste; yet when salty, bland, sweet, and pungent flavors combine and arise together, their various changing characteristics would constitute a single flavor, and there should be no discrimination.
If discrimination is absent, it cannot be called consciousness. How, then, can it again be called the tongue-consciousness of taste?

Regarding the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*): first, it is because the fault of consciousness being corrupted by excessive attachment to flavors is eliminated. Furthermore, the term is repeated to restate the previous calculation;

that is, if this consciousness were produced by flavor, it would arise from all flavors collectively rather than from a single substance, just as the sweet taste arises from sugarcane, whereas bitter taste [arises from something else].
[The flavors arise] from yellow myrobalan (*harītakī*) and so forth. However, since multiple flavors arise from multiple substances, these multiple substances are able to produce multiple flavors.

Taking this as an analogy, multiple flavors should likewise give rise to multiple consciousnesses. If that were the case, the consciousness would have multiple entities, which contradicts worldly experience;
for it is universally accepted in the world that gustatory consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*) is a single entity. [Section on the Nature of Consciousness]

The inferior consciousness has the fault of being subject to destruction by tastes. Saline, bland, sweet, and pungent include sour and bitter; these are the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the six tastes.

Their combination, simultaneous arising, and transformation constitute the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the six tastes. "Combination" refers, for example, to the blending of beans, flour, and salt to form a sauce.
"Simultaneous arising" refers, for example, to sugarcane being sweet from the moment it grows, or to *hāng-lián* (Coptis chinensis) being bitter from the moment it grows.
Regarding "suffering and so forth," as for "transformation," it is like when raw food is processed into cooked food, its original flavor changes.

The refutation of the [notion of] the mental aggregate (*manas-kalāpa*) means that if consciousness were a single entity, its substance would not arise from flavor, because cause and effect are not of the same kind.
If its substance must indeed arise from flavor, it must necessarily be derived from the six flavors—salty, bland, sweet, pungent, and so forth—as well as their combinations.
The various co-arising marks of transformation become conflated into a single flavor; since many have already formed one, that one is without fault.

However, if they are all equally a single flavor, there should be no differentiation, which contradicts worldly experience, for the world universally accepts that flavors are established through differentiation.
Regarding the phrase "differentiation": it refers to the fault of the destruction of consciousness when inferior flavors are consumed. It says:
Since the discrimination of the nature of taste is absent, the consciousness produced from it cannot be called "consciousness," for there is nothing to be cognized.
How, then, can the world further designate this consciousness as the "element of consciousness between the tongue and taste"? This is all the more evident as it contradicts worldly convention.
Thus concludes the refutation that neither [taste nor tongue] alone constitutes the object-field. Third, the refutation that both together do not constitute it.
It should not be that space gives rise to your mind-consciousness. When the tongue and flavors combine, there is fundamentally no self-nature within them;
how, then, could they give rise to an element?
Fearing that the claim that it arises from either the sense organ or the object would fail in both cases, you have instead reckoned that it arises from space. Therefore, the World-Honored One [said]:
This is because it should not be obstructed. To say that emptiness lacks the nature of consciousness—how could that possibly give rise to your mental consciousness?
This follows from the preceding text to prevent divergent views. The discussion of the union of tongue and flavor is the actual refutation of the two extremes.

Since tongue and flavor have already merged, the tongue is no longer the tongue, and flavor is no longer flavor; as they mutually cancel one another out, both vanish, and thus it is said: "immediately."
"In this, the middle has no self-nature. Here, "this" refers to the middle between the tongue and flavors;
"no self-nature" means there is no distinct self-nature for each. Since even self-nature does not exist, it is known that consciousness cannot arise.
Therefore, it is asked: "How can the elements (dhātus) arise? This concludes the analysis of delusion regarding consciousness. Third, the conclusion of the analysis and the demonstration.
Therefore, you should know that with the tongue and flavors as conditions, the tongue-consciousness element arises; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent.
Thus, the tongue, the flavors, and the tongue-element—these three are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.

The tongue-element (*jihvā-dhātu*) is the tongue-consciousness-element (*jihvā-vijñāna-dhātu*). This is named after its faculty (*indriya*). The following two elements should be understood accordingly. [This concludes] the section on the tongue, taste, and consciousness elements.

Regarding the five [remaining] elements—the body, touch, and consciousness—there are three parts: first, establishing the elements according to provisional teachings; second, discerning delusion based on consciousness;
third, concluding the discussion by providing a summary indication. First:
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that body and touch serve as conditions to give rise to body-consciousness—this consists of two parts:
first, identifying consciousness to examine its realm; second, analyzing the text to refute it point by point. First:
As for this consciousness, does it arise from the body and thus have the body as its constituent element (*dhātu*), or does it arise from contact and thus have contact as its constituent element?

The text refutes these two positions respectively in three parts each: first, the refutation that [the consciousness] is not established by being tied to the sense organ; second, the refutation that it is not established by being tied to the object.
Third, the two conditions are mutually contradictory and thus cannot be established. First:

Ānanda, if consciousness were produced because of the body, there would necessarily be neither conjunction nor separation. When the two—vitarka and vicāra—take the body as their object, what is it that cognizes?
Vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) refer to consciousness itself. Gross mental discernment is called vitarka; subtle mental discernment is called vicāra.

This corresponds to what was stated previously: "discerning vitarka and vicāra. They are divided into two types based on their relation to the objects of the senses—namely, combined vitarka-vicāra and separated vitarka-vicāra—and both are capable of being cognitive subjects (*ālambaka*). To refute this [position], one might argue that this consciousness arises from the body.
This must not rely upon the two objects of conjunction and separation; for one must know that these two objects do not exist.

Even if consciousness were produced and gave rise to the two types of vitarka and vicāra as its cognitive conditions (*ālambana*), if the body alone existed without an object, what would there be to cognize?
Thus, we know that the claim that consciousness arises because of the body is erroneous. Second, the refutation of the attachment to objects as being established.
If this consciousness were produced solely from contact, it would necessarily have no dependence upon your body. Who, indeed, could know contact and its absence without depending on the body?
To refute [the opponent's] view: if you claim that this consciousness arises from contact, it must not rely upon your body;
yet it is universally acknowledged in the world that one must depend on the body to know contact. Who is there who knows conjunction and disjunction without depending on the body? It is known.
Since [the object] is not yet established, how much less can it be cognized? Thus, one should know that the claim that consciousness arises from contact is also erroneous.
The three refutations and two dependencies are not established.
Ānanda, objects do not touch cognition; it is the body that knows there is contact. To know the body is itself to know contact, and to know contact is itself the body. This is precisely contact.
That which is not the body is itself the body, yet it is not contact. The two characteristics of body and contact are fundamentally without location.

To join with the body is to constitute the very nature of the body itself; to depart from the body is to be like the characteristic of empty space. Since neither internal nor external can be established, how could a middle be posited?
Since the middle [section] no longer establishes internal or external natures as empty, from whom would your consciousness arise to establish the sense-fields (*dhātu*)?
Having first refuted that there is no locus for its arising, fearing that a false attachment might still arise, he calls out its name and addresses it again, saying:
"If you falsely reckon that this consciousness arises through the co-arising of the faculty and the object, then there must necessarily be a tangible object that comes into contact with the body."
In contrast, you must understand that within the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), there are also external objects that do not come to touch your awareness;
it is only your own body that constitutes the "touched. As previously stated, when one rubs one's head with the hand, both the head and the hand are one's own body.
If this is so, then the body that is the knower is identical to the touch that is the known. The known—
Contact is precisely the body that knows; since the body is identical to contact, it is not the body. Since contact is identical to the body, it is not contact.
As they mutually negate one another and both vanish, the two characteristics of body and contact originally have no location; thus, that which is capable of producing [contact] cannot be found.
The section beginning with "合身" (uniting with the body) below negates the lack of substance in that which is produced. It says: since that which is capable of producing...
Since there is no locus, it is a mere pretense to say that consciousness cannot arise. Even if consciousness were to arise, would it be conjoined with the body or separate from the body?
If you say it is conjoined with the body, then it is simply the self-nature of the body itself and can no longer be called consciousness.

If you say it is separate from the body, then it is identical to the characteristics of empty space and the like, and likewise can no longer be called consciousness. Furthermore, that which is produced [in this manner] is untenable.

It is attained. ○ Regarding "internal" and "external," the conclusion is that both are unattainable. To speak of internal, external, and intermediate [realms], these are established in mutual dependence.
Now, since the internal and external are not established, how can the intermediate consciousness-element (vijñānadhātu) be established?
Since the intermediate is no longer established, the nature of the two elements—internal and external—is likewise empty. Thus, both the producer and the produced are unattainable. Then...
As for your statement regarding the arising of consciousness, from what basis is its realm established? It merely expresses that there is only emptiness.
This concludes the analysis of the falsity of consciousness. Third, following this analysis, the conclusion is presented.
Therefore, one should know that when body-contact as a condition gives rise to the body-consciousness element, these three locations are entirely non-existent;
thus, the body, contact, and the body-element—these three—are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

The section on the element of body-contact consciousness is concluded. Regarding the six elements of mind, phenomena, and consciousness, there are three parts: first, establishing the elements according to provisional teachings;
second, discerning delusion based on consciousness; and third, concluding the analysis to demonstrate the fetters. First:
Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified—that with the mind and dharmas as conditions, mental consciousness arises—this consists of two parts:
first, identifying the consciousness to examine its source; second, analyzing the text to refute it point by point. First:

As for this consciousness: does it arise from the mind (manas) and thus take the mind as its constituent element (dhātu), or does it arise from phenomena (dharma) and thus take phenomena as its constituent element?

Each of these two textual divisions refutes three [positions]: first, the refutation that [the consciousness] is tied to the sense organ (indriya) and thus fails to be established; second, the refutation that it is tied to the object (viṣaya) and thus fails to be established.
Third, the discussion of the two dependencies lacks textual evidence. First:

"Ānanda, if [consciousness] arises because of the mind, then within your mind there must be something thought of that brings forth your consciousness. If there were no prior phenomena, the mind would have nothing from which to arise.
Apart from conditions, it has no form; for what purpose would consciousness then exist? Furthermore, your conscious mind and...
Are the nature of mental deliberation (*manas*) and the nature of discernment (*vijñāna*) the same or different? If they were the same, then what would be produced by the mind (*manas*)?

If they were different, then since the mind would not be identical [to discernment], there would be no object of cognition. If there is no object of cognition, how can the mind arise? If there is an object of cognition, how can one cognize the mind?
Thus, neither the identity nor the difference of these two natures is established. How, then, can the realms (*dhātu*) be established?

First, this is refuted by means of the lack of substance in that which produces [consciousness]. If you claim that this consciousness arises from the mental faculty (*manas*), it should not depend upon the mental object (*dharmāyatana*).
One must know that within your mind there is necessarily some contemplated object before one can manifest your mental faculty.

If there were no contemplated prior object, the nature of the mental faculty would have nothing from which to arise. Thus, it is known that the nature of the mental faculty is devoid [of inherent existence].
Since conditions have no form, how can consciousness arise? Even if your consciousness were to arise, if there is no substance [to serve as its object], what would it be used for?

Being useless, it is merely an illusion; who then could say it arises from the sense-faculties (*indriya*)? Furthermore, the following section refutes [the arising of consciousness] by means of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in that which is produced.

"Consciousness-mind" (*vijñāna-citta*) refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). "Discernment" (*cintā*) refers to the mind-faculty (*manas*). Since the mind-faculty is precisely the *manas*, discernment is taken as its defining characteristic.

The term "name" (ming) implies "also" (jian), meaning "the same as" (tong). This is because the mental consciousness (yìshí) and the mental faculty (yìgēn) share the same nature of discernment (*vijñapti*).

To refute the notion that [this consciousness] arises from the faculty: if you insist that this consciousness is produced from the faculty, then your mental consciousness and the mental faculty of deliberation are both of the same nature of discernment;
tell me then, are they the same or different? If you say they are the same as the mind...

This is precisely the mental faculty (*manas*). How is it produced from the mind? If one says that it is distinct from the mind, yet not different from the mind in its capacity for discernment, then there would be no object of cognition.
If there were no object of cognition, it would be entirely separate from the mind; how then could it be said to be produced from the mind?
If, on the other hand, one claims there is an object of cognition, then by relying on that [object], it would be identical to the mental faculty. How then can they be distinguished?
If one speaks of consciousness (*vijñāna*) in relation to the mind (*manas*), is it different from the mind?

Thus we know that even the two natures—the mind being identical [to itself] and the mind being different [from itself], or having the capacity for discernment and lacking the capacity for discernment—cannot be established. How much less, then, can the "element" (*dhātu*) be established? Furthermore, how could an element be established at all?
Therefore, what was previously called the "consciousness-element" (*mano-vijñāna-dhātu*) in the ancient teachings is an error.
Second, it is established that [the mind] cannot be bound by sensory objects.
If [the mind] arises dependent on dharmas, then all worldly dharmas do not exist apart from the five sense-objects.

Observe these dharmas of form, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles; their characteristics are distinct and correspond to the five faculties, and they are not subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas*).
Your consciousness is certain to arise in dependence upon dharmas. Now, observe closely: what is the nature of each dharma?

If one is separated from form and emptiness, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction, union and separation, and arising and ceasing—transcending all these characteristics, nothing at all can be found.

When they arise, form, emptiness, and all dharmas arise together; when they cease, form, emptiness, and all dharmas cease together. Since the cause itself does not exist, how can there be that which arises from it?
What is the form and characteristic of consciousness? Since its characteristics do not exist, how can the realms arise?
First, it is refuted by showing that the producer lacks substance. If you claim that this consciousness arises because of dharmas, then those dharmas must possess substance.
However, all worldly dharmas are not apart from the five sense objects—namely, form, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
Observe that the dharma of form is what is confronted by the eye; the dharmas of sound are what are confronted by the ear; the dharma of fragrance is what is confronted by the nose;
the dharma of flavor is what is confronted by the tongue; and the dharma of touch is what is confronted by the body.
All of these have distinct characteristics that confront the five sense organs; they are not subsumed under the faculty of the mind. If your mental consciousness is determined...
Concentration arises based upon dharmas. Now, observe closely: what are the characteristics of these dharmas as objects?

They are merely the shadows of the five sense-objects that have passed away, arising and perishing. Both form and emptiness are the object of form (*rūpa*), for emptiness is simply one manifest color.

Movement and stillness are the object of sound (*śabda*). Permeability and obstruction are the object of fragrance (*gandha*). Contact and separation encompass both the objects of taste (*rasa*) and touch (*spraṣṭavya*).

Regarding "dust" (*dhūli*): it is because one knows [the object] exists when both types of dust are in contact, and knows it does not exist when they are separated. Arising and ceasing are precisely the *dharmadhātu-dhūli*.

When the shadows of the five sense-objects fall upon the stage of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), it is called "arising. When they fall beyond the reach of the objective field, it is called "ceasing. "Transcending" (*yue*) is synonymous with "separating" (*li*).
To break through the mind, suppose that the shadows of the five sense-objects—such as form, emptiness, and so forth—were to arise and... [separate].
When the shadows of the five sense-objects have ceased, can there still be a dharma-object to be apprehended? One must know that apart from these various marks, ultimately nothing is obtained;
thus, that which could produce them has no substance. The section beginning with "As for production" refutes [the notion of production] by means of the produced being formless.
It says: "As I have explained above regarding the reason why the dharma-object arises, it does not exceed the dharmas of form and emptiness."
The arising of mental objects (dharmas) is like the arising of shadows; the cessation of mental objects does not exceed the cessation of the shadows of phenomena such as form and emptiness.
There is no separate mental object that serves as their supporting cause.
Since the supporting cause is absent, what ultimate form or characteristic could there be for the conscious mind that arises from such a cause? If one knows its characteristics—
It does not exist. Having already stated that the elements (*dhātu*) are inherently false and illusory, how can one further claim that they arise? This only serves to reveal their error.
Third, regarding the two dependencies, there is no textual authority for them.
Zhengmo says: "This lacks the section that distinguishes the union of faculty and object" (i.e., as in the current commentary, there is no text refuting the two being mutually dependent;

while the preceding five sections all exist, this section alone is missing, hence Zhengmo says it is lacking). I, the humble writer, say: The mind and dharmas are inherently without characteristics, unlike the first five faculties and their objects which possess real natures and realms.
Furthermore, within the individual refutations of each part, their falsity and lack of substance are explained most clearly. As for [the notion of] co-arising—

In reckoning, they are naturally non-existent; nor is it necessary to refute them, for there is no omission in the text. Having concluded the discernment of delusion regarding consciousness, the third section follows as a conclusion to demonstrate the point:

Therefore, one should know that with the mind (*manas*) and phenomena (*dharma*) as conditions, the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) arises; yet these three locations are entirely non-existent. Thus, the mind and phenomena...
Furthermore, the three—the mind-element (*manodhātu*), its objects, and consciousness—are fundamentally neither causal conditions nor spontaneous natures.

The meaning of this concluding indication follows the previous explanation. Now, sentient beings, failing to understand the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as being formed from mind and matter, differentiate the gates of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and manifest the realms of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). When the faculties and their objects mutually induce one another, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) arise.
Once the internal and external are thus established, consciousness arises within them, and the boundaries of the eighteen realms cannot be shifted.
Within the *tathāgatagarbha*, these are firmly illusory and merely provisional designations; yet, from the perspective of sentient beings, they ultimately become solid and stubborn attachments.
By calculating others and calculating oneself, afflictions arise in an instant. By being deluded regarding principle and phenomena, one suddenly obstructs the knowable.
This serves as the cause for birth and death and hinders right knowledge and vision; thus, there is no path to realize nirvana—by what means could bodhi be attained?

Now that each of these characteristics has been refuted as false and their true nature revealed, one understands that the *dhātus* and *āyatanas* do not exist and that the *vijñāna-skandha* and *āyatanas* are fundamentally empty.
When grasping is exhausted and calculations eliminated, the characteristics are opened and the nature manifests; thus, Bodhi and Nirvana may be hoped for.
This concludes the synthesis of the four categories to return to the hidden nature.

Third, the fusion of the seven great elements (mahābhūta) to sweep away emotional attachments and conceptual calculations. (Zhengmo’s Commentary states: "Everyone knows that the principles and scope of this section must surpass the preceding one; yet, in truth, few are able to compare why it is superior.

The old commentaries claim that the former takes the body as its proximate object while the latter takes external objects as its remote object; they further say that the former realizes the single body while the latter fuses the myriad dharmas. Both are incorrect. This is because the four sections are the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) within the seven great elements, whereas the seven great elements are the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) upon those four sections.

The dharmas are fundamentally no different; however, while the four sections discuss how each individual thing is the true nature (*dharmatā*), they never state that each individual thing pervades the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It is like pointing to fragrant wood, coal, or..."

To speak briefly, it was said that fire can burn; yet it had not been stated that each individual spark can utterly incinerate forests and wilds. Now, the seven great elements are discussed such that each one individually pervades the entire Dharma-realm; therefore, they are collectively termed "Great. This is like when the various fires are described: each single spark possesses the ultimate capacity to utterly incinerate.

Generally, the preceding section revealed that the substance of every phenomenon (*dharma*) is truly eternal; this section, however, reveals that every phenomenon is perfectly interfused and all-pervasive. Therefore, the current commentary uses the heading "Interfusion and Greatness" to explain it.

As for the phrase "to sweep away emotional calculations," it is because Ānanda has already heard the principle that the manifesting vision transcends the emotions and is detached from the faculty of sight, and thus knows that the nature of seeing does not belong to either causes and conditions or to spontaneity. However, the four categories [of phenomena] encompass all dharmas, as if...

One cannot escape the realm of causes and conditions. Furthermore, there are those with perverse knowledge and erroneous understanding who, following their own sentiments, cling to the notion of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Now, hearing again that [the nature of phenomena] is neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature, they find it contradicts their former teachings and disturb their provisional attachments.

Therefore, the World-Honored One uses the passage beginning with "The true emptiness of the nature of form" (*prakṛti-rūpa-śūnyatā*) to sweep them away. [This section consists of: 1. Ānanda presents his doubts and makes a request; 2. The Tathāgata rebukes his delusion and grants permission to teach; 3. Ānanda follows the instruction and awaits the teaching; 4.
The Tathāgata establishes the foundation and explains it for him. First: [Ānanda presents his doubts and makes a request.]
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often spoken of the principle of the harmony of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

All the various transformations in the world are manifested through the harmony of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Why then does the Tathāgata now reject both causes and conditions as well as spontaneity (*svabhāva*)?
I do not now understand to which category this meaning belongs. I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and reveal it to the assembly."
It gives rise to the Middle Way, the definitive meaning, the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
First, it recounts what was previously taught; because [the teaching] is in harmony with and related to causes and conditions, these are mentioned together.

"Constantly taught" refers to establishing one's own school by overturning external calculations. "All worlds" comprehensively includes both the sentient and insentient realms; "sentient" refers to the seven destinies.
Rising and sinking; as for the vessel, the eight phases revolve and return, hence it is said there are "various transformations.

All of these are manifested through the mutual conditioning and harmonious integration of the four great elements, such as the earth element. That which is called "constant preaching" is precisely based upon this.
