Furthermore, although it is said to be constant preaching, there are also degrees of depth and shallowness, such as "emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle Way" being simultaneous.

It is so. ○ Regarding the phrase "How can...": this expresses doubt concerning what is currently being discarded. "To cast out" (*pai-bin*) means to expel; it signifies not employing [a certain view].

Although the terms "causes and conditions" (*yin-yuan*) and "spontaneity" (*ziran*) appear superficially equivalent, their underlying intent is solely to express doubt regarding the casting out of causes and conditions.

This is because, in the external schools that advocate spontaneity, there is no room for such doubt as to whether they should be cast out. Thus, one knows that this sentence is intended to express wonder at the fact that both [positions] rely on causes.
This refers to simultaneous exclusion (*ubhayapakṣa-nirākaraṇa*). This meaning is precisely the sense of simultaneous exclusion. "Belonging" (*shǔ*) means to be subsumed under.

It is said that causes and conditions are established through mutual dependence; they do not belong to this [side] and thus belong to that. Since both sides are simultaneously excluded, one does not know to which category they belong.
I only pray that you will deign to show us the Middle Way. What was previously asserted is now being excluded; the former and latter contradict one another.
It contradicts [my own position]. Since it is encompassed by neither my own school nor the external doctrines, I am unable to decide whether to advance or retreat;

I am at a loss regarding compliance or opposition. Like a rat caught between two doors or a sheep at the edge of a fence, I cannot bear this state of indecision. Therefore, I pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately grant me instruction: that which is impartial in its reasoning is called the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*);

that which reaches the ultimate of its meaning is called the Definitive (*nītārtha*); and that which speaks in accordance with reality is called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca-dharma*).
Their intention is that falling into existence through causes and conditions, or naturally sinking into emptiness, does not accord with the Middle Way.
They hold that naturalness is certainly not right view, and that causes and conditions likewise belong to the provisional teaching;

both are ultimately non-final and are alike mere childish talk, or like an empty fist—none of them are dharmas free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Because the Buddha rejected both [extremes], they instead seek it by reversing these positions. Later it says:
The nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form; this is the meaning revealed through equal and correct instruction.
Second, the Tathāgata rebukes delusion and permits instruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "You previously felt weary of and detached from the various Hinayana teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas."
Having resolved to diligently seek unsurpassed bodhi, I shall now reveal the ultimate truth for you.
Why, moreover, do you entangle yourself with worldly conceptual proliferation and delusive imaginings?

Though you have heard much, you are like a man who knows how to describe medicine but cannot distinguish it when the actual medicine appears before him. The Tathāgata says such a person is truly pitiable.
"Have compassion. Listen attentively now; I shall analyze and reveal it for you, so that those who cultivate the Mahāyāna in the future may also penetrate the true reality (*tathatā*).
First, it is shown by what has already been said: 'At that time' refers to the moment Ānanda made his request; 'addressing Ānanda' means—"
Because he responded immediately, he first directed [the Buddha] to return to the chamber of lust. At that time, he felt self-reproach for not yet having perfected his power of the Way;

this was the sound of his weary detachment from the teachings of the Śrāvakas and others, for the teachings of the Śrāvakas and others all cling to signs and are hindered by names, making it difficult to fully perfect the power of the Way.
Furthermore, at that time, his earnest invitation of *śamatha* and the other two [meditations] was the arousal of the bodhicitta.
One diligently seeks Bodhi, for the three [practices] beginning with *śamatha* are the sublime concentrations for attaining Buddhahood, through which one may proceed toward Bodhi.

Now, pointing this out after the realization [of the Truth], it is shown that the True Nature revealed by the ten sections and the Essence realized through the four categories is precisely the Middle Way;
it is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); it is the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Therefore, in summary—
To designate it by means of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): because "one" is precisely the Middle Way, whereas that which is not the Middle Way becomes dualistic;

because "the foremost" is precisely the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), whereas that which is not definitive has what precedes it; because "truth" (*satya*) is precisely the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), whereas that which involves conceptual proliferation is not truth.
"How can one... and below criticizes [this view] as being based on delusion and error. The phrase "How could one again take... and so forth expresses deep indignation at it.
It should not be so. "The world" refers here to the world of those who are learners within the Two Vehicles.

Because they do not realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), their verbal articulation of causes and conditions is termed "futile proliferation" (*prapañca*), and their mental contemplation of causes and conditions is termed "delusive conceptualization" (*vikalpa*).
Since their causes belong to such futile proliferation and delusive conceptualization, the Tathāgata repeatedly provides instruction to enable them to transcend this.
Regarding the Dharma, Ānanda instead asked, "How can they both be excluded? and so forth; thus he entangled and ensnared himself.
It was only natural, then, that the World-Honored One should find this deeply strange. The phrase "Though you are of great learning," and so on, serves as a metaphor to manifest his pitiable state.
This means that although Ānanda possesses the wisdom of great learning and is skilled at making requests, it does not go beyond what has been said.
To such a person, the Tathāgata reveals the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) so that they may realize it; this is precisely the true medicine appearing before them.
Yet Ānanda remains entangled in causes and conditions, clinging to expedient means as if they were reality, utterly unable to distinguish between them.
Being unable to distinguish, he will surely discard the true medicine to take up a counterfeit one, thereby deceiving both himself and others. This is...
Therefore, it is said that they are truly to be pitied. From "You now" onwards, he grants permission to provide an exposition.

Having already stated that many fail to awaken due to a lack of attentive listening, he now exhorts them to listen attentively. His granting of permission to "discriminate" and so forth is for the benefit of those present in the assembly.
"Discrimination" means to analyze the causes and conditions of non-comprehension so as to enable their transcendence. "Exposition" means to open [the way].
This demonstrates the definitive meaning of the Middle Way so that they may realize it, and it also benefits those of the future, thereby aiding later generations.
"True Reality" (shixiang) refers to the subsequent meaning of the Great Nature (*mahābhūta*); it encompasses all that was previously manifested and realized, for these are of one identical essence.
Because it remains unchanging while following conditions, it is called True Reality. Those who do not comprehend this, even if they practice, do so falsely.
All who are to practice the Mahāyāna in the future must necessarily attain thorough penetration; therefore, this is also intended for them. As it says below:
"Just as water becomes ice, and ice returns to water," this briefly demonstrates the meaning of the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Third, Ānanda followed the instruction and stood waiting to listen.
Ānanda remained silent, receiving the Buddha’s holy command.
His silence was one of a mind held empty and contemplative; his reception of the command was a respectful awaiting of the imperial edict. What is called "listening" is being upright...
Regard it as one who drinks when thirsty; with single-mindedness, enter into the meaning of these words. Second, the four Tathāgatas press him down and speak for him, which has two parts:
first, based on his attachments, briefly indicating the Middle Way; second, categorizing the gates to explain in detail the seven great elements. First:
Ānanda, it is as you have said: the four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world.
Ānanda, if the essential nature of those great elements were not itself a combination, they could not intermingle with one another, just as empty space does not combine with material forms.

If they were indeed combined, they would be identical to the transformations [they produce], such that their beginning and end would mutually constitute one another, and their arising and ceasing would likewise be mutually constitutive.
The succession of birth and death, death and birth, continues like a whirling firebrand, never finding rest.
O Ānanda, it is like water forming ice, and the ice returning to water.
First, examining what is falsely grasped: according to Ānanda’s previous statement, "All the various transformations in the world are manifested through the combination of the four great elements.
Now it is said, "The four great elements combine to manifest the various transformations of the world.
Although the subject and object are inverted, their meaning is no different; this is simply based on what was stated.

I have examined and determined this; therefore, I say: "As you have said. ○ From the passage beginning with "Ānanda," he proceeds to refute [the opponent's] cognition by means of inference (*anumāna*).
He states that the words "the four great elements combine to manifest the world" and so forth are spoken according to conventional perception and the grasping of signs.

If one were to argue from the perspective of ultimate nature (*dharmatā*), combination certainly belongs to the provisional teachings (*upāya*); yet even non-combination would fall into the views of externalists (*tīrthika*). Therefore, he briefly sets forth these two types.

This is not a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding "the nature of the great elements" (*mahābhūta-svabhāva*): its essence is non-composite, which means it is permitted only as unchanging and not permitted to follow conditions (*pratyaya*).
Because it does not calculate following conditions, it cannot intermingle with the various great elements.

Speaking in terms of the general characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the great elements, that which cannot harmonize with them means that its nature is itself the nature; it does not follow conditions to constitute a characteristic (*nimitta*). As it is said:

This would then fall into the view of spontaneous origination (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it should be like empty space, which does not blend with various forms. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

"The nature of the great elements (*mahābhūta-svabhāva*) is a subject that possesses existence; it is the thesis that it does not mix or blend with the various great elements. The reason (*hetu*) is: because its essence is not a composite."

The concordant example is like space, which does not harmonize with various forms; the Great Nature (Mahat) is not thus, and for this reason it is considered non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), causing one to realize its true nature.
If the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) still refers to the Great Nature, then as for "harmonizing," it is permitted only to follow conditions (*pratyaya*), but not to remain unchanging.

Because remaining unchanging is not permitted, it should be identical to the characteristics of the various great elements (*mahābhūta*), undergoing migration, transformation, and alteration. Only then...

The final four lines provide a comprehensive and detailed explanation of the states of transition, change, and transformation regarding both the external vessel-world and the internal bodies of sentient beings.
"Beginning and end mutually constituting" means that there is an end because of a beginning, and a beginning because of an end; they are successively and reciprocally constituted.

"Arising and ceasing continuing" means that generation and completion lead to destruction, and destruction leads to generation; these proceed in continuous succession from one to the next. This refers to the external vessel-world.
It is said: "Birth-and-death" (saṃsāra) refers to death resulting from birth, and birth resulting from death; these also mutually establish one another.
"Birth-and-birth" (jāti-jāti) refers to being born again after having been born, and dying again after having died;

these also continue in succession before and after. This is explained with reference to the internal body. Thus, one knows that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), both internal and external, are all characterized by transformation. Great!

That which has a nature identical to this does not have a nature that is self-existent; it is able to follow conditions to form characteristics. If it were thus, one would fall into the conceptualization of causes and conditions.

Therefore, it should be like a whirling firebrand, never having a moment’s rest. The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: "The Great Nature (*mahābhūta*) is a subject that possesses existence" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it possesses the meaning of combination. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: "like a whirling [firebrand]."

The fire-wheel has no rest, yet the nature of "Greatness" (mahat-tattva) is not like that; therefore, it is also considered non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*) [as a proof]. This is intended to cause one to realize for oneself.

Ānanda, the following analogy clarifies the correct principle: since the nature of "Greatness" is neither like empty space nor like the blending [of elements], and furthermore is not like the revolving fire-wheel, with what, then, is it ultimately identical? Therefore, he again uses a different analogy to provide a counter-argument.

This is clarified as follows: the analogy of water forming ice illustrates that the nature of the Great [Element] (*mahābhūta*) is unchanging while following conditions; the analogy of ice returning to water illustrates that the nature of the Great [Element] follows conditions while remaining unchanging.
Because it follows conditions while remaining unchanging, it does not fall into the trap of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);

because it remains unchanging while following conditions, it does not fall into the trap of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Not falling into either of these two is called the Middle Way and the Correct Principle.

Detailed Explanation of the Seven Elements according to the Two Divisions (Question: Ānanda inquired only about the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); why did the Tathāgata fully elucidate the seven elements? Answer: It is because he wished to encompass all phenomena exhaustively.

This is because, among the five aggregates (*skandha*), the four great elements only encompass the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) in its aspect of shape and color; among the six sense bases (*āyatana*), they only encompass the derivative [elements]; among the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), they only encompass the six objects and the derivative [elements] within the six faculties; and it is the same for the eighteen realms (*dhātu*).

As for the manifest color within the aggregate of form, as well as the remaining four aggregates, the nature of the faculties within the six bases, the nature of the faculties within the twelve bases, and the nature of the faculties and consciousness within the eighteen realms—none of these can [be encompassed by the four great elements].)

[Included]. Now, by adding the three great elements of space, seeing, and consciousness, all things are encompassed. Furthermore, fearing that Ānanda’s questions might not reach this depth, these are added to prevent various doubts.
7. First, the earth element; second, the fire element; third, the water element; fourth, the wind element; fifth, the space element; sixth, the seeing element; seventh, the consciousness element.
The first section has four parts: 1. Establishing the characteristics based on the nature; 2. First refuting the notion of combination;
3. Detailed demonstration of the Middle Way; 4. Simultaneously sweeping away both views.
Regarding the first: "Observe the nature of earth: grossly it is the great earth, subtly it is minute particles; down to the *paramāṇu* (limitless atom), analyze those ultimate infinitesimals."

The characteristic of the limit of form (*rūpa-paryanta-lakṣaṇa*) is composed of seven parts. When these are further analyzed down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), they are in fact the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
When the teaching instructs one to contemplate the nature of earth, it is intended to make known that the nature of the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is none other than the *tathāgatagarbha*.
This *tathāgatagarbha* follows conditions; moved by the collective ignorance (*avidyā*) of sentient beings, it manifests as coarse characteristics and becomes the great earth. As it is said:
It was previously stated that "obscuration and darkness constitute emptiness (*ākāśa*)," and that "within the obscurity of emptiness, darkness coagulates to form matter (*rūpa*).

This results from the practice of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), who analyze matter back into emptiness. Consequently, subtle characteristics manifest as minute particles (*paramāṇu*). As the *Prajñāpāramitā* states:

"The trichiliocosm is crushed into minute particles. The commentary explains: the Two Vehicles employ the contemplation of analyzing emptiness (*vibhāvanā-śūnyatā-bhāvanā*) through the use of mental imagery (*parikalpa*).
Wisdom. First, the great earth is divided into seven parts; thus, from coarse to subtle, it is successively divided into seven parts until one reaches the minute atom (*paramāṇu*).
At that point, the world no longer exists as such. If those atoms were further divided into seven parts, they would become the ultimate atom (*aṇu*).
What is called the "ultimate atom" is the most extremely subtle limit of form (*rūpa*).
This is the limit [of form]; hence it is called "the characteristic of the limit of form. If this characteristic were further divided into seven parts, it would become a *paramāṇu* (atom).

Now, instead of saying that one analyzes down to the *paramāṇu* and then to the *anu* (subtle particle), the World-Honored One has used these skillful, unimpeded, and elegant phrases—"analyzing those *paramāṇus* down to the *anu*"—which are both fresh and refined.
Consider this point: even the "adjacent atom" (paramāṇu) still retains the designation of "dust" (rajas); if it were further analyzed, even the name "dust" would be lost.
Therefore, it is said that if one further analyzes the adjacent atom, it is simply the nature of actual emptiness. Second, the refutation of the composite [atom] has two parts:
first, the direct refutation of how space combines to form matter; second, taking an example to further reveal its fallacy. First [the direct refutation].
Ānanda, if these neighboring atoms were analyzed until they became empty space, you should know that empty space gives rise to the appearance of form.
Now, as for what you have asked—how the various changing phenomena of the world arise through combination—you should observe this single neighboring atom:
by how much empty space must it be combined to exist? It is not possible for neighboring atoms to combine to form another neighboring atom.

Initially, it enters through concentration and emerges from it. If one follows the Hinayana, they must claim that when these atoms (*paramāṇu*) are analyzed and enter into emptiness, it is the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) entering into emptiness.
If this were indeed the case, then one should understand that empty space gives birth to the characteristics of form;
for where there is necessarily an entry, there must also be an emergence. "From 'If you now' onwards, he bases his argument on their attachment to raise an objection, saying:"
Now you have come forward and asked me this: "Because of combination, the various manifested forms of the world arise.
If this were so, then all manifested forms would exist through combination.
Setting aside for a moment the combination of other things, you should first observe that even a single atom (*paramāṇu*) must likewise be a combination.
There is. However, since the neighboring atom (*paramāṇu*) moves toward the direction of formlessness, it must employ space as its adjunct.
Now tell me: how many spaces are used to combine and produce this neighboring atom? This is because one clearly knows that space has no quantity and is fundamentally incapable of being combined;
thus, the question is posed as a challenge to make known that the neighboring atom does not exist through combination. ○ "It should not be... below.

Anticipating a mistaken defense, [the author] fears that one might raise the objection: "How can several instances of empty space combine to form a *paramāṇu*? Consequently, he offers a mistaken defense, saying:

"What I mean by 'combination' is simply the combining of material forms (*rūpa*) to constitute matter; it does not mean the combining of space to constitute matter. It is for this reason that he offers this pre-emptive refutation.
He states that the *paramāṇu* is the most subtle among all material forms, such that there is nothing subtler than it. If it must necessarily be a combination of material forms...
Regarding the formation of matter (*rūpa*): it must be formed by the aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Even if one were to grant this, there would be three fallacies:

First, while the formation of others through aggregation may accord with their own inherent nature, the formation of oneself through oneself is necessarily impossible according to the principle of self-nature.
Second, while the aggregation of many to form a single entity is consistent with reason, the aggregation of one to form a single entity is contradictory. Third, as for the aggregation...
That the minute forms aggregate to form the coarse is a calculation common to the world; that they aggregate to form the minute is not a calculation common to the world.
Because of these three fallacies, one should not refute [the position]. By taking these as examples, the fallacies are further revealed.
Furthermore, regarding those atoms of the neighboring dust that are analyzed into emptiness: by how many material forms (*rūpa*) are they synthesized to constitute empty space?

If it were synthesized by material forms, then when joined with form, it would be form and not emptiness; if it were synthesized by emptiness, then when joined with emptiness, it would be emptiness and not form. Since material form can still be analyzed away, how could emptiness be synthesized with it?
First, regarding the refutation based on emptiness: you have already established "conjunction" as your thesis; therefore, all things ought to exist through conjunction.
Furthermore, in the teachings of the Hinayana, when the neighboring atoms (*paramāṇu*) are analyzed into emptiness, this emptiness must necessarily be a synthesis of material forms (*rūpa*).
Now tell me: how many material forms must be synthesized to constitute empty space? Indeed, the Tathāgata, by means of analysis...

That it is difficult to reconcile upon entry is because analyzing form and returning it to emptiness is the specific teaching of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), whereas the harmonious combination of all characteristics is Ānanda’s own statement.
By following his own teaching to challenge his own words, he was rendered unable to offer a rebuttal.
If one were to use the analogy of "form" and below to reveal the error: suppose I were to ask you just now, and you—since...
One cannot offer a counter-argument. You surely know that when form (rūpa) is joined, the joined form is not empty.
If you already know that when form is joined, the joined form is not empty, then you must also know that if it were empty, then at the time of joining, what is joined would be empty and not form.
If this is so, then both form and emptiness are neither in combination nor existent through conjunction. The final two lines definitively conclude the refutation.
It says that although form cannot combine with emptiness, it can still be analyzed and dissolved into it; yet if emptiness were to combine and become form, how could they ever truly combine?
This decisively states that form is not a product of conjunction, thereby concluding the meaning of the correct refutation. — *Zhengmo* (The Correct Pulse)

It is said: Space briefly possesses four meanings that preclude the possibility of conjunction: first, it is formless and unobstructed; second, it is without measure or number; third, it is without boundaries;
and fourth, it is without change or fluctuation. Originally, the element of earth depends upon the aggregation of matter, and matter depends upon space.
Since emptiness cannot be joined, form is not a composite. Since form is not a composite, how could the earth element be a composite?
By applying this reasoning by analogy, all notions of "combination" can be refuted together. Thus, the refutation of combination is complete.
Third, a detailed exposition of the Middle Way has two parts: first, the direct exposition of the Middle Way; second, verifying it through empirical phenomena. Regarding the first:

You fundamentally do not know that within the Tathāgata-garbha there is intrinsic form which is true emptiness, and intrinsic emptiness which is true form—pure and quiescent from the beginning, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Regarding the statement, "The fundamental is not a combination; it is falsely conceived as a combination":

this is because you have been consistently ignorant and fundamentally did not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha there is the principle of "changing according to conditions while remaining unchanging" (*ananyathābhāva*) and "remaining unchanging while changing according to conditions.

As for "intrinsic form" (*prakṛti-rūpa*), it is the self-nature changing according to conditions that can manifest illusory form. Although it can manifest illusory form, its essence ultimately does not change. Therefore, it is said:
"True emptiness. True emptiness means that the true substance is itself empty. This clarifies the meaning within the *tathāgatagarbha* of being unchanging while following conditions.
"Intrinsic emptiness" means that the intrinsic nature is unchanging and its substance is fundamentally empty. Although its substance is fundamentally empty, its function is never lost;
therefore, it is called "true form. True form means that form is established based on the true. This clarifies the [meaning of the] *tathāgatagarbha*.
Within the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) lies the principle of remaining immutable while following conditions.

Because it possesses the principle of following conditions while remaining immutable, it is called "pure and fundamental. This means that form cannot obstruct it; its self-so-coming has been thus from the beginning.

Because it possesses the principle of remaining immutable while following conditions, it is said to be "pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. This means it completely fills the Dharma-realm on all sides without exception.
Therefore, it is known that among the ten realms, whatever possesses substantiality and obstruction within the midst of the true nature is the pervasiveness of the earth-element.

Yet, since it is pure and fundamental by nature, it does not fall into the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); since it is all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, it does not stagnate in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
One who understands this meaning realizes that the Middle Way, the Supreme Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), is right here and now. (Question: This section...)

When explaining that the element of earth (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) is all-pervasive, why does the detailed exposition of the Middle Way instead speak of "the true color of nature" (*prakṛti-rūpa*)? Answer: The element of earth fundamentally relies upon an aggregation of matter (*rūpa-skandha*). Since the nature of matter itself is already the Middle Way, the nature of earth can likewise be known as such.

Furthermore, in the preceding section refuting the combination of elements, earth was already transformed into matter; therefore, it is spoken of here in immediate succession for the sake of textual convenience. This is verified by the fact that the two [grasping] objects are established through experience.
It manifests according to the minds of sentient beings and in accordance with the scope of what they know, appearing through the power of their karma.

While the previous passage described the state of being "pure and fundamental" and "pervading the Dharma-realm" as referring to the inherent perfection of principle (*li-jù*), this passage verifies it through the actualization of phenomena (*shi-zào*).
It shows that whenever sentient beings desire to see something according to their own minds, they see it; and it appears in accordance with the capacity of their knowledge.
Thus one comes to know that from the beginning there was neither a sender nor a creator; how could it be anything other than the fundamentally pure?
Furthermore, one sees that according to the karma of one person, the appearance of one person manifests;
according to the karma of ten people, the appearance of ten people manifests; and so on, up to the karma of a thousand million people, the appearance of a thousand million people manifests.
From the outset, there is neither obstruction nor limitation; how could this not be the Dharma that pervades the entire dharma-realm?
One who understands this meaning will naturally no longer be confused by the notions of causality or spontaneity. The detailed exposition of the Middle Way is hereby concluded.
The four pairs and eight classes [of noble ones] sweep away the two types of views.
The world is ignorant and deludedly regards causes and conditions as well as spontaneous nature; all of these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discerning mind.
They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.
Although the term "worldly" is broad in scope, in this context it refers specifically to those of the Two Vehicles and the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), as they are currently under delusion.

Because they do not comprehend the principle that within the *tathāgatagarbha* there is the meaning of "changing while remaining unchanging" and "remaining unchanging while changing," they are termed "ignorant.
Seeing only the manifest forms that arise according to karma—unobstructed and limitless—they consequently become deluded.

Because they act as causes and conditions, they bind one to and cause one to fall into provisional teachings. Furthermore, some see the color-form that arises in the present and, following their minds and according to their measure, fail to recognize its non-substantiality and non-action, thereby deluding themselves into thinking it is spontaneous; thus they sink into heterodox paths. Since these all belong to false conceptualization, it is said:
"All are the mind of consciousness," and so forth. Since none are anything other than frivolous proliferation, it is said: "There is only verbal expression," and so forth. [The Ground]
The Great [Chapter] concludes. Part Two: The Fourfold Great Fire. First, the characteristics established according to their nature; second, the prior refutation of combination;
third, the detailed demonstration of the Middle Way; fourth, the simultaneous brushing away of the two views. First [section].
Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self; it depends upon various conditions. Observe, for instance, when a household in the city that has not yet eaten wishes to cook its meal:
they take a magnifying lens in their hand and seek fire from the sun.
First, the nature of fire follows conditions. This nature of fire is the *tathāgatagarbha* (Buddha-nature). Although its essence is unchanging, its function is able to follow conditions;
therefore, it is said to be "without self" (*anātman*), meaning there is no fixed sovereign or controller. It is also a matter of dependence.
Although the nature of fire is said to be without self, it must necessarily depend upon conditions such as wood, a drill, tinder, or a mirror to manifest its form. Observe this, [you].
The following passage cites an actual event as proof: [the monk] had not yet eaten and required food, so he wished to cook it—meaning to kindle a fire beneath the cauldron to ripen the food.
A *yangsui* (sun-stone) is an instrument for obtaining fire. Cui Bao’s commentary states that it is made of copper and shaped like a mirror;
when reflecting a person, the image appears inverted, and when facing the sun, fire emerges. The *Huainanzi* says: "The *yangsui* is fire."

Furthermore, Wang Chong’s *Lunheng* states: "On the day of Bingwu at noon on the fifth month, the stones of the five directions were smelted and refined into spheres like mirrors with depressions in their centers.
When the weather was clear, one could face the sun and produce fire from them.

This is merely a brief citation of one instance used as evidence to serve as the basis for the refutation and establishment of arguments against the theory of combination (*saṃghāta*) that follows. Part Two: First, the Refutation of Combination; Sub-part One.
This section restates the opponent's position and provides an illustration; secondly, it refutes that position based on its own premises. First:
"Ānanda, as for what is called 'conjunction,' it is like me and you and the one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus now forming a single assembly.
Although the assembly is one, when its basis is examined, each individual possesses a body, and all have their respective ancestral lineages."
Names, such as Śāriputra of the Brahmin caste, Uruvilvākāśyapa of the Kāśyapa caste, and so forth,
up to Ānanda of the Gautama clan.
Wishing to refute the notion of a "combination," he called out his name and said to him:
"If you claim that this fire exists as a 'combination,' let me clarify this through an analogy so that you may see your error for yourself. Now, various conditions combine to produce fire;
it is just as I and you, along with these one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, now constitute a single assembly. You must understand that although the assembly is one..."
If one examines their fundamental basis, each has its own body; furthermore, each possesses its own lineage of origin, clan, and name. Fire, too, should be like this:
although it is but a single fire, when tracing back to its original conditions, it should likewise each have its own substance.
Moreover, there should be categories and names for each, such as "this fire belongs to a mirror," "this fire belongs to moxa," or "this fire belongs to the sun."
...and so forth. If it were not so, then their harmonious union would not be established.
For instance, [the names] such as Śāriputra indicate their clan names. Śāriputra is here translated as "Son of the Śārikā Bird"; he was of the Brahmin caste, of the lineage of the Brahmans.
Uruvilvā is here translated as "Papaya Grove"; he was of the Kāśyapa caste, of the lineage of the tortoises. Ānanda—this...
It is said: "Ānanda, you belong to the Gautama clan, the Ikṣvāku lineage. The Buddha's progenitor was born from the sun-baked sugarcane and was thus named Gautama;
therefore, Gautama is translated as "Sun-lineage" (Sūryavaṃśa) and also as "Sugarcane. Later, after four generations, it was changed to Śākya.
This [title] merely traces back to its source. Zhengmo says: "There must first have been the appearance of a division."

[They] consider this to be the basis for conjunction; only then can conjunction occur. Therefore, they take the example of a single assembly being divided such that each member has their own clan as a fixed rule.
However, in the subsequent text, it is shown that fire is not like this; this is the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Second, refuting [the opponent's position] by addressing their adherence to it. First, refuting the individual characteristics; second, subsequently refuting...
The Analysis of Combined Characteristics. [This section has] two parts: first, examining the root of each instance of grasping; second, refuting them one by one according to their conditions. First:
"Ānanda, if this nature of fire exists because of combination, then when that hand holds a mirror toward the sun to seek fire, where does this fire [arise]?"
Does it emerge from the mirror? Does it emerge from the tinder? Or does it come from the sun?
If the essential nature of this fire were determinately produced through a combination [of causes], it should have possessed the characteristic of being already separate prior to that.
Now, when a person holds a fire-mirror (i.e., a *sūryakānta* or "sun-crystal") toward the sun in search of fire, does this fire exist [prior to its emergence] from...?
Regarding the fire emerging from the mirror: does it emerge from the tinder, or does it come from the sun?
It must be that fire emerges from each of these three locations; only then can it correspond to the analogy that Śāriputra and the others each possess their own bodies.

Therefore, this inquiry [is made] in two parts to pursue the conditions one by one for the sake of refutation: first, the refutation of its coming from the sun; second, the refutation of its emerging from the mirror.
The third [case of] destruction arises from the moxa.
First, Ānanda, if the sun were to come here, it would naturally burn the moxa in your hand; the forests from which it originated should all likewise be consumed by fire.
If you claim that there is fire coming from the sun, then it should not require a mirror; it should be able to burn the tinder in your hand by itself.
Furthermore, if it could burn the tinder, then all the trees in the forest from which it comes should also be consumed by fire.
Since the trees in the forest at its point of origin are not burned when the mirror is used, we know that no such fire comes from the sun.
The three types of destruction emerge from the mirror.
If they emerge from within the mirror, then since they can indeed emerge from the mirror, why does the moxa not melt the mirror?
○ Even when you hold it in your hand, there is no sign of heat; how then could it ever liquefy or dissolve?
At first, the fire emerges from the mirror itself. If one were to claim that the fire comes from within the mirror, it should not require the sun;
it ought to be able to emerge from the mirror by itself and ignite the tinder. Furthermore, if it can ignite the tinder, it should likewise be able to melt the mirror.
Since the mirror exists, why does it not melt itself? Now, as the mirror does not melt and the tinder must necessarily face the sun to burn, we know that this fire has no [inherent source].

There are those who emerge from within a mirror. [The Master] anticipates that you might offer a mistaken defense based on the objection, "If hearing that a mirror does not melt is a refutation, then one might falsely argue:
'Incense is easy to burn, but a mirror is difficult to melt. Since at that time the incense could indeed be burned," and so forth. This serves to simultaneously block such erroneous defenses.
Over time, it would naturally be able to melt the mirror; therefore, this objection is raised. It is a circuitous argument.

The intent of the refutation is that if it were indeed able to melt the mirror over time, there must first have been signs of heat. Yet, even now, when you bend your hand to hold it, no sign of heat is present.
"How can it be that after a long time it suddenly melts away? This is merely a mistaken calculation. 'Melting away' (rongpan) is synonymous with dissolving (xiaojie).
The three types of destruction arise from tinder (ai).
If they arose from the tinder itself, why would one need to rely on the continuous conjunction of the sun, a mirror, and light for fire to be produced?"

If it is claimed that fire arises from the tinder, then the fire would emerge from the tinder itself; why then would it depend upon the meeting of the sun, the mirror, and light before the fire arises?
Now, we see with our own eyes that those seeking fire hold a mirror toward the sun. From this, we know that this fire does not arise from the tinder.
Thus, by refuting [the notion of arising] through the three locations where fire is individually absent, one knows that it does not arise from their conjunction. By...

It is not as you claim, for Śāriputra and the others each possess their own distinct bodies; thus, having first finished refuting the notion of distinct characteristics, we shall next refute the notion of a combined characteristic.
Furthermore, observe closely: the mirror is held by the hand, the sun comes from the heavens, and the moxa is produced from its original site—whence does the fire come?
Wandering here. ○ The sun and the mirror are far apart; they are neither joined nor blended. ○ It should not be that the fire-light exists of itself from nowhere.
First, examine the direction from which it comes. "You must again observe closely" means he instructs you to observe in detail so that nothing is missed.
The fire was hidden within; because the mirror was held by the hand, he was taught to observe the hand. Because the sun comes from the heavens, he was taught to observe the heavens.
Because the moxa grows from the earth, he was taught to observe the earth. Thus, through careful and thorough investigation, he found no place where the fire had been hidden.
From what direction, then, did the fire travel here? Although his wisdom was like that of Śāriputra, [he could not discern it].
The Master’s argument is modeled after Pūrṇa’s inability to know or speak [of fire]. ○ Below, under the section on the sun and mirror, he correctly refutes their conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

He states that since the sun and mirror do not possess fire, and the hands and so forth likewise lack a place where fire is stored, one might fear it is said that the sun and mirror, through their conjunction, together ignite the tinder.
Therefore, he offers this refutation, stating that we clearly see the sun and mirror are far apart and are not [in contact].
If it were not a combination of these, how could it ignite the moxa? Thus, we know that the claim that there is fire within the combination is erroneous.

The final sentence anticipates and precludes a fallacious defense; fearing that upon hearing "neither a combination nor a non-combination," one might instead calculate that fire exists spontaneously without a source, this preclusion is made.
Originally, Ānanda took "combination" as his fundamental tenet; if, in truth, there were no source...

Since this would contradict our own tenets, it should not be refuted. Thus, we know that for one who does not understand the nature of the *ālayavijñāna*, it is not only the case that the combination [of conditions] is unestablished;
rather, their non-combination is even more untenable. This is what is meant by the subsequent passage stating that "there are merely words, but no actual meaning.
Having thus completed the refutation of the combination [of conditions], section three provides a detailed exposition of the Middle Way in two parts.
First, the direct demonstration of the Middle Way; second, taking phenomena as evidence for its realization. Regarding the first:
You still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of fire is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true fire;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
The preceding section on terminology is similar. It states that not only is the earth element unknown to you, but the fire element is likewise unknown.
This is because their natures and characteristics are analogous; the nature of fire is identical to what was previously discussed, differing only in that "fire" replaces "form.

These two points are verified through empirical observation. (In the section on the earth element, this category was not divided separately; however, as there is now an added passage here, it is not convenient to explain them together. Two: first, verification of purity; second, verification...
It is known to be all-pervasive.
First, it accords with the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they know. "Ānanda, you should know that when people hold a mirror in one place, fire arises in one place;
when they hold it throughout the Dharma-realm, it arises filling the entire world. Since its arising fills the entire world, how could it have a fixed location?"
First, he uses direct perception as verification. He states that even the fire produced by an act is likewise responsive to the mind and conforms to its measure;
thus, the meaning of its being fundamentally pure can be understood. *Ānanda*, [the Master] continues below, simultaneously refuting and redirecting his doubts.

Fearing that upon hearing the words "responsive to the mind and conforming to its measure," Ānanda might further doubt, saying: "The great element of earth, which meets the eye everywhere, can all be said to be responsive to the mind and conform to its measure."
Whether the fire-element is seen or not seen, it currently possesses a specific location; thus, the principle that it conforms to the capacity of the mind does not seem to be fully established.
Therefore, this is refuted as follows: to say that a mirror is held in one place while fire arises in another is merely because sentient beings see it according to their own mental inclinations.
To say that it is held throughout the entire dharma-realm and arises filling the world is to accord with the capacity of what is known.
If you know it, then you know it. However, since it has already arisen pervading the entire world, how could there be such things as "this" or "that," or specific locations?
What you call "sometimes seeing and sometimes not seeing" with apparent spatial dimensions is merely a failure of the capacity of your mind's cognition.
Second, it is verified that [the nature of phenomena] is all-pervasive and manifests according to karma.
To say that fire produced by physical causes is also a manifestation according to karma means that its pervasive circulation throughout the *dharmadhātu* can be understood.

[Verification] (Question: The arising of fire when holding a mirror seems to follow one's karma (*karmānuparivartin*). Since this has already been categorized under the preceding section, what then is meant by "following karma"? Answer: The arising of fire when holding a mirror is explained in terms of present conditions;

that is, when sought, it appears according to the mind and is known through its corresponding measure. "Manifesting in accordance with karma" is explained in terms of past causes; for example, the simultaneous presence of bodily warmth at birth or smoke from a cooking hearth. One is a temporary manifestation, while the other arises constantly.
They appear similar but are actually different. The detailed exposition of the Middle Way is concluded. The four pairs [of opposites] sweep away the two views.

The world is ignorant, deludedly taking [conditions] to be causes and conditions or inherent natures; all of these are merely the conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating consciousness-mind.
They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no real meaning whatsoever.

The meaning is as explained in the section on the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). This concludes the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*). Now for the water element (*ab-dhātu*) and the fourth [element], the air element (*vāyu-dhātu*):

1. Establishing the characteristics based on their intrinsic nature; 2. First, refuting the notion of combination; 3. Detailed demonstration of the Middle Way; 4. Simultaneously sweeping away the two views. First:
Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flowing and ceasing have no constancy.
For instance, in the city of Śrāvastī, there were great illusionists such as the seers Kapila, Kāpya, and Padma Mahāsāta, who sought the essence of the moon to mix with their magical elixirs.
During the day of the waxing moon, these masters would hold a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) in their hands to catch the water from the moon.

First, the nature of water follows conditions. This nature of water is also the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; while its essence remains unchanging, its function is able to follow conditions, and is therefore called "indeterminate.
Regarding the phrase "flowing and ceasing without constancy": the flow is not a constant flow, as it ceases in accordance with conditions.
The breath is impermanent; the breath flows according to conditions. This precisely reveals its instability.
○ Below, the passage beginning with "Like a room" cites an actual event as proof. Kāpiḷa is translated here as "yellow," or "yellowish-red," because his hair was both yellow and reddish.
Zhengmo (the Correct Pulse) states it is "blue"; perhaps this is based on a different source. Cakraka is translated as "wheel."
Because one’s own adherence to the perfected principle of their view is able to refute the doctrines of others, the *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) likens this to a mandārava flower;
the meaning is that the wheel must possess two [halves], just like a mandarin duck (*ranyang*). "Padma" is translated here as "red lotus," which is the name of a pond.
It is named after the pond because it dwells near it. "Bodhisattva" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term. "Abhiṣeka" means consecration.
It says: *Akāśamudrā*. This translates as "Sea Water. Because they dwell depending upon the sea water, they are practitioners of the Water-Outer Path (*udaka-tīrthika*).
Briefly, four sages are mentioned, with the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) encompassing the remainder.

Because they skillfully employ illusory arts (*māyā*), they are called "Great Illusionists. "Lunar Essence" refers to the water within the moon, which is used to compound medicines. From oneself... [text ends]
Regarding the pursuit of longevity through the taking of elixirs: because such empty claims lack empirical proof, the world refers to them as "illusions" (*māyā*).

Furthermore, as for "illusory medicine," it may rely on this drug to conjure various realms that dazzle and delude the eyes and mind. Regarding the phrase "the white moon and the day," the *Zhengmai* (Correct Pulse) states: the fifteenth night is the full moon (*pūrṇimā*);
the period before the full moon is the "white moon" (*śukla-pakṣa*), and the period after the full moon is the "black moon" (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*). As for the moon itself...
At midday, the light was as bright as day. Regarding the *fāng zhū* (the "square-jade" or concave mirror), the *Huainanzi* states:

"When the *fāng zhū* sees the moon, it exudes moisture that becomes water. Gāo Yòu says: "The *fāng zhū*, also known as the 'yin-suil' (negative fire-drill), produces water when directed toward the moon. Xǔ Shèn says: [The same].
"These are various pearls. [The others] are square stones. Zhengmo says, "They are crystal beads. Wang Chong’s *Lunheng* states:

"On the day of Renzi at midnight on the first day of the eleventh month, one smelts stones from the five directions in the north to produce them. Their shape is like that of a cup or basin; they receive the essence when facing the moon.
The current statement that they "receive the water from within the moon" is largely the same as this calculation. All of these [interpretations] fail to grasp the truth.

This refers only to the meaning of the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* following conditions (*pratyaya*). Second, first refuting the combined state (based on the *Mahābhūta-agni*, where there is a passage citing the opponent's position and providing an analogy;

it is not included here because it can be inferred from the preceding examples). This has two parts: first, refuting the individual characteristics; second, subsequently refuting the combined characteristic. The first of these has two parts.
First, examining the source of the water; second, refuting it by tracing its conditions. Regarding the first:
does this water emerge from within the jewel, exist spontaneously in space, or come from the moon?
The Buddha’s intention was that the meaning of "conjunction" (saṃnipāta) is only established when water emerges from each of these three locations.
Therefore, he raised this inquiry: "Does this water emerge from within the jewel? Does it arise spontaneously from space? Or does it come from the moon?
This must certainly be examined with care. Second, [the Buddha] refutes the three [possibilities] by following their respective conditions.
First, the refutation that [the water] comes from the moon; second, the refutation that it emerges from the pearl; third, the refutation that it arises from space. First:
Ānanda, if it came from the moon, then since it could cause water to emerge from the pearl even at a great distance, all the trees and forests it passed by should likewise discharge flowing streams.

If they were to flow, what need would there be for the *fangzhu* (the concave mirror used to collect dew) to produce it? Since they do not flow, it is clear that the water does not descend from the moon.
At first, when the moon is eclipsed, if one were to claim that water comes from the moon, this argument is incorrect.
For the moon is in the sky while the gem is in the hand; they are far apart. Yet, it is still able to come from such a great distance to cause water to emerge from the gem.
In that case, all the trees encountered along the way ought to emit and flow [water]; could such a thing truly exist?
If they did flow, it would reveal two fallacies. If one claims that the trees emit and flow [the water], then it should be collectible at every location;
why then wait for it to be produced by the *fangzhu* (concave mirror)? If one claims that the trees do not flow [the water], then it is clear that this water does not descend from the moon.

Because it is illogical for something to leave behind what is near in order to reach what is distant. Second, [the opponent's view] is refuted by showing that [the water] cannot emerge from the pearl.
If it were to emerge from the pearl, then water should constantly flow from within this pearl; why then wait for the middle of the night under the white moonlight?
If one were to claim that the water comes from within the jewel, it would not depend on other conditions.
If it did not depend on other conditions, water should flow from the jewel at all times. If this were so, one could receive it at any moment; why wait for midnight?

It would necessarily have to be received during the bright moonlit day—or rather, at midnight, which is the dead of night. This argument refutes the [opponent's] intention by demonstrating that [the water] must indeed await midnight to be received.
On a bright moonlit day, it is clearly understood that this water does not emerge from the pearl. Third, [the opponent] refutes the claim that it arises from space:
if it were to arise from space, then since the nature of space is boundless, water would likewise be limitless; from humans up to the heavens, all would be submerged together.
Furthermore, what of those who travel by water, land, and air?
If it were claimed that there is water produced from space, then since the nature of space is boundless, the water produced from it would likewise be limitless.
If this were so, then from humans up to the gods, all should equally be submerged in a vast flood and sink together into drowning.
There should not be any other substance remaining; how then could there be beings that move in water, on land, or through the air within that interval?
Thus, we know that the claim that water is produced from space is erroneous. First, the refutation of individual characteristics is concluded;
second, the refutation of combined characteristics follows.
Examine this further with careful attention: the moon ascends from the heavens; the pearl is held in the hand; the water basin that receives the pearl was originally set out by a person.
From what direction does the water flow here? The moon and the pearl are far apart; they are neither blended nor joined.
It cannot be that the water-crystal has arisen of itself from nowhere.
"First, 'carefully examining the direction' means to observe with close scrutiny. 'Ascend' (*zhì*) means to rise; the moon rises from the heavens, yet the heavens have no place to store water.
'Jewel' refers to that which is held in the hand; the hand has no place to store water. 'To receive' (*chéng*) means to support;
the bowl for receiving the jewel-water was originally set out by a person, yet the bowl has no place to store water. Since all three [directions] are thus..."
There is no place where water is stored, yet from what direction does this water flow here? This must not fail to be examined thoroughly.
○ The passage beginning with "The moon-jewel" directly refutes the notion of combination (*saṃghāta*).

Since there is no water in the moon and so forth, and furthermore no place for water to be stored in the sky and so forth, one might fear that water is produced through the combined action of the moon and the jewel; therefore, [the author] provides this [refutation].
Refutation: You claim that the moon and the water-crystal are distant from one another, neither conjoined nor combined; how then could they together produce water?

Thus, it is known that the so-called "conjunction" which produces water is erroneous. The final sentence anticipates and preempts a fallacious defense, fearing that one might offer "having no source" as a rebuttal;
therefore, it is refuted by stating "it should not be so," because such a defense contradicts one's own tenets. As for the water-crystal, it is compliant [with the argument].
Regarding their calculation: they reckon this water to be the essence within water. Having already refuted the notion of combination, [the following] details the Middle Way in two parts:
first, the actual demonstration; second, the verification through knowledge. First [the actual demonstration].
You still do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of water is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true water;
it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
This is known through two proofs.
In accordance with the minds of sentient beings and the extent of what they can know: if one person grasps the pearl, water appears in that one place;
if it is grasped throughout the entire Dharma-realm, water arises filling the entire Dharma-realm. When it fills the world, how could there be any fixed location? It manifests according to karma.

First, one verifies and knows [the nature of] purity. Within this, there are two meanings: verification through inclusion and verification through the resolution of doubt; both are explained according to the preceding analysis.
The final phrase, which verifies and knows its pervasiveness, is also based on the preceding. This concludes the detailed exposition of the Middle Way.
The four pairs and eight classes [of noble ones] sweep away the two types of views.
The world is ignorant, deludedly taking causes and conditions as well as spontaneous nature to be real; these are all merely conceptual constructions and calculations of the conscious mind.
They consist only of verbal expressions and possess no actual meaning whatsoever.

The section on the water element concludes. There are four sections on the four great wind elements: first, establishing their characteristics based on their nature; second, first refuting the notion of combination;
third, providing a detailed demonstration of the Middle Way; fourth, simultaneously brushing away both conceptual extremes. First:
Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant.
When you regularly adjust your robes upon entering the great assembly, the corner of your saṃghāṭī moves against those nearby, and a slight breeze then brushes their faces.
Initially, the nature of wind follows conditions; the nature of wind is also the nature of the storehouse (*ālaya*). "Having no substance" means having no fixed substance.

Because it has no fixed substance, it moves according to conditions and is still according to conditions; therefore, it is said to be "not permanent. From "You always... onwards, he cites actual events as proof.
Regarding matters such as begging for food and preaching the Dharma, one should wear the *kāṣāya*; therefore, it is said to be "always properly adjusted."
One enters the great assembly in accordance with the custom of the *saṃgha*. Regarding the *saṃghāṭī*, the Tang translation is "repeated-layered robe" (*chóngfù yī*).
Qingliang says its meaning is translated as "harmony" (*héhé*). A new one consists of two layers; an old one consists of four layers.

Because it is formed by layering, it is called "harmony. It is the first of the three types of robes based on their function. It is also called the "patchwork robe" (*zàsuì yī*), as it is made from cut and pieced fragments.

Because it possesses many characteristics of being a continuous thread, it comprises the three grades and nine levels, as explained in the section on the names and characteristics of the robes and alms bowl in the *Śrāmaṇera-vinaya*.

It exists only when the cloth moves; conversely, this implies that it does not exist when there is no movement. Through this, the meaning that it is not eternally present and lacks a substantial essence can be seen.
Second, first refuting the composite [whole], which has two parts: first, refuting the individual characteristics; second...
Next, the characteristics of combination are refuted in two parts: first, examining the wind in its source; second, refuting it by tracing its conditions. Regarding the first:
does this wind emerge from the corner of the *kāṣāya* robe, arise from empty space, or originate from that person’s face?
*Kāṣāya* is translated here as "dyed-in-uniform-color robes" (*huài-sè yī*). Qingliang (Xuanzang) says they are "robes of non-primary colors.
According to the Vinaya, these three colors—blue, black, and madder—are used to "ruin" the beautiful primary colors. Paramārtha says this is the general name for the three robes;

alternatively, they are called "dust-detaching garments" because they sever the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), or "emaciating garments" because they cut through the afflictions (*kleśa*). They are also referred to as "lotus... [garments].
Because the flower-garment is free from attachment. Herein, the intent of the inquiry is likewise to require that there be individual characteristics first, and only then can they be combined.
Second, refuting [the sound] by following its conditions, which consists of three parts: first, refuting [the sound] as emerging from the garment;
second, refuting it as originating from space; third, refuting it as being produced from the face. First:
"Ānanda, if this wind were to emerge from the corner of your *kāṣāya*, you would be wearing the wind; as the robe flutters and shakes, it should be separated from your body.
Now, as I preach the Dharma in this assembly with my robe hanging down, look at my robe: where is the wind?
There should be no place within the robe where the wind could be hidden."
When first tearing open the robe, wind emerges; since the wind comes from within the *kāṣāya*, it is difficult to wear when there is wind.
However, wind has movement as its inherent nature; if one were to actually wear it, the garment would naturally flutter and sway.

Therefore, it is difficult to refute [the argument] that [wind] is not separate from the body. By refuting the notion [of wind being separate], the point that one perceives wind while wearing a robe—without the robe being separated from the body—is established.
It is not the case that there is no wind within the robe; thus, it is clear that this wind does not emerge from the *kāṣāya*.

The section beginning with "I now" (我今下) serves to prevent erroneous arguments. Fearing that upon hearing the difficulty regarding separation from the body, one might erroneously argue: "If the robe is moving..."
Then the wind emerges; when the robe hangs down, the wind merely conceals it. How can one raise the objection that the wind causes it to flutter and detach from the body?
Therefore, this precaution was established. If you claim that when the robe hangs down, the wind merely conceals it—
"Just as my robe hangs down here within this Dharma assembly, it should likewise conceal the wind. You should observe for yourself where the wind is in relation to my robe.
To speak according to reality, there should be no place within the robe to conceal the wind, for the robe is made of cloth and possesses no pores. Second, the refutation arising from space.

If wind were produced from empty space, why does your robe not move when there is no breeze? Why is it not brushed by it? Since the nature of emptiness is eternally abiding, wind should be constantly produced.
If there were times when there was no wind, then empty space would have to perish. If wind could be seen to perish, what would the appearance of perishing empty space be like?
If there were arising and ceasing, it would not be called "empty space. Being named "empty space," how could wind emerge from it?
First, the refutation based on the absence of clothing: Wind arises from space and is not inherently related to clothing.
Therefore, it is difficult to argue that when the clothing does not move, for what reason is there no fanning [of wind]. This is the principle that space is devoid of the production of wind.

Next, the refutation based on the dissimilarity of cause and effect: The nature of space is eternally abiding. If it were to produce wind, it would necessarily produce it constantly, because the cause...

Because a permanent effect must necessarily be permanent. If that were so, then space (*ākāśa*) would also have to perish when there is no wind, since the cessation of an effect necessitates the cessation of its cause.

However, at the time when the wind ceases, this is visible to everyone. If you ask what form the cessation of space might take, we know that space does not cease, whereas the nature of wind does cease. How can an effect that is dissimilar to its cause arise from it?
This is certainly an impossibility. ○ Regarding the passage "If there were," he refutes it by showing that the name and its meaning do not correspond.
Space is originally defined by the meaning of being neither born nor ceasing. If it were subject to birth and cessation, it would no longer be called space.
Since it is now designated as "space," it should naturally be without birth or cessation. If wind were to arise within it, the name and the meaning would be inconsistent.
Therefore, it is difficult to say how the wind arises; for that which arises is precisely birth, and whatever is born must necessarily perish. Guanding says:
"Ordinary and small-minded practitioners constantly cling to the notion that wind is produced from space. Thus, [the text] refutes this point by point in detail.
The three types of "striking" arise from the face.

If the wind were produced spontaneously and then brushed against your face, it would indeed strike you from that face; yet, while you yourself are adjusting your robes, why do you brush them away in such a disorderly manner?
If you claim that wind arises spontaneously from the face being brushed, this argument is also untenable.
For if it were produced from that face, it ought to brush you; since we do not see it brushing you, we know it is not produced from that face.
Now, when you yourself are adjusting your robes, why does it instead brush your face? This demonstrates the principle that it is not produced from that face.
This can be seen even more clearly. Having finished first refuting the characteristic of individuality, secondly, we shall refute the characteristic of conjunction.

You should observe with careful discernment: the adjustment of the robe resides in you, while the face belongs to that other person; empty space is quiescent and does not participate in their movement.
"From which direction does the wind come, stirring itself to reach here? The nature of wind and space are distinct; they are neither blended nor conjoined.
It cannot be that the nature of wind exists of its own accord without a source.

First, examine the direction from which it comes. As for your instruction to 'examine with discernment,' this means to observe with careful discrimination and clarity regarding the reality of things. Do not..."
You have understood the matter upon merely seeing it. You stand there with your robes adjusted, yet you have no place to hide from the wind.
Your face belongs to that person, yet he has no place to hide from the wind. Space is tranquil and equal to emptiness, yet it too has no place to hide from the wind.
Since all three directions offer no place to hide from the wind, from which direction does the wind itself stir and come here? Furthermore—
One might fail to examine this thoroughly. ○ Regarding "wind and space," the following section correctly refutes their conjunction. Fearing that one might say:
"Since there is no wind in the space between the garment and the face, and upon careful observation there is no place where wind is stored, it stands to reason that they exist through conjunction;

thus, there should be no doubt. Therefore, this refutation is made: we see with our own eyes that the wind moves while the space remains still; their natures are mutually exclusive, and there is no conjunction.
Because this is the case, it is said that there is neither conjunction nor combination. By analogy with this, one may understand that clothing obstructs while wind passes through;

in all such instances, there is no sense of conjunction or combination. This sentence serves as a preemptive refutation of erroneous defenses, following the previous method; thus, the refutation of conjunction is now complete.
Third, a detailed exposition of the Middle Way, which has two parts: first, the direct exposition; second, the verification through knowledge. Regarding the first:
You simply do not know that within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of wind is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true wind.
It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

The character "wan" (宛) carries a profound sense of strangeness. It means that while the natures of earth, fire, and water have been demonstrated in detail through three successive stages, the nature of wind can be inferred by analogy.
Yet, observing your movements and stillness, you clearly do not understand the principle of the Tathāgatagarbha’s unchanging nature conforming to conditions.
The rest may be inferred according to what precedes.

Second, it is verified by knowing that [the wind] accords with the minds of sentient beings and corresponds to the measure of their cognition. Ānanda, it is like when you, as a single person, slightly move your robe;
a subtle breeze arises, sweeping through the entire Dharma-realm and filling the lands, pervading the whole world—how could it have a fixed location? Following...
The manifestation of the karma that initiates [rebirth] is first verified as pure. The Dharma-realm and the worldly realm of lands are of one and the same meaning; this refers to the sweeping motion.
"Sweeping throughout the Dharma-realm" means that all people within the Dharma-realm are subtly moving their garments. This brings forth birth throughout the entire land.
This means that winds arise everywhere throughout the entire land. Thus we know that these winds pervade the world; how could they have a fixed location?
The final phrase allows one to verify through experience that their pervasiveness is evident. This concludes the detailed exposition of the Middle Way.

These four pairs and two ranks are swept away by the world’s ignorance, which deludedly regards causes and conditions as well as spontaneous nature as real. All of these are merely conceptualizations and calculations of the discriminating consciousness;
they consist only of verbal expressions and possess no actual substance.

The section on the wind element concludes. Regarding the four great elements of the five voids: first, establishing the characteristics based on their nature; second, first refuting the notion of combination;
third, providing a detailed demonstration of the Middle Way; fourth, simultaneously sweeping away the two types of conceptualization. First:

Ānanda, emptiness has no form; it is manifested through matter. It is like a place in the city of Śrāvastī far from the river, where various Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, as well as Pahlavas and Caṇḍālas, have newly established a residence and dug a well in search of water.
When they have excavated the earth for one foot, there is then one foot of empty space within it. Thus it is.
Thus, even when one excavates the earth to a depth of one *zhang*, one regains one *zhang* of empty space within; the depth of this emptiness corresponds exactly to the amount excavated.

Initially, the nature of emptiness follows conditions. The two characters "nature of emptiness" (*kōng-xìng*) provisionally point to the unchanging essence. Because it is unchanging, [it can manifest through conditions].

This is called "formlessness. It means that there are no forms such as long, short, large, or small; rather, form is manifested through color. This refers to the function of following conditions (*pratyaya*).

Because it follows conditions, it is called "manifestation through causes," meaning that due to the distinctions among those colors and forms, space itself is revealed to have its own distinct differences.
As in the passage below, the city of Śrāvastī is cited as an illustration to provide proof. The ground of the city of Śrāvastī...
The population is vast and dense; being close to the river, there is no need to dig wells, so [the text] refers only to remote locations.
In the Western Regions, the social classes are divided into four castes (*varṇa*). *Kṣatriya* is abbreviated as *Kṣatri*; this translates as "Lord of the Fields," referring to the royal lineage.
*Brāhmaṇa* translates as "Pure Conduct"; they preserve the Way, abide in rectitude, and maintain pure integrity in their conduct, resembling [sages].
In this region, there are the Confucian and Daoist traditions. Vaiśya is translated here as "merchant"; these are those who trade by traveling and sell from their stalls.
Śūdra is translated as "farmer"; these are those who plow fields and cultivate the land. Outside of these four castes, there are separately two clans: the wise and the ignorant.
Therefore, it is said that they are "comprehensive. *Pārala* is translated here as "sharp faculties," such as those belonging to the six arts and the hundred crafts.
*Caṇḍāla* is translated here as "rigid insignia," such as butchers and executioners. When establishing a new residence or undertaking construction, water is required;
because carrying it from a distant river involves great expense and labor, one must seek it by digging a well. [For every] foot dug, [one obtains] a foot [of water].
"Empty. It emerges from the measure of emptiness; the meaning that its manifestation is dependent upon form can likewise be seen for itself.
The final two lines reiterate the preceding meaning and serve as the introduction to the following inquiry. Second, first, the refutation of combination (saṃghāta). Two.

First, the individual characteristics are refuted; second, the combined characteristic is refuted. Regarding the first [of these two], there are two parts: first, investigating the source based on emptiness;
second, refuting it by tracing its conditions. As for the first:
Is this emptiness produced by the earth as its cause? Does it exist because of the act of digging? Or does it arise spontaneously without a cause?
That which arises because of the earth is produced from the earth; that which exists because of the digging is produced from the tools of digging.

"Arising spontaneously without cause" means that there is no other cause, and it arises from its own essence—this is like saying that the space within a well emerges from the space pervading the entire world.
Second, refuting [the view of arising] by following conditions has three parts. First, the refutation of arising from self.

Second, it emerges by breaking through the soil; third, it emerges by being hewn out by a chisel. The first [case]—according to its underlying meaning—is actually the breaking [of the earth] so that [the water] arises from space; however, space is its own essence.

Therefore, it is said that [the effect] arises spontaneously. While many ancient masters have interpreted this as a refutation of causelessness (*ahetuka*), the present commentary does not do so, because such an interpretation would contradict the meaning of the refutation of combination (*saṃghāta*).
Ānanda, if this space were produced spontaneously without a cause, why was there no obstruction before the earth was excavated?
Why did one see only the great earth, with no passage or penetration at all?
To refute this intention: if you reckon that this emptiness arises independently from its own essence without any other cause, then it should not depend upon the act of digging or the earth itself.
If that were so, there should have been no obstruction even before the earth was dug; why then is it unable to be unobstructed?
Not only is it unable to be unobstructed, but one perceives only the vast expanse of the great earth, with nothing else at all.
This is the characteristic of thorough penetration. It is known that the claim that things arise spontaneously without a cause is erroneous.
Second, refuting [the idea that space] emerges from earth:
if it emerged from earth, then at the time the earth emerged, one should have seen space entering; yet if the earth emerged first without space entering, [this is impossible].
How can it be that empty space emerges from soil? If there were no entering or exiting, then space and soil would fundamentally have no different causes.
If they were not different, they would be identical; if they were identical, why would space not emerge when the soil emerges?
