At the beginning, when the earth is first broken and emerges, if you claim that this space emerges because of the earth, then at the time the earth comes out of the well, one should see empty space entering from the outside, because the earth was previously outside.
If the earth first emerges from the well without any empty space entering from the outside, how can you say that empty space emerges because of the earth? ○ If...
There is no need for a preemptive refutation of potential fallacious defenses. Fearing that Ānanda might defend [the position] by saying, "Space originally arises within;

it truly lacks the sense of emerging from the earth or entering a well," this refutation is made. If one claims that space lacks the sense of emerging from the earth or entering a well, then prior to the excavation of the earth, there would be no original cause for the distinction between space and earth. "Cause" (hetu) refers to dependence (āśraya). There would be no distinct cause.
This means that space and earth depend upon one another for their existence; there is no separate basis for them.

"If there is no difference, then they are identical" means that since there is no distinct cause, they are of a single substance. Since they are of a single substance, when one emerges, both emerge together.
Therefore, it is difficult to explain why space does not emerge at the same time as the earth emerges when it is excavated. Third, the refutation of the cause by means of excavation.

If it were produced because of the digging, then the space produced by the digging should not be the same as the earth removed. If it were not produced because of the digging, then since the digging itself merely brought forth the earth, how could one see the space?
First, this directly refutes the cause of digging: if you claim that this space is produced through the presence of digging, then the mere act of digging alone should suffice.

If emptiness were to emerge, it should not depend upon being excavated from the earth. Since it is now necessarily required that it be excavated from the earth to become empty, we clearly know that this emptiness does not arise because of the act of digging.
The phrase "does not depend" (bù yīn) serves as a simultaneous challenge to the claim of non-dependence.

Fearing that the opponent’s argument might be refuted by the necessity of digging, they may resort to the counter-argument that it does not depend on being excavated. Therefore, this challenge is raised: if you claim that this emptiness does not depend on being produced by the digging, [then...]
Then the excavation itself emerges from within and extends outward. How, then, can one perceive emptiness within it? This is not only because the excavation is not established through causes;
it is also not the case that it is not established through them. In short, failing to understand that nature is inherently complete—whether it be "thus" or "not thus"—is entirely incorrect.
First, the refutation of individual characteristics is concluded. Second, the refutation of the combined characteristic follows.
Examine this further with the utmost precision and scrutinize it thoroughly: the chisel follows the hand as it moves in various directions, and the earth shifts according to the ground.
From what source, then, does this empty space emerge? The hollowing out of space and the solidity of the earth do not function for one another;
they are neither blended nor joined. It cannot be that empty space arises from nowhere on its own.
First, examine the direction from which it came. The Buddha’s intention was that what I have taught is that it does not arise from three locations.
Even if you are not yet convinced in your heart, examine it more closely. What is meant by "examining closely"? It means to investigate thoroughly and discern its origin;
to observe carefully and visualize its location. From which direction could there be another hidden space? As for the hole dug by human hands—
I instructed him to observe his hand; when he moved it according to the various directions, I instructed him to observe those directions.
When the ground shifted as the earth moved, I instructed him to observe the earth. Once he had observed all three directions and found no place where the void was hidden, I asked:
"Now tell me, from what source does such a void ultimately arise? You must explain this clearly to me; do not be vague. [He] bored through the void.
Below, the refutation of conjunction is presented. As with the three aforementioned locations where [space] does not arise, there is likewise no hidden space within the three directions.
Fearing that one might claim they arise together through conjunction, this refutation is made. It is observed that the excavation and the space are respectively solid and void;
as such, they do not function for one another, and thus there is no sense of conjunction. Therefore, it is said: "It is neither conjoined nor combined. As...
Since the voidness of the "hollow" is thus, the voidness of the "earth" is likewise so; in both cases, there is no sense of combination.
One should understand that it is improper to preemptively block erroneous defenses. This concludes the refutation of combination. Third, a detailed exposition of the Middle Way, in three parts.
This consists of three parts: first, an illustration by analogy; second, the formal demonstration of the Middle Way; and third, verifying through empirical facts.

Regarding the first two [of these], there are two sub-sections: first, using emptiness as an analogy for the four great names of grasping; second, using the four as an analogy for emptiness to reveal the meaning of perfection. Regarding the first [sub-section]: [The text continues with the specific analogies.]
If this nature of empty space is perfect, pervasive, and fundamentally unmoving, one should know that the earth, water, fire,

and wind currently manifest before us are all equally termed the "five great elements. The Buddha’s intention was that, according to the aforementioned explanation, this empty space neither exists through combination nor—
It does not emerge from anywhere; one clearly knows that this is the nature which is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unmoving. Zhengmo (The Correct Pulse) says:

"In the three characters 'perfectly pervasive' (*yuán-zhōu-biàn*), the character 'perfect' (*yuán*) is the emphasis. This is because when ordinary people discuss emptiness, they also speak of its pervasiveness;
however, where there are obstructive dharmas of form, it is not interfused. Thus, while they say it is pervasive, it is not perfect."
"Universal" (*zōubiàn*) means all-pervasive. Now, it is said that the nature of emptiness is universal, and form does not obstruct it; therefore, the meaning of "perfect" (*yuán*) is added to it.
Furthermore, the phrase "unmoving" (*bùdòngyáo*) corresponds to the subsequent meaning of being without arising or ceasing.

That is to say, "universal" indicates that it is not the case that something exists here while it is absent there, or that it is absent here while it exists there; this is the sense of "perfect. "Unmoving" indicates that it is not something that existed previously [and then changes].

That which was non-existent now exists; that which now exists will later cease to exist—this is the meaning of "permanence. This is merely established as a premise, and what follows serves as an illustration:
ordinarily, people know only that earth, water, fire, and wind are called "great," but they do not realize that space (*ākāśa*) is also great.
Now, since its nature is perfect and all-pervasive, and fundamentally unshakable, it naturally gives rise to infinite functions.

Taking this as an analogy, one should know that this space is called one of the "five great elements" (pañca-mahābhūta) equally with the present earth, water, fire, and wind, because they all share the same meaning of being "great.
Second, by using the four [elements] as an analogy for space, the meaning of perfection is revealed.

The nature is truly perfect and harmonious; all are the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally without birth or extinction. Ānanda, your mind is deluded and confused, failing to realize that the four great elements are originally the Tathāgatagarbha.
You should contemplate whether space comes out or enters in, or whether it neither comes out nor enters in.
Since they are equally designated as the "five great elements" (pañca-mahābhūtāni), the nature of the element of space is true, and the natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are likewise true.

The element of space is perfectly interfused, and earth, water, fire, and wind are also perfectly interfused. This is because they are all the Tathāgatagarbha, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing. (Question:

You use the name "space" as an analogy for the other four, because people already do not understand it; yet you use the four to illustrate space in order to manifest their perfect interfusion—what is the intended meaning here? (Answer: There are two reasons for this. First, it is easier to understand.

The nature is true. Second is the ease with which one understands their perfect interfusion. Regarding the ease with which one understands that the nature is true: it was previously stated that "dark obscurity becomes space," and later it will be said that "space arises within great enlightenment. Thus, we know that the empty space before us directly depends on the nature for its arising; if one speaks of the nature being true, it is easy to believe.

As for earth, water, fire, and wind, people merely see them as depending upon space, yet they do not know that they arise from the nature. If one speaks of the nature being true, this is difficult to perceive. Regarding the ease with which one understands their perfect interfusion:

it was previously stated that if one digs out a foot of earth, there is a foot of empty space therein; if one digs out ten feet of earth, one likewise obtains ten feet of empty space. Later it will be said that "the substance of space is not the various phenomena, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those phenomena. Thus, we know that...

The preceding space was itself unobstructed; if one speaks of its perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), it is easy to believe. As for earth, water, fire, and wind, people only see them as mutually overcoming and extinguishing one another, yet they do not know that they mutually penetrate and contain one another. If one speaks of their perfect interfusion, it is difficult to perceive. For this reason, an analogy is drawn;

this is to use what is easily known to illustrate what is difficult to see, thereby making that which is difficult to see become easily understood. This is merely establishing the analogy; what follows is the instruction for contemplation. The name is called out repeatedly to signify a sense of awakening and alertness. Thus, I now provide this revelation... (Note:

This may be inferred and elucidated through analogy. Suppose your mind remains as before, clouded by provisional teachings and deluded by external doctrines, such that you cannot awaken to the fact that the four great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha.
In that case, you should contemplate whether the aforementioned empty space comes out or goes in, or whether it neither comes nor goes.
It is not as if it does not exist at all; for the Buddha’s intent is that if there were coming and going, one would fall [into the error of dualism].

Regarding causes and conditions: if there were no exiting and no entering, one would fall into the view of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). However, [the Buddha] was unwilling to explain it clearly and directly;

he only required that one observe for oneself and awaken for oneself. One must wait until one gains conviction that empty space has neither exiting nor entering, yet is not without exiting and entering, and that it is fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha*.
By applying this analogy, one will realize that the four great elements are likewise not obscure. Having thus completed the elucidation through such analogies:
Second, the correct demonstration of the Middle Way:
You do not understand this at all. Within the Tathāgatagarbha, the nature of awareness is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true awareness.
It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

The Master was also deeply perplexed by this meaning. He said: "I have previously and repeatedly revealed [the truth], and finally instructed you to practice contemplation, leading you to believe that awakening is attained through emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Yet, you remain entirely ignorant of the meanings within the Tathāgatagarbha, such as 'the true emptiness of intrinsic awareness' and 'the true awareness of intrinsic emptiness.
(According to the preceding [passage], earth, water, fire, and wind all employ their own primary elements in contrast to space; now, [we speak of] the emptiness of nature and the true emptiness.)"

The characters cannot be distinguished; therefore, the character "awakening" (*jue*) is substituted for it. To speak of "intrinsic awakening" (*xing jue*), awakening itself is movement. It possesses the sense of "following conditions.

Because it possesses this sense of following conditions, it can become "stubborn emptiness" (*wan kong*). Although it can become stubborn emptiness, its essence ultimately does not change; thus it is called "true emptiness" (*zhen kong*).
This is because what is called stubborn emptiness—having no substance—is precisely true emptiness. To speak of "intrinsic emptiness" (*xing kong*), emptiness itself is...
This is tranquility. It possesses the meaning of immutability; because it possesses the meaning of immutability, it perpetually maintains its own nature (*svabhāva*).

Although it perpetually maintains its own nature, its functioning never becomes obstructed; therefore, it is called "True Awakening" (*bhūta-avabodha*). This means that by relying on the nature, emptiness is realized, which is precisely True Awakening.
The above section differs slightly in phrasing from what precedes it, so it has been explained in sequence. The following two phrases follow the same principle as those above.
The three types of grasping are known through empirical verification;
they correspond to the minds of sentient beings and accord with the measure of what is to be known. Ānanda, it is like a single well being hollowed out within empty space:
the emptiness in the ten directions is likewise so. Since it fills the ten directions, how could it have a fixed location? It manifests in accordance with karma.
The detailed exposition of the Middle Way is complete. The four pairs [of practitioners] have swept away the two extremes of calculation.

Those in the world are ignorant and deludedly regard things as being produced by causes and conditions or by a nature of spontaneity; all of these are merely conceptualizations and estimations of the discerning mind.
All that exists is mere verbal expression; there is no real meaning whatsoever.

This concludes the Great Element of Space. VI. The Great Element of Seeing (*darśana-mahābhūta*). (Zhengmo says: This is the Great Element of the Faculties (*indriya-mahābhūta*). It subsumes all six faculties, yet only the faculty of the eye is cited as an example.
