Nor is it otherwise. Second, the aspiration to repay the debt of gratitude:
"May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King; may I further deliver as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges. I shall offer this profound resolve to every dust-mote world;
this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness."
The first phrase expresses the aspiration to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. The word "jin" (今) is an abbreviation for "jin er hou" (今而後), meaning "from now on.
Since Ānanda has already gained faith that the *dharmakāya* is primordially present and knows himself to have the capacity to achieve Buddhahood, he makes this vow:

from this moment forward, through successive acts of service and cultivation, may he attain the ultimate fruit, sit upon the great jewel-flower throne, and preach all *dharmaparyāyas*, thereby becoming a Buddha.

This is the King of Flowers. The second phrase expresses the vow to deliver sentient beings; it means that although one has attained the state of Ratnasambhava, one does not abandon the gate of compassion, but returns to the realm of worldly toil (*saṃsāra*) to perform the work of delivering beings.
One must surely continue in this way until every single being, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, has been delivered, with no end to the vow.
These two phrases are dedicated for the sake of repaying kindness; it means that having already attained the fruit of Buddhahood, furthermore—
To enter the realm of worldly toil (*saṃsāra*) to deliver sentient beings is called the profound mind (*gambhīracitta*).

To further dedicate this profound mind toward all sentient beings throughout the dust-like lands of the universe so that they may all together attain Buddhahood—this is what is meant by repaying the Buddha’s kindness even by a ten-thousandth part.
These three vows accomplish the three virtues;
I humbly entreat the World-Honored One to serve as witness. I vow to enter first into the evil world of the five turbidities;

so long as even a single sentient being has not attained Buddhahood, I shall never take *nirvāṇa* here. O Great Hero, Great Power, Great Compassion! I pray that you will further examine and eliminate my subtle [faults].
"May my subtle afflictions [be exhausted], so that I may quickly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment and sit at the site of awakening throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
First, I vow to fulfill this compassionate virtue. Regarding "humbly entreats" (*fùqǐng*): it means to bow down and request, expressing the sincerity of the petition.

Regarding "bears witness" (*zhèngmíng*): it means to know clearly and distinctly, ensuring that the vow is not false. This is because the preceding section concerns the arousal of the aspiration to deliver sentient beings.

This concerns matters subsequent to attaining Buddhahood. Furthermore, he reflected that even prior to becoming a Buddha, one must take the salvation of sentient beings as the requisite for enlightenment;

thus, he requested the Buddha to act as his witness. Regarding the "five turbidities" (*pañca-kaṣāya*): they are the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), and the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*).
Lurong said: "The turbidity of the eon is a provisional designation established in relation to the latter four turbidities. And:
They have no separate substance. The fact that the four turbidities intensify and converge at this time is precisely their characteristic.

The turbidity of views (dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya) has the five sharp afflictions (kleśas) as its substance, and the blazing intensity of various views as its characteristic. The turbidity of afflictions (kleśa-kaṣāya) has the five dull afflictions as its substance.

The three calamities (*tṛkalpa*) have the function of summoning and manifesting [suffering] as their characteristic. The defilement of sentient beings (*sattvakāṣāya*) takes the retribution of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), views, and pride as its essence;
ill repute and foul reputation constitute its characteristic. The defilement of lifespan (*āyuḥkāṣāya*) takes the continuity of matter and mind as its essence;

the shortening of years and the reduction of longevity constitute its characteristic. However, this differs from what is stated later in the sutra. That [passage] refers to the root, whereas this refers to the branches and secondary factors.

This is because their subtle characteristics and coarse characteristics differ. According to the teachings, when the human lifespan is twenty thousand years, one enters the *kalpa-kṣaya* (degeneration of the eon).

As it progresses and intensifies until the human lifespan reaches one hundred years, all evils flourish; people become stubborn and difficult to transform, at which point it is further termed an "evil age.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "In the period of turmoil during the degeneration of the eon, sentient beings have heavy defilements and accomplish all manner of unwholesome deeds."
This refers to the roots of virtue. However, most people in this world are timid about entering [the path]; therefore, one who first enters does so for two reasons:
first, to lead the multitude with a courageous mind; second, to rescue those suffering most severely with a mind of compassion.

*Nirvāṇa* (in Chinese, *nièpán*) is a variation in the weight of the Sanskrit pronunciation. One who has not yet attained Buddhahood shall never realize final liberation (*sākṣātkriyā*) within this [limited] state.

This is the vast mind. This constitutes the great benefaction toward sentient beings through the accomplishment of the *nirmāṇakāya*. Regarding the two phrases "Great Hero" (*mahāvīra*) and so forth, they vow the accomplishment of the perfection of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
One who can crush the deep delusions of sentient beings is called the Great Hero; one who can eliminate the seeds and habitual tendencies of deep delusion is called the One of Great Power;
one who can bestow the bliss of the two adornments is called the Greatly Compassionate One; and one who can uproot the [suffering of] the two deaths...
"Suffering" refers to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Because one seeks to attain the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*), one must rely upon the power of empowerment;
thus, it is designated according to the meaning of wisdom and abandonment. "To hope and seek" means this. "Subtle afflictions" refers to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Once inverted perceptions have been eliminated, one proceeds from this point to apply effort and practice; the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) can then naturally be severed. As for those subtle [cognitive] obstructions...
Since delusions have no objective conditions that can be extinguished, I hope you will examine this further and eliminate them.

This means that I seek from the Buddha a more thorough analysis of the dharmas for severing subtle delusions. Thus, through the great virtue of severance regarding ignorance, one achieves the Dharma-body.
The final two lines vow the achievement of the virtue of wisdom. "Unsurpassed enlightenment" refers to ultimate bodhi; "may I ascend it early" is the aspiration.

The meaning of attaining Buddhahood swiftly through the compassionate empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha is as follows: "In the worlds of the ten directions" refers to the universal entry into the Flower Treasury World (*Ghanavyūha*).
"Sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) refers to possessing the adornments and preaching the Dharma, thereby becoming the King of Jewel Flowers.

This constitutes the accomplishment of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) through the virtue of great wisdom regarding Bodhi. Once these three virtues are complete, the three bodies (*trikāya*) are perfected. From this point on—
In the future, I shall turn back the compassionate vessel and re-enter the realm of worldly toil to deliver all sentient beings so that we may together achieve Buddhahood;
only then will my vow to repay the Buddha’s kindness be fulfilled. (4) This concludes the application of the non-retrogressive resolve.
"Śūnyatā (the nature of emptiness) may perish, but the śakara (indestructible) mind does not waver.
Wénlǐng says: "Śūnyatā is translated here as 'emptiness' (*śūnyatā*); *śakara* is translated as 'solid' (*dṛḍha*).
This means that while the nature of emptiness, being without substance, may still perish, my own mind is solid and shall never regress. Guǎngdìng says: "[It] eliminates existence."
There are two meanings. First, emptiness can never be dissolved. As it says below, "Emptiness cannot be created, for it is indestructible.

Now, if one says that even emptiness can be dissolved while the mind remains unmoved, this refers to the meaning of the inexhaustible virtues of the Buddhas, which are like space that could be measured.

Second, when one awakens to the truth and returns to the source, empty space itself vanishes; when the bubble ceases, the emptiness from which it arose is fundamentally non-existent, let alone the various triple worlds.
There is. In principle, while emptiness may be dissolved and extinguished, the mind cannot be destroyed. For example, when the kalpa is destroyed, the oceans dry up and the mountains collapse;
yet how could the *tathāgatagarbha* mind ever be exhausted? Furthermore, it is said that in the Secret Mantra section, *śakara* and *kṣakara* are translated together as "vajra.
Since the mind is like a vajra, how could it ever be destroyed? Zhengmo says: "This generally summarizes what preceded."
Seeking enlightenment above and transforming those below, he made a profound vow in his heart: "Even if empty space should come to an end, my vow shall never cease.
From the time Ānanda requested the samādhi until this present teaching of the Dharma constitutes one complete cycle, titled the Cycle of Destroying Delusion and Revealing Reality.
In summary, it serves to eliminate inverted perceptions. The exposition of the *Gaganagañja* (Empty Treasury) is now concluded.
Commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: Pointing at the Palm (Lengyan jing zhizhang shu), Fascicle Three; Fascicle Four.
Respectfully composed by the junior disciple Dàtiāntōnglǐ of Xiánzōng at Niànhuá Monastery in the Capital.
The Dharma-heir (Xingzong Zuwang Tengqing Huairen Zu Yu Jiaozi): Second, regarding the explanation of the two *piṭakas* for the removal of subtle delusions.

(As stated above, once inverted thoughts have been eliminated and the treasury of emptiness has been believed, if one can cultivate practice through successive events, the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) may naturally be severed.

However, as for the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they still require careful discernment; how much more so for the ignorance of the arising-phase (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*), which is the most subtle among the subtle! Therefore, the previous statement that one "hopes to further discern and eliminate" was intended for the Tathāgata to exercise careful discernment and sever [them].)

The method for their removal involves eliminating them along with the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*). The Buddha, in order to respond to this, employed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra’s inquiry as a pretext to explain the latter two *piṭakas*. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) states: "The ancient masters’ explanations of the three *piṭakas* have two meanings.

First, the *Yuanjue shu* (Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra) takes 'concealment,' 'inclusion,' and 'production' as the three. Second, the *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sutra) explains the three *piṭakas*—Emptiness and so forth—in sequential order according to the three greatnesses (*mahattva*) of essence, attributes, and function.

The present [text] seems to follow the latter meaning, yet it differs slightly. The upper section on the *piṭaka* of Emptiness is entirely identical; however, because the true essence revealed therein is solely the Greatness of Essence (*dharmatā-mahattva*), its intent differs from that of the following two *piṭakas*. Thus, it explains the three *piṭakas* of Emptiness and so forth by synthesizing them through the single and double aspects of essence and function. And so it continues.

[Their] mutual application is likewise without deficiency. (2) First, Pūrṇa follows upon the preceding [discourse] to raise two doubts; second, the Tathāgata resolves these doubts by expounding the two Piṭakas.

Regarding the first, Zhengmo (Zheng-mo) says: "The fact that this is requested and initiated by Pūrṇa indicates that what is discussed below concerns subtle afflictions, profound principles, and the deep stage of those beyond training."

All should investigate this with their whole hearts; it is not merely for the sake of those still in training (śaikṣa). Therefore, I now present two aspects that surpass what was previously appropriate for the occasion: first, the excellence of having exhausted the delusions of the four abodes, which surpasses the previous state where such delusions were not yet exhausted;

second, the excellence of being able to expound through the four analytical knowledges, which surpasses the previous ability to merely memorize them. Three [sections follow]: first, a general praise of the wondrous instruction; second, a general narration of the presence of doubt; third, a formal presentation of the request. First:
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat amidst the great assembly;
he bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, you have skillfully expounded for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth."
"At that time" refers to the period when Ānanda and the others had already eliminated their inverted conceptions and had gained faith in the Treasury of Emptiness;

however, as subtle delusions still remained and they had not yet gained faith in the two treasuries, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra was about to pose a question. Rising from his seat in the midst of the assembly represents the manner of his inquiry:
with shoulders bared and kneeling cross-legged, his physical actions were reverent; with palms joined in homage, his mental activity was single-mindedly focused.
He addressed the Buddha, praising his virtuous verbal karma with great earnestness. Because he had moved the Buddha through this, the Buddha would surely respond;
thus, he praised him with great majestic power to subdue and dissolve his beginningless inverted conceptions.

He praised him as being "virtuous" and so forth, because the Buddha had long ago received him within the treasury of emptiness and caused him to have faith. As for the "Ultimate Truth," it refers to that which was previously requested by Ānanda.

The Way is the definitive meaning, the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). It shatters consciousness to open the path and points to the sense faculties to guide those of initial capacity.
It aligns the sections to reveal the hall and harmonizes the great to manifest the chamber. Because it proceeds step-by-step in orderly sequence, it is said that he is skilled at expounding it.
Regarding the fact that the "First" is crowned with the title "Tathāgata," it is because this principle of truth is that which all Buddhas [uphold].
Because of this realization. Second, a general discussion of having doubts, which has two parts: first, recounting one's own doubts; second, recounting the doubts of others.
Regarding the first: Although the World-Honored One has always ranked me as the foremost among those who preach the Dharma, now I have heard the subtle and wondrous sound of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
It is like a deaf person trying to listen for the sound of a mosquito from more than a hundred paces away; what they cannot see, how much less can they hear?

Although the Buddha has proclaimed this clearly to enable me to eliminate my delusions, I still do not yet fully understand the ultimate meaning of this principle and have not yet reached a ground free from doubt.

First, to manifest the excellence of the Dharma: the *Ekottarika-āgama* states that among all disciples, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is foremost in skillfully explaining the various meanings and principles of all dharmas.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Pūrṇa is preeminent among those who preach the Dharma;
it further says that he is foremost in preaching through various causes, conditions, and parables to benefit sentient beings. Thus, we know that Pūrṇa was the one who preached [the Dharma].
The Dharma is that which the Tathāgata has always commended; thus, he describes himself as being constantly commended by the World-Honored One and others.

The "subtle and wondrous sound of the Dharma" refers collectively to what has been explained above, because each instance of destroying the false to reveal the true is extremely subtle and utterly refined.
The "deaf person with dull hearing" is a metaphor for one who has not yet attained the wisdom of the Mahāyāna; they are as far away as a hundred paces.
I compared myself to one who has not yet reached the realm of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Due to these two conditions, although I heard the subtle and wondrous sound, I only grasped its coarse and superficial meaning; thus, I likened my listening to that of a mosquito or a gnat. "Ling" means to listen.
"Mosquitoes, gadflies, insects, gnats, and *kṣudraka* (tiny flies)" refers to the past. "Those who did not see" means they had not witnessed this assembly. By this—

The initiation and establishment [of this teaching] are inherently different from those of the past; therefore, even the dharma and its meaning as expounded here are still unprecedented compared to what existed before.
Thus it is said, "How much more so for one who hears it? This is why it is like listening for the sound of mosquitoes from a hundred paces away.
Although the Buddha’s [teaching] below is brief and clarifies that awakening is shallow, "proclaiming and illuminating" refers specifically to shattering delusion to reveal the truth.
Since the beginning of the True Teaching, [the Buddha] has repeatedly proclaimed and repeatedly elucidated it.

Although the one for whom the teaching was intended was Ānanda, the Buddha’s intention actually encompassed the entire assembly; thus, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra also said, "May you cause me to eliminate my delusions.

To "eliminate delusions" is spoken here in terms of severing doubts and giving rise to faith. This meaning still refers back to what was previously explained; those who have not yet understood are unable to understand in detail.

[The doubt] is exhausted because one merely believes in the *śūnyatā-garbha* (the womb of emptiness) while still not yet knowing the meanings of the non-empty (*aśūnya*) and that which is both empty and non-empty (*śūnyatā-aśūnyatā*).
However, since one has not yet been able to believe [in these] completely, one has also not yet reached the ultimate stage free from doubt. For this reason, there arise the lower forms of doubt:
the arising of doubt, the continuity of doubt, and the obstruction of doubt. Second, the narration of others' doubts.
“World-Honored One, although those such as Ānanda have attained awakening, their habitual outflows have not yet been eliminated.

As for us who have ascended to the state of no-outflows within this assembly, though we have exhausted all outflows, even now, upon hearing the Dharma-sound preached by the Tathāgata, we still harbor lingering doubts and regrets.”
The initial passage concerning the doubts of those still in training (*śaikṣa*) refers generally to a class of practitioners in training.
Their previous self-declaration of awakening was merely in conformity with the Buddha’s words, as it did not yet fall within the scope of their own wisdom;
thus they said, "Although [I have awakened], in truth I have not attained awakening," because the residual taints (*vāsanā-āsrava*) had not yet been eliminated. These residual taints are...
The afflictions of thought (*cintā-kleśa*) arise spontaneously through the accumulation of habits since beginningless time.

Since these afflictions of thought still persist, and the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) has not yet been entirely abandoned, it is certain that the previous awakening was not true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
○ We shall now describe the doubts of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). "We" refers to a certain class of persons beyond training speaking of themselves.

They previously claimed for themselves that their outflows (*āsrava*) were exhausted, yet this was merely a temporary severance of views and afflictions (*kleśa*), not true outflowlessness. Therefore, the word "although" is employed;

it means that although they claim to have exhausted all outflows, in reality they have not yet been able to exhaust them, because even upon hearing the Dharma being preached now, they still remain hesitant.

This is due to doubt and regret. "Doubt" refers to doubting that [the state] is pure; "regret" refers to lamenting the error of pervasiveness. Both of these constitute attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Because one is currently entangled by them, it is said that "one is still constrained. "Constrained" (*yú*) carries the meaning of being bound.

However, since attachment to phenomena has not yet been relinquished, the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) must naturally persist as well. Thus, it is certainly known that the aforementioned exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) was not yet attained.
This is not the ultimate truth. Thus, Ānanda and others, because their habitual outflows (*āsrava*) had not yet been eliminated, knew that their awakening was not genuine;

Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and others, because they still harbored lingering doubts and regrets, knew that their realization of the exhaustion of outflows was illusory. Both groups were alike in not having fully investigated this meaning;
both had simply not yet reached the stage free from doubt. This concludes the general discussion on those who harbor doubts.

The third section consists of two parts: first, the definitive presentation of two doubts; second, the request for the Buddha’s compassionate instruction. The first of these [two] has two sub-sections:

first, the definitive presentation of the doubt regarding the continuous arising of the myriad dharmas; second, the definitive presentation of the doubt regarding the pervasive presence of the great elements.
First: "World-Honored One, if all the world’s faculties, objects, aggregates, bases, and elements are the Tathāgatagarbha, pure and fundamental from the beginning,
why do the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise, undergoing successive transformations until their end?"
And yet it begins again.

First, it summarizes what was previously shown; furthermore, it establishes certainty. "The mundane" is distinguished from the "transcendent," because the faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) all belong to the mundane conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and are not the transcendent unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas. All faculties and objects...
"All are the Tathāgatagarbha" summarizes the intent of the preceding section on the manifestation of seeing;

for within that section—which was not divided into sub-sections—there is the passage beginning with "this seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi," which is summarized here according to its meaning.

Regarding the four categories of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), three are explicitly mentioned; the six sense bases and seven elements are all subsumed by the term "etcetera" (*diǎng*).
All of these are the Tathāgatagarbha, inherently pure. This summarizes the meaning of the previous sections and the intent of the "Fusion of the Great" chapter.

For within the previous sections, each individual phenomenon was permitted to be the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, while in the "Fusion of the Great," it is further permitted that they possess [this nature].

Because of the meaning of being fundamentally pure and quiescent. ○ "How can it be... and so forth follows this to form a doubt. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) commentary states: "This doubt has two aspects:
first, the doubt regarding its sudden arising at the beginning; second, the doubt regarding its subsequent continuity.
If one reads the preceding section again in sequence, these two doubts become manifest. "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth" refers to the world that follows. All...
The conditioned characteristics, together with the karmic fruits of sentient beings—up to this point, doubt first arises suddenly. The thought is:
"Since all these are stored within the mind, then from time immemorial they ought to have been inherently pure;
why then do worlds, sentient beings, and karmic fruits suddenly arise without cause? The second phrase, moreover, encompasses the aforementioned worlds.
Speaking generally of the karmic fruits of sentient beings: they undergo birth, abiding, change, and cessation;

they shift, transform, and circulate, with their preceding and succeeding limits never overstepping one another. Thus it is said that they "successively flow on. Because they cease and then arise again, it is said that they "end and then begin anew.
This passage addresses doubts regarding subsequent continuity, intending to suggest that since all things are stored within the mind, they ought naturally to be pure.
This is the fundamental nature. Even if [the mind] were to arise suddenly, once it has ceased, it should not continue in succession.

Furthermore, how could it eventually undergo a gradual transition from end to beginning? Regarding these two questions—on arising and on continuity—you shall see the answers for yourselves when we reach the relevant section below.
Second, to definitively state the doubt regarding the all-pervasiveness of the great elements:
Furthermore, as the Tathāgata has said, the fundamental natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are perfectly interfused, pervading the entire dharma-realm, serene and eternally abiding.
“World-Honored One, if the nature of earth is all-pervasive, how can it accommodate water? If the nature of water is all-pervasive, then fire cannot arise;

how then can it be explained? Furthermore, if the two natures of water and fire both pervade empty space without one subduing or extinguishing the other, World-Honored One, since the nature of earth is obstructive while the nature of space is vacuous and penetrating, how can both be all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm?”
The initial section summarizes what was previously stated; it is called "furthermore" (*yù*) because he restates his profound doubts.

Although the text is restricted to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), its meaning actually encompasses empty space (*ākāśa*). This will become clear when we reach the point where the objection is raised below. According to the text on the great element of space (*ākāśamahābhūta*):
If this nature of space is perfectly pervasive and fundamentally unmoving, one should know that the earth, water, fire, and wind presently manifest are all equally termed the "five great elements.
For the aforementioned "perfectly pervasive nature" is precisely the present "fundamental nature of perfect fusion," which belongs to the reality of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*).
The aforementioned "pervasiveness" is precisely the present "pervasiveness of the dharma-realm," which belongs to the reality of universality (*sāmānya*). The aforementioned...
That which is fundamentally immovable is precisely this present state of profound stillness and eternal abiding; it belongs to the reality of permanence (*nitya*).
Since all are equally termed the "five great elements" (*pañca-mahābhūtāni*), then earth, water, fire, and wind should likewise possess these three meanings of reality.

Therefore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra takes this as a precedent to resolve his doubts regarding the mutual obstruction of the natures of water and fire, and so forth. [The passage] beginning with "The World-Honored One" below follows this to establish the point.

Doubt: The nature of earth is solidity and obstruction; the nature of water is fluidity and dissolution. Since solidity and obstruction have already been established, fluidity and dissolution must necessarily destroy them.
Therefore it is said: "If the nature of earth were pervasive, how could it accommodate water? Not accommodating water means that the nature of earth cannot be perfectly integrated."

That which melts, dissolves, and disintegrates is the nature of water, which cannot abide permanently; this is the first doubt. The nature of water is moist and humid, while the nature of fire is dry.
Since moisture gives rise to existence, dryness must lead to its extinction. Therefore it is said that where the nature of water is pervasive, fire does not arise.
That fire does not arise means the nature of water cannot be perfectly integrated; that dryness leads to extinction is the nature of fire.
They cannot abide permanently; this is the second doubt. Just as earth does not contain water and water does not contain fire, so too fire does not contain water and water does not contain earth.
If this were the case, the principles of perfect interfusion, omnipresence, and serene permanence would all fail to be established.
How then can one clarify these matters? For now, let us consider them by way of water and fire.
It is difficult. To say that the Buddha’s words are not false and must necessarily reveal a profound meaning is correct;
however, it is not known by what means this revelation is made, such that the principle that fire and water both pervade all things without one subduing or extinguishing the other can be established.

Since the nature of earth and water can be understood by analogy, the obstructive nature of earth and so forth is employed to manifest the Great Element of Space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*), thereby completing the five great elements.
The meaning is this: when obstruction arises, pervasion and penetration are exhausted; when pervasion and penetration are attained, obstruction is lost.
This is like water and fire, which cannot coexist with one another. This is the third doubt. Why are these two phrases also used to pose a challenge based on doubt?
Having thus fully set forth these two doubts, [the Bodhisattva] secondly requested the Buddha’s compassionate instruction:
"I do not know where this meaning leads; I only pray that the Tathāgata will spread his great compassion and dispel the clouds of my delusion."
When the great assembly had finished speaking these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, thirsting for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction.
The phrase "this meaning" refers to the previously mentioned meanings of being fundamentally pure, perfectly pervasive, eternally abiding, and so forth; it signifies that which is sought after.
"Going" means to return to and take refuge in. To say that mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so forth possess continuity through birth seems to contradict their inherent purity;
yet the Tathāgata says they are "pure by nature. That earth, water, fire, wind, and so forth possess mutual obstruction seems to conflict with their perfect pervasiveness;
yet the Tathāgata says they are "all-pervading, perfect, and eternal. Since Pūrṇa did not dare to deem the Buddha's words erroneous, he directly—
One may lay the blame upon oneself; thus it is said, "I did not know," and so forth. When doubt is deep and remorse is heavy, none but a Buddha can provide release;
therefore it is said, "I only pray that the Tathāgata... Because great compassion is like the wind, it is called "proclaiming" (xuán) and "flowing" (liú).

Because delusion obstructs wisdom, it is called "opening" (kāi) and "clouds" (yún). This continues below with the passage on the Tathāgata’s manifestation, which proceeds without contradiction from the principle of purity.

Because purity and luminosity are all-pervasive, they do not deviate from perfect permanence; thus, the breeze of compassion spreads and the clouds of delusion disperse, while the sun of wisdom shines brightly and the sky of the nature is revealed.
The phrase "and the great assembly" serves as a general request for the multitude:

those in training (*śaikṣa*) have not yet eliminated their outflows (*āsrava*), so even if they have attained realization, it is not yet ultimate; those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) still harbor lingering doubts and regrets, so although they have severed [afflictions], they have not reached the limit.
"Since we are equally obscured by the clouds of delusion and all alike await the blowing of the wind of compassion, I pray that [your grace] extends to us as well.

Having spoken these words, he requested with his mouth; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he requested with his body; and yearning for your compassionate instruction, he requested with his mind.
There are two meanings for the title "Supreme Compassionate Teacher. First, "supreme compassion": the Buddha’s compassion is ultimate, as nothing can surpass it.

Second, "supreme instruction": it is able to empty attachment to phenomena and exhaust the marks of birth. Having thus followed up on the previous points, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra has finished posing his two doubts.

Second, the Tathāgata resolves doubts by teaching the two treasuries (*dvaya-garbha*): [he resolves the doubt regarding the generation stage by clarifying that the arising of delusion from the ultimate truth is precisely the teaching of the treasury of non-emptiness;

he resolves the doubt regarding pervasiveness by clarifying that essence and characteristics are non-obstructive, which is precisely the teaching of the treasury of emptiness-and-non-emptiness]. Third: first, the universal permission for obtaining benefit; second, the admonition to listen with reverence and compliance.
Third, the specific explanation based on doubt. First:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa and all the Arhats in the assembly who were free from outflows and had attained the stage of no-more-learning:
"Today, the Tathāgata shall universally proclaim for this assembly the true ultimate nature within the ultimate truth, so as to cause you..."
Within the assembly, the śrāvakas of fixed nature, as well as all those arhats who had not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness and were turning toward the Mahāyāna,
all obtained the ground of quiescent extinction of the One Vehicle— the true araṇya, the place of correct practice.
First, he specifically addresses those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Zhengmo says: "The Sūtra designates 'those beyond training' specifically to manifest the profundity of the Dharma.
"From 'The Tathāgata' [onward], he universally grants permission for the supreme Dharma. Zhengmo says: "The Buddha’s words are universal, yet they further reveal the vastness of his compassion.

Because it is universal, it does not concern only those beyond training; rather, even those still in training (*śaikṣa*), as well as the classes of humans and devas, are all among the sentient beings to whom it is addressed."
Regarding "the ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) and so forth: the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* verses state: "This ultimate reality of all phenomena is also suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, there are four kinds of ultimate truth: first, the worldly ultimate truth, which refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*);

second, the ultimate truth of principle, which refers to the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering; third, the ultimate truth of realization, which refers to the suchness of the two-fold emptiness; and fourth—

"Ultimate among ultimates" refers to the One True Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This topical outline is restricted to the beginning of the two *piṭakas*, yet its meaning extends throughout the latter parts of the three *piṭakas*; therefore, it is said to be "the true ultimate nature within the ultimate.

This is because the subsequent text fully reveals that the three *piṭakas* are not separate from the one mind (as the name of the *Ākāśagarbha* is "the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind," the name of the *Anākāśagarbha* is "the originally luminous and wondrous mind," and the name of the *Ākāśānākāśagarbha* is "the wondrously luminous and original mind").
This is precisely the one true *dharmadhātu*. The phrase "causing you" and what follows below is a preliminary indication of profound benefit.

"Those of fixed nature among the *śrāvakas" refers to those of the two vehicles who do not turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]. "Those who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness" refers to those of the two vehicles who have already turned their minds.

This means that while those of the two vehicles have already attained the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), although they possess the aspiration for the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), they have as yet been unable to attain it; even though they have been unable to attain it...

Having already grown weary of the Lesser Vehicle and turned toward the Greater, it is said that they "turn toward the Mahāyāna. Since they have already turned toward the Mahāyāna, they are indeed Bodhisattvas;
yet they are still called Arhats because the name is applied according to their outward manifestation (*traces*). The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) also includes those of no lineage (*agotra*).
Because all sentient beings possess a mind, and all who possess a mind shall become Buddhas—since the definitive teaching makes no such distinctions—all shall attain the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This means that once they have heard this Dharma, they possess the capacity to ultimately achieve Buddhahood;
thus, they are equally members of those who follow the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*). Although they are equally members of the Buddha Vehicle, while...

Entering [this state] according to individual capacities is briefly divided into three names. If one has already turned the mind [toward the Mahāyāna] and desires to swiftly attain Buddhahood, then this very place is the site of *śamatha-vimokṣa*. This is because the *dharmatā* of quiescence is itself the *bodhimaṇḍa*.
If those of the two vehicles with fixed natures loathe clamor and seek stillness, then this very place is true *araṇya*. This is because, even amidst clamor...

Because in tranquility there is no need for further aversion. If there are icchantikas devoid of the [Buddha] nature who are deeply attached to false views, this very state is the locus of correct practice;
that is to say, by being able to abandon false views and give rise to right and wholesome roots.

If one were to provide an exegesis based on the Tripiṭaka, the emptiness and non-emptiness of the Tathāgatagarbha is beyond "being" and "non-being," and is neither identical nor different—beyond all verbal expression.
The path is severed and the sphere of mental activity ceases; by relying on this, one can attain Buddhahood. This is the site of quiescent extinction.
The non-empty Tathāgatagarbha is all dharmas, for there is no dharma that is not the Buddha-dharma.
Abiding and maintaining the whole body, and utilizing the whole body, is true *araṇya*. The empty Tathāgatagarbha is free from all dharmas, yet all dharmas [are it].
There is nothing that can bind him. With a staff slung over his shoulder, he enters directly among the thousand peaks—this is the place of true practice.
One must know that the Tripitaka does not depart from the one mind, and the three stages do not depart from the One Vehicle; therefore, the One Vehicle is used as the overarching title for all.
The One Vehicle is identical to the One Mind. Second, the admonition to listen with reverence:
"Now listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Pūrṇa and the others, revering the Buddha’s Dharma-voice, listened in silence.
First, he exhorted them to listen and granted permission to speak. "Listen attentively" means to listen with a true mind, not with a mind subject to arising and ceasing.

○ Pūrṇa bowed low and respectfully received the instruction. "Respectfully" means to honor and comply. "The Dharma-sound" refers here to the sound of the exhortations and commands of the Buddha-dharma.
"Silently" means to stifle all external conditions and bind the mind to a single object. "Receiving the instruction" means to comprehend it with the mind.

Although the principles herein resemble the meaning of the mutual generation of the five elements found in external treatises, they are actually not entirely the same and cannot be matched point by point. There are two inconveniences: first, the sequence of the five elements is reversed in this scripture...)

The meaning, conversely, becomes obscure. Second, it causes those outside our teachings to believe that [our doctrine] does not transcend their own views. For while those outside our teachings mostly attribute the transformation of the faculties to yin and yang, our school directly points to the fact that life is fundamentally rooted in the nature and mind; thus, they obscure this truth.

To extrapolate from the internal to the external is the height of error in calculation. The text states: "The traditional interpretation based on the Five Elements (*pañca-dhātu*) of production and overcoming is profoundly contrary to the intent of the Sūtra. The Sūtra reveals that all things are but mind; why resort to worldly false reckonings as an explanation?

Consider, for instance, the case of mountain rocks supporting flames or melting water according to the theory of the Five Elements: if one takes rock to be metal, since metal can produce water, why would it also produce fire? If one takes rock to be earth, then neither water nor fire should be produced from it. Furthermore, when a forest burns to ash, one might say fire produces earth;

yet when [water] is squeezed out by twisting [a cloth], how could this be wood producing water in reverse? Thus, we know that those [worldly theories] should not be used to explain this. Question: The meanings such as "trembling arises in dependence on emptiness" and "solidity and clarity establish obstruction" are vast and profound. Who, moreover, [can fathom them]?

I believe this. He replied: "This is indeed the inconceivable power of the numinous mind and the inevitable principle of karmic response. Only a Buddha perceives and knows this through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For ordinary people of the mundane world, it is truly rare to believe in it; yet when they see it manifest before them, if their distress is extreme and cannot be relieved, their minds stir and their bodies move;

if their attachments are firm and their desires unfulfilled, their breath becomes stifled and their bodies stiffen. There are even those who strike the table or smash objects, or who fixate their minds until they become as hard as stone. This is further proof that what is 'empty' can lead to agitation, and what is 'solid and clear' establishes obstruction."

He asked again: "Islands, sandbars, rivers, and streams are things commonly seen by all people; but who else could see the fire within the great ocean? He replied: "Those on a sea vessel anchored at night certainly see it often. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* provides proof of this:
after the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, the Dragon King of the Great Ocean took the fire from within the water to the site of the cremation (*caitya*). This is precisely that evidence.
The three fetters form a continuity;
their mutual delusions arise and serve as seeds for one another. By these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession.
The first phrase concludes the initial formation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). "Interpenetrating" refers to the aforementioned wind, gold (earth), fire, and water—the four great elements.
Although they arise in succession, when tracing them back to their source, they are also seen to depend upon deluded awakening and deluded luminosity;
thus it is said that "delusions arise in mutual interaction. The next phrase concludes this by stating that the four abodes—water, land, mountains, and forests—interchange with one another.
This means that although the aforementioned four abodes take the Great [Element] as their seed, their natures are each all-pervasive, such that they also mutually serve as one another's basis.
Because they serve as causes and bases, it is said that they mutually act as seeds for one another. For example, when fire arises from the sea, the sea is the seed of the fire;
when rivers flow through an island, the island is the seed of the river; and even when a forest is burned into soil, the forest is the seed of the soil.
"Thickets and marshes condense to form water; thus, thickets are the seeds of water," and so forth. The final two lines conclude the continuity of causes and conditions.
This means that through the mutual production of delusions, the four great elements act as the cause, serving as seeds for one another, while the four abodes act as the condition.
From this point on, mountains, rivers, nations, and all worlds undergo a continuous succession of arising and ceasing, ceasing and arising, without end.

This is a detailed explanation of the preceding section from "the arising of the world" up to "if it were stilled, it would become empty space. This refers to the absence of a world, which need not be stated explicitly as it is self-evident.
[The first of the three parts concerning] the continuity of the world is complete. Second, the continuity of sentient beings has three sections:

first, the initial formation of the four natures; second, the transformation into the four modes of birth; third, the conclusion regarding their continuity. First: [The initial formation of the four natures.]

Furthermore, Pūrṇa, this delusion of clarity is not caused by another; the fault lies in the awakening of clarity itself. Once that which is delusory has been established, the principle of clarity cannot transcend it.
For this reason, hearing does not go beyond sound, and seeing does not surpass form. Thus, the six delusions of form, fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth are accomplished.
From this, the distinctions between seeing, perceiving, hearing, and knowing arise.

The first part is the general introduction. Regarding the phrase "Furthermore," etc., it means that following the previous explanation of the world-system, he again addresses the audience to demonstrate the meaning of the continuity of sentient beings.

The two lines beginning with "To clarify delusion" state that in order to clarify why true conditioned phenomena successively become delusive, there is no other cause; they arise through the blending of true awakening and deluded illumination.
This merely results in the fault of [conceptual] synthesis. ○ Regarding "that which is falsely imagined" (*so-wàng*), this is explained separately below.

"That which is falsely imagined" refers to the false consciousness that serves as the basis (*āśraya*) formed through the conjunction of the real and the false; this is precisely the *karmalakṣaṇa* (the phase of karma).

"Since it has been established" means that once the *karmalakṣaṇa* has been established, the "perceiving subject" (*darśana-bhāga*) emerges from upon that *karmalakṣaṇa*. This is intended to clarify the fundamental awakening (*mūla-ajñāna*).

The principle (*li*) is precisely the evolving aspect (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*). However, although the evolving aspect originally exists to clarify the principle, it is obstructed by the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) and cannot transcend it.
Because of these causes and conditions that prevent transcendence, when one wishes to hear and clarify [the principle], one cannot escape the sounds of the fundamental consciousness;
when one wishes to see and clarify it, one cannot surpass the forms of the fundamental consciousness. This is the manifested aspect (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, according to the *Awakening of Faith*, "manifestation" refers to the five sense objects appearing as soon as they encounter their respective faculties.

Here, however, we clarify only the two objects of sound and form by way of hearing and seeing; the others may be understood by analogy. Moreover, this hearing and seeing is exclusively the inherent nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*).
The roots have not yet been established. Sound and form are merely manifestations of delusion and are not yet summoned by karma.

When the six kinds of false objects—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—summoned by karma are fully accomplished, their coarse characteristics become fixed, and one clings to the existence of external objects outside the mind.
From this, the clarity of stillness becomes adhered to, giving rise to vision; as the essence of vision reflects these forms, it coagulates with them to form the eye. Thus...
When the extreme viscosity and profound stillness give rise to cognition, and the essence of cognition reflects the dharmas, the mind is then formed from those dharmas.
This is how, from within a single seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), there are differentiated divisions that constitute seeing, awareness, hearing, and cognition. As it says later:
"Originally relying on one refined spirit, they divide to form the six harmonious combinations. Second, these transform to form the four modes of birth.

Beings of similar karma entwine one another; through union and separation, they undergo transformation. Seeing light and perceiving color, they give rise to the manifestation of views and the formation of thoughts.

Divergent views produce hatred, while shared thoughts produce love. The flow of love becomes the seed, and the reception of thought constitutes the womb. Through their mutual encounter, they bring about birth, attracting those of similar karma.

Thus, by means of causes and conditions, there arise the stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth; whether born from a womb, an egg, moisture, or transformation, they follow their respective [conditions].
It should be understood that those born from eggs arise solely through thought; those born from wombs are due to emotional attachment; those born from moisture result from a response to union;

and those born by transformation respond to separation. This first section provides a general heading. Although the preceding section concluded on the formation of the sense organs from sensory objects, it spoke specifically in terms of human beings, because at the initial stage when delusion arises from the Truth, there is as yet no entanglement with mixed karma to be summoned. Now, this present section concerns human beings.

Sentient beings create karma individually, and thus their retributions differ. Therefore, it is said that "those with similar karma entangle one another; through union and separation, they form transformations.

"Those with similar karma entangle one another" means that when the parents and the child share a common karma, they mutually attract and entangle one another to undergo birth from a womb or an egg, such as in the cases of humans, animals, tortoises, snakes, and the like.
The phrase "through union and separation, they form transformations" is taken here for its underlying meaning.
It should be said that they are "formed through combination" or "transformed through separation. This means that they do not depend on parents but arise solely from their own karma.

Some take form through the union of moisture and thus undergo moist-birth, such as the class of wriggling insects; others leave this place to transform elsewhere and undergo transformation-birth, such as the classes of devas and hell-beings who fly about.
○ Regarding "seeing the light" and below, there is a detailed explanation, which is further divided into two parts. First, the detailed [explanation].
This clarifies birth from a womb. The *Hezhe* (合轍) states: "When the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) enters the womb, all places where it has no affinity appear as black as ink;
only at the place where it has an affinity for its parents does a single point of luminous color manifest. This refers to what is now called "seeing the manifestation of luminous color.
Furthermore, it says that this intermediate state body immediately proceeds to that location; this refers to what is now called "clearly seeing."

This refers to the statement: "When consciousness perceives form, perception is formed" (meaning that conceptualization arises spontaneously). Regarding "different perceptions" and so forth, *Abhiṣeka* states:

When a male enters the womb, he perceives the father as a man; because this is a different perception, he feels aversion. He perceives the mother as his wife; because this is a shared perception, he feels attraction.
For a female entering the womb, it is the reverse. According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are two types of ignorance (*avidyā*): first, that which initiates karma, which refers to the past.
The afflictions. Second, "moistening birth" refers to the arising of thoughts of aversion and attachment toward the parents at the moment of entering the womb.

When the mind of attachment flows toward the parents, it serves as the causal seed for taking birth; when the mind of conceptualization enters the gateway of the sense organs, it serves as the basis for the fetal stage.
Once the two drops of red and white have conjoined and generated [the embryo], it further draws in [the consciousness] to be of one kind with them.

Karma shall become its son. For this reason, with one's own karma as the cause and the parents as the conditions, once the embryonic state is established, it passes through the stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, and so forth.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that there are generally five stages within the womb.
The first week is called *kalala*. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states: *Kalala* is translated here as "congealed mucus," also as "thin curd," and also as "solidified butter.

In terms of meaning, it is translated as "impure mixture. This means that the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood is called "mixture" (*miśra*), while its own nature being unclean is called "impurity" (*aśuci*).
The second week is called *arbuda*, which is translated here as "blister"; it is like a blister on a sore.
The *kalala* (embryo) is so named because its internal and external aspects are like clarified butter (*sarpis*) before flesh has yet formed.

At the third week, it is called *arbuda*, which here means "coagulated" (*niṣyanda*), also translated as "soft flesh," because it has coagulated into something like soft flesh. At the fourth week, it is called *peśī*, which here means "thickened."

It is also called "solid flesh" (*ghanarasa*), meaning that the flesh gradually coagulates, thickens, and becomes firm. The fifth week is named *praśākhā*, which is translated as "the stage of form" (*ākṛti-avasthā*) and also as "limbs and joints.
This refers to the differentiation of the positions of the various sense organs, the body's shape, and the four limbs, as well as the skeletal joints.
Furthermore, the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* mentions a sixth and seventh week, termed the "stage of hair, body hair, nails, and teeth."
This refers to the gradual arising of the four dharmas. The seventh week is called the stage of "possessing the faculties" (*indriya-samanvāgata*) because all the sense-faculties are fully developed.
In this sutra, only the first two stages are mentioned briefly, while the others are subsumed by the word "etc. (*ādi*). The *Zhengmo* (The Correct Pulse) states:

"To provide such detailed and thorough exposition specifically regarding the womb-born [beings] is, on one hand, due to the urgency of teaching for the sake of humans, and on the other, because all sentient beings arise through sexual desire."
This correctly explains the nature of existence. Because viviparous birth is particularly prominent, the four modes of birth are briefly clarified below.
The *Zhengmai* states: "Viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and transformation-born are all responses; emotional attachment and conceptual thought, union and separation, are all inducements.

"Responding according to what is appropriate" means that one responds with the four modes of birth according to the specific inducement. Regarding "the oviparous are born solely from thought," it refers to thinking with longing.

"Conception through thought" (*saṃjñā*) refers to sentient beings born from eggs who, while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), falsely perceive a superior and wondrous place and give rise to a longing thought;
it is solely because of this that they undergo birth. "Birth from a womb is due to emotion" (*sneha*): "emotion" (*qíng*) refers to affectionate attachment.
This means that when sentient beings born from a womb are in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), they falsely perceive objects of sensual desire and a mind of affection arises toward them;
because of this, existence (*bhava*) is brought about as a result. Regarding those born from moisture who are "brought about by union," "union" refers to the new [state].

This means that when sentient beings born from moisture are in the intermediate state, they falsely perceive a new environment as something upon which they can rely, and they urgently desire to attach themselves to it.
It is through this that they are moved and receive a physical form. Regarding "transformation through detachment" (*li-ying*): "detachment" refers to the loathing of the old.

This means that when beings born by transformation possess a body within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), they falsely perceive their former environment as loathsome and urgently desire to detest and abandon it;

it is through this movement that the response is brought about. Although the order of stimulus and response may vary across the latter two types of birth, the underlying principle remains essentially the same.

They are mutually complete; one should understand this through personal realization. However, while the womb-born (*jarāyu-ja*) has already been explained in detail above, this [mode of birth] is briefly clarified here according to precedent.

The reason for the detailed explanation was to include all contributing conditions as a model for the other three modes of birth; the reason for the brief explanation here is to manifest that each [mode] possesses its own primary cause.
This is intended to enable sentient beings to practice before birth, so as to transcend the four states of attachment, aversion, union, and separation.
When the mind thus severs the paths of the four modes of birth, one may emerge from saṃsāra. Through the three fetters, continuity is established;

as feelings and perceptions join and separate, they undergo mutual transformation. All karmic retributions follow their ascent or descent. By these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.

The first two lines conclude the four types of "sensing" (*saṃvedana*). "Mutually transforming and changing" refers to instances such as when feeling (*vedanā*) changes into perception (*saṃjñā*), or when perception shifts into feeling, and so forth.
The next two lines conclude the four types of "responding" (*prativedha*). "Receiving karma" (*karmopabhoga*) refers to the retributive form (*vipākadeha*);

this is because the retributive form serves as the locus for the mastery of receiving karma. "Flying and sinking" signifies the meaning of "above and below," as flying and sinking possess the characteristics of upward and downward movement.

Therefore, it is said that since the four minds capable of inducing [rebirth] are subject to change, the physical forms of the four types of birth they induce follow one another in succession, resulting in higher or lower states.
This refers to ascending by means of wholesome karma and descending by following unwholesome conditions.
The final two phrases serve as a conclusion based on what has been stated; "for this cause and condition" refers to the aforementioned four natures.
With these four modes of birth as conditions, there is thus the continuity of sentient beings.

Regarding the continuity of sentient beings, the continuity of the fruits of the three types of karma is threefold: first, the establishment of the root; second, the development of the branches and twigs.
The three fetters form a continuous succession. Regarding the first three: first, desire-greed is the root; second, killing-greed is the root;
third, stealing-greed is the root. As for the first, Pūrṇa:
when perception and craving are bound together as one, and one cannot separate from this craving, then throughout the world, fathers, mothers, sons, and grandsons [are thus linked].
Birth is uninterrupted. These [four modes of birth] take desire and greed as their root.
One already knows that the distinctions among the four births depend solely upon a single thought-moment at the time of rebirth;

yet one does not yet know that the cyclical wandering through successive kalpas is even more fundamentally rooted in the indulgence of greed. To clarify this now, I address Pūrṇa once again. Having received the preceding...
When sentient beings exist, there arises the emotional attachment between self and other. Due to this emotional attachment, when they have not yet met, they harbor distant longings for one another;
once they have met, they become mutually affectionate and entwine so closely that they cannot be parted—hence it is said, "thought and love are bound together.
It is like a magnet attracting iron, or like glue adhering wood; hence it is said, "love cannot be separated. Because they cannot be separated by this, [the cycle continues].
They transform their forms and exchange their retributions, mutually serving as causes for kinship. Therefore it is said:
"Thus, throughout all worlds, fathers, mothers, sons, and grandsons are born one after another without interruption. These terms collectively refer to parents, children, and grandchildren.

Since they are thus born in succession without end, lustful desire constitutes greed, which serves as the basis for the continuity of subsequent karmic fruits; second, killing constitutes greed, which likewise serves as the basis.

When craving increases together with greed such that greed cannot be stopped, then all beings in the world—whether born from eggs, metamorphosed, from moisture, or from a womb—devour one another according to their relative strength and weakness. These acts are rooted in the greed for killing.

Furthermore, as established above, since sentient beings exist, there are their respective bodies and lives. Because of these bodies and lives, as long as they are not exhausted, one greedily seeks vigor and strength;
once they are exhausted, one again craves long life. Since the nourishment of these emotions is equal, it is said that "greed and craving grow together.
Knowing only how to protect them while disregarding cruelty, it is said that "greed cannot be stopped. From this...

Because they cannot refrain from doing so, those of different species devour one another. Since they kill wantonly and without restraint, it is said that those born from eggs, by transformation, from moisture, or from wombs, swallow and eat each other according to their relative strength and weakness.
The phrase "these beings" refers collectively to those born from eggs, by transformation, from moisture, or from wombs.

Once they have begun to devour one another based on strength and weakness, they establish greed through such killing; this becomes the fundamental basis for the continuity of the results of lower-tier karma.
The third [evil] has greed as its root.
Because humans eat sheep, when the sheep dies it becomes a human, and when the human dies they become a sheep.

In this way, even among the ten classes of living beings, death follows birth and birth follows death as they prey upon one another. These evil karmas arise together and persist until the end of the future; such beings are thus...
Theft has greed as its root.
Furthermore, since there are sentient beings as mentioned above, there is mutual oppression and plunder. Because of this oppression and plunder, one cannot repay them in the present life;

instead, one changes into the body of a sheep to discharge that debt by providing nourishment for their mouths and bellies. Therefore it is said: "In the future, one will eat sheep as a person. Hereafter...
The text states: "When the karmic retribution of the ghost has been exhausted, it encounters its original creditor with whom it shared a grievance;
it takes birth as a beast to repay its past debt. If the creditor seeks more than what is due and the debtor feels such injustice is unbearable, then the sheep dies and is reborn as a human.
The subsequent text states: "If that which is repaid exceeds what was owed, these sentient beings will again become human and be required to repay the surplus.
This refers to the case where, since the debt has been reversed and claimed back, the original debtor must necessarily return it. Furthermore, there are two ways in which this reversal occurs.
First, it concerns those with merit who suffer harm at the hands of others; second, it concerns those without merit who fall and are reborn as animals.
When it is now said that "a person dies and becomes a sheep," this refers specifically to those lacking merit. As the subsequent text states:
"If one possesses both power and merit, then among humans one shall not relinquish the human body to repay that power. If...
Those without merit return as animals to repay the remainder of that debt; this refers to the aforementioned humans and sheep.

This principle applies equally to all ten types of births. Regarding the categories of the ten births, among the twelve types of birth, those that are empty, scattered, dissolved, or submerged—such as earth, wood, stone, and metal—are excluded because they cannot be eaten. However...
Since this applies to all ten classes [of beings], the dead die and the living are born in an endless cycle of coming and going; thus, the karma of theft does not cease. Therefore it is said:
"Death after death, birth after birth, they come and devour one another. Such evil karma, accumulated through habituation, arises simultaneously with birth.

If there is no cause and condition—[wherein one's own power acts as the cause and the Buddha's empowerment acts as the condition]—to sever it, it will certainly persist until the very end of the future. (The subsequent passage...)
It says: "If one uses money or goods, or employs their labor, and once the debt is fully repaid, one stops;

yet if, in the interim, one should take their life or eat their flesh—and so on, even continuing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, devouring and slaughtering one another—this refers to such cases.

(Question: How does this differ from the greed for killing? Answer: The greed for killing arises from a mind intent on killing, while the greed for stealing arises from a mind intent on stealing. Although the karmic retribution may appear similar, the causal minds are distinct; therefore, they are spoken of as two separate categories.)

The phrase "these [beings]" refers collectively to the ten classes of living beings. Since they have already gone back and forth in mutual retribution, taking what is not given through theft constitutes greed;

this serves as the fundamental basis for the continuity of the fruits of lower karmic actions. [Question: In the worldly teachings, when discussing killing, the gravity of the offense is held to lie solely in the killing of humans, while the harming of other creatures is not considered so. Why is this?

The treatises on theft consider only the robbery of wealth to constitute a crime, yet they do not include the eating of meat. Now, this sutra discusses killing as extending to the ultimate harm of living beings; why then does it single out the eating of meat in its discussion of theft? Answer:

Worldly teachings are urgent in their desire to stop disorder and seek to nourish the people; therefore, they prohibit only killing humans and robbing them of property, but do not regulate the harming of living beings or the eating of meat. This sutra, however, seeks to sever the cycle of birth and death and must exhaust all karmic conditions; thus, it must sever both simultaneously. Furthermore, if one investigates the deep root of worldly disorder, it mostly arises from the harming of living beings and the eating of meat.

For example, when the Śākya clan suffered the slaughter by Virūḍhaka, people only knew of the immediate cause—the insults—but did not know the remote cause was the eating of fish. Therefore, peace is not long-lasting in this world, for during times of peace, people indulge their desires.

As for eating [meat]: after three or five hundred years, those humans who enjoy blessings will see their fortune end and calamity arise; those animals who have repaid their debts will be reborn as humans. When such karmic adversaries meet, chaos ensues. Thus we know that this present sutra possesses profound and far-reaching sagely wisdom, intended to uproot the foundation and block the source [of suffering].

An ancient virtuous one said: "If the world wishes to avoid the kalpa of swords and spears, it must be that sentient beings do not eat meat. Lay practitioners of external teachings, please rely upon these words of the Buddha. Even if you cannot completely abstain, you should at least maintain a slight sense of compassion when fishing, hunting, or slaughtering.

By gradually cultivating benevolence and kindness, you will ultimately achieve a state of gracious magnanimity. Do not recklessly give rise to slander or criticism, lest you incur sin and transgression. (The Initial Formation of the Roots)
The first part concludes. Second, the root transforms into the branches and twigs:
"You owe me my life, and I shall repay you for your debt. Because of these causes and conditions, one remains constantly within birth and death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
"You love my heart, and I cherish your form. Due to these causes and conditions, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you have remained constantly bound in entanglement.

Building upon the preceding discussion of the two karmas of killing and stealing, which perfume and form the habit-energy of greed, when enemies encounter one another, this [habit] manifests and erupts.
Hence it is said: "You owe me my life; I shall repay your debt. As the *Guanding* (Consecration) states: "The two lines beginning with 'You owe' are an elliptical abbreviation of many [verses]."
The verses consist of eight lines. They should be recited as follows: "You owe me my life; I return your life to you. "I owe you my life;
I return your life to you. This pertains to the greed of killing. "I owe you my debt; I return your debt to you.

"You owe me my debt; you return my debt to me. This pertains to the greed of stealing. With the lineage-seed (*gotra*) acting as the cause and present activity acting as the condition, by means of this—

Because causes and conditions mutually support one another, life after life one does not escape the cycle of saṃsāra; thus it is said that "through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one constantly remains in birth and death.
This refers to the culmination of the outflows of killing and stealing. Building upon the preceding discussion, the karma of sexual desire perfumes and forms the habit-energy of greed.
When affectionate bonds meet, this [feeling] manifests; hence it is said: "You love my heart, I cherish your form.
Within this, there is also an elliptical expression. Fully stated, it should read: "You love my heart, I love your heart;
I love your heart, you love my heart. This is spoken in terms of *en* (affectionate debt), meaning that because the heart is what constitutes the weight of such debt, I cherish you.
"O Form, you love me; O Form, I love you"—this is spoken in terms of emotional attachment.
That is to say, because emotion regards form as weighty, the causes and conditions are the same [as before]: life after life, from age to age, one fails to attain liberation.

Therefore it is said that "throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, one remains constantly in bondage. This refers to the final stage of the flow of sensual desire. However, what was stated above—that "one is constantly in birth"—[refers to the preceding stages].
"Death. Here, "those who are constantly in bondage" refers to those for whom enemies meet face-to-face and vow not to coexist; they must reach the point of one living and one dying.
Or those whose affectionate ties and mutual recognition vow not to part; they must reach the point of being eternally entangled and eternally bound.
In reality, birth and death are also called bondage, and bondage is also called birth and death; each term is used according to what is most prominent.

Furthermore, within this context, killing and stealing are presented together, while sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is explained separately because it relates to the distinction between enemies and kin. [Question:

Since both the fundamental and the derivative aspects of the text encompass multiple lifetimes, how are the meanings of "fundamental" (*mūla*) and "derivative" (*anta*) to be distinguished? [Answer: The "fundamental" refers to the accumulation of habituation over many lifetimes that forms the root of greed; the "derivative" refers to the continuous cycling through rebirths over many lifetimes without end.
This is like the difference in temporal boundaries between arising and abiding versus change and cessation. Thus, the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) form a continuity.
Only killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the three fundamental roots. By these causes and conditions, the fruits of karma continue in succession;
bearing the burden and returning [to rebirth] without ceasing, one remains constantly within birth and death.

That one is endlessly filled with affectionate attachment and remains perpetually bound is not due to any other cause, but solely because of the prior habituation to the three types of greed: killing, stealing, and sexual desire.
It serves as the root. If sentient beings hear of this power and eliminate the habituation of greed, then once the root is exhausted, the branches and twigs will not arise.
Regarding the phrase "by these causes and conditions": the root is the cause and the branches and twigs are the conditions.

Because cause and condition support one another, the continuity of karmic results exists through this. (Question: What is the difference between the continuity of karmic results and the continuity of sentient beings? Answer: The continuity of karmic results...)

The subsequent [section] then elaborates based on sentient beings. However, the continuity of sentient beings refers only to the single moment of taking birth, whereas the continuity of karmic results encompasses the accumulation of habits over successive kalpas. Once these habits have become deep-seated, the cycle of transmigration ceases not; yet with the slightest lapse of a single thought-moment, change and transformation become unstable.

If one can suddenly sever the single thought-moment and gradually remedy the accumulated habits, then transformation can be stabilized and the cycle of transmigration can be brought to rest. One must understand that sentient beings are not separate from karmic results, and karmic results are not separate from sentient beings; they are spoken of separately for the sake of accomplishing two benefits.
Together with the preceding discussion on the continuity of sentient beings, this provides a detailed clarification of truly conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The detailed explanation of the continuity of birth is concluded. Fourth, the response to the inquiry:
"Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted continuities are all the nature of the clarity of awakening that knows with perfect lucidity.
Because this lucidity gives rise to appearances, they emerge from deluded vision; thus do the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena successively flow and change."
Therefore, this delusion ends and begins again.
"The three kinds" at the beginning refers generally to the causes of delusion; "the continuity of these three kinds of sudden arising" refers to the aforementioned continuity of the three types.
Since there is no distinction in their continuity, it is simply the continuation of that which suddenly arose.
It is simply that within the midst of sudden arising, karmic fruits are joined with sentient beings; within the continuity [of consciousness], empty space is joined with the world.

In reality, there is no distinct dharma [between them]. "Awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*) refers to true clarity; it is what was previously called "the nature of awakening is wondrously clear" (*xing-jue miao-ming*) and "fundamental awakening is clear and wondrous" (*ben-jue ming-miao*).
"Clear understanding of the nature" (*ming-liao zhi xing*) refers to deluded clarity; it is what was previously called "the nature of awakening must be clear" (*xing-jue bi-ming*).

"This is what is meant by 'delusively taking [the mind] to be enlightened awareness. The two characters 'all' (皆) are terms used to refer downward from what was mentioned above, speaking of both the initial sudden arising and the subsequent continuity.
If one investigates its profound root, it all stems from the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment (本覺妙明), where, without cause, the mind arises with the desire to be enlightened.
It is the fault of delusively adding the nature of knowing that constitutes the transgression. [The character] "Because" (因):...

This concludes the response to the two questions. Regarding "the cause for the manifestation of clarity": this refers to the three phases of karma—projecting, evolving, and manifesting—which arise through the increased clarity of delusion.
Regarding "arising from false views": this refers to the generation of the three types—identity, difference, and non-existence—from the false views of the continuity of consciousness and so forth.
The phrase "mountains, rivers, and the great earth" cites the world as an illustration.

Space is characterized by both difference and identity. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—the categories that encompass sentient beings, their karma, and its fruits—are neither identical nor different.
This answers the question of how [things] could arise abruptly. However, wherever there is arising, there must be abiding;
wherever there is abiding, there must be change; and wherever there is change, there must be cessation. Thus, it is said that they "successively flow on. It is because of this succession that...
