An ancient master said: "To take a single blade of grass and manifest it as the sixteen-foot body"—this is the ultimate exertion to bring forth this meaning. ○ Regarding the "dharmas that are identical with the mind" mentioned below, there are also two:
first, those identical with the mundane; second, those identical with the supramundane. Within the identity with the mundane, the former is explained first.
Regarding the "identity with the seven great elements": as stated previously, their substance is not the manifold phenomena themselves, yet they do not obstruct the manifestation of all phenomena.

Next, regarding the "identity with the three categories": matter and mind are nothing other than what is manifested by the mind. Regarding the "identity within the supramundane," first is explained the identity with the Hīnayāna teachings:
there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm, and there is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm.

Regarding the "Dhātu" (Element/Realm): next, to clarify that this is precisely the Mahāyāna Dharma—since all causes and effects are established based upon the one mind, as seen in the fact that the three types of awakening and the five stages do not depart from the one true Dharma-realm;
the meaning of this is evident. Since it is both mundane and supramundane, the six classes of ordinary beings cannot escape its illumination, nor can the four classes of noble ones...
It is able to surpass that illumination. Therefore, the *Zhengmai* says: "The phenomena of the ten realms, apart from this mind, cannot be found as even a single thing;

this is called 'dust upon dust merging' and 'every land being perfectly penetrating. One who understands this meaning, though remaining unmoved within the one true reality, will have no lack in their responsive application.
[The section] beginning with "By this" concludes the meaning of clarity, referring to the previous answer given by the Buddha.

Regarding why the *Asaṃgata-garbha* (the Non-empty Treasury) is specifically taught as the basis for the continuous arising of all phenomena, it is because this very [treasury] possesses the meaning of being both simultaneous and identical.
Third, the *Śūnyatā-aśūnyatā-garbha* (the Empty-and-Non-empty Treasury) is taught based on the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous source of the mind. It is "separate from both being and non-being," yet it is "both being and non-being.
At the outset, this was able to harmonize and sweep away the [dualistic] mind; here, the word "is" (ji) doubly traces back to the two preceding [notions of] the treasury.

According to the above, it is neither mundane nor supramundane, revealing only the wondrousness of the Tathāgatagarbha-mind; yet it is both mundane and supramundane, revealing only the Tathāgatagarbha-mind.

"Clear. Since the wondrous clarity is manifest and its essence and function are distinct, why do the Buddhas and Śākyamuni, within their various explanations of universal pervasiveness, all speak of the meaning of both emptiness and non-emptiness?
Therefore it is said: "This is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously clear mind-source.
This means that this very Tathāgatagarbha is also the fundamental source of the two wondrous clarities. [The passage] beginning with "separate from" refers to what follows.

The method of "melting away" (róngfú) is as follows: Since the mind alone is taken as the fundamental source, the primary characteristics (zhèngxiàng) are not of the temporal realm and thus immediately vanish;

hence it is said they are "separated from being" (líjí). Because the primary characteristics are not of the temporal realm, they do not vanish when the time is present; hence it is said they are "separated from non-being" (lífēi).

This explains the meaning of the "double brushing away" (shuāngfú) by means of their mutual negation and simultaneous disappearance. Furthermore, since it possesses both the meanings of wondrous clarity (miàomíng), the primary characteristics are absent where [the source] resides.

Because they are not obstructed while being simultaneous, it is said that "they are identical. At the very point where they are mutually identical, because they are not obstructed while being simultaneously non-identical, it is said that "they are not identical.
This explains the meaning of dual integration by establishing two positions through mutual formation.

However, since both are simultaneously negated and integrated, such that existence and cessation are sovereign and free, it is beyond the reach of words and the scope of thought; this is called "only" (wei).
Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively fathom this; one who understands this meaning will not be disturbed in their contemplation even when confronted by a thousand difficulties.
According to the previous two sections, there should likewise be a passage that concludes and establishes the fundamental principle.

That it is not fully provided here is because, as soon as the mind-source was pointed out, the state of both "immediate" and "separate" emerged; since this did not involve extensive textual elaboration, there was no need for further conclusion.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that these three collections (Tripitaka) are all explained according to the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching]: this means that the three collections are in essence but the One Mind.
Since the One Mind perfectly encompasses the three collections, whenever one collection is mentioned, the other two are simultaneously and fully present.
When faith reaches this point, one will no longer be deceived by the tongues of others. Thus, the Three [Collections] are perfectly revealed.
The [section on] the treasury concludes. Second, the universal reproach for conceptual deliberation:

How can sentient beings within the three realms of existence in the world, as well as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have transcended the world, use their minds of limited knowledge to fathom the unsurpassed bodhi of the Tathāgata, or employ worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? It is like a lute...
Although the se, konghou, and pipa possess exquisite sounds, they cannot produce them without skillful fingers.
You and all sentient beings are likewise so: the precious, awakened true mind is fully complete in each and every one of you.

Just as when I press my finger, the Sea-Seal manifests its radiance, if you momentarily raise your mind, the afflictions of the mundane world arise first. This is because you do not diligently seek the path of supreme enlightenment, but instead cling to—
[The Buddha] rebuked those who, adhering to the Hīnayāna, consider a minor attainment to be sufficient.
"Worldly" refers to the container-world (*bhājana-loka*). "Beings of the three realms of existence" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).

"Transcendental [beings], such as those who have heard or attained realization," refers to the world of the Perfectly Awakened Ones (*samyaksambuddha-loka*). He did not mention Bodhisattvas because he was speaking specifically to Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. Thus, it is correct.
This is for the purpose of inclusion and for the sake of both [cause and fruit]. The phrase "how can this be? is a term of wonder and reproach.
The Buddha’s intention is that what was explained above—the three piṭakas and the single mind—are perfectly complete. When realized within the fruit, they constitute unsurpassed bodhi;
when awakened to within the cause, they constitute the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Yet, since they are simultaneously one within the three and three within the one, they are fully present at once.
It is inconceivable. It can only be known through wisdom (*jñāna*); it cannot be cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*). It can only be sealed by the mind;

it cannot be clarified by words. How could the beings of the three realms of existence in the world, upon hearing the conditions for transcendence, seek to fathom it with their deluded minds of knowing (referring to the conceptualizations of the six consciousnesses), employing the worldly language of frivolous proliferation?

(Regarding the fact that causes and conditions arise spontaneously and continue without interruption, etc. To wish to gain awakening and entry [into this truth] is like attempting to measure the ocean with a pint-measure or to illuminate the night with a firefly’s glow—is it not difficult?
○ To explain this by way of analogy: the *qin* had five strings in antiquity; today it has seven. "Qin" means "to restrain";
it signifies restraining and subduing depravity and lust, leading one toward the refined and correct. The *se* had fifty strings in antiquity; today it has two.
The *shu* has fifteen strings; it is a type of *xiao*. It is so called because its sound is *xiaoxiao*—meaning it is clear and resonant. The *konghou* has fourteen strings;
it was created by Shi Yan as a music of decadent indulgence (*mimi*). Later, it emerged from the region of Sangjian and Puxiang.
Because this is the preserved sign of an empty land, it is named after the "empty sign" (*kōkō*) and bamboo.

As for the four strings of the *pipā*, pushing them forward with the hand is called *pí* (forward), and drawing them back is called *pá* (backward); these names are derived from the movement of the fingers during performance.

All four are musical instruments, serving as a metaphor for the nature of the conditions heard by sentient beings. That which possesses "wondrous sound" refers to the wondrous sound being internally contained within.
This metaphor illustrates that when sentient beings hear of the nature of conditions, each possesses the meaning of the three Tathāgata-garbhas;

this can be called bodhi, and it signifies the capacity for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. "Lacking a skillful finger" refers to failing to act with skill; this metaphor illustrates sentient beings' hearing and conditioning.
One uses the mind that knows to gauge and enter through worldly language. "Unable to bring forth" means that the wondrous sound does not produce it;
this is a metaphor for sentient beings who, despite hearing the conditions, cannot realize supreme bodhi nor awaken to and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
[The phrase] "You and the following dharma" corresponds: "you" refers to Pūrṇa, while "sentient beings" also encompasses those who hear the conditions.
Each possesses its own nature, identical to those four kinds of musical instruments; therefore, it is said, "it is likewise so.
The stainless essence of the jewels is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. The pervasive and perfect function of awakening is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
The true mind, fully endowed with both meanings, is the empty-and-non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*. That each is complete in itself is a metaphor for sentient beings hearing [the Dharma].
Within the nature of conditions (*pratyaya*), these are inherently and spontaneously complete. This accords with the previously mentioned meaning of "wondrous sound" (*sughoṣa*).

Pressing the fingers is a brief representation of the sign of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), for it is free from conceptual discrimination and transcends language. "Ocean Seal" (*Sāgaramudrā*) is the name of a *samādhi*.

As stated in the "Chapter on the Honorable Head" (*Bhadrapāla-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: "The forms of sentient beings are each different; their karmic actions and voices are likewise immeasurable. In this way..."

All things can be manifested through the majestic spiritual power of the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*). Thus we know that the concentrated mind, being pure and limpid, manifests forms in response to objects;
it is like the seawater, which is profoundly still yet reflects images as if they were sealed within it—hence its name.
As for "Emitting Light," based upon that Sea-Seal Samādhi, it brings forth the light of Bodhi-wisdom, pointing out what the Buddha knows and what the Buddha sees. This...

The "mind" (*manas*) here seems to refer to the teaching on the profound and subtle meaning delivered while seated in peaceful composure prior to the discourse; however, there is no such text in the analogy itself.

If one were to supplement the analogy with the eight characters—"though there be exquisite sound, it must have exquisite fingers to produce that exquisite sound"—then both the Dharma (the subject) and the analogy would be complete.
As for "you momentarily raising your mind," this refers to the previously mentioned application of clarity to awareness.
Awakening has not yet become clear, yet ignorance is already blazing; therefore it is said that "dust-like afflictions arise first.

Once these dust-like afflictions have arisen, they obstruct Bodhi and hinder knowledge and vision. In this combined metaphor, if there were not a skillful finger, one could never bring forth the meaning.
○ The phrase "By reason of... concludes the censure. Above, it was stated: "If you momentarily raise your mind, dust-like afflictions arise first. Furthermore—
The reason for this was not previously made explicit; it is now set forth to demonstrate the intent of providing exhortation.
The unsurpassed path of awakening is a fruit that is neither born nor extinguished. Those who diligently seek this must employ the nature of non-arising and non-extinction as the causal mind.

Because they do not diligently seek [the truth] and do not employ a mind free from arising and ceasing, they are unable—like the Buddha—to cause the Ocean-Seal Samādhi to radiate light at the mere touch of a finger.
The nirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna possesses the fruit of arising and ceasing (because it has not yet transcended the *pariṇāmi-śarīra*).

Those who cherish this [state] employ only a mind subject to arising and ceasing; therefore, as soon as they intend to raise their minds toward clear awakening, afflictions (*kleśa*) arise first. They rejoice...
The temporary rest at the conjured city leads one to form the thought that it is the final destination; hence it is said, "to consider a little as sufficient.
Upon hearing this censure, one should give rise to deep reflection. Subsequently, Pūrṇa’s inquiry regarding the cause of delusion likely stems from this very point.
Having completed the formal exposition of the *pitaka*, there are two further sections to resolve doubts: first, resolving Pūrṇa’s doubt regarding the existence of a cause for delusion; second...

Śāriputra and Ānanda cling to reality and thus give rise to self-doubt; this constitutes the first two sections. First, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra clings to diligent seeking and doubts that there is a cause for the illusory;
second, the Tathāgata demonstrates the absence of cause and teaches through sudden awakening. The first [of these two].
Pūrṇa said: "I and the Tathāgata are identical in the perfect clarity of precious awakening, the truly wondrous, pure mind, which is non-dual and complete.
Yet, in the past, I encountered beginningless delusion and have long remained in saṃsāra; though I have now attained the Noble Vehicle, I have not yet reached its ultimate consummation.
World-Honored One, all your delusions are completely extinguished, leaving only the wondrous, true, and eternal. I venture to ask the Tathāgata about all things."
For what reason do sentient beings have delusions? Why do they obscure their own wondrous clarity and undergo this drowning in samsara?

When one first investigates the root, there is originally no duality. Regarding Pūrṇa’s words: after the Buddha previously rebuked him for not seeking [the truth], he spoke these words to pose his question.
As for the phrase "I and the Tathāgata," Zhengmo says: this is a deduction based on oneself in contrast to the Buddha, used as an analogy for all beings.
There is no being that is not thus. One sees that the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) of both sentient beings and Buddhas is without difference.

What was previously called the "precious awakened true mind" (*ratna-bodhi-tathatā-citta*) is here termed the "precious awakened perfect clarity" (*ratna-bodhi-paripūrṇa-vidyā*) and the "truly wondrous pure mind. "Precious" (*ratna*) is designated by "perfection" (*paripūrṇa*), taking the sense of being pure and all-pervasive;
it still belongs to the treasury of space (*ākāśagarbha*). "Awakened" (*bodhi*) is designated by "clarity" (*vidyā*), taking the sense of manifesting all phenomena through its function.
These still belong to the *asaṃskṛta-garbha* (the treasury of the non-empty). As for the true mind being designated as "wondrously pure" (*miāojìng*):

"wondrous" takes the simultaneous illumination of both emptiness and existence; "pure" takes the simultaneous negation of both emptiness and existence. These still belong to the *śūnyāśūnya-garbha* (the treasury of the empty-and-non-empty).
In reality, the three treasuries do not depart from the one mind; therefore, they are collectively concluded with the character "mind. Regarding "perfectly non-dual," they are all...
The endowment of their nature is each and every one perfectly complete; however, while the former refers to sentient beings, this refers to the Buddha.
○ As for "but I," the comparison below shows a vast disparity. The word "past" generally refers to kalpas of antiquity.

"Delusive thoughts" refers to coarse consciousness, because the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not know of the existence of subtle consciousness; yet they are still said to be "non-existent. "From the beginning" means that although it belongs to...

Because one investigates coarse consciousness and cannot find its initial characteristic, and because one relies upon it to give rise to delusions and create karma, thereby being unable to escape birth and death, it is said that one has "long remained in saṃsāra.
Precisely because one has long remained in saṃsāra and constantly suffered its harms, it is said that one has "encountered" them.
Now, those who have attained the Holy Vehicle have already realized the four fruits in the present life; they merely remain at a distance from the Buddha’s Bodhi.

"Ti-shang is still far off"; therefore, it is said that "ultimate attainment has not yet been reached. This is because Pūrṇa himself admits that he has returned from the mundane level but remains only halfway there.

As for "the various delusions being completely extinguished," this means not only can one sever the afflictions within the coarse consciousnesses, but even the most subtle *lakṣaṇa-utpāda* (the mark of arising) is entirely eliminated.
As for "only the wondrous, true, and eternal [remains]," this means not only can one depart from the *pariccheda-bhava* (segmented existence).
From birth and death up to the final transformation at the end of life, all are universally transcended. This praise of the Buddha by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra has reached its ultimate realization.
Viewed from this perspective, the comparison between the Buddha and Pūrṇa is indeed as vast as that between heaven and abyss.
[The Master] said: "I venture to ask. Below this, he requests the cause of delusion. He ventures to state his feelings, saying: "I venture to ask. No.

This question regarding sentient beings is asked for the sake of seeking [the truth] for oneself. As for the question, "By what cause do delusions arise?": one wishes to eliminate delusion by first exhausting its cause.
That which obscures the wondrous clarity is due to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); it covers and conceals true awakening (*tathatā*).

Those who undergo this drowning—ordinary beings drowning in the *paricchinna-vedanīya* (segmented) realm and those of the Two Vehicles drowning in the *pariṇāma-vedanīya* (transformative) realm—all encounter this.
Error. One should seek to completely eliminate [this]. This is precisely where Pūrṇa’s intention in inferring the cause lies.
Second, the Tathāgata demonstrates causelessness and teaches through sudden awakening. This has two parts: first, the formal explanation of causelessness;

second, the conclusion that demonstrates sudden awakening. The first [section] has four parts: first, citing the delusion to pose the question; second, clarifying through the integration of dharma and parable; third...
It is shown that there is no need for cessation. Fourth, the response to the inquiry:
First, the Buddha told Pūrṇa, "Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain. I shall now question you again regarding various matters present before us in the world."
Zhengmo says: "Although you have removed your doubts"—this single phrase grants that your great doubts have already been exhausted.

This is because, by tracing back to the root that there is no duality, you believe in your own original reality; by extolling the Buddha’s perfect permanence, you believe in the Buddha’s eternal realization.
Thus, doubts regarding the arising and continuity of the myriad dharmas, as well as delusions concerning their universal pervasiveness, have all been eliminated. As for remaining delusions...
Those who have not yet reached the end do not yet understand that ignorance is without cause; they merely seek it through force.

"Present phenomena" refers to those things currently seen by the eyes and heard by the ears in common experience. Among these various phenomena, there is this one instance that serves as an analogy, rather than being a mere hypothetical construction.
Now, I ask you again to demonstrate that the inquiry is based on actual facts, so that [you may] rely upon them.
This is because the meaning that delusion is fundamentally without cause is known through analogy. Second, the combination of the dharma and the analogy is explained in two parts:
first, providing an analogy based on phenomena; second, correlating the meaning with the dharma. First [the analogy based on phenomena]:
Have you not heard of Yajñadatta in the city of Śrāvastī? One morning, he suddenly looked at his face in a mirror.

He became attached to the head in the mirror, whose features were clearly visible, and grew resentful toward his own head for failing to show its face and eyes. He consequently regarded it as a malevolent spirit.
"He runs about wildly without cause. What do you think? For what reason does this man run about wildly without any apparent cause?
Pūrṇa replied, "This man’s mind is deranged; there is no other reason."
"Do you not hear?"—this rhetorical question is used to resolve the matter of what must be heard, as it pertains to the phenomena present before one.

The inhabitants of Śrāvastī and the Buddha share the same basis; this is a metaphor for the jewel-like awareness that is perfectly luminous, the truly wondrous and pure mind, which is non-dual and complete.
Yajñadatta (演若達多), here translated as "Sacrifice-Granted" (Cishou), was a madman in the city because he had obtained [his name] by begging from a deity;
this serves as a metaphor for Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, who, though born from the Truth, became a deluded person. "Suddenly" refers to Pūrṇa suddenly giving rise to a single thought;
since a single thought marks the beginning [of delusion], it is compared to the early morning. "Using a mirror to reflect one's face" is a metaphor for consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Taking the Buddha as an object: because one takes the Buddha as an object, the image of the Buddha arises as a transformation within one's own consciousness, just like the head in a mirror.
Failing to comprehend the correct principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), they do not realize that the external Buddha is entirely an image within their own consciousness.

On the contrary, they instead envy the fruit of Buddhahood, falsely seeking to extinguish the true and eternal. Therefore, it is likened to the head seen in a mirror, where the eyebrows and eyes are visible.
One’s own head is a metaphor for the Buddha within one's own mind; because the self-mind is fundamentally the Buddha, it is compared to one’s own head.
Failing to realize that the self-mind is fundamentally the Buddha, one instead laments having encountered delusion and being submerged in suffering.

Because they obscure the wondrous clarity, it is compared to the metaphor of angrily blaming oneself for not being able to see one's own face and features. Regarding "chimei" (魑魅), ancient commentators explain them as ghosts of the mountains and marshes.

I, however, suggest that the character "chi" (魑) contains the radical "li" (離), which can be used as a metaphor for the Two Vehicles who have attained transcendence; the character "mei" (魅) contains the radical "sun" (未), which can be used as a metaphor for ordinary beings who are deluded and obscured.
Ordinary beings recklessly consider themselves ordinary and have not yet emerged from the realm of segmented existence (*bhavāgra*). As for the Two Vehicles...
He reckons his own minor transformations to be flourishing intensely, just as that [other] person considers himself a shapeless *chimei* (demon) running wildly.
Thus we know that Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, though claiming for himself that he has now attained the Noble Vehicle (*āryayāna*), has not yet reached its ultimate consummation;

he remains, in essence, of the same class as that shapeless demon running wildly. Question: For what reason does this person run wildly without cause? [This question] was posed by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra directly to the Buddha.

Regarding the statement, "For what reason do all sentient beings have delusion? and so forth, the Buddha’s intention was likely to use the mouth as a metaphor to lead them to understand the meaning within the Dharma.
The answer, "It is because these people's minds are deranged and for no other reason," was already understood by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra regarding the metaphor;
however, he likely had not yet fully grasped that within the Dharma, delusion has no underlying cause.
Second, regarding the synthesis of meaning and phenomena, the Buddha said:
"The wondrous enlightenment is perfect and bright; it is fundamentally perfect, bright, and wondrous. Since it is designated as delusion, how could it have a cause?
If it had a cause, how could it be called delusion?"

"Wondrous enlightenment, luminous and perfect" is spoken in reference to the Buddha-mind. All delusions are completely extinguished, leaving only the wondrous, true, and eternal; therefore, it is called "wondrous enlightenment.
"Luminous" takes its meaning from its capacity to illuminate, and "perfect" takes its meaning from its capacity to pervade—this is what was meant in the preceding passage:

"Only wondrous enlightenment, luminous and perfect, shines universally upon the Dharma-realm. "Fundamentally perfect, luminous, and wondrous" is spoken in reference to the arising of the mind; it means not only...
The Buddha-mind is wondrous, luminous, and perfect; the mind that arises is likewise fundamentally perfect, fundamentally luminous, and fundamentally wondrous.

If one can give rise to the mind free from discursive thought, that very mind is the Buddha-mind. Thus we know that Pūrṇa envied the Buddha-mind and regretted his own mind, for both were equally products of deluded thought.
This accords in meaning with the previous analogy of loving the head in the mirror while hating and rebuking one's own head.
Since both that craving and hatred are equally delusions, they are identical to Pūrṇa’s envy and regret, which are likewise false.
According to Pūrṇa’s previous question, "By what cause do all sentient beings have delusion? whereas here it says, "Since these are called 'delusions,' how can they have a cause?
This is a concluding demonstration of Pūrṇa’s words. Based on the intent of Pūrṇa’s prior question, it was intended to investigate the matter deeply.

One should utterly sever it because its cause is false. This statement—"if there were a cause, how could it be called false?"—is a reductio ad absurdum that demonstrates its cause is definitively non-existent;

thus, there is no need for a false severance. In terms of meaning, this corresponds to the preceding section where the Buddha questioned Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra using a metaphor, and Pūrṇa answered using a metaphor.
Although the phrasing of the correspondence here is brief, the meaning is fully contained within it. From antiquity, all such cases have been treated in this manner.
This has been explained in a general way. Now, following the detailed and concise meanings within the analogies asked by Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, I shall provide a detailed analysis.

Having completed the combined clarification of the Dharma and the analogies, [the text] thirdly demonstrates that there is no need to extinguish the two. First, it rebukes [the opponent] for failing to return to what has already been said;

second, it demonstrates that there is no need to desire extinction. Regarding the first: "Now, to give rise to a thought toward the Buddha is precisely the same as previously adding clarity to Awakening. Since previously..."
It has already been said that they still cannot turn back; therefore, he rebukes them.

From these various deluded thoughts, which act as causes for one another, they have accumulated delusion upon delusion throughout countless kalpas. Even though the Buddhas have illuminated this for them, they still cannot turn back.
Continuing from the preceding section, one gives rise to the thought of taking the Buddha as an object.

Since this is identical to the case of Yan-ruo (Shan-shan) looking into a mirror, it can be understood that the beginningless movement of the mind and the luminous awareness are likewise analogous to this. Indeed, from the movement of the mind, subtle delusive thoughts (*parikalpita*) are established;
thus, from the subtle to the coarse, they arise in succession. Therefore, it is said that they "mutually cause one another. Once the coarse characteristics are established...
Thus, delusion has already been established. From this established delusion, one further develops successive delusions and attachments, thereby forming three kinds of continuity.
Hence it is said: "From delusion, delusion accumulates. Once this continuity is established, the cycle of transmigration turns without cease.
Therefore it is said that they have passed through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.

Although the Tathāgata has already elucidated such meanings for you in the past, observing the cause of your deluded question, it is evident that you have still not been able to return to the root and revert to the source;
how profound is your delusion! Second, he shows that there is no need to extinguish desire.

Thus, the cause of delusion arises from delusion itself. Since the consciousness of delusion has no cause, it is a false construction with nothing upon which to rely; since there is not even arising, what is there to be extinguished?
"Thus" refers to Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, who, having admired the Buddha and repented, asked: "What is the cause of this delusion? Although he spoke these words...
The delusion of today is likewise identical to the false conceptions of beginningless time. One must understand that such a cause for delusion does not truly exist as something separate;

rather, because of delusion, one fails to recognize it as false and thus perceives it as having a substantial body of its own—this is what was meant previously by the statement that "there is a semblance of the awareness of delusion.
To "recognize that delusion has no cause" means that once one recognizes this delusion, it is found to be entirely [without substance] in its very essence.
Emptiness—how could there be any further cause? This refers to what was stated previously: that when consciousness is deluded, its delusion ceases.
Regarding "delusion has no basis," it means that just as today’s delusion is thus, so too is primordial delusion;

by taking this as an analogy for that, all delusions are seen to have no basis. Since they have no basis, there is nothing that can produce them; since there is no producer, there is nothing produced.
How could there be [any such thing]? This shows that since even all delusions have no arising, what could one possibly intend to extinguish by seeking their cessation?
Thus, it is demonstrated that there is no need for extinction. Fourth, the question and answer are concluded.

One who attains Bodhi is like a person upon waking recounting the events of a dream. Even if the mind were sharp and brilliant, for what cause or condition could one seek to grasp an object within a dream?

How much more so when there is no cause and it was originally non-existent? It is like that city-dweller, Yan-ruo-da-duo (Śaṇḍaka), who had no cause or condition for suddenly fearing his own head and running away; when his madness suddenly ceased, the head was not obtained from without. Even if his madness has not yet ceased—
What loss could there be even in madness? ○ Pūrṇa, since the nature of delusion is thus, on what basis could it exist?

At the outset, one should inquire and demonstrate the nature of delusion. The Buddha’s intention was that because you previously asked the Buddha why delusion exists—thinking that once the Buddha had attained Bodhi, all delusions would have been extinguished, and that he must surely be able to explain both delusion and its causes and conditions—you felt it necessary to know the attainment of Bodhi.
Although one who has awakened can speak of the delusions [of a dream], it is like a person awake describing the events of a dream; fundamentally, nothing exists there.
If one were further asked to explain by what cause those delusions arose, even one endowed with the eloquence of a Buddha’s wisdom could not do so.
It is just like that person who has awakened: no matter how sharp and brilliant their mind may be, by what causes and conditions could they possibly retrieve the objects from within the dream?
"And yet it is shown to people. This shows that one who wishes to extinguish all delusions need not seek a cause;
how much less so when there has been no cause from the very beginning, because fundamentally nothing exists. ○ As for "like that" below, this uses a metaphor to clarify.

Although there was a metaphor above, it was merely a statement made within the context of the Dharma; here, however, the point is further elucidated specifically through the metaphor of Yan-luo-da-duo (Śaṇḍha).

How could there be such a thing as running away in fear of one's own head due to some external cause? This clearly demonstrates that frantic running has no cause, serving as a metaphor for how all delusions are without a source.
Why do we see that this frantic running is causeless? Because when the madness suddenly ceases, the head is not something acquired from the outside.
Not only does it cease upon the ending of the madness; even while the madness has not yet ceased, the head could have been lost at any time. Based on this:
Thus, the True Reality is fundamentally without loss. What was previously called "encountering delusion and undergoing immersion" is likewise merely a false calculation.
○ Regarding the phrase "the nature of delusion is thus," it means that the nature of delusion is fundamentally non-existent, just as I have explained.
As for the question "How can it exist?"—since even delusion does not truly exist, how much less so when one further investigates its source?
The cause itself would necessarily have no existence. This concludes the formal explanation of the absence of a cause. Second, the summary and demonstration of sudden enlightenment has two parts:
first, the explanation by way of Dharma; second, clarification by way of analogy. First [the explanation by way of Dharma]:
If you simply do not follow after the three types of continuity—the world, karma and its fruits, and sentient beings—then because these three conditions are severed, the three causes will not arise.
Thus, the madness of your own Yajñadatta within your mind will naturally subside; this subsiding is itself Bodhi.

The supremely pure, luminous mind is coextensive with the entire Dharma-realm; it is not obtained from others. Why, then, rely on arduous toil and the cultivation of proof through the "tender and the tough"?
The initial teaching provides the method for sudden awakening: when it says, "You need only not follow [delusions]," it means you need not seek further after delusion.
As for the cause: it is simply that one does not follow after delusions. "Discrimination" refers to the first five of the six gross phenomena (*ṣaḍ-audārikāḥ*);

"worldly karma, its fruits, and sentient beings" refers to the last one of the six gross phenomena. When these six gross phenomena are combined, they can give rise to the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
these constitute the conditions for the three [karmic paths]. If one can simply refrain from following after them, the coarse appearances will be eliminated, and—
The conditions for the arising of these three have been severed. The "three causes" refers to the subtle characteristics (*sūkṣma-nimitta*).

Because the seeds of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are contained within these subtle characteristics, they constitute the causes of the three. A cause must rely upon conditions to arise; therefore, it is said:
"Because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise. This is like the seeds of the five grains of the world, which necessarily depend upon soil and water.
It serves as a condition. If there were no water or soil, then even if one sows the seed, it would not sprout.

The "madness" of Da-da refers precisely to a single moment of deluded movement, for it is the initial arising of fundamental ignorance. To "rest of itself" means that it does not require the application of effort;
it naturally subsides and ceases. This is because, just as a seed that has failed to sprout will have its capacity for growth naturally destroyed if left alone.
Simply by being free from deluded thoughts, one is the Tathāgata. Therefore it is said: "Resting is itself Bodhi. Bodhi is the Buddha-mind.

To transcend all things is called "supreme" (vishaya). To be free from all defilements and afflictions is called "pure" (viśuddha). To be fully endowed with the illumination of wisdom is called "luminous" (vidyā).
To embody all phenomena without exception is called "originally pervading the Dharma-realm. To say it is not a transmission outside the Buddhas and Patriarchs is called "not obtained from others.
The final two lines conclude by clarifying that there is no need for diligent seeking: since it is not obtained from others, one is originally Buddha;
as it does not involve effort or achievement, how could one rely on toil and labor? Thus it is said, and so forth. This is the essential point.
This is from the *Zhuangzi*. The chapter "On Nourishing the Lord of Life" states: "The joints, sinews, and knuckles had never been touched [by his knife].
Wuxing says: "The meat between the bones is called 'ken' (肯); the places where muscles and sinews knot together are called 'qǐng' (綮).

According to my limited view, this is taken to mean the sense of arduous practice through laboring the sinews and suffering for the bones. I, however, believe that "ken" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), meaning to sever it as if splitting the meat between the bones.
"Meat. "The sinews and tendons" refers to the afflictions; it means severing them according to the principle, like cutting through the knots of muscle and sinew. The general meaning is:
why must one laboriously sever delusions as if cutting through sinews and tendons, practicing falsely and seeking false realization? This second analogy clarifies this point.
It is like a person who has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within his own garment, yet remains unaware of it.
Wandering through distant lands, exposed to the elements, he runs about begging for food; though he is truly impoverished, the jewel has never been lost.

Suddenly, a wise person points out the jewel to him, and his every wish is fulfilled from the heart, bringing him great abundance. Only then does he realize that the divine jewel was not obtained from the outside.
The first analogy illustrates fundamental non-awakening (*abodhi*). Some scholars interpret this as a general metaphor for ordinary beings and those of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Zhengmo states:

"The clothing symbolizes the three conditions of inverted discrimination, the three causes of subtle and flowing thoughts, and the fundamental ignorance of the nature of madness—the manner in which these layers upon layers envelop [the mind].
The pearl symbolizes the supremely pure and luminous mind of *bodhi*. From this, the branches and leaves [of delusion] arise together with the root."
Ignorance wraps [the mind] layer upon layer; therefore, although it exists, one does not perceive it. ○ The metaphor of "exhausted and exposed" below illustrates that delusion is not a loss.
Zhengmo says: To be entangled in emptiness while lacking wondrous function is called "exhausted. To be stagnant in existence with nowhere to retreat and hide is called "exposed.
Since both emptiness and existence are peripheral lands, they are like other regions; seeking the pleasures of humans and devas is likewise.
To seek only partial and minor benefits is like rushing about to beg for food. While ten thousand delusions race across one another, the single truth remains perfectly present;
it is like being poor yet possessing a pearl. This is what is meant by: "Even if you do not cease your madness, what have you lost? Regarding the passage beginning with "Suddenly there is...
which uses an analogy to illustrate awakening rather than attainment, Wuxing says: "The Buddha is like the wise man, and the teaching is like showing him the pearl. Zhengmo says: [as above].
The metaphor of attaining great wealth illustrates that the root is the fundamental dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The final two lines illustrate that it is not obtained from others.
My humble opinion is that "not obtained from others" clarifies that it is inherently and spontaneously present from the beginning; there is no need for laborious cultivation or realization.

Thus, we know that for a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanren*), practice places sole emphasis on sudden enlightenment (*dunwu*). The Zhengmo (Correct Pulse) says: "If one's enlightenment has not yet reached great penetration, yet they recklessly dismiss [the teachings]..."
To cultivate the practice [of the self] and yet fall into error is also the height of folly and delusion. This concludes the first section:
Śāriputra’s adherence to the notion that there is a cause for delusion. Second: Ānanda’s adherence to the notion that the True [Self] constitutes his own doubt. This has two parts:
(1) Ānanda adheres to the Buddha’s words and doubts whether the True [Self] constitutes his own; (2) the Tathāgata clarifies that it is not the self and teaches him gradual cultivation. Part One.
Two parts: first, he expresses his doubt by referring to what was just said; second, he presents his request by contrasting it with the past. Regarding the first:
at that moment, Ānanda prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet amidst the great assembly, then rose and addressed the Buddha:

"World-Honored One, you have just stated that because the three conditions for the karma of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are severed, the three causes do not arise. Consequently, the madness of Citta has naturally subsided."
"Cessation is itself Bodhi; it is not obtained from others. This principle of cause and condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is thus clear and manifest.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata suddenly discard cause and condition?
"At that very moment" refers to the time when the Buddha answered Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. It was precisely when Pūrṇa’s doubts were resolved that Ānanda [arose his own].

Doubts regarding this further arise; therefore, I state my position before the assembly: what is currently being discussed refers generally to the preceding section’s statement, "You need only not follow [the six coarse objects]," etc.
The karmic actions of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct take the six coarse objects as conditions and the three subtle states as their causes.
Once the six coarse [delusions] have been eliminated, the three subtle [delusions] become useless. Thus it is said: "Because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise.
Since the three subtle [delusions] are no longer functional, ignorance naturally turns to ash. Thus it is said: "Within the mind, the nature of Madhyāntika’s madness naturally subsides."
All these delusions are extinguished together. Because the true manifests when the delusory is extinguished, it is said that "resting is itself bodhi.

Since this is not obtained from others, what need is there to rely on the arduous labor of cultivation and realization? If even a person is not required, how much less so the words of effortful practice and verification.
There is no need to further cultivate or realize it. This single word "this" (斯) serves as a summary of the preceding discourse, as in the expression "if one relies on this teaching.
Ānanda’s intention was that if one relies on this teaching, then bodhi is attained through the cessation of false causes and conditions;
thus, would not the meaning of causes and conditions be perfectly clear and evident? However, once the principle of causes and conditions has been established...
Why does the Tathāgata suddenly and completely abandon the principle of dependent origination, and instead say that [enlightenment] is not obtained from others and does not rely on arduous effort?
Second, this is a request made by turning away from the past.
"World-Honored One, it is through causes and conditions that my mind has attained awakening.
Is this principle not true not only for us junior, trained śrāvakas, but also for those in this assembly such as Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and Subhūti?

Having heard the Buddha’s teaching on causes and conditions from an aged brahmin, they resolved their minds on awakening and attained the state of being free from outflows (anāsrava). Now, you speak of bodhi..."

If it arises from causes and conditions, then what was taught by King Śreṇika of Rājagṛha and others—that things are spontaneous (*svayambhū*)—would naturally constitute the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
We only pray that you will, out of great compassion, dispel our confusion and delusion.

The first section describes the causes and conditions that bring about benefit. "I attained awakening through causes and conditions" means that by hearing the Dharma of causes and conditions, one realizes the path of the first fruit (*srotāpatti*).
The passage beginning with "World-Honored One, this meaning... serves to demonstrate most emphatically that these causes and conditions must not be disregarded.
Its intent is that if awakening were achieved through causes alone, it would not be considered particularly significant.
"Because our years are still young, we have likely attained only the fruits of those in training (*śaikṣa*), or our realization is shallow and superficial.
This interpretation is incorrect; therefore, why does [the text] say "only [we]" and so forth? Here, in this assembly, it refers specifically to those who are elderly and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Among them, three individuals—such as Mahāmaudgalyāyana—are mentioned by name, while the rest are encompassed by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). All of these had previously relied upon false paths.
The Master practiced the teachings of non-Buddhist paths; therefore, it is said that he followed an old brahmin, just as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana previously studied under the brahmin Sañjaya.
Other cases may be understood by analogy. It was when he heard the Buddha’s words regarding causes and conditions—concise yet profound—that he abandoned heterodoxy and returned to the Right Path.
This is somewhat lacking in clarity compared to the preceding sentence. If one reads it with a brief pause at the midpoint, the meaning will not be confused.
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment, in order to refute the theories of no-cause and false causes, he taught the principle of true causes and conditions;
thus [the teaching] was heard. This hearing involved a great multitude of people; some heard it directly from the Buddha, while others heard it through successive transmission. All [of them...]
It can be said that because he heard [the Dharma], he gave rise to the resolve for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*). There are two types of such resolve: first, the resolve to leave the household life;

second, the resolve to transcend the boundaries [of worldly existence]. "Attaining awakening" refers to awakening to the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. By relying upon this, one severs the afflictions of views and mental formations (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-āsrava*) and realizes the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*);

therefore, it is said that one attains the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*). Thus, even the attainment of the stage of no-more-learning in old age is accomplished through causes and conditions, and these causes...
How could one suddenly turn one's back on conditions? Now, by saying "the present teaching," it clarifies that the present teaching turns its back on the past.
The previous statement, "resting is itself Bodhi," etc., refers to the principle of not following causes and conditions.

Thus, the mention of Rājagṛha and so forth not only reveals this turning away from the past, but also serves to prevent confusion with heterodox views; for Kuśārī is the name of a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). To cite one example:
The inclusion of such terms as "spontaneity" (svabhāva) is because it is their primary tenet. However, causes and conditions and spontaneity are established in mutual dependence;

since causes and conditions are not the ultimate principle, spontaneity is considered the superior teaching. Thus, for them, this [doctrine of spontaneity] conversely becomes the *paramārtha-satya* (ultimate truth).
How could this possibly be acceptable? ○ [I] only entreat you to bestow these two lines [of verse] out of great compassion.
"Developing" means: "opening" refers to opening up the delusions of dualistic divergence; "developing" refers to dispelling the stagnation of confused unity.
Ānanda clung to the Buddha’s words and his doubts regarding the reality of the self were thus resolved.

The Tathāgata clarifies that [enlightenment] is not attained through self-effort alone, but must be taught as a gradual cultivation. (This is because principle is realized through sudden awakening, whereas phenomena must be cultivated gradually.

If one clings to gradual cultivation while being deluded regarding sudden awakening, one will never attain the true fruit throughout kalpas of dust-like time. Conversely, if one clings to sudden awakening while being deluded regarding gradual cultivation, then even if one speaks extensively, it will all result in mere madness. Therefore, when the World-Honored One previously resolved the doubts of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, he emphasized sudden awakening;

now, in dispelling Ānanda’s delusions, he places particular weight on gradual cultivation. It is like a skilled physician administering medicine: by alternating between depletion and replenishment according to the occasion, there is no person who cannot be saved, and every ailment can be treated. This is followed by the selection of faculties for direct entry and the sequential traversal of stages.)

This constitutes clear evidence for the principle of sudden enlightenment followed by gradual cultivation). Two: First, the formal clarification that [the self] does not exist inherently; second, the conclusion exhorting gradual cultivation. Regarding the first:

(Although the text simultaneously refutes both *hetu-pratyaya* [causes and conditions] and *svabhāva* [inherent nature], the Master’s intent lies solely in refuting the latter. The topical outline follows the primary focus. Three: First, restating the attachment and refuting its logic;
second, clarifying through analogy that it does not exist inherently; third, the appropriate inquiry and concluding demonstration. Regarding the first:
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Just as when the causes and conditions for the madness of Rāvaṇa in the city are extinguished, the state of non-madness naturally emerges.
The principles of causes and conditions and of spontaneity are fully exhausted in this."
First, he restates their position; he speaks thus because he wishes to resolve their doubts. "That which is such" refers back to the analogy:
the madness of Datta is itself ignorance, and because it can obstruct bodhi, it is called a causal condition (*pratyaya*).

If it is extinguished and eliminated, one realizes that delusion is fundamentally empty; this restates the previously held view that because the three conditions are severed, the three causes [are likewise severed].

This means that the nature of madness does not arise and subsides of itself. The non-mad nature is itself Bodhi; because the delusion is extinguished, it is the Real, and thus it is said to "emerge spontaneously.
This restates the previously held position that the subsiding of madness is itself Bodhi and is not obtained from another.

The final two phrases refute the principle based on doubt. The Buddha’s intention was to explain that the nature of madness is caused by me— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Conditions are fundamentally not causes; I say that cessation is itself bodhi, yet it is also not something produced spontaneously.
That you do not understand this and instead falsely employ the principles of causes and conditions or spontaneity to exhaustively investigate the truth—how can this be so utterly erroneous?
Two analogies clarify that [the three] are not self-existent: first, an analogy for how awakening (*bodhi*) is not self-existent; second, an analogy for how ignorance (*avidyā*) is not self-existent;
third, an analogy for how original enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*) is not self-existent. Regarding the first two: first, the primary analogy for how awakening is not self-existent;
second, an auxiliary analogy to prevent misconceptions. Regarding the first:
Ānanda, the head of Yaśodara was originally natural. Since it was originally natural, there was no "becoming so" that was not itself natural.
For what reason and by what causes did he become terrified of his own head and run about in a frenzy?
To clarify this further through analogy so that its falsity may be easily revealed: previously, one's own head was used as a metaphor for the Buddha of one's own mind;
here, it serves as a metaphor for *bodhi*, because the Buddha of one's own mind is itself *bodhi*.

Within the analogy, if it were claimed that the head is inherently natural (*svabhāva*), then it should have been naturally so from the beginning, without any change or transformation. This is the correct explanation of the subsequent phrase.
This is an implicit negation (*paryudāsa*). "There is none that is so" means there is no such principle. Since there is no such principle, it is not something produced by itself (*svayam*).
By implication, that which is produced by itself must necessarily be immutable. The same applies to *bodhi* within the dharmas:

if the fruit is spontaneous (*svayambhū*), it should likewise be inherently so from the beginning and devoid of change. If this were the case, then all sentient beings would not [be able to attain it].

Having encountered delusion, one sinks into suffering; therefore, the text continues with the analogy, posing the question: "For what cause and condition does one run about in a frenzy, fearing for one's head?
This is because Pūrṇa’s own remorse over encountering delusion and sinking into suffering is precisely identical to the matter of Udāyin running about in a frenzy, fearing for his head.
When the Dharma and the analogy are revealed together, it is clear that Bodhi is not something that arises spontaneously.
Second, using a metaphor to prevent further misconceptions:
If this head of yours went mad due to causes and conditions, why did it not naturally lose its head due to causes and conditions? Your original head was never lost;
madness and terror merely emerged delusively. Since there has been no change whatsoever, what need is there for causes and conditions?

Fearing that upon hearing the previous analogy, they might further calculate that Bodhi belongs to causes and conditions— just as that natural head can also become crazed because it has causes and conditions—
the World-Honored One used this to prevent such a view. The Buddha’s intention was that if one were to say the natural head becomes crazed due to causes and conditions,
then when the crazed mind ceases, why does it not simultaneously return to its original state?
The loss of his head was due to the conditions of his madness; now that one sees where his mad mind has ceased, one realizes his original head was never lost.
It is clear that his frantic fear was a false projection, and his head never underwent any change. How could this head have existed by depending on causes and conditions? Awakening is also like this:
when all delusions are extinguished, it is inherently and spontaneously manifest; it does not depend upon causes and conditions.

There is. If one must abandon spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and resort to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is like leaving a pen only to enter a net; in the end, it is not a plan for liberation.
Thus, the first metaphor shows that awakening (*bodhi*) is not self-originated; the second metaphor shows that ignorance (*avidyā*) is not self-originated.
Madness is natural by nature; madness and fear have existed from the beginning. Before one was mad, where did the madness lie latent?

Because the Buddha previously answered Pūrṇa that delusion has no cause, fearing that Ānanda might not understand and would instead cling to the view that ignorance belongs to the "natural" (svabhāva), he uses the metaphor of "original madness being natural. His intention is to use original madness as a metaphor for ignorance.
This is clear. In the analogy, if one were to hold that the original madness was natural, then it would follow that Daṭṭha inherently possessed a nature of madness and fear from the very beginning.
Let us ask: prior to his becoming mad, where did this mad nature reside? Surely such a thing could not be.
It is the same with ignorance (*avidyā*) among phenomena (*dharma*). If it were natural, then sentient beings would inherently possess delusion.
Regarding the nature: when not even a single thought has arisen, where could the deluded nature possibly be hidden? Surely such a principle does not exist.
By combining the teaching with the analogy, it is clearly revealed that ignorance is not self-originated. Third, the analogy shows that fundamental awakening is not self-originated.
"Not mad" means "spontaneous. Since the head is fundamentally without delusion, why would one run about in madness?
Fearing that upon hearing the previous analogy, they might further calculate that original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) is spontaneous, [the text] addresses this;

for it has already been clarified previously that original enlightenment and *bodhi* are non-dual and are not self-originated. Now, because they again cling to this view, [the text] uses "not mad," "spontaneous," and so forth to prevent it. Not...
The nature of one who has not yet gone mad is a metaphor for original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*). However, when one has not yet gone mad, the head is inherently as it is;
thus, it is said to be "without delusion. This is a metaphor for how, when abiding in original enlightenment, bodhi is fundamentally real and not something conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This is first established by means of the metaphor; below, its non-self-nature is revealed. It is said that if the state of not being mad were indeed natural, it should not... [be subject to change].
One becomes insane; yet since one does not actually become insane, the original head is without delusion. Why then do you act so recklessly by running about like a madman?
This metaphor shows that the fruit of original enlightenment is spontaneous and should not result in confusion. Since confusion does not actually occur, bodhi is clearly present.
Why, then, do you wander aimlessly and deludedly? By combining the dharma and its metaphor, it is clearly revealed that fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is not self-originated.

(Question: The preceding metaphor—that bodhi is not of itself—was sufficient to resolve Ānanda’s doubt. Why, then, is there a subsequent metaphor stating that ignorance (*avidyā*) is not of itself and that fundamental awakening is not of itself? What is the intended meaning? (Answer: Externalist theories of "self-nature" (*svabhāva*) must be refuted until they are completely exhausted.

Ignorance is the source from which delusions arise; fundamental awakening is the foundation for realizing the truth. Since these two are both not of themselves, it follows that everything is not of itself. The section clarifying that [all things] are not of themselves is concluded.
Third, one should seek to demonstrate the binding.
If one awakens to the fact that the original head was merely consciousness perceiving a frantic run, then causes and conditions are naturally both mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Therefore, I say that when the three conditions are severed, that itself is the bodhicitta.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra clings to the delusion that there is a cause for existence; Ānanda suspects that the Truth might be confused with the self.
Both stem from their failure to realize that the original head has never been lost, and they do not know that their frantic running is but delusion.

If they were to awaken to the fact that the original head is found and recognize that their frantic running is delusion, then Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra’s clinging to causes and conditions and Ānanda’s suspicions would naturally both become mere frivolous discourse, devoid of any real meaning.
This serves both to resolve Ānanda’s present doubt and to preempt Pūrṇa’s potential attachment, awaiting the point where he will establish his own reasons;

such a development was inevitable. Therefore, because both [of these] are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), my words refer to the previous response of the Buddha to Pūrṇa: "Because the three conditions are severed, it is precisely bodhicitta."

Both [of these] are words of negation. By the character "hence" (故), it is shown that [the self] is not spontaneous; by the character "that" (即), it is shown that it is not produced through causes and conditions.
Previously, because Ānanda did not understand the meaning of the character "hence," he sought to establish spontaneity based on the absence of a cause.

Subsequently, fearing that Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra would not understand the meaning of the character "that," and might instead cling to causes and conditions in opposition to non-self, [the Buddha] therefore...

This is concluded and indicated by two statements, intended to lead one toward deep reflection and self-realization. This completes the section clarifying that [the goal] is not attained through oneself alone.
Second, the exhortation to gradual cultivation, which has three parts: first, developing based on what preceded; second, providing direct exhortation;
and third, using examples to issue a rebuke. Regarding the first (which refers to developing the practice of progressive advancement as the basis for the subsequent exhortation):
When the bodhicitta arises and the mind of arising-and-ceasing ceases, this is merely arising and ceasing. When both cessation and arising are exhausted, that is the path of non-effort (anābhoga).
If there were such a thing as spontaneity (*svabhāva*), then it would follow that the spontaneous mind arises and the mind of arising-and-ceasing ceases; this too would be arising and ceasing.
That which is without arising and ceasing is called spontaneity. It is just like when various worldly phenomena are blended together to form a single whole.
"Essence" refers to the nature of synthesis; that which is not synthesized is termed the nature of suchness. Suchness is not "such," and synthesis is not "synthesized.

When both synthesis and suchness are abandoned, and both the abandonment of synthesis and suchness are transcended—this phrase alone is called the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*)."

First, one is sent to practice through awakening. The aforementioned statement that "resting is itself bodhi" refers to the mind of sudden awakening to bodhi; this is termed the "arising of the bodhi-mind.

By relying on the power of this mind, one gradually subdues and eliminates the coarse manifestations of the two obstacles and the mind of arising and ceasing—this is termed the "extinction of the mind of arising and ceasing.
This refers to the fact that from this point onward, the coarse, manifest mind of arising and ceasing [is extinguished].

It is "extinction. According to the stages of the Final Teaching (Jiaojiao), this corresponds from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh. In the Final Teaching, the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) suppresses the manifest [afflictions].

Upon entering the first stage, the active manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa-samudācāra*) is first eliminated; by the seventh stage, the active manifestations of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-samudācāra*) are likewise exhausted.
This is merely "arising-and-extinguishing" because it refers to extinction in dependence upon arising; it remains, in essence, arising-and-extinguishing.

The mind-listener. Relying on this power of the mind to advance toward the subduing and removal of the seeds of the two obstacles, the subtle arising and ceasing of the mind is called "the simultaneous exhaustion of arising and ceasing.
This means that the mind characterized by the subtle arising and ceasing of seeds is also simultaneously exhausted.
According to the stages of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhāyāna*), from the first *mūrdhan* (Summit) up to the tenth *prayoga* (Preparation):

because the practices and stages of the Final Teaching subdue the seeds [of affliction], upon entering the first *mūrdhan*, the coarse seeds of the two obstacles are first eliminated; by reaching the tenth *prayoga*, the subtle seeds of the two obstacles are entirely exhausted.

From this point onward, one spontaneously subdues the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); therefore, it is called the Path of Effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*). "If there is... and below refers to the partial entry into fulfillment.
If it is still "resembling," this is because what was stated above regarding the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*) possesses a sense of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Based on this meaning, it is revealed that there arises a certain spontaneous mind; riding upon the power of this mind, one advances to subdue and eliminate residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*).
This most subtle mind of arising and ceasing is called the "extinction of the arising and ceasing mind," meaning that the habit-energies are the most subtle.
The mind of arising and ceasing also ceases. According to the stages of the Final Teaching (Jiao), this corresponds to the beginning of the ten bhūmis.

Through the four stages of "overcoming and subduing" (jiafu) in the Final Teaching, one eliminates the habitual tendencies (xi) stage by stage throughout the ten bhūmis; upon entering the initial mind of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), eleven parts [of these tendencies] are exhausted.
Yet, it is said that even this is still "arising and ceasing," because subtle marks of thought (nianxiang) have not yet been entirely eliminated.
Therefore, by relying on this initial mind and proceeding to sever one portion of the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the Buddha-ground, one becomes "without arising or ceasing.

This means that even the most subtle marks of thought are no longer present. According to the position of the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), at the stage following the *samyagjñāna* of Equal Enlightenment (*samalaṃbuddhi*), one spontaneously attains Buddhahood without further obstruction;
thus it is called "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*). It is just as when [the lower stages] are successively discarded.
"Waiting for entry into cessation": when various characteristics combine to form a substance, it is like a multitude of medicinal herbs combined into a pill;

this metaphor illustrates the two preceding layers of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), wherein arising and ceasing establish the state. Because there is no difference from that which is like the medicinal herbs forming a pill, it is called the "nature of combination.
That which is not a combination is like the pill becoming empty once the medicine is exhausted; this metaphor illustrates the [two] above... [the subsequent layer].

It emphasizes spontaneity (zìrán). Because it establishes its position through spontaneity—just as when medicine is exhausted, there is no difference from empty space—it is said to accord with the fundamental nature (běnrán xìng).
Phrases such as “the fundamental is not fundamental” employ metaphors to sweep away and dispel [conceptual attachments].
As for the previous statement that “resting is itself bodhi,” it appears to carry the sense of a fundamental nature; yet, while the mind of bodhi arises, the mind of birth-and-death ceases.
Thus, the "original suchness" mentioned above is not truly original suchness.

Next, it is said that although this [process] of arising and ceasing appears to possess the meaning of conjunction, when both cessation and arising are exhausted, then this subsequent conjunction is not true conjunction.

The phrase "conjunction and suchness are both transcended" further follows upon the previous tracks to negate them again. It means that what was said above—namely, that cessation and arising are both exhausted—is itself without...

The path of effortful cultivation (*yònggùndào*) also seems to possess the sense of being "original" (*běnrán*). Yet, when the mind of spontaneity arises and the mind of birth-and-death ceases, that which is "original" is likewise departed from.
Next, it is said that this [effortful path] is also subject to birth-and-death and thus seems to possess the sense of "conjunction" (*héhé*).
However, that which is without birth-and-death is called "spontaneous. Thus, that which is "conjunctive" is likewise departed from.

It is "separation. Because these two types of separation are unified, it is said that they are merely "together. The phrase "neither separation nor union" is the state where emotional attachments are exhausted through the transcendence of all dependencies.
As for what was stated above—that "non-arising and non-ceasing" is called "spontaneity"—it still seems to imply a sense of separating from causes and uniting with effects.
However, having separation and having union is itself a form of duality. If one were to maintain this [notion of] separation...

When both [the positions of] "neither" and "not-neither" are unified, all dualistic oppositions are exhausted. According to the final teaching (zhōngjiào), this corresponds to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (miàojiào).

Because in the wondrous enlightenment of the final teaching, all manifest seeds, latent seeds, and habitual tendencies are exhausted, that which is illusory is entirely true. Thereafter, there is no further stage; there is nothing further to be separated from, nor anything further to be unified with.
Since dualistic opposition has been severed, all types of causes and conditions—whether harmonious or non-harmonious, natural or otherwise—are likewise extinguished.

All various false conceptualizations and attachments cannot reach it; therefore, it is said to be "the dharma free from frivolous proliferation" (*niṣprapañca*). [Question: This sutra also encompasses both the Sudden and Perfect teachings;

why then is its classification of stages restricted solely to the Final Teaching (*paryavasāna-naya*)? [Answer: Because this sutra follows the latter half of the *Prajñāpāramitā* assemblies, serving as a bridge from the Gradual to the Sudden and from the Final to the Perfect, thereby constituting the capacity for receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

The preceding section on "Opening the Development" is concluded. Second, the main section on "Exhortation," which has three parts: 1. Cultivating what is unprofitable; 2. Hearing in vain without... [text fragment].
Section Three: Encouragement Regarding Practice. First:
"Bodhi and Nirvana are still far away; they cannot be realized through your diligent cultivation and verification over kalpas alone.

Although you may remember and uphold the pure and wondrous principles of the twelve divisions of the sutras of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, this will only increase your frivolous arguments."

The passage above states that because the three conditions are severed, it is the bodhicitta; this is a realization through awakening (*pratyakṣa-sākṣātkāra*), not a realization through cultivation (*bhāvanā-sākṣātkāra*).

According to the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), this is limited to the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*); it remains separated from the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue-guo*) by forty-five stages (namely, the stages of dwelling, practice, direction, application, and the grounds).
Therefore, it is said: "Bodhi and nirvāṇa still lie far away. The word "not" (*fei*) is a term used for contrastive clarification. The word "you" (*ru*) is a form of direct address.

"Passing through kalpas" means proceeding from here onward through yet more kalpas. "Diligently practicing and realizing" refers to laboriously and assiduously cultivating and purifying the manifest, latent, and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), thereby attaining entry into the sublime and wondrous stages of the worthies and sages (*ārya*). This is as previously described:

through successive stages of negation and establishment, one arrives at the state of non-conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). The Buddha’s intention is that only by hearing [the Dharma] in this manner will it be truly beneficial.
If it were not so, even to recite much would be in vain; hence it is said, "Though one may remember and uphold [the teachings]," and so forth.

To "remember and uphold" means not only being able to hear them, but also being able to retain them in memory. As for "the Tathāgatas of the ten directions," this refers to what has been taught by more than just a single Buddha.

Furthermore, they are able to record all that the Buddhas have spoken; it is not merely a single sūtra among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, but they are also able to record the twelve divisions of the scriptures in their entirety.

Regarding the pure and wondrous principles, it is not merely the coarse and manifest doctrines of the out-flowing (sāsrava) Lesser Vehicle, but they are also able to record the great, untainted (anāsrava), pure, and subtle principles within the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna scriptures.
These are what is remembered and upheld, layer upon layer without end, far exceeding the sands of the Ganges River.
Yet, even if one can do this, it serves merely as material for idle talk and ultimately yields no real efficacy; thus it is said that it "only increases frivolous discourse.
This is clearly seen in the saying of the ancient masters: "A foot of practice is better than ten feet of talk."
The two disciples heard this in vain.

Although you discourse upon causes and conditions with such clarity and certainty that people of the world call you foremost in erudition (*bahuśruta*), even through the habitual cultivation of such vast learning over many kalpas, you could not escape the peril of the Mātanga woman. Why then wait for me?

Regarding the Buddha-śikhara-dhāraṇī, it was previously stated that Ānanda’s failure to practice was of no benefit; fearing he might not yet be fully convinced, the matter is now verified through actual events.
Thus it says, "Although you [are as such]," and so forth. This discourse on causes and conditions and spontaneity concerns manifest phenomena; the words leave nothing further to be said.

The meaning is not at fault; therefore, it is said that he is "decisively clear. Among humans, the reputation you have earned as one of great learning is such that no voice can surpass it nor any peer equal it; thus, you are granted the title of being preeminent in this regard.

However, the Buddha’s intention is that although you are able to do so, it does not pertain to spiritual cultivation or realization, for this is merely due to the power of the habitual perfuming of extensive learning accumulated over many kalpas.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Buddha and Ānanda both resolved their minds [on enlightenment] together under the Buddha Śūnyarāja.
It can be verified by this fact that while the Buddha was always diligent and energetic, Ānanda always delighted in extensive learning (*bahuśruta*) and so forth.

The phrase "unable to escape" (*bùnéng miǎnlí*) precisely reveals his lack of merit. The characters "héxū" (what need) likely contain a scribal error for the character "shàng" (still/already); otherwise, it would not make sense.
The meaning was slightly inconsistent; however, when lecturing, it is also acceptable to adapt and modify the phrasing as needed.
Third, regarding exhortation through actual events:
the lustful fires in the mind of Mātanga were instantly extinguished, and he attained the stage of Anāgāmin, becoming a "grove of diligence" within my Dharma.

The river of craving shall be dried up, bringing you liberation. Therefore, Ānanda, though you may maintain the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrous adornments throughout kalpas, it would not equal practicing untainted karma for a single day, thereby distancing yourself from the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love.
As soon as he was touched by the power of the mantra, the fire of lust was suddenly extinguished; this demonstrates that the power of the mantra can destroy obstacles.

Not only did his lust cease, but he also attained the stage of Anāgāmin; this demonstrates that the power of the mantra can bring about benefit. "Anāgāmin" is the name for the third fruit of the Hīnayāna, which here is translated as "Non-returner.

This means that he has transcended and severed the eighty-eight *kleśas* (afflictions) associated with the delusions of views, and has suddenly severed the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm.
[He] contemplates: because he will no longer be reborn in the desire realm, from this point forward he shall advance in the Buddha-dharma and cultivate the untainted (*anāsrava*) path.
Because he has successively severed the higher [afflictions] through contemplation, it is called "the Forest of Diligence" (*vīryavana*). "Forest" implies a boundless expanse when viewed from afar;
this metaphor indicates that his diligence shall not stop at merely attaining the four fruits of arhatship. Regarding the phrase "the river of craving dries up," "craving" refers to—
