The three realms are craving; it drowns sentient beings like a torrential river. Since Dengga has already severed the craving of desire, it is like the water remaining when a torrent has been halted.
As he proceeds to sever the [cravings] of the two higher realms, both the waters will likewise dry up.
Having already detached from the entanglements of craving, he is thus freed from the pull of the hook. Therefore, it is said: "I shall cause you to attain liberation. For this reason, Ānanda—
[The passage] beginning with "etc. concludes the account of the *ḍākinī* mentioned above and addresses Ānanda to provide him with encouragement. It says:

"Although you have, throughout kalpas past, remembered and upheld the secret and profound teachings of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as well as their subtle, wondrous, solemn, and pure principles, it is not equal to giving rise to the resolve for enlightenment for a single day and advancing in the cultivation of untainted, supreme karma; [for by doing so], one can immediately..."
One who is far removed from the two sufferings of hatred and attachment—how could that person, such as the Gaṅgā, be subject to difficulty?

Furthermore, while the preceding passage spoke only of "attachment," this one includes both "hatred" and "attachment. This is because hatred and attachment are relative; where there is attachment, there must necessarily be hatred.
Thus, the suffering of encountering hatred is like Ānanda’s encounter with the Gaṅgā, while the suffering of separation due to attachment is like [the Gaṅgā’s separation] from...
Ānanda, for this reason both are called suffering. This concludes the section on exhortation. Third, the refutation by way of analogy:
For instance, Mātaṅgī was formerly a courtesan; through the power of the divine mantra, her lustful desires were eliminated. In the Dharma she is now known as the Bhikṣuṇī Śīlabhadrikā.
Together with Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, she has likewise realized their past causes and knows the causal conditions throughout successive lifetimes.
Craving is suffering. Because one may, in a single thought-moment, cultivate untainted goodness, one may either transcend the bonds of affliction or receive a prediction of enlightenment.
How can you deceive yourself by still lingering to watch and listen?
Taking Mātanga as an example, it is shown that she was a courtesan not only in this life but in previous existences as well;

this demonstrates the intensity of her lustful desires and how the power of the divine mantra can eliminate them. Because the fruit arises from the practice, the efficacy of cultivation and realization is made manifest.
Furthermore, for one who eliminates craving, the fire of lust is instantly extinguished and the river of desire dries up; this is the benefit of destroying evil, which is the Dharma.
The "Middle" refers to establishing a forest of diligence within the Buddha-dharma, which immediately gives rise to the benefit of goodness;

this is called the "nature," whereby one attains the stage of Anāgāmin and gradually enters the enlightened nature, which is the benefit of entering into principle. The "Bhikṣuṇī" refers to being able to enter the pure assembly and not being subject to expulsion by the Saṃgha, which is the benefit of joy.
This clearly demonstrates that the divine mantra possesses the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*; therefore, it is identical to [the aforementioned benefits].
Furthermore, Rāhula’s mother was named Yaśodharā; she was formerly the Buddha’s wife and has now likewise left the household life as a bhikṣuṇī.
The term "one and the same" (yīyàng) means identical. This indicates that the Bhikṣuṇī Śailā also attained awakening regarding the causes of her past lives just as Yaśodharā did.
This constitutes the attainment of the supernormal power of recollecting past existences (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna). Previously, before awakening to these past causes, she spoke at will.
One does not personally believe that craving is suffering; it is only through awakening that one is able to know this.

"Experiencing many lifetimes" refers to the causes spanning from time immemorial, undergoing birth and death throughout many successive lives. Because it is due to craving that one brings about birth and death, it is said to be suffering.
"Cultivating for a single thought-moment" means that, having grown weary of suffering, one gives rise to a desire for detachment and suddenly arouses superior resolve.

The thought of progress refers to the cultivation of meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the higher stages. Because the concentrations of the higher stages can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) of those higher stages, they are called untainted wholesome dharmas (*anāsrava-kuśala-dharma*).

The word "or" (*vā*) is a term of uncertainty. If one considers a small attainment to be sufficient, one may "emerge from entanglement," meaning that one realizes the four fruits and emerges from the entanglements of the three realms. Alternatively, if one turns from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, one may then receive...
Regarding the "bestowal of prophecy" (*vyākaraṇa*): this refers to the bestowal of prophecy by a Buddha upon one who has resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*).

Its intent is to show that the future [attainment] is not yet fixed. Now, Yaśodharā was long-practiced, while Śīlavatī was a beginner. By equating a beginner with one long-practiced, the Buddha’s intention was solely to praise Śīlavatī;
it was not intended as a simultaneous praise of both Yaśodharā and Śīlavatī. Reflect on this. The ancient masters saw this point here.
Because there is a prophecy [regarding this], it is concluded that this sutra must follow the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Furthermore, you wish to change the character "or" (或) to "ji" (即).
If one were to rely on that, it would subvert the Buddha’s sutras. How so? These two lines are precisely words of reprimand directed at Ānanda, stating:
"A woman's body is defiled and is not a vessel for the Dharma; how much more so for a nun who has been such since her previous lives."
A lewd woman is the most base and inferior of beings; yet, through a single moment of cultivation, her future destiny may be immeasurable.

How is it that you, a dignified man of illustrious lineage, do not strive for true cultivation and actual realization, but instead deceive and delude yourself, remaining mired in what is seen by the eyes and heard by the ears, fixated solely on the literal text?
To give rise to knowledge and understanding from within words and language—how could this not surpass the capacity of inferior women?
This concludes the resolution of doubts; may the three groups of followers develop perfect faith.

Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, had their doubts and delusions eliminated. Their minds awakened to the true reality (*dharmatā*), and their bodies and minds attained a lightness and ease such as they had never experienced before.
Weeping again with deep sorrow, they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet; kneeling with palms joined, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Unsurpassed One of Great Compassion, Pure and Precious King! You have skillfully opened our hearts, being able to employ such a kind [of teaching]."
Through various causes, conditions, and skillful means, he exhorted and inspired them, leading those who were submerged in darkness out of the sea of suffering.
At first, they rejoiced in their awakening and realization; Ānanda and the great assembly were all included within this Dharma gathering. These are those who heard the Buddha’s instructions.

Having heard the clear exposition of the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) and further hearing the instructions on sudden awakening and gradual cultivation, my doubts were eliminated and my mind realized the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
This true mark is precisely the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca); it is also the one mind, the threefold Tathāgatagarbha.
This is because the empty Tathāgatagarbha is a non-conjunction through conjunction, while the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha...
It is inherently neither "is" nor "is not. The Tathāgatagarbha, whether empty or non-empty, is likewise both united with and detached from these states.

It is solely this One Mind, which is neither united nor detached, transcending all false discrimination, inversion, and frivolous proliferation; therefore, it is collectively designated by the name "True Reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Thus, one should know that although [this teaching] appears after the tenfold manifestation of the seeing-nature and before the universal pervasiveness of the seven elements, it has already been set forth.
The name "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is not yet its perfect designation; it is like using a ladle to show someone a single drop of the ocean and calling it "the ocean.
Now, since true reality is identical to the three *tathāgatagarbhas*, those who do not attain awakening even after it has been fully revealed do so for two reasons:
first, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra suspected that delusion had a cause, and second, Ānanda clung to the truth as being self-existent. One of these is a matter of fact.
Obstruction: the first is the obstruction of principle (*dharma-āvaraṇa*). Having not yet gained self-confidence, by what means could one achieve awakening?

Now, by means of the Tathāgata’s demonstration of sudden awakening, the doubts of Pūrṇa are dissolved; and by clarifying gradual cultivation, the delusions of Ānanda are removed. Since the entire assembly hears this, their doubts and delusions are eliminated.
As for "the mind and body become light and at ease through faith and awakening," it means knowing that delusion is non-existent.
Because one is no longer obstructed by phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*), one suddenly realizes that the body is light and understands that the self is not real.

Because one is no longer obstructed by principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), one suddenly realizes that the mind is at peace. Although this is not yet true awakening, such perfect faith has likewise only begun to arise today.
Therefore, it is said that they "attained what they had never before. Ancient worthies immediately granted this as true awakening.

However, I, the humble one, maintain that if it were indeed true awakening, there would have been no need for the subsequent invitation to the Flower Gate. Thus, we know that in the former case, they merely gave rise to faith in accordance with the words.

As for the statement in the sutra that he "attained awakening," it means that starting from this point, he first realized for himself that his own mind possesses the meaning of the Tathāgata’s secret cause.

He wept again and again out of compassion and offered his thanks; because his faith and realization had become so profound, he felt all the more that the Buddha’s grace was difficult to repay, hence his sorrowful tears.
The term "again and again" (chóngfù) is used in contrast to the four previous occasions. Regarding "prostrating at the feet and kneeling long," it refers to...
This section primarily expresses gratitude for what has preceded; yet, in view of the subsequent text, it also includes a request for what follows.
"Supreme Great Compassion" refers to the Buddha’s ultimate compassion. "Pure Jewel King" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s true and pure loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
It is called "pure" because it is truly pure and unstained; it is called "Jewel King" because it possesses sovereign power to bring benefit and joy. "Skillfully opening my mind" means...
To dissolve subtle and deep-seated delusions and to develop the fundamental ground of the mind is called the Buddha’s true and pure compassion, which is able to bestow true and pure bliss.
To employ causes and conditions and so forth is to raise up events and establish skillful means;
to guide, sustain, and encourage others is called the Buddha’s ultimate pity, which is able to extract ultimate suffering. Causes and conditions.
Examples such as Yanruo losing his head, Dengga dissolving her love, and Ayeshu knowing the cause, are cited in succession;
thus they are called "various. These are all cases where the Tathāgata observes the capacities of beings to provide instruction, prescribing remedies according to their ailments;

for this reason, they are termed "expedient means" (*upāya*). As for "lifting up and encouraging": when the frantic mind immediately ceases, that cessation is itself *bodhi*. This clarity points toward the ultimate.
To uphold [the teachings] and maintain them through successive kalpas is not equal to a single day of authentic cultivation. Yet, he again encourages and exhorts us with composure;

everything is for the purpose of leading ordinary beings who are submerged in samsara and those of the Two Vehicles who dwell in silent quiescence out of the bitter sea of the two deaths, so that they may reach the other shore of the two adornments.
Truly, the grace of the Tathāgata, whose eyebrows trail upon the ground, is difficult to repay even in billions of kalpas.
Since Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra began his inquiries, this exposition of the Dharma has reached another cycle, titled "Searching Out the Subtle and Exhausting the Perfect Cycle.
Combined with the previous cycle, this constitutes that which Ānanda requested as *śamatha*.

According to the conventional understanding, *śamatha* is translated as "cessation," taking "quiescence" as its meaning. Now, from the time Ānanda first requested meditative concentration (*samādhi*)...
To dissolve inverted perceptions, eliminate subtle delusions, and reach the ultimate point where both separation and union are transcended is true quiescence.
The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* explains this as "obliterating appearances to clarify the spirit. Obliterating appearances corresponds to the meaning of "stopping" (*samatha*).

Now, within this sutra, the nature of vision is revealed and the storehouse-consciousness is pointed out; reaching the ultimate point where all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) ceases is true [quiescence].

This clarifies the spirit. Zhengmo says: "It takes the *dharmatā-nature* (*正因佛性*, *zhengyin foxing*) in its entirety and briefly incorporates the *enlightenment-factor* (*了因*, *liaoyin*) as the essence of *śamatha*.
This is because the *dharmatā-nature* is precisely the essence of the *Tathāgatagarbha*;

that Ānanda and the others hear the Dharma and awaken with faith is what constitutes the brief incorporation of the meaning of the *enlightenment-factor*. Within the title, the meaning of the 'Secret Cause of the Tathāgata' encompasses all."
This concludes the first major section: the exposition on the development of faith through *śamatha*.

Second, the exposition on the development of understanding through *samādhi*, which has two parts: (1) direct entry for those of superior faculties, and (2) preparatory practices in the ritual site (*maṇḍala*).
The first part has three sections: (1) Ānanda’s metaphor of seeking a door within a house; (2) the Buddha’s demonstration of the two doors for deep entry.

The assembly at the third convocation received his instructions and obtained benefit. This consists of three parts: first, acknowledging the sound and recounting the reproach; second, explaining a parable to express one's feelings;
and third, requesting instruction while awaiting the teaching. First:
“World-Honored One, although I have now received such sounds of the Dharma, I know that the Tathāgatagarbha— the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind—
pervades the worlds of the ten directions, containing and nurturing the pure, jewel-adorned lands of the Wondrous Enlightened Kings throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
Yet the Tathāgata further rebukes me for my lack of merit in mere learning, stating that it does not equal the practice of cultivation.”
"Initially receiving the Dharma-sound": this "Dharma-sound" generally refers to what has been explained previously.

Although the term "receiving" indicates that one has not yet fully mastered it, even within this state of incomplete mastery there is some subtle understanding; hence it says, "knowing the Tathāgatagarbha," etc.

That the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind pervades the ten directions is precisely what was previously described as the "empty and non-empty treasury" (śūnyatā-aśūnyatā-garbha). This concludes the latter section.
This is the meaning for generating faith that is difficult to conceive. As previously stated, "Only the wondrous enlightened clarity perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm.

From this, one understands that the mind pervades the ten directions. Since the mind pervades the ten directions, the lands of the transformation Buddhas and their transformation lands, as well as the lands of the reward Buddhas and their reward lands, are contained within the mind alone and nurtured by the mind alone;
therefore, it is said that the Tathāgatas, etc., are "contained and nurtured" (*han-yu*). "Tathāgata" here refers to the manifested [Buddha].
The "Transformation Body" (nirmāṇakāya) refers to the lands of transformation throughout the ten directions. The "King of Sublime Enlightenment" refers to the Body of Real Reward (sambhogakāya).
The "land upon which it relies" refers to the Land of Real Reward. Because this body possesses myriad virtues and the land is filled with the seven treasures, it is called "Adorned with Pure Jewels.
From "The Tathāgata... onwards, the previous censure is recounted. Previously, it was said: "In the human world, you are called foremost in learning..."
First, it states that despite the熏習 (*vāsanā*) from extensive learning accumulated over many kalpas, one could not escape the danger posed by the Mātangī;

this rebukes the futility of mere extensive learning. Furthermore, it says: "Though you have throughout kalpas retained the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrously adorned [teachings], they are not equal to a single day of cultivating untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) to distance oneself from the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love. This is a rebuke.

This is because they have not yet attained proficiency through cultivation. The second explanation employs a metaphor to express their inner sentiments (as soon as they realize that the mind is all-pervasive and that subtle awakening is beneficial, yet upon hearing further exhortations and reproaches, they still find no basis for progress;
thus, desiring to aspire toward true realization, they speak a metaphor to express their feelings).
"I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King. Although I have obtained this great residence, I must enter it through its gates.
Ānanda, still being in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), compared himself to a traveler; for a traveler has not yet arrived [at his destination].
It is one's own home. The Buddha said that Bodhi and Nirvana are still far off; this can be used to demonstrate this meaning.
As for the "Heavenly King," he serves Heaven and receives its mandate as Emperor or King, just as the Spring and Autumn Annals refer to the Son of Heaven of Zhou as the "Heavenly King.
This is used as a metaphor because the Buddha is the king among all dharmas. "Bestowing a magnificent house" is a metaphor for showing [the way].

"The hidden mind" (*zangxin*): This is illustrated by the "flowered mansion" because the mutual integration of its patterned and plain aspects can be used as a metaphor for the meaning of the perfect fusion of the essence and function of the hidden mind.
Such a revelation is truly beyond expectation; hence it is likened to being "suddenly favored," meaning to receive a gift unexpectedly.
"Although one obtains a great residence, one must enter through the gate" is a metaphor for the fact that although one knows the mind is all-pervasive, one must rely on the gates of contemplation.

"Awakening and entry. This is because he realized that his own extensive learning had been fruitless; he requested to seek awakening and entry through the gates of contemplation and to exert himself in authentic cultivation.
He made three requests for instruction, waiting for the teaching:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will not abandon his great compassion, but will show me how those of us in this assembly who are shrouded in darkness may relinquish the Lesser Vehicle."
He fully attained the path of the original aspiration for the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa without remainder.

He caused those in training to know from what they should subdue their former objects of attachment, so that they might attain dhāraṇī and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground;
remaining in the assembly with single-minded devotion, he awaited the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.
At first, I requested instruction, yet I could not find a gate of contemplation through which to enter, nor was there a path for me to cultivate toward Nirvana.
Unable to receive the guidance of Great Compassion, I remained in darkness with no means to attain illumination. Therefore, I only pray that the Tathāgata will not abandon his Great Compassion.

This is shown for those present in the assembly and others; it is requested specifically for those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as there are those still in training (*śaikṣa*) mentioned below.

"Obscured" (*bì*) refers to being hindered by provisional teachings (*upāya-yāna*); "darkened" (*mèi*) refers to being ignorant of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). "To cast aside" (*juānshě*) means to cause them to abandon the limited mind (*hīnayāna*);

"to fully attain" (*bìhuò*) means to cause them to achieve the great resolve (*mahāyāna*). When it says "the Tathāgata has no remainder," this distinguishes it from the "remainderless" (*anupadhiśeṣa*) of the two vehicles, because they [only]...

"Leaving behind the segmented [birth-and-death]" refers to the simultaneous exhaustion of both the segmented and the transformative [forms of rebirth]. As for the phrase "completely attaining," it signifies that the aim lies in ultimate attainment.
Although the aim lies in ultimate attainment, one proceeds from the near toward the distant; therefore, we shall first seek the path of the original arousal of the bodhicitta.

"Original" refers to the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*), and "path" points to the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mukha*). Thus, it is known that the "perfect penetration of the ear-faculty" mentioned below is precisely this causal stage.
The ground is the great gateway for the arousal of the bodhicitta. For those in training (*śaikṣa*) and others, they are requested in succession by the practitioners in training.

Those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), having already severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), need only turn their minds [toward awakening]. Because the攀缘 (*ālambana*, objective clinging) of those in training is still intensely active, they inquire:
"By what means should it be restrained? "Restraining" (*saṃvāra*) means to gather in and subdue; that which has not yet arisen is not allowed to arise, and that which has already arisen...
Because they must be swiftly extinguished, "clinging to objects" (ālambana) refers specifically to the six consciousnesses.

Although both the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*) take the six consciousnesses as their substance, the former clinging seems to be distinguished separately from the latter; this is because the category of thought functions spontaneously and has coexisted with [the mind] since beginningless time.
This is stated in the second fascicle of the *Dhāraṇī-śāstra*, in the passage "Analyzing the False to Reveal the True," which says:
As one is about to expound [this teaching], this request must be granted. Thus, it is known that the three Tathāgata-garbhas in the preceding section are precisely what is to be expounded.
The subsequent "selection of faculties" and "direct entry" are taught as the means by which [the goal] is necessarily attained.
Once this has been attained, the knowledge and vision of sentient beings becomes the knowledge and vision of a Buddha; this is the meaning of "entry. ○ Below this, he prostrates.

The Buddha awaits his instruction; those present in the assembly are single-minded, as is the hope of the great multitude. They await the compassionate decree of the Buddha, respectfully biding for his teaching.
Ānanda has finished using the analogy of the house to seek its door.
The two Buddhas demonstrate the profound entry into a single gate in four parts: first, opening the gate to distinguish the two meanings;
second, verifying through evidence to resolve two doubts; third, tying the cloth to show the sequence; and fourth, imparting the hidden teaching to select the fundamental root.
The first two [sections]: first, indicating for the sake of the audience; second, raising a question to provide an explanation. First:
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for those among the assembly—both pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—who were not yet masterful regarding the bodhicitta.

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings in the final dharma period after the parinirvāṇa of future Buddhas, he has brought forth the bodhicitta and opened the path of sublime practice of the Unsurpassed Vehicle. He proclaimed to Ānanda and the great assembly:
"You all must resolutely bring forth the bodhicitta and never grow weary in the Tathāgata’s wondrous samādhi. You should first clarify the initial stage of awakening."

Regarding the two definitive meanings of the mind, the first is presented by the narrator [the sūtra compiler]. Within the assembly, he specifically points to those pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas of indeterminate nature;

because their minor training has not yet been transformed and their great resolve is difficult to stabilize, they are objects of the World-Honored One’s compassion regarding the bodhicitta. As for the [text] that has not yet...

The Sovereign One correctly perceives this as the state of indefinite nature (*aniyata-gotra*). This means that although one has already resolved upon the path, one may regress when encountering adverse conditions, because there is no portion of inherent freedom at all.
This description primarily concerns the present, while the subsequent description also extends to the future. It is already pitiable that there will be no reliance after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
how much more so is it to be lamented that those with dull faculties during the Final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*) are still worthy of compassion? Furthermore, [the text continues:]
Now, the arousal of the bodhicitta is difficult to advance upon but easy to retreat from; thus, the Sage’s mind also takes this into account.
"The Vehicle of the Unsurpassed" refers to the fruit toward which one proceeds, namely the aforementioned *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

"The Path of Sublime Cultivation" refers to the cause by which one proceeds, namely the aforementioned "path of the original arousal of the mind. Furthermore, "perfect penetration" (*yuan-tong*) constitutes the path of cultivation; the word "sublime" (*miao*) alone—

He takes up the gateway of the ear. Because the faculty of hearing is perfectly penetrating, surpassing the twenty-four sages and being uniquely sublime, this path once opened allows one to ascend to Nirvana;
hence it is called "the path of the Unsurpassed Vehicle. ○ Regarding the phrase "proclaimed and shown" below:

it refers to the Tathāgata’s careful demonstration to Ānanda and the great assembly. Furthermore, the term "you all" specifically addresses those present as the immediate recipients of the teaching. It also...
This includes the future as well, because the preceding section of the sūtra states that the capacity of the practitioner (*yogin*) extends to both the present and the future.
"One who has resolutely resolved to attain bodhicitta" refers to one who vows to take up enlightenment and never regresses. "One who does not give rise to weariness in samādhi" means...
This means that one should cultivate the gateway of the ear with diligent application without ceasing. Thus, one knows that *samādhi* is the general name for all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
By selecting it with the word "wondrous" (*miao*), it specifically refers to the *samādhi* requested by Ānanda. Furthermore, the word "wondrous" has already distinguished it from other gateways;
the three characters "Buddha," "Tathāgata," and "Rulai" (Thus-Come-One) still clarify that this is merely the path of cultivation, taking the *samādhi* of the ear-gateway as its basis.
Because the Bhagavāns of the ten directions all share this single path to the gate of Nirvāṇa, this section establishes the definitive causal mind;
below, the thematic gates are indicated. That which ought to be clarified first must be explained, for if it is not, one will practice in confusion and ultimately achieve no real fruit.
Thus, the Confucian classics state: "Knowing what comes first and what comes last brings one close to the Way. This is precisely the initial mind that gives rise to awakening.

One gives rise to the initial resolve for bodhi; since the Sanskrit term for "bodhi" is *bodha* (awakening), and because an indeterminate initial resolve leads to many deviations along the way, the *Two Determinate Meanings* (*Niścaya-dvaya*) is opened.
Regarding the meaning of "determinate": it refers to the fact that the initial resolve relies upon this determination and cannot be altered.
This section has two parts: first, the interrogation; second, the explanation that establishes [the meaning]. First, the interrogation:
Second, the explanation and establishment. First:
"How are the two meanings of the initial mind determined?
The term "how" has the sense of an inquiry. That is to say, it is an inquiry directed at Ānanda as to why there are two [meanings] for a person who first resolves their mind [on awakening].
Regarding these various meanings, should one definitively rely upon them? This explanation consists of two parts:

first, the definitive meaning that because the cause is identical to the fruit, one enters *nirvāṇa* suddenly by clearing away turbidity; second, the definitive meaning that from the roots one unties the knots and releases the entanglements, thereby entering perfect penetration suddenly.
The first part has two sections: first, teaching that the cause is identical to the fruit; second, demonstrating the clearing away [of turbidity].

The turbid enters into nirvāṇa. First (Zhengmo says: "To take the cause as identical to the fruit is the primary, definitive tenet (*siddhānta*). To clarify the turbid and enter nirvāṇa is the purpose (*prayojana*) of this tenet. Since the tenet precedes the purpose, the tenet is clarified first.
There are three parts: 1. Using analogies to cause one to examine the causal mind; 2. Using reductio ad absurdum to reveal that it must be identical to the resultant awakening.
The third section clarifies the two aspects of difference and identity.

First: "Ānanda, regarding the primary truth (*paramārtha*), if you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the śrāvakas, cultivate the bodhisattva vehicle, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical to or different from the awakening at the stage of the resultant fruit."
The "Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha) is the heading that introduces the subject matter. "If one wishes to relinquish" refers to the mind generated by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

"Wishes" (*chanda*) means aspiration; it carries the sense of generating the resolve. "Relinquishing" (*utsarga*) means to cast off. Generating the resolve to abandon the Śrāvaka path and cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle is precisely what is meant by turning away from the Small toward the Great.
Entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is precisely what is meant by gradually reaching the ultimate fruit. This is taught by...

One should examine this carefully, for fear that a discrepancy in the cause will lead to an error in the result. "The mind of the causal stage" refers to the mind that initiates practice on the causal stage;
"the awakening of the resultant stage" refers to the awakening realized upon the resultant stage. If the causal mind is identical to the resultant awakening, it is like fashioning a vessel from gold.
If the causal mind differs from the resultant awakening, it is like steaming sand in an attempt to make rice. Are they identical or different?
This must be examined with careful scrutiny. Second, by way of contrast, it is essential that [the cause] be identical to the awakening of the fruit.
Ānanda, if one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation while seeking the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible.

The "mind of arising and ceasing" refers to the mind of the six consciousnesses. As for "taking this as the fundamental cause of cultivation," it means taking the mind that cultivates the fundamental ground as the cause.
"Buddha-vehicle" (buddhayāna) refers to the awakening of the stage of fruition; because one attains Buddhahood and delivers sentient beings by relying upon this, it is called the Buddha-vehicle.
Because its essence is truly eternal, it is said to be neither born nor extinguished. "There is no such place" means there is no such [state].

This passage uses these [examples] by way of contrast to clarify that, precisely because one seeks the Buddha-vehicle, it is only when employing a mind that is neither arising nor ceasing that there is such a possibility.
These three examples clarify the two aspects of difference and identity.
For this reason, you should illuminate that all conditioned phenomena within the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) are subject to transformation and extinction.
Ānanda, observe the world: among all conditioned phenomena, what is there that does not decay? Yet, one never hears of empty space (ākāśa) rotting or decaying.
Why is this? Because space is not a conditioned phenomenon; therefore, from beginning to end, it is without destruction or extinction.
The first example clarifies the distinct characteristics. "For this reason" means that because one takes these [phenomena] of arising and ceasing as a cause, one cannot attain the Buddha-vehicle.
"You should illuminate" means that you should clarify the analogy to distinguish between the mind of arising and ceasing and the mind that is neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
The various vessel-worlds are analogous to the six sense-bases and the consciousness-mind; when they encounter objects, [they arise].
Because it manifests, it is illustrated by the example of that which is produced. Because it ceases when separated from its object, it is illustrated by the example of that which perishes.

This causes one to observe that among all produced phenomena, who is there that does not undergo disintegration? Fearing that they might not believe the teaching and instead seek self-awakening, [the Buddha] shows that upon awakening, one realizes that produced phenomena ultimately undergo disintegration;
thus, one comes to know that the six sense bases and the arising and ceasing of consciousness are impermanent. This is certain.

However, because it cannot be employed [as an analogy], the subsequent section clarifies the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) by using space as an example for the nature of the sense organs (*indriya-svabhāva*).

Since the nature of the sense organs is eternally abiding (*nitya*), it is illustrated by the fact that they do not hear [sounds] nor undergo decay; the intended meaning of this inquiry is thus evident.

The examples such as "space is not something produced" illustrate that the nature of the sense organs does not arise dependent upon conditions (*pratyaya*). Consequently, from the beginningless past until the ultimate limit, its...

The nature is eternally abiding and without arising or ceasing. Based on this, if one wishes to take the causal mind as the basis for grasping while abandoning this [nature], there is nowhere to turn.
The teaching concludes that the cause is identical to the fruit. Second, showing how to clarify the turbidity to enter Nirvana:
First, the formation of the faculties from matter; second, the gradual manifestation of the signs of turbidity; third, a detailed exposition of the method for clarification. Part One.
Thus, within your body, that which has the characteristic of solidity is earth; moisture is water; the sensation of warmth is fire; and movement is wind.
By means of these four entanglements, your profoundly still, perfect, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind is divided into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
Once the causal mind is settled, one can advance toward clarifying turbidity. Turbidity does not become turbid of its own accord; it arises from the sense-faculties (*indriya*).
Therefore, it is said: "Within your own body... and so forth. That which has the characteristic of solidity is earth (*pṛthivī*), such as bone, flesh, nails, teeth, and so on.
That which is moist and wet is water (*ap*), such as mucus, tears, blood, marrow, and so on. That which has the sensation of warmth is fire (*tejas*), such as dryness, heat, mildness, and so on.
That which moves and vibrates is wind, such as the circulation of the breath and so forth.
"By means of these four entanglements" refers to how the body's form is produced through the mutual binding together of these four great elements. Where there is a bodily form, there are sense-gates;
where there are sense-gates, there is distinctness between self and other. Furthermore, their natures function according to each respective gate. Therefore, it is called "division."
"Your profoundly still, perfect, wondrous, and luminous mind"—the word "mind" here refers to the *ālayavijñāna*, meaning the essence of the union of the true and the false.
Because it was originally pure and all-pervasive before being conjoined with delusion, it is called "profoundly still and perfect.

Although it has already been conjoined with delusion, its luminous awareness remains undiminished; thus, it is designated as "wondrous. It serves as the seeing-essence (*darśana-viśuddhi*) of the eye.

For the listener, it is the auditory essence within the ear-faculty; for the perceiver, it is the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile essences, all equally termed "perceiving essence," because they are combined as a single faculty of cognition.

For the investigator, it is the cognitive essence within the mental faculty. Here, the term "investigator" (察) clarifies that this is the illuminating investigation of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), distinguishing it from the discriminative cognition of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). As stated later: "It originally depends on one pure, bright essence to divide and form [the various faculties]."
Sixth is "conjunction," which refers precisely to the meaning of this section. Second, the gradual manifestation of the signs of turbidity (the formation of the sense organs from the elements;

once the five aggregates are complete, the signs of the five turbidities gradually manifest thereafter based upon those five aggregates). This has two parts: first, the general presentation of the signs of turbidity; second, the specific demonstration of their gradual manifestation. Regarding the first:
From beginning to end, these five turbidities are a state of total confusion. ○ What, Ānanda, are these turbidities? For example, pure water is by nature clean and pristine.
Yet, things such as dust, soil, ash, and sand possess an inherent substance that is obstructive. These two entities are natural laws; their natures do not accord with one another.
Suppose there were a person in the world who took that dust and soil and threw it into the pure water. The soil would lose its obstructive quality, and the water—
Lacking purity, their appearance is turbid; this is called "turbidity. Your five layers of turbidity are likewise thus.

First, there is a general indication of the five turbidities: since sentient beings first bound form to create the sense organs, from the beginning their perception of emptiness was undifferentiated, and by the end they had lost the standard for distinguishing the same from the different. Including that intermediate period, there are five overlapping layers of confusion.
The characteristic of turbidity is that which causes this ocean of consciousness not to be clear and still, such that the pure virtues of *nirvāṇa* can never be realized.
Regarding the phrase "How so? (*katham*), it interrogates the characteristic of turbidity; the meaning of the interrogation is as can be understood.

Within the analogy, the clear water represents the mind of pure truth, which is also the very essence of the fruit of *nirvāṇa*. Because it has been unstained from the beginning, it is fundamentally clean and pure.

"However, 'analogy' (yu) refers to a category (lunlei). The category of dust, soil, ash, and sand is used as an analogy for the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their four characteristics (*dharmatā*), because they have long served as obstructions;
thus, they are compared to the obstructive nature of the physical substance. 'Conformity' (xunshun) refers to the two substances, water and earth, which are respectively clear and obstructive;
therefore, it is said that their natures do not conform to one another, serving as an analogy for the pure and true."

The nature of the mind is distinct from the nature of true and false as seen in views such as emptiness. There are people in the world who, like Ānanda and those born [in ignorance], take up earth and cast it into water;

this is a metaphor for grasping at the false and thereby confusing the true. Once one grasps the false and confuses the true, one will inevitably mistake the false for the true and the true for the false.
Therefore, it is illustrated by the loss of the earth’s obstructive solidity and the disappearance of the water’s purity. This is the turbidity.
Thus, it is a state of chaotic and unsettled appearance; since its physical form is such, it is called "turbidity.
Within the Dharma, the intermingling of the true and the false is exactly like this, which is why it serves as a metaphor. The final two lines can be understood by synthesizing them with the Dharma.
Second, the specific demonstration of the gradual manifestation has five parts: first, the kalpa-turbidity; second, the view-turbidity; third...
The turbidity of afflictions; the fourth, the turbidity of birth; and the fifth, the turbidity of lifespan. First, Ānanda:

you see that empty space pervades the worlds of the ten directions. There is no distinction between the perception of emptiness and the emptiness itself; there is emptiness but no substance, and there is perception but no awareness.
These interweave to falsely form what is called the first layer of turbidity, known as the *kalpa-turbidity*.
Once form has already been aggregated to constitute the sense organs, there arises that which sees and that which is seen. That which sees takes the eye as its primary faculty;
that which is seen takes space as its foremost object. Therefore, seeing space is taken as the essence of the kalpa-turbidity. As for "seeing space pervading the realm":
It is not only that space is pervasive, but vision is also pervasive. Because both space and vision are pervasive, they cannot be divided.
Since they cannot be divided, space is itself vision and vision is itself space. If space is itself vision, then there is only the name "space" without the substance of space.
If vision is itself space, then there is only the name "vision" without the awareness of vision. Thus, their characteristics [are one].
The weaver of emptiness is without substance; this is emptiness woven into views. The weaver of views is without awakening; this is views woven into emptiness.
Those who falsely establish them as a single entity do not realize it, taking it to be the sign of the beginning of the kalpa.
Therefore, it is said that this first layer is named the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). In other sutras, the turbidity of the kalpa is defined as the convergence of the four turbidities.

As for the substance: when the human lifespan was one hundred years, one would enter [the state of ignorance] only then; now, however, one enters immediately after binding form (*rūpa*) to create the sense faculties (*indriya*), with the manifestation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-darśana*) interwoven as the substance.
Furthermore, in other sutras, the four [defilements] are the agents of turbidity and the kalpas are the objects of turbidity;

here, however, the kalpas are the agents of turbidity and the pure, true nature is the object of turbidity. This is because one recognizes the chaos of the kalpas as the nature itself, just as if one were using...

This is because earth is cast into water. According to this, when the subsequent aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is shattered, one immediately transcends the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).
Since there is no form, there is no space; since there is no space, the vision has nothing upon which to weave. Therefore, Mount Gu Shan said that this turbidity depends upon the aggregate of form.
Second is the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).

Your body presently manifests as a composite of the four great elements; seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are congested and obstructed, while water, fire, wind, and earth revolve to produce cognition.
These interweave delusively to form this second layer, which is called the turbidity of views.
First one sees empty space; next, one sees one's own body. Therefore it is said: "Your body now manifests as a composite formed by the four great elements.

"Composite" (tuan) means to gather together. This means that you now take this perfectly profound, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind to gather together the four great elements to form the root-body.
Once the root-body is complete, it differentiates into seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, while harmonizing with water, fire, wind, and earth.
Therefore, the four natures and the four great elements constitute the substance of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
"To obstruct and cause stagnation" means that while the four natures are originally interpenetrating, they become blocked by the four great elements, resulting in stagnation and obstruction;
this refers to such states as not transcending form or hearing, and not emerging from sound and so forth. "To cause revolving awareness" means that the four great elements are originally insentient.
First, the four natures rotate and thereby achieve sentience, just as water is perceived to have moisture and fire is perceived to have heat, and so forth.
Regarding their interweaving: the four natures form obstructions; these natures weave themselves into the great elements, and the four great elements possess sentience.
This great weaving is of the nature of delusion; that which is falsely accomplished is an illusory achievement.

Sentient beings do not know this, and based upon it, they establish the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), which serves as the root of all views. Therefore, it is said that this second layer is called the turbidity of views (dṛṣṭikaṣāya).
In other sutras, the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*) is defined as having the five deluded views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) as its essence; thus, the views themselves constitute the turbidity.

However, in the present context, its essence consists of the fundamental nature and the gross characteristics interwoven, which is the turbidity of the true nature itself. According to this, when the subsequent aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is destroyed, one transcends the turbidity of views.

This is because where there is no feeling, there is no grasping (*piṇḍa*); and where there is no grasping, the fundamental nature and the gross characteristics do not interweave. Therefore, Gushan said: "This..."
The turbidity depends upon the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). There are three turbidities of affliction.

Furthermore, within your mind, there is the nature of recollection, cognition, recitation, and study, which gives rise to knowledge and vision; it allows the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) to appear, yet apart from these objects, there is no sign (*nimitta*).
Apart from discernment (*vitarka*), there is no intrinsic nature. These [aspects] interweave and falsely constitute what is called the third turbidity, that of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*).

Once the faculties (*indriya*) are fully equipped, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) arises spontaneously; hence it is said: "Furthermore, within your mind, there is recollection, cognition, and rehearsal. Here, "mind" refers to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*);
"recollection, cognition, and rehearsal" points specifically to the mental factor of perception (*saṃjñā*) among the six consciousnesses. "Recollection" means perceiving past objects.
"Recollection" means that consciousness arises as one brings past objects to mind. "Cognition" (*vijñāna*) refers to the arising of consciousness to grasp objects present before one.

"Recitation" (*svādhyāya*) refers to the arising of recitation-practice by taking future objects as one's focus. "Recitation-practice" means reading thoroughly so as not to forget, thereby anticipating [the object]. Regarding "the nature giving rise to knowledge and vision":
this means that the nature of the six consciousnesses arises from the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Among these six organs, only "knowledge and vision" are mentioned.

This is because by mentioning the last and the first, the middle is included. "Capable of manifesting the six objects" means that the six consciousnesses are capable of manifesting within the six sense-objects.
Thus, one knows that the delusive thoughts of the six consciousnesses externally rely upon objects to manifest; apart from the objects, there would be no characteristics of consciousness.

When internal consciousness arises dependent upon the sense faculties, it is devoid of the nature of awakening; being devoid of the nature of awakening, its nature is interwoven with characteristics (*nimitta*). When separated from objects, there are no characteristics;
thus, characteristics are interwoven with nature. In this way, false constructions are established. Sentient beings do not know this and, based upon it, give rise to various afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, it is said that this third layer is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*). In other sutras, [it is referred to as] "affliction" (*klesha*).

The turbidity of affliction (*kṣobha-kaṣāya*) takes the five dull underlying tendencies (*pañca mṛdu-kleśa*) as its essence; it is also the case that the afflictions themselves are the turbidity. Now, however, it takes the mutual entanglement of nature and characteristics as its essence;

it is also the turbidity of the true nature (*dharmatā*). According to this, when the subsequent aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is destroyed, one immediately transcends the turbidity of affliction.

Because in the absence of perception (*saṃjñā*), the six consciousnesses would be useless, and only the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) would fail to constitute affliction (*kleśa*).
Therefore, Mount Gu Shan said: "This turbidity depends upon the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); it is the turbidity of the four modes of birth."
Furthermore, you arise and perish morning and evening without ceasing; your perceptions and views constantly desire to remain in this world, yet the force of karma perpetually shifts the lands.
These delusions interweave to form existence—this is the fourth turbidity, known as the turbidity of sentient beings.
If there is a conscious mind, one immediately falls into birth and cessation. Therefore it is said: "Furthermore, you are born and cease from morning until evening without ceasing.
The *Renwang jing* states: "Within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) there are ninety *kṣaṇas*; within a single *kṣaṇa*, there are nine hundred instances of birth and cessation."
Moreover, from morning until evening, thoughts continue in uninterrupted succession; hence it is said that "arising and ceasing do not cease.

This is precisely the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), which is also termed "karma" (*karman*). "Cognition and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*) refers to the deluded and inverted cognition and vision of the six consciousnesses.

"Wishing to remain in the world" means to be attached to the three realms and not seek liberation from them. "The movement of karma" refers to the subtle shifting of the *saṃskāra-skandha* throughout the four [periods of the day].
The mutual alternation and transmigration between realms refers to the transformation of form and the shifting of retribution as one dies here and is born there.

However, while cognitive perception remains like the straight warp of a cloth, the movement of karma constantly shifts like the horizontal woof. When the warp and woof interweave, the various realms of existence are falsely formed.
Sentient beings do not realize this and instead regard them as truly existent; therefore, this is called the fourth layer of names.

The turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). In other sutras, the turbidity of sentient beings takes as its essence the retribution of views and pride; it is simply called "turbidity" because their individual characteristics are muddled and disturbed.

Here, however, it takes as its essence the weaving together of the characteristics of consciousness and mental formations (*saṃskāra*); it is called "turbidity" because it muddies and disturbs the true nature (*dharmatā*).

According to this, when the subsequent aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is destroyed, one immediately transcends the turbidity of sentient beings; for where there are no formations, there is no birth or cessation.

When there is no arising or ceasing, consciousness and perception are exhausted and the cycle of transmigration comes to rest. Thus, Gushan said: "This turbidity depends upon the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
Regarding the five turbidities of life:

you all see and hear with an original nature that is without difference; though various objects obstruct one another, they arise in diverse ways without form, yet within their nature they know one another."

Within their functions, they oppose one another; losing the standard for identity and difference, they interweave into delusion. This is the fifth layer, called the turbidity of life-force (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).

Consciousness, perception, mental formations, and karma all rely upon the eighth consciousness. Therefore, this section treats only the essence and function of the eighth as the turbidity of life-force.
Seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are originally one refined spirit; thus it is said that fundamentally there is no differentiation in nature. This refers to the eighth.
The substance of consciousness is the same. "Various objects" refers to the six kinds of objective phenomena.

"Separated and distinct" means being partitioned and mutually exclusive, such as form being visible alone and sound being audible alone. The eighth consciousness functions spontaneously and without intentionality, perceiving its respective objects individually.

Therefore, it is said that there is no "formless difference" (*wùzhuàng yìshēng*). This statement means that while the eight consciousnesses differ in their functions (*yòng*), they are identical in substance (*tǐ*).

"Mutually knowing within their nature" refers to their sharing a single cognitive awareness (*zhījué*). Because their functions differ, they are mutually exclusive; that is to say, what is seen is not heard, and so forth.

In their phenomenal aspects (*lakṣaṇa*), they turn away from one another and cannot be said to be identical; in their essential nature (*svabhāva*), they know one another and cannot be said to be different.
Thus it is said that "identity and difference lose their standard. This means that speaking of identity or speaking of difference are both unsuitable as standards.

Regarding their interweaving: if identity cannot serve as the standard, then the substance interweaves with the function; if difference cannot serve as the standard, then the function interweaves with the substance. [This is] delusion.

That which is established is a false construction; because sentient beings do not know this and instead cling to it as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), it is called the fifth turbidity, known as the turbidity of life (*āyuṣkaṣāya*).
In other sutras, the turbidity of life is defined as having the three factors of lifespan, warmth, and respiration as its essence, which sustain both matter and mind;
furthermore, it is called "turbid" simply because its own characteristics are confused and disturbed. Here, however, it refers to the eighth consciousness, whose essence and function are interwoven.

It constitutes the essence [of the life-faculty]. Furthermore, because it turbidly disturbs the true nature, it is called "turbidity. According to the later section on the destruction of the *vijñāna-skandha*, one then transcends the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
This is because, without this consciousness, there can be no continuous maintenance of the physical and mental life-faculties, and thus they would be severed. Therefore, Gushan said:

These turbidities depend upon the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Among these five turbidities, many ancient masters have taken the four great elements and the six sense objects to represent the preceding "ash and soil," while taking the four natures and the six faculties to represent the preceding "clear water.

However, the six faculties and four natures are precisely the vision accompanied by delusion; to take them as a metaphor for clear water seems inconsistent with the text regarding the clarification of turbidity. Now, I shall explain this clearly: the four natures, the six faculties, the four great elements, and the six sense objects are taken as metaphors for the ash and soil, whereas the fundamental, original self-nature is taken as the metaphor for the clear water.

Thus, the five layers arise from the pure mind, just as clear water becomes mixed with sand and soil. Since the True is not truly true, and the deluded is not truly deluded, it is exactly like soil losing its stability.

When obstructed, water loses its clarity; is it not so that we call it turbid? (End of Part Three: Manifesting the Signs of Turbidity. Part Two: Detailed Demonstration of the Method for Clarification.
Section One: Direct Demonstration by Means of the Dharma. Section Two: Manifestation through Analogy and Application. First: [The direct demonstration follows.]

Ānanda, if you now wish to cause your seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to reach far back in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity, you should first select the root of birth and death and rely upon that which is non-arising and non-ceasing—the perfected nature of perfect stillness.

By means of this stillness, turn back its false notions of extinction and arising to subdue them and return to original enlightenment. Attaining this original, luminous enlightenment, take this nature free from birth and death as the mind for the causal ground.
Thereafter, one will fully realize the cultivation and realization of the stage of fruition.
At the beginning, when intending to demonstrate the Dharma, you now wish to bring about equanimity; first, therefore, I shall stabilize your aspiration.

"Seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition" are spoken of here in general terms as the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), as yet without distinguishing between consciousness and the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*). "Distantly accords" means to correspond with the signs from afar.
This is the meaning of "conformity. However, seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are the causal mind; permanence, bliss, self, and purity are the resultant virtues.
To conform from afar to the resultant virtues by means of the causal mind is to make the cause identical to the result. Having already taught this previously, it is now further confirmed:
"Do you now desire and delight in this? If one desires and delights in this, one must not fail to [practice it].
Therefore, it is said that one should first select the root of birth and death. The root of birth and death refers to the six consciousnesses.
Since these two roots consist of the deluded root, which belongs to the realm of arising and ceasing and does not accord with the fruit-nature of virtue, one should select and eliminate them.
The nature of perfect stillness refers to the nature of the sense-faculties. Since this is the true root among the two roots, and...
Non-arising and non-extinction are identical to the awakened fruit; one should rely upon them to accomplish it. "Accomplish" means to perfect the mind of the causal stage.
Regarding the passage beginning with "By means of tranquility," one accomplishes through reliance on the Dharma. One must fix one's attention on the two characters "tranquility" (*zhan*).
This refers to the nature within the six sense faculties. Although it is named "perfectly tranquil non-arising and non-extinction," nevertheless, while in the state of a sentient being, it remains...
Views accompanied by delusion interweave with the four great elements, the six sense objects, and the various consciousnesses to form turbid appearances.
If one wishes to take these as the cause [of liberation], how can one gain entry? Therefore it is said: "By means of stillness. "Stillness" (zhan) has the meaning of immovability;

it means that one must simply remain unmoving, which refers to such things as the eyes not observing forms and the ears not hearing sounds. This is the turning away from false and illusory [perceptions].
"Cessation and birth" refers to a portion of deluded vision within true vision, as well as the four great elements, the six sense objects, and the various consciousnesses.
However, the character "tranquil" (*zhan*) represents the practice; the character "revolve" (*xuan*) represents the efficacy.

It means that if one can remain long in tranquility, one can thereby revolve and eliminate that false cessation and birth. This is what is meant in the following passage: "Deeply still and unmoving, like sand..."
The earth sinking of its own accord is precisely a metaphor for this. "Subduing the returning primordial awakening" indicates the scope of the process of "revolving.

When it says, "revolving that which is false and extinguishing birth," this does not mean immediate severance; rather, it merely temporarily subdues the active manifestations of the two obstacles, momentarily restoring the luminous nature of original awakening.
This corresponds to what is described in the following text as "clear water appearing before one," which serves as a metaphor.
This is the ear. One who attains the primordial luminous awareness (mūla-vidyā) thereby perceives the nature of that primordial luminous awareness.

This is what is meant by "initial awakening" (ādi-bodhi) arising based upon "original awakening" (mūla-bodhi). This constitutes true non-arising and non-ceasing, which far accords with the virtues of the Buddha. Therefore, it teaches that this [awakening] serves as the causal mind.

According to the stages of the Final Teaching (niṣṭhā-naya), this corresponds to the completion of the stage of faith (śraddhā-pūrṇa), because one is able to simultaneously suppress the two obstacles (āvaraṇa) in their manifest form.

This is because of practice. Only then do the causes become perfect and the fruits fulfilled. In the Ten Abidings, the manifest [afflictions] are eliminated; in the Ten Practices, the seeds are suppressed;

and so on until Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment, where the manifest, the seeds, and the habit-energies are all exhausted. There is no delusion left to be severed, and no Truth left to be realized.

Therefore, it is said that one "perfects the cultivation and realization of the ground of fruition. This is precisely what the subsequent passage means when it says, "removing the mud to reveal pure water."
The second [section] uses a metaphor to illustrate the point.
It is like settling turbid water by storing it in a still vessel. As it remains still and deep without movement, the sand and silt naturally sink, and the clear water appears before one;
this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*). When the mud is removed and only pure water remains, this is called the permanent severance of the root.
Ignorance. When the essence of clarity is pure, all transformations appear without becoming afflictions; they all accord with the pure and wondrous virtue of Nirvana.
This initial metaphor of concentration is intended to reveal the Dharma, saying that Ānanda desires his seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to reach far in accord with the eternal and blissful.

"Purity of the self" is like a person wishing to clarify turbid water. By selecting away the root of birth and death and relying upon the nature that is neither born nor extinguished, it is accomplished—just as one places water in a still vessel, away from all agitation.

Regarding "profound stillness," the following metaphor illustrates accomplishment through reliance on the Dharma: if one can indeed abide in this profound clarity, one may naturally revolve [the mind] so that its delusions are extinguished.
Birth. To subdue [the mind] and return to primordial awakening is like still, deep, and unmoving water where the sand and soil settle of their own accord, and the clear water manifests before one.
Having attained the primordial, luminous awareness as the mind for the causal stage, one’s position corresponds to the fulfillment of the stage of faith (*śraddhā*).

Because both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) have been simultaneously subdued in their active manifestation (*samudācāra*), it is said that this is called "for the first time subduing the adventitious afflictions" (*āgantuka-kleśa*). This is according to the section on "The Manifestation of Vision is Unmoving" in the first fascicle.

The metaphor of "guest-dust" refers to the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Here, it is used as a metaphor for the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), because these manifestations are unstable and fleeting, much like guests or dust.
The passage from "removing the mud" downward serves as a metaphor for the perfection of the cause and the fulfillment of the fruit.

It means that once the causal mind has gradually suppressed and eliminated [the afflictions], until even the manifest, the seeds, and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted, one attains the full realization of the ground of fruition. This is as follows:
Removing the mud is pure water; because there is no delusion that is not exhausted, it is called the "permanent severance of the root of ignorance.
Because there is no unreality that is not perfected, it is called the "purity of the marks of clarity. Turning the vessel of compassion against the current, one returns to deliver sentient beings.
All manifestations of supernatural powers—such as greed, anger, and ignorance—are no longer afflictions; it is like using gold to [fashion ornaments].
Since every vessel is made of gold, it is said that all are in accord with the pure and wondrous virtue of nirvāṇa.
This concludes the preceding summary of the principle that the cause is identical to the fruit, whereby one clears away turbidity and enters nirvāṇa instantaneously.

The second [section] concerns the meaning of decisively resolving the knots through the sense organs and immediately entering perfect penetration; it has two parts: first, teaching how to resolve the knots through the sense organs;

second, demonstrating how to escape the entanglements and enter perfection. Regarding the first (Zhengmo says: "Resolving the knots through the sense organs is the core principle of the second decision;

escaping the entanglements and entering perfection is the ultimate aim of this principle," and it also clarifies the core principle at the outset), there are three sub-points: first, urging one to examine with meticulous scrutiny; second...
By contrast, it is revealed that one must know the locus [of practice]. Third, the correct clarification of the certainty of arising from the faculties. First:
Regarding the second meaning, you all must certainly resolve to generate the bodhicitta and give rise to great courage within the Bodhisattva Vehicle.

One must resolutely abandon all conditioned marks and carefully examine the root of afflictions: throughout beginningless time, who has created and who has received these karmic actions that give rise to and moisten rebirth?

Regarding the second meaning: the phrase "the gate indicated" serves as a topical heading. The section beginning with "You all" below refers to the generation of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
This accords with the first meaning mentioned previously, which spoke of "renouncing the stage of a *śrāvaka*"; here it speaks of "generating the resolve for enlightenment.

However, renouncing the stage of a *śrāvaka* is precisely what constitutes generating the resolve for enlightenment. The former statement, "if one so desires," was intended to establish this through deliberation; the present statement asserts that it "must" be so.
He reiterated his instructions with great earnestness, fearing that their resolve might lack sincerity and that they would repent as soon as they had generated it.

Furthermore, whereas previously he spoke of "practicing the Bodhisattva vehicle," here he says "to give rise to great courage and vigor regarding the Bodhisattva vehicle," again fearing that their aspiration might lack firmness and that they would regress as soon as they had begun to practice.
Moreover, whereas previously he spoke of "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," here he speaks of "abandoning..."
"Abandon the conditioned. To enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one must indeed discard the conditioned;
thus, the words "decidedly" (*niścaya*) are added. The earnestness and urgency of this exhortation are already evident. An ancient master said:
"If you are not a swordsman, do not give him a sword," because it would be of no use to him. Now, the Tathāgata first urges the arousal of the bodhicitta, and afterwards...
This demonstrates the method for unraveling the knots; thus, the extraordinary teachings are not bestowed in vain. One should issue an order to carefully examine the location of the knots.
It is said that if one wishes to abandon conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), one must depart from afflictions (*kleśa*); if one wishes to depart from afflictions, one must sever their root.

Therefore, the teaching instructs that one should investigate with thorough scrutiny. Afflictions are the branches and the secondary, while ignorance (*avidyā*) is the root—that is, the initial phase of arising. The most...
From its initial arising, it is conjoined within the eight consciousnesses and bound within the six sense organs. Because it can give rise to the branches and twigs, it is termed the "root";
this refers to the ignorance of the branches and twigs. If one were to discuss the branches and twigs, they would also encompass the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
However, in addressing Ānanda now, we speak in terms of the afflictions (*kleśa*), as their functional manifestation is most prominent.

Since beginningless time, there have been two functions: first, the initiation of karma; second, the moistening of rebirth. The initiation of karma refers, for example, to past ignorance and present craving and grasping among the causes and conditions.
The moistening of rebirth refers, for example, to the development of aversion through distorted views at the moment of entering the womb.
The same perception gives rise to craving. To ask "who acts and who receives? is precisely to interrogate its fundamental basis.
This refers to these two kinds of afflictions—those that initiate karma and those that nourish rebirth—and seeks to determine who ultimately causes them to arise and who ultimately accepts them.
The intent here is to point toward the nature within the six sense faculties; however, it does not explicitly reveal this, awaiting one's own realization.
Second, it is revealed by contrast that one must know the locus.
Ānanda, if you cultivate Bodhi without carefully examining the root of afflictions, you will not be able to know where the false roots and objects are inverted.
If you do not even know the locus, how can you subdue them to attain the rank of Tathāgata? Ānanda.
[Ananda] said: "It is difficult. You observe that a person in the world who unties a knot does not see the knot itself; how then can they know it is being untied?
Furthermore, we have never heard of empty space being torn asunder by you. Why is this? Because emptiness has no form or characteristics, and thus there is neither knotting nor untying."

First is the explanation by way of the Dharma. Following the previous point that you must certainly be instructed with thoroughness and detail, this is because you have resolutely resolved your mind to become a person who cultivates Bodhi.
A person who cultivates Bodhi must necessarily sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). To sever the afflictions, one must first investigate their root.
Therefore, it is shown [in the text] that "if one does not examine carefully," and so forth. Although the sense bases (*āyatana*) and objects (*viṣaya*), though...
Although both are equally termed "false and delusory," the locus where they arise resides in the sense faculties (*indriya*).
The Buddha did not explain this explicitly, but merely taught that one should carefully observe these two locations to investigate from which source the delusions arise.

Since delusion is itself affliction (*kleśa*), "the location" refers to investigating its root. This must be known through careful observation; therefore, [the text] says, "if one does not carefully observe," and so forth.
This is revealed by way of contrast. Furthermore, in severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), the force must be like that of suppressing a rebellion:

one must first strike at their lair and eliminate their leaders, leaving them with nothing to rely upon and nothing to hide away. Only then will they perish and disperse of their own accord, submitting without being coerced.
Thus, it must be understood that this can only be achieved through knowing the proper locus; for if one does not even know the locus, how could one subdue them?

By suppressing [the literal meaning], one reveals its true implication. To attain the stage of the Tathāgata means that when the faculties are exhausted and afflictions eliminated, Bodhi can be established and realized;
it is like a realm being pacified and borders settled, allowing one to face south and style oneself "The Orphan" (the Son of Heaven). ○ "Observe this below" introduces a simile.
One who unties a knot in the world is a metaphor for one who cultivates bodhi.

Since those who cultivate bodhi must inevitably sever afflictions (*kleśa*), they are compared to the untying of a knot. "Not seeing that which is knotted" means not seeing the place where the knot arises;
if one does not even know the location, how could one know how to untie it? This refers to not knowing the method for unraveling and tearing it apart.

How does one subdue [the mind]? Below, the text cites scriptural evidence. Since it was previously stated that one does not perceive what is being bound, one might still not fully comprehend how to understand this;
therefore, the metaphor of space being uncrackable is cited again as proof. Space serves as a metaphor for the pure and true mind.
Because the pure and true mind is something that cannot be severed or removed, the metaphor of "not hearing" its being torn asunder is employed.
Why is this verified by means of the phrase? "Empty and without the form of characteristics" is a metaphor for the true mind being free from delusive appearances.
Since it is already free from delusive appearances, one naturally does not perceive any place of origination. This proves that there is no knot to be seen.
Since no place of origination is perceived, there should naturally be no delusion to be severed; therefore, it is illustrated by the metaphor of having no knot to be untied. This is the verification.

How is this to be understood? Furthermore, although this analogy serves as proof for what precedes it, it also teaches one to remain detached from arising and ceasing, and to maintain the true permanence.
If one maintains this true permanence, the constant light will manifest before one; the sense organs, objects, consciousness, and mind will accordingly dissolve away.
Once this occurs, what affliction remains to be severed, and what faculty remains to be eliminated?
Third, the explicit clarification of the three types of definitive entry through the faculties (*indriya*). First, a brief demonstration of how bondage is formed by means of the faculties;
second, a detailed exposition of the number of their qualities; third, the instruction on entering through the perfect [faculty]. Regarding the first:
Thus, your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these six acting as intermediaries for thieves—plunder the family treasures themselves.
Because of this, sentient beings have been bound by entanglements since beginningless time, and thus they are unable to transcend the physical world of the vessel.
The phrase "then" (*ze*) directly承接 (*jǐngchéng*) the preceding text. This means that if one wishes to know the locus of bondage, it is the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

"The eye" refers to the nature of seeing; "the ear" refers to the nature of hearing; and so on, up to "the mind," which refers to the nature of cognition. These are spoken of in terms of their manifest functions to reveal that they are, in essence, accompanied by delusion (*moha*).
As for "the six being the intermediaries for thieves": they not only entice external thieves, but can also act as their agents and provide them with shelter.

What was previously stated as "who acts and who receives" is now explained. That which seizes the treasures of one's own household refers to that which causes one to tolerate and accept inverted afflictions;
because it disturbs the nature of the mind, damages the wealth of the Dharma, and extinguishes merit. This passage merely indicates its locus;
what follows reveals its binding nature. The phrase "due to this beginninglessness," etc., refers to these six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
This is neutral. Since beginningless time, it has resided within the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
