"The world of sentient beings" refers to the four internal great elements (*mahābhūta*), as this pertains to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) among the three worlds.

"Those who give rise to fetters" means that from lifetime to lifetime they grasp [these elements] as a body and cling to them as a self (*ātman*). "The receptacle world" (*bhājana-loka*) refers to the four external great elements.

"Those who cannot transcend" refers not only to being unable to achieve liberation throughout successive lifetimes, but also to being obstructed even in the present moment—such as when one sees but cannot transcend form, or hears but cannot transcend sound. This has been a brief explanation of the two fetters of sense organs and objects.
If analyzed in detail according to the process of returning from delusion to truth, then the six fetters are fully present. Is this not true?
The locus where the fetters arise consists solely of the faculties and their neutral states. Part Three: Fully Manifesting the Quantities of Merits. One:

Investigating and Explaining the Sentient Beings and the World. Two: Establishing the Original Quantities. Three: Distinguishing and Showing the Presence or Absence of the Six Faculties. First [Section].
Ānanda, what is meant by the "world of sentient beings"? "World" (*loka*) refers to the flow of time; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial directions.
You should now know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the realms;
the past, future, and present constitute the worlds. There are ten directions and three periods of time. All sentient beings are woven together by delusive ignorance.
They are mutually constitutive. Within the body, worlds trade with one another and interpenetrate.
One wishes to borrow the mutual interpenetration of worlds to cumulatively reach the number twelve thousand; therefore, one proceeds from the preceding "sentient beings" and "worlds."
Thus they are defined and established. Regarding the explanation that "time" (*kāla*) refers to flux: this is because the past, present, and future undergo transformation, change, and transition.

Regarding the explanation that "world-system" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation: this is because it is the locus of positions in the east, south, west, and north. Having thus explained their meanings:

This principle should be clearly understood. Therefore, the teaching states: "You should now know that 'east,' 'west,' 'south,' 'north,' and so forth, are designated by the name 'direction' (dis) based on external spatial orientation;
while 'past,' 'future,' and so forth, are designated by the name 'time' (adhvan) based on external temporal flux.
The two phrases concerning direction summarize the enumeration of external worlds above, serving as an analogy for the internal time below.

Regarding the enumeration of the realms (*dhātu*): since external enumerations are easily perceived while internal enumerations are difficult to clarify, the external enumeration is first established and fixed.
When we reach the internal enumeration below, there will be no need for further elaborate explanation. However, the world is fundamentally illusory;

because sentient beings grasp it and take it as their body, and because they interweave themselves with the characteristics of that body, it is called "interwoven illusion" (*jiewang*). This means that the world is woven by the realms, and the realms are woven by—
Although the world is illusory and false, it appears as if it were truly existent. As for "mutually establishing," they establish one another:

because without the world (*loka*), the realm (*dhātu*) would have no basis; and without the realm, the world would have no means of manifestation. Regarding the shifting and exchanging within the body:
that which originally belonged to the external world now enters into the internal body; thus, the characteristics of the realms are exchanged and are not fixed. For example:
The turning of the left into the right and the front into the rear, and so forth—such is the characteristic of the world (*loka*), which flows and changes without ceasing.
This is like the transformation of the present into the past and the future into the present. Regarding the mutual interpenetration of worlds and realms:

when the world interpenetrates the realm, the realm subsumes the world; when the realm interpenetrates the world, the world subsumes the realm. These statements are provided here as a summary for the subsequent text.
This is merely the fundamental principle of numerical interpenetration. Second, regarding the penetration of the numbers of realms and worlds: first, explaining the mutual penetration of the dharmas;

second, reiterating the measure of their virtues. First (fearing that one might doubt that the number of realms is ten while the number of worlds is only three, such that their quantities are inconsistent and thus cannot interpenetrate, this section explains it by reducing the realms to four to establish the point).
Although the nature of this realm may be clearly defined by fixed positions even throughout the ten directions, the world merely refers to east, west, south, and north;
there is no fixed position for above or below, and the center has no fixed direction. These four numbers must be clear, as they intersect with worldly conventions.
The "nature of the realms" (*dhātu-svabhāva*) refers to the essential nature of the realms. "Establishing" (*saṃvidhāna*) means setting up a marker or establishing a direction;

it is like a person using a marker to designate a center and then looking around based on that marker. The word "although" (*yady api*) implies a lack of total acceptance, meaning that because the ten indeterminate [factors] are not fixed, one speaks here in terms of those that can be clarified by way of fixed positions. That is to say, among the ten directions, there actually exist fixed positions that can be...
Regarding "to clarify and reveal": people of the world merely perceive east, west, south, and north;
"perceive" here refers to verbal designation. Regarding "up and down having no fixed position": this indicates that up and down are simply the vertical dimensions of the four quarters;
since there is nothing else besides these, they are said to have "no position. Regarding "the center having no fixed direction": "center" refers to the intersection of east, west, south, and north.
To join them refers to what are called the southeast, southwest, northeast, and northwest. When combined they seem to exist, yet when separated they are truly non-existent;
therefore, it is said they have no fixed location. The final two lines conclude by demonstrating the method of mutual interpenetration.
It states that regarding the aforementioned mutual interpenetration of worlds, one merely takes the four directions—east, west, south, and north—as these four numbers are necessarily determinate.
The "Manifestation" (Famíng) refers simply to the mutual interpenetration of the three cycles of the world-numbers. Two multiplied by three reveals the measure of virtue;
three times four and four times three revolve to form twelve; these flow and transform through three cycles. One, ten, hundred, and thousand encompass the beginning and the end.
Within each of the six sense organs, there are one thousand two hundred merits.
As for "three times four," this refers to the involvement of the four directions within the three periods of time; thus, the three periods of time encompass the four directions.
Regarding "four times three": by means of the three periods of time, one enters the four directions; thus, within the four directions, the three periods of time are subsumed.
Regarding "twelve through winding turns": this describes the manner of winding turns and reciprocal movement. It refers to the reciprocal movement of three times four and four times three.
All constitute the number twelve; this is the first cycle (*āvalī*). Regarding the three cycles of flux and transformation:

taking the number of the aforementioned first cycle as the basis, they evolve and transform from the root to the branches, changing the few into many to form the second cycle, continuing thus up to the third cycle.
The first cycle results in twelve; the second cycle results in one hundred and two; the third [cycle results in...]
When multiplied three times, it becomes twelve hundred. Because the scriptural text rounds off for brevity, omitting the fractional remainder, it says "one, ten, hundred, thousand.

"One ten" refers to the number ten; this is as in the common vernacular expression where the number ten is called "one ten. The method of the threefold multiplication differs from previous explanations.
Here, I shall first clarify the threefold multiplication by beginning with the inclusion of the mundane world within the square, proceeding through a circular progression. That is to say, first—
The four directions—east, south, west, and north—each encompass a world-system (*loka-dhātu*);
as each world-system consists of three [layers], they form a total of twelve, constituting the first layer. Next, based on these twelve world-systems, each is able to encompass a direction;

as each direction consists of ten [sub-directions]—meaning that although there are four major directions within one side, when subdivided minutely, there are further the zenith, the nadir, and the four intermediate corners (as all the sūtras state that there are "ten directions")—they form a total of one hundred and twenty, constituting the second layer.

Layer three: Next, based on the one hundred and two directions, each is able to encompass a world-system (*loka*). Within each world-system there are ten [worlds] (meaning that although the general characteristic within a single world is threefold, if divided subtly, each of these three further becomes three, thus forming nine;

this constitutes a "long kalpa. Adding the present single thought-moment to this is called a "short kalpa"; combining the long and short makes ten, as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the existence of ten times).

These form the number one thousand and two, constituting the third layer. Since the manner of encompassing worlds within the directions is thus at the outset, the manner of encompassing directions within the worlds is likewise.
One may begin by reflecting on this analogy. The reason for necessarily taking three cycles is as follows: first, the square encompasses the world; next, the world encompasses the square;
and finally, the square again encompasses the world. This is intended to convey the meaning of completing the cycle and returning to the beginning.
Fearing that this may still not be clear, a diagram is provided below.

This diagram begins by subsuming the world within the square. If one begins the first layer by subsuming the square within the world, then the second layer subsumes the world within the square, transforming it into twelve hundred.

The third layer subsumes the square within the world, transforming it into twelve thousand. The method for increasing the numbers may also be illustrated according to the above. This summarizes the whole.
"From beginning to end" means to encompass the total number of the three repetitions from start to finish.
"Among the six sense organs" refers to within the six types of sensory natures; it means that the six types of sensory natures of sentient beings each pervade the body and mind.
Since the body and mind are interwoven with the world, they transform into twelve hundred equal parts, and thus there are six types.
The faculties and their natures likewise each transform according to those bodies and minds into one thousand two hundred modes of cognition;
hence it is said that each possesses one thousand two hundred merits. Here, "merit" refers precisely to cognition—that is, functional capacity and virtuous utility.

(Question: Is this [the teaching on the six faculties] the same as or different from the "merit of the six faculties" in the *Lotus Sūtra*? Answer: This [teaching] refers to the inherent nature (*li-jù*), meaning it exists inherently within the fundamental nature. That [teaching in the *Lotus Sūtra*] refers to phenomenal manifestation (*shi-zào*), meaning it is manifested through the power of the sūtra’s merit. If that [merit] did not rely on the power of the sūtra, it would also be merely inherent;

if this [inherent nature] were already understood as the resolution of the knots of the faculties, it would also be equivalent to phenomenal manifestation. Thus, there is difference within sameness, and sameness within difference. One cannot say they are the same, nor can one say they are different. Contemplate this.

The section on the original quantity of the faculties is concluded. Part Three: Distinguishing and Showing the Presence or Absence of the Six Faculties. Section One: General Inquiry and Determination.
Second, the specific demonstration of their completeness or deficiency. First:
"Ānanda, you should further determine the relative superiority and inferiority among them.
*Ke* (克) means "to be able" or "capable. This means that although the natures of the six sense faculties each possess twelve hundred merits, in the state of delusion—

Being constrained by the sense organs and limited by their respective objects, there is no absence of superiority and inferiority. Can you, moreover, definitively evaluate what is superior and what is inferior among them?
The Tathāgata, clearly knowing [the answer], intentionally poses this question as a prelude to the detailed examination and demonstration that follows.
Second, the specific demonstration of the presence or absence of the six [faculties] has two parts: first, the deficiency and inferiority of the eye faculty; second, the ear faculty...

1. The faculty of the eye is complete and excellent; 2. the faculty of the nose is deficient and inferior; 3. the faculty of the tongue is deficient and inferior; 4. the faculty of the tongue is complete and excellent; 5. the faculty of the body is deficient and inferior; 6. the faculty of the mind is complete and excellent. Regarding the first:

it is like observing with the eyes that which is dark behind and bright in front, where the area before is entirely bright and the area behind is entirely dark, while looking to the left and right in the intermediate directions.
Two-thirds. Generally speaking, the meritorious functions performed are incomplete; of the three parts of merit, one part lacks virtue.
One should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits.
"Observing and seeing" refers to the merit of seeing the nature. Because sentient beings perceive through the eye, it is said that "it is like the eye observing and seeing.
"Front, back, left, and right" refer to the south, north, east, and west of the body. This is the worldly application of directions, wherein the direction manifests while the world remains implicit;
thus, the number of merits is distinguished by means of front, back, left, and right. Here, "front" specifically indicates the south.
This includes both the southeast and southwest corners. "The rear" refers to the true north and includes both the northeast and northwest corners.
Since the front and rear each include two corners, their spatial extent should each possess four hundred merits.
As for the "darkness at the rear," this refers to the merits of the rear direction; because they are restricted by the physical organ [the eye], they are obscured and thus not seen.
The "former" refers to the merits of the front direction. Because one can see through the clarity of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), it is called "clear.
Furthermore, fearing that they might not understand the inclusion of both corners, the full characters are added to each to clarify this.

This is also to demonstrate that while the merits of the front direction are fully present, the merits of the rear direction are entirely lacking. "Left" and "right" refer exclusively to true east and true west. This is because...
Because the four corners are explained according to what precedes and follows them, and since their boundaries are narrow, they should each possess only two hundred merits;
this is because those observing from the side are able to look left and gaze right. Regarding the "two-thirds":
since the front and rear sides each possess four hundred merits, they should each constitute one part. As for the two lateral sides, since each...
Possessing two hundred merits, it ought to constitute one complete portion. When the latter part is excluded, it becomes entirely dark;
the remaining merits consist of only two out of the three portions.
Based on this, since the eye’s own merits are still deficient, it is said that "when considered as a whole, its functional skillfulness is incomplete. "Functional" (所作) refers to all its activities.
Regarding the statement that "one-third [of the light] constitutes its merit": this means that the one thousand two hundred merits are divided into three parts.
One part lacks merit and thus should be deficient by four hundred merits; this refers to what is called the "entirely dark" rear portion.
Since one part is thus deficient, only two parts remain, and therefore there are only eight hundred merits; these refer to what is called the "entirely bright" front portion and...
Those looking on from the left and right are such people. Second, the faculty of hearing is fully endowed.

Just as the ear listens in all ten directions without omission—whether moving, it reaches both near and far; whether still, it is boundless—one should know that the faculty of hearing is complete with one thousand two hundred merits.

"Universal hearing" (*zhou-tīng*) refers to the functional merit of the nature of hearing. Because sentient beings gather and hear through the ears, it is said to be "like the ear’s universal hearing.
This means that hearing is simultaneous and all-pervasive. Because hearing is simultaneous and all-pervasive, nothing is omitted throughout the ten directions.

As stated later: "If drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, they are heard at once in ten places. This also describes how the temporal is manifested through the spatial, while the temporal remains implicit.
Discussing this: when movement seems near or far, it is because the nature of hearing that movement appears to have distinctions of distance and proximity.
Since there are such distinctions of distance and proximity, it should possess only four hundred merits.
When stillness is without boundaries, it is because the nature of hearing that stillness truly has no limits or borders. Since there are no limits or borders, it should be complete with [all merits].
There are eight hundred merits. According to this, one-third of these constitutes the "merit" (referring to hearing movement as one part and hearing stillness as two parts).
Since there is not the slightest deficiency, it is able to fulfill the one thousand two hundred merits. Third, the faculty of the nose is deficient and inferior.
Just as the nose’s act of smelling involves both exhalation and inhalation, yet lacks the intermediate junction between them;
when examining the three parts of the olfactory faculty, one finds it deficient by one. Thus, one should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits.
"Olfactory smelling is the merit of the nature of smelling. Because the assembly of sentient beings smells with the nose, it is said that "it is like the nose smelling.
"Pervading both exhalation and inhalation" means that the merits inherent in the nature pervade both the outgoing breath and the incoming breath.
That which goes out has the function of universal exiting, meaning it exits to escort away the old;
that which comes in has the function of universal entering, meaning it enters to inhale the new. Both "new" and "old" refer to the sensory object of fragrance (*gandha-viṣaya*).

Since both exiting and entering possess these functions, they should each be endowed with four hundred merits; as for the deficiency regarding the intermediate junction, this refers to the point of transition between them.
At the juncture where there is a brief pause in the movement of inhalation and exhalation, the functional activity is not manifest.
Since the functional activity is not manifest, the intermediate junction is rendered useless; thus, one should expect a deficiency of four hundred merits.

To verify this through the faculty of the nose (*ghrāṇendriya*), one should examine the merits of the nasal faculty with a settled mind. "Lacking one-third" means that while three parts of the merit are present, one part is absent.
As for "virtue" (*guṇa*): since one part lacks virtue, only two parts remain. As each part consists of four hundred [units], there are only eight hundred merits.

Herein, the discussion of virtue is based on the intersection of the "entering," "exiting," and "middle. It should be understood that this refers to the sequence where the directions (*diś*) engage with the world (*loka*), such that when the world is manifest, the directions are hidden.
The intention behind beginning with the inclusion of the directions within the middle of the three cycles is precisely this.
Fourth is the excellence of the faculty of the tongue.
Just as the tongue proclaims all mundane and supramundane wisdom, its speech possesses proper method and its principles are inexhaustible.
One should know that the faculty of the tongue is complete with one thousand two hundred merits.
"Proclaiming" refers to the merit of the nature of the tongue. There are two aspects to this merit of the tongue's nature:

first, its function of tasting flavors is inferior, because it perceives only what is in contact; second, its function of verbal expression is superior, because it articulates meanings and principles.

Here, referring to the function of verbal expression, it is said that "it proclaims like the tongue. Regarding the phrase "exhausting all worlds," this means proclaiming conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Thus, one can exhaustively master mundane wisdom; by proclaiming the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one can exhaustively master supramundane wisdom.
Regarding the statement that there are "directions and limits" (*dig-bhāga*): this means that the ultimate and the conventional each have their own respective directions and boundaries.

This is because once one falls within the realm of verbal expression, the relative shallowness and depth of these two differ from one another. As for the statement that "principle is inexhaustible": [this refers to] the ultimate and the conventional...
Both truths are without end; that is to say, when the fruit can be spiritually realized, there is nothing—whether near or far, shallow or deep—that can limit it.

However, while it is said that there are spatial divisions, [the tongue-root] should possess only four hundred merits; yet, since its principle is inexhaustible, it should universally possess eight hundred merits.
Therefore, it is said: "One should know that the tongue-root is perfect with one thousand two hundred merits."
Virtue. According to this, what are called "directions" (fang) and "parts" (fen) manifest both spatially and temporally; when the three are superposed, they may all be subsumed as appropriate.
As for the five physical sense-faculties, they are deficient and inferior.

Just as the body perceives touch through consciousness—discerning whether it is adverse or favorable when in contact, yet being unable to know it when separated—the separation of one part and the union of two parts proves that the body-faculty lacks one-third of its three components.
One should know, therefore, that the body possesses only eight hundred merits.
The awareness of touch is the merit of the nature of the body. Because the collection of awarenesses resides in the body, it is said that "the body is aware of touch.
Regarding "cognizing the adverse and the favorable," this means that based on the touch being perceived, consciousness cognizes the two objects of the adverse and the favorable.

Regarding "being able to perceive when in contact," this means that although one cognizes the adverse and the favorable, one is only able to perceive them when various touches come into contact with the body.
"Knowing. Regarding "not knowing when separated": this means that when various tactile objects are separated from the body, one does not perceive them individually.
"Separated" refers to a single object; "combined" refers to both together, meaning they simultaneously reach two objects.
When a single object is perceived, it possesses four hundred qualities; when two objects are perceived, it possesses eight hundred qualities.
Now, since it is separated from the internal [consciousness] and lacks cognition, it should be deficient by four hundred merits.

Therefore, it is said that when examined in relation to the body-faculty, one-third is missing. Since one-third is missing and only two parts remain, it should be known that the body possesses only eight hundred merits.
However, since this discussion is based on the states of separation and union, it is also included within the worldly [conventional] perspective.
Furthermore, the sixth, the faculty of mind, is fully endowed with excellence.

Just as space silently accommodates the ten directions and the three periods of time, including all mundane and supramundane phenomena—encompassing both the holy and the ordinary without exception—it reaches to the very limits of existence.
One should know that the faculty of mind is thus complete with one thousand two hundred merits.
"Silent acceptance" (*mo-rong*) refers to knowing the merit of the nature of awareness. Because this accumulation of knowledge resides within the mind, it is called "as one wishes" (*ru-yi*).

This means that while the mouth speaks not, the mind itself communicates. The "ten directions" refer to the horizontal pervasiveness of the nature of awareness; the "three periods of time" refer to the vertical completeness of the nature of awareness.
These are the spatial orientations and temporal divisions upon which all phenomena—both mundane and supramundane—rely. Now, since this is already...

Both are manifested simultaneously; when they are layered, they may also be subsumed as desired. Worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*) comprehensively include the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*);

supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*) comprehensively include the truths (*satya*), conditions (*pratyaya*), and perfections (*pāramitā*). Since each category comprehensively includes [its respective members], they are collectively termed "all" (*sarva*).

These are merely words. "Sages" encompasses the four types of holy beings; "ordinary beings" encompasses the six realms of existence. Taken together with the preceding phrase, they refer to both phenomena (*dharma*) and persons.
That there is nothing not encompassed is the natural state of the inherent virtue of nature (*xingde*).

If one further includes the aspect of phenomenal creation (*shizao*), then regarding each and every person and phenomenon mentioned above, one is able to exhaust their limits and reach their boundaries. Thus, one knows the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*).
Perfect illumination is naturally all-encompassing without omission; thus, it is able to fulfill one thousand two hundred merits. This concludes the detailed exposition of the number of these merits.
Regarding the three teachings that enter the Two from the One, and the one teaching that uses self-verification to confirm the perfect faculty:
second, showing how by entering the One, one understands the Six. First [the entry from the Three into the Two].

This is a difficult question. If you now wish to go against the current of the desire-flow of birth and death and trace it back to its root until reaching the state of non-arising and non-extinction, you must examine these six faculties of sensory reception:
which are conjoined and which are separated; which are deep and which are shallow; which constitute the faculty of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), and which are not yet complete.
If you can, through this, awaken to the faculty of perfect penetration, you will be able to go against that beginningless flow of fabricated delusive karma and attain [liberation].
Following the path of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), one’s progress compared to those with imperfect faculties is multiplied by the factor of days and eons.

This was initially intended to provide verification; "contrary" (*ni*) here implies returning. Birth and death are the fruit of the flow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), while the flow of desire is the cause of birth and death.
Thus it is said that all sentient beings wander through the realm of desire by means of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Therefore—
This leads to the cycle of birth and death within the six realms. Now, regarding the Tathāgata’s definitive teaching on those who wish to turn back from desire and so forth:

this means that if you now wish to reverse the bitter fruits of birth and death, wish to turn back from the causes of wandering through the realms of sensory objects, and further wish to reverse the root of that wandering to reach the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, you must personally immerse your mind in examination. Otherwise, you will merely drift along.
If one practices indiscriminately, one will not achieve swift efficacy. The six sense organs (ṣaḍāyatana) are termed "receptive" because they are able to experience the objects of the six desires.
As for "who joins and who separates," this is intended to test which among the six sense organs possesses the faculty of cognition through conjunction.
What constitutes "knowledge through detachment"? It is because the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body involve combined knowledge and are thus difficult to cultivate;
whereas the three faculties of ear, eye, and mind involve detached knowledge and are thus easy to enter. As for what is deep and what is shallow:

let us examine among the faculties of detached knowledge which are superficial, manifest, and easy to clarify, and which are profound, hidden, and difficult to know. This is because the two faculties of eye and ear are superficial and manifest.
They are simply not employed; their mental faculties are deeply hidden and thus not readily utilized. Who possesses perfect penetration? Who lacks full perfection?
Let it be examined within these shallow and manifest faculties who has fully perfected their capacity and who lacks the necessary function and remains incomplete.
This is because the faculty of the eye lacks efficacy and should be discarded, while the faculty of the ear possesses efficacy and should be adopted.
By examining each of these one by one through deep verification, you may know what to adopt and what to discard, so as not to labor in vain.

The passage beginning with "If one can" reveals the supreme excellence of the perfect transcendence; it means that if one can awaken within this state where the six faculties are free from the superficiality of ordinary cognition.
Having attained a single faculty of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), one relies upon it for cultivation.

This reverses the deluded wheel of birth and death that has been interwoven since beginningless time, as well as the drifting through saṃsāra driven by karma and desire. One then attains compliance with perfect penetration, harmonizing with the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Thus, in a mere snap of the fingers, one transcends the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), whereas those with incomplete faculties labor in vain despite their efforts.
When these are compared, their ease and difficulty are incomparable; thus it is said that "a day and a kalpa multiply each other.

This means that the merit of one day for those with complete faculties (*paripūrṇendriya*) is twice as superior as that of one kalpa for those with incomplete faculties. Furthermore, "multiplied" (*bei*) is synonymous with "opposed" (*bei*).

This means that while those with complete faculties are as swift as a single day, those with incomplete faculties are as slow as a long kalpa; their slowness and swiftness are so opposed that they cannot be reconciled.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī subsequently made a selection, stating that their speed and slowness do not belong to the same class.
Second, showing how to enter the one to understand the six:
"I shall now fully reveal the fundamental merits of the six profound, perfect, and luminous states; their quantities are such that you may choose among them as you see fit."
As for those who may enter, I shall clarify and illuminate it so that you may advance.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions all cultivated the eighteen realms one by one and attained the perfect, unsurpassed Bodhi;
among them, there was no distinction of superior or inferior. However, because you are of inferior capacity and have not yet attained the perfectly sovereign wisdom therein, I proclaim this for you.
Simply enter deeply through one gate; once you have entered one without delusion, those six faculties of cognition will all become pure at once.
First, the text cites these virtues to prompt detailed discernment. "Fully manifesting" means to completely reveal and display which aspects are perfect and which are deficient.
The "six" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). "Profoundly perfect clarity" (*zhan yuan ming*) points to the nature within the six faculties.

That which has been pure from the beginning is called "profound" (*zhan*); that which is naturally all-pervasive is called "perfect" (*yuan*); and that which is inherently non-obscured is called "clear" (*ming*). As stated previously:

"Due to these four entanglements, your profoundly perfect, wondrously enlightened, and clear mind is divided into seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing. Thus, one knows that [this clarity] resides within the six faculties.
The nature itself is simply the nature of profound, perfect clarity. "Original merits" refers to those inherently present before one, which do not depend on cultivation for their attainment.
Regarding the "number and measure," whether it be twelve hundred or eight hundred, these have already been clearly distinguished and demonstrated previously;

therefore, they are merely restated here as such. As for the phrase "choose from among them according to your preference," the Buddha’s intention is that since the number and measure are already clear...
Furthermore, this shall be verified so that no further explanation is required; simply examine and select according to your own judgment, and you will find it is so.

That which may be entered is secretly pointed out as the faculty of hearing (*śrotra*), because among the six faculties it is characterized by detached cognition (*viveka-jñāna*), and within detached cognitions, it is the most shallowly manifest.

Because it is the root of perfect penetration within the superficial and manifest, "I shall now elucidate" means that once you have made a definitive choice, I will further clarify the gradual stages therein.
Once these stages are clarified, you can practice according to your capacity;

by yourself, you will be able to untie the knots and enter the perfect state—hence it is said, "to cause you to progress. The section beginning with "In the ten directions" demonstrates the impartiality of the holy nature.
"Thus," and so forth. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions refer to this when speaking of the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*) of all Buddhas.

Because their faculties and capacities are exceptionally superior, they are able to cultivate and realize each and every one within the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*); therefore it is said that "all are attained in perfection," and so on.

Regarding the phrase "in the midst of these," this still refers to the eighteen realms. Since every gate [of the realms] can be cultivated and realized, there is naturally nothing [that cannot be perfected].
Regarding "superior" and "inferior," the subsequent verse by Mañjuśrī states: "The nature of the Sage is all-pervading; both the direct and the inverse are skillful means.

This is precisely that meaning. The passage beginning with "But you... applies the teaching according to the capacity [of the practitioner] for single-minded cultivation. The passage beginning with "But you who are inferior...

suppresses those whose faculties do not match the transcendent excellence of the Buddhas' capacities. Within the eighteen realms (*dhātus*), [the teaching] is universally applicable when confronted with the various capacities [of beings].
If it is not correct, then it is obstructed. Therefore, it is said that one has not yet attained the sovereign wisdom that is perfectly complete within the center.
Sovereign wisdom is such that, as with the Tathāgatas, one may enter through every gate. Thus, my proclamation refers to the preceding instructions to "test" and "discern.
These instructions to test and discern are collectively intended to teach exclusive reliance upon the perfect faculties (*indriya*). Therefore, it says: "to cause [them] to..."
You need only enter deeply through a single gate. To "enter deeply" means that one must reach the point where all six knots are completely untied;
hence it is said, "Entering one, there is no delusion. As the verse by Mañjuśrī later states: "Once a single faculty returns to its source, the six sense bases achieve liberation."

Therefore it is said that those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified, because they fundamentally rely upon a single luminous essence. This section consists of two parts: first, teaching the method for untangling the knots from the faculties;
second, demonstrating the liberation from entanglements to enter the perfect state. Part one contains: A. Ānanda following the previous discourse to request further instruction;
B. The Tathāgata expanding and elucidating the teaching. Regarding the first: [The text continues with the specific dialogue.]

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it that by flowing against the current and penetrating deeply through a single gate, one can cause the six faculties to become pure simultaneously?
The phrase "how is it" is the wording of the inquiry; the meaning of what is asked consists briefly of three sections. As for the previous statement, "If one is able... [the text continues].
Regarding this awakening to the faculty of perfect penetration, one must flow against the current of that beginningless, interwoven stream of deluded karma.
Now you ask: "How does one flow against the current? Previously I said: "Therefore, I proclaim it so that you may enter deeply through a single gate.

Now you ask: "How does one enter deeply through a single gate? Previously I said: "Entering into the one state where there is no delusion, those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified. Now...
Question: How can one cause the six sense faculties to become pure simultaneously? According to this, the phrase "how can" (*yǒu yú hé*) should appear in all three sections.

Now, it is only placed at the beginning because the general meaning is unified while the specific intentions differ. This is because the preceding Buddha indicated the realms (*dhātu*) and [the disciple] requested further instruction.
Second, the Tathāgata expands upon and elucidates [the teaching], in four parts: first, exhorting according to the capacities of the disciples.

[The text consists of four sections: First, the cultivation [of the path]; second, questioning the faculties to dispel delusion; third, the formal answer to the question; fourth, the conclusion showing the benefits. Regarding the first:

The Buddha told Ānanda, "You have now attained the fruit of Srotāpanna; you have already extinguished the afflictions to be abandoned through insight regarding the world of sentient beings within the three realms.
However, you still do not yet know the beginningless, empty habitual tendencies accumulated within the faculties. Those habits..."
The acquisition [of these] is abandoned through cultivation. How much more so regarding the distinctions and enumerations of their arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing?

First, it is proclaimed that the afflictions of view have been extinguished. A *srotāpanna*—translated here as "Stream-enterer"—is so called because, having first seen the True Truth, they have for the first time entered the stream of the Noble Ones.
They are also called "those who have entered the stream. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states: "A *srotāpanna* is named..."
"Stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) refers to the first fruit of the Hīnayāna. Ānanda has realized this through direct experience; therefore, it is said that he "has already attained" it.

"Sentient beings of the three realms" is a general term for those within the realms who are training toward transcendence. In training for transcendence, one first severs the delusions of the mundane world.
There are two types of mundane delusions: first, the delusions of view, which consist of the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).

The first refers to the afflictions of the conceptual views of self-grasping (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). The second refers to the eighty-one grades of innate afflictions of thought associated with self-grasping.
Here, "those abandoned by seeing" (*darśana-heya*) refers to the afflictions of seeing (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), because they are abandoned during the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Since Ānanda was at the stage of the First Fruit (*srotāpanna*), which corresponds to the Path of Seeing, it is said that [these] have already been extinguished. However...
"Furthermore, 'suppressing' refers to the fact that his thoughts and delusions have not yet been severed. 'Among the present faculties' (*mūla*) refers to the faculties manifest before one.

'Accumulated over lifetimes' (*saṃcita*) refers to the period spanning kalpas since beginningless time. 'Beginningless' (*anādi*) refers to the very first limit. 'Empty habituation' (*śūnya-vāsanā*) refers to false habitual tendencies; that is, the afflictions of thought.
This means that although these afflictions are present within the current faculties, they have persisted since the accumulation of lifetimes."
It exists together with [the afflictions] from beginningless time; it is only after the second fruit (*dvitīya-phala*) that it is severed. Therefore, it is called "unknown" (*ajñāta*).

The phrase "attained through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya-prāpti*) refers to that which is severed during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The statement "must depend on... precisely clarifies that it cannot be severed without entering the path of cultivation.
The section beginning with "how much more so" illustrates [the process] from the subtle to the coarse. The term "herein" (*atra*) still refers to [the aforementioned context].
Regarding the faculties (*indriya*), arising, abiding, change, and cessation are spoken of collectively by way of progressing from the subtle to the coarse.
This means that even these illusory habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) must still be cultivated for their abandonment;

how much more so for those [phenomena] from the subtle to the coarse, which possess the fourfold demarcations of arising, abiding, change, and cessation? Furthermore, within these demarcations, there are many subtle sub-classifications. If...
If one does not deeply enter against the current, how can one escape the fetters and enter perfect penetration? This is something that cannot be left unknown.
According to the *Awakening of Faith*, among the three subtle states, the state of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*) gives rise to birth, because at the very first moment the mind moves.

The two aspects of manifestation and transformation, along with the six coarse elements, constitute the continuity of wisdom; these two aspects abide because the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha) is firmly established.
One clings to and discriminates these two aspects as distinct because the grasping at a personal self (pudgala-grāha) is distinct. The fifth stage, the arising of karma, constitutes cessation.
Because it exhausts the ultimate limit [of suffering]. The sixth category, the suffering associated with karmic fetters, pertains to future results;

it is not subsumed under afflictions or karma. "Quantitative divisions" refers to the broad categories, namely the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). "Numerical counts" refers to the detailed subdivisions.

Just as within the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), there are further contained the repeated characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, so it is even for the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).
The number of these various aspects is such that even a heap of sesame seeds or millet cannot serve as a metaphor for its magnitude.
2. Examining the Sense Organs to Shatter Delusion.
Now, you should observe these six sense organs before you: are they one, or are they six? Ānanda, if you say they are one, why does the ear not see?
Why does the eye not hear? Why does the head not tread? Why do the feet not speak? If these six organs were truly...
"It is fixed that there are six [faculties], as in my assembly here today. As I proclaim the subtle and wondrous Dharma to you, which of your six sense faculties comes to receive it?
Ānanda replied, "I hear with my ears. The Buddha said, "If you hear with your ears, what concern is this for your body or mouth?"
The mouth comes to inquire about the meaning, while the body rises to show reverent acceptance. Therefore, you should know that it is not one that ends in six, nor six that ends in one;
ultimately, your faculties are neither one nor six.
The initial instruction to contemplate the whole is a general inquiry. The four phases [of existence] cannot be severed abruptly; one must necessarily enter through a single gate.
Therefore, the teaching directs one first to contemplate the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*). This is because one intends to select a single gate from among these six as the point of entry.
The question as to whether it is "one" or "six" is intended to demonstrate that it is neither one nor six, thereby leading the practitioner toward...
To recommend and grasp the wondrous nature of universal penetration. ○ From "Ānanda" downward, there are six sections for the specific refutation, which further contain two meanings:

first, the refutation that the "one" is not established; second, the refutation that the "six" are not the correct principle. In the refutation of the "one," [the text] first restates [the opponent's position] and then presents the challenge.
The Buddha’s intention is that if one says it is "one," then the ear could become the eye, and the eye could become the ear; therefore, he challenges [him]: why does the ear not [become the eye]?

[The opponent] sees with the eyes; why then does one not hear with them? If it were the case that the eye and ear communicate with one another, by this analogy one could know that the head might become the feet and the feet might become the head.
Since even two distinct sense organs communicate, how much more so for a single body? Therefore, it is further difficult to ask: why do the feet not walk?
How can it be that there is no speech? Yet, even a single body does not possess mutual communication, let alone the six sense organs being distinct from one another.
Thus we know that what is called "oneness" is an error. In refuting the six [organs], first the six are cited to question the one;

next, the answer resolves the difficulty regarding the one. Regarding the citation of the six to question the one: the Buddha’s intention is that if these six organs were definitively established as six, they should...
Since they were unable to understand one another, he asked: "Regarding the six sense organs that now receive this teaching, which one comes to perceive it?
He replied, "I hear with my ears," which was an answer given from the perspective of using a single organ.
The Buddha said, "If you say your ear hears by itself," even granting that it uses a single organ, then using a single organ should not...
Because [the sense-faculties] communicate with one another, it is difficult to determine which are related to the body and speech.

However, we observe that when the mouth comes to inquire about a meaning, the body initiates respectful reception; this clearly demonstrates that the ear communicates with the body and speech, and by extension, the same applies to the other faculties.
Thus, we know that the claim that the "definitive establishment of six" is fixed is also incorrect. This section below generally dispels such false conceptualizations. This is [the conclusion].
Therefore, it should be understood that because these are both "neither," one should further understand that saying they are "not" is also not [the case].
The three final characters are all used as terms for "ultimately. The meaning is that if it is indeed not one, then it is ultimately six;
hence it is said: "not one, ultimately six. If it is indeed not six, then it is ultimately one; hence...
It is said that "the six ends are not one. This is because the former [position] uses "non-being" (fei) to dispel "being" (shi), while this [position] in turn uses "being" to dispel "non-being.

Fearing that if one hears of using "being" to dispel "non-being," one will revert to the original calculation and claim there is "one origin and six ends," the latter uses the inequality of the ends to dispel such views;
it means that, ultimately, one cannot speak in such a manner. This is the third, the correct answer to what was asked.

The question has four parts: first, establishing the principle; second, citing an analogy; third, applying the teaching to the case at hand; and fourth, providing the concluding answer. Regarding the first:

"Ānanda, you should know that these faculties are neither one nor six. Because of the inverted and fluctuating states since beginningless time, the meanings of 'one' and 'six' have arisen within the perfect and湛 (zhàn—tranquil and profound) reality.
"You, Śrotāpanna, although you have attained the dissolution of the six [faculties], have not yet eliminated the one."

First, following the reasoning established above, since it cannot be said that they are one or six, and yet it also cannot be said that they are neither one nor six, one should know that there exists a specific logical path for each of these cases.

This is truly because the sense-faculties have not yet been formed and thus transcend all numerical categories; therefore, they are said to be "neither one nor six. Precisely because they are neither one nor six, I—
As stated above, it is not permitted to say that these are one or that they are six. Since beginningless time, they have been bound to these faculties;

because they turn their backs on awakening and unite with sensory objects, they are called "inverted. From this point on, they have sunk into the realms of form, fragrance, taste, and touch, alternating between seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Within the stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), having already grasped at sensory objects to form the six [consciousnesses], once they have entered the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), then—

Detached from their respective objects, they become one. Therefore, within that perfected and tranquil state, there is fundamentally no nature of "one" or "six," yet the conceptual meaning of "one" and "six" arises.

Since there is both "one" and "six," I have, in what precedes, likewise not permitted the assertion of being "neither one nor six. [O] You must now provide a human witness to prove its existence. Vajra.

The *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "Not entering into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas is called a Srotāpanna. However, since the objects (*viṣaya*) are no longer engaged, the sense organs (*indriya*) have nothing with which to pair;

this is what is meant by the "extinction of the six [senses]. Although it is said that one has attained this, there is a sense that true extinction has not yet been achieved, because the state of mutual dependence has not yet been severed.
The six functions are merely temporarily suppressed, appearing as if they were a single entity; therefore, it is said: "Still..."
"One has not yet perished. Since one has not yet perished, there is still something upon which to depend; thus we know that what is called the "extinction of the six" is not true extinction.
It must be that even the "one" perishes for it to be true extinction. Zhengmo (The Correct Pulse) says:

This applies not only to the first fruit, but likewise to the fourth fruit. For in those cases, the path is perfected as the exhaustion of the six functions, which constitutes the nirvana of the severance of the ashes.
Second, an illustration:
It is like the great void of space merging with various vessels; because the shapes of the vessels differ, they are called "different spaces.
If one removes the vessels and contemplates the space, one says that space is one. How could that great void of space be either the same or different for you? How much more so, furthermore...
Names are both one and not one.

First, the primary analogy illustrates the preceding principle: the vast void represents the nature of perfect stillness; because it relies on the sense organs and conditions through objects, it is compared to its admixture within various vessels.
The differing shapes of the vessels represent the distinctness of the six sense-objects, while the nature of these six sense-objects remains distinct.
They also appear to be different. Because ordinary beings falsely cling to them as six, they are designated as "different" and compared to empty vessels.

When one sets aside the vessels to contemplate emptiness, this is like forgetting the objects to contemplate the nature. When one forgets the objects to contemplate the nature, that nature appears to be one.

Because those in the first fruit [of the path] falsely reckon it as one, emptiness is spoken of as being "one" and used as a metaphor for it. ○ Regarding the passage beginning with "That is too... below:
This metaphor dispels [your] conceptual attachment. To say that when empty space is precisely removing a vessel, it does not "become the same" as you by removing the vessel for you;

and when it is precisely placing a vessel, it does not "become different" from you by placing the vessel for you—this means that the removal of the vessel is the vessel’s own removal, and the placement of the vessel is the vessel’s own placement.
How then can that empty space be said to "become the same" as you by removing the vessel, or "become different" from you by placing the vessel?
They are not the same (non-identity implies difference). Based on this, even the perception of sameness and the perception of difference already belong to deluded sentiment;
how much more so when one further establishes conventional designations to say that they are "one" or "not one" (not one being synonymous with different)?

Does this not only serve to further reveal their delusion? This meaning is essentially similar to the preceding text; it ultimately does not accord with your fundamental doctrine of "one root and six consciousnesses. Therefore, [the author] explains:
This is done to dispel conceptual attachments by means of an analogy; the meaning within the Dharma can be realized through the mind.
There are two ways in which the three dharmas correspond: first, a general correspondence; second, a specific correspondence. Regarding the first:
"That which you clearly perceive—the six faculties of experience—is likewise so."

The two characters "liǎo zhī" (to know/thoroughly understand) have two interpretations. First, they are words of instruction, meaning that since the analogy has already been stated, one is taught that the nature of the faculties is likewise identical to great empty space.

Second, they are words for summoning the faculties, referring to the essence of constant knowing and the function of receptive experience; because their meaning is identical to great empty space, it says "likewise."
Thus it is. There are two distinct ways of combining these two: first, combining the three vessels to form a distinction; second, combining them while excluding the vessel to form a unity.
Regarding the first six: first, sight is established by reason of form; second, hearing is established by reason of sound; third, smelling is established by reason of fragrance;
fourth, tasting is established by reason of flavor; fifth, tactile awareness is established by reason of touch; sixth, cognition is established by reason of mental objects. First.
Due to the mutual conditioning of the two aspects of light and darkness, within the wondrous perfection, the stillness becomes adhered to and gives rise to vision.

The essence of vision reflects forms and binds with them to form the sense organ. The fundamental source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements. For this reason, the substance of the eye is said to be like a cluster of grapes.
The floating faculties, with their four objects, flow and rush toward form (*rūpa*).
"Light and darkness" refers to the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the object-field of form; the word "etc. (*ādi*) is included because it subsumes many specific types.
Although it subsumes many types, in total there are only two; therefore, it is still said to be "of two kinds. "Mutually manifesting" means they reveal one another, as when contrasted with darkness.

"Manifesting" refers to the confrontation with light, darkness, and so forth. "Sublime and perfect" (*miaoyuan*) means the sublime awakening is perfectly luminous; this refers directly to the True Mind (*zhenshin*).
"Adhering" (*nian*) signifies "inducing. It means that the True Mind is originally profound and calm, fundamentally devoid of such characteristics as seeing and hearing.

Because it encounters the contrasting phenomena of light and darkness, it induces a state of profound stillness and immobility from within its sublime perfection, and this manifests as the faculty of perception.
Because the essence of seeing [reflects] objects. "The essence of seeing reflects objects" means that once the essence capable of seeing has been activated, it further reflects and manifests objects.
This is precisely what was previously described as being like the great void merging with various vessels; this is the metaphor for this very point.
"Forming the sense organ by binding to form" means that having already reflected and manifested objects, it is naturally able to bind and grasp them, thereby forming [the faculty].
It floats as the supreme faculty (*indriya*). Regarding the statement that "the root-source is designated as 'equality'": "designation" refers to the initial formation of the name;

when the supreme ultimate faculty first arises, its source is simply called the "pure four great elements" (*mahābhūta*), and it does not yet possess the designation of "turbid defilement. Zhengmo says:
Regarding the statement "the eye is the pure [element] among the four great elements": this clarifies that although it belongs to the four great elements, its characteristic is most subtle;
only the noble eye or the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) can perceive it, while ordinary beings cannot behold it. It is not comparable to what can be grasped by the physical sense-organ (*māṃsacakṣus*).
As for the phrase "therefore it is called the essence of the eye," Guanding says: "That which is visible to the noble eye is not without a formal characteristic. Thus...
It is shaped like a cluster of grapes so that those who do not see it may know that it possesses subtle form (*sūkṣmarūpa*). The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"The atoms of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya-paramāṇu*) reside upon the pupil; because their substance is transparent, they are like autumnal spring water.
Regarding the four impurities of the floating root: whenever the floating root is formed, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) perceive it together with the four impurities, which are turbid and defiled.

There is no longer any name for "purity. Guanding says: Although the two faculties—the physical organ and the subtle faculty—differ in their coarseness and subtlety, both take as their essence the eight dharmas consisting of form, odor, taste, and touch, which are produced by earth, water, fire, and wind.

Now, when it is said that the four great elements are the "producers" from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), while the four sensory objects are the "produced" from the perspective of the physical organ (*audārika*), these are merely mutual reflections of their respective names.
The ignorant take "dust" (*rajas*) to mean turbid defilement. In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), at the initial stage of formation, turbid defilement does not manifest;

therefore, it is simply called the "four great elements" (*mahābhūta*). "Great" (*mahat*) is a name derived from being causal seeds. Once the physical sense organs (*mūla-indriya*) have become formed, they then accumulate [the elements].
Just as when peach or apricot fruits have matured, the causal seeds capable of producing them are accumulated within; therefore, it is simply called "four."
"O you with dusty ears! As for those whose faculties flow out and rush toward forms: once the floating roots have formed, they are daily confronted by the objects of form.
Consequently, the essence of vision becomes dissipated and unrestrained, rushing daily toward forms and unable to transcend them.

From this point on, it becomes forever opposed to the ear and the other faculties. What was previously called 'the differentiation of space due to the differences in the shapes of the vessels' is a metaphor for this."
Second, hearing is accomplished through sound.

Due to the striking of two types of phenomena—movement and stillness—a resonance arises from the attachment to the profound stillness within the wondrous perfection. This essence of hearing reflects sound and, by coiling back the sound, forms the sense organ.
The fundamental source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements. Because of this, the substance of the ear is said to be like a freshly curled leaf.
The floating faculties of the four sensory objects flow and rush toward sound.

The textual passages concerning the five faculties below share the same general meaning as those for the eye faculty; they need not be explained in detail, requiring only a brief clarification of the shifting terminology.
"Movement and stillness" refers to the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*); it is a collective designation that subsumes many specific types of sounds.
In summary, movement and stillness are said to constitute the two [aspects]. "Mutually striking" means attacking one another;

for instance, when movement attacks stillness, the dust of stillness is concealed, and when stillness attacks movement, the dust of movement is extinguished. "Rolling up" has the meaning of gathering and collecting;

it refers to the fact that while sound is empty and dispersed, its apprehension consists solely in being gathered and collected. "Newly rolled leaves" refers to lotus leaves that have just emerged from their sheaths.
The *Xianzong lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the Doctrine) states: "The atoms of the ear-faculty reside within the ear cavity, arranged in a circular fashion like a rolled birch-bark scroll.
They are composed of three causes and produce the sense of smelling."

Arising from the two aspects of penetration and obstruction, within the wondrous perfection, it adheres to the stillness to produce the sense of smelling. The essence of smelling reflects fragrance and receives fragrance to form the faculty.
The fundamental source of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements. Consequently, the substance of the nose is named after its shape, resembling a pair of hanging claws.
The floating faculties of the four sense objects flow and rush toward fragrance.

"Penetration and obstruction" refers to the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the object of fragrance. The term "etc. subsumes the various specific fragrances; the general [characteristic] consists only of penetration and obstruction, hence it is called "the two."
"Mutually manifesting" (*xiàngfā*) means that they reveal one another, such as when openness is revealed by virtue of obstruction, or obstruction is revealed by virtue of openness.
"Attracting" (*nà*) has the meaning of drawing in; this refers to the fact that the sense-object of fragrance belongs to the element of air, and its apprehension consists solely of being drawn in.

"Double-hanging claws" (*shuāngchuí zhǎo*) refers to a pair of claws hanging downward. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Xiǎnzōng lùn) states: "The atoms of the nose-faculty reside within the nasal bridge, upon the back [of the nostrils]."
The surface below is like a pair of hanging claws. The four causes arise from flavor to form tasting.

Through the intermingling of the two aspects of tranquility and transformation, within the wondrous perfection, turbidity adheres to stillness to produce tasting. The essence of tasting reflects flavor, and by condensing flavor, the sense organ is formed.
The fundamental source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements. Consequently, the substance of the tongue is named after its shape, resembling a crescent moon.
The floating faculties flow toward the four sensory objects and rush toward their flavors.
"Tranquil" (*tian*) signifies stillness; this refers to the state when [the faculty] is disengaged. "Transforming" (*bian*) signifies movement; this refers to the state when [the faculty] is engaged.

This is the general characteristic of the object of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*); specifically, it encompasses many individual tastes such as sweetness and so forth. Taken collectively, there are only two names: "tranquil" and "transforming. As for "mutually intermingling," they alternate with one another.

They correspond to one another; that is to say, by comparing [the states], one knows tranquility through change, and one knows tranquility through change. "Twisting" (*jiao*) has the meaning of revolving and coiling.

This means that because the object of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*) lacks a fixed form, it must be revolved and coiled before it can be known. Therefore, the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) perceives taste solely by means of revolving and coiling.
The "initial crescent moon" refers to the moon that has just begun to appear as a slanted, recumbent shape, such as it is on the third or fourth day after the new moon.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The atoms of the tongue faculty (*jihvendriya-paramāṇu*) are distributed across the tongue, their shape being like a half-moon."
The five [senses] produce cognition through contact.

Through the mutual friction of two things, such as separation and union, within the wondrous perfection, the stillness becomes adherent and cognition arises. The essence of cognition reflects the contact, and by grasping that contact, the sense-organ is formed.
The fundamental source of the organ is termed the "pure four great elements"; because of this, it is called the body, shaped like the head of a waist drum.
The floating faculties and the four objects flow and rush toward the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*).

"Joining and separating" refers to the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the object of touch; "equality" encompasses its specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The term "two" refers exclusively to the general [characteristic].
Because these are distinctions within the general category, they are called "mutual friction" (*saṃgharṣa*), meaning they mutually intersect and pass over one another.
This refers to departing while the other comes together, or coming together while the other departs; it is like two hands rubbing against each other, intersecting and passing over one another.

"Grasping" (*piṇḍana*) has the sense of taking up or receiving. It means that when the object-field (*spraṣṭavya*) meets with consciousness, there is no need for external conditions; there is only the act of grasping itself. [The character] *yāo* (waist).
Regarding "drum-head" (*gǔsàng*), the *Guǎngdìng* (Abhidharmakośa-śāstra) states: "The 'drum-head' refers to a drum-shaped vessel; it is round and wide at both ends, while narrow in the center.
This is the same as the *zhànggǔ* (staff-drum) used today. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*) are distributed throughout the entire body.
In women, they are like the surface of a drum-head; in men, they are like a finger-sheath. Knowledge is established through the six causes (*ṣaddhetu*).

Through the two kinds of continuity—arising and ceasing—the stillness of the wondrous perfection becomes adhered to, giving rise to cognition. This essence of cognition reflects phenomena and grasps them to form the sense organs.
The source of these organs is termed the "pure four great elements. Consequently, they are called the "mental faculty," like seeing within a dark chamber.
The floating faculties and the four objects flow and rush toward mental objects (*dharmas*).

"Arising and ceasing" refers to the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of mental objects; the same principle applies as before. Since they are collectively only arising and ceasing, it is said there are two kinds.
It is called "continuous" (*saṃtati*) because arising and ceasing do not stop; that is to say, having arisen it again ceases, and having ceased it arises once more.

"Grasping" (*parigraha*) has the meaning of "total maintenance. This means that since phenomena are merely reflected images, one must first maintain them as a whole before one can take them as objects. "Mental intention" (*manas*) refers to the faculty of mind.
Based on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the support is now made manifest by means of that which depends upon it, in order to demonstrate its existence.

The sense-base of mind (*manas-āyatana*) is precisely the ultimate faculty (*paramārtha-indriya*). As for "one who sees in a dark chamber," this refers to the internal illumination of mental objects (*dharma-viṣaya*), because it perceives objects that resemble those seen within a dark room.
The "floating root" (*tūla-indriya*) of the four sensory objects refers to the physical heart-mass; it is shaped like a lotus flower, opening in the morning and closing in the evening.
This differs from the *lakṣaṇa-yāna* (Dharmalakṣaṇa school), which takes only the deliberation of the manas to be the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*).
Therefore, the three vessels have been completed as distinct entities. Second, by merging and removing the vessels, they become one. Ānanda, so it is with these six faculties:
through that awakened clarity, there is clarity and the clarity of awakening; yet this loses its essential discernment, and by clinging to delusion, light is emitted.
It is for this reason that you now have no essence of seeing when separated from darkness or light, nor when separated from motion or stillness. Fundamentally...
Without hearing, there is no substance; without penetration or obstruction, the nature of smelling does not arise. Without change or tranquility, tasting has no outlet.
Without separation or union, the perception of touch is fundamentally non-existent. Without cessation or arising, one understands where peace resides.
At the outset, the six delusions are most clearly revealed. These six faculties still refer to the nature within the six faculties;

that nature also arises from the addition of "clarity" (*jue-ming*) to "awakening" (*jue*), which through successive transformations becomes delusion. Therefore it is said: "From that awakening-clarity," and so forth.

The two characters "awakening-clarity" first present the True as its basis, namely, the wondrous clarity of fundamental awakening (*ben-ju*). "There is clarity and there is awakening-clarity" follows next.
This refers to the delusion arising from what is called "clarity," meaning that one falsely takes it to be enlightened awareness (*vidyā*). However, this is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*);

because it obscures the true mind, it is said that "one loses that essential lucidity. This means losing that fundamental, wondrously luminous, pure, and truly manifest essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-vidyā*).
Through the union of the real and the delusive, the *ālaya-vijñāna* is formed. Once the *ālaya-vijñāna* has been established, it transforms—
The two aspects of seeing and appearance arise. Because the seeing aspect follows and differs from the appearance aspect, it is said that "clinging to delusion gives rise to [light] first.
This means that within the defiled appearance aspect, the delusions of the six sense-objects give rise to the light of the six natures within the seeing aspect.
According to this, even the luminous and clear awareness is already false; how much more so when one loses that essential clarity and, clinging to delusion, gives rise to light? It is still...
This is the ultimate point of delusion. Thus, the following correctly accords with the preceding metaphor:

since the six natures arise from clinging to delusion to emit light, if one does not cling, the light sinks into the six states of stillness. Therefore it is said: "Detached from darkness and detached from light, there is no essence of seeing.
Even to the point of "neither extinction nor arising," where can the awareness be lodged? This means that the six natures have already been dissolved. The six natures...
Once [the other consciousnesses] have been eliminated, only the *ālaya-vijñāna* remains. The followers of the Two Vehicles do not recognize this and instead take it to be *nirvāṇa*;

this is the first instance of their failure to eliminate [delusion]. What was previously stated—that "removing the vessel and contemplating emptiness" and "expounding emptiness as one"—is precisely a metaphor for this.
This concludes the synthesis of the preceding dharmas. Fourth, the conclusion and response.

You need only not follow after these twelve conditioned characteristics—motion and stillness, union and separation, tranquility and agitation, penetration and obstruction, birth and death, light and darkness.
By uprooting even one of these, you will detach from clinging and settle inwardly; as this settling returns to the fundamental reality, the original radiance will manifest.
Once that radiant nature has been made manifest, all other remaining attachments will be spontaneously and completely severed, arising no longer from the external objects before you.

Regarding "knowledge and vision": the initial response addresses the question, "What is the counter-flow? (Based on the three questions previously posed by Ānanda, the first was "What is the counter-flow?"; now the World-Honored One answers it with: "It is simply that you do not follow [the objects]," and so forth).
The Buddha’s intention is that there is no separate "counter-flow" other than this: simply not following after sensory objects. Thus, it is simply that you do not follow...

These four characters constitute the fundamental practice for attaining perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). They are similar to the two characters "tranquil" (*zhan*) used in the first principle [of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*], both of which are direct expositions of the teaching.

The reason that the sensory objects such as movement and stillness are not listed in their usual order is that the Buddha’s intention was to secretly indicate that the ear-gate is the primary point of entry, while the others can be understood through mutual correspondence.
The fact that they are all termed "conditioned characteristics" (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) is because of their essence...
Because these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) can also bring about the fruits of birth and death, it follows that the conditioned inherently contains birth and death.
To follow after sensory objects is to follow the flow of desire; not to follow them is to go against it.

This explanation not only corresponds to the point where Ānanda raised his question, but also accords with the passage in the previous section on "The Buddha Teaching Self-Verification of the Perfect Faculties," which speaks of desiring to go against birth and death.

The discourse on the flux of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is also thereby further clarified. ○ Following the extraction [of one sense-faculty], the answer addresses "entering deeply into one gate" (the second question asks:

"How does one enter deeply into one gate? Now the World-Honored One answers this by saying: "By extracting one root, etc."). "Extracting" (*ba*) has the meaning of selecting. The Buddha’s intention is that there is no fixed rule regarding the single gate;
rather, one may simply select one root from among the six sense-faculties according to one's own individual capacity (*yathā-yoga*). This is to become detached from clinging (*visaya-saṃsarga*).
"Internally subduing" (*neifu*) and so forth indicates the method of liberation. "Detaching from stickiness" (*tuozhan*) means to free oneself from attachment to sensory objects;
this is "entering the stream and losing the object," wherein motion and stillness do not arise. "Internally subduing" means to internally subdue the nature of the faculties;

this is "thus gradually increasing until what is heard and that which hears are both exhausted. "Subduing and returning to the original reality" means to subdue again and again, until even the act of subduing is discarded.
Returning to the fundamental source, the true essence, one reaches the point where hearing is exhausted and does not abide; that which perceives and that which is perceived are both empty.

This continues until birth and death are extinguished and quiescent extinction manifests before one. "To give rise to the original radiance" means that when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere; silent illumination encompasses the void.
This is the pinnacle of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), wherein one attains two supreme qualities and gives rise to three functions. This is the method of entering deeply through a single door.

The meaning is fully evident herein. ○ Regarding the passage "The luminous nature shines forth," this answers the question of the six sense organs being pure. (The three questions asked were: "How can one cause the six sense organs to become pure simultaneously?

Now, the World-Honored One answers with "the luminous nature shining forth," etc. The Buddha’s intention is that if one wishes to attain the perfect liberation of all faculties, it is realized immediately simply by the shining forth of the luminous nature.
The phrase "the luminous nature shining forth" reiterates the preceding meaning, referring to the fundamental...
The nature of radiant essence, having already been brought forth and made manifest—this refers to the "constant light appearing before one.
