As it says later: "When the constant light appears before one, the faculties, objects, consciousnesses, and mind dissolve simultaneously.

This means that all other five-fold attachments should be uprooted and completely liberated; the severance [of these bonds] can thus be known. The "five-fold attachments" refer to the remaining five faculties which are attached to their respective objects. They should...
"Uprooting" refers to one aspect of what is to be uprooted. "Perfect liberation" means that at that very moment, one is completely liberated and detached.

Although there is perfect liberation and detachment at that very moment, it is not as if nothing exists at all; rather, from that point forward, the cognitions and views that arise do not depend upon external objects.
This concludes the direct answer to the question. Part Four: Concluding Remarks on the Benefits (which is the wondrous function of perfect penetration). Section One.

"Clarity does not follow the sense organs, yet it manifests by relying upon them. Thus, the six organs function interchangeably for one another.

Building upon the previous point that cognition and vision do not arise from external objects, but rather that their illuminating function issues solely from the fundamental nature, it is said that "clarity does not follow the sense organs.
This means that the primordially inherent clarity no longer follows those six organs; "seeing" and "hearing" are merely different designations. "Relying upon" (ji) is as follows: [it means]...

This is a matter of entrustment. "Entrusting the faculties so that clarity may emerge" means that when knowledge and vision arise, they are entrusted to whichever one of the six faculties is appropriate, and the six types of clarity emerge together.
This is because it does not depend on external objects. For this reason, the six faculties are equal.
This means that because the six types of clarity can simultaneously arise based on any single faculty, one may employ the eye as the ear, or the ear as the eye, and so forth;
since they can all function according to need, it is called "the mutual functioning of the six faculties.
This supreme and wondrous application of perfect penetration has already been briefly demonstrated here. Second, [this is] verified through knowledge.
Ānanda, do you not know? Within this assembly, Aniruddha sees though he has no eyes; the Nāga Upananda hears though he has no ears;
the goddess of the Gaṅgā perceives fragrance though she has no nose; Gavāmpati knows flavors through his tongue; and the Śūnyatā-deva perceives touch though he has no body.
They have been made to appear momentarily by being reflected within the light of the Tathāgata. Since they have...

The substance of the wind-nature is fundamentally non-existent. All those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and achieved tranquility, such as Mahākāśyapa here in this assembly, whose mental faculty has long since ceased, possess a perfect and clear understanding that does not depend on mental ideation.
The reason for calling Ānanda again is that he wishes to use the present assembly as a witness to prove the reality of their mutual functioning.
"How could you not know? is a rhetorical question, implying that since they have been gathered together day and night, it is impossible that he would not know.
Aniruddha was the son of King Śuklodana; this name is translated as "Without Poverty," because he was immensely wealthy throughout many kalpas.
Name: When he first left the household life, he was fond of sleep; because he disparaged diligence, he lost his eyesight.
Later, by the power of samādhi, he possessed a distinct divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Because it emerged from half of his head, it is said that "he sees despite being sightless.
This vision does not follow the physical eye, but is manifested through the clarity of the head. Upāli (here called *Bhadanta*, meaning "Good Joy") was a dragon of the kingdom of Magadha.
Regarding the name: since the character for "deaf" (聾) is composed of "dragon" (龍) and "ear" (耳), we know that dragons are not without ears;

however, they cannot hear sounds, as if they were deaf. Some say they use their horns for hearing; this means that when they hear, it does not follow through the ears, but is manifested clearly through the horns.
The name of the Gaṅgā River is the same as the Ganges. A goddess presides over it as the deity of the river, just as [in the previous case].
These are comparable to the Goddess of the Luo River or the Consorts of the Xiang; they are not those who perceive fragrance by smelling with the nose.
Pārvatī—here translated as "the Cow-Chewer"—would chew emptily after eating like a cow. The Buddha feared that people in the world might give rise to slander.
An imperial decree commands that he dwell long in the heavens. One who knows flavors with a "different tongue" perceives flavor apart from the tongue.
These two aforementioned types of persons do not follow their original sense-faculties; they manifest clarity by relying on other [faculties]. *Śūnyatā* (舜若多) is translated here as "emptiness."
The deity is named "Emptiness" (Śūnyatā). This refers to the deity who presides over emptiness. Regarding the phrase "one who perceives touch without a body":

there is no physical form, yet the mind alone is capable of perception. This perception does not follow the body; rather, it manifests clearly through the mind to which it is entrusted. Fearing that one might ask, "If there is no body, who knows that a deity exists? he says:
"It is reflected within the light of the Tathāgata, causing it to appear for a moment. This is because the deity of Emptiness suffers from having no body.
The physical form cannot prostrate before the Buddha; it is only through the Buddha’s compassionate empowerment and the radiance of his light that it is made to appear.

Although it is made to appear by the radiance of his light, its substance is like the wind, vanishing in an instant. Therefore, it is said that since its substance is of the nature of wind, its essence is fundamentally non-existent.
It further states that the *ḍākinīs*, the deities, the Wind Devas (*vāyu-rāja*), and the gods of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) simultaneously prostrated;
all were made manifest by the reflection of light. The "attainment of cessation" (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is the name for the final stage among the nine successive attainments;

it is also called the "attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception" (*saṃjñāveditanirodhasamāpatti*), because both the aggregates of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) do not function therein. Furthermore, among the nine successive attainments, the first eight are mundane.

The stages of cultivation: the latter refers to that cultivated at the final stage of an ārya. Because this samādhi, once attained, leads immediately to the realization of nirvāṇa, they are called "śrāvakas who have attained tranquility.
Among the disciples of the Buddha, many have accomplished this; therefore, the word "all" (sarva) is placed at the beginning.
In this assembly, the example of one individual is cited to represent the whole. Mahākāśyapa—here translated as "Great Kauruṣya"—was a cousin of the Buddha.
Among the disciples, he was the foremost in dhūta practices. Regarding the phrase "the faculty of mind has long been extinguished," the "faculty of mind" refers to the seventh consciousness.

When Kāśyapa attained the samādhi of cessation, the six consciousnesses ceased to function, and the seventh consciousness’s act of deliberation also came to an end; hence it is said that [his mind] has long been extinguished.
As for the phrase "perfectly and clearly knowing," it means that among his remaining five faculties, each is perfectly clear and bright, such that all are capable of discerning and knowing.

From the outset, this does not depend upon the seventh mind-faculty (*manas*) or the sixth faculty of discursive thought (*manovijñāna*); hence it is said that "it does not rely on mental conceptions.
This knowledge does not follow after the mental faculty but is manifested through the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).

Now, regarding the six individuals mentioned above, three attained their realization through the ripening of karmic retribution (*vipāka*), while three attained it through the cultivation of the Hīnayāna. If they were already able to exercise such mutual mastery, how much more so for one who has attained the Truth?

This is truly perfect penetration. Entrusting this to the faculties so that clarity may manifest, the wondrousness of their mutual functioning naturally implies there must be something else inconceivable.
This concludes the section on the mutual functioning of the faculties. Second, both faculties and objects are simultaneously eliminated.
Ānanda, if your faculties are now fully extracted and their inner radiance shines forth, then these superficial phenomena and the various changing appearances of the vessel-world will,
like ice melting in hot water, be transformed in an instant into supreme awareness.
Selecting one sense organ encompasses all six; because the one is identical to the many, it is called "the faculties are completely uprooted.
Even if one proceeds from the objects of the senses to the cessation of the fetters, understanding them sequentially is what is meant by "having completely uprooted them.

"Internally luminous and radiating light" refers to the manifestation of function from a pure essence. "Dust-like objects" refers to the internal body of the sense organs, while "the vessel world" refers to the external [environment].
The world—both of these belong to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and ultimately revert to destruction; therefore, they are called "all manifestations of transformation.
Yet, since they belong to transformation, their entire substance is entirely empty and is nothing but the single mind.

It is because one fails to realize that it is mind-only and clings to things as being substantially real that the internal and external realms, the sentient and the insentient, become divided. Now, since the various faculties are perfected...
When the single nature is uprooted and made perfectly penetrating, it shines forth with inner clarity; the six delusions do not arise.

Because the single nature is perfectly penetrating, principle can be harmonized with phenomena, as it is said: "like hot water dissolving ice. Because the six delusions do not arise, all phenomena are entirely principle, as it is said:
"transforming into awakening in a single thought-moment. Even that which the Buddhas realize does not lie outside of this; therefore, it is further designated as "unsurpassed."
These three examples reveal the perfect subtlety.

Ānanda, it is like when people of the world gather their vision in the eyes; if one were to suddenly close them, the appearance of darkness would manifest before them, and the six sense organs would become dark and indistinct, with the head and feet appearing as one.
If that person were to run their hand over the outside of the body, although they do not see the head...
It is sufficient to discern that perception and cognition are identical. When visual consciousness conditions sight, it arises in dependence on light and darkness, thereby forming non-seeing.

If it were not for the spontaneous manifestation of light itself, then all appearances of darkness would never be able to obscure it. When the faculties and their objects have both been dissolved, how could the luminous awareness of enlightenment fail to be perfectly wondrous?

The initial statement regarding the "inherent principle" appearing as if obstructed refers to the preceding section where the "sentient beings and their environment" already encompass the sense organs and their objects;

yet, because people might doubt the claim that these are transformed through mindfulness and awakening, he first cites worldly people as an example. "Worldly people" here refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
"Gathering the vision in the eye" means that since the physical body has already formed a mass, the nature of vision is concentrated within the eyes. "Suddenly closing [the eyes]"...

This refers to the appearance of being tightly shut. Because one does not perceive clarity, it is said that "dark signs appear before one. This seems to be an obstruction caused by the sense organs (*indriya*).

Due to the darkness of the sensory objects (*viṣaya*), one realizes that all six sense organs are simultaneously obscured; hence, it is called "gloomy" (*ānran*). "Gloomy" describes a state of total blackness.
As for "the head and feet being of a similar kind," this means being of one type in having no conscious perception; this seems to be an obstruction caused by the sensory objects. ○
The passage uses the example of a person who lacks visual obstruction to illustrate this point. "That person" refers specifically to one whose eyes are closed.

"Tracing the body with the hand and circling it" means stroking and rubbing the body in order from head to foot. The phrase "although he does not see" indicates that it is not the case that he truly does not see;
rather, it is simply because he has not yet discerned [the specific parts]. "Once the head and feet are distinguished" means that the head and the feet have been identified.
Together they distinguish the hand that can touch; once the head perceives it as a hand, the feet likewise perceive it as a hand.
Thus it is said that perception is the same throughout. Since perception is the same and does not depend on the eyes at all, the sense organ is certainly unimpeded by its nature.
If this is so, why is it that one does not see when the eyes are actually engaged? Therefore it is said: "Perception depends on the presence of light."
And so forth. This means that when one relies on seeing light, it arises because of that light; yet when the appearance of darkness manifests before one, it seems as though seeing has ceased.
How could one know that at the moment of non-light, the nature of seeing darkness arises spontaneously? Darkness cannot obscure it.
If that is so, how could sensory objects (dust) obstruct the nature? Thus we know that for ordinary beings, the principle-as-endowment is already itself unobstructed.

Using this as an illustration, one can then envision the perfect subtlety of the subsequent "phenomenal creation" (shizao). [The section] beginning with "Roots and Objects" reveals the perfect subtlety of phenomenal creation.
Since roots and objects have been dissolved, the text refers to the Perfectly Penetrating Sage. "Roots" refers to the physical sense organs (the floating dust), which...

The preceding refers to the world of sentient beings. "Dust" (*rajas*) refers to external objects, which are the aforementioned receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*). Since it was previously stated that "it is like hot water dissolving ice," it says "having been dissolved.
Furthermore, since it was said that "upon recollection, it transforms into supreme enlightenment," it asks, "how could it not become perfectly wondrous?
Thus, one should know that "how" (*yīhuì*) is not an interrogative term but a declarative term. This refers to the faculties and dust of ordinary beings.
If its nature has not yet been dissolved, it is already unimpeded; how much more so for a Perfectly Enlightened Sage whose faculties and objects have both been dissolved?

How could there be any principle by which his enlightened clarity would fail to achieve perfect wondrousness? This is certainly impossible. (The *Zhengmo* says: "Discussing this in light of the two preceding meanings:

the former meaning briefly demonstrates the complete efficacy of cause and effect, enabling one to know in advance the ultimate fruit. The latter meaning provides a detailed demonstration of the expedient means for the beginner, enabling one to clearly understand the practical application of the effort. Summary.)
The first major section, which classifies the divisions to establish the two meanings, is concluded.
Second, verifying through evidence to resolve two doubts. First, verifying and explaining the doubt regarding the annihilation of the root-nature;

second, providing evidence to explain the doubt regarding the existence of a separate source for the fetters. The first [of these two] has two parts: first, Ānanda’s erroneous interpretation and mistaken objection; second, as...

The following is an explanation based on verifying the matter through scriptural evidence, consisting of three parts: first, an objection regarding the contradiction between cause and effect; second, an objection regarding the discrepancy between earlier and later teachings;
third, a request for the Great Compassionate One to reveal the truth. First:

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said, if one wishes to seek the permanently abiding awakened mind within the causal stage, it must correspond in name and designation with the resultant stage.
World-Honored One, within the state of the Tathāgata, there are these seven names and designations:
Bodhi, Nirvāṇa, True Suchness (Tathatā), Buddha-nature (Buddhadhātu), Amala-vijñāna, the Empty Tathāgatagarbha, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom."
Although they are distinct, their pure and perfect essence is firm and solid, like a diamond king, eternally abiding and indestructible.
If this seeing and hearing were to be separated from light and darkness, motion and stillness, and penetration and obstruction, they would ultimately have no substance;
they would be just like the thinking mind, which has no inherent existence apart from external objects. How can you take that which is ultimately subject to cessation as the cause for cultivation?

Desiring to attain the seven fruits of the Tathāgata’s eternal abiding, one first establishes the primary principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-siddhānta*). When the Buddha speaks as he does, it refers to what is taught within the gateway of the ultimate truth.

He said: "If, at the stage of the causal ground, one takes a mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation, yet seeks the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible.
This reveals that the causal mind must correspond with the resultant awakening. Now, Ānanda takes the meaning of that statement;
thus he says, "the awakening-mind at the causal ground," and so forth. As for "the awakening-mind at the causal ground," it means:

The initial mind of awakening generated within the causal stage is precisely the mind previously cultivated as the cause. "Desiring to seek" refers to the aforementioned Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*).
"Permanently abiding" refers to the aforementioned meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing. Regarding the correspondence of names and terms, it is not necessary for the names to be identical;
it is simply that the meaning accords with that name. [The passage] beginning with "World-Honored One" below cites and clarifies that the name of the fruition is "permanently abiding."

The fruit of bodhi-wisdom is the transformation of afflictions; this is what is designated by the term "Buddha-nature. The fruit of the cessation of nirvāṇa is the departure from birth-and-death and its realization;
this is what is designated by the term "True Suchness" (*tathatā*). True Suchness is non-false and unchanging; it is the essence of the aforementioned nirvāṇa.

Buddha-nature is pure awakening without insentience; it is the essence of the aforementioned bodhi. Thus, these two [above]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

These are named after their emergence from the entanglements (*paryutthāna*). These two refer to the essence (*svabhāva*) as their designation. *Amala-vijñāna* (the immaculate consciousness) is translated as "stainless" (*vimala*);
it is the aspect of the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) being purely pure. The "empty *tathāgatagarbha*" signifies being free from defilement;

it is the aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā*) being purely pure. These two are also named after their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is the transformation of the eighth [consciousness].
The mental complex associated with consciousness arises simultaneously with the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*).

Its universal illumination of the ten directions and its perfect manifestation within all lands and atoms constitute the sublime function of the stage of fruition. This [category] is further designated by a name based on its function, which encompasses both the names "emerging from entanglement" and "liberation.
It also includes two names that indicate its essence, two names that reveal its characteristics, and one name that invokes its function; therefore, it is called the "sevenfold."
These are names for it; it is called *bodhi*, or it is called *nirvāṇa*, and so on, even being called "mirror-like wisdom" (*ādarśajñāna*).

Therefore, it is said that although the designations differ, the fact that they differ reveals that they are not truly distinct. This is because they all equally possess the meaning of being pure, perfect, firm, solid, and eternally abiding.
"Pure and perfect" distinguishes this from the causal stage, as ordinary beings are defiled and thus not pure. (2)
The Bodhisattva’s [wisdom] is pure but not yet perfected; only the Buddha is uniquely pure and uniquely perfected.

Furthermore, among the seven names, the "pure consciousness" (amalavijñāna) and the "mirror-like wisdom" (ādarśajñāna) are excluded, as all the others pertain to the causal stage (hetu-bhūmi); it is for this reason that they are distinguished here.
Regarding the phrase "its essence is firm and concentrated": "firm" means solid and stable, which carries the meaning of being eternally abiding and immovable—like the Vajra and the jewel of Śakra.

Its substance is most firm; it is called "King" because it is supreme. This serves as a metaphor to reveal that the aforementioned seven names are likewise eternally abiding and indestructible, realized only by the Buddha.

If one were to hold the erroneous view below that the nature of the faculties is subject to annihilation—just as it was previously stated that when separated from light and separated from darkness there is no essence of seeing, and when separated from motion and separated from stillness, fundamentally...

There is no hearing, substance, and so forth. This clarifies that apart from the objects of perception, there is only a single brilliant essence. By removing the vessel [of the physical body] through contemplation, one perceives emptiness;
thus, emptiness is used as a metaphor for "oneness. This does not mean its ultimate annihilation. Ānanda, not understanding this, said:

"If this seeing and hearing (citing two natures to encompass all six natures) are apart from brightness and darkness, motion and stillness, and penetration and obstruction (citing three objects to encompass all six objects)..."
Ultimately, it has no essence. This is because you have erroneously interpreted the Buddha’s words to mean that the root-nature (*indriya-svabhāva*) is subject to annihilation.

Having already misinterpreted them, you further provide a mistaken proof, claiming: "It is like the mind of recollection; the mind of recollection is the mind of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).

To say that there is nothing apart from sensory objects is the meaning [the Buddha] intended when refuting the [existence of] consciousness. Now, the root-nature is truly not like that. Its thesis and reason are [invalid].
Once accomplished, it can be known by oneself. ○ [Question: How is it that the following objection contradicts the Buddha’s own school?
To take annihilation as the cause while seeking an eternal fruit is for the awakening-mind of the causal stage to be entirely inconsistent with the terminology of the resultant stage.
Therefore, the objection states: "How can one take this ultimate annihilation... and so forth. This concludes the objection regarding the contradiction between cause and effect.
Second, the difficulty regarding the differing accounts of priority and sequence:
"World-Honored One, if vision is ultimately empty when separated from light and darkness— just as when there are no external objects, the nature of thought itself ceases—

and when one investigates through progressive and regressive cycles with subtle discernment, finding that there is fundamentally no self-mind nor any mental factors of the self, then by what could a cause be established for seeking [the truth]?"
Unsurpassed Enlightenment. The Tathāgata previously taught that it is profoundly refined, perfect, and eternal. To deviate from these sincere words would ultimately result in frivolous discourse.
How, then, can the Tathāgata be said to speak words of truth?

First, this reiterates the meaning of the erroneous interpretation. The intent is that if, indeed, apart from objects such as light and darkness, the nature of seeing, hearing, and so forth were ultimately empty and non-existent—such that, as previously refuted regarding consciousness, the six consciousnesses lack prior objects and their own-nature ceases—there would still be a great error.
I venture to speak thus before the World-Honored One. [This concludes] the consideration of the lower [position] through progressive and regressive analysis.

Both their causes and conditions are likewise non-existent. "Advancing and retreating" refers to prior thoughts and subsequent reflections. "Cycling" means returning to the beginning after completion.
"Subtle investigation" refers to applying one's attention to trace the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. "My mind" refers to the *vijñāna* (consciousness) mind;
"mind" here points to the faculty (*indriya*), because the faculty serves as the basis for consciousness. Thus it is said, "Ānanda, at first..."

Taking the six consciousnesses to be the mind, he was refuted three times and dared not acknowledge them; subsequently, seeking a true mind elsewhere, the Buddha pointed out to him the seeing-nature (darśana-svabhāva).
Now, due to his erroneous interpretation of the Buddha’s words, he dares not even acknowledge the seeing. Therefore, it is said:
"Fundamentally, there is no self-mind nor any mental factors (caitta) belonging to the self. Since both of these are absent, the Dharma-body would be annihilated. It would be non-existent.
The Dharma can serve as the cause for the mind; therefore it is said: "For whom shall one establish the cause to seek unsurpassed enlightenment?

The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata" below is a summary and restatement of the discourse on the manifestation of seeing (*darśana*). That which was previously explained refers specifically to what was taught within the context of the manifestation of seeing.

To be unmoving and unmixed is called "clarity" (*zhan*); to transcend emotion and leave behind views is called "purity" (*jing*); to be unobstructed and undivided is called "perfection" (*yuan*); [and] to be neither extinguished nor lost...
It is replied that this refers to "permanence" (*nitya*). Although these four meanings encompass the essential points, they all ultimately derive from the meaning of being "ultimately uninterrupted.
Regarding the objection below—that it contradicts the Buddha’s own words—the point is that the Tathāgata has always pledged his teachings with truthful speech.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata speaks what is true; he speaks what is real. Fundamentally...
The preceding text of this sutra also states: "The Unsurpassed Dharma King speaks words of truth.

Now, observing what the Tathāgata has currently taught—that there is no essence of seeing apart from light and apart from darkness—yet previously he taught that it is profoundly pure, essential, perfect, constant, and ultimately uninterrupted:
do these differing statements before and after not contradict his truthful words? To "contradict" means to turn one's back on and depart from; thus, it would be a departure from his truthful words.

Having recently engaged in such evasive and confused speech, will you not ultimately fall into frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*)? Frivolous proliferation is deceptive, false, and without substance;
therefore, it is difficult to ask how the Tathāgata and others [attain their state]. I beseech you three times with great compassion to reveal and explain this.
I only pray that you will bestow great compassion to dispel my ignorance and stinginess.
Although I have presented these two difficult questions, I ultimately do not dare to definitively doubt the Buddha; therefore, I continue to seek your compassionate revelation.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "Though you have studied much and possess great learning, you have not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
In your mind, you merely know the causes of inversion, but when true inversion actually manifests before you, you are truly unable to recognize it.
Fearing that your sincere heart may still not be fully convinced, I shall now test you with various mundane matters to eliminate your doubts."
First, he rebukes their perversion: those who study much learning are rebuked for being preoccupied solely with memorization;
"study" here means the diligent application of one's will to investigate and practice the meaning. Those who have not exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) are rebuked for being lax in cultivation;

among the four outflows, they have only exhausted the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*), yet three remain, hence it is said they have "not exhausted them. All of this stems from a lack of cultivation.
The power is weak and wisdom is severed, lacking vigor. "Inversion" refers to the conscious mind (*vijñāna-citta*); "the cause" refers to the nature of the sense-faculties (*indriya-svabhāva*).
This means that consciousness manifests through the faculties because the faculties serve as its supporting cause (*āśraya-hetu*).

As seen in the preceding passage, Ānanda identified the nature of the faculties as the locus of the mind; this principle is already known, yet because his understanding is not yet complete, it is said to be "in vain. Truly...

Counting backward from the perspective of regarding the faculties (*indriya*) as being severed: although the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) is called "inverted," it merely revolves within birth and death.
However, if the nature of the faculties were truly severed and extinguished, one would fall forever from the lineage of the Buddhas.
Thus, we know that those who cling to the faculties as being severed are precisely experiencing true inversion. Observe how Ānanda cites the consciousness-mind to demonstrate his correct view.

Because they do not realize this for themselves, [the Buddha] rebukes them on the grounds that they have not yet truly recognized it. ○ The passage beginning with "I fear you" (*kō nyō*) correctly permits the removal of doubts.
The Buddha’s intention in rebuking their lack of recognition is that although they appear to be submissive through faith, it may not necessarily arise from a sincere heart.
Therefore, he says, "I fear your sincere heart has not yet submitted in faith. If one were to rearrange the phrasing according to the underlying meaning, it should read: "I fear you have not yet..."
"Sincere faith and submission" means that one knows [the truth] and is not merely pleased by it; it is a state of genuine and heartfelt compliance.
When I say, "I shall now try to use such means," I am employing expedient means to further inspire them, with the aim of ensuring they achieve sincere submission.
"Various worldly matters" refers to striking the bell to induce a dream; for both striking the bell and inducing a dream are mundane, secular activities within the realm of defilement (*saṃsāra*).
Regarding the "accident": when it is said that one's doubts shall be removed, this implies that by means of a causal event, the doubts will certainly be dispelled;

thus, the intention to inspire sincere faith and submission is already contained therein. Part Two: Verifying the Permanence through Specific Events. This has two sections: First, verifying permanence by striking a bell;
Second, verifying permanence by citing a dream. The first section has three parts: First, questioning about hearing and answering about hearing. Second...

Questioning with sound and answering with sound; three detailed expositions and refutations. Regarding the first two: one consists of three rounds of question and answer, and the second consists of a dual examination and determination.
As for the first: immediately thereafter, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula to strike the bell once and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear it now?"
Ānanda and the great assembly all said, "We hear. When the bell ceased and there was no sound, the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now?
Ānanda and the great assembly all said, "We do not hear it. Then Rāhula struck it once more, and the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear it now? Ānanda and the great assembly all said, "We hear it."
The first exchange establishes that hearing exists. The question asks whether one hears or not, thereby causing him to verify for himself its presence or absence.
The answer, "I hear," verifies for himself that hearing exists. The second exchange, following the cessation of the bell, establishes that [hearing] does not exist.

Since the cessation of the bell is not a case of truly having no hearing, it is known that he must have misunderstood; therefore, he is questioned again for confirmation. The answer, "I do not hear," is indeed [the truth].
However, this is a misunderstanding. At that time, the questions and answers below clarify the contradiction:
if it were truly the case that there was no hearing, then the nature of hearing would be annihilated; since this is not actually the case, he poses three questions for this reason.
Furthermore, the statement "both hear" clarifies that the previous claim of not hearing was still not self-aware. These two points are used together to examine and determine the truth.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "What do you hear? What do you not hear? Ānanda and the great assembly together replied to the Buddha, saying:
"If the bell is struck, I am able to hear it. When the striking has ceased and the sound has faded, when both the resonance and the echo have utterly vanished, that is called 'not hearing.'"
First is the dual inquiry. Because Ānanda might not realize that the nature of hearing is truly eternal and does not arise from conditions, the Buddha makes this dual inquiry.
From "Ānanda" onwards is the dual determination. If you say, "I hear the sound of the bell when it is struck," you still misunderstand;
there must be a sound for there to be hearing. When the striking has ceased and the sound has vanished, you then say, "there is no hearing. This, too, is a misunderstanding.

Where there is no sound, there is no hearing. What remains after the sound is called "tone" (*yin*); what remains after the tone is called "echo" (*xiang*). This has been provisionally established for the sake of examination;

the refutation will follow after the response concerning sound. Having finished the first pair of questions and answers regarding hearing, we now proceed with the second pair of questions and answers regarding sound.
This consists of two parts: first, three rounds of question and answer; second, a dual examination. First:
The Tathāgata further commanded Rāhula to strike the bell and asked Ānanda, "Do you hear the sound now?
Ānanda and the great assembly both replied, "There is a sound. After a short while, when the sound had faded, the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear the sound now?
Ānanda and the great assembly answered, "There is no sound. After a moment, Rāhula came again to strike the bell, and the Buddha asked once more, "Do you hear the sound now?"
"Is there sound? Ānanda and the great assembly all replied, "There is sound.

The initial question and answer established the existence [of sound]. By asking, "Is there sound?", he caused them to verify whether sound exists or not, so that they might realize that hearing is neither existent nor non-existent.
That they all said, "There is sound," was because they only knew that sound exists, but did not realize that hearing is not non-existent.
After a brief moment, he asked again: "Is it certain that there is no sound? "A brief moment" (*shaonian*) refers to a short duration of time.

When sound has vanished, it is naturally without sound; it is not that hearing itself is absent. Fearing that [the disciple] might become confused, he questioned him once more. The answer was: "There is no sound."
One simply knows that while sound is absent, awakening is not; one realizes that hearing is not non-existent.

○ After a short while, a question and answer clarify the confusion. "After a short while" means within a brief moment. Since the sound has vanished, it is only that the sound is non-existent, not that hearing is non-existent.

When struck again, there is only the presence of sound, and thus there is the presence of hearing. Because one knows this state is inevitably confused, he asks three times to bring it to a conclusion, saying: "Both..."
Those who perceive sound merely know how to respond verbally; they do not realize that the "drunken old man's" intent does not lie in the wine.
This pair of lines is used for definitive examination.
The Buddha asked Ānanda: "What is sound? What is the absence of sound? Ānanda and the great assembly together addressed the Buddha.

He said: "If the bell is struck, it is called 'having sound. When the striking has long ceased and the sound has vanished, such that both word and resonance are utterly cut off, it is called 'no sound.
At first, he examined both cases to determine that sound is impermanent and that existence and non-existence arise from conditions. He examined them both because he feared they might not understand."

○ Ānanda descended from his state of dualistic concentration. When he answered that sound exists when struck and does not exist when not struck, it was clear that he understood sound to be impermanent, and that existence and non-existence arise from conditions.
However, because he failed to realize that the nature of hearing itself is truly eternal—neither existing nor non-existing through conditions—he ultimately did not attain awakening.
This concludes the section on answering by means of hearing sounds; it constitutes the third detailed exposition and refutation.
First, he rebukes him for his evasive equivocation; second, he refutes his erroneous discourse; third, he provides a general summary and censure. Regarding the first:
The Buddha said to Ānanda and the great assembly, "How is it that you now engage in self-contradictory equivocation?
The great assembly and Ānanda simultaneously asked the Buddha, "In what way, sir, do we name this 'evasive equivocation'? The Buddha said, "I ask you: Do you hear?"

When you are asked, "Do you hear?", you say, "I hear. When you are asked, "Is it sound?", you say, "It is sound. Since your answers regarding hearing and sound are not fixed, how can this not be called evasive equivocation?
At the beginning, the Buddha rebuked his evasive equivocation. The phrase "how can this be? is a term of strange reproach.

It clarifies that while he speaks of the existence or non-existence of sound, he claims to hear its existence or non-existence; this is not a forced statement born of ignorance, but is certainly a confused account made despite knowing the truth.

Therefore, he rebukes him for his self-contradictory equivocation. Regarding the passage "The great assembly... and so forth: the assembly had not yet submitted their hearts. The phrase "how can this be? is a word used to distinguish and rectify the truth.
[The Opponent’s] Words: "If sound exists, it is heard; if it does not exist, it is not heard. When a bell is struck, there is sound; when it is not, there is no sound.

Answering according to reality, this is clear and distinct, without confusion. Therefore, how can this be called "confused speech" (*vikṣepa*)? [The Buddha’s] Words: Below this, the Buddha refutes [the argument] through principle.
The Buddha’s intention is that whether hearing exists or does not exist, and whether sound exists or does not exist, the principle is non-dual. Thus, they are one and the same.
Previously, when I asked you whether hearing exists or does not exist, you answered me that hearing exists and does not exist.
Again, when I asked you whether sound exists or does not exist, you likewise answered me that sound exists and does not exist.

You have merely responded in a muddled manner regarding the existence or non-existence of this hearing and the existence or non-existence of sound; since both lack definitive reality, how can such forced confusion be considered correct?
Is it not called "evasive confusion" to insist on debating this? Second, I shall refute your erroneous argument.

Ānanda, when the sound has vanished and there is no resonance, you say that there is no hearing. If, in reality, there were no hearing and the nature of hearing had already ceased, you would be like a withered tree.
When the bell is struck again, how could you know it? To distinguish between existence and non-existence is simply a matter of the auditory object (śabda-viṣaya) or...
Whether it exists or not, how could that nature of hearing be subject to your existence or non-existence? If you truly say there is no hearing, who is it that knows this "no"?
This initial statement was made for the purpose of refutation; the intent of the refutation was to dissolve the absence of sound by means of sound.
Yet you then claim there is no hearing. If hearing truly did not exist, then the nature of hearing would have already perished, becoming like withered wood, utterly devoid of the potential for life.
When the bell is struck again, the resonance occurs without conscious awareness.

How then can you claim to know it? Your assertion that there is no sound and no hearing is erroneous. ○ "Knowing existence" below explains this according to its underlying principle. To explain the principle:
since your faculty of hearing knows existence when sound exists and knows non-existence when sound is absent, it follows... [self-evident].
This sound-object may either exist or not exist within your faculty of hearing; how could that faculty of hearing itself be subject to existence or non-existence as a result of your sound-object?
This is the discussion according to the correct principle. The final two lines serve to prevent erroneous arguments.

(Fearing that one might say: "When there is knowledge of existence, one can distinguish the object, so it may be said that there is hearing; but when there is knowledge of non-existence, one does not distinguish the object—how could there truly be hearing?
To prevent this, he says: "If hearing were truly non-existent, who would know its non-existence? The word "yu" (still/also) means "is still.

This means that if the nature of hearing were truly non-existent, then knowledge should likewise be non-existent, because fundamentally they are one refined spirit (*ekasamprajanya*). If, as a result, both knowledge and [hearing] were non-existent, then...
Who is it that comes to know non-existence? Since there must be one who knows non-existence, there must likewise be one who hears non-existence.
Your claim that at the time of knowing non-existence, hearing cannot exist, is merely a fallacious argument.
Third, this is a general summary and refutation:

"Therefore, Ānanda, it is within hearing itself that sound has arising and ceasing; it is not that the arising of sound or the ceasing of sound causes your nature of hearing to become existent or non-existent.
"You are already inverted and deluded, mistaking sound for hearing; how can you wonder at being confused?"
The deluded take the permanent to be the intermittent. One should never say that apart from all movement and stillness, or closure and openness, there is hearing without intrinsic nature.

This first restates and concludes the correct principle. As stated above: "Knowing existence and knowing non-existence is simply because the auditory object (śabda-dhātu) is sometimes present and sometimes absent."
Now you say that within hearing itself, sounds have their own arising and ceasing. Previously, it was asked: "How could that nature of hearing be subject to your existence or non-existence?
Now you say that it is not the case that the arising of sound and the ceasing of sound cause your nature of hearing to become existent or non-existent.
"Clarifying" (ming) here refers to restating what was previously explained to conclude the correct principle of permanence.
"You still," and so forth, is a profound censure of delusion and confusion. "You still remain inverted" censures the absence of correct knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*).

Because you lack correct knowledge and vision, when it is clear that sound exists or does not exist, you claim instead that hearing exists or does not exist; therefore, it is said that you mistake sound for hearing.

Since one is already deluded by mistaking sound for hearing, and upon hearing no sound immediately concludes that there is no hearing, what is so strange about the previous state of being dazed and bewildered, whereby the true, eternal nature of hearing was taken to be ultimately annihilated—just like the thinking mind?
This is why the Tathāgata severely rebukes their extreme perversion; although his words seem not to express surprise, it is precisely for this reason that he is deeply surprised.
Ultimately, it does not descend to the extreme of manifesting a permanent nature [that exists] regardless of whether the sounds of movement or stillness are clamorous or silent;

nor does it depend on whether the faculty of hearing is obstructed or open, deficient or complete. One must say that this nature of hearing is not only beyond the movement and stillness of objects such that its lack of nature cannot be predicated, but even when separated from the obstruction or openness of the faculty itself, its lack of nature likewise cannot be predicated.
Because there is no such nature, one must ultimately refrain from using [the term] "etc. to exclude it. This concludes the demonstration through the striking of a bell to prove permanence.

Second, citing dreams as proof of permanence (Since the principle that the faculties and objects are both absent is profound and difficult to believe, this section cites the fact that hearing is not non-existent within dreams.

Furthermore, it uses this example to demonstrate the meaning that even when the physical form dissolves and life passes away, the nature of hearing does not cease to exist). Three points: 1. There is hearing during sleep and dreams; 2. One still remembers it upon waking; 3. To the utmost...
This reveals that the nature [of consciousness] is permanent. First:
it is like a person in a deep sleep, lying soundly upon a bed and pillow; while that person sleeps, someone in the house pounds cloth or husks rice.
In his dream, the person hears the sound of pounding and husking, yet perceives it as something else—either as the beating of a drum or the striking of a bell.
In that dream, he wondered to himself how his bell could have sounded like wood or stone.
One who is in deep sleep distinguishes himself from one who is lightly asleep; one who is in a state of profound slumber distinguishes himself from one who is merely momentarily drowsy.

It is said that a person who is lightly asleep, though in a state of profound slumber, will certainly wake upon hearing a sound; likewise, a person in deep sleep, if momentarily drowsy, will also wake upon hearing a sound. Only the one in deep sleep [remains unaware].

Only when one is a human being and fast asleep—failing to wake upon hearing a sound—does it truly constitute a dream experience. Therefore, the terms "deep" and "mature" (re-shu) are used to distinguish this state.

Beating clothes with a mallet and anvil is called *daolian* (beating the linen); pounding fine grain with a pestle and mortar is called *chongmi* (threshing rice). Both of these are sounds that clamor the ears.
Hearing such sounds within a dream reveals the true permanence of the faculty of hearing; the purpose is to demonstrate that it is distinct from other things.
Consciousness is obscure; although it is called "obscure," it is still a form of *anusmarana-vikalpa* (recollection-based conceptualization).

As for the statement, "either as if striking a drum or as if hitting a bell," this further belongs to *abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa* (discriminative conceptualization). However, the reason consciousness must be mentioned alongside [the sense organs] is that consciousness manifests in dependence upon the faculties (*indriya*);
because the presence of consciousness serves to reveal the existence of the faculties. This principle is then extended even to dreams and so forth.
This refers to shifting one's conceptual calculations. One marvels at why the bell does not speak while the drum does; this is presented in contrast with the following section.

Because in the state of dreamy obscurity, the bell and the drum are both indeterminate, and the sounds of wood, stone, pestles, and mortars are fundamentally indistinguishable within the dream, one thus marvels at them.
Upon waking, he still remembered it;

suddenly awakening, he immediately recognized the sound of the pestle and told his family members: "While I was dreaming, I was confused by this sound of pounding rice and took it to be the sound of drums."

"At that time, 'suddenly awakening' means to wake up oneself from a great deal of clamor. 'Swiftly' (*chuan*) means speed; because one understands immediately upon waking, it is called 'swift knowledge.

'Ablé' (*chu*)—meaning to pound and to husk—both may be referred to by the term *chu* (mortar/pestle), as the meanings of these two characters are identical. 'To inform one's family' refers to recounting the events of the dream.
The character for 'husking' (*chong*) also encompasses the sound of 'pounding' (*dao*), as the meanings of these two characters are the same. [He was] deluded.
Regarding the drum sounding without speaking and the bell likewise, they appear alternately as described above.

Furthermore, because one cannot fully recall or perfectly reproduce a dream after waking, if one necessarily relies on post-waking speech, then since one does not remember [the dream] after waking, what was heard within the dream might be considered unreliable.
However, since one is still able to recall and recount it after waking, this further demonstrates that what was heard within the dream is indeed real.
It is empty. The three poles manifest the constant nature.

Ānanda, while this person is dreaming, how could they recall stillness or movement, opening or closing, penetration or obstruction? Although their body is asleep, the faculty of hearing is not darkened.
Even if your physical form were to dissolve and the radiance of life were to depart, how could this nature be extinguished for you?

The initial realization is trustworthy; "stillness" refers to the cessation of movement and dust, while "opening and closing" refer to the permeability and obstruction of the sense faculties (*indriya*).
Generally speaking, closing is obstruction and opening is permeability. Alternatively, "closing" may refer to the hindrance of illness, while "obstruction" refers to the blockage by external objects;

"opening" signifies the departure of illness, and "permeability" denotes the separation from objects. As for the phrase "how could one remember," it means that when one is in deep sleep, both the faculties and their objects are forgotten.
Moreover, how could one possibly retain memory within a dream? Since one can hear even when there is no recollection, it is indeed true what was said previously:
that while both the sense organs and their objects are detached, the nature of hearing is not absent. ○ Regarding the phrase "its form lies below," this uses sleep as an analogy for death;
it means that according to my previous explanation, when a person is in deep sleep, although their physical form is dormant, the nature of hearing remains.

It does not grow dim. Taking this as an example, one knows that while the physical form may dissolve, it does not truly perish; and while life may pass away, it does not truly cease. Therefore, it is said: "Even if your physical form dissolves," and so forth.
The "light of life" refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). It is called "light" because it possesses the quality of false clarity.
This nature refers precisely to the faculty of hearing. As for the phrase "How could it be for you [and others]? it serves as a reductio ad absurdum (a counter-argument) to clarify the point.
These words are intended precisely to demonstrate that the faculty of hearing does not perish along with your physical form or cease when your life ends;

rather, it continues to exist alongside them without being extinguished. (Zhengmo asks: "If this root-nature is unrelated to movement and stillness, and unimpeded by birth and death, why did the Tathāgata say that apart from movement and stillness there is no essence of hearing?

The answer is: When the Buddha said there is no essence of hearing apart from objects, he meant that there is no accumulated hearing within the ear that coagulates to form the essence of hearing as a root. If this essence is forgotten, then the nature of hearing, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm, will finally [manifest]. )

This is clearly demonstrated; how could it be allowed to result in the doctrine of annihilation? This passage clarifies that from the very beginning there was no substance for hearing; it reveals that this was Ānanda’s own erroneous interpretation, rather than a contradiction within the Buddha’s own words. Wuxing said:

"Previously, Ānanda had generally raised doubts regarding the six sense organs being without substance when separated from their objects, while the Tathāgata specifically revealed the nature of hearing as permanent. This truly serves as the catalyst for the faculty of the ear-root (śrotrendriya) as the means of perfect penetration.

Section Three: Conclusion and Demonstration of Cause and Effect. Part One: Conclusion and demonstration of the cause and effect of birth and death. Part Two: Conclusion and demonstration of the true and eternal.

Cause and effect. First [it was taught that] the nature is truly eternal and each person possesses it inherently; yet we currently see sentient beings falling into impermanence. Since there must be cause and effect for this, [the text] here concludes and demonstrates [this point].
Because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed after forms and sounds, flowing along with every thought, they have never awakened to the nature that is pure, wondrous, and eternal.
Failing to follow what is constant, they pursue all that arises and perishes; thus, life after life, they transmigrate amidst defilement.
"From time immemorial" is said to express the extreme length of its delusion.
"Following forms and sounds" means that upon seeing forms one rushes toward them, and upon hearing sounds one pursues them; these two of the six sense-objects are cited to encompass the rest.

"Flowing and turning with every thought" means that once one follows forms and sounds, one must necessarily pursue deluded thoughts (the six consciousnesses). Once one pursues deluded thoughts, there arises birth and abiding.

"Differentiation" refers to the incessant flow of arising and ceasing. It is precisely because this incessant flow obscures the true permanence, and because the proliferation of deluded thoughts contravenes the pure and wondrous, that one regards [the nature] as if it were lost forever;
hence it is said, "one has never awakened. "Nature" (*xing*) refers to the fundamental original self-nature.

Speaking from the perspective of the time before the sense-faculties (*indriya*) had formed, it is called "pure" (*jing*) because the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) cannot defile it, and the faculties cannot...

The commentary says: "Subtle" means that birth cannot give rise to it and cessation cannot extinguish it; thus it is called "constant. Although these three meanings are mentioned together, only the character for "constant" (常) is emphasized.
As will be seen in the following text, "not following what is constant" means not following the existing nature of constancy, but rather flowing against the current to enter deeply.
"Chasing after all that arises and ceases" means merely following the six sense bases, with the consciousness-mind wavering inwardly and outwardly.
"Running" refers to both the paths of delusion and karma, which serve as the causes for birth and death. The phrase "by this" refers back to the aforementioned causes of birth and death;

it means that by virtue of these causes of birth and death, one transmigrates through the six realms of existence amidst the defiled phenomena of birth after birth, cycle after cycle, without rest. This pertains to the path of suffering, which constitutes birth.
The fruit of cessation. Second, the summary indicating the true and eternal cause and effect:

If one abandons arising and ceasing and maintains the true and eternal, the constant light will manifest before you; the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind will accordingly dissolve at that moment.
Conceptualization is the dust and the conscious mind is the defilement. When you distance yourself from both, your Dharma-eye will become clear and bright at that very moment;
how then could you fail to achieve unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?
If one abandons arising and ceasing, one does not pursue the delusory objects of the攀緣 (pān-yuán) consciousness that arises and ceases.

To maintain the true and constant is to rely solely on the nature of true constancy, thereby extinguishing the dust of sensory objects and exhausting the sense-faculties; this is what was referred to in the preceding text as "detaching from external attachments and subduing within.
As for "the constant light appearing before one," it refers to the radiance of perfect illumination emanating from the essence of true constancy, shining forth with brilliant clarity.
It is vividly clear, neither obscured nor darkened; this is what was meant in the preceding text by "submitting to the original truth and manifesting the fundamental radiance.

As for the phrase "the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind dissolve simultaneously," it means that once the constant light has appeared before one, all things are integrated upon encounter, such that the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind can no longer be apprehended.
This is what was meant in the preceding text by "the luminous nature manifests its brilliance, and all..."
The roots are uprooted completely. All floating dust-like appearances and the various transformed phenomena of the vessel-world are like ice melting in boiling water.

(The reason consciousness was not mentioned previously is that consciousness has no self-substance; it manifests in dependence upon the sense organs and their objects. Since even the organs and objects are being dissolved, it need not be mentioned. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is itself consciousness (*vijñāna*);

the objective phenomena (*ālambana-dharma*) perceived therein are the "dust" within the Eye of Dharma (*dharmacakṣus*). Consciousness is itself perception; the emotional sense organs (*indriya*) upon which it relies are the "dust" within the Eye of Dharma.
The Dharma-eye is defiled by impurities. When both [the eye and its objects] are distanced from these, then impurities cannot stain it and dust cannot darken it;
therefore, it is said to be "lucid and clear according to the occasion. The Dharma-eye is the Eye that Sees the Path (*darśanamārga*). When lucid and clear, the path ahead is easily discerned;
this also encompasses the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), for this is the cause of true permanence. As for the phrase "how could it not achieve equality," there are two meanings. First:
The Dharma-eye is clear and bright; whatever meets the eye is none other than the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
This is what was meant in the preceding passage: "In response to thought, it is transformed into supreme awakening. Second, the path ahead is easy to discern, and unsurpassed *bodhi* can be realized.
This pertains to the realization of the Way and constitutes the fruit of true permanence. However, these two demonstrations, if based on the perspective of arising and ceasing, do not...
One departs from saṃsāra; by relying on the true and eternal, one is able to achieve perfect enlightenment. The intent behind these alternations of suppression and encouragement is already evident.
Thus concludes the examination of the nature of the faculties and the severing of doubts regarding annihilationism.
*The Commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: Pointing at the Palm (Lengyan jing zhizhang shu), Fascicle Four and Fascicle Five.
Respectfully composed by the junior disciple Dàtiāntōnglǐ of Xiánzōng at Niànhuá Monastery in the Capital.
The Dharma-heir successor (Xingzong Zuwang Tengqing Huairen Zuyu Jiaozi), Second Witness, provides a separate commentary on the two points concerning the source of the knot:
first, Ānanda separately seeks the source of the knot; second, the Tathāgata certifies that there is no other substance.
The first [of these] has three parts: first, following the previous [discussion] to present the principle; second, describing the deluded seeking for the source.
The third instance of prostration and standing in attendance. First:

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained the second gateway of meaning, when I observe those in the world who attempt to untie knots, if they do not know the origin from which the knot was tied, I believe such people will ultimately never be able to untie it."

The Tathāgata previously explained the second method of teaching—that one must untie the knots by following their roots—and Ānanda, realizing he did not know the origin of the knots, set them aside despite having spoken.
This means that although he spoke, it was of no benefit. Now, with the passage beginning "Observe the world," etc., [the Buddha] clearly explains the reason for that lack of benefit.
"The origin of what is knotted" refers to the actual substance that constitutes the knot. As the subsequent text says:
"You know that this cloth was originally but a single strip; this is correct. One who understands how to untie a knot must know that the cloth is a single strip.
If one unties it at the very center of the knot, it will immediately unravel.

If one does not know this, one will inevitably pull and tug to the left and right, laboring in vain without success; therefore I say that such a person can never untie it. Thus we know what constitutes a knot."

The "origin" (*yuan*) here refers precisely to the true mind. Nevertheless, it does not depart from the nature within the six sense faculties. Ānanda, unaware of this, presumed there was something else;
thus, he follows up on the previously explained points of doctrine to clarify the futility of his ignorance regarding the origin of the knots.
Second, the description of deluded seeking for the origin.
“World-Honored One, it is the same for me and the śrāvakas in this assembly who are still in training. Since beginningless time, we have co-arisen and co-perished with various forms of ignorance.
Although we have attained such roots of goodness through extensive learning and are called ‘those who have left the home life,’ we remain like those suffering from quotidian malaria.
We only pray that the Great Compassionate One will take pity on us who are drowning in suffering. Today, what constitutes the fetters of our body and mind? From [where do they arise]?”
What is meant by "understanding"? It is that which enables sentient beings suffering from future afflictions to escape saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence.
First, a category is raised to describe delusion; one at the profound stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) would not dare claim not to know this.
Therefore, the text specifically cites the class of those still in training (śaikṣa). Just as that person who untied the knot did not know the origin of the knot, it is said, "it is likewise so."
Regarding "from the beginningless limit": according to this present sutra, it refers to the deluded state of taking what is not awakening to be awakening;

according to the *Awakening of Faith*, it refers to the moment when the mind arises through non-awakening (*abodhi*). Taking what is not awakening to be awakening, one establishes an objective realm based on that perceived clarity.

This aspect of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*) is itself the inseparability of the true and the false, co-arising with birth and cessation. Therefore, it is said that it "perishes and arises together with all ignorance. One must understand the true mind.
This is precisely the root of the knot. It is because [the mind] has been coexistent with ignorance since beginningless time that it is deluded and fails to know.
Since it does not know the Truth, merely hearing of it is of no benefit. Therefore, it is said: "Though one may attain such roots of goodness from extensive learning.

This is intended to reveal that such a person cannot untie the knot through cultivation and realization; being unable to untie the knot and achieve realization, they merely claim to have undergone the tonsure and donned the dyed robes.
Therefore, it is said that he is called "one who has left the home-life," because he lacks the actual substance of leaving the home-life. *Jiao* refers to malarial fever;
this illness involves alternating periods of cold and heat, with some cases recurring once every day and others recurring every other day.

Now, although Ānanda had personally severed the delusions of views and partially realized the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-nairātmya*), his confusion regarding the womb-existence and the darkness following the transition between bodies still remained.
It is unavoidable; therefore, it is likened to malaria that recurs every other day.

I only pray that after you have bestowed your instructions upon me, my true mind—which has sunk into ignorance and is submerged in birth and death—may be rescued by the great sage’s genuine compassion.

Therefore, I only pray that the Greatly Compassionate One will take pity on me. Having already transcended the realm of ordinary beings through the first fruit of the path, yet not having reached the stage of no-more-learning, let us for now set aside what preceded this and what follows it;
I simply request that the Tathāgata speak concerning my body and mind as they are today.
I report that my body and mind are currently well in their six fundamental aspects.
The Buddha previously instructed me to untie the knots from their roots, yet I do not know what constitutes a knot. May the Buddha explain this for me. A re-knotting does not arise spontaneously;
there must be a source from which it is knotted. Furthermore, I do not know where that source resides, nor from where one should begin the work to achieve liberation.

To explain: the Buddha also spoke of this for my sake. Once these instructions are put into practice, they will not only enable those currently in training to emerge from the depths of delusion, but will also be transmitted to the Dharma-ending age to eternally rescue sentient beings from the wheel of suffering. Therefore, it is said that they "will also cause future [beings]," and so forth.
Sentient beings in hardship refers to those whose bodies are currently within the cycle of saṃsāra, for they do not transcend saṃsāra.
Because suffering and hardship cannot be avoided, he strenuously taught the cultivation of the path to transcend birth and death; thus it is said that one may escape saṃsāra.
The "three realms of existence" (trai-dhātu) are the very locus of saṃsāra. Once saṃsāra has been escaped, one rides upon vows to deliver sentient beings, and naturally does not fall back into them.
Third, he prostrated and waited for instruction.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the great assembly. Shedding tears and raising his mind in sincere devotion, he awaited the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata.

Although the words of his request were addressed specifically to those still in training (śaikṣa), his intention also encompassed the entire dharma assembly; therefore, it is said that he "reached the entire great assembly. This is indeed so.

Because the practice and realization for resolving the knots is a profound stage even for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is something that even Bodhisattvas of the Perfectly True [Teaching] must seek.
"Prostrating with the five limbs" means to bow down so that the four limbs and the crown of the head touch the Buddha’s feet.

"Showering tears with uplifted sincerity" means shedding tears of gratitude and remorse while raising the body to kneel on both knees. "Waiting" has the meaning of looking expectantly. Unsurpassed opening...
Regarding "The Demonstration": what is to be explained below is the single path to nirvāṇa for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.
First, Ānanda finished his separate inquiry regarding the demonstration of the knots; second, the Tathāgatas testified that there was no other substance [to the knots];
fifth, first, the Original Teacher compassionately comforted him; second, the Buddhas manifested signs to testify and demonstrate; third, Ānanda, not yet clear, requested further instruction.
IV. The Tathāgata’s Explanation to Remove Doubts; V. The Great Assembly’s Receiving of the Teaching and Attaining Enlightenment.

First: At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still in training, and also for the sake of all sentient beings of the future—to serve as the cause for transcending the world and as eyes for the coming age—used his hand of Jambūnada purple-gold light...

He stroked Ānanda’s head out of compassion for Ānanda and all those still in training (*śaikṣa*). Because Ānanda had previously made this request, and because he was acting specifically for the sake of those in training—whose faculties and fetters remained intact such that they were still unaware of them—he taught that liberation comes from the very roots; for they were still racing their minds elsewhere in search [of a teacher].
The World-Honored One took pity on them and felt compassion for future sentient beings who are currently within the cycle of saṃsāra and have not yet escaped suffering and hardship.
By relying on the Dharma to untie their knots, they can transcend birth and death; therefore, it is said that this serves as the cause for transcending the world.
This accords with Ānanda’s request to be spared from saṃsāra: by following these teachings to practice and realize them, one may transcend the path of delusion.
Therefore, it is said that he acts as the eye for the future. This accords with Ānanda’s request not to fall into the three realms of existence.

The touching of the crown of his head with the hand signifies receiving and comforting him; it also symbolizes that what is to be taught below is the most supreme *uṣṇīṣa* (Crown) Dharma, while simultaneously responding to Ānanda’s request for unsurpassed instruction.
Second, the manifestation of signs by the two Tathāgatas to provide certification and demonstration.
First, the manifestation of signs by all Buddhas; second, the demonstration for sentient beings to hear and realize. Regarding the first:
immediately, the Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions shook in six ways, and Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust dwelling in those worlds [appeared].
From each of their crowns, precious lights issued forth. Simultaneously, these lights came from that world to the Jeta Grove and descended upon the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.
The great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.
The sixfold trembling of the Buddha-worlds in the ten directions signifies that once this Dharma is practiced, the six knots of all sentient beings can be simultaneously untied.

Since there is a Buddha presiding over each and every world, and when considered collectively their number is like the dust motes of the great earth, they are called "Tathāgatas as numerous as fine dust.
Because they are manifestly seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), excluding those of the past or future, it says "abiding."
Regarding the world: the fact that each has a jewel-light emerging from their crown signifies that their faculties are perfected and internally luminous;
it also signifies that what is to be explained below is the most supreme and wondrous Dharma.
That these lights simultaneously appear in that forest of arrival signifies that the various transformations of the mundane vessel-world are manifested through the power of mindfulness.
Because it is unsurpassed awakening, the consecration of the Tathāgata’s crown signifies the granting of authorization for realization.
This great assembly rejoices that there shall be immense benefit, for this auspicious omen is extraordinary. The two assemblies hear this demonstration of realization.
Thereupon Ānanda and the great assembly together heard the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, speaking with one voice:

"Excellent, Ānanda! If you wish to recognize and know the root of affliction that causes you to revolve in birth and death—the fundamental source of co-nascent ignorance—it is none other than your six sense faculties; there is no other thing. Furthermore, if you wish to know unsurpassed Bodhi..."
It shall cause you to swiftly realize the blissful liberation of wondrous, eternal tranquility. Furthermore, these six sense faculties of yours are not other things;
having attained what was never before experienced, you feel the Buddha’s empowerment. Thus, Ānanda and the great assembly were all able to hear from afar.

The fact that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions speak with one voice in different mouths reveals the identity of the Way and clarifies its trustworthiness. [The *Avataṃsaka* says] "the ten directions together..."
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* shows that all Buddhas teach this in common; Amitābha’s exhortation to believe in the six directions is also of this same intent.

He addresses Ānanda alone because he is the host who requested the teaching. "Excellent" (*sādhu*) is a term of praise, used because what he has asked constitutes the pivotal point for resolving the knots and practicing realization.
"If you wish to know and realize... [proceeds] by establishing that the knots reside solely within the sense faculties (*indriya*). [End of preceding section].
Ānanda asked how these fetters are to be understood as desire; it is simply that innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) is what this sutra refers to as the deluded "clarity" within false clarity.

It is called "innate" because it has coexisted with [sentient beings] from the beginningless past—this is what was previously stated regarding its simultaneous arising and ceasing with all forms of ignorance.
Once this delusion stirs, the three subtleties and six gross states unfold in succession.
Because they arise [from this], it is said that they cause you to revolve in birth and death.
Thus, one knows that the meaning of co-nascent ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) corresponds to the primary knot; the remaining five knots arise in dependence upon this, and are therefore called "roots.

Their substance is contained within the eight consciousnesses, while their function manifests within the six sense organs. There is no possibility of these knots existing apart from the roots; hence, it is said: "Only..."
Your six sense organs are nothing other than this; how can this proof be interpreted as having the meaning of "knots"?

Furthermore, when you wish to know [the nature of] the proofs regarding liberation, it is simply because you follow the sense organs. When Ānanda previously asked from what source liberation is named, that was precisely because he wished to know further.
One must not sink into the realization of the fruit regarding unsurpassed Bodhi; rather, let us speak in terms of the causal mind.
Since the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, there is no impediment to designating it as "unsurpassed. This true essence of the six natures is identical to the original cloth that binds them.
By taking this as the causal mind to untie the knots through cultivation and realization, one does not pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* but suddenly attains the two fruits.
Therefore, it is said: "It causes you to quickly realize [the fruit]," and so forth. Bliss is precisely the fruit of wisdom; one enjoys all...
Because it is the Dharma, liberation is the fruit of abandonment, for it is the distancing from all suffering; these two are spoken of in terms of cultivated virtue (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*).
Quiescence is also the fruit of abandonment, meaning that its nature is inherently unmoving in its profound stillness and tranquility;
wondrous permanence is also the fruit of wisdom, meaning that its subtle, true, and eternal nature is inherently unimpeded; these two are spoken of in terms of innate virtue (*asamskṛta-guṇa*).

However, since it is said that "swift realization" seems to pertain to cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), one must speak of it as necessarily encompassing innate virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), because the fruit penetrates back to the source of the cause.
Furthermore, since true nature (*tathatā*) is the very root of bondage, when bondage exists, nature itself exists.

Although liberation follows along with this nature, it still does not depart from the sense-faculties. Therefore, it is said: "It is none other than your six faculties; they are not some other thing. From what is this realization named?
This explains the meaning. The Buddhas have finished manifesting signs to provide certification and instruction. Third, Ānanda, not yet having attained clarity, requests further instruction.
Although Ānanda has heard such a Dharma-sound, his mind is still not clear. He prostrates himself before the Buddha and says:
"How can it be that my cycle of birth and death and the wondrous, eternal bliss are identical to these six sense faculties and nothing else?"
The "Dharma-sound" mentioned above refers to what has been taught by all the Buddhas. There are two meanings regarding those who hear this but do not yet understand clearly:
first, they doubt why it is that among the aggregate of the sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), only the sense organs undergo binding and liberation;

second, they doubt that if binding and liberation belong to the sense organs alone, then since the sense organs must be the fundamental source, why is it instead that the nature of Bodhi is taken [as the basis]?
