These doubts will be resolved below at the point where the World-Honored One provides his explanation.
"I have seen it myself. Why should I cause you to harbor doubts and ask such questions?

Herein, the "Peaceful Bliss, Wondrous Permanence" and the "Nirvana of True Purity" from the subsequent section are each presented separately because the principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*) are of one essence and can mutually encompass one another.
Second: The Tathāgata’s Explanation to Remove Doubts (that is, explaining what the Buddhas have taught in order to remove Ānanda’s unresolved doubts). 2.
First, the prose section. Second, the verse section. Regarding the first:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "The faculties and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual. The nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky."

“Ānanda, knowledge arises from objects, and characteristics exist because of the sense faculties. These characteristics and the faculty of seeing lack inherent nature; they are like two reeds leaning against each other.

Therefore, when you now establish a further cognition upon your own knowing and seeing, this is the very root of ignorance. When knowing and seeing are free from the act of seeing, this is nirvana—taintless, true, and pure. How could any other thing be admitted within this?”

First, the commentary explains why the doubt regarding the binding and liberation of the *indriyas* (faculties) alone is raised. In this text, "bondage" (*bandhana*) and "liberation" (*mokṣa*) are synonymous with "binding" (*grantha*) and "untying" (*vimocana*).

The reason the Buddha’s intention does not focus on the *viṣayas* (objects) is that although the faculties and objects differ in being internal and external, they both involve the subsumption of the derivative under the fundamental, as they arise from a single source;
that is to say, both the perceived characteristics (*nimitta*) and the seeing faculty (*darśana*) arise based upon self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*). Thus, when the faculties are bound...
Dust also constitutes bondage; when the faculties are liberated, the dust is likewise liberated along with them. From the very beginning, there is no duality between them.
Therefore, one takes only the faculties of sentient beings and not the objects of the insentient world, because sentient beings possess cognition and are thus proximate to the fundamental nature.
If that were so, then consciousness (*vijñāna*) would also be sentient; why, then, is it not included?

Because consciousness is merely the false conceptualization of the characteristics of external objects, like flowers in the sky—arising and ceasing without source, neither capable of being bound nor capable of being liberated.

This is why the binding and the untying pertain only to the faculties (*indriya*). [The Buddha] now explains, below, the doubt as to why the root of bondage is taken to be the nature (*dhātu*). This is the Buddha’s intention.
Because cognition arises from objects, in the absence of objects, cognition and vision do not exist.

Because there are appearances due to the sense organs, in the absence of the organs, the appearances of objects are fundamentally empty. Thus, objects, appearances, cognition, and vision all lack a real nature;

they are like the intertwined stalks of a reed (a type of plant whose stalks must grow in pairs, leaning against one another, for if solitary, they cannot stand on their own). For this reason, [they are] only the self-...
The true nature is genuine knowledge and genuine vision, existing alone; there is no room for further establishing knowledge or vision.

If one were to establish knowledge or vision upon this genuine knowledge and genuine vision, it would be like the inherently luminous nature of awareness becoming falsely conceptualized as "luminous awareness.

Therefore, it is said that this is the very root of ignorance. If one realizes that genuine knowledge and genuine vision involve no further establishment of knowledge or vision, it is like returning to the source.
Awakening. Because one attains the primordial enlightened awareness (*ādi-bodhi*), it is said that "this is precisely nirvāṇa, the untainted, truly pure.

This serves to conclude the section on the origin and to grasp the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*). Nirvāṇa is the general name for the fruit of cessation; "untainted, truly pure" is the specific characteristic of the fruit of cessation.

"Untainted" refers to the previously mentioned liberation, which is the fruit of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*); "truly pure" refers to the previously mentioned quiescence, which is the fruit of inherent nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*). [The text] does not say...
The fruits of wisdom are as explained in the preceding section. What is meant by "sentence" (*pada*)? It refers to the words that conclude and indicate swift realization.

Since it is said that the fundamental source (*mūla*) consists solely of the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), if one attains this nature, then the very mention of "roots" (*indriya*) is already incorrect.
How, then, could other things be further admitted within this to act as fetters and bonds? One who understands this meaning will find peace, liberation, and the wondrous tranquility of *śānti*.
This can always be established through proof. There are two verses in praise [of this], consisting of: first, the introductory verse; second, the main verse. Regarding the first:
at that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The purpose of the reiteration is that the meaning of the prose (*gadya*) was not yet fully exhaustive. The purpose of speaking in verse (*gāthā*) is that it serves as a string of flowers, making it easy to remember and uphold.
Alternatively, it is established for those whose faculties and natures are somewhat dull. The section on the actual verses is divided into two: first, the verses that correspond to the prose;

second, the verses that conclude by demonstrating the excellence of the Dharma. The former consists of two parts: first, verses explaining the initial doubt; second, verses explaining the subsequent doubt.
[Opening Prose: The initial doubt is immediately resolved, yet the doubt regarding the faculties remains.

The true nature of conditioned phenomena is empty; because they arise through conditions, they are like illusions. Unconditioned phenomena have no arising or ceasing; they are as unreal as flowers in the sky.
False speech reveals all that is true; yet both the false and the true are equally false. Since it is neither true nor not true, how can there be a seer and something seen?

In the interval between them, there is no real nature; they are like two reeds leaning against each other. Both bondage and liberation share the same cause; for the sage and the ordinary person, there are no two paths.

The initial verse transcends the nature of consciousness as being illusory. There are two kinds of consciousness: first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), which arises for ordinary beings in relation to existence;
second, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which arises for those of the Two Vehicles in relation to emptiness. In the verse, the first two lines first praise the conditioned.
The two characters "True Nature" (*zhēn xìng*) generally indicate the reality upon which both depend; below this, both the conditioned and the unconditioned are [discussed].
Because it arises based on true nature (*tathatā*), consciousness that blazes forth in relation to objects is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*). "Empty" (*śūnya*) means lacking reality.
Now, as for why it is said to be both "blazing forth in relation to objects" and "empty and without reality": it is because it is a phenomenon produced from conditions, like an illusion.

The consecration (*abhiṣeka*) establishes the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "The conditioned within true nature" is the subject (*dharmin*); "emptiness" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); [the reason] is...
It is said that because they arise from conditions, they are like illusions as a common analogy. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) states: "Illusory phenomena arise from conditions;

illusory phenomena are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature. Conditioned phenomena arise from conditions; conditioned phenomena are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature. Regarding the two lines on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), these follow the verse on the unconditioned:
"That which is forcibly immovable is called unconditioned consciousness. Because it is unmoving, there is no arising. This is because movement and arising are [mutually]..."

Because of this cause, there is no arising, and therefore no cessation. Since arising and cessation are mutually dependent, that which does not arise has nowhere from which it comes, and that which does not cease has nowhere to which it goes.
Because its entire substance is illusory, it is called unreal; being unreal, it is empty.
The difference lies only in the use of negation (*paryudāsa*) versus affirmation (*vidhi*). To express this through a metaphor, it is like a flower in the sky. If one were to...

The three members of this inference—the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—are inverted. The Consecration [Master] establishes the inference as follows: "The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) ultimate reality is the subject;
its non-substantiality is the thesis; the reason is 'because it is without arising or ceasing'; the concordant example is like a flower in the sky.

This is because a flower in the sky has no arising or ceasing, and a flower in the sky has no substantiality; the unconditioned is likewise so. Thus, the thesis is set forth through the process of inference.
The sūtra verses establish their propositions based on these causes; thus, there is no contradiction in meaning. If the term "true nature" (*tathatā*) were not included, what fault would there be?
It would lead to confusion with the school of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*), and furthermore, it would result in the loss of the principle of "mind-only.

The two lines concerning "falsehood" and "delusion" serve as a preemptive defense against potential questions. (One might fear someone asking: "In the provisional teachings of the Hīnayāna, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are generally regarded as false and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) as true. Why, now, do you reject even the unconditioned as unreal? Therefore, this defense is provided.)

Examining these provisional and minor teachings, they hold that the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is false and that the manifestation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is true. This clarifies that truth is established in dependence upon falsity.

Since truth is established in dependence upon falsity, that truth is certainly not true. Thus, both falsity and truth together constitute two forms of falsity. As the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (Pal-zhen lun) states:
"If there were conditioned phenomena, then there would be unconditioned phenomena. And as the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: [If there were something produced, there would be cessation.]
If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself becomes dependent; this sufficiently proves the point. [The phrase] "Yet it is not yet...

is a retrospective verse summarizing that the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) share the same source. It says: "Since consciousness (*vijñāna*) certainly lacks a substantial body, it is appropriate that it does not grasp [its object].

But the object can induce the organ and currently possesses functional efficacy; why then does it also not grasp? This is because both the organ and the object equally rely [on the same source]. Thus, regarding this very reliance...
The statement that the ālayavijñāna is "neither real nor unreal" is likewise so. The initial negation "not" (非) is a term of universal negation;
it means to universally negate both "real" and "unreal. This is because, being a synthesis of reality and delusion, it cannot be called real, nor can it be called unreal.
Since both "real" and "unreal" are inexpressible, it follows that the ālayavijñāna has no fixed nature from the outset.
How much more so regarding the two divisions of the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*), which are even less substantial.

How can one then distinguish between the faculty that sees and the object that is seen? Based on this, the faculty and the object rely upon one another, and in the interval between them there is no real nature whatsoever.
For this reason, I previously stated that they are like two reeds leaning against each other; since they are like two reeds, they share a single source and are not two distinct entities.

Therefore, both the binding of afflictions and their liberation take the six sense faculties as their basis and cause; thus, whether one becomes a sage or an ordinary person, all depend upon the cultivation of the six sense faculties.

Cultivating them in accordance with the truth leads to sagehood, while cultivating them in opposition leads to ordinariness—there are no two paths. This concludes the verse-commentary on the first doubt.
Second, the verse-commentary on the second doubt (the prose commentary’s second doubt concerns the doubt regarding the fundamental source of the knots and the grasping of their nature).
Observe that within the nature of their intersection, both existence and emptiness are absent; delusion and obscuration constitute ignorance, while clarity and illumination constitute liberation.
When you observe the "nature" within their intersection, I am instructing you to apply effort to investigate within the point where the sense faculties and their objects intersect.
Ultimately, what is this fundamental, original self-nature of the pure mind? When one speaks of its emptiness, all phenomena manifest through form;
when one speaks of its existence, even that "one" cannot be grasped. Therefore, it is said that both emptiness and existence are negated.

Within this state where both emptiness and existence are negated, there is the pure truth of the Middle Way, which is precisely the fundamental, original, true mind of self-nature. As soon as a single thought arises—

The formation of delusion and obscurity is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). This is what is meant in the prose section by "establishing knowledge within knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana-viddha-jñāna*), which is the very root of ignorance.
If, however, not a single thought arises, one naturally manifests clarity and thereby achieves liberation.

This is what is meant in the prose section by "knowledge and vision being without seeing" (*jñāna-darśana-nir-darśana*), which is *nirvāṇa*. One who understands this meaning realizes that the source of all knots is solely...
One need no longer harbor doubts regarding the grasping of true nature. This concludes the verse summary of the prose section.

Second, the conclusion and demonstration of the excellence of the Dharma, in four parts: first, the excellence of the attainment of the fruit; second, the excellence of the manifestation of principle; third, the excellence of the accomplishment of practice.
Fourth, the Subtlety of Establishing the Teaching. First:

Understanding the Sequence of the Causes for Untying the Knots; "When the Six Are Unraveled, Even 'One' Perishes"; Selecting the Root for Perfect Penetration; Entering the Stream to Attain True Enlightenment.
The preceding section has already demonstrated the origin of the knots; now we shall proceed to demonstrate the untying of the knots.
However, the binding proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, like a person putting on clothes; the untying proceeds from the coarse toward the subtle, like a person taking off clothes.

Therefore, it is said that this follows a sequential order. Regarding the six knots, it is taught that their source is one. Since the knots do not exist, what further name can be given to the source? Thus it is said:
When the six are resolved, the one also perishes; when the six are resolved and the one has perished, the pure truth manifests.
However, among the six faculties, some are complete and others are not, and their cultivation differs by factors of ten million. Therefore, one must select from among the faculties.

Having chosen a single faculty that is perfectly penetrating, rely upon it to enter the stream and cause the objects of perception to perish. Thereby, one can gradually untie the knots until the state of perfect enlightenment is attained.
How wondrous, then, is the fruit toward which it tends! Second, the wondrousness of the revealed principle:
"The subtle *ālayavijñāna*, whose habitual tendencies form a violent torrent; fearing that [beings] might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly expounded it."
Building upon the previous discussion regarding the selection of superior faculties, it is granted that those with the faculty of "perfection" (pariniṣpanna) enter the stream and achieve awakening.
This is because the nature within the faculties is precisely the *ādāna-vijñāna*. *Ādāna* is a synonym for the *ālaya-vijñāna*;

its full name is *ādhāna*, which translates as "grasping and maintaining. It possesses three meanings: first, grasping and maintaining the physical body so that it does not decay; second, grasping and maintaining the seeds [of existence].

The Son [of the Buddha] commands that it not be lost or scattered. Third, grasping brings about the continuity of rebirth. Some may interpret this as the *amala-vijñāna* (stainless consciousness), but that is not the intended meaning of this sutra.

Regarding the term "subtle" (*sūkṣma*): it is not like the preceding six consciousnesses, whose modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and manifest, such that they are known by all ordinary people and those of small capacity.
"Habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) refers specifically to ignorance (*avidyā*). Ignorance is called a "habitual tendency" because it has coexisted with [the mind] since beginningless time.
It is precisely because [the mind] has coexisted with beginningless [ignorance], undergoing successive mutual perfuming and transformation, that its arising and ceasing never cease;

thus, the various fetters gradually arise like a violent torrential stream—this is what is meant by "forming" them. Now, since the formation of these fetters arises from the false perfuming the True, their unraveling requires only the True to perfume the false.
Since both the True and the False reside within this same consciousness, the unraveling of the knots is as easy as turning over one's palm. So it is said:
This refers to the faith that enters the stream and achieves perfect enlightenment. If this is so, why does the ordinary sūtra not speak of it exclusively?

It is because this consciousness is a synthesis of the true and the false; were it to be taught at an inappropriate time, there is fear that sentient beings of sharp faculties might grasp the false as true and fall into the pride of superiority, while sentient beings of dull faculties would mistake the true for the false.
Out of delusion, they give rise to fragmented views. For this reason, I have never expounded [this] in my ordinary discourses, as it would be without benefit and even harmful.
Now that the proper time has arrived, I shall speak according to the needs of those who are ready.
The extinction of delusion and the restoration of truth depend entirely upon this single act. Is not the principle revealed thereby all the more wondrous?
Third is the wondrousness of the perfection of practice:

the mind grasps at its own mind, whereby that which is non-illusory becomes illusory phenomena; yet when there is no grasping, there is nothing that is not non-illusory. Even the non-illusory does not arise.
How is the illusory dharma established? This is called the Wondrous Lotus Vajra King Jewel-Awakening, the Samādhi of Illusory-like [Reality].
With a single snap of the fingers, one transcends the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding what was mentioned above—namely, that "habitual tendencies form a violent torrent"—this refers to the power of the perfuming of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*). At this point...
The *ādāna-vijñāna* transforms to give rise to the two divisions of the perceived (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiver (*darśana-bhāga*).

Since these are both the same self-mind divided into the grasping subject (*grāhaka*) and the grasped object (*grāhya*), it is said that "the self-mind grasps the self-mind. Because they are both the same self-mind and fundamentally lack subject and object, they are not an illusion.

Yet, because they transform to give rise to the perceived and the perceiver, with subject and object established as distinct entities, they constitute an illusion. Thus, one knows that what is "not an illusion" is [only] in relation to [the illusory].
The designation "illusion" is established through conceptual construction. If one does not grasp at it, then subject and object vanish and merge into the same as one's own mind;

because the dependent designation of "illusion" is lost, there is nothing that is not illusion. Since there is nothing that is not illusion, the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) does not arise.

If even the *ālayavijñāna*—which is not itself an illusion—does not arise, how much less can the illusory phenomena of seeing and appearances be established? In this way, the true mind alone shines forth in clarity.
This is called the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*). Taking this as its cause, it is likened to a lotus flower because the cause encompasses the ocean of fruits;

that is, the flower itself is the fruit, which can be compared to the meaning of the cause encompassing the ocean of fruits. Relying on this, one severs delusions such that there is no delusion left unsevered;
therefore, it is likened to a diamond (*vajra*), for it is taken to mean that whatever it strikes is immediately destroyed, comparable to the state where no delusion remains unsevered.
Because it has the meaning of severance: relying on this, one subdues Māra, and there is no Māra that is not crushed;
therefore, it is likened to a king, for a king can defeat his enemies and all submit wherever he goes. Because it benefits sentient beings: relying on this, there is no being that is not benefited;

therefore, it is likened to a treasure, for a treasure can provide relief to things in distress and reach everywhere. Because it contemplates phenomena: relying on this, there is no phenomenon that is not understood.
Therefore, it is named "Awakening" (*bodhi*); for Awakening is precisely the Buddha, who possesses all-encompassing wisdom.

Cultivating based upon this is cultivation that is itself non-cultivation; hence, it is said to be "like an illusion. Since there is no cultivation in this cultivation, the source of movement is fundamentally unmoving;
thus, there is no impediment to designating it as *samādhi*. One who attains this *samādhi* obtains two kinds of excellence and gives rise to three sublime functions. Therefore—
One who can practice for even the duration of a finger-snap may transcend the stage of no-more-learning; how marvelous, then, is the perfection of their conduct!
Fourth, the excellence of establishing the teaching:
this Abhidharma is the single gateway to Nirvana for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.
This refers to that which the aforementioned former teachings could not reach; therefore, it is designated as *Abhidharma*.

*Abhidharma* is translated as "Incomparable Dharma" (*anupama-dharma*). *Bhagavān* is another name for the Buddha; it is briefly translated as "Holy Honored One" (*ārya-bhaṭṭāraka*), but in detail it possesses six meanings:
mastery (*vaśitā*), brilliance (*tejas*), majesty (*śobhā*), renown (*yaśas*), auspiciousness (*śrī*), and nobility (*prabhutva*).

Among the five reasons for not translating, the "many meanings" (多義) reason applies here as well; the ten directions also encompass the three periods of time. The subsequent verse distinguishing the Perfect [Teaching] states:
"The Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate; the Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter the perfect clarity;
those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this Dharma. Thus, we know that the Bhagavans of the ten directions are the same.
One practices in accordance with this teaching; therefore, it is called "the single path. There is no other Great Nirvana to be attained beyond realizing it through this teaching;

thus, it is called "the gate. How wondrous indeed is the establishment of this teaching! Having finished explaining and removing doubts, the five great assemblies received his instruction and attained awakening.
Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the unsurpassed compassionate instruction of the Buddha Tathāgata—
consisting of geyas and gāthās, interwoven with refined brilliance, exquisite and lucid— their minds and eyes were opened and enlightened, and they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Previously, Ānanda and the assembly shed tears while awaiting instruction; this present awakening is likewise so.
One should know that the previous shedding of tears was precisely the catalyst for this awakening. "Buddhas" refers to all Buddhas; "Tathāgatas" refers to one's own original teacher.

The demonstration of realization has no other [purpose]; the explanations that dispel doubts are all unsurpassed compassionate instructions. *Geyya* is translated here as "Verses in Response" (*yingsong*), because they correspond to the meaning of the prose (*gadya*).
It is also called "Repetitive Verses" (*chongsong*), because they are repeated for the sake of those with dull faculties or for the assembly arriving later.
*Gāthā* is translated here as "recited praise" (*fēngsòng*), because it praises merits through recitation; it is also called "direct praise" (*zhísòng*), because it is spoken directly in verse form;

it is further termed "isolated verse" (*gūqǐsòng*), because it does not correspond to the prose narrative (*chángxíng*). *Geya* refers to verses such as those on the emptiness of conditioned phenomena within true nature.
*Gāthā* refers to verses such as those on the sequence of causes for unraveling the knots. *Vyākaraṇa* concerns the mixed [verses].

The term *miśra* (mixed) refers to verses alternating with prose before and after. The term *saṃkīrṇa* (intermingled) means that verses are intermingled with prose and broken down into distinct sections.
Regarding *suvyakta* (polished and clear), this refers to the *gāthā* (verses). "Polished" (*su*) means pure and unmixed with prose;

"clear" (*vyakta*) means transparent and lucid, as single verses are immediately manifest and penetrating. Because they are mixed and intermingled, they express meanings that are profound and subtle; because they are polished and clear, they reveal them.
The Dharma is luminous and clear; thus it is said that its wondrous principle is pure and transparent. Those who have not yet awakened through the prose awaken because of the verse;

those who have already awakened through the prose increase their realization further because of the verse. Therefore, it is said that the mind and eyes are opened and clarified. "Mind and eyes" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*);
for it functions by relying on the mind to discern phenomena and distinguish cultivation. Because it possesses the significance of having "eyes," once awakening has been attained, clarity increases.
Not only were both doubts simultaneously dispelled, but he also rejoiced that he was destined for the two fruits of the path; thus, he sighed over this unprecedented occurrence.
Having verified the facts, his two doubts were finally resolved.

He tied the cloth three times to demonstrate the sequence of order. (The Master said: "To untie the knots follows a sequence; when the six are untied, even the one perishes. Because Ānanda had not yet attained realization, the Tathāgata took a single cloth and tied it into six knots to show him.

He caused him to recognize the sequence in which the knots were formed within the roots by following the sequence of tying the cloth. Once he understood the sequence of forming the knots, [the Master] further used that as a basis to demonstrate the sequence for untying them.

The meaning of "when the six are untied, the one perishes" is contained in the phrase regarding the two pillars. Therefore, in this section, only the sequence of order is indicated. (○Zhengmo says: Previous commentators saw that the number of knots coincided with the number of sense organs, and thus claimed that the six knots were a metaphor for the eyes, ears, and so forth.)

Sixth: You argue that while the six knots in the analogy have a definite sequence, the six roots in the Dharma have no such sequence; thus, you claim there is the fault of the Dharma and the analogy being inconsistent. Yet, you do not dare to attribute this fault to the Buddha, instead forcibly instructing later generations that they must not use analogies to challenge the Dharma. What kind of statement is this?

The Buddha is titled the "Omniscient One," yet if his exposition of the Dharma already carries such flaws, how could he subdue demons and heretics, or serve as a model for humans and devas? This is certainly not the case.

It is because the Buddha’s teaching of the six knots was not intended as a metaphor for the six sense organs arranged horizontally. Rather, it describes how, by tracing back from the false to the True, one proceeds through six successive layers—from the subtle toward the coarse—until the characteristics of the faculties are fully manifested.

Furthermore, when returning from the false to the True, one likewise proceeds through six successive layers—from the coarse toward the subtle—until the characteristics of the faculties are dissolved. Moreover, the sequence of tying the knots and the sequence of untying them are both recorded with great care in the sutra; however, the phrasing is concise and does not explicitly reveal these details.

When one traces them backward through the "Perfect Penetration" (*yuan-tong*) of Avalokiteśvara, the six knots appear clearly. To take that [description] and apply it to this [teaching], how could there be any fault of discrepancy between the dharma and its metaphor? Let the wise examine this closely. (3.1)

1. Ānanda recounts what he has heard and requests further instruction. 2. The two Tathāgatas skillfully demonstrate through both Dharma and parable. 3. Ānanda, having received this instruction, is free from doubt. First:

Ānanda joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him: “I have now heard from the Buddha that the Great Compassion which is without obstruction is by nature pure, wondrous, and eternal.”

These are the words of the true Dharma. Yet our minds have not yet attained realization. The six knots have been untied, but the one remains; we pray you will explain the sequence for loosening and binding them.
We beseech you to bestow great compassion once more upon this assembly and those of the future, granting us the sound of the Dharma to wash away our deep-seated defilements.

The initial statement of the intent to hear [the teaching] and the expression of thanks—"joining the palms in prostration and making this request"—is a ritual gesture of gratitude for what preceded and a formal petition for what follows.

It is called "unrestricted great compassion" because it aims to uproot the suffering of the fetters and extend its benefit universally to all beings, both present and future. Furthermore, there are two types of "unrestricted":

first, the "personally unrestricted," which means bestowing the supreme Dharma upon all without discriminating between the superior and the inferior; this is intended to exclude those who are not suitable vessels, lest they be described [as recipients].

Regarding these two dharmas, there is no obstruction. Without stinginess or secrecy, the subtle and wondrous is presented openly, like placing it upon a single platter. This is distinguished from that which is not ordinarily expounded.
Only when the mind of great compassion possesses these two meanings can one bring forth the true dharma-words of nature-purity, subtlety, and permanence.

“Naturally pure, wondrous, and eternal” refers to what is explained in the prose (*gadya*). Regarding the explanation of the origin of fetters (*saṃyojana*), it means that while in bondage, one is unstained, for the nature is inherently pure.
Regarding the explanation of the liberation from fetters, it means that upon emerging from bondage, one is supreme, wondrous, eternally abiding, and indestructible.

This is stated specifically with reference to the expressed meaning (*vācya*). “True Dharma phrases” refers to the repeated exposition in verse (*śloka*). Since the prose has already been explained, the verses are now explained once more.
This arises from the Tathāgata’s true mind and sincere heart as he expounds these five-worded phrases of the Dharma. This explanation focuses specifically on the expressive words (*vyañjana*);
one must understand that the expressive and the expressed (*artha*) are necessarily inseparable. Prose and verse mutually encompass one another without obstruction.
According to this, while it is "great compassion," it is called "unrestricted" (*asaṃvara*); while it is "Dharma-phrases," they are called "true reality."

Although he does not explicitly express thanks, his intention is already conveyed therein. ○ As for the phrase "my mind is still [unresolved]," it is like a subordinate making a request for further instruction.

Regarding the principles heard above, although I have gained a rough grasp of them, my understanding of their meaning remains incomplete; therefore, it is said that "my mind has not yet attained full comprehension."
There are two points regarding the meanings not yet fully understood: first, the six interpretations and the single disappearance; second, the sequence for unraveling the knots.

These will be seen for themselves in the section below where the Tathāgata provides his response, so there is no need for further preliminary explanation. Since I have not yet deeply grasped these matters, how could I bear to abandon them? Therefore, I seek the Buddha’s compassionate grace once more out of pity.
This request is made on behalf of those present at this assembly as well as those of the future, for both the present and the yet-to-come. This is truly because—
If the sequence is not clarified, the defilements and fetters will be difficult to eliminate. To establish only one [category] in contrast to the six would further deepen the immersion in affliction.
Therefore, I request that you bestow the sound of the Dharma and demonstrate the two meanings to cleanse this.

Second, the Tathāgata’s skillful demonstration through both dharma and parable, which consists of two parts: first, the skillful demonstration of the sequence of forming a knot and answering that "six knots dissolve into one";

second, the skillful demonstration of the expedient means for untying it and answering the sequence of "unfurling the knots. The first part has two sections: first, the initial demonstration of the sequence of forming the knot;
second, the subsequent answer that "six knots dissolve into one. The first of these has three sections: first, from... [text continues].
First, there are six parts. Second, they are collectively termed "knots. Third, their sequence is not disordered. Regarding the first two: first, picking up the cloth from the table;
second, tying a knot and engaging in dialogue. First [of these two]: [The text continues with the detailed narrative of the dialogue.]
At that moment, the Tathāgata, upon his lion throne, adjusted his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robe, gathered his *saṃghāṭī*, and took up a seven-jeweled stand.
Extending his hand over the stand, he took the flowered cloth offered by the *karpāsa* devas.
"Immediately" refers to the time when Ānanda requested further instruction; it is used here to show that one should respond as soon as the opportunity arises.
*Nirvāṇaka* (Nepali: *nivāsana*) is translated as "inner garment"; in the Tang language, this means a skirt or lower robe.

*Saṃghāṭī* is translated as "variegated fragments robe"; it is the great outer robe (*mahākāṣāya*). Because it becomes loose and droops after sitting for a long time, one should adjust and gather it up.
"Zheng" means to adjust; "lian" means to gather and collect. This is because one intends to grasp the small table and take up the handkerchief, fearing that they might be obstructive.
The "seven-jeweled table" refers to the desk before the seat; its body is made of the seven precious substances.
"Lan" means to draw near to the body for the convenience of leaning upon it. "Yinshen" (extending) means stretching out the hand toward the table to lean on it for the ease of taking [the cloth].
The cloth was knotted; *karpāsa* (劫波羅) is also called *yama* (夜摩), which translates as "time" (*kāla*). This is the third heaven of the Desire Realm.

Because jeweled layered flowers and silk cloths are what the inhabitants of that heaven offer, the Buddha took this cloth to serve as a metaphor for the nature of pure truth—the very "original knot" mentioned in the preceding text.
This constitutes the second section: the questions and answers regarding the knots in the cloth.
Before the great assembly, he tied a knot in the cloth and asked Ānanda, "What is this called?
Ānanda and the great assembly together replied to the Buddha, "This is called a knot. Thereupon, the Tathāgata folded the layered cloth again and tied another knot.
He asked Ānanda once more, "What is this called? Ānanda and the great assembly again replied to the Buddha, "This is also called a knot."
[He] tied [them]. Thus, in this sequence, he knotted and folded the flower-scarf until six knots were formed in total.
As each knot was completed, [the Buddha] took the knot formed in his hand and held it up, asking Ānanda: "What is this called?
Ānanda and the great assembly likewise answered the Buddha in succession: "This is called a 'knot'."
The first exchange of question and answer constitutes one completion. To "tie" means to interlace and bind together.
The instruction to ask what it is called teaches that one should state the name of the knot oneself as a metaphor for the extinction of knots.

The response, "This is called a knot," indicates that while the name "knot" exists, the original state of the cloth’s spread-out form has been concealed. From "Thereupon" onwards, the second exchange of question and answer constitutes another completion. It involves folding and...

The same applies to the *dié* (a type of fine woolen fabric). Zhengmo says: "The *diéhua* is a silk cloth from the Western Regions; its value is immeasurable, and even today it is still considered noble and precious.
This can be known by observing that the character 'jewel' (*bǎo*) is added in the subsequent text. Furthermore, the formation of a second knot serves to pose the question, "What is this?
thereby causing him to speak for himself regarding the name of the second knot as a metaphor for the "knot of emptiness" (*kōngjié*). He answers that it is also called...
Regarding "binding" (*bandhana*): it has already been shown that two [factors] are bound together at one time according to their sequence.
○ Thus, the sixfold sequence of questions and answers is completed. Regarding the phrase "such a sequence, etc.": this refers to reflecting upon the first and second sequences mentioned above.

Furthermore, four knots were tied again, forming six knots in total. One by one, as each knot was formed, he asked what its name was, requiring him to state the names of the fourth, third, fifth, and sixth knots.
These were used as metaphors for the four knots of the sensory faculties' stillness and movement, which arise in succession.
When he replied to the Buddha that these were called "knots," it was because he already understood that the phenomena of the fourth, third, fifth, and sixth [knots] are naturally so.
The preceding and succeeding [sections] are complete. *Guanding* says: "In this manner, each question of name and answer of binding constitutes a sequence that exists from the very moment of binding;
thus it is clearly known that these are not metaphors for the six aspects such as the eye, for those arise simultaneously rather than with the eye first and the ear last.
First, the formation of the six from one is concluded. Second, they are collectively termed 'bindings'."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "When I first tied this cloth, you called it a 'knot. This folded flower-cloth was originally but a single strip;
as for the second and third [folds], why do you and your followers again call them 'knots'? Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,"
This precious cloth, woven from flowers into a headcloth, is originally a single entity;

yet as I contemplate it, when it is knotted once, it receives the name of "one knot," and if it were knotted a hundred times, it would ultimately be called "a hundred knots. How much more so in this case, where the cloth has only six knots?
○ It does not ultimately reach seven, nor does it remain at five. Why is it that the Tathāgata permits only the first instance?
Why are the second and third instances not called "knots"?

Regarding the first instance, the Tathāgata permits the objection regarding the latter; the principle that the first winding is called a "knot" is indeed permissible. For this reason, [the cloth] was previously...
In reality, there is only one strip of cloth; because one knot and one strip correspond exactly, once the strip has already formed a knot, it loses its name as a "strip.
Since the strip no longer retains the name "strip," then two or three loops likewise should no longer be called "knots."

Therefore, it is difficult [to explain] by means of the second or third [case]. "How is it that you all further name them 'fetters'? Here, "cáo" (曹) is synonymous with "bèi" (輩), meaning "class" or "group.
○ Below, Ānanda answers in six points regarding the hundred illustrations. "Jeweled layered flowers" likely refers to flowers from the heavens.
Because it can be spun and woven, it is said that "spinning and weaving produce a headcloth. "Spinning and weaving" is synonymous with "weaving.
Although they are originally one entity, this is a reversal of the Buddha’s earlier statement that it was "a single thread.
This is because the Buddha permitted only one loop to be called a "knot," while two loops or three loops were not permitted. Ānanda, although it is indeed one—
The substance is not as the Buddha has described; however, according to my own contemplation, it seems worthy of consideration.
Since the Tathāgata has already granted that one twist constitutes one knot, by this analogy we know that if a hundred twists were formed, they would ultimately be called a hundred knots.
How much more so in the case of this cloth, which has only six knots—how could these not be permitted? [He] finally did not stubbornly insist on disputing.

He granted this. Since there are only six knots, and these six knots already exhaust the dimensions of the cloth, while five knots still leave a remainder of the cloth, once the dimensions of the cloth are exhausted, it cannot be knotted again; therefore, it ultimately does not reach seven.

Since there is still a remainder of the cloth, it must necessarily reach six, and thus it does not stop at five either. It ultimately does not reach seven, for if it did, seven would not be called [a knot].
If it were still called a "fetter" (saṃyojana) even when five or six [fetters] remain, then the sixth would still be named a fetter;
why then does the Tathāgata permit this only for the first stage, while the second and third stages are not called fetters?
This is truly something I do not understand; surely there must be some reason to instruct me on this. Examining this, the Tathāgata intentionally poses a challenge to Ānanda.

I offer this argument to contest [the objection], not without reason. It accords with the explanation of the six layers of knots in the "Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ" (*Ārya-śrī-śarīra-guṇa-vyūha-nirdeśa*) found in the subsequent text.
From the perspective of their arising, they proceed from the subtle toward the coarse; from the perspective of their cessation, they proceed from the coarse to the subtle.
Even if the coarse characteristics were not explicitly termed "knots," I fear that beginners might neglect the coarse and thus fail to find an entry point for initial practice.
If one were not to designate subtle characteristics as "fetters" (saṃyojana), there would be the fear that those who practice deeply might dwell in the subtle and never reach ultimate realization.
Therefore, by means of Ānanda’s persistent debate, it is demonstrated that both coarse and subtle states are equally termed "fetters.
This is so that beginners may proceed from the coarse without the fault of skipping stages, while those practicing deeply may exhaust the subtle without the flaw of halting midway.
The three sequences were not disordered.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "This precious flowered cloth: you know that this cloth originally consists of only one strand.
When I tied it six times, there were six knots. Examine this closely: the substance of the cloth is the same, but differences arise because of the knots. "What do you think?"
"What? The first knot tied was called the first. In this way, up to the sixth knot being formed. Now I wish to take the name of the sixth knot and establish it as the first.
"No, World-Honored One. As long as the six knots exist, the name of this sixth one can never be the first.
Even if I were to spend my entire life applying the utmost discernment, how could I make this sixth knot [the first]?"

[This concerns] the confusion of names. The Buddha said: "It is so. Although these six knots are distinct, when one traces them back to their original cause, they were all fashioned from a single piece of cloth;

to try to make them chaotic and disordered will ultimately never succeed. "In this same way, your six sense faculties are also like this: within that which is ultimately identical, you have produced ultimate differences."
First, he instructs them to examine the similarities and differences. When the knots have not yet been tied, it is clearly a single cloth; thus, he allows that this is already known.
Once the six knots are formed, they appear distinctly different; therefore, he names them as "six.

Once the one and the six are established and the similarities and differences are distinguished, he further teaches them to observe closely and so forth, in order to make them know that difference arises from identity, and that by extinguishing difference, one returns to identity.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "What do you think? (*yad iha manyase*) which follows the word "intention" (*abhiprāya*), it intends to first discuss the sixth name.
If one were to tie the first name as "one," then the second would be tied as "two," the third as "three," and so on, up to the sixth;
thus, the sixth knot would constitute birth. This clarifies the sequential order.
This is a fixed sequence. Since the order is established, it is impossible for one to wish to combine the six names into one;
rather, he intentionally poses the question to have Ānanda determine it. One character in the following text is slightly incomplete;
if the character "得" (to obtain) were added, the intent of the question would then become manifest. ○ "No," and so on: Ānanda does not permit it, directly judging that it cannot be so.
He answered with "No. The passage beginning with "If the six knots still exist" clarifies the reason why it cannot be so.
The phrase "Even if I were to pass through many lifetimes," etc., further resolutely asserts that the names and meanings cannot be confused. The intent is this:

since the Buddha asked me, I thought that as one who possesses extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), I would certainly be able to name the six as one; yet I failed to realize that it is as the Buddha [has explained].

Regarding what you have asked: even if I were to rely on the power of my extensive learning and, through many more lifetimes, exhaust the brilliance of wisdom and the eloquence of speech, I would still find no principle by which to justify it. How could I suddenly cause these six knots to change their names?
Truly, I do not dare to deceive myself. ○ The Buddha’s words below are the Tathāgata’s seal of confirmation. As...
This is exactly as you have said. As for the six knots being different, we see that they are distinct from one another.
Although they are distinct, if each were a single, independent entity, it might be possible to exchange one for another;

yet, upon examining their original cause, they were all fashioned from a single piece of cloth. Since they were fashioned from a single piece of cloth, their sequence of before and after cannot be altered.
Therefore, one desires that their confusion shall ultimately never be established. ○ Thus, in the passage below, he combines them by means of the Dharma.

Although it speaks of the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), it actually refers to the "knots" within those six faculties—namely, the movement and stillness, the faculty and its perception, and emptiness and cessation.
Before the knots were produced, they were fundamentally identical; this cloth was originally but a single strip. Once the knots had been produced... [the text continues].

These are ultimately distinct; yet, by uniting them, one cannot confuse their names. However, since it is known that difference is established through identity, one gains confidence that by extinguishing difference, one returns to identity.
Thus, how could the merit of unraveling the knots be slight? First, the sequence for forming the knots has been demonstrated.
Second, the subsequent answer explains that when the six are untied, the one perishes.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you insist that these six knots cannot be made into a single one, how else could it be achieved? Ānanda replied:
"If these knots persist, disputes will arise like sharp blades. Within them, the notion will naturally occur: 'This knot is not that one.'"
Those knots do not exist here. If the Tathāgata were to untie them all today, and if the knots did not arise, then there would be neither "this" nor "that";
they could not even be called "one," so how could "six" be established? The Buddha said: "The dissolution of the six and the disappearance of the one are likewise thus."
The initial inquiry is established by means of a metaphor. "Resenting that the six do not form" means harboring an aversion toward the six knots being distinct and not desiring their formation.
"Rejoicing that the one forms" means admiring the fact that the single cloth was originally one and wishing for it to be restored as such. Furthermore, the question "How can this be achieved?
clearly indicates that understanding requires untying; thus, the question is intentionally posed to lead one to personally realize the meaning within the Dharma.
Therefore. ○ Below, Ānanda’s questions are answered according to his inquiries. If these knots remain, it means he does not know how to seek their resolution.
To desire to disarray six knots without knowing how to seek their resolution is something no one would permit;

hence it is said, "Right and wrong arise like a sharp edge," meaning the momentum of asserting right and asserting wrong has already been set in motion, like two armies whose blades have not yet clashed but whose points are already raised.
When the sharp edges arise, the two armies naturally clash; thus it is said, "within this, they spontaneously give rise to equality.

This means that within the six knots, there spontaneously arises the dispute of mutual contradiction between self and other. "To resolve them all" means to untie them completely through the sequence from the sixth down to the first.
When they are fully resolved and no longer arise, one returns to the original cloth; therefore, it is said, "then there is none."
This and that. Because there is neither "this" nor "that," all oppositions are severed. To speak of "one" is also a forced designation; therefore, it is said that one cannot even be named "one.
This is because the name "one" is established only in dependence upon "six. As for how the "six" could possibly be formed:
since even "one" cannot be established, how much less so the "six"? They naturally cannot be established. The passage beginning with "The Buddha said" below points to the Dharma to conclude.
Combined. It appears that Ānanda previously used the metaphor of a house seeking a door because he was dissatisfied with these six knots and wished for them to become one.

He did not know that one must untie the knots from their root; ordinary beings and those of limited capacity each abide in their own positions, and as long as these knots remain, they mutually contradict one another.
When the Tathāgata has untied all six knots, the pure truth is free from all relativity—this is the general principle.
"Unbinding. Yet, this is still not what is called "one. The Tathāgata wished to lead Ānanda to a complete understanding equal to his own;

therefore, he referred back to Ānanda’s question regarding the "six unbindings and the disappearance of one," and joined them together. When he speaks of the "six unbindings and the disappearance of one," it does not mean that the true essence is simultaneously lost;
rather, it simply means that the names of relative distinctions are no longer established. This is a skillful demonstration of the principle of forming knots.

Next, the response to "six being resolved and one ceasing" is concluded. Second, the skillful demonstration of the expedient means for resolving [the knots] and the response regarding the sequence of loosening the knots has two parts:
first, demonstrating the expedient means for resolution; second, subsequently responding regarding the sequence of loosening the knots.

The first part has two sections: first, citing the Dharma to initiate the discourse; second, pointing it out by means of an analogy. The first of these has two sections: first, the subtle characteristics; [the rest follows].
The three fetters. Regarding the second, the coarse characteristics of the three fetters:
first, because your mind-nature has been deluded from beginningless time, false perceptions have arisen.
To demonstrate the method for liberation, one must first identify the source of the fetters; thus it is said, "Because of your beginningless [delusion]," and so forth. "Mind-nature" refers to...

The true substance that serves as the basis is the root of these fetters; thus, a single thought of deluded movement is called "madness," which corresponds to the initial arising of ignorance and should be extinguished as the fetter.

Because it is the characteristic of the exhaustion of liberation, the union of the real and the deluded is called "confusion," which corresponds to the subsequent formation of the karmic phase and should be emptied as the fetter, for the evolving consciousness and the manifested objects have not yet been differentiated. As for the deluded emergence of knowledge and vision:

The false arising of the seer and the seen constitutes the two aspects of transformation and manifestation; in meaning, this corresponds to the fetter of awakening (*bodha-bandhana*), because awakening possesses the characteristics of subject and object.
These are the second coarse aspect and the third fetter.
When deluded thoughts arise without ceasing, the wearying faculty of sight gives rise to dust. It is like when the eyes are fatigued, there appear floating flowers;

these arise without cause within the pure, brilliant clarity due to agitation. All that exists in the world—mountains, rivers, the great earth, birth and death, and nirvana—is none other than the inverted appearance of floating flowers born of weary delusion.

First is the explanation by way of the Dharma. "The arising of delusion does not cease" means that based upon the subject (the perceiver) and the object (the perceived), one gives rise to false discrimination.
This continuity without interruption constitutes the two aspects of the continuity of cognition; it still belongs to the fetter of perception, though its mode of activity is somewhat more manifest.
Once it has become manifest, it inevitably leads to the agitation of the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*). By binding form into a root, one then clings to it.
"Grasping at signs" (quxiàng) corresponds in meaning to the "root-fetter" (gēnjié). This is because the characteristics of the roots first become manifest;

once the characteristics of the roots are manifest, one calculates names and gives rise to karma, thereby giving rise to worldly toil (chénláo). There are thus the characteristics of suffering bound by worldly karma, which correspond in meaning to the two fetters of movement and stillness.

This is because where there is the world, there are the various sensory objects (chénxiàng) such as movement and stillness, light and darkness. [This is] clarified by the following analogy concerning exhaustion.

"Exhaustion of pointing at the eyes and binding the brow" refers to the seeing that binds the root of delusion; this is because the exhaustion consists in taking delusion to be the very nature of seeing.
"The profound clarity and brilliance" refers to the nature within the sense organ; this is a metaphor for the pure fundamental mind.

Thus, in the analogy, although the exhaustion resides in the organ, the arising of the flower actually obscures the seeing-nature. In the Dharma, although the delusion resides in the seeing, the dust...
These arise and obstruct the pure mind. The Buddha’s intention was to clarify, through the metaphor of wildflowers appearing without cause, that the defilements and knots are illusory.

To know their illusoriness and not follow after them is precisely the point where the beginner first gains entry and begins to untie the knots. "All dharmas below" refers to the integration [of all things].
"All worlds" encompasses the three worlds in their entirety; "mountains, rivers, and the great earth" specifically points to the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*).

The realms (*dhātu*). Birth and death specifically refer to sentient beings; nirvāṇa specifically refers to perfect enlightenment. Both are equally dust-like fetters and are identical in their appearance to flowers.
They arise by depending proximately on the exhaustion of wisdom, giving rise to inverted views (this refers to seeing existence where there is none, grasping at names, and initiating karma).

They arise by depending distantly on ignorance, whereby non-awakening causes karma to revolve and manifest birth. Therefore, it is said that they are all "madness and exhaustion," and so forth. (Question: The Buddha raised the subtle...)

Conversely, why is it that the brief [explanations] are concise while the coarse characteristics are detailed? Answer: For those at the initial stage of practice, although the coarse aspects are difficult to comprehend, they are therefore explained in detail through both doctrine and parables. Once the coarse characteristics are understood, one enters into profound cultivation;

from that point forward, the practitioner will naturally be able to know the limits of the path through inference, rendering further detailed analysis unnecessary. This concludes the section on "Initiating by Citing the Dharma. Second, "Pointing Out by Means of Parables," which has two parts:
(1) those on the left and right do not understand, and (2) only the central person understands. First:
Ānanda said, "This knot is identical to the [original] knots; how can it be untied?
The Tathāgata took the knotted cloth with his hand and pulled it to the left, asking Ānanda, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One.
He then turned the cloth over and pulled it to the right side, again asking Ānanda, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One."

The initial inquiry asks for the method of liberation. Regarding the statement that "this affliction (*láo*) is identical to the fetter (*jié*)," it should be said: this refers to the progression from madness (*kuáng*) to affliction;
furthermore, when these share the same characteristic as the sensory objects (*chén*), they are collectively termed "fetter. However, the translated terminology here is somewhat deficient;

one should simply understand it by means of its underlying meaning. Since they are equally fetters, they must be resolved; yet, not knowing the method for their resolution, the questioner asks: "How [is this done]?"

The Tathāgata’s subsequent demonstration that [the knot] cannot be untied by partial means is as follows: pulling the tied cloth to the left from one side alone is a metaphor for ordinary beings who, deluded regarding their nature, mistakenly perceive it as existent and thus dwell exclusively in the conditioned;
dwelling exclusively in the conditioned makes it clear that they are incapable of untying it.
He then intentionally proceeded to question him by means of an analogy. Ānanda, having already understood it within the analogy, answered directly with "No.

He then immediately followed through. Subsequently, he again used his hand to pull specifically toward the right side; this was an analogy for the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) who cling to their own nature as non-existent and dwell exclusively in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The questions and answers may be understood according to the above. Within these two [analyses], his mind finally attained liberation.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I now pull at this knot with my hands from both the left and the right, yet I cannot untie it. By what skillful means could you untie it?
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, one should untie it at the very center of the knot, and then it will immediately fall apart."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "So it is, so it is. If you wish to eliminate the fetters, you must do so at the very heart of the fetters.
To begin by employing separate expedient means is to dwell exclusively in the conditioned; since this remains in motion, it can never achieve stillness."
Abiding one-sidedly in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), though free from movement, is still not true liberation. Thus, if the final knot cannot even be untied, how much less so the preceding ones?
Therefore, using the analogy to demonstrate that pulling from both the left and right simultaneously cannot untie it, you have established two propositions in the Dharma’s correct teaching:
to abandon the two extremes and seek another expedient means. How could this possibly be?
Only through understanding can [the knot] be resolved. ○ Below, Ānanda, the answer is given that it should be at the "knotting point.

The "knotting point" refers to the original place where the cloth’s top was exposed; it is a metaphor for the place where self-nature manifests. When self-nature manifests, its "top" resides within the object.
However, because one is obstructed by the movement of sensory objects (*viṣaya*), it is necessary to enter the stream and cause the objects to vanish;

thus, the knots of movement are untied and the nature of stillness manifests. As for "untieing is dispersal," not only are the knots of movement untied in this manner, but as they are released from within, the five knots of stillness and the others are dispersed along with them.
There is a profound reason why the Buddha had you speak of this yourself. The Buddha said:
He issues this seal of instruction to cause them to awaken to it for themselves. The repetition of "thus and thus" expresses deep approval.

Having already granted his deep approval, he further seals his teaching with this weighty confirmation to show that apart from this, there is no other expedient means by which one might immediately realize the meaning within the Dharma through analogy. Thus concludes the demonstration of the expedient means for liberation.
The second part, the subsequent answer, consists of four sections in sequential order: first, demonstrating that the Dharma is trustworthy; second, clarifying that knots must be untied;
third, establishing the certainty through analogy; fourth, applying the analogy to the Dharma. Regarding the first:
Ānanda, I teach that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions; it does not grasp at the coarse characteristics of worldly conjunctions.
The Tathāgata illuminates both mundane and supramundane phenomena, knowing their fundamental causes and how they emerge according to their respective conditions.

Thus, even a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he knows its very number. Before his eyes, he discerns every variety—whether pines are straight or thorns are crooked, whether cranes...
The white crow and the black crow both fully understand the fundamental source.

First, the precautionary note addresses lingering doubts from the past: (Fearing that these lingering doubts might arise—namely, that since [the Master] pointed out that "this mind is it," he has repeatedly refuted the doctrine of causes and conditions; yet now, hearing the analogy of untying the knot, it seems as though the Buddha-dharma also arises from conditions.
How can these preceding and succeeding statements be reconciled? Therefore, this precaution is made. The Buddha’s intention is that the Dharma for attaining Buddhahood which I am now expounding...

It is likewise produced from conditions; that is to say, the inherently pure fundamental mind serves as the cause, while the unraveling of knots and the cultivation of realization serve as the conditions.
Their wondrous union within the Middle Way constitutes the true cause and condition.

As for the coarse phenomena of worldly conjunction, such as a clay vessel formed through the conjunction of the causes and conditions of the wheel, cord, water, and earth, or the conjunction of semen, blood, and karmic consciousness—

These combine to form sentient beings. Ordinary people grasp at them as existing; those of the Two Vehicles grasp at them as empty. Such false conceptualization, rather than being true, is called "coarse appearance.
This should be shattered accordingly. What is presented here is not that [coarse appearance]. The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata" below reveals that the Buddha’s words are free from falsehood.
"Worldly dharmas" refer to the six classes of ordinary beings within the defiled Dharma-realm; "transcendental dharmas" refer to the four classes of noble ones within the pure Dharma-realm.

Regarding the realms: mundane phenomena take as their cause the seeds of defiled dharmas inherently present within the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), and as their condition, the wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable karmas performed in past lives.

Supramundane phenomena take as their cause the seeds of pure dharmas inherently present within the *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature), and as their condition, the practices of the truths, the bases of power, and the six perfections cultivated in past lives. [This applies to] ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle.
They do not know this; even if they were to have some insights, these would all belong to false conceptualizations and lack any basis for reliance.
Whenever the Tathāgata has an insight, he is truly able to know its fundamental cause and also knows how it arises from its respective conditions; thus, his principles are worthy of trust.
This applies not only to the coarse appearances within the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—but extends even beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
One can even know the number of drops in every single drop of rain.

As for the various distinctions within the phenomena of the present—such as how pines grow straight while thorns grow crooked, or how cranes are born white while crows are born black—one likewise understands their underlying causes, for each possesses its own specific causes and conditions. Based on this, both the environment and its inhabitants...

If even the most subtle among the two types of retribution can still be discerned and accurately explained, how much more credible must this present exposition of the causes and conditions of the Buddha-dharma be?
Second, it is clarified that what is bound must be liberated.
Therefore, Ānanda, follow your own inclination and choose one among these six faculties. Once the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of external objects will naturally cease.
When all delusions have been extinguished, what need is there for that which is not real?
Building upon the above, because these words of the Buddha are trustworthy, the fetters of the sense-faculties must be untied.
However, each of the six faculties corresponds to its own specific capacity. Now, you should select from among the six faculties according to what accords with your own mind;

once you have realized which faculty can serve as an entrance, you may proceed to practice accordingly. If you practice in this way, the six knots within the faculties will naturally be removed. As for these knots of the faculties...
If these are removed, then the two objects of motion and stillness will no longer arise. The faculties will perceive emptiness, all delusions will be extinguished, and they will perish forever.
If this were not true, what else could one rely upon? Those who are determined to restore their original truth must not neglect this.
Third, the definitive analysis by means of analogy:
"Ānanda, I now ask you: regarding this *karpāsa* cloth with six knots appearing before us, can they all be untied and removed simultaneously?
"No, World-Honored One. These knots were originally tied in succession; today they must likewise be [untied] in succession."
They are untied in succession. ○ Sixth, the knots share the same substance, yet they are tied at different times; therefore, when they are untied, how can they be removed simultaneously?
Thus, the initial question asks about simultaneous untying. By first citing the *kārpāsa* cloth, it is shown that its source is originally but a single strand, serving as a metaphor.
The fundamental mind is pure. Next, by raising the six knots appearing before one, it is shown that their karma has already formed six;
this is a metaphor for how delusive appearances have become fixed, entangling and binding. It is clearly known that these six knots cannot be untied all at once;
therefore, he asks whether they can be obtained simultaneously, causing [the interlocutor] to examine this for himself so as to understand the meaning within the Dharma. "No," [he replies]. Below...
He judges that it is impossible. Because Ānanda already understood this from the analogy, he simply judges it with "No.
Having already determined it is "No," he must still clarify the reason for it; therefore, he says: "Since they were originally tied up in sequence, they ought to be untied in sequence.
[Section 6] Following the tying, one should ask about the tying and answer regarding the tying. Suppose one wished to untie them simultaneously—[the text continues].
The one who unties must regard each of the six knots as a distinct entity; perhaps it would be possible if their initial formation as knots had occurred simultaneously.
However, since the six knots share a single substance and yet their formation was not simultaneous, how could they possibly be removed all at once when they are being untied?
This is certainly not the case. Fourth, the analogy of binding with the Dharma.
The Buddha said: "The liberation of the six sense faculties is likewise so. When this faculty is first liberated, one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

When the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous, it constitutes the liberation from phenomena (*dharma-vimokṣa*). Once phenomena are liberated, both [person and phenomenon] are empty and do not arise.
This is called a Bodhisattva attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) from within samādhi."
First is the general synthesis. Because Ānanda already understood this through the analogy, it was first presented as a general synthesis so that he might grasp its essential point.
This is like the statement: "If one pulls out any single root among the six sense organs, all six knots will be untied; it is just like untying the knots to restore the cloth.
This is followed by the specific synthesis beginning with the words "this root. Having already provided the general synthesis, there is further concern that...
Because they are confused regarding the boundaries [of the stages], they are subsequently categorized separately to allow for a detailed understanding. Within this, there are three parts;
first, the coarse fetters are resolved. According to the later passage on "Perfect Penetration" (*yuan-tong*), it says: "First, within hearing, one enters the stream and loses the object."
One immediately resolves the knot of motion. Once that which is entered is tranquil, and neither motion nor stillness arises, one then resolves the knot of stillness.
Increasing in this manner until both hearing and the object heard are exhausted, one resolves the knot of the faculties (*indriya*).

When it is now said, "this faculty is first resolved," it means that based on this nature of the faculty, one first resolves the knots of motion, stillness, and the faculties themselves. When objects vanish and the faculties are exhausted, the person has no [basis for] existence.

Based on this, it is said that one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Following this, one next understands the two fetters of "awakening" (*jue*) and "emptiness" (*kong*) among the subtle fetters.

According to the later passage on perfect penetration, it says: "When hearing is exhausted and one does not dwell [in it], awakening and that which is awakened to are empty; this is the liberation from the fetter of awakening.

When emptiness and awakening are perfectly fulfilled, that which is emptied and the act of emptying are extinguished; this is the liberation from the fetter of emptiness. What is now called "the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness" is precisely this.

This refers to the meaning within the subsequent section on Perfect Penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-vyūha*), where "the emptiness of that which is perceived by awakening" and "the extinction of that which is emptied by emptiness" are discussed.

It means that only when one reaches the emptiness of both the perceiver and the perceived does the nature of emptiness become perfect; only when that which is emptied by emptiness itself is extinguished does the nature of emptiness become clear.

This is because, in contrast to the aforementioned [stages] where one merely attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*)—which is a partial emptiness and a deluded emptiness—this state is both perfect and clear, and thus one is no longer confused by phenomena (*dharma*). Therefore, it is so called.
One achieves liberation through the dharma. Only upon the liberation of these two phrases does one resolve the final knot within the subtle fetters.
According to the subsequent text on perfect penetration, it says: "When birth and death are extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests"—this refers to resolving the knot of extinction.

The present statement, "Having achieved liberation from dharmas, both are empty and do not arise," refers precisely to the "birth and death are extinguished" and "quiescent extinction" mentioned in that later section on perfect penetration.
This refers to the meaning of "manifest presence" (*pratyakṣa*). It means that once the dharma of liberation has been established, the dharma of bondage can no longer bind;

this is termed "liberation. When one reaches this state, both person and dharmas are empty; hence it is called "universal emptiness" (*ubhaya-śūnyatā*). However, this universal emptiness still belongs to the realm of dependent establishment.
Birth and cessation still persist. If one knows that existence does not remain and emptiness does not stand, then both are empty and non-arising;
this is what is meant by "when birth and cessation have ceased. In this way, the six knots are completely untied, and True Suchness shines forth in solitary brilliance.
This is precisely the state where quiescence manifests within perfect penetration. This is called the "Concluding Verification. Indeed.
To abandon this and cultivate other gates is not true samādhi; to reach the state where both [subject and object] are empty and non-arising is not true *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.

Therefore it is said: "This is called the Bodhisattva," and so forth. (According to the judgment of the ancient masters, the stage at this point belongs to the Ten Faiths. However, upon careful examination of its meaning, it seems to correspond only to the third gradual stage.

As that text says: "When objects are no longer perceived, the faculties have nothing with which to pair. Flowing back to the source, they become entirely one, and the six functions cease to operate. This is precisely what is meant by "the initial liberation of these faculties, first attaining the emptiness of persons. Next...

It says: "The lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure, like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli. Body and mind are wondrously perfect and attain great peace and stability. This refers to the realization that the emptiness-nature is perfectly luminous, thereby achieving liberation through the Dharma.

It further says: "The secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [qualities] of all Tathāgatas all manifest therein. This refers to the state where the Dharma of liberation has already coalesced with emptiness and does not arise. Moreover, its concluding statement—that such a person immediately attains the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)—is identical to the present conclusion and verification.

By comparing these two, their respective scopes are exactly equal. Thus, we know that herein, attaining the emptiness of persons, achieving liberation through the Dharma, and attaining the patience of non-arising are merely realizations of awakening; they are not yet the realization attained through cultivation. In principle, this can truly penetrate to the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (sūkṣma-bodhi); in terms of actual practice, it still does not even reach [the level of]...

Regarding "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*): if one can practice gradually from this point, one may then be established in the stages of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*). Because practicing with the realization as the goal might lead to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), I have therefore briefly analyzed it based on the ancients.
Thus concludes the Tathāgata’s skillful demonstration through both Dharma and parables. Third, Ānanda received this instruction and was free from doubt.
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction, attained the perfect penetration of wisdom and awareness, becoming free from all doubt.
