"Having received the instruction" means they were guided and pointed toward by the Buddha. This refers to the meaning of the sequence of "the six being resolved and the one vanishing," as well as the order of "untying the knots.
"Perfect penetration of wisdom and awareness" means that through the wisdom of hearing, they realized that the nature within the six sense faculties is inherently perfect and complete.
It is pervasive, just as the jewel-flower cloth was originally but a single strip. The Dharma and its analogy are skillfully demonstrated, and the understanding is clear and distinct;
therefore, it is said that one attains freedom from doubt. Having finished demonstrating the sequence by tying the cloth.
IV. The Secret Bestowal for the Selection of the Fundamental Root. 1. Ānanda Requests Instruction on the Fundamental Root. 2. The Tathāgata Secretly Bestows the Ear-Gate. Section One: Three Parts. A.

Describing the Benefit and Expressing Doubt. B. Rejoicing at the Encounter and Fearing Misunderstanding. C. Sincere Petition through the Three Karmas. Subsection A. *Note: This is a structural outline (pīn-tí) of a commentary on the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* or related Mahāyāna sūtra exegesis concerning the practice of the "ear-door" (er-men) as the fundamental root of cultivation.*
At that time, they joined their palms, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Today our bodies and minds are radiant and clear, having attained unimpeded ease.
Although we have realized the meaning of the 'one' and the 'six' being lost, we have yet to reach the fundamental root of perfect penetration."
First, the prostration of gratitude describes the benefit. "At one time" means that the assembly gathered at the same moment.

"Joining the palms" means holding the mind in focus. "Prostrating at the feet" signifies the height of reverence. This is because, through the Buddha’s perfectly penetrating wisdom-awakening, he expresses gratitude for his instruction.
Because one does not internally cling to a self, body and mind are luminously clear. To be "luminously clear" means to be pure, pristine, and free from defilement.

Because of the hindrance of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one does not grasp at external phenomena; thus, one swiftly attains non-obstruction. Non-obstruction means being liberated from the bonds of phenomena.
Because one is free from the hindrance to the known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), this too is merely a temporary attainment of such [realization] through the perfect penetration of wisdom-awakening.
Although [the text says] "nevertheless," below this, he expresses his doubt based on his realization. Previously, Ānanda had answered the Buddha, saying: "If this knot still exists, it is..."

It does not arise abruptly. It continues until it says: "If one completely releases [all distinctions], then there is neither 'this' nor 'that. One cannot even be called 'one,' so how could 'six' be established?
This means that he has already been able to realize the principle that both "one" and "six" have vanished.

As for the phrase "even though" (*sui-fu*) used after he has already realized this, it reveals that although he knows [the truth], it is of no benefit as long as he has not yet reached the fundamental source of perfect penetration; therefore, it speaks of the "fundamental."
Regarding the "root" (mūla), there are two interpretations: first, in terms of the mundane world; second, in terms of the suitability of the faculties.
As for the mundane interpretation, within the worlds of the ten directions, each practice of perfect penetration has its own root.
Here, the fundamental root of this Sahā world is indicated, as in the verse from Mañjuśrī’s selection: "The true essence of the teaching in this region / Is pure in sound and hearing. To seek this...

Mati, it is truly through the faculty of hearing that one enters [enlightenment]. Thus we know that the ear-faculty’s perfect penetration (*karṇendriya-vyatikrama*) alone serves as the fundamental root for this Sahā world.
Regarding the suitability of capacities: since the capacities and inclinations of all sentient beings differ, they each cultivate and realize according to their own specific faculty.
Now, pointing to Ānanda’s fundamental root, as the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī, saying: "I now wish to cause Ānanda..."
"Among these twenty-five practices for awakening, who is suited to be its root? Mañjuśrī selected it, saying:
"I pray that you will bestow your grace upon the future, so that they may have no delusions regarding this gate; through skillful means, it is easily accomplished and is fit to be taught to Ānanda.
Thus we know that the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty is also the fundamental faculty of Ānanda. As the Tathāgata previously stated: "I shall now fully reveal..."

The six profound, perfect, and luminous original merits are such in their number and measure. As you examine and select those among them that you can enter, I shall clarify them for you so that you may progress.
At present, because you lack self-awakening wisdom, you are unable to discern them.
Therefore it is said: "Even so, we have not yet attained realization.
We two, Qingyu and Kongcuo, World-Honored One, have drifted through drifting kalpas, orphaned and exposed. With what heart or what concern could we have anticipated becoming kin to the Buddha?
It is like a nursing infant who suddenly encounters its compassionate mother. "If, moreover, the Way is accomplished through this encounter, then the secret words obtained [thereby] shall..."
If one awakens to the same fundamental reality, there is no difference from those who have not yet heard [the teaching].
First, one laments the past; "those of us who have drifted" refers to lamenting our own former drifting through birth and death and falling into various realms of existence.
To be "solitary" means to fall into various realms without obtaining the compassionate protection and salvation of the Sage. Drifting through birth and...
At death, there is no Nirvana to rely upon; one is left utterly exposed. To speak of "accumulated kalpas" is to manifest most clearly the long duration of this solitary exposure.
That such long-term exposure does not result in eternal sinking into the evil realms would be a great blessing indeed. How could one still possess the capacity for thought?
How could one still possess the capacity for wisdom, daring to hope to join the ranks of the Buddha’s celestial kin? Thus, those who now join the Buddha—
To be granted the fellowship of the heavenly kin is truly beyond all expectation. There is no metaphor that can adequately describe such an unexpected blessing. Thus it is said:

"Like a child who has lost its mother’s milk suddenly encountering a compassionate mother. This means that losing the mother’s milk and being on the verge of death is a metaphor for one's former state of drifting and wandering;

the precariousness of one's spiritual life (*jīvitendriya*) being restored through meeting the mother is a metaphor for now being included among the heavenly kin, receiving transformation, and reviving once more. Such is the nature of this unexpected joy.
The auspiciousness of this matter can already be seen for itself. Regarding Ānanda’s self-designation as a "heavenly kinsman" (*tiantun*) of the Buddha, Zhengmo says:
"Father, son, and brother—those who are united by Heaven constitute the heavenly kinship; ruler and minister, and friend—those who are united by righteousness constitute the human kinship.
As for the passage beginning with "If again," I fear it may be an error in the current text. It means that to be included among the Buddha’s heavenly kin was certainly beyond all expectation.
This is a source of celebration. If one can further rely on this opportunity to realize the fruits of the Path, it would truly be not failing the encounter.

Even if there were no new realizations regarding the secret words obtained today, if one were to merely understand them through the literal text as before, there would be no difference from having never heard them at all.
I fear that if this pivotal moment is missed, it may not be encountered again.
"I only know what it is like. With these threefold sincere petitions of body, speech, and mind, he prayed:

"May you, out of great compassion, bestow upon me the secret adornment and fulfill the Tathāgata’s final instruction. Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground;
then, withdrawing to conceal his secret intent, he awaited the Buddha’s silent transmission.
This opportunity having been missed, one continues to drift and fall as before; therefore, I only pray that the Tathāgata will act out of his great compassionate heart.
To cut off this drifting and falling, one must rely upon the secret adornment (miyan); thus, I seek both his compassion and his grace.

The two characters "secret" (mi) and "adornment" (yan) secretly point to the ear organ, for it is a secret, profound, subtle, and pure dharma. Regarding the phrase "to accomplish the Tathāgata," etc.:

His intention was that by bestowing this grace upon me, not only would those present at the assembly receive its benefit, but it could also serve as an instruction for the Tathāgata to provide for sentient beings at the final limit of time. It is like a compassionate father who originally composed a family code for his immediate descendants;
yet when it is transmitted to later generations, even distant scions and collateral branches still regard it as if they were face-to-face with him.
"Life. This means that one does not expect to achieve success in future lives, yet it is naturally accomplished. All of the above belongs to oral entreaty.
Having spoken these words, "prostrating with the five limbs on the ground" refers to bowing down with utmost sincerity, making the request through the action of the body.

Since one is thus able to fully know all things, there is no illness in the world that cannot be cured, and no life that cannot be sustained by the hand;
this refers to being able to treat physical illnesses. Second, the mind awakens to the medicine of the Dharma.
Serving the Tathāgata, one thoroughly understands the nature of taste: it is neither empty nor existent; it is neither identical to the body and mind, nor is it separate from the body and mind.
Through this, one awakens to the causes of taste by means of discernment.
Serving the Tathāgata may refer to Śākyamuni himself; for it is clarified in such texts as the *Brahmajāla* and the *Ratnakūṭa* that Śākyamuni attained buddhahood in this realm from time immemorial.
Since Bodhisattvas have likewise cultivated the causes in this realm from time immemorial, they are thereby able to serve him.

Having received the Buddha’s instruction through his compassionate acceptance, one realizes the nature of taste because one has tasted its principle; thus it is said that "one thoroughly knows the nature of taste.
Regarding the phrase "neither empty nor existent," Zhengmo says: "Because the tongue and the medicine touch, the taste manifests vividly, and therefore it is not empty."
Although it burns intensely, taste is non-existent because it lacks intrinsic nature; thus, it is not "existent.

Furthermore, as an object (*viṣaya*), taste is a form that possesses resistance (*sapratigha-rūpa*). Because it possesses resistance, it is not empty; because it is not seen [as a substantial entity], it is not existent.
When this initial awakening of consciousness arises and realizes its lack of substance, the body and mind—namely the tongue and the tongue-consciousness—are neither identical to nor separate from it.

Zhengmo says: Since the various medicines do not come [to the tongue] and the tongue-consciousness does not manifest of its own accord as suffering and so forth, it is not identical with the body and mind.
Since the tongue-consciousness would not taste the various medicines, how could it manifest suffering and so forth of its own accord? Therefore, it is not separate from the body and mind.
Subsequently, through contemplation, one realizes that it has no source. Furthermore, since it is not identical to the body and mind, it does not arise from the sense organs;
since it is not separate from the body and mind, it does not arise from external substances. Thus, when analyzing the cause of taste, one finds that it comes from nowhere.

When departing, there is no attachment; one should realize that all is entirely empty, such that even emptiness does not stand. Discrimination is utterly absent, and non-discriminative wisdom manifests radiantly before one.
Therefore, it is said: "From this, awakening is opened. Furthermore, this opening of awakening is not an emptiness that destroys the view of nihilism.

Awakening is not something that exists [as a separate entity], thereby shattering the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Awakening is not identical to the body and mind, thereby shattering the provisional schools' calculations regarding causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Awakening is not apart from the body and mind, thereby shattering the external schools' doctrine of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). This is what is meant by "that which can cure the disease of the mind.
The account of awakening and realization is complete. Second, the account of cultivation and realization.

Having received the seal of approval from the Buddha Tathāgata for the names of my brothers, the two bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, we now serve as Dharma princes within this assembly;
through the awakening to the clarity of flavors, our rank has been elevated to that of bodhisattvas.
The "seal" (mudrā) bestowed previously still referred to the past; what follows, stating "now within this assembly," refers to the present. "Kun-ji" (昆季) means brothers.
Because they were able to cure the two illnesses of body and mind, the Buddha conferred upon them the names Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata.
This was also to fulfill their power of past vows; thus, although they received the Buddha’s seal, they did not consent to attain a lesser [attainment].
To fulfill [the requirements], benefit sentient beings, adorn the lands, and advance in the practice of the Dharma King, he now manifests in the assembly of the Buddha as a Prince of the Dharma.
He further cultivates his previous contemplation, again taking flavor as the cause for awakening to clarity.

That is to say, while previously he analyzed the cause of flavor and realized only that all things are ultimately unobtainable, he now takes the sensory object of flavor as the cause and simultaneously awakens to the awareness of it.
The self-nature is perfectly luminous; because one spontaneously delivers sentient beings from this point onward and never regresses, it is said that "the stage of Bodhisattva has been attained.
The phrase "stage attained" reveals that this is genuine cultivation and actual realization, not merely an initial awakening based solely on the Buddha’s seal of approval.
According to this, although the points of awakening for the three individuals previously mentioned, such as Dharmapāla, were consistent with the Mahāyāna, their cultivation and realization...

[The previous practitioners] briefly attained the minor fruits; now, the two realizations of Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata are both great. Having completed the detailed narration of these two realizations, [the third section] concludes with the answer regarding perfect penetration.
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied that, according to my own realization, the cause of the sense of taste is supreme.
Initially, he offered medicine to the Buddha and the Sangha, vowing that in the future he would cure the dual illnesses of body and mind for all sentient beings.

Since both his practice and vow were centered upon the sense-object of taste (*rasa*), and since taste served as the primary cause suited to their specific capacity, he considered this the most excellent.

This concludes the section on the Medicine King’s sense-object of taste. Next, regarding the five *bhadra* brothers’ sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), there are three parts: first, prostrating and making a formal declaration; second, [the recitation of] the...
This section has two parts: the testimony and the conclusion of the perfect penetration.
First: Bhadrapāla, together with his sixteen companions, Bodhisattvas, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

Bhadrapāla is translated here as "Good Protector" (Shànshǒu) or "Good Guardian" (Shànhù). This means that he is able to protect himself through wholesome dharmas and is also able to protect others through wholesome dharmas;
alternatively, because he possesses specific skillful means for both protecting himself and protecting others, he is called "Good" in both respects.
He is also translated as "Worthy Head" (Xiánshǒu), as his rank is that of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), making him the foremost among the worthy ones. He is a companion.
"Those who practice the same path together" refers to companions on the Way. "Kaisa" (開士) is an alternative name for a Bodhisattva. The *Zhengmai* (正脈) states:

"It is a title for one who is able to awaken themselves and, simultaneously, is able to awaken sentient beings. Second, a detailed account of the two types of realization: first, the account of awakening-realization (*wu-zheng*);
second, the account of cultivation-realization (*xiu-zheng*). First [the account of awakening-realization]:

In the past, we heard the Dharma from the Buddha Vimalacandra and left the household life. While entering the bathhouse according to custom during the time for bathing the Sangha, we suddenly awakened to the cause of water:
it neither washes away dust nor washes the body; in the interval between these two, one attains a state of tranquil non-existence.

"I" refers to myself; "others" refers to my companions. We were all members of the arrogant assembly during the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja who later encountered the edification of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging.
"In the past" refers to the past, specifically the time of the Buddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja. Regarding why the Buddha is called Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"His divine wisdom is immeasurable, and he leads all beings. The *Yāoyì* (Essential Explanation) says: "Because of his greatness..."
His voice pervades the world because he fearlessly preaches the Dharma as a King of the Dharma.
According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there were twenty trillion Buddhas following the Buddha Vimalasvararāja in succession.
Bhadrapāla was to be among the disciples of the first Buddha’s Dharma-period, as he was a contemporary of Maitreya (Aśoka). As that sūtra concludes by identifying them: "At that time..."

The Bodhisattva Never Disparaging was none other than myself. Those among the fourfold assembly who at that time constantly disparaged this bodhisattva were none other than the bodhisattvas Bhadrapāla and others in this present assembly.
Initially they were a haughty multitude, but later, having witnessed the supernatural power of Never Disparaging, they became faithful and submissive, following him.
Thus, they were able to hear the Dharma, leave the household life, and attain realization. This was indeed because...
It is not that he was lightly inclined to hear the Buddha’s bequeathed Dharma and leave the household life.

In the present text, it is stated directly that he heard the Dharma from Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja Buddha and left the household life; this is because past events are described briefly rather than in full detail.
"When bathing the Sangha" refers to the time when the assembly of monks uses the bath every half-month. "Entering the room according to custom" means following the assembly of monks.
For example, when entering the bathhouse to receive a wash, one should follow the Vinaya rules for the seven classes of followers regarding pure bathing established by the Buddha.
To "suddenly awaken to water as a cause" means to suddenly realize that tactile sensations such as roughness or smoothness have water alone as their cause and possess no inherent nature.
This is like feeling a sensation of roughness when first washing away dust, and subsequently feeling a sensation of smoothness when washing the body.

Regarding contact: if one neither washes away the objects nor washes away the faculties, and if between the faculties and objects there is only ordinary stillness and composure, such that nothing exists and discrimination naturally does not arise, then as for awakening and realization, one is already equal to those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
This was not attained through cultivation. Second, the account of cultivation and realization:
my past habits were never forgotten, and thus until this present time, I have followed the Buddha into the homeless life and attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
That Buddha called me Bhadrapāla; through the manifestation of sublime touch, I dwell as a son of the Buddha.

"One who has not forgotten their past habituation" means that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from awakening and realization in previous lives have not yet been forgotten during the intervening period.

According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, from the time of the first Buddha Vipaśyin, through two trillion successive Buddhas of the same name, and further through those such as Candrasūryapradīpa and Meghasvararāja, one finally encounters the appearance of the present Buddha. This is stated thus by way of abbreviation and omission. Therefore, it says: "Now..."
Up to the present time, because he was a disciple who personally entered the gate, it is said that he "left home following the Buddha.

Because he received the teachings, severed his delusions, and realized Arhatship, it is said that he "caused him to attain the stage of no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*). However, since it is stated that his past habits were not forgotten, his realization must have already existed;
that it is now said he "caused him to attain" it upon the Buddha’s appearance in the world clearly indicates that this was a matter of cultivation and realization, without any doubt.
"That" refers to the time when one attains the state of *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning).

According to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, those with arrogant dispositions who, out of malice, despise Avalokiteśvara for not despising them, shall for two hundred billion kalpas never encounter a Buddha, never hear the Dharma, and never see the Saṃgha;
furthermore, for a thousand kalpas they shall undergo great suffering in the Avīci Hell. Yet, even so, they are still able to cultivate their former wholesome habits.
Because he had forgotten to guard his roots of goodness, the Buddha named him Bhadrapāla. Although he received the Buddha’s seal of approval, he did not abide in the Lesser Vehicle;

rather, he advanced to contemplate that the subtle and wondrous objects of touch are fundamentally the manifestation of the Tathāgatagarbha nature, and thus he was called Xuānmíng (Proclaiming Clarity).
Since "proclaiming clarity" carries the meaning of "manifestation," from then on he spontaneously delivered sentient beings according to their needs.
Because they dwell in dependence upon the world, it is said that they dwell as children of the Buddha. This concludes the sequential narration of the two proofs.
Third, the conclusion and response regarding the perfect penetration:
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I replied that, according to my realization, the cause of touch is supreme.

Observing the sense-base of touch (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), one enters the Path; because past habitual tendencies are not forgotten and one now easily attains self-awakening by taking touch as the cause, it is called "supreme.
As for the phrase "as I have realized," this is spoken solely from the perspective of one's own experience, not to force others to conform to oneself.

This concludes the section on the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavyaviṣaya*) by Bhadra. Third, the three sections on the sense-object of mental phenomena (*dharmaviṣaya*) according to the Kāśyapa school: first, performing prostrations and making a formal declaration.
Second, the sequential narration of the two proofs; third, the conclusion and response regarding perfect penetration.
First: Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī Golden Light, and others rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Mahākāśyapa—here translated as "Great Kauruṣya"—is his clan name. His ancestors practiced the Way until they moved the spirit of a divine tortoise to carry forth a celestial chart;
consequently, they took this as their surname. His personal name was Pipphala, because his parents prayed to the deity of this tree and he was born therefrom.
He is also translated as "Drinking Light" (Pītabhāsa), because the radiance of the Venerable One's body eclipsed all other light.
The nun Suvarṇaprabhāsā was his wife; the karmic connection between husband and wife will be explained in detail below. The term "etc. refers to her followers. As he describes them later himself:
"They are my own retinue who simultaneously resolved their minds [for enlightenment]," referring to those who followed him into the homeless life.
Part Two: A detailed account of the two types of realization, divided into: 1. An account of realization through awakening; 2. An account of realization through cultivation.
The first two [sections]: first, receiving retribution according to causes; second, attaining the fruit through the contemplation of dharmas. Regarding the first:
In a past kalpa, there was a Buddha who appeared in this world named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp). I was able to draw near to him.

Having heard the Dharma, he practiced and studied it; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he made offerings to the śarīra, lit lamps to maintain the light, and coated the Buddha’s images with purple-gold.
From that time forth, in birth after birth and life after life, his body has always been perfectly complete as a mass of purple-gold light.
These bhikṣuṇīs, such as Cīrṇābhāsottama-prabhā, are my own retinue; they resolved their minds for enlightenment at the same time as I.
Regarding "in past kalpas," according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this refers to immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas ago.
"In this world" indicates that it was not in another land. "The Buddha’s name was Candrasūryapradīpa" means that his light shone like the sun.

The sun causing people to engage in their labors during the day is a metaphor for conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) illuminating phenomena. The moon illuminating the night to bring people coolness is a metaphor for ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) illuminating principle.
The lamp that connects the sun and the moon is a metaphor for unimpeded wisdom (*asaṅga-jñāna*). Principle and phenomenon are illuminated simultaneously, being neither different nor identical.

This is the title for the perfect illumination of the three types of wisdom (*trividya*). According to that sutra, there were twenty thousand Buddhas, such as Candrasūryapradīpa, who succeeded one another.
The Buddha mentioned by Kāśyapa here appears to be the very last of them; for he speaks directly of the events after that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and does not mention any others.
If he had intended to speak of other Buddhas directly, he would have had to provide a brief account of them. As for my having attained the opportunity to draw near [to him]...

It was only upon first encountering the Lamp of Wisdom (Dīpaṃkara), hearing the Dharma, and practicing it that one first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). "Śarīra" translates as "sacred relics.

Those who make offerings after [the Buddha's] parinirvāṇa receive transformation and gratitude, as if the Buddha were still present. Thus, lighting lamps to continue the illumination and gilding images with purple gold are all matters of making offerings.
Regarding the conferral of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), the *Dharmaguptaka-dharmakośa-śāstra* states: "When Vipaśyin Buddha passed into extinction..."
Later, the gold on the stūpa and image became chipped and damaged. At that time, a poor woman obtained a gold coin by begging and hired a craftsman to apply it as a thin layer.
The goldsmith was delighted; once he had finished polishing and adorning the Buddha image, he vowed to become her husband.

For ninety-one kalpas, their bodies were constantly golden in color among humans and devas, and their minds constantly experienced bliss. Based on this, the application of purple-gold to images occurred at a later time.
Regarding this matter, it is possible that the text concerning the era of Vipaśyin was omitted during translation;
otherwise, since the subsequent passage states "from that time until now" (*ataḥ prabhṛti*), there would be no occasion for the events involving the poor woman and the goldsmith.
Furthermore, as the fundamental ground is inconceivable, it is not obstructive to accept different accounts as long as they yield spiritual benefit. As for the phrase "from that time until now":
From the time the image was naturally illuminated by lamps until the present day, its body has remained perpetually perfect as a mass of purple-gold light;
this is because, following causes, results must correspond to those causes. Thus, the nun of purple-gold light was none other than the poor woman of former times.
That goldsmith is none other than the present Kāśyapa. Because of his vow in the past, they have now become husband and wife;
therefore it is said, "He is my own kinsman. The word "etcetera" (等) is explained as before. Regarding those who resolved their minds [for enlightenment] at the same time, there are two meanings:
first, it refers to the past, meaning they resolved their minds simultaneously while painting the image; second, it refers to the present, meaning they resolved their minds simultaneously.
Regarding the two meanings of "leaving home" (pravrajyā), the latter principle is more profound. By contemplating phenomena, one attains the fruit.

I contemplate how the six sense objects in the world are subject to decay and transformation; by cultivating cessation through emptiness and stillness alone, body and mind can transcend hundreds of thousands of kalpas as easily as a finger-snap.
Regarding the statement that one contemplates the dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*) while speaking of the six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*): this is because it includes the aforementioned five [objects].
This is truly because the dharma has no separate essence; it is merely the reflected shadow of the preceding five.

If the external five objects are not extinguished, then the internal shadow-phenomena will ultimately never be fully eliminated. Therefore, the contemplator must proceed from the preceding five objects; that is, one first contemplates the five.

As sensory objects shift and change without constancy, one should immediately abandon discursive thought. When the "shadowless" phenomena naturally fall away from the mental consciousness, observe the dharmas once more;
they will spontaneously perish all at once. As for the phrase "only through emptiness and stillness," once the object of perception has ceased, the perceiving subject also dissolves.

From this point on, the six consciousnesses no longer function; this is called the concentration of non-mind. When the concentration is long-sustained and its power deepened, one advances toward cessation.
The coarse portion of the seventh manas is called the "attainment of cessation. When this attainment is cultivated, one specifically detests sensation and perception;

it is therefore also called the "attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception. When this attainment is accomplished, only the eighth ālayavijñāna remains to sustain the body, along with the subtle deliberation of the seventh manas.
Because it is no longer pulled by karma, one can transcend hundreds of thousands of kalpas. There is nothing... [text ends].
Due to his mental exertion, he emerged from this state of awareness in the time it takes to snap one's fingers. Guanding says:

"The present holding of the golden-threaded *kāṣāya* at Mount Kukkuṭapāda while awaiting Maitreya’s descent is precisely this samādhi. Furthermore, this samādhi is that in which the four fruits of the path abide.

This is obtained solely through the intensity of awakening the mind and is not related to gradual cultivation or realization. Even when the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is about to dissolve, one must still maintain it with effort.
This concludes the account of awakening and realization. Second, the account of cultivation and realization.

I have attained arhatship through the dharma of emptiness. The World-Honored One has declared me the foremost among those who practice dhūta. Through the illumination of the sublime dharma, all outflows (*āsrava*) have been extinguished.

Although I previously resided in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it was solely by awakening to the dharma of emptiness that I became an arhat; it was not [through that attainment].

This refers to cultivation and realization. Desiring to reach the stage of cultivation and realization through the endurance of ascetic practices (*duṣkara-caryā*), he was thus granted the seal of approval by the World-Honored One, who declared that his practice of *dhūta* is supreme.
*Dhūta* is also called *dhuta*; this translates as "shaking off" or "purifying. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: The Buddha said, "You are advanced in years;
you may now relinquish the twelve *dhūtas*. Kāśyapa did not relinquish them. The Buddha said, "Excellent! I...
Within the Buddha-dharma, Mahākāśyapa is foremost among those who practice the dhūta austerities. Regarding the twelve [dhūtas], the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
first, the forest hermitage (*āraṇya*); second, sitting in charnel grounds; third, dwelling at the foot of a tree; fourth, sitting in the open air;
fifth, constant sitting; sixth, always begging for food; seventh, eating in one sitting; eighth, moderation in food; ninth, not drinking liquids after midday.
10. Begging for alms in successive order; 11. Wearing rag-robes; 12. Possessing only the three robes.
By practicing with endurance, these are sufficient to shake off the dust of worldly toil; therefore, they are called *dhūta* practices.

Once the dust of toil is purified, one advances to contemplate the subtle and wondrous dharma-dust of the Buddha-fruit, which is revealed and made manifest within the *tathāgatagarbha*. Upon awakening and realization, one attains a profound resonance with the Buddha.
Regarding the fruit: examining the cultivation and abandonment [of defilements], it is limited only to that of the Two Vehicles; therefore, it is said that "all outflows (*āsrava*) are extinguished.

This means that the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) are forever exhausted.

Thus, one should know that the cultivation and realization herein are identical to those of the three individuals such as Dharmadinnā and others, and not the same as those of the three types of practitioners such as Bhaiṣajyarāja and others. This is because the two realizations of these three types of practitioners are both "Great" (*mahat*); hence, they proceed through...
The two proofs have been concluded. Third, the conclusion and response regarding the perfect penetration.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration; according to what I have realized, the causal factor of the Dharma (*dharmahetu*) is supreme.

According to the *Ekottarika Āgama*, his family was immensely wealthy—ten thousand times that of King Bimbisāra—and yet he was ultimately able to renounce it all and leave the home life. This is [the third proof].

Because their past roots have already been able to empty all that exists, they observe the transformation and decay of phenomena as the cause; since they should naturally enter [the path] with ease, this is considered superior.
This concludes the section on the perfect penetration of the six sense objects. Second, the perfect penetration of the five faculties (Zhengmo says: "If one of the six faculties is lacking...")

The faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) is retained as the rearguard to respond to the spiritual capacities of those in this realm; thus, one should examine how among the five faculties, four of them contain the term "revolving" (*xuanfan*). This is because the Dharma-gate of the nature of the faculties consists entirely of revolving the faculties to detach from objects;

the objects and consciousnesses do not function in this way, which can be seen through careful contemplation. Five [faculties]: first, the eye-faculty of Nanda; second, the nose-faculty of Cūḍapanthaka; third, the tongue-faculty of Gavāmpati.

Fourth is Pilindavatsa’s faculty of the body; fifth is Ākāśagarbha’s faculty of mind. Regarding the first three: first, prostration and presentation of the petition; second, a detailed recounting of the realization attained; third, the conclusion and response regarding perfect penetration. First: The faculty of the body is the most subtle and wondrous among the six faculties; it is the basis for all activities. It is through this that one perceives the forms of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, hears their sublime teachings, and experiences the bliss of samādhi. Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke of the faculty of the body as the means to attain perfect penetration. At that time, the Venerable Pilindavatsa rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, when I was formerly a Brahmin, I was well-versed in the Vedas and served as a teacher to five hundred youths. At that time, I had a disciple who was arrogant and disrespectful. Because he was difficult to manage, I struck him on the head with my staff. He immediately fell to the ground and died. I felt great remorse and, fearing the retribution for this karmic offense, I traveled to various places seeking a way to atone. I visited many sages and holy ones, yet none could provide me with a means to eliminate my transgression. Later, I encountered the Buddha Śākyamuni. Seeing me approach, he addressed me by name and said: 'Vatsa, you have committed a grave offense. You must now repent before the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja. I then went to the place where that Buddha resided, prostrated myself before him, and confessed my fault. That Buddha then placed his hand upon my head and said: 'Vatsa, you have already committed a transgression. You must now go to the world of Sahā and serve Śākyamuni Buddha; there you shall be able to exhaust your karmic obstacles. I followed his instruction and returned to this Sahā world. Having arrived, I saw the Buddha Śākyamuni and paid homage to him. The Buddha then asked me: 'Vatsa, where have you come from? I replied: 'World-Honored One, I have come from the world of the Buddha Bhaiṣajyarāja. The Buddha then asked: 'What did that Buddha say to you? I replied: 'That Buddha placed his hand upon my head and told me: "Go to the Sahā world and serve Śākyamuni Buddha; there you shall be able to exhaust your karmic obstacles. The Buddha Śākyamuni then said to me: 'Vatsa, you should now cultivate the practice of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra. I then cultivated the practice of Samantabhadra and, in accordance with the Buddha's teaching, contemplated the faculty of the body. After seven days, I attained the Samādhi of the Universal Radiance of the Body. By means of this samādhi, I was able to see all the Buddhas of the ten directions. Those Buddhas each extended their hands to touch my head and said: 'Good man, because you have cultivated the practice of Samantabhadra, you have been able to exhaust your karmic obstacles. You should now return to the Sahā world and preach the Dharma for all living beings. Having received these instructions from the Buddhas, I returned to this Sahā world and preached the Dharma for all living beings. Because I have attained this samādhi, I am able to see all the Buddhas of the ten directions. Therefore, I take the faculty of the body as the means to attain perfect penetration. World-Honored One, if there are living beings whose faculties are dull and obstructed, they should contemplate the faculty of the body; they will then be able to attain liberation. The Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Vatsa, you have indeed attained the faculty of the body and have been able to exhaust your karmic obstacles. You should now return to the Sahā world and preach the Dharma for all living beings. At that time, the Venerable Pilindavatsa, having received the Buddha's praise, circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid homage at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. (End of the first section.)
Aniruddha then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Aniruddha is also called Anuruddha or Aniruddhu; this is translated as 'Free from Poverty'."

He is also called Yìrú (Sukhāvatī) and Wúmíè (Aniruddha). Because in the past he offered millet porridge to a pratyekabuddha, from that time forward for ninety-one kalpas he has not suffered poverty; he has always attained his every wish and enjoyed inexhaustible blessings.
Thus, he is now the son of King Śuklodana, the Buddha’s maternal cousin and the elder brother of Ānanda.

2. Sequential Account of the Combined Realizations (Since the realization through fierce and sharp diligence encompasses both cultivation and realization, they are not treated separately; rather, they are clarified in combination).
When I first left home, I was constantly fond of sleep. The Tathāgata rebuked me, saying I belonged to the class of beasts. Hearing the Buddha’s reproach, I wept and reproached myself;
for seven days I did not sleep, and thereby lost both my eyes. The World-Honored One then showed me the Vajra Samādhi of Delightful Vision and Illumination.
Without using my eyes, I perceive the ten directions; their essential purity is transparently clear, as if looking at the palm of my hand.
The Fruit: The Tathāgata has certified me as an Arhat.
He first recounted how he was rebuked for losing his sight; how he initially left the household life; and how, failing to understand the Dharma he heard, he constantly delighted in sleep.
His being rebuked as one who is like an animal was intended to stir him by seeing the extreme depth of his ignorance. Upon hearing this rebuke, he felt shame.
Because he was deeply remorseful, he wept and reproached himself. His reproach was not in vain; it gave rise to such intense vigor that for seven days he did not sleep.
Because his vigor was excessive, his physical faculties were impaired, and thus he lost both his eyes. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
While the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park preaching the Dharma to the assembly, Nanda lay asleep therein. The Buddha spoke a verse in reprimand, saying: "Alas! Alas!"
What is meant by "sleep"? Creatures such as snails, whelks, clams, and oysters sleep for a thousand years and do not hear the name of the Buddha.
Aniruddha practiced with such diligence that for seven days and seven nights his eyes did not blink; consequently, his physical organs perished. This is a brief account related by Aniruddha himself.
[The passage] from "World-Honored One" downward describes how he received the teaching and attained the fruit. The World-Honored One took pity on him because of his blindness.
Therefore, he demonstrates this through samādhi. The name of this samādhi is "The Vajra of Joyful Vision and Illumination.
This means that when first initiating contemplation, one need only rely on the nature of joyful vision and illumination; it is also the state of entering the stream and losing the object.
Once the entry-point has become still and light and darkness no longer arise, and as this gradually increases until both the seer and the seen are exhausted, one then receives the name "Vajra."

This means that by relying on the power of the faculty of exhaustion (*kṣayendriya*), one advances to shatter deep delusions; its universal penetration and severance of remaining fetters is as sharp as a vajra.
It is also identical to the *karṇa-dvāra-samādhi* (ear-gate samādhi), and thus bears the meaning of the "Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening.

Once this samādhi is perfected, the fundamental luminosity is manifested; therefore, it is not perceived through visual observation. As stated in the *Abhiṣeka*: "The ten directions refer to the trichiliocosm."
This refers to the ten directions within [the mind]. Because it is utterly detached from the sense organs and their objects, it is called "the refined and true nature, penetratingly clear.
This means that the seeing-refined true nature is penetratingly clear and unobstructed; if one were to use a metaphor to describe it, it would be like observing fruit in the palm of one's hand.

Based on this, even the celestial eyes obtained as karmic retribution by devas and humans likely could not compare with the Venerable One’s [vision] to determine which is superior or inferior. Thus it is sealed and confirmed.

As for the Arhat, because his vigor and sharpness were such that both types of realization arose simultaneously, he did not need to continue practicing toward further realization after his initial awakening and certification, as was the case with Cienana and others.
This concludes the third response regarding the perfect penetration of the path.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties. "As I have realized it," [Ānanda] said, "to revolve the seeing and follow back to the source is the foremost.
'Revolving the seeing' means to turn back that seeing which pursues external objects, thereby becoming free from the burdens of those objects.

'Following the source' means to follow back to the original, true seeing, thereby becoming free internally from the knots of the sense organs. This accords with the meaning of the Perfect Penetration of the Ear-faculty, where both the hearing and the heard are exhausted.
Following the previous sequence of unfolding and binding, the meaning corresponds to this root being first liberated. The samādhi is named "Joyful Vision Illumination" (Lèjiàn zhàomíng).
By riding upon this superior progress, the subsequent knots can then be established and liberated; the samādhi is named "Vajra" (Jīngāng).
However, Naluo (Aniruddha) was specifically afflicted by delusion regarding sensory objects, so the World-Honored One instructed him to turn back his vision and forget external objects. Naluo...

The Vinaya masters primarily concern themselves with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasya*), which destroys the teachings of the World-Honored One; by following the source and detaching from the faculties, one naturally enters [the path] when correctly matched to their specific capacities.
Therefore, it is said that this is the foremost. This concludes the section on the eye-faculty of Nanda. Second, the nose-facity of Cūḍapanthaka.
First, he pays homage and makes his declaration; second, he recounts the two proofs; third, he concludes with the answer regarding perfect penetration. Part one.
