This is because, from beginning to end, they witnessed it with their own eyes and saw it directly; thus, they gained faith in the benefits of transcending the world and developed a sense of renunciation toward worldly existence.
In the midst of this impermanence, he deeply realized that craving is the root of all outflows (*āsrava*). His frantic mind suddenly ceased;
where cessation occurs, that is *bodhi*. Thus, he was able to liberate himself from the outflows of worldly craving.

Regarding these "worldly" outflows of craving, they are here discussed specifically in terms of the two delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*). However, these too are merely eliminated simultaneously with awakening, and are not [separately extinguished].
This concludes the sequence. Second, the account of cultivation and realization:

Having received the Buddha’s teachings on the precepts, from these [rules] up to the three thousand modes of deportment and the eighty thousand subtle *śīlavipatti* (transgressions of conduct) and *pratikṣepaṇasāvadya* (prohibited actions), all were completely purified.
Body and mind attained quiescence, and he became an Arhat. ○ I am the pillar within the assembly of the Tathāgata.
Record: Kinkin was held in high esteem by the assembly for his observance of the precepts and cultivation of the person.
Initially, when he attained the fruit through the observance of the precepts, he believed that this was sudden enlightenment (*tongo*). It was not known that it was gradual cultivation;

therefore, following the Buddha’s teaching, he was instructed in the observance of the precepts. To instruct him in the observance of the precepts was precisely intended to lead him toward gradual cultivation. Thus did he follow the Buddha.

The instruction is to practice and maintain it in this way; not only must the articles of the *pien-chü* (the *prātimokṣa*) remain unimpaired, but even the three thousand modes of deportment and eighty thousand subtle details must not be neglected.
This is merely to say that one must guard against transgressions with strictness and maintain the precepts with secrecy. Wén-líng says:

"In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, there are two hundred and fifty rules of discipline for each; when paired with the three aggregates (*tri-skandha*), they constitute three thousand. (This is...)
The three thousand modes of deportment (*tri-sahasra-īryāpatha*), when further multiplied by the seven branches of body and speech, become twenty-one thousand.

These are then multiplied by the four categories of afflictions—greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth—to become eighty-four thousand. (The sutra text abbreviates the remainder, mentioning only "eighty thousand subtle [afflictions].
According to what is recorded in the *Dharmasaṃkhyā* and as taught in the *Abhiṣeka*, these do not entirely coincide with this; however, they are roughly both based on the number two.

The mutual correspondence between the vehicles (*yāna*) and the precepts (*śīla*) has been paired out; although the numerical totals have thus been assembled, the underlying principle appears somewhat unsatisfactory.
Being of little learning and having not yet consulted the Vinaya-piṭaka, I do not dare to offer a definitive judgment.

However, since it is said that "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*) seems to pertain only to the maintenance of the body, it may perhaps refer to the minor details of conduct found outside the precepts of the Hīnayāna; and since it is said to be "subtle," it seems to involve the maintenance of both [body and mind].
As for the mind, it may refer to subtle practices external to the Mahāyāna precepts; let us set this aside as a point of doubt for further reference.

The categories of natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) encompass the precept systems of both vehicles. Regarding natural offenses: their nature is inherently sinful, independent of the Buddha's prohibitions.

Upholding [the precepts] is good; violating them is evil. Violating them incurs two kinds of offenses: first, an offense against the path of karma (*karmapatha*); second, an offense against the disciplinary regulations (*prajñapti*).

This applies to acts such as killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. Regarding prohibited actions (*vāritakarma*), there is no offense prior to their being regulated, but one commits an offense after they have been regulated.
For those who violate them, only an offense against the disciplinary regulations is established. Examples include drinking alcohol, tilling the soil, and so forth. "All are pure" means as follows:
If even the subtle practices mentioned above are not neglected, how much more so should one’s natural karma (*prakṛti-karman*) and prohibited karma (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya-karman*)?

One should naturally be like water that has removed its sediment, or like jade that is free from flaw. As for the quiescence of body and mind: in the Hīnayāna, the body is restrained, so the body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) is tranquil and unmoving;

in the Mahāyāna, the mind is restrained, so the mental faculty (*manas*) and consciousness (*citta*) are extinguished and do not arise. This pertains to the two delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought (*vitarka-kleśa*).
From this point on, [defilements] are forever exhausted; therefore, it is said that one has become an Arhat. ○ Regarding the passage "I am the head of the assembly...":

"Presiding over" is called *gāng* (the mainstay), and "maintaining" is called *jì* (the discipline). Because Upāli was able to uphold the precepts, the Buddha ordered him to inspect whether they were observed or violated, and to adjudicate between grave and minor offenses.
Since he presided over the Buddha’s assembly and maintained the study of the Vinaya, he said of himself, "I am... and so forth.
Furthermore, because the Mahāyāna practice of disciplining the mind can only be known by a Buddha, he personally received the seal of approval [from the Buddha].

Because the Hīnayāna practice of upholding the precepts and cultivating the body is universally acknowledged by all, the assembly recommended him as supreme. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Among the five hundred arhats, the Elder Upāli was foremost in the mastery of the Vinaya. Based on this, [the superiority of] the Mahāyāna discipline...
The mind is its secret practice; the discipline of the body in the Lesser Vehicle is its outward manifestation.
Now, by lingering among the weeds, his true guilt is finally laid bare. This concludes the two proofs. Third, the conclusion and response regarding perfect penetration.

The Buddha asked about the method of perfect penetration. I attained mastery over the body by concentrating on the body; I attained penetration into the mind by concentrating on the mind in succession.
Thereafter, my body and mind became entirely functional and beneficial, which I consider to be the foremost.
First, by means of the Hīnayāna, one holds that the body and body-consciousness do not function, thereby attaining great mastery over the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*).

Subsequently, by means of the Mahāyāna, one holds that mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are without distinction, thereby attaining wondrous penetration into the sense-object of phenomena (*dharma*).

Thereafter, the body and mind are mutually interchangeable, such that all [faculties], including the eye- and ear-consciousnesses, become entirely capable of penetrating and functioning with ease. Based on this:
This constitutes the first phrase. Although the wording appears general, the intent actually specifically points to the grasping of the body, as this is the primary expedient for entering the path.
Furthermore, this section is specifically intended to highlight the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*). Upāli’s discussion of body-consciousness is concluded. VI.
Maudgalyāyana’s discussion of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has three parts: (1) prostrating and making a formal statement; (2) a detailed narration.
II. Testimony. III. Conclusion and Response on Perfect Penetration. First:
Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Maudgalyāyana—here translated as Caishushi—is his clan name. He was a distinguished member of that lineage, and because his supernormal powers were so great, they are detailed in the Introduction.
Yet while everyone knows of Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal powers, they do not know the cause by which he attained them.
Now he himself recounts the cause: through the returning of consciousness to its profound stillness, the light of the mind was manifested and proclaimed.
Second, a sequential account of the two types of realization. First, the account of realization through awakening; second, the account of realization through cultivation.
Regarding the first: "In the beginning, while begging for food on the road, I encountered the three Kāśyapa brothers—Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa."
He proclaimed the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causes and conditions. I suddenly attained the mind [of awakening] and achieved great penetration.

This first instance refers to the time before he had left the household life; according to the *Ekottarika-āgama*, it concerns Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, who were fellow disciples of the brahmin Sāriputta.

They mastered all of his arts. However, as he was about to die, he smiled. When asked the reason for this, he said, "I saw King Kinnara of Suvarṇabhūmi and his consort cast themselves into the fire, vowing to be reborn together in one place. Later, seeing a merchant from Suvarṇabhūmi, he confirmed that this was indeed so.
The two men regretted not having fully mastered the arts; seeking further superior methods, they found no teacher to serve. One—
On his way, he encountered Aṅgīrasa and heard his account of the causes and conditions; he followed him to where the Buddha was, attained liberation, and left the household life.
That he later encountered the three Kāśyapas on the road has already been explained in the section on the Perfect Penetration of the Śarīra.
Uruvilvā means "Pumpkin Grove" (*kapitthavana*); because they dwelt by the grove, it is also called "Pumpkin Tumor. This refers to a tumor on the chest that resembles a [pumpkin].
The names "Upaga" (木瓜), "Gayāśīrṣa" (伽耶山), and "Nadī" (那提河) were established as titles based on their respective residences in order to distinguish them from others of the same clan.

All were disciples of the Buddha who propagated [the teachings] according to what the Buddha had spoken; therefore, it is said that they "proclaimed the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s causes and conditions.
However, if one discusses the meaning of "causes and conditions" in its general sense, it appears to function primarily as an antidote.
Whether it be causelessness or false causes, if one investigates them to their ultimate limit, they can truly lead one to the Buddha Vehicle.

As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Those phenomena produced through causes and conditions, I declare to be empty; they are also designated as conventional and are termed the meaning of the Middle Way.
Since these three contemplations are raised together and the three truths are illuminated simultaneously, what teaching would not be subsumed? What...
The Way does not stop here; it is not confined to the provisional teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, and thus its meaning is said to be profound.

"I suddenly arouse the mind" means to suddenly arouse the resolve to reform one's errors and return to the correct path. "Attaining great penetration" means to achieve perfect enlightenment into the principle that emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are identical.
From this point on, one turns back the discriminative consciousness of false delusions and returns to the state of profound stillness and immovability.
Regarding the nature [of enlightenment], through realization and testimony, it may be equal to the realm of the Buddha. Second, regarding the description of cultivation and realization:

the Tathāgata bestowed upon me the *kāṣāya* robe, which I donned upon my body; my beard and hair fell away of their own accord; and as I traveled throughout the ten directions, I attained freedom from all hindrances.

My supernormal powers have been manifested and proclaimed as unsurpassed; I have attained arhatship. Not only does the World-Honored One do so, but the Tathāgatas of the ten directions praise my spiritual power as perfect, clear, pure, sovereign, and fearless.
Upon seeing the Buddha for the first time, he immediately received the Tathāgata’s compassionate grace. As soon as the Buddha called out, "Welcome, Bhikṣu," he was endowed with the marks of a monk;

thus it is said that the *kāṣāya* robe was donned upon his body and his beard and hair fell away naturally. From that moment, the light of his mind was manifested and proclaimed, enabling him to travel through all quarters without obstruction.
This was truly because his supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) arose from the clarity of his own nature, such that he was ranked as supreme among the assembly. He traversed...
Since one has long observed the world and attained eternal quiescence through contemplation, it is said that one has "attained the state of an Arhat.

This is the preliminary realization and proof through which one first obtains the efficacy of the four fruits of the path. It is not only the World-Honored One who speaks thus; when he says, "My spiritual power," does this refer solely to the World-Honored One’s own approval?
No; even all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions praise my spiritual power, as I travel everywhere throughout the ten directions performing [these deeds].

It is called "perfectly luminous" (*pariśuddha*) because it performs the deeds of all Buddhas. It is called "pure" (*viśuddha*) because the single reality is immovable and not disturbed by even a speck of dust;
this praises its virtue of being unimpeded in engaging with the world. It is called "sovereign" (*vaśavartin*) because its spontaneous activity does not depend on deliberate mental effort.
It is called "fearless" (*abhaya*) because all demons are subdued and all enemies are crushed; this praises its spontaneity.
This is the virtue of subduing. For example, in the *Nāgāvatāra-sūtra*, when the Buddha ascended to Tuṣita Heaven, a venomous dragon created obstacles;
Maudgalyāyana manifested various large and small forms, and the dragon, terrified, bit him until he finally submitted.

Furthermore, in the *Cittavajra-sūtra*, when an externalist attempted to move a mountain, Maudgalyāyana rendered it motionless and leveled it into the great earth, removing the affliction for the people. Such instances all demonstrate his sovereign mastery and fearlessness.
Verification. Having finished recounting these two proofs, thirdly, he concludes by answering regarding perfect penetration.

The Buddha asked about perfect penetration; I replied that I attained it by turning back the stillness of the mind, whereby its radiance was manifested, like clearing a turbid stream until it becomes long-lasting, limpid, and crystalline.
This is the first [point].

The opening phrase restates the question; "I" and what follows provide the concluding answer. "Whirling back into stillness" means that through perfect awakening, causes and conditions have no further need for discrimination;
one whirls the mental consciousness back into the state of the inherently tranquil nature. This is simply because the preceding section contained this meaning implicitly.
"Speaking forth" means that when the light of the mind is proclaimed, one sees the Buddha renounce the world;
having long since returned to stillness, one differentiates and transforms the light of the mind-ground. Because this is brought forth and applied, there are supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

This is also what was previously contained within the "mind," which is now spoken forth. "Like clarifying a turbid stream" refers to the returning of consciousness to stillness, just as one clarifies a turbid flow.

The "flowing and returning" refers to the stillness of water. That which has been clear, pure, and translucent for a long time means that because the mind’s radiance has been manifested through prolonged stillness, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) arise;
this is like how water that has been clear for a long time becomes a translucent liquid capable of reflecting images.
This constitutes the first phrase; although the wording appears general, its intent actually specifically points to "revolving stillness. This is truly because of the Perfect [Enlightenment].
Awakening to causes and conditions serves as the precursor to the revolving tranquility; the radiance of the mind’s luminosity serves as the subsequent achievement of that revolving tranquility.
Thus we know that without revolving tranquility, perfect awakening would result in nothing but deluded understanding; the radiance of the mind is permitted only where the nature exists.
Since one cannot engage in gradual cultivation amidst the defilements of worldly toil, by what means could one sever the afflictions of views and thoughts to achieve actual realization?
It is therefore appropriate that taking the "revolving of the stillness" as primary. This follows the meaning of the phrase "previously containing no intention" according to the ancient masters.
In that case, terms such as "revolving and tranquil" (*xuánzhàn*) would have no basis here. This concludes the section on the Perfect Penetration of the Six Consciousnesses.

IV. The Seven Great Perfect Penetrations. (The *Zhengmo* [Correct Pulse] commentary states: "The first five 'greats' are the sense objects (*viṣaya*); the latter two 'greats' are consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the faculties (*indriya*). Although they do not transcend the previous three categories of faculties, objects, and consciousness, they specifically possess the characteristics of being all-pervasive and vast;
therefore, they are individually designated by the name 'Great' [*mahā*]. VII. 1. The Fire Great of Ucchuṣma; 2. The Earth Great of Dharaṇīdhara; 3. The Moon...

1. The Great Element of Light-Water; 2. The Great Element of Lapis Lazuli Wind; 3. The Great Element of the Space-Treasury of Emptiness; 4. The Great Element of Maitreya’s Consciousness; 5. The Great Element of Avalokiteśvara’s Faculties.

Regarding the first three [methods], there are three parts: first, prostrating and making a formal declaration; second, recounting the two proofs in detail; third, concluding with the answer regarding perfect penetration. First:
[The passage continues with the specific details of the first method.]
Ucchuṣma joined his palms before the Tathāgata, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
[Wenling says: "Ucchuṣma" means "Fire-Head. *Guanding* says: He is the Vajra-spirit Huoshou (Fire-Head).
Manifesting as a protector of the Dharma, he should not sit; therefore, it does not say he rose from his seat, but states directly that he was "before" the Buddha.]
The reason for specifically noting "palms joined" (*añjali*) at the beginning is that previously he was holding his fists and a vajra, which does not involve joining the palms.
Furthermore, the reason for specifically noting "bowing at the Buddha’s feet" is that, compared to the other sages, his prostration to the Buddha included an additional degree of reverence.

Second, the sequential narration of the two types of realization. First, the narration of the realization through awakening; second, the narration of the realization through cultivation. Regarding the first:
I constantly recall that in the distant past, during many kalpas ago, my nature was characterized by much greed.

There was a Buddha who appeared in the world named King of Emptiness (Kongwang), who taught that those with excessive lust become a mass of fierce fire. He instructed me to contemplate everywhere throughout my hundred bones and four limbs all sensations of cold and warmth.
Qi. The divine light condenses within, transforming many lustful minds into the fire of wisdom.
From this, all Buddhas have summoned me and named me Huotou (Fire-Head).
In the distant past, my nature was largely characterized by lust; "chang" (常) here means "formerly," as in "once.
I always first recall those things from long ago, personally recounting events from kalpas long past as recorded in my previous lives. My nature was one of great greed and desire.
This refers to those who, having been attached to lust throughout successive lifetimes, have formed a habitual nature such that they are born with abundant greed and desire from birth;
this is as described in the "Universal Gate" chapter regarding those with much lustful desire. Regarding the passage beginning with "There was a Buddha," the Buddha taught the contemplation of fire.

The Buddha’s name is King of Emptiness (*Śūnyarāja*), because he has profoundly realized the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) and attained mastery over all phenomena. This is from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The *Ānanda-ben-yun* (The Original Account of Ānanda) states: "I and Ānanda together resolved our minds for enlightenment in the presence of the Buddha Śūnyarāja.

From this, we know that Ucchuṣma also resolved his mind for enlightenment at the same time as the Buddha; however, he manifested the traces of a powerful warrior (*mahābala*) solely for the sake of protecting the Dharma.
To investigate his profound origin from afar is truly inconceivable. As for the statement that those with excessive lust become a mass of fierce fire, it is intended to...

To know how to fear and cease excessive lustful thoughts is likewise to apply medicine according to the specific ailment. *Guanding* says: "Lust is fundamentally triggered by the pressure of warm contact;
when lust is excessive, it constitutes an abundance of 'fire,' and is thus called a 'mass of fire. Fire takes burning as its defining characteristic.
However, the fire of desire not only burns away all roots of goodness, but through the mutual resonance of the internal and external, it is truly capable of burning all [virtues]."
The physical body and life-force provide clear evidence for this, as seen in practices such as self-immolation at celestial shrines or sitting upon beds of fire.

The instruction to contemplate the pervasive nature of cold and heat is intended to allow one to verify this for oneself: when the mind has not yet been stirred by lust, the hundred bones and four limbs are inherently cool;
yet, as soon as a single thought of desire arises, the entire body becomes parched and hot. Thus, the form is cold...
He realized that his own words regarding the "mass of fire" were not false. As for "divine light" (shenguang):

when the contemplation of fire was perfected, lustful thoughts were suddenly extinguished. Since the fiery energy could no longer leak outward and instead nourished the spirit, it was called "divine light.
Regarding "concentrated within": it is gathered and retained internally without being dispersed externally, much like the vital essence of a youth in the world.

That those who desire often find their bodies light and their physiques robust is a testament to the inner concentration of spiritual radiance (*śubha-prabhā*). As the proverb says, "When the essence is full, one does not think of desire.
Now, since the spiritual radiance is concentrated within, the thought of desire should naturally and permanently vanish; thus it is said that it transforms the lustful mind.
Furthermore, when the lustful mind is intense, it inevitably leads to delusion, agitation, and feverish heat; once the lustful mind is transformed, [these states] should naturally cease.

It transforms delusion into the clarity of wisdom and transmutes aridity into the flame of prajñā; because it illuminates the stage of the *bhūmi* and burns away the fuel of afflictions, it is said to "accomplish the fire of wisdom.
From this point upward, one accords with the Buddha Vehicle and attains a profound resonance with the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas;
thus, one receives from the Buddhas the name "Fire-Head" (*Agnimukha*). As for the term "Fire-Head," it precisely signifies this very origin.
Entering through the contemplation of fire is the foremost among the methods of perfect penetration. Second is the description of cultivation and realization:

"By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi, I attained Arhatship. Thereupon, I made a great vow: 'When all Buddhas achieve enlightenment, may I serve as a powerful attendant to personally subdue their demonic adversaries.'"

Because one contemplates fire until it becomes meditative concentration, it is called the *Tejovatī-samādhi* (Fire-Light Samādhi). By means of this power of concentration, one first severs the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava*), thereby attaining the state of an Arhat.
Regarding the phrase "the mind gives rise to a great vow," this refers to not abiding in the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
The vows of the Mahāyāna should have many gateways; here, the protection of the Dharma is taken as the gateway. Thus, it says: "When all Buddhas attain the Way, I..."
They were *malla* (wrestlers). The *malla* are, in fact, the *vajra*-deities (*vajrapāṇi*). Regarding those who personally subdue the enemies of Māra, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states:
"In the past, there was a king whose principal queen gave birth to a thousand sons.
Desiring to test the order in which they would attain Buddhahood in the future, K Krakucchanda drew the first lot; Śākyamuni drew the fourth lot; and so on, until Ruci drew [the final one]."
One thousand tally-sticks. The second wife gave birth to two sons: one vowed to become a Brahmā King and entreat his elder brother to turn the Wheel of Dharma;
the other vowed to become the Secret Trace Vajra Deity (*Guhyapada-vajra*) to protect his elder brother’s teachings.

When it is now said that "all Buddhas attain enlightenment," this may refer to the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa. My being a *malla* (wrestler) likely refers to the Secret Trace Vajra. This is because...

When the Way is esteemed, Māra is exalted; when conduct is fragrant, one encounters jealousy. Thus, whenever Buddhas attain enlightenment and preach the Dharma, there are often celestial Māras who perversely arise to create obstacles.

[The Bodhisattva] vows to personally subdue them, never tolerating them with leniency. His intention is to utilize this to adorn the land, benefit sentient beings, and bring the bodhisattva practices to completion.
This concludes the second section, the recounting of the two proofs. Third, the conclusion and response regarding the perfect penetration.

The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. I replied: "By clearly observing that the sensations of warmth within my body and mind flow unimpededly, all outflows were extinguished and a great jewel-flame arose, whereby I ascended to supreme enlightenment. This is the foremost."
Physical heat and mental agitation both constitute the sensation of warmth (*uṣmagata*). It is through both body and mind that this is called "contemplative observation" (*vipaśyanā*).

Therefore, while the previous stage—marking the initial arising—taught only the contemplation of the body, this stage includes deep cultivation and thus mentions the contemplation of the mind as well.

Only when one reaches the point of contemplating both body and mind together is *samādhi* perfected. Regarding its unimpeded circulation: once *samādhi* is achieved, it extends simultaneously to both body and mind without obstruction.
It is able to obstruct the sensation of warmth. When descending from above, the flow of awareness becomes supple and pervasive;
this is what is meant by "the divine light condensing within. It transforms a mind of excessive lust, whereby all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted.

Because it produces the fire of wisdom, it is said to "give rise to the great jewel-flame. Subduing demonic adversaries is called "Great"; protecting the Dharma and benefiting sentient beings is called "Jewel. It incinerates delusions.
"Shining upon the Truth" is named "Flame," which refers to the Fire-Light Samādhi (*tejodhipati-samādhi*).

As for his traces, because he was originally a powerful being who entered the Buddha-vehicle, it is said that he "ascended to Unsurpassed Enlightenment. However, greed is the root of affliction, and lust is called the foremost culprit;
since both are extinguished through the contemplation of fire, this is said to be "the foremost. This concludes the section on Ucchuṣma and the Great Element of Fire.
Second, the Earth-Holding Ground (Dharaṇīdhara-bhūmi), Part Three: 1. Prostration and Statement; 2. Detailed Account of Cultivation and Realization;
3. Conclusion and Response on Perfect Penetration. First:
Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
According to the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, the bodhisattva named "Earth-Holder" (*Dharanīdhara*) possesses ten meanings of "earth": first, vastness; second, being the support for sentient beings;
third, being free from likes and dislikes; fourth, receiving great rains; fifth, producing grasses and trees; and sixth, being the basis for seeds.

Seventh, it produces various jewels. Eighth, it produces various medicinal herbs. Ninth, it is unmoved by the wind. Tenth, it is not startled by the lion’s roar. The Bodhisattva maintains the mind as such.
If these qualities are considered individually and collectively, they are able to give rise to the vast bodhicitta;
they are able to serve as a refuge for sentient beings in saṃsāra; they do not discriminate among sentient beings; and they receive all [teachings].
Because it is the great Dharma rain of the Buddha; because it causes all merits to grow; because it is that upon which the seeds of bodhi rely;
because it gives rise to the teachings that benefit sentient beings; because it gives rise to the teachings that counteract afflictions;
because it is unmoved by the eight winds of the world; and because one does not feel alarm or doubt upon hearing the exposition of the profound Dharma—according to this fundamental sūtra:
Leveling the external realm and leveling the internal mind-ground; taking this as the cause to seek the fruit of Buddhahood—this is the meaning of the name.

Second, the sequential account of cultivation and realization (since this Bodhisattva begins by relying on formal practices, unlike the previous sages who first realized and then cultivated, these are described directly as "cultivation and realization"). This has two parts: first, the sequential cultivation of formal practices;
second, the realization of the fruit through awakening. The first part has three sections. First, initial cultivation consists solely of formal practice.

First, leveling the ground. Second, during the interim, concurrently performing acts of substitution and maintenance. Third, in subsequent cultivation, further including the salvation of those drowning.
Regarding the first: I recall that in the past, when the Tathāgata Samantaprabhā appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu.
Whenever there were dangerous roads, river crossings, or narrow passes where the terrain was uneven and caused harm to carts and horses, I always leveled and filled them all.
Some built bridges, while others carried sand and earth.
"In the past" refers to a previous life; the Buddha named Samantaprabhāsa (Universal Radiance) possessed both physical radiance and the radiance of wisdom that were all-pervasive.
He was the first of the fifty-three Buddhas. Upon seeing this Buddha, [the practitioner] resolved his mind on enlightenment, left the household life, and received full ordination.
Therefore, it is said: "I am a bhikṣu. A "crucial path" (*yāolù*) refers to a vital thoroughfare for land travel, as it is the route necessarily traversed by those coming and going.
A "ford" (*jīnkǒu*) refers to a junction where land and water meet, as it is the point necessarily passed through when crossing over.

A "field" (*tián dì*) refers to the ground for planting within a field, as it is the place where the activities of plowing and harvesting are conveniently carried out. That which is uneven, with elevations and depressions, is called "precipitous" (*xiǎn*).
A narrow passage where the banks of a ditch press closely together is called an "obstruction" (*ai*). Such places exist not only on main roads and ferry crossings, but also in fields;

it is not limited to these alone. Whenever there is anything improper, it will inevitably cause damage to carriages and horses—such as the danger of a carriage losing its linchpin or breaking its axle, or the suffering of a horse sinking its leg or losing its footing. If even carriages and horses are damaged, what need is there to mention other things?
This can be understood. "I level and fill them all" means to level the high and fill the low, smoothing them according to their natural incline.
"In some places I construct bridges" means to span with timber and support with stone, diverting the flow to avoid its force.

"In others I carry sand and earth" means to dam the water and cover the mud, counteracting the current to manage it. My efforts ensure that the treacherous becomes level and the narrow becomes broad for carriages.
"It is no hindrance; the horse will suffer no harm. Furthermore, during the interval between those two, I have concurrently performed services as a substitute.
Thus, through diligent toil, I have passed through the appearance of immeasurable Buddhas in the world.

There were sentient beings in the marketplace who required someone to carry their goods; I would first carry them for them. Upon reaching their destination, I would set down the goods and depart, taking no payment."
"Thus diligently laboring" means that leveling the roads, constructing bridges, and damming rivers can be called the height of toil and the utmost hardship.
"Passing through the appearance of immeasurable Buddhas in the world" reveals that one practices constantly without ceasing;
thus it is known that the gradual cultivation of the Bodhisattva’s practice is beyond the reach of the multitude of sages. This is...

This concludes the preceding section on leveling the ground. The following section concerns the simultaneous maintenance of the ritual implements during the Ming dynasty. Regarding the phrase "if there should be sentient beings":

this refers to the time when one is performing the preliminary practices, and should one encounter sentient beings—referring specifically to those who are weak and lacking strength—who require assistance in carrying items through a crowded marketplace (*huan-hui*).
As for the term *huan-hui*, Guanding states that *huan* refers to the city wall and *hui* refers to the city gate. I, however, [suggest it refers to] the marketplace itself.
Both were places of trade. Regarding "a person requiring assistance to carry an object," this refers to when an object acquired through trade could not be carried by one's own strength.
As for "I first offered to carry it," when a person requested the price, the Bodhisattva volunteered to carry it first.
This encompasses the three types of giving: first, the gift of material wealth by physically carrying it, as the body itself constitutes an internal treasure;

second, the gift of the Dharma through the conversion of those who request it; and third, the gift of fearlessness, wherein the owner of the object grants safety. "To go" (*yì*) means to arrive at the destination where one is headed.
"To release the object" means that the practitioner does not demand its price; "not taking its price" refers to the act of giving.
Nor do I grasp at this. Furthermore, within the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), the meaning of external wealth is fully realized.
Third, in subsequent practice, one further provides relief to those who are drowning.
During the time when the Buddha Viśvabhū was present in the world, there was widespread famine; I served as a porter for people, regardless of whether the distance was far or near.
He took only a single coin. Or, when oxen drawing carts were mired in the mud, I used my supernatural power to push their wheels and relieve them of their suffering.
"Bhīṣma" is the name of the Buddha; it is a term from the Sanskrit language meaning "Pervasive Sovereignty over All," referring to his mastery over all phenomena.
Because he attained mastery therein, he was the final Buddha of the past *Vyūha-kalpa*.
According to this account, Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara first resolved his mind for enlightenment under the Buddha Samantaprabhāsa;
thereafter, he passed through fifty-three Buddhas and nine hundred and ninety-nine Buddhas of the *Vyūha-kalpa*, until the appearance of the final Buddha, Viśvabhū.
At that time, he constantly practiced walking on level ground and the practice of substitution. Thus we know that the aforementioned mention of "immeasurable Buddhas" is stated in broad terms;
it may be that beyond the thousand Buddhas, there are other Buddhas who complete the number of immeasurable ones.
This is also not yet definitive, as it refers specifically to the period of the present age and excludes events occurring after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. Regarding the frequent occurrence of famine:
this means that grain was insufficient for cooking and food was not available. As for the earlier mention of "carrying" and "bearing," this implies that when light, one carries it in the hands;
when heavy, one bears it on the back. Although these appear separately in different passages, in reality they are mutually inclusive, referring generally to the act of carrying throughout one's life.
Regarding practice, there are two types of distance: first, the distance of the physical path; second, the distance of mental attitude. In both cases, the lack of questioning serves one purpose:
the former reveals that ease or difficulty is not to be compared, while the latter clarifies the equality toward enemies and kin. In sum, there is but a single mind free from discrimination.
As for taking only a single coin: this was because, during a time of famine when alms were difficult to obtain, he took only what was necessary to sustain his body out of a lack of excessive greed.
All that precedes belongs to his former conduct; what follows further includes his acts of saving those in distress.
For instance, there were carts and oxen mired in the mud; since a cart is drawn by oxen and lacks the agility of horses, it became especially stuck in the mire.
Then the driver would share in that misfortune. As for my supernormal powers, they are the result of vows and practices accumulated over many kalpas and are moved by the ripening of merit.
When I push the wheel to help the ox get out of the cart, it is not only the ox that is freed from the mire;
I also cause the one holding the reins to be released from their burden. This is the result of having cultivated such deeds throughout successive lives.
[The section] concludes. Second, awakening through realization of the fruit has two parts: first, awakening through receiving instruction; second, gradual entry into realization. Regarding the first:
at that time, the great king invited the Buddha to a vegetarian feast. At that moment, I leveled the ground to await the Buddha. [This was] in the city of Vaiśālī.
He came and placed his hand upon my head, saying to me: "If you level the ground of your own mind, then the ground of the entire world will be level.
At that moment, my mind opened; I saw that the minute particles of my own body and all the minute particles that constitute the world were equal and without distinction.
The self-nature of these minute particles does not touch one another; even weapons of war do not come into contact with them.

At first, he continued to practice his original vows; this was by invitation. As for the king inviting the Buddha, it was because he humbled himself before the supreme dignity of the Five Emperors to welcome the Sage of Ten Thousand Virtues for the sake of cultivating merit for the nation. Because he extensively arrayed rare delicacies and unsurpassed exquisite flavors, it is called "establishing a feast" (*zhāi*).
Leveling the ground was his original practice; furthermore, knowing that the Buddha was descending, he acted accordingly at that very moment.

Wait for him. ○ Regarding "Viśākha" (毗舍), the Buddha instructs him to maintain an even mind. As for "touching the crown of the head" (摩頂), it signifies the Tathāgata’s compassion for his long-standing toil in practice;

he bestows empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) to enable him to harmonize all matters through principle. One should keep the ground of the mind level because the *tathāgatagarbha* is fundamentally devoid of high and low.
When a single thought momentarily arises, pure and defiled states proliferate in abundance. If one can truly remain free from such thoughts—
When the internal mind is balanced, external manifestations become level. Though mountains and valleys may shift and change, one remains ever as they are;
though the tides rise and fall, the path has always been smooth. Therefore it is said that the world and all lands are entirely level.
As Vimalakīrti said: "If you wish to attain a pure land, you must purify your own mind; for according to the mind..."
"When the [mind] is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. Tiantai said: "The perilous state of the mind in the Sahā world evokes the high and deep terrain of hills and valleys;
the level state of the mind in Sukhāvatī results in ground as flat as the palm of a hand. Both of these express this same principle.

"I immediately attained great awakening" and "I immediately had my mind opened" mean that upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching on leveling the mind, one realizes that the phenomenal marks of thought have departed and the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) has been revealed.

It means to open and reveal. When the *ālayavijñāna* (the storehouse consciousness) opens and reveals the tranquil non-discriminative wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world transform in accordance with thought into supreme awakening.
Therefore, it is said that one sees the minute particles of the body and all the minute particles that constitute the world as being equal and without distinction.
Since they are equal and without distinction, the entire ground of the world becomes level.

However, both the body and the elements are designated as "subtle particles" (*paramāṇu*) because they are both composed of subtle particles; thus, by referring to the derived (*bhautika*), the primary (*bhūta*) is revealed.
This is also intended to demonstrate that they share the same great earth (*mahāpṛthivī*). Regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of subtle particles:

since there is no distinction among them as described above, one proceeds to observe that the subtle particles of the body and the elements possess a single, identical intrinsic nature. Since they possess this same single intrinsic nature...

In its true nature, there is in fact neither that which touches nor that which is touched, neither that which rubs nor that which is rubbed; therefore, it is said that they do not touch or rub one another.
How much more so for the body and the sensory realms—they do not touch or rub. Even when the body encounters weapons such as swords and spears, there is nothing to be touched.
This is evidenced by the Sixth Patriarch extending his neck as an assassin struck thrice with a sharp blade, each blow being like cutting through a shadow. This is precisely the proof.
Furthermore, when these [stages] above are universally understood through the four dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), their meaning becomes even clearer. As previously stated:

simply leveling the external world and exclusively devoting oneself to the cultivation of phenomena is the *phenomenal dharma-realm* (*shifenjie*). Relying on the teaching to level the mind and using principle (*li*) to subsume phenomena is the *principle dharma-realm* (*lifajie*).
When the mind opens and one perceives sensory objects (*viṣaya*), then principle does not obstruct phenomena; when the realm of the body is without differentiation, then phenomena...
There is no obstruction to principle; this is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.

As for the fact that even within the dharma-realm of a single atom there is no mutual contact or friction, yet they are mutually inclusive—such that when weapons are brought against one's body, there is no injury from contact—it is because they mutually interpenetrate.
This is precisely the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). This is merely stated in terms of the locus of vision;
it is by means of this that one attains great awakening. Second is gradual realization and entry.
I realized the patience of non-arising regarding the nature of phenomena and attained arhatship; subsequently, turning my mind toward enlightenment, I have now entered the stage of a bodhisattva.
Having heard the Tathāgatas proclaim the ground of the Buddhas' wondrous Lotus wisdom and vision, I was first appointed as a witness and served as their leader.
The body-element and its two objects encompass all phenomena. Since they share the same single self-nature, all phenomena likewise share that same single self-nature.
Who, then, is the producer? Who is the produced? By means of this, one awakens to the principle of the non-arising nature of all phenomena, accepting it with patient faith and without doubt.
Having reached the point of awakening, one is already equal to the eighth stage; it is merely a matter of subduing and severing [the remaining afflictions].

Because the limits of the afflictions of view and thought have been fully exhausted, he is said to have "attained the state of an Arhat. Since his realization is profound, he does not abide in shallow attainments;
thus, during the Bhadrakalpa (the Auspicious Aeon), he turned his mind [toward Bodhi] and has remained forever within the rank of a Bodhisattva until the present day.

When the various Tathāgatas refer to the three Buddhas prior to the Bhadrakalpa, they include all Buddhas from other directions as well. "The Wondrous Lotus" refers specifically to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Because this sutra is also titled *The Great Vaipulya King of the Wondrous Lotus*, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision refers to the Tathāgatagarbha mind revealed within the sutra.

When it resides in the eye, it is called "vision"; when it resides in the mind, it is called "knowledge. These two functions of the six senses are mentioned to encompass the rest, as they share a single essence.
Regarding the phrase "I first provide witness and proof," it means to lead the way in cultivation and to guide others toward it.
Because he was a junior [to the Buddha], yet because he was honored by all as one who draws in and guides those of later generations, he is called the "foremost leader.
This refers to his period from when he first turned his mind toward enlightenment during the Bhadrakalpa until now. The detailed account of his cultivation and realization is hereby concluded.
Third, Śrīmatī answered regarding perfect penetration.
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, she said: "I have observed with clarity that the two objects—the body and the sensory field—are equal and without distinction;

they are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha. It is only through delusion that these objects arise. Once the objects are dissolved, wisdom becomes perfect, and one accomplishes the Unsurpassed Way. This is the foremost."

Zhengmo says: This merely provides a comprehensive account of the previous realization. The two characters "thoroughly observing" (dìguān) refer to the opening of the mind upon receiving instruction as previously mentioned;
it means to examine and observe with non-discriminative wisdom. Because one realizes that the two objects are without difference, one knows they are rooted in the *tathāgatagarbha* nature.
Since one seeks the derivative based on the fundamental, there is no separate self-substance; therefore, it is said that "falsehoods arise as objects. However...
Although the arising of sensory dust belongs to the realm of delusion, the mere stirring of thought constitutes an obstruction.

If one can rouse diligent effort and forever leave behind the marks of conceptualization, then once delusory dust is eliminated, true wisdom will become perfect. What need is there to wait for the unsurpassed path of enlightenment to be realized?
This is based on the practice and realization of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who took the leveling of the ground as his gateway; therefore, it is said that this is the foremost.

The section on the Earth Element of the Ground of Holding is concluded. Regarding the Water Element of the Radiance of the Three Months, there are three parts: first, prostrating and presenting the petition;
second, recounting the process of cultivation and realization; third, concluding with the answer regarding perfect penetration. First:
The youth Candraprabha immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the name 'Candraprabha' (Moonlight), the moon is the essence of the water element.

Therefore, it was previously said that various Brahmins combine magical elixirs and, holding a *fangzhu* (a concave mirror) in their hands, receive the water of the moon. It is by means of this that the Bodhisattva contemplates the entry into water."
It has fully attained the essence of water; receiving this quintessence, it illuminates the Dharma-realm and brings benefit to all sentient beings.
It is named "Moon" for this reason. This explanation follows the meaning of the original sutra.
If one relies on the *Avataṃsaka*, the moon possesses four kinds of wonders: first, eclipsing the stars; second, manifesting its waning and waxing; third, [having...]
Water reflects images; the four types of vision all face one's own eyes. The Bodhisattva eclipses the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) and manifests wisdom and abandonment;
whenever there is an invocation, there is a response, and sentient beings each perceive him facing themselves. This is similar in meaning to the moonlight. Zhengmo says:
"Child" (*dāraka*) is an alternative name for a Bodhisattva, signifying the virtue of "childlike innocence" (*kumārabhūta*). It may also be said that the child is the Dharma itself.
The son of the king—just as Mañjuśrī is also referred to by the title "Child" (*kumāra*)—secondly, the account of his cultivation and realization (wherein the Bodhisattva himself says:

"I have now attained the path of an Arhat; I have long been free from the conditions of illness"). Based on this, he has turned from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, cultivating both principle and phenomena together;

unlike other sages who first attain awakening and then cultivate, he speaks directly of cultivation and realization. This consists of two parts: first, encountering Buddhist teachings and contemplation; second, cultivating and realizing according to those teachings. First:
I recall that in the past, as many eons ago as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Water-Deity (*Varuṇa*).
He taught various Bodhisattvas to practice the contemplation of water (*āp-kṛtsna*) to enter samādhi. They contemplated that within the body, the nature of water is not to be displaced.

Starting first from the mucus and saliva, they investigated in this manner until exhausting the lymph, marrow, blood, and the major and minor excretions; thus, everything within the body returns to the single nature of water.
The same. One perceives that the water within one’s own body is no different from the various fragrant oceans of the Floating Banner King lands outside the world-system.
The initial teaching uses the contemplation of water; because the event occurred in the past, it is called "of old," and because many eons have elapsed, it is called...
"Sand Kalpas" refers to the number of kalpas passed from this point to that point when counting backward, which is as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
The Buddha named Jaladeva (Water Heaven) attained the realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) by contemplating the nature of water;
he is one of the thirty-five Buddhas, as clarified in the *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā Sūtra*. His instruction of all bodhisattvas is not intended for a single individual alone.
Because he spoke according to [his own] realization to deliver a specific class of practitioners, he taught only the cultivation of the water-contemplation (*āp-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Since they attained patience (*kṣānti*) upon completing this contemplation, it is said that they "entered samādhi. The section below provides a detailed exposition of the method of practice.
Furthermore, there are two meanings. First, one first contemplates internal water. External water is distant and difficult to focus the mind upon;

therefore, one is first taught to contemplate within the body. Regarding the meaning of "water-nature being unassailable": because the water-element within the body cannot be overcome by the other elements.
Initially, starting from mucus, saliva, and so forth, the meaning of "unassailable" is explained. That which is in the nose is called *mukha* (mucus); that which is in the mouth is called...
Saliva. This water is that which is near the exterior, manifest and easily seen: when it is swallowed down the throat, it is called *jin* (essence-fluid);
when it overflows outside the throat, it is called *ye* (liquid). This water is that which is near the interior, hidden yet perceptible:
that which resides in the bones and marrow is called *jing* (vital essence); that which resides in the tendons and flesh is called *xue* (blood). This water dwells within.
That which is subtle, difficult to see, and difficult to perceive is the transformation and discharge of food and drink, known as the excretions of feces and urine.
Furthermore, this is water that enters the upper body, circulates, and flows downward.

Thus, from the outside to the inside and from the top to the bottom, if one investigates each part to its ultimate limit, there is nothing that does not flow throughout the entire body. Therefore, it is said: "within the body."

"Revolving. "Revolving" means the sense of flowing. Regarding "the nature of water is one and the same," the *Zhengmai* says: mucus, saliva, digestive juices, and lymphatic fluids are the clear aspects of water;
semen, blood, excrement, and urine are the turbid aspects of water. Although the clear and turbid differ, the nature of water is no different.
I, the fool, say that "one and the same" means they share a single essence throughout, such that earth, fire, and wind cannot overcome them.
"Extinction. This refers to what was stated above: "The nature of water cannot be usurped. Regarding the phrase "seeing the water," one next contemplates external water.

Although it is of the same substance and universally identical, it is nonetheless obstructed by the body; therefore, one must extend the contemplation outward, which is why it says, "seeing the water within the body," etc.
This means that one exclusively observes the water existing within the body, and furthermore, contemplates its relationship with the world.
This refers to the external fragrant waters. The *Ruzhufeng Zhaimai* (Picking the Veins at Milk Peak) states:
"According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, beneath the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean, there is a great lotus named 'Various Radiant Filaments Fragrance Banner.
This flower grows within the Universal Light Maṇi Fragrant Water Ocean. Within this flower are fragrant water oceans as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields. One.
Within each ocean there is a single world-system (*kṣetra-vyuha*). Each world-system consists of twenty tiers of Buddha-fields stacked high like a banner.
A fool further supplements this by saying that because they rise up preeminently like a king, they should be called "King-Banner World-Systems" (*dhvaja-rāja-kṣetra*).
Now, within this central world-system, "the outer" refers collectively to the Fragrant Ocean, namely the Universal Radiance Mani.
This ocean is so designated because it lies beneath the Great Lotus of the Flower-Array Banner and belongs to the exterior of the world-system.
"The Floating Banner King Land" refers to the individual fragrant oceans, namely those numbering as many as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields. These oceans lie beneath the Flower-Array Banner...
Because the Buddha-fields—resembling banners and resembling kings—float within the great lotuses of the banners, they are collectively and generally referred to as "all fragrant water oceans.

If discussed analytically, one should say: "the general fragrant water oceans outside the worlds, and the specific fragrant water oceans of the floating Banner-King fields. Regarding the phrase "equal and without distinction," it means that [they are identical].
Because the essence is universally pervasive and identical. Since the internal and external are of one identical essence, one does not perceive the body as an obstacle.
If one can further transcend the realms (*dhātu*), then one's nature merges with true emptiness.

However, regarding this passage, while the ancient masters from above interpreted it as observing within the body and below as a direct explanation of practicing contemplation to grasp the essential meaning, a careful examination of the text reveals that there is no mention of "grasping the essential meaning" (*ling-zhi*) therein.

The meaning of this is as follows: it is because the Tathāgata Water-Heaven (Vāri-deva) has already taught the practice of the water-contemplation (*āp-smṛtyupasthāna*), and now provides a detailed exposition of the method for its cultivation.
Upon completing the Buddhist teaching on contemplation, there are three parts: second, practicing and realizing according to the teaching; first, the initial accomplishment of internal contemplation;
second, the subsequent cultivation of external contemplation; third, the realization of the merging of water and space. First:
At that time, I had first accomplished this contemplation; I saw only the water, yet had not yet attained the state of being bodiless.
While I was practicing dhyāna in my room as a bhikṣu, a disciple of mine peered through the window to observe the room. He saw only clear water filling the entire room and could see nothing else.
Being young and ignorant, he took a piece of tile or rubble and threw it into the water, causing the water to splash.
With a glance, he departed. After I emerged from samādhi, I suddenly felt a pain in my heart, like that experienced by Śāriputra when he was struck by the malevolent ghost.
I thought to myself: "I have now attained the path of Arhatship; I have long been free from the conditions of illness. Why does this heart-pain arise all of a sudden today?
Could it be that I am falling away from my realization? At that moment, the youth came quickly before me and spoke.
Regarding the matter mentioned above, I told him: "If you see water again, you may open the door and enter this water to remove the tiles and debris.
The youth followed my instructions. Later, when he entered meditative absorption, he saw the water once more, and the tiles and debris were still there exactly as before.
He opened the door and removed them. Afterward, when I emerged from absorption, my physical body was restored to its original state.

"First, one realizes the body as limited to water. This "time" refers to the period of practicing according to the instructions. When the object and wisdom correspond, this is called the initial accomplishment of this contemplation.
Because one realizes that the nature of water is identical to the other great elements and cannot be displaced or extinguished, it is said that "one sees only its water.
Although one sees only its water, because it still revolves and returns within the body, it is said that [the realization] is not yet complete.
"He has attained the bodiless state. Although he knows there is no self within the body, he has not yet fully realized that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are all empty.
○ "He shall act as a bhikṣu" is said below to manifest that the body serves as an obstruction. Since he has not yet attained the bodiless state, he remains a follower of the Lesser Vehicle;
therefore, it says "he shall act as a bhikṣu," meaning that at that time he was still in the rank of a bhikṣu. As for "sitting in meditation within the chamber," it refers to...

This refers to the practice of the aforementioned contemplation. As for why meditation (*dhyāna*) is called "tranquility" (*ānā*), it is because the object and wisdom are in accord, such that one hits the mark without effort.
A "disciple" (*śiṣya*) is one who attends to the master by carrying his towel and water jar;

seeing him remain in the room for a long time, he does not dare enter directly, but merely peers through the window to observe the room, intending to ascertain whether the master is moving or still. The word "only" (*wei*) serves to exclude others.
It is said that earth, water, fire, and wind are all of one single nature; they do not arise without conditions, and their arising must depend upon conditions.

Now, by taking the contemplation of water as the condition, other conditions no longer give rise [to their respective appearances]. Therefore, one sees only pure water filling the room, while nothing else is perceived at all. Guanding stated:
"This is precisely the 'form resulting from meditative concentration' (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*). Later, during the Liang dynasty, there was the Chan Master Fachong.
The Master Shui-guan of Hanzhou had his quarters flooded by water; this can serve as proof of this principle. "Child" (*tóngzhì*) refers to a young boy;
generally, anyone from eight years of age up to fifteen may be so called. Because they have not yet mastered the facts and principles, they are said to be "ignorant.
Due to this ignorance, two kinds of doubt arise: first, the doubt that a bhikṣu who clearly knows [the situation] is at peace.
Chan asked, "How is it that there is no one in the room? The second doubt was that he clearly knew the room was a meditation hall; how could he see only water?

Because these two doubts were intertwined in his mind, he took tiles and rubble and threw them into the water. This was merely to test whether there was anyone there or not, and whether it was water or not.
He stirred and shook it to make it rise; once the water made a sound, he knew for certain it was water. Although...
He knew for certain that it was water, yet he remained fearful that someone might be there; thus, as he looked back and moved forward, it is said that "he departed while glancing back.

Regarding "suffering pain upon emerging from meditative concentration": although there were only tiles and pebbles within [the vessel], because he had not yet attained the bodyless state (*anātman*), he was obstructed by his physical body.
This is like Śāriputra encountering the malevolent *vetāla* spirit; Guanding says that Śāriputra, at the Ganges...
While dwelling in an araṇya on the riverbank, he entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*). A malevolent spirit struck him with its palm, causing him headache upon emerging from concentration.
Now, his heart is pained upon emerging; both are due to the same bodily obstruction.
○ "I myself do not know, yet I harbor doubt" refers to the mind that is self-doubting and self-astonished. "Now that I have attained [this]" refers to his own claim of having attained *Arhatship*.
The path of Arhatship was not only attained today; it had already been attained long ago. Thus, there are two kinds of causes for illness:

first, those induced by past karma (*pūrvakarma*); second, those summoned by present karma (*vartamānakarma*). As for the statement that [the Arhat] has long since departed [from such conditions], since one who has already attained Arhatship should naturally be free from present karma, and since it was attained long ago, one should also be free from past karma. If this were so, then—
Because there ought to be pain, he doubted himself, wondering how it could have arisen so suddenly; he marveled at himself, fearing he might have fallen away from his practice.
He did not realize that this was merely because he had been unable to extinguish the self and was thus hindered by the body.

○ At that time—used here as a verification for the removal [of doubt]—"at that time" refers precisely to the moment of his own doubt and self-marveling. "The youth came swiftly" means he wished to resolve his doubts.

"Because of his strange thoughts. "Quickly" means speedily. "To relate the aforementioned matters" refers to reporting in detail each of the events mentioned above, such as seeing water filling the room and throwing pebbles into it. "'I then said,' etc.

means that because he himself perceived the obstruction caused by the body, I instructed him to see the water again, open the door, and remove the pebbles, in order to test whether he still [perceived them].
"Are you in pain? The youth and his companions merely understood the instruction to remove the pebbles; they still did not know the underlying purpose for removing them.
It was only after I later emerged from meditative absorption that I realized this through personal experience.
The reason my heart was pained was because I possessed a body. Thus, he practiced the second stage: external observation.
He encountered immeasurable Buddhas. Proceeding in this manner until he reached the Tathāgata King of Sovereign Penetrations of Mountains and Seas, he finally attained the dissolution of his body.

He realized for himself that the pain in his heart was caused by attachment to the body. Desiring to extend his gaze outward and seek the Buddhas' acceptance, he again encountered immeasurable Buddhas.
Thus, in the presence of these immeasurable Buddhas, he extended his outward gaze as far as the mountains.

The Tathāgata Sāgaravaradharavikrīḍitābhijña first manifested his external appearance at this point. The name of the Tathāgata, Sāgaravaradharavikrīḍitābhijña, is also a title for the Great Perfect Penetration of Water.
This is because water is fundamentally fluid and pervasive, yet it encounters obstruction when meeting a mountain.
The Buddha, through the perfect penetration of the water element, fused mountains into water; thus, whether it be mountains or seas, they are equally subject to his sovereign mastery and circulation.
Now, mountains belong to the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*); since the earth element has been fused into water, the remaining elements may be understood accordingly.
Thus we know that this Buddha is called the "King" because he alone, through the perfect penetration of the water-element, transcends all other gates.

That Moonlight Bodhisattva’s cultivation of external observation must reach this Buddha before it is perfected is likewise according to the principle of "like seeking like" and "like responding to like.
Once external observation is perfected, one sees within the body of water and beyond the world a floating [lotus].
The various fragrant water seas of the Cakravarti-dhvaja world-systems are without distinction. Therefore, it is said that one only then attains the dissolution of the self.
Third, the realization of water merging with space:
the nature of the fragrant water seas of the worlds of the ten directions merges with true emptiness, being non-dual and without differentiation. Now, before the Tathāgata...
One attains the name of "Celibate Youth" (Kumārabhūta) and joins the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
Although the preceding section extended the discussion of external observation, it was limited to the various fragrant seas within a single Flower Treasury World-realm (*kusumagarbha-lokadhātu*).
Thus, while one has succeeded in losing the self, one has not yet lost the realm, because the characteristics of the realm have not yet been emptied. Now, following the loss of the self...

Furthermore, by the power of profound contemplation, one expands the external water until it becomes of one essence and identical with all the fragrant water-oceans of the Flower Treasury Adorned Worlds throughout the ten directions.
Beyond this, there are no boundaries to be dissolved and no water to be contemplated.
It is simply that one sees it relying upon true emptiness; because its substance is conjoined with true emptiness, it is said that "its nature is conjoined with true emptiness.

Since its nature is conjoined with true emptiness, emptiness and water are fused and identical, and thus it is said that "they are non-dual and without distinction. This refers to what was stated in the preceding text:
"The nature of water is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true water; pure and fundamental from the beginning, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm."

Thus, the ultimate realization has been attained. Regarding the Tathāgata here—where "Tathāgata" refers specifically to the present Buddha—although he had previously succeeded in transcending the body, he had not yet been able to transcend the realm; his name and status remained those of an Arhat.

Now, through the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world, he has finally attained the title of "Celibate Youth" (Kumārabhūta) and is permitted to participate in the assembly of Bodhisattvas. This is because I have realized the nature of water.

I merged with emptiness, having already reached the ground of the dharma-realm of emptiness. Having thus completed the account of my cultivation and realization, I conclude by answering the question on perfect penetration.
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: "By means of the single flavor of the water-element flowing through me, I attained the patience of non-arising and have perfected Bodhi."
This is the first [stage]:
the division of flavor and vapor. The meaning of the answer is that I contemplate the nature of water within and without as being of one single vapor-division;
it is merely flowing and pervasive, yet the water has not yet ceased to exist. When, however, this nature merges with true emptiness, even the water vanishes.
Extinct. By this, one realizes the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Once this patience is established, enlightenment is not far off.
If one wishes to realize it, there is no need to seek other gateways; therefore, it is called "the perfection of Bodhi. This is the foremost.
[The section on] Moonlight and Water is concluded. Fourth, [the section on] Lapis Lazuli and Wind, Part Three. First, prostrating and making a formal declaration. Second, proceeding through...
This describes the cultivation and realization, followed by the third section: the conclusion and response regarding perfect penetration. First:
The Dharma Prince Vairocanaraśmiprabha immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
Lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya) is transparent and radiant both inside and out, pure and free from blemish.

The following passage, in which the Bodhisattva describes his own body and mind as emitting light, penetratingly clear, and unimpeded, explains the reason for this name. Thus, the *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) states:

"Because he later realized a state of penetrating clarity, he received the title 'Lapis Lazuli'. Furthermore, the Sanskrit term *vaiḍūrya* is translated here as "blue-colored jewel. From this, the Bodhi...
Sā always emits a blue light that resembles lapis lazuli; therefore, he is named accordingly. *Guanding* (Consecration) states:
"This refers to the Bodhisattva Vairocanaraśmiprabha in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, who emitted blue light until it reached the seat of Śākyamuni.

Second, the chronological account of his cultivation and realization (the Bodhisattva’s own narrative states: "Not long after meeting the Buddha, I attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Its meaning is identical to that of Sudhana’s single lifetime of perfection...")

Realization cannot be discussed in terms of awakening first and cultivation later; therefore, it is also spoken of directly as "cultivation and realization. There are two parts: first, encountering the Buddhist teachings and contemplation; second, cultivating and realizing according to those teachings. Regarding the first:
I recall that in the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Immeasurable Sound (*Amitaghoṣa*).

He revealed to bodhisattvas the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment, observing that this world and the bodies of sentient beings are all produced by the turning of false conditions—wind, direction, and location.
The Buddha named Immeasurable Sound (Amitaghoṣa) took the cultivation of the contemplation of wind as his designation.
He taught that among all phenomena, there is none that does not possess sound; yet sound does not sound of itself—it exists because of the wind.

If one were to contemplate the wind directly, one fears that its appearance and disappearance would be inconsistent, making it difficult to achieve meditative realization. Therefore, one must use sound to contemplate the wind. Since sound is immeasurable, so too is the wind.
It is also immeasurable. Observing in this manner, it becomes the object of contemplation everywhere.

Therefore, the Buddha gave it this name so that those practicing the contemplation of wind may know its source. Furthermore, when the contemplation is perfected, the wind dissolves and returns to its fundamental nature.
Thereafter, based on the fundamental wind-nature (*dhātu-vāyu*), it issues forth as immeasurable sounds.

Because it preaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of beings, the Buddha designates it by this name, so that those who have perfected the contemplation of wind may understand its application. "Opening" (*kai*) means to reveal and manifest the rational nature (*dharmatā*).

"Indication" (shi) refers to pointing out the method of contemplation; the "bodhisattva" is the sentient being who is the recipient of this teaching. The phrase "fundamental awakening is wondrously luminous" (benjue miaoming) precisely clarifies the principle that is revealed.

That which has been spiritually discerning from the beginningless past is called "fundamental awakening" (benjue); that which has never been obscured since the beginningless past is called "wondrously luminous" (miaoming).
This refers to what was stated in the preceding passage: "the nature-awareness is wondrously luminous; the fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous.
The contemplation regarding "observing this world" and so forth precisely clarifies the contemplation being demonstrated. The character "contemplate" (guan) points to the observing wisdom (*jñāna*).

"Worlds and sentient beings" refer to the objects of observation. "Delusion" refers to the single thought-moment of false movement. Worlds and sentient beings exist in dependence upon this; therefore, it is termed a "condition" (*pratyaya*).

Furthermore, regarding what is called the "power of wind": because deluded movement belongs to wind and is able to serve as a condition for the body and the vessel-world (the physical universe), it is termed "power.

"Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) means change. This refers to how, based initially on the wondrous clarity of fundamental awakening, a single thought of deluded conditioning arises through the power of wind, resulting in the "mark of karma.
Due to this karma, it transforms into the capacity to see, which constitutes the "mark of transformation. And due to this capacity to see...
When objects falsely appear within the realm of consciousness, the subtle characteristics of worldlings and sentient beings manifest.

When the continuity of cognition clings to these through conceptualization and gives rise to karma, the coarse characteristics of worldlings and sentient beings—consisting of the marks of suffering bound by karma—become attached.
Thus, one knows that the world and its sentient beings originate from a single moment of deluded conditioning.
Because they arise through the shifting transformations of the power of wind, it is said that "all are equal," and so forth.

Nevertheless, although that Buddha sought to reveal the wondrous luminosity of original enlightenment (prakṛti-bodhi), he instead demonstrated this contemplation; for although enlightenment is inherently possessed and luminosity is wondrously perfected, [without such practice, they remain unmanifest].
Due to the wind-power of a single moment of deluded conditioning, the root-body and the vessel-world arise through constant transformation. Within, one is sealed by the grasping of self;

without, one is bound by the fetters of phenomena. Wandering aimlessly, one forgets the source; as one proceeds further and further downward, fundamental enlightenment conversely becomes non-enlightenment, and wondrous luminosity sinks forever into ignorance.
The Buddha reveals this contemplation to cause one to know that the power of the wind has no basis, and that the body and the vessel-world...

Empty from the beginning. Internally, by not clinging to a self, the segmentation [of existence] lacks cause; externally, by not binding to phenomena, the transformations of change sever their fetters.
One realizes original enlightenment and suddenly attains wondrous enlightenment; following the wondrous luminosity, one turns toward and enters perfect luminosity.

The ultimate limit of perfect penetration is exhausted herein. Second, practicing and realizing according to the teachings, in four parts: first, contemplating that the substance of wind is identical [to the nature of mind].
Second, realizing the nature of wind is empty; third, through the completion of contemplation, one attains patience; fourth, with the opening of the mind, one realizes the fruit. First:

At that time, I contemplated the establishment of the elements, contemplated the movement of the world, contemplated the movement and stillness of the body, and contemplated the movement and thoughts of the mind.
"All movements are non-dual and without distinction.
As for "at that time," it refers to the moment when that Buddha revealed the rational nature and pointed out the gate of contemplation.
To rely on the contemplation of wind in order to restore the wondrous clarity of fundamental awakening, one observes the world, the body, and the mind in their entirety.

Regarding the observation of the establishment of the realms: this means first observing the four cardinal directions—east, west, south, and north—and the four intermediate directions, as well as above and below;
