first, the former is called the "rhinoceros-like" (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*) and the latter is called the "group-dwelling" (*vargacārin*); second, the former does not encounter a Buddha [during his training].
This person encounters a Buddha. Third, whereas previously one attained awakening through self-realization alone, here one attains awakening by relying on the teachings.
Fourth, whereas previously one contemplated external objects, here one contemplates internal conditions. Fifth, whereas previously one’s faculties were sharp and keen, here one’s faculties are dull.

The present mention of "those in training" refers to a class of individuals seeking pratyekabuddhahood who have not yet entered the path of realization; they receive the teachings and contemplate conditions.

There are two gates: first, observing the flow of saṃsāra in its forward direction to know the causes of birth; second, observing the cessation of saṃsāra in its reverse direction to awaken to the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
What is now called the severance of the twelve links of dependent origination is explained according to the gate of reversal, because it is the direct cause for awakening;
thus, it is mentioned specifically. "Supreme nature" (*śreṣṭha-dhātu*) refers precisely to the principle of non-arising. Because it transcends the world, it is so named.
Supreme Nature (*paramatattva*). Because this nature is manifested through the severance of conditions, it is called "Supreme Nature manifested through the severance of conditions.

However, while the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is already termed "supreme," within the stage of the Path of Realization (*darśanamārga*), it is not merely supreme but reaches the state of subtlety. Thus, it is said:

"The Supreme and Subtle are Manifested and Perfected. This means that within the stage of the Path of Realization, the particularly superior and subtle nature is prefigured in its perfect manifestation.

Regarding the marks: manifesting the body and preaching the Dharma so that they may attain liberation follows the same principle as above, because the two types of awakening—through abandonment and realization—are identical.
Fourth, he is able to respond to the śrāvakas:

if those in training (śaikṣa) realize the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths, and through the path of cultivation enter cessation such that their supreme nature manifests in perfection, before them I [appear].
He manifests in the form of a śrāvaka and preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

Those prior to the fourth fruit—namely, those in the three fruits and four stages of the path—are all called "those in training" (śaikṣa), because they still have afflictions to be severed and truths to be investigated.
One who attains the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths is one who has first heard the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths from the Buddha.
...and the principle of emptiness and non-self. Because one hears the Dharma of the Four Truths, one knows the suffering of the triple world.

By cultivating the supramundane path, one partially severs the afflictions of views and thoughts and partially realizes *nirvāṇa*; thus it is said that "one enters extinction through the path of cultivation. Regarding "the supreme nature manifests its perfection":

this refers to the most excellent nature of extinction within the stages from the candidate for the fruit of Arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*) up to the four fruits; because the signs of its complete fulfillment are already manifest therein. Manifestation...
Regarding the bodies of the śrāvakas, he casts himself according to their inclinations; for those who preach the Dharma, he teaches the dharmas of superior progress;

and for those he causes to attain liberation, he effects their release from the bonds of views and afflictions (*kleśa*) as well as the suffering of the limited分段 [birth-and-death]. Thus he has fulfilled his responsiveness to the four types of noble ones.

Second, there are seven types of beings who can manifest as the seven celestial deities: first, those capable of manifesting the body of Brahmā; second, those capable of manifesting the body of Śakra;
third, those capable of manifesting Maheśvara; fourth, those capable of manifesting Maheśāna; fifth, those capable of manifesting the celestial general;
sixth, those capable of manifesting the Four Heavenly Kings; and seventh, those capable of manifesting the celestial crown prince. First:
If there are sentient beings who desire clear awakening of the mind, refrain from the defilements of desire, and wish for purity of body,
I manifest before them in the form of a Brahmā King and preach the Dharma to them, causing them to attain liberation.
If "all sentient beings" refers to those in the desire realm who aspire to be born in the Brahma Heaven:

although "desire" generally encompasses the five [objects] (the three being food, sleep, and sexual intercourse; and the five being forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles), because sexual intercourse is the foremost, the term is used specifically to denote the "desirous mind."
This refers to the mind of lustful desire. One who possesses clear awakening is not deluded by matters of desire. The *Zhengmo* states:
"It means to penetrate deeply that lustful desire is the root of all suffering. Because lustful desire has defilement as its nature, it is called a "dust" (*rajas*).
To permanently sever ties with a wife constitutes non-transgression. While the preceding phrase refers to deep understanding, this phrase refers to [the realization of] pain.
It is for the sake of the precepts. For one who desires purity of body, it clarifies the reason for not transgressing;

thus, it serves to manifest purity of body in the present as a cause for rebirth in the Brahma realm in the future. One who manifests a Brahma-body therein does so in accordance with their aspirations.

Regarding the consecration (abhiṣeka): its full name is *brahma*, which translates as "freedom from bonds" (*visaṃyoga*). This means that by leaving behind the bonds of the lower realms, one ascends to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
It is also called "Pure Conduct" (*brahmacarya*), meaning that one is able to practice the virtue of Brahmā because both desire and conceptualization are absent.

It is further termed "Exalted Purity," meaning that one transcends the defilements of the Desire Realm so thoroughly that they do not arise. As for the term "King," it refers to the devas of the Form Realm.
The Lord then expounds the Dharma of the four dhyānas and the sequence of cultivation and realization for those who preach the Dharma, as clarified in the section on the heavenly realms below.
He causes them to attain liberation so that they may be freed from the fetters of the lower realms and accomplish the ascent to the Form Realm.
The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) states: "This liberation is the accomplishment of the definitive relinquishing of desire to be born in the Brahma realm."
Regarding this matter: although both relinquishing and seeking are present here, the emphasis lies on aspiration; thus, it is equivalent to the "Accomplishment" section below.
Furthermore, the *pratisaṃvid* (liberations) one cultivates is also termed *vimokṣa* (deliverance). As the *Abhiṣeka* cites the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*:

"The Great Brahmā King expounded the *Vairāgya-śāstra* (Treatise on Detachment from Desire) to cause others to leave desire and be born in the Brahma world. This refers precisely to the meaning of the Dharma.
Second, he can manifest the body of Śakra.
If there are sentient beings who wish to become the Lord of Heaven to rule over the devas,
I appear before them in the form of Śakra and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.

If there are sentient beings who, among those in the human realm, aspire to be born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—*Trāyastriṃśa* being a Sanskrit term meaning "Thirty-three," which is the second heaven of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*)—this heaven is situated atop Mount Sumeru.

On each of its four sides there are eight heavens, with the Sudarśana Heaven at the center, where the Lord of Devas resides; including both the sovereign and his ministers, they constitute the Thirty-three Heavens.
Now, when it says "desiring to be the Lord of Devas," it refers not only to aspiring for birth there, but to desiring to become the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven itself.

Because he is the Lord. As for "the one who rules over all devas," this refers not only to his ruling over the Trāyastriṃśa devas, but also to the fact that the Great Generals of the lower heavens and the Four Heavenly Kings are all his subjects and likewise under his command.
Because he accords with their requests, he manifests in the form of Śakra before them. "Śakra" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit; in its full form, it is called Śakra-devendra.
Śakra-devendra is here translated as "Capable Ruler" (Nengzhu), because he is able to serve as the Lord of Devas.

Regarding the Dharma-preacher's exposition of the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths of action, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "This refers to the various virtuous discourses of Śakra-devendra."
The Accomplished One: By relying on the cause of the ten wholesome paths of action, one accomplishes the fruit of Śakra.

Third, he can manifest as the Lord of the Heaven of Free Enjoyment of Manifestations (Vaśavartin): if there are sentient beings who desire to travel freely through the ten directions with their bodies, I manifest before them as the Lord of the Heaven of Free Enjoyment of Manifestations.
He manifests in bodily form to preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
Regarding the *Īśvara-deva* (Lord of the Gods), the ignorant previously clung to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, asserting it was the *Nirmāṇarati-deva* (Gods who Delight in Emanations).
This is because when these gods wish to experience the pleasures of the five desires, they can transform at will and attain mastery. Guishan said: "This is desire..."
The Heaven at the Pinnacle of the Realm (*Kāyāgra-deva*). In Sanskrit, it is *Paranirmita-vaśavartin*, which means "Mastery over the Creations of Others.

This refers to the Māra-heaven, so called because one’s own pleasure is accomplished by relying on the creations of others. Alternatively, it is said that there is a separate dwelling place for the Māra-king atop the Six Heavens of Desire, which is also subsumed under the Heaven of Mastery over the Creations of Others.
The present text says: "If sentient beings seek to be born in the Heaven of Mastery over the Creations of Others..."
This refers to those who undergo transformation. Those who desire mastery over their bodies pray for the fulfillment of their primary retribution (*vipāka*).

Those who travel through the ten directions further seek unimpeded secondary retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*). The *Zhengmai* states: "The ten directions consist of the six heavens of the desire realm and the four continents.
As for "accomplishing the teaching," it means preaching the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade to enable them to achieve the most supreme state within the desire realm.
This is because it is the retribution of the Heaven of Mastery over Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*). According to the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), this heaven was originally above;

the former Śakra and the latter four kings of the gods were below. Although it does not appear in the middle [of the current arrangement], its position relative to above and below can be known by analogy.
Fourth, the ability to manifest as Maheśvara:
if there are sentient beings who desire mastery over their bodies to fly through the void,
I appear before them in the form of the deity Maheśvara and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goal.
Mahādeva, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, is said to be the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
this is because when the gods of this heaven wish to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses, other gods manifest them for them, and his sovereignty is superior to that of the former. Guishan says:

"This is the Mahesvara Heaven at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpāvacara*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "He has three eyes and eight arms, rides a white ox, and holds a white fly-whisk."
As for the previous mention of "wandering" (*parikrama*) and this current mention of "flying" (*vihāra*): wandering may involve detours or curves, whereas flying is invariably direct and swift.
Furthermore, when traveling through the ten directions, one may rely on high ground or descend to lower levels; however, when moving through space, one only rides upon clouds and controls the winds.
The superiority or inferiority of these two heavens’ sovereign powers is self-evident. If sentient beings desire this state, they should vow to be born in Mahāśvara.

This refers to the gods (*deva*). Regarding the "accomplishment of the teaching," it refers to the teaching of the four *dhyānas* and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), which brings about the fruition of the supreme Great Sovereignty (*maheśvara*) at the Peak of Form (*rūpāvacara-agra*). According to this, these gods occupy the highest level of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

Since the Brahmā King of the first *dhyāna* occupies the lowest level of the realm of form, the intermediate levels can be understood by analogy. Furthermore, they are not unmanifest. [Question: Regarding the two higher heavens, there are three ancient interpretations.

There are those who allocate the five and six heavens of the desire realm [respectively], such as the *Fahua wenju* (Textual Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), upon which the *Dacheng* (Great Commentary) relies. There are also those who subsume them all within the four heavens of Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Māra, and Maheśvara, such as the *Cien xuanzan* (Profound Praise of Ci'en).

Changshui followed this [interpretation]. Some explain it as referring to the two heavens of the Peak of Desire (*kāmadhātu-śikhara*) and the Peak of Form (*rūpadhātu-śikhara*); this is the *Avalokiteśvara-yi-shu*. Gushan and Wenling followed this. However, both the *Wenju* and the *Yi-shu* record the teachings of Zhiyi. The *Wenju* states:

"Regarding Maheśvara, some say he is the Maheśvara at the peak of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). This [being] should not transcend [the desire realm] to reach that [peak]. The *Yi-shu* further states: "Because he is Maheśvara, he is not [a resident of] the sixth heaven. Since the statements in the earlier and later texts contradict one another, which should one ultimately follow? Answer:

When I was formerly annotating the *Lotus Sūtra*, I relied on the *Dacheng* (Great Commentary) for my explanation and felt some doubt in my heart. Nevertheless, because it was a tradition inherited from Tiantai, I did not dare to change it arbitrarily. Now, based on Guanding’s analysis, which is extremely thorough, I shall rely on the latter of Tiantai’s two explanations.

The same applies as before. This is because the previous explanation may have been incorrect, and it was subsequently understood that this was not different from the prior statement. Furthermore, many sūtras and śāstras refer to Maheśvara as a deity of the Peak of Form (Bhavāgra). The *Zhengmo* states: "In general terms, all heavens may be included;

Brahmā encompasses the four dhyānas, while Śakra, the Four Kings, and others encompass the six heavens of desire. The two 'Masters' (Maheśvaras) are mentioned separately to distinguish between the limits of the Desire Realm and the Peak of Form. However, the four formless realms (ārūpyadhātu) are omitted, because in these realms one does not manifest a physical body, and thus [the Bodhisattva] does not manifest there.

Even if there were other skillful means for benefiting beings in those realms, they would not fall under this category. The *Guanjing* says: "In truth, the Bodhisattva’s benefit of sentient beings is difficult to fathom with ordinary sentiments."
Although the devas of the desire realm, the form realm, and the empty space are not listed together here, they are all fully included within the eight classes of spirits mentioned below.
Fifth is the Deva General who can manifest himself.
If there are sentient beings who love to command ghosts and spirits to protect their lands, I appear before them as a great celestial general.
He assumes a military form to preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
Regarding the "Great General of the Heavens," Zhengmo states that each of the four kings’ commanders has eight generals, with Weituo as their leader.
Guanding, citing the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, identifies Sanji as the Great General who patrols the twenty-eight divisions.

All who roam the world are governed by Saṃjñeya. The present statement that he "lovingly presides over ghosts and spirits" refers to seeking the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of Saṃjñeya and others.
Regarding "ghosts and spirits," they are the gods among ghosts. Zhaò says: "Gods receive mixed retributions of both good and evil."
They manifest forms superior to humans and inferior to devas; because their bodies are extremely subtle and light, they are difficult for humans to see.
This is the realm of ghosts and spirits (*piśāca*). Those who protect the land are those who traverse the world to eliminate calamities and bring down blessings and auspiciousness.
Those who achieve the preaching of the Dharma expound the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, as well as the secret methods of mantras and mudrās for summoning ghosts and spirits.
I cause them to achieve the rank of celestial generals so that they may protect the land according to their intentions.
Sixth, I am able to manifest as the Four Heavenly Kings;
if there are sentient beings who desire to govern the world and protect its inhabitants, I appear before them in the form of the Four Heavenly Kings.
He preaches the Dharma to them in person, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
(Regarding the Four Heavenly Kings, see the commentary in Volume Two. *Guanding* says: "These are the military ministers and generals of Śakra, who dwell on the mid-slope of Mount Sumeru;
each leads two classes of spirits and ghosts to ensure they do not harass people. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "We..."
The Four Kings, the twenty-eight divisions [of yakṣas], and hundreds of thousands of spirits and deities constantly observe and protect this Jambudvīpa with their pure divine eyes.

For this reason, we are called the World-Protecting Kings (*Lokapāla*). Now, you speak of "lovingly governing the world," which means we wish to serve as Heavenly Kings and govern the four continents in our respective divisions, ensuring that spirits and deities do not afflict or harm human beings. This is precisely...
To protect sentient beings, the one who accomplishes the teaching expounds the ten supreme wholesome actions and the methods for protecting the state and bringing peace to the people,
thereby fulfilling the vow of the Four Heavenly Kings to govern the world and protect living beings according to their respective jurisdictions.
Seventh, for those who aspire to be born as celestial princes and to command spirits and deities within the heavenly palaces,
I manifest before them in the form of a prince of the Four Heavenly Kings' realm and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goal.

If "all sentient beings" refers specifically to those within the human realm, it means that because they have witnessed ghosts and spirits causing calamities, harassing the people, and disrupting the state while in the human realm, they make a vow to be reborn in the palace of the Four Heavenly Kings to subdue these spirits and prevent them from causing harm;
hence it is said they "love being born in the heavenly palaces. Even if there are those who violate this [vow] and continue to cause calamities, they can still be driven away and controlled.
By his power, he subdued the ghosts and spirits; hence it is said that he "drives and commands the ghosts and spirits.
He manifests according to what beings delight in; hence it is said that he "manifests the body of a prince of the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Wēnlíng says: "The princes of the Four Heavenly Kings are of the same class as Nātha. The *Mahā-śrī-sūtra* states: "Each of the Four World-Protecting Kings has ninety-one [thousand]..."
"Son, the four kings together have three hundred and sixty-four sons. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also speaks thus.
According to Guanding, during the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, five kingdoms of the Western蕃 (Tibetans) came to raid Anxi.

Emperor Xuanzong summoned the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra to enter the palace to recite the *Rājanīya-pariṇāmanā-dhāraṇī* for the protection of the state. After only fourteen recitations, he suddenly beheld a deity."
He led five hundred men bearing halberds before the palace and addressed the Emperor, saying, "The second son of the Northern Heavenly King, Du Jian, went to rescue Anxi.

Subsequently, a memorial was submitted, and by imperial decree, images of the Heavenly King were installed in the northwestern corners of all prefectures, provinces, and districts to protect the national borders forever.
Thus, it is clear that this Heavenly King has sons. As for those who have achieved success through the Dharma, they speak of returning [to the source].

Through the methods of precepts, fasts, virtues, talismans, mantras, and seal-diagrams, he causes the sons of the Four Heavenly Kings to achieve success, thereby fulfilling his wishes to command spirits and deities;
this can respond to the seven heavens in their entirety.
Third, they are able to manifest before ten types of persons. First, they can manifest in the body of a human king; second, they can manifest in the body of a householder;
third, they can manifest in the body of a lay merchant; fourth, they can manifest in the body of a government official; fifth, they can manifest as a Brahmin; sixth, they can manifest as a bhikṣu;
seventh, they can manifest as a bhikṣuṇī; eighth, they can manifest as an upāsaka; ninth, they can...
Manifesting as an upāsikā: tenth, being able to manifest in the body of a woman.
First, if there are sentient beings who delight in being human kings, I manifest before them in the body of a human king and preach the Dharma for them.
To cause them to achieve their aim:
those who delight in being kings, possessing virtue and harboring benevolence, yet unable to endure the chaos of the world, resolve to become rulers of the Way in order to govern the state.
To explain the teachings so that they may succeed: for them, one explains the causes for birth into noble status and...
The virtue and achievements of an emperor serve merely to perfume the seeds for future lives.
If one does not measure oneself and recklessly covets the divine vessel [the throne], seeking the means to usurp it—how could a Bodhisattva respond to such a person? Wénlǐng says:

From the Golden Wheel-turning King down to the King of Śāṇakalpa, all are kings of men. If one follows the *Pumen pin* (Universal Gate Chapter), they are exclusively Kings of Śāṇakalpa, for that text refers to them as "lesser kings.
Second, he can manifest in the body of an elder (*śreṣṭhin*).
If there are sentient beings who cherish birth into a noble clan and are esteemed by the world, I manifest before them in the body of an elder and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve fulfillment.
Within the human realm, there are those who possess high rank and great virtue, who are revered by their own kin;
therefore, they also love and cherish their clan. As Mencius said: "In the court, nothing is as esteemed as rank; in the local community, nothing is as esteemed as age;

in assisting the world and leading the people, nothing is as esteemed as virtue. Thus we know that those who possess high rank, advanced age, and profound virtue do not merely [hold these attributes].
He is honored by his own kin and is also esteemed by the world; that is to say, wherever he goes, he is highly regarded and offered the seat of honor to his left.
Zhengmo says that in the Western Regions, the title "Elder" (*sthavira*) does not refer merely to one who is advanced in years.

Rather, it is an appellation for a high minister or a great family head who possesses both virtue and reputation. As for "one accomplished in preaching," this refers to one who preaches extensively to bestow benefits upon and rescue the masses.
The method for loving one's kin and extending benevolence to the people enables the accomplishment of elders so that they may fulfill their ancestral lineage and the aspirations of the world.
Third, he is able to manifest in the body of a layperson (*gṛhapati*):
if there are sentient beings who delight in discussing names and terms and dwell in self-purification, I manifest before them in the body of a layperson.
He preached the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve realization.
Regarding his discourse on names and terminology, he spoke with affection because he wished to instruct the world through the classics and precedents of antiquity and the present.

Regarding his self-positioning, he remained pure and secluded because he wished to preserve the Way by not pursuing fame or achievement. He was consecrated to establish words for instructing the world and to dwell in the preservation of the Way.

The *zhengyin* (upright recluse) maintains pure conduct and is commonly referred to as a *jushi* (lay practitioner); they are simply categorized as superior, middling, or inferior according to their respective levels.

Regarding those who achieve success in preaching the Dharma, this refers to the methods of concealing one's brilliance and remaining obscure, as well as composing writings to establish precedents, thereby enabling the *jushi* to fulfill their aspirations for instructing the world and upholding the Way.
Fourth, they are able to manifest in the form of a civil or military official (*zai guan*).
If there are sentient beings who love to govern a kingdom or administer a district, I manifest before them in the body of a high official and preach the Dharma for them,
enabling them to achieve their goals.

The "state" (*guotu*) refers to the royal capital. Those who "govern with love" assist the sovereign in cultivating the administration; Wénlǐng identifies these as the Three Dukes and high ministers. The "districts and towns" (*bāngyì*) refer to the feudal fiefs.
Those who "divide and judge" manage the people and adjudicate lawsuits; Wénlǐng identifies these as the Governors of Prefectures, District Magistrates, and County Chiefs.
"Ruler" (*zǎi*) carries the sense of dividing and judging; therefore, the preceding text states that they "divide and judge the districts and towns," for their offices encompass such governance.
This summarizes the meaning. Thus, it was said above that "love governs the land. Furthermore, a "ruler" (*zǎi*) is also called an "official" (*guān*).

To "decide cases" (*pòduàn*) implies both governing and managing; an "official" (*guān*) is also called a "ruler" (*zǎi*). To "manage and govern" (*guǎnshè*) implies both deciding cases and governing.

Therefore, from those who have received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) up to the three ranks of ministers and high officials, down to the provincial governors and the hundred functionaries, all are designated as "ruling officials" (*zhíguān*). Regarding the phrase "the accomplishment of preaching the Dharma," this refers to cultivation.

The methods for achieving "equilibrium and order," "loyalty and affection," "integrity and clarity," and so forth, are intended to enable one to become a minister of state, thereby fulfilling the aspiration to serve the sovereign and benefit the people.
Zhengmo says: "The first three categories are similar to those encompassed by Confucianism."
Fifth, I can manifest as a brahmin.
If there are sentient beings who delight in various arts and sciences and seek to maintain themselves through such means,
I appear before them in the body of a brahmin and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.

Astrology, geography, yin-yang, and calculations of the degrees are called *shu* (calculative arts). Witches, physicians, physiognomists, diviners, and those who employ talismans, water, incantations, and seals are called *shu* (practical arts).
"Loving" refers to taking pleasure in and diligently practicing these, because they can uplift the world and save oneself.

Refining the spirit, cultivating the elixir, and maintaining the life-force is called *she* (gathering). Fortifying the essence, nourishing the vital breath (*qi*), and guarding against injury is called *wei* (protecting).
Those who dwell in self-reliance do not pursue external studies, for they believe it can prolong their lives and preserve their physical forms.
*Brāhmaṇa* is translated here as "Pure Lineage" (*Jìngyì*); these people claim to have been born from the mouth of Brahmā and are thus his descendants.
Alternatively, they are called *Brahmacārin* (translated as "Vanzhì"); these people claim to inherit the dharma of Brahmā and are resolved to be born in the Brahma realm.

Because they are celestial beings, they are also called "Pure Practitioners" (*śuddhacārin*). Their lineage possesses its own distinct scriptures, which have been transmitted from generation to generation;

they take the study of the Way as their profession. For those who have achieved success in preaching the Dharma, he explains the methods of differentiated wisdom, refining the spirit, and regulating the breath, so that they may achieve mastery in the arts of numerology and self-protection. Zhengmo says: "This section seems..."
This [teaching] is subsumed under medicine, divination, and various arts. (Question: The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle;

there is no second, nor is there a third. It further says: "Only this one thing is real; the other two are not true. From this we know that even the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas belong to the illusory city. How much more so for the various devas, humans, kings, ministers, elders, and lay devotees, and their methods for governing and instructing the world?

And how much more so for the various Brahmins and their diverse heterodox studies? Why does the Bodhisattva not reform these old habits and demonstrate the supramundane Right Path to them? Instead, why does he preach the Dharma according to their inclinations, thereby fulfilling their tainted aspirations? Is this not so?)

"Is this the act of one who possesses a heart of compassion? He replied: "Among *sāsrava* (outflowing) phenomena, there are both good and evil. Even if one cannot yet accomplish the good, the momentum will inevitably flow toward evil.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva temporarily accords with their desire to achieve virtuous fruits, waiting until their faculties (*indriya*) have matured before revealing the supramundane Right Path. This is what is meant by: 'First, lead them with the hook of desire; afterwards, cause them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. The following sections are all modeled after this. (6) He can manifest in the body of a *bhikṣu*.
If there is a man who delights in study, leaves the household life, and upholds the various precepts,
I will manifest before him in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for him, causing him to achieve success.
Householder men, weary of the dust and toil of worldly life, take pleasure in studying the path of renunciation.

This involves the various precepts and codes of discipline, namely the ten precepts for *śrāmaṇeras* and the two hundred and fifty precepts for *bhikṣus*. The term *bhikṣu* is translated here as "mendicant" (*qǐshì*):

it means that above, one begs for the Buddha-dharma to sustain the life of wisdom, and below, one begs for food and drink to sustain the physical body. Alternatively, it is translated as "remover of famine."

This means that those who have left the household life and maintain the precepts are a noble field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), capable of producing wholesome roots in sentient beings and removing the famine [of suffering].

The "preacher of the Dharma" speaks on the teachings for those who have left the household life, such as by extolling the maintenance of the precepts and praising the holy life (*brahmacarya*). As for "accomplishment":
Having accomplished five virtues, he is the honored one among the assembly. Seventh, he can manifest as a bhikṣuṇī:

if there is a woman who delights in study, leaves the household life, and upholds the various prohibitions and precepts, I will manifest before her in the body of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for her, causing her to achieve accomplishment.
Having grown weary of the defilements of household life, and further detesting the five obstacles inherent to women, they aspire to the study of renunciation.

Regarding the various prohibitions, there are the three hundred and forty-eight precepts; furthermore, the eight respectful rules (*gurudharma*), the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts, and others are all included among these prohibitions.
The *Upāyika-vinaya-sudarsana* states: "Ni" means woman; it refers to a woman who has left the household life and received [the precepts].

She is fully entitled to be called a bhikṣuṇī. The exposition of the Dharma is as above. As for "attainment," it means that by relinquishing the dharma of the household life and receiving the dharma of renunciation, she transforms her body—which was subject to the five obstacles—into a companion endowed with the five virtues.
Eighth, he can manifest as an upāsaka.
If there is a man who delights in upholding the five precepts, I will manifest before him in the body of an upāsaka and preach the Dharma for him,
causing him to achieve success.

Because they desire to seek the superior rewards of humans and devas, they joyfully uphold the five precepts; for these five precepts serve as the cause for rebirth among humans and devas. The five precepts are:

abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants. Of these, the first four are natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), meaning their very nature is that of a transgression.

Drinking alcohol is a *pratikṣepaṇasāvadya* (prohibited offense) because it violates a prohibition and thereby constitutes an offense. Furthermore, it is called a prohibited offense because it can obstruct the first four [precepts].
For example, violating the five precepts due to alcohol is such a case. An ancient master said: "The five precepts are identical to the Five Constants."

Through benevolence (*maitrī*), one does not kill living beings; through righteousness (*artha*), one does not steal; through propriety (*dharma*), one does not engage in sexual misconduct; through faithfulness (*satya*), one does not speak falsely;
and through wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not drink intoxicants. Therefore, an *upāsaka* is also called an *upāsaka*; translated into Chinese as "male lay follower" (*jìnshì nán*).
This refers to one who draws near to and serves the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. When the preacher speaks of the dharma for householders, he speaks of these rules.
As it is said: "One performs the Buddha-work without being separated from worldly defilements; one cultivates the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) without abandoning wife and children.
Those who achieve [this] follow the teachings and practice them accordingly. By achieving [this], they take refuge in the precepts and plant the causes for rebirth among humans and devas.
Ninth, I can manifest as an upāsikā.
If there is a woman who abides by the five precepts, I will appear before her in the form of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma for her,
enabling her to achieve accomplishment.
Not only did she seek a superior rebirth, but she also wished to escape the female body; therefore, she took the five precepts upon herself.
"To take [the precepts] upon oneself" means that although there was no teacher to confer them, she assumed them as if they had been personally bestowed.
An *upāsikā* is also called an *upāsikā*; this translates as "female lay follower. "Lay follower" (*upāsaka*) is the same as above, differing only in gender.

The teacher of the Dharma does not merely expound the rules for laypeople; he further explains that although one may abide by the five precepts, they must necessarily be received from a master to constitute the status of an upāsaka.

This accomplishment not only fulfills the role of an upāsaka as a cause for rebirth among gods and humans, but also brings liberation from the female body and the attainment of the male form. Thus, the empowerment leads to the reception of the precepts.

The *Xiāozāi jīng* (Sūtra on the Elimination of Calamities) states: In India, there was a man who strictly observed the five precepts. While traveling abroad, his friends earnestly urged him to drink alcohol.

He traveled far to another land and stayed at the home of a woman who was a wife to a malevolent spirit. Although he violated the precept against intoxicants, the other four precepts remained entirely intact.
The celestial deities protected her so that the demon could not devour her.

He then explained the five precepts of the Buddha to the parents of the demon’s wife, leading them together to see the Buddha to eliminate all calamities and obstacles. Thus we know that both men and women should uphold the precepts;
there is indeed a profound reason why Bodhisattvas manifest themselves in these forms. Tenth, they can manifest in the body of a woman.
If there are women who manage internal affairs and establish themselves to cultivate their families and states, I will appear before them in the form of a female ruler,
a state lady, a titled consort, or a great matron, and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.

To serve those above and below with filial piety, respect, benevolence, and kindness is called "internal governance" (*neizheng*). This is because what is practiced within moves outward and brings about transformation.
To cultivate feminine virtue through integrity, stillness, diligence, and frugality is called "establishing oneself" (*lishen*).
This is because when one's virtue is without blemish, one can establish oneself; it refers to cultivation and rectification. Zhengmo says: "The inner chambers are the source of all transformations."
Therefore, regarding the order or chaos of the family and the state: "family" refers generally to those from the rank of Great Officer (daifu) downward;

"state" refers generally to those from the rank of Feudal Lord (zhuhou) upward. Gushan says: "The female ruler" refers to the consort of the Son of Heaven; "the state lady" refers to the wife of a feudal lord.
"Commanded Ladies" (*mingfu*) refers to wives who, by virtue of their husbands' honors, have received official edicts and mandates (*gao-ming*).

"Family Instructor" (*jia-xun gu*) refers to a lady of great standing whose talent and virtue are so complete that she serves as a teacher within the inner quarters. An example is Ban Biao’s daughter from Fufeng during the Later Han dynasty, who was the wife of Cao Shishu;

Emperor Huan repeatedly issued imperial decrees for her to enter the palace, where the Empress and the noble ladies were commanded to take her as their teacher. The world referred to her as "Lady Cao."
This is the household. As for "expounding the Dharma," it means expounding the methods of the three obediences and four virtues to rectify social customs and correct oneself.

As for "accomplishment," it refers to the internal resonance and external trust that accomplish the tasks of cultivating and governing the household and the state. Thus, one is able to respond to the ten types of people. End of section.
The four [powers] correspond to two youths and two [aspects]: first, the ability to manifest in the body of a young man; second, the ability to manifest in the body of a young woman.
Regarding the first:
if there are sentient beings whose male organs are not impaired, I manifest before them in the body of a young man and preach the Dharma for them.
To cause them to achieve this:
"not losing the male organ" means that regarding all objects of desire, one has never committed an offense through defilement; this refers to being a *kumārabhūta* (a perpetual celibate).
Fearing that those who have the resolve to maintain this for their entire lives might be unable to do so, the Bodhisattva acts according to their inclinations.
He manifests in the form of a young boy. As for the teacher of the Dharma, he preaches the Dharma of detachment from desire.

He causes the practitioner to maintain sincerity and embrace simplicity, so that by consolidating the essence and preserving the primal source, they achieve the state of a true youth. Second, he can manifest in the form of a young girl.
If there is a maiden who delights in her own body and does not seek to violate others, I will manifest before her in the form of a young girl and preach the Dharma for her,
causing her to achieve fulfillment.
"Chǔnǚ" (virgin) is also called "chǔzǐ" (maiden). It is a term for a young girl who has not yet married.

One who "delights in dwelling as a virgin" vows to remain a maiden for her entire life, maintaining her integrity and self-restraint. This is as the *Shijing* says: "Even unto death, I swear I shall never be otherwise."
For men, the wish is for a household; for women, the wish is for a family. This is the common sentiment of humanity.
Yet now, they regard marriage as an invasion and betrothal as a violent abandonment, giving rise to deep aversion and distress. Therefore, it is said that they do not seek such things.
Although they do not seek them, there is fear that invasions and violence may be forcibly imposed upon them against their will. For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests as a youth for their sake.
As for the female body: the speaker of the Dharma teaches the dharma of detachment from desire;

the practitioner causes her to increase in steadfastness and resolve so that she may maintain herself, and because she cannot be forcibly violated by aggressors, she achieves the state of a pure maiden’s body.

She is able to respond to two youths. [The section on] the five abilities to respond to the nine divisions ends here. First, she is able to manifest the bodies of various devas; second, she is able to...
1. They manifest the bodies of various nāgas. 2. They can manifest the bodies of yakṣas. 3. They can manifest the bodies of gandharvas. 4. They can manifest the bodies of asuras.
5. They can manifest the bodies of kiṃnaras. 6. They can manifest the bodies of mahoragas. 7.
They can manifest the bodies of ordinary humans. 8. They can manifest the bodies of non-humans. First:
If there are devas who desire to leave their celestial status, I manifest a celestial body and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goal.

Among these devas, there are two types: first, those not previously mentioned above, which this category collectively includes; second, those who specifically desire to leave their celestial status, to whom this response is particularly directed.
That is to say, while the former should seek entry [into the path], the latter should seek exit [from it]. Although I manifest [the same form] to both...

Because the manifestation of a celestial body and the preaching of the Dharma constitute distinct accomplishments. *Guǎngdìng* states: "The preacher of the Dharma preaches such teachings as impermanence, suffering, and emptiness. *Zhèngmò* states:
"'Accomplishment' means causing them to achieve the fulfillment of their vow to transcend [the celestial realm].

[Question: If they transcend the celestial order, what retribution do they achieve? [Answer: There are two meanings to this. First, because the various devas are attached to pleasure and cannot hear the Dharma, those who vow to be born among humans cause them to achieve the human order. This is because, among the six realms, [humans] are able to rectify the mind.

First, because one contemplates the pursuit of Bodhi, and only the human path is capable of it. Second, when the five signs of decay appear, those who feel weary of and seek to leave behind outflows (*āsrava*) and aspire for the non-outflow state are caused to achieve the ranks of the Noble Ones (*ārya*), for although the death-and-rebirth of the mundane realm (*prabandhaja-jarāmaraṇa*) cannot be avoided even in the heavens, only by entering the state of a Noble One can one escape it.
The same principle applies to the various classes such as the *nāgas*. Second, they are able to manifest the bodies of various *nāgas*.
If there are nāgas who wish to leave the nāga realm, I manifest in a nāga body and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.

Regarding the consecration (abhiṣeka), it says: "In the Sanskrit language it is *nāga*; here it is translated as 'dragon' (*long*). There are four types: first, those who guard the celestial palaces; second, those who raise clouds and send down rain;
third, those who open channels and divert rivers; fourth, those who guard hidden treasures. Because their categories further differ, they are so called."

Furthermore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* clarifies that there are five sufferings for dragons: namely, birth, sleep, lust, anger, and death; during these five times, they cannot escape their serpent form.
Moreover, there are three further sufferings: first, although they may eat food of a hundred flavors, the very first mouthful transforms into a toad;
second, when rain falls upon the scales spread across their backs, the pain is so intense it reaches their hearts; third, centipedes devour their brains.
Fine parasites bore into their bodies. The *Dīrgha Āgama* also clarifies that dragons have three afflictions: first, their bodies are scorched by hot sands;
second, their palaces and robes are destroyed by winds; third, they are devoured by garuḍas. Because they endure such manifold sufferings, they delight in leaving their class.
The *Mānastava Sūtra* states that there are four causes and conditions for falling into the dragon realm: first, giving; second, anger; third, despising others; and fourth, [the fourth cause].
Regarding self-exaltation: the Āgamas state that those who were previously full of anger, crooked and dishonest in mind, and who violated the precepts and engaged in strife, fell among the dragons.
However, by the power of the merit from having practiced great generosity, they possess palaces made of the seven treasures.

Based on this, it follows that when a Dharma teacher expounds upon such dharmas as giving, morality, benevolence, compassion, uprightness, harmony, and respect, those who achieve them will perfect their human relations.
If one can practice giving, precepts, and so forth without dwelling on signs, then the ranks of the noble ones may also be accomplished.
Third, he can manifest in the body of a yakṣa;
if there are yakṣas who wish to be delivered from their own class, I manifest before them in the form of a yakṣa and preach the Dharma for them.
May they achieve [this].
Regarding the consecration (*abhiṣeka*): *yakṣa* is here translated as "swift," because their movement is swift;

it is also called *rākṣasa*, which is here translated as "valiant and robust," because they are courageous, fierce, and strong. Alternatively, it is translated as "violent and evil," because their form is violent and evil. There is a [text] on the ground...
The modes of movement—walking, flying, and soaring—are not the same. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:

"All these yakṣas love and delight in the Tathāgata’s true Dharma and protect and uphold it with a profound mind. As for the current statement that they "delight in delivering their own kind," this is also due to being permeated by the Buddha-dharma;
they recognize violence and evil as causes for falling [into lower realms] and thus feel deep revulsion toward them. "Delivering" (*du*) likewise means emerging together and transcending [suffering].
The meaning of liberation. As for the "preacher of the Dharma," they preach such dharmas as gentleness, compliance, kindness, charity, upholding the precepts, and cultivating merit.
As for "accomplishment," it refers to accomplishing the human way; if one further cultivates wisdom in conjunction with these, one accomplishes the noble way.
Fourth, I can manifest as a gandharva.
If a gandharva desires to be liberated from their kind, I appear before them in the form of a gandharva and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve accomplishment.

The *Guanding* (Consecration) Sutra states: "Gandharva" is translated here as "Fragrance-Body" (*xiangyin*). Because they do not consume wine or meat but sustain their bodies solely through fragrance, the *Qingliang* (Coolness) Commentary says:
"They eat fragrance," because they dwell on the Ten Treasure Mountains and consume various powdered fragrances. Alternatively, it is translated as "Seeker-of-Fragrance" (*xunxiangxing*).
They reside in the Vajra Cave to the south of Mount Sumeru; when Śakra desires music, he burns aloeswood incense for them.
A deity arrived seeking incense. Kumārajīva said, "This is the deity who topples the banner of the Lord of Heaven (Indra) for worldly pleasures.

However, since he is a pleasure-deity of Śakra, he must naturally be inferior to the various devas. If even those devas delight in liberation that transcends their station, how much more so this deity?
Therefore, he too delights in emancipation. As for his preaching the Dharma, he spoke of being free from negligence and the ten wholesome actions of the middle grade.
The Dharma. One who achieves it is liberated from their original nature and achieves the nature of humanity. By being free from negligence, one is no longer bound by that original nature;
through the middling grade of goodness being perfected, the nature of humanity can be attained.
Fifth, I can manifest as an asura.
If an asura desires liberation from their kind, I manifest before them in the body of an asura and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve fulfillment.
Asura is translated here as "Neither-Ugly-Nor-Handsome" (*amūrdhaka*), because among their kind there are handsome women but no handsome men.
They are also called "Non-Gods" (*asura*), because while their kind possesses celestial fortune, they lack celestial virtue.
According to the original sūtras, they differ in being born from a womb, an egg, moisture, or by transformation; these are seen among the seven destinies in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
The Sūtra says: "Within the Vajra Mountains of Jambudvīpa, there is an Asura palace six thousand yojanas in extent, with railings and rows of trees.
Yet, three times each day and night, they undergo suffering; instruments of torment come of their own accord into their palace.
Thus we know that even those who seek to escape their station must likewise experience suffering, which gives rise to a mind of weary detachment. The Abhidharma-śāstra says:
Because they cannot endure what is good, cannot humble their minds, and fail to contemplate various forms of instruction, they are not virtuous heroes;
yet because they possess celestial-like conduct, they are called *asura*. The *Mingyi ji* (Compendium of Names and Meanings) states:

"Because, while in the causal stage, although they practiced the five constant virtues, they harbored a mind of suspicion and jealousy, desiring to surpass others; thus, by performing the ten wholesome actions of an inferior grade, they experience the retribution of being an *asura*."

The body of the asuras. Thus one knows that the teacher of the Dharma preaches such dharmas as gentleness, goodness, compliance, compassion, patience, humility, respect, a mind open to receiving instruction, and the ten wholesome actions of the middle grade. Those who achieve these fulfill their human relations;

by transforming the cause into the fruit through self-transformation—(note: according to various sūtras, there should follow the section on garuḍas after the asuras; they are not included here because they are subsumed under the non-humans later).
Sixth, he can manifest as a kiṃnara.
If a kiṃnara desires liberation from his kind, I manifest before him in the body of a kiṃnara and preach the Dharma for him,
causing him to achieve accomplishment.

*Kiṃnara* is translated here as "Doubtful Deity" (*yíshén*). Their form resembles that of humans, yet they have a horn upon their heads; because those who see them experience doubt, they are so named.

In Chinese, it is translated as "Singing Deity" (*gēshén*), for they are the deities of the Dharma-music of Śakra Devānām Indra. The *Bodhisattva-tsaie-jīng* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Abiding in the Womb) states:
"To the north of Mount Sumeru, amidst ten mountains of precious jewels, there are Kiṃnaras who govern and transform within them. This is due to their past practice of giving."

By the power of this [deity], he dwells in a palace of the seven treasures and possesses an exceedingly long lifespan. When the devas wish to perform music, sweat flows from his armpits and he ascends to heaven of his own accord.
It is this very deity who, when Śakra invited the Buddha, sang and chanted praises of the Dharma-gate with the celestial hosts.
Those among his kindred who desire liberation do so, perhaps, due to the power of the habitual cultivation of chanting and praising the Dharma-gate. As for the one who preaches the Dharma:
It explains the methods for calming a distracted mind through song and verse, the impermanence of sensual desires, and the ten intermediate wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*).
By accomplishing these, one is liberated from one's original class and achieves the human condition; thus, one rectifies the mind and thoughts to advance toward Bodhi.
Seventh, I can manifest as a mahoraga.
If a mahoraga wishes to be liberated from their kind, I appear before them in the body of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma for them,
causing them to achieve accomplishment.
Mahoraga is translated as "Earth-Dragon" (Dilong). Zao [Sengzhao] calls them "Great Python Deities. Changshui [Zongjing] says they are "field-crawlers," a class of beings that moves on their bellies.

Yet, even though devas and nāgas possess sovereign power and unimpeded freedom, they still endure many sufferings; how much more so for Earth-Dragons who move on their bellies—their suffering is naturally doubled.
Therefore, they too delight in liberation from their kind. Furthermore, this class is deaf, dull-witted, and ignorant, yet they harbor poison.

Harm to living beings mostly arises from ignorance and hatred. For their sake, the Bodhisattva manifests his body and teaches them such dharmas as the cultivation of wisdom and the cultivation of loving-kindness, causing them to forever abandon ignorance and hatred and to fulfill their human nature. Thus, by rectifying their mental deliberations, they may hope to advance toward Bodhi.
Eighth, he can manifest in the form of a constant human being.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being human and cultivating as humans, I manifest in a human body and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.

"Sentient beings" is a general term for those in the six realms of existence; here, however, we speak specifically of the human realm. According to the former [classification], kings, ministers, and officials are all called "humans.
Here, we refer to those who have no other seeking; such people, from birth to birth throughout their lives, have no other pursuit.
Because worldly aspirations reside within humans, they are called "delighting in humans" (*manuṣya-rata*) and "cultivating humans.

The *Fayuan* states: "Human" (*ren*) means "endurance" (*kṣānti*), for one is able to endure both adversity and favor. Mencius said: "Humans are benevolent; those who lack a heart of compassion are not human. The *Cūḍābharaṇa-rāja-sūtra* says:
"Human" means "intention" (*manas*), for one is able to engage in skillful reflection and recollection. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Humans can..."

Because one who can still the mind is able to cultivate the Way and attain the stages of penetration, it is known that both the internal (Buddhist) and external (non-Buddhist) teachings value human ethics;

therefore, one should joyfully cultivate them. Furthermore, the *Abhiṣeka* states that joyful cultivation encompasses eight meanings: first, because a human body is difficult to obtain, one seeks not to lose it;
second, being a human being in successive lifetimes makes cultivation and realization easy; third, the sages of the Three Vehicles are born together [in this state].

1. Among the realms of beings, these four are found only within the human world: the possibility of encountering the Buddha-dharma; 2. the five classes of divine beings (pañca-deva-nikāya) all admire humans—how could they not wish for this [human state]?
3. Only within the human path can one proceed toward Bodhi; 4. while the various devas are attached to pleasure, the other realms abound in suffering.
The paths of the eight Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are all attained through human beings. Based on this, those currently existing among humans should know to value themselves.
As for "expounding the Dharma," it means that the intermediate grade of virtuous precepts is taught as the concordant cause (*niṣyanda-hetu*).
As for "accomplishment," it means that the intermediate grade of form and mind is achieved as the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). Ninth, they are able to manifest in non-human bodies.
If there are non-human beings— whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception— who delight in transcending their own kind,
I manifest my body before them all and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.
The preceding category subsumes the human realm, including kings, ministers, and other such classes not fully enumerated here.

This present category subsumes the non-human realm, including devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and other such classes not fully enumerated here, because all those not included in the former are gathered within this one.
Changshui said: "Those with form include the 'refined and intelligent' who respond to omens of good and ill; those without form include the 'empty, dispersed, and dissolving.'"

Those with consciousness, such as ghosts, spirits, and numina; those without consciousness, such as spirits transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone—these are explained in the latter seven fascicles.
As for manifesting their bodies, each follows its own kind; as for preaching the Dharma, each responds to the capacities of beings;
and as for bringing about accomplishment, each fulfills their respective vows. This concludes the detailed explanation according to number.
The three knots are formed by the body;

this is called the "Exquisite and Pure Body of the Thirty-two Manifestations Entering into Buddha-lands. All are accomplished through the sovereign power of effortless wondrous efficacy, achieved through the cultivation of hearing and the permeation of hearing via samādhi.

This phrase "pointing to what is above" should correspond to what precedes it; that is, pointing to the specific enumeration above, one should conclude by correlating it with the number previously stated in the general heading.
To manifest all at once is called "wondrous" (miao). To respond universally without partiality is called "pure" (jing).

The thirty-two manifestations and the Universal Gate Chapter (Pumen pin) alternate in their appearance and disappearance, just as in this [text] there are four princes of the Heavenly Kings, while in that sūtra...
There are none. Among the women, this [text] includes the Queen Mother and the State Lady, whereas that sūtra is likewise brief.
Among the eight classes of beings, it contains the name of the *garuḍa*, and outside the eight classes, it contains the Vajrapāṇi deity; none of these are listed here.

This is because the Bodhisattva’s wondrous responses are boundless and his spiritual transformations are unfathomable; moreover, there are no sentient beings—whether human or non-human—to whom he does not adapt.
Thus, from these two sūtras, one may freely select and arrange [the names] to complete the number thirty-two. Indeed, each is inexhaustible, so do not be overly rigid or dogmatic.
Because he manifests throughout all lands and atoms, he is called the "Body that Enters All Lands. This is for the sake of the Universal Gate Chapter.
In response to the inquiry of Akṣayamati, it is stated that he "travels and transforms" only in Sahā; this does not mean that the wondrous response of the Bodhisattva is restricted solely to Sahā.
Therefore, in the subsequent verses, it is also said: "In the lands of the ten directions, there is no field where he does not manifest his body.
The phrase "all by means of samādhi," etc., explains the reason why he is able to achieve such wondrous responses. Samādhi...

This is the Samādhi of the Ear-Gate. Regarding "perfuming through hearing and cultivation through hearing": perfuming transforms the habitual tendencies of grasping, while cultivation treats the self-nature by employing only "turning back to hear.
Once the six knots are untied, the wondrous function manifests spontaneously; because it does not rely on artificial effort, it is called the "unconditioned wondrous power.
Because it responds effortlessly and naturally, it is called "spontaneous accomplishment. Based on this upward union, the three [realms] are formed.
The twelve [fearlessnesses] are concluded. Second, based on the subsequent [section], they are combined to form fourteen fearlessnesses. Three parts: first, citing the source and stating the number;
second, explaining them individually according to that number; third, concluding with the power to manifest the benefits. First [part].
World-Honored One, by means of this power of the effortless, wondrous Vajra Samādhi— perfumed by hearing and cultivated through hearing—
and because I share in the same compassionate longing as all sentient beings of the ten directions, the three periods of time, and the six realms,
I cause all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of meritorious qualities of fearlessness within my body and mind.
Initially, it is accomplished through the power of cultivation. "Hearing and practicing what has been heard" is as explained above. Being able to resolve all fetters is called the Vajra Samādhi;
its ultimate purity, extreme radiance, and pervasive penetration are termed the "Wondrous Power of Non-action. ○ From "and with all [beings]" below, one attains superior accomplished function.

With ultimate purity, extreme radiance, and pervasive penetration, tranquil illumination encompasses the void, such that worldly dharmas cannot act as obstructions. This corresponds to the arising of the mind below. Therefore...
He is able to share the same compassion and longing as all sentient beings. For this reason, he can manifest the functioning of the same sense organs as those beings;
thus it is said that he causes all sentient beings to be equal [to him]. The fourteen fearlessnesses are as explained below.
The term "I" is the Bodhisattva’s self-reference; it means that the Bodhisattva, through the empowerment of body and mind, is able to bestow fearlessness.

He bestows [these] upon sentient beings, causing them to obtain fourteen kinds of fearlessness within the body and mind of the Bodhisattva, thereby accomplishing the merit of liberation from suffering.
This merit is precisely benefit. Second, the fourteen [types] are explained individually according to their number.
First, fearlessness regarding suffering and affliction; (up to) fourteenth, fearlessness in upholding the name. First:
First, because I do not observe by means of an observing subject, those suffering sentient beings of the ten directions who observe my voice shall immediately attain liberation.
One who does not contemplate their own voice is no different from sentient beings who follow after sensory objects exclusively.
The phrase "contemplating with contemplation" means that by means of that capacity for contemplation, one turns back to contemplate one's own nature.

When one can cultivate oneself in this way, one can also cause those suffering sentient beings to be moved upon hearing the name and to invoke it, saying, "I call upon your name. Therefore, it is said: "Contemplate their sounds."

Regarding the statement that one "contemplates the sound" rather than merely "invoking the name": invoking the name belongs solely to the practice of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*), whereas contemplating the sound also encompasses the maintenance of principle (*tattva*).
This is because the Bodhisattva’s power of compassion bestows its grace, enabling the simultaneous cultivation of both phenomenon and principle.

Thus, in the "Universal Gate" chapter, one invokes the name with a single mind. Ancient masters have also stated that there is both the phenomenal and the principled aspect; however, cultivation based on phenomena alone does not necessarily [lead to the ultimate goal].

It accords with principle (*yukti*). Since the cultivation of principle (*tattva-bhāvanā*) encompasses all matters without exception, the term "contemplating sound" (*śabda-vipaśyanā*) alone simultaneously includes the designation "reciting the name.

However, in the cultivation of matters (*vastu-bhāvanā*), the mind of the practitioner and the mind of the Sage intersect; in the cultivation of principle, the forgetting of objects and the nature of suffering are both quiescent along with the nature of sound.
Therefore, it is said that one immediately attains liberation. This is why this sutra and the Universal Gate Chapter (*Samantamukha-parivarta*) are not entirely identical.
Because this sutra emphasizes the exhortation to practice, "observing their sounds" refers to the responsive resonance of the sentient beings (the *ki*).

Because the Universal Gate (*Pumen*) is intended solely to manifest the function [of the Bodhisattva], "observing their sounds" refers to the response of the Sage (*sheng*). Although there is identity within this difference, do not unfortunately "mark the boat" [i.e., cling to literalism].
Zhengmo says: "Although suffering and affliction are universal, it is also acceptable to distinguish them according to body and mind. That is to say, 'suffering' refers to its..."
It refers to the body being afflicted and its mind disturbed. Furthermore, it is said that while these are listed separately, they do not exhaust all forms of suffering;
rather, all afflictions are subsumed within this category. *Abhiṣeka* states: "This first [category] is the general, while the following thirteen are the specific.
Within the specifics, the first seven are 'sufferings' (*duḥkha*) and the latter six are 'afflictions' (*upāyāsa*). Second is fearlessness regarding the calamity of fire."
Second, through the revolving of knowledge and vision, one causes all sentient beings such that even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them.

"The revolving of knowledge and vision" refers to the mutual interpenetration of the six sense faculties. Once the Bodhisattva has revolved the faculty of hearing back to its original nature, his knowledge and vision likewise revolve back along with the hearing.
This is what is meant by "the reversal of a single faculty to the source, whereby the six locations are liberated. However...
The faculty of seeing belongs to fire and is thus interconnected with all fiery natures. Therefore, when the activity of seeing intersects [with fire], one perceives fierce flames.
Now, knowing that seeing has already revolved back, it can likewise respond to conditions by revolving toward other fires; this enables sentient beings to enter fire without being burned.
What is called "the power of majestic spiritual authority" in the Universal Gate Chapter (*Pumen pin*) also arises from the supreme and extraordinary merit of this revolving-back.
There are similar cases that must be properly understood. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) states: "Having realized the ultimate Dharma-realm, his majestic power is immeasurable;

therefore, those who single-mindedly invoke his name are immediately embraced by the majestic light of his great compassion and do not fall into the calamity of fire, just as entering the shade of a mountain prevents the heat from invading.
Third, there is fearlessness regarding the calamity of water."
Third, by reversing the flow of hearing, one causes all sentient beings who are adrift upon great waters not to be drowned.
"Reversing the flow of hearing" means to turn back and contemplate the nature of hearing; it is the reversal of deluded hearing to restore true hearing.
However, since the faculty of hearing belongs to water and is thus interconnected with all watery natures, when the activity of hearing engages, one perceives a great body of water.
Now, as hearing returns to its original nature, it can likewise respond to conditions by returning to that remaining water;
therefore, it causes sentient beings who enter the water not to drown, and they have no fear of the four classes of hungry ghosts.
Fourth, by severing deluded thoughts and being free from the intent to kill, one causes all sentient beings to enter the realms of ghosts such that the ghosts cannot harm them.
The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) says: "Ghosts and spirits take hidden, obscure states as the cause of their conceptualization and killing as the condition for their downfall. Now, the Bodhi..."

When Samantabhadra hears [the name], he internally extinguishes deluded thoughts within; his mind is free from killing or harm, and he completely transcends the mental activities of ghosts and spirits.
By the power of this complete transcendence, he can cause those who invoke his name to escape the calamities of ghosts.
Fifth is fearlessness regarding weapons.

Fifth, when the cultivation of hearing perfects the hearing and the six faculties are dissolved and restored to function as one with sound-hearing, it can cause sentient beings who are about to be harmed by weapons to have their bodies severed piece by piece;
yet it makes those weapons and spears feel like cutting through water or blowing across light, for their nature is non-existent.
"Shaking and moving.
"Perfuming the hearing to become true hearing" means that by the power of reverse-hearing (*pratyāśravaṇa*), one perfumes and cultivates false hearing to achieve ultimate, solid, and true hearing.
"The six faculties dissolve and return, becoming identical with the hearing of sound" refers to the dissolution of the remaining five faculties.

The delusion and the truth are likewise like the hearing of those who specialize in sound; for they are originally one refined spirit—when dissolved, they dissolve together, and when restored, they are restored together.
Because they are restored together, the ultimately firm and solid nature pervades everywhere in response to stimuli;
thus it can cause that blade to break into pieces. Because they are dissolved together, the principle of ultimate emptiness and stillness merges upon encountering circumstances.

Therefore, it is as if one were cutting through water or blowing upon light; since it is like cutting through water or blowing upon light, the person’s nature remains as-it-is (tathatā), neither perceiving nor knowing it, and thus it is said that there is no agitation. Furthermore, regarding the mention of "being harmed" herein:

It is as if Wuqi had been ensnared by the net of the law and mistakenly entered the gate of his enemy; or as if one who speaks of war and weapons were personally standing on the battlefield, surrounded by the enemy's onslaught.
At such moments, in a single instant, head and body might be separated; in a mere moment, life itself could not be preserved.
Yet, in these circumstances, Wuwei was able to manifest even more clearly his spiritual wonders. When the Six Ghosts beheld Wuwei, they saw him thus.
Sixth, the permeation of hearing is brilliant and its clarity pervades the entire Dharma-realm; thus, the nature of all dark obscurations cannot prevail.
It can cause yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, pretas, piśācas, pūtanas, and the like, so that even when they draw near, their eyes are unable to see.

Zhengmo says: "The first two lines describe the culmination of the practice of 'listening inwardly,' whereby the fundamental luminosity is manifested, shining forth to universally illumine the Dharma-realm.
The subsequent two lines describe the subtle, hidden habitual tendencies of ghosts and spirits; because they face darkness and turn their backs on light, they cannot endure such radiance.
This is like the owl, which sees at night but is blind by day, or the rākṣasa, who cannot see when facing the sun."—Guanding.
It is said: Yakṣas are male ghosts; rākṣasīs are female ghosts. Both of these are ghosts that devour humans.

If human corpses become foul-smelling, they use mantras to preserve them so they remain fresh. They are governed by the god Vaiśravaṇa (Multihearing). Kumbhāṇḍas—translated as "jar-shaped"—are ghosts that cause nightmares and bewitchment.
They are governed by the god Virūḍhaka (Growth-increasing). Piśācas—translated as "consumers of vital essence"—are able to devour humans and the five grains.
Vital essence (*ojas*) is under the jurisdiction of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. *Pūtana*—translated here as "stench-ghouls" (*chou-egui*)—are those who preside over febrile diseases;
they are under the jurisdiction of Virūpākṣa. The phrase "and so forth" includes others, for since the classes of ghosts (*preta*) are numerous, they cannot be fully enumerated.
Those whom one cannot see from nearby, such as a local deity not seeing [the monk] Dongshan, or a ghost-messenger not seeing a serving monk, are included therein.

Regarding the category [of ghosts]: since one cannot naturally avoid harm from them, [a question is asked: "How does this differ from the 'difficulty of ghosts' mentioned in the preceding text? [The answer is: The former refers to a single class [of ghosts], while this refers to many classes.

Furthermore, the former refers to entering a ghost realm by bodily means, whereas this refers to encountering them unexpectedly and by error. Although both constitute the difficulty of ghosts, it is not contradictory for each to appear in its respective context. Seventh: Fearlessness toward shackles and fetters.

Seventh: when the nature of sound is perfectly dissolved and the faculty of hearing is turned inward, one becomes free from all defilements and delusions, such that the shackles and fetters of sentient beings cannot bind them.
"The nature of sound is perfectly dissolved" means that the sense-object of sound has been extinguished. "The faculty of hearing is turned inward" refers to the ear-faculty.
It is "revolving. That which is free from all defilements and delusions means that the various objects such as form (*rūpa*) likewise dissolve and vanish along with sound;

the various delusions such as seeing likewise revolve back upon hearing. Once these delusions have returned [to their source], one uses the Truth (*tattva*) to protect them, enabling the shackles to be severed and destroyed.
Once the various objects have been extinguished, one uses Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to integrate them, enabling the imprisonment to become identical with space.
Therefore, it is said that they cannot be attached to. Regarding "the fearlessness against the eight thieves":

the eighth is the extinction of sound and the perfection of hearing, which universally generates the power of compassion; this can cause sentient beings to pass through perilous paths without being plundered by thieves.
When sounds are extinguished and voices have vanished, sensory objects cannot obstruct it. When sensory objects cannot obstruct it, the nature of hearing becomes perfectly pervasive.

Because the nature of hearing is perfectly pervasive, wherever sound reaches, one universally generates the power of compassion. Because one universally generates the power of compassion, one protects living beings everywhere, responding to conditions to transform the violent.
Thus, one can cause all sentient beings to encounter bandits without being robbed. (From the *Lotus Sūtra*)
Zhu Cheng says: Whether it be a vast and desolate wilderness or a narrow and secluded pass, or a path where bandits and enemies suddenly emerge—all such places are called "dangerous roads.
"Road" (*dao*) here means "path. Ninth: the fearlessness of the poison of greed.

Ninth, it perfumes the faculty of hearing so that it is detached from sensory objects and cannot be plundered by forms. This enables all beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greedy desire.
"Perfuming the hearing" means cultivating the nature of hearing until the six sense-faculties achieve perfect penetration. "Detached from objects" means being free from all sounds.
This means that both the defilements and the six objects are simultaneously liberated. When the six objects are all liberated, illusory form loses its power.
When the six faculties are perfectly penetrating, the true nature gains its power. That which lacks power cannot naturally withstand that which possesses power; it is as the saying goes:
"If the host awakens, then the various guests and devils cannot find their opportunity. Although this is [the realization] of the Bodhisattvas themselves...
This is the realized object. Nevertheless, by the power of combined efforts, the cause is able to lead those sentient beings who are excessively lustful to distance themselves from desire.

Regarding the term "excessively lustful" used for these beings: it refers to those whose habitual tendencies toward desire are particularly heavy, such that they repeatedly give rise to it in the presence of objects.

When slight, it damages the body and ruins one's virtue; when severe, it leads to the loss of the physical frame and the end of life. Furthermore, it brings about in future lives wives who are not chaste and virtuous, as well as [unruly] kinsmen.

This is contrary to one's wishes; indeed, it is most extreme. When retributions such as the copper pillars and iron beds manifest at the moment of death, and when one must personally endure the accumulated cold and solid ice of the hells from head to foot, the Bodhisattva’s true compassion is great enough to enable one to distance oneself from such suffering.
Tenth is Fearlessness Regarding the Poison of Hatred.
"Tenth" means that the pure sound is free from dust, and the faculties and their objects are perfectly interfused; there is neither the subject that opposes nor the object that is opposed.
This can cause all sentient beings who harbor anger and resentment to be free from all hatred.

Pure sound is that which is free from the names and signs grasped through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*); it consists solely of the sounds arising from the dependent nature (*paratantra*).
Although other sounds exist, they lack the power of defilement or obscuration; therefore, it is called "dustless" (*anāsrava*).
