Since the sound is thus neither defiled nor obstructed, the sense faculty (*indriya*) likewise lacks limitation and is unimpeded. In this way, the faculty and its object merge into a single nature.
As it is with the faculty and object of the ear, so it is with the remaining five; therefore, they are said to be "perfectly interfused" (*yuanrong*). As stated previously:
"The seer and the objects of seeing, along with the perceived forms, are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent.

This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. This refers to the absence of subject and object, meaning that since they are one, there is no opposition.
By nature, the faculties lack the quality of being opposed, and objects likewise lack the quality of being opposed;
thus, anger should naturally not exist, for anger arises from opposition and resistance. That it can cause all [beings] to be equal also results from the combined power of the Bodhisattva’s descent.
When sentient beings speak of "resentment," it refers to a habituation to anger that has become particularly heavy.
Do not suppress your senses toward objects. If you do so lightly, you will injure your vital energy and incur disgrace; if heavily, you will forget yourself and your kin.
Furthermore, it will lead to being sought out by others for their arsenic in future lives, and being tormented and harmed by them.

Most particularly severe are the appearances of the mountain of knives, iron spikes, the sword-tree, and the wheel of swords, which manifest before one at the moment of death, along with such matters as gouging, cutting, hacking, mincing, piercing, and beating.
One should personally accept [the blame], for this can cause one to leave behind anger. The great compassion of a Bodhisattva is profound.

However, among the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), anger (*krodha*) has distinctions of lightness, heaviness, and equality. When light, it is merely fury (*kopa*); when heavy, it further brings about resentment and malice (*upanāha*);
when equal, it does not exceed vexation (*pratigha*). These three all arise following anger; such is the relationship between the root and its derivative (*anuvyañjana*).
Based on the single, general poison of hatred (*dveṣa*), one speaks of being "free from all ill-will" with respect to sentient beings who harbor anger and resentment;

yet in reality, those who harbor anger and resentment also possess ill-will, and being "free from all ill-will" likewise includes freedom from anger and resentment. This is merely a case of mutual clarification and subsumption.
Eleventh is the lack of fear regarding the poison of delusion (*moha*).
Eleventh is "Dissolving Dust and Revolving Clarity. The body and mind of the dharma-realm are like lapis lazuli, transparently penetrating and unobstructed.
This enables all those with dull natures, hindrances, and *icchantikas* to forever leave behind the darkness of ignorance.

Wenling says: "Delusion arises from being obscured by false objects and covered by ignorance. To dissolve these objects is to be without obscuration; to revolve back to the light is to be without covering.
Thus, regarding the external dharma-realm and the internal body and mind, they become concentrated, pure, and brilliantly penetrating, thereby departing from the darkness of delusion.
However, this also belongs to self-realization; the meaning of how it can bring about this state may be understood according to what was explained above."—Zhengmo.
It is said: being fully possessed of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) constitutes "obscurity"; being fully possessed of the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) constitutes "dullness";

and being fully possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*) constitutes the "obstruction of nature" (*prakṛti-āvaraṇa*). *Adīnaka* means "lacking a virtuous mind" (*asat-citta*); furthermore, it is the most severe form of delusion (*moha*).

"Folly" (*mūḍha*) refers to the nature of obscurity and dullness, which is itself delusion (*sammoha*). This is because the nature of delusion consists precisely in darkness, dullness, and stagnation. For this reason...

Because their wholesome minds are forever obstructed and severed, they are called *icchantikas*. This is also due to the habitual preponderance of delusion (*moha*), which causes them to be confused regarding correct knowledge and vision.
On a minor scale, this results in the confusion of phenomena and principles; on a major scale, it leads to the inversion of the false and the true.

Furthermore, it causes them to be reborn in future lives into families of wrong views, with minds that are sycophantic and crooked. Most extreme among these are those who act as royal envoys or chief clerks who provide false testimony.

The signs of grasping at books and other such objects manifest before one at the time of death. One must undergo the entire sequence of interrogations, deceptions, examinations, and cross-examinations from beginning to end;

the Bodhisattva’s wondrous power can cause one to be forever freed from these. (Question: While realms such as water and fire are manifest states of suffering and can thus be called fearsome, greed, hatred, and delusion follow the movements of one's own mind—what is there to fear regarding them?
Answer: There are two reasons why they may be said to be fearsome. First, poison is a cause of suffering that can summon the fruit of suffering. Second, [they arise] in relation to external objects.)

The power of the frequent arising [of thoughts] is not free; this is said with reference to those who, based on faith in the cause and recognizing the fruit, know fear and seek liberation. (12) The twelfth is the fearlessness of seeking a son.
The twelfth refers to one whose form is fused and who, having heard of the Immovable Bodhimanda, enters into the world without destroying the world-systems.
They are able to universally make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, and at the side of each Buddha, they act as a Dharma Prince, being able to...
It causes those beings within the Dharma-realm who have no sons and desire a male child to give birth to a son endowed with merit and wisdom.
"Melting the form and restoring hearing" means that by dissolving the illusory body, one returns to true hearing;

that is to say, the sense faculties are completely uprooted, the inner clarity radiates light, and the faculties, the physical body, and the vessel-world are transformed at will into supreme awakening. This is...

It is principle realized through phenomena; by realizing principle through phenomena, one does not deviate from the ultimate while responding to the conventional. Thus, without leaving the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one enters into the mundane world.
"The site of enlightenment" refers to the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), for it is that upon which the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) relies.

"The mundane world" refers to the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), for it is that wherein the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) pervades. Thus, without moving, one enters [the world].

This is the realm of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma-avyāghāta*). Furthermore, because phenomena are non-obstructed with respect to principle, phenomena themselves are mutually identical in terms of their breadth and narrowness according to that principle.
Thus, without destroying the world-system, it can pervade the ten directions. "World-system" refers to the field of transformation of a single Buddha; in relation to the ten directions, it is narrow.
"The ten directions" refers to the fields of transformation of many Buddhas; in relation to a single world-system, they are broad. Not...

This is the realm of the "destructive omnipresence" (*bhaṅga-vibhu*) and the "unimpededness of phenomena and phenomena" (*dharmadharmāpratīghāta*). Furthermore, by virtue of this unimpededness of phenomena and phenomena, the body also manifests as both one and many according to the respective realms.
Thus, one is able to make offerings to all Buddhas and serve as a Dharma Prince (*dharmarāja-putra*) at the side of each Buddha.
A "Dharma Prince" refers to one who currently assists the Buddha in propagating the transformation [of sentient beings] and will succeed him as the next Buddha.
Regarding the position [of the text]: as the *I Ching* says, "To rectify the troubles left by one's father—this is the righteousness of having a son.

As for the phrase "capable of causing [others] to be equal," this means that because the Bodhisattva is the son of the Dharma-King, he causes his remaining merit and wisdom to benefit those sentient beings who are childless.
According to the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Pumen pin*), the desire for [a son] refers specifically to women; for women who are childless, there are three kinds of suffering. First:
First, one is abandoned by her own husband; second, she is despised by other wives; third, she is ridiculed by those around her.
Because of such fears regarding partiality and imbalance, the term "sentient beings" is used here generally, encompassing both men and women alike.
For it is said that among the three forms of unfiliality, having no descendants is the greatest; thus, all equally desire sons. Those who possess merit and virtue shall be wealthy.
Thus, those who are worthy, possessing wisdom and insight, are esteemed as sages. When these four excellences are fully realized, one further perceives the boundless nature of the Sage’s grace.
Thirteen: Seeking a Wife Without Fear.
Thirteenth: The six sense faculties are perfectly penetrating and luminously illumined without duality, encompassing the worlds of the ten directions.

This establishes the Great Perfect Mirror, the Empty Tathāgata-garbha, which receives and upholds the secret Dharma-gates of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions without loss.

It can cause those beings in the Dharma-realm who have no offspring, and those who desire daughters, to give birth to children who are upright, endowed with merit and virtue, gentle and compliant, and [possessed of all] excellences.
People love and revere women who possess auspicious marks.

When the six sense faculties function interchangeably, it is called "perfection" (yuan). When each functions without obstruction, it is called "pervasion" (tong). Because they function interchangeably, their luminous illumination is non-dual.
Because it is unimpeded, it encompasses all realms without exception. Because its luminous illumination is non-dual, it is designated by the name "Mirror-like Wisdom" (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

Because it encompasses all realms without exception, it is given the title "Space-Treasury" (*gaganagañja*). By virtue of the meaning of "mirror," it accords with the Tathāgata’s secrets and illuminates them without contradiction;
by virtue of the meaning of "treasury," it receives the Tathāgata’s secrets and contains them within itself.

There is no error. Regarding the phrase "capable of causing [others] to be equal," it means that because the Bodhisattva, through the residual merit and benefits remaining from having received the Dharma-gates in accordance with the various Buddhas, extends this to all sentient beings who lack sons. Although the text says "lacking sons" (*mǔ* = mother/son), it refers to those lacking sons because a daughter is considered half a son.
This is truly because a son inherits the internal lineage while a daughter forms external kinship; thus, there may be sons but no daughters.

Nor was she perfectly beautiful; thus, there were also those who sought a woman for her physical perfection to serve as a wife, her merit and virtue to bring about honor and prosperity, and her gentleness and compliance to fulfill the way of a wife. Because she possessed these three qualities, she won the love and respect of all people:
her physical perfection brought love, her merit and virtue brought respect, and her gentleness and compliance brought both love and respect together.
Thus, those who possess these marks do not have distinct characteristics; rather, they possess the mark of physical excellence, the mark of merit, and the mark of gentleness.
Among women, wisdom is not mentioned separately because it is subsumed within gentleness;

for it is only through the possession of wisdom that one can be truly gentle, thereby perfecting the Way of the Earth and fulfilling the virtues of a woman. Fourteenth: Holding the Name brings fearlessness.

(Question: Since holding the name arises from one's own mind, what is there to fear? Answer: One fears that it may be ineffective or that it may not surpass other names; all such things are feared. Now, by holding the single name of Avalokiteśvara, one gains more merit than many names, and thus there is no such fear. 3.
First, the collective manifestation of virtues; second, the narration of the origins to clarify equality; third, the resolution of doubts to prevent questioning. Regarding the first:
"The fourteen" refers to the ten billion suns and moons within this trichiliocosm.

Among the various Dharma-princes currently existing in the world, there are as many as sixty-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sands) in number. They cultivate the Dharma, establish models, and transform sentient beings.
The skillful wisdom that accords with sentient beings varies from one to another.

First, the vastness of the environment of support (*niśraya-vipāka*) is revealed; this refers to the Sahā world-system, comprising the three thousand great thousandfold worlds, which collectively describe the sphere of transformation of a single Buddha—the area illuminated by ten billion suns and moons. *“Manifestly dwelling”* and the following passages reveal the multitude of holy beings.

Because they are distinguished from the past and differ from the future, it is said that they "dwell manifestly in the world. Because they transcend the three stages of worthiness and surpass the ten levels of sainthood, they are called "sons of the Dharma-king" (*dharmarājaputra*).
The number of sixty-two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sands) is actually what is perceived through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the Bodhisattvas;

it is not a merely hypothetical number. The section beginning with "cultivating the Dharma" (*xiūfǎ*) reveals that their transformative virtues (*huàdé*) are each distinct. "Cultivating the Dharma" refers to their own cultivation.

There is a teaching. As for "establishing a model," it means establishing a standard of conduct to serve as a paradigm. Regarding "transforming and teaching sentient beings," this refers to perfecting oneself so as to bring others to perfection;

for when one's own benefit is fulfilled, the benefit of others is naturally achieved. "Accordance with sentient beings" means that within the trichiliocosm, one occupies a particular region and accords with the capacities of the beings in that region. It is for this reason that one engages with the world through skillful means and teaches.
The wisdom of the Dharma varies from one to another, as exemplified in the subsequent text by the twenty-five sages, each corresponding to their respective faculties, and so forth.
Second, the explanation of the arising through clarity and so on.

Through the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained, I have developed this wondrous gateway of the ear. Thereafter, my body and mind became subtle and wondrous, encompassing and pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

This enables sentient beings who uphold my name to possess a merit equal and no different from those who together with them uphold the names of as many Dharma princes as there are grains of sand in sixty-two Ganges Rivers.

The "original root of perfect penetration" has two meanings. First, it means that among all forms of perfect penetration, this alone serves as the original root for the Sahā world, because it is stated later:
"In this land, the true essence of the teaching is pure within hearing and sound. This explains the meaning of "original" by way of direct correspondence.
Second, it means that what was attained by Avalokiteśvara remains the original root of perfect penetration, because it is stated later: [and so forth].
This is because it is the single path to nirvana for all subtle-dust Buddhas; this is explained by subsuming the others to clarify the fundamental meaning.

Furthermore, the phrase "the original root of perfect penetration" is merely a provisional heading, while what follows sets forth its name and essence. Regarding "opening the wondrous gate of the ear":
this refers to developing the hearing-nature of the ear-gate to realize the true samādhi. Now, as for the three [aspects] of the ear-gate...
Regarding the fact that this alone is called "wondrous": it is because it possesses the meaning of inclusion and universal pervasion.
Once this gate is opened, it encompasses the other gates, making them identical to its own subtlety and identical to its own inclusion and pervasion.
Therefore, it enables one's own single name to be held together with the many names of others; their merit is perfectly equal, without any distinction. Thus we know:
The distinction between those with complete faculties and those with incomplete faculties is indeed a matter of days versus kalpas. Third, resolving doubts and preventing questions:
"World-Honored One, my single name is no different from those many names. It is because I have cultivated and attained true perfect penetration."

First, the resolution of doubts. (The doubt states: One name versus many names; individual recitation versus communal recitation. When comparing the conduct of these two individuals, they differ as much as heaven and earth;

yet when comparing their merit, they do not differ by so much as a hair’s breadth. What is the reason for this? [Fang] says: My single name is no different from his many names. ○ From "Because of my...

onwards, Fang poses a question. (The question states: A single name manifests only a single virtue, whereas many names should manifest many virtues. Since the one and the many are vastly distinct, how can you say they are no different? [Fang] says: Because of my cultivation and practice...

They attained true *pariṇāmanā* (perfect penetration). However, the *pariṇāmanā* of Avalokiteśvara alone is designated as "true" because it possesses the threefold reality of being perfect, universal, and constant.
This serves as a counter-illustration: the various skillful means and wisdoms of the sixty-two sons of the *saṃgha*, who followed the capacities of sentient beings, were each different;
thus, the *pariṇāmanā* they attained was merely similar to perfection rather than truly perfect, and merely similar to universality rather than truly universal.

This is not true supernormal hearing. Having finished the detailed explanation according to the numerical categories, the third section clarifies the benefits through the power of the fetters (*saṃyojana*):
this is called the fourteen powers of fearlessness that provide blessings for all sentient beings.
According to the preceding passage concerning the enumeration of numbers, it states: "It causes all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of fearless merits within my body and mind.
This indicates that the Bodhisattva’s body and mind are the agent of giving (*dāyaka*), while the fourteen fearlessnesses are the object given (*deya*).
As for the current phrase "this is called," etc., it means that what has been described above is termed "the Bodhisattva, by means of his own body and mind, [bestowing...]"

This refers to bestowing the power of fearlessness upon sentient beings who undergo the fourteen kinds of suffering. This constitutes the power of the conclusion. The phrase "endowed with merit" (*puji*) reveals the benefit;

it signifies being protected by merit. "Endowed" (*bei*) means complete. "Sentient beings" here specifically refers to those in the eight difficult circumstances (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), those afflicted by the three poisons, those subject to the two types of seeking, and those called by name (human beings).
Sentient beings in the eight difficult circumstances currently experience extreme suffering and fear that their lives cannot be preserved.
When sentient beings possessed by the three poisons manifest deep delusions and fear that their roots of goodness will be lost,
the Bodhisattva protects them through merit and preserves those roots of goodness.
When sentient beings seeking [worldly things] lack children and fear that their lineage will be severed, the Bodhisattva protects them through merit and preserves their progeny.
Sequel. Sentient beings who currently hold the name may fear that their own merit is not sufficient;
the Bodhisattva, however, protects them with his own merit to ensure their merit is complete. In this way, there is a means to bless them and a means to provide for them;
thus, the benefits of the Bodhisattva are universal. Based on the following sections, the fourteen fearlessnesses are completed.

The three [aspects] encompass the two excellences to form the four inconceivabilities. (Question: Regarding the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it corresponds to the "upper convergence," and regarding fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), it corresponds to the "lower convergence.

Since these are explicit statements in the text, there is nothing to be questioned. Now, in clarifying that the four inconceivabilities encompass the two excellences, what is the basis for this? Answer: The text states, "I have further attained this perfect penetration and cultivated the realization of the unsurpassed path. Thus we know that the two characters "cultivation" (*xiū*) and "realization" (*zhèng*) do not precede perfect penetration;

rather, the cultivation and realization of the stage of contemplative practice (*guānxíng*) occur after attaining perfect penetration. Based on the two excellences, one undergoes cultivation through various phenomena and attains realization through the successive stages, ultimately reaching the unsurpassed path. Furthermore, the text below says, "to rescue and protect sentient beings.")

"World-Honored One, because I have further attained this perfect penetration and realized the unsurpassed Way, I am also able to skillfully attain the four inconceivable and effortless sublime virtues.
The phrase 'further attained' (*you huo*) reiterates what was previously gained; that is to say, I have furthermore attained the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing. [End of upper section]

"Harmonizing below and harmonizing above" means practicing through successive stages and attaining realization through successive positions; because one's merit is perfected and practice is fulfilled, leading to ultimate Buddhahood, it is called the "Unsurpassed Way.
Not only can one obtain wondrous responses and the power of fearlessness, but it is also said that one "furthermore obtains" them.
The term "good" (*shan*) is used because the upper and lower [realms] are harmonized together, and compassion and wisdom are practiced in tandem—one obtaining and one [bestowing].
Regarding "attaining all": the *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) states that the virtuous characteristics listed below are so wondrous as to be inconceivable and so divine as to be beyond deliberation.
Regarding "unconditioned wondrous virtue" (*amala-guṇa*): the *Zhengmo* states that this distinguishes it from being produced through conditioned volition;
rather, it is spontaneously and freely accomplished. Second, the detailed explanation according to number.
Four: first, the inconceivability of the single-body form mantra; second, the inconceivability of the distinct-body form mantra;

third, the inconceivability of overcoming stinginess and fulfilling requests; fourth, the inconceivability of making offerings to the Buddhas and benefiting sentient beings. The first two are as follows:
First, the essence is established to indicate its function; second, the characteristics of that function are briefly set forth.

Regarding the first: because I initially attained the wondrously wondrous mind of hearing, the essence of the mind abandoned its hearing, such that seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing could no longer be partitioned off, becoming a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening. Therefore, I am able to manifest many wondrous forms and am able to preach.
Regarding the boundless secret mantras:
"First attaining the wondrously wondrous hearing-nature" refers to when a bodhisattva first cultivates the samādhi of the ear-gate and attains the nature of the mind that is capable of hearing.
Because it transcends other gates and is the most wondrous among all wonders, one should understand this in terms of movement and stillness.

The two fetters: when that which was heard has been exhausted, one is able to hear the manifest. "The refinement of the mind" means advancing in understanding, whereby the faculties awaken to emptiness and the four fetters are extinguished;
because once the hearing-mind is realized, one returns to the essence of refined and true reality.

"Leaving behind hearing" means that at the time when quiescent extinction manifests before one, that beginningless, false nature of hearing within the faculties is abandoned and never manifests again. However, as for delusion...

Since hearing has already been discarded, false seeing, false cognition, and so forth are likewise discarded along with it. Therefore, it is said that seeing, hearing, cognition, and knowledge cannot be separated one from another.
Because there is no separation, there is the single, true, perfectly湛 (zhan) and profound state. Thus it is said: "One attains a single, perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening.
"Perfectly interfused" means that dependent origination is without obstruction; this is the sense of "following conditions. "Pure" refers to the profoundly湛 (zhan) and still nature.
Yet it is immovable; this is precisely the meaning of "unchanging. Because the unchanging follows conditions, it is like gold and golden vessels;
therefore, it is called the "Precious Awakening. The word "precisely" (gu) simultaneously bears the two meanings of following conditions and remaining unchanging.
It is exactly because arising through conditions is mutually dependent and that unity and multiplicity are without obstruction, that within a single body one can manifest many wondrous forms.

Precisely because it is pure and profoundly serene, this true secret is manifested therein; thus, from among its manifold wondrous countenances, it is able to proclaim boundless secret divine mantras.
Second, the characteristics of the abbreviated manifestations of function (the functions being inexhaustible and impossible to describe fully;

what is stated below is but a small portion extracted from the inexhaustible—observe the two characters within it to understand). This has two parts: first, manifesting forms to symbolize the Dharma; second, transforming the countenance to provide protection.

First: Among them, some manifest one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, nine heads, eleven heads, and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, ten thousand heads, or eighty-four thousand *śakara* heads. Second: two arms.
Four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, up to twenty-four;
and so on, even unto one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms, and eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms.
Two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, nine eyes, and so on, even unto one hundred and eight eyes.
A thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, and eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes.
"The first can manifest a wondrous head" refers to the initial appearance; "among them" points to the midst of the many wondrous countenances.

Since their number is indefinite, it is said that they "may manifest. A single head is the fundamental count and thus need not be manifested. [This is accomplished through] compassion, majesty, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Because they are indeterminate, there is no impediment to speaking of them as being manifest. The same principle applies to the two arms, two eyes, and so forth.
Furthermore, since the head is fundamentally singular in number, it increases from this odd number until it reaches one hundred and eight.

Again, the progression up to eighty-four thousand is intended to correspond to the number of afflictions (*kleśa*) and worldly defilements (*pāriplava*). *Śakara* is translated here as "firm" (*kṣāra*).

It is firm; because it cannot be destroyed by sword wounds or axe blows. If one treats this as a symbolic teaching (*saṃketa-dharma*), "head" signifies the meaning of transcendence, representing the practice for one's own benefit.
Because self-benefit is uniquely excellent, it is initially symbolized by an odd number.
The progression to one hundred and eight, and further to eighty-four thousand, symbolizes that the Bodhisattva is personally capable of transcending.
The one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*) and the eighty-four thousand dust-laboring defilements represent the fulfillment of practices for one's own benefit.
○ Regarding the two arms below, he can manifest the "Wondrous Arm. Since the arms are originally two in number, they increase from this even number.
That the count reaches its limit at one hundred and eight, and further extends to eighty-four thousand, may be understood by analogy with the head [of the Buddha]. *Mudrā*.
This is called "seal" (mudrā). It means that each arm has a hand, and each hand forms a seal.

If it is intended to symbolize the Dharma, the hand carries the meaning of protection and sustenance, representing the practice of benefiting others; since benefiting others is inherently virtuous, it is first represented by an even number.
Regarding the enumeration reaching one hundred and eight, and further extending to eighty-four thousand:

this symbolizes the Bodhisattva’s protection and sustenance of sentient beings, enabling them to escape the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*) and the eighty-four thousand dust-labors (*rajas*).

This signifies the perfection of altruistic practice. ○ Second, regarding the "Eyes": below [the head] are the "Marvelous Eyes. As for the fundamental number of these eyes, there are two and three. Two is as follows: [text continues].
Ordinary people [possess] three [eyes], like Maheśvara; thus, they increase from the dual number to the singular.
Increasing further to one hundred and eight, and then to eighty-four thousand, these numbers correspond to the count of samādhis and dharma-gates.
As for "pure jewels," it is because the deep blue eyes are as pure as lapis lazuli. If this is interpreted as a symbolic teaching, the eyes...
The term "taking up and illuminating" signifies the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate; for provisional wisdom awakens others while ultimate wisdom awakens oneself.

These are represented by pairs and singles. The increase to one hundred and eight, and further to eighty-four thousand, represents the Bodhisattva’s use of the two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate to awaken both self and others, such that self and others together realize the hundred [truths].
The eight samādhis and the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates constitute the perfection of his awakening and practice.

Second, regarding the transformation of his appearance for the sake of rescue and protection: whether through compassion or majesty, whether through meditative concentration or wisdom, he rescues and protects sentient beings, attaining great mastery.

"Kindness" (*maitrī*) has the meaning of gathering and supporting. This means that toward those who should be gathered and supported, one manifests a compassionate countenance to gather and support them, as in the case of virtuous persons, the righteous gods, and so forth. "Majesty" (*tejas*) has the meaning of subduing.

This means that toward those who should be subdued, one manifests a majestic countenance to subdue them, as in the case of wicked persons, malevolent spirits, and so forth. "Composure" (*sthiti*) refers to abiding in tranquility.

The aspect of *maitrī* (loving-kindness) is for the sake of those whose deluded minds are distracted and scattered; the aspect of wisdom (*prajñā*) is the aspect of contemplative observation, for the sake of those who are mired in the darkness of ignorance and dullness.
Because these states are subject to change and instability, the word "or" (*vā*) is placed after each. Furthermore, regarding *maitrī*, the head, arms, and eyes—these three—are all compassionate.
It is said that they bestow secret mantras (*mantra*) for the purpose of gathering and supporting virtuous people, the righteous deities (*deva*), and others.
Regarding their enhancement: as for majesty, the head, arms, and eyes—these three—are all majestic;

they proclaim secret mantras of subjugation to subdue evil persons, malevolent spirits, and the like, causing them to depart. As for meditative concentration, the head, arms, and eyes—these three—are all concentrated.

It is taught that the Secret Mantra of Quiescent Abiding is for the purpose of counteracting sentient beings whose deluded minds are distracted and scattered, causing them to gather their mindfulness.

Since the head, arms, and eyes are all wisdom, it is taught that the Secret Mantra of Illuminating Wisdom is for the purpose of counteracting sentient beings who dwell in the darkness of ignorance, causing them to contemplate the mind.
Thus, having displayed both subduing and gathering, as well as the dual forms of śamatha and vipaśyanā, there is no [duality].
Suffering is not left unrescued; no one is left unprotected from birth. Therefore, it is said that he "rescues and protects sentient beings.

Because his power to extinguish evil and establish goodness is like a blade gliding through butter, it is said that he "attains great mastery. Since all these manifestations appear within a single body, this is called the "Mantra of the Identical Body Form" (*tongti xingzhou*).
As the *Text on the Great Compassion Repentance* (*Dabei chanwen*) says: "Within one body and mind, a thousand hands and eyes appear, illuminating..."
To perceive the dharma-realm and to protect and sustain sentient beings is this [practice]. Thus concludes the inconceivability of the homogenous-form mantra.
Second is the inconceivability of the heterogeneous-form mantra.
Second, because I have emerged from the six sense-objects through hearing and reflection, it is like a sound passing over a wall that cannot act as an obstruction; therefore, I—
I am skillfully able to manifest each and every form and recite each and every mantra; these forms and mantras can bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
For this reason, throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, I am known as the One Who Bestows Fearlessness.

Regarding "hearing and contemplating," two of the six natures are mentioned; since they are fundamentally one entity, whether they are cited individually or collectively, each encompasses them all, and either approach is acceptable according to the context.
"Transcending the six dusts" means that when the power of "listening inwardly" reaches its peak, the six natures become perfectly still and profound, such that the dusts can no longer bind them.
"Sound" refers to audible voices, serving as a metaphor for the nature of hearing; "walls" refers to enclosures, serving as a metaphor for the six [sense objects].
"Dust" refers to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). "To transcend" means to pass beyond, as in the metaphor of escaping;

it means that the six natures have escaped the six dusts such that the dusts cannot bind them, just as sound passes over a wall such that the wall cannot obstruct it. The correspondence between the dharma and the metaphor is thus clearly evident.
Therefore, regarding the phrase "I am skillfully able," etc., it means that because defilements cannot bind [the Buddha], he manifests in response to conditions.
Manifesting each individual form means manifesting different forms in response to different capacities. Reciting each individual mantra means preaching different mantras for different bodies;
thus, these are called "mantras of distinct physical forms. Alternatively, he may manifest a body to liberate them from their suffering and affliction, or...
The recitation of mantras accords with their specific aspirations; thus it is said that their forms and mantras are able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.

This "fearlessness" is the same as the fourteen types mentioned previously, differing only in that it should be distinguished as either implicit or explicit. Therefore, regarding the phrase "the ten directions," etc., the title is established based on his virtues.

To say that these titles pervade the lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions correctly demonstrates that the Bodhisattva’s actual virtues have moved and responded with sincerity.
There is nowhere it does not reach. How could it be that its fame and reputation spread only throughout China?
Third, by breaking through stinginess and responding to requests for the inconceivable:
these three arise from my cultivation of the fundamental, wondrous, perfect, penetrating, and pure root, such that all worlds where I travel are caused to be...
Sentient beings relinquish their bodies and precious treasures to seek my compassion.

"Fundamentally wondrous and perfect penetration" (*ben-miao-yuan-tong*) specifically refers to the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty. It is designated as "fundamentally wondrous" because it has inherently possessed the three meanings of "leaving," "shallow," and "perfect" from the very beginning.
However, although this wondrous nature is fundamentally present, as long as the six knots have not been untied, [the true nature remains obscured].

If one clings to and upholds these bonds, one cannot attain purity. Through the power of cultivation, the Bodhisattva unties the six knots, transcends the three voids, and spontaneously achieves the purity of the fundamental root. Once the fundamental root is pure, there is no attachment to anything.
Moved by this resonance, wherever they travel, they are able to cause sentient beings to [perceive] the treasures worn upon their own bodies.

One should treasure it and offer it as a gift. This is evidenced by the passage in the "Universal Gate" chapter where the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati unties from his neck a pearl necklace worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold and gives it to him.

Those who seek my compassion fear that [the recipient] might not accept it, whereby the merit of the gift could not be realized; this is as described in the "Universal Gate" chapter regarding Avalokiteśvara.

When the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati earnestly entreated him, Avalokiteśvara remained hesitant; he would only accept [the offerings] once the Buddha had spoken, out of compassion for Akṣayamati and the others—this is precisely the proof of that.
Zhengmo (Zheng-mo) says: "The stingy mind of sentient beings is the most difficult to break;
the mind of renunciation is the most difficult to arouse; the mind of seeking cannot be brought forth by force. Now, what has been passed over..."
Immediately, sentient beings were moved to abandon their stinginess and offer gifts in response to his entreaties; this is truly the work of inconceivable majestic spiritual power.
If one investigates its profound source, it arises simply from the purity and non-attachment of the faculty of hearing through long-standing practice, which is thus able to produce such a resonance.
Based on this, those who are stained by attachment to worldly affairs, who guard their wealth with parsimony, and who resent others for not providing them with offerings [stand in stark contrast].
One should also understand what is implied by this. Fourth, the inconceivable benefit of making offerings to the Buddhas and aiding sentient beings:

having attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate, one is able to use various precious treasures to make offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm.
For those who seek a wife, they obtain a wife; for those who seek a son, they obtain a son; for those who seek [the third... [text fragmentary].
One who seeks samādhi attains samādhi; one who seeks long life attains long life; and so on, up to one who seeks great nirvāṇa attains great nirvāṇa.

Because the faculties and nature serve as the cause, and the mind-cause is identical to the fruit, it is said: "I have attained the Buddha-mind. Thus, the bonds of conditions are severed and liberated.
Having attained wondrous awakening, this awakening is identical to realization; therefore, it is said that one realizes the ultimate.

Since one has awakened and realized equality with the Buddha, there is no virtue not perfected and no dharma to which one can cling. Thus, one is able to offer precious jewels and other such things to the Tathāgata.
It is because one is endowed with virtue that one is able to possess; it is through non-attachment that one is able to offer.

This is evidenced by the passage in the "Universal Gate" chapter where Avalokiteśvara receives a necklace and divides it into two parts: one he offers to Śākyamuni, and the other he offers to Prabhūtaratna.

That which extends to others is not the primary offering; rather, it is the merit of the act of giving that is dedicated to all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*, so that they may possess [it].

All requests were fulfilled. This is evidenced by the passage in the "Universal Gate" chapter where Avalokiteśvara accepts the offering of necklaces from the Buddha out of compassion for the fourfold assembly, as well as for humans and non-humans alike.
Indeed, the six realms of the Dharma-realm also encompass the four classes of noble beings.
In general, all that is sought does not exceed two types: first, worldly happiness; second, supramundane happiness.

Now, the pursuit of wife and children is restricted to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Samādhi and longevity, however, extend through the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

This is because "longevity" does not merely refer to a long life among humans, but includes the long-term rewards of both immortals and devas. Although samādhi extends to the supramundane, [the pursuit of wife and children does not].
However, since it is listed alongside one's wife, children, and long life, and is discussed in terms of worldly samādhi, this belongs to worldly happiness.
In this manner, even up to surpassing and abbreviating the provisional fruits of the Three Vehicles, the actual fruit of the One Vehicle may likewise be sought.
Therefore, it is said that by seeking great nirvāṇa, one attains great nirvāṇa; this is the supramundane [attainment].
Joy! Furthermore, worldly pleasures are finite and should not be sought after recklessly; how much less can the unconditioned bliss of the supramundane be attained so abruptly?

Now, by means of the inconceivable power of the Bodhisattva, one is able to perform vast and most excellent offerings and make vast and most excellent dedications of merit, thereby ensuring that all the sentient beings within the Dharma-realm have their prayers fulfilled. Thus we know that [this is the true] temple sacrifice.
Throughout the entire realm, the practice of ritual veneration and mindfulness extends from the highest to the lowest levels; this is not at all surprising. Zhengmei (Correct Pulse) says:
"The thirty-two manifestations are the gift of Dharma; the fourteen fearlessnesses are the gift of fearlessness; the four inconceivables comprise both gifts, including the gift of material wealth.
Thus, it is truly believed that *dāna* (generosity) encompasses the ten thousand practices. This concludes the summary of the two proofs previously detailed.
[The account] concludes. This was the third response concerning the perfection of penetration.

The Buddha asked about the perfection of penetration, and I replied: "Through the gate of the ear, I attained the samādhi of universal illumination; by focusing the mind on its conditions, I gained mastery.
Because of this entry into the stream of dharmas, I attained samāpatti and achieved Bodhi; this is the foremost. "World-Honored One, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised [this method]."
I have skillfully attained the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration. Within this great assembly, I was granted the prophecy that my name shall be Avalokiteśvara.
Because I contemplate and listen to the ten directions with perfect clarity, the name "Avalokiteśvara" pervades the worlds of the ten directions.
First, one should ask the question and provide the answer. The Buddha’s interrogative phrase establishes the basis for the Buddha’s inquiry.

I shall now correctly provide the answer by way of a summary: when in motion, it reaches both near and far; when still, it is boundless. Because the nature of hearing leaves nothing unperceived, it is called "universal illumination" (*yuanzhao*).

Based on this universally illuminating nature of hearing, one achieves right concentration; therefore, it is called *samādhi*. This is the naming of the concentration. As for the word "mind": *Note: The original text contains a fragmentary reference to the character "mind" (*xin*) at the end.*
He again points to the nature of hearing; because it can hear through walls without obstruction in the ten directions, it is called "sovereign.

Taking this sovereign nature of mind as the essence of contemplation, one does not pursue external objects but turns the hearing back in a single flavor; therefore, it is called "entering the stream."

Therefore, the cultivation of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) constitutes contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Based on the essence (*tattva*), one establishes practice; by means of practice, the essence is revealed.
When practice is perfected and the essence is fully realized, it is called "attaining *samādhi*. This clarifies the characteristics of this cultivation.

Should one wish to achieve enlightenment (*bodhi*), relying on these perfect faculties (*indriya*) is many times more effective than relying on those that are imperfect—day and eon after day, the difference is multiplied. Therefore, it is said: "This..."
This is the foremost. [The passage] beginning with "World-Honored One" below cites and reveals his transcendence. That Buddha is none other than the ancient Avalokiteśvara.
Because he saw that I in the past entered samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, he praised me, saying I had "well attained perfect penetration.
He said "well attained" because, compared to other methods, this requires little effort while yielding great results. This is recorded as being the same.
Regarding the title: first, it reveals the harmony between teacher and disciple; second, it reveals the reality attained. It must take place within a great assembly for three reasons:
first, to cause the ocean-like multitude to realize it together; second, to cause those of like practice to emulate the cultivation; and third, this represents the excellence of self-benefit.

"The nature of hearing is perfectly clear through contemplation" means that by turning back to contemplate the nature of hearing, one returns to the truth and leaves behind ordinary listening. Thus, the ten directions are illuminated in their entirety all at once.
This is clear understanding. Such clarity is not merely luminous; it must be able to respond perfectly to sounds.

It is because of this that sentient beings throughout the ten directions all know how to invoke his name. Thus, the name of Avalokiteśvara pervades the worlds of the ten directions. This is the excellence of benefiting others.
Both self-benefit and benefit for others are fully present within a single gateway of the ear. This is what is called the accomplishment of Bodhi.

The first [of the four dharmas] is faith. Furthermore, although each of the twenty-four sages spoke of their own as the foremost, they stated that it was not a method for universal cultivation, being limited to what they themselves had realized and known. Now, Avalokiteśvara speaks directly of the foremost without saying it is according to his own realization;
this reveals that it is indeed a method for universal cultivation. This distinction is already implicitly contained within the text itself, even without waiting for Mañjuśrī’s words.
This is merely a different intention. This concludes the section on the fundamental causes according to the various preceding explanations.

Regarding the third part, Mañjuśrī’s selection of the three [kinds of people], there are three sections: first, the Tathāgata first manifests auspicious signs; second, he commands Mañjuśrī to select them;
third, Mañjuśrī, in accordance with the imperial decree, speaks in verse. Within the first of these, there is one section: awakening to the characteristic of the essence containing its function.
Second is the characteristic of awakening and cultivation for those of the Two Vehicles; third is the characteristic of the fulfillment of the fruit through the three practices.

The first [section] has three parts: first, to manifest the essence and function of the faculty-nature; second, to manifest the essence and function of the other gates; and third, to manifest that the ear-gate is easy to awaken to. Regarding the first:

At that time, from his five limbs, the World-Honored One emitted jewel-like light, which reached far to moisten the crowns of the heads of the Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, as well as the Bodhisattvas who are Dharma Princes. Those Tathāgatas likewise emitted jewel-like light from their five limbs;

from those directions as numerous as motes of dust, this light came to moisten the crown of the Buddha’s head, and simultaneously moistened the crowns of the heads of all the great Bodhisattvas in the assembly.
As for the Arhats, according to the treatises on their deeds, each of the holy ones spoke of their own original causes; thus, the "Flower Hall" has gates through which one may enter.

Because both the Buddha himself and other Buddhas experience great joy, each emits light from the five parts of the body to manifest their self-congratulation, mutually pouring water over the crowns of the Buddhas' heads.

Regarding the phrase "and all those at the summit": this both demonstrates self-congratulation and demonstrates congratulating others. For when the gateway of perfect penetration has been opened, the original intent of all Buddhas can be fulfilled;
thus, all members of the assembly can be received and all may be congratulated. If interpreted as a symbolic representation of the Dharma:
the World-Honored One, as the fundamental Buddha, represents the fundamental root of this realm. Once that fundamental root is opened, then cultivation...

Because one abides in fearlessness through the cause and the attainment of the fruit, this is symbolized by the teacher’s seat. Not only does one abide in fearlessness, but one is also liberated through the five faculties;

thus, this is symbolized by the five limbs being suffused with light. That the light streams upward to drench the crown of the Buddha’s head symbolizes that, above, one shares the same power of compassion as all Buddhas;
and that it streams downward to drench the crowns of the Bodhisattvas symbolizes [the connection] below with sentient beings.
They share the same compassion and yearning. This is because once the fundamental root is opened, the essence necessarily contains its function.
What is called "the non-differentiation of the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings"—can be seen herein. Those Tathāgatas are Buddhas of other realms;
they represent that the remaining five faculties likewise possess this nature, for when one faculty returns to its source, all five faculties are simultaneously liberated.

Furthermore, the five limbs being simultaneously bathed by light symbolizes this; that the water comes to drench the crown of the Buddha’s head as well as the crowns of the assembly’s heads also symbolizes the meaning of "uniting above" and "uniting below.

Based on this, although the five sense faculties do not reach the level of the ear-faculty, they are still far superior to the various forms of perfect penetration involving objects and consciousness.
These two points symbolize the essence and function of the other gates.
The forest trees, groves, ponds, and marshes all emit the sounds of the Dharma; their interlacing lights entwine like a net of precious threads.
Since this event has occurred, both the Buddhas and the world rejoice, and even Heaven and Earth should manifest auspicious signs.

Therefore, the forest trees, groves, ponds, and marshes all emit the sounds of the Dharma and interlace their lights. If these are interpreted as symbols of the Dharma, then the forest trees, groves, ponds, and marshes all proclaim the Dharma.

The term "sound" signifies that the sense objects, consciousnesses, and so forth are all endowed with the nature of the Sage (*ārya-dhātu*). Since they are all endowed with this sage-nature, every gate interpenetrates with every other;
thus, it is represented by the mutual interlacing of light. Those who attain this light can adorn their own bodies and embrace all living beings;
therefore, it is represented by a net of jewel threads. Here, "jewel" takes the sense of adornment, while "net" takes the sense of gathering and sustaining.
The three marks alone are sufficient for the gateway of the ears to be easily understood.
This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before; all universally obtained the Vajra Samādhi.

According to the Discourse on Affairs, since they have both witnessed the shared celebration of living beings and Buddhas, and observed the manifestation of auspicious omens from heaven and earth, they have all attained what was unprecedented.
There has been such a moment. Because from this point on they have resolved their minds with never again regressing, they achieve the Vajra Samādhi.
If one interprets this as a symbolic teaching: the "great assembly" refers to the sentient beings of this realm within this gathering.

When these beings of this realm hear the Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ but once, their capacity and the teaching meet in harmony; thus, it is symbolized by the phrase "attaining what was never before attained. Since...
When the faculty and the teaching harmonize, it is easy to attain awakening and entry. Therefore, this is symbolized by the universal attainment of the Vajra Samādhi.
What was previously called the "Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening Illusion-like Samāpatti" is precisely a cryptic reference to the Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ.
Thus we know that both the "expresser" (the means) and the "expressed" (the goal) are equally termed the Vajra-samādhi;

however, the expresser refers solely to the non-retrogression of the initial resolve, whereas the expressed takes the unimpeded severance of hindrances as its mark—their difference lies merely in depth.
Now, these three preceding sections clearly demonstrate the superiority and inferiority of the dharmas they express. One who understands this meaning need not trouble Mañjuśrī further.

The selection is complete. The section on the realization of the essence containing its functions and characteristics is finished. Regarding the second point, the realization and cultivation of the Two Vehicles:
at that moment, it rained down lotus flowers made of a hundred jewels—blue, yellow, red, and white—intermingled and variegated.
In terms of the actual event, the assembled multitude benefited; thus, the heavens rained down precious flowers as offerings.
As for their "intermingling and profusion," this refers to the blue, yellow, red, and white colors being interspersed and falling in a chaotic, variegated mixture;

even the densest clusters of blossoms or the most intricate brocades would not suffice to match such beauty. If one interprets this as a symbolic teaching, it signifies that once the faculty of hearing has been awakened...
In perfect interfusion (*yuantong*), the nature-heaven (*xingtian*) is limpid and luminous; cultivating the causal practice based upon this contains all myriad functions.

Since cause and effect are thoroughly pervasive, it is symbolized by the rain of precious lotuses from the heavens. When discussing sequential progression (*xingbu*), the four stages of abiding, practice, transference, and realization (*zhuxingxiangdi*) are distinct and far apart;
thus, they are symbolized by blue, yellow, red, and white. When discussing perfect interfusion, one is identical to all, and all are identical to one.
All things are thus one; therefore, they are represented through their intermingling and complex entanglement. Qingliang (Chengguan) said:
"The myriad practices unfold like flowers blooming upon brocade"—this is precisely the same meaning. These three practices constitute the mark of the fulfillment of the fruition.
The empty spaces of the ten directions turned the color of the seven treasures. At that moment, the great earth, mountains, and rivers of this Sahā world all vanished from sight;
one saw only the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions merged into a single realm. Chanting and hymns were spontaneously performed and offered.
In terms of the phenomenal reality, the four flowers are in the void, reflecting one another to form the colors of the seven jewels;
like rain falling everywhere across the world, they pervade it so as to obscure the forms of mountains and rivers. Therefore, it is said that they do not appear simultaneously.

Yet, since the mountains and rivers no longer appear, the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) are no longer prominent; thus, one sees only the lands of the ten directions’ atoms merged into a single realm.
At this moment of auspicious response, all the devas offered praise and celebration; thus, one also heard the sounds of *brahmaghoṣa* and spontaneous chanting being performed.

*Brahmaghoṣa* refers to praises and eulogies in the Brahma-sound; "chanting" (*yongge*) refers to the recitation and singing of verses. If these are interpreted as symbolic representations of the Dharma:
when awakening gives rise to cultivation, one proceeds from the ultimate truth into the mundane world; therefore, it is symbolized by the formation of form from empty space. From...
When truly engaging with the mundane, the mundane is itself the ultimate; thus, it is symbolized by the non-appearance of mountains and rivers.
Since the ultimate and the mundane are mutually integrated, they wondrously coincide with the Middle Way; thus, it is symbolized by the unification of the dust-motes and the lands.

Abiding in the fruit while gathering in sentient beings, the Dharma-sound universally pervades; thus, it is symbolized by the chanting of *brahma*-melodies. Responding according to conditions, acting spontaneously and effortlessly...
Thus it is said. Therefore, this is expressed by means of "spontaneous unfolding and presentation" (*fuzòu*). "Unfolding and presentation" refers to the proclamation of the rhythmic progression.
When viewed in conjunction with the preceding section, the signs of cultivating the causes and realizing the fruit have already manifested their auspicious omens.

Having concluded the Tathāgata’s initial manifestation of auspicious signs, part two consists of the command to Mañjuśrī to select [the disciples]. First, a general discussion on cultivation according to practice.

It seems there is no need for selection [in this general sense]. However, in the second part, which specifically addresses the original capacity of the audience, one must indeed exercise discernment. First: therein, the Tathāgata addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī:

"You should now observe these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas and Arhats beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), each of whom has spoken of the skillful means (*upāya*) by which they first attained the Way; all have said that they practiced..."
They practice the true and perfect penetration; in their cultivation, there is truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or sequence.
These manifested signs symbolize the Dharma and are secretly shown in a manner difficult to clarify. Because they must be explained explicitly, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī.
The Buddha does not speak for himself because the return to the source is non-dual and admits of no discrimination;
to discriminate would result in partiality and contradict his own teaching. Since this present sutra expounds the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), he must address Mañjuśrī.

This is because while there are many gates of skillful means (*upāya*), failure to discriminate would lead to confusion, whereas discrimination requires wisdom. Mañjuśrī alone is designated for this purpose, as all other sutras...
Because Pu-meng (Maitreya) possesses great wisdom, although he had previously heard [the teachings] in a general way, he had not yet attained detailed contemplation.

Therefore, he was instructed: "You must now contemplate this. This is because one must surely contemplate in accordance with what has been heard in order to fully realize the reality of what is realized.

As for the fact that all twenty-five sages are called "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), there are two meanings: first, in relation to their remote origins; second, in relation to their fundamental dharma. Regarding...
From the perspective of the remote origin, although they have long since realized the fruit of Buddhahood, they manifest as abiding in the stage of the cause;

for example, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara was the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa in the past. From the perspective of the fundamental dharma, their realization is equal to that of the Buddha, meaning they are identical in both cultivation and realization.
This is because for practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching], cultivation is itself non-cultivation.

Regarding the phrase "each spoke," it means that each [practitioner] spoke of their own initial method for entering the path and attaining enlightenment; this refers, for example, to how the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses each rely upon a single gateway.
Regarding the phrase "all said," it means that all the sages declared what they themselves had practiced to be the true, perfect penetration (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). As for example...
It is as stated: "The twenty-five sages each claim to be the foremost; in reality, there is no superiority or inferiority. There are four reasons for this:
First, although the skillful means are manifold, they all return to the same source without duality, just as the thousand paths and nine thoroughfares all converge at the royal city.

Second, generally speaking, each direction follows its own appropriate suitability, such as the flavor-particles of the Fragrant Accumulation [Buddha-land] or the non-blinking of the eye-faculty. Third...

Because past habitual tendencies differ, each person selects that which is easy for them to enter; for example, as with Śūnyatā-utpāda (Subhūti), whose mind attained non-obstruction after kalpas of practice.
Because the habits of the four delusions differ, each selects their respective antidote; for example, as with those who have excessive lust, the Buddha taught the contemplation of fire and so forth.

Thus we know that what accords with the specific ailment is an excellent medicine, and that what allows for easy entry belongs to a wondrous gate. Moreover, the faculties vary according to different dispositions.
The gathering and transformation [of beings] does not rely on a single path; since the nature of the sages is equal and ultimate, how could there be two different outcomes?
As there is neither superiority nor inferiority, one should practice according to what is foremost, such as Pūrṇa, who has possessed unimpeded eloquence from the beginningless kalpas.
Regarding subsequent cultivation—such as Upāli following the Buddha in his renunciation of the city, receiving the precepts, and so forth—there is likewise no distinction.
Therefore, it is generally said that there is truly no superiority or inferiority, nor priority or posteriority, and so on.
Based on this, the twenty-five gates would seemingly require no selection. Second, when specifically addressing the original capacities [of the practitioners], one must indeed exercise discernment.
I now wish to cause Ānanda to attain awakening. Among the twenty-five practices, which one corresponds to his faculties?

Furthermore, after my parinirvāṇa, for the sentient beings of this world who enter the Bodhisattva vehicle and seek the unsurpassed path, by what gate of skillful means can they achieve success with ease?
At the beginning, this was specifically for Ānanda. Desiring to bring about his awakening, it was necessary to select a teaching that accorded with his capacity;
therefore, Mañjuśrī was specially commanded to discern, among twenty-five lines of verse, who possessed the corresponding root-faculty. Later, Mañjuśrī’s verse says:
"That he is capable of instructing Ānanda" precisely accords with this intention. "Furthermore, for my sake" refers to the future;
after my parinirvāṇa, those of dull faculties will find it difficult to attain awakening. The sentient beings of this world have particularly sharp faculties of hearing;

even if they do not apply themselves to these faculties, though there may be those who enter the Bodhisattva vehicle and seek the Unsurpassed Way, they will still find it difficult to reach the ultimate goal. For this reason, he further commanded Mañjuśrī.
To determine which gateway of skillful means leads to easy accomplishment, the subsequent verse by Mañjuśrī states:
"And during the final eon of sinking and delusion," which precisely accords with this intent. After Mañjuśrī had completed his selection as commanded, there are two parts:
first, the narrator describes the ritual setting and introduces the discourse; second, Mañjuśrī elaborates on the verses in detail. Regarding the first:
Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, having received the Buddha’s compassionate command, immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and,
sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha.
This is the essential intent. The Buddha’s command to select [Mañjuśrī] was intended to awaken Ānanda and to bring far-reaching benefit after his passing; thus it is called the "Compassionate Intent.
When a Most Honored One issues a mandate, a wise minister should receive it accordingly; therefore, Mañjuśrī received and honored it, responding with these verses.

Rising from one's seat to pay homage to the Buddha is the constant protocol for receiving his instructions. To "rely upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power" means to speak by depending on the Buddha’s empowerment.
Indeed, among the twenty-five sages, there have been those whose realization was equal to that of Mañjuśrī;

yet, were it not for the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, how would one dare to independently deliberate upon these matters? Furthermore, responding with verses rather than prose makes it easier to string the flowers together [into a garland].
Uphold this so that, having heard it, one may contemplate and practice it. Part Three: Mañjuśrī’s Detailed Explanation of the Verses.
One: Preliminary Opening of the Selection. Two: General Exclusion of Other Gateways. Three: Exclusive Selection of the Ear-faculty. Section One: Three Parts. One:
A General Clarification of the Arising of Delusion from Reality. Two: A Brief Demonstration of Returning from Delusion to Reality. Three: Following the Clarification, the Necessity for Selection.

Selection One: The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect; this perfect clarity makes awakening fundamentally wondrous. When primordial luminosity shines forth, it gives rise to an object; once that object is established, the nature of the illuminating subject perishes.

Through delusion and false imagination, empty space arises; based on space, the world is established. As thought becomes settled, the land is formed; through cognition and awareness, sentient beings come into being.
The two characters "Juehai" (Ocean of Awakening) manifest both the dharma and its metaphor simultaneously. As Wuxing said: "The nature of true awakening is like the great ocean.

The meanings of "clarity and roundness" (*chengyuan*) and "roundness and clarity" (*yuancheng*) apply to both the dharma and the metaphor. In the metaphor, it means the nature of the ocean is clear and still, perfectly manifesting the myriad phenomena.
In the dharma, it means the nature of awakening is limpid and tranquil, perfectly containing all existence. However, regarding the clarity and roundness of the ocean...

The ocean is easy to perceive, but its clarity and perfection are difficult to know. To cause one to realize that enlightened awareness is like the ocean, it is therefore designated by the term "clarity and perfection.
This is precisely "stillness yet illumination. Furthermore, although the nature of the ocean is perfect and manifests all phenomena, it remains clear and still without change.
Although the nature of enlightenment is perfect and contains all existence, it remains limpid and tranquil without shifting. For this reason, it is further described as "perfectly clear."

Observe this: it is precisely illumination within stillness. Because it is illumination within stillness, the nature of awakening is fundamentally wondrous; for "wondrous" carries the meaning of immutability (*avikāra*).
Because it is stillness within illumination, the nature of awakening is fundamentally luminous; for "luminous" carries the meaning of following conditions (*pratyaya-anuvartana*).
Since it is said to be fundamentally wondrous and fundamentally luminous, then even when a single thought does not arise, these qualities are naturally and inherently complete. If...
If one then gives rise to the thought of wanting to illuminate [it], this is the sudden arising of ignorance (*avidyā*).

From this, the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) is further produced, and all objective appearances are formed. As stated previously: "Awakening is not that which is illumined; because of illumination, the object is established.

Regarding the phrase "the object established," it means that once the characterized object (*lakṣya*) has been falsely established, it in turn gives rise to your false subject (*lakṣaka*), namely the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), which in turn takes that object...
The nature that was intended to illuminate becomes increasingly obscured and darkened; therefore, it is said to have "perished. Regarding the phrase "deluded confusion" and so forth:
since the nature that was to be illuminated has perished, the nature-awareness of true emptiness becomes lost amidst delusive afflictions, and its entire substance becomes entirely inert and void;
hence it is called "empty space. This is as previously stated: "Obscured darkness becomes space. Regarding the phrase "relying on space" and so forth:
This refers to the object-condition of firm attachment arising from the confrontation with the view of emptiness.

Since the essence of emptiness is fundamentally ungraspable as an object, it is due to this firm attachment that one falsely perceives the appearance of a world within empty space; hence, it is called "establishing realms."

This is as previously stated: "In the midst of empty darkness, the coagulation of obscurity forms matter. The two phrases beginning with "The ideation clarifies" separately clarify the characteristics of how realms are established based upon space.
It is said that there are two kinds of worlds: first, the coagulation of the clarification and condensation of deluded thought forms the land, which is called the *bhājana-loka* (the vessel-world);
second, the grasping of cognition and movement forms sentient beings, which is called the world of emotion (*sattva-loka*).

Regarding the world: furthermore, although this refers to the complete array of sentient beings and their environments, it speaks specifically of the subtle aspects within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
The coarse aspects are not mentioned because it is intended to show that those on the path of delusion have not yet traveled far, and thus it is easy for them to see how to return to the source.
Second, a brief demonstration of returning to the truth by reversing delusion:
"The void arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean. The minute dust-like lands of the outflows are all produced in dependence upon the void."
When the bubble perishes, emptiness is fundamentally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three worlds!
As stated above, "due to delusion and falsehood there is empty space," which means that empty space arises from within the awakened mind.
Yet, while everyone knows that empty space is vast, they do not realize that the awakened mind is even vaster. If one compares empty space with the awakened mind...
When compared, empty space is like a bubble and the awakened mind is like the ocean; thus it is said that "from the one ocean, a single bubble arises.
Furthermore, there are two reasons for using the ocean as a metaphor for the mind and the bubble as a metaphor for space:

first, the substance of the ocean is one while bubbles are many, which serves as a metaphor for the mind having a single essence while the manifestations of emptiness are manifold; furthermore, the single bubble specifically represents the One.
The emptiness of a single realm (*dhātu*) is the smallest [unit]. Second, the substance of the ocean is eternally abiding while the characteristics of bubbles arise and perish;

this is a metaphor for the awakened mind being beyond dependence, whereas empty space is established through dependence. Furthermore, using a single bubble as a metaphor for the emptiness of a single realm illustrates that it is the ultimate delusion.

The two characters "outflow" (*āsrava*) correspond to the aforementioned world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), while the "micro-dust lands" correspond to the aforementioned world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*).
Regarding the world: previously it was said that the realms are established based on space; here it is said that they all arise from space.
This is likely a reiteration of the previous point to demonstrate that, compared to empty space, these realms are even more minute and even more utterly illusory.

Since empty space is already like a single bubble, by knowing that the bubble is easily extinguished, one understands that space itself is fundamentally non-existent. If even space is fundamentally non-existent, [how much more so are the realms].
How much more so the three realms of sentient beings and their physical environment! Furthermore, how could these truly exist within empty space?
One who understands this intent will transcend both the realm of emotions and the realm of objects; with both emptiness and form exhausted, this is the essential secret for returning to the source.
Third, regarding the transmission of the brightness, one must exercise careful discernment.
The nature that returns to the source is non-dual, yet there are many gates of expedient means. The sacred nature has no obstruction; both following and reversing are expedient means.
For those at the initial stage entering samādhi, the speed of progress differs according to their individual capacities.
The first two lines clarify that one must select [the appropriate method] according to the faculties [of the practitioner].

It is said that if the fruit can be as described above—sudden enlightenment and immediate return to the source—then the nature of awakening is fundamentally without duality. However, because the capacities of sentient beings are not uniform, there are many paths of expedient means to correspond with their specific dispositions;
indeed, it is impossible not to exercise such selection. The section beginning with "The Holy Nature" below clarifies the difficulty.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) requires careful selection. It speaks of the nature that achieves sagehood as being such that there is no dharma through which it does not pass.

One may cultivate by following one's nature through the six sense faculties, or one may cultivate by turning against one's nature through the objects and consciousnesses; both serve as skillful means.

However, for those at the initial stage who wish to enter samādhi, some will require many kalpas while others will achieve it quickly in a short time; their ease or difficulty is naturally of different orders. Furthermore—
It may be that selection is not required. This concludes the second general section, which opens the topic of selection from above.

Within this, there are four parts: first, the exclusion of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*); second, the exclusion of the five sense faculties (*pañca-indriya*); third, the exclusion of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*).
The fourth section distinguishes the six from the seven elements. The first six are as follows: first, distinguishing the dust of form (rūpa) of Śāṭha;

second, distinguishing the dust of sound (śabda) of Cienā; third, distinguishing the dust of fragrance (gandha) of Xiāngyán; fourth, distinguishing the dust of flavor (rasa) of Yàowáng; fifth, distinguishing the dust of touch (spraṣṭavya) of Bādutuó.
Sixth, Kāśyapa’s Dharma-dust. First:
"The aggregate of form-perceptions constitutes dust; my refined discernment could not penetrate it. Why was I unable to attain clarity? It was therein that I attained perfect penetration."
Regarding the statement that "the perception of form binds together to form an object": it means that form alone cannot constitute an object.
It is only through the firm attachment of consciousness and perception, which bind and entangle one another, that there arises the sense of defilement and obscuration; thus, it becomes an object.
Once it has become an object, it defiles and obscures the fundamental root, such that one cannot clearly penetrate its essence of subtle purity and luminosity. It is like... [long duration]...

A traveler in a foreign land, though they have the road back home, does not know it. When you ask "how," you mean that perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) can only be entered through clarity and transparency.
How could one achieve such perfect penetration by means of material objects (*rūpa-dhātu*) that lack clarity and transparency?
This is certainly difficult to accomplish, as is known even without further deliberation.
Second, to exclude the auditory objects of Dignāga:
sounds are mixed with speech; they consist merely of phonemes, phrases, and sentences. Since one does not contain all, how can one attain perfect penetration?
