Regarding the two characters "yīn" (sound) and "shēng" (voice): analyzed separately, "yīn" refers to that which is winding and circuitous, while "shēng" refers to that which is direct.
Taken together as a compound, "yīnshēng" means "a voice possessing sound," as it specifically adopts the sense of being winding.

"Zá yǔyán" (various languages) means that based on those voices possessing sound, various utterances emerge to form a multitude of languages. "Yī" (like/as for) is used here as a particle of comparison. However—
These two phrases should be read in a single breath. That is to say, the names, phrases, meanings, and flavors are each distinct and manifest individually;
one name cannot contain multiple names, and so on, up to the point that one flavor cannot contain multiple flavors.

This indeed demonstrates that the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*) is not complete [in itself]. Within this context, what are called "names" (*nāman*), "phrases" (*pada*), and "syllables" (*vyañjana*):
names express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For example, "fire" expresses only the nature of burning. Phrases express distinctions (*viśeṣa*).

For example, "ragweed fire" as opposed to "charcoal fire," and so forth. These two are both the signifiers (*vācaka*). Syllables are the meanings (*artha*), which constitute the signified (*vācya*). Thus, they are the signifiers.
The reason "words" (*vyañjana*) are not mentioned among the [three] is that they are merely the conjunction of names and phrases and do not possess a separate substantial entity.
The reason "principles" (*artha*) are not mentioned among the "signifieds" (*abhidheya*) is that they are only known after awakening and are not a provisional means.

Furthermore, since principles are capable of universally encompassing everything, if they were included, the exclusion of "meaning" (*artha*) would be untenable; therefore, only "names," "phrases," and "syllables" (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*) are mentioned. [End of section.]
Since the phrasing does not encompass everything, it contradicts universal penetration; how then could one obtain [enlightenment] through this?
This is a rhetorical inversion used for exclusion. Third, it excludes Xiangyan’s olfactory dust.
"Olfaction is known through contact; when separated, it fundamentally does not exist. Since that which is perceived is not constant, how can one attain perfect penetration?
'Olfaction is known through contact' means that the olfactory object must necessarily meet with the nose before it can be known."
"To be separated means that from the very beginning there is nothing": this refers to how, when not in contact with the nose, the characteristic of fragrance fundamentally does not exist.
Thus, the objective field of fragrance is certainly not constant. "That which is perceived is not constant" means that since fragrance is sometimes present and sometimes absent, it cannot be eternal;
consequently, the nature of perception within the faculty also cannot manifest eternally. This is not because of the act of smelling... [and so forth].

Regarding the term "awakening" (*jue*): because they are fundamentally one essence, they may be spoken of interchangeably. Furthermore, since the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body all perceive through contact, they can all be termed "awakening.
The final phrase speaks of "perfect penetration" (*yuantong*), taking the nature of awakening as its essence.
If one were to contemplate based on fragrance, that awakening would lack constancy; how then could one rely upon it to achieve attainment?
Fourth, he examines the King of Medicines (Bhaiṣajyarāja) regarding the realm of taste:
"The nature of taste is not inherently existent; it exists only when there is something to be tasted. Since this perception is not constant or uniform, how can one attain perfect penetration?"
That "the nature of taste is not original" means that the essential substance of the objective field of taste does not exist inherently from the beginning.
That "it exists only when there is tasting" means that since it is not original, it must necessarily depend upon the time of contact with the object of taste before it can exist.
Thus, it exists only when there is contact and is absent when there is no contact; this shows that the objective field of taste is first of all not constant or uniform. [End of] Section.
Since the flavors mentioned in these two lines cannot remain constant, how much less can the nature of perception within the sense organs naturally remain eternally uniform?
How could one attain perfect penetration by relying upon them? It is clear that this is impossible.
Fifth, Bhadrapāla selects the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*).

Touch is clarified by that which is touched; there is nothing it does not clearly perceive. Yet, its nature as either union or separation is not fixed. How can one attain perfect penetration through this?

In the first phrase, the character "touch" (chù) above refers to the object-field of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), namely the characteristics of cold, warmth, roughness, smoothness, resistance, compliance, and so forth.
The character "touch" below refers to the object-field of form (*rūpa*, specifically the tangible); this means the physical substance that is touched and contacted by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

The underlying intention is that the characteristics of cold, warmth, roughness, smoothness, resistance, compliance, and so forth can only be manifested through the physical substance that is touched and contacted by the body-faculty.
[The text] manifests. The second line states that if there were no contact, one would be unable to discern the characteristics of the sense-object of touch;
therefore, it is the same as the two preceding objects in being known through conjunction. The final two lines state that the beginner values single-mindedness.
Now, since this sense-object of touch exists only when in conjunction and is absent when separated, its essential nature is not even fixed.
By depending on what can one attain perfect penetration? Sixth, Kāśyapa selects the dust of dharmas.
Dharmas are called internal dust; relying on dust necessarily implies an object. Since subject and object do not pervade all things, how can perfect penetration be attained?
Zhengmo says: "The dharma-object (dharmāyatana) is not the substantial reality of the five external sense-objects, but rather the shadow of the five sense-objects as they pass away.

It is perceived solely by the mental consciousness and belongs to the category of 'solitary shadows' (duoying-jing); therefore, it is called an 'internal object. Regarding the phrase 'relying on the object,' this does not follow the interpretation of Zhengmo.

According to Zhengmo, when the mental consciousness arises to perceive an object, focusing exclusively on a single realm is what is meant by 'relying on the object' and having something to depend upon."
Now, regarding that which relies on the "dust" (viṣaya): since it belongs to the internal dust, it must rely upon the external dust as it falls away.

Since it relies upon the external dust as it falls away, there must be a reflection of that which has fallen away for it to be termed "internal dust. Thus, the external dust is the agent of falling away, while the internal dust is the object of falling away.
However, since the external dust consists of five [sensory objects], its falling away necessarily occurs with a sequence of priority and posteriority. The internal...

The objects of the senses (*viṣaya*) also consist of five shadows; they are not without their respective distinctions of "A" and "B. Thus, both the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived clearly possess these five characteristics;
they do not interpenetrate or mutually pervade one another. Now, since the objects themselves are not perfect, how could they enable one to attain perfect penetration?

They should therefore be excluded. Having finished the exclusion of the six objects, the second part is the exclusion of the five faculties (since the ear faculty is to be selected from among them, they are now excluded).
(Only five within the middle: Five. First, distinguishing the eye-faculty of Nanda; second, distinguishing the nose-faculty of Cūḍapanthaka; third, distinguishing the tongue-faculty of Gavāmpati;
fourth, distinguishing the body-faculty of Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja; fifth, distinguishing the mind-faculty of Ākāśagarbha. First.
Although the seeing-nature is transparently clear, it is bright before one but not behind; the four directions are deficient by half. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
The first phrase, "even granted that it is transparently clear," means even granting that its illumination of objects is distinct, transparent, and unmixed.
The following two phrases refute the possibility of partial deficiency. According to the preceding [explanation]:
"the front is entirely bright" refers generally to the direct front and the two adjacent corners; "the back is entirely dark" refers generally to the direct rear and the two adjacent corners.
This can be understood from the word "entirely" (*quan*). Now, when it says "bright in the front," it refers exclusively to the direct front.
Regarding the regional dialects: since they are not clearly defined, hereafter we shall rely solely on the standard dialect, as neither contains complete characters.

The four intermediate directions (*vidiś*) refer to the four corners; while the two corners of the front side can be clearly identified, the two corners of the rear side cannot, which is why it is said that "one half is deficient.
As for the failure to mention the left and right sides, the verse is too concise to accommodate them, but they may be understood through oral explanation.

Just as clouds cannot illuminate what lies behind them once they have cleared, and since the four intermediate directions are also deficient by half, even if one were to look around to the left and right and calculate the total merit, it would amount to only two-thirds. Since one part is lacking, it is not complete or pervasive;
therefore, he uses the phrase "how could" to exclude it. Second, he excludes the olfactory faculty of Cūḍapanthaka.

The inhalation and exhalation of the breath are pervasive; yet, in the present state, there is no mingling of these airs. They remain fragmented and do not interpenetrate. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
"Nose-breath" refers to the air within the nostrils. "Pervasive in inhalation and exhalation" means that when exhaling to expel the old, it penetrates outward;
when inhaling to scent the new, it penetrates inward. This is as previously stated: "there is outflow and there is inflow. However...
Exhalation belongs to the past; inhalation belongs to the future. The brief moment when inhalation and exhalation pause is called the present.
That which has no "intermingling breath" (mixture of breaths) possesses no continuity of breath. Since there is no continuity of breath, there is no merit.
This is as previously stated: it is like being missing the central intersection. According to this, the three parts of the analysis of merit lack one part;

thus, the meaning of "round" (perfect) is already lost. Furthermore, regarding the branches of entry and exit, which are currently severed and separated such that the three time-periods do not interpenetrate, the meaning of "pervasive" is also lost.
How then can one attain perfect penetration through this? It is clearly understood that this is not easily achieved.
[The Buddha] said: "Third, to exclude the tongue faculty of Kauṇḍinya:
The tongue is not an entrance by itself; it gives rise to cognition because of flavors. When flavors cease, cognition has no existence. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"
The first sentence states that the tongue does not enter into the taste; there is no basis for the arising of cognition.

The second sentence states that it must depend on the object of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*) for the nature of cognizance to arise. The third sentence states that when the taste has vanished, the nature of cognizance remains as before and is no longer present.
This is identical to the previous case where cognition is not constant; thus, it is also examined by means of the phrase "how could" (*kathaṃ*). (Question: As for the ear faculty...)

[Objection: You admit that *śānti* (tranquility) is permanent; why then do you not admit that the tongue-faculty perceives a bland taste when separated from [other] flavors? [Response: Because *śānti* is not sound (*śabda*), it can still be heard even when separated from sound. Blandness (*mṛdu*), however, is fundamentally a flavor (*rasa*); therefore, when separated from flavor, there is absolutely nothing to be tasted.
This is the difference between these two regarding whether their nature is permanent or impermanent. Fourth, the exclusion of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) of Piṅgala.
The body and its objects of touch are likewise each distinct from the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment; their boundaries do not merge. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?

"Objects of touch" refers here to the sense-object of touch. As stated previously, "touch is clarified by the object of touch," and there is no aspect of touch that is not clarified; now, the same applies to the body-faculty.
Therefore, it is said to be "the same as the objects of touch," meaning that the enlightened nature of the body also arises in dependence upon the objects of touch.
The characteristics of things emerge and become manifest. If there were nothing to be contacted, they could not be brought to manifestation.
Mañjuśrī’s subtle eloquence uses concise words to provide an illustration. In the second line, the word "each" (ge) generally refers to both the exemplar and the exemplified;

it directly excludes that which is not the perfect penetration of *vitarka* (initial inquiry) and *vicāra* (subsequent investigation). [Initial mind arising in cultivation is called *vitarka*; subsequent mind corresponding thereto is called *vicāra*]. Therefore, it says "not. This is the section on the limits of measurement.

The fifth selection excludes the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) by means of the "dust-transcending" principle. This means that this body, when in contact with objects, exists; when separated from them, it does not. Its nature is therefore indeterminate.

It cannot be in profound accord or harmonious union with the boundless and measureless limits of that perfect, wondrous essence. Since this principle renders it subject to exclusion, the concluding phrase may be understood as the summary of this selection.
The fifth selection thus excludes the mental faculty by means of the "dust-transcending" principle.
"Knowing the faculty of the mind is a confused thought; even with profound clarity, one ultimately has no vision. If thoughts and perceptions cannot be shed, how can one attain perfect penetration?

'The faculty of knowing' refers to the faculty capable of cognition, which is the mental faculty (*manas*). This mental faculty is precisely the *manas-vijñāna* (the seventh consciousness), which constantly and critically deliberates.

Because it is confused with the discursive thoughts of the *mano-vijñāna* (the sixth consciousness), and because its coarse mind is difficult to discern, it is called 'confused. Even with profound clarity..."
Regarding "that which cannot be seen": this refers to that which one relies upon for cultivation, yet despite seeking its clarity and lucidity, it can ultimately never be seen.
If even such false thoughts and deliberations cannot be escaped, how could one attain perfect penetration? This must not fail to be examined.
Having finished the examination of the five sense organs, third is the examination of the six consciousnesses. First, the examination of Śāriputra.
1. Eye-consciousness; 2. Distinguishing from Samantabhadra’s ear-consciousness; 3. Distinguishing from Sundara’s nose-consciousness; 4. Distinguishing from Pūrṇa’s tongue-consciousness;
5. Distinguishing from Upāli’s body-consciousness; 6. Distinguishing from Maudgalyāyana’s mind-consciousness. First.

"Consciousness and seeing are mixed with the three harmonies; when their source is scrutinized, they are called 'without marks. Since their own essence has no fixed nature from the outset, how can one attain perfect penetration?

Regarding 'consciousness and seeing': eye-consciousness perceives objects according to thought, being coarse and superficial. It lacks extensive deliberation and is roughly similar to the faculty (the root) in its perception of objects;

therefore, there is no impediment to calling it 'seeing. Regarding 'mixed with the three harmonies': this refers to the internal reliance on the faculties and the nature of the faculties, and externally..."
It relies upon the dust of form; internal and external factors intermingle, and because it arises through the conjunction of these three conditions, one must interrogate its origin.
To "interrogate its origin" means to exhaustively investigate its source among those three conditions. When one investigates its origin, it is found to be entirely absent from all three locations:
first, it does not arise from the sense organ, for the organ alone, in the absence of the object, cannot produce it by itself. Second, it does not arise from the dust of form... [the dust of form].
Ignorance is not the cause of consciousness. Third, it does not arise from the nature (*prakṛti*), because the nature is tranquil while consciousness is active;

they are not of a similar kind. Since it cannot be found in these three locations, it is empty and false, lacking reality; therefore, it is called "non-characteristic" (*alakṣaṇa*). Its own essence is the very essence of consciousness.
It appears to exist when conditions combine, yet when its root is investigated, it is truly non-existent. Thus, for now, there is no fixed reality upon which to rely.
Because such cultivation ultimately yields no real fruit, the final verse asks how to distinguish it:

"The ear-consciousness of Samantabhadra—hearing with the mind penetrates the ten directions; this arises from the power of great causal roots. Those with their initial resolve cannot enter it; how can they attain perfect penetration?"

The first phrase means that the consciousness-mind accords with its true nature (*dharmatā*). Being identical in nature, it hears perfectly; thus, it can penetrate through the ten directions with sovereign non-obstruction.
"Born from the power of great causes" means that one is born as a result of what has been induced by a Bodhisattva’s cultivation of vast vows and practices over many kalpas.
The cultivation of such dharma-gates must be undertaken by Bodhisattvas of the profound stages; those at the initial stage [cannot].
Because my cultivation was shallow and my aspiration insufficient, I was unable to enter. The final line concludes the selection; this may be understood.
Third, the selection of Sunda’s nose-consciousness:

"The mental activity of the nose is fundamentally a provisional device, intended only to cause the mind to abide. Once abiding is achieved, the mind has found its dwelling place. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?"

Regarding "contemplation of the nose": it is like observing the tip of the nose as white to evoke the nasal consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*), thereby mentally visualizing the breath within the nostrils.
As for "the provisional mechanism," this refers to the fact that the original Buddhist contemplation was established as a remedial measure against Nanda’s distracted mind;

it is a provisional application of a skillful means, for the nasal consciousness itself does not inherently possess such a functional capacity. The next two phrases state that what is called the "provisional mechanism" is simply...
To gather his scattered mind and cause it to abide in a single object: if he were to abide in a single object, then that single object would become the locus where the mind dwells;
this would mean the mind has a fixed location. The final sentence states that if the mind has a fixed location, it is not universally pervasive (*aviprakṛṣṭa*);
how then could it attain [liberation]? Fourth, this distinguishes Pūrṇa’s tongue-consciousness.

"Explaining the Dharma by manipulating sounds and characters—how could one who has already attained awakening through this method achieve perfect penetration? Names and phrases are not themselves untainted;

how then can they lead to the attainment of perfect penetration? The first two lines state that the tongue-consciousness explaining the Dharma merely involves playing with sounds and characters, which is inconsistent with attaining great awakening.
Yet, it was through this very means that Pūrṇa attained great awakening and became an Arhat.
This person is one who, having long since perfected eloquence through the cultivation of past kalpas, uniquely excels in preaching the Dharma;

it is simply because the present season has arrived and the necessary conditions have converged that such a thing is possible. The latter two phrases state that if a beginner relies on the preaching of the Dharma, the Dharma being preached consists merely of names and phrases, which still belong to conditioned non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and are not [unconditioned].
To practice the untainted dharmas while being at odds with perfect penetration—how could one possibly attain them?
Fifth, he rejects the body-consciousness of Upāli:

"Observing precepts and transgressions merely restrain the body; they do not restrain that which is beyond the body. Since this [body-consciousness] does not originally pervade all things, how can it achieve perfect penetration?"

"Observing and transgressing" refers to the non-arising of physical consciousness regarding the acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. It means to maintain the precepts by not allowing oneself to commit the offenses of violating them.
At the initial stage, one relies on this [precept] merely to restrain the body; it does not go beyond the mere holding of the body in stillness.
If, however, [an action] is not subsumed under the body— such as false speech, frivolous talk, harsh speech, or double-tongued speech—
then consciousness has nothing from which it may be bound. Thus we know that even the bodily consciousness and its grasping do not pervade the two karmas of speech and mind,
let alone the pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) of a Bodhisattva, including the three thousand majestic deportments and eighty thousand subtle practices of all dharmas.
"Gate. Because it is naturally not all-pervasive, it is said to be "originally non-existent," meaning that it is fundamentally not pervasive.

Since it is not pervasive, it is not perfect; therefore, this phrase is employed to exclude it. (Master Wuxing asked: "Upāli adhered to the sequence of body and mind, both of which he mastered thoroughly.

Why does the present text speak only of 'restraining the body'? The commentary answers: "This is spoken from the perspective of the beginner. Generally, when a beginner observes the precepts, they first sever lust, killing, stealing, and lying. While lying may still be deferred, those matters most urgently requiring restraint are exclusively lust, killing, and stealing.")

[The text continues: ...but because it is truly difficult to control the mind, one first uses body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) to restrain the body. If body-consciousness does not give rise to perverse perceptions and remains free from evil contacts, then naturally there will be no further acts of killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct; this is what is meant by "restraining the body.

As for when the mind moves toward the mechanisms of lust, killing, or stealing, or when the mouth utters false speech, frivolous talk, and so forth—it is not that one does not wish to sever them, but it is not possible for body-consciousness alone to maintain such restraint. Not everyone is as capable as Upāli; how could they rely on this [method] to enter the Perfect [Samādhi]?
(Master Yue’s response was already noted by Zhengmo as being confused and is therefore not recorded). Sixth, distinguishing Maudgalyāyana’s mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

"Supernatural powers originate from past causes; what connection have they to the discrimination of dharmas? If mindfulness depends on conditions rather than being detached from objects, how can one attain perfect penetration?

The first line states that although Maudgalyāyana’s supernatural powers were manifested through the revolving of consciousness and the restoration of the mind’s luminosity, when one investigates their profound origin, they are the result of long-cultivated past causes.
Consider his initial encounter with the Buddha, when his hair and beard fell away of their own accord and the *kāṣāya* robe...
By observing the robes upon his body and feet, one knows there must be a cause for this.

The next phrase states that since it arises from past causes, it has no connection whatsoever with the discriminative mental consciousness arising upon present objective phenomena (*dharmas*); therefore, it asks:

"How could it concern the discrimination of phenomena? The phrase regarding "recollection as an object" means that discrimination regarding phenomena belongs to deluded recollection and clinging; although...
According to the dharma-object (dharmālambana), it truly relies upon external things; if one were separated from external things, then even the dharma would not exist, let alone consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that it is not separate from things. The final phrase states that since it is not separate from things, it is constrained by those things.
How can one attain perfect penetration? Having finished the examination of the six consciousnesses, there follows the fourth section:

the examination of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*). 1. Examination of Kṣitigarbha (Earth) regarding the earth element. 2. Examination of Candraprabha (Moonlight) regarding the water element. 3. Examination of Aghaniṣṭha (Ucchuṣma) regarding the fire element. 4.

Examination of Vairocana (Lapis Lazuli) regarding the wind element. 5. Examination of Gaganagañja (Space Treasury) regarding the space element. 6. Examination of Maitreya regarding the consciousness element. 7. Examination of Śrī-Prabhāsa (Potaraka).
The faculty of earth is primary.

If one contemplates it through its nature as earth, it is solid and obstructive rather than penetrative; it is conditioned and not of the nature of the noble ones. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates through the nature of earth, then because the nature of earth is solid and obstructive, it cannot be penetrated by the initial mind. This is so.
"One must practice for a long time before attaining penetration; this distinguishes the essence from analytical contemplation (*vibhāvanā*).

If one takes 'leveling the ground' as one's achievement, then leveling the ground is a conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*) and does not accord with the nature of the Sage. It is only by leveling the mind that one accords [with it]; this distinguishes the practice of leveling the ground."
According to this, both contemplation and practice fail to achieve the meaning of perfection; how, then, could one attain perfect penetration?
Second, regarding the selection of Moonlight’s water-element:
if one contemplates through the nature of water, then thoughts and perceptions are not real, and suchness is neither observation nor reflection; how, then, could one attain perfect penetration?

If one contemplates by way of the nature of water: as when the youth Candraprabha first contemplated that the nature of water within his own body was not lacking, and subsequently contemplated that it was no different from the ocean of fragrant waters; thus, all such things are objects formed through mental ideation.
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, there is only the body and no water—sufficient to know that these are not real. If one must certainly seek to accord with reality:

The principle of suchness must await the realization of water merging with space to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*); it cannot be attained through the initial mind’s discursive observation (*vitarka-vicāra*).

This is because the principle of suchness is free from thought and immovable; were there even a single movement of discursive observation, the appearance of motion would manifest and suchness would become obscured.
The meaning of the final phrase can be understood as a distinction. Third, the exclusion of Ucchuṣma and the fire element.
If one contemplates by way of the nature of fire, one becomes weary of existence as being non-real and seeks to depart from it; this is not a skillful means for a beginner.

How, then, could one attain perfect penetration? If one contemplates by way of the nature of fire—as in the case of Acala—this is because he perceived the appearance of fire due to his weariness with desire.
Were there no mind of weariness with desire, the appearance of fire would simply not exist. Thus, one knows that this method of contemplating fire [is not the universal path].
This is merely a temporary remedy for those with excessive lust and does not constitute the true ability to transcend desire.
However, since the beginner's mind cannot fully accommodate those whose afflictions are so rampant, how could it necessarily rely on this as a skillful means?
Even if one relies on this beginner's mind, it is not a true transcendence; how, then, could one attain the Perfect Way? One must truly believe that it is no easy matter.
Fourth, the selection of the wind-element of lapis lazuli:
If one contemplates the nature of wind, movement and stillness are not without their opposites; yet opposites are not the Unsurpassed Awakening. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates the nature of wind as being like the light of lapis lazuli, first one observes that all movements are non-dual and without distinction.
Next, one observes that they come from nowhere and go nowhere; thus, one enters stillness through movement.

Because entering stillness through movement constitutes a contemplation based on mutual dependence, it is not without a counterpart. Since it is not without a counterpart, it is inherently with a counterpart.
If phenomena were established through the mutual opposition of subject and object, how could they be called the essence of unsurpassed enlightenment? They would naturally not be so.

Since they are not the essence of enlightenment, cause and effect would be dissimilar; yet, because perfect penetration is itself the essence of enlightenment, how can the preceding statement be taken as a valid standard?
Fifth, distinguishing it from the emptiness of the treasury and the great element of space:

If one contemplates with the nature of emptiness, that which is dull and dark was originally not awakening. Since the absence of awakening differs from Bodhi, how could one attain perfect penetration?
Regarding those who contemplate through emptiness: they observe that the four great elements are without support, like the treasury of space;
they see that the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts are non-dual with space. However, space has the characteristics of darkness, dullness, and rigidity;
its own essence is fundamentally not awareness. That which is not awareness is the absence of awareness. Since it lacks cognitive awareness, it differs from bodhi. By means of Brahma...
"Bodhi" (菩提) is translated here as "the path of awakening" (覺道). Since this differs from [the conventional sense of] bodhi, it is difficult to enter through perfect penetration.
Therefore, [the text] selects [a specific faculty] to explain how one can attain it. Sixth, Maitreya’s selection of the element of consciousness (識大).

If one contemplates by means of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), one observes that consciousness is not permanent; yet to fix the mind upon it is merely false and delusive—how, then, could one attain perfect penetration?

If one contemplates by means of the nature of consciousness, it is like Maitreya Bodhisattva’s profound contemplation that the ten directions are *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), taking the nature of consciousness as the causal mind.
However, the consciousness that is the object of observation arises and ceases without ceasing; its own substance is fundamentally non-existent from the outset.

Although it is eternally abiding, if one maintains the mind to contemplate it, it is like steaming sand to make rice; this belongs to the realm of delusion. Therefore, he distinguishes it by asking, "How can it be obtained?
This is the seventh distinction concerning the faculty of Great Power of Avalokiteśvara.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; the nature of mindfulness is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing. Since cause and effect now yield such disparate results, how can one attain perfect penetration?
All movement and activity belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); therefore, they are called "all formations.

As soon as anything involves flux and transition, it is not permanent; therefore, they are called "impermanent. Furthermore, the nature of mindfulness also belongs to the flux of the aggregate of formations and is likewise impermanent. Therefore—
This refers to the fundamental arising and ceasing. To take this as the cause and thereby give rise to the vision of the Buddha is not necessarily impossible.

However, if one wishes to realize perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*) and achieve the fruit of permanence, then the perceiving subject and the perceived object are inherently and fundamentally distinct.

Therefore, the final phrase serves to exclude [the ear-faculty]. (Question: Śrī-Prabhāvatī gathers all six faculties and maintains pure mindfulness in succession; since the ear-faculty is included therein, why is it also excluded? Answer: Although Śrī-Prabhāvatī gathers all six faculties...)

However, one does not take the sense-faculties (*indriya*) as the entrance gate. Furthermore, once one has taken up the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth, one has already fallen into the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations); therefore, [these methods] are excluded. (The *Zhengmo* states: "In general discussion, the profound realization of the twenty-four sages must equal that of Avalokiteśvara.

Yet, when tracing their respective entrances, there are briefly four reasons why they should be excluded: first, they do not accord with the suitability of the region; second, they are not convenient for beginners; third, they require separate auxiliary supports; and fourth, they are not the standard mode of cultivation. By contrast, this reveals that the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) accords with the suitability of the region.")

This is the beginning of the initial stage. It does not require external resources and can be practiced at all times (as will be seen in the subsequent verse). Having concluded the general exclusion of other methods, [the text now] specifically selects the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) for four reasons:
first, it is precisely suited to the conditions of this region; second, it does not require external resources; third, it can be practiced and studied constantly;
and fourth, it is most convenient for beginners. Regarding the first three points: first, it is specifically suited to the conditions of this region; second, it is praised...
This reveals the Dharma for people. Third, it refutes deluded cultivation based on the teachings. First:
"I now address the World-Honored One: when the Buddha appeared in the Sahā world, the true essence of the teaching in this region was pure within hearing and sound."
To truly attain samādhi, one must enter through hearing.

Having already excluded other gateways, it is appropriate to determine the fundamental basis; thus, he again addressed the World-Honored One. To determine the fundamental basis, one must consider what is suitable for the specific situation;
therefore, he first stated that a Buddha appears in Sahā. According to the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, there may even be buddha-fields where...
They perform the Buddha-work through the light of the Buddha. In some buddha-fields, they perform the Buddha-work through the Bodhi tree of the Buddha;

even up to performing it through circular groves and terraced pavilions, or through the shadows and echoes of empty space, or through sounds and speech, or through silence and the absence of discourse—each according to what is appropriate for that region, as the substance of the teaching differs. Now, regarding this...

Because it is spoken for the sake of the Sahā world, it is called "the teaching-body of this region. It is called "true" because these three faculties universally benefit all and are suitable for the entire realm;
since those [teachings] that correspond only to a single capacity are excluded and not called "true," they are thus designated as such.
Regarding "purity residing in sound and hearing": among the three realities, if even one is incomplete, it is not pure. This is because there are obstructions and...
From the perspective of the phenomenal realm (*loka*), it is turbid and not clear; because it possesses arising and ceasing, it is defiled and not pure.
Based on this, the two characters "sound" (*yin*) and "hearing" (*wen*) refer to hearing as a corresponding sound, for a mere sound without hearing is not the true essence of the teaching.
Therefore, as previously stated by Dignāga, the sound-object (*śabda-viṣaya*) has already been excluded.

Here, we wish to select those who first practice concentration through the gate of hearing—those who truly enter by way of hearing—and we specifically designate the faculty of the ear alone as the fundamental root for this Sahā world.

This is because if one abandons this, *samādhi* is difficult to achieve. [Question: In the section concerning the essence of the teaching (*deśanā-dharma*) that expresses [truth], you initially selected sound, name, phrase, and sentence. Why do you now exclusively select the nature of hearing while omitting the actual sound? Is it not [the case that...]?

Did Qingliang not yet understand the essential purport of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*? In response: Qingliang established ten sections for the essence of the teaching, in which the preceding are inferior and the succeeding are superior; since vocal sound was already listed at the very beginning, it was already evident that it is not the true reality. Guifeng subsequently condensed these into four sections.

Furthermore, while sounds, names, phrases, and syllables are merely one aspect within the gate of following appearances (*anuvyañjana*), since they are said to follow appearances, they are known to be provisional designations (*prajñapti*) within an expedient teaching that resembles the ultimate. Returning to the true nature (*dharmatā*), the ultimate reality must be unimpeded; this constitutes the final, true essence of the teaching.

Now, hearing that the three types of reality are inherently complete (*prakṛti-sampad*) is precisely this unimpeded state. Thus, what Mañjuśrī selected accords perfectly with the views of Qingliang and Guifeng, like two halves of a tally fitting together. Therefore, there is no contradiction in selecting [this teaching] exclusively. [The section on] "Resolving the Appropriateness" is concluded. Second, praising the person and manifesting the Dharma, which has two parts:
first, praising the excellence of the person; second, manifesting the truth of the Dharma. First, praising the excellence of the person. Second, manifesting the truth of the Dharma.

Truly so. First, you who have left suffering behind and attained liberation—how excellent, O Avalokiteśvara! Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you enter Buddha-lands as many as motes of dust;
having attained the power of great mastery, you bestow fearlessness upon sentient beings. O Wondrous Sound Avalokiteśvara, your Brahma-voice is like the tide of the ocean.
Sound. The Savior brings all to peace; by transcending the world, one attains eternal abiding.
First, self-benefit is perfected: having untied the six knots and transcended the three voids and two deaths, one is no longer bound; thus it is called "freedom from suffering."
Because they transcend the mundane world and possess all manner of supramundane unimpededness, they are said to have "attained liberation.

This truly has two meanings. First, it signifies "sincerity" (*śraddhā*); it is a term used to indicate reality. For example, when one says, "Having left suffering behind, one attains deliverance"—truly, this is not in vain—it refers only to Avalokiteśvara.
Second, it signifies "excellent" (*kuśala*); it is a word of praise. For example, when one says, "Excellent, O Avalokiteśvara! its—
The benefit for oneself is already such as this. Regarding the subsequent section on the excellence of benefiting others:

the *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) commentary states that "kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" indicates that time is extremely long, thereby manifesting permanence; "lands as numerous as motes of dust" indicates that space is extremely vast.
This reveals pervasiveness. "Attaining great mastery" (mahāvaśitā) encompasses, in meaning, both the thirty-two manifestations and the foremost inconceivable virtue.

This is because following the thirty-two manifestations, there is the phrase "accomplishment through the mastery of effortless, wondrous power," and following the foremost inconceivable virtue, there is the statement "attaining great mastery in protecting and rescuing sentient beings. This constitutes the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*).
The meaning of "arising" subsumes the fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) and the second inconceivable quality. This is because following the fourteen fearlessnesses, there is the statement:
"By the power of bestowing fearlessness, he is fully equipped with the merit to benefit sentient beings. And following the second inconceivable quality, there is the statement:
"He is able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings. These two phrases regarding the "wondrous voice" are sufficient to complete the aforementioned thirty [qualities].
In the second [response] and the two preceding inconceivable [responses], there is the sound of preaching the Dharma and reciting mantras.

In the aforementioned passage concerning entry into lands as numerous as motes of dust, while there appears to be the sense of manifesting bodies and forms, there is nonetheless no mention of the sound of preaching the Dharma or reciting mantras.

Now, this [text] is supplemented to manifest the teachings on the body and to present them together. As for "Wondrous Sound" (Miaoyin): it is a mantra of identical essence (*tongti*), wherein a single sound contains all wonders.
As for "Avalokiteśvara" (Guanshizizai): it is a mantra of distinct essence (*yiti*), wherein one contemplates the world and manifests diverse explanations.

Through the thirty-two transformations, he breaks through the obstacles of others while manifesting the Brahma-voice; he speaks as required, never missing the proper time, and thus accords with reality.
The ocean tide. The fourteen fearlessnesses are solely responses to the hidden; therefore, their sounds are not described.

According to the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Pumen pin*), there are further superior worldly sounds, which collectively manifest that the four aforementioned sounds cannot match the World-Hearer (*Lokanātha*).

Here, the specific is cited to briefly represent the general. The two phrases beginning with "saving the world" encompass the latter two inconceivable virtues, as worldly people are stingy [with their suffering].
The affliction of greed for accumulation leads to the anxiety of gain and loss; even when one’s wife and children live long lives, if their desires are not fulfilled, it results in total unease.
Yet, within the third inconceivable power, stinginess is destroyed and requests are granted;

within the fourth inconceivable power, all that is sought is fulfilled, such that the world is entirely saved and brought to peace. This extends to the point where it says: "Seeking great nirvāṇa, one attains great nirvāṇa."
"Transcending the world, one attains eternal abiding. These are all the internal meanings of Avalokiteśvara’s own self-exposition, which Mañjuśrī has recounted in detail.

This is intended to cause those seeking perfect penetration to look up to and emulate this person. Having concluded the praise of the person's excellence, [the text proceeds to] secondly, reveal the reality of the Dharma in three parts:
first, the reality of perfection; second, the true jewel of penetration; third, the reality of permanence.
Truly so. First: I now declare to the Tathāgata what was spoken by Avalokiteśvara. For example, suppose a person is dwelling in stillness, and drums are struck simultaneously in all ten directions;
they hear them at once from all ten locations. This is the perfection of true reality.
"I" refers to Mañjuśrī himself speaking. "Addressing the Tathāgata" is intended to manifest the quest for the ultimate truth and to seek the Buddha’s certification.

The subsequent phrase, "desiring to seek the true root, it is exactly as Avalokiteśvara has said," indicates that Mañjuśrī first granted a general assent rather than referring to the following verses.
This is because what is set forth in the following verses does not constitute the internal meaning of Avalokiteśvara's own statement.

Therefore, it is like a single verse. This refers to Mañjuśrī taking up the meaning from within the previously mentioned merit of the ear-faculty—namely, that the ear listens to the ten directions without omission—to reveal the meaning of the perfect reality (*pariniṣpanna*).

He provisionally borrows the single instance of hearing a drum to illustrate the hearing of all sounds; hence, he says "it is like. The term "one who dwells in stillness" excludes times of clamor, for [in such] clamor...
At that time, although hearing is always pervasive, one does not realize it oneself. The *Zhengmai* (Correct Pulse) says:
"Beating drums in the ten directions simultaneously" means striking them all at once; "hearing in ten places at once" means there is no sequence in the hearing.
The final phrase establishes, based on this, that it is indeed pervasive (*yuan*); furthermore, it is true pervasiveness, real pervasiveness, and not a false claim of pervasiveness.
Because they can be compared [to one another]. Second, both penetrate the reality.

The eyes do not perceive what is beyond the obstruction; the mouth and nose are likewise so. The body knows through contact; thus one understands that mental thoughts are disordered and without sequence.
Hearing sounds through a wall, one can perceive them both from afar and nearby. That which is not limited by the five sense organs is the penetration of reality.

First, it distinguishes that the five organs are all restricted; "pointing at the eye" refers to the visual faculty, such as when one cannot see what is beyond an obstruction, like looking through window paper.
One does not see external objects and colors; one does not see the internal organs through the skin. This is restricted rather than pervasive. The same applies to the mouth and nose:
this merely illustrates their restriction and lack of pervasiveness; it does not illustrate their inability to see what is obstructed from outside.
Therefore, Guishan stated that the two lines concerning the mouth and nose are inverted. If one were to take the latter line as the former...

The meaning follows the principle of conformity. Since these three are all cognitions within the center [of the body], they are termed "restricted" (*jù*) because they are isolated and do not communicate with one another.
Furthermore, the character "mouth" (*kǒu*) should be "tongue" (*shé*); the term "mouth" is used as a substitute for "tongue" because the tongue is located within the mouth.

"Mind" (*xīn*) refers to the faculty of thought (*manas*), which is called "mindfulness" (*niàn*) because its constant and deliberative reflection is roughly similar to the functioning of consciousness (*vijñāna*). As stated previously: "Cognition..."
This refers to the confusion of the sense-faculties. That which is chaotic and lacks order is being entangled by discursive thought (*vitarka*).

One merely perceives arising, abiding, change, and cessation in a state of total disorder, without any beginning or end. This is as previously stated: "Even in profound clarity, there is ultimately nothing to be seen.

If this is the case, one cannot even escape from such conceptualization; how then could one attain penetration? Below the section on "the partitioned wall," the ear-faculty is revealed as being uniquely superior.
Regarding "penetration": one who listens to sounds through a partitioned wall is like someone hearing the sound of jade pendants across a wall; this demonstrates that obstructions cannot confine it.
That which can be heard both near and far—whether moving, it seems close at hand, or still, it is boundless—demonstrates that separation can also allow for penetration.
Since obstructions cannot confine it, the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) has no comparison; since separation can also allow for penetration, [this applies to] the other three faculties.
It has no peer. Furthermore, it is quiescent, boundless, and not of the same nature as the sense-faculties; its essence is profoundly lucid and free from seeing.
Therefore, it is not on the same level as the five faculties. Based on this, the five faculties are all restricted, whereas the ear alone is pervasive.
This pervasiveness may be called truly and substantially real. Third, it is eternally true and real.

The nature of sound fluctuates between movement and stillness; within hearing, it may be present or absent. When there is no sound, one speaks of "no-hearing," yet this is not a true absence of the nature of hearing.
Since sound is non-existent, there is no cessation; since sound is existent, there is no arising. When both arising and ceasing are perfectly transcended, this is the eternal reality.
"Even if one is in a dream, it is not the case that non-thought does not exist. Awakening and contemplation transcend discursive thought;
body and mind cannot reach them.

This first section clarifies permanence by means of sound (this takes the meaning from the "Verification of Permanence through Striking a Bell"). Regarding the nature of sound being movement or stillness, it is as previously explained in the case of Rāhu.
When striking a bell, at the very moment of the strike, the nature of the sound vibrates. As the sound fades after a long time, one speaks of "stillness" in contrast to that vibration.

Thus, because this single nature of sound manifests in form and possesses the characteristics of movement and stillness, those who perceive within hearing as being either existent or non-existent refer to the two characteristics of movement and stillness as they circulate and alternate within the profoundly tranquil essence of the nature of hearing. When it moves...
When there is clearly audible sound, it is "existence"; when it is still and silent with no sound, it is "non-existence. Worldly people are deluded and do not understand this principle;
thus, at the moment of silence, they label it "no-hearing. They fail to realize that during the time of silence, one perceives even more clearly that the nature of hearing is boundless and limitless.
Therefore, it is said that it is not the case that the nature of hearing truly becomes non-existent when there is no sound. Sound is absent.
The second statement means that as explained above, when sound is absent, the nature of hearing is already non-existent and thus has no cessation;

by this analogy, one knows that when sound is present, the nature of hearing likewise does not undergo birth. Thus, one knows that the nature of hearing is profoundly still, remaining as it is whether sound exists or not, while its own essence is utterly devoid of arising and ceasing.
Since it is utterly devoid of arising and ceasing, these two aspects are perfectly integrated.
"Detached. This distinguishes it from being described as "permanent" in contrast to what is severed; because [otherwise] it would be deemed empty or false, it is called "permanently real.

○ "Even if," etc., reveals permanence through the dream (this is an excerpt from the section on using dreams to verify permanence), stating that worldly people do not know that the nature of hearing is eternally abiding.

One might think that the realm of dreams is manifested solely by the solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and that since there is no thought at all regarding external objects therein, there should likewise be no hearing;

thus, the nature of hearing should cease. Yet, one fails to realize that even while in a dream, although there is no thought of external objects, this nature of hearing is not rendered non-existent by that absence.

When thought ceases, it simply vanishes. This is like the person in the aforementioned dream who, hearing the sound of pounding and threshing, was deluded into thinking it was the sound of bells and drums;
he then marveled at how his bell could produce the resonance of wood or stone. Based on this, even during a dream, thought still arises due to hearing.
What is called "no-thought" (wu-si) merely means that there is no object to be heard; how could it mean that hearing itself is extinguished? The final two lines anticipate a potential doubt:

[Fearing that one might follow the previous question by saying: "Let us set aside for now the argument that objects and consciousness are not permanent; however, as for the seven elements and the five faculties, are they not all entirely impermanent?

Why then do you alone grant that the nature of hearing attains the meaning of permanence? Therefore, Mañjuśrī and others offer this verse to prevent such a misconception. It states that the seven elements all belong to the realm of discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), as previously mentioned: "If one [perceives them]..."

The contemplation of the nature of the earth and so forth can be understood accordingly. Since these belong to vitarka and vicāra, they arise from the deliberations of the mental consciousness and thus fall entirely within the realm of arising and ceasing;

how could they be truly eternal? As for the awakened nature of the body and the cognitive nature of the mind, both fail to reach the state of dreaming, because that which is truly capable of awakening and knowing cannot constitute a dream. The same principle applies to the three faculties of the eyes and so forth.
This can be understood; therefore, it will not be stated again. Thus, it is clear that the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) are likewise neither truly eternal.

Generally discussing the three kinds of reality, there are briefly three analogies for their characteristics: Perfect Reality (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*) is like the bright sun in the sky, illuminating all phenomena simultaneously;

Penetrating Reality (*paratantra-tattva*) is like the waters of the four great rivers flowing from the Anavatapta Lake, universally benefiting all; and Constant Reality (*parikalpita-tattva*) is like the Great... [text ends].

Being empty and formless, it cannot be destroyed across the three time periods. For this reason, it can universally encompass the three faculties and accord with all realms, serving as the true essence of the teaching.
Having finished praising the person and manifesting the Dharma, [the text] now proceeds to the third section: Refuting Delusion regarding the Practice of the Teaching.

Now, in this Sahā world, the treatises on sound and language may be proclaimed and clarified. Sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; because they follow sounds, they wander through the cycle of rebirth.

Even though Ānanda possesses powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into deviant thoughts. Is it not the case that by following the place where one sinks, one must turn back the current to attain freedom from delusion?

First, it is shown that the faculty of hearing is particularly acute. Having established above that one possesses the three kinds of reality and may thus rely upon them for cultivation, it is even more evident here in this Sahā world:

since all matters, whether pertaining to principle or phenomena, are transmitted, proclaimed, and elucidated through sounds and speech, it is clear that the faculty of hearing is especially acute. [The text] now rebukes those who are deluded regarding hearing and follow after sounds. It says:
Since the faculty of hearing is particularly acute, all sentient beings should attain awakening through it.

That this is not the case for everyone is due solely to sentient beings' own delusion regarding their inherently existing true hearing; they merely follow sounds in a single flavor, flowing and turning in transmigration.
This applies not only to sentient beings: even someone like Ānanda, despite his powerful memory, could not avoid following sounds in transmigration and falling into heterodoxy.
Consider this, Ānanda; other cases may be known by extension. Regarding the final two lines, which teach the disappearance of the stream into which one enters:

it must surely be that the reason sentient beings and Ānanda have been unable to attain awakening is that they follow after the characteristics of the objects of perception (*ālambana-viṣaya*) and thus naturally sink into delusion. Since we know this must be so, one should cause those characteristics to vanish.
By returning that nature of cyclic flow to true hearing, one may gradually advance and attain the true, non-delusive nature.
This concludes the section on "Applying Oneself Appropriately. Second, "Not Requiring External Resources," part four.

First, the instruction to listen and state the title; second, pointing out faults and exhorting to practice; third, revealing the essential subtlety of the Dharma; fourth, concluding by showing what is not required.
Regarding the first: "Ānanda, listen attentively! Empowered by the Buddha's majestic strength, I shall proclaim the Vajra King, which is illusory and inconceivable."
The Mother of Buddhas’ True Samādhi:
In the first line, her name is invoked and she is exhorted, saying: "If you now truly wish to turn back the flow [of saṃsāra], you should listen attentively to my words.
In the subsequent line, it is stated that the method for turning back the flow is not easy to explain; if you truly listen attentively to me—
You should seek the Buddha’s empowerment; relying upon the Buddha’s majestic power, I shall proclaim it for you.
You, too, should conceive the thought that this is difficult to encounter. The Dharma of the Revolving Stream that I shall explain has, briefly, five names.
The first is called the Vajra Samādhi, because by means of this one cuts off delusions, such that there is no delusion left uncut. The second is called the King Samādhi, because by means of this...
First is the Samādhi of Subduing Māra, because there is no Māra that it does not subdue. Second is the Samādhi of Non-arising, because by relying on this, one realizes that arising is non-arising.

Third is the Samādhi of Illusion-like, because by relying on this practice, cultivation is itself non-cultivation. Fourth is the Samādhi of the Inconceivable, because by relying on this, the revealed principle transcends all words and thought.
Fifth is the Samādhi of the Mother of Buddhas, because by relying on this, one attains Buddhahood, and there is nothing that the Buddha cannot accomplish. Thus it is complete.
These five meanings are called the true samādhi, because it does not require the labor of seeking external supports.
Second, pointing out faults to encourage cultivation:
"You have heard all the secret gates of countless buddhas; yet, if you do not first eliminate the outflows of desire, your accumulation of learning will become a fault."
Error. ○ Regarding the phrase "Hearing and holding [the Dharma]—why does the Buddha not hear his own hearing?":
the first two lines set forth the cause. As the Buddha says in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "I and Ānanda together resolved our minds for enlightenment under the Buddha Śūnyarāja.
I have always been diligent and energetic; Ānanda has always delighted in much learning. According to this, Ānanda...
Since the time of the Buddha King of Emptiness (*Ākāśarāja*), the number of Buddhas he has encountered is equal to the atoms of dust.

At the abode of each and every Buddha, he has upheld the treasury of the Dharma through the power of his great learning. Therefore, it is said that he has heard all the secret gates of as many Buddhas as there are atoms of dust.
"Secret" has two meanings: first, it specifically refers to profound teachings; this implies that if even such profound teachings were heard, how much more so [the others].
The "shallow" refers to the manifestation that there is no dharma one has not heard. The second [category] encompasses both the shallow and the deep;

its intent is to manifest that because individuals have different understandings upon hearing the same thing, they do not know each other's insights, thereby forming a mutual secret. Next, the two phrases point out the error. The character "xian" (先) should be read as "zao" (早).

This means that Ānanda’s stage was at the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), where he had only severed the outflows of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*), while the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) remained entirely intact. Upon reaching the ultimate...

The reason they were unable to eliminate it early was simply that they had consistently accumulated much learning; by following after sensory objects and wandering in transmigration, they committed errors.
Thus one knows that their failure to understand the revolving stream was not limited to worldly dharmas, but extended even to the Buddha-dharma;
and their failure to understand the Buddha-dharma extended even to the profound secret teachings.

All these are merely following along with sensory dusts in the cycle of transmigration; they are entirely cases where the accumulation of learning has resulted in error. The final two lines offer an exhortation to practice:
since one knows that the accumulation of learning leads to error, rather than using the ears to hear and thereby maintain the teachings of all Buddhas, [one should instead apply oneself to practice].
Why not use the ear to hear and observe the nature of hearing itself? Would this not be somewhat essential and subtle? III.
Revealing the Essential Subtlety of the Dharma, in three parts: 1. The Dharma-exposition; 2. Clarification by analogy; 3. Synthesis. First [the Dharma-exposition].
Hearing is not produced spontaneously; it exists because of sound. When hearing turns back and detaches from sound, who can then be named?
Once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation. Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky.

When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the sense-faculties are removed, the dust is extinguished and awareness becomes perfectly pure. When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere; in silent illumination, one contains the void.
Emptiness. ○ Returning to observe the world, it is like a matter within a dream. Māraṅgaka is in a dream; who can detain your form?

The first [verse] explains the six liberations. (This reveals the essential meaning. The two lines beginning with "Hearing" state that the primordial one-essence-splendor is fundamentally without delusion.

As for "hearing": false hearing does not arise spontaneously; rather, it is due to the movement and stillness of sound that it adheres to the clarity [of the mind] and triggers the faculty of hearing.
By grasping at sound, the sense-organ is formed, and thus the designation "hearing" comes into being. This constitutes the three knots of the organ of movement and stillness.

The two lines beginning with "revolving the hearing" mean that if one can revolve the observation toward the nature of hearing itself, one should naturally lose the objective dust of sound; therefore—
It means that clouds are detached from sound. Once the sensory object of sound is detached, both motion and stillness vanish;

and since the faculty of hearing—the very nature capable of detaching itself—is no longer called "hearing," it is said: "Whom would one name? That is to say, whom would one name as "hearing"? There is nothing to which this could apply;
this is the resolution of the three fetters regarding the faculty of motion and stillness. The first line concerning the single faculty states that once the single faculty has already...

Returning to the root and reverting to the source, the awakened nature manifests before one; no longer following after sensory objects to form attachments, the six sense faculties all become liberation.

This is as stated later: "When objects are no longer engaged, the faculties have nothing with which to pair; flowing back to the source, they are entirely unified, and the six functions cease. (This clarifies the wondrous meaning.
Regarding the four lines beginning with "seeing and hearing," these manifest the function of the essence. They are: [seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting].
This further clarifies the superior intention to give rise to the meaning of the "purity of the ultimate luminous penetration" for those below.
It states that the original single pure brilliance gives rise to delusory seeing and hearing, which is analogous to how a pure eye gives rise to illusory cataracts.

Because of this delusory seeing and hearing, the triple world of the environment and its inhabitants arises through transformation, which is analogous to how illusory cataracts transform to produce flowers in the sky. Now...
Since the nature of hearing has already returned to its original source, the six sense organs are all liberated; thus, the deluded root of illusory cataracts is eliminated.
Since the illusory cataracts are eliminated, the "flowers in the sky" no longer exist; thus, the deluded objects of the triple world are dissolved.

With the root eliminated, the nature is free from partiality or restriction; with the objects dissolved, the essence is free from defilement. Therefore, it is said that awakening is perfect, pure, and clear. Pure.

The two final lines state that although awakening is considered "perfect" when the faculties are eradicated and "pure" when objects are eliminated, as long as there remains a subject that awakens and an object that is awakened, it is still termed a "knot.
Thus, while one may speak of perfection and purity, one has not yet reached ultimate perfection or ultimate purity.

It must reach the point where both the subject that awakens and the object that is awakened are empty, and even that emptiness is extinguished, so that quiescent extinction manifests before one; only then is it ultimate.

Purity. When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light spontaneously penetrates; this is what constitutes the ultimate perfection. It is like clouds parting to reveal the moon, whose light illuminates the ten directions.

If one considers this in conjunction with the previous teaching on "the single faculty returning to the source" and the "liberation of the six faculties," that [previous teaching] represents the ultimate of the essential, while this represents the ultimate of the wondrous.
This is what is meant by the phrase "quiescent illumination" when it says that "light penetrates. It is because of this.
Light is thus quiescent yet illuminating; it accords with the nature and encompasses the void. This is the ultimate limit of perfect penetration, and here it reaches its consummation.

Yet, when returning to descend into the world, one is unimpeded. "Yet" (què) implies a withdrawal. This means that having already attained the complete essence, one further acquires the great function;

thus, one has already equalled the fruit of Buddhahood. If, however, one does not wish to take realization as the final goal, but instead rides upon their vows to engage the world, this is called [the Bodhisattva path].

"Returning" means retreating and coming back; it refers to engaging with the world to deliver sentient beings. Having already transcended the three emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), one contemplates the world by relying on those three emptinesses.
Because it is entirely existent and entirely empty, it is said to be "like the events of a dream.

One who understands this meaning will, throughout the day, deliver sentient beings without seeing any sentient beings to be delivered. These two lines concerning Māra’s daughter (Mādrī) are intended to rouse Ānanda.

...these words. He said: "If you had been able to contemplate the world in this manner at that time, then the woman Mātaṅgī would have been clearly a person within a dream, and the incantation of the Brahmā-deva would likewise have been nothing more than words within a dream.
A person within a dream cannot unite with a form outside the dream, and words within a dream cannot draw one toward anything outside the dream."
As for this mind, even if one wished to preserve its form, who could possibly do so? Nevertheless, while the past cannot be remonstrated against, the future can still be pursued.
From now on, you should know to exert yourself. These two parables clarify this.
Just as a skillful worldly illusionist conjures various men and women, whose various faculties appear to move though they depend on a single mechanism;
when that mechanism ceases, all returns to stillness, and the illusions become devoid of intrinsic nature.

The skillful illusionist serves as a metaphor for true nature (*tathatā*), because true nature possesses the function of responding to conditions, just as a worldly illusionist possesses the art of craftsmanship.
Men and women serve as a metaphor for the *ālaya-vijñāna*, because the *ālaya* is a synthesis of the real and the false, just as worldly men and women possess the sense of union.
Since it is formed by responding to conditions, it is compared to an illusory creation.
The various sense organs (*indriya*) are metaphorically likened to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the *ālaya-vijñāna*. Bound by the six organs, they are divided into six natures;

reflected upon the six objects (*viṣaya*), they are termed the six essences (*ṣaḍ-viśuddhi*). Therefore, they are illustrated by the meaning of "movement. A single mechanical device represents the illusory man and woman;

the presence of a message within it illustrates the movement-phase within the union of the true and the false in the *ālaya*. As soon as this movement-phase arises, the seeing-division [is activated].
Suddenly it arises, just as when the illusory man or woman conjured by another stirs, all the sense-faculties are moved simultaneously.

The cessation of mental activity is likened to turning back from hearing to return to the source; returning to the source means that the *ālayavijñāna* remains unmoving, and thus it is compared to the metaphor of returning to stillness.

Once the mechanisms of activity have ceased and one has returned to quiescence, then the various sense organs that are illusory manifestations, as well as the illusory phenomena they produce, all simultaneously dissolve and subside.
Therefore it is said that "all illusions have no inherent nature. This metaphor illustrates that when the *ālayavijñāna* is unmoving, its seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) becomes tranquil;

the sense organs are eliminated and the sensory objects are dissolved, so that the essence of awakening is perfectly pure. As stated previously: "The seeing and the objects of seeing, along with the characteristics of what is conceived, are like space."
It is like flowers in the sky, which fundamentally do not exist—this is it.

Third, the union: the six sense organs are likewise. Originally, they depend on one refined spirit to divide into six harmonious unions. When one part attains rest and restoration, the functions of the other six cease to operate.

As soon as the thought arises, defilements dissolve, and one achieves perfect, bright, pure, and wondrous clarity. As for those who still have residual defilements, they remain at the stage of learning.
Ultimate clarity is the Tathāgata.
The first phrase speaks of the nature within the six sense faculties; this is also like the various faculties of an illusory person.

"Vital clarity" (jingming) is precisely the ālayavijñāna, which arises in dependence upon the Truth (tathatā). This corresponds to the metaphor above, wherein the man and woman are created by a magician.
Based on this, it is divided into six natures; because the faculties and their objects are combined, it is called "the accomplishment of the six harmonies.
These six harmonies arise from a single movement of the *ālayavijñāna*. This is analogous to how the movement of the male and female organs results from the pulling of a single string.
To achieve rest and return to the source in a single place means that hearing is turned back to its origin and the *ālayavijñāna* is unmoving. As for the analogy in this context...
The illusory man and woman have ceased their activity and returned to stillness; as the ālayavijñāna remains unmoving, its seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) likewise becomes tranquil.
Therefore it is said that the six functions are no longer established. As previously stated, "conceptual appearances are the dust, and the consciousness-emotions are the defilement.

Now that the six functions are no longer established, the appearances upon which conceptualization depends do not exist. When the appearances upon which conceptualization depends do not exist, the emotions upon which consciousness depends [likewise cease].

They are securely deposited; thus it is said that "dust and grime dissolve upon being brought to mind. Once the characteristics of the supported (the objects) have dissolved through this realization, the consciousness and perceptions that support them likewise no longer arise.
This precisely accords with the metaphor in the text where "all illusions are established as having no inherent nature.

As for the final three lines, there is no corresponding text in the metaphor; one need not force a correspondence. Perfectly luminous, pure, and wondrous is precisely the brilliant, essential awareness.

Regarding its essence: previously, it was termed "perfect" (*yuan*) simply because it is not restricted by the sense organs; here, it is further termed "luminous" (*ming*) because it is not obscured by sensory objects.

Furthermore, previously it was termed "pure" (*jing*) simply because the objects have dissolved and there is no defilement; here, it is further termed "sublime" (*miao*) because consciousness is exhausted and conceptualization is empty.
The three fetters of coarse characteristics have already been resolved, yet the three fetters of subtle characteristics have not [yet been resolved].
Because they are exhausted, they are called "remaining dust. This means that there remain subtle traces of fetters, like dust in the air;
this refers to what was previously stated in the commentary as "not yet having reached ultimate perfection and purity. Regarding these various terms:

since there is still "remaining dust," one must continue to revere study in order to advance toward the understanding of the final three fetters. "Ultimate clarity" refers to the manifestation of quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa). Purity.

Regarding the meaning of the "Ultimate Penetration of Light": although the Tathāgata did not attain this through a gradual process of cultivation and realization to reach equality with the Buddha-fruit, according to the discourse on the Dharma, there is further meaning below this concerning unimpeded engagement in the world, which was spoken specifically to inspire Ānanda.
Since these points are already contained within the preceding synthesis, there is no need for further prolixity. This concludes the manifestation of the subtle and wondrous essentials of the Dharma.
Fourth, the conclusion showing that [the other senses] do not assist:
"The great assembly and Ānanda, turn back your inverted hearing-faculty; by turning back the hearing to hear your own nature, that nature will accomplish the Unsurpassed Way.
Such is the true reality of perfect penetration."
Having already demonstrated the essential and subtle [truth], he wished to cause them to practice it; thus he called upon the great assembly and Ānanda to instruct them.

Upon encountering sound, the faculty of hearing immediately activates—this is called the "auditory mechanism. To follow objects exclusively is termed "inversion" (*viparyāsa*). "Revolve" (*xuan*) means to turn back.
This means to turn back from inversion so that the auditory mechanism no longer follows external objects. "Turning back the hearing to hear one's own nature" means that one desires to revolve...
Regarding the faculty of hearing, which is subject to perversion, one employs only the practice of "hearing back" (*fanwen*) to contemplate the nature of that which hears.

There is no need to laboriously seek other resources or alternative paths; this is what is meant by "the cause of cultivation not relying on external aids. As for "the nature accomplishing the unsurpassed Way," it means that if the nature of hearing does not manifest, so be it;
once it manifests, the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition. Thus, based on this very nature, one can achieve the unsurpassed.
The Way: since the nature itself is the Way, there is no need to rely further on other dharmas; this refers to the fact that the realization of the fruit does not depend [on them].

The final sentence provides a concluding demonstration, stating that the reason both the cultivation of causes and the realization of the fruit do not depend [on external aids] is that because the nature of hearing is both perfect and pervasive, the power of these two realities is capable of such [a result]. The reason "constant reality" is not mentioned is because of its power.

This is also discussed in the following section. It concludes that, generally speaking, one need not rely on external resources. There are three points regarding what can be constantly practiced and studied:

first, clarifying what can be constantly practiced; second, demonstrating conformity with the Buddha’s injunctions; and third, distinguishing other practices as being incorrect. First: [The original text continues here.]
This is the single path to nirvana for countless buddhas. All tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this door;
all bodhisattvas of the present now each enter its perfect clarity; and those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this very dharma.
I, too, have realized it through this—it is not only Avalokiteśvara who has done so.
