First, by severing lust, one will surely transcend birth and death; second, by not severing it, one will surely fall into the path of Māra. First:

Ānanda, what is the gathering of the mind that I call precept? If the sentient beings of the six realms throughout all worlds do not harbor lustful hearts, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
"How many? is a general interrogative phrase used to introduce the inquiry. It is said that the precepts have many aspects;
though minor points may be omitted, the major ones should still encompass all four [categories]. Since the text here mentions only "precepts," it is termed "general.

This should properly constitute a separate section, but as the text is too brief, it is not convenient to do so and is therefore appended here. The passage beginning with "If there are... specifically clarifies the meaning within the main subject matter. Worldly...

Throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions, among the six classes of beings—comprising the two paths (the three good paths and the three evil paths)—and among men and women, those whose minds are free from lust do not merely refrain from physical misconduct;
they also restrain their minds so that such thoughts do not arise.

One who acts thus does not follow the cycle of birth and death, for lustful desire is the root of birth and death. As the subsequent text states: "The craving of desire has been dried up; its roots..."
Objects do not coincide; the remaining physical substance manifest before you will no longer continue to arise. This can serve as proof of this principle.
Second, if you do not sever [the afflictions], you will inevitably fall into the path of Māra.
You have cultivated samādhi fundamentally to escape from worldly toil; if the lustful mind is not eliminated, you cannot escape from the dust of the world. Even if you possess much...
When wisdom and meditative concentration manifest before one, if one does not sever lust, one will inevitably fall into the paths of Māra. Those of the highest grade become Māra-kings;

those of the middle grade become Māra-subjects; and those of the lowest grade become Māra-maidens. These various Māras also have their own followers, each of whom claims for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

First, it clarifies not emerging from the dust. Your cultivation of the two phrases refers precisely to the time when, while practicing samādhi, your contemplation of principle (li) accords with reality;
internally you are detached from body and mind, and externally you leave behind the world. Since the afflictions of the dust have no basis to arise, it is said that they are "originally emerged."
The two phrases concerning "the lustful mind" mean that if the lustful mind is not eliminated, then worldly afflictions (*rajas*) will still remain.

Since the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*) is slightly deficient, [the affliction] arises in a mere flash and thus cannot be escaped. Furthermore, lustful desire is the foremost of all afflictions;
since the leader is present, its various categories will follow and arise. How, then, could one escape? "Even if... and so forth is a preemptive refutation of errors.

(Fearing error, the *Bian* [Discrimination] says: "The above explanation seems to refer to those whose wisdom is insufficient and who have not gained power in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). If one is indeed a person of great wisdom, at the time of correct practice they realize that the nature of desire is fundamentally empty;

for one who has gained power in meditative concentration, the practice manifests immediately after the task is finished. If this were the case, even if one did not sever lust, how would it concern worldly toil (*kleśa*)? Why then say they cannot transcend it? Such views are common among those of 'wild wisdom' in the study of doctrine (*yixue*) and those blind practitioners of the school (*zongtu*).

Therefore, the Tathāgata used the passage beginning with 'Even if one has much wisdom' to guard against them. One who possesses much wisdom may do so either because their faculties (*indriya*) are sharp from the start, or by seeking the teachings.

They arise [from this]. As for the manifestation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it may involve the stillness of the absence of objective referents, or it may correspond to rational contemplation (*yoniśomanasikāra*);

both of these constitute wholesome objects. Even if one does not sever lustful thoughts, they all constitute demonic activity (*mārakarman*). Therefore, the above states: "Even if one possesses wisdom and concentration..."
It is said that such a person will certainly fall into the path of Māra. Based on this, there is no harm in asserting that desire is non-existent while adhering to the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

However, those who rely on their mastery of meditative concentration to claim that sexual conduct poses no obstacle are, in fact, deceived by their own wisdom and concentration. (Question: Why is it that they do not fall into other paths?)

Answer: Because cause and effect are of different natures. This is because those in the realm of Māra who desire victory seek only sensual pleasure; however, because their merit is strong and their minds are not yet settled in dhyāna or wisdom, such states cannot arise [spontaneously]. Now, by using dhyāna and wisdom to assist a lustful mind, one will inevitably fall into the path of Māra—without doubt.

This is like those among the *skandha-māras* who practice the dhyāna of emptiness, yet remain attached to worldly toil and increase their retinue of beautiful women. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse/Commentary) says: "The categories of superior, middling, and inferior are merely gradations based on the thickness or thinness of one's merit.
I, the humble writer, say that the "King of Māra" refers to the Lord of the Heaven of the Pinnacle of Desire (*kāmadhātu*).
That which is induced by meditative wisdom (*dhyāna*) and insight (*prajñā*) surpasses that induced by a lustful mind. As for the followers of Māra, they belong to the realm of the Māra King;
they are induced by a state where meditative wisdom and the lustful mind are exactly equal. As for the Māra maidens, they are those governed by the subjects of the King;
they are induced when the lustful mind surpasses meditative wisdom. ○ Below that, they fall into pride and do not return. That the various Māras also have retinues is because of the world...
Foolish and deluded, they fail to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox; they surrender their hearts in refuge and follow [these paths] as their teachers and lineage.

Just as the ninety-six types of schools in the Western Regions and the various heterodox sects and side-gates in this land are all the followers of Māra, each claiming to be equal [to the truth], they have formed the habit of *māna* (conceit).
They regard what is not the fruit as the fruit. As the text on receiving from Māra says: "That person does not even realize they are under the influence of Māra."

[This refers to] those who, claiming for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, are exactly such [persons]. First, the presentation of the benefits and harms of observing and violating [the precepts] is concluded.

Second, a preliminary distinction between the demonic teachings and the Buddhist teachings and rituals. First, the demonic teachings [promote] greed and lust, misleading the world; second, the Buddhist teachings [teach] the severance of lust to achieve meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding the first:
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such followers of Māra will flourish in the world.
They will widely practice greed and lust while posing as "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra), causing sentient beings to fall into the pit of craving and false views and lose the path to Bodhi.

The two phrases beginning with "After my extinction" reveal that the time since the Sage’s passing is remote. Because false teachers preach the Dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, these demonic followers are said to be many.
Furthermore, many due to various conditions will undergo delusion and, upon death, become subjects of Māra. This is as stated in the *Maming wen* (Text on Becoming a Subject of Māra):
"After the end of their lives, they will inevitably become subjects of Māra. Regarding the phrase "the flourishing world," it refers to the multitude of demons.

They arise in competition to bring harm to the people, like a blazing fire that erupts with great intensity; the entire world suffers its incineration. Thus, the subsequent passage on the Māra-text states:
"In this way, evil spirits bewitch their hearts and viscera. For some, it lasts for nine lifetimes; for many, it exceeds a hundred generations.
It causes those who practice true cultivation to all become the retinue of Māra. Those who extensively engage in greed, lust, and the like are called the teachers of Māra."
The younger brothers of Māra transmitted their lewd practices to one another, even taking those who engage in widespread misconduct as their spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Thus, the later *Māravijaya-sūtra* states: "They praise sexual misconduct and do not condemn coarse behavior;

they take all manner of vulgarities as the transmission of the Dharma, causing sentient beings to regard lustful desire as the foremost among all desires, and regarding false views as the summation of all views."

Since they take lustful desire as their teaching, they cause people to fall into craving; furthermore, since they take false views as their spiritual friends, they cause people to fall into dogmatic views.
Because one becomes submerged within them and cannot emerge on one's own, they are likened to a pit.
As it says later: "A Bodhisattva views desire as he would avoid a fire-pit; the Buddha regards evil views as [the same]."
This is what is called the "Pitfall of Views. Because it violates and distances one from perfect penetration and turns one's back on the city of Nirvana, it is said that "the path to Bodhi is lost.
Second, the Buddha taught the severance of lust to achieve meditative concentration;
you teach worldly people to practice *samādhi* by first severing the lust of the mind. This is called the teaching of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Ones of previous Buddhas.
This is the first definitive and pure instruction.

As for your teaching of worldly people: this is the Buddha’s command to Ānanda that, when delivering sentient beings in the final age, you should teach and guide worldly people to rely on the Buddha’s instructions and act in opposition to Māra.
To cultivate *samādhi*, one must first sever sexual desire; this is because sexual desire—

Because it constitutes an obstruction to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "the mind’s lust. In the Mahāyāna, one does not merely restrain the body; it is only when the mind is extinguished that true severance is achieved.
This phrase clarifies that based on this [principle], it is called the Buddha’s instruction; otherwise, as in the former case, it would belong to the conduct of Māra.
"The Tathāgata" refers to the present Buddha, while "the World-Honored One of previous Buddhas" refers to those of the past. What follows...
This means that the present Buddha speaks thus, and the Buddhas of the past have already spoken thus; this makes it all the more evident that it is trustworthy.
That "the first" stands at the head of the four grave offenses (catvāraḥ pārājikāḥ) indicates that one must be definitively pure and that there must be no transgression.
"Clear instruction" means clear and manifest teaching. Since the Buddha has already provided such clear and manifest instruction, should those who are disciples of the Buddha not follow it?
This concludes the preliminary discernment of the ritual protocols for the teachings of Māra and the Buddha. Third, the determination of the success or failure of attaining Bodhi.
First, if one does not sever desire, enlightenment will surely be destroyed; second, only by severing lust can enlightenment be achieved. Regarding the first:
Therefore, Ānanda, if one practices meditative concentration without severing lust, it is like steaming sand and gravel in the hope that it will become rice.
Even after hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it shall be known only as "Hot Sands. Why? Because this is not rice; it is composed of sand and gravel.

You seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood with a lustful body; even if you should attain wondrous enlightenment, it will all be rooted in lust. If the root itself is formed of lust, how can there be liberation?
One will inevitably cycle through the three miserable realms and be unable to escape them. By what path can one cultivate and realize the Nirvana of the Tathāgata?

First, a metaphor is employed to illustrate this; therefore, Ānanda—because he had received the Buddha’s teaching on severing lust—is addressed once more by name to serve as the primary recipient of the instruction.
"If one does not sever lust and so forth" means that if one were to deliberately violate the Buddha’s command.
If one does not sever the mind of lust while practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), all such efforts merely provide sustenance for the works of Māra.

To illustrate this by analogy, you should see for yourself the error in this: it is like steaming sand in the hope that it will become rice; though it be done for kalpas, it remains nothing but hot sand.

This illustrates how even sublime awakening, when accompanied by lustful conduct, entirely becomes the work of Māra. Since the works of Māra are brought about by the accumulation of lust, as [the scripture] says:
As for the hot sands, they are formed from steamed sand; thus their origin can be known.
In the explanation, it is said that even these hot sands are not the fundamental substance of rice, because they were originally composed of sand and gravel. This serves as a metaphor:

the karmic activities of Māra are not the cause of Buddhahood, because they are brought about by the accumulation of lust. ○ From "You" onwards, the Dharma is applied to the analogy. You, through lust...

"Regarding 'the body and so forth': this means that even if you do not sever the lust of the mind, yet seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood through the body of lust, it is like the example of steaming sand in the hope that it will become rice. Regarding 'even if one attains wondrous awakening':

this means that even if one practices for many kalpas and attains wondrous enlightenment, it is all the work of Māra; as it is said in that [sūtra], even after a hundred thousand kalpas, it is merely called..."
It is like hot sand. Rather than calling it "the karma of Māra," it is called the "root of lust" because Māra can bring about lustful acts precisely by means of this root of lust.
Regarding "the root that accomplishes lust and so forth": since it is the very root of lustful desire, it itself can successively bring about lustful acts.
Through the daily accumulation of such evil karma, one will inevitably undergo transmigration through the three miserable realms. Not...
One is able to attain liberation. Since even a human body is difficult to obtain, how much more so is the cultivation and realization of the fruit of Buddhahood? Therefore, it is rebuked by asking:
"By what path can the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata be cultivated and realized? Nirvāṇa is the principle of suchness (*tathatā*); Bodhi is the wisdom of suchness.
Since principle is not realized, wisdom is not perfected; thus the commentary states that bodhi is destroyed.
Second, when lust is severed, bodhi is achieved.
One must ensure that both the faculties of lust and the body and mind are severed, and even the nature of severance is absent; only then can one hope for the Buddha’s bodhi.

The "mechanism of lust" refers to the very moment a desire first sprouts. At this time, one should first restrain the body so that it does not act, and subsequently restrain the mind so that it does not arise;
therefore, it is said that both are severed. Because nothing other than this can accord with the fruit [of enlightenment], it is said that one must "certainly cause" this to happen.
As for the phrase "the nature of severance is also non-existent," it means that if there were a nature of the agent who severs and a nature of that which is severed, [severance would be impossible].

It is still a matter of strenuous suppression and restraint; if one's maintenance falters even slightly, [the affliction] arises instantly, like grass pressed down by a stone or a thief bound with a rope.
Because this is not true severance, the nature of severance will ultimately not be attained. Rather, it means transforming the many lustful minds into the fire of wisdom;
there is no need for further application of restraint, as transgressions will naturally cease. It is like grass that has already withered.
By suppressing [the afflictions], they do not arise spontaneously; it is like a thief who changes his occupation—he does not depart of his own accord unless he is bound.
Through the precepts, concentration arises; through concentration, wisdom is developed. When concentration and wisdom are equalized, one flows into [enlightenment] spontaneously.

Therefore, it is said that one may hope for the Buddha’s bodhi. Now, as for why the previous section spoke of *nirvāṇa* while this section speaks of *bodhi*: it refers to the principle-wisdom (*li-zhi*).
This is because it is taught through the analogy of mutual reflections. The determination of the arising and perishing of bodhi is thus concluded.
Fourth, the summary judgment regarding what is relied upon or contradicted, and what is correct or erroneous:
"What I have spoken in this way is called the Buddha’s teaching; that which is not spoken in this way is the teaching of Pāpīyān."
Although this section consists of words for concluding and judging, it also serves as an instruction for Ānanda on how to distinguish between demons and Buddhas.

The Tathāgata’s intention was this: regarding what you previously said—that in the final age sentient beings will gradually distance themselves from the Buddha and false teachers will preach the Dharma like the sands of the Ganges—it was because he feared that false teachings would disrupt the correct path and that it would be difficult to distinguish between demons and Buddhas; therefore, I...
I have already explained in detail for you the rituals and teachings of Māra.

If, in the future age at the end of time, there are sentient beings who, following my instructions, practice samādhi by first severing the lust of the mind and so forth, this shall be known as the teaching of the Buddha.

One should urgently follow this advice. If, however, someone were to speak otherwise—claiming that practicing lust and greed extensively constitutes being a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra)—this is the speech of Pāpīyān.
One should sever such views deeply. Pāpīyān is an alternate name for Māra;
it means "the Killer," because he disturbs and confuses right practice, wounds the Dharma-body, and harms the life of wisdom. This concludes the precept against sexual misconduct.

Regarding the four points on the precept against killing: first, an exposition of the benefits and harms of observing it; second, the preliminary arrangement of the ritual protocols for the Buddhas and spirits;
third, the determination of the gains and losses regarding liberation; fourth, the concluding judgment on compliance and violation, as well as the heterodox and the orthodox.

Of these, the first two consist of: first, that by severing killing one will certainly transcend birth and death; and second, that by not severing it one will certainly fall into the realm of spirits. Regarding the first:
Ānanda, furthermore, if the sentient beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor the intent to kill, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
Guǎngdìng says: "The Buddhas establish their transformation through teaching with compassion as the foundation; Bodhisattvas benefit others by making salvation their priority."
How could one possibly harm living beings and wound compassion, or kill and thereby bind oneself in enmity? Therefore, next comes the precept against killing.

One whose mind does not kill neither kills by oneself, nor instructs others to kill, nor even rejoices in seeing others kill—thus departing from all such acts. Furthermore, this also serves as an illustration where the light case implies the heavy:
if the mind itself does not kill, how much more so when the body is confronted with the act of killing; one should naturally and forever abstain.

[This is] severed. Previously it was said: "You owe me my life; I shall repay you for your debt. By reason of these causes and conditions, one remains constantly in birth and death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Thus we know that the single matter of killing life binds together resentment and brings forth calamity, sufficient to invite birth and death.
Therefore, by not killing, one does not follow [this path]. Second, if one does not sever [killing], one will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits.
"You have cultivated samādhi originally to escape from worldly toil; yet if you do not eliminate the murderous mind, you cannot transcend the dust of the world.
Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the habit of killing, you will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits.

Those of the highest grade shall become powerful ghosts; those of the middle grade shall become flying yakṣas, various ghost generals, and the like; those of the lowest grade shall become earth-walking rākṣasas."
Kṣetra. ○ Those various ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each of whom claims to have realized the Unsurpassed Way.

First, regarding the clarification that "not emerging from the dust": not removing [the defilements] while not emerging [from them] means that the intent to kill belongs to greed and is further compounded by hatred;

it is also the very root of worldly toil (*kleśa*). ○ Even if there were [such a claim], the following anticipates erroneous arguments (fearing that one might erroneously argue: "A person of great wisdom understands that the nature of killing is fundamentally empty...").

When one gains mastery in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the power to kill manifests immediately; it appears to have no connection to worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). Many clever elders and lay practitioners who, having eaten meat until satiated, seek out monks to discuss Chan, hold such views.

Therefore, the Tathāgata also used the passage beginning with "Even if one possesses much wisdom" to prevent this. Spirits that subsist on blood and flesh take the karma of killing as the cause for their downfall;

those possessing supernatural powers and merit take meditative concentration and wisdom as the cause for their birth. Now, because one uses meditative concentration and wisdom to assist in killing, one will inevitably fall.
As for the Way: those of the superior grade possess meditative concentration and wisdom that surpass their karmic burden of killing;

since their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are great and their merit is likewise superior, they become ghosts of great power. In comparison to those of the lower and middle grades, they should be considered *yakṣas* who frequent the heavens and various lords of ghosts, such as the mountain deities and Yama.
Those of the middle grade possess meditative concentration and wisdom that are exactly equal to their karmic burden of killing.
Since their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and merit (*puṇya*) are next in rank after those above, they serve as leaders of the flying yakṣas and various spirits (*bhūta*).

"Flying" refers to moving through the air; "leaders of spirits" refers to the commanders and subordinates among the ghost-lords, such as those dwelling in mountain forests, city walls, or the Ox-Headed Hell-wardens (*gośīrṣa-yama-puruṣa*).
For those of inferior grade, whose meditative wisdom is weaker than their karmic activity of killing, their supernormal powers—[are as follows:]...
Because their merit is slight and inferior, they become terrestrial rākṣasas.
Such beings include those who consume the vital essence of humans, eat human flesh and blood, as well as various *pīśācas*, *yātudhānas*, *bhūtas*, *vetālas*, and *skandhas*.

These beings, having developed pride through their attainments, do not return [to the path]. They delude people with supernatural powers, kill living beings for sacrificial offerings, and devote themselves wholeheartedly to seeking spiritual efficacy.
Because they take refuge [in such powers], there are those among their followers who can foresee good and ill fortune, and whose words are invariably fulfilled.
Without self-reflection, they falsely give rise to the pride of being Buddhas; thus it is said that each and every one of them claims to have attained the supreme path of Buddhahood.

Whenever one sees the heterodox sects of this world claiming to have realized the fruits of enlightenment (*phala*), remaining complacent and unaware of fear—is this not also the work of demonic power? First, I shall set forth the maintenance [of the precepts].

The refutation of their harmful interests is concluded. Second, the preliminary clarification of the ritual protocols for the teachings on ghosts and the Buddha’s teachings. First, the teaching of ghosts permits the eating of meat without hindrance;
second, the Buddha’s teaching prohibits killing and establishes it as a fixed rule. The first [section] has three parts: first, the formal exposition of the teaching of ghosts;
second, the prevention of anticipated objections; third, the severe condemnation of its errors. The first [part]: [Text continues...]
After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma (mofa), many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, claiming that by eating meat one can attain the path to Bodhi.

This is the time when the Buddha has passed away, the Dharma is in its final age, and the Way has declined and become faint; as the world declines and the Way becomes faint, many people seek out hidden practices.
Because of these anomalies, ghosts and spirits flourish. Some manifest their numinous power by taking refuge in temple sacrifices; others appear as wonders by possessing human bodies.
Just as with the licentious sacrifices and spirit-mediums of the world, who among them are not driven by ghosts and spirits?

They themselves claim to eat meat and incite people to slaughter living beings for offerings, indulging in their own greed and gluttony. Furthermore, they claim to have attained the path to Bodhi and urge people [to follow them].

He imitated the conduct of those who fall into the realm of ghosts in order to support his own faction. As the proverb says, "Wine and meat pass through the intestines, but the Buddha sits upon the heart.
This is truly the speech of a ghost. Second, he poses questions and challenges.
Ānanda, I have permitted the bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat. These meats are all produced through my supernatural power; they originally possess no life-force.
You, O Brahmin, live in a land where the soil is mostly damp and humid, and because it is further infested with sand and gravel, grasses and vegetables do not grow.
It is by the addition of my great compassionate supernatural power that [these things are made possible].

First, the objection regarding the permission to eat pure meat (*śuci-māṃsa*). (Fearing that an objection might be raised: "If eating meat is a teaching of the *asuras*, then Buddhism itself should strictly prohibit it. Why did the Tathāgata also permit bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat?

Therefore, the World-Honored One provided this defense by means of the concept of "birth by transformation" (*upapāduka*), which lacks a life-principle. Regarding "pure meat": excluding humans, snakes, elephants, horses, donkeys, dogs, lions, foxes, pigs, and monkeys;
any other meat that one has not seen, heard of, or suspected was killed for one's sake constitutes the three types of pure meat. Furthermore...
Furthermore, birds that die naturally constitute the "five kinds of pure meat. In the past, within the provisional teachings, eating was permitted as a means to restrain the mind;
thus, those who eat "pure meat" do so because it is not actual flesh. All such meat is produced through my supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*);

it is fundamentally devoid of consciousness, warmth, and breath—these three—and merely consists of the union of form and mind (*rūpa-citta*) sustained as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). It is like a wooden puppet operated by a mechanism; even if one were to kill it, it is not a living being.
It is unobstructed. What harm is there in eating it? [Objection: You, Master Ba, prevent this by saying that grain and vegetables would not digest. (I fear you might further object:

"If it is through the Tathāgata’s supernatural power, why did he not transform it into grain or vegetables, but instead into pure meat? This merely provides an excuse for those who eat meat in the future; how could such an act be performed by one who is compassionate?

Therefore, the World-Honored One used the fact that [the land] mostly does not produce [such things] as a defense. Guǎngdìng says: In the Five Indias of the Western Regions, they are collectively called the Kingdom of the Brāhmaṇas. Because...
This was the place where those from the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended at the beginning of the kalpa. Since all those people belonged to a pure lineage (*śuddhavaṃśa*), the country was named after them.
What is now called "your" (*yuǒu*) Brahmin country is still referred to as "you" (*rǔ*) Brahmin country. Furthermore, the word "you" excludes oneself;
it means that the Buddha manifested his birth there but was not related to that pure lineage. If one did not make this distinction and exclusion, [the following] would be feared:

This is because they give rise to the conceit of belonging to that class. Furthermore, the body of a Tathāgata is not a body sustained by impure food; this is revealed because the fleshly body is manifested solely for their sake.
"Damp" refers to excessive heat from kilns, while "moist" refers to excessive humidity. Since there are places where the soil is neither of these, the text specifies "mostly.
As for the addition of "sand and stones," it means that it is not only mostly damp and moist, but also characterized by an abundance of sand and stone.
For these four reasons, grasses and vegetables would not grow. To prevent this, he established the cultivation of grain and vegetables;
yet people instead gave rise to suspicion and wonder, not daring to eat them because they were contrary to their usual habits.

For this reason, out of great compassion and pity, the Buddha empowered them through his supernatural power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), so that whatever grew from the earth appeared as transformed sustenance, thereby providing for them in advance.
The questioning was concluded. [The Buddha] thrice sternly rebuked his errors, stating:
"Out of great compassion, meat is merely a provisional name. You have tasted its flavor;

how can you, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, eat the flesh of sentient beings and yet still call yourself a son of the Śākya? You all should know that even if such meat-eaters should happen to attain the mind..."
Appearing as if they were in samādhi, they are all great rākṣasas; when their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the bitter sea of birth and death.
They are not disciples of the Buddha. How could such people ever escape the three realms, given that they continue to kill, devour, and consume one another without end?
At the outset, I received his severe rebuke. He stated that according to what was said above, those "pure meats" were actually manifested through my compassion;
they originally possessed no life-force and were merely designated by the name "meat.

This was done only to allow you, in the land of the Brahmins, to temporarily obtain their flavor to alleviate famine; it is not the eternal Dharma. Since it is not the eternal Dharma, for any ordinary person...
If one cannot even go to places where grain and vegetables grow, how much less so after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa—who would manifest transformations for them? Alas!
After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, there are those who still eat the flesh of sentient beings and yet call themselves disciples of the Śākya (Śākyaputrīya).
They wear the robes of the Buddha while destroying the Buddha’s teachings; they are like worms within the body of a lion that turn back to devour the lion itself.

"This is the flesh of one's own son. [The circle indicates a pause. "I command you all to know that you will surely fall" means that he taught what you must understand so that the words of the Tathāgata might be transmitted to the final age for the urgent purpose of providing salvation and correction.

He says that those who eat meat speak deceptively and cannot attain the opening of the mind; even if their practice manifests before them and they momentarily achieve such an opening, it is not genuine.
Furthermore, this is merely a semblance of *samādhi* and does not constitute the attainment of true *samyak-samāpatti*.

This is because, as long as the craving for killing is not eliminated, one acts as a *rākṣasa* in the present life; when the retribution ends and life concludes, one will inevitably sink into the ocean of suffering of birth and death.
One will remain forever among the class of ghosts and cease to be a disciple of the Buddha, for one is unable to transcend the triple world. Thus, the following passage indicates this.

Because they fall [into lower realms]. (Fearing that someone might ask: "Since these individuals call themselves sons of the Śākya and have already received the seeds of Buddhahood within the field of consciousness, even if they encounter transmigration, they will still be children of the Buddha. Why then do you say they must surely sink into birth and death and are not disciples of the Buddha?

Is this not too extreme a judgment? Therefore, the World-Honored One demonstrates this by means of mutual killing and devouring. It is said that these people and all other sentient beings harm and kill one another, and devour one another, as previously stated:
when a sheep dies it becomes a human, and when a human dies it becomes a sheep, dying again and again.
"Life after life, they come to devour one another; as long as this mutual consumption has not ceased, the cycle of retribution will never end.

As for those who speak of "leaving the realm," it is simply said that they are incapable of leaving it. Thus we know that those called "not disciples of the Buddha" have truly severed themselves from the path;
what connection do they have with the Buddha? This concludes the teaching of the ghosts regarding the lack of impediment to eating meat.
Second, the Buddha taught that the cessation of killing constitutes a fixed rule.

You now teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi by first ceasing the taking of life. This is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One of former Buddhas.

Although one has already previously severed sexual desire of the mind, if the karma of killing is not eliminated, it will ultimately remain within the semblance of meditative concentration; therefore, the teaching instructs that one must next sever the taking of life.
The remaining [precepts] are all to be understood according to the above. Having thus completed the preliminary clarification of the Buddhist ritual for the hungry ghosts.
Third, the determination regarding the gain and loss of liberation is twofold: first, if one does not cease killing, liberation will certainly be lost;
second, by ceasing killing, liberation is attained. Regarding the first:
therefore, Ānanda, if one practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) without ceasing killing, it is like a person who blocks their own ears.
He cried out in a loud voice seeking help, yet no one heard him; this is what is called "the more one seeks to conceal, the more it is revealed.
A pure bhikṣu and all bodhisattvas do not even tread upon living grass when walking on a forked path, much less pull it up with their hands.
How could those of great compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to serve as food?
The initial metaphor clarifies that [the precept] must be lost, following the preceding Buddhist teaching on the severance of killing. He calls out to the audience once more to address them again:
if one does not sever killing while practicing dhyāna, one cannot attain liberation. This shall be understood by oneself through the illustration that follows.
For example, "a person" refers to one who practices dhyāna while maintaining the habit of killing. "Blocking one's own ears" means employing...
Plugging the ears with the hands to avoid the disturbance of sound is a metaphor for practicing dhyāna to cultivate the mind and avoid the encroachment of worldly defilements (*rajas*).

Loud shouting and clamor are especially capable of deafening the ears; this is a metaphor for how the karma of killing, if not eliminated, uniquely serves to permeate the mind with worldly defilements.
Having already deafened one's own ears, one fears being overheard by others who might come to cause further disturbance; thus, one seeks someone who will not hear.
This is a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśa*) permeating the mind, where one fears being invaded by the murderous ghost of impermanence and seeks liberation.

One must know that plugging one's ears and shouting loudly cannot prevent others from hearing; therefore, the more one tries to conceal, the more it is revealed. This is a metaphor for the cultivation of dhyāna.
Even if one maintains the precept against killing, it cannot prevent impermanence from invading; thus, seeking tranquility only serves to increase disorder.

Based on this, it is clear that liberation cannot be attained through faith if one does not cease taking life. ○ Regarding "Pure and Clean" (*qingjing*), the following is intended to preempt erroneous questions (fearing someone might ask:).

Killing living beings violates compassion and must certainly be strictly prohibited. If one were merely to take their flesh and blood, it would seem not to harm great compassion; why, then, did the World-Honored One previously prohibit even "pure meat" for both [vehicles]?
Therefore, he established prohibitions using "pure bhikṣus" and so forth as examples. "Pure bhikṣus" and "bodhisattvas" refer to those who uphold the precepts in the two vehicles.
A "forked path" is a branching side road. On such a small road, people are sparse and green grass grows easily. Those of the two pure vehicles walk upon it.
One still maintains a sense of care for them and cannot bear to trample upon them; how much more so when using one's hands to pull them out—this makes it even more clear that such an act is improper.
For this reason, the destruction of "villages of spirits" was prohibited by the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, and the cutting of grass and felling of trees were also censured by the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

This is not only the case in Buddhism; even among the disciples of Confucius, there were those who would not kill insects emerging from their cocoons and would not pluck branches while they were in full growth. How could this be...?

Is it not because they fear offending the harmony of Heaven that they wish to avoid it? Thus we know that those who uphold the prohibitive precepts cannot bear to kill even the grass that grows upon them.
How then could those possessed of great compassion bear to take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to satisfy their hunger?
Although one does not kill oneself, one can still act as a cause for the killer. You ought to sever this practice immediately; do not let it continue.
[This is] a doubtful error. To sever the two [types of killing] and attain liberation, one must fulfill two conditions: first, encountering a disciple capable of being taught;
second, teaching them through profound severance. Regarding the first:
if there are bhikṣus who do not wear silks, cottons, or flosses from the East, nor the boots, leather shoes, furs, or woolens of this land...
Milk, curd, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*); thus, O Bhikṣu, one who has attained true liberation from the world repays past debts and no longer wanders within the three realms.
Why is this? Because by partaking of their physical forms, they become bound by those very conditions; it is like a person who eats the various grains of the earth—their feet never leave the ground.

First, one attains liberation by severing the conditions [for killing]. (Wearing silk and consuming milk both constitute conditions for killing, because excessive acquisition and use lead indirectly to the act of killing. In the Mahāyāna, the wearing of silk and consumption of milk may be permitted. Therefore, this is discussed specifically in relation to the bhikṣu.
For example, when later establishing a *maṇḍala* and performing offerings, clarified butter (*sarpis*) and honey (*madhu*) are used;
and when hanging banners, are they not made of silk? The essential point is that the mind must be free from the impulse to kill; if this is so, one will likely attain the goal.

It is acceptable. The character for "clothing" (*fú*) has two meanings: first, wearing or adorning oneself, as with silk, cotton, and the like; second, consuming or ingesting, as with milk, curd, and the like.
One does not wear [such items] because they are causes of killing. Silk, thread, cotton, floss, brocade, and gauze mostly originate from the various countries of Zhendan (China);
hence it is called the "East. Raising silkworms and boiling cocoons harms living beings and violates compassion.

They are produced. Leather boots, hide shoes, padded jackets, and garments made of coarse wool or hair mostly come from the various kingdoms of India; therefore, they are said to originate from "this land.

These are brought about by the peeling of skins, the shearing of fur, and the infliction of injury and cruelty upon living beings. "Milk" refers to cow's milk. When processed, it becomes curd (*dadhi*); processed again, it becomes butter (*navanīta*).
At its ultimate refinement, it is called clarified butter (*ghṛta*), or *maṇḍa*. Although this does not involve the fault of killing, it nevertheless involves taking [the product] improperly.
It harms the cow; how much more so when one seizes the calf’s food for the sake of one's own body—how could this be appropriate for one who possesses compassion?
For this reason, a bhikṣu does not wear garments made of silk, wool, and the like, nor does he consume milk, curd, and other such products.
Such a bhikṣu must have severed the bonds of his children; therefore, it is said that he is truly [liberated] in the world.

"Released. Although they remain bound by the fruits [of past karma], this is no more than the repayment of old debts. Once the residual physical form is exhausted, there is no further continuation of birth;
hence it is said that "they do not wander through the three realms. This shows that the conditions for killing must be severed.

The section beginning with "How" serves as an inquiry, an explanation, and a citation of evidence. The intent of the inquiry is that while severing the conditions for killing may lead to liberation in the world, such a matter is difficult to believe.
Furthermore, the commentary states that although silk, cotton, and fine fabrics are not the body in its entirety, they are nonetheless a small portion of it.
Wearing such garments or consuming them can all serve as conditions for creating a karmic connection with those [beings]. Consequently, one is unable to transcend their category.
As cited in the supporting evidence, at the beginning of the kalpa, the bodies of humans emitted flying light and their feet were like treading upon clouds; because of this—

Consuming the essence of the earth, they were unable to lift themselves up. Later, they gradually began to eat the hundred grains within that earth—rice, millet, beans, wheat, panicled millet, broomcorn millet, and so forth, each of various types, collectively termed the "hundred grains.
Because their karmic conditions became heavy through this attachment to the earth, their bodies gradually became solid and heavy, and their feet no longer left the ground.
However, even the insentient earth-element becomes difficult to lift when consumed; how much more so for the sentient body, which could never attain liberation by ingesting it?
Thus we know that those who do not consume it can naturally achieve liberation, and they are the ones fit to be taught.
Second, teach through profound renunciation:

you must ensure that, regarding all sentient beings, whether in their entirety or in their individual parts, neither your body nor your mind—through either of these two paths—shall serve them or consume them.
I declare such a person to be one who has attained true liberation.
Since the conditions for killing have been severed, one should cause the cessation of the karmic act of killing; thus it says, "one must ensure.
This means that one must certainly cause it to be so, and by no means permit its transgression. "Body and mind" refers to the body and mind of this person.
"Sentient beings" refers to sentient beings who possess feeling. As for the "body," it may mean harming the entire body; as for "parts of the body," it may mean damaging its limbs.
As for the "body," this refers to its flesh, blood, and so forth; in these matters, there must be no transgression whatsoever.

Regarding the "two paths of body and mind," it means that the bodies of sentient beings and their various parts are both paths through which one commits killing of body and mind. As for "not wearing and not eating," [it refers to these same objects].

Not only is there no karmic action of killing in the body, but even the thought of killing in the mind is absent. Since the thought of killing is absent, there is no further possibility of severing anything.

This carries the meaning that both body and mind are severed together, and even the nature of severance is non-existent. In this way, when entering the realm of worldly toil (*rajas*), one is no longer entangled;
riding upon one's vows, one encompasses all things and attains great sovereignty. Therefore, it is called "true liberation."

(Question: What is the difference between this true liberation and the true liberation mentioned above? Answer: The former is liberation by departing from the world; this is liberation while remaining within the world. They are certainly not the same.

The phrase "that which I have taught" is used to manifest its certainty and lack of falsehood; for even if the sun could be made cold and the moon could be made hot, there can be no variation in what the Buddha has taught.

Having thus concluded the determination of the attainment and loss of liberation, [the text] fourthly provides a summary judgment on dependence versus independence, and the heterodox versus the orthodox.
What I have spoken in this manner is called the teaching of the Buddha; that which is not spoken thus is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
The explanation of the meaning follows the above. The precept against killing is concluded.

Third, the precept against stealing (*adattādāna*). [Zhengmo says: This theft does not refer merely to the secret pilfering of another's property; rather, it includes all instances of practicing fraud, deception, or intimidation, even down to a single thought of seeking gain or offerings.]
It is so. Fourth: First, an exposition on the benefits and harms of maintaining or violating [the precepts]; second, a preliminary clarification of the ritual protocols of heterodox teachings;

third, a definitive determination of the true and the counterfeit regarding samādhi; fourth, a concluding adjudication of compliance and violation, as well as heterodoxy and orthodoxy. Regarding the first two: first, if one severs theft, one will certainly transcend birth and death;
second, if one does not sever it, one will certainly fall into heterodox paths. Regarding the first:
Ānanda, furthermore, if the beings within the six realms of this world do not harbor a mind of theft, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death.
The practice of a Bodhisattva is to benefit others while forgetting one’s own body; to direct evil deeds toward oneself and give good things to others. Suppose...
If the mind of theft is not eliminated, one cannot avoid harming others for one's own benefit, which violates the conduct of a Bodhisattva.

Therefore, although one has already severed [the habits of] sexual misconduct and killing, one must ensure that the mind does not steal. It is not mentioned specifically regarding the body because if the mind is temporarily unmoved, how much more so when the body encounters the act of stealing?
One should naturally sever it forever; if one does not sever theft, there will be repeated demands for restitution throughout successive lifetimes.
Death. Because you did not steal, you have not followed [the path of the spirits]. Second, if you do not sever it, you will inevitably fall into a deviant path.
You practice samādhi originally to transcend worldly toil; if the mind of theft is not eliminated, you cannot escape from the dust of the world.

Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever the mind of theft, you will inevitably fall into a deviant path—becoming a high-grade spirit or a medium-grade demon.
Māras. These are persons of inferior grade who are possessed by various māras. These various evil ones also have their own followers, each of whom claims to have realized the Unsurpassed Way.

The first section clarifies not giving rise to worldly defilements (*rajas*). When one is properly practicing samādhi, the object of meditation and the contemplation are in harmony, and thus worldly afflictions have no cause to arise;
hence it is said that they "originally do not emerge. If, however, the thieving mind is not eliminated, it is no different from pressing grass down with a stone.

If rational contemplation (*yuanli guan*) slightly falters, one will immediately give rise to afflictions upon encountering objects; the eighty thousand worldly afflictions will then follow one after another and blaze forth, as occurred in the past with a certain person.
The Master heard that the fragrance of lotuses produced defilement. Another deity rebuked him, saying: "Why do you steal this fragrance?

Because of attachment to the fragrance, all fetters arise. Thus one knows that the dust of worldly toil cannot be escaped. [This section] below, even if there were, serves as a precaution against erroneous arguments. (Fearing that someone might erroneously argue:

"A person of great wisdom thoroughly understands that the dust of worldly toil is fundamentally empty. When meditative concentration manifests, they can transcend to the stage of No-More-Learning in a mere snap of the fingers. Although they have not severed the theft of worldly toil, it does not bind them. Once the proper time has arrived, they must emerge.")

He then departs. How can you say he cannot depart? Shameless practitioners of Chan often use this as a pretext to gloss over their errors; therefore, the Tathāgata used such passages as "Even if one possesses much wisdom" and so forth to guard against it.

In the hidden ways of heterodox paths, the mind of theft serves as the condition for falling into ruin. These heterodox arts deceive the world; they cannot be mastered without the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Now, if one uses *dhyāna* and wisdom to assist in theft, one will surely fall among those of such a kind. Those of superior grade and spiritual essence steal the essence of the sun and moon.

The "Flowers" (Huā) secretly appropriate the spiritual excellence of Heaven and Earth; clinging to mountains and relying on waters, they delude people’s sacrifices. They belong to the class of malevolent deities.
Those of the middle grade, the "Seductive Spirits" (Yāomèi), steal the vital essence of human things and pilfer the moisture and vapors of mountain forests;

appearing as *wǎng* or *liǎng* spirits, they watch for opportunities to commit calamities. They belong to the class of malevolent ghosts. Those of the lower grade, the "Malevolent Persons," are by nature treacherous and crooked.
Those whose mental dispositions are depraved and who are possessed by various demons are those to whom spirits have attached themselves;

they are deluded by malevolent spirits, uttering false words to deceive the world and practicing eccentric conduct to惑惑 (delude) the common people—such are the class of heterodox outsiders (*tīrthika*).

These individuals also experience differences of superior, middling, and inferior grades due to the mutual dominance or subordination of their karma regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). ○ Among them, the inferior ones fall into arrogance.
They do not return. Successively and reciprocally they become attached to one another; later ones regard earlier ones as teachers, and earlier ones regard later ones as teachers.

Thus it is said: "Those various heterodox groups also have their own followers. Being possessed by and increasing in heterodoxy, they remain unaware of it themselves; sitting upright and receiving offerings, they appear exactly like Buddhas.
Therefore it is said: "Each and every one of them claims to have attained the Unsurpassed Way. This concludes the first exposition on maintaining [the precepts].

The section on violating interests and benefits concludes. Second, the preliminary clarification of the demonic Buddhist rites has two parts: first, how the demonic teachings deceive the world and increase greed; second, how the Buddhist teachings advocate relinquishing the body and severing theft. The first part has three sections: first, a formal exposition of the demonic teachings; second, anticipating and preventing objections; third, a forceful condemnation of their errors. The first [section]: [The demonic teachings] claim that by performing sacrifices and offering up one’s own flesh, one may obtain blessings and long life. They say that if one can offer up one’s own limbs, one will receive rewards from the gods. They further claim that if one can sacrifice one’s own children, one will obtain the fulfillment of all desires. They also say that if one can sacrifice one’s own wife, one will attain the rank of a noble lord. Furthermore, they say that if one can sacrifice one’s own parents, one will attain the position of a high official. They also say that if one can sacrifice one’s own siblings, one will obtain wealth and status. They also say that if one can sacrifice one’s own servants, one will obtain abundant grain. They also say that if one can sacrifice one’s own horses and cattle, one will obtain many mounts. They also say that if one can sacrifice one’s own dogs and pigs, one will obtain many livestock. They also say that if one can sacrifice one’s own birds and beasts, one will obtain many fowl and game. They also say that if one can sacrifice one’s own fruits and grains, one will obtain many provisions. They also say that if one can sacrifice one’s own clothing and ornaments, one will obtain many garments and decorations. They also say that if one can sacrifice one’s own houses and buildings, one will obtain many dwellings. They also say that if one can sacrifice one’s own lands and fields, one will obtain many estates. After my parinirvāṇa, during the age of the Dharma’s decay, many such demonic and heterodox beings will flourish in the world.

They will secretly harbor deceit while claiming to be "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra), each asserting for themselves that they have attained the dharmas of a superior person (*uttarapudgala*). They will entice and delude the ignorant, seeking to cause them to lose their minds.
In every place he passes through, households will suffer depletion and dissipation.

This is the time when, after his passing, the Dharma of the Buddha declines during the Final Age (*mofa*). Because the Dharma of the Buddha declines, malevolent spirits and heterodoxies find opportunity;
thus, they flourish extensively throughout the world. "Latent" means hidden in darkness; "deceitful" refers to fraud, lewdness, and delusion. This is as described in the *Māravijaya-sūtra*.
It is said: "They move in secret, harboring greed and desire; in their mouths they love to speak of calamities, blessings, and supernatural anomalies.

This refers to secretly concealing fraud and deception. Believing in their teachings, one's mind becomes agitated and unsettled; thus, they are called "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*) by them, though this is merely a false claim by these heterodox followers.
Once their disciples have been addressed as "spiritual friends," those teachers then presume for themselves the title of "Bodhisattvas. Therefore...
Each of them claimed to have attained the state of a "superior person" (*uttarapudgala*); here, "superior person" refers to a Bodhisattva, as they dwell above the level of the Śrāvakas.

This is the self-conceit of such false teachers. As for those who lack discernment, they are the ignorant and deluded of the world; those who deceive and惑惑 (delude) are the ostentatious, the fraudulent, and the seductive disturbers.
As stated in the *Māra-vikalpa-sūtra*: "Some say that the Tathāgata has appeared in such-and-such a place; others speak of the kalpa-fire."
Some speak of the calamity of weapons; this is merely to entice and delude the ignorant.

Fearing that they might lose their minds means causing those before them to be so terrified that they lose their original mind and forfeit their right view. Upon hearing that a Buddha has appeared in a certain place, they seek his guidance;
upon hearing of the fires of the kalpa or the calamity of weapons, they look to him for salvation. They exhaust their wealth in offerings, accepting it with a willing heart.
How regrettable! This causes the households through which they pass to suffer depletion and dissipation. This is precisely what is meant by summoning various malevolent spirits to pray for blessings;
how could one know that, were it truly real, one would ultimately be unable to escape?

Second, the prevention of objections. (Fearing that someone might raise this objection: "The households through which [monks] pass suffer depletion; since this is caused by the practices of heretical teachings, Buddhism should naturally prohibit it.

Why then did the Tathāgata allow the bhikṣus of his own teaching to beg for alms according to their directions? Is this not causing the households they pass through to suffer depletion? Therefore, the World-Honored One established these rules to prevent such occurrences among the bhikṣus of his teaching.)
I teach the bhikṣus to wander for alms according to their direction, so that they may abandon greed and accomplish the path to Bodhi.
To "wander for alms according to one's direction" means that regardless of whether food is refined or coarse, one simply begs and eats whatever is available in that direction.
One seeks only what is necessary to sustain the body, neither seeking falsely nor seeking in excess, and remains free from the four types of wrong livelihood; therefore, it is called "abandoning."
[They] crave. Yet craving is the root of afflictions (*kleśa*). Once the root is abandoned, the branches and twigs do not arise;

once afflictions are severed, Bodhi can be realized. Since Buddhism instructs one in this manner, how could it be compared to heterodox teachings that exhaust the world by indulging greed? Third, he severely rebukes their errors.

The bhikṣus do not cook for themselves; they rely on the remnants of their remaining lives. They are travelers adrift in the three realms, demonstrating a single coming and going, after which there is no returning.
How can these thieves, wearing my robes, peddle the teachings of the Tathāgata like a merchant, creating all manner of karmic deeds while claiming them all to be the Buddha-dharma?
Yet they denigrate the bhikṣus who have left the home life and observed the precepts, calling them followers of the Hīnayāna path. Because of this...
Such doubts and errors cause immeasurable sentient beings to fall into the Avīci Hell.
First, following the previous section, the correct view is revealed: "As I have explained above, the reason why bhikṣus do not cook their own food is as follows."

He has taken this final body as a vessel for accomplishing the work of the Way. Since he practices the Way in this final body for only half a lifetime remaining, it is called "the remainder of life" (*zansheng*).
Because he dwells in the world for only this remainder of life and will not remain long, it is said that he is "a traveler in the three realms" (*lübo sanjie*).
Zhengmo says: "To lodge on land is called 'traveling' (*lü*); to lodge on water is called 'mooring' (*po*. This means that his dwelling within the three realms is like...
A traveler passing through who stays for a night as a guest—what concern could they have for food?
Since he has no concern for food yet still begs for it, he demonstrates that his coming to this human world is like a one-way journey with a return;

because the residual traces of desire in the realm of form remain, he still requires the nourishment of solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). If those residual traces were exhausted, he would depart and never return again.
Thus, even the single matter of begging for alms arises only out of necessity. ○ [The text] asks: "How so? This section below refutes the false to reveal the non-authentic.
"Thieves" refers to those of heterodox schools among the ordained, for they can plunder and harm the Buddha-dharma.
"Wearing my robes" means that they physically don the *kāṣāya* (monastic robe) prescribed by the Buddha. "Dealing in imitation of the Tathāgata" means dealing in imitation of...

This is because, without wearing the Buddha’s robes, one cannot inspire confidence in others, and thus it is difficult to sell the Dharma. Regarding the performance of various kinds of activities:

this refers to using deceptive speech and eccentric conduct to entice and delude the minds of people, reaching no limit in their deviousness. All those who claim to speak the Buddha-Dharma refer to themselves [in this manner].
The Buddha-dharma ought to be thus. This [attitude] is precisely to peddle the Tathāgata’s non-Dharma as if it were the Dharma.

As for those who have left home with right faith, bhikṣus endowed with the precepts who observe the Buddha’s regulations, begging for food and renouncing greed—yet they instead slander them, claiming that adhering to minor details is the path of the Hīnayāna.
This, moreover, obstructs the correct practice of the Dharma and misrepresents the Dharma as non-Dharma.
Furthermore, the opening question "How can this be? is a word of severe censure. Its intended meaning is that even when a bhikṣu goes for alms, it is still done out of necessity;
how then could there actually be such thieves? The Avīci Hell is indeed established for those like you.
○ From "By this" onwards, he shows how they mislead others, meaning that by means of this dharma, they preach what is not the truth.
With doubts regarding the Dharma, immeasurable sentient beings destroy what is correct and take it to be false.

Because they preach what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma, they mislead immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to grasp at the false as true. Both disciple and teacher alike sever the seed of the Buddha;
once this body has perished, both shall fall into the Avīci Hell. This is what is meant by "one blind man leading a multitude of blind men, pulling one another into [the pit]."

This is precisely what is meant by the "fire pit. The demonic teachings entice the world and indulge greed to the end; the two Buddhist teachings, however, involve relinquishing the body and severing theft.
First, one teaching involves repaying debts by relinquishing the body; second, one teaching involves completing transformation by severing theft. Regarding the first:
If, after my parinirvāṇa, there should be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind to cultivate samādhi, and who, before an image of the Tathāgata,
lights a single lamp with his own body, burns a finger joint, or applies a single stick of incense to his body;
I say that such a person has, at once, repaid their karmic debts from beginningless time; they bid a final farewell to the world and are forever liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*).
Although they have not yet clearly realized the path to supreme enlightenment, this person’s mind is already resolved upon the Dharma.

If it were not for this slight cause of sacrificing their body, even if they were to attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they would inevitably be reborn as a human being to repay those old debts—just like my horse.

In the time of King Māndhātṛ and others, there was no such thing; at the beginning, one could completely discharge one's debts. During the Buddha’s lifetime, people possessed deep wisdom and shallow afflictions; thus, some might sacrifice their bodies while others might not.
Therefore, this is specifically discussed in reference to the period after his parinirvāṇa. There are bhikṣus and others who should appropriately cultivate the practice of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
He is a human being. "To resolve the mind" means to give rise to the Mahāyāna mind. "Decisive" means being firm and unshakable.
"Cultivating samādhi" refers to practicing the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, for by this one can remotely accord with the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed bodhi and pure nirvāṇa.
The Brahmajāla Sūtra says: "If you see a newly initiated bodhisattva, you should explain to them everything..."
As for asceticism: one may burn the body, the arms, or the fingers. If one does not burn the body, arms, or fingers as an offering to the Buddhas, one is not a renunciant bodhisattva.
Thus, it is known that those who have resolved their minds and are determined to cultivate samādhi should first practice the conduct of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
Standing before an image is for the purpose of making offerings to the Buddha; it is also to rely upon and sustain the power of the Buddha to eliminate [afflictions].
This is due to the influence of past obstructions (*pūrvāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, it is for the purpose of seeking the Buddha’s witness to eliminate present attachments.
Those whose attachment-obstructions are light kindle a single lamp; those whose attachment-obstructions are heavy burn a finger-joint (referring to one segment of a finger, specifically the tip);
and those whose attachment-obstructions are moderate burn a single incense stick. Generally, whether kindling a lamp, burning a finger, or burning incense, these acts are all performed by oneself.
The degree of one's offenses depends on the lightness or heaviness of the obstructions one clings to; the primary goal is simply to eliminate and sever them.

Even if one were unable to eliminate and sever them, though one might burn one’s entire body as an offering to the Buddha, the Buddha would not accept it; one would merely undergo extreme suffering in vain, with no benefit whatsoever.
If, moreover, one seeks fame or profit through this, it is called further increasing the greed of theft, which is a grave evil.

This is even more profound. My statement—that it is clearly sealed by the Buddha’s own personal certification and thus cannot be false—is because those karmic debts from beginningless time that are settled all at once refer to all outstanding debts from the beginningless past up to this present life;
through the empowerment of the Buddha's power, they are all settled at once, for this constitutes true diligence.

Because one makes offerings to all Tathāgatas with the true Dharma, this is spoken in terms of eliminating hindrances. When ego-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) is exhausted, the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are forever severed;
hence it is said, "one takes a long farewell from the world. A "long farewell" means a permanent parting. When clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is exhausted, ignorance (*avidyā*) also perishes;
hence it is said, "one is forever liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*). "Forever liberated" encompasses the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*). This is spoken in terms of exhaustion.

To speak of this directly: although it is said that obstacles are dissolved, one still relies upon the Buddha’s empowerment; although it is said that attachments are exhausted, they are merely the emptiness of essence.
This is because one has not yet been able to open the subtle ear-gate, nor has one attained the immediate illumination of the path to Unsurpassed Enlightenment.

For the path to Unsurpassed Enlightenment—consisting of the fifty-five stages—is a matter occurring only after the stage of Perfect Penetration. Thus, regarding these dharmas, this person has already...

A "resolute mind" refers to the state of self-realizing that one's obstructions are exhausted and, while holding to emptiness, having faith and knowledge that one will certainly attain [enlightenment] through any of the various dharma-gates of perfect penetration;

it is a mind free from doubt and hesitation. "If one does not descend, one must not abandon [the vow] and must surely repay [the debt]"—to say one "does not do so" means being attached to the notion of "self" and "what belongs to the self," being unable to sacrifice one's body as an offering, and failing to obtain the empowerment of the Buddha's power. Thus he spoke.

The "subtle cause" refers to speaking of the cause in relation to its fruit; thus, the cause is subtle. This is because it can suddenly eliminate past obstructions and attain a mind of certainty as its primary function.
Even if one attains the unconditioned (*asamskrta*), one may still be reborn among humans to repay karmic debts, because past obstructions have not yet been entirely eliminated.
Fearing that others might lack faith, [the Buddha] cites his own past events as proof (according to the *Udānavarga*).

Formerly, in the city of Vairaṇyā in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, King Ajātaśatru invited the Buddha and five hundred bhikṣus for a three-month period of offerings and almsgiving. At that time, a Māra deluded the king’s mind; he entered the palace and became addicted to the five desires, so that the offerings lasted only six days.

Furthermore, as the region was suffering from famine, the monks were unable to obtain almsfood. There was then a horse trainer who reduced his own portion of barley by half to provide for the Buddha and the Saṅgha until the ninety days had passed. Only then did the king awaken to his error and seek repentance before the Buddha. Śāriputra asked about the causes and conditions of this, and the Buddha said: "In the past, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, there was a king who invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha.

After the Buddha and the Saṅgha had finished eating, [the king] requested a portion of food on behalf of a sick bhikṣu and sent it over a mountain to a brahmin. When the brahmin smelled the fragrance, he reviled them, saying: 'These shaven-headed śramaṇas ought to eat this!'"

"Barley? How can it compare to delicacies? He taught five hundred youths, and they spoke in the same manner. At that time, the brahmin was my current self; the five hundred youths are now the five hundred arhats. Thus, even because of past insults toward the Buddha and the Sangha, one cannot escape retribution;

how much more so for stealing another's wealth or violating their person? One must naturally repay such debts. However, one must know that a manifested Buddha does not belong to the realm of karmic birth, and the True Buddha transcends all sensory measurements. Whom, then, could one call upon to receive retribution?

This is because [the Buddha] manifested the existence of karmic retribution for the sake of sentient beings who create karma, in order to instill in them a sense of dread; thus, he now cites this to prove that past debts must inevitably be repaid, and furthermore, to show that one must not fail to cultivate the practice of renunciation.
The second teaching establishes transformation by means of severing theft.

You teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi* first, and only thereafter to sever theft; this is called the third definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
If one does not relinquish the body, one will ultimately have to repay past debts; therefore, the instruction was given to teach the world how to sever theft.

By severing theft, there will be no debt to be repaid, and thus there is no need to relinquish the body. The statement that [theft] is to be severed later indicates that sexual misconduct is a fixed obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whereas killing violates compassion (*maitrī*);
therefore, it should be severed first. The phrase "and so forth" indicates that such a teaching is in accord with the Tathāgata’s intent.
The ritual for purification has been brought forth, and thus the path of transformation is accomplished.

Having completed the preliminary arrangements for the rites of the heterodox Buddhist teachings, there are three points for determining the true and the semblance of *samādhi*: first, that which is uninterrupted ultimately belongs to semblance-determination;
second, that which severs [the continuity] is called true. Regarding the first:
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not cease stealing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person pouring water into a leaking cup hoping to fill it;
even if they pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be restored.

It can be understood from the preceding invocation of the name. Although one may practice dhyāna without abandoning theft, it ultimately belongs to a semblance of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Fearing that this may still not be clear, the point is clarified through a metaphor. For example, "a person" represents the individual who practices dhyāna while still harboring theft; "a cup of wine" refers to the vessel [of the semblance of concentration].
The leaking cup is a metaphor for a mind harboring theft; the water is a metaphor for the water of the principle of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

To pour the water of the principle of meditative concentration into a mind harboring theft while hoping to achieve perfect penetration is like pouring water into a leaking cup while seeking to fill it.

As the water is poured, it leaks away accordingly; even through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, there will never be restoration. This is a metaphor for being scattered just as one attains concentration.
One will ultimately be unable to achieve meditative concentration; what is called "semblance samādhi" is not true samādhi.
Only when one has severed these two forms of theft can it be called genuine.

If, O bhikṣus, you do not store even a fraction of what remains from your robes and alms bowls, and give whatever remains from your begging for food to hungry sentient beings, [you shall attain true concentration].
In the great assembly, one should join the palms and pay homage to the multitude; if someone strikes or reviles one, it should be regarded as identical to praise.
One must ensure that both body and mind are completely relinquished, sharing one’s own flesh, bones, and blood with all sentient beings.
One must not take the Tathāgata’s teachings of provisional meaning and twist them into one's own interpretations to mislead beginners. The Buddha seals such a person as having attained true samādhi.
At the outset, one encounters those with the capacity for instruction. As for "those bhikṣus," this refers to those bhikṣus who may exist during the final age.
They must certainly not lack the three robes and the alms-bowl; as for anything beyond these, they do not accumulate even the slightest fraction of it.
Such persons will certainly not steal the clothing or belongings of others, but will wander from place to place begging for food, accepting whatever is obtained.
Supporting their own bodies, they would even give away any remaining parts to hungry sentient beings. Such persons will certainly not steal the food of others.

They constantly join their palms in prostration before the fourfold assembly within great congregations, realizing deeply that all people are equal as Buddhas through the realization of true reality (*tathatā*).
Such persons will certainly not harm others for their own benefit. If there is someone...

If one receives with joy and acceptance being reviled, beaten, or scolded—treating such treatment no differently than praise—it is because one has deeply realized that enemies and kin are of one essence and that honor and disgrace are irrelevant. Such a person will certainly not harm others for their own sake;
these are the types of individuals who can be taught. One must ensure that when encountering such a disciple, the teaching is imparted so that they may practice it deeply.
One should be taught to cultivate this deeply; hence it is said that one must "certainly cause both body and mind to be equally renounced.
This merely means that for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, one does not spare even toil and hardship. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra, states:
"May my thoughts continue in succession without interruption, and may my actions of body, speech, and mind never grow weary. The two lines concerning the body and flesh are the ultimate [conclusion].

Pushing this to its ultimate limit, one advances with instruction. This means that not only do both [the teacher and student] renounce [self-interest] without sparing labor or hardship, but they must certainly cause their own flesh, bones, and blood to be offered through vows to share with all sentient beings.

If one can truly act in this way, how could there ever again be acts of theft committed for one's own sake, or thoughts of theft conceived within one's own mind? ○ [The section beginning with] "Not taking... [follows].

The four fetters depend on whether one conforms to or opposes what is correct or erroneous.
That which is spoken by me is called the word of the Buddha; that which is not spoken in this way is the word of Pāpīyān.

The Fourth Precept Against False Speech (Zhengmo states: There are two types of false speech. To speak words that are untrue constitutes minor false speech; to falsely claim to have realized the fruits of the path constitutes major false speech. That which is severed here is major false speech). Four parts: First, a detailed exposition of the harms of false speech;
