Second, a preliminary clarification of the Tathāgata’s pedagogical methods; Third, a definitive determination regarding the possibility of realizing the fruits;

Fourth, a concluding judgment on compliance versus violation, and the heterodox versus the orthodox. Part One (In the previous three precepts, the benefits and harms of both maintaining and violating were presented together. Herein—):

The reason for not explicitly stating that [the roots] are "held" (*dhṛta*) or "beneficial" (*hitā*) has two meanings: first, to avoid excessive prolixity; second, because it can be understood by analogy with what precedes. Third, [the section on the cutting off of the roots of goodness] consists of three parts: first, following the previous discussion to indicate the harm; second, listing and explaining the meaning of the words;
third, concluding by pointing to the cutting off of the roots of goodness. First:

Ānanda, it is thus with the sentient beings of the six realms in this world: although their bodies and minds may be free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—such that these three practices are already perfected—if they engage in great falsehood, their *samādhi* will not attain purity; they will become demons of craving and views and lose the seed of the Tathāgata.
"Those who are thus" refers collectively to the aforementioned three types of people who have already abandoned lust, killing, and stealing.

Since they have not yet fully realized [the nature of] birth and death and still belong among those within the world—whether they have resolved their minds from the heavenly realm or resolved their minds from the human realm—they are called "sentient beings of the six paths.
When body and mind are free from killing, the practice of compassion is perfected; when body and mind are free from lust, it is Brahma-... [purity].

The practice of renunciation (*tyāga*) is accomplished. When body and mind are free from theft, the practice of renunciation is fulfilled; therefore, it is said that "the three practices are already perfected.
Previously, it was granted that one would transcend birth and death (*saṃsāra*); now, because this [falsehood] seeks to seize that [attainment], the words "even though" and so forth are employed.
If one commits a great falsehood (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*), one's non-birth in *saṃsāra* is immediately seized. As for "samādhi being impure," it is because there still remains...
Because the mind craves offerings, long-standing craving causes deluded attachment to intensify daily; long-standing delusion causes false views to arise secretly.

Thus, Māra finds his opportunity, and his essence flies to possess the body, resulting in the formation of the Māras of craving and views. Once they have become Māras, they do not realize it themselves;
while alive they are like those in a drunken dream, and at death they sink into the abyss. Even if the Buddhas appear in the world, it is difficult for them to provide salvation.
Sunk forever in birth and death, they have no prospect of seeking liberation; thus it is said that they have "lost the lineage of the Tathāgata.
Second, the explanation of the meaning of the listed statements:

this refers to those who claim to have attained what they have not attained, or say they have realized what they have not realized, or who seek worldly eminence and supremacy, as mentioned previously.
People say, "I have now attained the fruit of a srotāpanna, the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of an anāgāmin, the path of an arhat,
or the vehicle of a pratyekabuddha," or they claim to be bodhisattvas at various stages prior to or within the ten bhūmis. [They] seek prostrations and repentance from others,
coveting their offerings.

First, the terms are listed individually. The phrase "so-called" (*yǒu suǒwèi*) is a term used to introduce an explanation; it points to what is listed below and explains the aforementioned "great false speech.
As for what is called "great false speech," what are its words? They are precisely such things as "claiming to have attained what one has not attained," and so forth.
Regarding "claiming to have attained what one has not attained": this refers to one who has not attained *bodhi* yet claims to oneself that one has already attained *bodhi*.
"Ti. Regarding "claiming to have realized what has not been realized": this refers to one who, having not realized *nirvāṇa*, says of themselves, "I have already realized *nirvāṇa*.
Later, [the text] asks, "How much more so for the Dharma King? and thus bitterly rebukes such false usurpation. Alternatively, regarding "seeking worldly [attainments]," etc.:
This refers to those who do not dare to falsely claim *bodhi* or *nirvāṇa*, but merely seek to be honored as the most supreme and excellent within the world.
For this reason, it is said that they speak of what is currently before them. What do they say?
It means that among ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), they see only the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) as superior, and thus claim for themselves that they have already attained it.

Regarding the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*): next, within the state of a stream-enterer, because they perceive another fruit as superior, they claim for themselves that they have already attained the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).

Next, within the state of a once-returner, because they perceive another fruit as superior, they claim for themselves that they have already attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). Next, within the state of a non-returner, they perceive yet another fruit as superior...
Because they consider themselves superior, they claim to have already attained the path of an Arhat.
Next, because they see the Pratyekabuddhas and Solitary Realizers as superior among the Arhats, they claim to have already attained the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha.
Finally, because they see the Mahāyāna as superior within the Hīnayāna, they claim to have already attained the rank of a Sage of the Ten Stages or those prior to the stages.
The various stages of the three sages and the bodhisattvas—later, when it says "how could one claim for oneself the dharmas of a superior person?"—it is a pointed rebuke of this very point.
The final two lines provide a general explanation of its meaning, stating that such a person must necessarily utter such great false speech;
this is because they seek to have those before them prostrate and repent toward themselves, thereby taking advantage of the opportunity.
This reveals that he coveted their offerings; according to this, it is not merely false speech but also includes theft.
Therefore, the subsequent text designates this as an *ānantarya* (immediate) offense. The third bond refers to the severing of the roots of goodness.
Such an icchantika extinguishes the seed of the Buddhas. It is like a person cutting down a tāla tree with a sword;

the Buddha has declared that such a person’s roots of goodness are forever destroyed, they shall have no further knowledge or vision, and they will sink into the sea of the three sufferings, never attaining samādhi.
This first case specifically refers to one who severs the roots of goodness. With his mouth he utters false speech, and with his mind he covets offerings;
thus, the sins of falsehood combined with theft cause him to lose the roots of goodness forever. Therefore, it is said that this is an *icchantika*. *Icchantika* is also called *ichantidai*;

this translates as "one who has severed the roots of goodness. Since the roots of goodness are severed, there is no possibility of attaining Buddhahood; hence it is said that the seeds of the Buddha are extinguished.
This is illustrated by way of an analogy: to the north of the kingdom of Jālandhara in South India, there is a Tāla forest extending over thirty li.
The leaves of these trees are long, broad, and glossy; no country for writing employs them more than this one.
If that tree were cut with a blade, it would not grow back again. Now, taking this as a metaphor, it refers to those who sever their roots of goodness and extinguish the seed of the Buddha.

The Buddha’s prediction (vyākaraṇa) follows below, which uses the Dharma to provide the application. He specifically uses the term "Buddha’s prediction" to manifest that it is certain and without deviation.
Their roots of goodness are forever destroyed, and they no longer possess right knowledge or right view. This is precisely what is meant by: [The text continues...]

"To extinguish the Buddha-seed" corresponds to the aforementioned "cutting down the tala tree. "Sinking into the ocean of the three sufferings" means to be submerged in the cycle of birth and death within the triple world;

even if one possesses meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they will all serve as the karma of Māra, and thus it is said that "one does not achieve samādhi. This concludes the first section:

the exposition on the harm of false speech. Second, the preliminary clarification of the Tathāgata’s ritual protocols (as for the failure to distinguish demonic teachings and the like, since the orthodox teaching has already been clarified, [the demonic is understood by implication]).

(4) Not being deluded by the teachings of Māra and others. First, the Buddha’s command to transform beings through the secret teaching of the two vehicles. Second, as commanded, gathering and transforming beings without leaking [the truth].
Third, preventing inquiries by responding opportunistically with refutations. Fourth, using the teaching to sever delusions so as to accomplish transformation. First:
After my parinirvāṇa, I shall command all bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest their bodies within that age of the final dharma;
assuming various forms, they shall deliver those wandering in the cycle of rebirth.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Māra will be powerful and the Dharma weak;

therefore, he commanded Bodhisattvas and Arhats to manifest their transformation bodies there to pull back the Dharma of the Final Age and support the True Teaching, to crush heterodox sects and save sentient beings.

Those who assume various forms appear in accordance with the categories of beings to deliver those wandering in saṃsāra and cause them to transcend birth and death—namely, whatever body they should manifest.
Regarding those who have attained deliverance, he manifests whatever body is required to preach the Dharma. Second, as commanded, he gathers and nurtures sentient beings without fail;
he may appear as a śramaṇa, a layperson (śrāvaka), a householder, a king, a high official, a boy, or a girl—and even as a courtesan, a widow, a thief, a butcher, or a merchant.
In these capacities, he engages in their common activities, praising the Buddha Vehicle and causing them to... [attain it].

The mind enters samādhi. One must never say of oneself, "I am a true Bodhisattva" or "I am a true Arhat," lest one leak the Buddha’s secret causes and speak lightly of those who have recently studied.
First, both the forward and reverse orders are manifested together. "Manifesting as equals" refers to assuming various forms just as the Buddha commanded.
"Śramaṇas" refers to the two groups of those who have left the household life; "white-robed ones" refers to the two groups of laypeople.
Laymen and even maidens are all as described among the thirty-two manifestations. This is the practice of the forward order. As for courtesans and widows, they are like [the case of] Dharmodgata.
Those such as mother and daughter; those who engage in debauchery, theft, slaughter, or trade, like Aṅgulimāla—these are examples of "inverse conduct" (nigamana).
To "share the same activities" with them means to guide and transform them through *sāmānyārtha* (sharing the same purpose), which is one of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

This refers to the fact that one shares in their activities—whether inverse or conforming, defiled or pure—and so forth. Zhengmo says: "If one shares their class but does not share their activities, then..."
Because their minds were perverse and they would not comply with him, he temporarily joined them in their activities, intending to win their favor so that he might praise the Buddha Vehicle to them.

He thereby transformed those in the group of the wrongly fixed (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*) and those in the unsettled group (*aniyata-rāśi*), causing them to attain the rightly fixed group (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*).
Therefore, it is said: "He causes their bodies and minds to enter *samādhi*. [He] never degrades himself.
To leak such words—specifically, if one claims for oneself to be a true Bodhisattva or a true Arhat—one will inevitably disclose the reasons behind the Buddha’s secret instructions.
To speak lightly in this manner to students of the末法 (mofa/declining dharma) era results in two faults.

First, it would cause those with deluded thoughts to seek external reinforcement rather than apply themselves to genuine cultivation. Second, it would lead them to loftily defer to the sacred realm, thereby engendering self-imposed stagnation.
For these reasons, I did not speak of it myself. Third, it was to prevent questions that might have been used as an opportunity to issue a formal censure.
"Except for the case where, at the end of life, one leaves behind a physical legacy. How does such a person delude the masses and commit a great falsehood?

This is the first preventative inquiry. (This is included because there might be those who ask: "If these are transformed sages and worthies who descend to provide teachings and models, and do not personally leak [their own words], by what means are they to inspire faith in future generations? Therefore, the World-Honored One provides this preventative measure.)
It is said that when sages and worthies who manifest through transformation wish to inspire faith in future generations, they do so except at the moment of their passing;
yet even then, they must not reveal [the truth] too clearly, but may only entrust it within the hidden and subtle.
This is like the case of Fenggan’s loquacity or Dushun’s display of verses. [The text asks: "How is this?"—this concludes the refutation. Since it is merely...
It is permitted that life may end; this is merely the transfer of the aggregates (*skandhas*).

How can it be that such a person, before the moment of death has even arrived, openly proclaims themselves [to be enlightened]? This truly deludes and confuses sentient beings and constitutes a great falsehood (*mṛṣāvāda*).
The agonizing suffering of the Avīci hell will arrive before one knows it. The Four Teachings establish transformation by severing falsehood.
"You shall teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi, and thereafter eliminate all great false speech.
This is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past."

The Buddha’s instruction for the two vehicles is thus: when you teach worldly people to cultivate samādhi, they must, after having already severed the three preceding [precepts], further sever the great lie; only then will it accord with the Tathāgata’s pure and clear exhortation.

The preceding section constitutes the fourth [chapter]. Having completed the preliminary clarification of the Tathāgata’s pedagogical system, the third [section] concerns the determination of whether or not the fruit can be realized, which has two parts: first, that one cannot realize the fruit if [delusion] is not severed;
second, that one can achieve it only by severing delusion. Regarding the first:
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever this great false speech, it is like carving human excrement into the shape of sandalwood;
to seek its fragrance is impossible. I teach the bhikṣus that the hall of the direct mind is such that even within all actions during the four modes of deportment, there is no pretense whatsoever.
How then could one claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior man? It is like a pauper...
Ordinary people delusively style themselves emperors or kings and bring about their own execution and destruction; how much more so for the Dharma King—how could one delusively usurp his title?
If the ground is not true, the fruit will be crooked and obstructed. To seek the Bodhi of the Buddha while in such a state is like a person trying to bite their own navel—who can achieve anything?
The first analogy clarifies the inability [to achieve the goal]. One who practices dhyāna with the desire to attain bodhi, yet does not sever delusion, possesses a body of sin and evil.
To practice dhyāna with such a sinful body while desiring to attain bodhi is for cause and effect to be discordant;
therefore, it is illustrated by the analogy of carving human excrement into sandalwood. Although its form resembles sandalwood, its odor is actually foul.
It is evil; therefore, it is impossible to seek fragrant scents from it. This is a metaphor for those who practice meditation while harboring delusions:

though their outward appearance resembles that of a fellow practitioner of the Dharma, their inner confusion is actually identical to that of a demonic host. Thus, they can never hope to realize the fruits of the path or achieve liberation.
In my teaching, I have severely censured such transgressions. The Buddha’s intention was precisely that one cannot achieve Bodhi without severing false speech.
Therefore, since the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in ancient times, I have already instructed all bhikṣus to take a straightforward mind as the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
As the *Avataṃsaka* says: "The wondrous Dharma-tree of Bodhi grows from the ground of a straightforward mind. And as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* says: "Straightforward..."
"The mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) because it is free from falsehood. As previously stated, "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same path;

they all transcend birth and death by means of the straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*), and so forth. All such passages convey the meaning that the straightforward mind constitutes the site of enlightenment.
The four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) refer to walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. "All practices" refers to the practice gates of the two vehicles (*yāna*). It says:

“Bhikṣu Zun, you have followed my instructions. Within the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, and within the practice-gates of the two vehicles, if something exists, you say it exists;
if it does not exist, you say it does not exist. You do not harbor even a hair’s breadth of falsehood.

How can such a person intentionally violate the Buddha’s command and falsely claim to have attained the various superhuman states (uttara-manuṣya-dharma), such as that of a Srotāpanna? The gravity of his transgression is beyond measure.”
"How excellent are these words! For instance, the analogy of the destitute person is employed to manifest their transgression.

Because samādhi has not yet been accomplished and their inherent virtues have not yet been manifested, they are compared to a destitute person. While their inherent virtues remain unmanifested, they claim for themselves the status of sages."

Therefore, the false assumption of the title of "Emperor" is used as a metaphor. One who falsely assumes the title of Emperor brings upon themselves the calamity of execution and the destruction of their clan;
this serves as a metaphor for one who claims to be a "Worthy Sage" (xian-sheng) bringing upon themselves rebirth in Avīci Hell—the loss of the Dharma-body and the severance of wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, the two subsequent phrases express the principle of using the light to illustrate the heavy: they state that even the Worthy Sages of the Three Vehicles may not be stolen from.
How much more so for the names of Bodhi and Nirvana, which are the positions of the supramundane Dharma King!

How can one who has not attained them claim to have attained them, or who has not realized them declare that they have realized them, thus falsely usurping these titles? It should be known that their transgressions and evils are even more severe.
Because of this, it is concluded below that such a person is incapable; to call oneself a superior person while falsely usurping the title of Dharma King is entirely empty and false.

Because it is false, it is said that "the ground of practice is not true. Previously, it was stated that because the mind and speech are straightforward, from this point up through the intermediate stages of the grounds, there will forever be no signs of deviousness.
Now, since the ground of practice is not true, the resulting fruit will naturally entail circuitous detours.
Thus, while originally intending to achieve Buddhahood, one instead flows into the realms of Māras and externalists; in life one encounters the king’s law, and at death one falls into the hells.
This is a prison; how could it be anything other than a devious detour? A person such as this, though seeking Bodhi, will ultimately never reach it.

Therefore, it is said: "like a person trying to bite their own navel. "Bite" (shì) means to chew with the mouth. Since the mouth and the navel are far apart, one cannot reach them even if one tries to bite them.
This is a metaphor for how, due to delusion, one seeks the true reality, yet ultimately cannot realize it. Even if a Buddha were to appear in the world, it would be difficult to save such a person.
Therefore it is said: "Whom do you wish to accomplish? One who does not sever [delusion] cannot realize the fruit.
Only by severing delusions can one achieve accomplishment.
If the minds of bhikṣus are as straight as a bowstring, entirely true, and they enter samādhi, there will never be any demonic interference.
I certify that this person shall achieve the unsurpassed enlightenment of a bodhisattva.
"The mind is like a straight bowstring" means that the mind is as straight as a bowstring.
Since the mind is the master of the four modes of deportment, when the mind is like a straight bowstring, all the gates of practice within the four dignified postures are entirely true and real.
This refers to being forever free from all signs of crookedness. Regarding "entering samādhi and being forever free from demonic activities":
the conduct of demons is perilous and deviant; now, because the mind proceeds directly and uprightly, the true demons find no opportunity.

This means that one achieves the unsurpassed awakening of a bodhisattva, such that demons cannot disturb them; it is the achievement of the bodhisattva’s perfect and penetrating mind. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) says:
The unsurpassed awakening of a bodhisattva is precisely the mind of the true causal ground of perfect penetration;
yet, because the cause determines the fruit, this is also the unsurpassed bodhi that definitively establishes whether or not the realization of the fruit will be attained.
The fourfold judgment distinguishes between dependence and independence, and between the heterodox and the orthodox.
What I have taught is called the teaching of the Buddha; that which is not taught in this way is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
As for what I have taught: if there are people in the final age who possess the three precepts as I have taught them—
Furthermore, if one subsequently teaches the severance of delusions, this is called the Buddha’s teaching; one should immediately follow it.

If it is not taught in this way—for instance, if it says that since the three preceding types of false speech have already been severed, they need not be further severed, or if it says that when meditative wisdom (*dhyāna-jñāna*) manifests, false speech should seemingly pose no obstacle—this is the teaching of Pāpīyān (Māra). One should thoroughly reject it. This is what the Tathāgata intended to convey.
Ānanda transmits the Tathāgata’s words to the Dharma-ending age to protect those who practice authentically, ensuring that celestial Māras find no opportunity.
This concludes the separate clarification on upholding the precepts.
*The Finger-Possessing Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll Six;
*The Finger-Possessing Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
Respectfully composed by the junior disciple Dàtiāntōnglǐ of Xiánzōng at Niànhuá Monastery in the Capital.
The Dharma-heir (Xingzong Zuwang Tengqing Huairen Zuyu Jiaozi), Third Successor, shows how to distance oneself from demons in three parts.
First: maintaining the root and severing the branches. Second: cutting off worldly dust and distancing oneself from demons. Regarding the first:
Ānanda, regarding your question on the gathering of the mind: I shall now first explain the sublime gateway for training in entering samādhi to seek the Bodhisattva path.

One must first maintain these four kinds of restraint as clearly as ice and frost; then, all secondary branches [of transgression] will naturally fail to arise, and the three of the mind and four of the body will have no cause to be produced.

As previously stated, Ānanda asked: "Desiring to collect the mind and enter *samādhi*, how should one establish the site of practice (*maṇḍala*) so as to remain far removed from all demonic activities?
Since this was for the purpose of collecting the mind and entering *samādhi*, the Tathāgata steadied his intention and provided the instructions.
His meaning was that your previous question to me regarding the method for collecting the mind was intended—

Entering samādhi: what I have previously taught (referring to the four kinds of clear instructions) is precisely the most wondrous gateway for beginners to practice the gathering of the mind when entering samādhi. Therefore, for all who seek the bodhisattva path, [this is essential].
One must first maintain these four kinds of restraint, ensuring that body and mind are as pure and bright as ice or frost.
If this is so, then the roots are already withered, for lust, killing, stealing, and lying belong to the fundamental precepts.

Once the roots are withered, the branches and leaves have nothing to rely upon; therefore it is said that they cannot grow of their own accord. As for the three mental [transgressions], exclude those mentioned previously.
The three [karmas] of sexual misconduct, killing, and stealing; and all other differentiated afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion;

the four [vocal karmas], which, excluding the aforementioned great falsehood, include all other differentiated evil karmas such as lying, frivolous speech, harsh speech, and divisive speech—all these are merely branches and leaves.
Therefore, it is said that birth must have no cause. Based on this, one should strictly maintain [the precepts].
It is indeed appropriate to call these four prohibitions the sublime gateway for cultivation and study. Second, severing worldly dust and distancing oneself from demons:
Ānanda, if one does not neglect these four matters, the mind will no longer take as its objects form, sound, fragrance, taste, or touch;
how then could any demonic activities arise?
Among the four matters, if there is even a slight failure to maintain them, it is called "loss. If there is no loss, the mind dwells constantly in the precepts;
even when encountering sensory objects, it will no longer flow away or stray. Therefore, it is said that the mind does not even take as its conditions form, sound, smell, taste, or touch.
Of the six sense-objects, these four are mentioned because the remaining two can be understood by analogy. How, then, are all demonic activities [to be understood]?

Regarding the occurrence [of such thoughts]: it is stated with certainty that they can never arise, because when a demon relies on sensory objects (*viṣaya*) to enter, the objects do not serve as conditions for them, and thus the demon finds no opportunity.
Having thus instructed him to maintain the precepts to keep the demon at a distance, there are three further points: first, to have him recite mantras to eliminate habitual tendencies;
second, to point out to others and encourage them to recite mantras; and third, to demonstrate the efficacy of the mantras through their proven power. Furthermore—
To manifest that there is no difficulty in eliminating habitual tendencies: First, if there are those with past habitual tendencies whom you cannot eliminate,
you should teach such persons to single-mindedly recite my supreme divine mantra, the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa-vijaya-mahā-sātrapatra.
"Latent habits" (*pūrva-śruta-vāsanā*) refer to the seeds and habitual tendencies of deluded karma from past lives. They move spontaneously and cannot be restrained;

they are not like present karma, which can be extinguished solely through the power of observing the precepts. There are indeed those who maintain the precepts throughout their entire lives yet suddenly lose their resolve;
this is surely due to the influence of latent habits. One must therefore obtain divine mantras and not harbor [doubts].

Only through the power of deliberation can [afflictions] be eradicated; therefore, I exhort them to recite mantras. These mantras were spoken by the Transformation Buddhas from the Light on the Crown of the Head;
thus they are called "Buddhōṣṇīṣa-prabhā" (Light of the Buddha’s Crown). Furthermore, these are employed to symbolize the meaning of being honored and supreme, and of destroying delusions.
*Mahā-sattva-tra-pantra*. This is translated as "The Great White Parasol Canopy. "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*;

it is vast horizontally and exhaustive vertically, for it is great and without exterior. "White" (*śveta*) refers to the characteristics of the *tathāgatagarbha*; it possesses virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, for it is pure and unstained.
"Parasol Canopy" (*chatra*) refers to the function of the *tathāgatagarbha*; it gives birth to the Buddha-dharmas and provides shelter and protection.

Because it pertains to all sentient beings, and since it is identical to the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, one can attain Buddhahood by upholding it; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
Furthermore, its divine efficacy is inconceivable and no other mantra can surpass it—this too is the meaning of "unsurpassed. To recite the mantra while saying "with a single mind" means:

There is the phenomenal aspect (*vastu*) and the noumenal aspect (*tattva*). Regarding the phenomenal aspect, single-mindedness means that pure mindfulness continues in succession without being intermingled with various conditions.

Regarding the noumenal aspect, single-mindedness means clearly contemplating the hidden nature (*garbhadhātu-svabhāva*), such that thought ceases and subject and object are eliminated. This is because the mantra is a "mind-mantra"; it cannot be brought into resonance unless one is single-minded. Practice arises from the mind;
only by fully understanding the mind can [afflictions] be extinguished. When both the phenomenal and the noumenal are maintained together, [enlightenment] is accomplished.
The merit is easy to attain and the efficacy is swift. The second finger’s incantation is verified as effective;
this is the heart-mantra spoken by the Tathāgata from atop the Lotus Jewel Throne, emanating radiance from his invisible crown-mark (uṣṇīṣa) and the unconditioned mind-Buddha.
Furthermore, you and Mātangi have shared karmic conditions and bonds of affection throughout successive kalpas.
This power is not limited to a single lifetime or a single kalpa. Once I have proclaimed it, those with hearts of attachment shall forever be liberated and become arhats.

The initial reference to the mantra reveals its excellence; this refers to the superior mantra above, while the subsequent reference reveals what follows below. As for "the Tathāgata," etc., this reveals...
The speaker is supreme; it is said that the Tathāgata is most excellent, his vision is most wondrous, and his uṣṇīṣa-mark is most venerable.
The "unconditioned mind-Buddha" refers to the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) of the light from the crown.

Because this transformation Buddha of the crown-light manifests from the unconditioned mind of the Tathāgata, the three phrases beginning with "from the crown" reveal the supremacy of the mantra being taught. "From the crown" means from the transformation Buddha.

"From the crown" (*mūrdhan*): "emitting radiance" means emitting light again and again. Later it says, "from the crown, ten paths of light of a hundred jewels are emitted," because this indicates that the mantra being taught has the meaning of destroying delusion and accomplishing wisdom. "Seated upon a jewel lotus" refers to the emanation-buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*);
later it says, "there is an emanation-tathāgata seated within a jewel flower. The earlier statement, "within the light, a thousand-petaled jewel lotus is produced," [refers to this].

There is a transformation body of a Buddha, seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), manifesting the meaning that the spells he has taught possess the principle of the cause being realized through the seal of the fruit.
As for the "spells that accord with the mind" he has taught, they are the heart-seals (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas, for their essence is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
[The text continues: "Furthermore, you... [and so on], testing that they are efficacious; the power of these divine spells is inconceivable. For the time being, let us proceed...
One may verify this through recent events; thus it is said, "for now. The event occurs in the present time, while the causal conditions stem from the past;
hence it is called a "prior-life" (宿世) matter. According to the *Aṅgāraka-sūtra*, Ānanda was the husband of Aṅgulimālā for five hundred previous lifetimes.

The current statement regarding "causal conditions spanning kalpas" refers to this very fact: that the affection between husband and wife served as the causal condition. However, since it has already been stated...
It spans across kalpas and does not merely stop at five hundred lifetimes. Because the kindness is profound and the affection is heavy, it perfumes and conditions the mind;
from life to life and age after age, its influence is never forgotten. This is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*).

To say that it is not limited to a single lifetime or a single kalpa is to demonstrate that these habitual tendencies are so deep and substantial that they are difficult to liberate. As stated previously: "Your love for my heart, I..."

He took pity on your beauty. For this reason, throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, as soon as Ānanda and Ṭaṅga met, he ultimately reached the point of using his own body to caress her, nearly destroying his precept-body; such was the origin of his passion.
My previous statement, "I once proclaimed [the mantra]," etc., was slightly incomplete. It should have been stated fully as follows: "When Mañjuśrī held my divine mantra, as soon as..."
First, regarding the proclamation: Dengā suddenly realized the third fruit of the path; now, having forever severed her attachment to desire, she has become an Arhat.
How magnificent, then, is the power of the divine mantra! Third, it further demonstrates that there is no difficulty in eliminating habitual tendencies.
That man was a courtesan who lacked the intent for cultivation, yet through the secret assistance of spiritual power, he quickly realized the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
How much more so for you, Śrāvakas gathered here, who seek the Supreme Vehicle and are determined to attain Buddhahood—like raising a handful of dust with a favorable wind!
What difficulty or peril could there be?
Even that former courtesan, whose habitual craving was still intensely blazing and who had never applied herself to practice or cultivated remedies,
was able to swiftly realize the state of no-more-learning through the power of the Buddha’s divine mantra, which secretly nurtured her from within.
How much more so for those whose habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are subtle and thin, who already know the remedies, and who further add the recitation of divine mantras;

they should naturally eliminate their habits and attain Buddhahood. Therefore, he encourages them with such words. Those *śrāvakas* present in the assembly include both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Those in training have severed the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), while those beyond training have severed the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). This is not comparable to [the case of] Pūtigandha.
As for this courtesan, she sought the Supreme Vehicle; having already resolved her great mind, she was determined to attain Buddhahood and vowed never to regress.

She was not like Pañcaśikha (Dengjia), who lacked the intent to practice. [The phrase] "this section below should contain but does not recite the four characters 'zhoushi' (recites the mantra)" is likely an omission during the transcription process.
It is said that the Buddha’s intention was that because the courtesan had no prior cultivation, she attained realization only after receiving the mantra.
Regarding the realization of the fruit: why is it that you Śrāvakas, having resolved to attain Buddhahood, do not recite mantras?

This is intended to deeply exhort them to recite mantras in order to eliminate habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). If one indeed recites mantras, one will naturally be able to eliminate these tendencies and achieve Buddhahood;
therefore, the following uses a metaphor to clarify this: "For example, like dust," etc. Here, "minute particles" refers to the extreme subtlety of habitual tendencies. This is the correspondence.

The wind has power; this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s incantation. Just as when fine dust is scattered with a following wind, there is no dust that does not vanish, so too when habitual tendencies encounter the Buddha’s incantation, there is no tendency that is not eliminated.
What difficulty or peril could there be? This speaks most emphatically of the elimination of habitual tendencies to achieve Buddhahood, meaning there are no hardships or obstacles whatsoever.
Having first completed the instruction on distancing oneself from demons and eliminating habitual tendencies.

Second, the formal presentation of the altar-construction and the practice of the path, which has two parts: first, a brief presentation according to convenience; second, a detailed presentation in response to a request. The first [part] has two sections:
first, a brief presentation of the ritual rules for constructing the altar; second, a brief presentation of the ceremonial procedures for the practice of the path.
The first two [sections]: First, a reiterated instruction on the strict observance of the precepts; second, the recitation of mantras and the consecration of the ritual site. Regarding the first:
If there are those in the末法 (mofa) era who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they must first maintain the pure prohibitory precepts of a bhikṣu.
They must select a foremost śramaṇa whose precepts are pure to serve as their teacher. Should they not encounter a truly pure monk, [they should proceed as follows].
"You will certainly not achieve the discipline of the precepts.
In the final age, sentient beings face the intense burning of obstructive conditions; for them to cultivate *samādhi*, it cannot be done except at a site of enlightenment (*dharma-cakra*).

Therefore, you wish to sit [in meditation]. Since concentration arises from the precepts, I instruct you first to uphold the prohibitive precepts. As for calling the precepts 'prohibitions' (*jin*), it means:"

That which is prohibited by the Buddha ought to be restrained as a matter of principle, for there is not the slightest allowance for its transgression. "Clarifying" (qing) refers to clarifying the source;
"purifying" (jing) refers to purifying the flow. As stated above, this means that if one first maintains the four types of restraint, the various branches and leaves cannot arise on their own.
The reason for speaking only of maintaining the *bhikṣu* precepts is intended to lead those of the Lesser Vehicle into the Great Vehicle.
This is because the bhikṣu precepts serve as the very foundation for the bodhisattva precepts. Furthermore, there are two types of bhikṣus:
first, the bodhisattva bhikṣu; second, the śrāvaka bhikṣu. Thus, both vehicles are encompassed. The matter of upholding the precepts has already been explained in detail;
it is now presented again for convenience, and therefore is treated briefly here. As for the essential requirement of selecting a teacher, there is no need to elaborate further.
Because the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) is not easily established; it is like a mold for casting an image—the mold must necessarily be upright. Regarding the "foremost" one:

their virtue and seniority (*vṛddha*) are both prior, and they are recommended by the assembly. Such a śramaṇa can harmonize and accomplish the matter, and by using them as the preceptor (*ācārya*), the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is then successfully accomplished.
This is the truly pure Saṃgha, as described above. Even if one possesses the precepts, though they may be pure...
If one is pure but lacks seniority in virtue (*guṇa-vṛddha*), or if one possesses both virtue and seniority yet their precepts are not pure—both of these cases are not authentic.

Although they encounter [the ritual], it is as if they do not; thus, it is tantamount to not encountering it at all. There is merely the name of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual procedure), but no reality of accomplishing the task.
Therefore, it is said: "Your restraint of the precepts will certainly not be accomplished. Second, the recitation of mantras and the binding of the altar.
After the precepts have been completed, don new, clean robes, burn incense, and dwell in seclusion. Recite this divine mantra spoken by the Mind-Buddha one hundred and eight times.
Thereafter, establish the altar and set up the site of practice (*maṇḍala*).
Regarding "after the precepts have been perfected": once the vessel for the Path is complete, Māra cannot find an opportunity.

One adorns the body with new robes, perfumes the chamber with incense, and dwells in seclusion to restrain the mind. For one who recites mantras in this manner, spiritual efficacy can be attained and the habitual tendencies of delusion are easily eliminated.
"Universally settling the one hundred and eight" signifies the delusions and habitual tendencies that are to be remedied.

Regarding the number: because all sentient beings possess one hundred and eight afflictions, delusions, and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the method for establishing the boundary and the ritual site is as clearly explained in detail below.
Furthermore, there are two reasons why one must first recite mantras when establishing the boundary and the ritual site:
first, to purify the faculties by treating the habitual tendencies, so that the altar rites may manifest; second, to rely on the divine power of the mantras to keep distant all [obstacles].

Regarding the works of Māra: those who are determined to practice the Path must not remain ignorant of them. Having briefly shown the ritual rules for binding the maṇḍala, there follows the second section:

a brief indication of the ritual procedures for practicing the Path. This consists of three parts: first, seeking the Buddha’s empowerment; second, making vows within the site; [and third, the concluding rites].
The third path of practice is to invoke the Buddha. First (according to the subsequent text, this corresponds to the initial seven [stages]):
one seeks for the unsurpassed Tathāgatas currently residing in the lands of the ten directions to emit the light of great compassion and pour it over one’s crown.
According to the subsequent text, during the first seven days, there was prostration to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, as well as the recitation of mantras and circumambulation of the maṇḍala;

yet, the object of his request was not revealed. Now, however, only the object of his request is revealed, while the acts of prostration and recitation are not mentioned. In both cases, the preceding and succeeding accounts imply one another by way of ellipsis:

that the request was not made in vain, but necessarily relied upon prostration and recitation. These acts of prostration and recitation were no different from those performed for the purpose of seeking empowerment (abhiṣeka).

If one were to explain its meaning: seeking to move the mind toward ritual recitation with the expectation that a response will certainly be granted—this pertains to the "one who can evoke" (the practitioner).

"The ten directions" refers to east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below. "Presently abiding" means currently seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and having attained equal and perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Unsurpassed" means perfectly real, most venerable, transcending provisional and gradual methods—this pertains to the "one who is evoked" (the Buddha). Light...
It is emitted from the mind of great compassion; therefore, it is called "emitting the light of great compassion. This belongs to the responsive capacity (*nirmāṇakāya*).
As for the light coming to anoint their crowns: the light anoints them to increase their faith, and great compassion removes their obscurations, crowning both body and mind.

To consecrate their crowns brings benefit to both body and mind; this is what is appropriate. When the resonance between the practitioner and the response of the deity intersects, one may practice the Way without anxiety.
Second, making vows within the ritual arena (as per the later text, this occurs during the second seven-day period).

Ānanda, in this way, pure bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, or laywomen in the final age who extinguish lustful desire in their hearts and uphold the Buddha’s pure precepts shall give rise to the bodhisattva vow within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

Regarding the initial permission granted to the fourfold assembly: "in such a manner" refers to what I have explained above—that the establishment of boundaries and the construction of the altar are permitted for bhikṣus alone in this way.
Once the ritual procedures of the altar are completed, however, there are no restrictions on practice; therefore, permission is granted to nuns and others.
This refers specifically to the final age, as the purpose of establishing the altar and practicing the Way was originally for the sake of sentient beings in the final age.
The two groups who have left the household life have long been established in the observance of the precepts; therefore, they are collectively termed "the pure.
The *dānapati* (donors) are the two groups who remain in the household; as they do not wear dyed robes, they are collectively termed "white-robed ones" (*avadātavasana*).

However, regarding the establishment of boundaries (*sīmā*) and the construction of shrines (*caitya*), these are permitted only for *bhikṣus*, because the *bhikṣuṇī* community lacks the capacity for administrative management, and the white-robed laity lack the knowledge to demarcate boundaries. [End of] Platform.

Regarding the phrase "accomplishing cultivation" and the general permission for all four assemblies: because all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, all are capable of cultivation. *Zhengmo* (The Correct Pulse) states:
"Although there is no selection between monastics and laypeople, or men and women, each must certainly follow their own kind; they are not to be mixed together in a single assembly.
Regarding the section beginning with "the mind ceases," which strictly enjoins the precepts and the arousal of vows: the two lines concerning "the mind ceasing" are, at first glance—
This refers collectively to the fourfold assembly. It means that all should extinguish greed and all should uphold the precepts.
Since lustful greed is the root of affliction (*kleśa*), it is mentioned first. Alternatively, "extinguishing greed and lust in the mind" may refer specifically to the two lay assemblies;
for they cannot completely sever sexual desire, but it is sufficient for them to extinguish excessive greed and improper greed within their minds. To uphold the Buddha’s purity...
"Precepts" refers to the two groups of the renunciant community, for they ought to follow the Buddha’s regulations by maintaining both body and mind without allowing even the slightest transgression.
Furthermore, although this and the preceding section are alike in teaching strict precepts, their purposes differ:

the former was for the purpose of delimiting boundaries and constructing altars, while this is for the purpose of making vows and practicing the Way; thus, the instruction is to make vows within the ritual space.
This is because vows are able to guide practice. Vows may be extensive or concise, as will be clearly demonstrated in detail later.
Third, the path of practice brings about the manifestation of the Buddha (according to the subsequent text, this occurs at the third seven-day period).
Whether entering or leaving, bathing, or practicing the Way during the six periods of the day, they remained thus without sleep for twenty-one days.
I then manifested my own body before that person, rubbed their crown, comforted them, and caused them to attain awakening.
Regarding "entering and exiting for bathing": this means that if one encounters the two necessities (defecation and urination), after exiting one must re-enter and bathe the body;
the intention is that even the slightest impurity might make it difficult to achieve the desired response. Regarding "practicing the Way during the six periods":
practicing the Way is synonymous with reciting mantras. As detailed in the subsequent section, it states: "During the third seven-day period, [one practices] throughout the twelve periods."
Regarding the recitation of mantras: as for the present mention of "six periods," this refers to the twelve periods of the day.

It means that apart from the six periods during which one simply recites [the text], one specifically selects the other six periods to circumambulate the altar while reciting the mantra as a form of spiritual practice (*caryā*).

Thus, the fact that one does not sleep indicates that during the times outside of these six periods, one should likewise recite [the text]. Regarding the phrase "after three weeks": this means that once the first...
"Twenty-one days" refers to the final day; this shall be understood in detail from the subsequent text. Regarding "I myself manifest my body," etc.:
it means that having already made vows above, one now further practices the Path; since practice and vows support one another, they are sufficient to bring about a response.
Thus, he strokes the head to demonstrate his inclusion and guidance, and offers consolation to bestow fearlessness, thereby causing them to attain awakening—this is the teaching.
By exerting vigorous diligence, one unties the knots and practices for realization, until nirvāṇa necessarily manifests before one. This concludes the brief demonstration.
Second, the detailed demonstration in response to the request, which has two parts: first, Ānanda recounts his realization and requests a detailed explanation;
second, the Tathāgata provides the detailed demonstration of the method. First.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, having received the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction, my mind has been awakened.

I know for myself that I have cultivated and realized the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). In the final age, when practitioners establish a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), how should they perform the ritual of boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*)?"
In accordance with the pure protocols of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he first describes his own realization;
having previously been instructed to uphold the precepts to distance oneself from demons, and further commanded to recite mantras to eliminate habitual tendencies.
Finally, he further showed them how to form the altar and perform the ritual practice. These instructions all arise from the Tathāgata’s ultimate compassion;

therefore, they are called "the unsurpassed compassionate teachings. When he says, "I who have received [them]," he speaks of himself, for while others heard the same thing, their individual realizations differed.
As for the rest—whether they have awakened or not—it cannot yet be determined. Those whose minds have already attained awakening are as follows:
This is what the Buddha taught; I have briefly summarized its general outline. Regarding those who know for themselves that they have cultivated and realized the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*):

there are two such stages of no-more-learning. First, the four fruits of the Small Vehicle; second, the stage of Buddhahood in the Great Vehicle. Now, concerning Ānanda, we shall focus on the four fruits.
This means that since Ānanda has already attained awakening, he knows for himself that he must rely upon this to cultivate and realize them, even though he cannot do so immediately.

One reaches the stage of Buddhahood; thus, the path of the four fruits of arhatship and the state beyond training can finally be accomplished. Regarding the practice of the Dharma during the Final Age (mofa), please examine its methods carefully:
in this degenerate age, practicing the Way is like trying to produce a fathom-long wave from a foot of water; establishing a site for the Path (daochang) is by no means an easy task.
One must perform the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) according to the Dharma; only then can one ensure that no harm shall come. Therefore, the question is asked: "In what manner [should it be done]?

This means that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, while practicing on the causal stage (*hetubhūmi*), must naturally have had pure rules for distancing themselves from Māras and abandoning obstacles;

it is only by conforming to these that one acts in accordance with the Dharma. Second, the Tathāgata provides a detailed exposition of that method, which has two parts: first, the actual instruction; second, [the conclusion].
Detailed Explanation. Second, the inquiry and the formal response. This consists of two parts: first, the detailed explanation of the ritual rules for establishing the altar;
second, the detailed explanation of the ceremonial procedures for practicing the Way. The first part has five sections: first, smearing the altar and demarcating the boundaries;

second, internal and external adornments; third, the methods of making offerings; fourth, the rules for arranging images; fifth, the orientation of the empty mirror. First [section]: smearing the altar and demarcating the boundaries.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "If people of the末世 (final age) wish to establish a *bodhimaṇḍa*, they should first take a powerful white ox from the Snowy Mountains that feeds on the lush, fatty fragrant herbs of those mountains.
This ox drinks only the pure water of the Snowy Mountains; its dung is fine and subtle."
One may take its dung and mix it with *candana* (sandalwood) to plaster the ground. If it is not from the Snowy Mountains, the cow’s dung is foul and impure, and is unfit for smearing on the ground.

Instead, one should dig five feet below the surface of level plains and take the yellow earth, mixing it with *candana*, *agaru* (aloe), *sugandha* (frankincense), *turuṣka* (olibanum), *uragasāra* (ambergris), *kālānusāri* (yellow sandalwood), *sarjarasa* (resin), *devadāru* (pine), and *tagara*.
Using pine and *kakkola* (chicken-beak) incense, these ten kinds of fine incense are ground into powder. This is mixed with earth to form mud, which is used to coat the site of the ritual area.
A square and circular altar, sixteen feet in circumference, is constructed as an eight-cornered mandala.

This is the standard procedure for initially coating the altar (the "standard procedure" refers to the practice used in regions near the Snowy Mountains; as it must certainly be relied upon, it is called the "standard procedure").

In this degenerate age, obstacles are heavy, and it is difficult to practice unless one is in a formal ritual site (*maṇḍala*). Therefore, this vow is established. Since the ground where the position is established may be impure, it is necessary to apply a fresh coating separately.
In the Snowy Mountains there are oxen; they are white in color and possess great strength.

Those who first take them provide them with food and drink according to the proper method, and then collect their dung to mix with incense for smearing upon the ground. The fragrant herbs of the Snowy Mountains are abundant, rich, and oily;
when these are fed to the oxen, their dung becomes fragrant and oily. This is used to coat the ground not only to avoid odors, but also—
This is to increase its firmness. When the clear waters of the Snowy Mountains are neither turbid nor defiled, and one uses them to water an ox, its dung will be pure and doubly clean;
when used to smear the ground, not only will there be no impurity, but it will further enhance its cleanliness.
Regarding its "subtle excrement": it is refined, subtle, and exquisite; it encompasses superior fragrances, richness, and purity when considered as a whole.
Since it is said to be "acceptable," and furthermore that it is blended with sandalwood, this represents seeking the most refined within the already refined.

"Seeking the subtle and exquisite within the subtle and exquisite" means that because one seeks what is even more subtle and exquisite. "To plaster the ground" means to remove the old earth and cover it with fresh mud.

○ If it is not for the method of transforming the altar by applying a lower coating (it is said to be a "transformation method" because in distant lands such as the Snowy Mountains, yellow earth is used instead), then if the cows there are foul-smelling—as they have no fragrant herbs to eat and no pure water to drink—the [mud] from the cows [is used].

Furthermore, it is foul and filthy; how much more so its excrement! Fearing that one might commit an offense through improper use, it is selected for exclusion because it is unfit for smearing the ground.
One does not resort to high elevations, nor does one take from low depressions; thus it is said to be "separate from the level plain.

This is because high elevations are feared to accumulate impurities, while low depressions are feared to collect flowing filth. Regarding the phrase "digging away the surface soil," etc., it is because...

The surface soil is shallow; it is feared that this is not the original pure land (*śuddhāvāsa*). One must go down at least five feet (*pañca-hasta*) and take the naturally pure yellow earth (*pīta-mṛttikā*) for use.
Furthermore, regarding the blending with sandalwood (*candana*) and other fragrances: although the yellow earth is pure, it lacks fragrance.
The ten types of incense and their beneficial properties and origins await further investigation. As for grinding it finely into powder: if it were coarse, [it would be unsuitable].
It cannot form mud. Even if it were to form mud, it would not be fit for smearing upon the ground. ○ Regarding the characteristics of the altar boundaries (maṇḍala) within the square and the circle:
as for "square and circular," it is circular yet possesses corners. As for "one zhang and six chi" (approx. 5.04 meters), the diameter exceeds one zhang and six chi.
As for making an eight-cornered altar, since there are eight corners, there are eight sides; each side measures slightly more than six chi and four cun (approx. 2.16 meters).

The diameter is approximately one *zhang* and six *chi*. However, while the previous section mentioned "smearing the site," which refers merely to coating the ground surface, this section speaks of "constructing an eight-cornered altar" (*aṣṭakoṇamaṇḍala*), at which point the physical form of the altar is actually established. It need not necessarily involve piling up earth;
wood, stone, or other materials may all be used. One should simply act according to one's capacity and strive for excellence.
Second, the inner and outer adornments:
at the center of the maṇḍala, place a lotus flower fashioned from gold, silver, copper, or wood. Within the flower, set a bowl.

Inside the bowl, first fill it with dew collected during the eighth month; within the water, place whatever flowers and leaves are available. Then, take eight circular mirrors and place each in its respective direction.
Surround the flower bowl with a circle. Outside the mirror, establish sixteen lotus flowers, with sixteen incense burners interspersed among them.
Adorn the incense burners by burning only aloeswood so that the flames are not visible.

Regarding the adornment of the center of the first maṇḍala: although it is called the "center of the maṇḍala," one must still leave space on the outer perimeter to provide a place for offerings to Vairocana.
As for the flowers made of gold, silver, copper, or wood, they should be fashioned according to one's capacity, using either gold, silver, copper, or other materials.
Any of these may be fashioned. Alternatively, they may be made by combining gold, silver, copper, and wood.

As described in the "Chapter on the Wondrous Sound" (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*), there are lotus flowers made of various jewels, such as those with stems of Jāmbūnada gold, petals of white silver, filaments of diamond (*vajra*), and pericarps of *kiṃśuka* gemstone.
Regarding the placing of flowers at the center of the altar, one should prepare [them] in advance.
This is for the purpose of preparing the bowl. Placing the bowl within the flower is to prepare it in advance for holding water.
Filling the bowl with water and placing flower petals within the water is to use the water to soak the flowers, preventing them from withering. One must specifically use dew from the eighth month;
this is because dew is pure, the dew of the eighth month is thick, and it is easy to obtain. Furthermore, dew is inherently clean. Eight.
In the autumn sky, free from dust, the dew becomes even more pure. As for placing whatever flowers and leaves are available: in spring, one uses what belongs to spring;
in summer, what belongs to summer, and so forth—placing them according to the season with care to ensure the flowers and leaves are harmonious.
"Round mirror" refers to a circular mirror. Since the altar is modeled after the eight facets [of a jewel], therefore...
Take eight circular mirrors and one square mirror for each direction, suspending them in space; thus it is said that "each is placed in its respective direction.
They surround the flower bowl, which naturally implies being surrounded by the Buddha as well.

Taking the central image of the Buddha and the flower bowl, these are reflected in the eight mirrors, such that each of the eight mirrors bears the reflection of the Buddha and the flower bowl, mutually reflecting one another. These reflections...

"Manifesting in layers" briefly clarifies the fundamental realm. ○ "Outside the mirrors" and below refers to the outer adornments (the "outer" being still within the altar, but situated near its exterior).
"Establishment" has the meaning of placing offerings. It is said that the altar is divided into eight facets, each being narrow on the inside and broad on the outside;
therefore, there are only eight mirrors on the inside, while the lotus flowers outside the mirrors number sixteen—referring to the eight facets.
Regarding the eight branches in the center: this refers to the eight branches situated at the center of the eight corners.

As for the arrangement of flowers between the sixteen incense burners, it means that there are two burners on each side, placed between the two flowers at the central corners; thus, they are interspersed with the flowers. Regarding the adornment of the incense burners:
one should cover the fire with ash, ensuring they are kept neat and beautiful. As for burning only *agallochum* (sinking water): [this is the rule].

One should take its fragrance for its pure and subtle quality, which aids in awakening the concentrated mind. If it is mixed with other fragrances, they will become superficial and turbid, disturbing the concentrated mind.
Do not let anyone see the fire; place the incense upon the ashes and warm it until it ignites naturally.
If one sees fire and smoke arise, the fragrance will become coarse and turbid, and people will grow weary of smelling it, let alone the Buddhas and sages. Now...
Regarding local customs: they delight in burning large, perfectly shaped incense sticks; observing this, one should know that such practices are improper.
Regarding the ritual for the three types of offerings:
take white cow’s milk and place it in sixteen vessels; prepare milk pancakes, along with various sugar cakes, oil cakes, and milk porridge.
Sūhaka, honey, and ginger, along with pure ghee and pure honey—each sixteen [parts] outside the lotus, surrounding it—to be offered to the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas.
At every mealtime, [one should do this]. If it is at midnight, take half a *śoṇa* of honey and three *āḍhaka* of ghee;
place a small fire-pit separately before the altar and extract [the essence] by boiling *turuṣka* incense.

Bathe the charcoal with scented water and ignite it until it blazes fiercely. Cast this ghee and honey into the flaming furnace, burning them until the smoke has vanished, as an offering to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

This is the ritual for the first day’s daily offering. (Daily offerings all involve physical objects; they differ from the night offerings, which consist solely of burning the smoke of ghee and honey. [The offering of] white cow’s milk refers to:
Regarding the snow-mountain cow’s milk placed in sixteen vessels: it is used for making offerings because of its fragrant purity.
There are eight other flavors: first, milk used for fried cakes—meaning cakes made by frying milk; second, together with various granulated sugars.
1. Sugarcane juice boiled into sugar like sand, which is sweet in flavor. 2. Oil-cakes: cakes made by mixing oil with flour, which are oily and crisp.
3. Milk gruel: porridge made by mixing milk with rice, which is sweet and sticky. 4. *Sūhaka* (Suhāka):
a medicinal paste formed by blending various fragrant substances and boiling the liquid into a solid extract. 5. Honey-ginger: [a preparation] made with honey... [text truncated].

The flavor of soaked ginger is pungent and sweet. Seventh is pure ghee (*sarpis*), which refers to butter produced from the refinement of milk. Eighth is pure honey (*madhu*), which refers to honey produced from flower nectar.
"Each sixteen" means that these are likewise each placed in sixteen vessels, just as with the cow's milk.
"Surrounding the flowers from the outside" means that outside of the sixteen lotuses, there are nine flavors each, arranged in rows of three to encircle them.
"At every mealtime" refers to the time of eating, which is midday. Wēnlíng says:
"The Buddha accepts food at midday; therefore, every day he is offered sustenance at midday. If it is... [text ends]
The Ritual for the Night Offering (*rātri-pūjā*). (Regarding the "night offering": the Buddha does not eat at night; it is offered solely by burning incense of ghee and honey.
If it is said to be performed during the middle watch of the night, this means making the offering at the middle watch. Honey belongs to the flower’s pollen; its flavor is fragrant and clear.
Ghee belongs to the body’s constituents; its flavor is sweet and turbid. Taking half a *śu* of honey and using three *he* of ghee is intended to use the honey [to represent the essence].
This clarifies the turbidity of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*). As for the installation of a small hearth separately before the maṇḍala:
since the maṇḍala is divided into eight sides, one is installed on each side to prepare for the burning of the clarified butter and honey. The sacrificial vessels should not be excessively large.
Therefore, the brazier must be small; furthermore, if it were large, it would obstruct the path of practice and be inconvenient for its use.
As for *tūlūṣa*, this is translated as "white mugwort" (*śvetadūrvā*); water is boiled with this to bathe the charcoal because it is pure and fragrant.
Fearing that [the offering] might be extinguished by the butter and honey, he lit it until it blazed fiercely and cast [the offering] into it. This is the act of making an offering.
Since the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not partake of food during the middle watch of the night, he merely burned it until the smoke was exhausted, making the offering through its fragrance.
Regarding the fourth, the rules for the arrangement of images:

one should cause banners and flowers to be hung everywhere on the four outer sides. Within the ritual chamber, one should install the images of all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions upon the four walls.
One should then display Vairocana, Śākyamuni, and [Maitreya] facing the front.
Engrave Akṣobhya and Amitābha; the various great emanations, as well as the forms of Avalokiteśvara and Vajragarbha, shall be placed at their left and right.
Śakra, Brahmā, Ucchuṣma, and Lambodara, along with the Cāmuṇḍīs, Vighnāntaka, the Four Heavenly Kings, and Pināyaka, shall be arranged on the sides of the entrance, positioned to the left and right.

First, the sacred images of the outer altar (*bāhyamaṇḍala*). (The "outer altar" refers to the area outside the eight-cornered altar, within the altar chamber. Regarding the "four outer [sides]": this refers to the four exterior sides of the eight-cornered altar.
The instruction to "suspend banners and flowers everywhere" is for the purpose of adorning the altar chamber to prepare for the offerings to the sacred images.
The "altar chamber" is precisely the outer altar; the outer altar need not necessarily be eight-cornered, but may be like a hall or temple, and thus has only four walls.
Regarding "arranging": this means that for painted images, one spreads them out; for cast or carved images, one establishes them.

As for the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas, they may be arranged as principal figures with their attendants interspersed; beyond a count of ten, any number—more or less—is permissible, because the original sūtra does not specify a fixed number.
Furthermore, although it is said that the arrangement covers the four walls, if there are obstructions such as doors or windows, one should simply leave those spaces vacant.
It is merely a matter of setting out the empty space. Regarding the sacred images of the inner altar below:

those facing the sun should be positioned at the exact center of the altar, facing south (the direction of the sun), directly opposite the flower bowl at the heart of the altar. "To set out" (*kō*) means to arrange; it also carries the sense of establishing offerings.
Vairocana (盧舍那). Its full name is Vairocana, which has three meanings: first, "pervading all places," referring to the *dharmakāya*;
second, "perfectly pure," referring to the *svasaṃbhogakāya*; and third, "shining light everywhere," referring to the *parasaṃbhogakāya*.
These three bodies share a single name because they are equally the true body (*dharmakāya*); the True Body is the sovereign of the responsive bodies.
He resides within it. Below these are four images, followed by one outer enclosure, arranged so that Vairocana stands prominently high, visible from the front, back, left, and right.
Śākyamuni is positioned before Vairocana, sitting facing south, because he is the presiding lord of this world-system.
Maitreya is positioned behind Vairocana, sitting facing north, because he is the lord of the future.

Akṣobhya; in full, Akṣobhyeya. This translates as "Immovable. He resides to the left of Vairocana, sitting upright facing east, because he is the presiding lord of the eastern realm. Amitābha; in full, Amitābha. This means "Infinite Life."
He is also called Amitābha (Immeasurable Light). He is situated to the right of Vairocana, sitting facing west; this is because he is the presiding lord of the western realm.
As for the various great transformations, they are like the manifested images of the Vidyārājas, since Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and others all possess the forms of Vidyārājas.
Furthermore, among these various great transformations, Avalokiteśvara and Vajragarbha are specifically singled out.

It is essential to manifest these two Bodhisattvas. Avalokiteśvara is established as the master of perfect penetration (because Mañjuśrī selected the perfect methods from among the twenty-five sages and chose only Avalokiteśvara).

Vajragarbha is established as the master of the protective dhāraṇī (because it is stated later: "This dhāraṇī is always accompanied by a multitude of eighty-four thousand nayutas of Ganges-sand *koṭis* of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas;
each one has a retinue of various vajra-beings who attend upon them day and night"). Thus, they are placed at the left and right [of the Buddha].
These refer to the various great transformation-bodies, such as Avalokiteśvara and Vajragarbha, who are stationed to the left and right of the five Buddhas.

According to this, there are Buddhas in the five directions and Bodhisattvas in the four intermediate corners; as principal figures and their attendants intermingle, they form a solemn and wondrous realm.
○ Śakra stands at the side of the lower gate as a Dharma protector. Śakra is the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Brahmā... [is] the King of Brahmā.
The Lord of the Fourth Dhyāna; Ucchuṣma, the Fire-Headed Vajra; Nīladaṇḍa, the Blue-Faced Vajra;
and Kuṇḍalī—translated here as "Resolver of Enmity"—which is also an alternative name for a Vajra, as found in the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra*.
It is the Bodhisattva Vajrasenācārī who is this one. *Vikṛti* is translated here as "Pervasive Myriad" (*piānmàn qiānwàn*).
The *Vairocana-vikurvaṇa-sūtra* states: "On the right side is Vikṛti; her hand holds a rosary garland. She has three eyes and wears a topknot;
her venerable form is pure white. Regarding the Four Heavenly Kings: Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east, Virūḍhaka in the south, and Virūpākṣa in the west... [text continues].
[The deities] are Virūpākṣa and Virūḍhaka, who preside over the tribes under their jurisdiction. This is because each of the Four Great Heavenly Kings governs two classes of spirits.
Piṇāka means "pig-head" in this [language], and Nakula means "elephant-trunk"; these are the names of the two messengers.
As for those hung at the sides of the gate: "gate" refers to the gate of the outer altar, which may consist of either only the front and back, or both.
Left and right: simply provide offerings wherever there is a doorway. "Beside the door" refers to the two sides inside the entrance.
As for the method of arranging the offerings: generally, Śakra and Brahmā are placed at the front, one on the left and one on the right.
Ucchuṣma and Kṣitigarbha follow next, also one on the left and one on the right. Senāpati and Kuṭi follow again, likewise one on the left and one on the right.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings are positioned with two on each side, and the Pināyakas are provided for on both sides; therefore, they are collectively said to be "placed on the left and right.

Because these are all powerful external protectors, they are employed to guard the altar and protect the boundary, ensuring that Māras find no opportunity while the practitioner performs the path according to the Dharma. Fifth, the directions of the five mirrors of emptiness.
Furthermore, take eight mirrors and suspend them in the air, facing the mirrors installed within the ritual mandala,
so that their forms and reflections interpenetrate one another in successive layers.
The eight mirrors are likewise circular mirrors. Regarding "suspended inverted in space": they are tied and suspended above, hanging down with their faces turned downward;

because these mirrors are situated freely within space, the mirrors within the mandala surround Vairocana and the flower bowl at the center of the mandala—one mirror per direction—with their faces directed outward. As for the mirrors of the outer mandala, one per direction...
Each is a single mirror, yet they face inward; thus it is said that the surfaces face one another. To cause their forms and shadows to interpenetrate in successive layers:

formerly, the National Teacher Xianshou once arranged ten round mirrors for Empress Wu, placing them in the eight corners and at the zenith and nadir, all facing each other, with a Buddha image installed in the center. When lamps were lit to illuminate them, the reflections appeared in every mirror.
They interlace and reflect one another to manifest the principle that the ocean of *kṣetra* (world-systems) universally contains the ten realms in inexhaustible abundance.

This scripture is likewise so: just as the eight mirrors of the inner altar internally manifest the reflections of Vairocana’s lotus bowl and externally manifest the reflections of the four Buddhas and their various great transformations, as well as those of Avalokiteśvara, Vajragarbha, the lotus bowl, and the incense burner, these reflections penetrate into the mirrors of the outer altar.

Within the mirrors of the outer altar, the reflections of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions appear externally; the shadows of the Dharma-protectors flanking the gates appear externally;
and the reflections of the banners, flowers, and the practitioner’s prostrations and offerings appear internally, merging into the mirrors of the inner altar.
Furthermore, when the mirror of the inner altar enters into the mirror of the outer altar, its substance already carries the reflection of the outer altar.
When the mirror of the outer altar enters into the mirror of the inner altar, its substance likewise carries the reflection of the inner altar.
Moreover, the mirrors of the inner altar appear in succession to one another, and the same is true for the mirrors of the outer altar.
This is called the mutual interpenetration of layers upon layers. It enables the practitioner, without leaving their original place, to enter universally into immeasurable ocean-like assemblies;

to encompass the myriad phenomena, all returning together within the space of a single inch-square heart-mind. With a single incense offering or a single flower, one fully realizes the gate of non-obstruction;
with a single gaze or a single prostration, one suddenly enters the inconceivable realm. This is not merely for the sake of aesthetic beauty.

The ancient masters, following the ritual rules for establishing the altar (*maṇḍala*), explained everything solely through the symbolism of the Dharma (*dharmapratibimba*) while completely neglecting the practical details of its arrangement. Consequently, bodhisattvas who subsequently resolved to attain enlightenment established altars and performed practices that did not accord with the Tathāgata’s pure ritual rules;

furthermore, when seeking the Dharma symbolized therein, they remained utterly bewildered. Thus, having lost both the principle (*li*) and the phenomena (*shi*), they merely carried empty texts in vain.
