First, regarding the service of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): this is shown for those at the stage of the cause (*hetu-bhūmi*) to attract and guide beginners.

Therefore, one serves spiritual friends throughout the worlds of the ten directions, because they possess right knowledge and vision and can provide the necessary resources for beginners to advance on the path.
Regarding the four modes of deportment—namely, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—in each of these moments, there are specific [practices] that should be performed.

The objects offered are all made to accord with one’s wishes; hence it is said that the offerings are "as one desires" (*yirui*). The *Fahua Tianshou pin* (Devadatta Chapter of the Lotus Sutra) states:
"Gathering firewood, fruits, and melons, one offers them with respect according to the season. This is precisely that meaning. "According to" (*sui*) means "to accompany" (*dai*).
Now, one must necessarily accompany this mantra because it is intended for beginners; without this mantra, there would be no means to manifest spiritual penetration, nor could one reach afar.
Reaching throughout the ten directions, were it not for this mantra, there would be no means by which [the Dharma] could arise; one could not make offerings according to one's wishes.
Thus, those who wish to serve their spiritual friends and make offerings as they desire—should they not regard this mantra as an urgent priority?

○ From "As numerous as the sands of the Ganges" downward, [this mantra] enables one to draw near to all Buddhas, assisting them in spreading the transformation [of sentient beings] and guiding those of initial capacity. Therefore, it is present within the assemblies of the Tathāgatas.
Among them, he was made a Prince of the Dharma; he was promoted to a position of greatness because his wisdom and eloquence were fully perfected, such that none of his peers could rival him.
This, too, was brought about by the power of his mental concentration through mantras. These four are the proximate causes for his reception [into the assembly].
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, by practicing this mantra-heart, are able to gather and sustain their close karmic causes throughout the ten directions,
causing those of the Hīnayāna to hear the secret treasury without giving rise to alarm or fear.
"Practice" (*xing*) also implies "maintaining" (*chi*). It means that the Tathāgata and his kinsmen throughout the kalpas have been mutually dependent upon one another;

although he has himself attained Buddhahood, he remains mindful of those who are scattered throughout the ten directions and constantly maintains this [mantra] to gather them in. Therefore, it is said: "practice this mantra-heart."
"Regarding the phrase 'able [to act] throughout the ten directions,' and so forth: the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*) is precisely the Supreme Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Because the followers of the two vehicles do not know it, it is called 'secret. When those of provisional or inferior capacity first hear of it, they are often struck with alarm and fear.

For example, when Śāriputra of superior virtue heard the *Lotus Sūtra*—wherein the provisional was set aside and the real established—he still wondered, 'Could this not be a demon who has become a Buddha to disturb my mind? Many others were likewise."

It should be understood that [ordinary beings] are subject to fear and terror. What is now meant by "causing them not to be terrified" refers to those who have been one's close kin throughout successive kalpas;

even if they should enter into the provisional or inferior vehicles, they are empowered by this heart-mantra (cittadhāraṇī) so that their great aspirations are fulfilled and they become capable of receiving the Great [Vehicle].
This is like Ānanda in the *Lotus Sūtra*, who upon receiving his prediction, exclaimed: "I now have no further doubts; I abide securely in the Buddha."
The Way can be known by its lack of alarm and fear. Having concluded the demonstration of the two benefits through its traces, the second part demonstrates the realization of the fruit:
the Tathāgatas of the ten directions recited this mantra-heart, attained unsurpassed enlightenment, sat beneath the Bodhi tree, and entered Great Nirvāṇa.
In manifesting his final body, he recited mantras to sever residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*), transforming afflictions (*kleśa*) into the fruit of wisdom;

thus it is said that he attained unsurpassed enlightenment. Seated upright beneath the Bodhi tree, he remained tranquil and unmoving, transforming the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) into the fruit of cessation (*nirodha*).
Therefore, it is said that he has entered Great Nirvana. However, since this belongs to the manifestation of the traces, those who recite the mantra must still do so;
this is to show that even in his final existence, he must not forget this mantra. Third, the entrustment of the Dharma through the manifestation of traces.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this mantra-heart; after their parinirvāṇa, it is entrusted for the ultimate maintenance of the Buddha-dharma, ensuring that the precepts are strictly purified and rendered entirely stainless.
Having completed his worldly affairs by manifesting his final traces, he wished to benefit future sentient beings through this mantra;
therefore, he said, "Transmit this mantra-heart. After my parinirvāṇa, use this to protect the Dharma, so that the matters entrusted within the Buddha-dharma may endure.
This is ultimate upholding. By means of this protection of the precepts, those who strictly purify the monastic discipline are all rendered pure.
Based on this, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is possible to cause the True Dharma to endure long and the Vinaya to remain for a great length of time.
It relies entirely upon this mantra. Those who preside over the Dharma and the Vinaya must not neglect it. The detailed explanation of its two applications is concluded.
Third, the summary showing its inexhaustibility:
If I were to recite this Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Raśmi-Sañcaya-Pāṭala-Mantra from dawn until dusk with a continuous stream of sound, [it would never end].
The words and phrases do not overlap one another; even if one were to recite them for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they could never be exhausted.
Regarding my explanation of these phrases, there are two interpretations: first, the mere recitation of the mantra; second, the benefits of the mantra.
"From dawn until dusk" refers to the span of an entire day. "With sounds linked together" means that throughout the day, the recitation proceeds without interruption.
Therefore, the fact that the characters and phrases do not overlap means that each character and each phrase explains the Dharma differently from what precedes or follows it.

To say that one speaks in this manner for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is to most clearly demonstrate the vastness of the characters and phrases, as well as the extreme length of the days.
Even so, one could never exhaust the phrases; yet, if we consider the recitation of the mantra, by means of the mantra—
The meaning encompassed by this mind-mantra is inexhaustible and cannot be fully exhausted through speech;

it is like the "Single-Syllable Dharma Gate" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, for which even the ink of the oceans could not write out a single verse. If one were to speak of its benefits, they are as described above;

yet, even regarding the essential applications of the Buddhas, only a small portion has been briefly set forth. Even if one were to explain them in full, they would not be exhausted even after the passing of kalpas.
The reason why this mantra is essential for all Buddhas is not limited to this alone. Thus, the Zhengmo (Correct Pulse) states: "This inexhaustible method concerns what is essential for the Buddhas;
it does not pertain to the use of sentient beings. This concludes the section on what is essential for the Buddhas.
Second, the benefits and reliance of sentient beings, which has two parts: first, a specific explanation of the benefits and reliance; second, a general manifestation of the benefits.
Universal. Third, receiving benefits and being exhorted to faith. First eight [points]: 1. To distance oneself from demons and eliminate poison;

2. To accomplish wisdom and avoid harm; 3. To provide the resources for developing supernormal powers and clarity; 4. To remain far removed from the various realms of existence; 5. To constantly be born before the Buddhas; 6. To be able to accomplish all practices; 7.
To extinguish offenses and remove obstacles; 8. To have all requests fulfilled. The first two [points] concern the Śrāvakas.
Relying on this, one stays far from demons. Second, ordinary beings rely on it to eliminate poison. First:

It is also said that the name of this mantra is the "Crown of the Tathāgata. You who are in training and have not yet exhausted saṃsāra, if you resolve with sincerity to attain arhatship, do not sit in the place of practice without holding this mantra, which causes your body and mind to remain far from all demonic activities.
This is impossible.
Furthermore, it is said that there are two interpretations of these mantra syllables. First, the original name of this mantra is *Siddhārthapāṇḍarā*.
Because it is essential for all Buddhas, it is also called the "Crown of the Tathāgata" (*tathāgatamūrdhan*). This concludes the preceding section. Second—

Since this is named the "Crown of the Tathāgata," it is known to be supreme; thus, it is able to provide benefit and reliance for sentient beings. This refers to what arises after [the previous state].

"You who are still in training" specifically refers to those such as Ānanda; since there are still seven more rounds of birth and death remaining in the desire realm, how much more so in the higher realms?
Therefore, it is said that "saṃsāra is not yet exhausted. "To resolve the mind" means to resolve upon the mind of practicing the Path. Up to...

"Sincerity" means ultimate and profound sincerity. Those who seek arhatship desire to realize the emptiness of persons; yet to realize the emptiness of persons, one must also practice within the *dharma-cakra* (place of enlightenment).
Without upholding this mantra, one will mostly remain obstructed in the realm of the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

Therefore, it is said that "to cause them to distance themselves from demons is impossible"—this is an indirect indication (*paryudāsa*). To explain it directly: it means that one must certainly rely upon the upholding of the mantra. Thus...
One may thereby distance oneself from all māras. Second, ordinary worldlings rely upon it to eliminate poisons.

Ānanda, if in any world, in whatever land, there are sentient beings who—using birch bark, palm leaves, paper, silk, or white woolen cloth produced in that country—write down this dhāraṇī and store it in a fragrant pouch;
even if these people’s minds are dull and they have not yet attained [realization], [they shall be protected].
If one recites and remembers it, wears it on the body, or writes it within one's home, it should be known that throughout their entire life,
this person cannot be harmed by any poisons whatsoever.
As for "all worlds," there are ten directions with distinct differences. Regarding "the sentient beings in whatever lands":

regardless of which country or species they belong to—since lands have distinctions between central and peripheral regions, and sentient beings differ between the intelligent and the insentient—whichever country one is born in, and regardless of what kind of being one is born as, one may simply compose a book.
All of these may be used. Birch bark is available here in this land; it can be processed to make it thin and supple, and is suitable for writing upon.
Palm leaves (*pattraka*) originate from the Western Regions; their leaves are long and broad and can be used for inscribing characters. "Paper-surface" (*zhisù*) refers to the raw surface of paper.
In this region, bamboo is pounded to make a pulp; mulberry bark, paper mulberry bark, and the like may all be used for this purpose. "White *karpāsa*" refers to the white variety of cotton cloth.
*Yāma-karpāsa* flowers are like silk fibers, as are the *Gaochang* (Kucha) cotton seeds and the like—all of these may be used.

(Regarding the statement that *yāma-karpāsa* flowers are like silk fibers: *yāma* refers to the Kāpāla devas; they possess *karpāsa* flowers like silk fibers that can be spun and woven. As previously mentioned, these precious *karpāsa* flowers are woven together to form cloths. The *Gaochang* cotton seeds...)

As for this, Guanding said: "In the kingdom of Gaochang, there is a plant whose fruit resembles a cocoon; the silk within it is like fine thread and is called *máozi*. The people of the country harvest it and weave it into fine woolen cloth that is soft, white, and pure.
Regarding those who transcribe this dhāraṇī, they should use materials such as birch bark and so forth.

As for storing it in a fragrant pouch, one should fold it neatly and place it inside the pouch, so that it may be conveniently carried on one's person. If a person's mind is clouded, their innate nature will be dark and dull.
For those who are unable to recite or memorize it, they lack the power of hearing and retaining [the Dharma]. Alternatively, if one wears it upon the body, it should be worn at the chest;
if it is placed on the lower part of the body, one incurs fault. Or, if it is written within the home, it need not be on materials such as birch bark;
stone walls or plastered walls will suffice as convenient. However, it should not be kept in a low or defiled place. One should know that such a person...
One who wears this scripture upon their person for the duration of their life—meaning from birth until death—is such that all poisons, whether internal or external, cannot harm them.
Internally, those things that startle the mind at every turn, such as greed, anger, and delusion, are gradually transformed.
Externally, by the majestic spiritual power of the mantra, snakes, vipers, scorpions, and the like flee far away. Therefore, it is said: "That which cannot harm; it keeps demons at a distance."
The elimination of poison is complete. Second, the accomplishment of wisdom and the avoidance of harm. First, the world relies upon this to accomplish wisdom;
second, those in the final age rely upon this to avoid harm. Regarding the first:
Ānanda, I shall now further explain to you this dhāraṇī, which protects the world and grants great fearlessness, bringing it to fulfillment.
Sentient beings produce supramundane wisdom.
Because the benefits of the aforementioned incantations are not exhaustive, it is permitted to explain them further. Regarding the "Protector":

he rescues one from internal obstacles and protects against external obstacles. As for the statement that "worldly sentient beings desire to seek the supramundane," they are internally invaded by afflictions (*kleśa*).
Externally, one may be disturbed by malevolent spirits, constantly giving rise to fear and making accomplishment difficult.

By the power of the mantra, it protects against inner afflictions and guards against external malevolent spirits. Since the spirits do not cause disturbance, one is thereby enabled to attain great fearlessness.
Afflictions cannot invade them; thus, they are able to achieve supramundane wisdom. Second, [the section on] relying on this in the final age to avoid harm.
This has two parts: first, a specific explanation of avoiding harm; second, a general presentation of its causes. Regarding the first:
If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are sentient beings in the final age who can recite this themselves or teach others to recite it,
you should know that such sentient beings who uphold it through recitation cannot be burned by fire, cannot be drowned by water, and cannot be harmed by either great or small poisons.
In this way, even all evil incantations—whether from devas, nāgas, yakṣas, bhūtas, piśācas, or māras—cannot take hold.

His mind attains right concentration (*samādhi*). All curses, malevolent spells, poisons, gold poisons, silver poisons, and the poisonous vapors of plants, trees, insects, snakes, and all other things, upon entering this person’s mouth, become the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta*). All malevolent stars and...
Although various ghosts and spirits possess cruel hearts and seek to harm people, they cannot give rise to evil thoughts toward such a person.
At the beginning, one can thus avoid calamities and poisons; after his passing, sentient beings will be left without refuge, and in the final age, practitioners will face many obstacles.
To avoid one's own obstructions, one practices this heart-mantra; thus it is said, "if one is able to recite it oneself. To eliminate the obstructions of others, one transmits this heart-mantra;
thus it is said, "if one teaches others to recite it. Such beings who maintain [the mantra] through recitation refer to those who recite it themselves and those who recite it for others.
Fire is of two kinds: first, internal fire, which arises from the mind, such as the fire of desire and so forth.

Second is external fire, which arises from conditions, such as celestial fires and the like. Through the interaction of internal and external factors, minor instances involve the burning of houses and dwellings, while severe cases result in the scorching and rotting of one's body and head, even reaching the point where the kalpa-ending conflagration blazes forth and destroys everything up to the First Dhyāna Heaven.
All such things can be avoided through the power of mantras; therefore it is said that "fire cannot burn and water cannot drown. This principle applies by analogy to other elements.
This can be understood. Great poisons are like the spread of a pestilence; small poisons are like the stings of snakes and scorpions.
All such things can be turned back through the power of mantras; therefore it is said that they cannot cause harm. As for the passage "In this way," it means one can escape from evil spells.

The devas, nāgas, and spirits (deva-nāga-yakṣa) encompass the first six of the eight classes [of supernatural beings]. Because the yakṣas are termed "ghosts" (yakṣa), the two types of *rākṣasa* (delighting spirits) and the one type of *mahoraga* (serpent spirits) are all designated as "spirits" (*śen*).
That which possesses the numinous essence of heaven is called a *jing*; that which possesses the numinous essence of earth is called a *qi*.
Those who specialize in obstructing the Path are called *māra*; those who delude people are called *mei*. All of these are capable of performing incantations (*dhāraṇī*).
Because one uses mantras to harm others, they are called "evil. Once the mind encounters the mantra-heart, it is like ice melting in hot water;

thus it is said that [the evil] cannot adhere to it. This can be understood through the example of the *Daṅga* Brahmin’s mantra. When the mind attains the lower stage, one is able to escape various poisons.
By upholding this heart-mantra until both subject and object are forgotten, and one no longer undergoes any sensations, this is called the mind attaining *samādhi*.
Regarding "curses, *yangu* (sorcery), and toxic drugs": this refers to curses and *yangu*, as well as cursed toxic drugs. *Yangu* refers to corpse-poison (*shidu*).
The *Hanshu* states that [the practice of] *yan* killed more than four hundred families. "Toxic drugs" refers to material poisons.
The *Guangzhi* states that if the feathers of the *hen* bird drip into wine, one dies upon touching the lips with it. Based on this, both *yangu* and toxic drugs are capable of [killing].
It harms people. If one further employs malevolent incantations and curses, it will strike with certainty every hundred times. Regarding "poisons of gold and silver":

when gold and silver are heated in fire and their dross is leached away by water, drinking them can both poison a person. Regarding "plants, trees, insects, and snakes": these four poisons are mentioned briefly;
all others are encompassed by the toxic vapors of the myriad things. When these enter a person's mouth, they take on the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
Because the mind attains meditative absorption (*samādhi*), poisonous vapors cannot enter. ○ Regarding "all below": one can avoid harm from the five aggregates (*skandha*).
As for "malevolent stars," it refers to inauspicious planetary influences causing calamity. As for "ghosts and spirits," it refers to malevolent deities causing misfortune.

As for "those who inflict cruelty," it refers to those harboring malicious intent. All such things are imperceptible to humans, yet they secretly cause injury; by the power of the mantra, these calamities are transformed.
Because he performs meritorious deeds, it is said that he cannot give rise to evil. Second, the general reason for this is stated:
Piṇāyaka and all the other evil kings of ghosts, together with their retinues, have all received his profound kindness and constantly provide him with protection.

Pinnayaka. To briefly mention the names of two messengers: the various evil kings of ghosts who govern all malevolent spirits, together with their retinues—meaning that wherever the king of ghosts resides, the ghostly hosts follow him—all of whom have received profound grace;

that is, they have long been transformed by the Buddha’s teaching and have received the Buddha’s deep kindness. Therefore, in order to repay the Buddha’s kindness, they constantly [uphold] this mantra.
Furthermore, there is protection, because this mantra is the very heart of the Buddha. Yet, people only know that mantras can avert harm, without knowing the reason why they are able to do so;
it is further dependent upon these forms of protection. Therefore, they are specifically designated and set forth.
This concludes the summary of the wisdom for averting harm. Third, the development of supernormal powers and clear illumination. Part three. First:
The holy retinue attends upon him. Second, using the inferior to illustrate the superior; third, the formal explanation of the supportive conditions and their arousal.

Regarding the first: Ānanda, you should know that this mantra is always accompanied by eighty-four thousand nayutas of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* *koṭis* of the family of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas, each of whom has a host of vajra-beings as their retinue.
They attend him day and night.
This mantra is the heart of the Buddha; where the mantra is, there the Buddha is.

Therefore, he is always attended by a retinue of holy beings numbering *nayuta*—here translated as "ten billion"—and *koṭi*—here translated as "one hundred billion. These figures refer to the number of bodhisattvas. [The term] *koṭi*...
This was sufficient to exhaust [the count]. Counting again by means of the sands of the Ganges, even the sands of the Ganges and koṭis were insufficient to exhaust it.
Counting again by means of nayutas, even nayutas of the sands of the Ganges and koṭis were insufficient to exhaust it.
Counting again by means of eighty-four thousand, this is the ultimate expression of the vastness of their number. The Bodhisattva is named Vajragarbharāja.
He manifests a form of fierce wrath and possesses the power to subdue māras; thus he is named Vajra.
He embodies secret virtues and gathers the assembly of vajra-beings; therefore, he is called the King of the Treasury (Guhyarāja).
As for his lineage, these bodhisattvas are all of one kind and one clan. The various vajra-beings are precisely the assembly of those who are governed and protected by him.
Just as those such as Vajraśekhara and Nīlāmukha-vajra act as his retinue, obeying his commands and attending upon him day and night to provide constant protection, so it is with the mantra itself;
how much more so should it be understood that the practitioner who upholds it shall naturally receive its protection?
This is an inference from the inferior to the superior.

If there are sentient beings who, with a distracted mind and not in a state of samādhi, merely remember this in their hearts and uphold it verbally, this Vajra King will constantly follow those sons of good family. How much more so for those who possess the resolute bodhicitta!
First, the analogy is presented: "one with a distracted mind" refers to one who shifts abruptly from this to that; such a person belongs to the group of the indeterminate (aniyata-rāśi).

"One who is not in samādhi" refers to one who practices blindly and exercises recklessly; such a person belongs to the group of the wrongly fixed (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi). "The mind recollects" refers to a momentary recollection by the mind.

Because they do not maintain it with fixed or constant mindfulness. As for "holding it orally," this refers to holding it orally in a superficial manner, because they do not hold it in their minds through false concentration.

Since they do not maintain it in their minds with constant mindfulness, yet the Vajragarbha Kings constantly follow them, it is for the sake of repaying the Buddha’s kindness and providing protection and upholding beyond the ordinary.
Because they are neither fixed nor falsely concentrated, they are collectively addressed as "good sons."

Because one who is able to maintain the mantra already possesses roots of goodness and possesses the spirit of a true man (puruṣa-vīrya). How much more so for those mentioned below? This clarifies what is being illustrated:
it definitively excludes the indeterminate and selects for the non-erroneous determinate. That is to say, it belongs to the group of those with right determination (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi).
How much more so, then, for those with indeterminate or erroneous determination who, even by chance or through casual recollection, maintain the practice; they still receive its following benefits.

How much more so for those who have entered the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*)! One should constantly remember and maintain this in mind. Furthermore, it is not merely a matter of following along; this will be seen in the subsequent section itself.
Third, the actual clarification of the supportive conditions that bring about realization.
The refined essence of these Vajra Bodhisattvas, the King of the Treasury, secretly and swiftly awakens that divine consciousness.
At that moment, this person’s mind is able to remember eighty-four thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* eons; they come to know them all thoroughly and attain freedom from doubt.

He wields the vajra and upholds the secret treasury. He may be called Vajrabodhisattva, or Bodhisattvapiṭakarāja, or Vajragarbhārājābodhisattva, or Vajrabodhisattvapiṭakarāja, or Vajrarāja, or Vajragarbha;
any of these names is appropriate. "One of refined mind" refers to a mind of pure sincerity.
Above, they share the same power of compassion as all Buddhas; below, they share the same yearning of pity with all sentient beings.
Thus, they are able to stimulate that spiritual consciousness (*śen-shi*). The character "that" (*bi*) refers to a person who has resolved upon the bodhicitta and is capable of upholding the mantra.

"To stimulate" means to provide the necessary support and incitement, causing the spiritual consciousness to become penetratingly clear and luminous. Although the spiritual consciousness becomes penetratingly clear and luminous, that person still does not know it.
This is because these Bodhisattvas, with a mind of pure sincerity, swiftly bring forth [insight] even within darkness.
The phrase "this person, at that time," and so forth, refers to the simultaneous arising of both supernormal powers and clear insight (*abhijñā*). Zhengmo says:
"Memory seems to pertain only to past lives; however, by analogy from the past to the present and future, it certainly penetrates the three periods of time and is said to be all-pervasive."

Having understood this, one attains freedom from doubt and should simultaneously master the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). How much more so for those who have transcended eighty thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
these constitute the superior supernormal powers of a Bodhisattva. This concludes the section on the development of the supernormal powers.
Fourth, they remain far removed from rebirth in mixed realms;
from the first kalpa until their final body, in every successive birth, they are never born as yakṣas,
rākṣasas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, or any other hungry ghosts, whether possessing form or lacking form.

Regarding such evil realms as those of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," "from the first kalpa" means from the initial generation of the mind of awakening, passing through the first kalpa, up until the final body.
This refers to the period up until the final body before attaining Buddhahood. "Birth after birth" refers to the interval between two existences—the relinquishing of one life and receiving another.
"Non-birth" means not being born into the various lower realms, because one possesses supernormal clarity (*abhijñā*) and can thus know things beforehand.
*Yakṣa* (also called *rākṣasa*) refers to swift-moving spirits; *rākṣasa* here means "the terrifying," as they devour human beings.
They are *piśācas*. A *pūtana* is translated here as a "stench-demon" (*chou-e ghost*) and is the presiding deity of fevers.
A *kaṭapūtana* is translated here as a "strange stench-demon" (*qi-chou e-ghost*) and is the presiding deity of severe fevers. A *kumbhāṇḍa* is translated here as "jar-shaped."
The *yāma* is a ghost that causes nightmares and bewitchment. The *piśāca*, sometimes called *piśāca*, means "eater of essence.
This is because it can consume the vital essence of humans as well as the essence of the five grains.

Together with the various *preta*s—namely, hungry ghosts such as the Large-Bellied, Foul-Haired, Needle-Necked, and Torch-Mouthed—their having form means they possess color, as explained later in the text.
The retribution for refined spirits is as follows: those without form are without color, as described later in the text regarding "emptiness, dispersal, dissolution, and sinking.
Those with perception manifest as supernatural powers and strange transformations, such as the ghosts, spirits, and numinous beings mentioned later in the text.

Those without perception are stagnant, solid, and stubborn, as described later in the text regarding how "spirit and consciousness transform into earth, wood, metal, and stone. Each of these categories has its own particular suffering, which [the practitioner] must avoid.
Because it obstructs the Noble Path, it is called an "evil place. However, since birth has already ceased to arise, the Noble Path can be cultivated;
thus, it is fitting that one reaches the final body with causes perfected and fruits fulfilled. Furthermore, the five constant births occur before the Buddha.

If these good sons read, recite, copy, transcribe, wear, or preserve [this scripture], and offer various forms of worship, they shall not be born in states of poverty, lowliness, or unpleasantness throughout kalpa after kalpa.
Although these sentient beings may themselves fail to perform meritorious deeds, all the merits of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions shall be bestowed upon this person. By virtue of this—
One shall attain birth in the same place as all Buddhas for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, which are themselves unspeakably unspeakable;
with immeasurable merit like a cluster of akṣa fruits, one shall cultivate together in that same place, never to be separated.
First, by relying on this mantra, one is freed from suffering. This son of noble family refers specifically to those who possess the resolute bodhicitta;
they will not only avoid rebirth in the various lower realms, but if they rely upon this mantra, they will not even be born in those unpleasant places among human beings.

To face the text is "reading" (du); to turn one's back to it is "reciting" (song). To respectfully transcribe it is "writing" (shu); to cause another to write it is "copying" (xie). One should wear it upon the body.
"Name" refers to the labels [on offerings]. "Vessel" refers to the containers that hold them. "Various material offerings" refers to things such as incense, flowers, lamps, and candles.
Those who do not give rise to rebirth in states of poverty, low birth, or unpleasant conditions will certainly be born into wealthy, noble, and pleasant circumstances.

○ These [passages] below rely upon the Buddha’s perfected virtues. (Fearing that there might be a question such as: "Even if one relies on the power of the mantra, if one does not perform meritorious deeds, how can one be born in a place of happiness? Therefore, this explanation is given:

These sentient beings, even if they do not perform meritorious deeds, will not be hindered from being born in places of happiness, because all the merits and virtues of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are bestowed entirely upon these people.
To say they are "bestowed entirely upon these people" means that by means of this mantra...
This is the Buddha-mind; not to be apart from this mantra is precisely not to be apart from the Buddha-mind.
The merits of the Buddhas are inherent in one's own mind at all times. Because of this, one will be born before the Buddhas.

Regarding the phrase "because of this," it means that because the Buddha’s virtues are entirely bestowed upon them, they not only attain birth in a blissful place, but also encounter as many monks as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
For unspeakably many unspeakable kalpas, one shall be born in the same place as the Buddha; that is to say, one shall always stand before the Buddha.
Since one always stands before the Buddha and constantly relies upon this mantra, the virtues of the Buddha and the virtues of the mantra become identical to one’s own virtues.
Therefore it is said: "Immeasurable merits are like a cluster of akṣa fruits. This refers to the fruit of the akṣa cluster. Three.
The single seed and its stalk do not separate from one another; this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s virtues, the mantra’s virtues, and immeasurable merits being identical to one's own virtues.

The final two lines provide the explanation: as for why the Buddha’s virtues and the mantra’s virtues are identical to one's own virtues, it is because they are cultivated together in the same place and never become dispersed.
Since they are never dispersed, one constantly relies upon the Buddha’s virtues and the mantra.
One cultivates and refines virtue through practice to perfect one's own qualities; this is truly what is meant by the "cluster of akṣa fruits.
Sixth, it can accomplish all practices;
therefore, it can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify their roots of discipline, and enable those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them.
It causes those who have not yet applied diligence to attain diligence; it causes those who lack wisdom to attain wisdom;
it causes those who are not pure to swiftly attain purity; and it causes those who do not observe the fast and precepts to naturally fulfill them.
Building upon the above, because this divine mantra possesses such benefits, it is able to bring all practices to fulfillment.
As for a person who has broken the precepts—for instance, Ānanda, who among his eighty thousand practices violated only a single precept—if one's root of the precepts is pure...
Because his mind was pure, Ānanda had not yet been submerged; those who have not yet attained the precepts are like Dhaṅga, who was formerly a courtesan;
those who have caused others to attain the precepts are like Dhaṅga now, who is the nun Śīlā; and those who are not yet diligent...

Regarding Ānanda’s devotion to extensive learning and Daṅga’s partiality toward lustful desire: to cause those who possess diligence to attain it, [the Buddha] acted as when Ānanda earnestly requested meditative concentration;
to cause those who possess diligence to establish a forest of diligence, [he acted as when] Daṅga established the Forest of Diligence. Regarding those lacking wisdom:
to illustrate how Daṅga was ensnared by sleep and craving, not realizing that these are suffering; to cause those lacking wisdom to attain it, [the Buddha] acted as when Daṅga was with Rāhula.
The mother likewise realized her past causes. Those who were not yet purified were like Dhanagā before receiving the mantra, when the flames of lust flared up;

those who quickly attained purification were like Dhanagā after receiving the mantra, when the mind of lust suddenly ceased. Regarding the fasts and precepts, this refers to the Eightfold Precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa);
they differ vastly from the aforementioned five [precepts] in terms of superiority and inferiority. Using the former as a comparison for the latter, one would not maintain them oneself.

This can be understood through seven points concerning the extinguishing of offenses and the removal of hindrances: first, the extinguishing of present offenses; second, the removal of past hindrances.

Regarding the first [of these two], there are three sub-points: first, the simultaneous dissolution of both light and heavy offenses; second, the reduction of extremely light offenses to non-existence; third, the extinction of even extremely heavy offenses. First:
Ānanda, when these sons of good family maintain this mantra, even if they have violated the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them,
all the offenses of breaking the precepts— regardless of whether they are light or heavy— are simultaneously extinguished after they maintain the mantra.
When holding this mantra, one should naturally maintain the prohibitive precepts with solemnity, for the Buddha has given clear instructions on this matter.
Even if one has violated the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving and holding [the mantra], such acts belong to the past. Now that one is able to hold the mantra, one should renew oneself;

thus, the offenses of breaking the precepts previously committed against the assembly shall be extinguished all at once. The *Karmavācanā* says: "The evil committed by the former mind is like clouds covering [the sky]."
Later, when a wholesome mind arises, it is like a torch dispelling darkness. Since it is said that "it is like a torch dispelling darkness," what sin would not be extinguished?

Therefore, there is no distinction between grave and light [offenses]. (Grave refers to the first category of offenses in the Hīnayāna and the ten grave offenses in the Mahāyāna; light refers to the remaining categories in the Hīnayāna and the forty-eight kinds of light defilements in the Mahāyāna.
In both extremes of lightness, they are equally non-existent.

Even if one has consumed alcohol, eaten the five pungent roots, or engaged in various forms of impurity, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial immortals, spirits, and deities will not regard this as a transgression.
Even if one wears impure or tattered clothing, whether walking or staying still, one is entirely pure.
Even if one does not construct an altar, enter a place of practice, or engage in the Way, if one recites and maintains [the mantra]...
This mantra is identical in merit to entering the altar and practicing the Way; there is no difference between them. Regarding the consumption of raw onions and wine:

while there is no fault in [limited] use, wine has many disadvantages, as recorded in both the *sūtras* and the *śāstras*. As for eating the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*), they were censured by the Three Vehicles.
Regarding various impurities: apart from the three and five types of meat that are specifically excluded, all other [meats] are likewise [forbidden].
"It is impure; it should not be eaten. As for the current statement that "even if one has already [eaten]," this refers to the period prior to reciting the mantra.
Once the mantra has been recited, past transgressions are no longer culpable; therefore, from the Buddhas down to the spirits and deities, they will not regard it as a fault.
However, if at the very moment of approaching or during the actual recitation of the mantra, one still indulges freely in eating, then the celestial immortals will find it loathsome.
Foul and impure. Virtuous deities will not come to protect one; how much less so the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? The holy mirror is present here—how could one be without transgression?
Do not misunderstand this. Here, the "vajra-devas, celestial immortals, spirits, and ghosts" all refer to those who have made vows to protect the dharanis.

Regarding the point that "even if one wears [old robes], there is no offense for violating the teaching," this accords with the preceding text which states that the Buddha taught that one should wear new [robes].
[One should wear] clean robes, burn incense, and recite mantras; furthermore, one is instructed to practice the Way during the six periods [of the day] and remain awake for twenty-one days.
Now, it is said that one may even wear "unclean and tattered clothing," and it is also said to be "one act of walking and one act of standing.

Since it is called "unclean," it is not restricted to clean robes; since it is called "tattered," it is not restricted to new garments; and since it is called "one act of walking," [it is not restricted to formal circumambulation].
Thus, one is not restricted to the six periods [of the day]. Since it is said to be "one abiding," one is not restricted to the twenty-one days.
This is because for those who are impoverished and lack the leisure to escape from busy affairs, there is a fear that they might miss out on the benefits of reciting mantras;

therefore, it is permitted that even if this contravenes the Buddhist teachings, it is entirely equivalent to purity. That is to say, it is identical in its purity to those who strictly follow the instructions of the teachings.
Nevertheless, one must recognize for oneself that this violates the teachings and deeply purify the mind; it is simply not permissible to do so intentionally.

○ Even if one does not descend below the bounds of propriety and thus incurs no fault, one must still establish the altar according to the preceding text and perform the practice within the site in accordance with the Dharma, only then conforming to the Tathāgata’s pure rules of conduct.
As for the current statement, "even if one does not construct an altar," etc., it is also...

For those who lack the capacity to construct an altar, lack the conditions to enter the ritual arena, or lack the leisure to practice the Way, there is concern that they might lose the benefits of the mantra.

Therefore, even if one is permitted to recite and uphold the mantra according to convenience, there is no fault in deviating from the formal track—provided that it remains equivalent to the standard practice.
However, if one possesses the capacity, the conditions, and the leisure, it is still correct to construct an altar, enter the arena, and perform the Way. May you be fortunate.
Do not mistake change for permanence; otherwise, you will lose great benefit. Even the three most extreme [offenses] shall be extinguished.

If one has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution, or the four *pārājika* and eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses of monks and nuns, once this mantra has been recited, such heavy karma will be entirely eliminated and destroyed, like a heap of sand scattered by a fierce wind. Furthermore...
There is not even a hair’s breadth [of merit] remaining. As for the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*): first, killing one's father; second, killing one's mother; third, killing an Arhat;

fourth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha; and fifth, shedding the blood of a Buddha. One who commits these five heinous crimes shall fall into the Avīci Hell; among all sins, none is more grave than these.

In this regard, it is therefore called an "immediate grave offense" (*ānantarya*). The four offenses involving expulsion for a bhikṣu are the four *pārājika* rules: sexual misconduct, killing, theft, and false claims of spiritual attainment.

The Sanskrit term *pārājika* is translated here as "expulsion. This means that one who commits such an offense is forever cast outside the boundaries of the Buddha-dharma and may not dwell together with the pure Saṃgha.
As for the eight offenses involving expulsion for a bhikṣuṇī, the first four are the same as those for a bhikṣu.

The same as above. Furthermore, there are the eight acts of physical contact with concealment and acquiescence (*aṣṭau sparśāḥ saṃvaraṇānuvartanāni*). "Contact" refers to touching the body of a man with a defiled mind. The "eight" refer to: grasping the hand of a man with a defiled mind;

grasping his robe; entering a secluded place together; sitting together; speaking together; walking together; leaning against one another; and making appointments. "Concealment" refers to concealing the grave offenses of others. "Acquiescence" refers to providing robes, food, drink, and so forth for a monk who has been suspended (*utkṣiptaka*) by the Saṃgha.

Because these are all the most serious offenses of the first category, they are called "such grave karmas. If one recognizes them oneself and feels shame and remorse, one should recite mantras to seek repentance. By means of the mantra—
By the power [of this mantra], they should be extinguished upon mere recollection. Thus it is said: "It is like a fierce wind blowing away a heap of sand.

To say that the sand has already formed a heap implies that a gentle breeze could not blow it away; the wind is described as "fierce" to serve as a metaphor for the mantra being endowed with supernatural power.
Through the power of the mantra, grave offenses are extinguished; there is no offense that is not extinguished, just as when a fierce wind blows a heap of sand, there is no heap that remains.

Scattered. Therefore it is said that they are all extinguished and removed, without so much as a hair’s breadth remaining. Having finished the extinction of present offenses, second is the removal of past hindrances.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who, from immeasurable and incalculable kalpas ago, have committed all manner of light and heavy offenses—
Obstructions from previous lives that have not yet been repented— should one be able to read, recite, copy, or carry this mantra upon one's person,
or establish it within one's dwelling, house, garden, or villa— then such accumulated karma will vanish like snow melting in boiling water.
Before long, all shall attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
First, "past sins have not yet been repented" indicates that they were committed over countless and immeasurable lifetimes, not just in a single life.
"All light and heavy [sins]" indicates that the offenses are not of a single kind. Because they obstruct superior progress, they are called "hindrances.

Since these have persisted from previous lives and have not yet been repented, they will inevitably obstruct right practice; even if one practices *samādhi*, it will not be accomplished. One must necessarily...

"Extinguished by mantra. ○ If one is able to have [the obstacles] extinguished through the mantra below, and realizes for oneself that there were obstructions in past lives, one should uphold it with all one's might;
hence it says, "able to read and able to recite. Desiring that it not be forgotten whether rising or sitting, one should copy it out and wear it;
taking it so that it may strike the eyes and startle the heart, one should reside in a "zhuang-yuan" (莊園). "Zhuang" (莊) refers to a residence; this means to dwell in constant *an-gu* (安居, *ā-vāsa*).

"Place" refers to a garden or villa, meaning a location for occasional excursions and pleasure. "Thus accumulated karma" refers to the accumulation of light and heavy karmic obstacles over immeasurable and innumerable kalpas.
"Like hot water dissolving snow" is a metaphor for the swiftness with which they are eliminated.
The previous statement, "like hot water dissolving ice," implies that ice requires a short period of time; snow is not like that, for it merely encounters [the heat] and...
The water then immediately transformed; thus, it was extremely rapid. ○ Before long, one swiftly attains non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Since past obstructions have been eliminated and *samādhi* has been accomplished, it is said that "before long one attains patience" (*kṣānti*). According to the preceding context, this refers to the non-arising of both [subject and object] being empty;

according to the subsequent section, it corresponds to the third gradual stage. For now, it should not be interpreted as the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). This concludes the section on the extinction of offenses.
The removal of obstacles is complete. Eighth, all requests shall be fulfilled.

Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are women who have not yet borne children and desire to conceive, should they be able to recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, or wear this *Sītātapatrā* on their bodies, they will immediately give birth to blessings.
Virtuous men and women who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life; those who desire to swiftly fulfill their karmic rewards shall quickly attain fulfillment.
The same applies to their physical vitality, strength, and complexion. After the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the lands of the ten directions according to their vows;
they will certainly not be born in peripheral regions or among the lowly, much less in mixed forms.
Women do not give birth [easily]; in old age they have no support; moreover, they are currently abandoned by their husbands, ridiculed by others, and despised by other wives.
Therefore, all those who have not yet borne sons or daughters seek to conceive. "Conception" means to harbor a fetus within one's womb.
If one can recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, one’s desires should surely be fulfilled. Even if one’s wisdom and discernment are obscured...
If those who are dull-witted and unable to maintain mindfulness wear this *Siddhārthapāṇḍaravāsinī* upon their bodies, they will likewise share in the merit of such recollection.
Therefore it is said that sons and daughters of fortune and wisdom are born. Those sons and daughters who possess fortune and virtue are wealthy and benevolent;
those who possess wisdom and insight are sagacious and worthy. Thus, this fulfills the aspirations of men and women for offspring.
Furthermore, those who seek long life—ranging from the Son of Heaven above to the common people below—are all alike in this regard.
Because loving life and detesting death is the natural sentiment of humanity, those who obtain long life do so by the power of the mantra;

they extend their allotted years of heaven through the mantra’s efficacy, and by upholding it with a sincere heart, purifying the mind and diminishing desires, they avoid premature death. This is how it comes to pass.

"Longevity is what Qiu seeks. Those who wish to seek karmic fruition are said to practice extensive acts of giving in order to seek blessings and joy, further hoping that these results may be obtained immediately in the present life;
therefore, it is called "swift perfection. As for "swiftly attaining fulfillment," it is because their meritorious karma is already superior.
Furthermore, they are rescued by the power of mantras; this is accomplished entirely in the present, without waiting for the future. This is the pursuit of merit and happiness.
Regarding physical life, vitality, and strength, these are also spoken of in terms of those who seek them.

That is to say, although one possesses physical life, if one lacks vitality and strength, every movement and action will constantly be contrary to one's wishes; therefore, there are also those who seek robust health, and it is likewise so.
This is so. As in previous examples, one can know that it will be fulfilled. This "fulfillment" refers to the attainment of strength and vigor. The *Mahākaruṇā Sūtra* states:
"If, while reciting and upholding the Great Compassion Divine Mantra, anything sought in this present life is not fulfilled, then it cannot be called the *Mahākaruṇā-citta-dhāraṇī*.
Since the mantra is thus, its principle ought not to be false. At the end of one's life...
Regarding "thereafter": this refers to the period when the preceding aggregates (*skandha*) have already perished and the subsequent aggregates have not yet been formed.
As for "reborn in accordance with one's vows in the lands of the ten directions": it is said that among the lands of the ten directions, there are both pure and defiled ones.

If one maintains the mantra during life and vows to be reborn in a pure land, then after death, by the power of maintaining the mantra, one immediately attains rebirth in accordance with that vow. It is not merely a matter of being reborn in accordance with one's vows.
Furthermore, one is born into a noble family in a central land; thus it is said that one will certainly not be born in the borderlands or among the lowly.
Since one does not even take birth in the borderlands or among the lowly, how much less could one fall into the various forms and disparate retributions of the hells or hungry ghosts?
One should naturally not fall therein; this is the seeking of rebirth in the Pure Land. The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "Recite and uphold the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī."
"If I do not attain birth in the lands of all Buddhas, I vow not to achieve perfect enlightenment.

This is because that [vow] incorporates the power of the bodhisattva's aspiration, while this incorporates the mental power of all Buddhas; for this mantra is the heart-seal (hṛdaya-mudrā) of all Buddhas. Whoever upholds this mantra—
"Because they will certainly be protected and remembered by the Buddha. This concludes the detailed explanation of the specific benefits and advantages.

Second, the general manifestation of universal benefit has three parts: first, the elimination of all calamities; second, the abundance and joy of the myriad people; third, the non-appearance of malevolent stars. First [the elimination of all calamities]:
Ānanda, if there are kingdoms, prefectures, counties, or villages suffering from famine, epidemics, or the calamities of weapons, bandits, and strife,
as well as all other lands beset by misfortune— by transcribing this divine mantra and placing it at the four gates of the city,
or upon various *caityas* and *stūpas*, you shall cause all sentient beings within those lands to welcome and pay homage to this mantra.
Prostrate with reverence and offer worship with a single-minded focus. Cause the people to each wear it upon their person, or place it within each of their dwellings.
All calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished.

First, the difficulties of the lands are summarized in general. "Lands" (*deśa*) refers to the administrative superintendence of prefectures and counties. "Prefectures and counties" (*janapada*) refer to the divided governance of those lands.
"Villages" (*grāma*) refers to market towns and hamlets; these, in turn, are governed by the prefectures and counties.

"Famine" (*durbhikṣa*) means that households are as empty as hanging stone chimes and there is not a blade of green grass in the wilds; this is the difficulty of famine. "Epidemics" (*mārī*) means that the four seasons do not [function properly]...
"Correct. 'The prevalence of pestilence' refers to the calamity of epidemics. 'Arms' refers to the lack of tranquility on the frontiers.
'Bandits' refers to the lack of peace within the family and the state. 'Strife' refers to the chaos caused by petty elements; these are all the calamities of arms. As for the 'other calamities'..."
This includes all things that cause harm to sentient beings, such as uneven droughts and floods, or the occasional arrival of wind and hail.

Having written this below, one should establish it for offerings. As for writing the mantra and placing it at the four gates, this is so that all who pass to and fro may receive benefit wherever their eyes fall upon it;
furthermore, it is to ensure the protection of the hundred spirits against all calamities and evil matters.
Because one cannot enter [it]. *Cetiya* is translated here as "a place worthy of offerings. The *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states: "That which contains relics is called a *stūpa*;
that which lacks relics is called a *cetiya*. Based on this, a *cetiya* refers to things such as sūtra-stūpas and dharani-stūpas.
*Deva-kīla* is translated as "banner" (*dhvaja*), such as the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhvaja* and the *Dhāraṇī-dhvaja*. (In the *Xunwen*, *kīla* is glossed as *du*.)

The *Erya* calls it a *tai* (platform). A "detached" (*tuō*) structure refers to one where the accumulated earth has fallen away. We do not adopt that definition here because this is a term from the Sanskrit language.

Furthermore, these are places of veneration for all people. To cause all sentient beings within that land to welcome and receive this mantra and so forth—even those who reside at city gates or at *caityas* and *stūpas*, and even those who fear they might never enter a city or spend their entire lives without paying homage—[is the purpose].

As for the pagodas and temples, how could they possibly hear, see, or behold [the deity]? Therefore, it is necessary to employ the majesty of the state to compel the entire nation to welcome them with reverence, pay homage, and make offerings.
Furthermore, one should cause each person to wear [the image] upon their person and each to install it within their own dwelling.
○ All calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished; "all" refers collectively to these as described above.
What has been described above refers to famines, epidemics, and the like. The reason these things arise in such lands is entirely due to the ten unwholesome actions of the sentient beings therein.
Now, by making peaceful offerings with this mantra, they will gradually come to know how to reform their evils and turn toward goodness;
through faith, acceptance, and upholding, they will naturally invoke the blessings and protection of devas and nāgas, thereby transforming calamities and misfortunes into [auspiciousness].
Auspicious! Therefore, it is said that all [calamities] shall be extinguished. Second, the myriad people shall enjoy abundance and happiness.
Ānanda, wherever there are sentient beings in any land who possess this mantra, the devas and nāgas will rejoice; wind and rain will follow their proper seasons;
the five grains will be abundant; and the myriad subjects will dwell in peace and happiness.
"Wherever there are sentient beings in any land" means that regardless of where one may be, wherever there is a land and sentient beings, there must be this mantra.
This is because wherever this mantra exists, the devas and nāgas will immediately rejoice.
Furthermore, although it is said that the mantra exists wherever it is, one must necessarily believe in, accept, and uphold it in order to move the devas.

The dragons rejoice. Even if they do not give rise to faith and acceptance, but instead treat [the teachings] with contempt and defile them, it will still cause the devas and nāgas to manifest their wrath;
how then could there be any joy? As for wind and rain being timely: when it is appropriate for rain, it rains;
when it is appropriate for wind, it blows—there is neither excess nor deficiency. As for the five grains: millet, beans, hemp, wheat, and rice. "Abundant" means plentiful.
"Abundant and generous" refers to the great quantity of what was harvested; "shu" (庶) means the common multitude. In the Confucian classics, the people are termed "shu";
here, the term "zhao-shu" (兆庶) is used to manifest their vastness to the utmost, rather than restricting "zhao" to a fixed number of one billion.

This is similar to how "bai-xing" (百姓) and "wan-min" (萬民) are both used to denote the populace. "Peace and happiness" means that each person finds security in their own occupation and rejoices in what they possess.
Because there are no calamities. Second, the three malevolent stars do not appear. This has two parts: first, a brief indication; second, a detailed explanation. Regarding the first:
it is also able to suppress all malevolent stars and their various transformations according to the directions; disasters and obstacles do not arise, and people suffer no untimely deaths.
Manacles, fetters, cangues, and shackles shall not touch their bodies; they shall sleep peacefully day and night, never having evil dreams.
Regarding all malevolent stars, as described in the following sections: "able to subdue" means being able to suppress them so that they do not manifest signs of transformation or anomaly.

"Transformation" (*bian*) refers to deviating from the norm; "anomaly" (*guai*) refers to being different from the ordinary. This is as previously stated regarding comets, *bèi* (meteors), and falling stars.
This is so. As for the phrase "according to the direction," it means that [the response] manifests according to the specific direction of the stimulus.
This is because human affairs are enacted below while the Way of Heaven responds from above. Thus, once strange portents no longer arise, calamities and obstructions naturally do not occur.
When calamities do not arise, each person completes their natural lifespan; therefore it is said: "People suffer no untimely deaths. Obstructions.
If they do not arise, then all will be peaceful and free from affairs. Therefore it is said: "The cangue, shackles, and pillory shall not touch their bodies;

day and night they sleep in peace, without having nightmares. This means that since calamities and obstructions are absent and the punishments of hardship are not applied, one naturally sleeps peacefully and awakens peacefully, and even one's dreams are peaceful. Second, a detailed explanation.
Ānanda, in this Sahā world-system there are eighty-four thousand calamitous and malevolent stars, with twenty-eight great malevolent stars as their leaders.
Furthermore, there are eight great malevolent stars that act as their sovereigns;

when they manifest in various forms in the world, they are able to produce all manner of calamities and anomalies for sentient beings. Wherever this dhāraṇī exists on earth, they shall all be completely extinguished. 10.
An area of two *yojanas* constitutes the boundary of the consecrated ground (*sīmā*), into which no evil calamities or portents can ever enter.
Specifically, the Sahā world is singled out because it is a defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-bhūmi*); this serves to manifest that in the Pure Land there are no malevolent stars.
The number eighty-four thousand corresponds to the measure of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings. Evil does not become evil of its own accord; it transforms due to calamities. Therefore—
Regarding calamities caused by malevolent stars: if sentient beings can transform disaster into fortune, these shall be transformed into auspicious stars.
As for the twenty-eight great malevolent stars, when categorized according to the four directions, Buddhist scriptures and secular classics are largely the same with minor differences.
Their similarities lie in the fact that their names and numbers are identical; their minor differences lie in the shifting of their positions. For example, in the east...
The seven stars of the East: according to the *Mayūra* (Peacock), these are Mṛgaśirā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Śravaṇa, Svātī, Āśleṣā, Aśleṣā, and Anurādhā;

whereas the secular classics state they are Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśirā, Ārdrā, and Punarvasu. The seven stars of the South: according to the *Mayūra*, these are Jyeṣṭhā, Viśākhā, Citrā, Svātī, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, and Pūrvāṣāḍhā;
whereas the secular classics state they are Āśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, Hastā, Citrā, and Svātī. The seven stars of the West: according to... [text continues]
According to the *Mayūra* (Peacock) system, the seven stars of the north consist of Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Rohiṇī, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Uttaraphalgunī;

whereas according to the secular classics (*laukika-śāstra*), they consist of Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvabhadrapadā, Uttarabhadrapadā, Revatī, Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and Kṛttikā. According to the *Mayūra*, the seven stars of the south consist of Svāti, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Uttarāṣāḍhā;

This means that he is able to preside over eighty-four thousand [deities]. Because he is a great malevolent star, there are furthermore eight great malevolent stars.

(Question: Since following the right brings a response of blessing and following the perverse brings a response of disaster, why are they designated simply by the names of "malevolent stars"?

III. Receiving the Benefits and Exhorting to Faith (in two parts): A. Receiving the previously shown benefits; B. Exhorting to faith and attaining realization.

Regarding the first: For this reason, the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra to protect beginners and all practitioners in future ages as they enter samādhi, so that their bodies and minds may be tranquil and attain great peace and security, free from all demons, ghosts, and spirits.

Furthermore, regarding the harms caused by enmities and calamities from beginningless time, as well as the lingering debts of past karma that come to afflict and injure one—relying on the aforementioned divine mantra yields such benefits. For this reason, the Tathāgata proclaimed this mantra.
He did not speak of it in terms of the present life, but rather of the future life, because while the Buddha was in the world, Māra could find no opportunity to harm.
Because the obstacles of sentient beings are light, it does not say "protecting those who practice deeply," but rather says "protecting beginners.
This is because those who practice deeply possess the power to eliminate demons and the power to sever obstacles.

It does not speak of the state of distraction (*vikṣepa*) but speaks of "entering samādhi," because the state of distraction still belongs to the realm of demons; being possessed of obstacles, one remains unaware of them, and thus body and mind remain at ease.

"Those whose inner and outer selves are relaxed and unimpeded, who are liberated within and without, and have attained great peace and stability, truly abide in right concentration (*samādhi*) rather than in worldly enjoyment.

'There is nothing further that equals them' means they are protected by the power of the mantra. As for the various demons, ghosts, and spirits, they are as explained below in the section on the 'Shadow Demons' (*chāyā-māra*).

"Old karma and accumulated debts" refers to ancient karmic liabilities that have not yet been settled.
Following one since beginningless time, they afflict and harm the body and mind, prevent the attainment of *samādhi*, and constantly invade with manifold sufferings.

You, as well as all those among the assembly who are still in training, and all practitioners of future ages, should rely upon my maṇḍala and maintain the precepts according to the Dharma.

If these good sons do not attain mental penetration within this very body born of their parents, then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsely.

Since [the Buddhas] first encouraged faith, they will continue to provide protection in the future; it is therefore even more appropriate that you should believe and accept [this teaching] in the present. Thus, [the Buddha] addresses them collectively as "you."
As well as for those in training (*śaikṣa*) and all future practitioners, this section clarifies the conditions under which one does not incur the four transgressions:
first, deficiency in the ritual site; second, deficiency in the precepts; third, impurity of the master; and fourth, doubt and regret.

To commit even one of these constitutes merely planting a distant cause, making it difficult to attain realization in the present life. Thus, we know that the aforementioned permissions were merely skillful means and not the permanent rule.
This is the Dharma. I, the fool, say that among the four transgressions, doubt and regret are the root.

If one can truly believe without doubting and maintain [the precepts] without regretting, one will naturally refuse to tread upon the aforementioned transgressions; it is for this reason that they are called "those who encourage faith.

This refers to the body present before one, not awaiting the future. Wuxing says: Regarding "the mind penetrating," based on what precedes, there are no more than three meanings.

this person, at that time, is able to remember eighty-four thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas with their mind, comprehending them thoroughly and without any doubt.

What I call "penetration of the mind" refers to the opening and unblocking of the ground of the mind. As for the statement that one is able to refrain from the four [grave offenses] as described above—this is the fruit [of such penetration].

Zhengmai states that these are the Four Rectifying Officers (*sì-zhí-gōng-cáo*), which is also acceptable. However—

The mountain deity is the god who presides over mountains; the ocean deity is the god who presides over the ocean; the local deity is the god who presides over the earth.
"Water-dwellers" refers to those who move within the water; "land-dwellers" refers to those who move upon the land; and "sky-dwellers" refers to...

These include such as the water spirits, fire spirits, deities of medicinal herbs, forests, and crops. The Wind King (*fengshenwang*) is the presiding deity of wind. Because...
The upper realm belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are the four spheres of emptiness (*catasraḥ śūnyatā-vihārāḥ*).

The reason for not mentioning the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is that since the upper and lower realms already exist, the intermediate one can be understood by implication. Regarding the phrase "simultaneously bowing their heads," some say:

Thus, the prostration performed today need not be considered extraordinary. "Paying homage to the Buddha" is itself the act of making a vow; "protection" is as explained above.

At that time, eighty-four thousand nayutas of koṭis of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were Vajragarbha Kings, rose from their seats amidst the great assembly. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as for the meritorious deeds we have cultivated, we have long since attained Bodhi and do not enter Nirvana; we shall always follow this mantra to provide protection."

"Those who practice samādhi as correct cultivation during the final age"—the names and numbers of these bodhisattvas are all as explained previously. "Rising from their seats in the assembly to pay homage and address the Buddha" refers to making a vow before the multitude.
"Beings such as ourselves" refers to a specific class of bodhisattvas whose cultivated meritorious deeds have long since brought them to the realization of Bodhi.
"Attaining" means that one has already attained or shall attain nirvāṇa. "Not attaining nirvāṇa" refers to those who instead make a vow to remain as bodhisattvas.

"Protecting and guarding the final age" means that until the end of the future, they will never forget to provide protection and sustenance. "Practicing samādhi" refers to the cultivation of perfect penetration.
For such a person practicing the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*), one must first maintain the precepts and recite mantras, acting according to the instructions;
this is the true practitioner of cultivation. This clarifies that without these, protection cannot be attained. Second, a specific clarification of the protective sustenance.
World-Honored One, whenever such a person who cultivates the mind to seek right concentration is at a place of practice, or elsewhere walking for meditation,
or even when their mind is distracted as they wander through a village, we and our followers shall always follow and attend upon this person.

Regarding the phrase "thus cultivating the mind" and so forth: this refers to those who, as instructed by the Buddha, uphold the precepts, recite mantras, and practice samādhi in order to seek right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).

Having sought right concentration, whether they sit in meditation within the *maṇḍala* or walk in meditation elsewhere, they never depart from the recitation of mantras and the practice of "turning the hearing inward.
These are the ones belonging to the group of those destined for right concentration (*samyaktva-niyāma-rāśi*).
"Even those with distracted minds" refers to those who seek right concentration but are unable to collect their minds, reciting mantras only with a distracted mind;

these belong to the group of the indeterminate (*aniyata-rāśi*). "Those who sport in villages" refers to those who seek right concentration but do not know how to collect their minds, falsely claiming to attain stillness amidst movement;
these belong to the group of the wrongly fixed (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*). "We, the assembly of followers" refers to...
This refers to the retinue under one's command. It is as stated previously: "Each and every bodhisattva has a host of vajra-beings as their retinue.

Furthermore, it was said before: "Even if there are sentient beings who, with a distracted mind (the indeterminate group) or a mind not in samādhi (the wrongly fixed group), should remember [this] in their minds and uphold it with their mouths, the Vajra King will constantly follow them; how much more so [for those with a focused mind]?"
Those who have resolved upon the bodhicitta (the group of those fixed in rightness) are here said to be "constantly followed. This means that one shall attend and protect such persons.
