According to the preceding section on the delusions of sentient beings, there should have been a concluding subsection here on those delusions; that it is not provided separately now is as follows:
The world is analyzed by way of its divisions, each of which has a corresponding concluding statement, namely: "It is established because of this realm; it is formed because of this world.
Having concluded the analysis by raising and resolving these topical divisions, there are three sections on the gradual formation of the classes of beings:
first, the enumeration of the initial formation of the classes; second, the subsequent formation of cyclic existence; and third, the final formation of fixed existence. First:
The three periods of time and the four directions interpenetrate one another in harmony, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories.
"Periods" refers to the flow of transition; "directions" refers to spatial positions. There are three counts of this flow, hence they are called the "three periods," namely:
past, present, and future. There are four spatial positions, hence they are called the "four directions," namely: east, west, south, and north. Apart from the periods, there are the directions.
There is no basis. Where there are no realms, the world is no longer perceived. Because they depend on one another and are falsely established, it is called "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*).
Because they mutually intersect through conjunction, it is called "interpenetration.

Since "interpenetration" carries the meaning of entering into one another, those who transform sentient beings mean that sentient beings within the world should naturally undergo transformation along with the world itself. However...
The worlds interpenetrate one another, and the permutations of these transformations amount roughly to twelve.

For instance, if the world is applied to the directions, each of the four directions encompasses the three periods of time, resulting in a total of twelve permutations. Conversely, if the directions are applied to the world, each of the three periods of time encompasses the four directions;
the number of permutations remains the same. Among the sentient beings herein, those who undergo transformation according to the directions are born...
Born here and born there, their forms and types differ. According to the four directions, they are divided into four categories.

Within these four categories, there are births of the past, births of the present, and births of the future; as birth after birth differs, each category is further divided into three, thus becoming twelve.
If one follows the transformations of the world, there are the forms of those already born, those currently being born, and those yet to be born.
The categories differ. Within the three periods of time, they form three classes.
Among these three classes, there are those born in the south, those born in the north, those born in the east, and those born in the west; each birth is distinct.
Each class is further divided into four, thus forming twelve. This is merely a summary of how they become twelve according to direction and period; it speaks briefly of their forms.
The categories are not identical; they do not necessarily consist of the womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, or transformation-born types.

As for the womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born types mentioned below, these are further brought about by afflictions and karma, as will be seen in the section below. Second, the formation of the cycle of transmigration.
Therefore, in the world, sound arises from movement; form arises from sound; fragrance arises from form; touch arises from fragrance; flavor arises from touch;

and mental objects (*dharma*) are known through flavor. Because these six types of deluded conceptualization constitute the nature of karma, the twelve divisions [of the sense bases] revolve in this manner.
Building upon the preceding classification of categories, it follows that karma is produced through sensory objects (*viṣaya*), resulting in the phenomenon of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
As for the "world" (*loka*), it is the general characteristic of the six sense-objects; therefore, it is mentioned first. Regarding the statement that "sound arises from movement":
the flux of the world and the transformation of the realms are both termed "movement. Because movement necessarily gives rise to resonance, it is said that sound exists.
Regarding sound: it was previously stated that sound rolls up to form the ear; this occurs at this very moment. As for "having form" due to sound:

having already heard the sound, one necessarily seeks out its form; therefore, it is said to have form. It was previously stated that form binds together to form the eye; this occurs at this very moment.

Regarding "due to form there is fragrance": seeing a form gives rise to defilement, and one perceives fragrance within oneself; this is precisely the moment referred to previously as "receiving fragrance to constitute the nose.
Regarding "due to fragrance there is tangibility": smelling a fragrance and desiring to grasp it first gives rise to a distorted perception; hence it is said that "there is tangibility.
This is precisely the moment referred to previously as "grasping tangibility to constitute the body. Regarding "due to tangibility there is flavor": one perceives the tangibility.
Desire arises; the mouth secretes saliva of craving. Therefore, it is called "having flavor. What was previously described as "the flavor being twisted to form the tongue" occurs at this very moment.

As for "knowing dharmas because of flavor," it means that one does not forget the attachment to flavor, and the shadows of sensory objects constantly appear before the mind; therefore, it is called "knowing dharmas.
What was previously described as "grasping at dharmas to form the mind" occurs at this very moment. The "six chaotic delusions" refers to the six consciousnesses. This is because:

When the sense organs and their objects encounter one another, consciousness arises between them. Its function is indeterminate and thus termed "disturbance" (luan); its substance lacks reality and is thus termed "delusion" (wang).
Once deluded consciousness has arisen, discrimination follows, giving rise to various afflictions and creating manifold karmas;

this constitutes the accomplishment of the nature of karma. Once the nature of karma is established, retribution is experienced in accordance with that karma; hence it is said that there are twelve distinct divisions.
This means that they are categorized according to the initial formation of those twelve classes.
Thus, one knows that while the preceding twelve classes merely followed the transformations of the world, at this point they turn into the summoning of karma.
Those who revolve through this cycle do so because karma undergoes transition and retribution circulates; therefore, after the third [category], there are necessarily three fixed [classes].
First, the general summary from the preceding section; second, the detailed explanation according to categories; third, the concluding summary by enumeration.
Regarding the first: Therefore, the world of sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, exhausting twelve transformations, becomes a single cycle of return.

Because they ride upon this wheel of inverted characteristics, there exist worlds of egg-birth, womb-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth, as well as those with form and those without form.

Whether it be with perception, without perception, neither with nor without perception, or neither form nor non-form—therefore, regarding "the world and so forth," this refers to the revolving of these twelve wheels.
Consequently, the six sense-objects of the world also arise and transform according to their respective categories.
For example, as with the single object of sound, each category differs from the others; they necessarily undergo transformation in accordance with their corresponding categories.
Reaching the end of the twelve transformations constitutes one complete cycle. Once this cycle is completed, a further transformation begins again from the very start;
hence it is called "revolving and returning. "Revolving and returning" means that having gone through a full cycle, one begins anew.

However, it is essential to clarify these transformations of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), for the six sense objects serve as the conditions for creating karma, while the nature of karma is the cause of saṃsāric wandering. The six...
Since sentient beings (*jāti*) undergo transformations according to their respective categories, each category of being establishes its karma based on the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
This is why the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) does not cease and why sentient beings necessarily exist. Therefore, the following passage uses this very principle to provide a general summary.

"Riding upon" (*sheng*) means "by means of" (*hetu*). "Cycling" refers to the twelve cycles of rebirth. "Inversion" (*viparyāsa*) refers to [the process] of establishing [existence] based on sense-objects.
Regarding karma: although there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), if there is no inversion (*viparyāsa*), then cyclic existence can be stilled and the continuity of rebirth can be exhausted.
That "it exists" means that it certainly exists by virtue of inversion; this is what was previously referred to as the "world."
Because they serve as the basis, the four modes of birth (*yoni*) among those who depend upon them are considered constant. As stated previously: "The egg-born arise solely from thought;
the womb-born are due to emotion; the moisture-born are produced by contact; and the transformation-born respond through detachment. The latter eight [categories] are subject to change.

The previous statement that "emotion, thought, contact, and detachment mutually transform one another" indicates that differences exist merely according to the presence or absence of various conditions, just as in the case of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

It is said: There is union through passionate attachment, and separation through the absence of passionate attachment; transforming by depending on the womb, there is union through conceptualization and separation through the absence of conceptualization.
There is transformation by depending on the egg; it is not that there is form, for there is separation from passion and then union;

nor is it that there is no form, for there is union with passion and then separation. There is transformation by depending on moisture; it is not that there is conceptualization, for there is union after the departure of conceptualization; nor is it that there is no conceptualization.
They are conceived and then separated; they depend on transformation and then change. This is a general indication; the detailed explanation of their characteristics follows below.
There are twelve categories based on type: first, egg-born; second, womb-born; third, moisture-born; fourth, transformation-born; fifth, with form; sixth, formless;
seventh, with perception; eighth, without perception; ninth, neither with form nor... [text truncated].
They are not formless. Eleven are not with perception; twelve are not without perception.
First, Ānanda, due to the delusory cycle of the world, because of the inversion of movement, the combination of vital energies produces eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking.
Thus, there are egg-born beings, such as the *kalala*, which circulate through the lands.
Fish, birds, turtles, and snakes—these species fill [the world].

This has been briefly clarified at the outset. The meaning of "world" (*loka*) encompasses the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); as previously stated, these include sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch, exhausting the twelve transformations.
Now, in contrast to birth from an egg, this constitutes the first transformation. It is because of this transformation that false and delusive saṃsāra exists.

"False and delusive" refers to speculative conceptualization (*saṃjñā*); that is, when the six sense-objects of the world have not yet appeared before one, one forms distant and abstract mental images.
Because these are not real, there is "saṃsāra": as long as one does not comprehend these thoughts, birth from an egg will not cease. By means of the egg...

This is because they arise solely from perception (*saṃjñā*). Regarding "movement and inversion" (*dòngdiān*), the following provides a detailed explanation. Zhengmo says: "The essence of perception is light and buoyant; this is called 'movement-inversion.
It means that because of this movement, one inevitably comes to grasp the false as true; therefore, it is designated by the term 'inversion.'"
Regarding "the blending of vital energies" (*qi*): "energy" here refers to the intermingling of the male and female, the division of the *yīn-yáng* breaths.
However, this fundamentally belongs to the realm of delusion; due to inversion, one clings to it as real and blends with it. The *Zhèngmài* states:
"The egg is produced through the intersection of vital energies. "Accomplishment" (*chéng*) means to bring to fruition. As for the "eighty-four thousand," within this blending, all afflictions...
Because they are fully possessed of affliction (*kleśa*). Although they are fully possessed [of these], all arise from perception (*saṃjñā*);
since the mind of perception is unstable, fluctuating suddenly upward and downward, it is called "confused perception of flying and sinking. "Thus there are, etc.
means that by taking in the vital breath (*vāyu*) in this manner, form is produced; thus there are the egg-born and the *kalala*. The *kalala* is the first seven days of the fetal stage.

Regarding the "signs": because the formation of the egg occurs precisely at this stage. "Flowing through the lands" means the sense of saṃsāra. The final two phrases indicate the categories of beings:
those with thoughts of flight become birds; those with thoughts of sinking become fish; those possessing both become turtles and snakes.
As for "their kinds," this refers to all other classes that are not fully encompassed by these examples. Since they exist everywhere, it is said they "pervade and fill."
Second is birth from a womb.
Due to the defiled cycle of rebirth in the world, and because of the inversion of desire, eighty-four thousand transverse and vertical disordered thoughts are formed through union and nourishment.
Thus, there is the flow and turning within the realms of the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages, including those of humans and animals.
The dragon-sages (*nāga-ṛṣi*) of their kind fill [the world].
This has been briefly clarified above. Herein, the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) of this world correspond to the second transformation relative to womb-birth (*jarāyu-ja*).
Due to this transformation, there is the defiled cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). "Defiled" refers to deluded perception; that is to say, regarding this world—
When the six sense objects manifest before one, they are submerged in false emotions; because these are not pure, one wanders in saṃsāra.

This wandering arises because such emotions fail to realize the truth, and thus birth from a womb does not cease, for the womb is caused by emotion. [The section on] "the desire to fall" below provides a detailed explanation.
Zhengmo says: "Sentiment arises from craving; this is called the inversion of desire. This means that because of desire, one inevitably comes to grasp at the false as true;
therefore, it is also designated by the term 'inversion. As for 'nourishing through union,' 'nourishing' refers to the mutual moistening of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood.
This too is empty and false, yet due to inversion, one grasps it as real and unites with it."
“Combined. Zhengmo says: “This refers to the union of the essences (*śukra*) in the womb.

As for the ‘accomplishment of eighty-four thousand,’ it is because the afflictions (*kleśa*) are fully present within that union. Although the afflictions are fully present, they all arise from emotion (*qing*).

Because the emotional mind is unstable—sometimes horizontal and sometimes vertical—it is called ‘horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts. ‘Thus there are’ and so forth means that because of this...”

Taking the nourishment to form the body, there is the *arbuda* stage of the embryo. Because the *arbuda* marks the phase of the embryo’s division into two weeks, the stabilization of the embryo occurs precisely at this stage.
The final two phrases indicate the category: contemplating [the process] vertically constitutes the human mode.

Those with horizontal thoughts become animals; those possessing both [horizontal and vertical] become dragon-sages (*nāga-ṛṣi*), for the transformations of dragon-sages can be either horizontal or vertical.
Third are those born from moisture.

This arises from attachment to the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) within the world, due to the inversion of their destinies. Through the union of warmth, they are formed as eighty-four thousand [beings].
A thousand times over, inverted and chaotic thoughts arise. Because of this, there is the moist-phase *bīja-kalala* (the "coagulated corpse") that transmigrates through the realms.
Beings that crawl and wriggle, their species filling every space;

this briefly clarifies the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) within these realms, which constitute the third transformation relative to moisture-born beings. It is due to this transformation that [this state arises].

And there is attachment to saṃsāra. "Attachment" means clinging; that is to say, because one remains close to and joins with, rather than abandoning, the objects of the six sense-fields within the world.
"Saṃsāra" means the mind’s union [with these objects] such that it does not forget them.
Moisture-born birth does not cease, for it is brought about by the union of moisture and cohesion. Regarding the detailed explanation of "inverted pursuit" (*tiryag-ādi*):

"pursuit" (*gati*) refers to turning toward sense objects (*viṣaya*), while "inversion" (*viparyāsa*) refers to turning away from awakening (*bodhi*). As for "harmonizing with warmth," "warmth" here refers to the comparison of moist substances;

they mutually generate warmth through their interaction. This too is illusory, yet due to inversion, one clings to it as real. To take refuge within and rely upon that [union] is called "harmonizing" (*saṃyoga*).
This is the synthesis. Regarding the "accomplishment of eighty-four thousand": because the afflictions are fully present within this synthesis, the mind is unsettled;
at times it looks upward and at times it is overturned. Therefore, they are called "upside-down and disordered thoughts. "Upward" refers to looking up, while "overturned" refers to looking down.
Regarding the phrase "thus there is existence, etc.": it means that because form is constituted through the combination of such warmth, there is the moist characteristic of the *kalala*.
Since the *kalala* is the initial stage of moist-birth (*samsvedaja*), and it does not arise from a mother’s womb, the former two characteristics (the solid and the hollow) are absent.

The final two phrases indicate the categories: "covered" refers to those containing crawling insects, because their nature is devoid of cognition; "uncovered" refers to wriggling creatures, because their forms lack stability.
The rest is self-evident. Fourth are the spontaneously born (*upapāduka*).
Due to the causes of the world’s transformation and saṃsāra, and because of false inversions, the conjunction of contact produces eighty-four thousand discursive thoughts of the new and the old.
Thus, there exist transformed *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands;
they undergo metamorphosis and fly about, their species filling every space.
This is a brief initial clarification. Herein, the "elements and sense objects" (*dhātu-viṣaya*) constitute the fourth transformation relative to beings of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*).

Because of this transformation, there is the cycle of change and transmigration (*pariṇāma-saṃsāra*). "Change" (*pariṇāma*) refers to lightness and detachment; that is to say, regarding the six sense objects of the world.

The objects previously relied upon are hastily abandoned; because the mind is not constant, those who transmigrate do not change their hearts even as they depart from them, nor do they cease their rebirth through transformation, for they respond by transforming and departing. ○ Below, under "Pretending to be Upright," this is explained in detail:

departing [from objects] is called "false" because it is not true departure; considering it to be true is called "inversion. Upon contact, new objects manifest before one; this is the encounter with the old.
This is the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Even this new realm is false and illusory; yet, due to inversion (*viparyāsa*), one clings to it as real.

To transform one's will toward the higher [realms] is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). As for the accomplishment of the eighty-four thousand [afflictions], this is also due to conjunction being fully possessed of affliction (*kleśa*).

Although they are said to be fully possessed of affliction, there is no mind of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-citta*). Because the mind of renunciation is not settled, one fears attachment and fear obstruction. (Attachment means clinging to the old without shedding it; obstruction means...)
"Because the new obstructs and it is difficult for the old to proceed," it is therefore said that "the new and the old are in disarray. The phrase "Thus there is, etc.
means that through such a combination of contact, form is produced; thus there is the *kalala* (embryonic stage) characterized by transformation.

Since the *kalala* is precisely the initial sign of transformed birth (*upapāduka*), it signifies that the new substance has already been formed and has just emerged from its former husk, as it lacks the characteristics of the *arbuda* (obscured mass). The final two phrases point to the category [of beings].
Therefore, because one attains liberation from the old [body], one undergoes a transformation; because one attains the realization of the new [body], one soars through flight.

"Transformation" (蛻) is synonymous with "liberation" (脫). When a cicada sheds its skin, it flies; when a snake sheds its skin, it moves. Other cases may be inferred by analogy. Regarding the five types of beings with form (*rūpin*), [Guanding says: they possess form and unite with passion].

Due to the causes of worldly obstruction and the cycle of saṃsāra, because of the hindrance of perversion, they combine and become attached, forming eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of radiant brilliance.
Thus, there are beings with physical forms and *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands;
those who are spirits of auspicious or calamitous portents fill every category.

First, a brief explanation: herein, the "elements" (*dhātu*) and "objects" (*viṣaya*) constitute the fifth transformation in relation to that which possesses form (*rūpin*). Due to this transformation, there is obstruction and saṃsāra.

"Obstruction" means that regarding the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) of the world, one’s emotional attachment clings to them as one's own, desiring to retain them, thereby creating an obstacle toward others.
"Saṃsāra" means that emotional attachment is not eliminated; as long as there is that which possesses form...

They are severed because they are moved by form and emotion, for there is that which causes them to conjoin. ○ Regarding "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) and "inversion" (*viparyāsa*), the following provides a detailed explanation:

To create an impediment toward others is called obstruction; to desire to retain [them] for oneself is called inversion. "Attachment" (*abhiniveśa*) refers to a place of manifest prominence, for there is form that can be seen.
That there is form which can be seen belongs to the realm of delusion (*mṛṣā*); due to inversion, one clings to it as being real.
It is attached to that which is above; this is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). Within this conjunction, afflictions are fully present, thus forming eighty-four thousand varieties.
In total, because of the essence of craving and its radiant attachment, the mental continuum finds no rest; therefore, it is called "the confused thoughts of essential radiance."
"Thus, there is [the kalala], etc. means that by such conjunction and attachment, form is produced; therefore, there is the *kalala*, which is characterized by form.
Now, as for why it is called *kalala* (the "congealed"): because it is the first arising of form, and since all [subsequent forms] depend upon it, it is a manifest entity.

Thus, it does not yet possess the prior characteristics of the *arbuda* (the "obscured") and so forth. The final two phrases point to its category: it is a subtle essence of both auspicious and inauspicious [influences].
"Intelligent beings" refers to those who rely upon that refined brilliance to manifest omens of good or ill fortune, such as the celestial constellations.
Furthermore, there are spirits in the world who report auspicious or inauspicious events and frequently take possession of numinous objects; these are also included within this category.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the eighty deities are all formed from this refined radiance through the fundamental element of obstructive ideation (*saṃjñā*). This is sufficient to corroborate this point.
The six formless realms (the *Abhiṣeka* states that these are "formless" because they are devoid of color).
Due to the world’s causes dissolving into the cycle of rebirth, and because of deluded inversion, the union with darkness produces eighty-four thousand subtle, hidden, and chaotic thoughts.
Thus, there exist the formless *kalala* realms of transmigration. [This is] the dispersal into emptiness.
The dissolution of these categories fills [the realms].

This first briefly clarifies the "dusts" (*viṣaya*) of the realms herein, which, in contrast to the formless, constitute the sixth transformation. Due to this transformation, there occurs the cycle of dissolution and transmigration.
As for "dissolution," it refers to the state where one is weary of existence and seeks the stillness of craving regarding the six dusts of the world.
However, the desire to extinguish craving and stillness also belongs to *qing* (sentiment); the aversion to existence and the desire for dispersion also belong to *li* (detachment).

If sentiment and detachment do not transform one another, the formless realm will not cease; hence it is called "saṃsāra. This is because the cause of form is felt through sentiment, and there is no way to achieve detachment through it.

The section below, beginning with "delusion and inversion" (*huodian*), provides a detailed explanation. Craving, stillness, and aversion to existence are termed "delusion" (*huo*); the desire to extinguish and the desire to disperse are termed [the subsequent states].
"Upside-down" (*viparyāsa*) refers to a state of dark obscurity and lack of clarity. This dark obscurity and lack of clarity are themselves illusory;

yet, due to inversion, one clings to them as real. To pursue and follow after these is called "conjunction. Within this conjunction, afflictions are fully present, thus forming eighty-four thousand types.
Taken collectively, they serve to conceal the aggregates (*skandha*); when the emotions depart from them, the resulting confusion is manifold.
Therefore it is said: "dark, hidden, and deluded conceptualization. Regarding the phrase "thus there is [the kalala]," this means that by such a combination with darkness, form is produced;

thus there is the formless *kalala*. Now, although it is formless, it is still called *kalala* because, while it lacks manifest color, it possesses a subtle, dark color; it is simply named as such because it is not seen by the ordinary eye.

It is not that there is truly nothing. The final two phrases point to their respective categories: because they are perceptions of the *skandhas*, they become empty or dissolved, like the class of spirits who preside over space;
because they are perceptions of concealment, they become submerged or dispersed, like the class of ghosts whose souls are stagnant.
Seventh is the realm of those with perception (*saṃjñin*; the *Guǎngdìng* commentary states: "there is perception and one perceives, thereby merging").

Because the world’s causes involve the revolving of indistinct forms (*wangxiàng*), and because shadows are inverted, the combination of memories forms eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thoughts.
For this reason, there is the flow and transformation through the lands of the *kalala* stage characterized by the appearance of perception. [This includes] spirits and ghosts.
The various classes of spirits fill [the world].
This has been briefly clarified above. Herein, the "dusts" (*viṣaya*) of the realms correspond to the seventh transformation in relation to those with perception (*saṃjñā*).

Due to this transformation, there arises the cycle of the "insubstantial" (*wangxiang*). The term "insubstantial" refers to the state of fixating one's thoughts upon the six dusts of the world, desiring to unite with them.
This is because when mental projections are not true, they are called "non-existent" (wang); yet, because one desires to unite with what appears to exist, there are names and forms.

As for those in saṃsāra, their thoughts and unions never cease; though there is thought, there is no end to it. Taking thought and mental projection as causes, existence arises through attachment and formation, thereby producing karmic retribution.

○ This is explained in detail below under the section on "shadows and perversions. When things are not true but appear to exist, they are called "shadows"; this refers to the desire to unite with mental projections.

This is called "inversion. "Recollection" refers to the objects previously recollected; that which was previously recollected also belongs to the realm of falsehood, yet due to inversion, one clings to it as being real.
When the spirit wanders above these, it is called "conjunction. Within this conjunction, afflictions are fully present, thus they total eighty-four thousand.
In sum, the spirit is hidden within these sublime traces, and the vital energy (*qi*) is bound within the numinous.
"Trace" (zōng) means recollection and mindfulness; therefore, it is said that "hiddenly one forms disordered thoughts. Regarding the phrase "Thus there is... and so forth:

this means that by means of such a combination of recollection, form is produced; thus there is the *saṃjñā-nimitta-kalala*. Now, as for why the *saṃjñā-nimitta* is called *kalala*: [it is because]...
Because they were born with consciousness and all proceeded [to their respective realms], there are superior traces and numinous vestiges;
naturally, they would not possess characteristics such as *bhiṣa* (corpses). The final two phrases indicate the categories [of beings]:

through latent thought they become ghosts and spirits (*bhūta-preta*), such as the various classes of ghosts and spirits of mountains, forests, land, city walls, rivers, and peaks; through focused visualization they become *piśāca* (sprites), such as mountain sprites and sea sprites.
The essences of wind, the essences of rivers, the essences of earth, and various other classes of spirits—these eight types of "non-conceptual" beings (the *Abhiṣeka* commentary states:

"non-conceptual yet conceptualizing, and thus detached")—due to the causes of the world’s dullness and saṃsāra, and because of deluded inversion, combine with stubborn matter to form eighty-four thousand parched and disordered thoughts.
For this reason, there exists the land where the non-conceptual *kalala* transmigrates, [possessing] spirit and mind.
It transforms into earth, wood, metal, and stone, such that these types fill [the world].
This briefly clarifies the "dust" (*rajas*) of this realm. In contrast to the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*), this constitutes the eighth transformation.
Due to this transformation, there arises dull-witted saṃsāra. "Dull-witted" refers to those who have long since become firmly detached from the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) of the world.

This is because long-term conceptualization without transformation is called "ignorance" (*mūḍha*), and being firmly detached without returning is called "dullness" (*jaḍa*). As for "saṃsāra," it refers to conceptualization that is detached yet does not transform;

it is difficult to escape from the state of non-conceptualization. This is because conceptualization and long-term conceptualization form the causes, whereas firm detachment and non-returning form the conditions for rebirth.

○ The section beginning with "delusion and confusion" explains this in detail: long-term conceptualization and firm detachment are called "delusion," characterized by non-transformation and non-returning.
This is called "inversion" (*viparyāsa*). "Stolid" refers to insentient matter. Insentient matter is inherently illusory;

yet, due to inversion, one clings to it as real and becomes stagnant therein—this is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). Within this conjunction, afflictions (*kleśa*) are fully present, thus forming the eighty-four thousand [afflictions].
Because one cannot attain [liberation] through long-held conceptions, the mind’s thoughts are extinguished like ashes. Therefore...
Regarding the phrase "withered and chaotic thoughts" and "thus there is [the kalala]," this means that because such a combination of inert matter forms a shape, there exists the *asaṃjñika-kalala*.
Furthermore, the reason the state of being without perception (*asaṃjñika*) is also called *kalala* is that it already belongs to the category of combined inert matter.
The initial characteristic is that of firmness and rigidity. The final two phrases indicate related categories:
the refinement of essence into earth and wood, and spirit into metal and stone, such as the pillar of Hua-biao producing essence or Wang-fu becoming a mountain.
Ninth, the non-material form (the *Abhiṣeka* commentary states: "Non-material form refers to the separation and union of the passions").
Because the world of causes revolves through mutual dependence, and due to false inversion, they combine and become defiled, forming eighty-four thousand thoughts of causal reliance and confusion.
For this reason, there exists the state of non-material form that takes on material characteristics, becoming the *kalala* (embryonic stage) as it flows and transmigrates through various realms.
Earth. ○ Various sea squids and the like take shrimp for their eyes; such species fill the world.
This has briefly clarified the "dust-elements" (*dhātu-rajas*) within this realm. In contrast to those that are not material, this constitutes the ninth transformation.

Due to this transformation, there exists dependent co-arising (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and saṃsāra. "Dependent" means that regarding these dust-elements of the various realms, one feels passionate attachment and does not—
Self-assignment is union. Because one constantly desires to achieve one's own will by borrowing from others, it is called "mutual dependence.

When the mind of dependence does not cease, there is no retribution in the realm of form that does not halt; thus, it is called "saṃsāra. The section on "False Perversion" below clarifies depending on others while concealing oneself.
To have deceit and fraud as one's core disposition is termed "false perversion. "Defilement" refers to objects of emotional attachment; these are the objects of emotional attachment.
These are fundamentally illusory; yet, due to inversion, they are grasped as real. When the yang departs from the yin, it is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).

This conjunction possesses affliction, and thus constitutes the eighty-four thousand [afflictions]. Generally, these arise through the power of causes depending upon persons, and are formed through the mind’s thoughts and dependencies;
hence it is said, "causes and dependencies give rise to disordered conceptualization. The phrase "thus there are," etc., means that by means of such conjunctions...
"Defilement forms shape. Thus, there is that which is "not a form yet forms a color" (aśarīra-rūpa-saṃsthāna), namely the *kalala*. Regarding the term "not a form": it does not mean truly existent;
although it is not truly existent, it is nevertheless able to borrow from others to constitute its own substance and possesses utility in dependence upon things.
Therefore, it is called "forming a color *kalala*. The final three phrases indicate the category. Wēnlíng says: "The *shuǐmǔ* (the sea-slug) uses water foam as..."

Substance (is that which is established as substance by depending on others). Taking shrimp for eyes (is to have utility in dependence upon things); originally there is no color, but it acquires color in dependence upon things.
It cannot function on its own; it awaits external objects to have utility. As the subsequent text states: "A flying essence attaches itself to a person’s mouth and speaks the sutras and Dharma.
This is the superior type among such [spirits]. The "ten non-forms" (the *Guanding* commentary explains this as "non-form refers to the union and separation of passions").
Due to the mutual attraction of world-phenomena, beings cycle through saṃsāra. Because their natures are inverted, they combine mantras to produce eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of summoning.
Thus, there exist formless realms and formless *kalala* that flow and circulate within various lands.
Curses, incantations, and the rites of suppression abound, filling these classes of beings.
First, a brief explanation: herein, the "elements and sense objects" (*dhātu-viṣaya*) are contrasted with the formless (*ārūpya*) as the tenth transformation.

Because of this transformation, there is mutual attraction within saṃsāra. "Mutual attraction" means that regarding the various elements and sense objects, although one is emotionally attached to them, one is drawn toward and joins with them, and likewise drawn away from and separates from them;
hence it is called "mutual attraction. As long as the thought of such attraction is not eliminated, [it persists]. It is not...

Because the formless does not cease, it is called saṃsāra. ○ Regarding the nature of inversion (*viparyāsa*), this is explained in detail below. Long-standing habituation forms what is called "nature" (*svabhāva*);
sudden union and sudden separation are called "inversion. The mantra is the object that can induce [this state]. This inducing object is also illusory;
yet, due to inversion, one clings to it as real, becoming hidden or manifest with it—hence it is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).
Through the combination and aggregation of afflictions, eighty-four thousand [forms] are produced. Because they are collectively summoned and called upon to go and come, the mind finds no peace;

hence it is called "disturbed conceptualization through summoning. Regarding the phrase "thus there exist," etc., it means that because forms are produced through such combined mantras, there exist those that are not without color-form (*rūpa*) and those that are not without the *kalala* stage; thus it says "not without."

This is not that they are truly non-existent; rather, because they can come and go according to mantras, and although they come and go according to mantras, they are not seen by ordinary eyes, they are therefore still designated by the name "formless" (ārūpya). Since they are named formless, yet are also called "kalala," [it is for this reason].
Because there exists subtle form (rūpa). The final two phrases indicate the category [of beings]. Regarding "those who curse and suppress life":
this refers to those who curse spirits and deities, or who suppress death to preserve life. As the subsequent text states: "To encounter clarity and take on form is called 'employing ghosts.
I [the commentator] say that the world’s practices of writing talismans to summon immortals and reciting mantras to expel ghosts are all subsumed within this category.
Eleventh is the state of "non-existent perception" (the *Abhiṣeka* commentary states: "non-existent perception is the union of separation and integration").

Because the world arises from the conjunction of causes with delusive saṃsāra, and due to the inversion of ignorance, these disparate elements combine to form eighty-four thousand chaotic and intermingled perceptions.
Consequently, there exists the realm of the *kalala* and *arbuda*, where the characteristics of non-existent perception give rise to the perception of existence.
Earth. ○ Those such as the *pulu* (mud-worms) transform through different substances until their species fill the space;
this has been briefly clarified above. Herein, the "dust-elements" (*dhātu-rajas*) are contrasted with the state of non-perception to constitute the eleven transformations.
Because of these transformations, there arises the false conjunction of saṃsāra. This "false conjunction" refers to the suspended conceptualization of the various dust-elements, which does not...

"Self-seizure" (ziduó) means "appropriating for oneself. Because one constantly desires to ride upon emptiness to practice *yīnyīn* (divination), it is called "appropriating delusion" (*héwàng*), meaning that within the act of appropriation there is delusion.
When the appropriation of delusion does not cease, the retribution of having thoughts never stops; hence it is called "saṃsāra. Regarding "wǎngdiān" (deceitful delusion):

this is explained in detail below. "Gāng" (岡) is synonymous with "qī" (欺, to deceive). To seek fame without being dislodged from it, riding upon emptiness to occupy a name, is "wǎng" (deceit). This refers to feigned goodness (*yángshàn*).
Secretly evil: to deceive others and deceive oneself is called "inversion" (*viparyāsa*). To claim that something is not one's own refers to the illusory realm.
Since the illusory realm is not one's own, it is clearly characterized by falsehood; yet, due to inversion, one clings to it as real and employs it for higher scheming.
This is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). Because conjunction possesses affliction, it constitutes eighty-four thousand [types]. Taken collectively, these are contrasted with one's own avoidance;

because they dwell in the mind as things to be shunned, they are called "reciprocal and disordered conceptualizations. Regarding the phrase "therefore there are," etc.: this means that by virtue of such a combination of the different, forms are produced;
thus, there arise the characteristics of the perception of what is not yet existent, forming the *kalala* through perception. It is "not yet existent perception."
Regarding "form" (*saṃsthāna*): it is not definitively existent, for there is no desire to deny its convergence. Regarding "becoming an embryo through ideation" (*kalala*):
it is not definitively non-existent, for it proceeds by means of emptiness. The final three phrases indicate the category [of examples]. *Guǎndǐng* says: "The *púlú* is also called *guǒluó*;
it is the slender-waisted wasp. A poem says: "The *mínglíng* has offspring; the *guǒluó* carries them away. The commentary states: "The *mínglíng*..."

The *línglíng* is a silkworm from mulberry trees. The *guǒluó* (a species of wasp) gathers mud to construct a nest, carries the mulberry worm into it, and chants incantations for seven days until it transforms into its own offspring.
This describes the moment when the *guǒluó* receives birth; the nature and karma of the *línglíng* have already been transformed, and it thus takes on the empty husk of that [wasp].
Therefore, it is said that "different substances complete one another. I, the fool, say: [this arises...]

Vampires and the like are also included within this category. The twelfth is "Not Non-Perception" (the *Abhiṣeka* commentary states: "It is not non-perception; it is the union of perception and its separation").

Due to the cycle of enmity and harm in the world, because of the perversity of killing, they combine to form eighty-four thousand types of monsters who harbor the notion that they are eating their own parents.
For this reason, there exists the realm where the *kalala* and *arbuda* stages flow on, characterized by "Not Non-Perception" and "Non-Perception."

Earth. ○ For instance, creatures such as the earth-owl (*kṣitighoṇa*) fashion their young from clods of earth, while the "broken-mirror" bird (*ādarśabhañjana*) takes the fruit of a poisonous tree and embraces it as its offspring;
once the offspring have matured, both parents meet their end by being devoured by them. Such species abound.
First, a brief explanation: herein, the elements (*dhātu*) and sense objects (*viṣaya*), when contrasted with those who are not non-percipient (*asaṃjñin*), constitute the twelve transformations.
Because of these transformations, there arise enmity, harm, and saṃsāra. "Enmity and harm" refers to the initial conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) regarding the various elements and sense objects.
Subsequently, they align themselves; yet in the end, because they do not conform to their own intentions, desire and aversion separate. Thus it is called "resentment and harm.

When the mind of resentment and harm is not dispelled, there is no cessation of the retribution of non-perception (asaṃjñi-vedanīya). Therefore, it is called "saṃsāra. The section beginning with "killing" explains this in detail below.

"Harm" refers to that which can take away life, which constitutes killing. To place the enemy first and the relative second is called "reversal. "Monstrous" refers precisely to that which is resented and harmed.
Things are inherently extraordinary; therefore, they are called "strange" (*guài*). This strangeness is also illusory, yet due to inversion (*viparyāsa*), one clings to it as real.
Based on this, one gives rise to kin and enemies, which is termed "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). Conjunction possesses affliction; thus, eighty-four thousand [afflictions] are formed.
Generally, because one fails to contemplate profound kindness and instead desires malicious separation, harboring rebellion in one's heart, it is said that [such a person] "eats their father."
Regarding the "conception of a mother": it is not called "confusion" because it follows the convenience of the text and is understood by analogy with what precedes it.

As for the phrase "thus there is, etc.," it means that because such a combination forms a shape, there is [the kalala], which is neither non-existent nor characterized by the absence of perception (asaṃjñika), nor is it a *kalala* devoid of perception.
"Is not of the nature of non-perception" means it is not definitively non-existent, because it was originally intended to be joined [to the womb].
"The *kalala* of non-perception" means it is not definitively existent, because it ultimately results in the departure from evil. ○ The final six phrases indicate the categories.
Gushan says: According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Wu" in the *Shiji*, for the sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor, one *xiao* bird and a mirror were used. Meng Kang said: "The earth-*xiao*..."

The bird is named "Mother-Eater" (Mātṛ-bhakṣa); the beast is named "Broken-Mirror" (Khaṇḍa-ādarśa) and is said to eat its father. The Yellow Emperor, wishing to exterminate their kind, mandated that they be used in all hundred sacrifices.
The Broken-Mirror resembles a wild boar (*cchur*) but has the eyes of a tiger. That it is now called a "bird" is likely an error resulting from a mistake in oral transmission or translation.
Having completed the detailed explanation according to categories, the three fingers are now used for a final summary.
These are called the twelve types of sentient beings.
According to the preceding text, as the directions and worlds intersect, they become twelve. Although their forms and categories are divided, they are still not summoned by karma.

Furthermore, it is said that the six types of deluded false thoughts constitute the nature of karma; thus, although the twelve categories of beings are summoned by karma, they were not yet definitively existent.
Reaching this point, one becomes increasingly distant from the truth and pursues delusion ever deeper; wandering aimlessly until forgetting the source, they finally become definitively existent.
Therefore, this serves as a summary to conclude the meaning of this chapter. Moreover, regarding the remaining twelve classes of beings...

There are differing interpretations of this sūtra. According to the present text, the four modes of birth—womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—already encompass the three realms.
As for the latter eight [categories], they involve the mutual interaction and successive transformation of the four mental states; they do not belong exclusively to the four modes of birth.
Nevertheless, it is not necessary to further reconcile this with the various superior retributions such as form and emptiness.
This concludes the preceding section on how, based upon the True [Dharmadhātu], delusion arises to form the categories of sentient beings. *Lengyan jing zhizhang shu*, Fascicle Seven.

II. Extinction of Delusion and the Manifestation of Reality: Four Sections. 1. Correctly elucidating the various stages (*bhūmi*). 2. Concluding by revealing the method of cultivation. 3. Commending the initial resolve. 4.

Discerning the heterodox and the orthodox. The first [section] has ten parts: 1. The three gradual [stages]. 2. Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna*). 3. The Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). 4. The Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*). 5.
The Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). 6. The Ten Transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*). 7. The Four Additions (*catasraḥ pratyāyāḥ*). 8. The Tenth [Stage].

The Grounds. Nine: Equal Enlightenment; Ten: Sublime Enlightenment. Regarding the first two: first, pointing back to what preceded to initiate what follows; second, correctly demonstrating the gradual sequence. Regarding the first two [of these]:

first, pointing back to how mutual possession constitutes delusion; second, initiating the subsequent three to gradually achieve their removal. First: *Note: This is a structural outline (pīṭaka) for a commentary on the stages of enlightenment, likely from a Mahāyāna Buddhist treatise such as the *Awakening of Faith* or related texts.*
Ānanda, within each and every class of such sentient beings, there likewise exists twelve kinds of inversion.
It is like pressing upon the eyes so that illusory flowers appear; these inverted, false, and chaotic conceptions are fully present within the wondrous, perfect, truly pure, and luminous mind.
The initial reference points to the mutual inclusion [of the twelve categories] mentioned previously. This phrase "sentient beings" refers collectively to the twelve classes of living beings.

That each individual class possesses [the others] within itself constitutes their mutual inclusion. For example, in the case of the egg-born class, that which manifests is termed the "inversion of motion."
The remaining eleven inversions are not absent; they merely lie latent. When they encounter the appropriate conditions, they arise.
Just as it is with the "egg-born" category, so it is with the other eleven categories. Taken together, there should be one hundred and forty-four inversions.
Furthermore, within each of these inversions, there are fully eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts;
this is truly the ultimate of emptiness and the extreme of delusion. To illustrate this delusion by means of an analogy:

the eye represents the true mind, the squeezing represents a single moment of deluded movement, and the production of the chaotic flowers represents the twelve classes of beings, each of which mutually contains the others. This is because...
The true mind is fundamentally pure. It first arises from a single moment of deluded movement, which then transforms and gives rise to the twelve classes of beings.

Furthermore, each of these possesses inverted and chaotic thoughts. It is like the eye, which originally has no flowers; because it is empty, one falsely rubs it, and through this process, chaotic flowers appear.
Yet, one clearly knows that the eye originally had no flowers, and they exist only because of the rubbing. The rubbing, too, [is likewise empty].
It is not real. When one lets go of the hand, it returns to its original emptiness; even when pinched, it does not exist. How, then, could the flower stand?
One who understands this analogy can then contemplate and understand the meaning of inversion and delusion. Regarding "inversion," the following applies the Dharma to illustrate it:
"Unchanging" is named "wondrous," referring to the essence of the mind; "following conditions" is called "perfect," referring to the function of the mind. Although it follows conditions...
Unchanging, it is termed "True Purity. Although unchanging, it accords with conditions; thus, it is termed "True Illumination.

The union of this essence and its function is therefore called the "Wondrous, Perfect, Truly Pure, and Luminous Mind. In these analogies, the word "term" (mù) refers to inversion, which is precisely deluded movement.
Because the True is fundamentally unmoving, movement constitutes a departure from the True; hence it is called "inversion. Within these analogies...

Regarding the term "捏字" (niè zì): "confused thoughts" (*luanxiang*) refers to the eighty-four thousand [delusions]. For example, those born from eggs are called "confused thoughts of flying and sinking," while those born from wombs are called "confused thoughts of horizontal and vertical [orientation].
Since inversion (*dao*) already possesses all [delusions] mutually, confused thoughts should likewise possess them mutually. As for what is called "falsehood" (*xuwang*):
it originally arises from deluded movement and thus lacks substantial reality. Although it lacks substantial reality, it flourishes profusely within the state of delusion.

Therefore, it is said that they are "fully complete. In this combined analogy, disordered flowers come forth. Although these flowers have no fruit, one must wait until the hand is released to cause them to wither.
This illustrates that although thoughts are false and illusory, to eliminate thoughts one must necessarily depart from mental activity.
Thus, the text below demonstrates the three gradual stages. Once these are initiated, the latter three [stages] can be attained and eliminated.
As you now cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi, you must establish three gradual stages to eliminate the fundamental deluded thoughts that originally caused this confusion.
It is like removing poisonous honey from a clean vessel: one washes and cleanses the vessel with various hot water, mixed ashes, and fragrant perfumes, before subsequently filling it with ambrosia.

First is the explanation by means of the Dharma. "The Buddha’s samādhi" refers specifically to the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*). Through partial cultivation and partial realization, one attains the various stages;
through complete cultivation and complete realization, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood. This is an instance of speaking of the fruit within the cause, which is why the term "Buddha" is employed.
"Original deluded thoughts" refers to those possessed by sentient beings of the various classes, such as the so-called "deluded thoughts of flying and sinking," and so forth.

This is so. That which exists inherently within the state of delusion is called the "original locus" (*yuansuo*); that which serves as the cause in contrast to the subsequent fruit is called the "original cause" (*benyin*).

As for the statement that one must establish three gradual stages (*sanzhianci*) before they can be eliminated, this does not mean that they can be completely removed within those three gradual stages themselves.

Rather, it means that only after the three gradual stages, by progressing through the various levels (*wei*) and practicing severance (*xiuduan*), will the seeds and habitual tendencies (*zhongxi*) both be exhausted. [It is] like purification.
The following provides an analogy. The middle section of the text below is slightly insufficient; it should be stated in full as follows: "It is like a clean vessel filled with poisonous honey.
This metaphor illustrates a single moment of deluded movement within the True Mind, which constitutes a complete state of chaotic conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

"Removing the poisonous honey" is a metaphor for eliminating its auxiliary causes, excising its primary nature, and counteracting its manifest karma. "Hot water" is a metaphor for the various [remedies].
The "concentration within the stages" and the "concentrations within all stages" still do not depart from the preceding samādhi.
The metaphor of "ashes and incense" represents the wisdom within all stages; this wisdom within all stages still does not depart from the preceding perfect penetration.
"Washing and purifying the vessel" represents the complete severance of seeds and habitual tendencies within all stages. "Subsequently storing ambrosia" represents the pure mind of the Buddha-fruit.

Only then will one be capable of receiving the true flavor of the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle (Ekayāna). This concludes the section on "Pointing to the preceding to introduce the subsequent. Second, the main exposition of the gradual stages has two parts: first, the interrogation, introduction, and enumeration; second, the sequential explanation and establishment. The first [part]: [The text continues: "How could it be that those who have not yet severed their afflictions and attachments would suddenly attain the fruit of Buddhahood? The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "It is not so. Why? Because the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is eternally quiescent and free from all conceptual proliferation (prapañca). It is not something produced by causes and conditions, nor is it something that can be attained through effort. Mahāmati, it is only when sentient beings exhaust their afflictions and attachments, sever the continuity of their karmic seeds, and attain the stage of non-arising that they are called Buddhas. Mahāmati, this is why I say that those who have not yet severed their afflictions and attachments cannot suddenly attain the fruit of Buddhahood. This concludes the first part. Second, the sequential explanation and establishment: "Mahāmati, there are four kinds of gradual stages for entering the path. What are the four? First, the gradual stage of the five aggregates; second, the gradual stage of the twelve sense bases; third, the gradual stage of the eighteen elements; fourth, the gradual stage of the twelve links of dependent origination. Mahāmati, these are called the four gradual stages for entering the path. This concludes the second part. Third, the summary and conclusion: "Therefore, Mahāmati, you should know that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is not fixed. Depending on the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings, he teaches various gates of liberation. Mahāmati, if one relies on the gate of the five aggregates to enter the path, one should not cling to the five aggregates as being real. If one relies on the gate of the twelve sense bases to enter the path, one should not cling to the twelve sense bases as being real. If one relies on the gate of the eighteen elements to enter the path, one should not cling to the eighteen elements as being real. If one relies on the gate of the twelve links of dependent origination to enter the path, one should not cling to the twelve links as being real. Mahāmati, if one can thus practice without clinging, one will gradually advance toward the stage of Buddhahood. This concludes the third part. Fourth, the refutation of heterodox views: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of heterodox views regarding the self. What are the four? First, the view that the self is eternal; second, the view that the self is finite; third, the view that the self is both finite and infinite; fourth, the view that the self is neither finite nor infinite. Mahāmati, these are called the four heterodox views regarding the self. Mahāmati, because sentient beings are attached to these views, they wander in birth and death and cannot escape the cycle of transmigration. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should diligently cultivate the wisdom that transcends all views. This concludes the fourth part. Fifth, the encouragement to practice: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, you should know that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is like a great physician. Just as a great physician prescribes medicine according to the specific ailments of his patients, the Tathāgata also teaches the Dharma according to the specific capacities and dispositions of sentient beings. Mahāmati, you should not think that the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is contradictory. Why? Because the Tathāgata’s ultimate intention is to lead all sentient beings to attain liberation. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should rely on the Tathāgata’s teaching and diligently practice the path of the Bodhisattva. This concludes the fifth part. Sixth, the dedication of merit: "By the power of this merit, may all sentient beings quickly realize the supreme enlightenment and universally deliver all beings from the ocean of suffering. This concludes the sixth part. Seventh, the title of the chapter: "This concludes the Chapter on the Gradual Stages of Entering the Path. This concludes the seventh part. Eighth, the concluding verses: "The gradual stages are profound and subtle; they are difficult to fathom even by sages. Only by relying on the Buddha's power can one gradually advance. May all beings together attain the fruit of Buddhahood. This concludes the eighth part. Ninth, the seal of transmission: "Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī with a great assembly of monks and bodhisattvas. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the venerable Ānanda: 'Ānanda, you should now receive and uphold this Sūtra of the Gradual Stages of Entering the Path. Why? Because this Sūtra contains the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury. If there are sentient beings who hear this Sūtra and believe and accept it, you should know that such people have already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas. Then the venerable Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, respectfully accepted and upheld it. This concludes the ninth part. What are called the three gradual stages? First, through cultivation, one eliminates their auxiliary causes. Second, through true cultivation, one hollows out their primary nature.
Third, through further advancement, one opposes their manifest karma.
The opening phrase, which poses the inquiry, is clear. First, the section beginning with "The first" provides the enumeration.
Herein, the third, "Advancement," refers to the Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ. The second, "True Cultivation," refers to the expedient means for perfect penetration;

this is because taking the earnest observance of the precepts as true cultivation constitutes such a means. As for the first, "Cultivation and Practice," it serves as the expedient means for true cultivation.

This introduces the inquiry following the preceding section. There are two parts to the formal explanation: first, the teaching on clothing, food, and the abstention from pungent roots;

Ānanda, these twelve classes of beings in this world cannot sustain themselves independently; they abide by means of the four kinds of nutriment, namely:
edible food, contact-food, volition-food, and consciousness-food. For this reason, the Buddha taught that all sentient beings abide by means of nutriment.
"Ānanda, all sentient beings live because they consume what is sweet and die because they consume what is poisonous.
Therefore, those who seek samādhi should sever their consumption of the five kinds of pungent vegetables found in the world."
The initial teaching concerns abiding by means of nutriment for the twelve classes of beings, as described above.
Regarding those who cannot sustain themselves—that is, those unable to maintain their physical lives—they must rely on the four nutriments (*āhāra*) to support and preserve their bodies and lives.
This is the general indication; what follows is the specific enumeration. As for "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), it refers to the food consumed by human beings.
There must necessarily be distinct categories. *Guanding* (Consecration) states: "Most sūtras and śāstras refer to 'lump food' (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).

This definition is restrictive, for things such as syrups and drinks cannot be formed into lumps. As for "contact food" (*sparśa-āhāra*), this refers to spirits and the like who are satiated by touching the vital energy (*prāṇa*) of others;

since this constitutes their sustenance, it is considered food. These two types of food pertain to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). As for "volition food" (*manaḥsañcetanā-āhāra*), this refers to those in the dhyāna heavens who subsist solely on meditative reflection.

It serves as food. Furthermore, it is like hanging sand to stave off hunger or longing for plums to quench thirst; these are also included within the category of "food through thought" (*āhāra-saṃjñā*).

As for "consciousness-food" (*vijñāna-āhāra*), this refers to the four formless heavens (*ārūpya-dhātu*), where life is sustained solely by the concentration of consciousness (*vijñāna-samādhi*); because they possess the meaning of "food," they are so categorized.

Moreover, it is like the hells and hungry ghosts (*preta*), whose lives continue for kalpas based solely upon their karmic consciousness; these are also included within consciousness-food. These four types of food have been briefly summarized above.
The meanings in the *Wenling* [Commentary] and the *Guanding* [Commentary] are detailed in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. To avoid prolixity, they are not recorded here.

The reason for necessarily mentioning "four" is to encompass the three realms (*tridhātu*) and to counteract the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). As the *Guanding* states: After the Buddha attained enlightenment, in order to eliminate the non-Buddhists' ascetic practices of self-starvation, he taught that all sentient beings subsist upon nutriment (*āhāra*).

This is the correct awakening and the correct teaching, which others cannot know. The non-Buddhists mocked him, saying, "Even fools know this; why is it only the Perfectly Awakened One who knows? The Buddha asked them in return, "How many kinds of nutriment are there? The non-Buddhists were unable to answer. Thereupon, [the Buddha] explained that sentient beings depend upon four [kinds of nutriment].

"Regarding food and dwelling," and so forth—the Buddha’s words are thus cited from previous teachings to establish this proof. There are two reasons why this must be stated first in order to sever the consumption of the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*):
first, to demonstrate that since even eating for the sake of maintaining the physical life is impermissible, how much more so the eating of pungent roots;
one should therefore resolve to abandon them. Second, to demonstrate that since there are four kinds of sustenance (*āhāra*), why must one be restricted to a single fixed type?
Eating pungent vegetables brings about one's own calamity and affliction. ○ Ānanda, the following instructions teach the severing of the five pungent plants.

That which nourishes and sustains the physical life is called "sweet" (*gan*); this does not refer exclusively to sweet flavors. That which injures and destroys the physical life is called "poison" (*du*); this does not refer exclusively to lethal poisons or wine.

The statement that those who eat them are "born [in such states] or die [because of them]" clarifies that these pungent and aromatic plants are matters of vital concern to one's life and nature; for all sentient beings, they must never be consumed.
How much more so for those seeking right concentration, whose very existence depends upon the wisdom-life of the *dharmakāya*. It is therefore fitting to strictly prohibit them;

thus, one should sever [the use of] these five kinds of pungent vegetables in accordance with this teaching. Regarding the five pungent vegetables, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Onion, garlic, leek, scallion, and *hiṅgu*.

Master Ying said that "*hiṅgu*" is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound; the correct term is *xingyi*. (The Tripiṭaka Master Cimin stated: *Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment from a commentary on monastic discipline (vinaya) regarding the prohibition of pungent vegetables.*

It is said: "The root resembles a radish; when it emerges from the soil, it has a pungent odor. Because the Compassionate One went to that land during the winter solstice, he had not yet seen its sprouts.
Since this plant does not exist here [in this region], it was not translated. The *Tiantai Fanwang Jing Shu* states: "Hingu is *jizhi* (a type of thistle)."

they can obstruct the Path of the Sages and also obstruct the pure realms of humans and devas, let alone the fruit of Buddhahood.
These are precisely what must be severed. Second, clarifying the faults and afflictions of eating pungent roots.
These five kinds of pungent plants: eating them cooked arouses lust; eating them raw increases anger.

Thus, in this world, those who eat pungent plants—even if they can expound the twelve divisions of the scriptures—the celestial beings of the ten directions loathe their foul stench and all keep their distance.
Various hungry ghosts, because of their eating these things, lick the corners of their lips. They constantly dwell with ghosts, and their merit and virtue diminish day by day.

Such waxing and waning brings no benefit. When those who consume pungent roots practice *samādhi*, Bodhisattvas, celestial immortals, and virtuous deities from the ten directions will not come to protect them.

A powerful Māra will seize this opportunity to manifest in the form of a Buddha and preach the Dharma to them, reviling the prohibitions and precepts while praising lust, anger, and ignorance. At the end of their lives, they will themselves become members of the Māra’s retinue and undergo [retribution].
When their demonic merit is exhausted, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
Initially, the arousal of lust increases anger. The *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Pulse) states: "Cooked food necessarily strengthens the fire of the gallbladder, hence the arousal of lust;

raw consumption necessarily agitates the qi of the liver, hence the increase of anger. This is what is discerned by the Buddha’s wisdom, without the slightest error. One should therefore respect and believe this.
Be deeply cautious regarding this. ○ Thus, for those in the lower heavens, the distance to them is great while their proximity to ghosts is near.
The twelve divisions of the scriptures encompass all that the Buddha has taught; those capable of proclaiming them should be heard by celestial beings and immortals who draw near.

Yet now, because of the consumption of pungent foods, not only do they fail to come near to hear [the Dharma], but they even loathe its foul stench and all depart from afar, as if one were currently in a state of impurity.
Those who observe the fasts and precepts still avoid those who eat pungent foods; thus, it can be known that celestial immortals keep their distance.
Since hungry ghosts crave impurity, they lick the lips and mouths of those who eat pungent food in the dark realm, following them without ever leaving.
Consequently, such people always dwell with ghosts, while celestial immortals who increase one's merit all stay far away; therefore, their blessings and virtues diminish day by day.
Hungry ghosts bring about calamity; because one constantly dwells with them, there is long-term lack of benefit. That which lacks benefit is precisely the matter of disaster and misfortune.
○ This refers to being unprotected below the food and encountering Māra while practicing *samādhi*; this is the embryonic stage for attaining Buddhahood.
Bodhisattvas, celestial seers (ṛṣis), and benevolent deities should all provide protection; however, because one consumes pungent foods, they will all fail to come, as they also loathe its foul odor.
If they were to provide protection, Māra would be unable to approach. Because they do not come, it allows the powerful Māra King to find an opportunity.
This "powerful Māra" is the celestial Māra (devaputra-māra). He knows that [the practitioner] is cultivating the three...

Samādhi. Because there are those who aspire to seek Buddhahood, he manifests the body of a Buddha to dazzle and delude them. He disparages those who violate the prohibitions and precepts, deprecating the upholding of the precepts as the "Small Vehicle" (Hīnayāna).
He praises lust, anger, and ignorance, extolling the three poisons as the "Great Way. These are the self-justifications of the ignorant;
few are there who do not fall under their delusion. Alas! How can one not stand in awe? ○ [The section] following "At the end of life" establishes [the teaching].
The Māra falls into hell. Manifesting before others, he practices the teachings of Māra; at the end of his life, he becomes a follower of Māra himself.

All the *samādhis* he cultivates serve only as resources for outflows (*sāsrava*). Consequently, he enjoys the blessings of Māra; when those blessings are exhausted, calamity arrives, and he is thus reborn in the Avīci Hell. The *Zhengmo* says:

Why do you neglect them instead of courageously severing them? Furthermore, the reason why pungent vegetables are called "auxiliary causes" (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) for [unwholesome actions] can be seen within this very section:
giving rise to lust constitutes an auxiliary cause for sexual misconduct; increasing anger constitutes an auxiliary cause for killing.

When merit is exhausted and calamity grows, it inevitably leads to harming others to benefit oneself. Even if one were able to preach the sutras, such behavior would still belong to the realm of false discourse.
Prajñā. These [factors] further serve as auxiliary causes for theft and falsehood; how much more so when Māra arrives to preach perversely—what evil would he not assist?
Being a member of Māra’s retinue oneself, what transgression would not arise? It is therefore appropriate to designate them as "auxiliary causes.
This concludes the formal explanation. Third, the conclusion.
Ānanda, those who cultivate bodhi must permanently sever the five pungent roots. This is called the first stage of progressive cultivation.
Since consuming pungent roots carries such faults and afflictions as described above, anyone wishing to cultivate bodhi must first—
One must forever sever the five pungent roots; this refers to what was stated below regarding the fruit being able to sever the pungent roots.
This constitutes the first advancement from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), marking the gradual sequence of practice for a beginner until the auxiliary causes have been eliminated.

Second, [the section on] "excising their fundamental nature" has three parts: first, the introduction; second, the formal explanation; third, the conclusion. Regarding the first: "What is the fundamental nature?

This introduces the second point, which concerns the meaning of the gradual stages. Regarding the second, the formal explanation, there are three parts: first, the instruction to first sever [the afflictions].

[The text addresses] sexual misconduct and killing. Second, it demonstrates the progressive cultivation of the remaining precepts. Third, it provides a detailed explanation of the benefits of maintaining the precepts. First:
"Ānanda, when such sentient beings enter *samādhi*, they must first strictly maintain pure and clean moral discipline (*śīla*).
They must forever sever the mind of lust, abstain from wine and meat, purify their food with fire, and never consume anything that possesses life-force. Ānanda, this is the cultivation..."
If a practitioner does not cease sexual misconduct and killing, it is impossible for them to transcend the three realms.
This was the initial general instruction on upholding the precepts. The phrase "such sentient beings" refers to those who have already abandoned the five pungent roots.

Having abandoned the five pungent roots, one should enter *samādhi*; however, concentration arises solely from the precepts, for without the precepts, *samādhi* cannot be accomplished. Therefore, he taught [this].
Since one must first maintain the precepts, they are said to be "strictly maintained" because not even a hair’s breadth of transgression is permitted.

Furthermore, they are called "pure" because this involves not only the control of the body but also the control of the mind. Regarding the phrase "permanently severing," lust and killing are cited first;

for lust can obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while killing violates compassion (*maitrī*). Among the four fundamental offenses (*mūlāpatti*), these two are the most essential; therefore, they are mentioned first.

To raise this point: one who has permanently severed the mind of lust has exhausted both the manifest and the latent seeds; they are like a withered tree that does not sprout, or like cold ashes that do not flame.

Regarding the severance of killing, the text uses the expression of using the light to illustrate the heavy, stating that even wine and meat are not permitted to be consumed, and even living breath is not permitted to be eaten—how much more so the act of killing? One should naturally sever it forever, consuming food purified by fire.

The Vinaya clarifies that fresh, living things must be purified by fire before being eaten; if they have not been touched by fire, they are impure and may not be consumed immediately because they still possess life.
This is why the Confucian school does not pluck growing plants and does not clear away the grass in their courtyards.

Dàtóng’s intention is the same; all [these teachings] are merely for the purpose of preventing small faults and stopping them before they grow. ○ From "Ānanda" onwards, it demonstrates what ought to be severed.

Cultivation is fundamentally for the sake of transcending the realms (*dhātu*). If one does not sever lust and killing, one cannot transcend the realms, because there are matters of mutual generation and mutual killing.
By saying this, he correctly shows that these two are what must first be severed.
Second, he shows how to progress in the cultivation of the remaining precepts:
one should contemplate lust as being like a venomous snake or as seeing an enemy thief. First, one maintains the four parājikas and eight parājikas of the śrāvaka to keep the body unmoving;
subsequently, one practices the pure discipline of a bodhisattva to keep the mind from arising [with afflictions].

Among all the precepts, the specific instruction to contemplate desire is because it is so difficult to sever. Furthermore, it is because all sentient beings derive their very life and nature from sexual desire.
