It is like a venomous snake or a vengeful thief—both are merely harsh speech. A venomous snake injures the body and takes one's life;
a vengeful thief plunders wealth and seizes possessions; but this single matter of sexual desire destroys the Dharma-body and injures [the mind].

"O Āyuṣmat, because they damage the wealth of the Dharma and extinguish merit, these are used as metaphors. Yet, although the Tathāgata speaks such harsh words, sentient beings must likewise sever them with a resolute mind.
As for the Śrāvaka followers of the Hīnayāna, there are the four parājikas and eight parājikas, which constitute the Hīnayāna precepts;
for a bhikṣu, there are only the four parājikas, namely: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. To commit [any of] these..."

Because they are not permitted to dwell together [with the Sangha], they are called "abandonments" (*pārājika*). For a bhikṣuṇī, in addition to the four abandonments, there are further added the eight offenses of touching, concealing, and following;

these are called the eight abandonments. To first hold the great and then hold the small is the intention of "starting from what is distant and moving toward what is near," or "ascending the high starting from the low.
As for "holding the body without moving," it does not mean that the mind is not held; rather, it refers to the power [of the body].

This is not yet exhaustive. As for not mentioning the subsequent sections: when the foundation is established, the Way arises of itself; when the source is settled, the stream becomes clear of itself.
Having already mastered the "Small" [Vehicle], one ought to advance toward the "Great. Therefore, it says: "Next, the Bodhisattva’s Pure Code of Discipline.
A Bodhisattva is a person of the Mahāyāna; the Pure Code of Discipline is the Mahāyāna precepts. Even if there were but a hair’s breadth...
The moment a thought arises, it is no longer pure; therefore, it is said that one must not give rise to a grasping mind.
Third, a detailed explanation of the benefits of upholding the precepts:
when the prohibitive precepts are perfected, there will forever be no karma of mutual birth or mutual killing within the world, and acts of theft and robbery will not occur.
Free from the burden of karmic debt, one shall likewise not have to repay past debts in this world. This person of purity cultivates *samādhi*;
without needing the divine eye, their physical body naturally perceives the worlds of the ten directions. They behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and personally receive the holy teachings.
Attaining great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they travel through the worlds of the ten directions; with a pure past life, they encounter no difficulties.
Perilous!
At the outset, one accomplishes the causes for transcending the world. Although the prohibitions encompass all four parājikas, here they specifically point to sexual misconduct and killing.

Because these two are difficult to sever, they should be strictly forbidden even more so than theft and falsehood. Since both body and mind are severed [from them], it is said that "accomplishment" is achieved.
As for these: when lust is severed, they no longer give rise to one another; when killing is severed, they no longer kill one another. Therefore, it is said that they are "forever non-existent.
To take what is not given is called "stealing" (thief); to take by force is called "robbery" (plunder). Furthermore, both stealing and robbery are accompanied by false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*):

for instance, in the case of stealing, one employs artful words so that the victim does not realize it; in the case of robbery, one uses intimidation so that the victim is forced to endure it. To incur debt is [also a form of] stealing.
It is caused by robbery and theft. One returns debts because of the burden of what was owed. Now that there is no longer any stealing or robbing, one naturally has no burdens.
Since there are no burdens, one likewise does not repay past debts. This is as previously stated: "To take a long farewell from the world."

Furthermore, although the world generally encompasses the three realms, here it appears to refer exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because the cycle of birth, killing, debt, and repayment are matters pertaining specifically to the desire realm.
Based on this, a person who upholds the precepts will not be reborn in the desire realm in the future;
even if they are reborn there, they will do no more than cultivate further among human beings, as they are no longer subject to birth, killing, or debt.

This refers to the practice of returning to one's original state. This is the development of the "semblance" supernormal powers (abhijñā) by those who are pure. "Pure persons" refers specifically to those who uphold the precepts.

Because concentration arises from the precepts, and supernormal powers are developed through concentration, such a person can, by practicing *samādhi* alone, develop the five semblance supernormal powers.
Their "fleshly eye" (māṃsa-cakṣus) resembles the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), and therefore they do not need to employ the divine eye to see; it is naturally so.
Thus, without relying on deliberate mental effort, those in the ten directions—because they are all-encompassing and leave nothing out—possess divine ears that resemble fleshly ears;

therefore, they are likewise able to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma. As for the term "resemble," it means that through the superior power of their ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the superior power of the initial stage of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), this capacity arises for a brief duration; it is not a perfect, pervasive, or supreme function. Below...

The third point is understood by analogy. "Personally receiving the imperial decree" is analogous to the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*). "Wandering through realms by means of supernormal powers" is analogous to the supernormal power of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*).
"Knowledge of past lives" is likewise only analogous; yet, although it is called "analogous," it is nonetheless unimpeded throughout the three periods of time, and is therefore termed "pure.
Regarding the phrase "attaining freedom from hardship and peril": because of this knowledge of past lives, one never again falls into the three [evil paths].
The evil realms are places of hardship, peril, and obstruction. This concludes the formal explanation.
Third, the summary: this is called the second stage of progressive cultivation.
To say that "this fruit can adorn the precepts" refers to the second stage of progressive advancement from the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
This constitutes the gradual sequence of definitive practice; it is called the "second" in contrast to the aforementioned "first.

Furthermore, because the initial stage of learning is not yet fixed, this is explained as "definitive practice. Regarding the term "right nature" (*samyaktva*) used here for what is abandoned, it is in contrast to—
The above is spoken by way of assisting the cause. This is because the preceding [sections] merely assisted in bringing this forth; this, however, is precisely the nature of sin itself.

Having finished excavating its true nature, there are three parts to the contradiction of its manifest karma: first, the introduction of the inquiry; second, the formal explanation; and third, the conclusion. First:
[The text continues with the specific analysis of the nature of sin.]
"What is manifest karma?
This question addresses the third stage of the gradual process. Therein are three parts to the formal explanation: first, receiving the precepts and cultivating meditative concentration;
second, suddenly attaining the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*); and third, being taught to cultivate gradually. Regarding the first:
Ānanda, when one who thus purely maintains the prohibitive precepts has no mind of greedy lust, they do not flow excessively toward the six external objects.
Because they do not flow outward, they revolve back to the source and return to themselves. When the objects are no longer conditioned, the sense organs have nothing to pair with;
the flow is reversed and the whole becomes one, so that the six functions cease to operate.
This immediately follows upon the preceding text to establish the cause for the arising of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, speaking specifically of the person before us:
although they maintain all the precepts, it is singled out that their mind is free from lustful desire, because lust is the chief destroyer of concentration.

Regarding "the six external sense objects" (*ṣaḍ bāhyaviṣayāḥ*) and so forth, lust serves as the precursor that defiles these objects; it is like how sound arises when there is movement—thus, one remains [detached].

The mind lusts for sounds. Because of sound there is form; thus the mind dwells in lustful attachment to form. Because of form there is fragrance; thus the mind dwells in lustful attachment to fragrance.
Because of fragrance there is flavor; thus the mind dwells in lustful attachment to flavor. Because of flavor there is tangibility; thus the mind dwells in lustful attachment to tangibility.
Because of tangibility there are mental objects (*dharma*); thus the mind dwells in lustful attachment to mental objects. If the mind is free from greedy lust, then regarding all forms...

Since one does not direct the mind toward sounds and other objects, it is said that they do not "flow forth and disperse" (*pravisṛta*) to any great extent. To say they "flow forth and disperse" means that the spirit finds its escape therein, becoming unrestrained as it pursues sensory conditions.
To say they do not do so "to a great extent" does not mean they are entirely absent; it simply means that one does not fixate the mind upon them with greedy attachment.

Regarding the phrase "because they do not flow forth and disperse," this cites the aforementioned lack of excessive dispersion as the cause. This refers to the fact that since external objects—[the text continues]...
When the mind is tranquil, one can then turn back to contemplate the fundamental root and return to the original luminosity; thus, internal observation (*adhyātma-vipaśyanā*) is perfected.

Once internal observation is perfected, external objects are completely shed; hence it is said, "not conditioned. According to the *Āvarta-śrotra-mūla-pariśuddhi*, this corresponds to "entering the stream and losing the object," where movement and stillness do not arise.
The preceding discussion of "not allowing the flow to escape" does not yet avoid the alternation between movement and stillness.
This is to be entirely non-contingent; it is the simultaneous extinction of both movement and stillness. It is a matter of correspondence:

when one says that the sense organ corresponds to the object, if the object is not contingent, the organ has nothing to correspond to. When the organ has no correspondence, its nature likewise does not manifest.

According to the Ear-organ’s Perfect Penetration (*karṇendriya-pariśuddhi*), this corresponds to the stage where "that which hears and that which is heard are both exhausted. Upon reaching this, the six organs flow back and fully return to the One.
This is their inherent nature; hence it is said, "reversing the flow to restore the oneness. Once the flow is reversed and oneness is restored, there is no further function for the roots of bondage;

hence it is said, "the six faculties cease to operate. According to the Ear-faculty’s Perfect Penetration (*śrotra-indriya-pariśuddhi*), this corresponds to the knot of perception (*vijñāna-grantha*). If one clings to this as being correct, [one remains bound].
Then one will be obstructed by awakening. The Great Outline states, "contradicting their manifest karma," which refers precisely to this section.

Within this section, there are two types of manifest karma: first, the "dissipation" (pramāda) is manifest karma; if it is not excessive, it is only slightly contradicted. Second, the "six functions" (ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya) are manifest karma;
if they do not operate, they are completely contradicted. Second, suddenly attaining the Dharma abruptly.
The lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure, like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli.
Body and mind are blissful, wondrously perfect, equal, and attain great peace and security. All the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [realms] of all Tathāgatas manifest therein.
This person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Building upon the previous point that the six functions do not operate and only one remains, if one proceeds to observe this "one," it is merely a name established in contrast to the six.

Since the six do not exist, how can the one be established? This is the realization that the perceiver is empty. As for this seeing that realizes [emptiness]— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the source.*
Since the [subjective] perceiving part is empty, the perceived objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*) likewise does not exist. Therefore, it is said that the lands of the ten directions are "brightly pure.
"Brightly" means pervasive and transparent; "pure" means that not a single dharma is seen to be present before the mind.
Reaching this state, both the perceiver and the perceived are empty, and only emptiness remains. This accords with the Perfect Penetration of the Ear-faculty.
This should be resolved through emptiness. If one clings to this as being real, it will again be obstructed by emptiness.
If one proceeds to contemplate that this emptiness is not nihilistic, but rather that the nature of consciousness is luminously clear within the Great Awakened Mind, it is said:
"It is like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli. From this point on, body and mind are filled with joy, for one has been able to transcend the obstruction of emptiness.

Furthermore, when one transcends emptiness and obstruction, that which was emptied by emptiness ceases to exist, leaving only cessation remaining. According to the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, this corresponds to the cessation of the knots.
If one clings to this as being ultimate, it remains a subtle obstacle known as "falling from the summit.

If one further contemplates this cessation—that cessation is spoken of only in contrast to arising, and thus cessation itself is not the truth—then since both arising and cessation have ceased, one attains wondrous perfection.
Equanimity (*samatā*). For that which is without delusion and inexhaustible is called "wondrous" (*miao*); that which is without unreality and reaches the ultimate is called "perfect" (*yuan*).
That the beginning and the source are non-dual is called "equanimity. From this point on, the three voids suddenly clarify and the two deaths abruptly become empty;

hence it is said that one attains great peace and stability. Quiescence and illumination mutually merge, and wisdom and severance are fully perfected; hence it is said that all Tathāgatas are secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous.
All are manifested therein. This is because the "mysterious and perfect" (*mi-yuan*) is the fruit of wisdom: when gathered inward, it is mysterious; when released outward, it is perfect.
The "pure and wondrous" (*jing-miao*) is the fruit of cessation: when realized in its essence, it is pure; when applied in its function, it is wondrous.
These are what all Buddhas have realized; hence the term "all Tathāgatas. The cause of perfect penetration lies in the mind, which suddenly encompasses the ocean of the fruition. Therefore—

It is said that all things appear within it. According to the "Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ" (*śrotra-indriya-avavāda*), this corresponds to the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*).

When quiescent extinction manifests, not a single thought arises; therefore, it is said that such a person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Regarding the realization of awakening, one is already equal to the realm of the Buddhas. This is what is meant by: "The principle is realized through sudden awakening; riding upon that awakening, all is simultaneously dissolved. Regarding the actual practice of cultivation, only...
In the third stage of gradual progression, inverted and chaotic thoughts cease abruptly from this point on; false transmigration shall never again exist from here forward.
Thus, the three teachings cultivate through gradual stages.
From this point, one gradually cultivates; according to the practices undertaken, one establishes oneself in the stages of the sages.

Affairs are not eliminated all at once, but are exhausted through a gradual sequence; therefore, the teaching is that one should cultivate from this point onward. When defilements are exhausted, the mirror becomes bright.
As the water rises, the boat ascends; therefore, it is shown that according to the depth of one's practice, one is established in the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*).

That is to say, there are degrees of shallowness and depth in the practice, and distinctions of superiority and inferiority in the establishment of the stages. This will be seen for oneself in the subsequent scriptural text. The formal explanation is now concluded.
The three fetters are thus severed;
this is called the third stage of progressive cultivation.

This means that the fruit is able to oppose one's present karma until the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is [the transition] from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

The Ground. Third, the progressive advancement. This refers to the gradual sequence of contemplative practice; what was previously described as "like removing poison from honey within a clean vessel" is a metaphor for this very point.
This concludes the summary of the three gradual stages. Second, the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*).
Ānanda, these sons of good family have the craving for existence dried up and their faculties and objects no longer meet. Their remaining physical form before them will not continue to be reborn.

Their grasping mind is empty yet luminous, consisting purely of wisdom; the nature of this wisdom is bright and perfect, illuminating the ten directions. Because they possess this wisdom while still being dry [of defilement], it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśana-bhūmi).
In the second stage of gradual progression, the mind of lust is permanently severed; hence it is said that "desire and craving are withered and dried up.
In the third stage of gradual progression, one forgets sensory objects and exhausts the sense-faculties; hence it is said that "the faculties and their objects do not encounter one another.

This meaning corresponds to the initial loosening of the knots within the process of liberation, wherein one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which is equal to the stage of the four fruits of the Śrāvaka vehicle. Therefore, it is said: "The remaining physical form now present shall no longer continue."
Birth: the remaining physical substance constitutes the final body; "non-continuation" means that future existence is forever severed.

This above has explained the meaning of "drying up" (*khan*) according to the second gradual stage and the first half of the third. Furthermore, within the third gradual stage, the lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure;
therefore, it is said that the grasping mind is "empty and luminous. "Grasping mind" refers to the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
The mind: because the land is luminous, it is empty; because it is pure and devoid of phenomena, it is bright.

In the sense of "untying the knots," this corresponds to the perfect brightness of the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which constitutes the liberation of dharmas. Reaching this point, both person and dharmas are empty; therefore, it is said that it is purely wisdom.
Furthermore, in the third gradual stage, through wondrous perfection and equality, one attains great peace and security; hence it is called the nature of wisdom.

"Brilliant and Perfect" (*mingyuan*): The nature of wisdom is precisely the wisdom of the three voids; it is the nature of wondrous, perfect equanimity. Because one attains great peace and security, it is called "brilliant and perfect.

While "great peace and security" seems to refer to the ultimate consummation of the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa*), "brilliant and perfect" seems to refer to the ultimate consummation of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Since these are but a single mind, there is no contradiction in speaking of them individually. This meaning within the section on "untying the knots" corresponds to liberation (*vimukti*).

When all phenomena are simultaneously empty and unarisen, one attains their entire substance (*dharmatā*). This above has explained the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*) by means of the latter half of the three gradual stages.
Question: Since this refers only to the preceding meaning, why is it established as a separate stage? Answer: The former stage only involves the realization of the substance;
this stage additionally involves the arousal of its function. Therefore, it says, "polishing the ten directions. "Polishing" (*yìng*) means adorning; it refers to the act of adornment.
The meaning is that, according to its essence, it gives rise to function, adorning and purifying the retributive lands (*vipākakṣetra*) throughout the ten directions.

Within the "Perfect Penetration" (*yuantong*), one immediately attains two excellences and manifests three functions. Although one can act in this way, it still remains a state where wisdom exists in isolation;

therefore, this stage is established and named "Dry Wisdom" (*gānhuì*). [Section] Thirty: Faith Two. One: Tracing back from the preceding to generally introduce the subsequent stage. Two: Specific [analysis].
This clarifies the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) in their respective positions.

First: when the habit-energy of desire has begun to dry up but has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma, one immediately enters the central flow within this very mind, whereby the perfect and wondrous [nature] unfolds.

Previously it was said that while the craving for desire had been dried up, its habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) had not yet been exhausted. Now, within the stage of "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*), one uses the adornment of the buddha-fields to treat these desires and habits;
since they have not yet reached ultimate exhaustion, it is said that "the habit of desire has only just begun to dry.
Because Bodhi and Nirvana still lie far ahead, it is said that "one has not yet connected with the Dharma-stream of the Tathāgata. Here, "the Dharma of the Tathāgata" refers to Bodhi.
It speaks of nirvāṇa. In contrast to the flow of ignorance and saṃsāra, it refers to the flow of bodhi and nirvāṇa.

As for the statement "not yet having reached [it]," this means one must correctly perceive that one should proceed through successive stages of practice and cultivation; therefore, one cannot take sudden enlightenment through universal penetration as the standard.
This "mind" refers to the final mind of the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*). Regarding the phrase "flowing into the midst of the midst," there are two interpretations.

First, "midst" (*zhong*) refers to the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Since all subsequent stages do not depart from the Middle Way, it is called "the midst of the midst. Second, "midst" refers to the Mean (*madhyama*).
This is because in the subsequent cultivation, although one does not abandon phenomenal activities (*dharma*), one also does not fall into excessive attachment; it is simply this [balance].

"Centered" means being neither partial nor biased; it refers to flowing in spontaneously. "Perfectly and wondrously blossoming" means that while the flow remains undifferentiated, it is still that same perfectly penetrating and wondrous nature;
it merely advances through successive stages, like the layers of a lotus flower opening and gradually unfolding.
Second, specifically clarifying the ten stages of this position: the ten [faiths]. First, faith. Second, mindfulness... [and so on].
1. Mind; 2. Threefold progressive mind; 3. Wisdom mind; 4. Concentration mind; 5. Non-retrogression; 6. Protection of the Dharma;
7. Dedication; 8. Precept mind; 9. Vow mind. First.
From this true, wondrous, and perfect state, one again gives rise to the true and wondrous. Wondrous faith abides eternally; all delusive thoughts are extinguished without remainder.
This state of pure truth on the Middle Way is called the Abode of Faith.

From the awakening to true, wondrous, and perfect [enlightenment], one again gives rise to true, wondrous cultivation. Because one simultaneously believes in both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), it is called "wondrous faith.
Because it is never lost or regressed, it is called "ever-abiding" (*nitya*). Outsiders (*tīrthika*) incline toward the heterodox; ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) incline toward existence (*bhava*);

and those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) incline toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*). All these are mere false imaginings (*vikalpa*). Since all are utterly discarded, it is said that they are "extinguished without remainder. False imaginings are thus extinguished.
Because it is free from conceptualization, the Middle Way is true; because there is nothing remaining, the Middle Way is pure. Being both true and pure, the mind of faith is resolute;
therefore, it is called the "Abiding in the Mind of Faith. Second is the "Mind of Recollection."
With true faith and clear understanding, one realizes that all is perfectly interfused; the three categories of aggregates, sense-bases, and elements can no longer act as obstructions.
In this way, even throughout countless eons of the past and future, all habitual tendencies from the shedding and taking up of bodies manifest before one.
These good sons are all able to recollect without any loss; this is called the dwelling of the mind of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
"True faith" refers to the pure and genuine faith of the aforementioned Middle Way.
"Clarity" means being vividly and clearly aware, never being deluded by any phenomena (*dharma*). Because they are not deluded by any phenomena, regarding all things...
Regarding the Dharma, one is able to harmonize, integrate, and encompass it all through the correct principle of the Middle Way; hence it is said that "all are perfectly penetrating.
These two phrases entirely build upon the benefits achieved by the preceding stage of faith to serve as the cause for this present stage.

From here on, the stage itself is correctly elucidated. The fact that the three—aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—cannot act as obstructions is precisely due to this perfect penetration of all.

Therefore, the aggregates (*skandha*) cannot cover it, the sense bases (*āyatana*) cannot confine it, and the elements (*dhātu*) cannot separate it. "In this way" means that the aggregates and so forth do not obstruct it in such a manner.
The phrase "up to" (*yāvat*) abbreviates by skipping over the present. Since it has been stated that the aggregates and so forth are without obstruction, [the text proceeds].

Not only does he maintain mindfulness without forgetfulness regarding the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that ought to be severed within his present body, but even the habitual tendencies that have already been severed or ought to be severed throughout the countless kalpas of past and future lives—through the successive casting off and taking up of bodies—all manifest before him, and he is able to remember them all without forgetfulness.
This refers to the mind of unforgetting cultivation; it is as if one were saying, "I desire to diminish [them]."

Although he has transgressed and is not yet fully accomplished, because he does not forget the practice of cultivation and constantly maintains mindfulness, this is called the "abiding of the mind in mindfulness. Third is the "mind of progress."
The wondrous, perfect, and pure reality gives rise to transformation from its true essence. The habitual tendencies of beginningless time merge into a single luminous clarity;
this singular luminous clarity that advances toward true purity is called the mind of diligence.
Due to the manifestation of prior habitual tendencies, one's desire for their exhaustion remains unfulfilled;

nevertheless, by relying once more upon the previously attained wondrous, perfect awakening and the pure, true faith in the Middle Way, one confronts delusive habits and refines the genuine essence. After a long time, the genuine becomes increasingly refined.
Thus, the power to melt away delusion arises; hence it is said, "to initiate transformation.
Because this melting of delusion constitutes the True, one is able to cause those beginningless habitual tendencies to merge into a single, refined lucidity. "Beginningless" refers to the past;
the present and future are not mentioned because once the past has been melted away, the present and future will no longer arise. These are the aforementioned four lines.

This is entirely based on the power of the first stage of faith to assist in treating the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the second stage of faith, thereby establishing the causes for the present stage.

From this point downward, the text correctly elucidates the present stage itself. Since beginningless habitual tendencies pervade the single, refined spirit, one cultivates practice by passing through various phenomena solely by means of the principle of that refined spirit;
hence it is called "progressing toward" (*jinqu*). Although one cultivates practice by passing through various phenomena, one does not...
Because one abides in the conditioned, it is called "true purity. Thus, delusion is exhausted and principle is perfected;
whether effort is applied or not, this stage is therefore named the Mind of Diligence and the Mind of the Four Wisdoms.
When the essence of mind manifests before one, being purely characterized by wisdom, it is called the "abiding of the wisdom-mind.

Building upon the preceding stage, one advances toward true purity and does not dwell in the conditioned. The essence of mind manifests from time to time, and wisdom remains unclouded from time to time.
Upon reaching this point, the wisdom-mind becomes definitive; it engages with phenomena purely through wisdom. Therefore, it is called the "wisdom-mind."
It is called "abiding. Abiding has the meaning of determination. The five states of the determined mind:

when the clarity of wisdom is maintained and pervades all, being profoundly still and tranquil; this profound stillness, wondrous, and eternally concentrated is called the abiding of the determined mind.
The preceding stage is characterized purely by wisdom; that is to say, at the time of encountering affairs, one always maintains the illumination of wisdom to observe them.
By using wisdom to illuminate affairs, every matter accords with principle; hence it is said, "pervasive, tranquil, and profoundly still.
These two phrases also build upon what was realized in the previous stage to establish the cause for the present stage. The following two phrases then correctly clarify the present [stage].
In its state, it is profoundly still and does not abide; yet its great functioning flourishes profusely. Therefore, it is described as "wondrous" because of its stillness.

Although its great functioning flourishes profusely, it remains unmoving and undisturbed; therefore, it is described as "constant" because of its concentration. Qingliang said: "Wisdom is all-encompassing and eternally tranquil."
This refers to the principle that "the manifold activities are ever thus. Since it is said that [the mind] is constantly concentrated, there is no time when it is not settled;

therefore, this very state is called the abiding of the concentrated mind (Zhengmo states: "The first five levels of faith belong to the five faculties, like the seeds of a fruit tree whose roots have taken hold in the earth.

The latter five levels of faith belong to the five powers, like roots that, having been established for a long time, possess an inherent power that cannot be uprooted"). This is the sixth stage: Non-retrogression.
The light of concentration (*samādhi*) illuminates and penetrates deeply into the luminous nature. Advancing alone without retreating is called the "non-retrogressive mind.

The mind of wisdom seems to lean toward wisdom because it is purely characterized by wisdom; the mind of concentration seems to coincide with concentration because it is tranquil, wondrous, and eternally凝 (concentrated/still).
Thus, concentration serves as the support for wisdom; hence it is said that "the light of concentration illuminates and clarifies. As it is said:
"Pure, ultimate radiance and penetration" means that tranquil illumination encompasses empty space.

Furthermore, because wisdom can support meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "the luminous nature penetrating deeply," which refers to penetrating deeply into concentration. This is what is meant by "returning to observe the world as if it were a dream.
Based on this, concentration and wisdom support one another; as the former diminishes, the latter increases. Therefore, it is said: "Only advancing, no retreating."

It does not regress; for this reason, it is called the "non-regressive mind. The significance of this stage corresponds to the power of progress. Seventh is the "mind that protects the Dharma" (*dharmapāla-citta*):

with a mind of steady progress, one maintains [the Dharma] securely so as not to lose it. The meeting of the vital energy (*prāṇa*) of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions is called the "mind that protects the Dharma."
As for "advancing the mind," it means the concentrated mind advances day by day. As for "serene ease," it means not relying on strenuous effort.

Because of this, one is able to maintain it spontaneously and never lose the concentrated mind. Once the concentrated mind is perfected, one receives the compassionate light of the Buddha’s illumination.
Thus, one attains communion with the *dhātu* (spiritual essence) of the Tathāgata. This *dhātu* is precisely the *dhātu* of the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Based on this, because one is able to protect oneself internally and elicit the protection of the Buddha externally, it is designated by the name "the mind that protects the Dharma" (*dharmarakṣā-citta*).

The meaning of this stage corresponds to the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as it is brought about by the daily advancement of the concentrated mind. [This concludes] the eighth dedication.
Maintaining this awakened clarity, one is able to use wondrous power to turn the Buddha’s compassionate light back toward the Buddha and dwell therein.
It is like two mirrors with their radiance facing each other, wherein wondrous reflections interpenetrate one another in infinite layers; this is called the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*).

According to the preceding stage of non-retrogression, concentration and wisdom support one another. In the higher stages, because concentration is profound, it becomes the cause for protecting the Dharma;
hence it is said that "the mind advances and maintains. In this present stage, because wisdom is luminous, it becomes the cause for dedication.
Therefore it is said: "Awakened clarity maintains. This means that awakened wisdom becomes increasingly clear and is maintained without loss.
Precisely because it is maintained without loss, one is able to respond to the Buddha’s compassionate light through the power of wondrous wisdom. This response is not distinct [from the Buddha];
it is simply abiding toward the Buddha, meaning that every thought-moment dwells within the realm of the Buddha. However, those in the higher stages directly connect with the Buddha.
The realm of vital energy (*dhātu*). Having been graced by the Buddha’s compassionate light, there is the reflection of oneself within the Buddha’s heart;
at this stage, one turns back the Buddha’s compassionate light and abides facing the Buddha, whereby there are the reflections of all Buddhas within one’s own heart.
When the reflection of oneself is within the Buddha’s heart, one has entered the Buddha’s heart; when the reflection of the Buddha is within one’s own heart, the Buddha has already entered.
When one’s own mind enters the Buddha’s mind, it already carries the reflection of the Buddha; because when receiving the Buddha’s portion of vital energy, one’s own mind is already the Buddha.
When the Buddha enters one’s own mind, he already carries one’s own reflection; because when returning the Buddha’s compassionate light, the Buddha’s mind is already oneself.
Thus, one’s own mind and the Buddha’s mind enter into one another in successive layers.

Therefore, it is said: "It is like two mirrors facing each other. The two mirrors facing one another symbolize the mind of oneself and the mind of the Buddha in mutual correspondence through compassion and wisdom.
The wondrous reflections within them symbolize the reflection of oneself within the Buddha’s mind and the reflection of all Buddhas within one's own mind.
Their mutual interpenetration in successive layers symbolizes that when one enters the Buddha’s mind, one already carries the Buddha’s reflection within.
When the Buddha enters one’s own mind, he already carries his own reflection; thus, the mind of oneself and the mind of the Buddha are neither identical nor different.
This does not preclude the provisional establishment of dedication within the state of non-dedication.

Furthermore, at this stage, one’s own mind receives the Buddha’s vital energy, and the Buddhas respond to one’s own mind by directing their compassionate light toward oneself. In this stage, one is sustained by the grace of the Buddha’s compassion.
Light. The wondrous power responds to the Buddha’s compassion; because one directs one’s own mind toward the Buddha, it receives the name of “dedication” (*pariṇāmanā*).
Among the five powers, its meaning corresponds to the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*), as it is brought about by the further clarification of awakened insight. Ninth, the mind of precepts.

The light of the mind secretly turns back, attaining the Buddha’s eternally concentrated, unsurpassed, wondrous purity. Abiding in the unconditioned and achieving non-forgetfulness is called the "abiding of the mind in morality.

Here, "mind" refers to one's own mind; "light" refers to the Buddha-light; "turning back" (huí) is synonymous with "returning" (huí). This states that in the two aforementioned stages, one’s own mind turns back [toward the source].

They are directed toward the Buddha, and the Buddha’s light is directed back toward themselves; both belong to the realm of hidden penetration and mysterious response, hence they are called "secret redirection.
These two together inherit from the two preceding stages to serve as the cause for the present stage. From here on, the text correctly elucidates the present stage itself.
"Obtaining" (*haku*) means "attaining. This refers to attaining the Buddha-concentration (*buddha-samādhi*) by virtue of the power of the secret transformation.

Because the Great Concentration of the Nāga is never a state of non-concentration, it is said to be "perpetually凝" (*jō*, unmoving/still). It is not merely that one attains concentration, but that one is also able to attain the fruit; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed, wondrous, and pure.
"Wondrous" (*myō*) refers to *bodhi*, because it emerges from the entanglements of afflictions (*kleśa*). "Pure" (*jō*) refers to *nirvāṇa*, because it is free from birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Because it is free from defilement, that which is called "unsurpassed" is precisely the Buddha. From this point on, seeking the Buddha-way above, one knows with certainty that there is no Buddha to be accomplished;
transforming sentient beings below, one knows with certainty that there are no beings to be delivered. Therefore, it is said that one dwells peacefully in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As the power of faith increases, not even a hair’s breadth of a conditioned thought arises; therefore, it is said that one attains freedom from loss.

This stage is called "Abiding in the Mind of Precepts" (*śīlacittasthiti*). Because one attains the Buddha’s eternal constancy, this is the precept conjoined with meditative concentration (*samādhisamvara*);

because it is unsurpassed, wondrous, and pure, this is the precept conjoined with the Path (*mārgasamvara*); and because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and without loss, this is the precept of restraint (*saṃvarasamvara*).

Among the five powers, its meaning corresponds to the power of faith (*śraddhābala*), for through unconditioned right faith, there is no omission or loss. It consists of the ten aspirational minds (*praṇidhicitta*).

Abiding in the mastery of ethical discipline (*śīla-vaśitā*). Being able to travel throughout the ten directions, going wherever one wishes according to one’s vow, is called the dwelling of the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-citta-vihāra*).

Regarding "abiding in the mastery of ethical discipline": because the restraints associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samvara*) and those associated with the Path (*mārga-samvara*) are spontaneously pure, the precepts of concentration are ever-concentrated.

One attains the bliss of samādhi and the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) through right reception (*samāpatti*). (By the power of samādhi, one attains the bliss of mastery and enters all buddha-fields universally, moving unhindered according to one’s will. The Path.

Through the excellence of the precepts, one attains the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) that realizes the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. (Having realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is like an illusion and fundamentally non-existent, one is thus able to enter everywhere.

Through the discipline of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one attains the mind-made body that arises simultaneously with its class (*nikāya-sahaja*) and is devoid of volitional effort (*anabhisamskāra*).

(Manifesting forms according to the various classes of sentient beings, like reflections appearing in a mirror, yet without any deliberate action. By means of this, one is able to travel throughout the ten directions; indeed, it is not merely a matter of traveling through the ten directions.
Furthermore, that which is able to go and that which is gone follow one’s vow; that is to say, whatever place one vows to go to, one arrives there in a single thought-moment.

For this reason, it is called the "vowing mind" (*praṇidhicitta*), which in meaning corresponds to the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), because a vow is accomplished through recollecting without forgetting.

(Zhengmo states: "In discussing the ten minds generally, the first six cultivate one's own mind, while the latter four combine with the Buddha's virtues. Guanding states: 'The first is the fundamental substance of faith; the remaining nine are the virtuous manifestations of faith. Furthermore, the first nine belong to internal practice and virtue, while the last one belongs to external transformation.'"* )

[The Master] said: "I, the fool, believe that among the ten minds, six of them all include the character 'abiding' (zhù). One should know by analogy that the remaining four should likewise have it. This is because when the state of quiescent extinction (śānti-nirvāṇa) manifests before one, the realization and testimony are already equal to the Buddha-realm; how much more so for the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā)! How could there be any further regression?

Thus, we know that the name 'ten faiths' here borrows the gradual (anupūrva) to signify the sudden (akṣaya), and borrows the partial (prādeśika) to signify the perfect (pariniṣpanna). In reality, they are not at all like the ten faiths within the partial and gradual teachings, which are as light as a goose feather. The Ten Faiths conclude. The Forty Abodes (catvāriṃśad-vihāra): 1.
The Abode of Initial Resolve (cittotpāda-vihāra); 2. The Abode of Cultivating the Ground (bhūmi-parikarman-vihāra); 3. The Abode of Practice (caryā-vihāra); 4. The Abode of Birth...

The Abodes: 1. The Abode of the Noble; 2. The Abode of the Perfectly Pure; 3. The Abode of the Radiant; 4. The Abode of the Refulgent; 5. The Abode of the Difficult to Conquer; 6. The Abode of Presence; 7. The Abode of Right Mindfulness; 8. The Abode of Non-retrogression; 9. The Abode of the Youthful Truth;
10. The Abode of the Crown Prince; 11. The Abode of Empowerment. First:

Ānanda, these sons of good family, by means of true skillful means, give rise to these ten minds. The essence of their minds radiates brilliance, and as the ten functions interpenetrate one another, they perfect a single mind;
this is called the Dwelling of the Initial Resolve.
The full possession of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) is called "wholesome" (*kuśala*), because the roots of goodness are definitive.

The accomplishment of the five powers (*pañcabala*) is termed "manhood," because one is able to distinguish the subsequent stages. True skillful means refers precisely to the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing. As it was said previously: "The holy nature has no obstruction;
whether following or reversing [the flow], all are skillful means. For those of initial resolve entering samādhi, the speed of attainment differs beyond comparison. Thus we know.
The perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing is uniquely the true expedient means, for it is the single path to Nirvana for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.
All others are merely semblances, as they do not constitute a constant practice of study, and because their teachings are spoken according to varying levels of depth.
The ten kinds of faith do not depart from the wondrous nature of perfect penetration; thus it is said that "by means of this, one gives rise to [faith]. This is based on...
When these ten minds are refined, tempered, and cultivated, the mind of perfect penetration becomes increasingly subtle and increasingly luminous;
hence it is said that "the essence of the mind radiates brilliance. Regarding "the ten functions interpenetrate": the above was gradual development, whereas this is perfect fusion.
For example, when any one of the ten minds arises, the remaining nine minds all interpenetrate within this single mind—mind after mind.
All are thus. They mutually encompass and interpenetrate one another. Reaching this point, the bodhicitta is truly pure and free from delusion;
therefore, it is called the "perfectly accomplished single mind. The single mind is itself the bodhicitta. According to the *Awakening of Faith*, there are three kinds of bodhicitta:
first, the direct mind, because it correctly contemplates the dharma of suchness; second, the profound mind, because it delights in accumulating [virtues]... one.
Because it cuts through all wholesome dharmas; because the third is the mind of great compassion, which extensively delivers all sentient beings.
Among these ten minds, the first is the pure and true Middle Way, which is the *ṛjukacitta* (straight mind). From the second to the ninth, all are the *adhyāśayacitta* (deep mind).
The final one is able to traverse the ten directions, its meaning encompassing the mind of compassion (*karuṇācitta*). Since these ten functions engage with people, they arise accordingly.

The single mind is the complete fulfillment of the three minds; thus, one attains the mind that perfectly accomplishes bodhi. Because it is perfectly accomplished, it receives the name "Stage of Resolving the Mind.
Second is the "Stage of Cultivating the Ground."

The illumination within the mind is like the appearance of refined gold within pure lapis lazuli. Because one treads upon the ground by means of this prior wondrous mind, it is called the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground (*kṣitigarbha-vihāra*).
Based on the bodhicitta, true wisdom arises once more; therefore, it is said that "illumination is manifested within the mind. The bodhicitta is pure...
Because it is pure and brilliant, it is likened to lapis lazuli. Because the essence of true wisdom is refined and its function is luminous, it is likened to fine gold.
Regarding "using the aforementioned sublime mind to tread upon and form the ground":
this means that once true wisdom has arisen, one employs the ten preceding types of sublime mind to cultivate authentic practice, treading upon True Suchness (*tathatā*) to achieve progress.
The stage of the subsequent position is like a narrow path on a mountain trail;
by its persistent use, it becomes a road, and it is for this reason that it is named the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground. Third is the Dwelling of Cultivation.

When both the mind-ground (*citta-bhūmi*) and its cognitive engagement (*jñāna-praveśa*) are fully clarified, and one traverses the ten directions without obstruction, this is called the "Abiding in Practice" (*caryā-vihāra*).
"Mind" refers to the wondrous mind mentioned previously; "ground" refers to the ground previously traversed.

Since the wondrous mind already involves the interpenetration of the ten functions, the ground traversed likewise involves the cognitive engagement of the ten minds. Because of this cognitive engagement, the single mind is clearly understood. Mind...
The mind is likewise in all respects. Therefore, it is said that both attain clarity. Because both attain clarity, one realizes the Truth from time to time, and this Truth is nowhere not harmonized.
Thus, one is able to traverse the ten directions without obstruction or hindrance, and from this point on, manifests countless emanations of the body.
Pervading the lands of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas above and benefiting sentient beings below—this is called the Dwelling of Cultivation. (Question:

This is somewhat similar in wording to the passage in the "Dwelling of Vows" regarding being able to travel through the ten directions and going wherever one's vows lead; what is the distinction in meaning? Answer: That refers to the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*), while this refers to manifesting transformation bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).

Furthermore, that speaks of "following vows," which seems to imply traveling directly to a single direction; this speaks of "unimpededness," clarifying that one enters everywhere throughout the atoms of all lands. Thus, the distinction between superior and inferior is clearly established. The Fourth: The Noble Dwelling of Birth.

Their conduct becomes identical to that of the Buddha, and they receive the Buddha’s spiritual essence (*dhātu*). Just as an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) spontaneously seeks out its parents, their subtle faith communicates with the darkness of the world, entering the lineage of the Tathāgata;
this is called the Stage of Noble Birth (*janmaja-vihāra*).

By planting the seeds of true practice, the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition; therefore, it is said that "practice is identical to the Buddha. Because the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, the fruition penetrates back to the source of the cause;
therefore, it is said that one "receives the Buddha’s vital energy (*vāyu-bhāga*). As stated previously in the *Dharmapāla-hṛdaya-śāstra*:

"The vital energies of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions interconnect," which refers to the vital energy of the compassionate mind. The meaning of the present statement, "receiving the Buddha’s vital energy," is as follows: [it refers to the penetration of the causal source through the fruition].
It is said that their share of the *tathatā* (true suchness) is certainly not the same. The next two lines provide a metaphor:

the arousal of the mind in the first stage (*bhūmi*) is like the prior *skandha* (aggregate) giving rise to delusion; the cultivation of the ground in the second stage is like the prior *skandha* creating karma;

and the practice in the third stage is like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) maintaining seeds while wandering. Since this [third stage] involves activity identical to that of a Buddha, one receives the "breath" (*vāyu*) of the Buddha; therefore, it is compared to the intermediate state.

The hidden [faith] seeks its parents as a metaphor for this. Although the Buddha has not yet granted a clear prediction, by means of this hidden faith, one knows that his initial resolve does not regress.
Although he himself has not yet attained manifest realization, he has already attained secret communion;

perceiving that he will certainly realize the ultimate fruit, one knows that this hidden faith and secret communion are precisely the intersection of the path of resonance and response, like the mutual entanglement of those with similar karma. Thus it is bound.

This is the section on the formation of the embryo. Therefore, it is said that one "enters the lineage of the Tathāgata. Entering the lineage of the Tathāgata is like being entrusted to the womb of a king;
thus, it is called the Stage of Noble Birth (*janmaja-vihāra*). Fifth is the Stage of Full Endowment (*sambhṛta-vihāra*).

Having already entered the womb of the Way and personally received the lineage of the Awakened One, one is like a fetus that has already formed human features without deficiency; this is called the stage of "Abiding in the Fulfillment of Expedient Means.
What was previously termed "entering the lineage of the Tathāgata" refers to the formation of the womb of the Way; as for the term "wandering," it means relying upon this [stage].

Cultivating the cause, one attains sovereign non-obstruction, like a noble person dwelling in the womb—peaceful, joyful, and unrestrained. Yongjia said, "The profound spirit is hidden within the dharma-realm";
this refers precisely to this meaning. From then on, I have constantly been protected and remembered by all Buddhas, and the Dharma-body has gradually been realized and entered;
thus it is said, "I personally serve the lineage of the Awakened One," meaning that I personally serve the protection and mindfulness of the Great Awakened One for the sake of the Dharma.

It is the progeny of the body. Because skillful means and wisdom are gradually brought to full completion, it is likened to a fetus that has already formed and whose human characteristics are not deficient;
this refers to the fulfillment of the faculties and physical form when the forty-nine days within the womb have passed.
For this reason, it is called the "Abiding in the Fulfillment of Skillful Means. This is the sixth stage, the "Abiding in the Rectification of the Mind."
The physical appearance and the mental characteristics are both identical [to those of a Buddha], hence it is called the "Abode of the Rectified Mind.

Because expedient wisdom is manifested externally, it is termed "physical appearance"; because the means for gathering and transforming sentient beings are fully perfected, it is termed "like a Buddha.
This passage cites the preceding stage as the cause for the present stage. From here on, the present stage itself is correctly elucidated. By means of...

The provisional provisionally accords with the real; internally illuminating True Suchness (Tathatā), it is called the "characteristic of the mind" (*citta-lakṣaṇa*). Because wisdom and principle are perfected, it is said to be "also identical.

Being identical to the Buddha, one achieves correct knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*). Just as after the seven-times-seven stages within the womb, the characteristic of the mind gradually becomes manifest, it is therefore named "Correct Mind" (*samyak-citta*).
This is the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya-vihāra*).
The integration of body and mind, which increases day by day, is called the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avivartana-vihāra*).

In the fifth stage, provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) manifests externally; its appearance is like that of a Buddha, hence it is called "body" (*kāya*). In the sixth stage, true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) illuminates internally;

its mental state accords with that of a Buddha, hence it is called "mind" (*citta*). Taking these two meanings together constitutes the cause for the seventh stage; therefore, it is said they are "integrated. This refers to provisional [wisdom].
It is the perfection of the ultimate. It is the perfection of both the provisional and the ultimate. Since the two benefits are pursued simultaneously, it is said that "it increases day by day.
Being like one in the mother's womb, having fully passed through the ten months, it is perfected without decay; thus it is said to be "non-retrogressive. This corresponds to the six kinds of faith.
Although they share the same name, "Non-retrogression," there is a difference in their depth. That [stage] is non-retrogression of faith, whereas this is non-retrogression of abiding in the Path.
This is the eighth, the Stage of Youthful Truth (Kumārabhūta).
The simultaneous and complete possession of the spiritual characteristics of the ten bodies is called the Stage of Youthful Truth (*kumārabhūmi*).
Building upon the preceding stages, these increase day by day; while the provisional benefit is superior, the ultimate benefit is profound.

Therefore, it is said that the spiritual characteristics of the ten bodies are simultaneously and completely possessed. Here, the ten bodies serve as the particulars, while the two wisdoms—provisional and ultimate—serve as the general principle. This is as within the ten bodies themselves.

The three bodies—the Bodhi-body (*bodhi-kāya*), the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*), and the Majestic Power-body (*vibhūti-kāya*)—all belong to ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*), because they are objects of self-realization (*pratyātma-adhigama*).

The five bodies—the Vow-body (*praṇidhāna-kāya*), the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), the Sustaining Power-body (*adhiṣṭhāna-kāya*), the Mind-born-body (*manomaya-kāya*), and the Merit-body (*puṇya-kāya*)—all belong to provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), because they are objects for the transformation of others (*parārtha*).
The two bodies—the Marks-and-Excellences Adorned-body (*lakṣaṇavyañjana-saṃskṛta-kāya*) and the Wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*)—pertain to both provisional and ultimate wisdom.

Indeed, because the marks and embellishments (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) constitute the transformation-body of retribution, and wisdom constitutes both the self-realization and the transformation for others;

according to the *Avataṃsaka*, it is only at the eighth stage that the ten bodies are fully possessed. As for the fact that they are already complete at the eighth abode in this present sutra, it is because both sutras belong to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), and thus their earlier and later stages must necessarily be mutually integrated. Moreover, since one attains Buddhahood upon the fulfillment of faith in the *Avataṃsaka*, how could the ten bodies not be present?

It is not yet fully complete; however, its textual description is revealed within the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). Regarding the term "numinous characteristics" (*lingxiang*): it signifies the meaning of spiritual subtlety and boundless adaptability.

This is like a newborn whose gestation is full: although the six sense organs and four limbs are each perfectly formed, the primal integrity has not yet dispersed and the taints of emotion have not yet manifested;
therefore, it is named "Childlike Innocence" (*tongzhen*). This is the dwelling of the nine princes.
The formation of the emergence from the womb is called the "Abode of the Dharma Prince," wherein one becomes a child of the Buddha.
The phrase "the ten bodies of the higher stages are fully perfected" refers to this very formation of the emergence from the womb; this citation serves as the cause for what follows.
The subsequent sentence correctly clarifies the specific stage itself. Since one is still "wandering within the womb of the Way" among these five abodes, one remains constrained by the Way.
Previously, they had not yet attained great mastery; therefore, it was merely said that they personally received the lineage of the Awakened One, but it was not said that they were his sons.

Now, having attained great mastery and suddenly transcended the obstacles of principle (*li-zhang*), they are able to undertake the great tasks of the Buddha-dharma; hence it is said that they are personally the sons of the Buddha.
Just as a prince of the world, upon passing the age of fifteen and possessing some degree of discernment, comes to possess the bearing of a sovereign;
for this reason, it is called the Dwelling of the Dharma Prince (Dharmarājaputra-vihāra) and the Tenth Dwelling of Consecration (Abhiṣeka-vihāra).

Through these outward signs, one becomes a full person. Just as a great king of a nation delegates various state affairs to his crown prince, so too when that kṣatriya king’s heir apparent has reached maturity, he is consecrated with the ceremonial sprinkling; this is called "abiding in the consecration."
The "superior rank" is named *dharmaputra* (Dharma Prince). This signifies that he has attained full maturity; that is, it manifests him as one who is destined to become a Buddha.
This serves as a restatement of the preceding cause. As for the passage beginning with "Like a kingdom," this correctly clarifies his actual status:

because the Buddha wishes to bestow upon him a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), he first commands him to act on the Buddha’s behalf to proclaim the teaching and transform sentient beings; therefore, he is metaphorically compared to the great king of a kingdom.

"King of a country" refers specifically to a Kṣatriya king (Kṣatriya means "noble clan" in this context). Regarding the phrase "entrusting state affairs," it means that because the King considers state affairs to be of great importance, he fears [the candidate] might not be capable of handling them;
therefore, he first entrusts him with a small portion of such affairs to test his abilities.

"Entrusting" (wei) means to entrust or delegate. This metaphor illustrates that the Buddha, wishing to bestow a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa), fears that their intellectual power may not yet be sufficient;

therefore, he first has them act on behalf of the Buddha to propagate the teachings and perform the Buddha’s work. Once he perceives that their intellectual power has increased and they are no longer afraid of saving sentient beings, he immediately grants them the prediction.
Thus, it is compared to a Kṣatriya king and so forth; "heir apparent" (shizi) refers to the crown prince.
Because he has inherited the kingship through successive generations, the one who has reached full maturity is capable of managing the affairs of state;

this is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s increase in wisdom and power, whereby he is unafraid as he delivers sentient beings. As for "arraying," it refers to arraying the waters of the four great oceans; "consecrating" (abhiṣeka) refers to [the ritual sprinkling].

The crown of the crown prince is sprinkled with water to confer upon him the rank of king; this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s power of wisdom conferring its grace and bestowing a prophecy upon him, enabling him to be endowed with the ten powers and to be counted among the ranks of Buddhas. As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

"The crown prince born to a Wheel-Turning Sage King has a mother who is the principal queen," and so on, until it says: "He takes the waters of the four great oceans and places them in a golden pitcher."
Within [the palace], the King takes this vessel and pours it over the crown of the Crown Prince’s head. At that moment, he is said to have received the royal position.
It is the same when a Bodhisattva receives his office: because the waters of the Buddhas’ wisdom are poured upon his crown, this is called the Bodhisattva receiving the office of great wisdom.
Because he is endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, he is reckoned among the ranks of the Buddhas. This is the stage of the *Avataṃsaka*.

Regarding the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), the present scripture places them within the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*). This is because both scriptures share the same fundamental tenet, possessing the dual meanings of "perfect fusion" (*yuanrong*) and "gradual progression" (*xingbu*).

While there is no lack of distinction in terms of gradual progression, the former is likened to a prince of the *cakravartin* (wheel-turning king), whereas this is likened to a prince of the *kṣatriya* caste;
thus, they differ from one another. However, if considered in terms of perfect fusion, then the preceding and succeeding stages encompass and penetrate one another, as follows:
The preceding eight stages (*bhūmi*) have already clarified this; it can be understood that the final phrase establishes the name based on a metaphor.

This concludes the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*). Regarding the Fifty Practices (*pañcāśat-pratipatti*): [Zhengmo] says, "In the preceding ten stages, one is born into the Buddha-family and receives the family inheritance; these ten practices, however, involve undertaking the Buddha’s activities. Furthermore, from the very first moment of the Mahāyāna mind, one inherently practices both self-benefit and the benefit of others simultaneously."

However, within the stage of abiding in faith (*śraddhā-vihāra*), the benefit of others is not yet preeminent; therefore, among the preceding twenty-four stages, there is no explicit indication of the activity of delivering sentient beings. From this point onward, it is gradually made manifest. Now, when the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) are compared with the *Avataṃsaka*, they are clearly identified as the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

Furthermore, the latter five perfections are derived by expanding the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) into five, which also differs from the conventional ten perfections. 1. The Practice of Joy (*pramuditā-caryā*); 2. The Practice of Benefiting Others (*arthacaryā*); 3. The Practice of Non-Anger (*akrodha-caryā*); 4. The Practice of Inexhaustibility (*akṣaya-caryā*); 5.
The Practice of Freedom from Distraction (*avikṣepa-caryā*); 6. The Practice of Excellent Manifestation (*sudarśana-caryā*).
7. The Practice of Non-attachment; 8. The Practice of Reverence; 9. The Practice of Wholesome Dharmas; 10. The Practice of Reality. First:
Ānanda, once these sons of good family have become children of the Buddha, they possess the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas;
because they accord with the ten directions, this is called the Practice of Joy.
In the eighth stage, one is newly born; in the ninth stage, one gradually grows; and in the tenth stage, one receives office. Hence it is said, "Having become a son of the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas":

according to the *Avataṃsaka*, this bodhisattva studies what the Buddhas originally practiced and recollects what the Buddhas originally practiced, even to the point of saying that they maintain, manifest, and expound [the teachings].

To speak of the original practices cultivated by all Buddhas is to show that there is no Buddha-virtue they do not possess. To accord with the ten directions is precisely the extensive practice of giving.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In accordance with various lands, wherever there is poverty and deprivation, one takes rebirth there through the power of vows;
becoming noble, wealthy, and of inexhaustible riches, one practices the giving of material wealth, even unto one's own body."
Without sparing even their own flesh, they practice the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*), thereby teaching the equality of the three periods of time, up to and including *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*;
this is precisely what it means to accord with the meaning [of the name]. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) says:

"This constitutes the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), because the *Avataṃsaka* initially designates this bodhisattva as a 'Great Giver' (*mahādānapati*). He is designated by the name 'Joyful Practitioner' (*Nandika*) for two reasons. First, seeing that there is..."
Regarding those who come to beg: one should regard them as fields of merit and as virtuous friends, thereby giving rise to redoubled joy.
Second, one should grant whatever is requested, causing all sentient beings to be fully satisfied and to give rise to a joyful mind. This is also the meaning found in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
Second is the practice of benefiting others.
Being well able to benefit all sentient beings is called "beneficial conduct.
Having already attained joy, one then transforms others through the virtue of precepts; hence it is called "benefiting. Regarding the phrase "well able":
the virtue of the precepts is perfected within oneself and transformed outwardly; without expending effort, there is no benefit that is not universally provided.
Zhengmo says: "This is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), for the *Avataṃsaka* initially designates this bodhisattva as one who guards and upholds pure precepts.
It is termed 'one who acts for the benefit of others' (*anugrāhaka*) for two reasons: first, being able to abide oneself in unsurpassed ethical discipline, one benefits oneself well;
second, causing others to abide in unsurpassed ethical discipline, one also benefits others. This is detailed in the *Avataṃsaka*."
I shall not cite further examples here. Third is the practice of non-aversion (*adveṣa*).
To awaken oneself and awaken others so that there is no opposition or resistance is called the practice of non-aversion.
Having already benefited them, one continues to awaken others by means of the principle realized within oneself; it is like holding an axe-handle [to guide the cutting].
In hewing a handle for an axe, the model is not far off. Therefore, one gains others' lack of resistance; because there is no resistance, hatred has no cause to arise.
Based on this, if another cannot be awakened, that constitutes resistance; if one grows weary and abandons the transformation of others, that constitutes hatred.
Now, by awakening others through one's own awakening, it is easy for others to be awakened and oneself does not grow weary. For this reason, it is so named.

It constitutes the practice of non-ill will and non-hatred. Zhengmo (正脈) says: "This is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), because the *Avataṃsaka* initially designates this bodhisattva as one who constantly cultivates the dharma of patience.
However, there it is called 'the practice of non-opposition,' which refers to willingly accepting external hardships."
Non-opposition toward others is called patience (*kṣānti*). This is termed the practice of being free from malice. It refers to taking up for oneself the state of being free from malice;
enduring and accepting the teachings is called patience. These are the four inexhaustible practices.

The manifestation of various forms extending to the limits of the future, characterized by equality throughout the three periods of time and universal penetration across the ten directions, is called inexhaustible practice.
Being free from anger and resentment, the Bodhisattva nevertheless follows those sentient beings of all types, appearing wherever they may be and taking birth in every place;
hence it is said that "various forms are born. Since the realms of birth are inexhaustible, the vows and practices of the Bodhisattva are likewise inexhaustible.
It is inexhaustible; therefore, it is said to "reach the limits of the future. Since it can reach the limits of the future, it enters into the equality of the three periods of time.
Since it can give rise to all categories of beings, it penetrates and accords with all directions throughout the ten quarters. Thus, both horizontally and vertically, there is no exhaustion;
hence, it is named the "Inexhaustible Practice. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) says: "This is the stage of the Perfection of Vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*)."
The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra designates this bodhisattva as one who cultivates all forms of diligence (*vīrya*).

However, that [text] names it the "Practice of Unyielding Flexibility" (*anavamṛdyacaryā*), taking the sense that one cannot be bent, broken, obstructed, or hindered by any objective realm (*viṣaya*) to be "diligence.
This [text], however, names it the "Practice of Exhaustlessness" (*akṣayacaryā*), taking the sense that one is able to teach and benefit beings at all times and in all places to be "diligence."
Fifth is the practice of freedom from confusion.
All things are unified; attaining non-deviation amidst the various dharma-gates is called the practice of freedom from delusive confusion.
Being able to pervade horizontally and encompass vertically, one is naturally able to harmonize the minds of all sentient beings and accord with them.
Therefore, it is said that "all things are identical. Since all things are identical, one is naturally able to preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings;

hence, it is called the "various Dharma-gates. As the faculties of beings respond to the teaching to receive benefit, and the teaching responds to those faculties to effect transformation, it is said that "there is no error.
Thus, even when a thousand difficulties assail at once, their wisdom does not grow dim, and when ten thousand stimuli arise simultaneously—
He proceeds, yet his mind is not disturbed; for this reason, it is called the practice of being free from deluded distraction. The *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse) states:
"This is the perfection of dhyāna (*dhyānapāramitā*), because the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* initially characterizes the mind of this bodhisattva as being without distraction, firm, and immovable."
If one relies on the present sutra, then non-delusion and non-distraction constitute dhyāna.

As for the six wholesome manifest activities (*kuśala-samudācāra*), they reveal a multitude of differences within the same [state]; each distinct characteristic is individually seen as being equally termed "wholesome manifest activity."
The superior [Buddha] manifests bodies according to the species [of beings], such that all are unified.
This is the process from the root to the branches, like Avalokiteśvara, who can manifest thirty-two types of responses—manifesting as a deva for devas, as a human for humans, and so forth.

What is now called "manifesting difference within unity" is the process from the branches to the branches; it is like, within a single celestial body, further manifesting in response to various differences.
According to the various capacities of beings, they manifest in numerous diverse forms; the same is true for human bodies and so forth.

Therefore, it is said that "within the identical, a multitude of differences is manifested. Although a multitude of differences is manifested, those celestial hosts still perceive these various distinct characteristics as being identical to themselves;
the same is true for the human hosts and others. Therefore, it is said that "each distinct characteristic is perceived individually [as such]."
The same. Based on this, it means that a single body can manifest many bodies, and within those many bodies, a single body is manifested.

For this reason, it is called "skillful manifestation" (*sukhābhisaṃbodhi*). *Zhengmo* states: "This is the wisdom of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena" (which differs from the view of the present commentary).
*Guanding* says: "This is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). He further explains himself: "If it were not for the Great Dharma-realm..."

How can wisdom manifest in such perfect integration? The ignorant claim it is still merely the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), yet this is because the unimpeded wisdom of the bodhisattva skillfully employs its functions so that the one and the many are non-obstructive, and both identity and difference are simultaneously established. Thus it is manifested.
Seventh is the practice of non-attachment.
Thus, even unto the number of dust motes that fill the void of the ten directions, within each single mote one manifests the worlds of the ten directions.
Manifesting both the motes and the worlds without mutual obstruction or hindrance is called the practice of non-attachment.
The preceding section on the excellent manifestation of bodily forms has been thus explained. It is not only the bodily forms;

even the worlds are all excellently manifested without obstruction. The following section, "In the ten directions, throughout the empty space, as many as there are motes of dust," clarifies the vast number of motes of dust, thereby illustrating the narrowness of that which is capable of manifesting them. Each and every one...
"Manifesting the worlds of the ten directions within a mote of dust" indicates that the worlds are even more numerous; it clarifies that what is manifested is vast.
Both the manifestor and the manifested do not lose their respective characteristics; this is called "manifesting the mote and manifesting the world.

That is to say, the mote remains outside the world without losing its characteristic of narrowness, while the world remains inside the mote without losing its characteristic of vastness. They are manifested simultaneously; therefore, it is so stated.
"They do not obstruct one another. Zhengmo says: "When the realms enter the particles, the realms are not small; this means the small does not remain confined within the large.
When the particles contain the realms, the particles are not large; this means the large does not obstruct the small. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"Within every particle of all the worlds of Flower Treasury, the entire Dharma-realm is seen. This is the same principle. —Wenling.

It is said: "This arises from the excellent practice of Subhūti, which expands and perfects [his realization] in a seamless fusion. Thus he is designated as the "Practitioner Without Attachment" (*asaṅga-caryā*).

According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, this refers simply to being entirely without attachment. The *Zhengmo* states: "If there were even a single instance of attachment, how could one possibly achieve such a simultaneous fusion of the great and the small?
According to this sūtra, "non-attachment" is precisely the forgetting of objects. When the power of forgetting objects reaches its ultimate limit, one is then able to...
"Body and mind are perfectly luminous; the site of enlightenment is immovable.
Within the tip of a single hair, one can universally contain the lands of the ten directions," and so forth, as clarified previously in the section on the unimpeded manifestation of vision.
