Thus we know that the manifestation of objects and the manifestation of realms do not obstruct or hinder one another precisely because the function of forgetting objects has reached its ultimate limit; therefore, it is designated by the name "Practice of Non-attachment. Zhengmo says: "This is..."

The wisdom of the non-obstruction of all phenomena (*sarva-vastu-asangajñāna*). Guanding states: "This is precisely the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*)," citing the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* to show that this bodhisattva brings about transformation and deliverance through skillful means.

I [Yuan] say: that the realms of dust and worlds manifest within one another, and the large and small are mutually integrated, is precisely due to the operation of the bodhisattva’s unobstructed wisdom and the power of great skillful means. These constitute the eight practices of respect.
All these various manifestations are the first *pāramitā*, named the "Practice of Reverence.
Building upon the preceding [text], it is not only that bodies and lands are manifested; rather, all the immeasurable and wondrous practices of the bodhisattvas are fully perfected at once.
Therefore, it is said that "various things manifest before one. Whichever single practice one undertakes, it is capable of reaching the supreme ultimate.
Because they reach the ultimate end, it is said that all are the foremost *pāramitā*. "Foremost" (*prathama*) means "supreme";
"*pāramitā*" means "reaching the further shore. Furthermore, the Sanskrit term *pāramitā* is translated here as "reaching the other shore.
This refers to departing from this shore of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), crossing over the turbulent current of afflictions (*kleśa*), and arriving at the other shore of *nirvāṇa*. Indeed...
Nirvana on the other shore is the ultimate destination. Furthermore, although abiding in nirvana may be called ultimate, it is still not the foremost state;
for one must necessarily neither abide in nirvana nor abide in saṃsāra, but rather go back and forth to deliver sentient beings.
To dwell in non-dwelling is alone called the foremost. This is because it is the Great Nirvana of the place of non-abiding.
As the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "When a Bodhisattva dwells in this practice, they do not abandon the great vows of a Bodhisattva;
they do not dwell on this shore of saṃsāra, nor do they dwell on that shore of nirvāṇa, nor do they dwell in the middle stream of afflictions, yet they are able to ferry beings across."
The Bodhisattva goes from this shore to the other shore, the place free from sorrow and affliction, yet returns again and again without rest;
this is precisely the meaning of the first *pāramitā* in this sutra. It is called the "Venerable Practice" because such a practice is worthy of honor and respect.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is called the "Difficult-to-Attain Practice," as it is [unattainable] by those in the world...
"Venerable objects are difficult to obtain. Zhengmo says: "This is the wisdom of the ultimate other shore. Guanding says:
"This is precisely the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), for the *Avataṃsaka* states that this bodhisattva does not regress from the Mahāyāna aspiration.
I [Yuyi] say: "The various manifestations before one are all the first *pāramitā*; it is through this that the bodhisattva..."
This is the result of being guided by vows and practice. Regarding the nine practices of wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-caryā*):
when such practices are perfectly integrated and able to fulfill the norms of all Buddhas of the ten directions, they are called the practice of wholesome dharmas.
Building upon the various sublime practices mentioned above, when these are all unified within a single practice, it is called "pure" (*chun*);

yet, when a single practice fully encompasses these various sublime practices, it is called "mixed" (*za*). Because such purity and mixture are unimpeded, it is termed "perfectly interfused" (*yuanrong*).

Master Qingliang said: "The myriad practices bloom in profusion; this is like flowers blooming upon brocade. This refers precisely to this. Relying on these sublime practices, one traverses the ten [stages]...
Furthermore, by assisting the Buddhas in turning the wheel of Dharma and transforming sentient beings, it is said that one can "accomplish the norms of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
To conclude with the title "Practitioner of Wholesome Dharmas" means that every word and every action returns to the ultimate good;
as these are all the Buddha-dharma, they may be called a "track" (*vartman*) and may serve as a "standard" (*pramāṇa*). As the *Avataṃsaka* states: "This bodhisattva is able to purify himself..."
"Purity" refers to being able to universally benefit all sentient beings through the skillful means of non-attachment;
this is what is meant. Zhengmo (Zheng-mo) says: "This is the wisdom that gives rise to understanding in accordance with the rules. Guanding says: "This is the power of strength (*bala*).

His own commentary states: "It is fully endowed with three powers, namely: the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*), the power of analytical investigation (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*), and the power of transformation (*nirmāṇa-bala*); each has its respective textual authority."

The proofs are omitted for fear of prolixity. I, a fool, consider that the ability to accomplish wholesome dharmas is precisely due to the power of the practice of respect shown by those in superior positions. These are the ten practices of reality.
Each and every one is pure, untainted, the single true, unconditioned nature that is inherently so; therefore, they are called "true and real practices.
The two characters "each and every one" (一一) encompass the preceding nine practices, referring to the aforementioned wholesome dharmas as well as the previous eight.
Although great functions arise in profusion, it remains eternally as-it-is (*tathatā*); therefore, it is called "pure. That which is pure is precisely the meaning of *tathatā* being unmoving.
Being unmoving in *tathatā*, one is free from the marks of thought; being free from the marks of thought, one is equal to the realm of empty space.
This is the Tathāgata’s impartial *dharmakāya*; therefore, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). For, by giving rise to a [discursive] mind...
The slightest movement of thought deviates from the essence of the Dharma and constitutes outflow (āsrava). The two phrases regarding "one reality" explain the meaning of "all are.
When it says that all are pure and without outflow, it is because the nature of the one true unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is inherently so.
When it says "the one true unconditioned," etc., it means that the Bodhisattva should manifest within quiescence.
Prior to this, all was empty and non-arising; the One True alone was revealed, and one immediately realized the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). How could this not be pure?

Although later one attains two kinds of excellence and manifests three wondrous functions, having passed through the stages to reach this point, all are fundamentally inconsistent with the nature [of reality].
How could there be any further outflows (*āsrava*)? If that is so, why was it not explained before? It is because only when the practice of phenomena reaches this point does one dare to speak.
Because it is fixed. Based on this, every practice is true and every dharma is real. For this reason, it is called "true and real practice. *Zhengmo* says:
"This is the wisdom that integrates conditions to enter reality. *Guanding* says: "This is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."

Furthermore, I shall explain this by means of my own threefold wisdom: the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*), the wisdom of maturing sentient beings (*sattvaparipācana-jñāna*), and the wisdom of enjoying the dharma-bliss (*dharmasambhogajñāna*).

There are textual proofs for each of these as well, which I have not recorded here. I, the fool, maintain that purity and the absence of outflows (*anāsrava*) are achieved precisely through the fundamental wisdom of perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna-mūla-jñāna*).

(The ten lines listed to the right should be correlated with the Ten Mysteries [Daśamithyā] to manifest their perfect subtlety. First, having become a child of the Buddha, one is fully endowed with the immeasurable...)

The wondrous virtue of the Tathāgata is like a single drop of water in the ocean, yet it possesses the flavor of all hundred rivers; this is the Gate of Simultaneous Endowment and Correspondence. Second, the benefits received by all sentient beings are each distinct, with their mutual concealment and manifestation being like a crescent moon in the autumn sky.

First, the simultaneous presence of darkness and light constitutes the gate of the coexistence of the hidden and the manifest. Second, self-awakening and awakening others proceed without conflict, like gold and its golden color, which are never separated; this is the gate of the mutual identity and sovereign freedom of all phenomena.

Third, reaching to the limits of the future, the three periods of time are equal, like a single night’s dream spanning a hundred years; this is the gate of the distinct formation of the ten ages through the separation of dharmas. Fourth, among various dharma-gates, there is no error, like a lapis lazuli jar containing many mustard seeds; this is the gate of the minute containment and establishment of one within another.

Fifth, the identical manifests the diverse, and the diverse manifests the identical, like a thousand lamps in a single room where each ray of light interpenetrates the others; this is the gate of the mutual containment of the one and the many without their losing their distinctness.

Seventh is the manifestation of objects and realms without mutual obstruction; like a one-foot mirror reflecting images from a thousand li away, this is the gate of the sovereign freedom of breadth and narrowness. Eighth is the manifestation of all varieties before one, wherein each and every thing is the foremost *pāramitā*;

like raising a fist or knitting the brows, everything encountered is the Way—this is the gate of manifesting the Dharma by relying on phenomena to generate understanding. Ninth is this perfect interfusion, which can establish the norms for the Buddhas of the ten directions;

like two mirrors facing each other, transmitting light and reflecting one another—this is the gate of the realm of Indra’s net. Eleventh, every single thing is pure and untainted; like the North Star around which all the stars revolve—this is the gate of the sovereign and its attendants being perfectly luminous and endowed with virtue. These are based on the teachings of the ancient masters.

Ten Similes. Comparing this with the scriptural text, I have briefly provided this synthesis; in reality, each and every practice contains all ten gates. Although the text does not explicitly reveal them, their meaning may be investigated and sought.

The Ten Practices are concluded. Regarding the Sixty Dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), [Master] Guanding said: "The *Avataṃsaka* clarifies that dedication is precisely the making of vows. This is because if there is practice without vows, the practice will surely be aimless; if there are vows without practice, the vows are merely empty constructs."

When practice and vows support one another, one finally reaches the ocean of the great *nirvāṇa* of all Buddhas. The *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Pulse) quotes Guifeng as saying: "Dedication does not exceed three points: namely, sentient beings, the Buddha-way, and *tathatā*.

Although the text of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is extremely vast and its meaning extensively encompasses these three points, the text of the present sūtra is concise, with each point having its own hidden or manifest aspects. For instance, when sentient beings are manifest, the other two are hidden; the same applies to the Buddha-way and *tathatā*. That which is manifest is explicitly developed, while that which is hidden is also contained within the intended meaning.
It is not that they are entirely non-existent. (10) First, dedication free from signs; second, indestructible dedication;
third, dedication equal to the Buddhas; fourth, dedication reaching all places; fifth, inexhaustible dedication; sixth, impartial dedication;
seventh, dedication through equal contemplation; eighth, dedication to suchness; ninth, unconditioned dedication; tenth, immeasurable dedication. First:

Ānanda, when these good sons have perfected their supernormal powers and completed the work of attaining Buddhahood, they shall become pure, clean, and true, remaining far removed from all lingering afflictions.
They shall then deliver sentient beings while eliminating the very notion of "delivering" them; turning their minds toward the unconditioned, they proceed upon the path to Nirvana.
This is called the Dedication of Saving and Protecting All Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings.

This "good man" refers to the practitioner who has successively cultivated the ten stages of practice. In the first stage, one accords with the ten directions; in the second, one universally benefits all.
Continuing thus up to the seventh stage, where the manifestation of sense-objects and realms no longer obstructs one another, the wondrous function reaches its ultimate limit;
hence it is said that "supernatural powers are perfected. In the eighth stage, one brings various practices to final consummation; in the ninth stage, one attains Buddhahood.
The rules and regulations are thus fully prepared; therefore, it is said that the work of attaining Buddhahood is complete.

Because the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) are pure and free from outflows (*anāsrava*), they are pristine, refined, and true. Being the single truth of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), their nature is inherently so; therefore, they remain far removed from all lingering afflictions.
This entirely builds upon the preceding ten practices to initiate the meaning of the "Initial Direction" (*prathama-abhimukha*). Since there are no lingering afflictions, one proceeds spontaneously.
To save sentient beings: one does not perceive any sentient beings who can be saved; therefore it is said, "One should save sentient beings while extinguishing the mark of saving.
Yet, since it is called "saving sentient beings," this is turning the mind toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because one does not dwell in the unconditioned.
Since it is called "extinguishing marks," this is heading toward the path of *nirvāṇa*, because one is able to reach *nirvāṇa*. This concludes the title: "Rescue and Protection."
Regarding the term "etcetera": as stated above, there are two meanings to "saving sentient beings" (*duō shēng*). First, saving them so they may be free from suffering;

this is the meaning of "rescue. Second, saving them so they may attain happiness; this is the meaning of "protection. What was previously described as "extinguishing the marks of saving" refers to the perspective of the *savior* (*néng dù*).

What is here described as "leaving behind the marks of sentient beings" refers to the perspective of the *saved* (*suǒ dù*). This is because the relationship between subject and object (*néng-suǒ duìdài*) exists.

That which can characterize must have that which is characterized. Now, because one does not perceive oneself as the subject who crosses over, one likewise does not perceive others as the objects to be crossed over.
Since both the internal and external are empty, one also does not perceive a dharma for delivering sentient beings within the middle. This is the quiescence of the essence of the three wheels;
it is the true elimination of marks and the true detachment from marks. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "One does not perceive the mark of sentient beings."
This continues up to "perception and vision are non-perverted," and so forth. If one synthesizes this through the three points:

in this stage, one is directly oriented toward the Buddha-way because *nirvāṇa* is itself the Buddha-way; yet it also concurrently involves orientation toward the other two, because providing protection and succor is orientation toward sentient beings, and being free from signs is orientation toward *tathatā*. Second is the "Non-Destructive Dedication."
To destroy that which is destructible and to remain far removed from all forms of detachment is called the "Non-Destructive Dedication.

"Destruction" refers to the eradication of higher stages, while "that which is destructible" refers to the transcendence of characteristics in higher stages; this signifies the meaning of relying upon the higher stages to give rise to the present stage.
Since it is said that one destroys that which is destructible, the three spheres (trimaṇḍala) are empty in essence, and one is detached from everything.
It is named "Detachment from All" (*sarva-viveka*). If one merely maintains this detachment from all, there is still destruction; therefore, one must likewise distance oneself from this as well.
That which is termed "Indestructible" (*akṣaya*) eliminates the marks of transcendence through the higher stage.

Thus, emptiness destroys existence, and in this stage, one distances oneself from all forms of detachment, whereby existence destroys emptiness. When both emptiness and existence are destroyed, the essence merges with the True.
As for "Suchness" (*tathatā*): because Suchness is indestructible, this stage clarifies that it is a dedication toward Suchness; yet it also encompasses two aspects.

By destroying that which is destructible, the intention lies in dedicating [merit] toward the Buddha-way while remaining far removed from all forms of detachment. Furthermore, one again dedicates [the merit] to sentient beings. [Question:

The Middle Way of pure truth in the initial stage of faith—how does this differ from the present? [Answer: That refers to total interpenetration (*yuanrong*), whereas this refers to sequential progression (*xingbu*). Whenever there are similarities between preceding and succeeding stages, they should all be understood according to this principle.
[One] knows). The third is the dedication equal to all Buddhas.
Original enlightenment (*honkaku*) is profoundly still, its awakening equal to the awakening of the Buddhas; this is called the "dedication equal to all Buddhas.

In this stage, the essence is in union with True Suchness (*tathatā*). Because within this essential state there is complete illumination, it is designated by the term "original enlightenment" (*honkaku*). As for the essence...
Since it is neither destroyed nor altered, its illumination is clear and pure; therefore, it is described as "serene" (*zhanran*).
Because it is serene, there is no phenomenon that is not fully known and no principle that is not clearly understood; thus it is said that "awakening is equal to the awakening of the Buddhas.

The phrase "equaling all Buddhas" means that since the function of awakening is already equal, all aspects of compassion, wisdom, vows, and practice are likewise equal in every respect. This stage clarifies this point.
Dedicating [merit] toward the Buddha-way. If one considers the equality of compassion, wisdom, vows, and practice, it also encompasses the other two [perfections].
The fourth is the dedication reaching all places (*sarvatraga-pariṇāmanā*).
When the essence of reality is clearly manifested such that the ground is like the ground of a Buddha, it is called the dedication reaching all places.

Second, it turns toward the essence that accords with *tathatā*; having already attained the immutable essence, it is therefore called "refined and true" (*jingzhen*). Third, it turns toward the profound stillness of original enlightenment (*benjue*);

further attaining its function that accords with conditions, it is therefore called "manifesting illumination" (*faming*). These two [phrases] together take the preceding two stages as the causes for their respective positions.
Since it is said that one has already achieved refined truth and manifest illumination, one is naturally able to harmonize principle with phenomena through this...

When principle is harmonized with phenomena, then phenomena are harmonized with principle. Not only is awakening equal to the awakening of a Buddha, but the stages (*bhūmi*) are likewise equal to the stages of a Buddha.

When the stages are equal to the stages of a Buddha, one does not depart from one's original location yet reaches everywhere throughout the ten directions; therefore, it is called "reaching all places.
According to the *Avataṃsaka*, the Bodhisattvas at this stage extensively cultivate offerings and reach the presence of all Buddhas. Furthermore,
It is said that the three karmas universally enter all worlds to perform the Buddha-work.

Since it is stated that one extensively cultivates offerings and reaches the presence of all Buddhas, this must involve seeking what the Buddhas have realized; thus, there are two simultaneous meanings: first, dedication toward True Suchness (*tathatā*), and second, dedication toward the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, since it is said that one universally enters the worlds to perform the Buddha-work, this must necessarily be for the benefit of others.
To delight sentient beings is to dedicate [merit] to them.
The fifth inexhaustible dedication is called the dedication of the treasury of inexhaustible merit, wherein worlds and Tathāgatas interpenetrate one another without obstruction.

Third, when the three stages of enlightenment are equal to the Buddha’s enlightenment, one manifests the body without obstruction. Fourth, when the four stages of the grounds are like the Buddha-ground, one manifests the realm without obstruction.

When manifesting the body without obstruction, one is able to penetrate into the realms and sense-objects; when manifesting the realm without obstruction, one is able to penetrate into the pores of the body.
Therefore, it is said that worlds and Tathāgatas mutually penetrate one another, as it is said regarding "within a single pore."
The tip [of a single hair] manifests the realm of the Treasure King; seated within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Wheel of Dharma.

The one and the many are mutually inclusive, like a thousand lamps arranged within a single room. Broadness and narrowness are sovereign, like a cubit-long mirror reflecting a thousand li. Thus it is said that one attains non-obstruction.
Each and every Buddha-body and each and every world are all able to bring sentient beings to fulfillment and adornment.
Because it is one's own virtue, it is thus named the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* states:
"When abiding in this dedication, one attains ten inexhaustible treasuries: first, seeing the Buddha; second, entering the Dharma; third, recollecting and upholding; fourth, definitive wisdom."
Fifth, the comprehension of meanings and intentions; sixth, boundless realization; seventh, merit; eighth, courageous wisdom-awakening; ninth, eloquence;
tenth, the powers and fearlessnesses. Because these and others are all inexhaustible, if one were to synthesize them across the three locations:
To realize principle by means of this is dedication to True Suchness (*tathatā*). To advance toward the fruit by means of this is dedication to the Buddha-way.
To transform others by means of this is dedication to sentient beings. These are the six equal dedications.
Within the same Buddha-ground, each stage produces its own cause of purification; by relying on these causes, one manifests and takes up the path to nirvana.
This is called the dedication of roots of goodness that accords with equality.
Building upon the previous section, since the body relies upon the *dhātu*, it is said that "one abides in the same stage as the Buddha.
Because one accomplishes a treasury of inexhaustible merit, it is said that "within each stage, the causes for purity arise. Regarding the term "causes for purity":
because the aforementioned inexhaustible merit consists purely of the causes for Buddhahood and is not mixed with other vehicles, this entirely refers back to the preceding stages.
Relying on those pure causes, they are progressively expanded and extended; this is termed "manifestation. Because of this expansion, one proceeds directly toward the fruit of Buddhahood;

therefore, it is called "taking the path to nirvāṇa. As for the concluding designation "roots of goodness that accord with equality," it is because by allowing them to expand, extend, and manifest, one does not contravene the cause of Buddhahood;
thus, it is called "accordance. Furthermore, there is no discrepancy with the causes of all Buddhas.

Second, it is called "equanimity" because the inexhaustible merits of the Buddha-fruit all arise from this. It is called "wholesome root" because this stage clarifies the dedication toward the Buddha-way.

If one expands upon and elaborates its significance, it encompasses both self-benefit and benefit for others, as well as the other two [aspects], since self-benefit is directed toward True Suchness (*tathatā*) and benefiting others is directed toward sentient beings. In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is named "Firm."
Regarding the firming of the roots of goodness: it is precisely by relying on and cultivating the causal conditions that one becomes irreversible. As a verse in that sutra says:
"Thus dedicating all roots of goodness, they are equal, firm, and without regression;
realized by all Buddhas, they are entirely encompassed without exception. This is the seventh dedication, the Dedication through Sevenfold Contemplation.

Once the true roots have been established, all sentient beings of the ten directions are my own fundamental nature. When this nature is perfectly realized and accomplished, one does not lose sight of sentient beings;
this is called the dedication of merit through the contemplation that accords with the equal observation of all sentient beings.
Since the superior stage is able to accord with the roots of goodness that are equal, these true roots are thereby established.

From this, great compassion arises once more, whereby one regards all sentient beings with equanimity; thus it is said that "the sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own original nature," because the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is identical to one's own Buddha-nature. This is precisely what is called "compassion of identical substance."

"Nature is perfectly accomplished; one does not abandon sentient beings" means that since all sentient beings are the very nature of oneself, and one's own nature is perfectly accomplished, how could one possibly neglect those sentient beings and fail to deliver them? Therefore, one must not abandon them.
This concludes the section titled "Equally Contemplating All Sentient Beings," which begins by stating that the sentient beings of the ten directions are all oneself.
The fundamental nature is precisely equal contemplation. The concluding statement that "sentient beings are not lost" refers to compliance.
This stage clarifies dedication toward sentient beings; if one causes sentient beings to return to their fundamental nature, this is dedication toward True Suchness (tathatā).
If one causes all sentient beings to equally realize bodhi, this is precisely dedication toward the Buddha-way. As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says:

"The Bodhisattva universally makes equal vows; according to the meritorious deeds they have accumulated, may all throughout the three realms attain peace and stability, and may all fully achieve the unsurpassed fruit. This is the eighth, dedication through true suchness (*tathatā*).
That is to say, all dharmas are free from all marks; being neither attached to "being" nor to "leaving," this is called the dedication of the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Since it was stated above that one does not lose sight of sentient beings, one establishes the gate of transformative manifestation and does not abandon a single dharma; therefore, it is said:
It is precisely all dharmas. Although it is said to be "precisely all dharmas," one does not abide in those dharmas;
therefore, it is said to be "detached from all marks. This is because they are all one's own original nature. This refers back to what was stated regarding the higher stages.

Reaching this point, "precisely at the time of detachment, there is immediacy (ji)," and "precisely at the time of immediacy, there is detachment. Therefore, it is said that there is no attachment to either "immediacy" or "detachment. As it is said:

Detached from both being and non-being, it is both identical to and not identical with [the ultimate]. The path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity ceases. It is utterly severed from all delusions and eternally possesses no distinct essence;
therefore, it is summarized as the "characteristic of True Suchness" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*). This stage clarifies that this is the dedication toward True Suchness.
According to the title of this section, it is also a dedication toward the Buddha-way by means of the characteristic of True Suchness. If one follows the *Avataṃsaka*...
Veneration. This also includes the dedication for the sake of sentient beings. As a verse in that sutra says:
"All sentient beings and all phenomena abide therein, yet have no place of abiding. True Suchness is present everywhere; the non-apprehension of self-nature is the true nature.
By means of this mind, the Bodhisattva dedicates so that all sentient beings may be free from attachment.
The ninth is the unconditioned dedication (*asaṃbaddha-pariṇāmanā*).
Truly attaining that which is such as the ten directions without obstruction is called the "unconditioned liberation dedication" (*asaṃbaddha-vimukti-pariṇāmanā*).

Regarding the statement that the two [aspects] of the higher stages are without attachment and are named the "characteristic of true suchness" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), this refers to the practice of non-attachment, just as in that [preceding case].
Regarding the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness): this stage inherits the meaning from the preceding section, hence it is said that one "truly attains what is such.

This means that because one's practice is purely true, one has already attained that which is such as *tathatā*. Now, while the essence of *tathatā* pervades the ten directions without obstruction, since one's practice has already become that which is such as *tathatā*, it naturally corresponds to that which is capable of being such; therefore, it is also...
It is said that the ten directions are unobstructed. Because they are unobstructed, one cannot be bound; thus it is called "unbound.
Because one is unbound, one enters and exits with mastery; thus it is called "liberation. Zhengmo (Correct Pulse) says: "Only at the higher stages does one attain liberation from bondage."
In this stage, one attains mastery and liberation. The deluded person says: "In the higher stages, it is simply that I do not cling to them;
in this stage, however, it is that they do not bind me. It is precisely because I do not cling to them that they are unable to bind me.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* is titled "The Dedication of the Mind of Liberation, Unattached and Unbound. If one correlates this with the three points:

liberation means that Bodhi can be realized, which is the dedication toward the Buddha-way; being unbound means that gathering in sentient beings is without hindrance, which is the dedication toward sentient beings;
and being unattached means that not a single thought arises, which is the dedication toward True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The tenth is the Infinite Dedication.
When the nature-virtues are perfectly accomplished and the measure of the dharma-realm ceases, it is called the Infinite Dedication of the Dharma-realm.
This refers to the liberation from bondage in the higher stages, which is the perfect accomplishment of the inherent virtues and functions. Therefore, this is the support.

One cites this intention as the cause for its proper station. However, while it was previously stated that the ten directions are unimpeded, there still remained a delimited measure of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Now, however, the inherent virtues are perfectly fulfilled and the dependent origination is inexhaustible; even those measures of the ten directions no longer exist.
Therefore, it is said that "the measure of the dharma-realm is extinguished. When it says "dharma-realm," it refers specifically to the dharma-realm of the ten directions, and not [to anything else].
This refers to the ten dharma realms. Because these immeasurable virtues and functions are dedicated toward three destinations, they are designated by the name "immeasurable dharma realm.
The *Avataṃsaka* states: "O Son of the Buddha, one who skillfully studies this dedication shall fully accomplish immeasurable practices and vows;
grasping the entire dharma realm without exception, one is thus able to achieve the power of the Sugata. Now, since it is said...
To embrace the *dharmadhātu* is to dedicate [merit] toward sentient beings. Since it is said that one can thus become a Sugata, this is dedication toward the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, the character "power" (*bala*) also encompasses dedication toward *tathatā*; that is to say, the Sugata takes the self-nature of *tathatā* as the dependent origination of power.
When combined with the preceding text on the ten dedications, these follow one another in sequence, each depending on the former to give rise to the latter.

Furthermore, I do not follow the ancient masters in establishing ten intermediate stages (*daśāntara*) nor in forcibly correlating them with the ten mysteries (*daśa-gūḍha*). I trust that those with discerning eyes will distinguish this for themselves.
This concludes the summary of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Seventy-fourth, the stage of application (*prayoga*). (According to scriptures such as the *Ratnakūṭa-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, these stages are not listed separately; however, according to treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the preceding stage is the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*), the subsequent stage is the stage of penetration (*prativedha*), and this is the stage of application.)

Although these are now listed separately, they differ vastly in depth from the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only). This is because the sutra specifically designates them as "wondrous, perfect preparatory practices" (*prayoga*). To clarify this through analogy:

suppose an ordinary person and the Great King of his own country both simultaneously resolve to ascend Mount Tai, and together prepare their provisions and set out on an auspicious day. Yet, the provisions prepared by the ordinary person amount to no more than a few pieces of gold, whereas those of the King involve tens of millions.

When it comes to their departure, the ordinary person has no more than one steed or two horses, while the King departs with thousands of camels and tens of thousands of horses. Even the ordinary person’s single steed or two horses still encounter many obstructions, whereas the King’s thousands of camels and tens of thousands of horses clear the mountains and bridge the waters according to schedule.

One must surely ascend. Therefore, the provisions previously mentioned have already transcended the gradual teachings; how could these preparatory practices (prayoga) again resemble those provisional schools that explain the Dharma through metaphors? The relative depth and shallowness are self-evident. Thus, one knows that although the previous discourse was freely expounded as wondrous and perfect, [it remains distinct from this].

Ultimately, these are the provisions (*sambhāra*). This wondrous perfection is termed the "preparatory application" (*prayoga*), which also embodies the principle of sequential arrangement within the context of mutual interpenetration. (2) First, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one;
second, the formal explanation of the four preparatory applications. Regarding the first:
Ānanda, these good sons have fully perfected the forty-one pure minds. Next, they accomplish the four kinds of wondrous and perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
Following these three gradual stages, they are called "good sons" because they do not dwell in their wondrous realization and possess a mind directed toward further advancement. Furthermore—
Because it is the spirit of a great man (*puruṣa*), although one practices with fervent intensity, one does not abide in signs; therefore, it is called "pure.
Beginning from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) and ending with the tenth stage of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), these are thus called the "forty-one minds.

Since each position has been fully traversed, the term "exhaustive" is employed; this concludes the preceding section. Next, regarding "accomplishment": it is accomplished immediately thereafter. As for the "four kinds," they are as follows:

Although it is said that one applies effort and practice, this still does not depart from the wondrous, pervasive, and subtle nature; therefore, it is designated as "wondrous, pervasive, and subtle" (*miaoyuan*).

Furthermore, these two characters, "wondrous" (*miao*) and "pervasive" (*yuan*), contain two levels of discernment: first, they distinguish [this path] from the coarseness of the Hīnayāna, which is not "wondrous";
second, they distinguish it from the partiality of the provisional teachings, which are not "pervasive. As for the reason why it is able to perform such discernment, it is also...
Because this does not depart from the wondrous nature of perfect penetration, it arises subsequent to that. Second, the explicit explanation of the four stages of application (*prayoga*).

First, the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*); second, the stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*); third, the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*); fourth, the stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). First [the stage of Heat]:
One immediately takes the Buddha’s awakening as one’s own mind. Whether it has emerged or not yet emerged, it is like drilling wood for fire when the wood is about to ignite;
this is called the Stage of Warmth (*uṣmagata*).
This stage follows upon the meaning of the previous nine directions. It is said that within these nine directions there is neither bondage nor liberation, because of the mind—its causal nature.

The functioning of virtue has reached its ultimate limit; once it has reached its limit, there is nothing further to be employed. Therefore, in this stage, one takes the awakening of the Buddha as one's own mind.
This means that the essence—which corresponds to the marks and activities of the Buddha’s fruition—is taken as the mind that applies effort and practice.
However, because the causal mind has not yet perished though it seeks to perish, and the fruition-function has not yet manifested though it seeks to manifest, it is said: "If it emerges..."
It has not yet emerged. This is like the following analogy for clarifying the characteristics of having emerged and not yet emerged. "One who drills for fire" refers to drilling wood to seek fire;
it is a metaphor for the practitioner personally investigating the causal mind in order to seek the function of the resultant awakening.

"Wishing to ignite the wood" refers to the appearance of the sign of warmth; it is a metaphor for the sought-after function of the result that is about to transcend the causal mind, though it has not yet done so.
Yes. Its characteristics have already been briefly demonstrated. For this reason, it is called the Stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*).

[In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is stated that at this stage one enters the Samādhi of Attaining Clarity (*vidarśanā-lābha-samādhi*) and gives rise to inferior vitarka and vicāra, first observing that the four dharmas—the name, the object, the self-nature, and the distinction—are all empty; here, however, we simply observe the emptiness of the causal mind through the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*). Second is the Stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*).

Furthermore, one uses one's own mind to traverse the path realized by the Buddhas. Whether relying on something or not relying on anything, it is like ascending a high mountain where the body enters empty space;
yet, if there is even a slight obstruction below, this is called the "Stage of the Summit" (mūrdhan-bhūmi).

This stage follows upon the meaning of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). It is said that within the ten dedications, the measure of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) ceases and the ten directions are entirely realized as one's own mind.
Therefore, in this stage, one takes one's own mind as the ground traversed by the Buddha; that is to say, one contemplates the essence of one's own mind.
This is precisely the realm of the Buddhas. It directly relies upon the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), which is that which all Buddhas have trodden.
However, because the characteristics of the mind have not yet been entirely forgotten, one cannot truly coincide with the Buddha-realm. Therefore, it is said: "If one relies, it is not relying.

This illustrates the characteristic of "if one relies, it is not relying," using the metaphor of ascending and descending. The phrase "like ascending a high mountain, the body enters empty space" is a metaphor for this.

When the essence [of the mind] personally accords with the mind itself, it is the realm of the Buddha; it personally relies upon the *dharmatā*. This corresponds to what was said above regarding "relying" (*yi*).

However, there remains a subtle obstruction below; this is a metaphor for the mental characteristics not yet being entirely forgotten, such that one cannot truly accord with the Buddha-realm by personally relying upon the *dharmatā*.

This corresponds to what was said above regarding "not relying" (*fei yi*). For this reason, it is called the Stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan-bhūmi*). (In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this stage is described as entering the *vṛddha-vidyā-samādhi*.)

One gives rise to superior investigation and analysis, repeatedly contemplating that the four dharmas—name and so forth—are all transformations of consciousness-only. Now, by means of the power of wisdom gradually increased through preparatory application (*prayoga*), one contemplates one's own mind as being, in its essence, the realm of the Buddha. Question: Within the three stages of orientation (*tri-śraddhā-prasthāna*), original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) is profound and still.

Their awakening is equal to the Buddha’s awakening. Among the four stages of progress (*catur-yoni*), their refined and true illumination is like the stage of the Buddhas. In meaning, this is roughly similar to the two stages of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit). How are their relative shallowness and depth to be distinguished? Answer: The three stages of progress merely involve the manifestation of illumination within the essence itself.

Turning toward the four directions, one then integrates phenomena through principle; thus it is called "equality" (qi) and "suchness" (ru). Although these appear to possess two distinct characteristics, when one reaches this state, words become the realization of words, essential for dissolving the duality of separate entities. The progression from the former to the latter, from the shallow to the profound, is not difficult to discern.
The third stage is the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).

Here, the mind and the Buddha are identical, and one skillfully attains the Middle Way. Just as when enduring a person, one neither harbors resentment nor gives rise to [hostility], it is called the "ground of patience.

In the stage of warmth (*uṣmagata*), one takes the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind, yet is not yet fully able to do so. In the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), one takes one's own mind as the Buddha.
[The practitioner] has not yet [attained mastery of] the objective realm. Therefore, in this stage, the mind and the Buddha are identical, and one skillfully attains the Middle Way.

To say that "the mind and the Buddha are identical" means that the Buddha’s awakening merges into identity with the causal mind, and the causal mind merges into identity with the Buddha’s objective realm.
Although the mind and the Buddha remain distinct, cause and effect are fused and identical. Because cause and effect are fused and identical, neither is abandoned; one constantly [abides in...]
Within the state of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*), one perceives the Buddha’s enlightened activities and thoroughly penetrates one's own mind within the sphere of action of all Buddhas;
hence it is said that one has "well attained the Middle Way. Although it is called "well attained," it is merely a clear realization within the mind that cannot be fully expressed in words.

Therefore it is said: "one who endures the affairs of others. One who endures the affairs of others is one who is well able to endure such matters; this is a metaphor for a person who has skillfully attained the Middle Way.
"Neither harboring [resentment] nor expressing it" means that although they wish to appeal their grievances to others, they are unable to open their mouths.
This is an analogy for one who has well attained the Middle Way. Within the mind, there is clear understanding, and one also wishes to explain this to others;

yet, because the mind and the Buddha are identical, there is in reality neither a grasper nor a grasped, and thus it cannot be articulated. For this reason, it is called the Stage of Patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*).

(In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, this stage is said to enter the "seal-determining" concentration [*mudrā-niyama-samādhi*] and give rise to the "inferior suchness-contemplation" [*tathatā-yathābhūta-parīkṣā*], whereby the four dharmas are sealed as empty. Now, however, it is simply by means of the power of the wisdom of decisive application that one seals the preceding characteristics of the mind and the Buddha.)
This is simply the meaning. Fourth is the Stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

When the calculations of quantity are extinguished and one awakens to the Middle Way amidst delusion, there is nothing to which the two [extremes] refer; this is named the Stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma.

The first three stages involve shifting and changing from stage to stage, which is termed "worldly enumeration" (*saṃkhyā*). The distinction between the center and the periphery is termed "interval measurement" (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, in this stage, both number and measure are extinguished; because the stage of application (*prayoga*) is fulfilled, there is nothing further to shift or change, and neither center nor periphery is established.

Because no interval or measure can be apprehended; it is precisely because there is nothing that can undergo transition or change, and no interval or measure can be apprehended, that it is called the Middle Way between delusion and awakening.
"The two have no referent" means that regarding the Middle Way between delusion and awakening, this refers to the two stages of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Peak).
At the stage of Heat, one takes the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind; at the stage of Peak, one takes one's own mind as the Buddha’s realm. Thus, they are deluded regarding the Middle Way.

Because each falls into one extreme, upon reaching the stage of *kṣānti* (patience), one awakens to the Middle Way; for it is clearly stated in the sūtras that one has "skillfully attained the Middle Way.
Regarding the second point, "having nothing to refer to": delusion and awakening are both forgotten, and neither center nor periphery is established.

Because delusion and awakening are both forgotten, one transcends the temporal cycles of *parinirmita-vaśavartin*. Because neither center nor periphery is established, one severs the duality of self and other.
Regarding the measure of the interval: because it is so brief, it is called the "Supreme Worldly Stage" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
To say "Supreme Worldly" means that this person is called the foremost among those in the world; the intent is to show that upon entering this stage, one becomes a world-transcender.

(In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is stated that at this stage one enters the *ānantarya-samādhi* and gives rise to the superior *yathābhūta-pratyavekṣā*, sealing the emptiness of the two graspings. Now, however, we speak only of the power of wisdom achieved through application, which is unattached to the three aforementioned [aspects]. Question: Since these four subsequent applications (*prayoga*) are not identical...)

Regarding the attachment and citation of the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) teachings: why is this done? Answer: Since the terminology is identical to that [of the Consciousness-Only school], if they were not compared side-by-side, there would likely be confusion. Therefore, those explanations are cited so that the provisional and the real, the partial and the perfect, may be distinguished as clearly as a melon from a bean.

As for the *Ratnavyūha* and other sutras frequently not listing these four stages: it is because these four stages lie between the two pillars of the "stages of approach" (*prayoga*) and the "stages of realization" (*bhūmi*).

They should correspond to the mind emerging from the tenth stage of approach and the mind entering the first stage of realization; when combined with what precedes and follows, there are none that do not accord.
Those who are capable [of this]—the subsequent ones on the path of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi)—should follow this example.

This concludes the preceding four stages of preparatory application (*prayoga*). Regarding the eighty stages (*bhūmi*), there are three meanings: First, the meaning of "position" (*sthāna*): from the first to the tenth, the positions differ. It is like the earth itself, which is essentially one, yet its elevations and depressions are unequal.

Second, the meaning of "solidity" (*dṛḍha*): each stage takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its essence; it is immovable and indestructible. It is like the earth supporting Mount Hua and Mount Yue, and the rivers and seas; it does not weigh them down nor does it leak them away. Third, the meaning of "growth and development": because each stage is able to bring forth and develop the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*).

Regarding the merit: just as the earth is able to produce and grow all things. Question: Since the stage of application (*prayoga*) has already been designated by the name "earth," how does this differ from it? Answer: The former position is established in terms of the gradual deepening of the stages of practice; this position is established in terms of the gradual excellence of the stages of fruition (*phala*).

The former solidity is established in terms of the firmness of the power of practice; this solidity is established in terms of the true and eternal nature of the fruit-body. The former growth is established in terms of the functional efficacy of the stage of practice; this growth is established in terms of the merits of the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*). Although each possesses these three meanings, they are distinct.

Yet, these stages differ in their depth and excellence. To provide a further analogy for all these preceding and succeeding positions taken together: it is like a person wishing to enter the great ocean to gather various treasures. First, they must study the laws of the water and master the skills of the oars and rudders; this refers to the three *śrāmaṇeras* (gradual approaches).

Once the laws of the water are refined and the skills of the oars and rudders are mastered, this refers to *śuṣka-vipaśyanā* (dry wisdom). The ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are like choosing an auspicious day to set out on the journey. The stages of abiding, practice, and orientation (*daśa-vihāra*, *daśa-caryā*, *daśa-pratipatti*) are like preparing the necessary provisions.

The four stages of application (*catur-prayoga*) are like gradually entering the great ocean from shallow to deep. The ten stages of the bodhisattva (*daśa-bhūmi*) are like gradually traversing the sites of treasure, moving from inferior toward superior. The stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) is like having just arrived at the location of the most excellent and precious jewels. The stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*suviśuddha-bodhi*) is like having already obtained the various treasures and returning from the sea. Throughout...

To relieve distress and deficiency: the sixty stages of the sages correspond clearly to both the Dharma and its metaphors. Now, the ten bhūmis are clarified: first, the Stage of Joy; second, the Stage Free from Defilement.
3. The Ground of Radiant Light; 4. The Ground of Blazing Wisdom; 5. The Ground Difficult to Conquer; 6. The Ground of Manifestation; 7.
The Ground of Far-Reaching Progress; 8. The Ground of Immovability; 9. The Ground of Excellent Intelligence; 10. The Ground of the Dharma Cloud. First.

Ānanda, these sons of good family have attained thorough penetration regarding great bodhi; their awakening penetrates that of the Tathāgatas, exhausting the realm of the Buddhas—this is called the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).

In this stage, one is deluded regarding awakening and the Middle Way; both are without objective referents. This stage is, in its very nature, free from thought, and True Suchness (tathatā) manifests before one.
Therefore, it is said that "one has successfully attained thorough penetration into Great Bodhi," because True Suchness is the very essence of Bodhi.

Regarding what is called "Great Bodhi" (Mahābodhi): among the five types of bodhi—(1) the bodhi of generating the aspiration (*cittotpāda-bodhi*), corresponding to the stage of the ten faiths; (2) the bodhi of subduing the mind (*vinaya-citta-bodhi*), corresponding to the stage of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śukla*);

(3) the bodhi of clarifying the mind (*vidyā-citta-bodhi*), corresponding to the first seven stages (*sapta-bhūmi*); (4) the bodhi of emerging and reaching (*niṣkrama-prāpti-bodhi*), corresponding to the final three stages; and (5) the unsurpassed bodhi (*anuttara-bodhi*), corresponding to the fruit of Buddhahood—it must be this unsurpassed bodhi.

However, this is merely a thorough penetration (*prativedha*) and not yet actual realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). According to the treatise, it is only upon actual realization that one enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), at which point one has for the first time attained it.
"Clarifying the mind" refers to *bodhi*. As soon as one attains the *bodhi* of clarifying the mind, one is immediately able to penetrate the unsurpassed *bodhi*.
It is like how, through the light of a single crack, one can comprehend the myriad phenomena; therefore, it is called "skillfully attaining.
The two phrases beginning with "Awakening penetrates" explain the meaning of the preceding two phrases, stating that one has skillfully attained penetration into Great *Bodhi*.
This is because the wisdom that is capable of awakening reaches out to the wisdom of the Tathāgata from afar, and the principle that is awakened to encompasses the entire realm of all Buddhas.
Regarding the designation of this stage as the "Joyful Ground" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the various interpretations in the sutras and śāstras are so diverse that it is difficult to record them all here.
For now, I follow the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, which states: "That which was previously unattained is now finally attained, just as one had wished."
All are fully accomplished, giving rise to supreme joy and bliss; therefore, that sutra names this stage "The Ground of Supreme Joy.
Second is the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*):
when distinct natures enter into sameness and even those common natures are extinguished, it is named the Ground of Freedom from Defilement.

Having attained the superior penetration of the Buddha-realm, one no longer possesses the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) belonging to the nine realms; this is termed "the different nature entering the same.

At this stage, since the distinction between the ordinary being and the Buddha is confronted, the nature of the ordinary being does not exist. If the nature of the ordinary being is absent, how could the Buddha-realm persist?

Therefore, even the "same nature" is extinguished. This is designated as the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*). In various sūtras and śāstras, this is generally explained in terms of being free from the defilement of violating the precepts.

Now, it is only by realizing that the realm of the Buddha is empty that it is called "Free from Defilement" (vimalā). Because the realm of the Buddha still exists as an object of the mind, it remains a subtle mark of conceptualization;
thus, it is still a defilement within True Suchness (tathatā). This is the third stage, the Ground of Radiance (prabhākārī bhūmiḥ).
When purity reaches its ultimate limit, luminosity arises; this is called the Ground of Emitting Light (*Prabhākarī*).

The two characters "purity reaching its ultimate limit" (*jing ji*) refer back to what preceded; because even the commonality with the higher stages has been extinguished, one is free from the defilement of thoughts of [attaining] Buddhahood, which is termed "purity reaching its ultimate limit.
In this stage, True Suchness (*tathatā*) is pure and refined, and its spiritual discernment is unimpeded; therefore, it is said that "luminosity arises. It is like an ancient...
A mirror is polished again until its radiance shines forth. For this reason, it is called the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*). The scriptural text is most clear;
there is no need for further elaboration. Fourth is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
The ultimate perfection of clarity and the fulfillment of awakening is named the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
The two characters "ultimate clarity" (*ming ji*) carry over from the preceding [ground]. Because the wisdom of the principle of self-awakening is perfected, it is called "ultimate clarity.

In this stage, relying upon the wisdom of the principle of self-awakening, one gives rise to the flames of the True Dharma and generates the wisdom of skillful means, thereby incinerating the afflictions of sentient beings.

Because one accomplishes the merit of benefiting others, it is called "Fulfillment of Enlightenment" (*bodhiparipūri*). For example, just as a flame arises upon a flame, it is named "Blazing Wisdom" (*arciṣmatī*).
While many sūtras state that the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) burn the fuel of afflictions (*kleśa*), this is considered solely for one's own benefit.

Now, since the preceding stage of "Radiance" (*prabhākārī*) appears to be merely self-awakening, this is named "Blazing Wisdom"; it should be understood as encompassing both [self-benefit and benefit for others].

Awakening others. Furthermore, the sutras explicitly state that awakening is fulfilled. If it were merely for one's own benefit, how could it deserve such a title? For those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), there is no fixed rule;
each should be explained according to the manifest text, rather than being forced into conformity. Fifth is the Stage Difficult to Conquer (Duranjayā-bhūmi).
Because nothing—neither all that is identical nor all that is different—can surpass it, it is named the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).

On the third ground, one realizes the identity of the principle for oneself; on the fourth ground, one realizes the diversity of the dharmas for others. Therefore, it is said that "all identities and differences" [are surpassed].
In this state, both self-awakening and awakening others are not established; hence it is said that "it is that which cannot be reached.

This is because [in other states] there is difference and sameness, self and other, the subject who awakens and the object to be awakened—all of which strictly belong to the functioning of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Since neither of these two is established here, one transcends the conditioned; therefore, the functioning of the conditioned cannot reach it.
If one cannot even attain this, how much less so the superior? For this reason, it is called the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*).

Regarding the Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) perspective, on this ground the two wisdoms of the ultimate and the conventional possess mutually contradictory modes of activity (*ākāra*); yet they are brought into correspondence, which is extremely difficult to achieve.

Thus, while that [Vijñaptimātra] system and this Sūtra are roughly similar in their treatment of the ultimate and the conventional, there are differences. *Zhengmo* states: "That [system] represents the most supreme synthesis; this..."
Thus, they are far removed and difficult to equate; their essential purposes differ, being merely similar in appearance. As for the sixth stage, the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*):
because unconditioned *tathatā* (suchness) is by nature pure and clearly manifest, it is named the Ground of Presence.

The first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) is the realization of *tathatā* (suchness). However, this is still conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because it is manifested through the partial application of effortful activity.
Upon reaching the higher stages, the distinctions between sameness and difference cease; one transcends conditioned effort and accords with unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) *tathatā*.

This is merely intrinsically pure (*prakṛti-viśuddha*), yet it has not yet been fully revealed, because the shadows of habitual tendencies involving effort have not yet been exhausted. Upon reaching...
This means that conditioned cultivation has been exhausted and one is attached to the principle of the unconditioned; therefore, it is said that "the nature is pure and luminously revealed.

As for the designation of this stage as the "Manifesting Ground" (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*), it is named precisely because the unconditioned *tathatā* (suchness) is vividly manifest before one. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"In this stage, one realizes the undefiled and pure *tathatā*; that is to say, the original nature of this *tathatā* is undefiled, and it cannot [be defiled]."

It is said that purity occurs only subsequently; however, since it is stated that the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) is untainted, this is roughly analogous to the "innate purity" (*prakṛti-vyavadāna*) herein.

Since it is stated that [purity] is "realized," this is roughly analogous to the "manifestation" (*vibhūta*) herein. Nevertheless, because their natures and characteristics differ in their emphasis—whether partial or complete—the distinct purports of the Sūtras and Śāstras cannot be taken as entirely identical.
(7) The Seventh Ground, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*).
Reaching the limit of the reality-limit (*tathatā*) is called the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*).

Although the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) reality-limit of the higher stages is now clearly revealed, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) has not yet been able to travel far, because it is obstructed by the principle [of the lower stages].
Upon reaching this stage, one reaches the limit of the reality-limit; however, the reality-limit itself is without limit. Because...
All phenomena constitute the limit (*koṭi*). This is because the principle of being without boundaries completely pervades all things that possess boundaries;
this corresponds to the gate of the principle pervading phenomena within the framework of the gates of principle and phenomena.

Since the principle already pervades all phenomena, wisdom likewise pervades them accordingly, for the wisdom-principle is not distinct from it, just as a pearl is not distinct from its radiance. Therefore, one is able to exhaustively reach the limit of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus it is concluded.

It is called the Stage of Far-Reaching Travel because its name is derived from the far-reaching activity of wisdom. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "On this stage, one cultivates the ten skillful means of wisdom.
This means that although one cultivates the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one does not abandon sentient beings through compassion;
although one knows the equal Dharma of all Buddhas, one always delights in making offerings to the Buddhas; and although one enters the wisdom that contemplates emptiness..."
Entering the gates, they diligently accumulate merit and virtue. Though they remain far removed from the triple world, they adorn the triple world.

Even though they know that the three periods of time are but a single thought-moment, they deliver sentient beings according to their various conceptions of kalpas and their diverse mental inclinations and discriminations.
Based on this, they do not abandon sentient beings; they constantly delight in making offerings to the Buddhas, diligently accumulating merit and virtue, and adorning [the realm].
The three realms, up to the liberation of sentient beings according to their needs, represent the exhaustion of the limit of true suchness (*tathatā*) in this very sutra.
Regarding the eighth stage, the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*): the mind of true suchness is called the Immovable Ground.
The higher stage extends to the limit of the ultimate suchness (*tathatā*), not abandoning a single dharma. This stage does not abandon a single dharma until the very limit of suchness.
This is because phenomena that possess limitations are entirely identical to the principle (*li*) that is without limitation.

This corresponds to the "gate of phenomena pervading the principle" within the framework of the relationship between principle and phenomenon. Since phenomena have already pervaded the principle, the entirety of phenomena is the entirety of the principle. Therefore...
It is called the "one true suchness mind" (*eka-tathatā-citta*). According to this, although it pervades all phenomena, it does not depart from the limit of true suchness (*tathatā-koṭi*).
For this reason, it is named the "Immovable Ground" (*acalā-bhūmi*). The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "Entering into all phenomena, which are originally unarisen," etc.;
this is precisely the meaning of the one true suchness mind herein. Vajraghaṇṭa states: "The non-arising attained through the three gradual stages."

Regarding the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*): it is only upon reaching this stage that one attains direct realization and achieves perfect completion free from delusion. Ninth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
Part Two: First, the explicit clarification of the fundamental stage; second, the summary of cultivation. Regarding the first:
The stage where the function of True Suchness (tathatā) is activated is named the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (sādhumatī-bhūmi).
This is the interpretation of Zheng-mu (Zhengmai), which clarifies [the matter] as clearly as seeing the palm of one's hand; I shall now adopt it in its entirety. Zheng-mu states:

"The preceding stage is the attainment of the entire substance of True Suchness; this stage is the activation of the great function of True Suchness. Function arises from the substance. From this point onward...
As for the principle of this: while the *Avataṃsaka* and *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* sutras mostly point toward meritorious practice, this sutra seems to speak of the fundamental true essence acting by itself.
In the preceding stages, even a single speck of dust or a single hair is pure and fundamentally so;

in this stage, however, every speck of dust and every hair is omnipresent throughout the Dharma-realm, mutually interfusing and entering one another—simultaneously pervasive and simultaneously encompassing—and is thus fully perfected.
Because it possesses the ten mystic functions (*daśa-guhya-karma-prayoga*), it is said to "manifest the function of True Suchness" (*tathatā-vṛtti*).

As for the designation of this stage as the "Stage of Good Wisdom" (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*), it should be understood as the unimpeded wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-asangajñāna*). [Question: What distinguishes this from the mutual manifestation of the realms of dust-particles within the seven practices (*saptavidha-caryā*) and the mutual interpenetration of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) within the five directions? [Answer: Prior to the fifth stage, [such manifestations occur]...

Both belong to the stage of practice with effortful application; how much more so for those on the paths and stages (*mārga* and *bhūmi*)? How could they possibly be the same as this? Thus we know that the seven practices arise through the predominant power of practice, while the five paths and stages arise through the predominant power of aspiration.

Nevertheless, they are triggered simultaneously upon awakening, just as the two supreme and three functional powers of Avalokiteśvara were all manifested immediately after attaining perfect penetration. It further states: "Examining the characteristics of these ten holy practices, they differ significantly from those in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Therefore, I have relied on the words of the sages to seek the ultimate truth, not daring to arbitrarily adopt or reject anything. According to the *Avataṃsaka*..."
Yan Weishi’s *Jinguangming* all state that this stage possesses the four types of unimpeded mastery (*pratisaṃvid*), acting as a great Dharma-preacher who most excellently expounds the teachings.

Zizhong said: "The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* clarifies that this Bodhisattva possesses the four types of unimpeded wisdom (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) and serves as a great Dharma-preacher, expounding immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* phrases and meanings without exhaustion; therefore, it is called 'Manifesting the Truth' (*fa zhen*)."
Regarding its application: I maintain that while the preaching of the Dharma can indeed be described as an "application" (yòng), it is but one among the great applications.
Therefore, I now refer to these as the ten mysterious applications (shí xuán yè yòng), within which the preaching of the Dharma is naturally contained.
All of the above follows the *Zhengmài* (Orthodox Pulse), with only minor variations in the wording of certain characters; the only difference lies in the phrasing of the intermediate responses.

If one speaks in relation to the former two positions, then they constitute the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai*), whereas this constitutes the function of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*shi-shi wu-ai*).
Second, the summary of cultivation.
Ānanda, from this point onward, these bodhisattvas complete their cultivation and their merit becomes perfected;
therefore, this stage is also designated by the name "the Stage of Cultivation.
The phrase "these bodhisattvas" is a general term and has not yet been specifically identified. As for the phrase "from this point onward," it refers to—
This refers to all Bodhisattvas from the time they are designated for the second bhūmi onward.

Because they enter the stage of cultivation starting from their own second bhūmi and continue until the sixth bhūmi, they enter the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and complete their conditioned practices. In the seventh bhūmi, they advance further into the unconditioned;

in the eighth bhūmi, with the mind of true suchness (*tathatā*), their practice of non-action is also completed. Therefore, it is said that "the work of cultivation is finished," continuing thus through the ninth bhūmi.
Having already attained the total embodiment of great function, it is said that "merit is perfected. This implies that the ten stages (*bhūmi*) constitute the stage of cultivation (*śikṣā-bhūmi*).

In many sūtras and śāstras, these are largely categorized within the stage of cultivation; however, here, by setting aside the "emergence" [from the state of non-abiding] and retaining the "correct," the stages prior to this one are likewise designated as the stage of cultivation.
Yet, since it says "likewise designated," this does not refer to them with absolute certainty.

This stage marks the end of the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), though it may also be designated as such. Thus, one should know that the ultimate completion of cultivation does not pertain solely to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);

it must also include the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*). Since one has not yet reached the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*), it is improper to say that there is no longer any cultivation.
It is simply that the aspect of realization (pratyakṣa) is predominant while the aspect of cultivation (bhāvanā) is slight. Regarding the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi):
because the wondrous cloud of the canopy of compassion covers the ocean of nirvāṇa, it is named the Cloud of Dharma stage.
It was stated above that the practice has reached its completion and merit is perfected; thus, one should immediately realize and attain nirvāṇa. However, as for why...
As for "not taking up nirvāṇa," it is because one seeks to benefit sentient beings; thus it is said that the wondrous clouds of the compassionate canopy cover the ocean of nirvāṇa.
The character *yīn* (canopy) should be pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*). Regarding the phrase "wondrous clouds of the compassionate canopy":

this refers to the Bodhisattva, after the perfection of their merits, once again giving rise to true compassion to canopy and protect sentient beings, like a ten-thousand-li expanse of clear blue sky suddenly—
It raises subtle and wondrous clouds that shade and cover the world, so that all may equally bathe in the joy of refreshing coolness.
It is for this reason that it can obstruct the fruit of Buddhahood, preventing its realization; thus it is said to "cover the ocean of Nirvāṇa.
It is precisely because its true compassion is like a cloud that covers and veils the dharma of Nirvāṇa that this stage is named the *Dharmameghā-bhūmi*. The Ten Stages are concluded.

Regarding the ninth stage, the position of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambuddha), there are two parts: first, the explicit clarification of its fundamental position; second, the conclusion which confirms the preceding stages. First: "The Tathāgata flows against the current;

likewise, the Bodhisattva proceeds in accordance with it until he reaches [this stage]. When the limit of awakening and the boundary [of the previous stage] intersect, it is called Equal Enlightenment."

Those above [the stage of Bodhisattvas] benefit sentient beings while concealing their own entry into *nirvāṇa*. Once they have emerged from the gate of compassion (*maitrī*), they immediately enter the ocean of fruition (*phala-sāgara*).
The reason they are not called "Sublime Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is that the Tathāgatas flow against the current, whereas Bodhisattvas follow it.

To say they "flow against the current" means that having already reached the ocean of fruition, they reverse the direction of the compassionate vessel (*maitrī-naukā*), exiting *nirvāṇa* and entering the realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). It is said...
"Following toward arrival" means that, about to exhaust the ocean of fruition, one swiftly poling the boat of wisdom to turn away from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and head toward nirvāṇa.

This is spoken in terms of the fruit of cessation (*nirodha-phala*). If, however, it is considered in terms of the fruit of wisdom (*jñāna-phala*), then the Buddha emerges at the boundary of bodhi-awakening and the Bodhisattva enters the boundary of bodhi-awakening;
they meet precisely at this intersection, hence it is called "entering the intersection. Zhengmo says: "It is like entering..."
Regarding those who gather jewels from the sea: the first merchant had already obtained various treasures and emerged against the current, reaching the gateway of the ocean.
Only then did the second merchant advance to take his own share, entering with the current, also reaching the gateway of the ocean.

These two ships were exactly level, differing only in that one’s bow pointed outward and the other’s pointed inward. The *Yingluo jing* (Sutra of the Necklaces) says: "Equal Enlightenment illuminates quiescence. This is subtle...

"Awareness that is quiescent and illuminating" (jue-jizhao) also carries this same meaning. As for the designation "Equal Enlightenment" (Dengjue), its significance is taken to mean being equal to "Sublime Enlightenment" (Miaojue).
Some say that there remains one more stage before reaching the level of Sublime Enlightenment; however, this is not the intent of the present sutra. [Question:

Regarding these fifty-five stages above, it would be appropriate to set forth the boundaries for the severance of delusions so that the progression through the stages might be clearly distinguished. While it is certainly convenient to explain the meanings based solely on the text as it stands, within the ten practices and ten transferences of this sutra, the contemplative objects (*viṣaya*) resemble those of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Yet, there is no explicit delineation of the severance of delusions.

Question: Regarding the attainment of realization, whether it be shallow or deep, upon what does one rely? Answer: For a fool to attempt to fathom the realm of the sages with an ordinary mind is truly difficult to achieve self-confidence; thus, one must simply take the words of the sages as the definitive standard. As for that which is contained within the sutras, how could I dare not to elucidate it?

Who would permit the arbitrary addition of what is not found in the sutras? Upon careful examination of the stages and positions (*avasthā*) in the original sutra, it is evident that they not only differ from those of the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) system, but even the sequence of shallow and deep stages in sutras such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Śrī-garbha-vyūha* does not correspond to this [text].

This is because for one of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches back to the source of the cause. Thus, as in the *Avataṃsaka*, the stage of the fulfillment of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā-citta*) subsumes the positions and realizes awakening. In this sutra, however, the profound stage of Equal Enlightenment (*sama-saṃbodhi*) attains the mind of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-citta*). How, then, can their relative shallowness or depth be discussed merely in terms of chronological sequence?

Nevertheless, within the context of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), the Buddha has also implicitly included the principle of sequential arrangement (*xingbu*). Therefore, for now, I shall explain the text solely by following its literal expressions; that is to say, I dare not fail to bring forth the meaning contained within the Sūtra. As for the limits of severing delusions (*duanhuo*), this is briefly revealed only at the stage of faith (*xinwei*):
