In the first faith, it is said, "All false thoughts (*wangxiang*) are extinguished without remainder. This refers to the severance of active delusions and their seeds (*xianzhong*). In the second faith, it is said, "All habitual tendencies (*xiqu*) all manifest before one, being remembered without forgetfulness. This refers to the subduing of habitual tendencies (*fuxi*). In the third faith, it is said, "The habitual tendencies from beginningless time merge into a single brilliant clarity.

This refers to the total exhaustion of habitual tendencies (*jinxi*). This is truly because the Principle (*li*) is realized through sudden enlightenment (*dunwu*), whereby one rides upon this awakening to eliminate [delusions] simultaneously. However, because the habit-energy of desire (*yuxi*) has only just begun to dry up, it has not yet...

When encountering the flow of the Dharma, there are times when thoughts arise in response to objects; this occurs occasionally. However, by relying once more on the power of superior faith (*adhimukti*), one attains complete subduing and complete severance of delusions.

Upon reaching the third stage of faith, it is like wood turned to ash, never to flare up again. Therefore, from the fourth stage of faith onward, the texts do not mention a single word regarding the severance of delusions. How could a fool dare to add such things arbitrarily? This is what is meant by the saying: "Who permits the unauthorized addition of what is not found in the sutras? Someone may ask:

"If severance is like wood turned to ash and realization is like gold extracted from ore, it would seem that subsequent stages should no longer exist. Why, then, are the ranks still listed as they were before? The answer is: Once gold has been extracted from ore, it can be fashioned into vessels. Even after it has been refined, one may seek further refinement. There is...

To exert effort is [the stage of] "Suchness" (yathābhūta). Not seeking its refinement, yet naturally being without anything that is not refined, is "Non-action" (anabhisamskāra). To move the emperors and kings, to arrange the ancestral temples, to store the yellow river water, to hold the sweet dew, to revere Heaven and Earth, and to offer sacrifices to the spirits—this is the "Great Function of the Total Body" (sarvakāya-mahāprayoga).

That the altars of soil and grain protect it, and the myriad people receive its blessing, is the "Subtle Cloud of Compassionate Shade. To emulate ancient treasures of the utmost rarity and to awaken to the same awakening as the Buddhas is the "Formation of the Ultimate Jewel.

To settle the treasury and reach the ultimate state of wondrous enlightenment is the "Finality of Sublime Awakening. One who understands these metaphors will establish their position after cutting off [delusions], possessing no lack of rational basis. However, this is something not seen in other sutras or treatises, but is found only in this scripture; it is intended to lead those of gradual entry into the Sudden, and to lead those of partial [understanding] toward the Perfect.

This entry into perfection originates from the World-Honored One’s numinous wisdom and subtle discernment. How could those who mistakenly strike pillars, drums, or lutes be worthy of discussing this? Second, the conclusion confirms what preceded it.

Ānanda, from the stage of the Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-prajñā-citta) up to Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), this awakening first attains the initial stage of Dry Wisdom within the Diamond Mind (vajra-citta).

The phrase "from the Dry [Wisdom] up to Equal [Enlightenment]" clarifies the progression from the shallow to the deep; the phrase "this awakening first attains [Equal Enlightenment]" reveals what follows.
This is realized only at the preceding stage. This is truly because the initial mind of Dry Wisdom already possesses all the merits of the subsequent stages;
however, these have not yet been experienced through the process of actual cultivation. They exist solely as inherent nature rather than being accomplished through practice.
Now, proceeding from the shallow to the deep, one gradually cultivates until reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment, yet within that mind of Dry Wisdom, that which was possessed...
Only after all merits have been perfected does one personally realize [this state]; hence it is said that "this awakening is first attained," and so forth.
The "Vajra-mind" refers to the wondrous mind of perfect penetration. Because he previously untied the knots from the sense organs, the Tathāgata named it the "Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening.
Regarding the "Illusory-like Samādhi," Avalokiteśvara himself stated that it consists of "hearing-perfuming" and "hearing-cultivation."
Regarding the *Vajrasamādhi*, from the passage where it is selected by Mañjuśrī, it further states:
"It proclaims the Vajrarāja, the inconceivable illusory-like Mother of Buddhas, the true samādhi," and so forth. Based on this, it remains the initial stage of "Dry Wisdom" (*khan-hye*).

However, it is only at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) that one first attains direct realization and reaches its ultimate fulfillment. Qingliang says: "The arising of clarity is like the Eastern Temple; when wisdom is full, there is no [further] attainment."
This differs from the initial mind. As the ancient masters said: "The final secure barrier is not separate from the first step. All of this conveys this same meaning.
This concludes the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Next is the tenth stage, the stage of Perfect Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).
In this manner, through twelve successive layers of single and double stages, one finally exhausts the wondrous enlightenment and achieves the Unsurpassed Way.
The phrase "in this manner, through successive layers" refers generally to what has been explained from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) onward.

This means that starting from Dry Wisdom, there are successive layers, each consisting of either a single or a double stage, until the twelfth layer, at which point one exhaustively attains wondrous enlightenment.

This clearly indicates that awakening occurs in every stage; it is simply that what precedes [the first stage] is not yet wondrous, while upon entering the stages (bhūmi) one becomes wondrous but not yet exhaustive, reaching full exhaustion only at the stage of Buddhahood.

Thus, he speaks of the whole by tracing from the beginning to the end. Zhengmo [Zhengyan] takes the "single" to mean being restricted to a single stage, and the "repeated" to mean encompassing all ten stages in their entirety—this is most correct. However, he follows Wenling in selecting only the "one dry" [stage].

(Single items: 2. Faith; 3. Abiding; 4. Practice; 5. Orientation. (Combined items: 6. Heat; 7. Summit; 8. Patience; 9. Worldly Dharma. (Single item: 10. Ground. (Combined items: 11. Equality; 12. Vajra. (Single item:
In the present commentary, the "Vajra" stage is omitted and the "Sublime Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is added. Regarding the phrase "accomplishing the unsurpassed path":
since one has already exhausted the Sublime Enlightenment, the path reaches its ultimate consummation, and there is nothing further that can [be accomplished].
It is that which rides upon them all. This concludes the preceding section, which clearly elucidates the various stages. Second, the concluding summary reveals the method of cultivation:
these various stages are all observed through the ten profound metaphors of the vajra-like illusion within *śamatha*.
"By means of the vipaśyanā of all Tathāgatas, one purifies, cultivates, realizes, and gradually enters deeper;
these various stages" refers collectively to the aforementioned stages of the causal ground (hetu-bhūmi) and the resultant ground (phala-bhūmi). "All [are] by means of equality," etc.

This reveals that both the stages of cause and the stages of fruition do not depart from the wondrous mind of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), for the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty is itself the Vajra King Samādhi.
Regarding the phrase "contemplation" (*guan-cha*) and so forth: it means that as one passes through each stage, there must be the specific meritorious achievement of that stage;
if one does not contemplate, one fears the arising of attachment. Therefore, one must rely upon that Vajra [Samādhi].
One observes them through samādhi. Regarding the ten similes such as that of an illusion, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"Observe all karma as like an illusion; all phenomena as like a mirage; all bodies as like the moon reflected in water; exquisite forms as like space; exquisite sounds as like an echo;
all Buddha-lands as like a city of the gandharvas; the Buddha’s activities as like a dream; the Buddha’s body as like a shadow; and the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*)..."
Like a reflection; the Dharma-body is like a transformation, neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned, because all things are empty.
Although there are ten metaphors herein, the phenomena they illustrate do not go beyond saving sentient beings, preaching the Dharma, adorning the lands, and making offerings to the Buddhas.
However, since it is said that nothing can be grasped, there are no sentient beings to save, no Dharma to preach, and no land to adorn.

Adorn. Since there is no Buddha to be offered to, yet it is said that one must not abandon [the practice], then one spontaneously delivers sentient beings, spontaneously preaches the Dharma, spontaneously adorns the lands, and spontaneously makes offerings to the Buddhas. Since it is said that all things are empty, then both grasping and rejecting are forgotten;

even the mind that forgets is stilled. This is the attainment of *śamatha* (calm abiding) based on *vipaśyanā* (insight). If *śamatha* becomes long-drawn-out and stagnant, it obstructs further progress; therefore, once again—
Within *śamatha*, one employs the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas. The meaning of *śamatha* is translated as "cessation" (*zhi*), and the meaning of *vipaśyanā* is translated as "insight" (*guan*).
As the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-śāstra* states: "Settle the mind in right concentration."
This is precisely what is called "stopping" (*śamatha*). It refers to the correct abiding in the discernment of phenomena; this is termed the characteristic of "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "What is called 'stopping' refers to the cessation of all objective characteristics, in accordance with the meaning of *śamatha*.
What is called 'contemplation' refers to the discernment of that which arises from causes and conditions."

Regarding the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*): because it accords with the meaning of *vipaśyanā*, one now contemplates only the quiescence of the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) without abiding in its original state;
this is called *śamatha*. To further contemplate the merits ahead and induce superior progress is called *vipaśyanā*.
This constitutes the accomplishment of contemplation based on [the foundation of] stillness. Since *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are practiced in union, neither identical nor separate, it is thus said:
This is the pure cultivation and realization that proceeds from cause to fruit, traversing every stage; hence it is called "gradually entering deeper.
One who understands this Dharma avoids both the fault of halting midway and the practice of overreaching. This is revealed following the [preceding] stages.
There is indeed a profound reason for this. Ānanda,
by thus revering the initial resolve through these three progressive stages, one is well able to accomplish the fifty-five levels of the true path to Bodhi.

Continuing from the preceding discussion of the stages of cause and fruit, all are observed through the diamond-like contemplation (*vajra-vipaśyanā*). Thus, the merit accrues to the third gradual stage (*krama*).
Although the concluding text of the three gradual stages collectively refers to "progress," the heading of this section alone bears the name "Receiving Progress.
Furthermore, this third progress is precisely the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*karṇendriya-pariśuddhi*), which is also—
Regarding the Vajra Samādhi: if one does not rely on this contemplation, the subsequent stages will be difficult to accomplish.
Therefore, it is said that "all [stages] are accomplished through the threefold advancement," and so forth. Furthermore, at the very end of the third gradual stage, it says:
"From this point, gradually practicing according to the activities undertaken, one establishes the noble stages. Thus, we know that "skillfully accomplishing" refers exclusively to the third stage.

According to the conventional path, *dhyāna* (禪) is translated as *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (靜慮), taking "quiescent contemplation" as its primary sense. In the present sutra, however, it is for the purpose of extinguishing the twelve categories of sentient beings.

To rectify inverted and chaotic thoughts, three gradual stages are established; these constitute the meaning of "quiescence" (*śamatha*). Within the state of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*), there is dryness yet wisdom exists; this constitutes the meaning of "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
By means of this very mind, one flows into the center; this constitutes the meaning of "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*).

The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* explains this as the "insentient yet responsive mind that transcends all dependencies. In the present sūtra, every stage does not depart from the Middle Way; this is precisely the insentient yet responsive mind that transcends all dependencies.

It is the mind. Zhengmo says: "Taking the *dharmatā-nature* (正因佛性) in its entirety, while simultaneously incorporating both the *pratyaya-hetu* and *hetu-hetu* natures (緣了二因), constitutes the essence of dhyāna.
In this sutra, the three gradual stages of attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) correspond to the *dharmatā-nature*.
Within *śamatha*, employing the *vipaśyanā* of all Tathāgatas for pure cultivation and realization corresponds to simultaneously incorporating both the *pratyaya-hetu* and *hetu-hetu* natures."
This is the cause. All the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas mentioned in the title are subsumed under this meaning.
Up to this point, the section on the opening instruction for the cultivation and realization of *dhyāna* is concluded.

4. The Section on Revealing the Realization of the Śūraṅgama Sādhana. (Question: The Zhengmo commentary categorizes this as "Essential for Beginners," whereas the current sub-commentary categorizes it as the "Section on Realization. Why is there such a profound discrepancy between these levels of depth?)

Answer: For those of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren), cultivation and realization place their primary emphasis on the initial mind (chuxin). When this initial mind is vitalized and penetrated, one spontaneously and effortlessly enters realization. This is evidenced by the fact that when the subsequent consciousness-aggregate (shiyin) is exhausted and one enters the Stage of Dry Wisdom (qianhui di), it is stated:

"In this way, one transcends the ten stages of faith, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the four preparatory minds, the diamond-like ten grounds, and equal-enlightenment; becoming perfectly luminous, one enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment. This sufficiently proves this principle. If this is compared with the *Zhengmo* (The Correct Pulse), there is no contradiction.

The only difference lies in the fact that [the *Shoulengyan jing*] reveals the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* specifically for the purpose of shattering the obstacles within the preceding three parts and accomplishing the meaning of ultimate firmness. III. 1. Thorough Investigation.
The seven destinies (*sapta-gati*) are used to break obstacles within *śamatha*. Second, the five *māras* are detailed and distinguished to break obstacles within *samādhi*.

Third, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are again clarified to break obstacles within *dhyāna*. Regarding the first three [sections], there are: first, Ānanda’s inquiry; second, the Tathāgata’s praise and permission;
third, the actual exposition. Regarding the first of these three, there is: first, the expression of gratitude for what was previously stated.
[This section] provides further benefit. Second, [he] expresses doubts and requests instruction; third, he cites legal precedents to pose questions. First:
immediately rising from his seat, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, whose compassionate voice is all-pervading, you have skillfully opened up for sentient beings their subtle and deep-seated delusions, causing my body and mind today to experience great joy.”

Nevertheless, one obtains great benefit. Regarding rising from one's seat and prostrating at the feet, there are two intentions: first, to express gratitude for what has preceded; second, to request what follows. Joining the palms is reverence of the physical action (*kāyakarman*);

being respectful is reverence of the mental action (*manaskarman*); addressing the Buddha is reverence of the verbal action (*vākkarman*). To express gratitude for the past and request the future, such is the proper form of salutation.
Therefore, the inverted deluded thoughts of the twelve classes of beings are instantaneously and completely dissolved; thus, he is honored as the World-Honored One of Sovereign Power and Virtue.
Having fully revealed the sublime principles for advancing through the stages of sagehood, he is honored as the One of Compassionate Voice Who Is Without Obstruction.

"Subtle and deep-seated afflictions" refers specifically to the deluded thoughts of these beings; it is none other than a Buddha who can perceive them, and none other than a Buddha [who can eliminate them].
Do not speak of it; therefore, it is called "subtle. Because one is not self-aware of it and does not know it oneself, it is called "sinking into delusion.
It is likened to the flowers produced when pressing the eyes; the teaching employs the three gradual stages to eliminate it, all of which are skillfully revealed.

One rejoices that the holy stages can be cultivated and knows that birth and death are not binding; therefore, it is said that body and mind are "joyful and at ease. Thus, the name follows from the meaning.
The meaning is that because it can be upheld and relied upon, it is said that "one attains great benefit. All of this is attributed to the Buddha’s merit; therefore, it says, "to us.
Second, the expression of doubt and the request for instruction.
World-Honored One, if this wondrously luminous, truly pure, and sublime mind is from the beginning all-pervading and perfect—
such that even the great earth, grasses, trees, crawling insects, and sentient beings are fundamentally True Suchness (tathatā), which is the true essence of the Tathāgata’s Buddhahood—
and if the Buddha-essence is thus truly real, why are there further the paths of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas?
"World-Honored One, does this Way exist inherently from the beginning, or does it arise from the deluded habitual practices of sentient beings?

To first settle the mind and then realize its manifestation—if this 'wondrous brightness' and so forth refers to the meaning previously explained regarding the pervasive and perfect nature of the mind, then because the nature of the mind has the quality of following conditions, it is called 'wondrously bright'; yet the nature of the mind also possesses the quality of being unchanging."

This is its meaning; therefore, it is called "True Purity. Although it follows conditions, it does not change; although it does not change, it follows conditions; therefore, it is called the "Wondrous Mind.
It is precisely this that is indicated by the phrase "the secret cause of the Tathāgata" within *śamatha*, and the "perfectly penetrating wondrous essence" within *samādhi*.
The meaning of its original, pervasive perfection has already been explained repeatedly. However, within *śamatha*, one gives rise to faith through following the words.

Within samādhi, Ānanda and his peers likewise only attained a semblance of understanding. Now, following the practice of dhyāna, their minds have become tranquil and solid, and subtle delusions have been eliminated;
thus they have attained true awakening. Therefore, he summarizes what was previously explained to establish this point definitively.
"Thus, [arising] from the truth, one doubts the false. "Thus" refers to that which is originally pervasive and perfect.
Thus it is. The phrase "and so forth" (乃至) abbreviates the internal root-body (*mūla-kāya*). "The great earth" refers to the external receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*).
Furthermore, grasses and trees are the minute aspects of the receptacle-world, while wriggling, sentient beings are the subtle aspects of the root-body.

Since it is said to be both pervasive and perfect, there is no phenomenon that it does not encompass and no entity that it does not contain; thus, all root-bodies and receptacle-worlds—grass... [and so on].
Even wood and insects are all established from the mind; therefore, it is said that their fundamental source is true suchness (*tathatā*).

This means that when one traces back to their fundamental source, there is only the single nature of true suchness. Furthermore, this nature of true suchness is precisely the true essence of attaining Buddhahood.
Because True Suchness (tathatā) is itself the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), and one who realizes this can attain Buddhahood. Regarding the "reality of the Buddha-body":
since it is the very essence of a Buddha, it must correspond to reality. Now, observing the falsity and delusion of the seven destinies, one cannot help but harbor doubts.

Therefore it is asked: "How can there further be hells and so forth? This text explicitly mentions the six destinies (*ṣadgati*), while the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) encompasses the realm of the *ṛṣis*.
Thus, the subsequent passage clarifies that there are seven. The section beginning with "World-Honored One" follows up on these doubts by posing two questions:

first, asking whether [the realms] exist inherently within the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*); second, asking whether they arise from the habitual tendencies of deluded thought (*vikalpa-vāsanā*). The intention is that within the nature itself...
If [the nature] exists, then the seven destinies would not be false and illusory. If illusory habits arise, then the principle of "immediacy" (ji-xing) is not established.
Furthermore, if immediacy is not established, then there are dharmas external to this mind, which contradicts the present realization of the meaning of universal perfection.
This seems inconsistent. Therefore, I did not venture to fully grasp [your previous meaning] but instead posed this inquiry.

Later you say that the thorough investigation of the seven realms of existence reveals them all to be the signs of deluded conditioned phenomena; they are births through false conceptualization and followings of karma through false conceptualization.

Within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind of non-action, these are all like flowers in the sky—originally having no point of attachment, being nothing more than a single falsehood. Furthermore...

World-Honored One, for example, the Bhikṣuṇī Ratnaprabhā upheld the Bodhisattva precepts, yet she secretly engaged in sexual misconduct.

She falsely claimed that sexual conduct is not killing, not stealing, and carries no karmic retribution. Having uttered these words, a great, fierce fire first arose from her female organ, and subsequently, fierce fires burned through every joint of her body, and she fell into the Avīci Hell. [Likewise were] King Vairōcana and Sunakṣatra.
O Bhikṣu, because the Vaiḍūrya [King] slaughtered the Gautama clan, and because Sunakṣatra falsely proclaimed that all phenomena are empty,
he fell alive into the Avīci Hell.
Regarding the first case of falling through lustful falsehood: engaging in sexual misconduct while observing the precepts already constitutes a grave offense; moreover, it is compounded by lying.
Furthermore, this is not an ordinary lie, for one claims that engaging in sexual misconduct causes no harm to others, unlike taking the life of another being.
To steal another’s property, there is no retribution in the present life and none in the future;
yet to violate the precepts and mislead others is an even greater evil, and thus one must undergo both the immediate retribution (*hetu-vipāka*) and the ultimate retribution (*phala-vipāka*).

Since lust belongs to the element of fire, it causes the female organ to produce fire. That [the result] arises immediately after speech is due to the predominance of karmic power, for the retribution cannot be delayed. Section.

Regarding the burning of the joints: this is caused by the fire of desire pervading the entire body. As the *Ucchuṣma-sādhana* states, "It is said that those who indulge excessively in lust become a mass of fierce fire.
This is indeed not false. This is a manifest karmic reward (*puṣpa-vipāka*), yet such a reward is insufficient to repay the debt.
Therefore, at the end of life, their consciousness falls directly into hell. As it says below: "With nine thoughts of passion and one thought of the Dharma, they descend through the wheel of fire.
Their bodies enter the ground where wind and fire intersect; those with lighter karma are born in the *sāntara* hells, while those with heavier karma are born in the *avīci* hells.

Although Liánxiāng now claims that lustful desire carries no retribution, she still believes that killing and stealing do have retribution; this appears to be the case of "nine thoughts of passion and one thought," whereby one undergoes such suffering.

Retribution occurs at the junction of water and fire; however, because one who destroys the precepts and misleads others commits an extremely grave evil, it is said that they fall into the Avīci Hell.
○ Regarding "Vaiśālī... falling for killing and lying": Wēnlíng says, "King Virūḍhaka was the crown prince of the Vaiśālī kingdom.
Driven by long-standing resentment, he slaughtered the Śākya clan. The Buddha prophesied that in seven days he would enter hell. The King was terrified and [mounted his horse]..."
He entered the sea, where fire spontaneously emerged from the water and consumed him. This is detailed in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Vaiḍūryarāja Sūtra*.
Sunakṣatra is also called Shanxiu; the Āgama states that he was the son of the Buddha’s maternal cousin, while others say he was the son of Devadatta.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra associated with evil friends and fell away from the four dhyānas."
Having given rise to evil and false views, he speaks thus: "There is no Buddha, there is no Dharma, and there is no Nirvāṇa," and so forth;

this is to falsely claim that the Dharma is empty. Now, while Vairūḍyaka’s killing of people out of malice already constitutes a grave offense, the victim was moreover not an ordinary person, but one of the Gautama clan.
That Sunakṣatra falsely claims the Dharma is empty is itself a perverse delusion. If...
To further steal offerings while simultaneously committing theft constitutes a crime for both parties that is equally grave;
therefore, both are cast alive into prison. As it says below: "Those of pure emotion sink directly into the Avīci Hell.

If, within their sinking minds, they slander the Mahāyāna, violate the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, preach false doctrines through deception, or greedily and improperly consume the faithful's offerings—
Vaiśālī was full of reverence, yet he was reborn in the Avīci Hell of the ten directions;
now, Rāvaṇa slaughtered at will and Sunakṣatra indulged in falsehoods, appearing to be of pure emotion, yet they surely ought to sink into Avīci.

Moreover, Rāvaṇa attacked the Śākyas, seeking to sever the seed of the Buddha, while Sunakṣatra spoke falsely and vainly coveted offerings; since they both committed many such sins, they may well have been reborn again in the ten directions.
As for the hells, they are merely the physical bodies seen by all people, which briefly manifest the "flower reward" (the immediate retribution).
After falling into them, one undergoes the full fruit-reward for kalpas in the Avīci Hell. Second, the question is posed based on the hells.
Are these various hells fixed in specific locations, or do they arise spontaneously? Is it that each person, having generated their own karma, experiences the retribution individually?

We pray that you will bestow great compassion to enlighten us who are as yet ignorant, so that all sentient beings who uphold the precepts may hear this definitive meaning, receive it with joy and reverence, and remain pure and free from transgression.
First, two points are asked together. It is said that when viewed from the perspective of these three types of people, these various hells do not exist inherently;

rather, they arise from deluded habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). However, it is not known whether they have fixed locations, or whether they naturally manifest according to the karma produced by each respective individual, such that they privately undergo retribution in their own particular places. The intent of the question is as follows:
This means that if there were a fixed place [of rebirth], it would have no connection to the cause of karma; one would fear falling into nihilism.

If, however, existence follows from karma, then the manifestation of retribution will be evident, which is sufficient to inspire deep reflection. You likely already know this to be according to karma, yet you do not dare to decide for yourself.
Observing the wording of the petition below, it is clear that the emphasis lies on upholding the precepts. ○ May you graciously grant your compassionate response to this humble request.

[The practitioner] makes this aspiration: "Since the two meanings are not yet resolved and the false and the correct have not been distinguished, I am like a child. May you definitively point them out and establish the distinction between right and wrong;
this is what constitutes 'opening and developing. Because you would grant me this joy, I only pray that you will bestow your compassion.
This is the request for oneself. "May all [beings] likewise... is the request for others. For those who uphold the precepts, it is established for the sake of liberation from the suffering of hell.

There is a fixed principle: if one realizes for oneself that observing the precepts is of no benefit, one may instead give rise to doubt. However, if one hears that rebirth is determined by karma, one will naturally feel joy and exultation;
receiving and upholding this teaching with the highest reverence, one will become even more careful and pure, thereby avoiding the transgression of breaking the precepts.
When Ānanda had finished his inquiry, the two Tathāgatas praised and approved his words.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "How excellent is this question! It will cause all sentient beings not to enter into false views. Listen attentively now;
I shall explain it for you. Zhengmo (正脈) says:
"How excellent" is a term of praise expressing delight because the question accords with one's intent. "This question" refers to...

Regarding the two preceding questions, once these two have been resolved, the false and the correct are naturally distinguished; hence it is said, "causing all sentient beings not to enter into false views.
This is because by clinging to the existence of a fixed location and failing to believe in [the principle of] following karma, one immediately falls into false views.
The final two phrases, which admonish the listener and grant permission to speak, are easily understood. Third, the actual exposition consists of four parts. First, a brief indication.

I. The causes and conditions for ascending and descending. II. A detailed explanation of the transmigration through the seven realms of existence (*sapta-gati*). III. Answering and explaining the preceding questions in sequence. IV.

Concluding with praise to demonstrate the false and the correct. Regarding the first [section], there are three parts: 1. Ascending and descending based on internal and external meditative concentrations (*samādhi*);

2. The differentiation of realms and categories according to emotional thoughts (*saṃjñā*); 3. The fixed locations resulting from the conditions of karma. Regarding the first two [parts], there is one section: A general heading.
The internal division and the external division. Second, a specific explanation of how sentient beings fall through delusion and ascend through thought. First:
"Ānanda, all sentient beings are in truth fundamentally true and pure. Because of that false seeing, false habits arise.
Due to this, the internal division and the external division are distinguished."
The "all" and the "two phrases" refer to those who have attained awakening; "due to that false view" refers to those who are deluded. The Tathāgata’s intention is this:

if one truly awakens to the fact that the true nature is all-pervasive and perfect, then the great earth, grasses, trees, wriggling insects, and all sentient beings are fundamentally primordial True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, all sentient beings are in reality fundamentally true and pure; it is only because all sentient beings... [do not realize this].
Upon awakening to universal perfection, one falsely perceives the mark of sentient beings.
Because of this, false habit-energies arise through perfuming, just as when one constantly keeps the mark of sentient beings in mind.
Due to not forgetting the mark of sentient beings, one may develop a deep attachment within the bodies of sentient beings, or one may long for excellence outside of their bodies.

Excellent. Therefore it is said: "From this, one distinguishes between the internal division and the external division. Second, the separate clarification of the descent of sentient beings and the ascent of thought.
First, the separate clarification of the descent of sentient beings; second, the separate clarification of the ascent of thought. Regarding the first:
Ānanda, the internal element is precisely the constituent part of sentient beings. Because of various attachments and defilements, deluded emotions are aroused;
as these emotions accumulate without ceasing, they can produce the water of craving. For this reason, when a sentient being’s mind recalls delicacies, water flows from their mouth;
when their mind recalls a former person, whether with pity or resentment, tears fill their eyes; and when they greedily seek wealth and treasures, saliva of craving issues forth from their heart.
The body is glossy and moist; when the mind becomes attached and engages in sexual intercourse, fluids naturally flow from both the male and female organs.

Ānanda, although various forms of craving differ, their underlying fetters are the same: being moistened and unable to ascend, they naturally fall downward. This is called the "internal element" (antarbhauma).
First, the internal objects are indicated. Regarding "internal objects" (*adhyātma-viṣaya*): this refers to that which is within the constituent parts of sentient beings.
The phrase "due to various... clarifies the internal mind. "Due to various attachments and defilements" means that, based upon these internal objects, various attachments and defilements arise.
"Giving rise to deluded sentiments" means that because of such attachments and defilements, all manner of false and illusory states are produced.
"Sentimental views. "The accumulation of sentiment without ceasing" refers to the accumulation of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) through sentiment.

"Able to produce the water of craving" means that when craving reaches its peak, it becomes moistening; when moistening reaches its peak, it flows and congeals. This is the correct manifestation of the characteristics of the mind.
From here below, the matter is taken up for verification. "For this reason" means because it is able to produce the water of craving. "Delicacies... [text ends].

"Excellent and exquisite food and drink" refers to the two objects of fragrance and flavor; when one recollects them and gives rise to craving, water flows from the mouth—this can be understood by observing how one’s own saliva involuntarily swallows upon seeing someone eating delicious food. "The person before one" refers to a person previously encountered, encompassing the two objects of sound and form;
because both the sound and form were beautiful, they cause the mind to remember them, whether out of pity or resentment. As for "pitying him,"...
Sounds and forms may be indulged in; one regrets not hearing or seeing them, and this pity and regret do not cease.

The resulting grief is difficult to restrain, which is why tears fill the eyes—this is a common occurrence. When wealth and treasures have not yet arrived but the mind gives rise to greedy longing, this is the "dust of dharmas" (*dharmaviṣaya*).
When wealth and treasures are about to arrive and one’s craving for them nourishes the body, moisture and luster are produced, as follows:

When people in the world see that another’s complexion is moist and lustrous, they immediately congratulate them, knowing it can be inferred that they have acquired great wealth. When the mind becomes attached and one engages in sexual intercourse, this is the objective field of touch (*spraṣṭavya*).
Even before the two organs have made contact, the fluids have already begun to flow; thus, the principle that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is able to produce water is even more clearly demonstrable.
[The commentary] concludes the names of the internal constituents below [the section on Ānanda]: although various cravings differ, the objects grasped by them are only four.
The treatise states that "the objects [of the senses] encompass all six. Regarding the phrase "flowing and congealing are the same":
for example, when the entire substance is glossy and moist, this is water congealed within; tears from the eyes, saliva, and the fluids of the tongue-organ are all water flowing outward.
Whether in a state of flow or congealment, they all have moisture as their nature; therefore, it is said they are the same. Because they are moist, they cannot rise upward. Not...

Ascending from falling is what must inevitably occur according to principle; therefore, it is called "spontaneous" (*ziran*). This refers to the arising of an internal state of mind based on an internal object;
hence, it is termed "internal division. Second, to specifically clarify the perception of ascending.
Ānanda, the external division refers to that which lies beyond the realm of sentient beings. Because of their yearning and admiration, they give rise to empty conceptions;

as these conceptions accumulate without ceasing, they can produce a superior vital energy. For this reason, when sentient beings maintain prohibitive precepts in their minds, their entire bodies become light and pure;

when they maintain mantras and mudrās in their minds, their gaze becomes bold and resolute; when their hearts desire to be born in heaven, they dream of soaring upward; and when their minds dwell upon the Buddha-lands, they perceive the holy ones.

The objective realm manifests in stillness. One serves a spiritual friend while disregarding one’s own body and life. ○ Ānanda, although these various conceptions differ, their lightness and elevation are the same;
they fly and move without sinking, naturally transcending. This is called the external division.
First, the external objects are indicated. Regarding "external objects," this refers to that which is outside the constituent parts of sentient beings. Network Sharing:

Respectfully composed by the junior disciple Da-tian Tong-li of Xian-zong at Nianhua Monastery in the Capital.

The Two [Heavens of] the Four Dhyānas (*catur-dhyāna*). (Wen'eng says: The preceding six heavens, although free from the disturbances of sensory dust, have not yet been able to sever desire; therefore, they are collectively termed the "Desire Realm" (*kāmadhātu*). From here upward, the eighteen heavens are explained;

although free from the defilement of desire, they still possess material form (*rūpa*); therefore, they are collectively termed the "Form Realm" (*rūpadhātu*). They are also collectively termed the "Brahma-world," because they have already left behind the defilement of desire. They are also collectively designated as the "Four Dhyānas," because they have already left behind agitation and movement.

Zhengmo says: Although the bodies of the previous heavens have emerged from movement, the mind and its traces still intersect. It is sufficient to know that above this point there are absolutely no women; mind and traces are both severed, and there is nothing with which to interact. Furthermore, there is neither eating nor sleeping; the three desires are all forgotten. Should one encounter even slight hunger or fatigue, one immediately enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Upon emerging...)

In samādhi, one is satiated and becomes lucid and refined. This is because, by taking the joy of dhyāna as food and rest, one has already transcended the coarse and heavy body and mind. Briefly categorized, there are four stages, each with its own fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*). When detailed according to their superior and inferior qualities, there are eighteen. (2)

First, a detailed enumeration of the various heavens; second, a summary identifying them as belonging to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the first [section], there are four parts: first, the three heavens of the First Dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*);
second, the three heavens of the Second Dhyāna; third, the three heavens of the Third Dhyāna; and fourth, the nine heavens of the Fourth Dhyāna. Regarding the first two [of these four]:

First, a detailed explanation; second, a summary. The first part has three sections: first, the Heaven of Brahma’s Retinue (*Brahmapāriṣadya*); second, the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers (*Brahmapurohita*);
third, the Great Brahma Heaven (*Mahābrahmā*). Regarding the first:
Ānanda, among all those in the world who cultivate the mind, if they do not rely on *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) and lack wisdom, yet are nonetheless able—

Restraining the body, they do not engage in sexual desire. Whether walking or sitting, they are free from all such thoughts; since no defilement of passion arises, they leave no trace in the realm of desire.
Such persons should consider themselves companions of Brahmā. This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārṣadya).
The "world" here still refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because beings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) also cultivate [the path] from within the desire realm.
"All those who cultivate the mind" is a general term for all practitioners of cultivation.
Regarding the phrase "cultivating the mind," if one examines its original intent, it was fundamentally for the purpose of cultivating the mind; however, because they did not attain its...
The Dharma. It was merely an accidental entry into the heavenly realms. *Dhyāna*—translated here as "meditative concentration" (*jinglü*)—means to contemplate through stillness;
those who cultivate the mind should first rely upon it. That it is said here to be "not required" is precisely because one has not attained the Dharma.
Those without wisdom cannot achieve great enlightenment. To "arise cultivation from nature" while being able only to cling to the body... only.
One practices by relying on the characteristics of phenomena and strictly maintains the prohibitive precepts. Initially, through the power of firm resolve, one refrains from sexual desire;
however, this is not yet a state of mindlessness. Next, whether walking or sitting, both thoughts and perceptions vanish, and with them, the mind itself ceases to exist.
Finally, when no further defilement arises and one does not remain within the realm of desire, the cause for the higher realms is established. Once that cause is established, [the result follows].
The fruit follows the mind itself; therefore, in accordance with their thought of renouncing desire, they become companions of Brahmā (*brahmapārisadya*).

Having transcended the Heaven of Desire (*kāmadhātu*), yet not having reached the Heaven of Brahmā’s Ministers (*brahmapurohita*), they are called the "Assembly of Brahmā" (*brahmakāyika*). Zhengmo says: "They are the common people of the Brahma-world."
Second are the Brahmā-purohita devas.
Having eliminated the habituation to desire, the mind of freedom from desire manifests; they delight in and accord with all forms of discipline (vinaya).
Such persons are able to practice the virtues of Brahmā at the appropriate time; this class of beings is called the Brahmā-purohita devas.

Following from the previous point, because love and attachment do not arise, one does not remain bound to the desire realm; hence it is said, "The habituation to desire has been eliminated," meaning that the habitual tendencies toward sexual desire in the desire realm have already been subdued and removed.
Following from the previous point, such a person should consider their own body as a companion to the Brahma-world;
hence it is said, "Free from desire, the pure mind manifests," meaning that the pure mind free from desire has already become manifest. From this point onward, there is no further need for grasping.
He maintains it. Because he is able to harmonize with the rules of the Brahma-vinaya, it is said that he "delights in and accords with" them.

To say he "delights in" means there is no suffering from forced practice; to say he "accords with" means there is the joy of peaceful practice. Thus, the cause for being a Brahma-purohita is established.
When the cause is fulfilled and the fruit is realized, it is said that "this person is able to practice the virtues of Brahma at the proper time. The phrase "at the proper time" clarifies this.
The gods of this heaven ascend further than those of the previous heavens; they have left the lower realm to be born above, yet they still await a different time [for their full realization].
The perfection of the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) is what is termed "virtue" (*guṇa*); assisting those above and transforming those below is what is termed "conduct" (*caryā*).

Having already transcended the Brahma-multitude (*Brahmapārṣadya*) but not yet reaching the Great Brahmā (*Mahābrahmā*), they are therefore called the "Brahma-Attendants" (*Brahmapurohita*). Zhengmo says: "Since they assist in the transformation [of beings], they are effectively celestial ministers."
There are three kinds of Great Brahmā heavens.
Their bodies and minds are wondrously perfect and their deportment is flawless; they possess pure precepts and are further endowed with clear realization.
Such persons, at the appropriate time, are able to lead the Brahmā assembly as Great Brahmā Kings. This class of beings is called the Great Brahmā Heaven.
Building upon the preceding [state of] delight and compliance, it is said that "body and mind are wondrously perfect. Because of delight, the mind is without constraint;
because of compliance, the body is without limitation. Being without constraint and without limitation, they are thus termed "wondrously perfect.

Building upon the preceding ability to practice Brahma-virtue, it is said that "dignified deportment is unimpaired. Since it is said that one is "able to practice," this refers to walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.

Between these, there is a majesty that inspires awe and a deportment that one may look up to; therefore, it is called "unimpaired. Since even their majestic deportment is unimpaired, their prohibitions and precepts are naturally pure.

Upon reaching this heaven, they are not only pure, but are further endowed with clear realization—meaning they know what is maintained and what is transgressed, and they know what is permitted and what is prohibited. Being thus able to know what is maintained and what is transgressed, [they proceed further].

Knowing what is permitted and what is prohibited, he is able to personally adjudicate between heavy and light offenses, clearly demonstrating rewards and punishments, thereby fulfilling the cause of the Great Brahmā.

As the cause matures and the fruit is realized, he is accordingly able to preside over the assembly of Brahmās at the appropriate time. Because his rank transcends that of the Brahmā-purohitas, he is called "Great.
Because he is revered by the Brahmā-pariṣadyas, he is called "King. According to the first dhyāna, which covers the four continents, the Brahmā-king...
Each [of these] should naturally have its own distinct allotment. Now, those whose virtue and rank are equal are designated as a single class.
However, the reason they are called "kings" (rāja) while still being termed "devas" is to distinguish them from other realms; for instance, a human king is also called a "human.
This concludes the section on specific names. Second, the summary.
Ānanda, these three superior classes cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction.
Although they have not yet correctly cultivated the true *samādhi*, their pure minds remain unmoved by any outflows (*āsrava*); this is called the first dhyāna.

These three are called "superior streams" because they possess superior bodies and superior bliss, as they transcend the lower realms. All forms of suffering and affliction refer to the coarse and extreme pains of the lower realms;

since one has already abandoned such sufferings when the form-aggregate of the first dhyāna arises based on the *anāgamya* (preparatory) concentration, how much more so for the first dhyāna itself, which possesses both vitarka and vicāra?
How could it possibly oppress [the practitioner] again? Therefore, it is stated directly that it "cannot."
Since it was previously stated that one does not rely on *dhyāna*, it is not correct cultivation; furthermore, since it is said that there is no wisdom, it is not the true *samādhi*.
It is merely that within a mind of pure precept-keeping, one cannot be moved by the various outflows (*āsrava*) of the desire realm.
It is precisely because of this meaning of immovability that it is called the First Dhyāna. It possesses five factors of merit, namely:

vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), prīti (joy), sukha (bliss), and ekāgratā (one-pointedness of mind). Among the nine stages, it is called the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion;
this is because, by being secluded from the afflictions and various unwholesome dharmas of the lower realms, the wholesome dharmas such as the joy and bliss of the First Dhyāna arise. First...
The three heavens of the first dhyāna are concluded. Second, the three heavens of the second dhyāna. Part one: a detailed explanation. Part two: a general summary.
The first [detailed explanation] has three sections: 1. Parīttābha (Limited Light) Heaven; 2. Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light) Heaven; 3. Ābhāsvara (Radiant Sound) Heaven. First: [Parīttābha Heaven].
Ānanda, next there is the Brahmā Heaven, which governs the Brahmās and perfects the Brahma-conduct. With a tranquil mind unmoving, stillness and clarity give rise to light.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha).
Regarding "the next Brahmā heaven," this refers to the second dhyāna heaven, which originally derives from the Brahmā heaven of the first dhyāna.
This is because within that Brahmā heaven, he presides over the Brahmās. As for "one who has perfected the Brahma-faring":

having presided over them for a long time, his merit in transforming others is profound and his own practice is increasingly pure. Regarding "one whose mind is tranquil and unmoving": this refers to the Brahma-faring.

Once perfected, the power of the pure mind becomes firm, and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) becomes increasingly manifest. Because meditative concentration becomes increasingly manifest, the cause for the "Limited Light" (*Parīttābha*) is established.
When the cause is fulfilled and the fruit is realized, it is said that "tranquility gives rise to light. This means that while remaining tranquil and unmoving, one is profoundly clear and serene;
both internally and externally one is bright and pure, and body and mind radiate with brilliance. This is precisely because [the state] is restricted to...

Because their physical and mental radiance has not yet reached far-reaching reflection, they are named the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*). Second, as for the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*Apramāṇābha*):
their lights illuminate one another exhaustlessly, and their radiance reflects throughout the worlds of the ten directions, universally transforming them into lapis lazuli.
This class of beings is named the Heaven of Immeasurable Light.

"Light illuminating light" means that based on the preceding stage, the power of meditative concentration increases further, such that the physical light and mental light illuminate one another in succession, like passing a flame from one fire to another, burning with intense brilliance.

Once they burn with intense brilliance, their radiance becomes inexhaustible, and thus the supreme cause of immeasurable light is accomplished. Since the fruit follows the excellence of the cause, it is said:

It reflects throughout the worlds of the ten directions, universally becoming lapis lazuli. This refers to the supporting retribution (the environment), which—just like the supported retribution (the body and mind)—is transparent and pure from within and without, being free from all blemish or defilement. Zhenji said:

"Reflecting throughout the worlds of the ten directions" is spoken of in terms of the light of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) according to what is experienced and utilized, referring to the east, west, south, north, and so forth. Based on this, that which is called...

"The ten directions" refers here to the ten directions within the second dhyāna heaven; alternatively, it may refer to the small chiliocosm, as the second dhyāna heavens encompass the small chiliocosm.
It is termed "Immeasurable Light" (Amitābha) in contrast to the "measurable" light of the preceding heavens.
Furthermore, while the light of the previous heavens can be measured by this heaven, the light of this heaven cannot be measured by the previous heavens.

Because they possess energy, the third class, the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven), absorbs and sustains the circular radiance to accomplish the essence of the teaching; they manifest pure transformations whose applications are inexhaustible.
This category is thus called the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
The recipient of the teaching absorbs the meaning of the Dharma; the teacher of the teaching maintains the sounds.
This relies solely upon perfect radiance (*paripūrṇa-prabhā*), for this heaven accomplishes the essence of the teaching through perfect radiance itself. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"There are some Buddha-fields that perform the work of a Buddha by means of radiance. This may be cited as an analogy for the present case. According to the ancients who have cited various [scriptures]...

The sūtras and śāstras frequently state that from the second dhyāna upward, there is no method of verbal expression; they rely solely on Master Zhongyuan to explain this, yet I fear this may not necessarily be the case.
Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* also says: "From the Ābhāsvara and Śubhakṛtsna heavens, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)."
One hears all the sounds of speech. Thus we know that when the ancient masters cited the phrase "no speech," they meant only the absence of vocal eloquence;
for speech issues forth from light, as it will be said later: "The circular light produces sound.
As for "emitting transformation," it means relying upon the circular light to proclaim and expound the principles of transformation. As for "pure," it means...
This is the teaching of spontaneous accomplishment, characterized by non-action and non-conditioning.

It is for this reason that its application is inexhaustible, serving as the most excellent retribution among the second dhyāna. As for the designation "Light-Sound" (Ābhāsvara), it is so called because their perfect radiance constitutes their speech.
This concludes the specific explanation. Second, the general conclusion.
Ānanda, these three superior classes cannot be oppressed by any anxiety or distress.
Although they have not yet correctly cultivated true samādhi, because coarse outflows have been suppressed within their pure minds, they are called the Second Dhyāna.

These three are called "superior streams" (viśeṣa-bhāgīya) because they are not only superior to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but also superior to the first dhyāna, as each subsequent stage becomes increasingly excellent.
All forms of anxiety and apprehension refer to the subtle suffering of the first dhyāna;

having just recently departed from the suffering of the desire realm, one fears falling back into it, resulting in a state of constant worry and suspense. At times, one resists this with applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). Now, having reached...

In the second dhyāna, one becomes increasingly distant from desire; fearing that the mind might fall back, anxiety no longer oppresses, and one enters the state of non-discursive thought (avitarka) and non-discursive investigation (avicāra).
Although it is without discursive thought and investigation, it still belongs to the realm of outflows (sāsrava);
therefore, it is not the true samādhi of right cultivation. The "coarse outflow" refers to the craving within the first dhyāna; although it cannot yet be severed, regarding the second...
In the pure mind of dhyāna, nothing arises from external causes; therefore, it is said that [the afflictions] have already been subdued.
Based on this, one has already transcended the first dhyāna but has not yet reached the third; thus, it is designated by the name of the second dhyāna. It possesses four factors of merit, namely:

internal purity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind. Among the nine stages, it is called the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration (*samādhi*), because its concentration is superior to that of the first [dhyāna].
The first dhyāna possesses both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), and is accompanied by the joy and bliss of anxious anticipation.

Because one attains the second dhyāna, which is without vitarka or vicāra and characterized by the joy and bliss of internal purity, the three heavens of the second dhyāna are concluded. Third, the three heavens of the third dhyāna are two [in terms of their nature].
First, a detailed explanation; second, a summary. The first [section] has three parts: first, the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven; second, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven;
third, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven. Regarding the first:

Ānanda, these devas and humans have perfected the light of their circles and mastered the resonance of sound; they reveal the wondrous through this resonance, giving rise to refined practice that penetrates tranquility.
Extinguishing pleasure—this class of beings is called the Parīttābha (Limited Radiance) devas.

These celestial beings still refer back to the aforementioned Ābhāsvara (Luminous) realm; by building upon the previous state of "inhaling and sustaining the circular radiance," they achieve the essence of the teaching.
Thus it is said that "the circular radiance achieves sound," meaning that the perfect radiance achieves sound as the teaching.
This is the essence. Building upon the preceding [explanation], it issues forth pure transformation; its application is inexhaustible. Hence it is said: "Unfolding sound to reveal the wondrous.
This means that by unfolding and emitting sound, one manifests the principle of transformation to achieve wondrous function.

According to this, while the first dhyāna leaves movement behind to seek stillness, and the second dhyāna relies on stillness to manifest movement—though it manifests movement based on stillness—at the time of movement, it cannot avoid contradicting stillness. Thus, it issues forth...

The practice was still coarse. Now, having reached this heaven, the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) becomes increasingly profound; movement does not contradict stillness. Therefore, it is said that "the practice develops into refined conduct.

Based on this, both movement and stillness are simultaneously extinguished—this is called "quiescent extinction" (*śānti-nirvāṇa*). The bliss of quiescent extinction is more subtle and superior than what preceded it.
However, because one has only just entered this realm, it is described as "penetrating. It is termed "Limited Purity" (*parītta-śubha*) because [it is characterized by] quiescence...
"Cessation" (*nirodha*) is termed "pure" (*śubha*) because its object is exclusively [the pure]. It is also tentatively termed "limited" (*parītta*) because its magnitude is restricted.
Furthermore, it is called "pure" in contrast to what precedes it, and "limited" in contrast to what follows it. Second, the Heaven of the Immeasurable Pure (*apramāṇa-śubha*).
When pure emptiness manifests before one, it triggers boundlessness; with the body and mind becoming light and tranquil, one achieves the bliss of cessation.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇaśubha*).
Although the preceding heavens also generally involve cessation, because the realm of purity has not yet vanished, they are still constrained by that very purity.
This is the purity of finite measure. Now, having reached this heaven, the power of meditative concentration becomes increasingly profound; thus, both the pure and the empty become void.

Therefore, it is said that "pure emptiness manifests before one. Once pure emptiness has manifested, one uses emptiness to induce purity, and purity and emptiness arise together, equaling the vast void in their measure.
Hence, it is called "inducing the boundless," meaning that the purity induced by emptiness is then without limit.

It is the limit (*anta*). Since purity has no limit, one’s own awakened awareness manifests such that body and mind are like a single speck of dust in the great void—without burden and without constraint;
hence it is called "light" and "peaceful. To distinguish this from the initial stage of pervasive quiescence, it is said to be "accomplished.
The designation "Immeasurable Purity" is made with reference to the boundlessness of its pure realm. Furthermore, as for the pure realm of the preceding heaven...
These deities possess the power of measurement; because the preceding deities lack such power, their spheres are not pure.

As for the three Śubhakṛtsna (Pervasive Purity) heavens, the world, body, and mind are entirely and perfectly pure. Having accomplished the qualities of purity, they manifest supreme reliance and return to the bliss of nirvāṇa.
This class of beings is called the Śubhakṛtsna devas.

Although the previous heavens were pure and their objects of perception were boundless, the substrate of existence (āśraya) was not yet entirely eliminated, because they still possessed both body and mind.
Because there is a world, and since body, mind, and world already exist, although this purity is immeasurable, it is not yet perfectly complete and pervasive.

Now, having reached this heaven, the power of meditative concentration becomes even deeper; thus, together with all bodies, minds, and worlds, they are obliterated into a single essence, becoming vast and free from all admixture.
Therefore, it is called "all-encompassing purity. "Pure virtue" refers to the virtue of absolute purity.
Since it has already become perfectly pervasive, it is called "accomplishment. As for the pleasure of the outflows (*sāsrava*), it reaches its ultimate limit here;

because one realizes its own excellence as something worthy of reliance, it is said that "the supreme refuge is manifest. Yet, being unaware that it still belongs to the realm of outflows, one proceeds to abide therein without relinquishing it.

Therefore, it is said that one returns to the bliss of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*). If we were to combine the preceding two stages to distinguish their relative superiority and inferiority:

the first is the initial penetration, like finding the path; the second is the actual accomplishment, like entering the gate; and the present stage is already perfected, like ascending into and entering the hall.

The distinction between their shallow and deep levels is clearly discernible. As for the designation "Universal Purity" (*Śubhakṛtsna*), this refers to the fact that its pure objective realm is perfectly pervasive.

(Question: Regarding the six heavens of the desire realm, according to the passage on *samādhi*, they seem like the adornments of a bodhimanda; according to the passage on *dhyāna*, they seem like the two gradual stages of "carving away the nature.

Since entering the form realm, we have discussed this up to this point: according to *samādhi*, it seems like the concentration and wisdom of the bodhimanda; according to *dhyāna*, it seems like the deep cultivation through successive stages. Furthermore, *nirvāṇa* is translated as "quiescent extinction" (*jīmíè*), yet the exhaustion of fetters is also called "the manifestation of quiescent extinction.

Why is this quiescent extinction so vastly different in quality from that [of the heavens]? Please explain the profound reason for this, so that we may avoid practicing erroneously. (Answer: An excellent question! This is exactly what I wished to say. According to the previous Buddha’s instruction in the passage on *samādhi*, he said: "You all must resolutely resolve to attain Bodhicitta. Toward the Buddhas..."

To attain the wondrous samādhi, one must not give rise to weariness; one should first clarify the two definitive meanings regarding the initial aspiration for enlightenment. This shows that a person who practices correctly must first resolve upon bodhicitta and rely upon true samādhi, employing the mind of non-arising and non-extinction.

It is like a skilled goldsmith who, wishing to offer a vessel to the Supreme Deity, relies on a fine furnace and hammer to fashion a vessel from gold; what was initially made is already precious, yet once completed, it becomes an even more honored vessel.

This refers to the exhaustion of all fetters, where so-called "quiescence" (jīmè) manifests before one. That nirvāṇa is translated as "quiescence" (jīmè) is precisely this point. Now, the previous statement that "people of the world do not seek the eternal" means they do not resolve upon bodhicitta. Furthermore, the statement that "without relying on dhyāna, there is no wisdom" means they do not rely on true samādhi.

This is ignorance. Moreover, since the cause for birth in the heavens begins with pure thought (*saṃjñā*), one must not employ a mind subject to arising and ceasing when it is a mind beyond arising and ceasing that is required. It is like a clumsy cook who, wishing to satisfy a peasant, uses a cracked cauldron and stove to prepare rice out of sand; from the start, this was never the essence of rice, and through kalpas of dust-like time, it remains nothing but hot sand.

What is called "clarity and awakening" in the First Dhyāna and what is called "tranquil extinction" (*śānti*) in the Third Dhyāna are precisely this. Because one recognizes this depth, one will naturally avoid erroneous cultivation. Question:

Since the path ahead has already been mistaken, how can one rectify the practice? Answer: Within the Heaven of Merit and Love (*Puṇyaprasava*), there are two diverging paths. If one follows the Path of Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) and ascends through the stages of Non-returner (*Anāgāmin*), transcending the realm of space and exhausting all emptiness, both will result in the attainment of the correct fruit. Thus, the previous cultivation was not without some slight benefit.

If one lacks right mindfulness and fails to return to the ultimate emptiness, remaining deluded and leaking, one will enter the cycle of transmigration; thus, all past efforts will have been in vain. This is the distinction between cultivating what is wholesome and what is unwholesome. Question: In this world, body and mind are entirely perfect and pure.

"What distinguishes my emptiness from the emptiness of dharmas? He replied: "The two types of emptiness are realized through awakening; the two types of purity are suppressed through conceptualization. A difference of a hair's breadth leads to a loss of a thousand miles; they must be distinguished. Thus ends the clarification of the distinctions.
Second, the summary:
Ānanda, these three superior practitioners possess great conformity; their bodies and minds are at ease, and they attain immeasurable bliss.
Although they have not yet truly attained the genuine *samādhi*, because they are fully endowed with joy within a state of mental composure, this is called the third dhyāna.

These three superior streams should be understood as being even more excellent than the preceding ones. The first is called "conformity" (*ānulomika*) because it marks the initial penetration, like finding a path free from obstacles.
The second is called "peaceful security" (*kṣema*) because it constitutes actual accomplishment, like entering a gate free from dangers and difficulties.
When the third stage is perfected, it is called "attaining bliss. This is like ascending to the hall and entering the inner chamber; one dwells therein and constantly enjoys its benefits.

Furthermore, regarding the term "great" used in accordance with the context, this distinguishes [this state] from the Light-Sound Heaven (*Ābhāsvara*), whose practice has not yet been refined; for while they may possess a minor degree of compliance, it is not yet "great.

Regarding the term "peaceful and secure," the phrase "body and mind" distinguishes this from the initial attainment of the Minor Purity (*Parīttābha*) and the first entry into cessation (*nirodha*); for although the body may already be at peace, [the mind is not yet fully so].

Because the mind has not yet become obscured, the bliss obtained is said to be "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*); this distinguishes it from the "Immeasurable Purity" (*Apramāṇa-śubha*), for its bliss can still be measured.
As for the bliss of the "Universal Purity" (*Śubhakṛtsna*), there is nothing that can distinguish it;

therefore, it is universally distinguished as being neither primary nor true. Although it is neither primary nor true, worldly bliss reaches its ultimate limit therein; hence it is called the "mind of peace and security."
The perfection of joy within the middle [dhyāna] is the mind of tranquility, which is precisely the mind of the third dhyāna.

In the first and second dhyānas, because one is free from hindrances and excels therein, it is called the "pure mind. In the third dhyāna, because one attains the excellence of bliss, it is called the "tranquil mind.

Furthermore, in the first dhyāna, one rejoices because one is free from the suffering and affliction of the desire realm; in the second dhyāna, one rejoices because one is free from the anxiety and longing of the first dhyāna. Upon reaching...
In the third dhyāna, even those two types of joy (*prīti*) are absent; one perceives only bliss (*sukha*), and thus it is called "peaceful" (*kṣema*).
Although one perceives only bliss, within that state of peace there is also a sense of self-contentment—a joy that is not coarse. This is certainly not something that can be known by ordinary people;
therefore, it is specifically characterized as being fully endowed with joy (*prāmodya*) to manifest the excellence of its bliss. (2)
Above the first dhyāna and below the fourth dhyāna, one attains the name of the third dhyāna, which possesses five factors of merit:

equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*). Among the nine stages, it is called the stage of sublime bliss free from joy (*niḥprītika-sukha-bhūmi*).

This is because one has abandoned the coarse, fluctuating joy of the previous two dhyānas—which is easily perceived as being like suffering or grief—and has attained the natural tranquility of the third dhyāna itself.
Because the subtle marks are hidden and their wondrous bliss difficult to know.

This concludes the three heavens of the Third Dhyāna. Fourth, the Nine Heavens of the Fourth Dhyāna. (Wenling says: There are nine heavens in the Fourth Dhyāna in total; however, as for the realms of retribution in the Fourth Dhyāna, there are only three heavens. The fourth, the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), is a separate opening from the third, the Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*).

Beyond these, there are further five Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) heavens, which are separately cultivated by sages and worthies through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Because they all equally enter the dhyāna of equanimity (*upekṣā*), they establish their dwelling places within the same category of the mind of equanimity. 2. 1.

There are four external heavens in total. Regarding the five heavens of the non-returners (anāgāmin), there are two parts: first, a detailed explanation of the first two; second, a general summary. Within the first four, there are:

first, the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava); second, the Heaven of Merit-Love (Vṛhatphala); third, the Heaven of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala); and fourth, the Heaven of Non-Perception (Asaṃjñisattva). First: [The Heaven of Merit-Born]
Ānanda, furthermore, there are gods and humans whose causes for suffering—bodily and mental oppression—have already been exhausted.

Since pleasure is not permanent and will inevitably perish after a time, they simultaneously and instantaneously relinquish both the mind of suffering and the mind of pleasure. The coarse and heavy characteristics are extinguished, and the nature of pure merit arises.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Birth of Merit (Puṇyaprasava-deva).

Furthermore, O deva and humans, although the fourth dhyāna is indicated here, the narrative of its causes originally derives from the third dhyāna. In the first dhyāna, one is already free from suffering and distress;
in the second dhyāna, one is further free from anxiety and worry. Therefore, it is said that body and mind are not oppressed. In the first dhyāna, the various outflows (*āsrava*) are unmoving;
in the second dhyāna, the coarse outflows have already been subdued. Therefore, it is said that the causes of suffering are exhausted. This reveals that within the third dhyāna alone...

There is sublime bliss (*sukha*) and subtle outflow (*āsrava*). (The preceding text states: "Superior support manifests" refers to sublime bliss; "returning to the bliss of cessation" refers to subtle outflow.

Regarding the statement that "bliss is not permanent," it means that as the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) becomes increasingly profound, one further realizes that even the bliss of the third dhyāna is not permanent.

When the merit of one's karma is exhausted, it will inevitably perish after a long time. For this reason, one simultaneously subdues both the mind that dwells in the absence of suffering and the mind that dwells in bliss.

They are eliminated; therefore, it is said that they are abandoned all at once and simultaneously. This is precisely because the simultaneous abandonment of the two minds is termed the "extinction of the signs of heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*), for when these two minds are mutually dependent, they constitute the very nature of heaviness.
Regarding the phrase "the nature of pure merit arises": when the mind of relinquishment is unmoving, it is itself the nature of pure merit.
Because this concentration (*samādhi*) briefly manifests, it is termed "arising. As for the conclusion that it is named "merit-arising," it is essentially...
They are named for their birth from the nature of pure merit. Second are the gods of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*).
Their minds of equanimity are perfectly integrated and their resolute conviction is pure; within unobstructed merit, they attain sublime conformity that extends to the furthest reaches of the future.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Bliss through Equanimity (Pramoditā).
Although in the higher realms one simultaneously and suddenly abandons both the minds of pleasure and pain, one has not yet escaped the presence of subject and object;

thus, the mind of equanimity still possesses limitations and obstructions. Upon reaching this heaven, the meditative absorption of equanimity becomes even deeper, such that subject and object are forgotten. Therefore, it is called the "mind of equanimity."
"Perfect fusion. Within this perfect fusion, the mind of relinquishment is understood with complete clarity; this is called "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*).
To maintain this mind so that neither subject nor object may again give rise to conceptual thought is called "purity. Regarding the two phrases on "merit":
since the mind of relinquishment is perfectly fused, infinite, and unimpeded, the pure merit it evokes naturally should likewise be without obstruction or limitation.
According to this, it is clearly superior to what preceded it; thus, pure merit is now being produced.

Since it is said that "resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) is purified," one should naturally neither dwell upon nor cling to this merit that is free from obstruction. Therefore, it is called "attaining wondrous conformity" (*sūkṣmānukūla*); "wondrous" refers to excellence.
This means that regarding the subsequent "Extensive Fruit" (*bṛhatphala*), one has already been able to skillfully conform to and cultivate it. To the end... [text truncated]
Regarding "the limit of the future" (*āyatana-koṭi*): this refers to investigating the mind of relinquishment to see what its ultimate boundary in the future may be.
It does not mean that one can exhaustively reach the very end of the future through effort; rather, it is simply that the literal phrasing should not be allowed to distort the intended meaning.

Furthermore, the primary fruit of this heaven consists solely of pure merit without obstruction, whereby one attains sublime conformity. Moreover, it serves as a skillful means (*upāya*) for the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) heaven. If one were to exhaustively investigate the future...
The future limit (*āyatyanta*) is further a skillful means for the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*). Therefore, it is said below that this heaven has two diverging paths.
Regarding the designation "Loved by Merit" (*Puṇyaprasava*), there are two meanings: first, pure merit is unobstructed and is thus lovely and desirable;
second, having already attained pure, unobstructed merit, its fruit is vast, superior, and sublime. This is the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*).
