Dwelling on the side of Mount Sumeru, they are able to manifest bodies of various sizes within the realm of desire according to their will;
such is their class. Because their emotional attachments are heavy, they are demoted and consequently experience birth from a womb, for the womb arises due to the presence of emotion.

Since its lower region borders the sun and moon, and its lower part adjoins the human realm, and because its sentient beings possess desires similar to those of humans, it is subsumed under the human destiny (*manuṣya-gati*).
The three [upper regions] are subsumed under the heavens of miraculous birth (*upapāduka-deva*). (The former is superior.)
There are asura kings who uphold the world; their power penetrates all things and they are fearless, able to contend for authority with the Brahma King, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
These asuras, through their transformations, are subsumed within the realm of celestial beings.
This type does not emerge from the aforementioned causes; examining it through its effects, it appears to have come from among the human realm.

Because humans possess great merit and virtue, they ought to be reborn in the heavens; however, due to a heavy preoccupation with victory and defeat, they engaged in the enterprise of contending for kingship and plotting hegemony, clinging to the merit of establishing boundaries and dividing lands.
When their affairs did not accord with their wishes, anger and jealousy became bound within their hearts, and thus [they experienced this retribution].

He becomes a King of the Asuras; his karmic reward is equal to that of the devas. He is moved by the great fortune found among humans, yet his nature is inclined toward strife and contention, and his mind is driven by the desire for victory over others.

Because his ambition to contend for kingship and seek hegemony remains unfulfilled, and his habit of dividing borders and carving out territories still persists, he is thus moved to grasp and maintain the world.
The *Zhengmai* states: "As for 'grasping and maintaining the world,' he is also able to drive [it]."

They employ spirits and deities to bring calamity or fortune upon the human realm. This intention can be seen in the *Mayūra-jātaka*, which contains the account of the punishment meted out by an asura.
I, the humble writer, maintain that while the two characters for "world" (*jagat*) convey a general sense, their specific meanings differ;
for each of the seven destinies possesses its own world and its own sovereign who presides over it. Now, since he has become a king of the asuras, that which he presides over must be...
This refers to the world of the asuras. Those whose power penetrates all and who are fearless possess the power of supernormal faculties that penetrate everything without obstruction;
from the heavens above to the earth below, they have nothing to fear. This is also brought about by their possession of great merit and a courageous mind.
Regarding those who can equal them, the *Abhiṣeka* states: "The Brahmā King is the lord of the trichiliocosm; Śakra [is the lord of the desire realm]..."
The Honored One among the thirteen heavens is the sovereign over the Four Heavenly Kings and the four continents; each has his specific office.

The asuras are not included among them, yet out of envy they give rise to contention, desiring to usurp their authority. Thus they come at times to wage war. Furthermore, citing scriptural evidence, it is said:
when the asuras first come to battle, they first encounter the four heavenly deities, then the other scattered devas, and finally the Four Heavenly Kings. The power of the Four Kings—
The enemy could not prevail. He was then about to report this to the Lord of Devas (Śakradevendra), but the power of the Lord of Devas was insufficient to oppose him.
Thereupon, he successively petitioned for aid from the heavens above, down to the Brahmā King, who descended to assist him from heaven. However, he has not specified which sūtra this refers to;

it must surely be based on some particular vision. Nevertheless, since such beings are able to contend for power with Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings, they must belong to both the Form and Desire Realms.
All must possess their own corresponding spheres of experience (*sabhāga-viṣaya*). Because the power of their merit is great, they do not undergo birth from a womb;

rather, having merely departed from a human body of retribution, they immediately manifest an illusory form as an *asura*. Therefore, it is said that they exist through transformation (*nirmāṇa*), for they are manifested and separated [from their former state].
Since their meritorious retribution resembles that of the gods, they are subsumed under the celestial realm (*devagati*). Alternatively, because their dwelling place is adjacent to...
Celestial palaces. As stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*: "Those with great power and vast merit dwell amidst the mountains of various forms (*nānā-lakṣaṇa-parvata*).
These are included among the four types of moisture-born animals (the inferior).
Ānanda, there is another class of inferior asuras who are born in the heart of the great ocean and dwell at the mouth of a subterranean cavern.
They roam through the void by day and return to their watery abodes by night. These asuras, due to their moisture-nature, are categorized within the realm of animals.
This, too, does not go beyond the aforementioned causes. Examining it through its effects, it appears they have come from among the animal realm.
For instance, within the animal realm there are birds that take refuge and receive the precepts, and dragons that raise clouds and bring rain;

though they possess the causal conditions of virtuous karma, their animalistic habits have not yet been eliminated. Consequently, their retribution manifests as the inferior state of an asura, rather than being a separate category in its own right.
This refers to the inferior asuras. They are not limited to the single class of moisture-born beings; other modes of birth are even more numerous.
These moisture-born ones are but a portion of the inferior category; thus they are called "inferior.

This is because, in terms of their causal origins, they do not equal the [other] three superior classes, and in terms of their resultant abodes, merit, and spiritual power, they all fall short of the three superior classes. If one were to compare them with...

Regarding the comparison of superiority and inferiority among the aforementioned three pairs, those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) are like kings; those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*) are like ministers; those born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*) are like commoners;
and these moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*) beings are like the slaves of asuras. As for "born in the heart of the great ocean," the "heart of the ocean" refers to the seabed;
it is merely spoken of in terms of the middle [depth]. Regarding "sinking into the mouth of a water-hole," the "water-hole" may be...
This refers to the Tailgate (Weilu). However, according to secular classics, the Tailgate is located to the east of the Azure Sea and is the name of a river.

Now, it is called the "Heart of the Sea" (Haixin), seemingly because there is a distinct location at the bottom of the sea where water leaks out. Furthermore, these two phrases may also be divided into two categories:
for instance, due to the residual habit of the Golden-Winged Bird (Garuda) devouring dragons, it is caused to be born in the heart of the great ocean as a calamitous dragon (nielong).
Because they have not yet abandoned the residual habits of avoiding suffering, they are reborn at the mouths of underwater caves. Those who roam the void by day do so to provide their labor;
those who return to dwell in the water at night do so to rest from their toil. Thus, they are judged to be slaves of the asuras.
Although they consider the ocean to be superior and desire to associate with it, they are reborn there due to the presence of moisture, being produced by that very dampness.
This is because they share a common karmic affinity. Having come from among the animal realm, they still carry residual habits; therefore, they are subsumed within the destiny of animals.
Alternatively, their dwelling places border the realm of the nāgas, as the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:

"Those with little power and meager merit dwell at the bottom of the great ocean. (According to various sūtras and śāstras, the descriptions of the asuras' dwellings do not entirely coincide; however, only a Buddha can know them, and only a Buddha [can fully understand them]).

It is said that this [teaching] is likely beyond the reach of the mental capacity of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). For now, I shall explain it solely based on what is taught in the extant sutras, interpreting it according to the principle that cause and effect correspond to one another;

other matters will not be recorded here. This concludes the detailed explanation of the cycle of transmigration through the seven destinies. Third, answering the preceding questions in sequence, there are two parts:
first, answering the general question; second, answering the specific questions. The first part answers the general question concerning the seven destinies.

Ānanda, thus the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, seers and immortals, devas, and asuras—having minutely examined these seven realms, they are all but states of delusion, the characteristics of conditioned existence.
They undergo birth through false imagination and follow their karma through false imagination.

Within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind of non-action, they are all like flowers in the sky, fundamentally having no place of attachment. There is only this single unreality; there is nothing more.
The two characters "root" (gen) and "source" (xu) collectively refer to what has been explained above: the three evil destinies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals;
and the three virtuous destinies of humans, immortals (xian), and devas. In the conventional enumeration of the six destinies, there are no immortals; they are subsumed within the realm of the devas.

Because worldly people do not distinguish between humans, immortals, and devas, [the Buddha] spoke in accordance with worldly convention. Now, in this treatise, we discuss the seven destinies (*gati*);
therefore, he has distinguished them here. Generally, the asuras are placed after humans and devas when speaking according to the three grades of the good paths (*kuśala-mārga*).

Here, they are placed at the end because there are four destinies that are neither exclusively good nor exclusively evil. Thus, those who investigate the seven destinies in detail [should understand this].
He carefully investigated the fundamental causes of the seven destinies. Lack of awakening due to ignorance is called "obscurity"; giving rise to delusions and creating karma is called "sinking";
experiencing retribution according to karma is called "the various conditioned phenomena. The two phrases concerning "deluded thoughts" serve to explain the meaning of these conditioned phenomena:
they state that the division of destinies occurs solely through birth by means of deluded thoughts, and the cycle of transmigration likewise occurs solely through deluded thoughts following karma.
Since it is produced solely by deluded conceptualization, how could it be something conditioned? The fundamental mind is none other than the primordial *tathatā*.
What was previously called "the primordial *tathatā*" is precisely the true body of the Tathāgata’s attainment of Buddhahood;

therefore, it is said to be "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskṛta*). To be unobscured by deluded conceptualization is called "clarity"; to be unhindered by the seven realms of rebirth is called "perfection"; and to be unimpeded by karmic retribution—[is called "liberation"].

That which is transmigrated is called "the wondrous. It is precisely because one does not understand this mind that there are falsely the seven destinies. If one were indeed able to understand this, how could there be cyclic existence?
Therefore, it is said that all are like flowers in the sky; the intent here is to use empty space as a metaphor for the true mind.
The arising and ceasing of wild flowers is used as a metaphor for the transmigration through the seven realms of existence.
That which is fundamentally without attachment arises right where it is and perishes right where it is; how could there be any place of abiding?

Thus one knows that the seven realms are merely a single delusion, having no fundamental root or beginning from which they can be investigated. According to what Ānanda previously asked: "Does this path return to its original [source]?"
"Coming from existence" refers to its arising from the deluded habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of sentient beings;

the subsequent statement, "now it is said that birth arises from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and follows after karma," answers this by explaining that it arises from deluded habitual tendencies.

Furthermore, the statement, "it is merely a single falsehood, having no root or source," answers this by explaining that it does not exist from the beginning. These two responses address the previous specific questions (the previous specific questions concerning the hells).

As previously mentioned, although Ānanda asked specifically about the hells, he treated them as one example for all six [realms]. Therefore, the conclusion of the answer now proceeds by addressing all seven destinies.
"Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their original mind; they undergo this saṃsāra through immeasurable kalpas without attaining true purity.
This is entirely due to their compliance with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Conversely, by turning away from these three, they will instead give birth to the state of no-birth."

Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—these are known as the realm of ghosts; that which is nameless is the celestial realm. Where existence and non-existence oppose one another, the nature of saṃsāra arises.
If one attains the wondrous arousal of samādhi, then there is wondrous and eternal stillness; both existence and non-existence are absent, and even this absence of duality is extinguished.
Since there is as yet no abstaining from killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, how could one further follow after the acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct?

O Ānanda, if the three karmas are not severed, each has its own private tendencies. Because of these individual private tendencies, the collective sharing of these private tendencies has a fixed location that is not non-existent.
First, this also serves to resolve the preceding doubts. Regarding the phrase "these sentient beings," the Buddha also speaks of them collectively by way of the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*).

This is because he clearly knows that Ānanda’s question concerning the hells follows the pattern of the six destinies. Based on what Ānanda previously doubted, he asked: "The Buddha-body is truly real;
how can there still be such paths as those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, *asuras*, humans, and devas? Now...

The Tathāgata explains this by means of [the phrase] "failing to recognize one's original mind" and so forth. "Failing to recognize one's original mind" means not knowing the true reality of the Buddha-body (*buddhatva*).
Since one does not know the true reality of the Buddha-body, one naturally follows deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) according to karma and undergoes this cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
This is the reason why the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*) exist. Because the seven destinies exist, the cycle of birth and death continues without ceasing; therefore—
It is said that even after immeasurable kalpas, the evil realms are certainly impure, and the purity of the good realms is likewise not true.
Therefore, it is said that "true purity is not attained. This is because one fails to recognize the fundamental mind and ultimately remains within the realm of outflows (*āsrava*).
○ The following section clarifies how this follows from karma; it explains that the reason true purity is not attained is entirely due to conforming to and following along with killing and stealing.

Regarding sexual misconduct: among the ten non-virtuous actions, only killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are singled out because greed and the other [afflictions] belong to the category of mental delusions and are subsumed within the "conformity" [of the mind], while lying and the others belong to speech and manifest as the outward expression of one's own physical karma.
Since the primary cause for cyclic existence is the physical karma itself, those who turn away from these three [actions] recognize them as the causes of the evil realms and desire [to abandon them].
To contravene this is to give rise [to delusion]. "Giving rise" means gradually subduing and eliminating; by eliminating one portion of existence, one attains one portion of non-existence.
If one follows along until reaching total existence, then retribution will induce rebirth as a ghost or in hell; hence it is said that "those with names belong to the class of ghosts.
This is because the hells are also a category within the realm of hungry ghosts. If, however, one gives rise [to insight] and reaches total...

When there is no [existence], one is reborn in the higher realms; hence it is called the "Nameless Heavenly Realm" (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*). This is because it is entirely beyond anything that can be achieved by the heavens of the desire realm.
"Inclining" (*qīng*) means to usurp. Regarding "the existent and the non-existent incline toward one another":

this means that existence does not remain forever existent, for at times it is usurped by non-existence and gradually reaches the state of non-existence; non-existence does not remain forever non-existent, for at times it is usurped by existence...
Gradually tending toward existence, one revolves through the good realms—from the heavens down to the immortals and humans;
gradually tending toward non-existence, one revolves through the evil realms—from the hells down to the hungry ghosts and animals.
Thus, within the fundamental mind of non-action, inverted states continue in succession; therefore, it is said that the nature of saṃsāra arises.

Regarding "the cycle of rebirth accords with the nature": this is because it possesses the nature of conditioned arising and ceasing. "If one attains [this]" and below, the teaching is to cease the cycle.
"Miraculously giving rise to samādhi" means that without departing from the gates of the six sense organs, one directly perceives the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.

As for the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing: that which cannot be said to exist is called "wondrous" (miao); that which cannot be said not to exist is called "constant" (chang). This is in contrast to [dualistic] opposition.

Since both [existence and non-existence] are severed, the "middle" is not established either; this is called "quiescence. Now, since existence cannot exist, non-existence is not established in dependence upon existence;
since non-existence cannot be non-existent, existence is not established in dependence upon non-existence.

Therefore, it is said that both existence and non-existence are non-existent, meaning that both extremes of existence and non-existence are entirely absent. Since the two extremes are absent, the middle is not established in dependence upon those extremes.
Therefore it is said that "non-duality is also extinguished. This means that even the Middle Way of non-duality is extinguished along with all else.
From this point, purity reaches its ultimate limit, radiance penetrates everywhere, and tranquil illumination encompasses the void. Returning to observe the world, it is like a dream-event:

appearing according to conditions while being non-existent, yet not abiding in non-existence. Therefore it is said: "There is still no 'not killing,' 'not stealing,' or 'not committing adultery'; they appear according to conditions while existing."
Yet they do not abide in existence. Therefore it is said: "How could one further follow the acts of killing, stealing, and lust? This is that which does not revolve within the seven destinies;
thus the secret cause of the Tathāgata is ever present before one. [The text continues: "Ānanda, below this you should ask the question to receive the answer.
'The three karmas are not severed, each having its own private [nature]' means that the karmas are each different, and the retribution received is likewise..."
Each has its own private [karmic cause]. This answers Ānanda’s question regarding how each naturally initiates their respective karma and privately experiences its results.

Because of these individual privacies, there are "shared portions of various privacies," meaning that within these individual privacies, there are those whose karmas are identical who receive retribution together in one place; this constitutes the ground of shared portions among various privacies. This is also...

There are fixed locations; therefore, it is said that they are not non-existent. For example, among those in the hells, the lighter offenders are definitely reborn in the *antarā-kalpas* (intermediate hells), while the heavier offenders are definitely reborn in the *avīci* (uninterrupted) hell.

This answers Ānanda’s question regarding whether there are fixed locations. Having completed the sequential explanation of the preceding questions, the fourth section concludes with a summary and praise to demonstrate the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox.
Delusion arises spontaneously; its arising is without cause and cannot be traced. You must exert yourself in cultivation to attain Bodhi by eliminating the three delusions.
Even if you should acquire supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) without exhausting these three delusions, they will all be mundane, conditioned functions.
If habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not extinguished, you will fall into the path of Māra; though you wish to eliminate delusion, you will only redouble your falsehoods. Thus spoke the Tathāgata.
They are to be pitied. You have falsely created for yourself the fault that there is no bodhi; to speak thus is called speaking correctly.
If anyone else were to speak otherwise, they would be speaking as the Māra King speaks.

The first section reveals delusion and exhorts cultivation. Building upon the preceding point that although there are fixed locations for receiving retribution, when one investigates their remote origin, they all stem from a single moment of deluded movement, which transforms and gives rise to the objective realm of the *ālaya-vijñāna*. Therefore, it is said: "Arising spontaneously from delusion."
The single character "delusion" (wang) refers precisely to that initial thought, which is designated as ignorance (avidyā).
If one further investigates the source from which this ignorance arises, there is no other origin; therefore, it is said that the arising of delusion is without cause.
This is as previously stated: the nature of delusion has no substance and does not depend upon anything else. Since it does not depend on anything...
Based on this, the departure from thought is itself [the goal]; thus it is said that there is nothing to be sought or investigated. This is as previously stated:
"If one wishes to return to the True, once the True has been attained, even 'True' is no longer the True; such is the nature of True Suchness.

Since there is indeed nothing to be sought or investigated, one must proceed solely from the coarse toward the subtle, gradually subduing and eliminating [delusions]. Therefore, I instruct you to exert yourself in practice with the utmost diligence.
The term "practitioner" refers to one who practices the gradual subduing and elimination [of afflictions].
Since such gradual subduing and elimination are not easily attained, and one wishes to realize Bodhi, from where should one begin? Therefore, it is shown that one must eliminate the three delusions.

These three delusions refer specifically to lust, killing, and stealing. To be attached to and confused by these, failing to understand them, is what is termed "delusion. It is said that they must be eliminated.

This means that if one merely distances oneself from existence (*bhava*), it is not yet called "removal. One must reach the point where both existence and non-existence are absent, and even this absence of duality is extinguished;
only then is it called "removal. The section beginning with "not exhausting" [the afflictions] points out the faults and concludes with praise.

It states that if one does not exhaust the three delusions (*kleśa*), one will not only undergo the cycle of rebirth in the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*); even if one attains a semblance of realization through the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), [one will still fall].

Even with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one cannot transcend the world; because they have not yet achieved the wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), it is said that these are all worldly, conditioned functions (*saṃskṛta-kriyā*).
This is because habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not been extinguished and arise again in response to objects. Those of the highest grade will inevitably become demon kings (*mārāḥ*);
those of the middle grade will inevitably become subjects of Māra; and those of the lowest grade will inevitably become demonesses (*mārīcyaḥ*). Therefore, it is said that they fall into...
Regarding the path of Māra: when first beginning its cultivation, although one intends to eliminate delusion, once one has fallen into the path of Māra, one becomes doubly more hypocritical.
When the blessings of Māra are exhausted and karmic retribution manifests before one, the extreme suffering of Avīci is what one must return to experience for oneself.
For this reason, the Tathāgata calls such a person "one who is to be pitied. Yet, he also warns them most earnestly.
○ You have falsely cast aspersions, harbored doubts, and selected [yourself] as a demon. Based on what Ānanda previously doubted, he said: "The Buddha-body is truly real;
how can there still be the paths of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas? Now it is said: "You have falsely [assumed] yourself..."
This is not the fault of Bodhi; it merely refutes what is inappropriate in one's doubts.

The intent is to make [the interlocutor] realize that their own doubt is improper, thereby causing them to believe what the Buddha has taught. Thus, he shows that if someone were to speak in this way, it would be called "correct speech.
Conversely, if another were to say something such as, "It exists inherently from the beginning and is not summoned by karma," [that would be incorrect].
Since it contradicts the truthful word, one knows that this was spoken by the Mara King.

Thus, the Tathāgata, fearing that future generations would be deluded by Mara’s teachings and commit acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), provided this preliminary discernment and instruction.
This concludes the summary of the major sections, having thoroughly investigated the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*) to break through the obstacles within *śamatha*.
Second, a detailed examination of the five māras to break through the obstacles within samādhi, in three parts: first, the Tathāgata points out the māras and exhorts them to listen;
second, the assembly joyfully listens to the compassionate instruction; third, the Tathāgata explains it in successive order. The first consists of four sections.

First, turning back as the discourse was about to conclude; second, binding the discourse and identifying Māra; third, pointing out Māra to reveal his harm; fourth, admonishing the listeners and granting permission to teach.
Regarding the first:
at that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to leave the Dharma seat, he took up a seven-jeweled desk from his lion throne and turned toward the Purple Gold Mountain.
He then leaned back against his support and addressed the great assembly and Ānanda, saying:
"The seven realms of rebirth shall no longer revolve; the secret cause is free from hindrances. From this point on, samādhi can be cultivated and dhyāna easily accomplished.

My Buddha-mind is somewhat comforted, and my profound voice wishes to cease; therefore, it is said that he was about to conclude his session at the Dharma-seat. As for 'taking up the seven-jeweled desk,' this refers to..."
"Rising" refers to turning toward Mount Zijing and leaving one's seat; this is the sign that the Dharma-seat is about to conclude.
The "bed" is named after the lion because the lion represents fearlessness in preaching the Dharma; alternatively, it may be appropriate to represent the lion itself as the bed.
The "table" is named after the seven treasures because the treasures symbolize the universal benefit of the noble wealth; alternatively, one may use actual precious materials for it.

The small table is also appropriate. It represents the body of Tathāgata Zijin (Purple Mountain). His sixteen-foot golden form has a halo radiating in all directions, majestic and lofty like a mountain;
hence it is so named. As for "returning once more," it means returning after turning away. As for "leaning against," it means leaning upon the table and resting against the seat.
However, since he has already turned away from Mount Zijin and yet returns once more to lean against it, one fears that a demon might arise.
Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which obstruct the samādhi of reality, I wish to provide a detailed analysis.

I address the great assembly and Ānanda, saying that each person must recognize these subtle demonic activities so that they may be transmitted to the age of the Final Dharma; for Ānanda bears a heavy responsibility.
The second section explains the designation of Māra.
You who are still in training—whether pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas—today turn your minds toward great bodhi and supreme, wondrous enlightenment.
I have now taught the method for true cultivation. Yet you still do not recognize the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Regarding those subtle demonic activities:
previously, when the true Dharma was first established, it was announced to the entire assembly; here, however, he addresses the *śaikṣas* (those still in training) alone.

This is specifically for the sake of the *śaikṣas*, because the demons pose a grave threat to them, whereas the demons pose only a slight threat to the *aśaikṣas* (those beyond training), though they should also be included. You all—
Because it is subsumed under two characters: "turning the mind" means turning away from the mind of the Hīnayāna; "proceeding toward the Great" means heading toward the path of the Mahāyāna.

Since both the general request and the specific request previously mentioned involve the intention of turning away from the small vehicle and proceeding toward the great, and as they constitute a single assembly, there is no hindrance to speaking of them collectively in reference to today’s occasion.
Furthermore, within the Mahāyāna bodhi, there are distinctions between the provisional and the real, and between the partial and the complete; this is for the purpose of making such a distinction.

Because the powers are divided, it is called "unsurpassed wondrous enlightenment. To manifest that which the assembly aspires toward is precisely the ultimate, singular Buddha-vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the Perfect Teaching (*samyak-siddhānta*), which is the true realization.
*Śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna* are all methods for true cultivation, as has been fully clarified previously;
hence it is said, "I have now already explained. Based on this, there is a path for true cultivation—this is the unsurpassed wondrous [enlightenment].
One should awaken to that which is to be pursued. This is because in the preceding section there was the statement regarding the method for concluding the Dharma seat.
○ "You still" and below marks the subsequent lack of recognition of demonic activities. *Śamatha* is cessation within *samādhi*; *vipaśyanā* is contemplation within *samādhi*.

It is like the process of untangling the six knots, where the preceding and succeeding stages fully possess the meaning of both cessation and contemplation. Thus, it is the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Manifest before one, yet not recognized for what it is; therefore, it is called a "subtle demonic activity.

Since the Dharma assembly is about to conclude without having been analyzed, there is concern that [the practitioners] may still not have identified it. As future gatherings are not fixed, it would be better to point it out while seated;
thus, this is now clearly indicated. Below, it will be examined and analyzed in detail. Third, pointing to the demon to reveal its harm.
When demonic realms appear before you, you fail to recognize them; your purification of the mind is not correct, and you fall into false views.

Or perhaps it is your own *skandha*-māra, or a celestial *māra*, or you are possessed by a ghost or spirit, or beset by a *chī-mèi* (goblin); your mind lacks clarity, and you mistake a thief for your son.
Furthermore, within this state, you consider a small attainment to be sufficient—just as in the fourth dhyāna, where one who has heard nothing falsely claims to have attained it.

Having realized the state of sainthood (*ārya*), when his celestial retribution was exhausted and the signs of decline appeared before him, he slandered an Arhat and, having undergone subsequent existence, fell into the Avīci Hell.
The first two phrases of the initial [verse] cite his prior lack of recognition as the cause for falling into error. Next...
These two points: To claim that "washing the mind" is not the primary goal falls into false views.

Since the original purpose of practicing concentration (*samādhi*) is to wash the mind, failing to recognize demonic realms will obscure all correct views; even if one intends to wash the mind, one will not achieve its true correctness.
Failing to grasp what is correct, one will inevitably fall into the heterodox. As with the five *skandha*-demon realms described below, all arise from mistaking the heterodox for the correct;
these are all instances of false views. ○ From "Or perhaps you... onwards, he sequentially points out the demon realms;
however, it is not necessary to categorize them strictly according to the five *skandhas*. This is because within each of the five *skandhas* there are ten demons, and among those ten demons, some...
There are those who encounter only the demon of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*); there are those who, beyond the demon of the aggregates, also encounter the celestial demon (*deva-māra*);

there are those who, beyond the demon of the aggregates, further become possessed by ghosts and spirits; and there are those who, beyond the demon of the aggregates, further fall victim to mountain sprites and malevolent spirits.

For example, within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the first nine are like the *skandha-māra*, while the tenth is said to be "this is called a perverted mind that harbors goblins and demons," or being encountered by a celestial *māra* entering one's heart and belly.

Furthermore, within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*), the arising of inexhaustible compassion and so forth are all *skandha-māras*; by means of these, the *māras* of compassion and others enter one's heart and belly. And...
As for the "grief-demons" (*śoka-māra*) and so forth, it is uncertain whether they are celestial *māras* or *chimei* (mountain sprites).

This is especially true since the ninth [category] also mentions that the "ghost-heart" has long entered [them]. Thus, one knows that the *skandha-māras* pervade all fifty [categories], while among the celestial *māras*, ghosts, spirits, and *chimei*, there are those who possess [the afflictions] fully and those who do not; these are merely pointed out in general. This is the aforementioned...
What is called a demonic realm refers to that which is not clear within the mind; this is precisely a lack of recognition.

To mistake a thief for one's own son is to fall into perversion. These are spoken as metaphors. ○ Furthermore, regarding "descending to provide proof and falling into hell": as for those who are "within" it...

This also refers generally to the demon of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra*). As in the previous four [aggregates], there are all instances of speaking of having personally attained the state of a sage;
furthermore, within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), one even claims to have fully realized *bodhi*. These are all alike cases of being satisfied with a small attainment.
In one instance, he could not avoid the cycle of saṃsāra. Rather than being reproached for his mistaken practice, he instead slandered those with genuine realization;

thus, he was destined to undergo the extreme sufferings of the Avīci hell himself. Fearing that others might fall into doubt or error, the Buddha took this case as an example to provide a warning, saying, "It is like the bhikṣu who lacked learning in the fourth dhyāna," and so forth.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There was once a bhikṣu who followed his own mind in solitary cultivation..."

One who possesses extensive learning and wisdom, yet does not recognize the stages of the various dhyānas and the three realms, might attain the first dhyāna through cultivation and immediately claim it to be the first fruit (srotāpanna), continuing in this manner until they claim the fourth dhyāna to be the fourth fruit (arhat).

When their life is about to end, they perceive the signs of the intermediate state (antarābhava) and give rise to false views, slandering [the truth] by claiming there is no nirvana and that arhats are subject to rebirth. Due to these causes and conditions, they fall directly into the hells (niraya).
The "unlearned bhikṣu" mentioned here refers to a certain bhikṣu in the treatise who lacked extensive learning and wisdom, yet was designated as an "attainer of the fourth dhyāna.
That is to say, he had cultivated and attained the first through the fourth dhyānas, yet falsely claimed to have realized the state of an ārya.
That is to say, within the treatise it is stated that from the first fruit up to the fourth fruit, once the retribution of the heavenly realm has been exhausted;

within the treatise it is stated that when life is about to end, the signs of decay appear before one; within the treatise it is stated that one perceives the signs of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); within the treatise it is stated that those who slander Arhats will encounter future existence (*punarbhava*) in their bodies;
and within the treatise it is stated that those who slander the non-existence of Nirvana for Arhats and claim they are subject to rebirth will fall into the Avīci Hell. Thus it is said.

In the treatise, it is stated that by these causes and conditions one falls into the hells (*niraya*). This is essentially the same matter as in the sutra; the difference lies merely in the degree of detail.
[The Buddha] then instructed him to listen attentively, saying:
"You should listen with careful attention; I shall now analyze this for you in minute detail."
The instruction to "listen attentively" is because the works of Māra are subtle; they cannot be understood through coarse hearing alone.

The permission to "discern minutely" reflects a compassionate and earnest concern, fearing that a superficial explanation would be difficult to clarify. *Zi* (仔) means *zi* (孳), signifying unremitting diligence.
Zhengmo (正脈) says: "Not only does he permit discernment, but he further permits minute scrutiny, for one reason, [to guard against] Māra..."

The signs are profound and subtle, difficult to perceive; first, because the harm of Māra is so cruel as to be unbearable, the True Compassion (Bhagavān) has exerted himself to provide such detailed instruction.
After the Tathāgata had finished pointing out the Māras and admonishing the assembly to listen, the members of the second assembly joyfully listened to his compassionate teaching.
Ānanda rose together with those in the assembly who were fellow students; they joyfully prostrated themselves and waited in reverence for his compassionate instruction.

As for Ānanda’s rising: it was because he was startled and moved by hearing [the news of] the harm. That it was only the fellow students who did so: it was because Māra was particularly anxious on their behalf.
Because they had been granted permission to receive a detailed analysis, they joyfully prostrated themselves; having received the teaching, they listened with an open mind and a desire to hear.
I humbly await your compassionate instruction. The Tathāgata explains these three points in succession: first, causing awakening by revealing the origin;

second, discerning the characteristics to bring about recognition; third, following the ancients to provide a concluding exhortation. Regarding the first [of these], there are three parts: first, a general presentation of the root of delusion.
Second, each provides its own reason; third, failing to perceive this results in harm. First:
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly, saying: "You should all know that within the world of outflows, there are twelve classes of sentient beings."
The wondrous luminosity of original enlightenment, the perfect essence of the mind, is non-dual and indistinguishable from that of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Because of your deluded thoughts, you have erred regarding this principle; thus, ignorance and craving arise. From the pervasive delusion produced by these arising thoughts, the nature of space emerges.
As this delusion continues without ceasing, the world-systems come into being.
First, the True Nature that is the object of delusion is clarified. The treatise states that regarding demonic realms, those in training (śaikṣa) are particularly prone to them;

regarding the root of delusion, those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are equally deluded. Therefore, the Buddha told Ānanda and the great assembly: "The world of outflows" refers to the environmental retribution (adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka);

"the twelve classes of beings" refers to the personal retribution (ātmabhāva-vipāka). These arise distantly from afflictions and are proximately summoned by karma; hence they are called "with outflows. This serves to distinguish [them].

The nature of phenomena and the enjoyment body and land are not [subject to] outflows, for they are untainted. That which is free from the non-awakening of ignorance is called "original awakening" (*mūla-bodhi*).
That which is free from the confusion of deluded thoughts is called "wondrous clarity. That upon which all Buddhas rely for their emergence is called "the perfection of awakening.
That upon which worlds and sentient beings rely for their establishment is called the "essence of mind. Based on this, the arising of the mind is...

This is the Buddha-mind; therefore, it is said that it is non-dual and indistinguishable from the Buddhas of the ten directions. The passage beginning with "Because of you" (由汝) correctly clarifies the delusion that has arisen.

It arises proximately from the deluded thoughts regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and distantly from the ignorance (*avidyā*) regarding principle (*tattva*). Therefore, it says: "It is due to your deluded thoughts that you fail to realize the principle;
this is the fault. This is a general explanation; what follows is a detailed exposition. "Delusion" (*moha*) is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*). Because...
Because one does not know the Dharma of True Suchness as it truly is—namely, that it is one—it is called ignorance (*moha*).

Because one is not aware that the mind arises and possesses its thoughts, it is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*). As stated previously, "The nature of awareness is necessarily luminous; delusion takes this luminosity to be the act of awareness.
This refers precisely to the thought of desiring to clarify the essence of awareness as being craving. Due to this craving, the true and the false combine, and transformation arises.
The *ālayavijñāna* is called "origination" (*pravṛtti*). That is to say, because it relies on non-awakening (*avidyā*), the mind moves;

this is designated as "karma. As stated previously: "Awakening is not that which is illumined; by means of illumination, an object is established. This means that the establishment of an object constitutes origination.
"Origination" refers to the arising of the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of seeing, based upon the previously produced karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
What is meant by "because of movement, one is able to see"? As stated previously: "Since that which is perceived has been falsely established, your false capacity to perceive arises.

This refers to taking this false capacity as the source of arising and development. "Pervasive delusion" means that because of this capacity to see, the original, fundamentally awakened true mind becomes entirely obscured;
one no longer perceives true awakening, but sees only a stubborn void. This is why it is said: "Thereupon, there is [the world]."
Emptiness. As the preceding verse states: "From delusion, space arises. Regarding the phrase "the transformation of delusion does not cease":

this means that by confronting emptiness with one's vision, one becomes further confused and bewildered; yet, one again gives rise to the mind that transforms delusion, continuing without interruption.

Consequently, within that emptiness, one perceives the appearance of form and characteristics. This is called the arising of the world. As stated previously: "Relying on emptiness, [the world] is established."
This refers to the world-system. This emptiness and this realm are discussed here specifically in terms of the subtle characteristics of the land;
sentient beings are not mentioned because the cause for agitating Māra lies solely in the shaking and splitting of the land, which has no bearing upon sentient beings.

Furthermore, it is not said that coarse appearances [cause this], because coarse appearances are produced by karma and belong to the realm of individual karma; they result from deluded thoughts regarding phenomena.
Subtle appearances of affliction manifest and belong to the realm of commonality; they result from ignorance regarding principle.

When the realm of individual karma vibrates, it is insufficient to cause demonic interference, for it is merely one's own perception of individual karma. Only when the realm of commonality fractures is it sufficient to cause demonic interference.
Because they are seen in common by those of the same class (*sabhāga*), there are three reasons for each of the two: first, the reason for being moved by Māra; second, the reason for becoming Māra;
and third, the reason for transcending Māra. Regarding the first of these, there are three parts: first, receiving and manifesting the delusions of the realms.
Second, he shows the realm of dhyāna; third, he moves and transforms māras. Regarding the first:
these lands of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, are all established through deluded, stubborn, and false conceptualization, rather than being free from outflows (anāsrava).

"You should know that empty space arises within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky; how much more so, then, are all worlds contained within empty space?
If even one among you were to give rise to true realization and return to the source, this emptiness of the ten directions would entirely vanish and dissolve.
How could the lands existing within that emptiness not tremble and shatter?"
The initial "first" (*chū*) receives the preceding section by direct manifestation; thus, the character "then" (*zé*) closely connects with the text above.
"The ten directions" refers to the realm of the homogeneous portion (*sabhāgatā*). There are two meanings for "dust-motes": first, as a metaphor, it reveals the vastness of the lands;

second, regarding their substance, they are composed of dust-motes. If one discusses the homogeneous portion, the metaphorical sense is more primary. As the passage on the deluded vision of the homogeneous portion states: "Sahā..."
The worlds, as well as all the impure realms throughout the ten directions, are equally this enlightened, luminous, and untainted wondrous mind;
they are merely the illusory conditions of a disease. Since these realms pervade the ten directions, their number—equal to that of motes of dust—is not considered excessive.

If one takes the impure aspects, it is also appropriate to speak in terms of substance, for sentient beings, due to their unawakened attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), calculate them to be mere motes of dust.
It is established. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Suppose, for example, that the trichiliocosm were ground into fine dust.
Since the world can be broken down, its substance consists of these fine particles; this is what is being considered. Thus, both meanings coexist.

"You may take and use them as you please. That which is not untainted (*anāsrava*) is precisely that which is tainted (*sāsrava*), because there is a distinction between negation by exclusion (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*) and affirmation by inclusion (*vidhi*).
"All are established by deluded, stubborn conceptualization" means that due to pervasive delusion, there is stubborn emptiness;

as stated previously, "the arising of pervasive delusion" results in the existence of the nature of space. Due to the transformation of delusion through conceptualization, there is the establishment of the world-system.
As stated previously, "the transformation of delusion never ceasing gives rise to worlds. The meaning of this world being illusory can already be seen from this.
○ One should know that what follows uses emptiness as a metaphor for the realms. All sentient beings take empty space to be vast;
yet now it is said that [the world] is born within your mind. This indicates that the fundamental awakened true mind still lies beyond empty space.
The previous statement, "emptiness arises within great enlightenment," refers precisely to this meaning. Furthermore, all sentient beings collectively reckon that empty space is indestructible;
yet now it is said to be "like a fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity. Here, "vast clarity" (tàiqīng) refers to the reaches of the heavens.
According to the secular classics, the heavens are composed of pure qi and occupy the highest position; thus, they are designated as the "Great Clarity" (Taiching).
A single fragment of cloud is but a drifting cloud. A drifting cloud is exceedingly empty and consists of only a single piece, yet it is further dotted upon the Great Clarity.
How vast and yet how minute! How could it possibly endure for long? Using this as a metaphor for emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one can see that emptiness is easily destroyed.
If even emptiness is easily destroyed, how much more so the various worlds, which exist within that very emptiness?
Is not the meaning of their illusory nature made all the more evident? What was said previously regarding "a single bubble arising on the ocean" is likewise largely identical to this principle.
You all must understand that the following citations will necessarily undergo transformation. If there were birth, all would be proven; however, the realm of space has completely dissolved.

Since the subsequent passage speaks of "the land," it refers merely to its trembling and splitting apart; therefore, it speaks only in terms of a single person. To "give rise to the truth and return to the source" refers precisely to the practice and realization of untying the knots, as it is said:
"Entering the stream, one loses the objects of perception; movement and stillness do not arise; the faculties and their objects are both liberated. Awareness...

The mind alone is revealed; this is called the manifestation of truth. If one can further realize that the perceived object is empty, and that the emptiness which perceives it is extinguished, then with the cessation of both arising and ceasing, quiescent extinction manifests before one. This is termed "returning to the source.

When returning to the source, there is no delusion, and only then does empty space dissolve and perish, for empty space exists only because of delusory ignorance. As stated previously: "Arising and pervading delusion, there is empty space."

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is precisely this. Question: The Buddha attained enlightenment long ago, yet empty space still remains. How can the meaning of "dissolution" or "extinction" be reconciled with this? Answer:
What is called "dissolution" refers simply to the state where all is emptiness and all is reality (*tattva*). One who realizes it perceives the reality and does not perceive the emptiness;
thus, in terms of its meaning, it is called "dissolved. If one has not yet realized it, they continue to perceive the emptiness, just as [the people] did when seeing the *Lotus Sūtra*.

The burning of pure vision should be understood by analogy with this meaning. However, since the realized one perceives neither emptiness nor the elements, they have simply removed one portion from within the common objective field.
At that time, ordinary beings must necessarily perceive it as being torn asunder; therefore, he counters with the question, "How can there be emptiness?
etc., intending to demonstrate that there is absolutely no [element] that does not undergo transformation.
This is the principle. Question: Those who have realized [the truth] do not see emptiness (*śūnyatā*), yet those who have not yet realized it continue to see emptiness without change.

Those who have realized [the truth] do not see the world-system (*dhātu*), but for what reason do those who have not yet realized it see the world-system as quaking and splitting apart? Answer: Emptiness is fundamentally formless.
To remove even a single portion of it is due to a lack of awakening. It is like ten lamps illuminating a room; if one lamp is removed, the remaining nine lights [still shine].
It remains all-pervasive; since the realm possesses form, if even one part were removed, it should undergo change. It would be like ten streams of water poured together into a single vessel:
if one stream of water were removed, the water in the entire vessel would necessarily be stirred. This is an inevitable logical consequence.
One should not raise objections. These two causes demonstrate the realm of dhyāna:

when you practitioners cultivate dhyāna and adorn the samādhi, the minds of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the various stainless Great Arhats will penetrate in perfect harmony, becoming profoundly still and lucid at that very spot.
"You who cultivate dhyāna and adorn samādhi," he said, "you who wish to practice dhyāna in order to traverse the stages of sagehood must first adorn the realm of samādhi;
that is to say, you must untie the six knots and transcend the three voids."
If this faculty is first liberated and one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), then the essence of the mind manifests before one.
This is in perfect accord with the principle of the emptiness of persons realized by the novice Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the great Arhats free from outflows.
If one further reaches the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness, one achieves liberation through phenomena (*dharma-vimukti*) and is liberated from phenomena.
Once both are empty and non-arising, one will be profoundly still in that very place, becoming entirely identical with the Buddha-realm;
this is precisely the removal of one portion from within the common realm. Third, due to the demon of fluctuation.
All the Māra kings, spirits, ghosts, and ordinary devas saw their palaces collapse and split apart for no apparent reason. The great earth quaked and cracked open;
all creatures of water, land, and air were struck with terror. Ordinary beings, shrouded in darkness, did not perceive this transformation.
Although they had all attained the five supernormal powers—with the sole exception of the exhaustion of outflows—they remained attached to these worldly defilements. How [could they have known]?
This causes you to be torn asunder at that place; therefore, when you are in samādhi, ghosts, spirits, celestial Māras, *māṅliang*, and *yingjing* demons all come together to harass you.
At first, the Māras and others see the transformation.
All the Māra kings—referring to the Lord of the Desire Realm (*Kāmadhātu-pati*)—are meant here; it does not refer to the subjects of Māra or the Māra-demons.

"Women" refers to those who lead groups and include their attendants. "As well as ghosts and spirits" includes powerful ghosts and spirits, as well as flying yakṣas, earth-walking rākṣasas, and so forth.
"Ordinary worldly devas" includes those of the six heavens of desire and the four dhyāna heavens, as well as non-Buddhists and the gods of the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva).
However, although demons and spirits possess the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā), they cannot know [the Buddha's mind] for this reason.
This was before it had actually occurred; thus, they saw only their own palaces collapsing and cracking for no apparent reason.
The great earth shook violently, and ordinary beings were struck with alarm and cried out: "It is not only the palaces of demons and spirits that are collapsing;
even this entire great earth is trembling and splitting apart! Those who travel by water fled to the water, those who travel by land fled to the land, and those who fly took to the sky.

Regarding their movements: although there are three types of movement, they all reside upon the earth. Since the earth has now quaked and split apart, the sentient beings within these three realms of movement would naturally run about in disorder, fly about in disorder, and sink down in disorder;
hence it is said that "there are none who are not struck with alarm. To be "struck with alarm" (*jingjie*) is the appearance of being terrified and ill at ease.
Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) lack the wisdom of self-awakening and the clarity of foresight; therefore, they are called "obscured" (*hun*).
"Darkness. Because of this obscurity, one fails to realize that one is being shifted by external objects, leading to the propagation of erroneous and false teachings.
This includes such claims as "the Yin and Yang have lost their proper measure" or "the divine turtle moves its eyes," all of which are examples of this.

○ Regarding the phrase "those demons and others come to cause affliction": "those" refers specifically to Māra kings, ghosts, spirits, and the like. They cultivate tainted dhyāna and develop tainted supernormal powers.

Therefore it is said that they all obtain [it]. Because this is *sāsrava* (with outflows), there are only five types, as the *āsravakṣaya-abhijñā* (the supernormal power of the destruction of outflows) is excluded from among the six *abhijñās*.
Since the destruction of outflows is absent, one would naturally remain attached to these worldly afflictions (*rajas*) and not seek liberation.
How could you allow them to spontaneously attain the Way while simultaneously shattering their very foundation? This would be something they themselves would not accept. Therefore...

Building upon the preceding point that [the practitioner] cannot endure being torn asunder, this section explains the meaning of "arising to cause affliction. Ghosts, spirits, and celestial Māras specialize in afflicting and harming those engaged in correct cultivation.
The reason ordinary worldly devas (*pṛthagjana-deva*) are not mentioned is that although they may witness such rending and tearing, they do not engage in acts of affliction or harm.
*Wǎngliǎng* (wraiths) and *yāojīng* (sprites) are either dispatched by demons or ghosts; the term *qiān* signifies "all" or "every one."
They say, "You are currently in samādhi. They then see you trembling and tearing apart;
fearing that you will surely be destroyed in the future, they all come to proclaim lustful and delusive teachings to disturb and confuse you, so that your samādhi cannot be accomplished.
This concludes the first cause for the arousal of Māra. Second, the two causes for the accomplishment of Māra: first, Māra is inherently without malice; second, the mind is deluded.
Thus it was accomplished. First:

Although those various Māras may be filled with great rage, within their defilements and within your wondrous awakening, they do not touch one another at all—like wind blowing upon light, or like a blade cutting through water.
You are like boiling water; they are like solid ice. As the warmth gradually approaches, the ice will surely melt.
It will not take long before it is destroyed and perishes. To rely merely on one's own spiritual power is to be but its guest.
Since the other has already come to cause disturbance, anger naturally arises; furthermore, because it destroys his palace, this anger is no ordinary one, and thus it is called "great.
As for the word "although," it indicates that it does not harm me, but rather causes damage to him. That dust—
"To labor within" clarifies that one is still amidst the dharma of arising and ceasing. "Within your wondrous awakening" clarifies that one has already abided within the principle of true permanence.
Because one seeks to destroy true permanence by means of arising and ceasing, it is said: "It is like wind blowing upon light."
Because one wishes to disturb the concentrated mind with anger, it is said that "it is like a sword cutting water, such that they do not touch at all.

Just as light does not receive a blow and water does not receive a cut, this is a metaphor for the true and constant concentrated mind; even when encountering the afflictions of Māra, it remains uninjured.
Furthermore, regarding "within your wondrous enlightenment," it refers to the true and constant wisdom being perfectly luminous—perfectly luminous.
Therefore, it is like boiling water. Those within the realm of afflictions (*kleśa*) hold fast to views of arising and ceasing;

because they hold fast to them, it is like the freezing of solid ice. Just as the warm vapor of the boiling water gradually approaches the ice, the cold that binds the ice will not last long before it melts away.
This is a metaphor for how true wisdom, when it illuminates Māra, naturally possesses the power to destroy him.
[This is] merit. When false attachments confront the Truth, they naturally lack the power to endure for long and instead cause self-injury.
Based on this, even if Māras employ a hundred stratagems to harass you, they can do no harm to you, relying merely upon their supernatural powers;
even if they become greatly enraged, they are but guests who will depart before long. Thus, it is up to the practitioner alone—
It is appropriate to rely upon right knowledge and right view. The two minds become deluded and thus form;
the accomplishment of confusion and disorder arises from the five aggregates within your own mind acting as the master. If the master is deluded, the guest finds its opportunity.
Building upon the preceding point that Māra is fundamentally incapable of harm, we consider why he is able to fulfill his intent and cause you such disruption and confusion:
who, ultimately, is the one instigating him? Therefore, it is said: "It is due to the master of the five aggregates within your own mind.
This "master of the five aggregates" refers to the fivefold realms of the aggregates to be discussed below, as well as the mental state of contemplative wisdom (*samādhi*) during meditation. Indeed.
Because when the objects of the aggregates appear before one, the wisdom of contemplation is somewhat diminished, the Māra Pāpīyān and his like take advantage of this opportunity to enter.
Therefore, what follows uses the metaphor that if the host is deluded, the guest gains the upper hand.

In this metaphor, only that which remains is called the "host," and that which does not remain is called the "guest"; it need not necessarily be explained in terms of the conventional meaning of host and guest. This is because...
There is a sense of mutual resonance between host and guest; thus, the dharma and its metaphor are not entirely identical. Zhengmo says:

When demons disturb the practitioner, it is like a guest-thief plundering the host. If the host remains deeply secluded and unmoving, the thief cannot fathom him; the closer the thief comes, the more terrified he becomes.
This is what the worldly proverb means when it says, "A powerful thief fears a weak host. If the host fails to maintain his composure and instead panics and flees...
He fled, but was captured by bandits. Only then did he find the opportunity to respond with the Dharma through parables; thus it is clear that the source of affliction lies with the host.
This concludes the section on the causes for becoming a māra. Third, the causes for transcending māra.
If you remain in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and awaken without delusion, then those demonic affairs will be powerless against you.

When the *skandhas* (*yin*) dissolve and you enter into clarity, all those various evils will receive only their dark, subterranean energy. Since clarity can destroy darkness, they will first perish on their own;
how then would they dare remain to disturb your meditative absorption?

The initial emergence proceeds through manifestation and transcendence; as stated above, one should know that when the practitioner is properly situated at the stage of *dhyāna*, they should simply awaken without delusion.

Although one does not speak of *samādhi* here but rather uses the term *dhyāna*, this is because *dhyāna* is translated as "calm contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), whereas *samādhi* refers to the integration of both concentration and wisdom. Awakening...

This means: one perceives it as being Māra and realizes it is not a wholesome state. Having already perceived it as Māra and realized it is not a wholesome state, one naturally should not succumb to its delusion.
When one does not succumb to its delusion, then concentration becomes increasingly deep and wisdom becomes increasingly clear;

thus Māra finds it difficult to enter and evil finds it difficult to approach. Therefore it is said: "He can do nothing with you. [The following section] "The obscurations dissolve" provides a detailed explanation of this.
Therefore, because awakening is free from delusion, the realms of the *skandhas* gradually dissolve, while clarity and brilliance gradually manifest;
hence it is said that "as the *skandhas* dissolve, one enters into clarity. This is as previously stated: "the clarity refined by hearing permeates the Dharma-realm.

As for the "multitude of evils," this refers to demons (*māra*) and ghosts (*preta*), meaning that when they take form, they all receive and are sustained by the qi of profound darkness. As it is said:
The rākṣasa cannot see when facing the sun; this can serve as clear evidence. Based on this, your brilliant clarity is able to dispel their profound darkness.
If they should approach you, they will naturally be dissolved and destroyed. As stated previously, all such profound darknesses—
By their very nature, they cannot be entirely present. How could they dare to remain? This is a definitive statement that they cannot remain for long.

If they do not even dare to remain, how could they possibly disturb your meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*)? This concludes the preceding section, which has set forth the respective reasons for each case.
Third, failing to awaken leads to harm.
If you do not attain clear realization and remain deluded by the aggregates, then you, Ānanda, will surely become a son of Māra and achieve the state of a Māra-person.
As for the Mataṅga woman, she was exceedingly lowly and inferior; yet she merely used a mantra to destroy your Buddhist precepts and eighty thousand practices.
If one violates only a single precept, because the mind remains pure, one has not yet fallen into ruin; yet this [violation] destroys your entire body of precious enlightenment.
It is like a high minister’s family suddenly encountering a confiscation of their property: they will be reduced to utter destitution, beyond all hope of rescue.
At first, one is deluded and fallen into Māra. If one does not attain clear awakening, one cannot discern that this is Māra; one fails to realize it is not a wholesome state.
Since one cannot discern that it is Māra and realize it is not a wholesome state, one will inevitably mistake it for a realization of sainthood.

One is deluded by the realm of the aggregates (skandhas). Once deluded by the realm of the aggregates, external demons gain the opportunity to destroy your concentrated mind, cause you to lose right view, and lead you into perverse thoughts; therefore, it is said that one will inevitably become a child of Māra.
Having become a child of Māra, all that one cultivates becomes demonic karma, and in the future, one will achieve nothing but the state of those who follow the path of Māra.
The phrase "like Mātaṅgī" provides an example to illustrate the nature of harm. The Tathāgata’s intention is this:

when you first resolved to seek meditative concentration, you originally viewed Mātaṅgī as a source of harm. Comparing her to the present case, the harm posed by the woman Mātaṅgī was utterly insignificant;
"insignificant" (miǎo) means minute, and "inferior" (liè) means lacking power. This indicates that while she did cause some harm, it was not a great calamity.
It is powerless. How is this known? It is said that the Mātanga girl used only the ancient Brahma-mantra to enchant you, and possessed no other arts.
Compared to the successive emergence of the realms of the shadows and the hundredfold transformations of demonic forms, her ability to cause harm is already trivial and inferior.
Even if she were to draw you into a lewd encounter and touch your body with lustful hands, it would only break [your concentration].
Regarding the Vinaya discipline established by the Buddha, among the eighty thousand modes of conduct, it is subsumed within the three clusters.

Even if one were to violate only the single cluster of the *saṃvara-śīla* (the precepts of restraint), compared to becoming a son of Māra and achieving the state of a demonic person, the harm accomplished therein is exceedingly slight.
Furthermore, at that time, it was the very essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*) that was about to be destroyed; it was not that you intentionally gave rise to lust.
Regarding "attachment": because the mind is pure, one does not even sink into the three miserable realms due to the transgression of breaking the precepts;
thus it is seen that its harm is not great and its power to bring calamity is weak. This character specifically refers to the demon of the aggregates (skandha-māra).

When the realm of the *āyatanas* manifests before them, they are unable to awaken clearly. External demons find an opportunity to destroy their concentrated mind, causing their roots of goodness to perish forever and leading them deep into false views.
From this point, the Dharma-body is severed; from this, the life of wisdom is cut off. Therefore it is said:
"It ruins your entire precious awakening. "Precious" (*bao*) refers to the essence that does not change; "awakening" (*jue*) refers to the function that can adapt to conditions. This is...
This is the Dharma-body, which also encompasses the life of wisdom; therefore, it is designated by its entirety. ○ The following analogy serves as a warning:
a minister who formerly submitted to the King’s transformation represents Ānanda and others, who originally belonged to the Buddha-realm.
Once they fall into heterodoxy, they are no longer tolerated within the Buddha-realm, just as a minister who rebels against the King suddenly encounters the confiscation of his property.

Regarding the matter of "confiscation of records" (*jimen*): this refers to the forfeiture of one's family register (*jiguan*). It is as stated in the *Hanshu*: "to remove them from their clan register" (*chu qi shuji*).
Once their clan register has been removed, they ought naturally to be banished to distant regions and exiled to foreign lands;

even their closest kin cannot show them compassion, and righteous friends find it difficult to provide rescue or aid. Therefore, it is said: "Wandering and falling into ruin, there is no one to pity or save them. This is the intended meaning.

This is a metaphor for those who cling to false views; the Buddha-realm will not admit them. They will inevitably wander through the three miserable realms for aeons as numerous as motes of dust, with no possibility of return.
Even though there may be Bodhisattvas possessing a compassionate heart and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) with vows of pity, they have no means to rescue them.
How can one not be cautious! How can one not be cautious! This concludes the preceding section on "The Causes and Conditions for Awakening."

Second, distinguishing the characteristics to enable the recognition of the five [aggregates]: first, the demonic signs of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); second, the demonic signs of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*);

third, the demonic signs of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); fourth, the demonic signs of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); and fifth, the demonic signs of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Regarding the first four, there are three stages:

first, when one has just begun practice and has not yet broken through the aggregate of form; second, when the practice is finalized and the source of delusion is revealed; and third, the demonic signs that appear during the intermediate stages.
Fourth, the conclusion summarizes the matter as a warning and instruction. First:

"Ānanda, you should know this: when you sit at the site of enlightenment and eliminate all thoughts, once those thoughts are exhausted, then all states free from thought will be luminously clear and penetrating;
movement and stillness will not shift them, and recollection and forgetfulness will be one and the same. You should abide in this state and enter samādhi."
"Ti. It is like a person with clear vision situated in great darkness; though the essence of the mind is wondrously pure, its light has not yet been emitted.
This is what is called the domain of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).

As previously explained, the initial thought is the total purity of the mind. Since the demon of the aggregates (skandha-māra) possesses such faults and afflictions, it must not be [permitted to prevail]."
Because [the truth] is not yet known, he instructs that it "should be known" to provide a sense of awakening.

When you say, "you sit at the site of enlightenment," this refers to the initial sitting at the site of enlightenment by one who wishes to cultivate *samādhi*. At the time of first sitting at the site of enlightenment, one must first still the distracted mind;
hence it is said, "dissolve all thoughts. To "dissolve" means to forget all objects of perception through the power of "listening inwardly" (*pratyāśravaṇa*).

When the images of sensory objects are thus [stilled], the mind of discursive thought naturally dissolves away. This is not a case of there being a separate method for dissolution other than the practice of "returning to hearing.
If those thoughts are exhausted—meaning that objects have perished and thoughts have ceased—then for all those who are free from thought, there should naturally arise a distinct mind of non-thought.
This mind of non-thought is precisely the manifestation of the fundamental nature of the sense-faculties.
At all times, it is neither mixed nor obscured; therefore, it is called "pure" and "luminous. Regarding "unwavering amidst movement and stillness":
when movement departs and stillness arrives, its nature remains as it is—this is the meaning of being unmixed. Regarding "remaining the same whether remembered or forgotten":

when recollection arises and forgetfulness ceases, its essence is ever-constant—this is the meaning of being unobscured. Furthermore, "unwavering amidst movement and stillness" refers to the hearing-nature of the ear-faculty.
Recollection and forgetfulness are as one. This refers to the nature of the faculty of mind (*manas*). Of the six faculties, two are mentioned; the remaining four are included within the mind.
○ One should abide in the lower stage to manifest the sphere of form. "One who should abide in this place" means abiding the mind in the locus of the faculty-nature.
Since characteristics such as movement and stillness, or recollection and forgetfulness, do not arise at all, it is called entering *samādhi*. At this time—
At this juncture, although one's fundamental nature is luminous, one still does not know what kind of state it is. Therefore it is said:
"It is like a person with clear vision standing in great darkness. This is because the nature of the six essences is still shrouded by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);
though subtle and pure, the mind has not yet emitted light. Hence it is said: "This is called the realm of the aggregate of form."
"District" (*qū*) refers to a small hut. "Roof" (*yǔ*) refers to the four eaves of a house. The meaning is that the mind of the wondrously pure essential nature is fundamentally all-pervasive;
yet it is constrained and obscured by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), like the four eaves of a small hut.

[Question: If those thoughts are exhausted, it seems as though no form can be seen. Why, then, is it still called the "district of the aggregate of form"? [Answer: Although it appears as if there is no form, one has not yet entirely forgotten space. Here, "darkness" is used as a metaphor for "space. Since space has not been forgotten, form is not truly non-existent; it is simply...
Taste reverses hearing; when concentration is deep, the ears are no longer seen. Second, one ultimately destroys and reveals the source of delusion.
If the eyes are clear and bright, the ten directions open up like a cave, and there is no longer any darkness. This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form and name (*rūpa-nāma-skandha*).
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). One should observe its origin, which has the solidified false imagination (*dṛḍha-vikalpa*) as its root.
Previously, by extinguishing form and abiding in emptiness, although one’s faculties and nature were clear and bright, one did not know what kind of state this was;
thus it was likened to a person with clear vision situated in great, profound darkness. Now, as meditative concentration (*samādhi*) becomes increasingly deep, even emptiness is forgotten;
thus it is likened to when the eyes become luminous and the ten directions open wide, with no further gloom or obscurity. From this point on, one refines...
