The nature is wondrously pure; the light of the mind is all-pervasive and perfect. Therefore, it is said that the aggregate of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-skandha*) is exhausted.

According to the *Āvarta-śrotra-mūla-mantra* (the Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ), this corresponds to the non-arising of motion and stillness, whereby one can transcend the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kāluṣya*).

In this sutra, the essence of the turbidity of the kalpa is constituted by the interweaving of emptiness, views, and appearances. As the preceding passage on the turbidity of the kalpa states: "When you perceive empty space, emptiness and seeing are not distinguished; they interweave to form delusion."
This is called the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). It is known that this is like a person with clear vision situated in great darkness, unable to discern what kind of realm it is;

this is precisely the characteristic of the turbidity of the kalpa. Now, as the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) becomes increasingly profound, even emptiness is forgotten, and there is nothing seen to be woven together;
thus one is able to transcend. Having transcended, one turns back to observe the locus of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Regarding "arising from birth": this refers to the moment when one does not distinguish within the emptiness of vision; through the stubborn desire to see, material forms (*rūpa*) are consequently formed.
Thus it is said that "solidified false discrimination" (*dṛḍha-vikalpa*) constitutes its root. Previously it was stated that because the delusion of transformation does not cease, worlds arise;
indeed, this non-ceasing delusion of transformation is precisely solidified false discrimination.
There are ten signs of Māra that manifest during the intermediate state: first, the sign of the overflowing of vital essence (*śukra*) before the objective field;
second, the sign of the overflowing of vital essence from the physical form; third, the sign of the successive separation and union of the vital essence and the soul;

fourth, the sign of being defiled by the awakening of the conscious spirit (*puruṣa*); fifth, the sign of the power of suppression exceeding its proper limit; sixth, the sign of the mind becoming subtle and dense, thereby clarifying one's vision.

1. The sign of the seven particles aligning and merging into a great, pure form; 2. The sign of the deepening of joyful and loathsome contemplation through concentrated visualization; 3. The sign of the mind being so intensely pressured that it flies out; 4. The sign of a perverted mind harboring and receiving malevolent spirits (*chi-mei*). First: [The first sign:

The practitioner visualizes the seven types of subtle particles (*paramāṇu*) aligned side by side. As they merge and enter into one another, they become a single, vast, and purely characterized form. This is the initial stage.
Ānanda, if you investigate the wondrous clarity within this state until the four elements no longer entangle one another, you may find that for a brief moment the body can pass through obstructions.
This is called the overflowing of refined spirit into the external realm; it is merely a temporary attainment resulting from meditative effort and is not a holy realization.
If you do not conceive of it as a holy state, it is a favorable condition; but if you interpret it as a holy attainment, you will immediately be possessed by various demons.

"In this state" refers to the moment when [the eye] has not yet been destroyed but is on the verge of being destroyed. As mentioned above, it is like a person with clear vision situated in great darkness;
although it is said that [the eye] has not yet been destroyed, it is already at the point of destruction.

If one dwells in this objective realm, one falls into what the orthodox school calls the "extreme of a single color. Therefore, one must investigate the wondrous clarity within this state. As for "wondrous clarity":
This still refers to the neutral nature of the six sense faculties; one must simply study them with even greater refinement of mind.
When studying with such refined concentration, one temporarily forgets the objects of form (*rūpa-dhātu*). This is not only forgetting external forms, but forgetting them internally as well.

Therefore, it is said that "the four great elements do not interweave," because earth, water, fire, and wind all belong to the objects of form. "Interweaving" means mutual penetration, which is the meaning of combination.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "All sentient beings falsely identify the combination of the four great elements as their own physical form.
Since one no longer weaves [the threads of delusion], the physical form does not exist; hence it is said that in a brief moment, the body can pass through obstructions.
"Shortly thereafter" means after a brief moment. That the body can emerge from obstructions does not refer to the physical body present before one;
rather, because the four elements do not entwine, one perceives separately a clear and ethereal body that has transcended the obstructions of the four elements.
This clear and ethereal body is precisely the refined spirit; having transcended the obstructions of the four elements, it naturally flows and circulates freely.
It overflows upon the field before one. Therefore it is said: "This is called the overflowing of refined clarity onto the field before one.
That "this is merely a function" means that this field is not real; it is manifested solely by the power of the function of refining and investigating wondrous clarity.
If this function slightly diminishes, this field immediately ceases. Thus it is said: "One has temporarily attained such a state. Since it is not permanent, it belongs to—
This is false and illusory; therefore, it is said not to constitute a realization of sainthood (*ārya-siddhi*), for a true realization of sainthood is necessarily free from cessation.

If one does not mistake this for a realization of sainthood but continues to investigate the wondrous clarity with renewed vigor, this is precisely the precursor to breaking through the *skandhas* (aggregates). Therefore, it is called a "wholesome state.
If, however, one interprets it as a realization of sainthood, this is what the orthodox school calls "seizing and playing with the vital spirit," whereby demons find their opportunity.
Thus, they take advantage of a vulnerability to enter; hence it is said that one immediately receives the various evils.
Second, when the refined essence overflows from the physical form:
Ānanda, if this mind further investigates its wondrous clarity until it penetrates deep into the body, this person will suddenly, within that—
One may extract worms and *ōmi* from within the body, yet the physical form remains intact and uninjured. This is called the overflowing of refined essence through the physical body.
It is merely a temporary attainment resulting from refined practice and is not a realization of the Holy Path. To regard it as such without harboring thoughts of sanctity is a wholesome state;
however, to interpret it as a holy attainment is to fall prey to various demonic influences.
Although objects appear before one, one does not form holy interpretations of them; rather, one continues to employ the previous contemplation. Therefore it is said:
"Furthermore, with this mind, one minutely investigates the wondrous clarity. Here, "this mind" is the observing mind, and "wondrous clarity" is the nature that is observed.

It is simply that the mind becomes increasingly refined and the clarity becomes even more wondrous. As the contemplative illumination deepens, it no longer overflows outward; it turns back in a single flavor.

[The disciple] asked: "If hearing should naturally overflow within, it is said that 'the body is penetrated from within. [Question: Previously, these signs originally manifested through the refinement of the wondrous clarity (*prabhāsvara*) by means of functional effort.

Now that you have again used this mind to refine the wondrous clarity, the previous signs ought to become even more pronounced. Why do they not overflow outward, but instead flow inward? [Answer: "As previously stated, it is like a person with clear vision situated in great, profound darkness."

Although one may say that they have refined their subtle clarity, they cannot avoid feeling a sense of weariness and a desire to escape; thus, their refined brilliance overflows outward. Now, by not forming the understanding of being a sage and instead continuing to refine their subtle clarity, they cannot avoid having a mind that abandons the external to flow inward;
thus, their refined brilliance flows inward. As the ancient masters said, "Before the hall of the withered tree, there are many diverging paths"—this is indeed beyond doubt.

As for picking out *rāji* worms and roundworms from within one's body, this too is another instance of perceiving a body as pure and ethereal, yet it is not something picked out from within one's present physical body.
This refers to the physical body itself picking [the parasites] up. It is because the refined spirit (*jingming*) moves from the outside toward the inside;
by contemplating the physical body as being like a wooden puppet, one is able to pick out the *rui* and *hui* worms without causing any injury whatsoever.

This is because the aforementioned refined spirit follows that thought of turning inward from the exterior and returns to illuminate the internal organs; hence it is said that "it flows and overflows through the physical form."
This is merely a state experienced by those of refined practice; it is not yet the ultimate reality. Because their practice of investigation is more refined than before, this realm manifests.
One may briefly understand the preceding case by analogy with what follows. Regarding the "ascariasis and roundworms" mentioned in the text: these are parasites within the intestines and stomach.
Those that are short and thin are ascariasis (*yáo*); those that are long and large are roundworms (*huí*).
The three essences and spirits alternate between separating and uniting.

Furthermore, as one investigates this mind with refined intensity both internally and externally, the soul, spirit, will, and consciousness—excluding the body they grasp and sustain—all interpenetrate and act as guest and host to one another.
Suddenly, one hears the sound of the Dharma being preached in the air, or hears it from the ten directions.
We shall likewise expound the profound meaning of this: it is called the "successive separation and union of the vital essence," which brings about the perfection of wholesome seeds.

To briefly attain such a state does not constitute a realization of the holy; if one does not conceive of it as being holy, it is called a "wholesome realm. However, if one interprets it as a holy attainment, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.
At first, by means of investigating the wondrous luminosity, one slightly withdraws the mind directed toward external objects; consequently, the refined clarity overflows outward.
Next, by means of investigating the wondrous luminosity with a subtle admixture of thoughts directed inward, the refined clarity flows inward.
Now, adhering to neither of these two, one again employs the mind of contemplative observation to investigate the aforementioned two locations—the internal and the external—with refined precision.
This is the wondrously luminous fundamental substance. Therefore it is said: "Furthermore, with this mind, one investigates minutely both internally and externally.

At that time, through the power of this internal and external minute investigation, the wondrous luminosity becomes pervasive and integrated; thus, the six internal breaths interpenetrate and the two external sounds are presented together.

As for the soul (*hún*), spirit (*pó*), will (*yì*), intention (*zhì*), and consciousness (*shén*), these as recorded in non-Buddhist classics cannot be considered entirely identical [to the Buddhist categories]. According to...
The *Zihui* (Dictionary of Characters) explains the meaning of the character "zàng" (viscera) as follows: "Zàng means 'to store.

It refers to the essence being stored in the kidneys, the spirit (*shén*) being stored in the heart, the soul (*hún*) being stored in the liver, the魄 (*pò*) being stored in the lungs, and the will (*zhì*) being stored in the spleen.

This account omits the "mind" (*yì*) from the six [viscera] mentioned in the present sutra, yet it also fails to specify what entities the soul and so forth are, nor does it explain how they ought to be stored within the liver and other organs. This is one interpretation.
Zhengmei cites a medical classic which states: "The *hun* (soul) is stored in the liver; the *po* (spirit) is stored in the lungs; the *yi* (mind) is stored in the spleen;
the *zhi* (will) is stored in the gallbladder—or, according to some, in the left kidney; the *jing* (essence) is stored in the kidneys; and the *shen* (consciousness) is stored in the heart.
This corresponds to the names and numbers in the present sutra, though it differs slightly from the *Zihui*. These are the two explanations. Guanding cites Bian Que:

The *Nan jing* (Difficult Classic) states: "The five viscera have seven spirits; what does each one store? The answer is: "A 'viscera' (*zang*) is that which contains and stores the human spirit and vital energy (*qi*).
Thus, the liver stores the *hun* (soul); the lungs store the *po* (soul); the heart stores the *shen* (spirit); the spleen stores the *yi* (thought/intention) and *zhi* (wisdom);
and the kidneys store the *jing* (essence) and *zhi* (will). Compared with the current classic, it contains more wisdom and accords with the medical texts of the *Yi zihui*.
Each of these three accounts also differs from the others. Being a fool who has never been well-versed in non-Buddhist scriptures, I do not dare to offer a reckless critique;

I have merely recorded them here for reference. Nevertheless, the Buddha is called the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*); whatever he has taught is based on what he has directly perceived through direct cognition (*pratyakṣa*).

From this level downward, there is no way to determine the truth except through inference (*anumāna*). I shall now attempt to explain [the matter] by means of the six qi (*ṣaḍ-vāyu*). This is truly...
Since humans receive the qi of Heaven and Earth, and the qi of Heaven and Earth consists of six elements—namely, yin, yang, darkness, light, wind, and rain—humans likewise must possess these.
These are what are called the *hun*, *po*, intention, will, spirit, and consciousness.

It is said that the ascending aspect of the qi is the *hun*, while the descending aspect is the *po*, which closely resembles the two qi of yin and yang in Heaven and Earth. As for the contraction of this qi...
Stillness is the *zhi* (will/volition); dispersion and movement are the *yi* (mind/thought). These are like the two qi of darkness and light in heaven and earth.
That which is the full harmony of the qi is the *shen* (spirit); that which is the moistening of the qi is the *jing* (essence). These are like the two qi of wind and rain in heaven and earth.
However, speaking of this solely in terms of a single body, these six qi are what is grasped and sustained (*zhishou*), while the body is that which sustains (*neng*).
Regarding "appropriation" (*upātta*): the phrase "excluding the appropriated body" is used because this general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) has no point of intersection [with the specific].
As for "the rest all interpenetrate," it is like how the *hun* (soul) originally ascends yet can also descend, while the *po* (soul) originally descends yet can also ascend, and so forth.
Regarding their acting as "guest and host" to one another: if the *hun* descends, then the *po* becomes the host while the *hun* [becomes the guest].
As for being a guest: if the *po* ascends, then the *hun* becomes the host and the *po* becomes the guest. The remaining four cases can be understood by analogy with this.

However, this is still based on the mutual interaction between pairs of three and two. If we further consider the *hun* interacting with the five [elements], then all five become hosts while the *hun* alone acts as their companion.
The same applies when the *po* and the others interact with the five. Therefore, it is said that they "mutually serve as each other. This arises from...

The wondrous clarity is internally pervasive and harmonious; thus it is so. Regarding the phrase "suddenly hearing from within the void," etc., it means that wondrous clarity is fundamentally all-pervasive, and the Buddha-dharma has been manifest and complete from the beginning.
Previously, because of the universal delusion arising from the impulse of birth, there was the nature of space.
As the delusion transformed without ceasing, the world-system arose. Once the realm of space became manifest, the Buddha-dharma was thereby obscured. Now, by...

The aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is about to open; the realm of space is about to be exhausted; the Buddha-dharma inherent in one's nature is about to manifest; and the primordial perfect sound is about to provide its omen.

Thus, one suddenly hears the preaching of the Dharma in the midst of space, with principles unfolding throughout the ten directions. As these principles unfold and the Dharma is preached, space and the directions mutually reflect one another.
There is no need to forcibly distinguish between the Exoteric and Esoteric; this arises because the wondrous clarity penetrates and unifies with the external. Therefore...

It is indeed so. Regarding the phrase "this is called the refined essence (*sūkṣma-ātman*) and so forth," the six qi (vital energies) are mentioned by citing two; the remainder are subsumed through their underlying meaning.

As for "mutually separating and uniting," separation and union are precisely what constitutes interpenetration (*shèrù*). This is because, in common parlance, interpenetration necessarily involves departing from one's own original position to unite with another.
This extends even to preaching the Dharma within space and unfolding its principles throughout the ten directions, which proceeds from the Subtle [Wisdom].

The "bright, penetrating, and harmonious" [state] is a premonitory sign. It returns to permeate and perfect the six qi—such as the essence and spirit—thereby establishing the seeds of future goodness.
This is precisely why the subsequent section speaks of "the characteristics of what is permeated by the awakening of the mind, soul, and numinous spirit. It is for this reason.
Fourth is the sign of the mind-soul being defiled by what it perceives.
Furthermore, when this mind becomes clear and exposed, bright and penetrating, with inner light shining forth, the ten directions everywhere take on the color of Jāmbūnada gold.
All types of forms are transformed into Tathāgatas. Suddenly, one beholds Vairocana seated upon the Terrace of Celestial Radiance, surrounded by a thousand Buddhas;
ten billion lands and lotus flowers appear simultaneously. This is called the defilement of the awakening of the soul and spirit.
The light of the mind is polished and clarified, illuminating all worlds. To briefly attain such a state is not yet the realization of a Sage.
Not giving rise to the mind of holiness is called a wholesome state; if one forms a conception of holiness, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.

Previously, by using the mind of contemplative observation to investigate thoroughly within and without, the internal essence and spirit were made to alternate between separating and uniting, while the external realm of space was brought to fruition as wholesome seeds.
Now, one does not cling to those former objects, yet still employs contemplative observation.
The mind becomes serene and manifest within; it becomes bright and transparent without. Because it is serene and manifest within, inner radiance is produced and revealed.
Because it is bright and transparent without, the ten directions everywhere become golden in color, and all things are transformed into Tathāgatas.
This is because throughout the ten directions and the dharma-realm, among all categories of beings—
This is fundamentally the dependent origination of self-nature, established equally upon the Dharma-body. Previously, it was shrouded by the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);
as the sentient world and the physical vessel were not yet integrated, the golden hue did not manifest, and where did that wondrous essence abide?

Now, as the aggregate of form is about to open and the sentient world and the physical vessel are about to merge, the entire dharma-realm of the ten directions has already been transformed into a golden color, and all species have already been transformed into that wondrous essence. This...
The nature-realm of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is a sign that it will certainly be realized in the future.

Although this state manifests now, because contemplative observation is uninterrupted and its functional power increases, the retributive and transformational bodies (*saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*) begin to take shape; thus, at this time, one suddenly beholds Vairocana and others.
The name Vairocana has three meanings: first, "pervading all places," which seems to refer to the Dharma-body; second, "full" [of light].
"Purity" seems to refer to one's own retribution; "thirdly, universal illumination of light" seems to refer to the retribution of others.

Here, both types of retribution are encompassed. "Dwelling" (ju) means to rest upon or rely on. Regarding the "Celestial Light Terrace," the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "At that time, in the Lotus-womb Treasury World..."
The majestic celestial radiance of Vairocana Buddha upon the lion throne is none other than the present-day Vairocana;
that very Vairocana is this one. Thus, the *Abhiṣeka* states: "Vairocana and Rocana differ only in the phonetic transcription of the Sanskrit sounds.
Since it specifies "upon the throne," it implies he is seated there. What is now called the "platform" is that same [throne].
This refers to the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbhalokadhātu*); the translation here is merely abbreviated.

The two characters "Heavenly Light" (*Tianguang*) correspond to the "Majestic Heavenly Light Lion Throne" (*Hehetianguang Shizi-zuo*) mentioned therein. Since the throne rests upon the pedestal, it is called the "Heavenly Light Pedestal.
Regarding the phrase "surrounded by a thousand Buddhas," the verse in that sutra states: "Upon a thousand lotuses surrounding [the central one], there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis."
One flower contains ten billion lands; in each land is one Śākyamuni. This is because at the center of the Lotus-Womb World (Padmagarbha-lokadhātu) is a great lotus upon which Vairocana sits.
Surrounding it are further one thousand flowers, and upon each flower is a Buddha who serves as the presiding lord.
This refers to what is now called "surrounded by a thousand Buddhas. Furthermore, each flower contains ten billion [lands].
[The] leaves [contain] ten billion lands and ten billion Śākyamunis. Now, it mentions "ten billion lands and lotus flowers.
Since the lotus flower is that upon which the Buddha sits, although the Buddha is not explicitly named, he can be understood through the meaning.

However, Vairocana is the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (reward body) Buddha, while Śākyamuni is the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (transformation body) Buddha; they appear simultaneously. Thus, these are the lands of the reward and transformation bodies. As for...
This is an omen that one will certainly attain [the goal] upon its arrival. It is called "that which is permeated by the spiritual awakening of the mind-soul" (*citta-ātman-vijñāna*).

This is because within the previous object, two sounds were presented together, and thus it was permeated by the habitual tendencies of the spiritual awakening of the mind-soul. As for the term "mind-soul" (*citta-ātman*), "mind" (*citta*) is precisely "intellect" (*manas*).
Furthermore, the six breaths and the two [nostrils] are subsumed under this principle by virtue of their meaning. This is because the six breaths depend upon the wondrous clarity (*prabhāsvara*).

Since the two sounds are intermingled within that wondrous clarity, each of the six breaths possesses spiritual penetration and wise awakening, as well as the habitual tendencies of perfuming and defilement;
it is simply that humans do not perceive them themselves. If one does not perceive them oneself, how could they suddenly appear within the object of contemplation?
Manifesting, it is said that "the light of the mind is refined and bright, illuminating all worlds.
"The light of the mind is refined and bright" refers to the observing mind being clear and revealed within. "Illuminating all worlds" refers to the observing mind being pure and penetrating without.

What was previously called "internal light manifesting and clarifying" is precisely the appearance of the light of the mind being refined and bright. Throughout the ten directions, it universally manifests as gold.

All forms transform into Tathāgatas and the like, immediately illuminating the characteristics of all worlds. Even if one briefly attains the lower stage, it may be understood according to the previous explanation.
Fifth, the signs of the power of suppression exceeding its proper limit.
Furthermore, with this mind, one investigates the wondrous clarity with ceaseless observation, suppressing, subduing, restraining, and transcending it.
At that time, suddenly the empty space of the ten directions becomes the color of the seven treasures, or the color of a hundred treasures;
simultaneously filling all space without mutual obstruction, blue, yellow, red, and white each appear in their own purity. This is called the power of suppression exceeding its proper measure.

To temporarily attain such a state does not constitute a realization of the holy. To refrain from regarding it as a holy attainment is called a "wholesome realm. If one instead interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
Although one perceives these external objects, by not interpreting them as holy and continuing to employ the previous contemplation, it is said: "Furthermore, with this mind, refined..."
Investigating the wondrous clarity: although one may investigate this wondrous clarity with great refinement, the external objects before one do not vanish.

One should therefore observe them with the wisdom of contemplation. As the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "The practitioner should constantly observe with wisdom, ensuring that this mind does not fall into the net of heterodoxy.
It further says: "One should maintain the thought that [all is] mind-only, and then the objective realm will cease. Both of these passages convey the meaning of observation (*vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the statement that "the speech does not cease," this does not mean that the contemplation itself does not cease. It means that although one observes in this manner, the preceding object cannot be made to cease.
Because it cannot be made to cease, one modifies the practice by cultivating *śamatha* (calm abiding); hence it is said, "suppressing and subduing.
As for "suppressing," one must not suppress the preceding object; rather, one only suppresses and halts one's own mind, pressing it into stillness so that it does not move, as if rising [from sleep].
Xinxun said: "One must not follow the mind as it dwells upon external objects. He further stated: "When long-practiced cultivation becomes pure and mature, the mind attains stability.

Both of these refer to the meaning of suppression and restraint. By using this as an antidote, the preceding objects of perception are eliminated; this is precisely what constitutes subduing [the mind].

Furthermore, according to the tradition of the ancient masters, when a meditative state manifests before one, it should be verified by three methods. The first is to polish it with concentration (*samādhi*).
Second is cultivation based on the fundamental [nature]; third is observation through wisdom. As the Sūtra says:
"If one wishes to know genuine gold, one tests it with three methods—namely, burning, cutting, and rubbing. The practitioner is likewise so: observation through wisdom is like burning;

refining through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is like rubbing; and cultivation based on the fundamental nature is like hammering. Now, herein, this mind is further refined by means of these [methods].
"Wondrous Brilliance" refers to relying on the fundamental nature for cultivation and refinement. "Observation" refers to the observation of wisdom.
"Suppression and subjugation" refers to grinding through the power of meditative concentration. Once it has been subdued, one must once again refine that wondrous brilliance with precision.
When the aggregates naturally open and one's nature manifests, it is like lead being exhausted and gold becoming pure; this may serve as an apt analogy.

If one were to unilaterally suppress and constrain [the mind], this would constitute a hindrance to transcendent observational wisdom (*vipaśyanā*), resulting in the manifestation of inferior objective signs. At that time:

"At this very moment" and "suddenly," etc., means that the previous appearance of the Buddha arose as an illusory manifestation based on the mind of wisdom (*prajñā-citta*), while the previous appearance of the realms manifested falsely based on the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi-viṣaya*). Now, because one suppresses them through the single flavor (*ekarasa*), only the existence of the realms is perceived;
furthermore, because one employs transcendent observational wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), the appearance of the Buddha is no longer seen. Since the appearance of the Buddha...
Since [the Buddha] has already ceased to appear, the platform and the flowers have both vanished; thus, one sees only the empty space of the ten directions and so forth.

The seven treasures and the hundred treasures remain as the characteristics of the land of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*). Alternatively, these may be divided into "one's own retribution" and "the retribution of others":

that which is one's own retribution is what one personally enjoys, and thus consists only of the seven treasures; whereas the retribution of others corresponds specifically to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and thus includes the hundred treasures.

Although these arise through illusion and manifest as delusions, they are nonetheless capable of interacting and mutually accommodating one another; thus it is said that they are simultaneously pervasive and do not obstruct or hinder each other.
If one continues to feel aversion toward this mixture and attempts to suppress it, the manifestations will only increase.

Then, blue, yellow, red, and white will each appear in their own purity—meaning that suddenly pure blue appears, and suddenly pure yellow appears, and so forth. This is the *vipāka-kṣetra* (retribution land).

The marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are exhausted, and the marks of the land of intrinsic nature (*dharmatā-bhūmi*) appear. In the preceding section, the land of intrinsic nature was described as being solely golden; here it is said that the four colors are each pure.
This is because whatever is pure and without admixture is precisely the color of intrinsic nature. Regarding the phrase "this is called suppressing, etc.":
"suppressing" (*yī-àn*) means to restrain or prohibit; "exceeding the limit" (*yú-fèn*) means to transcend. This refers to what was stated above regarding restraint and transcendence.
This is because they have transcended the former state. The rest is the same as above. Sixth, the mind becomes subtle and refined, clarifying its perceptions and appearances.
Furthermore, by investigating with this mind until it is transparently penetrating, the refined light remains undisturbed.

Suddenly, in the middle of the night within a dark room, one sees various objects no different from those seen in broad daylight; yet the objects in the dark room do not vanish. This is called "refinement of the mind."
If you clarify your vision so that what you behold penetrates the profound depths, and you momentarily attain such a state, do not regard it as a holy realization.
To refrain from conceiving the thought of holiness is called a "wholesome state"; if you instead form a conception of holiness, you will immediately fall prey to various delusions.
Having already perceived the external objects before him, he realized that his suppression of the mind had been excessive; therefore, he again used this mind to investigate the wondrous clarity.

This is what is meant by "if the mind sinks, arouse it with contemplation. Having thus balanced concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), he once more clarified and stilled his vision so as to illuminate the objects before him.
This is what is meant by "examining the source to see from where it ultimately arises."
This arises from one's dwelling. That the refined radiance is not disturbed is brought about by clarifying and stilling one's vision.

That objects are seen in the darkness of night is brought about by the illumination that penetrates the realm before one. "Midnight" refers to the middle watch of the night; "a dark room without a lamp" refers to the absence of light.
That various objects are seen means that all the various forms and phenomena existing outside the room can also be seen, no different from the bright day.
This refers to what is seen in a dark room, perceived with such clarity and distinctness as if it were midday;

neither the room nor the darkness can act as an obstruction. Although they do not act as obstructions, the darkness, the room, and the objects within the room are likewise neither eliminated nor extinguished.
Being neither eliminated nor extinguished, there is no hindrance and no obstruction—this is the opening of the aggregates.
"The preceding signs have appeared. Regarding the phrase "this is called subtlety of mind" (*citta-sūkṣmatā*), it refers to the mind that contemplates and investigates with extreme refinement.
Although the manifestation of the nature (*dharmatā*) has not yet fully revealed itself, one nonetheless secretly attains clarity and stillness; hence it is said, "one secretly clarifies that vision.
What was described above as "the refined light being undisturbed" is precisely this sign. Having already secretly attained clarity and stillness, regarding the objects perceived...

Because one is able to penetrate the subtle and profound through one's own power, it is said that "what is seen penetrates the profound. What was mentioned above regarding seeing objects in the darkness of night is precisely this manifestation.
Such light and shadow arise and vanish in an instant; therefore, it is called "temporarily attained. This is distinct from the constant radiance of the realization of the Sage.
It shines through antiquity and soars through the present; therefore, it is not something that can be grasped. If one does not harbor attachment, even the heterodox becomes the orthodox.

How much more so when its original nature is a virtuous sign! Thus it is said: "If one does not give rise to the mind of holiness, it is called a wholesome state. If one gives rise to attachment, even the orthodox becomes heterodox.
How much more so when its original nature belongs to the realm of light and shadow! Thus it is said: "If one forms a conception of holiness, one immediately falls prey to all manner of heterodoxies."

When the seven dust-essences are aligned and enter the great pure mark, this mind again enters the sphere of pervasive emptiness and fusion; suddenly, the four limbs become like grass and wood, such that even if burned by fire or hacked with a blade, one feels nothing at all.
Furthermore, the flames cannot burn them, and even if their flesh is cut, it is as if wood were being pared away.

This is called the simultaneous merging of sensory objects with the nature of the four great elements, entering entirely into purity. To temporarily attain such a state is not a realization of the holy.
If one does not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm"; if one treats it as a holy realization, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.

Furthermore, as for "using this mind," one uses the mind of contemplative observation to investigate the wondrous luminosity. When the cultivation of this investigation reaches its ultimate, both body and environment are forgotten;
the internal and external become unified, becoming a hollow void free from obstruction. Therefore, it is said: "Perfectly entering the empty and harmonious."
Because the internal and external have merged as one, the four limbs suddenly become identical to grass and wood.
Because they are empty and unimpeded, even when burned by fire or cut by a blade, there is no sensation whatsoever. This refers to slight burning and light cutting;

that is to say, one does not perceive the scorching of slight burning, nor does one perceive the pain of light cutting, because [the body] has become identical to grass and wood. Furthermore, as for fire...
Regarding "light and so forth": it means that not only will a slight fire fail to burn him, but even if the flames were to blaze up intensely, they could not consume him;
nor will he be harmed by light cutting, for even if his flesh were sliced from his body, it would be like carving wood, leaving no trace.

(Question: What is the difference between this and the case where Avalokiteśvara’s fire cannot burn and his sword is broken into pieces? Answer: That is the supreme function of Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*), which manifests according to the capacity of the practitioner. This is the state when the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is about to open, achieved through the power of one's practice.)

The true and the false are utterly distinct; do not misunderstand this. What is called "the merging of objects" (*chenbing*) means that both the body and the objective realm are forgotten, such that internal objects and external objects merge into a single entity.
Although they have merged into a single entity, the natures of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) have not yet been entirely forgotten.
If, furthermore, through the power of investigation, one eliminates the natures of the four great elements until reaching a state of empty voidness and non-obstruction, then this is...
"Entering exclusively into purity" refers to what was stated above as "perfectly entering into emptiness and fusion.
Such signs as being burned by fire or cut by a blade without ever feeling it manifest from this. For the subsequent examples, one may infer the preceding case.
As the eightfold contemplation of joy and revulsion deepens through concentrated visualization,
and as this mind achieves the ultimate perfection of purifying the pure mind, one suddenly sees the great earth, the mountains,

and rivers of the ten directions all become Buddha-lands, replete with the seven treasures and filled with pervasive radiance; furthermore, one sees Buddhas and Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Palatial towers and halls fill the void, magnificent and splendid; looking down upon the hells and gazing up at the celestial palaces, one attains unimpeded vision.

This is called the deepening of focused contemplation through the practice of joy and revulsion; after long cultivation, it manifests as such. It is not a holy realization. If one does not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is known as an auspicious state;
if one interprets it as a holy realization, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
Although the above state has entered perfectly into emptiness and fusion, it has not yet reached ultimate purity, because there still remain such signs as being burned by fire or cut by a blade;
therefore, one feels weary of this and seeks to leave it. Consequently, one again uses the mind of contemplative observation to minutely investigate wondrous clarity.
This is done out of a longing to seek ultimate purity and to achieve a pure mind. When the function of purifying the mind reaches its peak, one contemplates in order to further purify that mind.
The function of illumination reaches its ultimate limit. "Suddenly seeing the great earth and so forth" means that the unimpeded realm of both defilement and purity manifests instantaneously.

"The mountains and rivers of the ten directions all become Buddha-lands" refers to the aspect of purity within defilement. "Complete with the seven treasures" [refers to the adornments of these lands].
"Clearly this is a pure land. That 'light pervades everywhere' means that the seven treasures intermingle and radiate within it.
Furthermore, 'seeing Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges' is because the mountains and rivers of the ten directions have all become Buddha-lands;
since there is one Buddha for each land, their number must be as vast as the sands of the Ganges. That 'pavilions and palaces fill the void with magnificent splendor' refers to the superior lands."
The earth constitutes the general retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*), while this palace is the specific retribution (*asādhāraṇa-vipāka*).

Since the general retribution already manifests as the interlacing brilliance of the seven treasures, the palace itself should naturally be adorned with exquisite splendor; for when one is pure, all becomes pure.

As for the statement that "one sees the hells below and contemplates the celestial palaces above," this is the aspect of defilement within purity. One might argue that since it is a Pure Land, it should be entirely devoid of defiled aspects.
Yet one still perceives both hell and heaven; this clarifies that the pure is itself defiled. Regarding "attaining non-obstruction," there are two interpretations.
If it refers solely to heaven and hell, it means that by observing above and seeing below, one attains non-obstruction.

If it is understood generally in terms of Buddha-lands, it means that because the defiled and the pure are mutually identical, one attains non-obstruction. [Question: The previous interpretation of the practitioner was originally for the purpose of accomplishing purity.

The mind should contemplate only the appearance of purity. Why do both defilement and purity appear together? Might this not be inconsistent with the nature of the mind? Answer: To become pure by departing from defilement is not true purity, for it involves a state of mutual opposition. It is essential that defilement and purity be without obstruction.

This alone constitutes true purity. When the practitioner awakens to this, they suddenly cease both longing and aversion; this is the accomplishment of the pure mind, which is itself a wholesome state. Regarding what is called "longing for and aversion toward" and so forth:

it means one feels aversion toward the preceding objects and longs to seek the pure mind, while employing the power of refined investigation into the wondrous luminosity to concentrate the mind and focus the thought.
One contemplates long entry into transformation, thereby realizing the realm of unimpeded defilement and purity that is truly pure and serene; it manifests from this.
Ninth is the sign of the mind being pressed and constrained to the extreme, causing it to fly out.

Furthermore, as one investigates with this mind into the profound and distant, suddenly in the middle of the night one may see from afar the markets, streets, and alleys, or the kinsmen and relatives, or even hear their voices.
This is called "the pressured mind," which, being driven to its extreme limit, flies out; therefore, it perceives many things that are obstructed.

This is not yet the realization of a sage. To refrain from conceiving oneself as a sage is called a "wholesome state"; however, if one interprets this as the realization of a sage, one will immediately succumb to various delusions.

Because the previous hindrance between defilement and purity has been resolved and the mind of longing and aversion has ceased, one suddenly awakens to the wondrously luminous true mind, which is all-pervasive and boundless, extending infinitely in both horizontal and vertical directions.
Therefore, with the mind of contemplative observation, one further investigates this wondrous luminosity to seek its profound depth.

This is a distant realm. At midnight, when it is pitch black, there ought to be no seeing. That it is now said one can suddenly see in the middle of the night demonstrates that darkness cannot obscure.
Furthermore, that it is said one sees from afar into the distance demonstrates that physical boundaries cannot obstruct.

This is the omen that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is about to open and the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) is about to become perfected. A place for exchange is called a market (*śreṇī*).

In ancient times, markets were often established at places where there were wells; thus, they were called "market-wells" (*shijing*). A main thoroughfare connecting these market-wells is called a street (*jiē*);

a winding lane branching off from it is called an alley (*xiàng*). "Relatives" (*qīn*) include both those on the father’s and mother’s sides—six degrees of kinship—while "clan" (*zú*) encompasses all members, whether distant or near.
Regarding "surname" and "retinue": this refers to all those who are included within one's circle of kinship, whether male or female, great or small.
If one hears their voices, it is because the nature of seeing is about to become perfected; the nature of hearing is likewise so, for they were originally a single, pure luminosity.
Zhengmo said: "I personally saw a monk from Henan while he was in Lu. As he happened to be sitting in quietude, he suddenly saw his hometown;
the marketplace appeared exactly as it was. He saw his elder brother being beaten by an official. Calculating the date and time, before long, a fellow villager arrived in Lu.
When he questioned him, it was indeed so. This must have been an unfolding of the Chan realm. It is roughly similar to this [case]. What a pity for that monk!"
They do not know how to value themselves. I, the fool, say that since it is said they are seen from afar, it need not necessarily be one's own kinsmen or relatives.
For wherever there are their kinsmen or relatives living together and conversing, all are able to see and all are able to hear.
Furthermore, if they can still see and hear at midnight, it may be known that they are even more so during the day. This is called "pressing."
"Regarding 'the mind and so forth': this refers to investigating the wondrous clarity in order to seek what is profound and far-reaching. This is precisely the application of effort and compulsion.
When such compulsion reaches its limit, the false principle accords with [the mind], and one perceives a semblance of the self-mind as having the appearance of flying out.

For this reason, darkness cannot obscure it, and objects cannot obstruct it. [Question: "The preceding commentary explains that because the prior non-obstruction between defilement and purity causes the mind of longing and aversion to cease, one suddenly awakens to the wondrously clear reality."

The mind is all-pervasive and boundless; it is limitless both horizontally and vertically. Since it is neither bounded nor limited, how could there be such a phenomenon as "flying out"? Answer: Previously, when joy and aversion were momentarily stilled, the shadow and echo appeared briefly. Yet, upon applying effort to investigate, it remained confined within the sense faculties.

Even this current state of extreme intensity where it seems to "fly out" belongs to the realm of shadows and echoes. As the ancient masters said: "The moon is clearly seen upon the plum blossoms; yet when one seeks it at the blossoms, the moon has vanished. This was likely their insight into this very point.
The ten kinds of deviant minds harbor and receive the forms of malevolent spirits (*chi-mei*).
Furthermore, when one investigates with such a mind to the utmost degree of refinement, one perceives the physical form of the *kalyāṇamitra* undergoing transformations;

in a brief moment, it shifts and changes in various ways without apparent cause. This is called the deviant mind harboring and receiving malevolent spirits. Alternatively, one may encounter a celestial Māra who enters one's heart and belly.

To suddenly preach the Dharma and penetrate subtle meanings does not constitute a sign of saintly realization. If you do not give rise to the thought of being a saint, demonic activities will subside;
if you take such experiences as signs of sainthood, you will immediately fall prey to various delusions.
Regarding the nine previous signs, they were all based on not conceiving a holy mind and further investigating the wondrous clarity as the cause.

Only this final sign, however, involves interpreting the preceding state of being driven to the limit and flying out as a realization of holiness, taking the pursuit of further refinement as the cause.
Therefore it is said: "Furthermore, with this mind, one investigates to the ultimate point of refinement. Although one wishes to investigate to the ultimate point of refinement...

[This is] the ultimate [explanation]. However, one version reads "the holy mind" (shèngxīn). Because [the practitioner] has long been influenced by various evil influences, upon encountering a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), their physical form undergoes transformation.
Regarding the term "spiritual friend," there are briefly two interpretations. First, it refers to a spiritual friend with whom one has long been acquainted;
seeing only that their physical form has undergone transformation, one realizes this is the work of demonic power. Second, it refers to one who originally lacked knowledge...

Consciousness merely perceives them through delusion. Furthermore, one sees their forms and bodies undergo transformation; these are manifestations produced by the power of Māra. The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"They may manifest as celestial beings, or manifest as bodhisattvas, or even appear as Tathāgatas and so forth. This refers to the phenomenon of the transformation of physical form.
"In a short while" means without waiting for a long duration. "Without cause" means without relying on any prior conditions or reasons.
Regarding "various transformations": suddenly a deva transforms into a Buddha, and suddenly a Buddha transforms into a deva, and so forth;

this refers to undergoing a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations in the space of a single moment. This is called "the deluded mind" and so on: first, it is a "sacred realization," which is in fact a deluded mind;
second, it "summons a multitude of demons," which is to say it "accepts and harbors" them. As stated previously: "If the host..."

The phrase "a wayward guest who takes advantage of the opportunity" is precisely a metaphor for this. As for the mention of "chi-mei" (goblins and specters), these are merely those dispatched by Māra;
if one can quickly awaken and immediately cease such thoughts, they will vanish of their own accord before long, and the harm they cause remains minor.
Should they fail to awaken to this themselves, they will further encounter celestial Māras entering their hearts and bellies;

not only will they manifest the forms of Māras externally, but they will also be internally tainted by demonic wisdom, enabling them to preach the Dharma without cause and appearing to have a superficial mastery of subtle meanings.
What was previously described as "certainly becoming a son of Māra and accomplishing demonic persons" refers precisely to this. It is merely being sustained by the power of Māra;

therefore, it is said that these are not signs of saintly realization (*ārya-siddhi*). If one awakens to this without delusion and does not give rise to the thought of being a saint, but instead practices according to the fundamental [teachings], then Māra will naturally dissipate.
If, however, one continues as before without understanding and interprets this as a sign of saintly realization, one will further succumb to various evils. As stated previously, it is clearly...
This refers to the transformation of decay into something beyond lamentation or rescue. This concludes the manifestation of demonic signs within the intermediate stages.
Fourth, a summary is provided as a warning and exhortation:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifest states during *dhyāna* all appear because the mind is in interaction with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)."

Regarding this matter, sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering these causes and conditions, they remain lost and fail to recognize them for what they are, claiming instead that they have attained the state of a sage.

Having committed such a great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. "You all should rely on this teaching after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, proclaiming and revealing its meaning during the Age of Dharma Decline.
Do not allow celestial Māras to find an opportunity to deceive you. Maintain and protect it so that it may be fulfilled."
The Unsurpassed Way initially emerges through vigilance. These ten kinds refer collectively to what has been explained above;
they do not speak of the manifest objects of *samādhi*, but rather speak of *dhyāna*. This is because although these objects exist within *samādhi*, when one investigates their ultimate nature...

"By being able to manifest" refers briefly to both tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), as previously stated regarding the subtle demonic activities in the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

All subsequent instances should be understood accordingly. "All of these belong to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)" indicates the period when [the aggregate] is about to be destroyed but has not yet been destroyed.
"The mind and its objects interact" means that the observation of the mind is not pure; it is the intermingling of right mindfulness and false thoughts.
They arise through mutual interaction. This is because if there were no wrong thoughts, demonic activities would not emerge;

yet if there were no right mindfulness, even if they did emerge, they would not reach the number ten. It is solely through the interaction of these two types of thought—arising and ceasing alternately, extinguishing and arising again—that they multiply until they reach ten.
For this reason, these phenomena appear. Those among sentient beings who are stubborn and deluded claim that...

By nature I am dull and stubborn; I am bewildered and confused regarding all matters. One who does not reflect upon themselves might say that while their station is among the ranks of ordinary beings, they have suddenly manifested a sacred realm.
Such a person ought to reflect: "Who am I that I could manifest such a sublime response?
It is because one is both stubborn and deluded that this is impossible. Those who encounter these conditions [should know] that the aforementioned ten types are all...
Regarding the phrase "the causal conditions for the destruction of the aggregate of form are about to arise; being deluded, one does not recognize it for oneself":

this means that one fails to recognize that this is a manifestation of the state of *dhyāna*, yet claims to have attained the stage of a sage (*ārya*). Without measuring one's own capacity, one considers oneself part of the common run of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

claiming what has not been attained as attained, and saying one has realized what has not been realized, it is therefore said that a great falsehood has been established. As for the statement that one falls into the Avīci Hell, this most clearly demonstrates that [the offender] is indeed [a perpetrator of such a grave transgression].
The harm is without end; this is merely to demonstrate a sense of vigilance. ○ "You all," and so forth, is an instruction to proclaim and protect [the teaching].

While the Tathāgata was in the world, Māra could do nothing; therefore, he taught that one should rely on the Tathāgata and others—meaning that one should rely on what the Buddha has spoken until after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
After the Tathāgata’s extinction, the True and Semblance Dharma periods were still viable; therefore, he further taught...
Because at this time within the Dharma of the Final Age, Māra is powerful and the Dharma is weak, it is necessary to proclaim this meaning so that one may know and take precautions;
thus, Māra will find no opportunity. Should there be negligence, the harm would not be slight. Therefore, he entrusts [this] so that Māra may not find an opportunity.
"To maintain and protect" means to maintain the Final Age and to protect those who practice correctly, thereby bringing them to fulfillment.
Regarding the Unsurpassed Way: by means of the ten minds, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is shattered and the fundamental nature is revealed;
proceeding to shatter the remaining four aggregates, the six knots are untied and perfect penetration is realized. This concludes the summary of the demonic signs of the aggregate of form.

The four aspects of the demonic signs of the second aggregate, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha-māra-lakṣaṇa*): first, beginning the cultivation before breaking through the aggregate of sensation;

second, finally breaking through it to reveal the manifest source of delusion; third, the demonic signs that appear in the interim; fourth, a summary conclusion to provide a warning and exhortation. First:

Ānanda, when that son of good family practices samādhi and the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is exhausted within śamatha, he perceives the minds of all Buddhas appearing like reflections in a clear mirror. Although there is something attained, he is not yet able to employ it;

it is like a person suffering from a nightmare whose hands and feet are perfectly present and whose sight and hearing are unconfused, yet whose heart is touched by an external malevolent spirit and remains unable to move. This is...
This is called the realm of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). That "good son" refers to one who has penetrated through the preceding objects. Zhengmo says:

Regarding the ten aforementioned objects, whether one has fully experienced them or not, or whether there are even more similar ones, if one is in no way deluded by them, that constitutes penetration.
The ear penetrates the external objects and further refines its focus; therefore, it is called the cultivation of *samādhi*.

Within this context, the cultivation of *samādhi* represents the final stage of cultivation relative to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), yet the initial stage relative to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*).

*Śamatha* still carries the meaning of "stopping. This is because, by penetrating the external objects through the cultivation of *samādhi*, one permanently severs divergent thoughts to achieve [this state].
Deep stillness: therein, the mind becomes refined and lucid, transcending emptiness and obscurity; this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Once the aggregate of form is exhausted, both emptiness and form are forgotten, and the light of the mind becomes universally pervasive and perfect, becoming similar to that of a Buddha.
Thus it is said, "one sees the mind of all Buddhas"—this means that one perceives the Buddha-mind within one's own mind. Although one sees the Buddha-mind, it remains...
Enveloped by the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), one does not transcend the temporary vision of the reflection of the Buddha-mind within a state of empty clarity;
therefore, it is compared to images appearing in a bright mirror. The phrase "if there are two lines" combines the preceding metaphor to introduce the subsequent metaphor.

Because one perceives something resembling the minds of the Buddhas, it is said that "if there is anything attained," which corresponds to seeing the image in the mirror; this is not direct realization.
Therefore it is said that one has not yet been able to employ [it]. This corresponds to the fact that although the reflected image appears in the mirror, one is actually unable to grasp it.

Although the analogy is not exhaustive, there must be a specific reason for its intent. Fearing that it may still not be clear, the text subsequently employs the analogy of a person suffering from a nightmare.
One who is "possessed by a nightmare spirit" refers to being oppressed by malevolent ghosts; this is a metaphor for the practitioner being shrouded by the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Although one is thus shrouded by the aggregate of sensation, the Buddha-mind and its meritorious qualities are inherently present within one's own mind, manifest and unclouded.

Therefore, it is illustrated by the fact that although one is possessed, the hands and feet remain intact and the faculties of seeing and hearing are not deluded. Yet, despite this integrity and lack of delusion, how can one withstand the touch of one's own mind?
Just as one is struck by external spirits and cannot move, so too is it with that which is shrouded by the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation).

Although the Buddha-mind and its meritorious qualities are inherently complete within one's own mind—vivid and never obscured—they are veiled by the *vedanā-skandha* and thus cannot manifest in accordance with conditions.
Since they cannot manifest in accordance with conditions, it is as if one has just left one room only to enter another; therefore, [one remains trapped].
This is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Second, when one finally breaks through and reveals the source of delusion—just as when the affliction of a nightmare ceases and the mind leaves the body to look back at one's own face, moving and staying with freedom and no longer subject to obstruction—this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), observing that its origin is but empty, luminous, and false conceptualization.
This is considered its fundamental basis.

Previously, it was covered by the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), like a person afflicted by a nightmare; if the aggregate of sensation is shattered, then the affliction of the nightmare ceases.

Now, the aggregate of sensation has no separate existence other than the illuminating function of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*); because there is this illuminating function, there is [the aggregate].
The "worn-out robe" (lingna) is called the fundamental aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha). For all that belongs to the aggregate of sensation arises from within this.
Because there is the fundamental aggregate of sensation, one grasps at form to form the sense organs and gives rise to the view of a self-body (satkāya-dṛṣṭi).

Even if the aggregate of sensation has not yet been destroyed, the view of a self-body will likewise not be entirely forgotten. One must wait until the aggregate of sensation is exhausted before finally escaping the cage of the body.
Therefore it is said that the mind is detached from the body. Not only is it detached from the body, but it can also reflect back upon its own face.
Not only can it reflect upon its own face, but it can also attain the "mind-born" (manomaya) state, moving and dwelling with freedom, no longer subject to obstruction or hindrance.

It is just as when the affliction of a nightmare has ceased; one's hands and feet, along with sight and hearing, are all capable of movement and purposeful action. One realizes for oneself that such is possible.

This is called the sign of the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). According to the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, this corresponds to the exhaustion of both hearing and that which is heard.

(Question: The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) was exhausted previously; how can there still be a body and face? Answer: What is meant by "exhaustion" refers only to the exhaustion of the aggregate itself, not the exhaustion of its form. If one were to insist on exhausting the form itself, then one whose aggregate of form is exhausted would be identical to those in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*); how could that be reasonable? Regarding the transcendence of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*):

in this scripture, the turbidity of views takes the interweaving of the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) and great characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as its substance, as described previously for the turbidity of views.

The text says: "Your body currently manifests as a composite of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) for its substance. The natures of these four elements obstruct one another, causing resistance; the four elements revolve, causing perception.

Their mutual interweaving falsely forms [the body], which is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Now, since the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has been shattered, there is no longer any grasping of form to constitute the sense organs.
The natures and the great elements do not interweave, and the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is also forgotten; therefore, you are able to transcend. This is transcendence."
Afterwards, turning back to observe the origin of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*): it is simply the illuminating function of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) that falsely experiences;
therefore, it is said that "empty clarity and false ideation constitute its root."
There are ten signs of Māra that manifest during the intermediate stage: first, the sign of suppressing and crushing through effort; second, the sign of overstepping through haughty haste;
third, the sign of losing oneself through meditative cultivation devoid of wisdom; fourth, the sign of constant scrutiny while losing mindfulness in the application of the mind;
fifth, the sign of failing in skillful means during practice; sixth, the sign of self-restraint through pliancy devoid of wisdom.

Seven: the characteristic of being superior through views while lacking wisdom to save oneself; eight: the characteristic of attaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom; nine: the characteristic of the settled mind sinking and losing its clarity; ten: the characteristic of the meditative object being peaceful and harmonious as it enters the mind. Regarding the first two [of these], there are: first, showing the characteristics to instruct and awaken; second, warning against delusion to reveal its harm. First [the instruction]: The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has taught that all phenomena are empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, unceasing, originally quiescent, and naturally parinirvāṇic. World-Honored One, if sentient beings hear this teaching, they will immediately give rise to fear and dread. Why is this? Because, World-Honored One, those who have not yet cultivated the roots of goodness, who have not yet accumulated merit, who have not yet purified their karmic obstacles, and who have not yet matured their faculties, upon hearing this teaching, will think: 'If all phenomena are empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, unceasing, originally quiescent, and naturally parinirvāṇic, then what dharma is there for me to attain? What dharma is there for me to cultivate? What dharma is there for me to abandon? Thinking thus, they will fall into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). They will say: 'If all dharmas are originally non-existent, then even the wholesome dharmas are originally non-existent. Since the wholesome dharmas are originally non-existent, how could there be an attainment of nirvāṇa? Therefore, there is no nirvāṇa. Because of this, they will abandon the cultivation of the roots of goodness and will not seek the path to liberation. The *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, there are those who, having heard that all dharmas are empty and without self-nature, give rise to a nihilistic view, thinking: 'If all dharmas are empty and without self-nature, then there is no cause for the arising of suffering, nor is there any fruit of retribution. There is no past life, nor is there a future life. There is no present life either. All dharmas are originally non-existent. Since there is nothing at all, there is no good and no evil; there is no cause and no effect. If there is no cause and no effect, then there is no need to cultivate the path to liberation. This is called the characteristic of the view of nihilism. Because of this view, one abandons the cultivation of the roots of goodness and does not seek the path to liberation. This is called the characteristic of being superior through views while lacking wisdom to save oneself. The *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* states: "What is the characteristic of the view of nihilism? It refers to the false discrimination that arises from the view of non-existence regarding the three times, which leads to the abandonment of the roots of goodness and the failure to seek the path to liberation. Ānanda, when that son of good family is within this state, he attains a great radiance and his mind becomes luminously clear.
However, because he suppresses [his emotions] excessively within, a boundless compassion suddenly arises in him. Thus, even upon seeing a mosquito or a gnat, he regards it as his own infant;
a heart of pity arises and he involuntarily sheds tears. This is called the overstepping of effort through excessive suppression. If he were to awaken...
There is no fault. This is not yet the realization of a sage. Once one awakens and understands, delusion will naturally dissipate over time.

That "good son" refers to one whose *skandha* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is about to break down but has not yet broken down. Being on the threshold between breaking down and not yet breaking down, they stand between the two pillars;
hence it is said, "it should be within this. Because the *skandha* of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the *skandha* of sensation has become clear, it is said that he "attains."

"Great Radiance. This is because the *vedanā-skandha* (aggregate of sensation) is itself the empty luminosity of the seeing-faculty; previously, it fell into the realm of form (*rūpa*), and thus its greatness was not manifest.
Now that the *rūpa-skandha* has been destroyed, the essence of empty luminosity is revealed; therefore, it is named "Great Radiance.
As for "the mind illuminating and clarifying," this means seeing the Buddha-mind within one's own mind. Not knowing this, one is still covered by the *vedanā-skandha*. Self-..."

This means being identical to the Buddha. It refers to deeply reproaching oneself for not liberating sentient beings; thus it is called "internal suppression" (*nèiyì*). "Suppression" (*yì*) carries the sense of self-reproach.
While this mind is inherently virtuous, if one remains solely in this state, forgetting the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), it becomes excessive.
"Suddenly [turning] toward that place" refers specifically to where sentient beings reside. "Giving rise to inexhaustible compassion" means that one’s sorrow does not cease.
One is able to restrain oneself. Thus, regarding all that is seen—even down to mosquitoes, gadflies, and maggots—one regards them as one's own only child;
therefore it is said, "as if they were an infant" (an infant at birth whose blood-red complexion has not yet faded). To give rise to a heart of compassion is likewise what is natural.
Yet, tears flow involuntarily; this is immediately falling into the view of attachment. This is called the "mind with effortful application.

By suppressing, rebuking, and inflicting injury, one exceeds one's proper limits, thereby causing these manifestations to appear. If one awakens to this, then one will benefit sentient beings in accordance with conditions without losing right concentration;
therefore, it is said there is no fault. Because the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) temporarily manifests, it is said not to be a holy realization. Do not mistake this for a holy attainment.
This means awakening to reality without delusion. If one’s right view is clear and distinct, then craving and views will naturally not arise;
thus it is said that they have long since been extinguished of their own accord. Second, warning against delusion to reveal its harm.
If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, then the demon of sorrow will enter their heart and viscera;
upon seeing others, they will weep boundlessly, losing right concentration and falling into ruin.

If one forms a sacred understanding of this, falsely claiming it to be identical to the great compassion of the Buddhas or the compassionate gaze of Avalokiteśvara, demons will find their opportunity.
Because like attracts like, the "compassion-demon" (*bei-mo*) enters their heart and viscera. This compassion-demon refers to the lingering soul of those who died in suffering;
it is a class of demon formed by the spirits of the aged. Once it has entered the heart and viscera and seized the conscious spirit, it causes [the practitioner] to see—
People then become sorrowful, weeping boundlessly. From this arise various perversions, giving rise to false views; therefore, it is said that one loses right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
At the end of life, one will inevitably become an attendant of the Māra King, wandering and falling into ruin; therefore, it is said that one shall undergo a downward fall.
This concludes the section on the faults of excessive suppression and crushing in the application of effort. Second, the faults of excessive haste and rashness in the application of effort.
There are two aspects. First, teaching through signs to bring about awakening; second, warning against delusion to reveal its harms. Regarding the first:

Ānanda, furthermore, when those good sons within that state of concentration perceive that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes clear, and as superior signs manifest before them, they may be so intensely moved that they suddenly give rise to boundless courage within that state. Their minds become fierce and sharp, and their resolve becomes equal [to the task].
Regarding the Buddhas, it is said that they can transcend three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* in a single thought-moment. This is called "surpassing and transcending through the exertion of effort.
There is no fault in this awakening, yet it does not constitute a realization of sainthood (*ārya*). Once one is fully awakened and no longer deluded, [this state] will naturally dissipate over time.
