The *Zhengding* says: "This refers to the spontaneous opening of the *māra* of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Once the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has opened, one continues to cultivate *samādhi* in order to exhaust the aggregate of sensation; therefore, it is again referred to by the term "man within concentration.

"Seeing the aggregate of form dissolve" means stripping away a layer of coarse objects that obstruct through form, like removing an outer garment. "The aggregate of sensation becomes clear" means revealing a kind of empty luminosity.
The "boundary" (viṣaya) is like the inner garment appearing before one; its meaning is the same as in the preceding section regarding the attainment of great radiance.
When superior signs manifest, one sees the minds of all Buddhas within one's own mind; its meaning is the same as in the preceding section regarding the illumination of that mind.

This is identical to the state of realization and awakening. Yet, being unaware, one is still shrouded by the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate); thus, one suffers in solitude for failing to exert oneself. Therefore—
"Clouded by agitation" means being moved by emotion and stimulated by inspiration, feeling regret that one has not achieved success quickly; this is the difference in the view that arises.
Nevertheless, this mind is also wholesome, yet if one persists in it exclusively, it becomes excessive. One must suddenly awaken from within it.
This refers to the stirring within the heart that gives rise to infinite courage; so intense is this valor that one cannot restrain it.

Thus, one ventures through hardships and traverses perils with total fearlessness, not even declining to tread upon boiling water or enter into fire. Therefore, it is said that "the mind is fierce and sharp.
One realizes for oneself that the ultimate fruit can be attained on this very spot; hence it is said that "one's resolve is equal to that of all Buddhas. About to...

How can the sudden gallop of a dragon compare to the slow crawling of an ant? Therefore, it is said that three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* must be traversed through thought. This is called the stage of "cultivated effort" (*sābhoga-prayoga*).
If one desires to leap over and surpass the Buddha-vehicle with reckless spontaneity, one cannot avoid exceeding one's proper station; thus, this manifestation occurs.

If one awakens to this, then seeking Buddhahood will proceed spontaneously, and one will not lose right concentration (*samādhi*); hence it is said there is no fault. [This concerns] the temporary state of the *vedanā-skandha*.
Because it manifests [as such], it is not a realization of the sages. To awaken to this and remain undeluded is, as before, clear right view;
one dwells in right samādhi, and after a long time, [the afflictions] naturally subside. Second, warning against delusion to reveal its harm.
If one forms a sacred understanding of this, then a mad demon will enter their heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, they will boast of their own pride as being beyond compare;
their mind will come to see neither Buddha above nor people below. Having lost right concentration, they shall surely fall into ruin.
If one forms a holy understanding, failing to examine oneself and reckoning it as a realization of sainthood, one will lose right concentration (*samādhi*) and Māra will find an opportunity.
Because like attracts like, a mad Māra enters the mind. As for a mad Māra, this refers to those who were madmen in the world who died with their ambitions unfulfilled;
their lingering spirits fail to be reborn and, having grown old, become Māras, thus entering the mind.
The *pūrvakāya* (the upper body) governs the consciousness; thus, when seeing others, it causes one to boast—that is, to take pride in one's own virtues.
"Arrogance beyond compare" means that because of the self (*ātman*), arrogance arises such that there is no equal to it.

Their minds not only lack the three vehicles, but even looking upward, they do not see the Buddha. Even if he were to become a Buddha, they would think nothing more than that he is equal to themselves. Looking downward...
They do not see people. Because these people remain in the realm of the ordinary, how could they know what I have realized?
From this, they give rise to various false views, lose their right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), and become demonic persons destined for downfall. Alas, how terrifying! (Guanding says:

"If even a sage who has broken through the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and transcended it can still cause a mad demon to enter his mind, then how much less do the followers of our school today—who claim to have 'broken through' [the barriers] and imitate others by reviling the Buddhas and scolding the Patriarchs—know how many aggregates they have actually broken? Yet they remain so complacent.")

"Do you not know fear? Thus, the function of the practice becomes arrogant and overreaches its bounds, concluding the section. Second, the characteristics of losing oneself through cultivating the mind without wisdom.
This has two parts: first, showing the characteristics to instruct toward awakening; second, warning against delusion to reveal its harm. First:
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear.
Having no new realization before them and having lost their former dwelling place, their power of wisdom declines and they enter a state of desolation where they see nothing at all.
Suddenly, a great parching thirst arises within their minds, and at all times they remain submerged in this recollection without distraction, taking this very state to be the mark of diligent vigor.
This is called "cultivating the mind while lacking wisdom, thereby losing oneself. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not considered a realization of the holy state.
The realm of awakening and realization is the same as before. As for the reason why it is not said that superior signs manifest:

the exhaustion of form must necessarily occur, but because the translated terminology is abbreviated, it is simply due to seeing the minds of all Buddhas within one's own mind, yet remaining unaware that one is still under the influence of the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation).
It is covered over; unable to advance and break through it, one says, "There is no new realization before me.

Although one has seen the Buddha-mind, if there is something grasped as an attainment that cannot yet be employed, one still thinks of returning for refuge to the physical body (rūpakāya) and increases one's application of effort and practice.

Furthermore, seeing that the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) has already dissolved, there is nothing upon which to rely; thus it is said, "The place of return is lost. However, since the aggregate of form has already been seen to dissolve, this is precisely—
It is better to rely on form (*rūpa*) for cultivation, because although one relies on it, it is not obscured (*anivṛta*).

Once the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is seen to be clear and bright, it is precisely the right time to proceed to break through the aggregate of sensation, because its empty clarity is not the ultimate reality.

If one is unable to do either, this is called the weakening of the power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*), because one has not realized the meaning that the aggregate of form is both empty and not empty, and that the aggregate of sensation is both existent and non-existent.
Therefore, by means of this, one extinguishes the heart and dissolves the will between the two pillars; hence it is said, "Entering the center, one ruins the ground.
From this point on, not a single thing is seen as something to be done; hence it is said, "Turning away, there is nothing to be seen. This vision that arises is different from the previous one.
As for "within the mind," this refers to the state within the mind where the center has been ruined; not a single thing is performed. Looking toward...
Because there is something to be attained, one gives rise to great parching thirst—meaning it is like a withered tree awaiting rain, or like a thirsty person awaiting water.
As for "sinking into recollection without distraction," this means settling the mind and recollecting the objects that were previously lost; at every moment, one dares not allow any lapse.
One thinks to oneself: "Since I have sunk into recollection for so long, I must surely attain something. Thus, one completely forgets the original practice of the three [samādhis].

Ma. Therefore, one takes this as the mark of diligent vigor. As for the phrase "this is called cultivating the mind," it means that once the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) has been exhausted, one should properly rely upon illusory form to further cultivate *samādhi* and refine the mind of empty luminosity.

Yet, lacking the wisdom of thorough penetration, one manifests the appearance of great parching thirst. Upon awakening to this, one suddenly abandons sunken recollections and returns to rely upon fundamental cultivation;

therefore, it is said that there is no fault. This is not considered a "sage-attestation" (sheng-zheng), because it differs from the sage-attestation which cuts off [delusion] before and after, and does not establish anything in the middle.
The two phrases regarding "awakening" and "realization" are missing from the text, likely due to the translator.
This is a brief summary. Second, warning against delusion to reveal its harm:
if one takes this to be a realization of sainthood, there is the "demon of recollection," which seizes the heart-faculty morning and evening and suspends it in a single location.
Having lost right concentration (*samādhi*), one shall fall into ruin.

Having no new realization before, one returns to lose one's former dwelling. One claims that both the preceding and succeeding states have been cut off, yet upon entering the middle state, the ground collapses;
seeing nothing at all, one claims that even the middle does not stand. At all times, one remains submerged in recollection without scattering, and considers this to be [enlightenment].

The characteristics of diligent vigor—indeed, all such states—are taken as signs of saintly realization (*ārya-vijñapti*). One thereby forgets and loses the original practice, and Māra seizes the opportunity.

Because things of a similar kind attract one another, the "recollection-māra" (*smṛti-māra*) enters the mind. As for this recollection-māra: it refers to those people in the world who are overly cautious and scrupulous;
when they encounter circumstances that weigh upon their minds, they die of internal depression. Their lingering spirits fail to be reborn, and having grown old in this state, they become māras.

It enters their heart and viscera and restrains their consciousness; thus, it causes them to "grip the mind from dawn to dusk," meaning that from morning until evening they constrain and narrow their minds.
To "suspend it in one place" means to bind it within the *fangcun* (the space between the eyebrows), so that they dare not let go for even a hair’s breadth.
Because they remain single-mindedly in this way, they cause them to lose right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) and lack the wisdom to save themselves; in the future, they will certainly...

From this, one falls into ruin. (Question: If concentrating the mind on a single point accomplishes everything, why does one instead lose right concentration (*samādhi*)? Answer: This was merely an instruction for beginners to gather their distracted minds by contemplating the "head-word" (*huatou*).

One who has already broken through the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) should not remain stuck here; moreover, this state is possessed by the power of Māra, so do not misunderstand it. The section on "The Culmination of Self-Loss of Characteristics through Mind-Cultivation Without Wisdom" ends.

Part Four: "The Characteristic of Constant Loss of Vigilance Through Use of the Mind. One: Showing the characteristics to instruct toward awakening. Two: Warning against delusion to reveal [the truth].

Harm. First: Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright.

Because the power of their wisdom exceeds the concentration, they lose its sharp intensity; harboring various superior natures within their minds, they themselves become suspicious that their own mind is already Vairocana.

To consider a small attainment as sufficient is called "losing constant discernment through the application of the mind," resulting in one being submerged in intellectual views (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*). If one awakens to this, there is no fault;
it is not yet a holy realization (*siddhi*).

Within the state of awakening and realization, there should also be the expression that "superior signs manifest before one. When the power of wisdom (*prajñā*) surpasses that of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), joy [arises].

Because the essence of joy is one of natural ease, one forgets to gather and restrain the mind; because one forgets to gather and restrain the mind, one does not know how to further cultivate the fundamental concentration and cannot penetrate through this state.

Therefore, it is said that one has lost "fierce intensity. When the essence of joy is one of natural ease, one regards one's own spirit with singular reverence, believing that the Buddha resides within one's own mind;
thus, one harbors the mind with a sense of superior nature, which is what is meant by being "excessively noble."
This is what is meant by "birth. As for the term "supreme nature" (prakṛti), it refers directly to the Buddha-mind within one's own mind.

Since one takes this as one's internal resolve, one may harbor doubts within one's own mind regarding Śākyamuni. Furthermore, previously, when the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) was exhausted, the ten directions opened up clearly.
There is no longer any darkness; it is as if a brilliant light shines everywhere.

Now, within my own mind, I see the minds of all Buddhas. Combining these two signs, this doubt arises. When it says "the doubt has already arisen," it means that such a doubt has already been produced;
there is merely a slight lack of peace. Although there is a slight lack of peace, one does not contemplate further cultivation; therefore, it is said that [this state] is attained.

"Being content with little" refers to those who apply their minds equally. This means that by exclusively employing the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā*), they become overly urgent in realizing the essence, thereby losing the constant examination of their own state.
They become singularly immersed in the views of realization and awakening, which leads to the manifestation of these signs.

If one awakens and does not remain immersed, but instead further cultivates the fundamental samādhi, it is said there is "no fault. This concerns the stage of the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate).
It is like a reflection appearing in a mirror; therefore, it is said that this is not a realization of sainthood. Second, as a warning against delusion to reveal its harm:
if you take this to be a realization of sainthood, then the demons of inferiority and complacency will enter your heart and entrails.
Seeing others say for themselves, "I have attained the Unsurpassed Ultimate Truth," you will lose your correct meditative absorption and fall into ruin.
If one forms a holy understanding, they will rely solely on their own *samādhi* (śamatha), clinging to delusion without returning to the truth.
Although there may be slight instability, they will no longer engage in further cultivation. Because like attracts like, there arises the demon of inferiority and easy contentment.
This demon of inferiority and easy contentment enters their heart and innermost being; it is like the world’s unlearned bhikṣus who hold the views of externalists (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Those who die without transformation and become demons in their old age are all like this.
They enter one’s heart and viscera and seize one’s spirit, causing them to claim to others that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* and the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

This is not merely the lingering habit of calculating results based on results; rather, by employing other people, they vent their own ambitions. Thus, they lose the state of right reception (*samyak-samādhi*).
If the mind follows the transformations of Māra, one shall surely fall into ruin; at death, one will descend into the three miserable realms.
This brings joy to the heart of the Demon King, while the worthy sages lament and sigh. Thus, through the application of the mind, one loses the constant state of discernment.
Second, the five types of practitioners who lose their skillful means. First, showing the signs of the teaching for awakening; second, warning the deluded to reveal the harm. Regarding the first:

furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear and bright, yet they have not yet attained a new realization.
Therefore, the mind has already perished. As one surveys the two limits [of past and future], difficulties and perils arise spontaneously.

Suddenly, within the mind, inexhaustible sorrow arises, like sitting upon an iron bed or drinking a lethal poison. One no longer desires to live and constantly seeks someone to end one's life so as to attain liberation early.
This is called practicing while losing the skillful means; though there is no fault in awakening to this state, it does not constitute a realization of the holy.

The first four lines are understandable. Regarding the two lines concerning "new realization" (*navādhigama*), the ancient masters all maintained that they are identical to the third vision (*darśana*).

I, however, maintain that they are half-identical and half-different. As for what is meant by "half-identical": since new realization has not yet been attained, this is equivalent to the prior absence of new realization. As for what is meant by "half-different":
the previous statement, "returning to lose one's former dwelling," refers to the desire to return and rely upon the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Furthermore—
Regarding the practice of effortful cultivation: one realizes for oneself that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been exhausted and there is nothing left upon which to rely.
This is what is meant by "the former mind having perished. Previously, when the aggregate of form was exhausted, the ten directions opened up clearly, and there was no longer any darkness;

it seemed as though the light of the mind was all-pervading. However, that was merely a temporary manifestation resulting from effortful application and would naturally dissipate after a time. Now, since the previous objective realm...
Once [delusions] have been extinguished, the habitual mind naturally ceases to exist again.
An ancient master said: "When first seeing the Way, mountains are not mountains and waters are not waters; after having seen the Way, mountains are again mountains and waters are again waters.
This is precisely that meaning. "One who surveys extensively" refers to one who observes thoroughly from beginning to end. "The two limits" refers to the limit of the past.
Regarding the future limit: new realizations have not yet been attained, so one does not know how to apply effort;
the past mind has already perished, so there is fear of its being lost or regressed. Therefore, it is said that "difficulties and dangers arise spontaneously within the mind."
That which suddenly gives rise to inexhaustible anxiety within a mind already beset by hardship is as follows: before realization, one is anxious that there is no progress;
after realization, one is anxious that there may be regression. Thus, it is like one sitting upon an iron bed: if cool, it freezes;

if hot, it sears—metaphor for being unable to sit or lie down in peace. It is like one who has drunk a poisonous drug: swallowing it was difficult, and vomiting it up is also painful—metaphor for drinking [the poison].
When one’s food is unsettled and the heart has no desire to live, one thinks that death would mean no further suffering;
thus, resentful of not dying quickly, one seeks someone to take one’s life. Since the intention is already for a swift death to leave behind sorrow, it is said: "May I quickly attain liberation."

Regarding the phrase "this is called practicing," etc.: it means that although there is mental practice, one has lost the skillful means and wisdom, leaving no path for transcendence, which results in the manifestation of these signs.
If one awakens to this, the former mind has already perished; it is precisely the right time to abandon the old and proceed toward the new.

Since new realizations have not yet been attained, it is precisely because one must further cultivate the fundamental samādhi that it is said there is "no fault. To seek liberation through the desire for death is clearly a delusion;
therefore, it is said that this is not a realization of the sages. Second, warning against delusion to reveal its harm.
If one forms a noble understanding [of these states], then a portion of the demon of constant sorrow will enter their heart and viscera.

Grasping a sword or blade with their own hands, they will cut their own flesh, rejoicing in the relinquishing of their life-span. Or they will be constantly sorrowful, fleeing into mountains and forests, unable to bear the sight of people.
Falling away from right concentration, one will surely descend into ruin.
If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, regarding empty clarity as a sacred attainment and clinging to the relinquishing of life as liberation, the Māra will find its opportunity.
Because like attracts like, the Māra of Constant Sorrow enters the heart and viscera; thus there is constant sorrow.
As for "Māra": it refers to those in the world who, out of deep loathing for worldly existence, lack the power to transcend it and die in a state of despondency;
their spirits remain stagnant and fail to transform. When they grow old, they become Māras.

They enter the hearts and viscera of others to alleviate their grief and sorrow, thereby causing them to cut off their own flesh and even rejoice in relinquishing their lifespan to seek a swift death. This is the most extreme form; there are also milder instances, but only...
Constantly harboring sorrow and anxiety, he flees into the mountains and forests, deeply wearying of worldly affairs and unable to bear the sight of people.

This mind is permeated by the habitual tendencies of Māra; unable to turn back on its own, it consequently causes one to lose right concentration (*samādhi*) and practice nothing but the works of Māra, naturally leading to a downward spiral.
Thus ends the section on losing the signs of skillful means in cultivation.

Sixth, the mark of self-restraint through lightness and ease but lacking wisdom. This has two parts: first, teaching the manifestation to awaken understanding; second, admonishing the deluded to reveal the harm. Regarding the first:

furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, those sons of good family see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear and bright, abiding in purity.

This is called "pliancy" (praśrabdhi), yet one restrains oneself through lack of wisdom. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a sign of saintly realization.
As before, when form dissolves, sensation becomes clear. Within this state of purity, because one has newly realized what was not yet attained, one does not regard it as difficult;

It is said that within the heart there is such rapture that it cannot be restrained. This is the perspective of our own school.
This is a great taboo. As for what is called "light ease" (*praśrabdhi*) and so forth, it refers to a temporary manifestation of light ease within a pure mind;
lacking wisdom, one cannot restrain oneself, resulting in the appearance of these signs. If one awakens to this, one should not regard it with joy.
One must urgently seek out one's original practice; therefore, it is said there is "no fault. These manifestations appear only momentarily and are not constant, resembling shadows and light;

If one forms a holy understanding [of these states], then a portion of the Mara of Delightful Pleasure will enter their heart and innermost being. Upon seeing people, they will laugh;

Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright.
Believing themselves to have reached sufficiency, they suddenly experience a groundless and great conceit (*māna*).

Thus, conceit (*māna*), excessive conceit (*atimāna*), and even surpassing conceit (*mānātimāna*), as well as overweening conceit (*adhimāna*) or inferiority conceit (*ūnamāna*), may all arise simultaneously. In their hearts, they still look down upon the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
How much more so for those of lower rank, such as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas? This is called "superior vision without wisdom to save oneself. If one awakens to this, there is no fault;
it is not a true realization of the holy state.

When one sees that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved, one takes this to mean that delusion is exhausted when it is not; when one sees that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is clear and bright, one takes this to mean that it is the absence of reality.
It is not complete. Not knowing that the squareness is the characteristic of the manifestation of form opening up to receive [objects], one considers oneself already sufficient.
Having considered oneself already sufficient, one will surely regard oneself as superior; thus, a sudden great *asmimāna* (great self-conceit) arises.
As for what is called "self-conceit" (*māna*), it means conceit arising because of the "self," such as saying, "I am the Buddha," and so forth; therefore, it is called "great. If...
If there were actual realization of a fruit, that would be the arising of pride based on existence. Now, because one calculates existence where there is none, it is called "without basis.
Taking this pride as its root, and so forth, up to regarding those who are inferior as superior to oneself, or regarding those who are equal as equal to oneself—this is termed pride (*māna*).
This is merely pride. Furthermore, regarding those who are equal, one calculates oneself as superior.
To conceive oneself as equal to those who are superior is called *abhimāna* (conceit); it is so named because it exceeds the previous form of conceit (*māna*).

Furthermore, to conceive oneself as superior to those who are superior is called *mānātimāna* (excessive conceit); it is so named because, compared to the previous *abhimāna*, this conceit is even more intense.
Furthermore, to claim one has attained what has not been attained, or to say one has realized what has not been realized, is done solely through an overweening mind (*adhimāna*).
It is also conceit toward others. Furthermore, when one does not show respect or seek [instruction] from those who possess virtue and wisdom, it is called "inferiority conceit" (*ūnamāna*).
This is to willingly accept one's own inferiority while, conversely, treating others with pride. An ancient sage said: "Among the seven types of conceit, only *mithyāmāna* (false conceit) is missing.
I, however, maintain that since these various forms of conceit arise simultaneously with what is fundamentally neither right knowledge nor right view, they are themselves false.
Pride. Since the seven types of pride are complete, being neither before nor after, it is said that they arise simultaneously.

To say they "arise together" means they are all present within the mind and manifest immediately upon encountering an object. The passage beginning with "Within the mind... explains the meaning of their simultaneous arising.
It states that [this person] still regards even the Tathāgatas of the ten directions as inferior; how much more so those below the rank of the Tathāgatas?
When one occupies the stage of a Bodhisattva or that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Lesser Vehicle, it can be known that all forms of pride arise simultaneously.
This is called "seeing oneself as superior" and so forth; it means seeing oneself as being superior.

Even if one were to illuminate with wisdom that all dharmas are equal in their single nature, one would not yet perceive even a single sentient being toward whom one could feel pride, let alone toward those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
They give rise to arrogance, relying solely on a lack of wisdom to save themselves, which results in the manifestation of these signs.

If one awakens to this, one will no longer see oneself as superior, and all forms of pride will dissolve; hence it is said there is "no fault. Because the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has merely temporarily manifested, it is said that this is not a realization of sainthood.
Second, the warning against delusion reveals its harm.
If one forms a holy understanding [of these things], then a portion of the great demon of self-conceit will enter their heart and viscera.

They will fail to pay homage to stupas and temples, and they will destroy scriptures and images, saying to donors: "These are merely gold and copper, or wood and clay; the scriptures are but leaves from trees or woven silk.
They claim that the physical body is truly eternal and thus do not respect it themselves, yet they revere wood and clay—this is truly a perversion.

Those with deep faith will take it from him and crush it, burying it in the ground; those sentient beings who harbor doubts and errors will enter the Avīci Hell and, losing right concentration, shall fall into ruin.
If one forms a firm conviction, seeing what is superior, they do not turn back; clinging in delusion, they do not return.

Because like attracts like, the demon of great conceit enters their heart and innermost being. As for what is called the demon of great conceit, it is like the non-Buddhist practitioners who possess the pride of superiority.
Those who die without undergoing transformation and become demons in their old age are precisely these beings. They enter the hearts and viscera of people, providing them with perverse arrogance;
thus, they cause them not to pay reverence to stupas and temples, even going so far as to destroy scriptures and images.
Should they encounter a donor who warns them in alarm, they will immediately claim, "This Buddha image was originally fashioned from gold and copper, or perhaps constructed from earth and wood."
This Dharma of the sutra was originally written on palm leaves or printed upon cotton cloth;
since these belong to the category of insentient matter, how could they possess spiritual efficacy? Furthermore, if one asks, "What is the Buddha? What is the Dharma?
and then asserts that the physical body present before us, which possesses sentience and awareness, is the true Buddha when it is revered and cherished—then [this is the case].
"This is the eternal Dharma. Why, then, do you not show yourself respect, but instead honor earth and wood? To abandon what is near to seek what is distant is truly a perversion.
This is the Demon King using people as his mouthpiece to sever the Buddha-Dharma, desiring to make his own teachings flourish.
When the *dānapati* heard this, doubt and faith were intertwined within them; those with deep faith listened to and followed his words.
To destroy and shatter scriptures and images, burying and discarding them in the earth, is to fall into the teachings of Māra, thereby committing the karma of Avīci Hell.
According to this, those who harbor both doubt and faith merely receive that doubt; those who believe his words with deep conviction directly encounter that error.
Thus it is said that he "doubts and misleads sentient beings. Doubt serves as the remote cause for hell, while error serves as the [proximate cause].
Because this is the proximate cause for hell, it is said in general that one enters the Avīci Hell. If even hearing such talk leads to such a result, how much more so for the person themselves?

They will surely lose their right reception (*samyag-samādhi*) and fall into ruin. (As the Zhengmo asks: "Under the gate of the Patriarchs, they reviled the Buddhas and cursed the Patriarchs; how does this differ from this [case]? Answer:

The Patriarchs most intensely desired people to awaken to the equality of the single nature and realize that there is no Buddha outside the mind, thereby severing all views of 'Buddha. How could they truly increase arrogance and, conversely, lose their equanimity? (○ Hezhe asks about Lin...))

Ji did not pay homage at the patriarchal stupa; Danxia burned the wooden Buddha; Deshan said that the entire Tripitaka is like a handkerchief for wiping snot; and Yantou said that the words and phrases of the patriarchs are like worn-out straw sandals. Is this not great arrogance? Answer:

These were spoken as a means of exhortation for those who cling to external seeking without realizing their own mind, and who cling to words and teachings while refusing to advance in practice. It was done with a single heart of true compassion; who would say it was a mind of pride?

If the patriarchs had truly possessed a mind of pride, they too could not have avoided the hells—how much less others! (○ Original Commentary Question: Regarding the various elders cited above, how do we know that demons did not enter their hearts? Answer: If one is stubbornly attached...)

This teaching states: "To be consistently non-returning is for Māra to enter one’s heart and viscera. As for the elders mentioned above, they all possessed the correspondence between practice and realization; it was merely speech adapted to the occasion.
This concludes the section on "Seeing Superiority Without Wisdom to Save Oneself. Second, the eight causes by which wisdom attains various marks of lightness and purity.
First, showing signs to instruct and awaken. Second, warning the deluded to reveal the harm. Regarding the first:
Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear and bright.

Within their refined spirit, they perfectly realize the principle of essence and attain great compliance. Suddenly, their minds give rise to immeasurable lightness and ease, leading them to claim they have become sages and attained great mastery.
This is called obtaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom; if they awaken to this, there is no fault, for it is not a true realization of sainthood.
As form dissolves, sensation becomes luminous; the objects perceived remain the same as before.

This brilliant clarity is one's own mind, because within the realm of sentient beings there is no purely true mind, and thus the fundamental clarity of the essence of consciousness is taken as one's own mind.
This essential principle is the Buddha-mind. Although it is said that the Buddha-mind is extremely subtle and refined, it does not depart from the midst of one's own mind. This...
These two lines likewise refer to seeing the minds of all Buddhas within one’s own mind; they merely alter the phrasing.

Because the causal stage of self-awakening encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition stage reaches back to the source of the cause, the causal mind and the resultant awakening do not contradict one another; hence it is said that "one attains great accordance.
Looking back, as the aggregate of form has already dissolved, one is transcendent and free from entanglement; thus, within that mind, there suddenly arises...
There is immeasurable pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). One directly perceives that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and luminous, brilliantly clear and transparent.

Therefore, one says of oneself that one has become a sage and attained great mastery. Regarding the phrase "this is called wisdom based on the cause": it means that within a mind of refined brilliance, one attains the wisdom that perfectly realizes the subtle principle;
turning back to contemplate the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and directly perceiving the aggregate of sensation, one obtains various states of pliancy and clarity.
Regarding these signs: if one awakens to them, one should not take lightness and ease as one's own standard, nor take clarity and purity as one's own burden.

By riding upon this wisdom of perfect awakening, one further cultivates the fundamental concentration; therefore, it is said there is "no fault. Yet, because one has fallen precisely into the realm of receiving [sensations], it is not a holy realization.
Second, warning against delusion to reveal its harm.
If one forms a noble understanding [of these states], then a portion of the "light-and-pure" māra will enter their heart and inner organs.
They will consider themselves satisfied and no longer seek further progress. Such individuals mostly become unlearned bhikṣus who mislead sentient beings and cause them to fall into the Avīci Hell.
One will lose right concentration and fall into ruin.

If one takes this as a realization of the holy, regarding awakened wisdom as Bodhi and lightness and purity as Nirvana, then because they are drawn by similar characteristics, a demon who delights in lightness and purity will enter their heart and entrails. Such a demon who delights in lightness and purity is like those in the world...
Without relying on true awakening to cultivate *samādhi*, one sits in meditation solely to collect the mind.
Having attained a slight degree of lightness and clarity, one gives rise to a sense of self-satisfaction; such a person dies without transformation and becomes a demon in old age.

This occurs because [the demon] enters one’s heart and entrails and seizes one’s consciousness, causing one to claim satisfaction and no longer seek further progress. One follows one's own whims and considers oneself right, remaining ignorant [of the truth].

Though they draw near to virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they do not hear the sublime and wondrous Dharma; therefore, it is said that many such individuals become "unlearned bhikṣus" (*aśrutavān bhikṣuḥ*).
At the time of their death, they realize there is no actual realization, and their disparagement of those practicing correctly proves useless.

They cry out, "The Buddha-dharma deceives people," or they develop doubt upon hearing it, or they directly accept its errors, thereby creating the cause for slandering the Dharma and severing their bodhi.

Therefore, it is said that one falls into the Avīci Hell. How much more so for a person who has already been possessed by a demon; such a person would naturally lose their correct meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Having misled oneself and misled others, how could they not suffer a downfall? Having concluded the section on attaining various signs of lightness and purity through wisdom, we now turn to the second part:
the nine stages of concentration where the mind sinks and the signs of appearance are lost. First, showing the signs to instruct and awaken [the practitioner].
Second, warning against delusion to reveal its harm. First:

Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear and bright.
Within this clarity of awakening, they attain a nature of empty luminosity, yet suddenly turn toward eternal extinction. They deny cause and effect and enter exclusively into emptiness.
The empty mind manifests before one, and eventually a thought arises that produces an understanding of long-term cessation and annihilation.

This is called the sinking of the concentrated mind, resulting in the loss of its illuminating response. (Note: Regarding the ten objects of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), as well as the first eight and the last one of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), these terms and phrases appear in all such instances.

They are generally stated by summarizing their characteristics; thus, the section titles are all established based upon them. Only this particular section lacks them, which may be due to an omission during transcription. Now, following the preceding and succeeding examples, I have summarized the intent of this specific section to supplement it. I do not dare consider this my own definitive conclusion, but await those of superior insight.)

Furthermore, distinguish these [passages] by enclosing both the preceding and following sections with circles, so that they may be differentiated from the Buddha’s own words. This shall cause readers to know they are later interpolations, thereby avoiding the sin of presumptuous fabrication. If one realizes this, there is no fault; it does not constitute proof of saintliness.
The first four lines are understandable. The preceding section stated: "Within the essence of clarity, one perfectly awakens to the principle of essence;

this is 'clear awakening. Here, within that clear awakening, one contemplates the nature of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), realizing it is nothing but empty clarity and deluded thought.
The substance upon which it relies is the nature that is quiescent and unmoving; therefore, it is said that one 'attains the nature of empty clarity. Recognizing this as..."
Truly, they forget their original practice and sink into a single flavor of emptiness; the characteristics of their minds become utterly still.
Therefore it is said that they suddenly turn toward eternal extinction within this state. Believing that this itself is the goal, they think there is no need for further cultivation or effort.

Thus it is said they deny cause and effect; from this point on, there is no Buddha to be realized and no birth from which to deliver others. Hence it is called "entering exclusively into emptiness," where the myriad phenomena...

Upon reaching this state, it is empty and nothing can oppose it; hence it is called "the empty mind manifesting before one. When the empty mind manifests before one, no reaction arises toward objects.
Even if the mind were to arise, it would only serve to increase the understanding of cessation and extinction. (Supplementary note:

This is called "the concentrated mind" because one has attained the nature of vacuous luminosity and is oriented toward ultimate stillness. However, one must avoid sinking into a state that exceeds one's capacity. If...
If one can illuminate this with the wisdom of contemplation, it is precisely the moment when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is about to be shattered.

Yet, failing to maintain this responsive illumination leads to the manifestation of signs such as the repudiation of cause and effect. If one awakens to this, one will not stagnate in eternal extinction nor dwell in a void mind;

when cessation and contemplation flow as a unified stream, the aggregate of sensation can be shattered. Therefore, it is said that there is no fault. To be "unified yet partial" is a state of imbalance; it is not [the proper state].
This is the Middle Way; therefore, it is said that this is not a sign of saintly realization. Second, as a warning against delusion to reveal its harm:

if one takes this to be a sign of saintliness, then the demons of emptiness will enter one's heart and viscera, leading one to slander those who uphold the precepts, calling them followers of the Lesser Vehicle.

Since a Bodhisattva has realized emptiness, what is there to be upheld or transgressed? Such a person may constantly drink alcohol, eat meat, and engage extensively in sexual misconduct before faithful donors.
By means of demonic power, they cause those before them to not give rise to doubt or slander. Once the mind of a ghost has long entered them, they may even consume excrement and urine;
for them, wine, meat, and such things are all equally empty. Thus, they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code and lead others into sin through error.
One will lose right concentration and fall into ruin.

If one takes this as a realization of the holy, they cling to emptiness as being correct; they will remain extinguished for a long time without returning. This leads to a single class [of beings] who, because an "emptiness-demon" has entered their minds, speak of it.
As for what is called the "emptiness-demon," it is like the worldly *cārvāka* heretics who cling to emptiness; though they die, they do not transform, remaining for years.

The aged and experienced ones are precisely those who have been possessed by demons. These demons enter their hearts and innermost beings, providing them with the interpretation of nihilistic annihilation;

thus, they cause them to slander the observance of precepts as being merely for the Śrāvakas, and to regard the realization of emptiness as the mark of a Bodhisattva, even claiming: "Since a Bodhisattva has realized emptiness, what need is there for observing or violating precepts?"
Suppose there is a faithful donor who has long harbored a distaste for the monastic community due to their drinking of alcohol, eating of meat, and sexual impurities.
Yet this person frequently indulges in drinking, eating meat, and engaging extensively in sexual misconduct.

Claiming that he practices what is contrary to the way to attain mastery of the Buddha-way, and by the power of demonic possession, he attempts to win over those present, asserting that [the monks'] conduct is "practicing in reverse" (*viloma-caryā*), and thus fails to give rise to [faith].

They harbor doubts and slander, unaware that they are merely being incited by Māra. (I personally witnessed a monk who claimed to be a descendant of the Dongxia lineage; he frequently drank wine and ate meat at the homes of donors, yet those donors revered him as if he were a Buddha.

When I inquired about the teachings he imparted to his patrons, I found that for the most part they were compliant with lust and filth. Alas! Māra has entered their hearts and viscera. Although the Sūtras provide clear evidence of this, it is truly lamentable that many in the world follow him without suspicion.
Originally belonging to the class of ghosts with lingering spirits, he has become a Māra through old age; thus, there is no harm in still calling him a ghost.

The mind has entered [this state] for a long time, and its habitual conditioning has become deep. Since the habits of ghosts delight in filth, they are made to eat excrement, urine, wine, meat, and the like.
Alternatively, this may be due to the hardships encountered by humans. Once the principle of emptiness is realized, one should understand that both purity and impurity are empty.
Since you have already consumed wine and meat, why not also consume excrement and urine? Thus, they consume both the pure and the impure, claiming that both are equally empty.
Such a person has already violated the Buddha’s code of discipline (*vinaya*) and, moreover, leads others into transgression through erroneous speech.
By causing both themselves and others to fall, they shall surely lose their meditative attainments (*samādhi*) and descend into ruin, their concentrated mind sinking into oblivion.
The section on "Loss of Vision" concludes. Part Two: The Ten States of Samādhi, the Tranquil Entry of the Mind into Its Characteristics. First: Teaching through Manifestation to Awaken Understanding.
Second: Warning Against Delusion to Reveal Harm. Regarding the first:

Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons see the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) become clear and bright; they savor its empty luminosity.
It penetrates deeply into the marrow of one's bones. Suddenly, infinite love arises in the mind; when this love reaches its peak, it becomes madness, which is then greed.

This is called the state of meditative concentration entering the mind with ease and serenity. Without wisdom, one maintains oneself and mistakenly enters into various desires; yet, if one awakens to this, there is no fault.
This is not yet the realization of a sage.

When form has dissolved and sensation becomes luminous, the objective realm remains the same as before. One who relishes this empty luminosity does not realize that this empty luminosity is the characteristic of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
They exert all their strength to investigate and savor it, wondering ultimately from where it arises. This state penetrates deeply into the marrow of the heart.

One knows that this is the pursuit of the stage of the ground of direction (*gati-bhūmi*). Because one investigates with a single flavor within the mind (*fangcun*) and throughout the joints of the bones, the void and luminosity reflect inwardly upon the mind and the joints;
they become refined, crystalline, and radiant, such that one spontaneously experiences a state of ease and natural harmony.
Therefore, within his mind, infinite love suddenly arises; when love reaches its peak, it generates moisture; the emotions are stirred and driven to madness;
the realm of lust appears before him, and he cannot restrain himself. Thus, he falls into greed and desire. This is what happens when people in the world do not know how to cultivate the mind.
One merely contemplates nourishing this illusory form; few fail to fall into this state.

What is called the "state of meditative concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to the condition within meditation where one investigates and relishes emptiness and luminosity, which internally reflects upon the very marrow of the mind, resulting in a state of tranquil compliance and ease.

When entering such a concentrated mind, if one’s attachment becomes extreme and emotions run wild, lacking the wisdom to maintain self-control, one may mistakenly enter into various signs of desire. [This must be] awakened to.
If you recognize this as empty clarity and investigate the true nature, it is precisely the time when the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation) is about to break down;
hence it is said, "no fault. Even if a sense of peace and compliance enters the mind, one will fall the moment one encounters external objects; hence it is said, "this is not a saintly realization."
Second, warning against delusion and revealing its harm:

If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, the demon of desire will enter their heart and viscera. Such a person will consistently claim that desire is the path to Bodhi, leading laypeople to practice desire with equanimity.
Those who engage in sexual misconduct will be called "sons of the Dharma," due to the power of spirits and ghosts.
In the final age, they will gather the foolish and ignorant, numbering up to a hundred;
thus it may reach one hundred, two hundred, or five, six, or seven hundred, eventually filling thousands and tens of thousands. The demons will grow weary and abandon their bodies;
lacking majesty and virtue, they will fall into royal calamities. They will mislead sentient beings into the Avīci Hell; losing right concentration, they shall surely descend into ruin.
If one forms a holy understanding [of this state], they do not realize that the brilliance of the body’s bones is merely a sign of internal radiance within emptiness.
Instead, they take the lump of flesh to be the master, reckon the skeletal frame to be their family treasure, and identify tranquility and compliance as their true enjoyment.

When attachment reaches its peak, it becomes desire; through the convergence of like with like, the demon of desire enters the mind. What is called the "demon of desire" is precisely the summit of desire.
This is the Great Sovereign Māra. As seen in the subsequent text where he is called a "spirit" (*śen*) or a "ghost" (*gui*), he appears to be an agent dispatched by Māra.
He enters their hearts and viscera to increase their lustful thoughts, thereby causing them to speak exclusively of desire.

He falsely claims that the incessant cycle of rebirth is itself the path of eternal Bodhi, and transforms laypeople into practitioners who engage in desire with equanimity, instructing them as follows:

Without distinguishing between self and other, and without discriminating between the beautiful and the ugly, they falsely claim that practicing desire with equanimity is itself the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Those who believe this teaching act out sexual misconduct in accordance with their instructions, calling themselves "holders of the Dharma" because they falsely believe they can thereby transmit the Dharma of Bodhi.
Fearing that someone might ask: "How can people believe in such things when they are so vulgar, lewd, filthy, and base as to be unworthy of reaching this state? [the author responds:]...
Therefore it is said: "By the power of spirits and ghosts. This refers to the power of māra-spirits and demon-ghosts.

Yet, even during the periods of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, such things did not yet exist. As for the midst of the Final Age, they ensnare the ordinary and the foolish, their number eventually reaching one hundred.
Thus, from few to many, they reach one hundred or two hundred, or even five hundred or six hundred.

There may even be many millions of them. Although they are encompassed by the power of Māra, it is because lust is what humans desire that Māra enters their hearts and entrails, using it as a pretext to engage in sexual conduct.
When their bodies grow frail and their strength diminishes, Māra’s mind becomes weary and he departs from their physical forms.
Once Māra’s power has receded, his followers disperse; therefore, this is called "majestic power" (*vaśitā*).
Since there were no prior offenses discovered, he was convicted solely for fanning the assembly; thus, he fell into royal peril. Some, suspecting him, slandered the orthodox;
others, being misled, entered into heterodoxy. Therefore it is said: "Suspecting and misleading sentient beings, they slander the orthodox and enter into heterodoxy."

All these constitute causes for the Avīci Hell; thus, one enters the Unrelenting (Avīci) Prison. Because all prior merits are utterly nullified, it is said that one has "lost right concentration" (*samyaksamādhi*).
Because one's future existence will inevitably fall [into hell], it is said that one "shall sink and descend. (The Zhengmo Commentary states: "In recent times, such cases have not yet been seen.

Even those with slight similarities have not reached such intensity. However, the Buddha’s words are not false; as the Dharma-ending age deepens in the future, they will surely exist. This concludes the manifestation of demonic signs during the intermediate stage.
Fourth, the summary and exhortation:
"Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifestations during *dhyāna* all appear because the mind is interacting with the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation).
Sentient beings are stubbornly deluded and fail to reflect upon themselves; encountering these conditions, they are confused and do not recognize them for what they are, saying:"
To claim sainthood is a great falsehood that leads to rebirth in the Avīci Hell.

You all should likewise take these words of the Tathāgata and transmit them after my parinirvāṇa during the Dharma-ending age, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find an opportunity;
maintain and protect [this teaching] so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
The initial emergence [of these phenomena] arises from vigilance. (The section beginning with) "You all... is an entrustment to ensure their transmission and protection. Zhengmo says:

This section is entirely identical to that of the *rūpa-skandha* (the aggregate of form). However, whereas in the former case these ten types were merely the initial stage of incitement, here the demonic activities have already been fully realized.

Furthermore, while the former spoke of demons arriving in their various forms, it did not specifically mention the *deva-rākṣasas* (celestial demons) manifesting their refined spirits. Based on this...
This, then, is the statement that one must not allow the celestial Māra to find an opportunity; it differs slightly from the previous section.

Previously, it was taught that because there is a fear that the celestial Māra might find an opportunity to enter if one does not exercise precaution, one should proclaim this meaning so that he finds no such opportunity.
Here, however, because the celestial Māra finds an opportunity and dispatches the ten Māras to come and cause affliction, it is taught that one should cause [the teaching] to be opened up everywhere.
Awakening. Do not allow them to find an opportunity; immediately dispatch a messenger. This concludes the summary of the demonic signs of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
Regarding the four demonic signs of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): 1. The initial cultivation before breaking through the aggregate of perception;

2. The final breaking through that reveals the source of delusion; 3. The demonic signs manifested during the intermediate stage; 4. The summary presented as a warning and exhortation. First [the initial cultivation]:

Ānanda, when that good man cultivates samādhi and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is exhausted, although his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet ended, his mind has left its physical form like a bird escaping from a cage.
He is already able to achieve [this state] and, from this ordinary body, ascend through the sixty saintly stages of the Bodhisattvas.
Attaining the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*), he proceeds everywhere without obstruction. It is, for example, as if someone were sleeping soundly and speaking in their sleep; this person...
Although there is no distinct object of cognition, their speech has already formed into melodic rhythms and sequential order, causing those who are not asleep to fully comprehend their words;
this is what is called the domain of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
That son of good family also refers to one who perceives people through the objects before them, whether they are complete or incomplete, as explained previously.
Because he continues to investigate thoroughly while perceiving through the objects before him, it is called the cultivation of *samādhi*.

Herein, this cultivation of *samādhi* is the final stage of cultivation relative to the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), and the initial stage of cultivation relative to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). It is the eternal severance.
The preceding ten states of mind gradually dissolve into empty clarity; this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Although the aggregate of sensation is exhausted, one is still shrouded by the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); therefore, the outflows (*āsrava*) have not yet been extinguished. As for the word "although," it is used because there is also an appearance of exhaustion.

When the mind is detached from its form, because there are no aggregates of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), there is no longer any receiving of [external objects]. No longer grasping at sensory objects to form the sense faculties, one directly perceives the essence that is free from the roots [of perception].
Fearing that this may still not be clearly understood, it is therefore further illustrated by the metaphor of a bird escaping from a cage.
This is because the bird is used as a metaphor for the essence that has become detached from the roots, while the cage is a metaphor for the roots that bind it.

Having attained the essence detached from the roots, it appears as if one has attained the supreme function of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); hence it is said, "has already been able to achieve," and so forth.

This means that one has already been able to proceed from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) on the broad ground, through the three gradual stages, ascending through all the levels of the Bodhisattvas, up to the sixtieth.
The stage of the Sage of Wondrous Enlightenment is so called because all the bodily marks and merits therein can be manifested.
As for what is meant by "capable of manifestation," it does not refer to a literal realization where the above and below merge; therefore, it is called the *manomayakāya* (mind-made body).

Among the three types, this should be the *manomayakāya* of the nature of the self-nature of dharmas (*dharmatā-manomayakāya*). Because its substance is free from the sense organs, it is the eighth [consciousness].
The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*): all phenomena arise through the transformation of this consciousness.
Once this consciousness is attained, one is able to realize that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is like an illusion, because they are merely transformations of consciousness.
Therefore, know that this is the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) that realizes the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. Having attained this body, not only can one manifest it, but furthermore—

Because one is able to enter all lands universally, it is said that "one proceeds everywhere without obstruction. Fearing that this may still not be clear, the text uses the analogy of "a person" and so forth.
"Deep sleep" refers to being fast asleep; "dreaming speech" refers to talking in one's sleep.

It does not say "extremely lucid speech," but rather "deep sleep and dreaming speech," because [the state] is covered by the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of mental formations) and is not a true realization; it is merely...
"Because it is mind-born; there is no separate object of knowledge" means that these are merely empty words, for regarding the matter being discussed, there is nothing further to be known.
This is like one whose aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not yet been exhausted: although they manifest as a sage or an ordinary person, these are only mind-born states;
since they have not yet personally realized the identity of the superior and the inferior, their speech merely conforms to the rhythms of sound.
"Succession and so forth" means that although there is no actual object of cognition, the words spoken possess established phonetic rhythms that can be heard and have a discernible succession;
they enable those present who are not asleep to clearly understand the speech.

This is analogous to one whose aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not yet been exhausted: although it is not a true realization of identity, what manifests is nonetheless solemnly present.

The physical characteristics are visible; one can distinguish between the stage of ordinary beings and the stage of sages. This causes those who have attained actual realization to know that what is manifested is not erroneous.
Since what is manifested is not erroneous, yet they have not yet attained actual realization, it is clear they are still shrouded by the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception).
Therefore, it is said: "This is called the domain of the *saṃjñā-skandha*. Second, at the conclusion, the false source is exposed and destroyed.
If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating perceptions are eliminated, it is like removing dust and grime from the awakened, luminous mind.

When one thoroughly illuminates the beginning and end of a single cycle of birth and death, this is called the exhaustion of the *nāma-skandha* (the aggregate of name). Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāluṣya*). One should observe its origin:
pervasive delusive conceptualization (*yōng-t'ong wang-mang*) serves as its root.

"Movement of thought" refers to the seeds of the six consciousnesses contained within the eighth consciousness. Because they possess a subtle characteristic of movement, they are designated as "movement of thought.
Movement necessarily entails ideation; this is precisely the fundamental aggregate of ideation (*saṃjñā-skandha*), for the floating thoughts of the six consciousnesses all arise from this ideation.
Once this ideation is exhausted, the secondary and derivative floating [thoughts] within the six consciousnesses [are likewise eliminated].

Thoughts have no point of origin; thus it is said that "floating thoughts are eliminated. The "awakened, luminous mind" (*jue-ming xin*) refers to the eighth fundamental consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*);

because it carries delusion, it is not called the "wondrously awakened luminous mind" (*miao-jue-ming xin*). Since stirring of thought has ceased and floating thoughts do not arise, it is said to be "like removing dust and grime.
This is because the nature of consciousness and its awakened luminosity are like a mirror, while the floating thoughts of the six consciousnesses are like [the dust].
"Dust" refers to the subtle characteristic of movement, which is like a defilement. "A single category of birth and death" refers to the twelve classes of beings;
it means the birth and death belonging to each respective class, because "category" (*lun*) is synonymous with "class" (*lei*).

"Illuminating from beginning to end with perfect clarity" means that starting from the beginning of birth from eggs and ending with the final stage of birth as non-percipient beings, one is able to illuminate them all perfectly, because the luminous clarity of awareness is manifest before one.

The root source of birth and death is revealed from this point onward, as stated in the subsequent text: "He perceives all twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category.
Thus, the root source of birth and death for these various classes of beings is precisely the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Once the *saṃskāra-skandha* manifests, one has transcended the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception); therefore, it is said that "the *saṃjñā-skandha* is exhausted. According to the *śrotra-indriya* (faculty of hearing) [of the *Śrotāpanna*],...

Because they are inherently possessed [of these qualities]. Those who listen to the Dharma do not refer exclusively to the practitioners; rather, it includes everyone present in the assembly.

Yet they secretly carry out these deeds. It is a pity that those who were once children of the Buddha have now become subjects of Māra.
This also clarifies that they themselves will suffer the harm; the phrase "fond of speaking of [the Buddhas] being equal" and so forth further clarifies that the world suffers their delusions.

This refers to faith. Regarding the phrase "the person sees what is already so" and so forth: "the person" refers to the individual being pointed out.

Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is no longer beset by perverse thoughts as his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination, he may, within this samādhi, develop a fondness for a lingering attachment.
He clarifies his refined contemplation, greedily seeking a point of resonance with the truth. At that time, a celestial Māra awaits an opportunity to exploit his weakness.

The first four lines may be understood according to what has preceded. Regarding "the mind loves the subtle and pervasive": this refers precisely to not encountering obstacles (*nālukya*), whereby one spontaneously realizes that the concentrated mind is dense and continuous;

as perfect concentration gives rise to illumination, one spontaneously realizes that its wondrous function is subtly pervasive. (This means it is subtly pervasive in accordance with the Bodhisattva’s virtue of being "above-same and below-harmonious.
Because of this, within *samādhi*, the mind gives rise to longing and attachment; this very state constitutes the summoning of demons.
For this reason, because one’s affection is already deep and pervasive, the mind will inevitably reach a state of clarity and concentration. One applies diligent contemplation;
yet, although the concentrated mind is subtle and continuous, its wondrous function remains harmonized with the flow [of worldly conditions], leading one to fear it may not be the ultimate reality.
Thus, one desires to seek a perfect accord with the true essence and function of reality. While this mind is inherently virtuous, as long as there is attachment, deliberation, and seeking, then—
This is of their own making; it is therefore fitting that the Demon King finds his opportunity. Second, he comes through a person who has been possessed.

A flying spirit enters a person’s mouth and speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. That person is truly unaware that they are possessed by a demon, yet they claim for themselves the attainment of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the place where the son of good family seeking harmony resides, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma. Their form and that [of the possessed person]...
Those who hear the Dharma remain externally unchanged; yet, before they have even heard the teaching, their minds spontaneously awaken. From moment to moment, their thoughts shift and transform:
some attain knowledge of past lives, some possess the power of knowing others' minds, some see the hells, or some come to know all manner of human affairs, both good and evil.
Some speak verses aloud, while others recite sutras themselves; each experiences joy and delight such as they have never known before.
The flying spirit’s possession of a person is the same as described previously. It seeks union with a man—that is, it targets a person who is currently seeking a harmonious fit.

As for the one who spreads seats and preaches the Dharma, the spirit should immediately preach for them the methods for attaining a semblance of harmony and the application of the essence of perfect penetration.
Among the second category of demons, the first type possesses a person and causes them to transform their own appearance; the second type possesses a person and causes others [to do so].
Transformation. Now, both his form and those listening to the Dharma have no external change or alteration.
The original intent of Māra was likely to demonstrate that the ordinary and the sage are one and the same—the meaning of the subtle continuity between their similar essence and function.
Those whose minds awaken of themselves are like those who attain the body of perfect penetration; those whose thoughts shift and change from moment to moment are like those who attain perfection.

This applies universally. Some may attain the knowledge of past lives and thus know the events of the past; some may possess the power of knowing others' minds and thus know the mental states of others;
some may see the hells and comprehend the conditions of extreme suffering; or some may see the human realm and recognize the divergent paths of rebirth.
All of these are merely similar reflections that accord with the ordinary mind. Or, those who speak verses do so spontaneously.

Whether reciting verses of praise with the mouth or personally chanting the sutras—meaning being able to recite the words of the scriptures from memory—all of these are in a manner that accords with the holy mind.
Being in accord with both the holy and the ordinary, they are roughly similar to the aforementioned "upper accord" and "lower accord.
Believing themselves to have already attained [realization], each rejoices; celebrating together with others, they experience what has never been before.
The three types of sensation lead to delusion and the formation of faults.
Such people, being foolish and deluded, claim to be bodhisattvas; they harbor deep affection for their own minds, violate the Buddha’s code of discipline, and secretly practice greed and desire.
They are fond of saying that among Buddhas there are great and small, that such-and-such a Buddha was earlier and such-and-such a Buddha was later, and that within them there is also...

Whether it be a true Buddha, a provisional Buddha, a male Buddha, or a female Buddha—the same applies to Bodhisattvas. Because such people see them, they cleanse their original minds only to easily fall into deviant understanding.
The meaning of this delusion and confusion is likewise as explained previously. It is simply that upon seeing them, they are able to preach the Dharma without cause. There is none.
"Causing people to attain enlightenment," and so forth. Because of these delusions, one becomes a "Bodhisattva.

Once one has become a "Bodhisattva" through such delusions, there will inevitably arise lingering intimacy and affection, which secretly binds the mind. Believing their teachings, one violates the Buddha’s Vinaya;
performing their practices, one secretly indulges in lustful desires. This also brings harm upon oneself. "In their mouths they love to speak," and so forth—this refers to the world.
Being deluded by this, they have not yet reached the perfection of awakening and thus cannot be called Buddhas. Once one is called a Buddha, there is no distinction between great and small.
To speak of Buddhas as being "great" or "small" implies that the desire-realm Mara is a "Great Buddha" while the ten Maras such as the "Monstrous" are "Small Buddhas.
The Way of every Buddha is identical; it is consistent across all time. If one discusses the Buddha by disregarding his traces, then—

There is no priority or sequence. Yet, when it is said that "a certain Buddha is a former Buddha" and "that Buddha is a later Buddha," the underlying meaning is that the two demons of *guai* (monsters) and *ba* (drought spirits), appearing first, are designated as the former Buddhas, while the seven demons such as *gu* (sorcery), appearing later, are designated as the latter Buddhas.

When delusion is exhausted and reality reaches its ultimate limit, one is then called a Buddha. Since they are called Buddhas, there is no distinction between true and false; yet, [the text] speaks of a "true Buddha" and a "false [Buddha]."

"Buddha" refers to the images of past Buddhas; those who are silent and speak not are the provisional Buddhas, while the physical bodies appearing before us, seated upon thrones and preaching the Dharma, are the true Buddhas.
Because their passions have been entirely exhausted, they are designated as "Buddhas. Since they are so designated, [they are called Buddhas].
How could there truly be men and women such that one speaks of a "male Buddha" and a "female Buddha"? This refers to those possessed by demonic spirits:
those who practice lust without satiety are called "male Buddhas," while those who receive their lust are called "female Buddhas" because they comply with the will of the demons.

Furthermore, it is claimed that men and women who undergo transformation imitate acts of lust and are thus Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is said that Bodhisattvas are likewise [of both genders]. As stated previously...
It is said that those who engage in sexual misconduct are called "sons of the Dharma-holders"; this is precisely the same meaning.

As for the phrase "that person, seeing [the signs], etc.," it means that because of what has been taught, they cleanse the mind they originally cultivated and alter their practice to demonic activities;
thus, false awakening is easily achieved, as it is triggered by the resources previously cultivated. This is the fourth point, titled "Calling Out to Awaken."
This is called a *māra* ghost, an old spirit that afflicts and disturbs this person. Once it has become satiated and its mind turns away, it departs from the person's body;

yet both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal peril. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

As stated previously: if, regarding their original cause, greed and delusion constitute an offense, once that person’s retribution for the offense is exhausted, they encounter a beast and take its form;
this is called a *māyā-ghost* (*mèiguǐ*). The rest follows the above pattern. When the *māyā-ghost* reaches old age, it completes its transformation into the appearance of a *māra*.
The four types of *gū* ghosts who, in their old age, manifest demonic characteristics: first, they provide an opportunity for demons; second, they possess people to cause delusion;
third, they receive this delusion and bring about calamity; fourth, they manifest names to awaken others. First:

Furthermore, when the son of good family’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and he is no longer beset by deviant thoughts as his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination, within this *samādhi* he comes to love the fundamental root.
He exhaustively examines the transformations of things and the beginning and end of their natures, refining his mind with vigor and greedily seeking analytical discernment.
At that time, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to exploit him.

The first four lines are the same as before. Regarding "the root of mental craving": it is precisely because the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts, that the subtle signs of movement are revealed;
yet one does not recognize them as the seeds of the six consciousnesses—the root of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

They erroneously claim that movement gives rise to existence, taking it to be the root of the myriad things. Consequently, their minds become attached, causing them to forget their fundamental cultivation.

They single-mindedly exhaust themselves in observing the transformations of things, their intention being to investigate the beginning and end of its nature, hoping to grasp both its total essence and its great function simultaneously.
Little do they realize that the moment this impulse is triggered, it is already an invitation to demonic interference.

This is the gateway. Since it is said that one must exhaustively survey [the teachings], one must ensure that the mind is diligent, refined, and swift, so that it remains free from laxity or negligence.
One must expect to attain [realization]; thus it is said: "eagerly seek analytical discernment. "Analytical discernment" refers to the differentiation of the principles of phenomena (*dharmas*).

One analyzes its nature. Yet this mind is already delusory; when the mantra further speaks of "mental attachment," "essence and spirit," and "greedy seeking," it provides yet another opening for exploitation.
Therefore, it is said: "At that time, the celestial Māra waits for his opportunity."
Second, the spirit possesses a person to cause delusion.
A flying essence enters a person’s mouth and speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. That person was previously unaware that they were possessed by a demon;
