they also claim to have personally attained supreme *nirvāṇa*. They come to the place of the good man who seeks the source, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma. Their body possesses a majestic aura.
The deity subdued those who sought [the Dharma], causing them to submit naturally in their hearts even without hearing the teaching beneath his seat.
These people took the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and bodhi-dharmakāya to be identical to their own present physical bodies;
they saw that fathers and sons, succeeding one another in birth, were themselves the eternally abiding and uninterrupted dharmakāya, pointing directly to the present as such.

In the Buddha-land, there are no separate Pure Abodes nor the golden-hued marks. Those people accepted this with faith; they forgot their former resolve and took refuge with their very bodies and lives, attaining what they had never experienced before.
Regarding those possessed by spirits who first take them as their masters: "previously unaware" means that they did not previously recognize themselves as being possessed by demonic spirits.

As for saying they have attained *nirvāṇa*, it is precisely because they were unaware. Even if they were able to become aware of it themselves, how could they go so far as to falsely speak in such a manner?
They should have sought [the Dharma] and come; when the seat was spread and the Dharma was preached, they should have immediately spoken falsely [of their attainment].
The transformation of things is their fundamental nature. ○ As for "the body possesses," it refers to gathering the multitude below as companions.

When possessed by demonic spirits, there are also manifestations of awe-inspiring majesty and the power of supernatural retention; therefore, it is said that "the body possesses majestic spiritual power."
It enables those who seek the source to dare not transgress; hence it is said that "it subdues those who seek.

Not only does it affect the seekers, but it can also cause the assembly seated below to collapse in devotion upon their arrival; hence it is said that "though they have not yet heard the Dharma, their minds naturally submit.
"These various" and below refers to the confusion shared by both the principal and the retinue. "These various people" refers to both the aforementioned principal and the retinue.

To speak of this: it is as if one were to say that *nirvāṇa* is the fruit of cessation and *bodhi* is the fruit of wisdom, and that the *dharmakāya*—which is the basis for wisdom and cessation, transcending birth and death and severing delusive defilement—is none other than this very fleshly body manifest before us.
This is surely because one uses a mind that seeks its origin through perverse knowledge and deluded vision, thereby falling into false confusion.
It is not only material things that are thus; even *nirvāṇa*, *bodhi*, and the *dharmakāya* do not exist apart from the present physical body as their basis.
Father and son, father and son, are born in succession to one another precisely because desire and greed serve as their foundation.
While karma and its fruits continue in this way, to claim that this is the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*—alas, how lamentable! To be thus entangled...
To claim that bondage is liberation and that the faculty of desire is the Buddha-nature is a false teaching that deceives people; its calamities will extend through successive kalpas.
Those with even a modicum of right view should cover their ears and avoid such views. To point to the present moment as being the very land of the Buddha—this is utterly misguided.

To falsely appropriate the Buddhist scriptures' teaching that "defilement is itself purity" and claim there are no distinct Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) or the golden-hued marks [of a Buddha] is to recklessly imitate the Chan school's talk of "no land and no Buddha.
It is like a fox or a rat taking refuge in a city wall or a shrine, causing people to dare not burn them down.
Yet, in the end, those with true insight can discern for themselves whether it is merely a fox or a rat, or the city wall and the shrine itself. Regarding this:
The people below received it with faith and returned in celebration. As for "those people," they refer to those who had sought [the Way] before.

Having witnessed his majestic spirit subduing the multitude, their hearts were already broken and humbled; hearing that what he taught was extraordinary, how could they dare to transgress it? Hence, it is said they "received it with faith.
Examining their original intent, they fundamentally wished to analyze the nature of the transformation of things, hoping thereby to attain the realization of the whole body.
This is a great misuse. Now, because he has been crushed by Māra, he conversely takes this present physical body as the source of the Dharma of life.
He claims that *nirvāṇa*, *bodhi*, and the *dharmakāya* are not separate from this. He claims that the mutual generation of father and son constitutes the uninterrupted *dharmakāya*.
He claims there are no other Pure Abodes or golden-hued Buddhas. His perversity is truly extreme.
Flowing along without returning, they are said to have lost their original mind. Mistaking the heterodox for the orthodox, they surrender their bodies and lives in refuge;
taking demons to be Buddhas, they rejoice in what they have never before experienced. Thus, the three types of sensation lead to delusion and the formation of faults.
These deluded fools take themselves to be Bodhisattvas; yet when their hearts are scrutinized, they have violated the Buddha’s precepts and secretly practice lust.
They delight in saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all pure lands, and that the two sexual organs of male and female are the true locus of bodhi and nirvana.
Those ignorant ones believe these defiled words.
The previous statement that "this person is deluded" referred specifically to the practitioner. The present statement that "these [people] are deluded" refers collectively to the assembly they lead.
Because the practitioner is subdued first and the led assembly is subdued afterward, all are deluded into regarding themselves as Bodhisattvas.
When one investigates their minds, they believe what they say; yet when one investigates their present physical bodies, there is only greed.
Regarding the mind of desire, they reckon it to be the source of transformation and birth; thus, they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code and secretly practice greed.
This first clarifies those currently suffering harm. The passage beginning with "In their mouths they love to speak of... further clarifies those who will subsequently be deluded.
If one were to provide a provisional teaching as an antidote, in order to lead them to realize their own fundamental capacities, one might say that the eyes, ears, and so forth are pure.
As for the "earth," it might perhaps be acceptable from a theoretical standpoint; however, if one speaks exclusively of what is pleasant, that is the heterodox view of non-Buddhists.
How much more so when one takes the male and female sexual organs—the source of filth and impurity—and claims them to be the true locus of bodhi and nirvana?

This is a sacrilege against the realization of the sages and a corruption of the Buddha-vehicle. Anyone possessing even a modicum of human conscience would surely find such a thing unbearable to utter.
Regarding the mouth: Zhengmo says, "The general meaning is nothing other than inciting people to indulge in lust, break the precepts, and destroy great samādhi.
Ignorant men and women only know how to follow their own passions and desires, unaware of what is wrong;
thus, they often believe these filthy words and fall into the ranks of Māra. Fourth is titled "Warning and Awakening."
These are known as the evil spirits of *gudu* (poisonous charms) and *yan-sheng* (hypnotic possession), who become demons through old age to harass and disturb this person.

Once they have become satiated and their minds turn away, they depart from the person's body; yet both the disciple and the master will fall into royal punishment. You should awaken to this first so as not to enter the cycle of *saṃsāra*.
Deluded and ignorant, they fall into the Avīci Hell.

This Māra originally comes from two classes of beings: namely, the *gudu* ghosts (poisonous spirits) and the *yansheng* ghosts (suppressive spirits). As previously stated, regarding their original causes:
if one commits offenses through greed and resentment, once that person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter insects and take form; these are called *gudu* ghosts.
Furthermore, it is said that those who commit the sin of greedy deception, once their retribution is exhausted, encounter the netherworld and assume a form known as a *yāma-ghost* (魘鬼).

The present mention of "victorious *yāma*" refers to the fact that the power of these ghosts to afflict people is supreme. Regarding the others: on the banks of the Huai River, the *gū-ghosts* (蠱鬼) reach old age and manifest the signs of a *māra*;
fourth, the *pañca-māraka-ghosts* (五癘鬼) reach old age and manifest the signs of a *māra*. Thus, they become one with the *māras*.
First, a person comes to delude them; second, they become deluded; third, they incur fault through this delusion; fourth, their name is proclaimed to awaken others. Regarding the first:

Furthermore, O son of good family, when the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) has become void and subtle, and one is no longer beset by deviant thoughts as perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes manifest, one may within this *samādhi* develop a fondness for suspended responses.
One circulates through these, investigating with refined intensity and greedily seeking mysterious resonance. At that time, the celestial Māra watches for such an opportunity.

The first four lines are the same as before. Regarding "in samādhi, the mind fondly longs for a responsive manifestation": one realizes that the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) has not yet been shattered and its superior function is not yet perfected.
Desiring to attain perfect, all-encompassing knowledge, the Bodhisattva at the stage of the Sages longingly awaits a responsive manifestation within their own minds.

This provides the resources for the development of divine wisdom. "Circulating and investigating with refinement" means manifesting a mind-born body (*manomayakāya*) that flows and circulates throughout the worlds of the ten directions, diligently seeking out various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and bodhisattvas.

"Craving and seeking through mysterious resonance" refers to the reason for this circulation; it is because one craves and seeks a mysterious response and harmonious accord in order to reach [the goal].

It is merely a matter of moving the sages through resonance and receiving their response; yet one fails to realize that once this aspiration arises, if the concentrated mind is not kept secure, there will be a vulnerability that can be exploited and a method by which one may be ensnared.
Thus, it allows the celestial Māras to watch for and seize the opportunity.
Second, the spirit possessing a person to cause delusion:

A flying essence possesses a person, who speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. That person has no prior awareness that they are possessed by a demon, yet they claim for themselves the attainment of unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the place of those good sons seeking a response, arrange their seats, and preach the Dharma. This can cause those who listen...
The assembly beheld his body for a brief moment as if it had been a hundred thousand years; their hearts were filled with attachment and they could not bear to let him go.

They served him as slaves, providing the four requisites of life without feeling weary. Each person caused those in their own retinue to realize that he was their former teacher and original spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*);
they gave rise to a distinct dharma-love that adhered like glue or lacquer, attaining what they had never experienced before.
When someone initially becomes possessed and manifests responses, speaking of the sutras and Dharma without end, this must be the work of a demonic spirit possessing them.
The reason they do not perceive it as strange is that the person originally does not realize they are possessed by a demon.
Not only are they unable to perceive this, but they instead increase their own perverse arrogance, even claiming to have personally attained *nirvāṇa*. They respond to those who seek them...
Come! Spread the seat and preach the Dharma. You should immediately explain for them the method of latent resonance and remote response.

"Able to cause" refers to gathering the assembly and manifesting immediate responses; it means that because they are encompassed by the power of Māra, even for a brief moment—meaning suddenly—those who hear this will be able to clearly see the person possessed by a māra-spirit, as if it were vividly present before their eyes.
Because they have practiced for a long time and attained realization, it is said that they are "like those of a hundred thousand years.
Due to this affectionate attachment, they do not abandon [the teacher], regarding themselves as servants and providing the four types of offerings without perceiving them as labor.

"Each and every one" below refers to leading their followers to take refuge. "Each and every one" points to the assembly previously gathered; "those under the seat" further refers to the disciples within this assembly.

Regarding the assembly gathered there: since they have already become his slaves and servants, he further reveals each of them individually, so that the disciples seated below may recognize those possessed by demons as having been their own teachers in previous lives and their original spiritual mentors (*kalyāṇamitra*).
A further kind of mind has arisen: a heart that loves the Dharma as if it were lacquer and glue, so adhesive that it cannot be untied.
This is something never before experienced, for which I am deeply filled with joy. Yet, when these three types of feelings are subject to delusion, they result in fault.
Such people are deluded by folly and mistake him for a bodhisattva; they draw near to his mind, violating the Buddha’s precepts while secretly indulging in lust.
They are fond of saying: "In a previous life, during such-and-such an existence, I first delivered such-and-such a person.
At that time, they were my wife, concubine, or brother; now I have come to deliver them. Come with me and return to such-and-such a world to make offerings to such-and-such a Buddha."
Some say there is a separate realm called the "Luminous Heaven" where a Buddha dwells, a place of rest for all Tathāgatas;
those who do not know this believe such claims to be false and deceptive, thereby losing their original mind.
Having heard his Dharma and seeing the assembly he had gathered, people led their followers to take refuge; such was the divine power of his transformation.
Therefore, they were deluded into thinking he was a bodhisattva. Once deluded into thinking he was a bodhisattva, they would certainly approach him with sincere hearts.
Therefore, it is said that they draw near to their [the demons'] minds and believe their false teachings; thus they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code (*vinaya*).

They are defiled by their perverse conduct and consequently engage in secret lustful desires; this is how they bring harm upon themselves. Furthermore, those below them in the world also inherit these delusions.
As stated previously, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he commanded all bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest in response-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) and be born [among them].
In that age of the Final Dharma, they will assume various forms to deliver those wandering in saṃsāra, yet they will never say of themselves, "I am a true Bodhisattva" or "I am a true Arhat.
This exception applies only to cases where, at the end of life, something is left behind as a testament;

since they have not yet reached the end of their lives, even such a claim is impermissible, let alone one made with a pleasant tongue. Thus, it can be known that what they say is heterodox and not orthodox. Furthermore, as for what they say:
"I, in such-and-such a birth, first delivered such-and-such a person," he says, solemnly assuming the role of his original teacher;
furthermore, he claims that at that time they were his wife, concubine, or brother, clearly using the hook of desire to entice them until he speaks of coming now to deliver them.
They merely follow their own suspended attachments and claim that one must return to a certain world to make offerings to a certain Buddha;
they further insist on the pursuit of mysterious spiritual responses. Such delusory speech confuses the masses and its evil influence oppresses others.

Alas, how lamentable it is that the ignorant and deluded in this world delight in claiming saintly realizations without any self-reflection! As for those who claim there are other [realms] and so forth, these are errors.

To point to the palace of Māra at the summit of the desire realm as the Heaven of Great Radiance (Mahābhāsvara), and falsely claim that the Māra-king at the summit of the desire realm dwells therein as a Buddha;
and further to falsely assert that those who believe his words and return to his teaching will be reborn together with him in this heaven,
which is the dwelling place where all Tathāgatas rest— such great falsehoods being established, the extreme suffering of Avīci will arrive before one has even turned a heel.
Those with even a modicum of knowledge would certainly refuse to believe it; hence it is said that those who lack wisdom believe this falsehood.
Because they are thus deeply attached to false views, they do not return to the truth until death; hence it is said that they have lost their original mind.
The fourth is called "Awakening through Alarm.
This refers to the *lì* ghost, who, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb this person. Once he has become satiated and his mind turns away, he departs from the person's body;
yet both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal calamity. You must first perceive this so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; otherwise, you will be deluded and remain unaware.
They fall into the Avīci Hell.

As previously stated, if among humans one commits the offense of covetous recollection, once that person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter a state of decay and take form as a *rākṣasa* (malignant spirit), known as a *pūtana*.
The rest may be understood accordingly. When these *pūtanā* spirits reach old age, they ultimately assume the appearance of Māras.

The six powerful *bala-rākṣasīs* manifest the appearance of aged demons (the following five demons differ in their thematic momentum from those in the preceding text). Three [points]: first, the demon gains an opportunity;
second, it attaches itself to a person to cause delusion; third, it reveals its name to awaken others. First: [Text continues...]

Furthermore, good son, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts as the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) gives rise to illumination, the mind within this *samādhi* may come to cherish deep penetration.
One exerts oneself with diligent toil, delighting in dwelling in the stillness of the aggregates and greedily seeking tranquil serenity.
At that time, the celestial Māra awaits his opportunity.
The first four lines are the same as before. Regarding "the mind lovingly entering deeply into samādhi":

this refers to one who has not yet broken through the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and whose superior function has not yet become perfected, yet whose mind loves to enter deeply into the sphere of perfect penetration.

This is identical to what was seen in the preceding section; however, the objective sought differs. In the preceding section, one sought the empowerment of others, and thus loved the distant response; in this section, one seeks...
Because one relies on one's own power, attachment penetrates deeply. "Overcoming oneself" means holding oneself accountable; "exerting effort" means seeking with arduous diligence.
"Delighting in dark seclusion" means that through dark and quiet places, one may advance in the quest.
"Seeking tranquility" means that through a state of stillness and serenity, one may enter perfection. Yet they do not realize that this is *samādhi*.
Within the state of the ground, there is no room for the arising of thoughts or mental activity. As soon as there is attachment or delight, the path of Māra opens;
once one engages in craving and seeking, the weapons of the demons enter. Therefore it is said: "At that time, the celestial Māras wait for their opportunity."
Second, the spirit possessing a person to cause delusion:

A flying essence possesses a person who speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. That person originally did not realize they were possessed by a demon, yet they claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvana.
They come to the place of the son of good family who seeks the aggregates, arrange seats, and preach the Dharma, causing him to listen.
Each person knew their own past karma. At that place, he spoke to one man, saying, "Though you have not yet died, you have already become an animal.
He commanded another man to step on the [man's] tail from behind, causing him to be instantly unable to stand up.

Thereupon, the entire assembly bowed their hearts in humble submission. If someone gave rise to a thought, he already knew its inception. Beyond the Buddha’s discipline (*vinaya*), he added further weight.
They practice asceticism with great rigor. They slander bhikṣus and revile their followers. They expose private matters without avoiding public censure.
They are fond of speaking of future calamities and blessings, and when the time comes, they are not off by even a hair’s breadth.

When those who first joined him preached the Dharma, the one who arranged the seats and preached the Dharma followed their inclination toward seeking the tranquility of the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*), and thus erroneously taught a profound realization of the method of perfect penetration; the rest is to be understood according to the above.

Regarding "causing them to submit to the power of Māra" and "each knowing their own karma": it is not that the listeners were truly able to know for themselves; rather, it was because he [the teacher] listened to what they [said].
He said: "Who were you in your previous life? What karma did you perform? Thus he claimed to know for himself.
This demonstrates his former supernormal knowledge of the past. "In that very place" means in the place where the Dharma was being preached.
"Speaking to one person" means speaking specifically toward a single individual. "Even though you have not yet died, you have already become an animal" is shown by...
"In the future, he will surely fall; I fear his mind has not yet been subdued. Furthermore, an imperial messenger was ordered to step on [the Buddha's] tail from behind.
Possessed by demonic power, the man was suddenly rendered unable to rise.

Because such a miraculous proof occurred, the entire assembly at that time bowed their hearts in total surrender and reverence. This demonstrates that [the Buddha's power] extends to the future. Even if...
Suppose there is a person who gives rise to a thought; one has already known the very beginning of that arising thought—originating from what conditions?

This demonstrates the establishment of supernatural power (*abhijñā*) regarding the present. Māra’s intention was to claim that being able to penetrate the three periods of time constitutes perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-abhijñā*);

yet he did not realize that the superior function of perfect penetration truly does not stop at this alone. Below this, the Buddha’s discipline further manifests deceptive wonders. The Buddha established [the precepts]:
The Vinaya rules are neither excessive nor deficient; one who practices in accordance with them is a practitioner of the Middle Way.
To now add further asceticism beyond this, deliberately adopting eccentric conduct to startle the world—this is what Guanding says.

"Practicing extreme asceticism" refers to such acts as renouncing the five flavors, baring one's four limbs, plucking out one's hair, fumigating the nose [with smoke], casting oneself into ashes, or lying upon thorns, and so forth.
"Slandering bhikṣus" means disparaging them for their inability to practice such asceticism.
"Abusing the assembly" is intended to demonstrate that one has no private attachments. "Exposing the affairs of others" means exposing the hidden secrets of people. Not...
Those who seek to avoid suspicion claim to possess a straightforward heart toward others; those fond of speaking of fortune and misfortune manifest their own lack of prior knowledge;
and those who declare that when the time arrives nothing can go wrong demonstrate that what they say must surely come true.
All such individuals intentionally employ strange and eccentric speech to deceive the world. Alas! These mediocre, common folk have, in a single moment, become demonic spirits.

Attached to these [views], they are able to speak such deceptive words and engage in such heterodox practices. Unless one possesses correct knowledge and correct view, there are few who are not deluded by them;
thinking they are bodhisattvas, many suffer great harm. Third is "Renown that Provokes Alarm."
This powerful ghost, having grown old, becomes a demon to harass and disturb this person. Once he has become satiated and his mind turns away, he departs from the person's body;

yet both the disciple and the teacher will fall together into royal peril. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
This powerful ghost merely possesses spiritual power and supernatural faculties, and its strength is capable of deluding people;
it does not belong to the class of superior-grade great-power ghost kings previously described. Thus concludes the section on the aged and accomplished demonic manifestations of powerful ghosts.

Third, regarding the seven ghosts and spirits who, having grown old, manifest the appearance of Māras: first, they take advantage of the opportunity to become Māras; second, they possess humans to come and cause delusion;
third, they manifest names to provide awakening and alertness. First:

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and one is no longer beset by deviant thoughts as the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes luminous, there may arise within this *samādhi* a craving for knowledge and views.
One then diligently and painfully investigates, greedily seeking past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*). At that time, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to exploit him.
To those whose hearts crave knowledge and views, he may cause them to encounter a lack of the four requisites while practicing *samādhi*, or he may cause them to [seek] worldly benefit.
Sentient beings, though lacking the necessary conditions, desire to know the gold and treasures left behind by their past lives and wish to see the hidden treasuries within the earth.
Because these habitual tendencies (vāsanā) reside in the mind, images of various mental cravings arise within meditative concentration (samādhi).
"Exerting diligent and arduous research" means to apply oneself with tireless effort and hardship, searching in various places.
"Craving for the remnants of past lives" means to greedily seek after the things left behind by one's former existences;

furthermore, this craving arises from specific objects and is more swiftly conducive to demonic interference than the previous attachment arising from abstract principles, thereby providing the celestial Māras with an opportunity.
Second, there is the manifestation through possessing a person to cause delusion.

A flying spirit possesses a person and speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. That person is utterly unaware that they are possessed by a māra, and they likewise claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
They come to the dwelling of those good sons seeking the Way, arrange their seats, and preach the Dharma. This person, for no reason...

At the place where the Dharma is being preached, he obtains a great precious jewel. At times, the Māra manifests as an animal with its mouth holding that jewel, along with various treasures, bamboo slips, tablets, and other extraordinary objects; he first presents these to the person and then attaches them to their body.
Or, he entices the listeners by hiding a bright moon-jewel (candrakānta-maṇi) beneath the ground, which illuminates that spot. All those who listen...
This person has attained what was never before possible. He eats many medicinal herbs but does not partake of fine delicacies;

at times he consumes only one grain of hemp and one grain of wheat per day, yet his body remains plump and robust because it is sustained by the power of Māra. He slanders bhikṣus and reviles the assembly, showing no regard for the censure of others.
In his mouth, he delights in speaking of hidden treasures in other regions and the secret dwelling places of the sages and worthies of the ten directions, according to their [desires].
In the latter case, one often encounters individuals who possess extraordinary qualities.

At first, a flying spirit directly attaches itself to them to cause delusion; this is what is meant by "extraordinary" (shu-jue). It means that they do not perceive it at all—that is, they are utterly unaware of it.

When such a person spreads their seat and preaches the Dharma, they cater to the inclinations of others' knowledge and views and to the long-held desires of their past lives, falsely preaching the practice of cultivation.
"Because they have practiced the methods of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). "This person" refers to one possessed by a māra. "Without cause" means that there is no apparent cause in the present;

it manifests as something left over from a previous life. "Obtaining it at the place where the Dharma is being preached" shows that the jewel does not belong to another, but was one's own possession from a former existence.
○ Regarding the preliminary signs of the māra’s descent and the subsequent delusion of attachment, sometimes...

Regarding "transforming into something equivalent": this refers to times when, instead of emitting an essence, [the spirit] directly attaches itself and first transforms into an animal, such as a *ruìfèng* (auspicious phoenix) or a *xiánglíng* (auspicious qilin).
These creatures carry its pearls and various precious treasures in their mouths, serving as auspicious omens for the manifestation of a sage.
This is like the dragon-horse bearing the *tú* (diagram), or the bamboo slips bound with leather cords known as *cè* (records). As for the carving of bamboo... [text fragment].
Simplicity: slips of bamboo were used as tokens (*fu*), and wooden tablets as documents (*du*). The *Preface* to the *Zuozhuan* states: "Great matters are recorded on bamboo strips (*ce*);
minor matters are merely noted on bamboo slips and wooden tablets. A token is a seal of trust;

according to Han regulations, it was made of bamboo, six inches long, with a notch carved into its center for verification. Two people each held one half; they would join them together to confirm their meeting.

The talisman (*fu*) may indeed be trusted. As for those various extraordinary objects—referring to things rarely seen in the world, such as the Dragon-Splendor Jewel Mirror (*nāgāloka-maṇi-ādarśa*) and the like—which first bestow [blessings] upon a person and subsequently manifest within their physical body: these are produced by the power of *māra*.
They manifest as talismans of the "Heaven-Riding Vehicle" (*devayāna*) in order to act as teachers who transform the world, or to entice those who listen, saying: [...the rest of the passage...]
To entice and gather those who listen to the Dharma and cause them to believe his teaching, he first conceals various extraordinary objects beneath the ground where he preaches.
Furthermore, there is a bright moon-like pearl that illuminates that place. When these listeners behold these omens with their own eyes, their hearts believe his words;
they naturally experience what they have never known before. [This is] the "Manifestation of Deceit" following the "Excessive Eating."
These were extraordinary delusions. Medicinal herbs are not things for ordinary consumption, yet he intentionally ate them in great quantities.

Fine delicacies are what all people delight in, yet he feigned indifference and did not eat them. To take but one meal at midday is something even ordinary people cannot manage, yet he willingly consumed only one grain of hemp and one grain of wheat daily;
and yet his body remained robust and full, never becoming thin or withered. This was Māra.
Because they are sustained by [supernatural] powers, these are all acts of eccentricity. To slander bhikṣus and others constitutes eccentric speech;
this may be understood by reference to what preceded. Those who delight in speaking of treasures in other regions delude people with worldly benefits;
those who delight in speaking of sages dwelling in seclusion delude people with supramundane benefits—these, too, are deceptive words.
Those who followed after him saw a different person; this was the work of demonic power, intended to manifest his non-ordinary nature.
Because he was protected by benevolent deities, it was likewise a deceptive manifestation. This is the third instance of him emerging to awaken others.
These are spirits of mountains, forests, lands, city walls, rivers, and peaks who have grown old and become demons.
Some indulge in lust and violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly practicing the five desires with those they serve; others are diligent and subsist solely on grasses and trees.
Unfixed actions will disturb and agitate this person; once a sense of satiety arises, they will depart from the person's body. Both disciple and teacher will then fall into royal peril.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
"Mountain forests" refers to those who preside over mountain forests. "Land, city-protectors, rivers, and peaks" all refer generally to those who preside over them.

Among these are both ghosts and spirits; these are what the preceding text referred to as the "powerful ghost kings," the "flying yakṣas," and the "earth-walking rākṣasas" who have attached themselves to the category of immortals (*xiānqù*). Now, since they have attached themselves to the category of immortals, why is this so?

They become demons. This is because they sacrifice blood at shrines; their pleasures do not equal those in the demon palaces. As they grow old, they develop a sense of weariness and desire to escape their original status.
Furthermore, endowed with intelligence and merit, they ascend to the realm of demons as soon as a thought arises; thus, they are able to achieve this state.
Those who delude people with their essence may briefly be categorized by three types of conduct. Some preach lewdness, thereby violating the Buddha’s pure precepts;
they serve as disciples to such [teachers] and secretly indulge in the five desires of the world—this is using desire to destroy the Dharma.
Others engage in useless diligence, practicing blindly out of ignorance, consuming only grass or wood—this causes people...

Imitating their conduct: this is the method by which delusion destroys wisdom. Or there may be those who frequently become angry and frequently rejoice; who frequently exert themselves and frequently become indolent; who frequently have faith and frequently harbor doubt;
whose actions lack constancy, and who, with a single-minded intent to cause vexation and confusion, cause such a person to lose their original practice.

This is the method by which distraction destroys concentration. The details regarding "weariness" and "satisfaction" can be understood by analogy with what precedes. When spirits and ghosts grow old, they become māras.
The section on signs concludes. Third, the three signs of an eightfold *jingmei* (spirit-demon) who has grown old and become a *māra*: first, providing an opportunity for the *māra* to gain entry;
second, possessing a person to come and cause delusion; third, manifesting names to provide awakening. First:

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts as the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes luminous,

if within this *samādhi* one develops a fondness for various supernatural powers and transformations, investigating the source of these transformations and greedily grasping at spiritual might, then the celestial Māra will watch for his opportunity and seize it.

Regarding "the mind’s love for supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth": this refers to one who has not yet personally realized the destruction of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and has not yet deeply attained the profound penetration of universal resonance (*yuan-tong*).

Because there is no means for divine function to manifest wondrously, the mind yearns for the Bodhisattvas' sovereign supernatural powers and various transformations, such as the thirty-two manifestations, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and the four inconceivables. It is by virtue of this that one investigates transformation.

The source of transformation consists of greed for the wondrous power of spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*). However, the source of transformation arises from perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), and the wondrous power of spiritual penetrations manifests through non-action (*wu-wo*).
Simply rely on fundamental cultivation until the subsequent layers of obscuration (*yin*) are completely shattered. When the proper time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself.
If you give rise to a calculating mind to investigate it, you immediately fall into perverse thought; if you fixate your intent with greed, you are lost.
They grasp at things; thus there is manifest activity. How could this not allow the celestial Māras and malevolent spirits to wait for an opportunity?
Second, they come through those possessed by spirits to delude others.

A flying spirit enters a person’s mouth and speaks of the sutras and the Dharma; the person truly does not realize they are possessed by a māra, and likewise claims to have attained realization themselves.
The Unsurpassed Nirvana. He comes to the place where that son of good family seeking supernatural powers resides, spreads his seat, and preaches the Dharma.
This person may then hold a flame in his hand and grasp that light, distributing it over the heads of the fourfold assembly who are listening.
On the crowns of the heads of all these listeners, the flames reach several feet in length; yet they possess no quality of heat and never burn them. Or, upon water—
He moved as if treading upon level ground. At times he sat unmoving in mid-air; at other times he entered into a flask or stayed within a sack.
He passed through windows and penetrated walls without any hindrance, yet alone he could not exercise mastery over blades and weapons.
He claimed to be a Buddha, wearing white robes while receiving the prostrations of this mountain monk. He slandered Chan and the Vinaya, reviled his followers, and exposed their secrets.
In his human affairs, he did not avoid scandal or suspicion. He constantly spoke of supernatural powers and mastery while in their presence, or even caused people to see Buddha-lands from the side.
Such demonic power used to delude people and lacked any reality. He praised sexual misconduct and did not condemn coarse behavior, taking various vulgarities as the transmission of the Dharma.

First, regarding the delusion concerning seeking the teaching of the Dharma: one should seek it, and when the teacher comes to spread his seat and preach the Dharma, one should immediately request him to teach the methods of supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*).
The rest is as above. Next, regarding the delusion concerning manifesting supernatural powers according to one's needs:

because mere verbal explanation is insufficient to inspire faith, and with the desire to cause [the practitioner] to see them directly, he next manifests supernatural powers. He holds a fire in his hand, and having done so...

This is already a divine marvel; how much more so when he gathers his radiance into fragments and distributes them over the heads of the fourfold assembly, each fragment several feet long, neither hot nor burning—this is the height of divine marvel.
To walk upon water is already enough to bewilder people, yet to do so as if treading on level ground is even more bewildering. Furthermore, these two matters...
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of fearlessness that resemble the overcoming of the perils of fire and water;

however, those [practitioners] achieve this through the wondrous power of revolving their sight and hearing, whereas here, it is through seeing karma and hearing karma that the power of karma manifests as fire and water—thus they are not the same.
Sitting unmoving in mid-air is like the mutual identity of form and emptiness; even a jar or a sack [can be used].

It accommodates the body, appearing as if the large and small were mutually contained within one another. However, that [state] is the dependent origination of the ocean of nature (*dharmadhātu*), whereas this is produced by the power of Māra;
thus, they differ in terms of duration. A person of wisdom can naturally discern between them. As for the window, it may be closed, yet one can still pass through.
A wall may be obstructive yet penetrable; this too resembles the supernatural power of the *ṛddhi-viṣaya*.

However, it is produced through the power of Māra and is fundamentally different from the powers developed through cultivation by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as well as those arising from the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) in the Mahāyāna. As for why one cannot attain mastery over weapons:
it is because Māra has not yet abandoned desire and the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) has not been extinguished, and thus he cannot cause weapons not to wound. ○
He himself declares that what he says below is manifested to reveal delusion; for the sake of those who are ignorant and confused, he claims to be a Buddha.
Should there be an unwise bhikṣu who believes his words and joyfully prostrates before him, that person will immediately don white robes while receiving the bows of bhikṣus.
Such a one slanders those who practice meditation and discipline, denigrating the Chan school as "mad practitioners" and disparaging the upholders of the Vinaya as "lesser beings."
Furthermore, those who do not reject such teachers of doctrine falsely claim that what they themselves have spoken is the very word of the Buddha, asserting that it should be followed and believed.
By claiming for themselves the status of a Buddha, they destroy the Jewel of the Buddha; by receiving the prostrations of bhikṣus, they destroy the Jewel of the Saṅgha;
and by slandering dhyāna and the Vinaya, they destroy the Jewel of the Dharma. Those who believe their teachings and imitate their conduct sever the lineage of the Three Jewels.
This is the seed of hell. Those who revile the assembly consider themselves impartial; those who expose the affairs of others consider themselves upright.
Deludedly claiming to be both impartial and upright, they ask, "Why should I fear criticism or suspicion? and thus do not avoid it.
They constantly speak of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) in order to comfort the hearts of seekers; they cause people to see Buddha-lands in order to provide proof of their own correctness.
The two phrases regarding "the Buddha" and "the power of ghosts" directly denounce [those views] as false and not true.

They praise those who engage in sexual misconduct, as when it is said that the two organs of male and female are themselves the true locus of bodhi and nirvana, and so forth; thus, they do not disparage such coarse practitioners.
For example, they claim that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue manifest as the Pure Land; they take vulgar, lewd, and debased matters to be the transmission of the Dharma;
and they say that those who can practice sexual misconduct are called "sons of the Dharma-holders."
Third is the emergence of those who cause alarm and awakening.
These are the mountain spirits, sea spirits, wind spirits, river spirits, and earth spirits of all plants and trees, as well as the accumulated essences and phantoms of many kalpas;
or else dragon phantoms; or spirits formed when immortals whose lifespans have ended are revived; or those whose period of immortality has expired.

When his allotted years have ended and he ought to die, yet his form does not decay, it is because another spirit has attached itself to him. As he grows old, he becomes a demon who harasses and disturbs this person.
Once the spirit has become satiated and the thought of departure arises, it leaves the person's body; both the disciple and the master often fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
The four characters "Heaven, Earth, Great Power" (Tiandi Dali) collectively refer to the five essences mentioned below.

Because these are the powerful essences within heaven and earth, it is said that the mountains, seas, rivers, winds, and lands each have their own presiding deities, who may be either orthodox or heterodox.
That which is correct becomes a *shen* (spirit); that which is perverse becomes a *jing* (essence). Because it is able to share power with the correct *shen*, its strength is the greatest.

Regarding "all grasses and trees" and so forth: this refers to extraordinary plants and strange woods that do not die for accumulated kalpas, receiving the essence of Heaven, Earth, the sun, and the moon to become *mei* ghosts.
Or again, as for dragon-ghosts (*long-mei*), they are not those that raise clouds or bring about [rain].
There are dragons of the rain, as well as those that guard the celestial palaces and those that guard the treasuries.

One class steals the spiritual essence of Heaven, while the other robs the vital essence of material things; both can manifest as *yao* (monsters) or *mei* (seducers). Alternatively, there are those who were originally immortals but, upon the end of their lifespans, returned to life as *mei*;
having originally sought longevity, they did not expect there would be an end, and dying with no peace in their hearts, they attach themselves to their former abodes.
They return to their physical substance and are revived; yet, they do not believe in the arts of the immortals and instead manifest as malevolent spirits, hence they are called *mèi* (demoniacs).

Regarding those who have completed their period as immortals and whose years for death have arrived, this refers to the duration of their immortal tenure—whether five hundred years, one thousand years, or three thousand years—and how, according to these calculations, there must inevitably come a time of exhaustion. Since there is such an end, one calculates their...

He was due to die by the laws of age; however, because he had refined his essence and nurtured his vital energy (*qi*), though his spirit had departed, his physical form had not yet undergone transformation.
Thus, he became possessed by strange spirits, who borrowed his substance to act as demons.

Yet, while the arts of the immortals are fundamentally for longevity and the refinement of the body originally aims at non-transformation, alas, when the appointed time has arrived, the consciousness is difficult to retain, leaving behind nothing but an empty shell.
One becomes possessed by a strange spirit. It is a pity that past meritorious practices are instead used to support such a malevolent apparition.
Those who do not cultivate *samādhi* but instead fix their thoughts to preserve the physical form should know to reflect with great urgency. Regarding the two phrases on "old age":

it means that the aforementioned spirits and demons reach maturity as demonic companions when they grow old; these demonic emissaries then attach themselves to the spirits to harass and disturb such persons. The rest may be understood accordingly.
Contemplation and Knowledge: The detailed account of how *jingmei* (spiritual apparitions) age and take on demonic forms.

Regarding the three ways in which the ninefold vital energy (*jiuqi*) ages and takes on demonic forms: first, it provides an opportunity for demons; second, it attaches itself to humans to cause delusion;
third, it manifests names to provide awakening and alertness.

Furthermore, good son, when the aggregate of sensation is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by perverse thoughts as the perfect concentration brings forth illumination, within this *samādhi* the mind comes to cherish the cessation of entry [into extinction].
One investigates the nature of transformation and greedily seeks the profound emptiness. At that time, the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to seize it.

Regarding "the cessation of craving for the mind": one personally realizes that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has already ceased, and the subtle movement of the fundamental aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is revealed within the substance of the eight consciousnesses. Because of this, craving for the mind ceases;
that is to say, it ceases together with that fundamental aggregate of perception and its subtle movement. All phenomena are like magical illusions, arising from movement.

That which exists is precisely its nature. What is now called "investigating the transformative nature" refers to investigating the fundamental *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) and its subtle, moving characteristics, with the aim of bringing them to total cessation.
This aim for total cessation is undertaken because of a longing for profound emptiness (*gambhīra-śūnyatā*).
By "profound emptiness," it is meant not only that both mind and objects are quiescent, but furthermore, that the hidden and the manifest are both sovereign and free. However...
Your resolve is indeed excellent; however, you have given rise to attachment and delight, forgetting your original practice.

By single-mindedly pursuing [external things], you first cleared the path for heterodoxy, allowing the celestial Māras to find an opportunity—this was only to be expected. Second, others have come to you to delude you.

A flying spirit takes possession of a person and speaks of the Dharma and its methods. That person never realizes they are possessed by a demon, yet claims for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the dwelling of a son of good family who seeks emptiness, spread out a seat, and preach the Dharma.

Within the great assembly, their form suddenly becomes empty and the multitude sees nothing; then, from the void, they suddenly reappear. Thus, they exercise mastery over appearing and disappearing at will.
Sometimes they manifest their bodies as transparent as lapis lazuli; sometimes they extend their hands and feet, emitting the fragrance of *candana*;
or their excrement and urine are like thick honey. They revile the precepts and hold those who have left the household life in contempt.

Constantly preaching in their mouths that there is neither cause nor effect, and that upon a single death one is extinguished forever with no further rebirths for either ordinary beings or sages, they secretly practice while claiming to have attained emptiness and stillness.
Regarding greed: those who indulge in desire also attain the emptiness of mind. Denying cause and effect, he first preached the manifestation of emptiness.
As for the one who prepared the seat and preached the Dharma, he responded to their request by erroneously teaching that both mind and objects are empty.
Relying on these empty words, fearing they might not believe him, he subsequently manifested emptiness; this was precisely during the Great [Assembly].
Suddenly, within the assembly, it became empty and nothing could be seen; this demonstrates that existence is itself emptiness.

When, while the forms were empty and invisible, they suddenly emerged from the void, this demonstrates that emptiness is itself existence. Such mastery over appearing and disappearing is roughly similar to "wondrous existence" (miao-you) within "true emptiness" (zhen-kong).
This was merely a deceptive manifestation intended to accord with the minds of those who crave profound emptiness.
Such signs of unimpededness are produced by the power of Māra; do not mistake them. Or, they may manifest inferior wonders to delude the masses:
their bodies, born of desire and craving, suddenly appear as transparent as lapis lazuli, demonstrating that they are pure while still stained;
yet their hands touch everything, and their feet are often covered in sweat and filth, while they suddenly emit the fragrance of sandalwood, though their excrement is foul-smelling.
Turbid urine may suddenly become as sweet as rock honey; these are all cases where what is foul becomes fragrant.

This is intended to demonstrate that just as existence can be empty, defilement can be purified, and the foul can become fragrant. Such supernatural wonders are most likely to startle the common folk.
Furthermore, since the body is the root of desire, they also intend to use this as a seductive technique to incite lust. Thus, they slander and destroy the precepts.
This refers to those who, while using the observance of precepts to restrain the body, fail to realize that there is no "body" to be restrained.

They disparage those who have left the household life, claiming they cannot achieve the emptiness of the body and are merely binding themselves in vain. This, too, is the dregs of the Tathāgata’s teachings, stolen by celestial Māras and used to bolster their own flow of rhetoric.
Should anyone be of this sort, they ought to know to feel ashamed. ○ [Regarding] the phrase "denying [reality] with the mouth": it refers to those who reject and negate [the truth].
Regarding cause and effect: previously, by means of the matter of a "similar emptiness," they led [beings] into the ranks of Māra;
this is also the doctrine of ultimate annihilationism, which gradually destroys the seeds of the Buddha.

Therefore, they constantly preach that there is no cause and no effect, and that after one death, there is eternal extinction—just as King Prasenajit previously saw Kātyāyana and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, both of whom said that after this body dies...
They advocate annihilationism and fall precisely into this view, claiming that there are no further rebirths and no ordinary beings or sages.
If there are no future bodies, then good and evil deeds have no retribution; if there are no ordinary beings or sages, then cultivation and realization are mere empty talk.

Thus, they take the total annihilation of all things to be the attainment of emptiness and the attainment of tranquility. Having taken annihilation as the attainment of emptiness and tranquility, they proceed to indulge in their desires.
To ensure they remain uninjured and unimpeded, it is said that although they have attained emptiness and stillness, they secretly practice lustful desires;
those who receive these desires are called "sons of the Dharma" who maintain the lineage. They secretly transmit the doctrine of annihilation, causing students to adopt the view of nihilism.
Thus it is said: "They also attain an empty mind, yet deny cause and effect. Yongjia said: "Vast and open emptiness, denying cause and effect—how vast and unrestrained!"
To act with dissipation invites calamity; how much more so when one is instigated by demons! Third is the name "Awakening through Alarm":

this refers to the vital essence of solar and lunar eclipses, precious metals, jade, cinnabar, fungi, qilin, phoenixes, tortoises, and cranes, which do not die for thousands of myriad years and thus become spirits.
They emerge within the lands; when they grow old, they become demons to harass and disturb people until their hearts become weary and satisfied.
When that person’s body departs, both the disciple and the teacher will likely fall into royal punishment. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth;
if you remain deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
Regarding the eclipses of the sun and moon: when dark vapors press against them, it is called "thinning" (*bó*); when they obscure their brilliant radiance, it is called "eclipsing" (*shí*).
This refers precisely to what we call solar and lunar conjunctions. Now, the sun is the essence of Yang and the moon is the essence of Yin;
each possesses a radiant aura that spreads and pours forth everywhere. At the moment of such an eclipse, this radiation cannot be dispersed, but passes directly through [the obscuring vapors].
As for the earth, its precious metals, jade, cinnabar, and rare herbs, as well as the qilin, phoenix, tortoise, and crane—by obtaining these, one may achieve longevity and cultivate excellence.
Thus it is said that those who do not die for thousands of myriad years are "spirits" (*ling*).
Those born within the human realm are "Immortals of Things," "Immortals of Birds," or "Immortals of Beasts"; they are distinct from the "accumulated kalpas of refined charms" mentioned previously.

...as well as those who have become demons through old age, etc., may be understood according to the preceding [sections]. This concludes the section on the signs of the spirit becoming a demon through old age.
Third, the signs of being instigated by the ten kinds of *māra* devas: first, providing an opportunity for the *māra* to gain access; second, possessing a person to come and cause delusion;
third, manifesting names to provide awakening. First:

Furthermore, son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become empty and subtle, and one is no longer beset by deviant thoughts as the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) becomes luminous, there may arise within this *samādhi* a craving for long life.

One laboriously investigates the subtlest points, greedily seeking eternal years, and abandons the coarse, fragmented birth to suddenly hope for the permanence of the subtle marks of the transformational body (*pariṇāmika-śarīra*).
At that time, the celestial Māra watches for his opportunity.
Once the aggregate of sensation has been shattered, the subtle movement of the fundamental aggregate of perception is revealed.
One realizes that the floating thoughts of the six consciousnesses arise from this, and that boundless birth and death are produced from this. Consequently, the mind develops a craving for long life.
This is because one must shatter the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) to emerge from birth and death. "Microscopic" (*wei*) refers to subtle signs of movement.

However, these subtle signs of movement cannot be investigated through a mind of intentional effort; rather, by relying on fundamental cultivation, they will naturally cease once meditative concentration (*samādhi*) becomes deep.
It is like settling turbid water in a still vessel: when it is profoundly still and unmoving, the sand and silt settle of their own accord. Now, by means of...
To labor so diligently and exhaust oneself in investigating the subtlest intimations is already a miscalculation.

Furthermore, to covet eternal existence while abandoning the birth-and-death of the segmented realm, and to suddenly hope for the transformation-body while longing for the permanence of subtle marks—this only serves to further increase one's delusions.
It is no wonder that the celestial Māras wait in ambush, finding their opportunity. Second, they come through human intermediaries to cause confusion.

A flying spirit takes possession of a person and speaks of the Dharma; that person does not realize at all that they are possessed by a demon, and claims for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the place where the son of good family seeking the Way resides, spread out a seat, and preach the Dharma.

They speak eloquently of traveling to and from other lands without hindrance, or of returning in an instant after having traveled ten thousand *li*, claiming to have actually obtained [the teachings] in those distant regions.

Furthermore, suppose there is an object located within a single dwelling, at a distance of only a few paces from one spot. If a person were told to go from the eastern side to the western wall, they might walk with great haste for many years and still not arrive.
Because of this, their mind may develop faith and yet harbor doubts as to whether the Buddha has truly appeared before them.
He constantly says with his own mouth: "The sentient beings of the ten directions are all my children; I have given birth to all Buddhas, and I have brought forth the worlds. I am...
The original Buddha appeared in the world spontaneously and did not attain it through cultivation.
That he came at first to preach the Dharma, yet they remained entirely unaware and unperceptive, contains a profound sense of wonder.
To say that such people were originally ordinary, worldly beings and that he spoke the sutras and Dharma without cause, clearly indicates they were possessed by demons. Thus...

That they do not perceive this at all is indeed strange. As for those who spread out seats and preach the Dharma, they comply with what others seek by erroneously claiming that there is a self-existent, eternally abiding dharma.

When they manifest spiritual powers to move and inspire those who speak of them favorably—such as by showing themselves traveling to other lands without obstruction, or returning from ten thousand *li* away in an instant—it is because they have manifested a body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Mere words have no basis for proof; it is because one causes [the object] to appear before one’s eyes that it is so.

As for those who obtain objects from distant places, this serves as testimony that their arrival was not in vain. (I have heard that among those who follow the Daoist teachings, Xue Daoguang cultivated nature but did not cultivate life-force; he could only manifest a shadow-spirit, yet could not retrieve objects from afar.)

Zhang Ziyang practiced the dual cultivation of *xing* (nature) and *ming* (life), and was further able to manifest a *yang-shen* (spiritual body) and retrieve objects from afar. Judging by this, even if one can retrieve objects from a distance, it still does not transcend the mere conjuring skills of celestial demons (*tianmo*).

How could such feats compare in quality or depth with the "Universal Manifestation of Physical Bodies" (*prabhāsvara-samādhi*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*, or the "perfectly penetrating and supreme function" of this very scripture? A single dwelling or house is but a few paces in extent; it is extremely close.
Yet, traveling from east to west at a rapid pace for many years, one fails to reach it; it seems as if it were very far away. However, above—
When clarity resides within oneself, what is distant is traversed as if it were near. When this clarity is directed toward others, it causes the near to appear as if distant.
This bears a slight resemblance to the "freedom of breadth and narrowness" among the Ten Mysterious Gates; even the illusory arts of demonic power are difficult to conceive.
Because of this, his mind was stirred with awe, and he nearly believed it to be real. However, because he had not yet reached a definitive certainty, it is said that he doubted the Buddha.
Manifest before them. Now, since it is said they have "faith" and yet also "doubt," it is fortunate that they still remain at the juncture where doubt and faith intermingle;
as they have not yet gone deep, they may perhaps be saved. ○ Regarding the phrase "constantly demonstrating permanence within their mouths":
this means that because they are constantly speaking [of permanence], one fears that their state of mixed doubt and faith will be habitually perfumed by demonic speech. All sentient beings...
My son, "I existed before there were sentient beings" clarifies that I existed even prior to the existence of sentient beings.

"I give birth to all Buddhas" clarifies that I gave birth even prior to the birth of all Buddhas. "I bring forth the worlds" clarifies that I brought them forth even prior to the emergence of the worlds.
Sentient beings exist in dependence upon me; all Buddhas are born in dependence upon me; and the worlds emerge in dependence upon me.
Therefore, it is said: "I am the Primordial Buddha. This refers to the Fundamental Primordial Buddha.
Since he is the Fundamental Primordial Buddha, he remains even to this day; as for the length of his lifespan, there likely could be none that surpasses this.

The concluding statement—that he appeared in the world spontaneously and did not attain it through cultivation—precisely reveals that the practice of his followers is useless, and it seeks to delude those who hold to the correct [teachings].
To cultivate [the mind] and yet deliver it into the net of Māra. Third is the name "Awakening through Renown.

This refers to when the sovereign Māras of the world and their retinues—such as the Cāmuṇḍas, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Piśāca youths who have not yet awakened their resolve—take advantage of one's empty clarity to consume their vital essence. Or, it may occur without such causes.

The Master said: "If a practitioner personally witnesses [this deity] being called Vajradhara and granted long life, yet manifests in the form of a beautiful woman and indulges in rampant lust, then before a year has passed, their liver and brain will wither away. They will speak to themselves alone, appearing like a malevolent spirit.
Those who encounter this person—of whom there are many whose details are unknown—will fall into royal calamities; they will dry up and die before even facing formal execution, causing great turmoil."
That person will eventually pass away; you should first awaken so as not to enter saṃsāra. If you remain deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Regarding the phrase "the first treading upon the former name is called 'manifestation'": Master Gushan says that this refers to the Māra of the Heavenly King of Desire (Kāmadeva) who dwells in the world.

Above the sixth heaven of the Realm of Desire (*kāmadhātu*), there is a separate dwelling place for the Māra King, which is also included within the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).

Because he lacks the mind of renunciation, he is designated by the name "Abiding in the World. However, when a practitioner has already destroyed the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and attained the realization of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and further desires to destroy the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) with the resolve for definitive renunciation, the celestial Māra cannot bear this and therefore causes [obstacles].
Their retinues dispatch spirits to possess people and delude them. Regarding those such as the Cāmuṇḍās and others, two categories from among their retinues are briefly cited here:
the Cāmuṇḍās—here translated as "jealous women" or alternatively as "wrathful goddesses"—who are so called because they are preoccupied with jealousy and anger and are female māras;
and the Piśāca youths, who are the Piśāca dark-demons, also known as Piśācas.
"Zhe" (遮). This is called "Consuming Vital Essence" (*chāyā-puṣṭa*). It means that they are able to consume the vital essence of humans and the five grains.
As for why their names are invariably linked with those of the Heavenly Kings, it is because they are under their jurisdiction.

Since they are governed by the Four Heavenly Kings, they ought to protect the world and sustain those who practice the true path; yet that they instead attach themselves to humans is because these ghost-children are ignorant and deluded. They have not yet...
This is because they give rise to the intention to protect the world and to preserve and sustain the mind of true cultivation.
However, they must cause Cāmuṇḍā to become intimate with them, so that by exploiting her empty eloquence and clear wisdom, she may provide resources for the arousal of false views;
furthermore, they must cause the Vaiśravaṇa youth to become close to them, so that he may devour their marrow, essence, blood, and vital energy.
To assist and nourish false deities is not only intended to destroy correct cultivation, but is also done simultaneously to benefit the retinues of Māra.

○ Alternatively, the phrase "or not" further clarifies that it is not necessarily due to a teacher. This refers to the previous statement about flying spirits possessing people and acting as their teachers, whereby the practitioner is deluded by following such a teacher; however, this is not invariably the case. Therefore, it says "or not."
Since it is not due to a teacher, and yet he is not without a teacher, why would he receive delusion? Therefore, it is said that he "personally observed and saw.

Regarding those who are called Vajradharas and the like: first, they manifest the appearance of powerful and steadfast warriors and grant them the art of longevity so that they do not fear bodily injury;
subsequently, they manifest as beautiful women and cause them to indulge extensively in lustful desires. Little do they realize—
The discourse on longevity is merely a hollow claim; the harm caused to the body, however, has actual and verifiable evidence.
Thus it is said, "not exceeding a year," meaning not more than one and a half years. By that time, the liver-blood, brain, and membranes have already become parched and depleted.
Nowadays, many who believe in sexual arts and indulge in licentiousness as being without hindrance encounter this very calamity. [End of] Oral [Testimony].
Regarding what is called "speaking alone": this refers to constantly speaking and conversing by oneself. There are two explanations for this:
first, Guanding says that it is the qi being depleted and giving rise to delirious speech. Second, Zhengmai says that one sees a manifestation of a māra and engages in sexual desire with it;
others do not see this, so it is called "speaking alone," yet in reality, one is speaking with a māra. What is said has no fixed content.
There are many strange and anomalous occurrences; thus, what one hears may seem like the speech of demons and specters—this refers precisely to the words and speech of Māra.
○ The preceding section concludes by clarifying that both parties are subject to harm.

It states that those who previously received delusions from their teachers, without discerning whether they were possessed by demonic spirits, often caused both disciple and teacher to fall together into royal punishment and calamity. If it is as such...
Those who do not rely on a teacher will die of dehydration even before they encounter the punishment; thus, their harm is even more rapid.
Both of these are sufficient to disturb and confuse those practitioners, leading them to the destruction of their bodies and the loss of their lives.
The remainder may be understood. This concludes the general summary of the demonic signs that have appeared throughout the preceding sections.
Part Four: A General Conclusion to Provide Warning and Exhortation, in four sections: (1) Anticipating the affliction of demons; (2) Exhorting one to rescue others through compassion.
The three fetters are to be overcome through vigilance; the four instructions are for the purpose of entrusting and protecting [the Dharma]. First:
Ānanda, you should know that in the final age, these ten kinds of Māras will go forth from home to practice the Way within my Dharma.
Sometimes they attach themselves to human bodies, or sometimes they manifest their own forms; in all cases, they claim to have already attained the realization of Perfect and Universal Wisdom.

They praise sexual desire as a means to break the Buddha’s Vinaya rules. Originally, evil Māra teachers and their disciples transmitted these lewd practices among themselves. Thus, such perverse spirits bewitch the heart and viscera of practitioners.
In the near term, this may affect nine lifetimes, and often it exceeds a hundred generations, causing those who truly practice cultivation to be entirely subverted by Māra.
Kuan, after his life comes to an end, he will surely become a subject of Māra. Having lost the Perfectly Complete Knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), he will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Regarding the ten types of those who falsely claim the ultimate fruit: the first nine are spirits, ghosts, and elemental beings who become Māras upon reaching old age and join the faction of the celestial Māras; the last one is a Cāmuṇḍā or a Piśāca youth, who is possessed by Māra.
They act as emissaries and become associates of the celestial Māras; therefore, among the ten types mentioned previously, it is said in each case that the celestial Māras find an opportunity.
This refers to the time of the final dharma (mappō), the period when the Buddha-dharma declines. When the Buddha-dharma declines, the path of Māra flourishes.

It is not necessarily the case that they will always wait for an opportunity to delude people as described before; there are also those who, riding upon their vows, destroy the teachings and manifest as renunciants. They remain...
Regarding those who cultivate the path within the Buddha-dharma, as cited in the Tongyi: "In the past, when the Buddha dwelt in the world, various māras sought to destroy the Dharma;
yet by the Buddha’s supernatural power, they were all unable to do so. The māras then made a vow: 'After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, [we shall destroy it].'"
Having left the household life in accordance with the teachings, they instead destroy the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha shed tears and said, "There is nothing I can do for you.
It is like worms within the body of a lion devouring the lion’s own flesh. Thus we know that those monks who today destroy the Dharma all belong to Māra;
they are all worms within the lion’s body. Those who have left the household life with right faith must distinguish them from such people. Furthermore:
One must not fail to guard against them. Some attach themselves to the human body, as explained generally throughout the ten [sections].
Others manifest their own forms, as clarified in the final one among the ten. Or they may exist throughout all ten, with only the last one making them explicit.
Within the first ten māras, each is said to have "attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa" on its own; this refers to the fruit of cessation (*nirodha-phala*). This [latter case], however, all say...

"Having already attained perfect and complete enlightenment" refers to the fruit of wisdom. This is because one fears that people might think it is either "erroneous" (*mithyā*) or "partial" (*pradeśika*);
therefore, one first declares for oneself that it is indeed "correct" (*samyak*) and "complete" (*sarva*). The courage of a thief is naturally such as this. As stated previously:
"How is it that these thieves, donning my robes, perform all manner of deeds while claiming them to be the Buddha-dharma and so forth?
It is precisely for their sake that I utter this bitter rebuke. As for the praise below regarding the proclamation of lust as a calamity:

those who praise lustful desire do so by conforming to worldly ways of teaching, because people easily follow such [teachings]. Those who violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code slander the correct path as being false, desiring to destroy the Teaching."
This refers to the past. It means that the various evil Māras and their disciples of the past all transmitted lust through lust;
hence it is said, "lust was transmitted from lust to lust. Since lust was transmitted from lust to lust, it was likewise inherited from lust to lust.
In this way, the former demonic spirits possessed the hearts and viscera of those who followed them, such that the whole world remained unaware as they gradually entered the realm of Māra.

Therefore, it is said that "if near, nine lifetimes; often more than a hundred generations," and so forth. These "nine lifetimes" and "hundred generations" are all calculated from the time after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
According to the records, when the Buddha was in the world, the human lifespan was one hundred years; generally, one century is reckoned as one lifetime.
Thus, "nine lifetimes" would correspond to nine hundred years. When the True Dharma (*saddharma*) was about to end, heterodox teachings were just beginning to arise.
There have indeed been times when those who have aroused the aspiration for awakening and engaged in practice have mistakenly entered the retinue of Māra;

thus it is said that "in the near term, nine lifetimes," meaning that within nine lifetimes, [the goal] will be attained. Regarding the statement that "many exceed a hundred generations," the General Commentary states that thirty years constitute one generation;

thus, a hundred generations would equal three thousand years. This is because we currently dwell in the age of the Final Dharma (*mappō*), when people are generally burdened by heavy defilements. The original...
If one expects true cultivation yet instead produces demonic karma—as in the ten types previously described—all such instances take true cultivation as a retinue for demons.
Having become a retainer of demons, one will inevitably become a subject of demons in the future;
descending further and further, one brings about the loss of right universal knowledge and falls into the Avīci Hell. Second, I exhort you to save them through compassion.

"You need not first attain nirvāṇa at this time. Even if you should attain the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), remain there by your vow and enter that age of the final dharma to give rise to great compassion.
Rescue those sentient beings who possess a correct mind and deep faith, so that they do not fall under the influence of Māra and may attain right knowledge and vision."
"I have now delivered you from birth and death. To follow the Buddha’s words is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
This was first shown as an exhortation. "One who has not yet attained deliverance for oneself but first delivers others is one who has resolved upon the Bodhisattva path.
Ānanda had long wished to learn the way of the Bodhisattvas; therefore, he was taught that he need not first attain nirvana himself. At this time, Ānanda—
Having severed the six grades of the path of cultivation within the three realms, one knows for oneself that the realization of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) has been accomplished;
