therefore, it is advised that even if one attains no-more-learning, one must still maintain a vow. One is taught to enter the age of the final Dharma (*paścima-dharma*), because this is a time when Māra is powerful and the Dharma is weak.
Those who give rise to great compassion bestow the joy of right knowledge and right view, uprooting false knowledge and false views.

This is the contemplation of suffering. "Rectifying the mind" means generating the bodhicitta. "Deep faith" means believing and knowing that the Buddha-nature exists within the minds of sentient beings;

thus, one seeks to deliver such beings by practicing the Samādhi of True Cultivation so as not to be attached to demons, and by opening the "wondrous gate of the ear" to attain right knowledge and vision.
This is precisely the power of great compassion. The *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Pulse) says: "Contemplating the Buddha..."
It can be known from this that Ānanda’s entry into parinirvāṇa in four parts was merely a provisional manifestation;
it is certain that he remained in the world in accordance with the Buddha’s entrusted vow to provide silent salvation. ○ From "I now" onwards, [the text] further serves to inspire and rouse [others].

Although Ānanda was at the stage of the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmin), he could have attained the Way through his own power; however, because he served the Buddha, he retained residual fetters. The Buddha knew that these were merely the fetters of limited existence (bhavāgra).
Therefore it is said: "I have now delivered you from birth and death. Having emerged from birth and death, you must repay the Buddha's kindness.
There is no other way to repay his kindness than to follow and rely upon the Buddha’s words. By following and relying upon the Buddha’s words, one brings compassion to save the world.
This is precisely what is meant by repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Zhengmo says: "To hear these instructions with reverence yet not feel heartache or shed tears is to be a person of wood or stone;
the three fetters are overcome through constant vigilance."
Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states appearing during *dhyāna* all manifest because the mind is engaged in a reciprocal interaction with the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
When sentient beings are stubbornly deluded and fail to reflect upon themselves, they encounter these conditions and, being confused, do not recognize them for what they are;
they claim to have attained the state of a sage. Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
This section is entirely identical to that on the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); its meaning may likewise be inferred accordingly. Fourth, the entrustment for transmission and protection:
"You must take these words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them to the Dharma-ending age.
Cause all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find an opportunity; maintain and protect them so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way."
This is also the same as in the case of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); however, while that [text] says "it should also be so," its intent in the exhortation is somewhat relaxed.

Here it says "it must be so," and its intent in the exhortation is even more urgent. This is truly because when practice is deep, demonic interference is heavy; to lose what is about to be accomplished all at once is indeed to be pitied.
This concludes the summary of the demonic signs of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
*The Finger-Pointing Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll Nine;
*The Finger-Pointing Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
Respectfully composed by the junior disciple Dàtiāntōnglǐ of Xiánzōng at Niànhuá Monastery in the Capital.
The Dharma-heir (Xingzong Zuwang Tengqing Huairen Zuyu Jiaozi), Section Four: The Four Aspects of the Demonic Signs of the *saṃskāra-skandha*.
First, beginning practice before breaking through the *saṃskāra-skandha*; second, the final breakthrough that reveals the source of delusion;
third, the demonic signs manifested during the interim; fourth, a summary to provide warning and instruction. Part One.
Ānanda, when that good man cultivates *samādhi* and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, his ordinary dreams and fantasies vanish;
whether awake or asleep, he remains ever one. His awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky. No longer are there coarse and heavy shadows of external objects.
He contemplates the great earth, mountains, and rivers of the world as if in a clear mirror: they appear without adhering to it, and pass away without leaving a trace.

As for its traces: it receives illumination in emptiness and is utterly devoid of habitual patterns; there is only the single, pure reality. From this point, the root-source of birth and death is revealed.
One sees all twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category.

Although one has not yet penetrated the individual origins of their destinies, one perceives their common basis of life, which is like a shimmering mirage—vibrant, clear, and turbulent—serving as the ultimate ground for the floating sense organs and their objects.
This is the pivot-hole; it is what is called the domain of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
That good man may also point to a person who perceives external objects, or one who never gives rise to craving or seeking from beginning to end.
The nature of permanence is fixed; or, when Māra arrives, one is able to perceive it immediately. Because the original cultivation is not destroyed, one continues to speak of "cultivating samādhi.

Herein, this cultivation of samādhi is the final cultivation in relation to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), yet it is the initial cultivation in relation to the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
As samādhi advances, the movement of thought is dissolved and floating perceptions are likewise eliminated; this is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*).
Regarding "the extinction of the aggregates": once the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted, there is no perception during the day and no dreaming at night;
therefore, it is said that "dreams and thoughts have been extinguished. Guanding says: "Daytime perceptions and nighttime dreams are both the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Thus, it is later stated: "When awake, it is the mind of perception; when asleep, it constitutes various dreams. Now, since there are neither dreams nor perceptions, one is always as if in sleep even while awake.
At that time, the state of sleep is always identical to the state of waking; therefore, it is said that "waking and sleeping are constantly one.

This is because in the state of waking there is no discursive thought, which is like the stillness of sleep, and in the state of sleep there are no dreams, which is like the clarity of waking. "Awakened clarity" (jue-ming) refers to the eighth fundamental consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

Having already departed from the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the preceding six [objects] are empty and quiescent; hence they are called "void and still. Because they are both void and still, they are likened to a clear sky.
"Coarse and heavy" refers to the objective realms of form (*rūpa*) and so forth; "reflected phenomena" refers to the solitary images of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Regarding the phrase "no longer," it means that objects manifest in dependence upon consciousness; since consciousness is now empty and still, the objects likewise [cease] along with consciousness.

Both are empty and both are quiescent. Since consciousness and its objects are both empty and quiescent, one simply uses the fundamentally enlightened and luminous primary consciousness to observe the worlds, the great earth, mountains, and rivers. Although the myriad phenomena all appear therein, there is no discrimination;
therefore it is said: "It is like the clarity of a mirror reflecting images; when they come, shadows appear within the mirror, yet the mirror itself is originally without them."
Whatever is grasped, once it passes, its reflection vanishes from within the mirror, and the mirror itself leaves no trace.

Based on this, the manifestation of objects within consciousness is nothing more than a hollow reception of a response. When the object ceases, there is clearly no lingering habituation within consciousness.
Because it is a hollow reception of a response, it is free from the defilements of the six sense-objects; because there is no lingering habituation, it distinguishes [itself from them].

Because consciousness is false and delusive, it is said that there is "only one pure reality. This is because "one" is spoken in contrast to the six [consciousnesses], "pure" in contrast to the mixed, and "real" in contrast to the false.
In fact, this refers only to the eighth fundamental consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), and is not yet ultimate.
The "root-source of arising and ceasing" refers to the seeds of the seven consciousnesses contained within the eighth consciousness, as they possess subtle arising and ceasing.
This is called the fundamental aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), for all aggregates of formations arise in dependence upon it.
Previously, because it was shrouded by the characteristic of movement, it existed yet was not seen; therefore, the subsequent text refers to it as "subtle and hidden deluded thought.

Now that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted and the characteristic of movement has already dissolved, these seven types are revealed; thus it is said that the root-source of arising and ceasing is here stripped away.
Lù: "The twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions, in their constant arising and ceasing, do not transcend this;
therefore, they are all able to see it, and can exhaustively describe its various types. 'Exhaustively' (bi) means to the limit (qìng); 'to the end' (dān) means to the utmost (jìn).

Each of their life-continuums is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), yet it is still shrouded by the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha); hence it is said that they have not yet attained penetration. 'Common basis of birth' still refers to the seven kinds [of beings]."
Because this is the root-source of arising and ceasing, none of the twelve classes of beings or all formations of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) are without it;

therefore, it is called the "common basis of arising. It is like a "wild horse" (*yemǎ*): a wild horse is the drifting vapor over fields that can be seen hovering above the ground on a clear spring day;
Zhuangzi called it a "wild horse," while Buddhist scriptures often refer to it as a "mirage" (*marīci*). Thirsty deer mistake it for water.
It is taken to be water, yet it is not actually water. Its shimmering brilliance is like a flame because it consists of the seeds of the seven consciousnesses.

Its clarity and turbulence have the appearance of water because they possess the principle of subtle arising and ceasing. Regarding its being "the ultimate pivot-hole for the floating sense-bases and objects":
the floating sense-bases and objects refer to the bodies of sentient beings; for the floating sense-bases consist of the four sense-objects.

Because they are produced from such conditions, the twelve classes of beings are each distinct. The mechanism of transformation relies solely upon the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations);
therefore, it constitutes the ultimate pivot-hole. The *Abhiṣeka* states: "The 'pivot' refers to the door-axle; the 'hole' refers to the place where the axle rests."

first, the calculation of two natures as eternal; second, the calculation of four natures as eternal; third, the calculation of three natures as eternal;
fourth, the calculation of one nature as eternal. The first [part]:
First, this person exhaustively investigates the nature of the mind and its objects, finding no cause for either.

This person wishes to exhaustively investigate the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Rather than desiring to examine each of the twelve classes of beings in detail, they seek the nature of the aggregate of formations by means of the mind and its objects.
Therefore, it is said that they "exhaustively investigate the nature of the mind and its objects.

When they reach the point where there is nothing further to be observed, they claim that both [the mind and its objects] are without cause. Since this person’s investigation is thus cursory, yet they rely upon...
In this cultivation, one knows only within twenty thousand kalpas; beyond twenty thousand kalpas, it becomes dark and there is nothing to be observed.
The sentient beings of the ten directions are precisely the scope of what is currently known within those twenty thousand kalpas.

All instances of arising and ceasing—when both mind and object are taken into account—are such that both mind and object belong to the transformations of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), and all possess...
Because there is arising and ceasing. Yet, arising and ceasing are precisely impermanence. However, they merely observe that arising ceases and ceasing arises, revolving without interruption;
consequently, they reckon the two natures of mind and object to be permanent.
Second, they calculate that the four natures are eternal.
These people exhaustively investigate the source of the four great elements and conclude that the four natures are eternally abiding.

Through cultivation, they are able to know all the births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within forty thousand kalpas; they perceive that these all possess an enduring essence that is never dispersed or lost, and thus they reckon them to be eternal.
This person wishes to exhaustively investigate the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). To investigate by following categories is the fault of being overly detailed;

to investigate by means of the mind and its objects is the fault of being overly brief. Therefore, they investigate solely by means of the four great elements internally and externally, until they reach a state of profound nothingness where nothing is seen.

Consequently, they take this to be the fundamental essence of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). Furthermore, they designate it as the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Because its arising and ceasing are not perceived, they name it "eternally abiding" (*nitya*).

Examining the merit of these people's research, since their treatment of detail and brevity is balanced, if one can know [the truth] within forty thousand kalpas by relying on this practice, then beyond those forty thousand kalpas, it is likewise so.
In the profound darkness there is nothing to be observed. The sentient beings of the ten directions are, within the span of forty thousand kalpas, the full extent of what is currently known;
all their arising and ceasing are likewise spoken of in conjunction with the four great elements.

This is because the internal four great elements constitute the physical bodies and faculties of sentient beings, while the external four great elements constitute the vessel-world of sentient beings; both are subject to the transformations of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), and both possess birth.

Because they cease. Indeed, arising and ceasing are precisely what constitutes impermanence; yet they [the proponents of permanence] maintain that beyond forty thousand kalpas, the essence remains eternally undestroyed, and thus they reckon the nature of the four great elements to be permanent.

It appears that in the preceding section, "permanence" was defined by the non-loss of the present cycle, speaking in terms of function; whereas in this section, it is because their past arising and ceasing cannot be perceived.
This refers to permanence; it is as if spoken in terms of the essence (*tattva*). These two views differ. Third, they calculate the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) to be permanent.

This means that these people exhaustively investigate the fundamental source and locus of the six sense organs, the manas, the grasping, and the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*), finding that their nature is eternally constant.
Through cultivation, they are able to know that all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas circulate in saṃsāra without losing [their identity].
Originally abiding eternally, one exhausts [the investigation] without losing its nature and reckons it as permanent.

This person has already destroyed the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and now seeks to investigate the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha). Thus, they examine each and every instance within the six sense organs and the manas that undergoes appropriation.
Therefore, it is said that they "exhaust the six sense organs," and so forth. It does not say "six consciousnesses" but rather says "six [organs]."

As for the "root" (*mūla*): because the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has already been destroyed, the modes of activity of the six consciousnesses are no longer manifest; one perceives only the nature of the root as profoundly still.

Since this is sought within the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), the *manas* is precisely the seventh consciousness. This is called "deliberation" (*manana*), because it constantly and critically deliberates.
"Appropriation" (*upādāna*) is the eighth consciousness, which grasps and maintains the seeds of the faculties and the physical vessel-world, taking them as its object.
In order to produce sensory-cognitive experience (*vedanā*), the three characters *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* are restated as the three aforementioned dharmas.

According to the conventional path, "mind" (*citta*) is defined as "arising through accumulation," because it gathers all seeds and gives rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*); this refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Here, however, "mind" (*citta*) refers to the nature within the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). "Intellect" (*manas*) is defined as "deliberation," referring to that which constantly and critically deliberates on the mark of self (*ātman*).

Therefore, while it is conventionally held that the six preceding consciousnesses are designated as "vijñāna" (cognition) because they each specifically discern their own respective objects—directly confronting the *manas*—here the eighth [consciousness] is taken as "vijñāna. Because it is the foundation of all these consciousnesses, it alone receives the name "vijñāna.
As for the phrase "exhaustively [discerning] the *manas* and its appropriation (*upādāna*)," this refers precisely to this mind and intellect (*citta-mati*).

Within consciousness, one investigates its fundamental origin and source. One must understand that even the six sense organs and the manas-consciousness are merely manifestations of the eighth consciousness;
how much more so for the skandha of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) within them—how could it have any further origin? Therefore, one knows the fundamental origin of the skandha of formations.

It exists solely within the eighth consciousness. This is because the seven types [of formations] within the eighth consciousness constitute the fundamental aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*);
all other aggregates of formations depend upon this. Investigate and examine in this manner until you reach the point where there is nothing further to be perceived.
Failing to perceive arising and ceasing, they claim that the nature is eternally constant; this is a false calculation that the substance of the past is permanent.
Relying upon this substance, they further apply investigation, which is called "cultivation.

As their effort becomes deeper than before, they are naturally able to know far back into eighty thousand kalpas, yet they see only the arising and ceasing of all sentient beings within those eighty thousand kalpas.
Upon arising, they claim that the cycle is never lost; this is a fallacious calculation that the functioning (*yòng*) in the present is permanent.

However, since such a person already clings to the past as being originally and eternally abiding, and further perceives the nature (*xìng*) as inexhaustible in the present, they consequently calculate that the three natures within mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*) are all equally eternal.
Thus, the two aforementioned calculations of permanence—one concerning functioning alone and the other concerning substance (*tǐ*) alone—are both erroneous.
This combines both essence and function. Furthermore, of the two preceding [categories], the first refers solely to the present, while the second refers solely to the past;
this [present category] speaks in terms of both temporal limits. The fourth [category] calculates that nature is eternal.
Fourth, this person has exhausted the source of ideation; in their fundamental nature, there is no longer any flowing, ceasing, or movement.

The mind of birth and extinction has now been eternally extinguished, and within this principle, non-arising and non-extinction is spontaneously realized. Based on what the mind has fathomed, they reckon this state to be permanent.
"Having exhausted the source of perception" means that the fundamental aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has already been eliminated.

Now, this fundamental aggregate of perception is precisely the aspect of motion within the eighth consciousness. Once the aspect of motion has dissolved, the source of activity is revealed and termed the "vital principle" (*shengli*).
Failing to recognize that there is still a subtle, continuous flow, they erroneously claim that there is no further movement, cessation, or circulation. Their intention is essentially as follows:

Because the mind that perceives arising and ceasing has now been eternally extinguished, one proceeds through the fundamental principle of arising; thus, non-arising and non-ceasing are spontaneously accomplished.

Yet, one does not realize that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists precisely of these seven types, which are in fact not the true reality. Its essence is a subtle, continuous flow;
it is truly not the genuine non-arising and non-ceasing. It is merely because of the mind’s estimations that one erroneously calculates the nature of formations.
It is considered permanent; that is to say, it resembles inference (*anumāna*) but is not true inference. Zhengmo says:
After this person has reached the stage where conceptualization is exhausted and practice is manifested, they lack the power of further investigation and thus reckon [the state] to be permanent.

Compared to the first [stage], this is already shallow and inferior; how much more so for the second or third? Therefore, one no longer establishes the ability to know the measure of kalpas, but merely estimates its duration.

It is certain that [the realization] will not be attained within twenty thousand kalpas. I, the fool, believe that the aforementioned three cases seem to pertain to those of dull faculties who cannot directly observe the *saṃskāra-skandha* (formative aggregate).
Therefore, they gradually investigate and exhaustively analyze the mind-objects, the four great elements, and the six sense organs along with the *manas* and its grasping;
based on the degree of their application—whether detailed, concise, or intermediate—they are distinguished according to what is known.

Regarding the measure of the kalpa: this [case] seems to pertain to those of sharp faculties who directly contemplate the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) without extensive investigation;

therefore, no kalpa-measure is established for them. It is only because they would otherwise fall into eternalist views—that they are categorized as such. This concludes the separate detailed explanation.
Second, the faults are summarized:
because of this adherence to permanence, one loses right universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and falls into the ways of external paths, becoming deluded regarding the nature of bodhi.

Failing to realize that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is a manifestation of mind alone, one loses right knowledge; obscured by the aggregate of formations, one does not see the truth.
The mind, then, lacks universal knowledge. Because it is subsumed under the eternalist view within the category of extreme views, it is said that one "falls into the ranks of the heterodox.
By clinging to this as permanent, one does not believe in the existence of a separate, truly eternal Bodhi; hence, it is said that one "is deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
Having completed the detailed explanation of each section, the third part concludes by establishing the discourse as an external treatise.
This is called the second type of externalist who establishes a doctrine of pervasive permanence (*paripūrṇa-śāśvata-vāda*).

With the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) already exhausted and the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) not yet destroyed, they dwell in the interval between these two pillars;

it is to this class that the following refers, hence the statement: "This is called the second," and so forth. To establish a doctrine of pervasive permanence means to assert four kinds of pervasive permanence.

Regarding this meaning, he composed that treatise. Guanding said: "In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, among the views of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the four theories of eternalism regarding the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) are fully explained as clarified in the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya* (Qingliang shu).

[The following] concerns the three modes of conceptualization arising within the context of the perfect and eternal, and the three modes of conceptualization arising within the context of self and others. First, the heading which indicates the fallacy; second, the detailed classification."
Commentary: These three points establish the external treatise. First:
furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, Māra finds no opportunity; they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.
Observing that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source, one who gives rise to conceptual calculations regarding self and others falls into the four inverted views,
specifically the doctrine that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent.
The first two instances both speak of "concentrated clarity" (*ning-ming*), which reveals that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) support one another.

This single instance speaks of "firm concentration" (*jian-ning*), which seems to belong exclusively to concentration. Although it appears to belong exclusively to concentration, it is nonetheless brought forth by the power of wisdom;

thus, the benefit of concentration becomes profound, firm, and concentrated. Being firm and concentrated, one does not engage in erroneous seeking; therefore, it is called "rectifying the mind. Mind...
Once it is rectified, Māra has no way to enter; thus he finds no opportunity.

To "exhaust the fundamental of the categories of living beings" means to thoroughly investigate the twelve classes of sentient beings in order to seek the profound root of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

Once that profound root is revealed, one may naturally advance to break through it by refining the wondrous clarity with single-minded precision. Yet, when one contemplates that profound root, it remains obscure and does not manifest.
It is clear and not turbid; yet, it is seen that its constant clarity is disturbed, serving as the fundamental source of all movements.
Since it is the fundamental source of all movements, the bodies and minds of self and others, as well as their environments and inhabitants, are all established in dependence upon it.
Consequently, based on these [views], one gives rise to various false conceptualizations regarding one's own and others' phenomena, thereby falling into the four types of inverted views.
Within these four types of inverted views, each contains the sense of being partly impermanent and partly permanent. As the *Hezhe* (The Concordant Commentary) states:
Within the state of equality, there is fundamentally no self or other, yet one falsely discriminates between self and other.

Within the definitive meaning of the Middle Way, which utterly transcends the two extremes, one erroneously clings to annihilationism and eternalism. How could this be anything other than a perverted view? This section consists of two parts:
first, a detailed explanation by way of individual analysis; second, a general presentation of the faults. The first part has four sections, the first of which is the contemplation of the self.

1. Observing another, one gives rise to two views; 2. Abandoning oneself and observing another, one gives rise to two views; 3. Abandoning another and observing oneself, one gives rise to two views; 4.
Without distinguishing between self and other, one gives rise to two views. First:
First, this person contemplates the wondrous, luminous mind as pervading the worlds of the ten directions, regarding its profound stillness as the ultimate *puruṣa* (divine self).
From this, he calculates that his self pervades the ten directions, being concentrated, luminous, and immovable;
he holds that all sentient beings are born and die within his own mind, and thus his own mind-nature is called "constant," while those who undergo birth and death possess a truly impermanent nature.

Unaware that this constant agitation within profound stillness is the source of all movement—the very fundamental *saṃskāra-skandha*—one erroneously claims that the wondrously luminous true mind does not transcend this.
Therefore, one relies upon this very state to contemplate the wondrously luminous mind; through the power of such contemplation, [the realization arises].
One contemplates this mind as vast and all-pervasive; through long-term contemplation, this becomes established, and thus one sees this mind pervading the worlds of the ten directions.
Furthermore, because one is unaware of its clarity being disturbed, one falsely claims it to be profoundly still (*zhanran*). That which is pervasive and unimpeded is called "spirit" (*shen*);

that which is profoundly still and unmoving is called "self" (*wo*); and calculating this to be supreme, one calls it "ultimate. These are the twenty [conceptions] calculated by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
This is the final of the five truths. They claim that from *māyā* (the primordial darkness) arises *mahat* (the Great One);

from *mahat* arises the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense); from the *ahaṃkāra* arise the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); from the five subtle elements arise the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*); and from the five gross elements arise the eleven sense organs. Finally, they posit a single divine self (*puruṣa*).
They erroneously reckon *māyā-prakṛti* as the agent of production, while the twenty-three intermediate factors are regarded as the objects produced.
[The *Śāstra*] states: "The *puruṣa* (spiritual self) is the enjoyer; the twenty-three intermediate factors are the objects of enjoyment.
As that treatise says: "Because the *puruṣa* possesses consciousness and is capable of deliberation, its nature consists of thought (*cintā*).
It enjoys the twenty-three factors, such as the *mahat* and so forth. This is because the seeds of the seven consciousnesses contained within the eighth consciousness are taken as the *puruṣa*.
I am also thus. Having established the divine self (*puruṣa*), one further relies upon that divine self to give rise to the notion of being omnipresent and eternal;
hence it is said, "From this, one then calculates [it to be] equal. That the self pervades the ten directions is because it possesses the quality of pervading the realm.

That it is "congealed and luminous, unmoving" is because it possesses the quality of being profoundly still (*zhanran*). "Profoundly still" means being like water that has become clear and translucent; therefore, one calculates it to be congealed.

[The Master] said: "It is clear. Although water is limpid and forms reflections, one does not perceive the mark of movement; therefore, one reckons it as non-moving. Non-movement is the meaning of permanence (*nitya*).
Being both pervasive and permanent, it constitutes true permanence (*tathatā-nitya*). This contemplation arises from the self and gives rise to the reckoning of permanence.

'All sentient beings are equal' refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) based on that pervasive permanence, whereby one proceeds to contemplate sentient beings. Since the self is already pervasive throughout the ten [directions]..."
In this way, all sentient beings of the ten directions are within my own mind. Since I am凝然不動 (nìngrán bùdòng, immutably still), all sentient beings are born and die of themselves.

When one contemplates birth and gives rise to the notion of impermanence, the nature of my mind is such that it simultaneously upholds both self and other to distinguish the meanings of permanence and impermanence.
Second, abandoning self-observation and observing others gives rise to two types of conceptualization.
These two people do not observe their own minds; instead, they universally observe the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
They see places where kalpas are destroyed and designate them as the nature of ultimate impermanence, while they see places where kalpas are not destroyed and designate them as ultimate permanence.
"The person" refers back to the individual previously mentioned. Since that person has already realized within their own mind that [the self] is permanent, they do not further contemplate that mind.
Regarding other phenomena, they have only known that sentient beings are impermanent, yet they were still unable to know whether the land is permanent or not;

therefore, this section contemplates only the land. "Contemplation" (*guan*) here carries the meaning of directing the mind toward mental visualization. After such visualization has persisted for a long time...

When the contemplation is perfected, one is indeed able to see everywhere. However, regarding the sands and soil of the ten directions that undergo formation and destruction, such a person sees only the places where the kalpa is destroyed;
they do not know that after destruction there is formation, and thus they designate it as having the nature of ultimate impermanence.
If they see a place where a kalpa has formed and is temporarily not destroyed, they do not know that it will ultimately be destroyed, and thus [they likewise fall into error].
This is termed the ultimately true and eternal *gotra*. One must understand that the nature of the *dhātu* is non-dual, such that its formation and destruction follow conditions.
If one clings to impermanence because of the existence of destruction, then the Bodhisattva’s aspiration to adorn the land with ashes would be undermined.
If one clings to true permanence because of the absence of destruction, then the ordinary person’s attachment to the world would increase. Such false views mislead people and must not be held.
They do not understand. Third, they abandon the contemplation of others and give rise to two views regarding themselves.
First, this person separately contemplates their own mind as being subtle, fine, and dense, like a minute particle;

it transmigrates through the ten directions, its nature remaining unchanging, and it can cause this body to arise and perish in an instant. This indestructible nature is called the "eternal nature of the self."
All birth and death flow forth from the self; this is termed the nature of impermanence.
Within this, there is a distinct contemplation. In contrast to the two preceding sections, there should be three meanings. For now, consider the second:

namely, setting aside the external support (the environment) and contemplating the self’s primary retribution (the individual existence). This primary retribution of the self consists of both mind and body; contemplate them distinctly.
"Contemplating the mind as equal" refers to the contemplation of the mind. "Being able to cause this body to be equal" refers to the contemplation of the body.
If one correlates this with the first [section], it possesses two meanings: first, regarding the externalist calculations of the self-characteristic (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*), there are three types.

The previous contemplation of the *puruṣa* (spiritual self) pervading the world was the "vast self"; this, however, is a distinct contemplation of the "subtle self" and the "self of indeterminate size. Second, the previous...
To contemplate that the primary retribution is one's own mind and the bodies of sentient beings is to separately contemplate one's own mind and one's own body;
it is likewise to set aside others and contemplate only oneself. What is called "subtle, refined, and profound" refers specifically to the fundamental aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
It is called "refined" because it is the seed of the seven consciousnesses; it is called "subtle" because it is stored within the *ālayavijñāna*. Whether it exists or...
It is called "subtle" (*miao*) because it has no [discernible] cause; it is called "dense" (*mi*) because the coarse mind cannot perceive it.
This refers to what was previously termed "hidden and obscure delusive thought. As for the metaphor of "fine dust" (*paramāṇu*), fine dust is taken as the seed of the world;
its minuteness has no interior, its substance is most subtle, and even weary eyes cannot behold it. Because the meaning is similar, if one considers only this sense, it is "subtle."
There is also the subtle self. Relying on this for its operation, it gives rise to delusions and creates karma, flowing through the ten directions while its nature remains unchanging.
This is the indeterminate self of varying magnitude. Although its nature remains unchanging, the movement of karma is constantly shifting, capable of causing this body to deteriorate in each moment;
therefore, it is said that it arises and perishes simultaneously. As for its indestructible nature, it is...
Together, they support both mind and body to distinguish the meanings of the fetters regarding permanence and impermanence.
Fourth, failing to distinguish between self and other, they give rise to two types of reckoning.

These four refer to one who, knowing the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has ended, perceives the flow of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because this aggregate of formations flows constantly, they reckon it to be of a permanent nature.
The fact that form, sensation, perception, and so forth have now been extinguished is what is called impermanence.
The reason no distinction is made between self and other is that, when comparing oneself to others, the general principle is always thus.

Therefore, one should know that whenever the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, one will necessarily perceive the shifting flow of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). This is an absolute certainty; do not let it be otherwise. The aggregate of mental formations is constant.
The section on "flowing" and so forth also doubly inherits the two preceding divisions to explain the meaning of permanence and impermanence.
Because a constant flow continues without interruption, it is reckoned as permanent; because it ceases and is no longer present, it is reckoned as impermanent.
Having completed the detailed analysis, secondly, the faults [of these views] are presented in general.

Because of this speculative reckoning that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) and become deluded regarding the nature of bodhi.
Although these four reckonings differ, they do not, in total, transcend the meaning of "one part impermanent and one part permanent.

Regarding those who fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists, the *Guanding* (Consecration) states: "Such as the masters of the Sāṃkhya treatises," and the *Zhilun* (Treatise on Wisdom) states: "One should not cling to all dharmas."
If it were eternal, there would be neither sin nor merit; there would be no killing or harming, nor would there be the granting of life.

There would be neither bondage nor liberation, and thus no nirvana. If one clings to impermanence, that is nihilism; likewise, there would be no sin or merit, nor would there be the causal conditions for the increase or decrease of karmic deeds.
Even the retribution of results would be lost. All of these are sufficient to delude the nature of Bodhi. [This concludes] the section on "Distinguishing the Branches."

The detailed explanation is complete. This concludes the third external treatise, which is called the "Doctrine of Partial Eternity" of the third class of non-Buddhist outsiders. Within the context of "the exhaustion of perception and the manifestation of formations," the word "third" refers to this category; thus it is named the third. As for the term "partial" (*ekadeśa*): [The text continues: ...because they maintain that while some phenomena are eternal, others are impermanent. Furthermore, because they do not admit the existence of a self (*ātman*) or a person (*pudgala*), nor do they fully comprehend the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are designated as "partial. This is because they assert that among the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), only a portion—namely, space (*ākāśa*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—is eternal, whereas the remaining four aggregates are impermanent. Therefore, this is termed the "Doctrine of Partial Eternity. It is called "external" because these views contradict the true Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha. It is called a "treatise" (*śāstra*) because they establish their own system of tenets through reasoning and scriptural authority. Thus, the detailed explanation of the third external doctrine is finished. The third section of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* is concluded. This indicates that the remaining one portion is a doctrine of impermanence (*anityavāda*).
Furthermore, the specific mention of "one portion" is because, among the two-part doctrines, the eternalist view is predominant, thereby highlighting its singular importance. *Abhiṣeka* states:

"It is subsumed under the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. *Qīngliáng* states: "Among the various views of extremes held by non-Buddhists, there is a self and a world."
The fourfold theory of being partly eternal and partly non-eternal concludes the section on the arising of conceptualizations regarding self and others.
This section consists of three parts: first, the presentation of the fallacy; second, the detailed explanation through categorization;
and third, the conclusion as an external doctrine. First: [The text continues with the specific arguments.]
Furthermore, when those good sons within samādhi maintain a firm and concentrated right mind, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure source which is yet constantly subject to agitation. If, within these various states, they give rise to conceptual calculations, such persons fall into the four theories of finitude.
Stabilizing and concentrating the upright mind is the same as described previously. However, the profound clarity is constantly disturbed;
since this is the source of all movement, all temporal divisions and spatial directions are established in dependence upon it. Consequently, regarding these temporal divisions and spatial directions:
They give rise to various false conceptualizations and fall into the four theories of finitude.
As will be seen below, among these four views, the first two arise based on temporal divisions, while the latter two arise based on spatial directions.

The reason the theory of "infinite" is not mentioned here is that those who hold such a view consider the infinite to belong to the realm of their own self-realization, whereas the finite belongs to the realm of others' delusion; this is likely their underlying intention.
To transform delusion into awakening, [the text] addresses those who are biased toward the extreme of existence (*bhava-anta*). This is explained in detail through two parts:
first, a specific analysis; second, a general exposition of their errors. The first part has four sections: (1) giving rise to two views regarding the temporal aspect of the mind;
(2) giving rise to two views regarding the temporal aspect of objects; (3) giving rise to two views regarding the location of cognition; and (4) regarding...
Seeing the directions, two calculations arise. First:
one is the calculation of the human mind that the source of life’s flowing function never ceases; calculating the past and future is called "having boundaries."

To calculate the continuous mind and name it "boundless" means that when one seeks to exhaustively investigate the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one traces them back to the very first moment of the arising mind.
Thereupon, one reckons this to be the source of birth and extinction; from that point onward, until the final exhaustion of a single lifetime, there is a continuous flux in the interim.
This armor never ceases. From the end of life until its exhaustion, one never perceives the function of shifting flux.
Not realizing that this is merely due to the insufficiency of one's own mental power, one then calculates that the past and future lack a continuous function, calling this "having limits.
That the present possesses a continuous mind is called "limitless. His intention was clearly intended to lead people...
They abandon the mind that has no limit regarding past faults, yet simultaneously negate both prior causes and subsequent effects.
They adopt a mind that perceives the present as limitless, asserting that the effect does not repay the cause and the cause does not summon the effect.

Those who argue based on this will surely abandon the principle of cause and condition and fall into the view of spontaneity (*svabhāva*). Second, they give rise to two views regarding objects and time.
Second, this person observes eighty thousand kalpas and thereby perceives sentient beings; prior to those eighty thousand kalpas, there is silence with nothing heard or seen.
That place where there is nothing heard or seen is called "boundless," while that place where sentient beings exist is called "bounded."
To exhaustively investigate the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one proceeds until eighty thousand kalpas have passed. One contemplates that state as the source of arising and ceasing;

from that point onward, one perceives the birth and death, and the cessation and birth, of sentient beings. Prior to those eighty thousand kalpas, however, there is a silence beyond hearing or seeing.
Therein, one sees only a place devoid of hearing and seeing—profoundly obscure and indistinguishable, vast and boundless, such that one does not know it to be anything other than oneself.
Because it cannot be reached by seeing or hearing, they consequently name it the "nature of the boundless.

Furthermore, because they see only where sentient beings dwell, with birth and death arising and ceasing as if there were distinct boundaries, they do not realize that these are merely the false manifestations arising from the karmic conditions of sentient beings;
they consequently name it the "nature of the bounded. Their intention is essentially to lead people to abandon what is manifest.
Those who take as their basis the nature of finitude prior to existence— which is free from arising and ceasing—
and instead grasp at the nature of infinity prior to the kalpa to realize true permanence, will surely fear birth and death and fall into the view of annihilationism.
Third, regarding the knowledge of directions, two types of calculations arise.
First, this person calculates that because "I" know everything pervasively, I have attained the nature of boundlessness. Yet, all those people are currently within the scope of my knowing;
I have never known their own nature of knowing. Thus, they are said not to have attained a mind of boundlessness, but rather to possess a nature of limitation.

If one wishes to exhaustively investigate the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one must fully illuminate the beginning and end of the life-and-death cycle for each of the twelve classes of beings.

Consequently, one calculates that "I" am capable of universal knowledge. Because of this universal knowledge, one falsely perceives that the measure of one's own mind pervades all things, and thus erroneously claims, "I have attained a boundless nature.
How could such a person know that both cessation and arising still remain within the boundaries of the aggregate of formations?
Furthermore, I see all those people manifest within the sphere of my own cognition;
I know only that they die here and are born there, each with a specific location. Yet, I am utterly unable to know their nature as cognition, which is without location.
For this reason, I cannot attain the mind that is boundless; if I were able to attain it, I would certainly know it myself.

Since I do not know [the ultimate], and that [self] is merely of a finite nature—furthermore, as we currently observe its death here and birth there, each having a specific location—it can be known to be finite.
How could one know that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is illusory, fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature?
One who makes such a calculation merely wishes to cause people to abandon that which exists.

The nature of being finite is devoid of spatial direction; to grasp at the nature of my own infinitude as being the state of perfect omniscience (samyaksambuddhatva) would surely cause one who relies on such a treatise to contradict the principle of identity and fall into overweening pride (abhimāna).
Fourth, regarding the observation of spatial directions, two types of calculations arise.

As for these four: this person, having exhausted the investigation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and found it to be empty, uses the path of his own mind to deliberate and calculate that within the single body of every sentient being, all things are half-arising and half-ceasing, thereby clarifying everything that exists within the world.
Half has limits and half is limitless.
"Exhausting the emptiness of the aggregate of formations" means that once the aggregate of perception has ceased, one perceives the flow of the aggregate of formations;
through the power of samādhi, one seeks to exhaust it into emptiness. "That which is seen by him is equal" means that while one is precisely within samādhi, one perceives the aggregate of formations.
When emerging from the samādhi of cessation, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) arises.

Not realizing that this is due to the impurity of one's spiritual practice, one merely uses the path of the deluded mind to speculate based on what was seen, falsely claiming that within the bodies of sentient beings there is always a state of half-arising and half-ceasing.
Generalizing from this single instance, one concludes that everything existing in the world is likewise half-existent and half-boundary-limited.
Half of it is boundless, because at the time of arising one perceives it as having limits, whereas at the time of cessation one perceives it as being boundless.
Those who rely on this treatise will surely become confused by positing cessation in opposition to arising, thereby falling into the view of imagining emptiness while closing one's eyes.
The detailed analysis is concluded. Second, the general faults are set forth:
by such conceptualizations of finitude and infinity, one falls into the ranks of external paths and becomes deluded regarding the nature of bodhi.

Based on these four types of conceptualization, they establish the existence of finitude and infinity; the Sāṃkhya teachers and others act as their companions, and thus it is said that they have fallen into heterodoxy.
Awakening has the Middle Way as its essence, whereas extremes are not the Middle, and for this reason, they are deluded.
Having completed the detailed explanation of each section, the third part concludes by establishing the nature of external treatises.
This is called the fourth heterodox school’s doctrine of the existence of limits (*antavāda*).

This phrase is intelligible; it does not speak of "limitlessness," as has already been clarified previously. *Abhiṣeka* states: "This is also subsumed under the extreme view of partiality (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Thus ends the section on the conceptualization of characteristics within the various states.
Fifth, regarding the arising of conceptualizations within knowledge and vision, there are three parts: first, the introduction showing the fallacy; second, the detailed explanation through analysis;
third, the conclusion establishing the external treatise. First:
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who maintain a firm and concentrated upright mind, Māra finds no opportunity.

Having exhausted the root of all living beings, they contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source. Those who give rise to conceptual calculations within their knowledge and vision fall into four kinds of inverted, "immortal" equivocation and pervasive false theorizing.

Since the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the fundamental source of all movement, and because within these movements there are differences in what is known and seen according to time and place,
one falls into four kinds of inverted views through such conceptualization. Regarding the term "immortal" (*amara*),
Zizhong quotes the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which states that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) reckon that the heavens are eternally abiding and thus name them "immortal."

One should not answer in a confused or evasive manner; by doing so, one may be reborn in that heaven. However, if one truly does not know and yet answers impulsively, there is a fear that it will become a deceptive evasion.
Therefore, when questioned, one should reply, "This is a secret term and should not be disclosed," or provide an indefinite answer.
The Buddha’s Dharma rebukes this, calling it "true equivocation. Zhenji said: "Non-Buddhists reckon the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) to be the Immortal Heaven.
Desiring to be born in that heaven, they respond [to questions] haphazardly, fearing they might fall into equivocation; yet they do not realize they are merely using forced words to claim secrecy."
One should not provide answers by mixing them with the indeterminate; to do so would fall squarely into the fallacy of evasive argumentation (*vāk-chala*). Guanding says:
It is called "pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpita*) because it is a false discrimination; it is called "vain discourse" (*tuccha-pralāpa*) because it possesses no real meaning whatsoever.
The detailed explanation of the two parts consists of two sections: first, the individual analysis; second, the general presentation of the faults.
The first [section] has four parts: first, generating evasive equivocation regarding the four pairs of meanings; second, generating evasive equivocation regarding the meaning of simple non-existence;

third, generating evasive equivocation regarding the meaning of simple existence; fourth, generating evasive equivocation regarding the meaning of both existence and non-existence. The first [of these]:
First, this person contemplates the source of transformation. Seeing the place where things shift and flow, they name it "change.

Seeing the place where things continue in succession, they name it "permanence. Seeing the place where there is something seen, they name it "arising. Not seeing the place where seeing occurs, they name it "cessation."

The state where the causal nature of the continuity is uninterrupted is called "increase" (*vṛddhi*). The point within the very process of continuity where it is interrupted is called "decrease" (*hāni*).
The place where each [phenomenon] arises is called "existence" (*bhava*). The place where they mutually cease is called "non-existence" (*abhāva*).
While observing through principle as a whole, their mental application results in fragmented views.

When seekers of the Dharma come to inquire about its meaning, they reply, "I am now both arising and ceasing, both existent and non-existent, both increasing and decreasing," thus confusing their speech at all times.
This causes the person before one to lose the chapters and sentences [of their own realization].
Regarding "observing the source of transformation": once the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) has been exhausted, the *saṃskāra-skandha* (volitional formations aggregate) is revealed.

To proceed in observing the *saṃskāra-skandha* as the source of transformation means that, since it is the source of transformation, its essence is precisely that of flux and movement; therefore, it is called "seeing."
The locus of transmigration: where there is transmigration, there is alteration; therefore, it is termed "change" (*pariṇāma*).

Although there is alteration, there is nevertheless a continuity between what precedes and what follows; therefore, it is called "the locus of continuity. Where there is continuity, there is no interruption;
therefore, it is termed "permanence" (*nitya*). This is the pairing of change and permanence. The locus of that which is seen is termed [the locus of] seeing.
"Arising" refers to that which occurs within eighty thousand kalpas; because there appears to be the arising of sentient beings in the locus of the seer and the seen, it is designated as "arising.

"Cessation," which refers to not seeing the locus of the seen, means that beyond eighty thousand kalpas, the locus of the seen is no longer perceived, appearing as if sentient beings have ceased to exist; therefore, it is designated as "cessation. This is the contrast between arising and cessation.
Furthermore, regarding the cause of continuity: as long as there are sentient beings, there is birth and death.
Within this process of the birth and death of sentient beings, they further give rise to the speculative view that there must be a distinct intermediate cause of continuity.

For instance, when the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) of the preceding life has already ceased and the *saṃskāra-skandha* of the subsequent life has not yet arisen, there must necessarily be a cause of continuity in the interval. However, as for this cause of continuity...
This refers to the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*). Its substance is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

Because they do not realize that there is a separate aggregate of consciousness outside of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), they merely perceive its nature as being uninterrupted and, seeing it as if an additional phenomenon has emerged, they designate it as "increase" (*vṛddhi*).

"Within the continuous succession" refers specifically to the succession of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). However, within that succession of the intermediate state, there is also a subtle aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*);
because that mind is coarse, it is not perceived, and one perceives only the place from which [the being] has departed.
If there is one fewer [characteristic], it is called "diminution. This constitutes the pair of increase and diminution. Regarding "the respective places of birth":

where there are sentient beings, there are distinctions. Furthermore, within these distinctions among sentient beings, one separately gives rise to the notion that each has its own specific place of birth;
for example, humans are reborn as humans, and birds are reborn as birds—each category having its own distinct characteristics.
Regarding the places of birth: although beings are born one after another, there are also instances where they change form and undergo a different retribution.

Because sentient beings do not understand this, they falsely claim that each distinct category has a fixed place of birth. For this reason, it is called "existence" (*bhava*). Regarding the mutual cessation of these states:
for example, humans are not born as birds, and birds are not born as humans. Although humans are not born as birds, among humans...
There is also the nature of birds; although birds do not give birth to humans, within the category of birds there is also human nature.

Because they do not recognize this, they falsely claim that "this" and "that" are definitively mutually exclusive. For this reason, it is called "non-existence. This constitutes the pair of existence and non-existence.
The first pair still uses the principle of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) for a general observation; therefore, it is said to be "by way of principle."
Observe all things universally, yet without partial attachment; this constitutes the attainment of right view.

This is because one perceives the nature of permanence within the realm of change, and perceives the characteristics of change within the realm of permanence. As for the latter three pairs, they involve using a deluded mind to hold distinct and divergent views;
if one becomes further attached to these, they will lead to increasingly fragmented and disjointed perspectives. This is in contrast to right view.
From within [that state], wrong views arise; because from within wrong views, one further gives rise to biased attachments.
There may be those who seek the Dharma, desiring to seek the Buddha-Dharma by practicing *samādhi*.

When they come to inquire about its meaning—asking about the meaning of what is practiced and realized—one answers with various distinct views. Fearing that they might fall into biased attachment, one says: "It also arises."
"Also extinguished," and so forth. The word "also" (*yi*) indicates a state of doubt where both possibilities are held; its intent is to manifest that one does not fall into partial attachment.

Yet, failing to realize that there is no sovereign master within the "Middle Way," one instead falls into the discourse of sophistry (*kuhaka-vāda*). The reason for not saying "both changing and constant" is that a specific term is used to replace a general one.
Furthermore, among the four pairs [of opposites], the first pair is still relatively close to reason, yet it is nonetheless discarded; this is precisely what constitutes right view.
"In that regard, there is no master. Regarding "at all times," this refers back to whenever anyone asks a question; it refers to those who always muddle their speech.
Regarding "citing words of doubt and ambiguity," this refers to the person standing before one who has come forward to ask a question.
Since the respondent’s answers are merely evasive and confused, the listener’s understanding naturally becomes vague and indistinct. This is a transgression.
The ear becomes empty; how could there be any phrases or sentences to be remembered? Therefore, it is called "losing.
Furthermore, one who loses the phrases and sentences does not merely lose what is currently being heard, but loses even those phrases and sentences previously studied.

This is not only useless; it is, on the contrary, detrimental. Second, regarding the single [position] that lacks meaning, one gives rise to evasive confusion (this and the following section represent the development of biased attachments within the prior discussion of existence and non-existence; this is precisely what is meant by "successively fragmenting").
Second, this person contemplates the mind with such precision that they find it has no fixed location; because it is non-existent, they attain realization.
When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying merely "non-existence. Apart from this "non-existence," they have nothing further to say.
"To contemplate their mind" means to contemplate the mind of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) among living beings.

One merely observes that humans do not produce birds and birds do not produce humans, and so forth; thus, in the state of mutual non-existence, they erroneously claim that their own minds lack the nature of other species.
Furthermore, they claim to have attained realization because of this absence. It should be understood that what they call "realization" is as follows:
This is a fallacious proof that does not accord with reason; it is not a genuine realization of the truth.

When someone comes to question him, he answers with only a single word because he fears inviting difficult inquiries and dares not speak much. Furthermore, he wishes to deceive others with secret terminology.
It is not the case that one should speak of everything as such. To say merely that something "does not exist" is to answer evasively based on one's own erroneous views.

As for those who, having excluded what is non-existent, have nothing further to say, they do not explain on what basis they claim non-existence, nor what the meaning of "non-existence" is; it is simply a forced and confused statement.
Third, they give evasive and confused answers regarding matters that are straightforward.

Third, these people carefully observe that their minds each have their own distinct locations; based on this, they claim to have attained realization. When someone comes to question them, [they respond with evasion].
He answered with only a single word, saying merely that it was so; beyond this, he had nothing further to say.
Upon closely observing their minds, they were seen to be the same as before: humans were still born from humans, birds from birds, and so forth.

Consequently, in each respective case, they erroneously claimed that within their own minds there existed a nature of its own kind, and they presumed that because such things exist, they could be attained.
"Realization" is also a mistaken realization, not a true realization. To answer with a single word, "Yes," is also as explained above.
However, by saying "it is so," since each thing possesses its own nature, humans are simply humans and birds are simply birds;
by analogy, I am simply I. Therefore, he only says "it is so," yet he does not dare to state it explicitly—of what is it so?
Regarding the meaning: for what reason is this spoken? Therefore, to eliminate it is non-speaking; it is seen all the more as a deceptive and confused discourse.

Fourth, generating deceptive confusion regarding the meanings of existence and non-existence (this refers to seeing non-existence within existence and seeing existence within non-existence; not daring to speak of difference, yet not daring to speak of identity;
having no rational basis to rely upon, one speaks with forced arrogance and confusion).
Fourth, there are those who hold views that both existence and non-existence coexist. Because their objective realm is fragmented, their minds are likewise distracted.

When someone comes to question them, they answer that "existence" is itself "non-existence," and that within "non-existence" there is not "existence. This is entirely evasive and confused, leaving no room for further inquiry.

Regarding those who hold the view that both existence and non-existence coexist: this refers to observing within the realm of sentient beings that they undergo transformations of form and shifts in retribution, such as a person changing into a bird, or a bird transforming into a person, and so forth.
When a person changes into a bird, then within that human there is no human nature, but rather the nature of a bird;
when a bird transforms into a person, then within that bird there is no bird-nature, but rather the nature of a human. For this reason, regarding each and every [instance]...
Within these categories, both existence and non-existence are perceived; how could one know that their nature is fundamentally non-dual, and that their transformation follows conditions?
As for "the objects being bifurcated," this means that within the single nature, one calculates existence and calculates non-existence, like a single trunk branching into two limbs.
As for "the mind also being distracted," it refers to not daring to definitively grasp [reality] as existent, due to the meaning of existence and non-existence.
Therefore, one does not dare to definitively maintain that [things] are non-existent, because there is the sense in which they exist; this is what is called "confusion.

When someone comes and asks, and one answers that "existence is itself non-existence," it is because that person does not understand transformation according to conditions, yet they insist on answering with a single identity.
Furthermore, when one says "non-existence is not existence," it is because that person does not understand that the nature is fundamentally non-dual, yet they insist [on such a view].
This is answered by means of a different entity. Suppose there were an objection stating: "For what reason do you say that existence is non-existence? One would then necessarily answer:
"Non-existence is also existence. Suppose one were to object again: "How can non-existence not be existence? One would then necessarily answer:
"Within existence, there is no 'also non-existence. All of this is merely forced speech; non-existence is not [existence].
These are mixed-up words; therefore, it is said that all such equivocation lacks any rational basis to rely upon and provides no meaningful principle to depend on.
Consequently, there is no room for further interrogation. Having finished the detailed analysis, secondly, the faults are presented collectively.
By means of this conceptualization, they resort to evasive and deceptive sophistry, falling into the ranks of external paths and becoming deluded regarding the nature of bodhi.
Regarding these conceptualizations, in their general form there are only four types; when analyzed in detail, however, there are four pairs.
"Two, one, neither, or both; evasive and confused" means being artfully stubborn and muddled. "Vain and non-existent" means being false and without basis.

[Concepts such as] transformation and constancy, arising and ceasing, existence and non-existence, increase and decrease, identity and difference, both and neither, and so forth—all belong to externalist calculations.
Since this [view] is identical to theirs, it is said that they "fall into the ranks of the heterodox. The bodhicitta takes the *tathāgatagarbha* mind as its essence, and is free from...

All characteristics are, in themselves, all phenomena. They are neither separate nor non-separate; they are both identical and not identical. The path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity ceases.
Since this is distinct from that, it is said that one is deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This concludes the detailed explanation by sections.
These three constitute the external treatises.
This is called the fifth heterodox school’s fourfold nature of inverted views—the futile equivocation of the "Immortal" (Amarāvikṣepa)—which is a pervasive false discourse.
Following the fourth, it is designated as the fifth; because it deludes right knowledge and vision while establishing false knowledge and vision, it is called the "four."
This is the nature of perversion. Like those non-Buddhists who calculate the existence of an immortal heaven, they provide evasive answers; hence they are called "the immortals' evasive wranglers.
Observing these various preceding heterodox calculations, one sees that they are not only like a rope appearing upon hemp fibers, but further resemble a snake appearing upon a rope;
thus they are called "pervasive false theories. This concludes the section on the arising of conceptual marks within knowledge and vision.

Sixth, regarding the arising of conceptualizations within the inexhaustible flow, there are three parts: first, the introduction showing the fall; second, the explanation of the characteristics and the emergence from faults; third, the conclusion establishing the external treatise. First: The term "inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*) means that it cannot be exhausted by any means whatsoever. It refers to the nature of the mind (*cittatva*), which is the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). This is because it is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and is not subject to arising or ceasing. It is called "flow" (*srotas*) because it is continuous and uninterrupted. It is called "inexhaustible" because it is not something that can be consumed or depleted. It is called "arising" (*utpatti*) because it manifests as various appearances. It is called "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) because it discriminates between self and other, and so forth. It is called "fall" (*patana*) because it falls into the states of birth and death. It is called "introduction" (*uddeśa*) because it points out the essential meaning. It is called "showing" (*darśana*) because it reveals the true nature. It is called "part" (*bhāga*) because it is a portion of the whole. It is called "introduction" (*uddeśa*) because it introduces the subsequent detailed explanation. It is called "showing" (*darśana*) because it shows the path to liberation. It is called "fall" (*patana*) because it falls away from the state of enlightenment. It is called "first" (*ādya*) because it precedes the other two parts. It is called "part" (*bhāga*) because it is one of the three sections. It is called "introduction" (*uddeśa*) because it introduces the topic of the inexhaustible flow. It is called "showing" (*darśana*) because it shows the error of clinging to signs. It is called "fall" (*patana*) because it falls into the pit of false views. It is called "first" (*ādya*) because it is the initial stage of the analysis. It is called "part" (*bhāga*) because it is the first of the three divisions. It is called "introduction" (*uddeśa*) because it introduces the method of refuting the opponent's position. It is called "showing" (*darśana*) because it shows the defects of their arguments. It is called "fall" (*patana*) because it falls into the trap of sophistry. It is called "first" (*ādya*) because it is the primary point of contention. It is called "part" (*bhāga*) because it is the first section of the critique. It is called "introduction" (*uddeśa*) because it introduces the refutation of the externalist doctrines. It is called "showing" (*darśana*) because it shows the logical fallacies. It is called "fall" (*patana*) because it falls into the error of dualistic grasping. It is called "first" (*ādya*) because it is the opening of the refutation. It is called "part" (*bhāga*) because it is the first of the three concluding sections. It is called "introduction" (*uddeśa*) because it introduces the final summary. It is called "showing" (*darśana*) because it shows the superiority of the Buddha's teaching. It is called "fall" (*patana*) because it falls away from the heterodox systems. It is called "first" (*ādya*) because it is the beginning of the conclusion. It is called "part" (*bhāga*) because it is the first of the three concluding segments.
