Furthermore, when those good sons within samādhi maintain a firm and concentrated right mind, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. Those who harbor conceptual calculations regarding this inexhaustible flow fall into the error of generating a perverted resolve concerning the existence of signs after death.

The beginning is the same as before. However, since it is said to be "constantly disturbed," its movement and transformation are inexhaustible. From this, within the flow of the inexhaustible, conceptualization arises;
there is no other conceptualization than this: namely, conceptualizing this very movement and transformation as the source of all agitation.

That which will arise in the future can produce all movements. Since that which will arise in the future can produce all movements, then that which has already ceased in the present must necessarily arise in the future.
Therefore, it is said that such a person falls into the view of "characteristics existing after death.

Due to this notion of characteristics existing after death, they further calculate that the two natures of affliction (*kleśa*) and awakening (*bodhi*) are both eternal, thereby becoming deluded regarding the transformation from defilement to purity within Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).

This is a correct critique. It contradicts the profound intent of the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* regarding the "unmoving nature following conditions" (*bùbiàn suíyuán*). Therefore, it is said that "the arousal of the mind is inverted.

Second, the refutation of the two interpretations of its characteristics has two parts: first, a specific explanation of those characteristics; second, a general presentation of the faults. First [the specific explanation]:
Some, in order to secure their own bodies, claim that "form is the self. Others perceive the self as encompassing and pervading the entire realm, claiming that "the self possesses form.

Others, following the prior conditions that revolve around them, claim that "form belongs to the self. Still others, based on the continuity within the process of formations, claim that "the self is within form.
All of these are conceptual reckonings asserting that there is a mark after death. Thus, revolving in this manner, there are sixteen such marks.
From this point, some may calculate that afflictions and enlightenment are two distinct natures that proceed side by side without ever touching one another;
or, those who cling to their own bodies may perceive that while the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is inexhaustible, the body itself is subject to exhaustion;

or, they may seek to preserve and cherish their thoughts, desiring to make their bodies firm. Although such individuals have previously transcended the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been exhausted.
It has perished; yet when meeting conditions, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) still blazes forth. However, where there is a body, there must be form (*rūpa*).

Although one has previously already destroyed the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the habitual tendencies have not been entirely eliminated; thus, when meeting conditions, the aggregate of form arises again.

Consequently, based on form, one establishes a self and says, "Form is the self. Although one has previously already attained the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), the habitual tendencies have not been entirely eliminated.
It perishes; yet when encountering conditions, the grasping at a self still arises. This is identical to the externalist view among the four propositions that "form is the self.

Based on this, what was previously called "shattering the aggregates and transcending turbidity," as well as what was stated in the fifth fascicle—"when these faculties first resolve, one first attains the emptiness of persons"—are all matters where the principle is realized through sudden awakening, and awakening and practice proceed simultaneously.

If the sequence of causes for cultivation through successive stages of practice is not completed, and one encounters sensory objects with a fleeting thought arise, there are few who do not fall into deviant knowledge and erroneous understanding.
The same applies to the two aggregates of sensation and perception; this should be understood accordingly. One should not raise the objection:
"Since the three aggregates have already been exhausted, how can one still cling to them? Or, as for those who calculate that the self is perfectly encompassing and pervasive throughout all lands.
To falsely conceive of the nature of the self as vast is not truly awakening to the mind that encompasses the great void and measures the entire realm of sand-grains.

To say "I have form" is because, in the absence of a self, form would have no basis for establishment. This is identical to the externalist calculation among the four propositions, which holds that the self is large and form is small, and that form is seen within the self.
Or, it refers to those who maintain that the preceding objects of perception revolve and return according to the self.

The preceding conditions are the sensory objects (*viṣaya*), which also belong to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Through false conceptualization, they revolve and circulate in accordance with the self, being employed and put to work.

This is not truly the ability to transform things like a Buddha, who possesses mastery over form. As for the statement "form belongs to the self," it means that form is not the self, yet it is used by the self.
This differs from the externalist calculation among the four propositions, which posits [the self] as distinct from form.

This is the same as the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*). Alternatively, regarding the phrase "the self that continues within the formations (*saṃskāra*)," the character *xing* (formation) should be the character *se* (form).

This means that the self conceived here takes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) as its substance and continuity as its characteristic, yet it relies upon the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Therefore, it says: "The self relies on the continuity within form. Only by explaining it in this way does it accord with the context.
The subsequent sentence says, "I am in form" (*rūpe*). Now, the phrase "relying on formations" (*saṃskāra*) is likely a scribal error resulting from following previous texts.
If one were to interpret it by forcibly conforming to the word "formations," it would mean that there is a separate self-entity (*ātman*) that relies upon the continuity within formations;
since formations manifest by depending on form, the self also exists in form by following those formations. Thus, one could say, "I am in form. This is an alternative interpretation.
Thus, one may attain mastery over the meaning; by not altering it, one comes to cherish the sutras. One should simply know this:
it is identical to the externalist views among the four propositions, which hold that "the body is large and the self is small, and the self dwells within the body.

All such views are speculative reckonings asserting that there is a form after death, because the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) flows constantly and serves as the source of all movement, inevitably giving rise to future existence.
Because all things are in motion, one calculates these four selves as all possessing characteristics that persist after death.

Just as it is with respect to the four characteristics of form (*rūpa*), so it is with respect to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Therefore, it is said that there are sixteen characteristics in this revolving cycle.

"Revolving" means that the four types of self-characteristics begin again after they have completed their cycle, corresponding to the four aggregates (*skandha*). [Question: Since the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has not yet been dismantled and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has not yet been revealed, why...

"Can one establish the fourfold propositions regarding consciousness? Answer: Although it is said that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has not yet been dismantled and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has not yet been revealed, this merely means its substance has not been seen; how could its name not have been heard? Even granting that its name has been heard, who can prohibit one from employing inference to establish it?

Are those who nowadays discuss the aggregate of consciousness all ones for whom the aggregate of formations has already been dismantled? The above constitutes the primary calculation regarding future existence. From here on, there follows the shifting calculation of two types of permanence.
"From this, some calculate ultimate afflictions, etc."—the intent is that [they believe] "I possess goodness."
There are two natures: the evil nature and the good nature. Evil is the nature of affliction (*kleśa*), while good is the nature of awakening (*bodhi*).
However, since there are characteristics that persist even after my death, the nature of affliction will ultimately remain affliction, and the nature of awakening will ultimately remain awakening.
The nature of affliction progresses daily toward evil, while the nature of awakening progresses daily toward goodness; therefore, they are called the "two natures."

"They drive side by side. "Drive" here means to advance. That they do not touch one another means that those with perfected unwholesome natures naturally fall into hell, while those with perfected wholesome natures naturally become Buddhas; thus, each does not obstruct the other. Those who hold this view—

Thus, the evil nature will ultimately never be exhausted, and the good nature will ultimately never become pure. Those who fall into hell will continue to exist as beings; as for attaining Buddhahood, that is not necessarily so. (Question:

Regarding the ancient interpretation of the sixteen phrases, many take the "divine self" (*puruṣa*) to correspond to the first four aggregates (*skandhas*), as it is said: "Form is the self; sensation is the self; perception is the self; formations are the self.

Now, in this commentary, you correspond [the self] to the first three and the last one, yet you do not mention its correspondence to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra*). What is the intent behind this? Answer: In the ancient interpretation, non-Buddhists regard the eight consciousnesses as the divine self. Since their fundamental substance is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), it naturally follows...)

Regarding the preceding four [aggregates], sixteen propositions were established. Now, this commentary addresses the practitioner of the Perfect Penetration (yuan-tong), who perceives the self-characteristic (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) through the seventh consciousness; since its substance is precisely the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one should establish sixteen propositions based on the first three and the last one.

Although the views of the non-Buddhists and the practitioner naturally differ, there is no need to force them into agreement. Having completed the detailed explanation of their characteristics (2), the faults are now presented collectively.
Because they speculate that there is existence after death, they fall away from the Way and become confused regarding the nature of Bodhi.
To speculate on existence after death is to fall into the extreme view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). Therefore, it is said that they "fall away from the Way" and become non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

How much more so when they speculate that the two natures are each eternal and do not believe that the defiled can be transformed into the pure; is this not indeed to be confused about the nature of Bodhi?
Yes. The refutation of the characteristics of the "sign of existence after death" is concluded. This completes the third section on the formation of external doctrines.
This is called the sixth heterodox theory established among the five aggregates: the perverted view of mind that asserts the existence of signs after death.

That which can face the characteristic of self is, in its essence, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Together with the three preceding and the one succeeding it that are faced [by it], all are said to be "existence after death.
Therefore, it is established that the characteristic of existence after death resides within the five aggregates.

Furthermore, the aggregate of formations acts as the "possessor" (*svāmī*), because its nature is constantly agitated and thus the source of movement. The other four aggregates act as the "possessed" (*sva*), because they arise in succession depending upon the aggregate of formations.

Since this is a combined discussion of the subject and the object, it is stated generally that there are signs after death. One must understand that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are unreal, like flowers in the sky;
to say that when the flowers vanish, only emptiness remains, is already a perversion. How much more so to calculate that they will be reborn—this perversion is particularly extreme.
This treatise is established based on such [views]; since it proceeds from mental perversions, how could it truly be that the heavenly demon Pāpīyān has come to delude and confuse one?

Ah! This concludes the section on the conceptualization of characteristics arising within the inexhaustible flow. Seventh, regarding the conceptualization of characteristics arising from prior cessation, there are three parts:
first, the heading that indicates the fallacy; second, the explanation of the characteristics and their transcendence; third, the conclusion establishing the external treatise. First:
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaust the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. If, while first eliminating form, sensation, and perception, they give rise to conceptual calculations, such persons fall into the inverted resolve of "signlessness after death."

The initial point is as before and should be considered accordingly. However, they perceive only the constant agitation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and do not see the preceding three aggregates.

Consequently, they form conceptual constructions regarding those three aggregates previously eliminated, asserting that while these three aggregates formerly existed, they have now ceased and no longer exist.

By analogy, they conclude that although the aggregate of formations currently exists, it too must cease and become non-existent in the future. Based on this calculation, they conceive of the relinquishing of their retribution.
Afterward, it ultimately returns to annihilation. Therefore, it is said that this person falls into the view of signlessness after death.
From this signlessness after death, they further calculate that all things are empty, establishing the false doctrine of the non-Buddhists that destroys permanence for the sake of nihilism.

This violates the sincere words of the Buddha’s teaching on cultivating causes and realizing fruits; therefore, it is called "inverted resolve. (Zhengmo says: This is the direct opposite of the preceding section.

In the former case, one beheld the unextinguished activity-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and saw its inexhaustibility, thereby reckoning that the preceding three aggregates and all phenomena were likewise inexhaustible. In this case, one beholds the already-extinguished preceding three aggregates and sees their signlessness.)

And because one calculates that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and all phenomena are likewise devoid of marks (*animitta*). Second, the explanation of the characteristics and the emergence of faults has two parts: first, the specific explanation of their characteristics;
second, the general presentation of their faults. First [the specific explanation].

Seeing that form has ceased, one finds no basis for its manifestation. Contemplating that perception has ceased, one finds the mind is unattached. Knowing that sensation has ceased, one finds no further continuity.
The nature of the aggregates dissolves; even if the processes of life persist, being devoid of sensation and perception, one is the same as grass and trees.

If this physical basis cannot be apprehended even while present before one, how could there be any further characteristics after death? By examining it through this reasoning, one finds that characteristics are absent after death;

thus, in this cycle, there are eight instances of the absence of characteristics. From this, some may calculate that the causes and effects of nirvana are entirely empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately resulting in total annihilation.
"Form" refers to the physical body; it exists because of matter (*rūpa*). Now that one sees that the aggregate of matter has already ceased, one knows that form has nothing upon which to depend.
This is the reckoning of "no body. "Mind" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*); it exists because of mental objects (*saṃjñā*).

Now that one contemplates that the aggregate of perception has already ceased, one realizes that the mind has nothing to which it is bound. This is the reckoning of "no mind. "Continuous connection" refers to the reception of external objects.
It benefits the body and mind. Now, knowing that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has already ceased, one thinks that the body and mind are no longer linked together;
this calculation implies that even if body and mind still exist, they cannot sustain themselves. Based on this, such is the nature of the [remaining] three aggregates.

All have already been dissolved and dispersed. Even if the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) remains as the principle capable of producing [phenomena], that which is produced consists only of the remaining *vijñāna-skandha* (the aggregate of consciousness).
Since there are neither sensation (*vedanā*) nor perception (*saṃjñā*), the *vijñāna-skandha* is of the same substance as grass and trees;
for the *vijñāna-skandha* relies upon sensation and perception to function. This "substance" does not merely refer to material form (*rūpa*), but rather refers to...
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) combine to form this illusory substance. The first three have already ceased, and the last one is useless;
thus, even while this substance is present before us, it cannot be apprehended, let alone after death. How then could there be any further characteristics?
This is a definitive statement that there is no self (*ātman*). As for the "examination based on this": because [the former] has already ceased, one examines and discriminates [the latter].
It ceases. By comparing the present state with what follows, one concludes that after death there is no further appearance; thus, the principle is fully established.
In this manner, one cycles through the aggregates from form (rūpa-skandha) to consciousness (vijñāna-skandha), contrasting the period before birth with that after death.

Because there is the sense of cyclic continuity. Regarding the eight instances of signlessness (*animitta*): the first three are signless because they have already ceased; the last one is signless because it is useless.
Between birth and death, logically there should be eight [instances], yet only the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is excluded.

This is because the aggregate of formations is directly perceived, and thus there is no fault in stating its existence. However, when it is established that the other four aggregates are all absent, then the aggregate of formations has nothing upon which to rely.
This requires no further words to explain itself. The above constitutes the correct calculation that there is nothing after death; from here on follows the shifting calculation that all is empty.

It is said that the manifest substance is empty, such that there is no one to cultivate the causes; after death, the marks are non-existent, such that there is no one to realize the fruit. Therefore it is said:
"From this point, some calculate that the causes and fruits of *nirvāṇa* are entirely empty. Since everything is empty...
If it were empty, then what are called the cause and fruit of nirvāṇa would exist merely as names. If one follows the name to seek the reality, there would be no reality corresponding to that name;
therefore, it is said to be ultimately annihilated. Second, this generally sets forth the faults [of such a view].
Because they speculate that there is nothing after death, they fall away from the Way and become confused regarding the nature of Bodhi.

To calculate that there is nothing after death is to fall into the extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), specifically the portion of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); therefore, it is said they "fall away from the Way" and become non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

This is especially true when they calculate that both cause and effect are empty and do not believe in *nirvāṇa*. Since the fruit of cessation is not established, how could the fruit of wisdom (*jñānaphala*)...
How could it possibly exist independently? Therefore, it is said that they "delude the nature of bodhi. This concludes the explanation of the characteristics and the exposition of their errors.
Third, the summary that establishes the external doctrine:
this is called the seventh heterodox school’s theory of the post-mortem non-existence of signs within the five aggregates, which constitutes a perversion of mind.

Form, sensation, and perception cease; the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) becomes useless. Even if the aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāra-skandha) persists, it has nothing to rely upon and will soon perish of its own accord.

Therefore, it is said that among the five aggregates, there is no sign after death. Furthermore, the first three [aggregates] are non-existent through direct perception; the aggregate of consciousness is non-existent by inference;

and the aggregate of mental formations is non-existent by implication. Thus, all five aggregates are non-existent. One must understand that worldly phenomena are eternally abiding and that all things...
There is no transition. If one seeks permanence by departing from characteristics, yet speaks of transition regarding phenomena, this is already a perversion;
how much more so to calculate annihilation? Such perversion is extreme; it is truly for the mind to be shrouded by false views.

To establish a treatise based on this, following the perversions of the mind, and to bring about evil fruits through wholesome causes—like pursuing the path of a Pratyekabuddha while trampling a wheel of fire—is truly pitiable and lamentable. Thus one practices meditation.

This person also knows how to examine the mirror. First, he eliminates and extinguishes the conceptual signs that have arisen. Eighth, regarding the conceptual signs arising within existence and cessation, there are three parts: first, indicating the cause and showing the fallacy; second, explaining the characteristics and exposing the error; third, concluding with the external treatise. The first [part]: [The text continues: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of self-nature: one is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and the other is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Among these, the imagined nature consists of the various forms of conceptualization based on the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, which are like a dream, a mirage, or a reflection. The perfected nature is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, free from the duality of grasped and grasper. [The text continues: "Mahāmati, if one does not understand this, one will fall into the views of eternalism or nihilism. Therefore, you should cultivate the wisdom that transcends words and letters. [The text continues: "At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse: 'If one clings to the imagined nature, One will never see the perfected nature. When the imagined is thoroughly understood, The perfected nature is revealed. [The text continues: "Thus, Mahāmati, you should abandon all conceptual proliferation and abide in the state of non-discrimination. [The text continues: "Having said this, the World-Honored One further addressed Mahāmati: 'Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three kinds of conceptual signs arising within the midst of existence and cessation: first, the sign of the self; second, the sign of phenomena; and third, the sign of the characteristics of birth and death. [The text continues: "Regarding the first, it indicates the source and demonstrates the downfall. [The text continues: "Regarding the second, it explains the characteristics and exposes the error. [The text continues: "Regarding the third, it concludes by establishing the external treatise. [The text continues: "As for the first: [the passage begins here]."

Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi*, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māra finds no opportunity. They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source.

Within the state of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), they simultaneously suppress sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*). By dualistically calculating existence and non-existence, their own essential natures cancel each other out.
Such persons fall into the nihilistic view that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence, giving rise to perverse theories.

Zhengmo says: "In the state where the activity-aggregate (saṃskāra-skandha) still persists," one sees that the activity-aggregate has not yet been extinguished, and the phenomenal world remains distinct.

"Simultaneously with the extinction of sensation and perception (vedanā and saṃjñā)," one sees that the preceding three aggregates have already ceased, and their very substance is entirely empty. "Dually calculating existence and non-existence" refers to...

To reckon existence regarding what persists and to reckon non-existence regarding what ceases; as for the mutual subversion of their own essential characteristics, it means using the existence of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) to subvert the non-existence of the preceding three [aggregates], and using the non-existence of the preceding three to subvert the existence of the *saṃskāra-skandha*.

The final statement regarding "falling into neither" means that by subverting non-existence, one establishes "not non-existent," and by subverting existence, one establishes "not existent. This is the explanation.
This is clear. However, in my humble opinion, it differs slightly from the *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse). Regarding the statement "reckoning both existence and non-existence":

this refers to reckoning that within the aggregates of form, feeling, and perception which have already ceased, there was previously existence and now there is non-existence; and within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) which currently exists, there is present existence and previously there was non-existence.
Precisely because that which previously existed is now non-existent, one may infer by analogy that that which currently exists must likewise have been non-existent in the past.

This is non-existence. Thus, within each of the four aggregates (*skandhas*), both existence and non-existence are present; therefore, they are reckoned as a pair. Regarding the mutual sublation of their own essential natures (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-viparyaya*):

this means that the three preceding aggregates already ceased and the currently existing aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) each possess the sense of mutually sublating one another’s essential natures.
For instance, since the three preceding aggregates that have already ceased each possess both existence and non-existence, if one considers them by way of their own essential nature—
If one uses the non-existence of intrinsic nature to refute the existence of intrinsic nature, then that non-existence is not a true non-existence, because it carries the sense of "existence.
If one uses the non-existence of intrinsic nature to refute the existence of intrinsic nature, then that existence is not a true existence, because it carries the sense of "non-existence."

Since it is thus for the three aggregates that have already ceased, it is likewise for the currently existing aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Since it is thus in the present, it will be so in the future.

Therefore, it is said that this person falls into the state of "neither-existence-nor-non-existence" after death. This constitutes the second explanation, which clarifies the characteristics and reveals the error of the two [previous] positions.
First, a specific explanation of their characteristics; second, a general exposition of their faults. Regarding the first:

within form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*), one perceives both existence and non-existence; within the flux of formations (*saṃskāra*), one contemplates that there is neither existence nor non-existence.

Thus, through this cycle, one exhaustively investigates the eightfold "neither-nor" characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*). Upon encountering any single condition, one claims that after death there is either a mark of existence or a mark of non-existence.

Furthermore, because one calculates that the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is subject to change and transformation, the mind gives rise to penetrating realization: they are neither existent nor non-existent, and one loses the distinction between the empty and the real.

Regarding the perception of existence and non-existence within form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*): this means that while form, feeling, and perception are non-existent in the present, they will necessarily exist in the future.
Yet, although they will necessarily exist in the future, they are nonetheless not existent. Within the flux of conditioned formations, one contemplates that there is nothing that is not non-existent.

This means that the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) exists in the present, but will certainly not exist in the future. Although it will certainly not exist in the future, it is nevertheless not non-existent.
Thus, that which goes from existence to non-existence returns to existence once it has become non-existent; and that which goes from non-existence to existence—[is likewise so].
Having existed, they return to non-existence; existence has the sense of coming and going, hence it is called "cycling" (*xúnhuán*). "Dhātu" (*jiè*) carries the meaning of "delimitation.

To speak of "exhausting the aggregates and elements" (*yīnjiè*) means that such existence and non-existence, coming and going in a cycle, proceed from the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and from before birth to after death; this constitutes the exhaustion of the various destinies (*gati*) within the four aggregates. However—

The four aggregates (*skandha*) prior to death already possess four instances of "neither-existence-nor-non-existence" (*naiva-saṃjñi-nāsaṃjñin*); the four aggregates after death should likewise possess four instances of "neither-existence-nor-non-existence.

Thus, eight aspects of "neither-existence-nor-non-existence" are established. Consequently, whenever one of these four aggregates is taken as an object of cognition, it is asserted that there is both existence and non-existence after death.
Based on this, the eight [aspects] thus reckoned— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the logical structure of the argument presented.]
"Neither" refers to taking the state of being "neither" during life as an analogy for the state after death;

its intent lies primarily in the period after death, which is why the concluding statement later says that both are "neither" after death. The above constitutes the eight aspects of the primary thesis.

From here on, one shifts to the thesis regarding all things, meaning the activity of the practitioner. Furthermore, one calculates regarding all practitioners, meaning one shifts to calculate all that exists.

This constitutes conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). "Shifting" refers to the alternating transition between existence and non-existence—namely, from existence to non-existence, and from non-existence to existence.
"Distortion" refers to the confusion of this and that—namely, that existence is not truly existent, and non-existence is not truly non-existent.

Because one falsely imagines that suchness is inherently so, one expands erroneous knowledge and fallacious understanding; thus it is said that the mind gives rise to [false] penetration and awakening, while clinging to existence and non-existence as fixed.
Neither is the case. Even if someone were to ask, "Which is empty and which is real? one would likewise be unable to provide an answer; hence it is called "being at a loss.
Second, this generally sets forth the faults [of these positions].

Because they calculate that after death there is neither [existence nor non-existence], and because the future limit is obscure and beyond description, they fall into the ways of external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
The phrase "by calculating such as these" generally refers to all the aforementioned calculations as the cause for establishing these faults. [The term] "future limit" (paścānta).

This refers to the future. To fail to distinguish between existence and non-existence is called "darkness" (*hun*); to lose one's bearings regarding the void and the real is called "blindness" (*meng*).

Because there is no correct principle by which to speak, it is said that "there is nothing that can be articulated. Because only false views are thereby nurtured, it is said that "one falls into the ways of external paths" (*tīrthika*).
The nature of *bodhi* does not fall into existence or non-existence, yet it is not separate from existence and non-existence. Now, since both existence and non-existence are present...
No; therefore, it is called "delusion. This concludes the explanation of the characteristics and the refutation of the error. Third, the conclusion of the external treatise:
this is termed the eighth heterodox doctrine, the theory of the mental perversion that asserts neither-existence-nor-non-existence after death within the five aggregates.
As it is with the three aggregates (*skandha*) that have already ceased, so it is with the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that have not yet ceased.

As it is with the aggregate of formations that has already manifested, so it is with the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) that has not yet manifested. As it was before birth, so it is after death.

Therefore, it is said that within the five aggregates, after death, there is "neither [existence nor non-existence]. The reason it does not say that before birth there is "neither" is that this clinging does not continue [prior to birth].
This is because it would entail the fault of non-establishment. It is simply due to the continuous arising of subsequent attachments that one becomes confused regarding the nature of Bodhi.

Therefore, the intent of the previous statement emphasized the period after death. One must understand that true emptiness does not obstruct wondrous existence, and wondrous existence does not obstruct true emptiness;
where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases, to now calculate that both existence and non-existence are neither is truly a matter of the mind.
This is a perversion. To establish a treatise based on this contradicts the Buddha’s correct teaching; it misleads oneself and others, and the harm is no small matter.

Having concluded the section on the conceptualization of characteristics regarding existence and non-existence, [the text now addresses] the third part: the three aspects of the conceptualization of non-arising in successive stages.
First, the heading indicating the fallacy; second, the explanation of the characteristics and the exposure of errors; third, the conclusion establishing the externalist doctrine. First:

Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration such that Māra finds no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings.

They contemplate that profound, pure, and eternally quiescent source of constant agitation; yet, regarding what lies beyond this, they fail to give rise to further discernment. Such persons fall into the seven theories of annihilationism.
Constant agitation causes every moment to shift and flow; shifting and flowing means there is no abiding. Because there is no abiding, whether near or far, there is inevitably cessation.

Based on this, one subsequently engages in speculative calculation regarding non-existence, reckoning that this retribution is simply annihilated, that the subsequent retribution is likewise annihilated, and so on through successive stages until there is ultimately an end. This is the seventh [view]: annihilationism.

The commentator [Zongmi], in the *Qingliang Chao*, combines these into three: first, those who hold that the self possesses form, being composed of the coarse four great elements as its nature, and is annihilated after death, because they see that the body exists before death but does not exist after; second, those who hold that the self is an inhabitant of the heavens of the desire realm who is annihilated after death;

third, those who hold that the self is an inhabitant of the heavens of the formless or empty space who is annihilated after death. The first category encompasses those in the hells, hungry ghosts, and humans.

The sentient beings are categorized into four groups: the first two are the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the latter three are the gods of the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*). These three groups, combined with the [other] four destinies (*gati*), constitute seven;
because they all undergo annihilation, they are called the "Seven Annihilations. The treatise that evaluates this meaning is termed the "Annihilationist Theory" (*ucchedavāda*).
Second, explaining the characteristics and exposing the faults has two parts: first, explaining the characteristics individually; second, exposing the faults collectively. Regarding the first:

some reckon that extinction occurs through the destruction of the body; some through the exhaustion of desire; some through the exhaustion of suffering; some through extreme bliss; or some through extreme equanimity.
Thus, as they circulate through the cycle until the seven limits are exhausted, they manifest and then perish; once perished, they no longer exist.

Alternatively, those who reckon that the body perishes falsely calculate that the pre-existences as hell-dwellers, ghosts, humans, or animals persist, and that when the body dies, they are extinguished.

Some who wish for extinction through the cessation of desire falsely reckon that the gods of the six heavens of desire take desire as the cause of their birth; thus, when desire is exhausted, they are extinguished.

Others who wish for extinction through the cessation of suffering falsely reckon that the first dhyāna takes the aversion to suffering as the cause of its birth; thus, when suffering is exhausted, it is extinguished.
Regarding "extreme joy ceases": one falsely conceives that the second dhyāna takes joy as its cause of birth; thus, when extreme joy ceases, [the state] ceases. Regarding "extreme equanimity ceases":
one falsely conceives that the third dhyāna takes extreme joy as its retributive form; thus, when extreme equanimity ceases, [the state] ceases.
Next, one should say: "or it ceases in the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana)," or "it ceases in the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana)," and so forth.

For the fourth dhyāna takes supreme equanimity as its resultant form; thus, when one falsely conceives of the sphere of infinite space, [the mind] ceases there. One should understand that for the sphere of infinite consciousness and the others, it likewise ceases in those respective spheres.
Now, rather than stating them all together, the phrase "and so forth" is used to speak of them collectively by means of an abbreviated leap. Thus, following...
"Cyclic" means that as the preceding perishes and the succeeding arises, birth and extinction follow one another in succession;

because there is this sense of circling, it is called "exhausting the seven limits"—namely, the six realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, humans, animals, and the three heavens, plus the limit of the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception. "Manifestly dissolving and extinguishing so that once extinguished they never recur" means:

The retribution already manifested has ceased. Once it has ceased, one then undergoes other retribution; there is no longer any further existence of this [specific] retribution. Thus, this retribution becomes subject to annihilation.

It is like the cessation of the bodies of the four realms of existence (*catur-gati*) in the present moment. Once they have ceased, one then undergoes the retribution of the desire heavens (*kāma-deva*);
there is no longer any further retribution of the four realms of existence. Thus, the four realms of existence become annihilated. Other cases may be understood by analogy.
It is known. The Āgamas also state: There are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, during the final age, give rise to the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).
Some reckon that my body, having arisen from causes and conditions, must inevitably return to destruction. (1) Some reckon that the self is annihilated in the desire realm heavens (*kāmadhātu*).
(2) Some reckon that the self is annihilated in the form realm heavens (*rūpadhātu*). (3) Some reckon that the self is annihilated in the emptiness of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
(4) Or one calculates that the self is severed at the sphere of infinite consciousness; (5) severed at the sphere of nothingness; (6) severed at the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
(7) This differs slightly from the opening and closing of the original sutra. Second, the faults are summarized and set forth.

Based on this speculative reckoning, one falls into the view that there is annihilation after death, thereby straying from the nature of Bodhi and falling into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
"Annihilation after death" means that once the present retribution has been exhausted, one will subsequently undergo other forms of retribution and never again receive this specific retribution;
thus, one gives rise to the notion of annihilation regarding this present retribution, as in the case of Makkhali Gosāla and others. Therefore, it is said that they have fallen [into error].
They fall into the ranks of the heterodox; they exhaust the seven limits [of time] and ultimately reach total annihilation, never again seeing anyone who attains Bodhi.

Therefore, it is said that they are deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This concludes the explanation of the characteristics and their transcendence. Third, the summary that establishes the external treatise.
This is called the ninth heterodox theory established among the five aggregates (*skandhas*), which is the inverted view that there is annihilation after death.

Since the four aggregates are all subject to transformation by the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), if the aggregate of formations is severed, how could the other four aggregates remain permanent?

Therefore, it is said that within the framework of the five aggregates, there is annihilation after death. One must understand that self-nature has no fixed essence; it revolves according to the conditions of karma.
Humans can indeed become Heaven, and Heaven can likewise become humans; the same applies to the other realms of existence.

If one clings to the notion that a single retribution is final and severed, this is already an inversion. How much more so when one is deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi, which ultimately has no such cessation?
This is not merely an inversion of speech, but a discourse arising from an inverted mind. Thus, there is no further arising of subsequent states.

The section on the characteristics of conceptualization is concluded. Regarding the tenth point, the threefold conceptualization regarding the arising of subsequent existence: first, the heading that indicates the fallacy;
second, the explanation of the characteristics and the demonstration of the error; third, the conclusion that establishes the external treatise. First [the heading]:
Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the origin of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. If, subsequently, they give rise to speculative calculations regarding existence, these people fall into the "Five Theories of Nirvāṇa."
This is the same constant disturbance as the preceding section, yet the views differ. In the former case, because there is constant disturbance, there is a shifting flow from moment to moment;

because there is a shifting flow, there is no abiding; and because there is no abiding, there is necessarily cessation. Thus, one engages in conceptual construction regarding the non-existence of subsequent moments.
In this case, because there is constant disturbance, there is a continuous succession from moment to moment; because there is a continuous succession, there is no interruption.
Because that which is uninterrupted must necessarily exist, one generates conceptual constructions regarding future existence (*paścima-bhava*).
"Future existence" refers to the fact that this retribution immediately gives rise to further retribution, continuing from one to the next until it reaches the ultimate state of eternal permanence.
Regarding the "Treatise on the Five Nirvāṇas," the *Ching-liang-ch'ao* states: First, seeing that one currently receives [retribution] as a deva...

1. If a person takes the pleasures of the five sensory desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) to be *nirvāṇa*. 2. Because they are weary of the five sensory desires, they dwell in the first dhyāna and take it to be *nirvāṇa*. 3.
Because they are weary of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), they dwell in the second dhyāna and take it to be *nirvāṇa*. 4.

Because they are weary of all applied and sustained thought and joy (*prīti*), they dwell in the third dhyāna and take it to be *nirvāṇa*. 5. Because they are weary of joy and bliss (*sukha*), and so forth...
Regarding inhalation and exhalation, they claim that abiding in the four *dhyānas* is equivalent to *nirvāṇa*. To investigate this meaning, it is called the "Five Theories of Nirvāṇa.

Second, the explanation of their characteristics and the refutation of those errors has two parts: first, the specific explanation of their characteristics; second, the general presentation of their errors.
First [the specific explanation]:
Either because one regards the desire realm as the true basis for transformation due to perceiving its clarity and brightness and thus giving rise to attachment;
or because the nature of the first dhyāna is free from sorrow; or because the mind in the second dhyāna is free from suffering; or because of the extreme joy that follows in the third dhyāna.

Alternatively, because both suffering and pleasure have ceased in the four dhyānas and one does not undergo the nature of birth and death within saṃsāra, one becomes deluded regarding the tainted heavens and conceives them as the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Taking the five abodes as a secure and supreme pure refuge, one thus cycles through these five abodes until the ultimate end.

Alternatively, taking the desire realm as the true basis for transformation (*parāvṛtti*) means that, upon seeing the extreme suffering of the four destinies and the bliss of the heavens of desire, one then conceives of transforming the four destinies to rely upon the heavens of desire;
this is equivalent to transforming birth and death to rely upon nirvāṇa, such that there is no further transformation.
Even if there were another transformation, this nature would not be destroyed; therefore, it is called "true. For what reason?
Thus they form such a conception. Because they perceive the perfect luminosity and give rise to attachment toward it, they speak of "perfect luminosity.
The Four Heavenly Kings are adjacent to the sun and moon; the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven surpasses the light of the sun and moon; how much more so, then, does the Tuṣita Heaven?

Generally ascending through the subtle and refined, one transforms and delights in surpassing the realm of Transformation (Nirmāṇarati), and further transcends the realm of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).

One may know that the radiance becomes increasingly perfect; yet, unaware that one has not yet transcended the Desire Realm (Kāmadhātu), where pleasure is the cause of suffering, one compares it to the higher realms.
The light then appears like a firefly, and upon seeing it thus, one gives rise to craving and admiration without end, calculating [it to be superior].

This is for the sake of attaining the correct transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Alternatively, as for the statement that "the nature of the first dhyāna is free from sorrow," this means that upon seeing the suffering of the desire realm, one feels profound sorrow and consequently conceives of the first dhyāna as *nirvāṇa*. For what reason is such a conception formed?
It is because its nature is free from sorrow. Regarding the term "free from sorrow," it means that it cannot be afflicted by the coarse and heavy suffering of the lower realms.
Moving about, they do not realize that they have not yet emerged from vitarka and vicāra; still being bound by anxiety and suspense, they claim to be without sorrow.
Because they are without sorrow, they reckon this to be nirvāṇa. Or, as for those who say that in the second dhyāna there is no suffering because the mind is free of it:
having perceived that in the first dhyāna there is anxiety and that there is still the suffering of vitarka and vicāra, they consequently reckon the second dhyāna to be nirvāṇa. For what reason?

They form such a conception because their minds are not afflicted by suffering. To say they are "without suffering" means that in the First Dhyāna, they cannot be oppressed by the anxiety of *daurmanasya* (mental distress).
Not knowing that while there is something to be experienced, it is said to be "non-existent," yet this non-existence is not a true non-existence, they simply claim to be "without suffering.

Because they are without suffering, they conceive of this as *nirvāṇa*. (Zhengmo says: According to the preceding section on the heavens of the Form Realm, in the First Dhyāna they are not oppressed by the afflictions of suffering (*duḥkha*), while in the Second Dhyāna they are not oppressed by the anxiety of mental distress (*daurmanasya*). Suffering is heavy and mental distress is light; this is the sequence.)

This is appropriate. Now, since the first dhyāna is without sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and the second dhyāna is without suffering (*duḥkha*), it is certainly a mistake or a reversal by the translator. I, the fool, maintain that where there is sorrow there must be suffering, and where there is suffering there must be sorrow;

however, they each have their own degrees of lightness and heaviness, so there is no hindrance to their appearing interchangeably. Therefore, this present commentary merely explains the text according to its literal sequence, and stops when it can be so understood.

As for the claim that "it is because the third dhyāna follows upon extreme joy," this means that one perceives the joy of the second dhyāna as being dependent on the cessation of suffering and thus not yet ultimate; consequently, one reckons the third dhyāna to be *nirvāṇa*. Because...
For what reason is such a calculation made? It is because of the "extreme delight and conformity. Regarding "extreme delight and conformity":

the gods of the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Parītta-śubha*) possess great conformity, yet they conform without being delighted; the gods of the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇa-śubha*) have peace and stability of body and mind, yet they are delighted without being extreme;
the gods of the Heaven of Universal Purity (*Śubha-kṛtsna*) attain immeasurable bliss, and thus reach the pinnacle of joy and extreme conformity—yet they do not know it.

However, that which is conditioned is nonetheless called "Ultimate Bliss" (*sukhāvatī*); because it is ultimate bliss, it is termed "Nirvana. Alternatively, regarding the statement that in the fourth dhyāna both suffering and pleasure have ceased:
this means that one perceives the bliss of the third dhyāna as not being permanent, for after a time it must inevitably perish and give rise [to suffering].
Consequently, they reckon the four dhyānas to be *nirvāṇa*. For what reason do they make such a reckoning?
Because both suffering and pleasure have ceased, and because they do not undergo the nature of saṃsāric birth and death.

Regarding the phrase "both suffering and pleasure have ceased," it means that they cannot be moved by any worldly objects of suffering or pleasure. Regarding the phrase "not undergoing the nature of saṃsāric birth and death," it means...
For when there is suffering and joy, there is necessarily longing and aversion; with longing and aversion, there is the cycle of birth and death.
Now that both suffering and joy have vanished, longing and aversion do not arise; this is the eternally abiding true nature that does not undergo the cycle of birth and death.
You do not realize that this is merely the state where the mind of grasping has been exhausted and its function has reached full maturity. This is precisely...
When one perceives arising and ceasing, one then claims not to undergo saṃsāra; because of this non-acceptance, one reckons it to be nirvāṇa. An ancient master said:

"The word 'or' (huò) is a term of indefiniteness, indicating that it is not necessarily a single person who universally conceives of these five locations. I, the humble writer, believe it must indeed be a single person;
however, depending on the duration of their practice, their conceptions change from before to after in an unstable manner. For this reason, the word "or" is employed.
At the beginning, one regards the four realms of existence as suffering and consequently reckons the heavens of desire as *nirvāṇa*.
As one’s cultivation deepens, one further perceives the heavens of desire as suffering and consequently reckons the first dhyāna as *nirvāṇa*, and so forth.

Therefore, initially taking the desire realm as the true basis of transformation (*parāvṛtti*) reveals that all subsequent stages are merely successive revisions and are not the true state. Furthermore, this applies generally to the five [realms].
All these abodes are, in fact, nirvāṇa; they differ only in their relative superiority and inferiority across time. "Delusion" refers to ignorance, while "action" refers to erroneous recognition.

To say that the various heavens originally belong to the outflows (*sāsrava*) and that nirvāṇa is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet now one takes the heavens to be nirvāṇa, is entirely due to not knowing what constitutes the outflows and erroneously taking them to be the unconditioned, thereby regarding these five abodes as secure and peaceful.
This is the realm where those who are most supremely pure dwell. It is not merely that they reckon these five places as being with remainder or without remainder;
rather, they also reckon themselves to be arhats, bodhisattvas, or even Tathāgatas.
Regarding such cyclic progression: as one moves from the inferior toward the superior, birth and cessation proceed without ceasing; thus, there is the sense of "cycling.
From the Desire Realm heavens up to the Fourth Dhyāna, each stage is considered supreme, and these are termed the "five ultimate stations."
Second, the faults are summarized:
by means of this conceptualization, one attains a semblance of nirvana in five ways, thereby falling into the ranks of external paths and becoming deluded regarding the nature of bodhi.
Regarding the "five semblances of nirvana," the character *xian* (present/manifest) has two meanings: first, manifestation, meaning that they appear as identical to true nirvana.

The nature [of these views] is such that they manifest differently across the five periods. Second, regarding their manifestation: this refers to the five kinds of *nirvāṇa*, as each is explained according to what is presently manifest.
To give rise to views based on [these provisional] teachings is to be subsumed under wrong views; therefore, it is said they "fall into the ranks of external paths.
Having already mistaken the false for the true, they will inevitably come to regard the true as false; hence, it is said they "delude the nature of bodhi. This explains their characteristics.
Transcending the realm of mind, these three constitute the formation of external treatises.
This is called the tenth heterodox school’s inverted doctrine of the five present nirvāṇas established within the five aggregates.
Among the demons of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), this [view] stands at the very end; therefore, it is called the tenth heterodox school.

They hold that form, sensation, perception, and consciousness all depend upon the shifting flow of the aggregate of formations. Since the aggregate of formations is eternal, the other four aggregates are likewise so.

That which has already ceased should naturally arise again, and that which has not yet ceased should naturally abide forever. This reckoning that the nature of the five aggregates is eternal is itself the nature of nirvāṇa. However—
These manifest according to five periods, each being proclaimed as supreme within its own context; thus it is said that "among the five aggregates, five kinds of nirvāṇa appear.
How could one know that they are deluded regarding the heavens of outflows (sāsrava), taking them to be unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)?

It is like mistaking hail for pearls—laboring in vain to treasure them. When the vessel breaks and the water spills, nothing remains but empty lamentation. How much more so when one relies upon these [delusions] to establish a treatise!

From mental inversion, one errs oneself and leads others astray; how could this not be discerned? This concludes the section on the manifestations of demonic signs that appeared during the intermediate period.

Part Four: A Summary to Serve as a Warning and Exhortation, in two sections: (1) concluding by means of a warning, and (2) exhorting to transmit and protect [the teaching]. First: [The text continues with the following: ...the mind becomes inverted. One deludes oneself and deludes others; can this not be discerned? This concludes the section on the demonic signs manifested during the intermediate period. Part Four: A Summary to Serve as a Warning and Exhortation, in two parts: first, concluding by means of a warning; second, exhorting to transmit and protect. Regarding the first:

Ānanda, these ten kinds of delusory insights regarding *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a conflicting manner within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), thereby manifesting these so-called awakenings.

Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. When these states appear before them, they mistake their confusion for enlightenment and claim to have attained the state of a sage.
Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell.
The first three aggregates (skandhas) all involve the manifestation of demonic realms; therefore, the ten types [of delusion] are all described as "manifested objects.
However, this aggregate is solely a state of perverse awakening and insanity; therefore, the ten types are all described as "insane understandings.

As long as the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) has not been broken, false thoughts and correct mindfulness arise in alternation; hence it is said that "the mind functions in mutual interaction. Because the false confuses the correct, then—
Right mindfulness lacks power. When one relies on the correct [state] to give rise to delusion, then deluded thoughts gain strength; thus, this perverse realization manifests.
If one can personally maintain awareness and exercise discernment, then even when encountering these manifestations, they will not exceed being like light or like shadows.

Before long, it will vanish of its own accord. Alas, sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they fail to reflect upon themselves. When encountering this manifestation before them, they mistake delusion for understanding.
Having mistaken delusion for understanding, they inevitably claim for themselves that they have attained the state of a sage.
Because they have thus committed a great falsehood, they shall fall into the Avīci Hell. Second, the instruction to entrust and protect [this teaching].
"You must all take these words of the Tathāgata and transmit them after my parinirvāṇa during the Age of Dharma-Decline.

Cause all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning, so that the demons of the mind do not give rise to deep calamities within themselves. Protect and shield them from the subtle influences of false views;
teach their bodies and minds to awaken to the true meaning, so that they do not encounter divergent paths on the Unsurpassed Way. Do not allow the mind..."
May one find contentment with even a small measure [of realization], acting as a pure guiding finger for the Great Awakened King.
First, it is taught that one must not cling to the heterodox. To "awaken to this meaning" refers to awakening to the meanings of the ten types of heterodox interpretations mentioned previously.
Once one is able to awaken to them, one will naturally be able to discern them; as soon as a deluded thought begins to sprout, one should immediately—
One should resist it with right mindfulness. Therefore, it is said: "Do not allow the demons of the mind to give rise to deep calamity.
For deluded thoughts are the demons of the mind, as they can harm right knowledge and vision; and false interpretations are deep calamities, as they can serve as the cause for rebirth in hell.
As the Book says: "Calamities wrought by Heaven may still be avoided; calamities wrought by oneself cannot be lived through. Now it is said:
"To arise of one's own accord" means precisely that one has created one's own calamity. ○ "Maintain and protect below" means to guard [the mind] so that it does not stagnate in the minor [delusions].

This refers to what I have said above: having already been able to maintain and shield [the mind], and having regulated and eliminated false views to break through the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one must still be instructed to experience this with body and mind, thereby awakening to the *ālaya-vijñāna* at the point where the formations shift and flow.
The ocean represents the true meaning of eternal abiding. "Branching off" refers to divergent side-paths; it is a metaphor for the Lesser Vehicle, as well as the paths of Māras and non-Buddhists.
Since one is able to awaken to the true meaning, one takes non-arising and non-ceasing as the causal mind and proceeds directly toward the fruit of Buddhahood, like the main thoroughfare to Chang’an.
Therefore, it is said that one does not encounter branching paths on the unsurpassed Way. Although...
It is said that one does not encounter further branching paths; however, because the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) has not yet been transcended, one must remain vigilant.

Therefore, it is said: "Do not let the mind pray for quick attainment, nor be satisfied with a little. One then regards it as one's own self-substance and calculates that its capacity to generate the affairs of sentient beings constitutes the fruit of having accomplished those activities.

Having lost their original cultivation, they are said to be "far removed from perfect penetration" and will ultimately sink into birth and death; thus it is said they "turn their backs on the city of Nirvana.

Therefore, they designate themselves as "Pervasive and Perfect" (Vibhu). Now, since the practitioner’s calculation is identical to theirs, he is born into their class;

arising is non-arising. This calculation holds that there is actual production. How could these two be the same? Furthermore, there is the good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), he has not yet perfected it.
The meaning is to be understood according to the previous [section]. These two erroneous interpretations constitute faults.
If, regarding that which is taken as refuge or reliance, one suspects that one's own body and mind flow forth from it, and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it;
then, regarding the ground from which all these arise and flow forth, one will conceive the understanding that it is the true, eternal body, free from birth and extinction.
Amidst arising and ceasing, they prematurely reckon it to be eternally abiding; thus they are deluded regarding non-arising and likewise confused about arising and ceasing.

Those who dwell securely in this infatuation and conceive a resolute conviction [of permanence] fall into the dualistic attachment of permanence and impermanence, reckoning the Lord (Īśvara) as their companion.
They have become deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.
In the preceding section, they took the consciousness to which they return as their own self-nature;

in this section, although there is a consciousness to which they return and upon which they rely, this is likewise the contemplation of losing the body to observe consciousness. Through long-term cultivation of this contemplation, they see only consciousness and no longer perceive a body.
He then calculated that his own body had entered into consciousness, thinking, "This is truly my place of refuge.
As his contemplative practice slightly declined, he again saw his body and the empty space; he then doubted that his body and mind had flowed forth from that [consciousness].
The empty space of the ten directions all arises from it; it goes without saying, then, that all things existing within that space do so as well.

Thus, regarding the passage beginning with "all arise," they further calculate that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is the true, eternal body. The character for "earth" (*dì*) also carries the meaning of "place.
However, since they have already asserted that the empty space and so forth all arise from it, they take the arising of the mind and other phenomena [to be the source].

Because it flows forth from there, the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) is taken as the locus where space and other elements arise, and the place from which the body, mind, and so forth are issued.
Those who conceive of this as a true, eternal body that is without birth or extinction perceive no body at the initial stage when their contemplation is perfected;
it is as if the body and mind have ceased within the consciousness. However, when their contemplative practice slightly declines, [the body reappears].
Furthermore, one perceives the body as if it were produced from within consciousness, appearing to arise and perish; thus, it is certainly impermanent.

Yet, as for that consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) to which [the body] returns, its beginning and end are never seen to arise or perish. Therefore, one forms the understanding that this very [consciousness] is the true, eternal body, free from arising and ceasing.
Those who recklessly calculate it to be permanent while it is still amidst arising and ceasing refer to the consciousness-aggregate.
Since this has already undergone transformation due to ignorance, it still belongs to the realm of subtle arising and ceasing. It is like a rapid current that appears tranquil;

because the flow is so swift, it is not perceived, yet it is not that there is no flow at all. Only when the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted can it be called the eternally abiding true mind.
At present, as long as the aggregate of consciousness is not yet exhausted, to conceive an understanding of non-arising and non-ceasing is itself within the realm of arising and ceasing.
Within consciousness, one prematurely calculates permanence, like seeing an egg and seeking the night-owl, or seeing a crossbow bolt and thinking of roasted owl meat—is this not delusion?
This is precisely because one does not understand the permanently abiding true mind and its nature of non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus it is said:

"Since one is already deluded regarding non-arising, one also fails to understand the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha), which still belongs to subtle arising and ceasing. Therefore, it is said: "Furthermore..."

Deluded regarding arising and ceasing, they are ignorant of both the true and the false; hence it is called "sinking into delusion. Being complacent and unaware of their error, it is called "dwelling in ease.
Yet, conversely, they form the notion that this [state] is superior; this is what is meant by "giving rise to a superior resolve.

Having formed such a resolve, they will inevitably regard the aggregate of consciousness as permanent, while their own body and mind are impermanent; therefore it is said, "this person then falls into..."
The attachment to permanence and impermanence concerns Maheśvara, who is the Māra-king at the summit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Kātyāyana states that all sentient beings are created by Maheśvara. In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the ash-smearing heretics (*bhasmaka-tīrthika*) reckon Maheśvara to be the cause of all things.
Now, since the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is declared to be the universal source of arising:
The "Flowing Ground" (liú dì) is similar to those who reckon that Maheśvara is the cause of all things; therefore, it is said to form their companionship.

Since they are deluded regarding the nature of non-arising and non-extinction, they naturally become confused about the Buddha’s Bodhi, for the nature of non-arising and non-extinction is the very essence of Bodhi.
Since they are confused regarding the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) of arising and extinction, they naturally lose their true knowledge and vision, because they [mistakenly] identify—
To falsely take the unreal as real is to fall into false knowledge and views. Third is the "Emergence of Names" as an awakening.

This is called the third establishment of causes based on the mind to produce the fruit of false discrimination. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.

One fashions a body of true permanence and lacks the understanding of non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus it is said: "Accomplishing the fruit of false discrimination.
Flowing into heterodox views, one naturally becomes distant from perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). At death, one follows the current into drowning; one naturally becomes distant from *nirvāṇa*.

The two disks face each other back-to-back. Not having yet attained the perfect true mind, one erroneously conceives of them as being circular; thus it is said that the seeds of inverted perfection are produced.

As stated above, the second error consists in forming a fault through misunderstanding.

If one establishes a view based on the knowledge that all objects of cognition are universally and completely known, then all plants and trees in the ten directions would be called sentient beings and would not differ from humans;
furthermore, when a human dies, they would become plants and trees in the ten directions once again. This would be a non-discriminating, universal knowledge.
Those who give rise to such superior understanding fall into the attachment of knowing non-knowing. Paṭa and Śāṇi cling to all-encompassing awakening as their companion;
they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.
According to the passage in the first section concerning the "sudden manifestation of the superior aspect," it says: "Awareness and cognition pervade and merge;

one is able to enter the perfect source. "Entering" means returning. The three preceding [sections] all involve giving rise to conceptual calculations regarding that which is returned to, yet these calculations differ from one another.

This present section concerns the arising of conceptual calculations regarding awareness and cognition pervading and merging. That is to say, upon suddenly seeing that awareness and cognition pervade and merge, one does not know [the true nature].
This is the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Furthermore, one proceeds to observe this cognition, which is able to universally know all phenomena.

Consequently, regarding the objects of knowledge, one calculates that the capacity for knowing is omnipresent and perfect. Thus it is said: "Because knowing is pervasive and perfect. Because knowing is pervasive, there is no phenomenon that is not included;
because knowing is perfect, there are no things that are not contained within it. From this, based on this pervasive and perfect knowing...

This establishes a false understanding. Grasses and trees of the ten directions are fundamentally insentient; yet, due to this false understanding, they are all called sentient beings, no different from humans.
Because one knows what is contained therein by virtue of knowing where it resides, the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* states:
"Sentient and insentient share a single essence; everywhere they are identical with the true Dharmadhātu. Now, regarding the calculation of the insentient and the sentient:

There is no difference. Furthermore, it may superficially appear to have some logic; yet, to reckon that grasses and trees are human beings, and that when humans die they return to becoming plants and trees, is truly a heterodox teaching.

By these two statements alone, the demonic form is fully revealed. "Universal" (*sarva*) implies possessing knowledge; "self" (*ātman*) implies profound realization.

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) has already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), he has not yet perfected it.
Two errors arise as faults:
if, within the mutual functioning of the perfectly interfused sense organs, he has attained compliance, he will then proceed toward the universal transformation that gives rise to all things.
They seek the light of fire, delight in the purity of water, cherish the circulation of wind, and contemplate the formation of particles;

each venerates their respective object and, taking these various particles as the fundamental cause of all manifestation, establishes a view of eternal permanence. Such a person falls into the attachment to birth and non-birth.
The various Kāśyapas and Brahmins diligently applied their minds and exhausted their bodies in serving fire and venerating water, seeking to transcend birth and death;
thus they became his companions, yet they were deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lost their true knowledge and vision.
According to the passage on the initial manifestation of the superior signs within the first stage, it says:

"It can cause the intervals between one's own sense organs to suddenly close and open. (The Commentary states: "One's own body" refers to one's own person. If meditative observation is clear and vigorous, the characteristics of the sense organs are not seen; thus, the intervals between the organs seem to suddenly close. If one slightly lapses into dullness or stagnation, the characteristics of the sense organs appear distinctly; thus, the intervals between the organs seem to suddenly open again.

This is not the same as the aforementioned dissolution of the six gates, wherein the characteristics of the sense organs are never seen again. Now, this section states: "Within the mutual functioning of the sense organs, one has already attained compliance."
This refers to the meaning of the primary faculties being separated yet occasionally joining and occasionally opening. Therefore, Master Huan said:

"One whose consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) is exhausted has worn away the six gates so that the various faculties function interchangeably. Now, as this [consciousness] is not yet exhausted, one merely attains compliance. Master Zhengmo said: "This interpretation is most correct.
The single character 'one' (yi) within 'contemplation' (guan) is sufficient to reveal the subtlety of their interchangeable functioning. It is contained therein, though not yet..."
It is "arising. For "following" means to rely without turning away, and "conforming" means to incline toward without opposing;

thus, while the characteristics of their mutual application are briefly established, they have not yet received a prominent designation. This is for the sake of that which easily brings about the complete transformation and arising of all things.
The two characters "yuan" (perfect) and "hua" (transformation) refer to the opening and closing of the sensory faculties.

Because the opening and closing of the faculties briefly embody the meaning of perfect fusion and transformation, the wondrous calculation of perfect fusion and transformation arises; it does not depend on a single condition alone, hence the term "all.
This implicitly refers to earth, water, fire, and wind as "all. Since these are capable of producing perfect fusion and transformation...
Each [element] should inherently possess its own preeminent nature (*viśeṣa-dharma*). Therefore, it is said that one seeks the "light of fire" and so forth.
The intent is that light is the preeminent nature of fire; all characteristics of light arise in dependence upon it.
Purity is the preeminent nature of water; all characteristics of purity arise in dependence upon it. Circulation is...
The preeminent nature of wind is that all pervasive characteristics arise in dependence upon it;
