because it accomplishes [the elements], it is the preeminent nature of the *dhātu* (here, earth). Since it is composed of many *dhātus*, it can produce everything and thus possesses the sense of "accomplishment.
All characteristics of accomplishment arise in dependence upon it. Therefore, those who seek it, delight in it, cherish it, and contemplate it do so in order to further progress.
This is because of the wondrous nature of its perfect transformation. Regarding the statement in the *Abhiṣeka* [Sūtra], "each honors and serves": "honor" (*chóng*) means to revere;

"serve" (*shì*) means to make offerings. Whether it be maintaining a single brazier of fire, arranging a basin of water, raising a single banner in the wind, or scooping up a cup of earth—surrounding them on all four sides and paying homage in the eight directions with these various mundane objects, one thereby...

He reveals the reason for his veneration of these objects: he regards these sensory objects as the fundamental cause of arising and conditioned activity (the term "multitude of objects" refers generally to earth, water, fire, and wind, all of which are external objects). He considers all that is produced to be impermanent;
because only this [consciousness] is eternally abiding, he establishes the understanding of permanence therein. Having established this as permanent, he will necessarily regard it as unarisen.

Since they regard that which is other as impermanent, they must necessarily regard that which is other as having birth; therefore it is said: "Such a person falls into the dualistic attachment to birth and non-birth.

"All Kāśyapas" refers specifically to Uruvilvākāśyapa and his brothers, who previously practiced fire-worship and later returned to the Buddha’s transformation, as well as including Brahmins and all other non-Buddhists such as those who worship water. With diligent minds, they exerted themselves...
As for the person: they labor their mind and employ their body. Those who serve fire and revere water offer worship to fire and hold water in high esteem.
It need not be explicitly stated that those who serve wind and revere earth can be understood by analogy.

The former act to seek liberation from birth and death; the latter act to advance toward perfect transformation. Although their purposes differ, their veneration and service are no different. Therefore, it is said: "Accomplishment."

Since that which his companions established was not truly eternal, how could the practice they cultivated have yielded any real fruit? Therefore it is said they were "deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi.
They venerated insentient things and established a view of permanence; therefore it is said they had "lost their right knowledge and vision."
Third is the emergence of fame and alertness;
this is called the fifth attachment to veneration. It is a deluded mind that establishes false seeking based on external objects, hoping for false results through such seeking.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of perverted transformation.
Zhengmo says: "To be attached to" means to cling to false delusions. "To honor and serve" means to devote oneself to false practices.

"One whose mind is deluded" is one who is confused about their own inherently true, numinous awareness. "To follow external objects" is to follow those insentient things composed of the four elements.
"To falsely seek causes" is to seek what should not be sought; it is to mistake what is not a cause for a cause. "To falsely hope for results" is to hope for what should not be hoped for...

"Ji" means to regard what is not the fruit as the fruit, and to regard what is not the cause as the cause; because one fails to attain the mind of perfect penetration, it is called "contrary and remote.
To regard what is not the fruit as the fruit means one fails to attain the actual realization of Nirvana; therefore, it is called "backing away. Guanding says:

"The seeds of inverted transformation" refers to the Buddha’s teaching that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only (vijñaptimātra). Thus, one knows that it is consciousness-only.
The mind is that which generates and transforms; the myriad phenomena of the three realms are that which is generated and transformed. This is the correct principle of generation and transformation.

Now, having inverted this principle of transformation, you grasp at the various sensory objects as the fundamental cause of activity, venerating water and fire, sacrificing to the earth, and invoking the wind.
Therefore, in the future, you will surely fall among those of perverted transformation, such as when the spirit is transformed into...
Regarding the category of those who engage with earth, wood, metal, and stone: they calculate, cling to, honor, and pursue the resulting marks of accomplishment.

Regarding the three aspects of the six circles of voidness and the mind’s accomplishment: first, the manifestation of consciousness when practice is exhausted; second, the fault of erroneous understanding; third, the emergence of names for the purpose of awakening. First: [The text continues with the detailed explanation of these points.]

Furthermore, if a son of good family has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth and death, yet has not yet perfected the subtle essence of stillness, two errors will result in fault.

If, regarding the perfect luminosity, he calculates that the void within that luminosity is not the extinction of the manifold transformations, and takes this permanent extinction as his refuge; [this is the first error].

Those who give rise to such a conviction fall into the attachment of taking refuge in that which offers no refuge; they become companions to the *śūnyatā* spirits among the non-conceptual heavens (*asaṃjñisattva*), becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing their true knowledge and vision.

This is the same as the object of reliance discussed in the preceding section. That section, in discussing the mutual functioning of the sense organs, stated that "conformity has already been attained," which briefly encompasses the meaning of perfect, integrated illumination and comprehension.
This section speaks of "perfect clarity" (*yuanming*), which likewise carries the meaning of perfect, integrated illumination and comprehension.
However, while the preceding section relies upon this object to reckon the arising of all things, this section reckons it within the clarity itself.

It is merely emptiness. This is what constitutes their difference. When they speak of "emptiness within clarity," they mean that although it is called perfect clarity, it is nothing more than alternating between opening and closing.
At the moment it opens, they conceive of it as clarity; at the moment it closes, they conceive of it as emptiness.
Thus, they not only conceive of clarity as being empty within, but further conceive of clarity as emerging from emptiness. Taking emptiness to be superior, they instead desire—
It is not that the transformative nature within their various faculties is extinguished so as to be made eternally extinct;
rather, their intention is to eternally extinguish the various faculties upon which they rely, leaving only a phantom-like, vacuous consciousness as the place of refuge.
This is precisely what is meant by being deluded regarding wondrous function and falling into vacuity; it is fundamentally a mistaken interpretation, yet they consider themselves superior.

Therefore, it is said that one who generates such a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*)—having already formed this conviction—will necessarily take the emptiness within me as having a refuge, while that which is the actual manifestation of reality is without refuge.
Hence, it is said: "This person falls into the attachment of taking what is without refuge as a refuge.

The Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*) refers to the various heavens of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) among the four dhyāna heavens. Regarding these various heavens of the non-Buddhists, for the most part they are exhausted [in their understanding].
Because emptiness does not return, they are further designated by the name Śūnyatā (Emptiness), as *śūnyatā* is translated as "emptiness.
Although the emptiness toward which they aspire differs, they alike reckon that non-existence (*vibhava*) is the place of refuge; hence it is said they become each other's companions.
Having fallen into non-existence, they naturally lose their way regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi. Since they are companions of the Non-conceptual (*asaṃjñin*), they naturally...
One should lose one's knowledge and vision. This third emergence is called "the awakening alarm.

This is termed the sixth: the mind of perfect voidness and non-existence achieves the fruit of empty extinction. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seed of annihilationism.

Within this perfect luminosity, they calculate it to be void and non-existent; based on this, they give rise to a mind that hopes to attain the true fruit. Thus it is said: "The mind of perfect voidness.
Exhausting the emptiness without returning, deluded and leaking with no hearing of the Dharma, they enter the cycle of rebirth. Thus it is said: "They achieve the fruit of empty extinction.

This means that even if one practices until reaching the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), when the retribution is exhausted, one returns once more to be scattered among the various realms.

This is precisely what is meant by "destinies. To single-mindedly speculate on emptiness and non-existence violates and distances one from perfect penetration; to ultimately fall into nihilism is to turn one's back on the city of Nirvana.

Since one currently dwells in a mind of annihilation, one will inevitably fall into the seed of annihilation in the future, such as Kātyāyana and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who falsely speculated on the categories of annihilation after death. (The Zhengmo asks: This and the following...)

What is the distinction between the ninth and the tenth? Answer: They are identical in their abandonment of existence (*bhava*), their grasping for emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and their views, understandings, and aspirations; however, their initial mental orientations differ. This former is the seed of ordinary worldlings and outsiders who suppress afflictions (*kleśa*) to grasp emptiness; that latter is the noble lineage (*āryagotra*) which eradicates afflictions to realize emptiness.
Thus, there is a difference between the mundane and the supramundane. [The section on] "The Perfectly Empty Mind Attaining the Mark of Fruition" concludes.
Seven: The Mark of Fruition Resulting from Attachment to the Origin of Life. 1. The manifestation of consciousness when karma is exhausted. 2. Attainment through erroneous understanding.
Fault. Third is the emergence of awakening. First:

Furthermore, a good man may exhaustively investigate the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), thereby extinguishing both arising and ceasing; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*), he has not yet perfected it.
Second, erroneous understanding leads to fault.

If one forms a resolute conviction that the body is solid and permanent, and that it remains eternally constant like a refined essence that never decays or passes away, such a person falls into the attachment of craving for what is not truly non-craving. They become companions to those Āsitas who seek long life.
They become deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision.
Since the preceding section established the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) as the place of refuge, they now falsely reckon this consciousness-aggregate to be perfect and eternal.
Because it is that to which all such categories return, it is "perfect" (*yuan*); because it is the source from which each life originates, it is "constant" (*chang*).

Being both perfect and constant, those who falsely reckon they have attained this believe they can preserve their physical form and enjoy eternal longevity. This, moreover, is a further transformation within the context of perfection and constancy, giving rise to the reckoning of a solidified body as eternally abiding.
This solidified body as eternally abiding is likewise identical to the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-bīja*) as perfect and constant.
The internal and external support one another; form and mind sustain each other like a mountain or an ocean. Therefore, it is said that they "do not long fall or pass away.
"Fall" (qīng) means to collapse; "pass away" (shì) means to depart. Because one considers this calculation to be correct, it is said that "one who produces resolute conviction" (adhimukti).
Having formed such resolute conviction, one will surely regard this as something desirable, while all else is not to be craved or sought after; hence, it is called "this" (shi).
Humans, however, fall into the attachment of either craving or non-craving. Asita—meaning "Incomparable" (Anupama) in this context—is the name of a long-lived ṛṣi.
The plural "the ṛṣis" is used because there were not just one such seers; they were all individuals whose lifespans were so extremely long that none in the world could equal them.
All these may be so designated. Since they greedily seek long life, they are similar to this [state]; thus it is said they "form its companions.
Shrouded by the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), they do not know to further seek true permanence; thus it is said they are "deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi.
Attached to long-term existence, they completely forget that this body is merely a temporary lodging; thus it is said they have "lost their knowledge and vision."
Third is the emergence of the breath as a sign of awakening;
this is called the seventh attachment to the source of life, which establishes a cause of solid delusion leading to the fruit of long-term toil.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of deluded prolongation.
The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is reckoned as the thread of continuity for each individual life; hence it is said that one clings to the source of life.
Taking this as a cause, what the ignorant call "solid" is called "empty and false" by the wise. Thus it is said:
"Establishing the cause of solid falsehood, one relies upon this to pursue its fruit. To the deluded, this is called "longevity"; to the awakened, it is called "futile toil. Therefore...

It is said that they head toward the fruit of long-term toil and lose what was originally cultivated. Therefore, it is called being far removed from perfect penetration; thus, one does not transcend birth and death, and is said to turn one's back on the city of Nirvana.
Since in the present life one makes the solidification of form one’s primary concern, in the future one will inevitably fall among those who falsely prolong their existence through seeds.
"Falsely prolonging" means not relying on true awakening to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead cultivating separate deluded thoughts while maintaining [the body].

The solidification of thought: this refers to the ten kinds of immortals previously mentioned. Having finished describing the signs of accomplishment resulting from attachment to the life-source, there are three signs of accomplishment resulting from the cause of giving rise to perverse thoughts: first, the manifestation of consciousness when karma is exhausted;
second, the formation of faults through erroneous understanding; third, the emergence of names and the awakening of awareness. Regarding the first:

Furthermore, there is the good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), he has not yet perfected it.
Two erroneous understandings lead to fault:
first, observing that life-force is interpenetrating, he instead clings to worldly defilements (*saṃkleśa*), fearing they might be exhausted; thus, at this juncture, he sits within a lotus palace.
They extensively acquire the seven treasures and increase their retinue of precious women, indulging their desires until they give rise to a sense of superior understanding;

such people fall into the attachment of "the real within the unreal. They become companions to the Ḍākinīs and Kālarātrīs, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing all true knowledge and vision.
As in the first of the preceding characteristics, the text regarding the initial manifestation of the superior characteristic states:
"It can cause one's own body's sense organs to join and separate, and it also enables universal awareness with all categories of beings throughout the ten directions.

Regarding these three sections above, the first two both involve the arising of calculations based on the joining and separating of the sense organs, yet their divergent attachments differ; the latter one still arises through a successive progression from the second.
This present section concerns the arising of calculations based on the universal consciousness common to all classes of beings.

Because one perceives that "I" and these various classes share a single conscious awareness, and yet this conscious awareness is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), which was previously referred to in the text as the "thread of individual life."

Therefore it is said: "Observe that life-spans are mutually interconnected. If one were to further investigate this, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) could naturally be broken through;
yet, instead, one retreats and remains stuck within worldly toil and affliction, never reaching ultimate exhaustion.

This is because there is a fear that if the aggregate of consciousness were completely dissolved, the life-faculties of both self and others would be severed. Thus, at this juncture, one simply halts and remains amidst the dust of the world.

Regarding the "aspect of toil": it is said that the afflictions (*kleśa*) have craving (*rāga*) as their root. This craving for the five objects of desire first requires the adornment of the *pariṇāmanirmita* (the environment).
Therefore, at this very moment, he sits within a lotus palace. The reason the palace is named after the lotus is to take its adornment, beauty, subtle fragrance, and purity as models.
This also refers to one who possesses great merit and virtue, who relies upon *dhyāna* to...
This refers to those who practice false paths. Were it not so, how could the Lotus Palace be easily reached? "Extensive Transformation" refers to the manifestation of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
The "Seven Treasures" are the seven precious gems (*saptaratna*). "Yuanmei" is a beautiful woman, peerless in the world.

They are called "treasures. Yet, since they were able to extensively gather the seven precious gems so that various jewels were arrayed within the flower palace, and furthermore increased the number of precious ladies so that beautiful forms attended upon them on all sides, it can be known that they indulged in the utmost luxury and desire, sinking into the intoxication of ignorance and afflictions.
Thus, at the outset, they sought to retain [these things].

As for "dust-labor" (kleśa), one will ultimately sink and drown within it; the entire body of precious awakening (*ratnabodhi*) is thereby destroyed from this point on. Is this not truly to be lamented? (Question:

The Bodhisattva’s retention of delusions to moisten rebirth—how does this differ from this [situation]? Answer: Retaining delusions to moisten rebirth is originally undertaken with the intent to teach and transform sentient beings. Here, however, one retains dust-labor until consciousness is exhausted and life is severed;

this is feared because therein lies the distinction between delusion and enlightenment, and the differentiation between bondage and liberation. The two lines concerning "indulgence and license" precisely reveal that one is submerged and drowning without realizing it.

Such a person falls into the attachment of "the real" within "non-reality. Erroneously believing that one must necessarily seek the Real, their consciousness is exhausted and their life severed, yet they find themselves instead devoid of the Real.
*Cakila* is an alternative name for a celestial Māra. In the Sanskrit language, *caki* means "bondage";
in the Sanskrit language, *kāla* means "that which is created by me. Such a person claims for himself [the status of] the Three...
"The realms, fetters, and bonds can only be created by me, for I am able to transform the objects of desire and thereby bind sentient beings.
Their current refusal to abandon worldly afflictions is roughly equivalent to that calculation; thus it is said they have become my companions.
Because they do not know that there exists separately the unsurpassed bodhi, which the Buddha knows and the Buddha sees, it is said they are deluded and have lost [the Way].
Third is the emergence of agitation and alarm;

this is called the eighth cause for generating perverse thoughts, which establishes the fruit of blazing dust. It is far removed from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seed of celestial Māras.
Not realizing that true reality is manifest before them, they fear only the severance of their life-force; thus it is said they give rise to the cause of perverse thoughts.
Seated within the Lotus Palace, they exhaust themselves in luxury and indulge in the utmost desires; thus it is said they establish the fruit of blazing defilements.

The mind of perfect penetration is from this point forever lost, and the wondrous fruit of Nirvana is thereby permanently forfeited; thus it is said they "contradict" and "turn their backs. They do not sever desire.
Yet if one practices dhyāna [under such conditions], one will inevitably fall into the path of Māra; hence it is said that one becomes a "celestial Māra species.

These are what are called the superior grade of Māra kings, the middle grade of Māra subjects, and the inferior grade of Māra women. This concludes the section on how the cause of perverse thoughts results in the manifestation of their effects.
Third, the three aspects of the fruit resulting from the perfect purity of the nine spheres corresponding to the mind: first, the manifestation of consciousness at the end of the practice;
second, the faults incurred through erroneous understanding; third, the naming and awakening. First:

Furthermore, there is the good son who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), he has not yet perfected it.
Two errors arise from his misunderstanding and become faults:

within the clarity of life, he discriminates between the refined and the coarse, and judges the true and the false. He regards the retribution of cause and effect as merely a matter of seeking a response through spiritual resonance.
They turn their backs on the path of purity—namely, the seeing of suffering, the abandoning of its origin, the realization of its cessation, and the cultivation of the path.
Having settled into cessation, they rest and no longer advance, giving rise to a fixed conviction; such persons fall into the category of those with fixed nature (niyata-rāśi) among the śrāvakas.
They become companions to those unlearned monastics who possess overweening pride (adhimāna). They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.

Since the previous section has already observed that life-force (*jīvita*) interpenetrates all things, it follows that all ordinary beings and sages, as well as the heterodox and the orthodox, are manifested based upon this life-root (*jīvitendriya*).
This constitutes the arising of conceptual discrimination and other calculations within the manifestation of the life-root.

Nevertheless, while they are equally manifested through the same life-root, the state of the sage is refined (because their transformation is subtle and minute), whereas the state of the ordinary being is coarse (because their segmented existence is gross and manifest).
Therefore, it is necessary to analyze and distinguish the origins of the refined and the coarse.

Furthermore, although they are equally manifested through the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the Path of the Sages is authentic (because there is no further existence), whereas that of the non-Buddhists is spurious (because there is no real fruit). Thus, it is necessary to clarify and resolve the differences between the authentic and the spurious.
As for the mutual retribution of cause and effect, both the refined and the coarse, as well as the authentic and the spurious, are all [subject to this].

Because causes elicit their corresponding effects, they naturally respond to one another. Once one understands this natural correspondence, if one wishes to transform the coarse into the refined and abandon the false for the true, one should simply seek resonance and response;
then such resonance will be swiftly accomplished, while those who remain obstructed will achieve only minor fruits.
Therefore, it is said that they turn their backs on the path of purity. "The path of purity" refers to the Buddha-way.

What is called "seeing suffering" and so forth refers back to the matters of seeking response and resonance, explaining them by way of reference. Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are the fruit and cause of the mundane world;

cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are the fruit and cause of the supramundane. "Seeing" and "abandoning" refer to loathing the fruit and eliminating the cause; "realizing" and "cultivating" [refer to the realization of cessation and the cultivation of the path].

This refers to establishing the cause based upon the fruit. That is to say, those who seek only for a response do so for this reason. "Having already rested in extinction" means they have ceased at the illusory city (*pratibhāsa-nagara*).
"No longer proceeding forward" means they do not seek the place of treasure. They consider what is meager to be sufficient.
Therefore, they give rise to resolute conviction [in their own state] and do not conceive even a single thought of delight in the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas;
thus they fall into the category of those Śrāvakas of fixed nature, namely, the dull-witted Arhats who do not turn their minds toward enlightenment.

The bhikṣus of the four dhyānas who have heard nothing wrongly regard what is not a fruit as a fruit, belonging to the stream of those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) within the Buddha’s assembly; claiming to have attained what they have not attained is roughly the same as this calculation. Therefore it is said:

They form its companions. Regarding the fruition of Buddhahood and Bodhi, they embrace delusion until their connection is severed; they stagnate in quiescence and sink into emptiness; their cognition turns to ash and their vision is extinguished.
Therefore, it is called "delusion" and "loss. Third, the emergence of names serves as an awakening.

This is called the ninth: the perfect essence responding to the mind to achieve the fruit of quiescent progression. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.
By perfectly contemplating the Four Noble Truths and seeking response with sincere devotion, one’s affairs accord with one’s vows; hence it is called "the perfect essence responding."

The mind, having ceased its activity, comes to rest; it does not advance toward superior resolve but instead willingly falls into a state of ash-like extinction. Therefore, it is said that one has attained the fruit of quiescence.
Shrouded by the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), one fails to obtain the cause for perfect penetration through the mind; therefore, it is said that one is "distant" from it.

Obscured by partial emptiness, one cannot reach the ultimate fruit of cessation; therefore, it is called "turning one's back. Since that which is present before one is now like a rotten seed, one’s physical form is reduced to ashes.

One will inevitably fall into the state of a withered sprout; hence it is said that one is "born entangled in the seeds of emptiness. This means being forever bound by emptiness, lacking the resolve to transcend and be liberated.
The section on the perfect essence responding to the mind to achieve the signs of fruition concludes.

Ten: The Manifestation of the Fruit through the Mind of Perfect Enlightenment [Yong-hui], Part Three. 1. The Exhaustion of Practice and the Manifestation of Consciousness; 2. Errors in Understanding and the Formation of Faults;
3. Naming the Title and Providing an Exhortation. First: [The Exhaustion of Practice and the Manifestation of Consciousness].

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth and death may still find that his subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected.
Two erroneous understandings lead to fault:
if he investigates the profound subtlety within the perfectly integrated, pure, and luminous awakening, he will establish himself in *nirvāṇa* and fail to advance further.

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the fixed nature of pratyekabuddhas; those who associate with their kind and do not turn their minds back [toward enlightenment] become their companions.
They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision.
The "clarity of awareness" (*jue-ming*) is precisely the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate). As previously stated, it is the "true consciousness of the clarity of awareness.

This is because the objects of consciousness have reached their ultimate limit at this stage; therefore, the text specifically cites the "clarity of awareness," which serves as its basis, to manifest its excellence.

The previous statement that "it can cause one's own body and sense organs to be separated or joined, or opened or closed" already briefly possesses the meaning of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*). Furthermore, it is said that "it also [interacts] with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions."

Penetrating awareness (*abhijñā*). To be aware of and know penetratingly is, in brief, to possess the meaning of purity. Those who investigate the profound and subtle do not realize that they are still within the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Based on two meanings, they resolve to investigate in order to awaken to two kinds of profundity and subtlety.
First, based on the principle of perfect interfusion (*pariniṣpanna*), they awaken to the truth that dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature (by means of the six roots).
These belong to the phenomena of dependent origination. Now, seeing them open and close momentarily, one awakens to the principle that dependently originated things lack intrinsic nature.

Second, by relying on purity, one awakens to the meaning of the stillness within turmoil. (Since all categories originally belong to the phenomena of turmoil, now seeing that their cognitive awareness is universally pervasive, one consequently awakens to the meaning of stillness within turmoil.

As for the establishment of *nirvāṇa*: it was originally the cultivation of perfect penetration; suddenly encountering a divergent awakening, one erroneously reckons it to be profound and subtle, and thus establishes it as such.

Nirvāṇa. Because they do not know to further seek the ocean of nature (*dharmatā*), the perfect fusion of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and its non-obstruction, as well as the immovable ground of true thusness (*tathatā*) and the field of quiescent extinction, it is said that they do not advance. This is precisely what is meant by "realizing [enlightenment] midway.

Therefore, it is said that those who produce resolute conviction establish nirvāṇa based on the lack of intrinsic nature in dependently arisen phenomena; their reckoning is identical to that of the *pratyekabuddhas*.

Establishing themselves in nirvana amidst the turmoil of the world, they are reckoned as being identical to the pratyekabuddhas; thus it is said that such persons fall into the fixed nature of a pratyekabuddha.
This is because the Sanskrit term *pratyekabuddha* fully encompasses the dual meaning of both "conditioned" (*pratyaya*) and "solitary" (*eka*) awakening.

Furthermore, because they do not advance further, they are designated as having a "fixed nature. Regarding those of the class of the conditioned and the solitary: "conditioned" refers to the *pratyekabuddha*, who receives the teachings [of others].

Regarding the class of those who contemplate conditions (pratyekabuddhas), they are called "solitary awakeners" because they attain enlightenment spontaneously without a teacher. Both classes contain those who do not turn their minds [toward full Buddhahood].
However, while the former rely on their specific category to practice directly, the latter achieve realization through the perfect penetration [of the six sense bases].
Although the causes differ, the result is identical; therefore, it is said that they become companions. The final two lines may be understood by analogy with the preceding section on the śrāvakas.
Knowing this, the third is called "emergence through alertness.
This is called the tenth fruit of the *yong* (swimming) mind becoming a profound clarity (*zhanming*). It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana;
it gives rise to a state of awakened, perfect luminosity—the unchanging seed of perfection.

The union and opening of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) is called "round" (*yuan*). The pervasive awareness and cognition is called "penetration" (*yong*). What are termed "awareness" (*jue*) and "mind" (*xin*) both refer to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

That which binds the faculties is named "awareness," because it possesses cognitive discernment. That which constitutes the essence itself is named "mind," because it is capable of gathering and initiating [mental activity].

Regarding the "fruit of profound clarity": tranquility is named "profound" (*zhan*), which refers to the fruit of solitary awakening (*pratyekabuddha*). Being devoid of intrinsic nature is called "clarity" (*ming*), which refers to the *pratyekabuddha*.
This refers to the fruit. The two phrases concerning "contradiction" and "remoteness" may also be understood by analogy with the preceding discussion on the śrāvakas.

Since it is so in the present, it will be so in the future; hence it is said: "The awakening is perfect and luminous, not transforming the seeds of the circle. Here, "awakening" (jue) refers to the pratyekabuddhas and the solitary awakeners (pratyekabuddhas).

Their two principles are perfect (yuan) and their two wisdoms are luminous (ming); thus they are called "awakening," "perfect," and "luminous. This is their own reckoning of the perfection of the qualities of the fruit.

Yet they cannot be transformed; they remain merely seeds of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*). [Question: Regarding these ten objects mentioned above: the first eight involve non-Buddhists and celestial seers who entangle practitioners and cause them to sink into birth and death; these may indeed be called demons (*māra*).

However, the latter two concern Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, both of whom belong to the correct vehicle of the Buddha’s teaching. Even if they possess a fixed nature, they are still able to transcend the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*). If you categorize them all uniformly as demonic realms, it would cause people to fear practicing [the path]. Should those of dull faculties encounter this, they might lose the opportunity for guidance.

Is this truly the conduct of one with a compassionate heart? [Answer: According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is said: "To forget the Bodhicitta while cultivating various roots of goodness," and so forth, even down to: "one whose resolve and intention are narrow and inferior. [This refers to such practitioners.]

To not seek the Dharma of the Great Bodhi of all Buddhas and so forth are all the works of Māra; how much more so now, when it is said that one is "contrary to and far removed from perfect penetration" and "turns one's back on the city of Nirvāṇa"—if this is not the work of Māra, what is it? One must know that the intent here is to extol and emphasize perfect penetration.

Generally speaking, anything that creates obstacles for the attainment of Perfect Penetration (yuantong) constitutes the work of demons (māra). This does not apply, however, to those who originally practiced according to other gateways; for example, even those with no nature for enlightenment (icchantika) as taught in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* are all permitted to achieve Buddhahood, and the subtle causes and scattered virtues mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra* equally serve to assist in its manifestation.

Within this present scripture, whether one follows the sequence or proceeds in reverse, the sacred nature is mutually pervasive. If one clings to the literal words to the detriment of the underlying meaning, not only will there be obstructions regarding other scriptures, but even within the preceding and succeeding sections of this very text, there will be points that cannot be reconciled.
[The section on] the demonic manifestations appearing in the interim concludes. Part Four: A Summary to Provide Warning and Exhortation, in two sections. First: The Manifestation.
Due to vigilance, there are two instructions regarding protection and proclamation. First:
Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* lead to madness midway through their practice due to delusion; this occurs while one has not yet attained fulfillment.
The arising of the realization of fulfillment is entirely due to the mutual interaction of the mind with the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), which gives rise to this stage.

Beings, stubborn and deluded, fail to reflect upon themselves; when this state manifests before them, each rests according to their own cherished prior habits and deluded minds, regarding it as the ultimate ground of refuge and peace.
They claim for themselves the fulfillment of unsurpassed *bodhi*, yet this is a great falsehood.
If one achieves these, one will be influenced by external paths and demonic forces; when the karma is exhausted, one will fall into the Avīci Hell.

For Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, this does not lead to further progress. These ten types, as previously described, belong collectively to the wholesome states of dhyāna before the demons have arisen.
Therefore, they were first designated by the term *dhyāna*. Before reaching perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), these are all merely intermediate stages.

If a demonic realm arises, one immediately becomes deranged; this refers to the attainment of a perverted and insane mode of cognition. Because one relies on such perverted and insane cognition, one fails to achieve self-awareness;
hence, it is called "delusion. Due to this delusion, one considers a small attainment to be sufficient; hence, it is said that regarding what has not yet been attained...

Within the feet, one gives rise to the realization of sufficiency. If one investigates the reason why this leads to madness, it is not because there are actually external demons coming to disturb one;
therefore, it is said that "it is all the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha)," referring to the moment when the consciousness-aggregate is about to open but has not yet opened.
"Mind and activity interacting" means that the application of mind is not pure; delusive thoughts and right mindfulness arise alternately.
Because of this, one attains realization midway. Therefore it is said, "one is born into this stage. "Stage" (wei) here refers to realization.
[The text] next warns of the manifest harm, saying that sentient beings are stubborn and deluded, failing to reflect upon themselves. This is a warning.

Whenever any object appears before you, you should reflect upon it yourself. It is further said that when encountering such appearances, each person grasps them according to what they personally cherish;

this is due to the deluded mind resulting from past habitual tendencies. Therefore, one should be cautioned that whenever such an object is encountered, one must remember one's original practice and not allow oneself to be governed by residual habits.
Now, since you do not reflect upon this yourself and are again deluded by past habits—
The mind no longer further investigates the wondrous clarity; therefore, it is said that it "rests of its own accord. This resting is twofold.
The first eight kinds regard their own calculated fruits as the ultimate ground of refuge and tranquility—such as the first fruit of refuge, up to the eighth fruit of burning afflictions.

The latter two kinds regard their own realized fruits... [self-]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, likely discussing the various stages of meditative attainment and their respective fruits.)
To claim that one has fulfilled unsurpassed bodhi is like the fruit of the ninth stage of pacification or the fruit of the tenth stage of profound clarity.
All such claims constitute what is called "great false speech," for they involve claiming to have attained what has not been attained and claiming to have realized what has not been realized.
Although all these are forms of false speech, their harm varies in degree, much like the eight types of heterodox paths mentioned previously.
The Māras and those with manifest merit all experience their results through outflowing (*sāsrava*) karma.

Once the karma that produced these results is exhausted and the retribution is finished, they will inevitably fall into the Avīci Hell. This is said in reference to those who commit the most severe harm.

As for the latter two types—Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—their manifest realization of the fruit does not belong to the induction of outflowing karma; when their retribution ends, they do not fall. They are merely...
One will not achieve further progress. This is said with reference to those instances where the harm is slight;
yet, although there are degrees of severity in such harm, it constitutes a demonic obstacle within *samādhi* because it can create hindrances to the realization of perfect penetration.
Second, entrust this to you for proclamation and protection.

You must maintain your resolve and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata; after my parinirvāṇa, transmit this Dharma-gate to the final age, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand its meaning.
Do not allow them to encounter Māra or bring about their own ruin; protect, sustain, and compassionately rescue them.
Eliminate distracting conditions and cause their bodies and minds to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. From the initial accomplishment, they shall not encounter divergent paths.
You who maintain your resolve, I instruct you to be attentive; do not be negligent. Uphold these words of the Tathāgata’s path.
The instruction on self-benefit is given because by upholding the Tathāgata’s path for destroying Māra, perfect penetration can be achieved.
The passage beginning with "After my parinirvāṇa" and so forth teaches altruism; this is truly because in the age of the Final Dharma after the Buddha’s extinction, [such practice is required].

The True Path has declined, and false views compete to arise. Compared to the time when the Tathāgata dwelt in the world and the periods of the True and Semblance Dharma prevailed, this era is indeed pitiable.

To cause all sentient beings universally to awaken to this meaning refers to awakening to the tenfold distinctions of how one becomes deranged midway through the path. Once this has been awakened to, then the distorted and deluded views—

They shall not be born again. Therefore, it is said: "Do not allow yourself to see Māra and create your own heavy calamity. What is called a "heavy calamity" refers to grave transgressions and karmic retributions;

this includes those such as non-Buddhists and malevolent spirits who fall into hell at the end of their retribution, as well as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas whose wisdom fails them at the "City of Illusion.
These all arise from the emergence of deluded views and do not come from without; hence it is said they are "created by oneself. To preserve [this truth]...
"Sui" (to soothe) means to preserve and sustain meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). "Ai jiu" (compassionate rescue) means to compassionately rescue the practitioner.

"Xiao xi xie yuan" (eliminating and stilling perverse conditions) means to eliminate and still the conditions for perverse views, so that their body and mind may equally achieve perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) in the present.

Because they have achieved perfect penetration, they are naturally able to transform the cognitive perspectives of sentient beings and enter the cognitive perspective of the Buddha. Having already entered the Buddha's [perspective]...
Through knowledge and vision, one establishes the stages of the noble ones (ārya-bhūmi) according to the practices undertaken;

beginning from this point, one gradually achieves perfection until the attainment of Buddhahood without encountering bypaths. This means that from beginning to end, throughout the stages and positions, there are forever no crooked or devious aspects.
This concludes the summary and analysis of characteristics for the purpose of recognition. Part Three: Following the Ancients and Concluding with Exhortation, Section Two.

First, three specific exhortations are presented; second, a general conclusion and entrustment. The first [section] has three parts: first, an exhortation regarding the practice of taking up [the teachings];
second, an exhortation regarding the discernment of demons; third, an exhortation regarding the use of mantras. The first [part]:

In this Dharma-gate, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust have ridden upon this mind to open it and attain the Unsurpassed Way.
When the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, your present sense faculties will function interchangeably.

From within this mutual functioning, one can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*). Within this state, the perfectly luminous and refined essence of the mind gives rise to transformation, like pure crystal.

Within the crystal, a precious moon is contained. Thus, one transcends the stages of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten dedications, the four preparatory minds, and the bodhisattva’s practice of the vajra-like ten bhūmis and equal-enlightenment;
entering the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment, one fulfills bodhi and returns to non-attainment.

First, the ancient [teaching] is cited to provide an exhortation. Although these phrases of the Dharma-gate are immediately proximate to the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate), their meaning encompasses the preceding four aggregates as well.

This is because the four aggregates are first opened up and the consciousness-aggregate is finally exhausted; once the consciousness-aggregate is exhausted, one knows that the preceding four are also exhausted.
"In the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" refers distantly to many kalpas. "Dust-like Tathāgatas" refers to Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust.
This is said because it expresses the extreme abundance of Buddhas. Previously it was said, "These are the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust; this is the single path to the gate of Nirvana.
Here it is said, "Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust ride upon this mind and, by its opening, attain the Unsurpassed Way.

This is truly because the total eradication of demons here is identical to the unraveling of the knots there; they are one and the same Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration. When the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted...
Then both "one" and "six" vanish, and the true nature manifests before one. One is all; all is one. Thus, it causes the various sense faculties to function as one another’s instruments.
This refers precisely to the point where the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate) is about to be exhausted.

From the phrase "mutually" (*hu*) downwards, he reveals the superior stage that should be cultivated: the *vajra-kṣānti* (diamond-like wisdom). This does not refer to what is described in the *Zhengmai* (Correct Pulse), for it points directly to—
The preceding stage is the initial Ground of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*). This is because the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing is termed the "Vajra Samādhi.
Since Dry Wisdom directly relies upon this for its establishment, the name "Vajra" is specifically designated for it.

As for the statement that one can enter from within the "mutual functioning" [of the faculties], it is because through mutual functioning, wisdom becomes powerful and superior, and the craving of desire begins to dry up and wither. This is the essence of perfect luminosity.
"Mind" refers to the essence of the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*). "The six sense faculties functioning interchangeably" is called "perfect clarity" (*vimala*);

"the craving for desire dried up" is called "refined mind. This means that once one has entered this stage, one must necessarily possess its essence. Since the essence must necessarily include its function, it is said that "within this, transformation is initiated.
This refers to the initiation of supernatural powers and transformations within this very state of perfect clarity and refined mind. Regarding what is... [text ends]
This means that having attained two excellences, one initiates three functions. The phrase "pure" in the two lines is spoken by way of analogy.

It refers to the perfectly luminous and subtle mind, whose nature inherently possesses spiritual transformation; its manifestation and application are unhindered, like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon within, which is unimpeded in its clear illumination of both the near and the far.
Since awakening and realization are already equal to the fruit of Buddhahood, it says, "Thus."

This refers to transcending the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and the ten abodes (*vihāra*). Its intent is that "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) serves as the agent of transcendence, while the intermediate stages serve as that which is transcended;
likewise, dry wisdom serves as the agent of entry, while the "Sublime Adornment" (*Sudarśana*) serves as that which is entered.
This is largely the same as the *Avataṃsaka*, with only minor differences. Since the *Avataṃsaka* does not establish dry wisdom prior to the ten faiths, it states that "the ten faiths are fulfilled."

The mind encompasses the stages and realizes awakening; thus, the stage of faith (*śraddhā*) serves as that which transcends. In this scripture, the ten stages of faith are derived from the stage of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*);
therefore, the stage of faith itself is also included among what is transcended. This is a minor distinction.

Generally speaking, for practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun*), the very first stage is taken as that which transcends. The birth of a prince from the womb serves as a clear illustration of this.

This analogy is largely the same. Zhengmo (The Correct Pulse) says: "The specific mention of 'that which is practiced' regarding the stages (*bhūmi*) intends to indicate that entering the stages constitutes the true cultivation of the noble ranks.

All are cultivated through the severance [of afflictions] by means of adamantine, sharp wisdom. (I, the humble writer, say: This "adamantine" is different from the two characters for "adamantine" in the preceding stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).
The latter refers to the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, which serves as the common basis for all stages; therefore, it was placed [there].)
Because it is the beginning of the Ten Grounds (daśabhūmi), it is called the "Vajra" of the Ten Grounds.

Regarding the term "perfectly luminous" (*yuanming*) applied to Equal Enlightenment (*samabodhi*), it means seeing that from beginning to end there is only this single mind; however, reaching Equal Enlightenment is the ultimate limit of transformative manifestation.

Based on this, Master Jiao already knew that within the stage of Equal Enlightenment, it is still the mind of "dry wisdom" (*ganhui*), having merely attained perfect luminosity. Why, then, did he previously—after the stage of Equal Enlightenment—forcefully open up "dry wisdom" as if he had not understood the statement that one only attains dry wisdom at the very beginning? This is what is called being habituated...

"Riding a horse"—is this not what is meant by the "master of the crossroads" (*jiaoshi*) for one who is accustomed to falling? I have already provided a revised interpretation of this in the preceding text; here, I shall again offer a supplementary clarification based on the term "master of the crossroads. As for the Tathāgata being called the "Ocean of Sublime Adornment" (*miaozhuangyan hai*):

it is because the adornments of the myriad virtues each reach their ultimate excellence, all of which arise through conditions (*pratyaya*) from the ocean of nature (*xinghai*), such that the one and the many are mutually unimpeded in a重重 (layered/interpenetrating) and inexhaustible manner. The two phrases concerning "perfection" (*yuanman*) serve to clarify the capacity for transcendence.

Regarding the meaning of "being able to enter": even if one proceeds through the stages of cultivation until the perfection of Bodhi, it does not exceed the perfection of all merits within the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*). Ultimately, not a single dharma comes into being anew.
Therefore, it is said that one returns to non-attainment. It is for this reason that one is able to transcend and enter.
Second, the exhortation to discern demons:
this is the analytical discernment of enlightened clarity within *śamatha* by means of *vipaśyanā*, as practiced by the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.
Subtle demonic activities and demonic realms manifest before you; you are able to recognize them. The defilements of the mind are washed away, and you do not fall into false views.
The *skandha*-māras are extinguished; the celestial *māras* are shattered. Great spirits and ghosts lose heart and flee; *chi-mei* and *chi-liang* demons can no longer be born.
Until you reach Bodhi, you shall lack nothing. Those of inferior capacity will advance toward Great Nirvana.
The mind remains settled and free from confusion.
First, he cites the ancients to provide encouragement: the past Buddhas were those who had passed through the realm of Māra.

*Śamatha* means "stopping" (*zhi*) and *vipaśyanā* means "contemplation" (*guan*). This refers to how the World-Honored Ones of former Buddhas, within the meditative concentration of *śamatha*, by means of—
Through vipaśyanā—the clear wisdom of discernment and investigation—one analyzes and distinguishes subtle demonic activities until realization is attained.
What I have now explained likewise merely follows the precedents of the former Buddhas; it is not a novel invention.
If you can indeed act according to my instructions, then when the realm of Māra appears before you, you will be able to recognize it. Once you are able to recognize it, [you will be liberated].

If one does not form a noble understanding (*ārya-adhimukti*), then the defilements of the mind are washed away, Māras find no opportunity, and one does not fall into the net of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

It is said that this right view is precisely what one must recognize regarding the realm of Māra. Regarding the "Māra of the Aggregates" (*skandha-māra*) below, its benefits shall be clarified and analyzed.

As for the Māra of the Aggregates, it refers to the manifest states appearing during *dhyāna*; for example, within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the body is able to pass through obstructions.

The ten [states] within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), such as attaining great radiance; the ten within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), such as the manifestation of perfect concentration;
the ten within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), such as profound clarity and agitation;

and the ten within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), such as the separation and union of the faculties, the opening and closing of awareness, and the pervasive flow of cognition—though these are wholesome states, they can still give rise to demons. One must observe them with the correct eye.
This is precisely the *skandha-māra*. If the practitioner can observe correctly and with clarity, it will naturally subside before long;
thus, the *skandha-māra* is extinguished. Once the *skandha-māra* has been extinguished, contemplative wisdom becomes increasingly refined and luminous.
Even if there were a *deva-māra*, it could not withstand such illumination; its mind would naturally be shattered and its courage crushed.
As for the powerful spirits and deities, they are the subordinates of Māra. "Tǐ" means to lose or to be deprived.

This implies that if even the celestial Māras are thus shattered and destroyed, how much more so the powerful spirits and deities; they should naturally lose their courage and flee beyond twelve *yojanas*.
If this is the case for the king’s ministers, what need is there to mention the minor spirits such as the *chī-mèi* and *wǎng-liǎng*? Furthermore, for them...
Driven by Māra, one should naturally conceal one's form and obscure one's traces; hence it is said that there is no further birth.
Based on this, both internal and external obstacles are simultaneously and secretly dissolved, whereby one is able to transcend all stages and proceed directly to Bodhi.
Although it is said that this state transcends and reaches the ultimate, there is no lack whatsoever of the merits of the various stages;
for one awakening is the awakening of all, and one realization is the realization of all.

Even those of the inferior Two Vehicles—such as the latter two types of the *vijñāna-skandha-māra*—can be transformed by it, so that they may rouse their resolve to advance and never turn back from the mind of Great Nirvāṇa.
To become bewildered and distressed is precisely what characterizes the work of Māra; how could one possibly treat this with negligence? Third, I urge you to employ mantras.
If there are sentient beings in the final age who are dull-witted and ignorant, who do not recognize *dhyāna* nor understand how to preach the Dharma, yet delight in practicing samādhi—
Fearing that you might fall into heterodoxy, I single-mindedly urge you to uphold this Buddha-uṣṇīṣa dhāraṇī mantra.
If you are not yet able to recite it, write it down in your meditation hall or carry it upon your person; then no demons whatsoever will be able to move you.

During the era of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), the Buddha-way was flourishing; many people attained realization through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Even if demonic activities (*mārakarman*) occurred, they could not act as obstacles.
In the age of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), the Buddha-way gradually declined. Although people still attempted to emulate that [direct] measure, demonic activities became numerous;

yet, there was no reason for deep concern. Therefore, this is specifically discussed with reference to the final age (*paścimakāla*). Those who are dull-witted and ignorant are the masses of the final age.
Born thus, they are foolish, deluded, and dull-witted; their wisdom is not clear and their faculties are not sharp.

Since their wisdom is not clear, they do not recognize the various distinct states within *dhyāna*. Since their faculties are not sharp, they do not know the Buddha’s taught gateways for discerning demons.
Lacking both these conditions—personal effort and the power of the Dharma—they yet delight in practicing *samādhi*. This is like one who sets out on a journey with only goods to trade.
"O you who possess many jewels, as you travel through perilous paths with no weapons of your own and no external rescue, it is inevitable that those who are close to you will worry for you.
You fear associating with the heterodox; fearing that you may fail to discern the truth and mistakenly join the ranks of Māra, you would then be the same as the heterodox.
Therefore, I instruct you to encourage yourself with single-mindedness; there is no need to employ any other methods."
One should simply encourage others by this means; this is the foremost dharma-gate for repelling Māras.

For since this mantra is called "Buddha-uṣṇīṣa," it is most honored and most supreme; and since it is called a "dhāraṇī," it encompasses all dharmas, as it possesses the meaning of being unsurpassed when upheld.
If one is unable to recite it—meaning even if there should be sentient beings who are utterly foolish and dull-witted and lack the ability to recite—[one should still encourage them].
Read this essence. Therefore, instruct that it be transcribed and kept in the meditation hall and worn upon the body. To demonstrate how one remains unmoved by various māras:
because this mantra is constantly accompanied day and night by the assembly of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattva and his retinue;
furthermore, because the ground for twelve *yojanas* surrounding this mantra becomes a consecrated boundary (*sīmābandha*). Thus, it is separately set forth.
The three exhortations are concluded. Second, the general summary and entrustment:
"You should reverently honor the ultimate practice and final instructions of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
Having already demonstrated the method for discerning demons, he further sets forth the meaning of the concluding exhortation; finally, he again instructs: "You should reverently honor..."
"Qin. Thus, the Tathāgata’s repeated and earnest exhortation is already profound and deep. Nevertheless, there are two meanings in teaching one to be reverent and respectful (*gongqin*).
First, this is the method for ultimate cultivation and progress from beginning to end by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions;
it should be practiced with reverence and respect. This is an entrustment to achieve one's own [enlightenment] in accordance with the Dharma.
This is beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*). Second, these are the ten directions’ Tathāgatas, who out of compassion for the final age of the Dharma’s end have bequeathed this model of conduct;
one should respectfully and reverently receive it and propagate it. This entrustment is intended to ensure that one accomplishes the practice of benefiting others by relying on the teachings.
This concludes the general summary and detailed analysis of the five māras, which has finished explaining the obstacles within *samādhi*.

The third section clarifies the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in order to break through the obstacles within *dhyāna*. Within this division of *dhyāna*, the myriad practices of the bodhisattva are revealed, with an emphasis on practical cultivation.

Fearing that practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching might become mired in principle—relying on sudden enlightenment to simultaneously eliminate all afflictions—and thus being unable to endure gradual cultivation, they might wish to discard the myriad practices, thereby creating obstacles within *dhyāna*. Now, by means of Ānanda’s inquiry, the limits of the five aggregates are once again clarified.

Finally, he further showed him that delusions are not removed instantaneously, but are exhausted through a gradual sequence. Once it is known that they are exhausted through a gradual sequence, one does not abandon the myriad practices, and the obstacles within *dhyāna* can be broken.
(3) First, Ānanda receives the instruction and asks again; second, the Tathāgata answers again based on the question; third, the conclusion, exhortation, opening of the path, and transmission.
First: Ānanda immediately rose from his seat. Having heard the Buddha’s instructions, he prostrated himself in reverent acceptance, memorizing them without loss.
Within the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more: "As the Buddha has stated, among the characteristics of the five aggregates, there are five kinds of delusion."
This is our original thought: we have not previously received the Tathāgata’s subtle and detailed instruction.
Furthermore, regarding these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), are they to be eliminated simultaneously or exhausted sequentially? Within these five layers, what constitutes their ultimate boundary?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will manifest his great compassion, purifying the minds and eyes of this great assembly, and for the sake of all sentient beings in the future age.

Acting as the eye for the future, he first received and upheld the essential intent. As soon as the profound sounds that discern demons had ceased, the divine realization appropriate to the occasion manifested spontaneously;
thus Ānanda rose from his seat. Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the ultimate nature of the five aggregates became perfectly clear. The five...

The characteristics of Māra’s conduct are clearly manifest; therefore, the one present at the occasion prostrated to the Tathāgata and reverently received the Dharma instructions, vowing to lead them for his own cultivation.

"To remember and uphold without loss" means to maintain mindfulness and grasp them in the present, so that they shall not be forgotten or lost in the future, vowing to lead others by means of them for the sake of transcending the world.
○ Below the section on "the Great," he restates the three questions; although he has received [the teachings],...
Still harboring doubts, he addressed the Buddha once more. His uncertainty was no different from before; he merely sought further instruction on what he had previously asked. Thus he said:

"As the Buddha has taught, regarding the five delusions within the five aggregates: within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), there is the delusion of solidity; within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the delusion of empty luminosity;
within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the delusion of interpenetration; and within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the delusion of profound concealment."

Perception (*saṃjñā*). Within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), there are empty and false conceptualizations. Based on these five kinds [of mental states], they are able to produce the secondary branches;
therefore, they are called the "original fundamental minds. For thirty years, I have never expounded upon them.

Even if I have spoken of them, it has not gone beyond briefly enumerating their names and characteristics. Therefore, you say, "We have not ordinarily received subtle and detailed instruction. This is the first question.

"Please explain in detail the source of delusion. He asked this again. "Regarding 'simultaneous elimination' (*bingxiao*): this refers to one who has already attained perfect penetration (*yuantong*);

because they ride upon awakening, all is eliminated simultaneously, as it is entirely empty in its very substance. Regarding 'gradual exhaustion' (*cijing*): this refers to one who passes through the various stages (*wei*), refining them through phenomena and practicing cultivation in successive order.

As for the two characters 'wei' (in *bingwei* and *cijing*), their respective meanings have not yet been resolved; I pray that you will clarify the meaning intended by the Buddha. This [is the request].
The second question requests a definitive clarification regarding the sudden and gradual [approaches]. "Thus, the five layers" refers to the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

"To arrive at" (*yi*) means to reach. The question, "By arriving at what does one define the boundary? is intended to know at what stage of realization one reaches the limit of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and so on, up to at what stage one reaches the limit of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). This is the [second]...
The three questions were asked because the realms [of sentient beings] vary in depth. From "I only pray" (*yuan*) onwards, he requests benefit for both the present and the future.

These three questions, as mentioned above, are all essential for rescuing the world and constitute the pivotal points for cultivation and realization; therefore, he seeks for the Tathāgata to manifest great compassion and provide further instruction.
Upon hearing this, one will fully comprehend the source of delusion, avoid falling into the obstacle of principle (*li-zhang*), and not remain stalled midway.
Therefore, it is said: "Clarify the mind and purify the eyes. When the ground of the mind is clear and pure, one will not err regarding the path ahead, just as the eyes can discern the way.
Having attained clarity of mind and eyes, one rides upon their vows to enter into that age of the Final Dharma (*mappō*), transmitting the words of the Tathāgata to future generations;
hence it is said: "Acting as the eye for the future."

Second, the Tathāgata’s repeated response to the questions. (Within the responses, the second and third points correspond respectively to the second and third points of the questions; these are interwoven before and after as the Buddha’s discourse proceeds spontaneously.
Third, [the section] has three parts: first, answering regarding the false source of the five aggregates; second, answering regarding the depth and shallowness of the causal realms;

third, answering that principle does not abandon phenomena. Regarding the first of these three: first, a general manifestation of how [phenomena] arise from delusion; second, a specific verification through grasping; third, pointing to the fundamental knot for demonstration. First...
Three. First, everything arises from delusion; second, the five aggregates are understood by analogy; third, the conclusion is presented to prevent further questioning. Regarding the first:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "The essence of the true, wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment is perfectly pure; it does not harbor birth and death, nor any defilements."
"Even down to empty space, all arise from the production of false conceptualization.
Originally, in the true reality, there was fundamentally no dharma. 'Essential truth' refers to the unchanging essence; 'wondrous luminosity' refers to the function that accords with conditions."

This is spoken in terms of the essence and function of the true mind. Possessing this essence and function, whether in a state of delusion or non-delusion, it is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūla-bodhi*).

It is all-pervading and pure, with no room for anything else within it; this constitutes its "perfect purity. Originally, there are neither sentient beings nor the various realms of the physical world;
therefore, it is said that it does not retain birth-and-death or any defilements. Birth-and-death refers to the fruit of sentient beings, while "defilements" refers to—

The "defilements" (*mala*) are precisely the afflictions and karma; they serve as the cause for sentient beings. Since these no longer remain, there are no sentient beings within the Truth (*tathatā*).
Consequently, there is no meaning of the "receptacle world" (*bhājana-loka*). This is implied by the intent of the following passage.

Regarding the phrase "down to the lower dharmas arising from delusion," the two characters "down to" (*zhì yǐ*) skip over the subtle dust-worlds (*paramāṇu-loka*). Subtle dust is taken as the cause of the receptacle world, and the world itself is the receptacle.

Because it is the fruit of the realms (*dhātu*). Since there are no sentient beings within the ultimate truth (*tattva*), then death, birth, and the defilements (*rajas*) all arise from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Not only do death, birth, and the defilements arise from false conceptualization, but even the subtle dusts of the world, up to the very space upon which they depend, all arise through false conceptualization.
Based on this, it goes without saying that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are produced by delusion.
The two [realms] and the five aggregates are to be understood by analogy.
This originally fundamental, wondrously luminous, true essence gives rise, through delusion, to all the vessel-worlds, just as Yajñadatta mistook his head for its reflection.
Delusion has no original cause; yet within this false conceptualization, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions. Those who are deluded regarding these causes and conditions—
It is called "spontaneous. That nature of space arises as a true illusion; both causes and conditions and spontaneity are all the conceptual constructions of the deluded minds of sentient beings.
This refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Since it is said that everything arises from false imagination, how much more so the five aggregates? Therefore, it says: "This..."

"Original enlightenment," "wondrous clarity," and so forth. "Original enlightenment" is as explained above. Previously it was said that the "subtle essence is wondrously clear"; here it is said that "the wondrous clarity is the true essence.
This is intended to reveal the meaning of the mutual fusion of essence and function—being neither identical nor different. This refers to the True [Nature] upon which they depend.
Since there is originally but one True [Nature], how could the five aggregates exist? It is simply because, at first, there was a single movement of deluded thought.
The union of the real and the false forms the ālayavijñāna. Depending upon this consciousness, the perceiving aspect (darśana-bhāga) emerges;
depending upon the perceiving aspect, the perceived aspect (nimitta-bhāga) emerges. Within the perceived aspect, the realm of space first takes shape;
therefore it is said that the false gives rise to the various vessel-worlds (bhājana-loka). Thus, space and the seeing are not yet distinguished, nor is form...

The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) arises simultaneously with the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*); its nature is a compaction of the four great elements. The aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) arises simultaneously with the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); it is the weaving together of the sense organs, their objects, and consciousness.
The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) arises simultaneously with the turbidity of affliction (*kleśa-kaṣāya*); while cognition desires to remain fixed, karmic forces are constantly shifting.

The aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) arises simultaneously with the turbidity of birth (*jāti-kaṣāya*); they correspond within the substance [of the mind] yet oppose one another in their functions. The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) arises simultaneously with the turbidity of life (*āyu-kaṣāya*).

It arises. In sum, because they do not understand that all is but mind, they employ various deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) to grasp at signs within objects, which are thus successively and falsely established.

Therefore, it is said that they are like the yakṣa *Yajñadatta*, who, being deluded, mistook his own head for its reflection. This uses the case of *Yajñadatta*’s delusion regarding his head as a metaphor for sentient beings’ failure to realize that all is but mind;
and his frantic running after the reflection serves as a metaphor for their employment of various deluded thoughts to grasp at signs within objects.

[This refers to] the characteristic of turbid aggregates arising through mutual succession. However, since the various receptacle worlds are said to have arisen falsely, they fundamentally do not exist;
how then could there be a creator who brings them forth? Therefore it is said that "the false has no original cause.

Thus we know that the five aggregates currently manifest are nothing but deluded thoughts. The followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand this, mistakenly calculating them as causes and conditions; hence it is said:

Within the realm of deluded conceptualization, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions; yet, as for the heterodox views of external paths that deny cause and effect, they are termed those who are "deluded regarding causes and conditions.
Having become deluded regarding causes and conditions, they will inevitably falsely calculate that things exist spontaneously;

thus, they are said to "proclaim spontaneity" (*svabhāva*). In reality, both causes and conditions and spontaneity are merely frivolous conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*); therefore, with reference to that empty space—
How much more so when it is manifested? As stated previously: "Emptiness arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the sea.

From this we know that even empty space is a substantial illusion born of delusion; how much more so the worlds, sentient beings, and even the five aggregates currently manifest before us, which exist within that space—how could they possess any reality?
Therefore, one should know that whether one speaks of causes and conditions or of spontaneity, [they are all ultimately unreal].
All of these are the conceptual constructions of the deluded minds of sentient beings; this is precisely what was meant previously by the statement that there are "only words and no actual meaning.
Third is the conclusion and demonstration in response to potential questions.

Ānanda, when one knows where delusion arises, one speaks of the causes and conditions of delusion. If delusion were fundamentally non-existent, then speaking of the causes and conditions of delusion would be fundamentally non-existent as well;

how much more so for those who do not understand and instead speculate that it arises spontaneously? Therefore, the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the original cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but false imagination.

First, the defense against questioning: (It may be feared that, following the previous question, one might say: "Since the five aggregates before us exist through deluded thought (*vikalpa*), it seems reasonable to claim that deluded thought constitutes their cause and condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
