Why, then, do you reject both 'cause and condition' and 'spontaneity' (*svabhāva*)? Therefore, the World-Honored One provides this defense. The Buddha’s intention is this: if one knows the place from which deluded thought arises, one may say that deluded thought constitutes its cause and condition;
however, if deluded thought fundamentally has no place of arising, then it is entirely empty in its very substance. If...

To further explain that these deluded thoughts serve as causes and conditions is to show that, fundamentally, nothing exists at all. Even within our own teachings on causes and conditions, there is nothing to be found;
how much more so for those of external schools who, not understanding causes and conditions, speculate about a "spontaneous nature"?

This only serves to demonstrate the ultimate extent of their delusion. Therefore, the following section concludes and clarifies this point. (Previously, in the discussion on the five aggregates, it was revealed that the five aggregates are formed by the five deluded thoughts. Fearing that [the reader] might not yet have a deep understanding...)
Faith. Therefore, this is concluded here as a demonstration: because of these causes and conditions, both [the self and the aggregates] are naturally neither of them.

Thus, when the Tathāgata previously elucidated for you the fundamental cause of the five aggregates, although there are five distinct designations—such as "solidity" and "empty luminosity"—they are all equally false imaginings;
they are utterly devoid of any substantial entity that can be traced or investigated. This collectively reveals that...

The section on Delusion concludes. Second, specifically verifying [the nature of reality] through grasping. (Previously, the five layers of delusive thought were explained; these were all discussed in terms of fundamental subtle characteristics. However, because these subtle characteristics are profound and distant, they are difficult for people to know.

Now, in response to Ānanda’s repeated request for a subtle and detailed exposition, we take easily understood phenomena present before us as examples to verify [the principle]. Five: First, verifying that form arises from delusion.

2. Verifying that sensation arises from delusion; 3. Verifying that perception arises from delusion; 4. Verifying that mental formations arise from delusion; 5. Verifying that consciousness arises from delusion. Regarding the first:
Your body was previously produced through the parents' conceptualization; if your mind were not conceptualizing, it could not have entered into that conceptualization to transmit life.

"As I have previously said: when the mind conceives of the taste of vinegar, saliva is produced in the mouth; when the mind conceives of climbing a high peak, a tingling sensation arises in the soles of the feet.
Although the precipice does not exist and the vinegar has not arrived, your physical body is certainly not of the same category as empty delusions.
How could the water in the mouth emerge simply because of speaking of vinegar? Therefore, you should know that your present material body is called the 'first of the firm and solid.'"
"Deluded thought.

First, the essence [of the body] is indicated by means of "thought. The Buddha's intention is that because the fundamental aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is subtle and difficult to perceive, he speaks for the time being in terms of the manifest aggregate of form;
thus he says, "your body. Since this body has substance and is visible, it is precisely the aggregate of form.
Furthermore, it is first due to the union of the father’s essence and the mother’s blood—the red and the white—that conception occurs based on the perception of the parents.
As stated previously, when the mind becomes attached and engages in sexual conduct, the fluids of the male and female organs naturally flow; this is the very proof of that principle.

Regarding the statement that "your mind is not [composed of] thought and so forth," the reason the paternal seed and maternal blood can be gathered to form one's own body is likewise due to the mutual resonance and union of one's own self-perception and the perceptions of the parents' minds, thereby transmitting and continuing the life-force.
If one were devoid of thought, there would be no response, and thus life could not be sustained; the red and white elements would collapse, and the physical body could not be formed.
This is precisely what was illustrated previously: "Diverse views give rise to hatred; shared thoughts give rise to love.
Retaining love as the seed and receiving thought as the womb"—this is the verification thereof. As for the passage beginning with "As I," it employs metaphors to reveal the nature of delusion.
As I previously stated, this analogy was already cited earlier within the section on the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); it is now being cited once again.

Although life is transmitted through perception as mentioned above, there still remain the "red and white" [semen and blood] that can be grasped. If one were to claim these are illusory, it would seem difficult to understand;
therefore, I have further cited the two analogies of the perception of sour saliva and the perception of height arising from acidity to provide a comparison.
In general, the known is used as an analogy for the unknown; here, moreover, that which is most easily known is used as an analogy for what is easily known above.

One contemplates the taste of vinegar, which illustrates how life is transmitted through mental perception; saliva arises in the mouth, which illustrates how a substance is formed by gathering droplets.
These two phrases regarding mental perception are understood by analogy. However, there is no precipice, nor is there the sourness of the vinegar.
This is empty. Since the sour object has not yet arrived, the saliva in the mouth is merely a delusion.

Taking this as an analogy, the substance of the present form is likewise entirely empty and utterly delusory, like the saliva in the mouth that causes the feet to ache; they belong to the same category.

Therefore, one may raise a counter-objection by saying "it certainly is not," etc., asserting: "Suppose that your own body were certainly not [empty] like the saliva in the mouth that causes the feet to ache."

Regarding those who falsely claim [the body] is of the same category [as consciousness]: your body arises from perception (*saṃjñā*). Salivation and the tingling in the feet should not likewise arise from perception.

Setting aside the tingling in the feet for a moment, how does salivation arise specifically from talking about vinegar? From this we know that salivation arises from perception. Since it is identical to your body in this regard, [your position is untenable].

Your substance is false and illusory; it should likewise be the same as saliva. Since this is so for the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) currently manifest before you, the fundamental aggregate of form that preceded it can be understood by analogy.

Therefore, the following points to the name of the aggregate of form. The Buddha’s original intention was that because the fundamental aggregate of form is difficult to comprehend, he cited the substance of the manifest form as an example. Furthermore, fearing that [the nature of] the substance of form...
It is difficult to understand. Furthermore, two more metaphors are cited as examples. Having already clarified this through metaphor, he now concludes by referring to the substance of form (*rūpa*).

"Therefore, you should know" means that, based on the preceding discussion of the substance of form—wherein the water and the void were shown to be illusory and mutually pervasive—he concludes and instructs Ānanda that this is what one must know.
"Your present physical body" refers to the substance of form before one's eyes; it has fundamentally no [independent existence].
All that exists is composed solely of deluded thoughts; therefore, it is directly termed "deluded thought. Because it stands at the head of the five aggregates (*skandhas*), it is called the "first.
As for the term "solid," it signifies a state of clarity and concentration that does not undergo transformation.
This is also the case with the fundamental aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Second, one verifies that sensation arises from delusion.

This very state you have described—whereby the mind’s contemplation of heights causes your physical form to truly experience a sense of distress—is born from the cause of sensation, which is able to move the substance of the body.

This present state of yours, where you are driven about by the two manifest conditions of what is favorable and beneficial versus what is adverse and harmful, is called the second delusive thought: "empty clarity."

At the outset, the metaphor is employed to reveal the nature of delusion. In the preceding section, that which is easily understood was first presented; subsequently, the most easily understood thing was cited as a metaphor.

In this present section, following the momentum of the preceding meaning, that which is most easily understood is taken as the exemplar (*dṛṣṭānta*), while that which is [initially] easy to understand is taken as the object of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*).
By means of these general analogies, the matter is elucidated to demonstrate its falsity; yet, the structural progression of the text varies in each instance.
Furthermore, that which is here explained refers to taking the aforementioned metaphors as the illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Among the two metaphors, one specifically takes the metaphor of the mind imagining oneself ascending a height; hence it says, "the mind imagining while facing a height. This means that although one has not actually ascended the height, it is merely a mental imagination (*saṃjñā-citta*).
This serves as a metaphor for how, within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), there is fundamentally no real object, but only sensation itself.
It is the mind. It is solely this conceptualizing mind that can cause your physical form to truly experience astringency and bitterness.

This is a metaphor for how it is solely the feeling-mind (*vedanā-citta*) that can move the substance of form (*rūpa*), manifesting as signs of the disagreeable, agreeable, painful, pleasant, or neutral.

Thus one knows that the signs of the disagreeable, agreeable, painful, pleasant, or neutral are identical to astringency and bitterness; they are merely false and illusory, as will be seen in the subsequent text. By...

The following is applied by means of the Dharma. Regarding "arising from causes": this refers to the fact that within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), there is fundamentally no real object;

when one investigates its causal origin, it is found to be merely the arising of a mind of sensation. This corresponds to the mental state of "imagining oneself at a height," which is capable of moving the physical body.

Regarding "manifesting upon the physical body": this refers to the manifestation of signs such as the disagreeable, the agreeable, suffering, pleasure, or neutrality upon the physical body. This corresponds to...
It can cause your physical form to truly experience astringency and bitterness. ○ Now, as you point downward, I shall name the fetters of sensation (*vedanā*).

That which accords with one and brings benefit is the present sensation of pleasure; that which opposes one and causes harm is the present sensation of suffering. "The two manifest" refers to the active manifestation of these two types, suffering and pleasure.
"Dashing to and fro" is the characteristic of their coming and going in mutual interaction. Indeed, the intersection of suffering and pleasure is precisely the middle way.

This is merely a conventional designation. To take the analogy of sourness or astringency: fundamentally, these have no inherent existence; their substance is composed solely of deluded thoughts, and thus they are named after those thoughts.
Occupying the position following the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it is called the second. As for the term "empty clarity" (*kha-prakāśa*):
Apart from the body, there is nothing; it is merely the awareness of a void and luminosity. The fundamental aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is also like this.
Third, one verifies that perception arises from delusion:

it is by your thoughts and reflections that you cause your physical body to exist. The body does not belong to the same category as thought; for what reason, then, does your body follow along with your thoughts?
It causes various forms to be grasped; the mind gives rise to the apprehension of shapes, which corresponds with mindfulness. When awake, this is the conceptualizing mind;
when asleep, it becomes various dreams. Thus, the movement of your conceptual thoughts and deluded emotions is called the third false discrimination, known as "interfusion."

At the initial stage of melting, there is as yet no differentiation. The preceding explanation of the fundamental *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) pertained to the seeds of the six consciousnesses within the *ālayavijñāna*;

this refers to what was previously described as "stirring thoughts. Because these are subtle and difficult to discern, the present discussion concerns only the *saṃjñā-skandha* as it manifests before one.
This manifest *saṃjñā-skandha* is precisely the mental deliberations (*manasikāra*) within the six consciousnesses; this refers to what was previously described as...
This refers to floating thoughts. As soon as a single thought-movement arises, the five sense organs all rush outward. Therefore it is said: "It is by your thoughts that you cause your physical body.
This speaks, for the time being, of the state before the merging and differentiation [of mind and body]; at that time, there is only deluded thought, devoid of any substantial reality.

The phrase "the body is not the lower part" indicates that [the essence] pervades all consciousnesses. The body belongs to the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), while thought belongs to the category of mind (*citta-dharma*).
Therefore it is said that the body does not belong to the category of mental factors (*citta-dharma*). Since it does not belong to that category, it should not follow after mental factors.

Thus, it is difficult to ask why your body is driven by what follows after mental factors. The various subsequent passages explain this by correlating the substance [of the body] with all the consciousnesses.
Perception (saṃjñā) has the grasping of images as its essential nature. It arises by grasping in accordance with its objects; since these images are not uniform, it is said to "grasp various images.
Due to grasping various images, it can cause various states of mind to arise, just as they correspond to the images thus grasped.

Visual consciousness arises conditioned by forms; auditory consciousness arises conditioned by sounds, and so forth. This substance pervades the five consciousnesses. Once the mind has arisen, the sense faculties also follow it toward their respective objects;
hence it is called "form-grasping" (*ākāra-grahaṇa*). By means of this, the physical body is constantly associated with mental deliberation (*vitarka-vicāra*);
it is for this reason that it is said to be "that which follows what is directed by mindfulness. Furthermore, regarding this mental deliberation:
"Waking" refers to the mind of mental imagery; this applies to the independent [mental consciousness] during the state of distraction.
"Sleeping" refers to the thought of dreaming; this further applies to the independent [mental consciousness] within a dream.

The reason it is not stated that this applies to "recollection" (anusmaraṇa) is that recollection is subsumed within the five sensory consciousnesses, because once the five consciousnesses have arisen, clear recollection also arises simultaneously with them.

It is not stated that this [state] applies to the independent [consciousness] within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because in this *sūtra*, *samādhi* does not refer to a concentration involving the contemplation of images, as the independent [consciousness] does not manifest therein.
Regarding the phrase "then you," it points to the name of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

As for "your perceptions and thoughts," this is spoken in reference to the present *saṃjñā-skandha* in its state of fusion before it has yet been differentiated. As for "the agitation of deluded sentiment," this refers to...

Regarding the essence of the present aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), when spoken of in relation to all consciousnesses, it is uniformly a false conceptualization and lacks any substantial reality;
therefore, it is called "delusive thought" (*vikalpa*). It occupies the position immediately following the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and is thus named the third.

As for the term "interpenetrating" (*yōutsū*), it refers precisely to this fusion wherein the essence has not yet been differentiated and thus permeates all consciousnesses. Although the fundamental aggregate of perception stands at the beginning...
Among the eight consciousnesses, the principle that their fusion and identity are undifferentiated and that their substance pervades all consciousnesses is likewise so.
Furthermore, although this [ālayavijñāna] and the two aforementioned [skandhas] share the same name, "delusive thought" (parikalpita), their meanings differ slightly:
the former two skandhas are called "delusive" because they are formed by delusive thought, whereas this *saṃjñā-skandha* is called "delusive" because its very substance is itself delusion.
Fourth, the evidence that practice arises from delusion:
The principle of transformation does not abide, but shifts and migrates in secret. Nails grow, hair grows, vital energy wanes, and the countenance wrinkles;
day and night they alternate, yet one never awakens to this. O Ānanda, if this were not you, how could it be that the body undergoes change? If it must be truly you...
"What is 'without awareness'? It is the fact that your various formations (*saṃskāra*) do not cease for even a single moment; this is called the fourth subtle and hidden delusion.

First, the characteristics of the fundamental aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) were shown to be subtle and difficult to perceive. Now, we shall examine it by means of the formations currently manifesting before you;
therefore, it is said that 'the principle of transformation does not abide. 'The principle of transformation' refers to the formations currently manifesting before you, because they are present."
Because the nature of the body is one of shifting, flowing, and changing, its substance belongs to the realm of arising and ceasing; therefore, it is said to be "non-abiding.
Although it is called non-abiding, the preceding moment ceases and the succeeding moment arises, occurring only as a continuous and subtle displacement that is not clearly visible.
Since it is not clearly visible, by what means is its existence known? It is because there are characteristics that can be verified, as in the case of a person...
At the time of birth, the nails gradually grow and the hair gradually emerges. By the time one reaches old age, the vital energy gradually dissipates and the complexion gradually wrinkles.
Who causes this? It is likely the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) that acts as its agent.
Day and night they alternate; within a single day and night, arising and ceasing, ceasing and arising, succeed one another in turn, never ceasing for a moment.
The Awakened One has observed that from antiquity until now, people have practiced [these habits] without examining them. As it is said in the *Bārsi*: "Transformations shift subtly;
I truly do not perceive them. And as the Brahmin says: "Am I still the person of old, or am I no longer that person? Both express this very same meaning.
○ Ānanda, the following passage reveals that the essence [of the mind] is illusory. These two lines mean:

if this aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) were not your mind, it would naturally undergo change on its own, independent of you; how then could it cause your essential body to undergo transformation?
"If it must be either of two [possibilities]" refers to the statement: "If this must be your true mind, then since it is capable of undergoing change, its substance should be self-aware.

Why is it that you now have no awareness? Thus, whether it is yours or not yours, both are unobtainable; it is clear, then, that its entire substance is empty and illusory. The phrase "Then your... below points to the activity to conclude the name. Then... (Note:
The original text contains a commentary on a section of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. The translation reflects the structure of the Chinese syntax and the logical progression of the argument.)
"Your 'all formations' (saṃskāra)" refers to the currently manifest aggregates (skandha). That they do not cease for even a single moment is their characteristic.
As the *Renwang jing* states: "Within a single thought-moment (citta-kṣaṇa) there are ninety kṣaṇas; within one kṣaṇa there are nine hundred births and cessations."
Thus, it can be known that every thought-moment is incessant; its entire substance is utterly illusory, and for this reason it is designated by the name "deluded thought" (*vikalpa*).
Furthermore, because its subtle shifting is imperceptible, it is given the title of "profound and hidden. The fundamental *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is likewise so.
There are five proofs that consciousness arises from delusion: first, identifying the root to mark the branches; second, definitively discerning that it is not real.
First, regarding the identification of the knots by means of the three fingers:
furthermore, that which you call "constant"—the place where your subtle essence is tranquil and unmoving—is not exempt from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within the body.
To be free from all conceptualizations is called "vivid clarity" (*jīngmíng*). To be without further arising or ceasing is called "tranquil and unshakable" (*zhànbùyáo*).

This refers to a distinct awareness of a state of vivid clarity and tranquility that exists after the exhaustion of conceptualization and mental formations; this is what is known as the fundamental *ālaya-vijñāna* (the aggregate of consciousness).
Its essence penetrates the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Within the stage of sentient beings, there is no other true essence apart from this. Therefore...
The provisional school regards [the self] as permanent; however, this sutra also provisionally permits it at the outset.
Because it is subtle and difficult to know, it is pointed out as being present before one; thus it is said that within the body it does not transcend seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition.
This refers to how the original single essence of spirit is divided into six harmonious combinations. Yet, because this is fundamentally difficult to know, it is pointed out here...

"Manifesting before one" also means that ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle do not know that seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition are of the same essence as the subtle spirit of consciousness (*vijñāna-śukra*).
Therefore, by relying on the root to indicate the branches, this is a skillful means of gradual introduction. Second, distinguishing and determining that it is not the true reality.

If this true essence were pure and real, it could not tolerate the habitual influence of delusion. For what reason, then, did you all once behold a wondrous object in years past, such that throughout the passing of those years there was neither memory nor forgetting;
yet later, upon suddenly beholding that same anomaly again, the memory returned perfectly clear, without the slightest loss?
If this essence is thus lucid, profound, and unwavering, how can it be subject to being perfumed by thoughts from moment to moment? What calculation can there be for this?

Consider this, Ānanda: you should know that this stillness is not the ultimate reality. It is like a rapid current that appears tranquil from a distance; because the flow is so swift, it is not perceived, yet this does not mean there is no flow.

If this were not the source of conceptualization, how could one ever undergo the habitual tendencies of delusion? As long as your six faculties do not function in mutual interpenetration, this false discrimination—this opening and closing—will never cease.
First, this is a hypothetical concession to the counter-argument. Since it has been established above that [the nature] is called "eternal," one must necessarily reckon it as being pure and true;

therefore, this is conceded for the sake of argument. If it were truly pure and unmixed, a true nature devoid of delusion, it could not possibly allow the defilements of the seeds of habituation to accumulate within it—this is a settled principle.
The phrase "for what reason" (*kena hetunā*) is a term used for a counter-objection. Previously...
"Years" refers to the distant past. "To see with one's own eyes" means to witness personally. When one witnesses a strange or extraordinary thing, one necessarily becomes biasedly attached to it;
this is the stage of the "seed of habituation" (vāsanā-bīja) having already been deposited within the field of consciousness (vijñāna-kṣetra).

"Having passed through years" means that after further passing through many years and many ages, one may still remember at first, but over time forgets; and after yet more time, one both remembers and forgets.
Both are absent. It is set aside in a state of total indistinctness, as if it were neither existent nor non-existent.

"Afterwards" refers to the period following the absence of both recollection and forgetting. "The former anomaly" still points to that extraordinary object from years past. "Suddenly beholding it again" means...
Unexpectedly, it is seen once again. That the memory is as vivid as before is due to the power of the internal perfuming of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
that nothing has been lost is because the seeds remain intact. Based on this, the fact that [the mind] receives perfuming and maintains the seeds seems to be neither subtle nor real;
therefore, he raises a counter-objection by asking, "By what cause... and so forth. Below this, he clarifies that this is delusion and not reality, and that it is not subtle or real.
This clarity and lucidity is precisely what is manifested as seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is of one undifferentiated nature, termed "tranquil and unshakable.
Since it is admitted that these share the same essence, there is no impediment to speaking of this in terms of the fundamental source.

The phrase "moment by moment receiving perfuming" refers to preceding and succeeding moments receiving perfuming and maintaining seeds without any cessation. This constitutes the specific measure [of its function].
As for the number of heads, they are immeasurable and boundless; hence it is said, "What calculation can there be? Based on this, it is certainly not the refined and true [nature].
Therefore, he specifically calls Ānanda by name and instructs him that he should know this stillness is not the true [nature].
Regarding the phrase "like a rushing stream," the Zhengmai (Correct Pulse) says: one must take a rushing stream that flows smoothly without waves; it is tranquil and peaceful. Looking toward...
It is like one who is tranquil, because there are no fluctuations of waves and no surging or receding of rapids.
The two phrases regarding the "swift current" clarify that its direct cause (the *samyag-hetu*) flows so rapidly that it cannot be perceived; it is not that there is truly no flow.
The intended meaning of the metaphor is that the reason the *ālaya-vijñāna* is called "constant" is merely because it is coarse to ordinary beings and followers of the Lesser Vehicle.
The mind looks toward it; in reality, every thought-moment is perfumed, undergoing subtle arising and ceasing without a moment’s rest or stillness.
It merely appears unmoving because the divisions and enumerations within it cannot be calculated; yet it is not truly eternal, for the root of deluded thought has not yet been exhausted.
○ "If it were not... below indicates what should be cultivated. "If it were not thought... [is the phrase].
Regarding the phrase "the original source" (*yuan*): it means that even if there were no root-source of deluded thought within this state, how could one still be perfumed by the habits of delusion?
This is a definitive statement that there is still a subtle level of deluded thought present.

To exhaust this thought, one must wait for the manifestation of quiescence (*śamatha*), when the six sense faculties function interchangeably, when the states of integration and separation are perfected, and when both the "one" and the "six" have vanished. Thus it is said.
I have addressed this not for your sake, but rather to reveal it by contrast. It is precisely because the perfect penetration of vision must be cultivated that the six knots must be untied.

By using three fingers to identify the knots of consciousness, you can now see within your own present seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing: how many of these habitual patterns are merely superficial, while deep within, they are turbid, obscure, and void.
The fifth is the subtle and refined perception of inversion.

The Buddha, following upon this, addressed him, saying: "Because you have not yet attained the mutual functioning of the six sense organs and have not exhausted the source of perception, you, Ānanda, are likewise a person who has not yet exhausted the source of perception.
How do we know that you have not yet exhausted the source of perception? It is as in your case..."
Within the nature of present seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing, that which is able to thread together and habituate the "ji" (ji refers to *vāsanā*, or habitual tendencies;

"ji" means subtle, referring to the seeds, as they are minute and not yet manifest) so that they are not lost, is a portion of ignorance within the *ālaya-vijñāna*—the profoundly serene and lucid consciousness—and is therefore called "formless" (*wangxiang*). This is because the ignorance within the *ālaya* acts as the threading agent.
Among the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), how many are practiced until they become habitual? They are in harmony with True Suchness (*tathatā*), being neither identical nor different;

therefore, they are called "void and non-existent. Because they follow the four aggregates (*skandha*), they are called the "fifth. Ordinary beings reckon them as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), while those of the Two Vehicles recognize them as *nirvāṇa*.
To take what is non-existent as existent and what is void as real is called "inversion" (*viparyāsa*). In contrast to the preceding four...
Because its modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and manifest, it is called "subtle. Although it is not the wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind, it is like a second moon;

therefore, it is called "subtle perception" (*sūkṣma-saṃjñā*). Based on this, when the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, one merely exhausts its delusion but does not exhaust its reality.
This is precisely why the Sūtra initially selected the faculty-nature (*indriya-prakṛti*). Having concluded the separate summary of the means of verification.
The Three Fingers showed Ānanda:
"These five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) are formed by the five kinds of false imagination.
They are collectively called the 'five aggregates of clinging' because, according to what is induced by karma, one experiences these five aggregates, and these aggregates obscure the true nature."
Furthermore, based on these five types, one experiences retribution in the present life, repays the karma of previous lives, and creates causes for the future;

because they mutually conceal one another's specific characteristics and are difficult to transcend, they are also called the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*). This means that by clinging to them as a self, they are provisionally gathered together.
Moreover, based on these five types, one grasps objects and gives rise to karma, gathering together the conditioned and unconditioned, as well as the tainted and untainted.
Because they serve as the causes for future lives, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are not exhausted, and one does not escape saṃsāra.
Observing their origin, one finds that the five kinds of deluded thoughts constitute their root; therefore it is said, "The five deluded thoughts are formed.
This concludes the response to Ānanda’s request for a detailed explanation of the source of delusion regarding the five aggregates. Second, the response concerning the depth of the causal realms.
If you now wish to know the depth of the causal realms: only form and emptiness are the limits of form; only contact and separation are the limits of sensation;
only recollection and forgetfulness are the limits of perception; only cessation and arising are the limits of mental formations;
and the profound entry into the merging with the profound is the limit of consciousness.
First, to establish the intent of the question: I understand that you now ask these five successive questions regarding what constitutes their boundaries.
Your intention is likely to know the limits of the causal succession from consciousness through to form (*rūpa*), as well as the meanings of their relative depth and shallowness therein.
"Only form" (*rūpa*) and what follows are explained in their proper sequence. Zhengmo says: "That which has characteristics is form; that which lacks characteristics is emptiness.
Thus we know that to exhaust only form is called "shallow," while to exhaust both form and emptiness is called "deep. If one abandons form to guard emptiness, [it remains shallow].
The Patriarchal House calls this "falling into the extreme of a single color"; the Vijñaptimātra school calls it "the single manifest color of emptiness.
Since neither has yet emerged from the boundaries of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), all such patiences regarding emptiness are not ultimate.

It is only when both emptiness and form are extinguished that the aggregate of form is truly exhausted. Contact (*spraṣṭavya*) comprises the two sensations of suffering and pleasure; detachment (*vairāgya*) is the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣāvedanā*). This is...
To know only the exhaustion of contact (*sparśa*) is called "shallow"; to exhaust it together with detachment (*vairāgya*) is called "deep.

If one cuts off contact while guarding detachment—just as the Brahmins take non-reception (*anupādāna*) as their tenet—one has still not emerged from the limits of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
Therefore, all forms of renunciation and relinquishment are not ultimate. It must be that both contact and detachment are extinguished for the aggregate of sensation to be exhausted. There is...

To have thoughts is to record; to be without records is to forget. Thus we know that merely exhausting what is called "recording" is shallow, while exhausting both recording and forgetting is profound.

If one abandons recording and clings to forgetting, the Patriarchal House calls this "no-mind," yet it remains separated by a further barrier and has not yet transcended the limits of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Therefore, all states of non-perception whatsoever are not ultimate. This is because...

When both memory and forgetfulness are abandoned, this constitutes the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). The coarse activity of the distracted mind is "arising" (*utpāda*);
the subtle activity of the concentrated mind is "ceasing" (*nirodha*). Thus one knows that exhausting only arising is called "shallow," while exhausting both arising and ceasing is called "deep.

If one departs from arising, abiding, and ceasing, the original sūtra describes it as "vibrant and turbid clarity," like a wild horse; it has not yet emerged from [the realm of conditioned phenomena].
This is the limit of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Therefore, all states of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) are not ultimate.

Only when both arising and ceasing have vanished can it be said that the aggregate of formations has been exhausted. "Serene stillness" (*zhan*) refers to the eighth fundamental consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*);

this is what was previously called "the state of serene stillness where there is no movement. To say "entering the serene stillness" means relying upon this eighth fundamental consciousness to turn back from discursive thought and enter into non-existence.

"Mindfulness. This is because one enters [samādhi] by means of stillness (*zhan*). "Uniting with stillness" refers to maintaining non-mindfulness and abiding in the eighth fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);

this is because one abides having united with stillness. Thus, it is known that entering by means of stillness is shallow if one merely exhausts mindfulness (*yǒu niàn*) but does not further abide in the union with stillness;
it is profound when one simultaneously exhausts non-mindfulness (*wú niàn*). If one enters by means of stillness, then...

It merges with the profound stillness (*zhan*). The ancient masters call this "the final falling from the summit. It has not yet transcended the limits of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*);

therefore, as long as the retributive consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) is not empty, none of these states constitute the ultimate. One must necessarily enter through the profound stillness without merging with it;
only then is the aggregate of consciousness exhausted. According to this, each of the five aggregates has its own limit, which must be completely eliminated.
Nevertheless, there are distinctions between the shallow and the profound. If one halts at the shallow level, the fruit will ultimately never be perfected;

if one exhausts the limits [of the shallow] without realizing [the profound], one’s efforts may be wasted in vain. The Dharma-eye is prized for its lack of obscuration, and the realization of the fruit must aim for perfect enlightenment.
This is why Ānanda asked, "To what limit does one proceed? and why the Tathāgata answered him by distinguishing between the shallow and the profound.
Third, the principle does not negate the phenomenon.
These five aggregates originally arise in overlapping succession; their arising depends on consciousness, and their cessation begins with the removal of form.

In principle, there is sudden enlightenment, and through that enlightenment, all is simultaneously dissolved. Yet phenomena are not suddenly eliminated; they are exhausted only through gradual stages. I have already shown you the *kṣapa* cloth.
[The interlocutor] asks: "What is it that you do not understand that you inquire about this again?
First, the direct answer: "These five aggregates" refers back to the fundamental five aggregates, because they are the source of the present five aggregates.
Regarding their "repeated arising": this means that due to ignorance and non-awakening, consciousness arises; and consciousness is...

There is that which is called "activity" (*saṃskāra*). Activity necessarily involves movement, which is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*). From movement, there arises the aspect of seeing characterized by empty luminosity, which is called "feeling" (*vedanā*).
From seeing, there arise the characteristics of empty form and shape, which is called "form" (*rūpa*). Thus, they arise through successive layers being superimposed upon one another.
According to this, birth has consciousness as its cause; proceeding from the subtle toward the coarse, it culminates in form. As it is said:

When a person puts on clothes, they must necessarily do so from the inside out, gradually dressing; thus, the cessation of the five aggregates proceeds by eliminating them starting from form, moving from the coarse to the subtle, until reaching consciousness.
This is like a person taking off clothes, which must necessarily be done from the outside in, gradually undressing.

Once perfect penetration is attained, one is equal to the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore it is said: "In principle, there is sudden enlightenment; the delusive thoughts of the five aggregates are suddenly [extinguished]."
Both are empty; hence it is said that "through awakening, both are simultaneously dissolved. However, habitual tendencies from beginningless time arise whenever they encounter circumstances.

One must ensure that they do not arise upon encountering circumstances, yet this cannot be eliminated instantaneously. Therefore, one must establish the stages of sagehood (*āryabhūmi*) and cultivate practice through successive experiences.

Only then can they be extinguished. Therefore it is said: "They are exhausted through successive causes. One who understands this meaning will naturally not be hindered by subtle awakening, nor will they reject the sacred stages of *dhyāna*, such that both understanding and practice are perfected. [The section] beginning with "I have already" below is a refutation of the question.
According to the previous analogy of tying a cloth to demonstrate sequential order, the text states: "Six different knots are made from a single cloth;
if they are allowed to become disordered, they can never be completed. These knots must be untied in a fixed sequence. Now, the exhaustion of the aggregates (*skandha*) is likewise so.
Because the exhaustion of the aggregates (*skandha*) is already contained within the unraveling of the knots, as previously stated, it says:
"I have already shown you the knots of the *karpāsa* cloth. Ānanda had also said earlier: "These knots were originally produced by being tied in succession;
today they must be untied in succession. Since he already understood that, he should have applied the same principle here; therefore, he is rebuked with:
What is it that you do not understand that you ask this question again? (Question: Previously, the six knots were shown as being prior to *āyatana-samudaya* [the convergence of the sense bases];

here, the gradual cultivation is shown as occurring after *āyatana-samudaya*. Why, then, are the previous six knots still taken as a metaphor? Answer: The characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are contained within these six knots. Once the six knots are untied, the five aggregates are thereby exhausted. One awakens to this within *samādhi*, and one cultivates this within *dhyāna*.

Since the sequence is identical and correct, there is no contradiction in still taking the six knots as a metaphor. However, within *samādhi*, they are entirely removed through the sole use of the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*) to grind them away; within *dhyāna*, they are entirely removed by employing both practical conduct (*kriyā*) and cultivation to refine them. The power of concentration grinds...)

Polishing [the mind] merely suppresses delusions and realizes emptiness; it is a practice of ritual cultivation that can truly sever delusion and realize the Real. This is the difference between the former and the latter stages. If we discuss the characteristics of the exhaustion of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) by specifically addressing the ranks of the Sages:

the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) should occur at the time of entering the stage of "Abiding" after the completion of "Faith," because by completing Faith and entering Abiding, one leaves behind illusory form and is born into the Buddha-family. The exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) should occur at the time of entering "Practice" after the completion of "Abiding," because by completing Abiding and entering Practice, one leaves behind deluded sensation and proceeds toward true cultivation.

The extinction of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) should occur at the stage of "fulfilling practice and entering toward" (*xingman ruxiang*). This is because fulfilling practice and entering toward means being free from deluded thoughts as one approaches the three locations. The extinction of the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) should occur at the stage of "entering the ground through application" (*youjia rudi*).

This is because entering the ground through application means that numerical calculations are extinguished as one gradually enters the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*). The extinction of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) should occur between the emergence from the grounds and the entry into the Equal and Wondrous [Wisdom]. This is because emerging from the grounds and entering the Equal [Wisdom] still involves subtle marks of thought;

only after the Vajra Path is reached does the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) become empty, and one enters the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). If one carefully examines the meaning of the text of this sutra, the principle is indeed thus. One must understand that the sequence of stages, their depth and shallowness, and their opening and closing within the Perfect and Sudden Vehicle (*yuantun jiaocheng*) cannot be entirely identical [to other systems]; it is not permissible to judge it by means of other sutras.
This concludes the Tathāgata’s response to the difficult question posed by the ancient masters. Third, he offers a summary exhortation for its transmission and dissemination:
"You should take this root-source of deluded thought and achieve a thorough understanding of it.

Transmit and reveal it to all practitioners in the future age of the Dharma's decay, so that they may recognize the profound falsity of their own nature, develop deep weariness with it, realize the existence of Nirvāṇa, and no longer cling to the three realms."

The five aggregates (*skandhas*) manifest before us, taking the fivefold deluded thoughts as their root source. As long as this root source is not eliminated, the five aggregates can never be exhausted.
Therefore, it is taught: "You should sever this root source of deluded thought," and so forth.

One whose mind attains penetration realizes that all is manifested by the mind alone and produced by consciousness alone; that apart from the mind there is no substance, and apart from consciousness there is nothing.

This is the nature [of the teaching]. Having a basis for one's own cultivation, one should consider benefiting others; therefore, the teachings are transmitted to show them to those who will come in the future.

The specific mention of the "Dharma-ending age" (mofa) is because in that age attachments are heavy and the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are difficult to eliminate; thus, it reaches only those who are practitioners.

Because they do not know how to practice, it is insufficient to speak of this to them. To cause them to recognize what is false and illusory means to cause them to recognize that there is only mind and no external substance, and that consciousness-only has no inherent nature.
Since the root source is already merely false and illusory, how could the branches and ends be real?
To mistake the false for the true, one wanders through vast eons; by knowing this and not following it, one is said to develop a profound weariness that arises spontaneously.

When the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) have been exhausted, the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing manifests; this is the true essence of *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is said that one "knows existence.
From this point on, according to the practices undertaken, one establishes the stages of the sages (*ārya-bhūmi*) and advances in pursuit of unsurpassed *bodhi*.

Hence, it is said that one "does not cling to the three realms. The purpose of reiterating the discussion of the five aggregates lies precisely here. Following Ānanda’s request to discourse on the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*).
From that time until now, this exposition of the Dharma has reached its conclusion, constituting another cycle known as the "Cycle for Breaking Obstructions and Dissolving Hindrances.

This cycle comprises the entirety of the preceding three parts and forms the primary *Śūraṅgama-rāja* (King of the Heroic March). According to conventional interpretation, *śūraṅgama* is translated as "ultimate solidity," taking the sense of being immovable and indestructible.
In this present sutra, the seven destinies are minutely investigated and shown to be nothing other than one's own karma.

That which is summoned: a detailed analysis of the five māras reveals they are all brought about by perverse thoughts. To further clarify the five skandhas, they are collectively rooted in delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Summoned by one's own karma, the seven realms of existence are formed while the secret cause is destroyed; brought about by perverse thoughts, the five māras arise while the definitive meaning is lost.
Rooted in delusive conceptualization, the five skandhas shroud the mind while the myriad practices collapse; the secret cause...
If [the mind] is destroyed, right faith will not be firm; if the definitive meaning is lost, right understanding will not be solid;

if the myriad practices collapse, true cultivation will surely fall away. Thus, there is destruction because from beginning to end one lacks firmness. Now, knowing that this is summoned by one's own karma, if karma is not created, the seven realms of existence are empty.
That which results from perverse thought—if thought is free from perversity, the five māras will flee. As for deluded imagination...

This serves as the root. When perception is free from delusion, the five aggregates dissolve; when the seven realms of existence are seen as empty, the secret cause is inherently present and right faith becomes firm.
When the five demons flee, the definitive meaning manifests before one, and right understanding becomes solid.

When the five aggregates dissolve, the myriad practices proceed without obstruction, and true cultivation is perfected. Once true cultivation is perfected, wondrous realization will surely be attained. Based on this—

This constitutes the generation of faith, the arousal of understanding, the initiation of practice, and the realization of the fruit—from beginning to end, it is ultimately firm, unshakable, and indestructible.

The three characters "Śūraṅgama" in the title encompass this entire meaning. From the time Ānanda requested the samādhi until the present discussion, this section constitutes the "Correct Main Body" (Zhengzongfen).

III. The Conclusion (The primary teaching having been completed, the immediate benefit has been realized. The true doctrine must now be transmitted; the bridge for future generations must be entrusted to it.

So that the ocean of Dharma may branch out and the waters of benefit may flow and moisten all, its grace shall soak the sands of the world-systems and its transformation fill the dust-motes of the ten directions. Since the merit lies in its circulation, it is placed at the end. Furthermore, the introduction is like the head, the primary teaching is like the body, and the conclusion is like the feet. By observing the head, one can discern the person’s entire life.)

If one examines his body, his physical strength is worthy of appraisal; yet there is no place he cannot reach on foot. His body and head are merely empty vessels. Since the exposition of the correct teaching has been concluded, its circulation should be detailed. (Three parts: First, comparing and evaluating the merit of transforming others;

second, manifesting the benefits of one’s own cultivation; third, the assembly receiving the teaching with joy and dispersing. The first [of these three] has three parts: first, citing an example to inquire about merit;

second, answering that it is inexhaustible; third, comparing and manifesting the merit of transformation. Ānanda, suppose there were someone who filled all the empty space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures, and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a mind that never failed. What do you think?
Would this person, by virtue of this cause and condition of giving to the Buddhas, obtain much merit?
As explained and transmitted above, its merit should naturally be inexhaustible. Therefore, it is said:
"If there should be another person"—meaning, suppose there were yet another kind of person—a single direction of empty space would still be impossible to measure.
How much more so when filling the voids of the ten directions; from this, one can know that space is inexhaustible.
If such empty spaces each contained the seven treasures—even if they were not filled—one could not calculate their number. How much more so when they are filled with the seven treasures;

from this, one can know that the jewels are boundless. If one were to offer these precious treasures to a single Buddha alone, that gift would already be vast; how much more so if [offered to all Buddhas].
To offer this to as many Buddhas as there are atoms in the universe, the vastness of this material gift can thus be known.
To serve these Buddhas with one’s person and provide them with material offerings is already extremely difficult; how much more so when the mind is free from any sense of futility.
Thus, it can be known that while externally he exhausted every ritual form in his giving, internally he depleted his very sincerity.
Desiring to use this merit to compare it with the merit of the circulation [of the teaching], he asked, "What do you think?
He did not speak of the inconceivable merit resulting from the causes and conditions of giving to the Buddha himself; rather, he wished to employ the words of those present to instruct the assembly.
Therefore, he asked whether the merit obtained would be great; the second [Vimalakīrti] answered that it would be inexhaustible.
Ānanda replied, "Space is inexhaustible, and precious jewels are boundless. [The Buddha said:

"In the past, there was a sentient being who gave the Buddha seven coins and, by relinquishing his body, still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King. How much more so now, when the space before us encompasses the entirety of the Buddha-fields!"
Precious jewels are bestowed everywhere, filling all space; even if one were to contemplate this for an entire kalpa, one could not reach its limit.

How, then, could there be any boundary to such merit? Initially, when establishing the prior giving, it was said that it fills the void of the ten directions; thus, empty space is inexhaustible. Furthermore, it is said to be overflowing—

Third, comparing and manifesting the merit of transformation.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The words of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are not false.

If there were another person whose body was burdened with the four grave offenses and the ten pārājikas, they would, in a mere instant, pass through this world and other worlds into the Avīci Hell, continuing until the end..."

He traverses all ten directions without interval, leaving nothing unexperienced. ○ He is able, with a single thought, to expound this Dharma-door to those who have not yet studied during the final kalpa.
○ This person’s karmic obstructions shall be extinguished at that very moment; the causes for suffering in hell they were to undergo are transformed into a Land of Peace and Bliss.
○ The merit they obtain shall surpass that of the previous donor by a hundredfold or a thousandfold.
It is ten million billion times greater; indeed, it is such that even calculation and analogy cannot reach it.

First, it is shown that one should believe what is taught: because the effort required to propagate this sutra is very slight, the destruction of sins and the acquisition of merit surpass those of the former.
This is difficult for people to believe; therefore, [the Buddha] pre-emptively demonstrates that his words are not false, so as to manifest what one should believe.
○ "If, moreover," and so forth, raises the barrier of heavy human obstructions. "If there should be another person" and so on means:

even if there were such a person who, in a single lifetime, fully possessed the four kinds of grave offenses of the Hīnayāna and the ten pārājika offenses of the Mahāyāna—these are the transgressions.
This is the ultimate gravity. Among these, if one commits even a single offense, one should immediately fall into hell; how much more so when committing them all together?

One should naturally fall swiftly. Therefore it is said that "in a mere instant, one passes through the Avīci hells of this world and other worlds," meaning that one is first born in the Avīci of this world for a full kalpa, and when that kalpa ends, one is reborn in the Avīci of another world. Thus it continues.
From one direction to another, they are reborn in succession; hence it is said, "extending even to the exhaustion of the ten directions without interval.
"Without interval" (wújiān) is the Chinese transcription of the Sanskrit term *Avīci*.

The phrase "there is none through which they do not pass" indicates that they traverse all ten directions simultaneously, experiencing every single hell, as they never depart from the realm of the hells. The section beginning with "Able to... clarifies the power of upholding [the precepts].
The merit is small. One who is able to apply even a single thought refers to one who, at the moment of impending downfall, suddenly awakens to this Dharma-gate.

Having already attained sudden awakening, they further vow to reveal and teach this Dharma-gate during the final kalpa to those who have not yet studied meditative concentration, so that they may become like themselves.
Based on this, the continuation of the Buddha’s life of wisdom depends entirely upon such a person.
If one were to discuss only his traces of transformation, his merit would appear very slight;

for his time was but a single thought-moment, his teaching but a single Dharma, and those he instructed were only those who had not yet studied. ○ As for the phrase "this person," it refers to one who turns suffering into happiness.

"Those with karmic obstructions" specifically refers to the four grave offenses and ten abandonments mentioned above. "In accordance with their thoughts" means responding to their sudden awakening to the One.
Consider this: at the very moment of sudden enlightenment, it is said that "this mind makes the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha. What hindrance would not be dissolved?

What transgression would not be extinguished? That which is called the sin accumulated over a hundred kalpas is instantly swept away in a single thought-moment, just as fire consumes dry grass until nothing remains. As for the phrase "transforming what is received," it means that it is not only oneself...
It eliminates karmic obstacles. Furthermore, one can use this dharma-gate to instruct those who have not yet studied, transforming the realm of Māra into the realm of the Buddha;
thus it is said that the causes of hell are transformed into a land of peace and bliss. Regarding "obtaining blessings," the blessings obtained here surpass those of the former.
The "person" referred to in the previous instance of giving refers to one who offers treasures filling the void of space to the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust. This person merely...

Regarding this single thought: although teaching this one dharma to those who have not yet studied it may seem to yield little merit, the statement that it "surpasses those who came before" contains briefly three meanings.
First, it concerns the Buddha, who does not take delight in honoring himself, but takes delight only in saving sentient beings.
Second, it concerns practice, which does not prioritize self-benefit, but focuses solely on benefiting others.
It is because it is more weighty. Thirdly, in terms of merit: the former consists of contaminated (sāsrava) merit, whereas this consists of uncontaminated (anāsrava) merit.
For example, a single wish-fulfilling gem surpasses a thousand kinds of oceanic treasures, and a single grain of elixir of immortality outstrips ten thousand varieties of medical prescriptions;
thus, its transcendence of the former merit is not at all surprising. Regarding the phrase "a hundredfold, a thousandfold," etc., it means:
It surpasses the previous merit; not merely by one or two times, but if explained briefly, it surpasses it by a hundred or a thousand times.
If explained in a moderate manner, it surpasses it by ten thousand, a hundred million, or even more. Thus, as one speaks further and further, the increase becomes ever greater.
It is even beyond the reach of calculation by multiples; it is beyond the reach of analogy by multiples.
To speak in general of the merit of those former people, however boundless and limitless one may describe it, it cannot remotely equal even a small fraction of this merit.

Furthermore, within this passage there is an implicit meaning intended to illustrate through external comparison: that even a person who has committed the most grievous sins, if they propagate this sutra for a single thought-moment—
If even this can extinguish sins and procure such merit, how much more so for those who propagate minor offenses or those that are not offenses over a long period?
How could the resulting merit and virtue possibly be conceived? This concludes the summary and comparative calculation of the merit of benefiting others.
Second, to demonstrate the benefits for one's own cultivation:
"Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra, my extensive explanation of them would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
Following my instructions and practicing according to the teaching, they will directly attain Bodhi, and no further demonic activities shall arise."
Regarding the benefits of initial recitation and retention, they have already been compared above; it is known that the merit of transforming others is superior.
Therefore, this section further speaks from the perspective of one who recites and retains [the text] for oneself. One who can recite this sutra maintains both the words and their meaning;

one who can retain this mantra achieves the correspondence of mind and speech. As the ancient masters said: "When the sound of the Dharma enters the ear, its meritorious retribution lasts through kalpas; even a single phrase..."

Tainted spirits shall all rely upon it to reach the other shore; how much more so for those who uphold both the text and meaning of the revealed sutras, or who coordinate mind and mouth through secret mantras.
These form the cause for ultimate firmness and penetrate the profound depths of the source of all phenomena.
Judging the fruit by its cause, their merit is inconceivable; thus it is said: "Were I to explain them extensively, even an eon would not suffice. Relying upon me...

Below, the reasons for this are set forth: if one is able to maintain both the letter and the meaning, such that mind and speech are in accord, and can personally rely upon my teachings to initiate practices for self-benefit, then by practicing according to the instructions, one will accomplish the merit of benefiting others.
Thus, one cultivates both the Exoteric and Esoteric paths, benefiting both oneself and others, like a sail catching a favorable wind or a lion’s lute being played amidst a multitude.
Through this sound, they naturally and directly attain Bodhi, and no longer possess demonic activities. This is why these merits are inexhaustible and why their praise is without end.
At the three times of day, the assembly received the teaching with joy and dispersed.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās;
all the worldlings, including devas, humans, and asuras; as well as the bodhisattvas, followers of the two vehicles, noble seers, and youths from other regions;
together with the powerful spirits and ghosts who had first resolved their minds—were all greatly rejoiced, paid homage, and departed.

Regarding the phrase "The Buddha, having finished speaking the sutra": from the time Ānanda first requested that [the teaching] be fixed until now, the Tathāgata has extensively discussed the four divisions [of the Dharma], further evaluated their merits, and praised the blessings of upholding it, thereby demonstrating his intention to conclude with exhortations for its circulation.
This is because all that ought to be spoken has already been fully expounded. Furthermore, within this, there are also instances where various Buddhas act as witnesses.

It is said that [the teachings] were spoken by the Buddha and by the bodhisattvas who assisted in the transformation of beings; because the companions follow the leader, they are collectively referred to as "spoken by the Buddha.
Regarding the enumeration of the fourfold assembly, only bhikṣus are listed; the other three may have arrived later.
That they now all appear together is because wherever the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, there must always be the fourfold assembly to serve as his inner protection. As for the devas...

Regarding humans and asuras, three of the eight classes have been mentioned; the others should likewise be present, for wherever the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, these eight classes invariably serve as its external protectors.

Their omission from the introductory sections is not due to negligence, as they are certainly included when one examines the "Hundred Spirits Protecting the Mantra," where Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Kings, the Yakṣa Generals, and others appear. Their presence can thus be clearly seen.

As for the bodhisattvas from other lands: in the introductory section, they are those who resolve their doubts through inquiry with the assembly already present, as well as those who arrive later through the resonance of the voice.
The reason it does not mention the bodhisattvas of this land is that these bodhisattvas are all, by nature, countless emanations pervading the lands of the ten directions;

thus, they are subsumed within the category of "other lands. Furthermore, regarding the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) from other lands, they are included because they follow and rejoice in the Mahāyāna, whereas those of this land are excluded.
They constantly follow this land; they constantly follow this land, for they are included among the fourfold assembly.

As for the "Holy Seer Youth," he has internally realized the Holy Path and externally manifests the traces of a seer; he does not lose his state of pure youth. He may come because of sympathetic joy, or he may arrive to protect the mantras;

therefore, he is not categorized in the same way as those who have merely resolved their minds [for enlightenment] or the powerful spirits and ghosts. Thus it is said. The "Great Power Spirits and Ghosts" refers to those who have already...
They resolve their minds on Bodhicitta and, riding upon great supernormal power, subdue Māras and external adversaries to serve as the assembly of outer protectors;
thus, they all experience great joy. Having heard the True Teaching (Abhidharma), they realize that the Buddha-way can be accomplished;
this joy is not ordinary, for they feel profound celebration. They prostrate and depart because, having further heard these sublime praises, they understand the entrustment of the Dharma.
"It exists. It does not depart in vain; it departs having performed prostrations and received the instruction. This concludes the section on the circulation of the teaching.
The verse of dedication says:
"The ultimate, firm, and most excellent Dharma, I have explained according to my capacity, as the Buddha taught."
Seeing, hearing, and rejoicing constitute the direct cause [for liberation], erasing my inverted offenses from billions of kalpas.

Now, as for this single commentary, *The Finger and Palm of the Śūraṅgama*, the Venerable Master Da of the ancient monastery Nianhua, out of compassion for future generations...

This "Finger Pointing at the Palm" is a commentary on the Great Compassionate Heart, intended for those in the darkness of ignorance. It demonstrates the benefit of the *loka-saṃvṛti-satya* (worldly standpoint).
Classified within the Vaipulya section of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it discusses all five teachings simultaneously. Its stages of severance and realization span the three gradual sequences (*śan-ci*).

Like fresh butter that, when the poison is expelled, transforms into the wondrous flavor of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), it is a teaching for those of superior faculties and sharp capacities to carry upon their shoulders to the very end.

Rarely do the ignorant and dark-minded find it difficult to grasp the household treasure. With a heart of ultimate compassion, the Elder has brought forth the ground of actual reality (*yathābhūta-bhūmi*).
At such profound and subtle junctures, he has dissected and elucidated each point one by one;

the phrasing is clear and simple, yet the underlying principles are profound and deep. Regarding the naming "Fingers and Palms": "fingers" refers to the clarity and simplicity, while "palms" refers to the profundity and depth. "Indicate" (*shi*) means to point out.
"Grasping" means to hold firmly. The text’s "seven locations for seeking the mind" and "eight returns to distinguish seeing" demonstrate the clear pointing [of the finger].
"If it is not you, then who? demonstrates the knowing that grasps and holds. The Dharma-body is inherently possessed; the Reward-body is manifested through cultivation.

Grasping refers to the inherent possession of the nature-virtues of the Dharma-body, which is neither born nor extinguished, neither identical nor different, and remains unchanging while following conditions, yet follows conditions without [losing its nature].

Transformation. Seeing with the eyes and hearing with the ears, moving the hands and lifting the feet—all these are the manifestation of the fundamental true wisdom and the nature-virtue of the *dharmakāya*, the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*.
This is the sublime function of the *Lengyanwang Samādhi* (King of Śrī Samādhi), the meditative absorption of the unconditioned transformation of transformations.
To point toward and clarify awareness while establishing a conscious subject is the root of birth-and-death and ignorance; it is the grasping of knowledge and sensation that lacks [liberation].
Awakening is precisely the fruit-virtue of nirvana. This principle is inherently possessed by every person; it is not lacking in anyone.
It is one's own biological mother within one’s own house, yet while people are unable to accept and recognize her, they instead go to another's home to bow before a stranger.
The Old Man has expounded and pointed this out: if the ground is not true, then one is no different from Śākyamuni Buddha himself—sharing the same nose.
Kong [Zhao-en] expounds the meaning, pointing out that non-arising and non-ceasing constitute the foundation.

One cultivates the cause by employing the wisdom of initial awakening (*shijue*) to return to the principle of original awakening (*benjue*), thereby grasping the fruition of perfected awakening (*chengjue*). The *Shu* (Commentary) establishes ten gates, all of which lead into the single gate of the "Flower Hall" (*huawu*).
While the Sūtra discusses twenty-five sages and their many gates of expedient means, the Layman [Li Tongxuan] grasps them all as returning to the source.

This scripture contains two dharma-gates. It establishes three contemplations to gradually remove the mud and reveal the pure water; it demonstrates ten causes, six retributions, and four layers of solemn instruction.

It shows that concentration arises from precepts, and wisdom is developed through concentration—thus defining the definitive stages of progress. It reveals fifty kinds of *skandha-māras* to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, the false and the true;
by removing the heterodox and the false, one masters the orthodox and grasps the true. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is a precious raft for crossing out of the mundane world.
The standard for the fruit of Buddhahood must be sought in the Venerable Ānanda, who manifested through great sovereign power to discern the capacities of beings in the final age;
apart from this dharma-standard, there will be no time for transcending the mundane dust. Śākyamuni, the Elder, with his Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, has clearly illuminated immeasurable kalpas;
through this unconditioned great compassion, he takes pity on the ignorant and dark-sighted sentient beings of the future and reveals to them—
There is that which is grasped. To be deluded about its finger is to lose its palm; the monk Wumen was reborn in the Hell of Limitless Suffering.
To understand its finger and observe its palm, the Venerable Ānanda attained the Dharma-body without passing through kalpas. Yet, one might fail to believe in its finger.
She did not recognize its palm. The bhikṣuṇī Bāoliánxiāng’s fire of lust blazed upon her body; she followed its fingers and beheld its palm.
When the bhikṣuṇī Xiàngxìng saw the Buddha, she immediately realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*. At that time, there was a lay disciple of the Śākya clan whose eye of the Path was perfectly clear;
reading these commentaries, he awakened to the fact that cause and effect are created by the mind. He sighed toward me, saying: "The enlightened one penetrates."
The realization of principle is the embodiment of the Dharma-body; "Heaven" (Tian) refers to the natural, innate virtue of the true mark (*dharmatā*) and the ultimate truth.
The Elder Da Tian invokes virtue by means of this name. Were it not for this Elder Da Tian, one would be unable to compose this commentary;

were it not for this commentary, one would be unable to bring forth the meaning of this sutra; were it not for this sutra, one would be unable to recognize the great significance of the West's arrival. Without clarifying the West...

How could those who come here recognize the original person, the lord and master inherently possessed within themselves? This name is assigned to indicate that one has pointed out the original person and taken hold of the lord and master.
There are many commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; their texts are voluminous and their meanings profound.

Even those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence are like mosquitoes trying to bite an iron stake—how much more so for those of dull and ignorant natures? Medicine has no distinction of noble or base.

As for "responding to the illness": the Elder Liang uses the *prajñā* of words and letters to point toward the *prajñā* of contemplative observation, and through the *prajñā* of contemplative observation, he grasps the *prajñā* of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
This is truly an excellent remedy for the final age and is truly suited for those who are ignorant and deluded.

The *Zhizhang yishu* (A Single Commentary on the Fingers and Palms) is truly the key to unlocking the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is the key for opening the gates of ignorance and darkness for those like me.
Although the principle may be realized suddenly, phenomena must necessarily be eliminated gradually. To leap over stages is to become an associate of the heterodox, the false, and the demonic;

there will be no cause for the fruit of the Bodhi path, and one will have a share in the three miserable realms. In life, one will encounter royal calamity; in death, one will fall into hell. My Buddha Śākyamuni...
This is the *Kāñcana-mukha-mudrā-samādhi*. One must not fail to widely disseminate commentaries and sub-commentaries regarding this manual throughout the world.
Both Confucians and Buddhists are capable of reciting it; those of the highest faculties will pass through its gates with ease, while even those of the lowest faculties can reach its domain.
I have heard that among all forms of giving, the gift of Dharma is the most supreme. Reflecting upon my own capabilities, however, I find them insufficient, and thus I cannot help but [proceed].

Upon hearing that fellow practitioners of both Confucianism and Buddhism, as well as virtuous men and faithful women, have valued the Dharma above gold and contributed funds for its printing so that this treatise may circulate—
like a seamless jewel-stupa rising from the vast ocean— I, Chao, have composed this postscript as a key to open the palm of the hand.
It was written at this time.
